patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to an assembly (100) for controlling multidimensional movement of a battery cell stack (108) within a battery pack (102). The assembly (100) include rectangular channels (104) integrated into a battery enclosure (106) to maintain consistent cell spacing and restrict lateral movement along a X-axis. A rectangular tube (110), positioned at top of the battery cell stack (108), applies uniform compressive force to control vertical displacement along a Y-axis. Cross-tube plates (112) are mounted over battery cells (108) to distribute pressure evenly across surface, preventing mechanical deformation and controlling movement along the Z-axis. The assembly (100) enhances structural integrity, prevents uneven cell bulging, and improves thermal regulation through consistent airflow channels. Bolted components secure structure, accommodating thermal expansion with precise tolerances. The assembly (100) is modular, scalable, and adaptable to various battery configurations, promoting longer battery life and simplified maintenance.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure relates to battery pack assemblies, and more specifically relates to an assembly for multidimensional movement control in a battery pack to improve performance and longevity in high-capacity applications. BACKGROUND [0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present disclosure. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed disclosure, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. [0003] A battery pack is an assembly of multiple battery cells configured to provide a specified voltage and capacity for various applications, including electric vehicles, renewable energy storage, and portable electronics. These battery packs include structural enclosures, electrical connections, thermal management components, and safety mechanisms to ensure efficient and reliable operation. The arrangement and mechanical stability of battery cells within the pack are critical for performance, longevity, and safety. [0004] One of the primary challenges in battery pack design is mechanical stress and deformation caused by expansion and contraction of cells during charge and discharge cycles. Without proper movement restriction and uniform pressure distribution, cells may experience uneven bulging, leading to reduced efficiency, compromised thermal management, and potential safety hazards such as short circuits or thermal runaway. [0005] Existing solutions often rely on foam spacers, adhesive bonding, or simple mechanical enclosures to hold battery cells in place. However, these methods lack effective multidimensional movement control, resulting in inconsistent pressure distribution and inadequate thermal dissipation. Over time, such limitations can cause cell misalignment, decreased cycle life, and increased maintenance requirements. [0006] There is, therefore, a need for a solution to enhance mechanical stability and thermal performance of battery pack. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0007] A general object of the present disclosure is to provide improved thermal management within the battery pack by maintaining consistent airflow between cells. [0008] An object of the present disclosure is to provide enhanced structural integrity under operational stress by controlling multidimensional cell movement. [0009] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide uniform pressure distribution across all battery cells, preventing mechanical deformation and uneven bulging. [0010] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide equal spacing between battery cells to optimize cooling and ensure consistent cell alignment. [0011] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a design that facilitates easy replacement of individual battery cells without disassembling the entire pack. [0012] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide quick access to individual battery cells for maintenance and inspection. [0013] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a cost-efficient, scalable design adaptable to various battery configurations and sizes. SUMMARY [0014] Aspects of the present disclosure relate to battery pack assemblies, specifically to an assembly configured to control multidimensional movement of battery cells. The proposed assembly improves structural stability, ensures uniform pressure distribution, and enhances thermal management, resulting in increased performance and longevity. [0015] An aspect of the present disclosure pertains to an assembly for controlling multidimensional movement in a battery pack, configured to enhance structural stability, pressure distribution, and thermal regulation. The assembly includes rectangular channels integrated within a battery enclosure to maintain consistent cell spacing and control lateral displacement of battery cells along an X-axis. A rectangular tube is positioned at the top of the battery cells to apply and sustain uniform compressive force, controlling vertical displacement along a Y-axis. Additionally, one or more cross-tube plates are positioned on top of the battery cells to distribute pressure uniformly across the cell surfaces, preventing mechanical deformation and controlling movement along a Z-axis. [0016] In an aspect, the rectangular channels are placed on bottom and side walls of the enclosure to secure the cells and maintain alignment along the X-axis. [0017] In an aspect, the rectangular tube is bolted to the enclosure and accommodates thermal expansion with a tolerance of ±0.5 mm. [0018] In an aspect, the cross-tube plates are fastened with bolts at each corner, ensuring equal pressure distribution and stabilizing the assembly against mechanical vibrations. [0019] In an aspect, the cross-tube plates are made from thermally conductive material to improve heat dissipation. [0020] In an aspect, the combination of rectangular channels, the rectangular tube, and cross-tube plates restricts cell movement along all three axes (X, Y, and Z), enhancing mechanical integrity and thermal management of the battery pack. [0021] Various objects, features, aspects, and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments, along with the accompanying drawing figures in which like numerals represent like components. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0022] The following drawings form part of the present specification and are included to further illustrate aspects of the present disclosure. The disclosure may be better understood by reference to the drawings in combination with the detailed description of the specific embodiments presented herein. [0023] FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, where force is applied along Y and Z axis to control vertical and surface displacement of battery cells, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0024] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, depicting cross-tube plates positioned on top of battery cells to restrict movement along a Z-axis, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0025] FIG. 3 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, depicting rectangular channels positioned on bottom and side walls of battery enclosure to restrict movement along a X-axis and secure battery cells in place, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0026] The following is a detailed description of embodiments of the disclosure depicted in the accompanying drawings. The embodiments are in such detail as to clearly communicate the disclosure. If the specification states a component or feature “may”, “can”, “could”, or “might” be included or have a characteristic, that particular component or feature is not required to be included or have the characteristic. [0027] As used in the description herein and throughout the claims that follow, the meaning of “a,” “an,” and “the” includes plural reference unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. Also, as used in the description herein, the meaning of “in” includes “in” and “on” unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. [0028] Embodiments of the present disclosure relate to battery pack assemblies, specifically to an assembly configured to control multidimensional movement of battery cells Various embodiments with respect to the present disclosure will be explained in detail with reference to FIGs. 1-3. [0029] An embodiment of the present disclosure pertains to an assembly for controlling multidimensional movement in a battery pack, configured to enhance structural stability, pressure distribution, and thermal regulation. The assembly includes rectangular channels integrated within a battery enclosure to maintain consistent cell spacing and control lateral displacement of battery cells along an X-axis. A rectangular tube is positioned at the top of the battery cells to apply and sustain uniform compressive force, controlling vertical displacement along a Y-axis. Additionally, one or more cross-tube plates are positioned on top of the battery cells to distribute pressure uniformly across the cell surfaces, preventing mechanical deformation and controlling movement along a Z-axis. [0030] In an embodiment, the rectangular channels are placed on bottom and side walls of the enclosure to secure the cells and maintain alignment along the X-axis. [0031] In an embodiment, the rectangular tube is bolted to the enclosure and accommodates thermal expansion with a tolerance of ±0.5 mm. [0032] In an embodiment, the cross-tube plates are fastened with bolts at each corner, ensuring equal pressure distribution and stabilizing the assembly against mechanical vibrations. [0033] In an embodiment, the cross-tube plates are made from thermally conductive material to improve heat dissipation. [0034] In an embodiment, the combination of rectangular channels, the rectangular tube, and cross-tube plates restricts cell movement along all three axes (X, Y, and Z), enhancing mechanical integrity and thermal management of the battery pack. [0035] FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, where force is applied along Y-axis and Z-axis to control vertical and surface displacement of battery cells, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0036] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, depicting cross-tube plates positioned on top of battery cells to restrict movement along a Z-axis, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0037] FIG. 3 illustrates an exemplary schematic view of a proposed assembly integrated with a battery pack, depicting rectangular channels positioned on bottom and side walls of battery enclosure to restrict movement along a X-axis and secure battery cells in place, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0038] Referring to FIGs. 1, 2, and 3, an assembly (100) to control multidimensional movement in a battery pack (102) is disclosed. The assembly (100) prevents unwanted movement of battery cells (108) (or battery cells stack) to avoid mechanical damage, maintain structural integrity, and ensure consistent performance. The assembly (100) includes one or more rectangular channels (104) that are integrated into a battery enclosure (106) of the battery pack (102). These rectangular channels (104) is essential in keeping the battery cells (108) properly spaced and aligned. Maintaining consistent spacing between the battery cells (108) is essential to prevent issues like cell-to-cell contact, which can lead to short circuits or inconsistent heat dissipation. By holding the battery cells (108) at a fixed distance from each other, the rectangular channels (104) help ensure even airflow and better thermal management. [0039] In addition, the rectangular channels (104) are specifically configured to control lateral displacement of the battery cells (108) along the X-axis. Lateral displacement refers to side-to-side movement, which can cause mechanical stress or damage to the battery cells (108) if left unchecked. The rectangular channels (104) act as physical barriers that prevent the battery cells (108) from shifting horizontally, keeping them securely in place even when the battery pack (102) experiences vibrations or external forces. [0040] Further, to provide complete lateral stability, the rectangular channels (104) are strategically positioned within the battery enclosure (106). A first rectangular channel (104-1) is placed at bottom of the battery enclosure (106), forming a stable base for the battery cells (108) to rest on. Meanwhile, a second rectangular channel (104-2) and a third rectangular channel (104-3) are positioned on side walls of the battery enclosure (106). This configuration creates a pocket-like structure that surrounds the battery cells (108) on multiple sides, ensuring they remain tightly secured and aligned along the X-axis. By combining bottom and side rectangular channels (104-1, 104-2, and 104-3) as shown in FIG. 3, the assembly (100) effectively locks the battery cells (108) in place, preventing lateral movement without compromising spacing or airflow. This structural arrangement enhances stability of the battery pack (102), reduces wear on individual battery cells (108), and contributes to longer cycle life and safer operation. [0041] In an embodiment, the assembly (100) includes a rectangular tube (110) positioned at top of the battery cells (108). This rectangular tube (110) is configured for applying and maintaining a uniform compressive force on the battery cells (108). The force controls vertical displacement of the battery cells (108) along a Y-axis, i.e. prevents the battery cells (108) from shifting or expanding upwards or downwards. Controlling vertical movement is essential because uncontrolled expansion, especially during charge and discharge cycles, can cause physical damage to the battery cells (108), lead to uneven pressure distribution, and increase risk of mechanical failure or capacity loss. [0042] In addition, the rectangular tube (110) is securely bolted to the battery enclosure (106). Bolting ensures the rectangular tube (110) remains firmly in place, even when subjected to external vibrations or mechanical stresses. This bolted connection reinforces structural integrity of the battery pack (102), preventing loosening over time and consistently maintaining necessary pressure on the battery cells (108). [0043] Further, the rectangular tube (110) is configured to accommodate thermal expansion. For instance, the battery cells (108) naturally expand and contract during operation due to heating and cooling cycles. Excessive pressure from uncontrolled expansion could damage the battery cells (108) or the battery enclosure (106). To mitigate this risk, the rectangular tube (110) is configured with a thermal expansion tolerance of ±0.5 mm. This built-in flexibility allows the rectangular tube (110) to adapt to cell expansion without compromising the applied compressive force or disrupting the alignment of the battery cells (108). [0044] In addition, the assembly (100) include one or more cross-tube plates (112), positioned on top of the battery cells (108), as shown in FIG. 2, for pressure management and movement restriction along a Z-axis. The cross-tube plates (112) help distribute pressure uniformly across entire surface of the battery cells (108). This even pressure distribution is essential because it prevents individual battery cells (108) from experiencing uneven force, which could cause mechanical deformation, such as bulging or warping of the cells. Such deformations may compromise cell performance, reduce lifespan of the battery pack (102), and even pose safety risks. [0045] Additionally, the cross-tube plates (112) are made of a thermally conductive material, which enhances heat dissipation from the battery cells (108). Efficient heat transfer helps regulate temperature within the battery pack (102), reducing likelihood of thermal hotspots and enhancing thermal management. To ensure the cross-tube plates (112) stay securely in place and provide consistent pressure, they are fastened with bolts at each corner of the battery cells (108). This bolted configuration ensures that pressure is applied uniformly across all battery cells (108), preventing any single cell from shifting or loosening. The stable structure created by this fastening mechanism also helps stabilize the battery assembly against mechanical vibrations, which can occur during transport or operation, especially in dynamic environments like electric vehicles or energy storage systems. [0046] Further, combination of the rectangular channels (104-1, 104-2, and 104-3), the rectangular tube (110), and the cross-tube plates (112) restrict the battery cells (108) movement along the X, Y, and Z axis. This multidimensional stabilization maintains cell alignment, prevents deformation, and enhances structural integrity of the battery pack (102). [0047] Thus, the proposed disclosure provides the assembly (100) to effectively control movement of the battery cells (108) along all three axes, ensuring structural stability, preventing deformation, and enhancing thermal regulation. These features collectively improve performance, longevity, and safety of the battery pack (102) in high-capacity applications. [0048] It will be apparent to those skilled in the art that the apparatus of the disclosure may be provided using some or all of the mentioned features and components without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. While various embodiments of the present disclosure have been illustrated and described herein, it will be clear that the disclosure is not limited to these embodiments only. Numerous modifications, changes, variations, substitutions, and equivalents will be apparent to those skilled in the art, without departing from the spirit and scope of the disclosure, as described in the claims. ADVANTAGES OF THE PRESENT INVENTION [0049] The present disclosure provides improved thermal management within the battery pack by maintaining consistent airflow between cells. [0050] The present disclosure provides enhanced structural integrity under operational stress by controlling multidimensional cell movement. [0051] The present disclosure provides uniform pressure distribution across all battery cells, preventing mechanical deformation and uneven bulging. [0052] The present disclosure provides equal spacing between battery cells to optimize cooling and ensure consistent cell alignment. [0053] The present disclosure provides an assembly that facilitates easy replacement of individual battery cells without disassembling the entire pack. [0054] The present disclosure provides quick access to individual battery cells for maintenance and inspection. [0055] The present disclosure provides a cost-efficient, scalable design adaptable to various battery configurations and sizes. , Claims:1. The assembly (100) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the rectangular tube (110) is bolted to the battery enclosure (106) and accommodates thermal expansion with a tolerance of ±0.5 mm. 4. The assembly (100) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the one or more cross-tube plates (112) are fastened with bolts at each corner of the battery cells (108), for equal pressure distribution across the battery cells and stabilizing the assembly against mechanical vibrations. 5. The assembly (100) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the one or more cross-tube plates (112) are made of a thermally conductive material. 6. The assembly (100) as claimed in claim 1, wherein combination of the one or more rectangular channels (104), the rectangular tube (110), and the one or more cross-tube plates (112) restricts movement of the battery cells along the X-axis, Y-axis, and Z-axis.

patents.abstract: The invention relates to a system and method for recycling spent lithium-ion battery black mass using natural acids such as citric acid or oxalic acid. The process involves mixing black mass with natural acid and a reducing agent at moderate temperatures (50-100°C) to extract lithium as soluble salts, while cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite remain as insoluble materials. The lithium solution is further processed to produce lithium carbonate, and the insoluble salts are treated with inorganic acids to regenerate natural acids, which are recovered through crystallization at low temperatures (-10 to 5°C). The system includes a closed-loop acid recovery unit, reducing natural acid consumption by up to 70% and cutting costs by 20%. The method achieves >95% recovery of lithium and other valuable metals, operates with minimal environmental impact, and supports industrial scalability, making it a sustainable solution for LIB recycling.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of sustainable recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries, specifically to a system and method for extracting lithium and other valuable metals using natural acids while minimizing acid consumption. It focuses on reducing processing costs, environmental impact, and improving resource recovery rates. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. [0003] Rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has significantly increased the demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), resulting in a growing volume of spent batteries that must be recycled to recover valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite. Current recycling methods primarily rely on hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processes. While these methods enable material recovery, they present significant environmental and economic challenges. For instance, the extensive use of strong inorganic acids, such as hydrochloric acid (HCl) and sulfuric acid (H2SO4), in hydrometallurgical leaching processes often leads to hazardous effluent generation and high operational costs due to the non-recovery of these acids. [0004] Several prior art references have explored alternative approaches to LIB recycling. For example, hydrometallurgical methods employing citric acid and hydrogen peroxide as a leachant and reductant, respectively, have demonstrated moderate leaching efficiencies for lithium and transition metals. These methods are environmentally friendlier than traditional processes but suffer from high costs and challenges in reclaiming and reusing the organic acid (Politecnico Di Torino et al, 2023). Similarly, oxalic acid has been successfully utilized in processes to selectively leach lithium from battery black mass and clay-type lithium ores. These processes achieve lithium recovery rates of up to 90% but face cost inefficiencies and complexities in recovering the acid for reuse (Journal of Cleaner Production, Volume 112, Part 4, 20 January 2016, Pages 3562-3570) [0005] Other strategies, such as sodium carbonate precipitation, allow lithium recovery in the form of lithium carbonate. However, co-precipitation with impurities often compromises the purity of the final product, posing significant challenges for its reuse in battery-grade applications. Furthermore, existing recycling processes frequently require energy-intensive pretreatment steps, such as roasting at 500°C, which exacerbate the carbon footprint of the operation. [0006] Despite these advancements, several critical issues remain. Many recycling methods lack closed-loop acid recovery systems, leading to excessive acid consumption and high operational costs. Processes frequently fail to prioritize lithium recovery, resulting in resource inefficiency and suboptimal environmental outcomes. Additionally, the reliance on strong acids and high-temperature pretreatments significantly increases the environmental and economic costs. [0007] Hence, in view of the above, there is a dire need to develop a sustainable, cost-effective recycling methodology that overcomes these limitations. An ideal solution should prioritize the recovery and reuse of leaching agents, minimize secondary pollution, and enhance lithium recovery efficiency. A closed-loop system capable of reducing the dependency on both harsh chemicals and energy-intensive pretreatments may represent a significant advancement in LIB recycling. Moreover, ensuring higher purity levels of recovered lithium and other metals is vital to meet the stringent quality requirements for reuse in battery manufacturing OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION [0008] The primary objective of the present invention is to develop a sustainable, efficient, and cost-effective process for recovering valuable materials, particularly lithium, from spent lithium-ion battery (LIB) black mass. [0009] Another objective of the present invention is the efficient extraction of lithium from the black mass using mild, environmentally friendly natural acids instead of harsh inorganic acids along with ensuring higher recovery rates while maintaining the purity of lithium salts suitable for battery manufacturing [0010] Another objective of the present invention is to reduce the consumption of costly natural acids, such as citric and oxalic acids, by implementing an innovative recovery mechanism, and in turn, reducing overall processing costs making the method economically viable for large-scale applications [0011] Another objective of the present invention is to a provide a process for recovering natural acids from the leachate via crystallization at low temperatures to minimize waste generation, reduces dependency on external acid supplies, and lowers the environmental footprint [0012] Another objective of the present invention is to provide a process which enables recovery of high-value metals such as cobalt, nickel, and manganese in their pure forms as soluble salt solution, facilitating their direct reuse in cathode manufacturing processes [0013] Another objective of the present invention is to eliminate secondary pollution caused by excess chemical use in traditional recycling methods by optimizing reaction conditions and adopting environmentally benign reagents. [0014] Another objective of the present invention is to address critical challenges associated with conventional LIB recycling methods, focusing on reducing acid consumption, improving recovery efficiencies, and minimizing environmental impact. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0015] The present invention relates to a sustainable and cost-effective process for recovering high-value materials, particularly lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite, from spent lithium-ion battery (LIB) black mass. The process prioritizes the use of mild natural acids, such as citric or oxalic acids, along with a reducing agent, to minimize the environmental impact and reduce operational costs. [0016] In an aspect, present invention discloses a system (100) for extracting lithium and recovering natural acids from spent lithium-ion battery (LIB) black mass, comprising: an extraction unit (101) configured to receive black mass, natural acid, and a reducing agent under pre-designed temperature and pressure conditions to produce a black mass dispersion containing soluble lithium salts and insoluble/sparingly soluble salts/metal salts; a filtration unit (102) configured to separate the soluble lithium-containing solution from sparingly soluble/insoluble salts, graphite, and another residue; an acid treatment unit (103) configured to treat insoluble/sparingly soluble salts with an inorganic acid to regenerate the natural acid and dissolve metal salts; a second filtration unit (104) configured to separate insoluble/sparingly soluble graphite from the solution containing regenerated natural acid and dissolved metal salts; and an acid recovery unit (105) configured to crystallize and recover the natural acid by reducing the solution temperature to a predetermined level, allowing reuse of the natural acid and reducing process costs. [0017] In another aspect, the present invention discloses a process for recovering lithium, natural acid, and other valuable metals from spent LIB black mass, comprising: mixing black mass with natural acid and a reducing agent in predetermined weight ratios and molar ratios; separating the lithium-containing solution from insoluble/sparingly soluble salts and graphite using filtration; treating the insoluble/sparingly soluble salts with an inorganic acid to dissolve metal salts and regenerate natural acid; separating insoluble graphite from the solution containing regenerated natural acid and dissolved metal salts; and crystallizing the natural acid by cooling the solution to-10 to 5°C, filtering the crystals, and reusing the recovered natural acid. [0018] Various objects, features, aspects and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments. Definitions: [0029] For the purpose of the present invention, LIB (Lithium-Ion Battery) may be defined as a rechargeable battery with lithium-based cathodes. [0041] For the purpose of the present invention, Cathode Active Material may be defined as Materials like NMC/NCA/LMO/LCO used in LIB cathodes. [0043] For the purpose of the present invention, Recovery Rate may be defined as Percentage of material successfully extracted or reclaimed. [0045] For the purpose of the present invention, Solubility may be defined as an ability of a substance to dissolve in a solvent. [0046] For the purpose of the present invention, Selective Precipitation may be defined as Isolating specific ions from a solution. [0047] For the purpose of the present invention, Environmental Impact may be defined as an effect of a process on natural resources and ecosystems. [0049] In a general embodiment, the present invention provides a comprehensive system and method for recycling spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that addresses several challenges in existing recycling technologies, including high costs, environmental impact, and inefficient recovery of valuable materials. The process is designed to extract lithium and recover valuable metals such as cobalt, nickel, and manganese while significantly reducing the consumption of expensive natural acids like citric acid or oxalic acid. [0050] In an embodiment, the present invention introduces a sustainable and cost-effective solution for recycling spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), focusing on reducing the reliance on expensive natural acids while maximizing the recovery of valuable materials like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. The process uses natural acids such as citric or oxalic acid, combined with reducing agents like glucose or hydrogen peroxide, to selectively extract lithium as a soluble salt under mild conditions (50-100°C for 1-5 hours). [0051] In an embodiment, the remaining materials, including cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite, are processed further using inorganic acids to ensure complete recovery. A key innovation is the integration of an acid recovery system that crystallizes and reclaims natural acids by cooling the solution to low temperatures (-10 to 5°C). This closed-loop process reduces natural acid consumption by up to 70%, significantly lowering costs while minimizing waste and environmental impact. [0052] In an embodiment, the system operates efficiently at moderate temperatures, avoiding energy-intensive processes like high-temperature pyrolysis. It achieves recovery rates exceeding 95% for all targeted materials, making it both environmentally and economically sustainable. Furthermore, the process is scalable and adaptable for industrial applications, ensuring high-purity outputs suitable for reuse in battery manufacturing. This invention provides a critical step forward in addressing the growing need for sustainable recycling in the electric vehicle and energy storage industries. [0053] In an embodiment, present invention discloses a system (100) for extracting lithium and recovering natural acids from spent lithium-ion battery (LIB) black mass, comprising: an extraction unit (101) configured to receive black mass, natural acid, and a reducing agent under pre-designed temperature and pressure conditions to produce a black mass dispersion containing soluble lithium salts and insoluble/sparingly soluble metal salts; a filtration unit (102) configured to separate the lithium-containing solution from insoluble salts, graphite, and another residue; an acid treatment unit (103) configured to treat insoluble/sparingly soluble salts with an inorganic acid to regenerate the natural acid and dissolve metal salts; a second filtration unit (104) configured to separate insoluble graphite from the solution containing regenerated natural acid and dissolved metal salts; and an acid recovery unit (105) configured to crystallize and recover the natural acid by reducing the solution temperature to a predetermined level, allowing reuse of the natural acid and reducing process costs. [0054] In an embodiment, the filtration unit (103) has a pore size in the range of 0.1 to 5 micrometers, enabling the separation of lithium-containing solutions from insoluble salts and graphite. [0055] In an embodiment, the filter is made of acid-resistant materials selected from polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), ceramic, reinforced carbon fibers or different grades of stainless steel. [0056] In an embodiment, the natural acid is selected from citric acid, oxalic acid, formic acid, or a combination thereof. [0057] In an embodiment, the reducing agent is selected from hydrogen peroxide, glucose, formic acid or a combination thereof. [0058] In an embodiment, wherein the acid recovery unit is configured to recover upto 70% of the natural acid used in the process. [0059] In an embodiment, the production cost is reduced by up to 20% compared to systems without natural acid recovery. [0060] In an embodiment, the present invention discloses a process for recovering lithium, natural acid, and other valuable metals from spent LIB black mass, comprising: mixing black mass with natural acid and a reducing agent; separating the lithium-containing solution from insoluble salts and graphite using filtration; treating the insoluble salts with an inorganic acid to dissolve metal salts and regenerate natural acid; separating insoluble graphite from the solution containing regenerated natural acid and dissolved metal salts; and crystallizing the natural acid by cooling the solution to-10 to 5°C, filtering the crystals, and reusing the recovered natural acid. [0061] In an embodiment, the black mass comprises 3-4% lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese in the range of 5-16%, 25-35% graphite with additional 1-10% impurities including aluminum, copper and iron. [0062] In an embodiment, the concentration of natural acid ranges between 1 M and 2.5 M, [0063] In an embodiment, the concentration of reducing agent ranges between 1% to 10% v/v. [0064] In an embodiment, the black mass is mixed with natural acid and reducing agent at the temperature ranging between 50-100°C for the duration ranging from 1-5 hours, [0065] In an embodiment, the natural acid includes citric acid or oxalic acid; [0066] In an embodiment, the inorganic acid is selected from hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, nitric acid or a combination thereof. [0067] In an embodiment, the lithium-containing solution is further treated with sodium carbonate to produce lithium carbonate. [0068] In an embodiment, the recovery yield of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese ranges from 95%-98%. [0069] In an embodiment, the metal salts solution is further processed to recover cobalt, nickel, and manganese as high-value products. [0070] In an embodiment, the recovered natural acid is reused in subsequent extraction cycles, forming a closed-loop system with minimal waste generation. [0071] Hence, disclosed invention addresses the critical challenges in the recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries, specifically focusing on reducing acid consumption, improving recovery rates, and minimizing environmental impact. By utilizing natural acids in a closed-loop system, the invention achieves a cost-efficient, sustainable, and scalable solution for the extraction and recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from black mass. The integration of an advanced acid recovery unit significantly reduces operational costs while ensuring environmentally friendly practices. [0072] Accordingly, the present invention not only overcomes the limitations of prior art, such as high acid consumption, inefficient recovery rates, and complex processes, but also aligns with global demands for sustainable battery recycling methods. With high recovery efficiency, low energy requirements, and the ability to produce high-purity lithium salts for reuse in battery manufacturing, the invention provides an innovative pathway to support the growing electric vehicle market and the circular economy. patents.abstract: The present disclosure provides a sustainable and efficient system for selective lithium recovery from electronic waste, industrial effluents, and other lithium-containing solutions. It employs functionalized cellulose-based adsorbents, including modified sawdust and cellulose beads, engineered with fusion proteins comprising Cellulose Binding Modules (CBMs) and Lithium Binding Peptides (LBPs). The CBMs anchor the proteins to the cellulose, while the LBPs selectively bind lithium ions. These adsorbents are used in a fixed-bed adsorption column to capture lithium ions selectively, with elution achieved using a pH-modulated buffer. The system operates under mild conditions, eliminating the need for high energy inputs or harsh chemicals, making it eco-friendly and cost-effective. The absorbents are reusable, further reducing operational costs. The modular design allows for customization to recover other critical metals like cobalt, nickel, and copper. This invention addresses global demand for sustainable lithium recovery while supporting a circular economy by minimizing environmental impact and waste.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [0001] The present disclosure pertains to the field of recycling technologies with special emphasis on lithium recovery. More particularly, the present disclosure focuses on a novel, selective, and eco-friendly system for lithium-ion recovery, leveraging functionalized cellulose-based materials modified with fusion proteins. The disclosure addresses critical challenges in lithium recovery, offering a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to conventional chemical and electrochemical methods, while promoting environmental sustainability and resource circularity. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. [0003] Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become indispensable in powering modern devices, including smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles. Their widespread adoption over the past two decades has led to a dramatic increase in the demand for lithium, a critical component in their manufacture. In 2017, global lithium production reached approximately 43,000 tons, and this figure continues to grow as industries embrace renewable energy solutions and electric mobility. However, sustainably meeting this demand presents a major challenge, making the recovery of lithium-ion from e-waste an urgent necessity. [0004] Current methods for lithium recovery, such as chemical precipitation, electrochemical extraction, and hydrothermal processes, have been widely studied but face significant limitations. For instance, electrochemical and hydrothermal processes are energy-intensive, relying on high heat and electricity, which drive up costs and contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, use of corrosive acids and harmful chemicals in these methods poses severe environmental and health risks. These processes also lack selectivity needed to efficiently isolate lithium ions from complex mixtures, resulting in low purity and additional processing steps. [0005] Another prevalent way for lithium recovery involves microbial systems employing Escherichia coli for selectively recovering lithium by engineering microbes to present specific peptides or proteins on their surfaces. For instance, methods disclosed in patents like KR20190009512A utilize microbial systems engineered to selectively bind lithium ions via cell surface display of metal-binding peptides. While innovative, this approach faces challenges such as difficulty of separating microbial cells from treated media, inefficiencies in protein folding and stability, and scalability issues for industrial applications. These limitations hinder their effectiveness in large-scale settings. [0006] In parallel, scientific literature highlights the potential of lithium-binding peptides and cellulose adsorption technologies in metal recovery. While these methods show promise, they are often limited in scope, addressing isolated aspects of the recovery process without offering comprehensive or integrated solutions. [0007] Given these challenges, there is a pressing need for innovative solutions that combine the strengths of existing methods while addressing their weaknesses. Therefore, developing a system and process capable of efficiently recovering lithium ions from e-waste without relying on high-energy inputs or harmful chemicals along with being cost effective and scalable is essential. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION [0008] The primary objective of the present disclosure is to provide a novel, eco-friendly, and cost-effective solution for the selective recovery of lithium from electronic waste (e-waste) and other lithium-containing solutions. [0009] Another objective of the present disclosure is to design a low-cost, energy-efficient system and process for recovering lithium ions from electronic waste and industrial effluents without relying on high-energy-intensive methods such as chemical precipitation, electrochemical extraction, or hydrothermal processes. [0010] Another objective of the present disclosure is to utilize bioengineered cellulose-based materials functionalized with fusion proteins to achieve high selectivity and efficiency in lithium recovery. [0011] Another objective of the present disclosure is to improve selectivity of lithium-ion capture from complex solutions, ensuring that lithium ions are efficiently separated from other metals and contaminants in e-waste or brine solutions. [0012] Another objective of the present disclosure is to develop cellulose-based adsorbents (such as sawdust and cellulose beads) functionalized with fusion proteins that can be reused multiple times without significant loss of performance. [0013] Another objective of the present disclosure is to develop a lithium recovery process that reduces the need for expensive or complicated technologies, making the recovery of lithium more affordable and accessible for industrial-scale applications. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0014] In an aspect, the present disclosure provides a system and a method involving integration of fusion protein technology with cellulose-based materials, creating an eco-friendly, scalable, and selective process for lithium recovery. [0015] In an aspect, the present disclosure provides a system for selective recovery of lithium ions from a lithium-containing solution. The proposed system comprises a cellulose adsorption column positioned as a vertical cylinder filled with cellulose-based adsorbent material, wherein the adsorbent material comprises any or a combination of cellulose beads or sawdust, each of which adsorbent material is functionalized with fusion polypeptides, wherein said cellulose beads or sawdust, both are functionalized in order to bind the proteins with cellulose/hemicellulose substrate present in cellulose beads or sawdust. [0016] The said system can further include a feed mechanism to introduce the lithium-containing solution into the adsorption column. Upon introduction of the lithium containing solution into the adsorption column, lithium ions are retained/extracted/isolated using a selective retention sub-system based on affinity between the lithium binding peptide (LBP) and lithium ions while allowing other ions to pass through. [0017] The said system can further include a selective retention sub-system to retain lithium ions based on affinity between the fusion polypeptides and lithium ions while allowing other ions to pass through; and [0018] The system further includes an elution mechanism to release the retained lithium ions based on alternation of one or more environmental conditions selected from any or a combination of pH or ionic strength, wherein the optimal range of adsorption by the protein ranges between pH 7-8, and wherein reduced adsorption occurs due to formation of salts with Li, which leads to elution when the pH is decreased to 6, [0019] In an aspect, the fusion polypeptides can be selected from any or a combination of a Cellulose Binding Module (CBM) domain designed to anchor the fusion polypeptide to the cellulose-based adsorbent material, a Lithium Binding Peptide (LBP) configured to selectively bind lithium ions, and a linker sequence joining the CBM and LBP to maintain structural stability and functionality. [0020] In an aspect, the present disclosure provides a process for recovering lithium ions, which involves several steps. First, a cellulose adsorption column is prepared, packed with cellulose-based adsorbent material functionalized with a fusion polypeptide. This fusion polypeptide comprises a Cellulose Binding Module (CBM) that binds to the cellulose-based adsorbent material, a Lithium Binding Peptide (LBP) that selectively binds lithium ions, and a linker sequence that joins the CBM and LBP to ensure structural stability and functionality. [0021] The said solution containing lithium ions is introduced into the column, allowing the lithium ions to bind to the LBP present on the functionalized adsorbent material. Subsequently, the lithium ions are eluted from the adsorbent material by altering environmental conditions such as pH or ionic strength. Finally, the eluted lithium ions are recovered and analyzed for their purity and concentration. [0022] In an aspect, the present disclosure provides a kit for selective recovery of lithium ions, comprising the system as disclosed herein, an elution buffer optimized for lithium-ion recovery; and an instruction manual for operating the system. [0023] An exemplary aspect of the present disclosure is to employ functionalized cellulose materials comprising sawdust and cellulose beads along with fusion polypeptides to selectively bind lithium ions from solutions, wherein fusion polypeptides are designed with a Cellulose Binding Module (CBM) and Lithium Binding Protein (LBP) to provide high specificity and binding efficiency. Hence, by leveraging properties of cellulose-binding modules (CBMs) and lithium-binding peptides (LBPs), the present disclosure offers a cost-effective and sustainable solution for lithium recycling from e-waste. [0024] Various objects, features, aspects, and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES [0025] The accompanying drawings are included to provide a clear understanding of the present invention and a detailed description, and they constitute a part of this complete specification. [0026] FIG. 1 illustrates a system for recovering the lithium ions from an e-waste or a lithium rich solution. [0027] FIG. 2 illustrates a method of recovering the lithium ions from an e-waste or a lithium rich solution. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [0028] The following is a full description of the disclosure's embodiments. The embodiments are described in such a way that the disclosure is clearly communicated. The level of detail provided, on the other hand, is not meant to limit the expected variations of embodiments; rather, it is designed to include all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives that come within the spirit and scope of the current disclosure as defined by the attached claims. Unless the context indicates otherwise, the term "comprise" and variants such as "comprises" and "comprising" throughout the specification are to be read in an open, inclusive meaning, that is, as "including, but not limited to." [0029] When "one embodiment" or "an embodiment" is used in this specification, it signifies that a particular feature, structure, or characteristic described in conjunction with the embodiment is present in at least one embodiment. As a result, the expressions "in one embodiment" and "in an embodiment" that appear throughout this specification do not necessarily refer to the same embodiment. Furthermore, in one or more embodiments, the specific features, structures, or qualities may be combined in any way that is appropriate. [0030] The headings and abstract of the invention provided herein are for convenience only and do not interpret the scope or meaning of the embodiments. [0031] All publications herein are incorporated by reference to the same extent as if each individual publication or patent application were specifically and individually indicated to be incorporated by reference. [0032] Groupings of alternative elements or embodiments of the invention disclosed herein are not to be construed as limitations. [0033] It should also be appreciated that the present invention can be implemented in numerous ways, including as a system, a method or a device. In this specification, these implementations, or any other form that the invention may take, may be referred to as processes. In general, the order of the steps of the disclosed processes may be altered within the scope of the invention. [0034] Various terms as used herein are shown below. To the extent a term used in a claim is not defined below, it should be given the broadest definition persons in the pertinent art have given that term as reflected in printed publications and issued patents at the time of filing. Definitions [0035] For the purpose of the present disclosure, lithium-ion recovery may be defined as a process of extracting lithium ions from various sources, such as electronic waste, industrial effluents, or brine solutions, for reuse in applications like battery production. Recovery focuses on efficiency, selectivity, and environmental sustainability. [0036] For the purpose of the present disclosure, cellulose may be defined as a natural, abundant, biodegradable polysaccharide composed of glucose units. It serves as the structural component of plant cell walls and is used in this invention as a base material for adsorbents due to its modifiability and availability. [0037] For the purpose of the present disclosure, fusion protein may be defined as a hybrid protein consisting of two or more functional domains linked together. In this invention, the domains are a CBM and an LBP. [0038] For the purpose of the present disclosure, Cellulose Binding Module (CBM) may be defined as protein domains that specifically bind to cellulose surfaces, aiding immobilization. [0039] For the purpose of the present disclosure, Ion Binding Peptide (IBP) may be defined as a peptide domain designed to selectively bind a specific ion. [0040] For the purpose of the present invention, Lithium Binding Peptide (LBP) may be defined as a peptide domain designed to selectively bind lithium ions. [0041] For the purpose of the present invention, linker sequence refers to a short chain of amino acids used in fusion proteins to connect different functional domains (e.g., CBM and LBP) while maintaining their structural stability and functionality. [0042] For the purpose of the present invention, fixed-bed adsorption column may be defined as vertical column filled with adsorbent material, such as functionalized cellulose or sawdust. The column facilitates the interaction between the solution containing lithium ions and the adsorbent for selective capture. [0043] For the purpose of the present invention, adsorption may be defined as a process by which molecules (in this case, lithium ions) adhere to the surface of a solid material (adsorbent). Adsorption in this invention is facilitated by functionalized cellulose beads or sawdust. [0044] For the purpose of the present disclosure, black mass may be defined as a mixture of shredded materials derived from discarded lithium-ion batteries. [0045] For the purpose of the present disclosure, adsorption column may be defined as a cylindrical setup used for separation processes, where a target compound binds to the column's adsorbent material. [0046] For the purpose of the present disclosure, e-waste may be defined as discarded electronic devices containing components like lithium-ion batteries. [0047] For the purpose of the present disclosure, selective retention may refer to a process where only specific ions (e.g., lithium in the present case) are retained on the adsorbent material, while others pass through, based on affinity. [0048] For the purpose of the present disclosure, elution may be defined as a process to release/elute the adsorbed lithium ions from the cellulose material by altering environmental conditions, such as pH, to facilitate recovery. [0049] For the purpose of the present disclosure, sawdust functionalization refers to the modification of sawdust to incorporate cellulose-binding modules, enhancing its ability to bind proteins and create specialized adsorbent materials. [0050] For the purpose of the present disclosure, reusability may be defined as the ability of the functionalized cellulose adsorbent material to retain its binding capacity and functionality over multiple recovery cycles, reducing waste and operational costs. [0051] For the purpose of the present disclosure, affinity-based purification refers to a purification method that relies on specific interactions between a target molecule and a binding site. In this invention, the selective binding of lithium ions to LBPs ensures high-purity recovery. [0052] For the purpose of the present disclosure, selectivity refers to the ability of the system to preferentially bind lithium ions over other ions or impurities present in the solution. High selectivity minimizes contamination and enhances the efficiency of lithium recovery. [0053] In an embodiment, a specialized sawdust, that acts like tiny sponges, is used to selectively capture target metals without using electrically intensive processes. In contrast, this invention operates under mild conditions (room temperature and neutral pH), reducing energy consumption and associated costs. [00141] Unlike microbial-based recovery systems that require the separation of microbial cells from the treated solution, this invention uses non-living cellulose-based adsorbents. This simplifies the separation process and eliminates the complexities associated with scaling microbial systems for industrial applications. [00142] The pH-based elution process ensures that lithium is efficiently recovered from the functionalized cellulose adsorbents. The system allows for precise control over elution conditions, enabling high recovery yields without the risk of damaging the adsorbent material or compromising lithium purity. [00143] With the increasing global demand for lithium, particularly in the context of the growing electric vehicle (EV) market and renewable energy storage, the need for sustainable and cost-effective recovery methods is greater than ever. This invention meets this need by offering a solution that is both economically viable and environmentally friendly. , Claims:1. patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a process for recycling of spent ternary lithium-ion batteries (LiB’s) via biomass assisted pyrolysis, comprising: a) mixing cathode powder <53 µm of a spent ternary LIB with lignocellulosic biomass powder having particle size <150 µm; b) pyrolyzing the mixture at a temperature in the range of 500 ? to 700 ? in an inert atmosphere (N2 gas) in a tube furnace to obtain a reduced char, pyrolysis gases, and pyrolysis oil; c) leaching the reduced char with water while simultaneously purging with the CO2 rich pyrolysis gas, and then filtering to obtain a Li rich solution and a leach residue; d) treating the leach residue with 2M citric acid at a temperature of 70 ? for 90 min and then filtering to obtain an acidic leach solution and a carbon rich leach residue; and subjecting to precipitation by addition of 1.10 times stoichiometric oxalic acid, and then filtering to obtain mixed metal oxalate and an acidic filtrate.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD The present disclosure relates to a process for recycling of spent ternary lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Particularly, the present disclosure relates to a process for recycling of spent ternary lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) via lignocellulosic biomass-assisted pyrolysis. BACKGROUND Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), having compact size, high specific energy, good capacity retention, and slow self-discharge rate, are one of the most crucial parts of portable electronic devices, electric vehicles, hardware tools, etc. for electrical energy storage. However, due to the presence of toxic and flammable components, spent batteries are not categorized as environmentally friendly or compatible. The current recycling processes of spent LIBs fall under three major categories, namely, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, and a combination of both. Pyrometallurgy based process includes smelting (at 1400-1500 ?), resulting in loss of Li values in the slag or gas produced, while the reduction-based processes work at lower temperatures (500-900 ?) and are followed by carbonated water leaching that use carbon sources (graphite, lignin, etc.) or hydrogen gas as reductant resulting in CO2 emission and higher economics of the process. Hydro-based processes demand high acid dosages with the addition of different reductants (H2O2, Glucose, etc.) and require higher flux (NaOH) consumption to recover Li values from the leach solutions. The use of graphite or other carbon sources, external CO2 gas flow in carbonated water leaching, and the inability to recirculate the acid solution add to the overall economy of the process. The combined process comprises reduction roasting of cathode active material or black mass at 500-900 ? to convert Li into water-soluble Li2CO3 or LiOH by utilizing graphite (30-50 wt%), straw (5-20 wt%), waste paper (5-20%), macadamia shell (10-40 wt%), and reductive gases (H2, CH4, CO, and biomass pyrolysis gas). The combined process also comprises leaching of the water leach residue in inorganic (1-6 M H2SO4, 1-3 M HCl, 1-3 M HNO3) or organic acid (1-3 M Citric acid, Tartaric acid) [US20230391632A1, CN111733326A, WO2023148760A1, CN115621597A, and CN115893511A]. Direct leaching of LIBs electrode powder utilizing H2SO4 (1-3 M, 60-90 ?, 20-50 g/L, 30-120 min), mixture of citric (0.6-0.7 M) and phosphoric acid (0.2-0.3 M) (S/L 15-40 g/L, 50-95 ?, 5-60 min) dissolves Li, Ni, Co, and Mn using reductants (H2O2, Glucose, Ascorbic acid etc.) [US20220149452A1; CN109065996B]. Leaching is followed by solvent extraction and selective or co-precipitation of Li, Ni, Co, and Mn using NaOH or Oxalic acid. Thus, there exists a need for a, simple, efficient, cost effective, carbon neutral, sustainable simple, efficient, cost-effective, carbon neutral, and environmentally friendly process for recovering Li, Ni, Co, and Mn values from spent lithium-ion batteries, to address the limitations of existing pyro and hydro-based methods. OBJECTIVES The main objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling ternary lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that utilizes lignocellulosic biomass-assisted pyrolysis. Another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that is efficient in extracting Li, Ni, Co, and Mn. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that extracts Li, Ni, Co, and Mn with high purity. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that is sustainable. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that utilizes two different waste streams, i.e., discarded LIBs and lignocellulosic biomass. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that utilizes the byproducts generated during the process. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that utilizes pyrolysis gas generated during the process as a CO2 source for carbonated water leaching. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that recirculates and reuses acid generated during the process. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process that fixes toxic and hazardous fluorine and provides pyrolysis oil that is free from toxic and hazardous fluorine and may be explored as a clean fuel source. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that is simple, economic and efficient. Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that is sustainable and environmentally friendly. SUMMARY In an aspect, the present disclosure relates to a process for recycling of spent ternary lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) via biomass assisted pyrolysis, said process comprising the following steps: a) mixing cathode powder, having particle size in the range of 1 µm to 53 µm, of a spent ternary Lithium-ion battery with lignocellulosic biomass having particle size in the range of 1 µm to 150 µm to obtain a mixture; b) pyrolyzing the mixture at a temperature in the range of 500 ? to 700 ?, by heating at a rate of 10 ?/min, under an inert atmosphere (N2 gas) in a tube furnace, for 15 mins to 60 mins to obtain a reduced char, CO2 rich pyrolysis gases, and pyrolysis oil; c) leaching the reduced char with water, at room temperature for 30 mins, while purging with the CO2 rich pyrolysis gas obtained in the pyrolysis step (b), and then filtering the leached char to obtain a Li rich solution and a leach residue rich in Ni, Co, and Mn; d) treating the leach residue rich in Ni, Co, and Mn, with 2M citric acid at a temperature of 70 ? for 90 min, and then filtering to obtain an acidic leach solution (rich in Ni, Co, and Mn) and a carbon rich leach residue; and e) subjecting the acidic leach solution to precipitation, at room temperature, by addition of 1.10 times stoichiometric oxalic acid, and then filtering to obtain mixed metal oxalate and an acidic filtrate. Figure 2: illustrates process flowsheet for the present invention. Figure 3: illustrates XRD spectrum of the reduced char at different conditions for the present disclosure. Figure 4: illustrates the XRD spectrum of the products obtained in the present disclosure; Figures 4(a), (b) and (c) illustrate the XRD spectrum (phase analysis) of the products (Li2CO3, Mixed metal oxalate, and Li3PO4 powder) obtained using the present process. Several existing methods for recovering Li, Ni, Co, and Mn metals from spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) fall under three major categories, namely, hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, and a combination of both. The existing pyro and hydro-based methods have limitations, such as the use of large amounts of carbon material with higher reduction temperature and high inorganic acid and base consumption, respectively. Further, these previous studies utilizing carbon or hydrogen-assisted reduction roasting did not consider the byproducts generated during the process for recycling and reuse. Furthermore, in the existing hydro-based methods, recirculation of the acid was not possible due to various reasons. The present invention provides a process for recycling lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that utilizes lignocellulosic biomass for pyrolysis, which is simple, efficient, cost effective, sustainable and environmentally friendly. The present method uses biomass, which is considered a carbon neutral source, as a reducing agent thereby supporting the carbon neutrality aspects of the process. The present process utilizes the pyrolysis gas, generated during the pyrolysis, as a CO2 source for carbonated water leaching, acid recovered after the leaching process, for recirculation, and fixates hazardous fluorine mostly as metal fluoride during the process, thereby adding to the overall economy and helps in minimizing the waste generation. The current process effectively extracts Li, Ni, Co, and Mn with purity comparable to the previously reported routes. Therefore, in an aspect, the present disclosure relates to a process for recycling of spent ternary lithium-ion batteries (LiB’s) via biomass assisted pyrolysis, said process comprising the following steps: a) mixing cathode powder, having particle size in the range of 1 µm to 53 µm, of a spent ternary Lithium-ion battery with lignocellulosic biomass having particle size in the range of 1 µm to 150 µm to obtain a mixture; b) pyrolyzing the mixture at a temperature in the range of 500 ? to 700 ?, by heating at a rate of 10 ?/min, under an inert atmosphere (N2 gas) in a tube furnace, for 15 mins to 60 mins to obtain a reduced char, CO2 rich pyrolysis gases, and pyrolysis oil; c) leaching the reduced char with water, at room temperature, for 30 mins with a solid to liquid (S/L) ratio of 1/50, while purging with CO2 rich pyrolysis gas obtained in the pyrolysis step (b), and then filtering the leached char to obtain a Li rich solution and a leach residue rich in Ni, Co, and Mn; d) treating the leach residue rich in Ni, Co, and Mn, with 2M citric acid at a temperature of 70 ? for 90 min, and then filtering to obtain an acidic leach solution rich in Ni, Co, and Mn, and a carbon rich leach residue; and e) subjecting the acidic leach solution rich in Ni, Co, and Mn, to precipitation, at room temperature, by addition of 1.10 times stoichiometric oxalic acid, and then filtering to obtain mixed metal oxalate and an acidic filtrate. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the spent ternary Lithium-ion battery is selected from the group consisting of NMC442, NMC532, and combinations thereof. In another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the spent ternary Lithium-ion battery is selected from the group consisting of NMC442 and NMC532. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the spent ternary Lithium-ion battery is NMC532. In a more preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the spent ternary Lithium-ion battery is NMC532. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the lignocellulosic biomass powder is selected from the group consisting of Walnut shell powder, pistachio shell powder, sunflower seed shell powder and pine nut shell powder. In another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the lignocellulosic biomass powder is selected from the group consisting of Walnut shell powder, pistachio shell powder, and pine nut shell powder. In yet another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the lignocellulosic biomass powder is selected from the group consisting of Walnut shell powder and pine nut shell powder. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the lignocellulosic biomass powder is selected from the group consisting of Walnut shell powder. In the present disclosure, cathode powder having particle size below 53 µm is necessary because above this size other impurities such as Al, Cu resides in the pure cathode powder. In the present disclosure, lignocellulosic biomass of walnut shell powder having particle size in the range of 1 µm to 150 µm is used for better reduction kinetics. If one uses lignocellulosic biomass of walnut shell powder having particle size above 150 µm then reaction kinetics might change and results will vary, i.e. particle size above 150 µm will slow down the reaction kinetics and would result in inferior results. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is in the range of 100:20 to 100:40. In another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is in the range of 100:22 to 100:38. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is in the range of 100:24 to 100:36. In a more embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is in the range of 100:26 to 100:34. In a most preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is in the range of 100:28 to 100:32. In another most preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (a), the weight ratio of the cathode powder to the lignocellulosic biomass is 100:30. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the temperature of pyrolysis is in the range of 500-700 ? with a heating rate of 10 ?/min. In another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the temperature of pyrolysis is in the range of 500-650 ? with a heating rate of 10 ?/min. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the temperature of pyrolysis is in the range of 500-600 ? with a heating rate of 10 ?/min. In a more preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the temperature of pyrolysis is in the range of 500-550 ? with a heating rate of 10 ?/min. In a most preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the temperature of pyrolysis is 500 ? with a heating rate of 10 ?/min. Temperature range of 500 ? to 700 ? is common for the pyrolysis and beyond this temperature the fixed carbon content produced will be more and it will convert the process more towards the solid-solid reaction. Apart from that the increase in temperature will result in loss of valuable Li in vapour form, and due to sintering lower dissolution of Ni, Co, and Mn in acid leaching. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the pyrolysis is carried out for 15 to 60 min. In another embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the pyrolysis is carried out for 25 to 60 min.
