There is no advantage of increasing the time beyond this range because the reaction is completed within this time. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, step (b) further comprises a step of evaporating the Li rich solution to obtain Li2CO3 powder. In the present disclosure, for evaporation of water from the Li rich solution, to obtain Li2CO3 powder, any known method may be used. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the pyrolysis oil obtained is free from hazardous fluorine and may be explored as a clean fuel source. In an embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (b), the Li2CO3 obtained is ~96-97% pure. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (d), the weight/volume ratio of the leach residue and the 2M citric acid is 1:40. In a preferred embodiment of the present disclosure, in step (e), the stoichiometric ratio of the acidic leach solution to the oxalic acid is 1:1.10. The leftover acid solution after precipitation can be recirculated at least 3 times for the acid-leaching of the water-leached residue to obtain a final barren solution containing a minimum of 2g/L Li. In the process of the present disclosure, the acidic filtrate obtained in step (e), is recirculated for the acid-leaching of the leach residue in step (d), and on final recirculation, a final acidic filtrate rich in Li (>2 g/L) is obtained in step (e); the acidic filtrate obtained in step (e), may be recirculated three times for the acid-leaching of the leach residue in step (d), and on three recirculation’s, a final acidic filtrate rich in Li (>2 g/L) is obtained in step (e); The step (e), further comprises a step of adding an alkali (NaOH) to the final acidic filtrate rich in Li (>2 g/L), to increase its pH to >10, and subjecting the final acidic filtrate (pH > 10) to precipitation (at 90 ?) by the addition of 1.05 × stoichiometric Na3PO4 and then filtering to obtain a second Li salt (Li3PO4) and a final barren solution (rich in Na). The final leach solution is treated with 1.05 × stoichiometric Na3PO4 at pH>10 to recover Li3PO4. In the process of the present disclosure, the Li salt (Li3PO4) from the final leach solution is recovered by precipitation using 1.05 × stoichiometric Na3PO4 having a pH>10. The precipitation efficiency was observed to be 50-70%. The final barren solution (pH>12 containing ~100-120 g/L Na, ~500-800 ppm Li, 300-400 ppm F, and <60 ppm Ni, Co, and Mn) obtained after Li precipitation can be reutilized as a pH modifier (till pH~7). In the process of the present disclosure, the 20-40% fluorine (F) in Li2CO3 is fixed as LiF, whereas 4-8% F in mixed metal oxalate is fixed as NiF2, CoF2, and MnF2, and ~60-70% F in the final barren solution, while obtaining almost fluorine-free pyrolysis gas and oil. The present invention is further illustrated by the following examples. These examples describe possible preferred embodiments for illustrative purposes only, but they do not limit the scope of the invention. These laboratory scale experiments can be scaled up to industrial/ commercial scale. EXAMPLES The following examples are given by way of illustration of the present invention and should not be construed to limit the scope of present disclosure. It is to be understood that both the foregoing general description and the following detailed description are exemplary and explanatory only and are intended to provide further explanation of the subject matter. Although the subject matter has been described in considerable detail with reference to certain preferred embodiments thereof, other embodiments are possible. As such, the spirit and scope of the subject matter should not be limited to the description of the preferred embodiment contained therein. Methods, Materials and Measurements All commercially available chemicals were purchased from appropriate sources and used as received unless otherwise mentioned. NMC442, NMC532 batteries were procured from Institute scrap warehouse. Citric Acid, Oxalic Acid, Na3PO4, and NaOH were purchased from local supplier (Rankem made). Walnuts were purchased from the market, and the shells were dried and ground to obtain the walnut powder. A conventional custom-made Tube Furnace having a 1.5 kW power rating and a silicon carbide heating source fitted with a PID controller was used. The elemental composition of the cathode active powder used in the present disclosure is presented in Figure 1(a). The elemental compositions (weight %) were measured with the help of MP-AES, Flame Photometer, and UV-visible spectrophotometer. The phase analysis (XRD Spectrum) of the cathode active powder was performed with the help of XRD analysis. XRD spectrum presented in Figure 1(b) confirmed the phase of cathode active powder as NMC 532. The SEM-EDS micrograph and elemental mapping analysis of the cathode active material is presented in the Figures 1(c) and (d). Elemental mapping confirms the uniform distribution of Ni, Co, Mn, and O in the cathode active material. The atomic ratio of Ni/Co/Mn in the EDS analysis confirms the phase present as NMC 532. The SEM-EDS micrograph of walnut shell powder, an image of walnut shell, and CHNS analysis of the walnut shell powder used in the present disclosure is presented in Figures 1(e) and (f) confirming the presence of C and H in the walnut shell powder. Example 1 – The extraction of Li salts (Li2CO3 and Li3PO4) and mixed metal oxalate (Ni, Co, and Mn) from spent Lithium-ion batteries (NMC 532): Spent Lithium-ion batteries (NMC 532) were discharged and their cathode material was dismantled, crushed/ground, and sieved to obtain a cathode powder having particle size <53 µm. The cathode powder (50 g, particle size <53 µm) was mixed with 30 wt% (15 g) lignocellulosic biomass (Walnut shell) powder having particle size <150 µm in mortar and pestle. The mixture was pyrolyzed at a temperature of 500 ? in a tube furnace while heating at a rate of 10 ?/min in an inert atmosphere (N2 gas) for 60 min to obtain a reduced char (Li2CO3, NiO, CoO, Ni, Co, C) (~50 g), pyrolysis gases, and pyrolysis oil. The reduced char was leached, at room temperature for 30 min, with water, while purging with CO2 rich pyrolysis gas obtained in the pyrolysis step, and then filtered to obtain a Li rich solution and a leach residue (~40 g). The Li rich solution was evaporated to retrieve the first Li salt as Li2CO3 powder (~10 g) having ~97% purity. The Li extraction efficiency via water leaching and evaporation observed to be ~86%. The 40 g leach residue was divided into 4 parts of 10 g each for further acidic leaching. 10 g leach residue was dissolved in 2M citric acid at a temperature of 70 ? for 90 min, with a solid/liquid ratio (S/L) of 1/40, and then filtered to obtain an acidic leach solution rich in Ni, Co, Mn and a minor amount of Li and a carbon (~65 wt%) rich leach residue (~1 g). The acidic leach solution was subjected to precipitation by addition of 1.10 times stoichiometric oxalic acid, and then filtered to obtain mixed metal oxalate (~23 g) and an acidic filtrate. The Ni, Co, and Mn precipitation efficiency was observed to be ~99% The acidic filtrate obtained was recirculated (instead of fresh acid solution) for the acid-leaching of the 10 g water-leached residue obtained earlier, followed by filtration and oxalate precipitation. The four parts of water leach residue (10 g each) were dissolved with the same acidic solution via recirculation of acidic filtrate while increasing the amount of residual Li with each recirculation. During the leaching process, fresh acid was used only once. After recirculating the acidic filtrate at least three times, a final barren solution containing a minimum of 2g/L of Li was obtained. The final leach solution was treated with NaOH to increase the pH of the solution to >10 and 1.05X stoichiometric Na3PO4 was added to recover Li3PO4 (2nd Li salt). The Li precipitation efficiency was observed to be ~70%. In the pyrolysis step, the hazardous fluorine was fixed as metal fluoride (LiF, NiF2, MnF2, and CoF2) during the reduction process and dissolved in the water leaching (LiF) or acid leaching (NiF2, MnF2, and CoF2) step. The pyrolysis oil obtained was found to be free of hazardous fluorine and can be explored as a clean fuel source. The carbon rich leach residue can be utilized as a catalyst in the biomass pyrolysis process. Li2CO3 and Li3PO4 salts were found to be ~96-97% pure, and the mixed metal oxalate dihydrates of Ni/Co/Mn were found to be ~99% pure and had an atomic ratio of 51/21/28, respectively. The above procedure was used to carry out the following experiments, using the parameters in the Table-1 below. patents.abstract: The present invention discloses the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation to inhibit thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, comprising a lithium salt, a cyclic carbonate compound, and a furan-based compound. The electrolyte is a mixture of lithium salt in a composition of cyclic carbonate compound and the furan-based compound in the specific molar ratio. The thermos-response electrolyte 10 composition at higher temperature undergoes a Diels-Alder reaction at a predetermined threshold temperature, thereby forming reaction products that inhibit ion transport and blocks thermal runaway in the Lithium-ion battery. patents.complete_specification: Description:A THERMORESPONSIVE ELECTROLYTE FORMULATION FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERY SAFETY AND PROCESS THEREOF FIELD OF INVENTION 5 The present invention relates to the field of battery technology. Specifically, the present invention relates to lithium-ion batteries. More specifically, the present invention relates to electrolyte formulation. for lithium-ion batteries. More particularly, the present invention relates to the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries to prevent thermal runaway and to enhance 10 the reliability of lithium-ion batteries. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION In recent years, llithium-ion battery technology is viable due to its high energy density and cyclic abilities. Different electrolytes are used in lithium-ion batteries 15 for enhancing their efficiency. These electrolytes have been divided into liquid, solid, and polymer electrolytes and explained on the basis of different solventelectrolytes. Aqueous electrolytes are preferable due to their preference over organic electrolytes having properties like non-flammability, low cost, and safety. However, many other factors like pH, corrosion process, oxidation-reduction side 20 reactions, and hydrogen gas evolution created limitations in their performance. Later, solid-state lithium-ion batteries are preferred over both aqueous lithium-ion batteries and organic-based lithium-ion batteries due to their outstanding electrochemical competencies. The electrochemical cycles of batteries can be increased by the creation of a solid electrolyte interface. Solid-state batteries 25 exhibited considerable efficiency in the presence of composite polymer electrolytes with the advantage of suppressed dendrite growth. In advanced polymer-based solid-state lithium-ion batteries, gel polymer electrolytes have been used, which is a combination of both solid and polymeric 3 electrolytes. The use of these electrolytes enhanced the battery performance and generated potential up to 5 V. In general, Electrolytes are categorized into weak and strong electrolytes based on conductivity. Conductivity depends on the concentration of ions in an electrolyte. Strong electrolytes dissociate completely 5 into ions on dissolution. Acids, bases, and salts fall into the category of strong electrolytes. Materials that partially dissociate into their ions; like CH3COOH, alkyl amine, etc. are placed in the category of weak electrolytes. Electricity discovery has led to the invention of various storage devices, like batteries capacitors, etc. Energy storage in batteries is considered an efficient and reliable form of storage. During 10 the charging process, electrical energy is stored at the anode, and chemical energy is stored at the cathode while during discharge, the energy is released in the form of electricity. Electrolytes act as a transport medium for the movement of ions between electrodes and are also responsible for the enhanced performance and cell stability of batteries. Cell voltage and capacity represent energy density, while 15 coulombic efficiency and cyclic stability indicate energy efficiency. These parameters are very important for investigating battery performance. High energy density and excellent performance make lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) an active candidate in this field of energy storage devices. John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino were awarded the Nobel prize in 2019 in 20 chemistry for their contribution to LIBs. Their theories regarding LIBs are now commonly applicable around the world. Rechargeable LIBs are promisingly used in aerospace, electrical vehicles, and many other advanced technologies due to their high energy densities. LIBs are now mostly used in electrical and hybrid automobiles. Several factors affect the performance of LIBs, among which 25 temperature is an important factor that influences the life cycle, cost, and energy density of LIBs. Another important aspect of LIBs is electrolytes, which are one of the core sections responsible for defining the efficiency of LIBs. Over the years, change in cell designs have necessitated the need for more efficient electrolytes to enhance the performance of LIBs, resulting in the innovation of 30 various electrolytes (liquid, solid, aqueous, organic, polymer, etc.). 4 There are few patents available in the state of art about existence and some of the most used electrolytes are discussed below: US9190698B2 discloses a Lithium-ion electrolytes with improved safety tolerance to high voltage systems, the invention also includes various embodiments of 5 electrolytes for use in lithium-ion batteries, the electrolytes having improved safety and the ability to operate with high-capacity anodes and high voltage cathodes. In one embodiment there is provided an electrolyte for use in a lithiumion battery comprising an anode and a high voltage cathode. The electrolyte has a mixture of a cyclic carbonate of ethylene carbonate (EC) or mono-fluoroethylene 10 carbonate (FEC) co-solvent, ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), a flame retardant additive, a lithium salt, and an electrolyte additive that improves compatibility and performance of the lithium-ion battery with a high voltage cathode. The lithiumion battery is charged to a voltage in a range of from about 2.0 V (Volts) to about 5.0 V (Volts). 15 US9166249B2 discloses a Fluoride ion battery composition, the invention also discloses anion-based charge transport electrochemical system that uses fluoride ion transporting electrolytes, including ionic liquids, with and without various additives to improve performance, is described. The fluoride ion transporting electrolyte can be wholly or partly an ionic liquid that is typically 20 liquid at temperatures less than 200 degrees Celsius. In other embodiments, electrolytes that remain liquid at less than 100 degrees Celsius are useful. Hubble et al., 2022, from Google Scholar discloses a Liquid electrolyte development for low-temperature lithium-ion batteries, the Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) power virtually all modern portable devices and electric vehicles, and their 25 ubiquity continues to grow. With increasing applications, however, increasing challenges come, especially when operating conditions deviate from room temperature. While high-temperature performance and degradation has been extensively studied in LIBs, sub-zero Celsius performance has received less attention, despite being critical for batteries in transportation roles. Although many 30 individual processes contribute to the capacity loss commonly observed in LIBs at 5 low temperatures, most of them are governed to some extent by the non-aqueous liquid electrolyte present throughout the cell interior. Therefore, electrolyte engineering presents an unparalleled opportunity to study and address the fundamental causes of low-temperature failure. In this review, we first briefly cover 5 the various processes that determine lithium-ion performance below 0 °C. Then, we outline recent literature on electrolyte-based strategies to improve said performance, including various additives, solvents and lithium salts. Finally, we summarize these findings and provide some perspectives on the current state of the field, including promising new areas of investigation. 10 However, thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries is a serious safety concern that can result in fires and explosions. Conventional safety mechanisms, such as shutdown separators and flame-retardant additives, frequently fail to respond quickly or lose effectiveness in extreme conditions. As a result, there is a need in the current state of the art to develop the present 15 invention, which addresses these limitations by introducing a thermoresponsive electrolyte that autonomously prevents thermal runaway at an early stage while maintaining the electrochemical performance of the batteries. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION 20 The major objective of the present invention is to provide a novel electrolyte formulation. Another objective of the present invention is to provide a novel electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries. Another objective of the present invention is to provide a thermoresponsive 25 electrolyte which undergoes a Diels-alder reaction at elevated temperatures, leading to a controlled thermal shutdown before the onset of catastrophic failure, this mechanism provides an intrinsic safety feature that actively prevents thermal runaway. 6 Another objective of the present invention is to design an electrolyte which functions effectively at room temperature under normal operating conditions, preserving the battery's capacity and cycle life while providing a reliable mechanism at elevated temperatures. 5 Yet another objective of the present invention is to utilize the components such as vinylene carbonate (VC) and 2,5-dimethylfuran (DMFu) that are either already used in commercial electrolytes or can be derived from renewable resources, enabling cost-effective and sustainable production. Yet another objective of the present invention is to provide novel electrolyte that 10 seamlessly integrated into existing LIB production lines without significant retooling, thereby avoiding high capital expenditures and facilitating widespread adoption. Further objective of the present invention is to utilize the developed thermoresponsive electrolyte formulation for thermal runaway in lithium – ion batteries. 15 SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION In one aspect, the present invention discloses a novel thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation to inhibit thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, comprising: a lithium salt; 20 a cyclic carbonate compound, and a furan-based compound, the electrolyte is a mixture of lithium salt in a composition of cyclic carbonate compound and the furan-based compound in predetermined molar ratio, The obtained thermos-response electrolyte composition, at higher 25 temperature undergoes a Diels-Alder reaction at a predetermined threshold temperature, thereby forming reaction products that inhibit ion transport and blocks thermal runaway in the lithium-ion battery. 7 The thermos-responsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries as mentioned above the predetermined molar ratio of lithium salt : cyclic carbonate compound : furan-based compound is in the range of 0.10-0.15: 0.9-1.0 : 0.75-0.8 5 In another aspect, the present invention also discloses the process of inhibition of thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, comprising steps: dissolution of lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in a mixed solvent comprising vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran at a 10 molar ratio of 0.15:0.8:1.0; blocks the micropores of a tri-layer polypropylene/polyethylene/polypropylene (PP/PE/PP) separator of the battery, thereby inhibiting the ion transport and blocking the thermal runaway. 20 In yet another aspect, the present invention discloses a lithium-ion battery, comprising: a positive pole piece/cathode; In further aspect, the present invention discloses the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries as mentioned above, the vinylene carbonate 30 forms a stable and protective solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the battery anode, reducing electrolyte decomposition and improving cycle life. 8 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS The accompanying drawings, which are incorporated in and constitute a part of this disclosure, illustrate exemplary embodiments and, together with the description, serve to explain the disclosed principles. 5 Figure: 1 depicts research objectives of the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation of the present invention. Figure: 2 depicts pouch cell performance of the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation of the present invention. Figure: 3 depicts thermal shutdown behaviour of the thermo-responsive electrolyte 10 formulation of the present invention. Figure: 4 depicts SEM Analysis of the thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation of the present invention. 15 20 9 DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention as embodied by “A THERMORESPONSIVE ELECTROLYTE FORMULATION FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERY SAFETY AND PROCESS THEREOF” succinctly fulfills the above-mentioned need[s] in the 5 art. The present invention has objective[s] arising as a result of the abovementioned need[s], said objective[s] having been enumerated herein above. The following description is directed to “a thermoresponsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion battery safety and process thereof” as much as the objective(s) of the present invention are enumerated, it will be obvious to a person 10 skilled in the art that, the enumerated objective(s) are not exhaustive of the present invention in its entirety and are enclosed solely for the purpose of illustration. The present invention therefore encompasses also, any improvisation[s]/modification[s] applied to the structural alternative[s]/functional alternative[s] within its scope and purview. The present invention may be embodied in other specific forms without departing from the essential attributes thereof. 20 Furthermore, the terms and phrases used herein are not intended to be limiting but rather are to provide an understandable description. Throughout this specification, the use of the word "comprises" and variations such as "comprises" and "comprising" may imply the inclusion of an element or elements not specifically recited. 25 The embodiments of present invention provide a novel thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation for thermal runaway inhibition in lithium-ion batteries. Lithium-ion Batteries hitherto had serious drawbacks, or safety concerns due to thermal runaway. LIB’s being extensively adapted in electric vehicles, portable electronics, and energy storage systems with risk of thermal runaway, can lead to 10 fires and explosions. trilayer polypropylene/polyethylene/polypropylene (PP/PE/PP) separators with intrinsic thermal shutdown mechanisms, commercialized by Celgard, are the most sought-after internal functional component that safeguards LIBs from thermal runaway. However, these PP/PE/PP 5 trilayer separators often fail to prevent thermal runaway in practical applications. This is because the melting point of PE (130 °C) is only 30 °C lower than the melting temperature of PP (160 °C). Thermal inertia after battery shutdown can easily cause the internal temperature of the batteries to reach the melting point of PP, leading to the separator shrinking and causing an internal short-circuit. In certain instances, 10 cells with thermal shutdown separators remain inactive for as little as three minutes before failing due to internal short circuits. On the other hand, the incorporation of flame-retardant (chemicals) additives into the electrolytes often deteriorates the battery performance. The present invention discloses a solution to intrinsically safer electrolyte that can 15 autonomously prevent thermal runaway at an early stage without compromising the electrochemical performance of the batteries and the dimensional stability of the separator, tremendously enhancing the LIBs safety, Present invention in various embodiments provides a novel thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries. A major motivational aspect of the 20 present invention is the adoption of Lithium-Ion Batteries (LIBs) in various applications which has raised safety concerns due to the risk of thermal runaway. The thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation of the present invention includes the electrolyte composition which comprises a lithium salt, specifically lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), dissolved in a mixture of VC and 25 DMFu at an optimized molar ratio of 0.15:0.8:1.0. The electrolyte formulation of the present invention is prepared by dissolving LiTFSI into a mixture of high-purity DMFu and VC, followed by continuous stirring until a uniform solution is obtained. 11 It includes the Thermal Shutdown Mechanism: Particularly, at room temperature, the electrolyte functions effectively in LIBs. Upon reaching a critical temperature (e.g., 120°C), the Diels-Alder reaction between VC and DMFu alters the electrolyte’s physicochemical properties, leading to a rapid increase in viscosity, 5 phase separation, or polymerization, effectively halting ion transport. Additionally, the reaction forms oligomers that occlude the micropores of the commercial trilayer polymer separator, ceasing battery operation. In first embodiment, the present invention discloses, a novel thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation to inhibit thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, batteries, 10 comprising: a lithium salt; a cyclic carbonate compound, and a furan-based compound, the electrolyte is a mixture of lithium salt in a composition of cyclic 15 carbonate compound and the furan-based compound in predetermined molar ratio, The obtained thermos-response electrolyte composition, at higher temperature undergoes a Diels-Alder reaction at a predetermined threshold temperature, thereby forming reaction products that inhibit 20 ion transport and blocks thermal runaway in the lithium-ion battery. In one embodiment of the present invention, the predetermined molar ratio of lithium salt : cyclic carbonate compound : furan-based compound is in the range of 0.10-0.15: 0.9-1.0 : 0.75-0.8. In one embodiment of the present invention, the lithium salt is lithium 25 bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI). In one embodiment of the present invention, the cyclic carbonate compound is vinylene carbonate (VC) and the furan-based compound is 2,5-dimethylfuran (DMFu). 12 In second embodiment, the present invention discloses, a novel process of preparation of thermo-responsive electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion batteries, comprising steps: dissolving a lithium salt is lithium 5 bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in a mixed solvent comprising vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran at a molar ratio of 0.15:0.8:1.0; with constant stirring at room temperature, to yield the reaction product. The the formulation is capable of undergoing a Diels-Alder reaction 10 between vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran upon reaching a threshold temperature in the range of 90°C to 120°C; In another embodiment of the present invention is provided a Lithium-Ion battery with the thermos-responsive electrolyte composition to prevent thermal inhibition 15 comprising: a positive pole piece/cathode; a negative pole piece/anode; a diaphragm spaced between the positive and negative pole pieces that contains the thermos-responsive electrolyte composition of the present 20 invention a lithium salt, a cyclic carbonate compound, and a furan-based compound, wherein the electrolyte is lithium salt dissolved in a solvent mixture of the cyclic carbonate compound and a furan-based compound which are capable of undergoing Diels-Alder reaction. 25 In another embodiment of the present invention is provided a process of inhibit of thermal runaway in lithium-ion batteries, comprising steps: Preparation of thermos-responsive electrolyte: 13 dissolution of lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in a mixed solvent comprising vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran at a molar ratio of 0.15:0.8:1.0; with constant stirring; providing a Lithium-ion battery with the thermos-responsive 5 electrolyte formulation in the compartment between the anode or negative pole and the cathode or positive pole, wherein the formulation solvents vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran upon reaching a predetermined threshold temperature in the range of 90°C to 120°C along with Lithium salt undergoes a 10 Diels-Alder reaction resulting in reaction product, and the formation of reaction products comprising oligomeric species that increase viscosity and induce phase separation or polymerization of the electrolyte thus blocks the micropores of a trilayer polypropylene/polyethylene/polypropylene (PP/PE/PP) 15 separator of the Li-ion battery, thereby inhibiting the ion transport and blocking the thermal runaway. In an embodiment of the present invention, the tri-layer separator is selected from the group comprising polypropylene, polyethylene, polypropylene (PP/PE/PP). The Diels-Alder reaction between vinylene carbonate and 2,5-dimethylfuran is 20 tailored to ensure normal electrochemical performance at operating temperatures while triggering a shutdown response only under overheating conditions. As per the present invention, the formulation functions effectively at room temperature, preserving battery capacity and cycle life under normal operating conditions. The vinylene carbonate forms a stable and protective solid electrolyte 25 interphase (SEI) on the battery anode, reducing electrolyte decomposition and improving cycle life. 14 WORKING EXAMPLE In commercial LIBs, thermal runaway is typically controlled using temperatureresponsive tri-layer polypropylene/polyethylene/polypropylene (PP/PE/PP) separators. However, because of thermal shrinkage at ~160 °C, these separators 5 often fail to prevent thermal runaway in practical LIBs. The LIB’s of the present invention comprises of thermos-responsive electrolyte composed of a lithium salt dissolved in vinylene carbonate (VC) and 2,5-dimethylfuran (DMFu) that functions effectively in batteries at room temperature. At high temperatures, VC and DMFu participate in Diels-Alder reactions, forming oligomers that significantly decrease 10 the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte and concurrently occlude the micropores of PP/PE/PP separators. These dual effects enable a two-step intelligent modulation of thermal runaway, with a warning phase activated above 80 °C and a complete thermal shutdown at 120 °C. Figure 1a illustrates that formation of oligomers from the vinylene carbonate (VC) 15 and 2,5-dimethylfuran (DMFu) at a temperature of 120°C leading to thermal protection by oligomers that significantly decrease the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte and concurrently occlude the micropores of PP/PE/PP separators. The electrolyte formulation presented here can be integrated into existing battery production lines in Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) without significant 20 retooling, avoiding high capital expenditures. Also, from the figure 1 illustrates experimental analysis of the present invention. Experimental Analysis of the present invention: The experimental analysis of the novel electrolyte formulation for lithium-ion 25 batteries (LIBs) focused on evaluating its performance, thermal shutdown behaviour, and structural changes under elevated temperatures. The experimental analysis provides the working of the electrolyte formulation of the present invention and its application in inhibition of thermal runaway in Lithium-Ion Batteries (LIBs) 15 The following key experiments were conducted and clearly depicted in Figure 1 to 4 which includes: From figure 2 Pouch Cell Performance is clearly explained: Objective: To assess the electrochemical performance of the electrolyte in a 5 practical battery configuration. Method: Pouch cells were assembled using the proposed electrolyte and tested under standard charge-discharge cycles at room temperature. Results: The cells demonstrated stable cycling performance with minimal capacity fade, indicating that the electrolyte maintains effective ion transport and 10 electrochemical stability under normal operating conditions. The present invention validates the potential of the thermoresponsive electrolyte in practical LIBs, a single-layer pouch cell was fabricated using the commercial LiFePO4 cathode and the graphite anode. From Figure 2a and 2b its schematically illustrates a configuration of the pouch cell and its working mechanism. From the 15 figure 2c its clearly depicts the charge-discharge profiles of the pouch cells for different cycles reveal nearly identical voltage polarization during cycling. Figure 2d explains the pouch cell exhibits an initial areal charge capacity of 1.27 mA h cm–2 and 1.15 mA h cm–2 during the following discharge, retaining 0.87 mA h cm–2 after 30 cycles. It's important to highlight that there is a significant 20 performance lack of correspondence between coin and pouch cells. The quantity of the electrolyte inevitably exists in excess in the coin cells, leading to distinctly better performance than that of the pouch cells. Figure 2 clearly shows the research analysis of the present invention, which discloses: Conventional lithium-ion battery (LIB) safety mechanisms rely heavily 25 on battery management systems (BMS), which have inherent limitations in response time and efficiency. These systems use external sensors and circuits to detect overcharging, but their response time may be insufficient to prevent failure. Furthermore, short internal circuits caused by dendrite growth or physical damage 16 are difficult to detect and address in real time. Furthermore, there is a growing shift from liquid to solid-state electrolytes to improve LIB safety. However, solid-state electrolytes face significant challenges, such as low ionic conductivity, high interfacial resistance, and complicated manufacturing processes. Scaling up their 5 production while maintaining cost efficiency remains a significant challenge. Illustrated in figure 3 Thermal Shutdown Behaviour: Figure 3 demonstrates the thermal shutdown behaviour of the thermos-responsive electrolyte when tested in pouch cells. 10 Objective: To evaluate the thermal shutdown capability of the electrolyte. Method: The electrolyte's response to elevated temperatures was tested by subjecting the pouch cells to controlled heating. Results: The electrolyte exhibited a two-step intelligent modulation of thermal runaway. A warning phase was activated above 80°C, characterized by a gradual 15 increase in internal resistance. Complete thermal shutdown occurred at 120°C, where the Diels-Alder reaction between vinylene carbonate (VC) and 2,5-dimethylfuran (DMFu) significantly decreased the ionic conductivity and occluded the micropores of the separator, effectively halting ion transport. The thermal shutdown characteristics of the thermoresponsive electrolyte 20 formulation were evaluated and compared with the conventional carbonate-based LP30 electrolyte using Swagelok cells. To ease the risk of parasitic electrolyte reactions with the lithium anode at elevated temperatures, a graphite||LiFePO4 fullcell configuration was employed. Initial cycling of the cells at a 0.1C rate and room temperature (25 °C) confirmed stable operation, followed by additional cycling at 25 80 °C and 120 °C. Both graphite/LiFePO4 cells displayed distinct multistep chargedischarge plateaus at 25 °C and 80 °C, as depicted in Fig. 3a. Notably, the LP30 electrolyte-containing cell-maintained functionality even at 120 °C, as evidenced by its charge profile. patents.abstract: The present disclosure provides a binder-free, zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoplatelet-coated polypropylene separator for lithium metal batteries. ZnO nanoplatelets are self-assembled on the separator surface from an aqueous suspension, avoiding the use of toxic binders or solvents. The ZnO coating facilitates uniform lithium ion flux and promotes in-situ formation of a stable artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the lithium anode, comprising Zn, Li2O, LiOH, and LixZny. The modified separator demonstrates improved electrolyte uptake, ionic conductivity, and thermal stability. Electrochemical testing shows reduced nucleation overpotential, enhanced reversibility, and over 500 stable cycles at 1 mA/cm². The separator further exhibits dendrite suppression and extended performance in anode-free lithium metal batteries. Post-cycling analysis confirms interfacial stabilization by inorganic SEI components. The method is simple, scalable, eco-friendly, and effective across a range of cell architectures, offering a practical solution for high-performance lithium metal batteries.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage devices. More particularly, the invention pertains to lithium metal batteries, and specifically to a modified separator structure comprising a binder-free zinc oxide nanoplatelet coating on polypropylene separators, facilitating enhanced lithium ion transport, suppression of dendritic growth, and stabilization of lithium metal anodes. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) are widely regarded as the next-generation energy storage systems owing to their high theoretical specific capacity (~3860 mAh/g) and lowest redox potential among all known anode materials. These attributes render lithium metal a promising anode for high-energy-density applications, including electric vehicles, aerospace technologies, and grid-scale energy storage. Despite their immense potential, lithium metal batteries have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, primarily due to safety and stability concerns associated with the lithium metal anode. [0003] A major challenge in the practical application of lithium metal anodes is the formation of lithium dendrites during repeated plating and stripping processes. These dendritic structures originate from the uneven deposition of lithium ions on the anode surface, which leads to the growth of filament-like protrusions that can eventually penetrate the separator and cause internal short circuits. Such short circuits result in rapid battery failure, thermal runaway and potential safety hazards including fire or explosion. [0004] In addition to dendrite formation, the lithium metal anode is prone to the formation of an unstable and non-uniform solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer due to continuous reactions between lithium and the electrolyte. The repeated rupture and reformation of this SEI layer during battery cycling not only consume active lithium and electrolyte but also result in the formation of "dead lithium," thereby decreasing the coulombic efficiency and cycling stability of the cell. [0005] Numerous strategies have been proposed to address these issues. One of the more promising approaches involves the modification of battery separators to regulate lithium ion transport and suppress dendrite growth. Conventional separator modification methods include the application of ceramic, polymeric, or composite coatings on commercial separators using techniques such as doctor blade coating, slurry casting, or dip coating. These coatings often include binders like polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) in organic solvents such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), which enable film formation and adhesion. [0006] However, the use of binders and organic solvents introduces several drawbacks. The presence of a binder can decrease ionic conductivity, block separator pores, and impede lithium ion flux. Additionally, organic solvents like NMP are toxic, environmentally hazardous, and not ideal for scalable industrial applications. Furthermore, the mechanical stability and thermal resistance of binder-based coatings are often inadequate under operational conditions, limiting their practical utility in lithium metal batteries. [0007] In certain reports, the application of lithiophilic materials, such as metals or metal oxides, has been attempted to homogenize lithium ion distribution and promote smooth lithium deposition. While this strategy has shown promise, its efficacy is often compromised by the use of thick coatings, insulating additives, or the lack of in-situ interfacial reactivity with lithium metal. [0008] Therefore, there remains an unmet need for separator for lithium metal batteries that enables uniform lithium plating and suppresses dendrite growth during cycling along with being binder-free, scalable, and capable of delivering high thermal stability, improved wettability, enhanced ionic conductivity, and most importantly, effective suppression of dendritic growth. The ideal separator system should also facilitate the formation of a robust, inorganic-rich, and electrochemically stable SEI layer directly at the lithium metal interface, thereby improving both the safety and performance of lithium metal batteries across a wide range of current densities. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0009] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies are as listed herein below. [0010] The primary object of the present disclosure is to provide a separator for lithium metal batteries that enables uniform lithium plating and suppresses dendrite growth during cycling. [0011] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a binder-free separator modification strategy that avoids the use of toxic solvents and insulating binders typically used in conventional separator coatings. [0012] Yet another object of the present disclosure is to improve the ionic conductivity, lithium ion transference number, and electrolyte wettability of polypropylene-based battery separators. [0013] A further object of the present disclosure is to enable the in-situ formation of an artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) comprising zinc, lithium oxide, lithium hydroxide, and LixZny alloys for enhanced interfacial stability. [0014] It is also an object of the present disclosure is to enhance the thermal stability and mechanical integrity of the separator at elevated operating temperatures. [0015] Still another object is to demonstrate the applicability of the modified separator in both lithium metal batteries and anode-free lithium batteries with copper current collectors. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0016] In accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure, a binder-free zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoplatelet-coated polypropylene (PP) separator for use in lithium metal batteries is provided. The invention involves immersing a microporous PP separator into an aqueous suspension of ZnO nanoplatelets and thermally treating the assembly to promote uniform adhesion of ZnO onto the separator surface. [0017] In another aspect, the ZnO-coated separator serves a dual function: (i) its lithiophilic nature homogenizes lithium ion flux to suppress dendrite growth, and (ii) the ZnO undergoes in-situ electrochemical reduction to form a Zn-rich, inorganic SEI comprising Li2O, LiOH, and LixZny. [0018] In another aspect, the modified separator exhibits enhanced electrolyte uptake, ionic conductivity, and transference number while maintaining thermal stability above 300°C. Electrochemical evaluation demonstrates lower nucleation overpotential, improved reversibility, and prolonged cycling life. The separator is also effective in anode-free lithium metal batteries, showing higher lithium recovery and reduced dead lithium formation. [0019] In an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a separator for a lithium metal battery, the separator comprising: a microporous polypropylene substrate; and a coating of metal oxide nanoplatelets disposed on at least one surface of the substrate, wherein the metal oxide nanoplatelets are applied via a binder-free self-assembly method, and wherein the separator is configured to promote uniform lithium ion flux and enable in-situ formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on a lithium metal anode. [0020] In another embodiment, the present disclosure provides a method of fabricating a separator for a lithium metal battery, the method comprising: preparing an aqueous suspension of ZnO nanoplatelets; immersing a polypropylene separator in the suspension; thermally treating the immersed separator to promote adsorption of ZnO onto the separator surface; and vacuum drying the ZnO-coated separator to obtain a binder-free ZnO nanoplatelet-coated separator. [0021] In another embodiment , the present disclosure provides a lithium metal battery, comprising: a lithium metal anode, a cathode, an electrolyte, and a separator positioned between the anode and the cathode, wherein the separator facilitates formation of a Zn-rich in-situ SEI on the anode surface during operation. [0022] In another embodiment, the present disclosure provides an anode-free lithium metal battery, comprising: a cathode, a copper current collector functioning as an anode during initial lithium plating an electrolyte, and a separator positioned between the cathode and the current collector, wherein the separator facilitates uniform lithium nucleation and deposition on the copper collector. [0087] The present disclosure reports a ZnO-decorated polypropylene separator as a bi-functional tool to suppress or mitigate dendritic proliferation. The ZnO-coated separator prepared via a binder-free strategy delivers two benefits. Firstly, the formation of a Zn-rich in-situ artificial SEI is expected due to the spontaneous reduction of ZnO on the lithium surface. Secondly, the lithiophilic ZnO will provide a uniform ion flux to counter Li+ depletion/non-uniform Li+ distribution near the anode surface. [0088] The modified separators are explicitly characterized to support the role of these benefits. The ZnO-coated separator exhibits improved wettability, higher electrolyte uptake percentage, improved ionic conductivity, and larger transference number and exchange current density. During electrochemical characterization, ZnO modified separators exhibit a substantially lower nucleation overpotential of 70 mV, superior cycle life of more than 500 cycles at a current density of 1 mA/cm2 in aggressive carbonate solvents, and better reversibility at elevated current densities up to 5 mA/cm2. [0089] With comprehensive electrochemical and post-cycling characterization, it is shown that ZnO-coated separators are potentially promising for mitigating dendritic growth and improving the interfacial instability, as observed from the HR-SEM and EDS analysis. The in-situ formation of Zn and LixZny SEI is confirmed from the post-cycling XRD and XPS analysis of the metallic anode. Ascribed to the synergistic effect of lithiophilicity and in-situ formation of anion dominant inorganic rich SEI, the proposed strategy enabled stable lithium metal deposition–stripping behaviour and can further be applied for anode-free batteries. [0090] Accordingly, the present invention discloses a binder-free ZnO nanoplatelet-coated polypropylene separator that addresses major challenges in lithium metal battery technology. Through enhanced wettability, ion transport, thermal stability, and interfacial chemistry, the invention significantly extends battery life, suppresses dendritic growth, and is effective even in anode-free systems. The approach is environmentally friendly and amenable to industrial scale-up, marking a substantial improvement over existing separator technologies. Example 4: ZnO engineered separator: [00107] The ZnO modified separator was prepared by allowing self-assembly of the synthesised ZnO nanoplatelets onto the polypropylene separator (PP 2500) using 1 mg/mL (ZnO-1) and 5 mg/mL (ZnO-5) ZnO suspension. Due to adsorption of white ZnO, the separator turned little opaque compared to the translucent blank separator. To better elucidate the ZnO decoration, the SEM images of bare and modified separators were captured. The bare separator revealed a porous structure as reported by celgard® (Figure 1(a)), whereas ZnO-1 (Figure 1(b)) and ZnO-5 (Figure 1(c)) evinced surface decoration with ZnO nanoplatelets. The elemental mapping and EDX featured the presence of ZnO in both the separators, with an obvious higher ZnO content (12 atomic %) in separator decorated using 5 mg/mL suspension. Interestingly, the surface decoration protocol did not lead to any pore shrinkage. The pores with comparable dimension were observed in the SEM images of the bare and modified separators. To have a fair comparison, the separator modified using the same protocol in absence of ZnO was also characterised (ZnO-0). The observation indicated that the anisotropy caused by ZnO nano-structure helped in preventing the pore blockage by penetrating into the pores of the separator. The successful decoration of separator with ZnO was further confirmed from the X-ray diffraction analysis. Figure 1(d) displays the XRD patterns of the ZnO nanostructures in its as-synthesized state. The diffractogram exhibited major peaks at 31.77°, 34.41°, 36.25°, 47.57°, 56.6°, 62.85°, 67.94°, and 69.08°. These angles correspond to the lattice planes (100), (002), (101), (102), (110), (103), (112), and (201), respectively. The observed pattern exhibits a strong correspondence with the data from the JCPDS (reference number 01-079-2205) corresponding to the ZnO with the hexagonal wurzite structure. The X-ray diffractograms of ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 featured the peaks of ZnO in addition to the PP separator peaks at 2? = 14.0°, 17.0°, and 18.5°, which are indicative of the presence of isotactic polypropylene. [00108] Thermal stability is an important property of a separator. The low thermal stability and thermal shrinkage of the separator is considered to be an intrinsic drawback which effects the safety of the cell. As a consequence of separator shrinkage, the cathode and anode comes in direct contact resulting in short circuit ultimately leading to fire and explosion. Therefore, it is crucial to improve or atleast retain the thermal stability of the separator during modification. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) is thus employed to ensure the thermal stability of the modified separator. Figure 1(e) presents the TGA curves for bare and ZnO-1, and ZnO-5. As seen from the TGA, the bare separator start showing weight loss as early as 270 °C whereas the onset potential for ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 were observed to be 315 °C and 325 °C, respectively. The higher onset potentials and inflection points of the modified separators manifests their enhanced thermal stability which can be attributed to high thermal stability of ZnO. In addition, ZnO-5 showed the maximum loss of 32 %, beyond which no further loss of mass was observed. This can be explained on the basis of higher ZnO loading which exhibits thermal stability of >900 °C. Thermal shrinkage analysis of the modified and unmodified separators was further performed by heating the separators of the same dimensions at 40°, 60°, and 100° C, respectively, for 1 hour. The images of the separators subjected to different temperatures are presented in Figure 1(f) for comparative analysis. It can be observed that the bare PP started rolling at 60° C, whereas it was completely rolled and shrunk at 100 °C. In contrast, ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 demonstrated stable behaviour up to 100° C. In accordance with the inferences made from TGA analysis, the thermal shrinkage analysis also revealed that modification with ZnO improves the thermal stability of the PP separator and the improvement was found to be more pronounced for higher loading of ZnO. [00109] Next, the effect of surface layer on the electrolyte wetting was investigated first by measuring the dynamic contact angle of the sessile electrolyte drop on the individual separator and later by investigating the percentage electrolyte uptake. When a liquid electrolyte was dropped onto the bare separator (Figure 1(g)), an initial contact angle of 62° was observed which was still as high as 59° after 45s (4% lower compared to initial angle) indicating poor wettability of the commercial PP separator. However, ZnO-1 manifested a slightly lower initial contact angle of 57° which reduced to 51° in 45s i.e. nearly 11 % lower than the initial contact angle. The electrolyte wetting was found to be drastically improved in case of ZnO-5 as witnessed from the initial contact angle of 47°. Furthermore, over a time of 45s, the contact angle reduced to 35° which is 25 % lower than the initial contact angle and 41 % lower compared to contact angle observed after 45s of wetting of bare separator. The dynamic contact angle measurement of the electrolyte drop clearly demonstrates improved wetting performance of the ZnO modified separator. The heterogeneous distribution of lithiophilic ZnO nanoplatelets over the pores of separator allows additional layer for electrolyte sopping offering better wettability. Furthermore, the electrolyte uptake studies were conducted using Bare PP and ZnO coated separators and the results calculated using ‘equation 1’ are tabulated in Table 1. The ZnO-1 exhibited an uptake of 462%, nearly 48% higher than the bare separator. Interestingly, the uptake percentage for ZnO-5 was found to be 448, slightly lower compared to ZnO-1. This is because of a higher ‘Wo’ of ZnO-5 ascribed to higher ZnO loading. The Nyquist plot observed for ZnO-1, ZnO-5, and bare PP separator are presented in Figure 1(h,i). The plot indicates that the bulk resistance of ZnO-coated separators is lower than that of bare PP, resulting in improved ionic conductivity. The observed ionic conductivities calculated using ‘equation 2’ are summarized in Table 1. The ZnO-modified separators exhibited nearly 2 times higher ionic conductivity than bare separators. Similar improvements were observed in the transference number of Li+ calculated utilizing the Bruce-Vincent method, as outlined in the experimental section. The transference number of Li+ with ZnO-1 PP was found to be 0.67, substantially higher than 0.41, corresponding to bare PP (Figure 1(j)). The increased ionic conductivity and transference number of ZnO-modified separators can be ascribed to the redistribution of the Li+ ions through their insertion in the ZnO layer. As such, the ionic conductivity of PP is solely dependent on the movement of liquid electrolyte through the pores and thus offers non-uniform Li+ flux to the anode surface. Adding a lithophilic ZnO layer, therefore, improves and homogenizes the Li+ ionic conductivity and allows more cationic charge conduction. Furthermore, the Tafel plots recorded for the symmetric cells containing ZnO-1 PP demonstrate a notably higher current density of 0.54 mA?cm-2, which is 1.45 times greater than that of the bare symmetric cells (0.37 mA?cm-2; Figure 1(k)) and 1.23 times higher than ZnO-5 (0.45 mA?cm-2; Figure 1(k)). These findings underscore the enhanced kinetics of Li+ in the presence of ZnO-1 PP. The impact of ZnO modification on the antioxidant stability of electrolyte was also studied by recording the current response of Li|ZnO-PP|Al and Li|Bare-PP|Al coin cell using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in the potential range of 3.0 – 5.0 V at a scan rate of 0.5 mV/s. The comparative voltammograms demonstrated suppressed oxidative current in the presence of a modified separator with nearly 0.31 V higher onset potential compared to bare PP. All these studies manifested improved wettability and faster Li+ diffusion/transfer kinetics in the presence of the ZnO-modified separators. These traits are anticipated to offer uniform Li+ flux, leading to homogenous nucleation and smooth lithium plating. The impact of ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 on the electrochemical reversibility of the Li|Li symmetrical cell was next investigated to validate these anticipations. Example 5: Electrochemical reversibility [00111] The nucleation overpotential observed during the Li plating is an important parameter for investigating the lithiophilicity of the material. Figure 2(a) present the comparative nucleation overpotential observed using unmodified, ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 separators. Interestingly, both the ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 resulted in substantially lower nucleation overpotential of 70, and 150 mV, respectively. In contrast, the cell with unmodified separator showed a nucleation overpotential of 240 mV. Furthermore, ZnO modified separators also exerted substantially lower growth overpotentials. The difference between nucleation and growth overpotential was found to reduce from 149 mV in case of bare PP to 19 mV for ZnO-1. This substantial decrease in nucleation and growth overpotential indicates facilitated nucleation and plating in presence of ZnO ascribed to its lithiophilic nature, improved wettability and uniform Li+ flux. [00112] To test the efficacy of the modified separators under more realistic conditions, the lithium plating/dissolution behaviour at elevated current densities were further investigated. It is well known, that dendritic proliferation becomes much more catastrophic at current densities > 2 mA/cm2 and thus it is crucial to test the modified separators at these demanding current densities. Therefore, Li platting/dissolution in presence and absence of modified separators were studied at increasing current densities of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 5.0 mA/cm2 and the results are presented in Figure 2(b-j). Interestingly, the improvement in case of ZnO modified separator was much more prominent at elevated areal current densities. The plating-striping polarization of the cell with unmodified separator increased from 160 mV to 419 mV as the current density was raised from 0.2 to 3 mA/cm2. In addition, the cell failed to exhibit any reversibility at current density of 5 mA/cm2 featuring an apparent short circuit in the voltage profile (Figure 2(g, h)). Whereas, in presence of ZnO-1, a voltage polarization of 197 mV was observed at 3 mA/cm2 which increased to 317 mV at 5 mA/cm2. Both the cells with ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 separators exhibited complete reversibility even at a high current density of 5 mA/cm2. On linear fitting, the voltage polarization was found to increase at a rate of 46 mV/(mA.cm-2) for ZnO-1 PP compared to 139 mV/(mA.cm-2) observed for cell having bare separator. The results clearly indicate the substantially improved rate performance of the modified separators. The lower overpotential and better reversibility in presence of ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 even at high current densities (> 2 mA/cm2) clearly manifests the ability of ZnO towards supressing the dendritic growth. [00113] As a result of increasing current density, the metal surface is expected to corrode with development of pits, dead Li and mossy growth. As a combined effect of these degradation processes, the recovery of plated Li is severely impacted. Therefore, the robustness of the cell was next investigated by letting the cells cycle at 1 mA/cm2 after the rate performance. [00114] As seen from the Figure 2(i), a rapid increase in polarization was observed for the cell having unmodified separator as well as control separator (ZnO-0). Whereas, the cell having ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 showcase stable plating/stripping behaviour without any substantial increase in voltage polarization till 300 hours. Nevertheless, the ZnO-1 was found to outperform ZnO-5, ZnO-0 and the unmodified separator which can be ascribed to its greater electrolyte uptake ability and higher ionic conductivity. Whereas, higher loading of ZnO in case of ZnO-5 can lead to thicker layer which might impede the charge transfer. [00115] Next, the cycle life of lithium plating/dissolution was tested by cycling the fresh cells having unmodified, ZnO-1 and ZnO-5 separators at 1 mA/cm2 current density with a capacity of 0.5 mAh/cm2. As showcased in Figure 3(a), the Li|Li symmetrical cells demonstrated a stable cyclability upto 500 cycles. The evolution of voltage polarization with the cycle number was monitored and plotted in Figure 3(b). The figure showcased a stable voltage polarization of 89 mV at 100th cycle for ZnO-1 compared to 195 mV for bare separator. The voltage polarization of ZnO-1 slightly rises to 112 mV after 200 cycle and 150 mV after 300 cycles. On the other hand, the symmetrical cell assembled using unmodified separator featured a significantly shorter cycle life showcasing a short circuit after 213th cycle. The prolonged cycle life and moderate cell polarization showcased by ZnO modified separators manifested the potentiality of ZnO coating for stabilizing and mitigating the interfacial instability associated with metallic Li anode. [00116] The galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) was next deployed to comprehend the effect of Li+ mass transfer complications on cell polarization. The mass-transfer complication originates due to the accumulation of dead lithium and depletion of Li+ at the electrode/electrolyte interphase. By providing a prolonged rest period of 3 minutes after 15 seconds of galvanostatic current, the GITT allows dilution of local concentration gradients so that the electrode/electrolyte interphase establishes a steady-state equilibrium condition and minimizes the contributions from mass-transfer complications. Thus, the comparative analysis of cell polarization in the GITT voltage profile sandwiched between the uninterrupted galvanostatic charge-discharge profile was carried out to deconvolute the effect of mass transfer complications on the growth of cell polarization. As presented in Figure 3(c,d), the first GITT cycle of both cells resembles the stripping platting voltages of the previous galvanostatic cycles. Nevertheless, in the second GITT trace (Figure 3(e)), the bare PP showcased significantly lower polarization than the corresponding uninterrupted galvanostatic voltage profiles of preceding cycles. The difference in total overpotential for GITT and galvanostatic cycles in the case of bare PP was ~27%, much more significant than 11% for the ZnO-1 PP. This demonstrates that ZnO-1 PP minimizes the voltage polarization associated with the Li+ mass transport complications. As the mass transfer complication arises due to the accumulation of dead lithium and the development of concentration gradients at the electrode/electrolyte interphase, the GITT studies reveal a more pronounced accumulation of dead lithium in the case of bare PP and highlight the superiority of ZnO-1 PP in minimizing the dendritic proliferation which is the primary reason for the accumulation of dead lithium layer. [00117] The substantially improved electrochemical performance is associated with the bi-functional role of the ZnO modified separator. Firstly, the lithiophilic ZnO layer offers an improved and uniform Li+ flux through the separators and overcomes the dendritic proliferation due to the localized Li+ density near the pores of separator. Secondly, ZnO contributes to stabilize the surface of lithium anode by reacting with metallic Li and resulting in an in-situ ASEI formation as per the following reactions: Li + ZnO ? Zn + Li2O + LiOH xLi + yZn ? LixZny [00118] Where the ASEI having lithiophilic Zn and LixZny can offer preferential nucleation sites and act as physical barrier between electrolyte and metallic lithium, the LiOH and Li2O can act as Li+ conductors to facilitate Li+ plating below the ASEI. Example 6: Post-Cycling Analysis [00119] To support the aforementioned explanations, the cycled lithium and corresponding separators were analysed using HR-SEM and XRD. The HR-SEM images of lithium extracted from cells cycled for 50 cycles at a current density of 1 mA/cm2 were recorded and are presented in Figure 4(a). The HR-SEM images of lithium cycled using unmodified separator demonstrated evident non-uniform lithium deposition and dendritic proliferation. On the contrary, in the presence of ZnO-1 and ZnO-5, a dense, uniform lithium deposition with much smoother topography was apparent from the HR-SEM images of the post-cycled lithium. However, ZnO-1 featured flat and smooth plating, whereas ZnO-5 resulted in entangled lithium nuclei merging into each other. Uniform deposition is likely to arise because of the lithiophilic ZnO and subsequent insertion of Li+ in ZnO, which facilitate uniform Li+ flux during stripping/deposition cycles. Furthermore, the EDX analysis of the cycled anode confirmed the presence of Zn on the surface, manifesting the in-situ formation of Zn-rich SEI, which eventually suppresses the continuous electrolyte degradation and stabilizes the reactive lithium metal/electrolyte interphase. Furthermore, the topographical changes in the cycled separators were also investigated, and the microscopic images are presented in Figure 4(b). The comparative images presented in the figure represent nearly blocked pores of the bare separator. Furthermore, the surface seems to be protruded. In contrast, ZnO-1 featured open pores similar to the pore sizes observed before cycling. In addition, the EDX analysis showed 6% of Zn in the post-cycled image, which is just 1 % less than the Zn content observed in the uncycled ZnO-1. These observations reveal the well-preserved structure and topography of ZnO-1, which explains its superior performance. Surprisingly, ZnO-5 features partially clogged pores and protruded surfaces. The partial clogging of the pores can be explained by the high ZnO loading in ZnO-5, which might have resulted in preferential lithium plating on the separator itself. Because of the partially clogged pores and thicker ZnO layer, a compromised Li+ diffusion is ascertained, which also explains the electrochemical behaviour of ZnO-5. In order to comprehend the interaction between Li and Zn, the post-cycled XRD characterization of both the separator and metallic Li was conducted. The XRD of Bare and ZnO-1 post-cycled separator (after 50 cycles). The PP separator exhibits only the peaks corresponding to the isotactic polypropylene. On the other hand, in addition to the PP peaks below 20°, the XRD of ZnO-1 showcased signature peaks of Zn and LixZny (JCPDS#03-0954) indicating the chemical/electrochemical reduction of ZnO to Zn and its further alloying with lithium (Figure 5). The distinctive peaks seen for the LixZny alloy provide evidence that the ZnO-coated PP material demonstrates the formation of an alloy with Li and facilitates an even distribution of Li+ ions to the anode surface. In order to better understand the interaction between ZnO and metallic Li, the XRD of cycled Lithium was also studied. The XRD spectra of metallic lithium cycled using the bare PP and the ZnO-1. The XRD spectra of lithium cycled in the presence of bare PP exhibit characteristic peaks corresponding to metallic lithium, lithium oxide (Li2O), and lithium hydroxide (LiOH). On the other hand, apart from the peaks typical of Li, Li2O (ICDD #01-074-6256) and LiOH (ICDD #32-0564), the XRD spectra of Li cycled in the presence of ZnO-1 exhibit peaks similar to those of Zn and LiZn alloy. Example 7: XPS analysis [00120] To validate the XRD analysis, XPS of the cycled lithium was performed. Figure 5 displays the Zn 2p, O 1s, and F 1s spectra of the Li anode after 50 plating stripping cycles in the presence of ZnO-1 PP (referred to as ZnO-1|Li) and bare PP (referred to as Li) at a current density of 1 mA/cm². Figure 5(a) presents the deconvoluted Zn 2p spectra of the lithium cycled in the presence of ZnO-1 PP. The Zn 2p exhibited doublet peaks corresponding to Zn 2p3/2 and Zn 2p1/2 at 1021.3 and 1044.4 eV. The broad Zn 2p3/2 was deconvoluted for better analysis, as shown in Figure 5(b). The deconvolution resulted in four peaks at 1022.0, 1021.3, 1020.7 and 1019.9 eV. The first three peaks correspond to ZnF2, ZnO, Zn. Meanwhile, the peak at 1019.9 eV implicated the formation of LixZny alloy. Considering the more pronounced electropositive character of Li compared to Zn, its alloying with Zn will result in increased electron density distribution in the vicinity of Zn atoms, thereby explaining its presence at binding energy lower than that of Zn metal. The Zn 2p spectrum confirmed the formation of LixZny and Zn-rich SEI on the lithium surface, which is in agreement with the inferences made from the XRD analysis. The O 1s spectra of both the ZnO-1|Li and bare|Li exhibited peaks at 530.78, 531.5, and 532.9 eV, which can be attributed to LiOH, Li2CO3, and LixPOyFz respectively, the decomposition product of carbonate solvents and LiPF6 (Figure 5(c,d)). The ZnO-1|Li had an additional peak at 529.7 eV corresponding to the Zn-O, thereby validating the presence of ZnO on the lithium surface. The F 1s (Figure 5(e,f)) spectrum shows the presence of LixPFy and LiF (~686.5 and ~684.03 eV). An additional peak at 684.6 eV appeared in ZnO-1|Li, indicating the formation of inorganic ZnF2 on the lithium surface. The Li 1s spectra of ZnO-1|Li and Li exerted four peaks at 54.3, 54.7, 55.3, and 56.0 eV corresponding to Li2O, LiOH, Li2CO3 and LiF, respectively. However, the ZnO-1|Li has a relatively larger percentage of Li2O and LiOH than bare, supporting the proposed stabilization mechanism of ZnO-1 PP. Furthermore, the C 1s of bare lithium have a more considerable contribution from the C=O, implicating more pronounced solvent residues at bare lithium. Following this, the F/C and P/C elemental ratios were also compared. As F and P correspond to the anion and C origins from the solvent, the F/C and P/C ratio can be interpreted as the indicator for predicting the preference towards anion-to-solvent ratio in SEI. The ZnO-1 PP had significantly larger F/C and P/C compared to bare Li, indicating lower solvent residues and preferred anion-to-solvent decomposition at the metal anode ultimately resulting in more robust inorganic SEI in the presence of ZnO-1|PP. Thus, the post-cycling studies of the separator and lithium confirmed that the modified PP separator reacted with metallic lithium, resulting in modulated SEI composition with more inorganic components like LiF, ZnF2, ZnO, and LixZny. The high lithiophilicity, shear modulus, and robustness of these inorganic ceramics explain the suppressed interfacial instability and improved electrochemical performance of Li anode in the presence of ZnO-modified separators. Additional Example: Comparison with conventional doctor’s blade coating: [00121] Composite coating using doctor’s blade is a conventional method for separator modification and has been reported extensively in literature. Though it offers a precise control over the uniformity and wet coating thickness of the surface layer over the separator, but it relies on use of binder, mostly PVDF in NMP which are associated with their own troubles like toxicity, instability and poor Li+ conductivity. In contrast, the proposed method relies on the self-adsorption/decoration of separator which features appreciable stability and reliability without use of any toxic solvent or binder. Therefore, the separators modified with proposed strategy were compared with the separators coated with the slurry composed of 80 % ZnO and 20 % PVDF using doctor’s blade fixed to 50 µm wet coating thickness. [00122] The doctor’s blade method resulted in a coating thickness of 22 µm. The separator coated using doctor’s blade are referred as ZnO-PVDF in the following text. Li|Li symmetrical cells were assembled using ZnO-1 and ZnO-PVDF separators and their comparative electrochemical performance were analysed for Li platting dissolution cycles as a function of increasing current densities and cycle numbers. Though, ZnO-PVDF showcase much stable voltage profiles at lower current densities ascribed to uniform distribution of ZnO nanoplatelets across the separator. However, the material exhibited a sharp increase in polarization at current densities > 1 mA/cm2 (Figure 6). The increase in overpotential can be ascribed to impeded Li+ transfer at fast rates due to dense layer of ZnO and binder. This dense layer can act as an additional barrier next to separators pores which can offer hindrance to the movement of Li+. In addition, the cell with ZnO-PVDF suffered from sharp increase in voltage at much early stage (nearly 200 cycles), whereas ZnO-1 reached the same overpotential after 450 cycles. Nevertheless, both the materials exhibited substantially improved performance compared to unmodified separator. However, the ZnO-1, the separators modified using proposed binder free approach outperforms the ones prepared using the slurry coating method ascribed to minimal yet optimum surface decoration of ZnO. Example 8: Li Vs Cu: Future directions for anode free metal batteries [00123] The efficacy of the ZnO functionalized separator was further investigated in the presence of limited lithium conditions, typically for extending the application of the proposed strategy in the format commonly known as “anode-free” lithium metal batteries. To do so, the 3.85 mAh equivalent lithium was plated on the copper current collector at a current density of 0.5 mA/cm2. It is well reported that the copper current collector offers much higher nucleation overpotential for lithium plating resulting in non-uniform lithium nucleation and further growth. Because of this, the SEI that results from the electrolyte reduction at the plated lithium is also non-uniform and unstable. As a result, the anode free lithium metal batteries are severely challenged with poor reversibility, compromised coulombic efficiency, and capacity fading. To study the reversibility of plating and lithium behaviour in presence and absence of ZnO, 50% of the initially plated lithium was dissolved and plated at a current density of 2 mA/cm2 for 10 cycles. After 10 cycles, all the lithium was allowed to dissolve without any time limitation. The results are presented in Figure 7(a). In contrast to a much higher nucleation overpotential of 303 mV, the cell with ZnO-1 exhibited facilitated nucleation with an overpotential of 174 mV (Figure 7(b)). The lower overpotential can be explained on the basis of the lithiophilic character of ZnO and its contribution to the uniform SEI formation. Furthermore, ZnO-1 showed slightly lower striping/plating overpotential growth compared to the bare separator. However, the signatures of soft short-circuits were observed in both the cases which can be ascribed to the high current densities. Nevertheless, after 10 rounds of continuous plating and dissolution, nearly 68 % of the plated lithium can be recovered in the case of ZnO-1. In contrast, the cell with a bare separator delivered only 53% of the plated lithium, indicating significantly higher dead Li content. [00124] The microscopic images of the Cu after the complete stripping of lithium were then recorded to visualize the surface changes and dead lithium deposits. As the Figure 7(c and d) shows, the Cu current collector from the cell, which had a bare separator, was filled with mossy dead lithium. Meanwhile, the Cu from the cell having ZnO-1 showcased a much smoother surface with undersized and flattish undissolved lithium. Furthermore, EDX confirms the presence of Zn on the copper surface. This study clearly outlines the advantages of ZnO in facilitating the nucleation of lithium, stabilizing the SEI, and preventing the dendritic growth and loss of lithium even under limited lithium conditions. Example 9: Full cell with LCO as cathode [00125] Encouraged by the improvements in the electrochemical performance of Li|Li symmetrical cells, full cells with commercial lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) cathode were assembled using bare PP and ZnO-1 PP as separators, respectively. The rate performance and cycle life of the cells were investigated to evaluate the practical efficacy of ZnO-1 PP. As shown in Figure 8, both the cells exhibited similar voltage profiles, delivering a specific discharge capacity of ~170 mAh/g at C/15. Nevertheless, substantial improvements were observed at rates higher than C/3. The cell with ZnO-1 PP delivered 140.28, 131.45, 116.5, 104.02, and 95.07 mAh/g at C/3, C/2, 1C, 2C, and 3C, respectively, showcasing up to ~25 % improvement compared to the cell with bare PP. Also, the LCO|ZnO-1|Li at C/3 for 100 cycles exhibited ~18 % improvement and 91.27 % capacity retention compared to LCO|Bare|Li, which showed 88.34 % capacity retention. The comparative rate study manifested the role of ZnO-1 PP in improving the charge transfer, which can be ascribed to higher ionic conductivity, larger transport number, and enhanced exchange current density. The effect of ZnO-1 PP on the cycling stability was next assessed by continuously cycling the cell at 1C for 100 cycles. Figure 8(b) showcases the discharge capacity as a function of cycle number. As can be seen from the figure, the cell with ZnO-1 exhibited higher discharge capacity in the beginning, which was consistently maintained till 100 cycles, exhibiting a capacity retention of 83.8 % with a ~13.2 [00126] Conclusively, the present disclosure provides a binder-free approach to modify the poly-propylene separators with ZnO nanoplatelets to stabilize the deposition-dissolution behavior of lithium. Ascribed to the high lithiophilicity and lithium insertion capability of ZnO, the additional ZnO layer on the separator offers lower nucleation overpotentials, uniform Li+ flux, and guided lithium deposition. Furthermore, the ZnO nanoplatelets in direct contact with metallic lithium get reduced on the metal surface, resulting in the in-situ formation of artificial SEI on the metal anode. Ascribed to these combined benefits, the modified separator showcased a substantially improved cycle life of more than 500 cycles in aggressive carbonate solvent, improved rate kinetics in current densities ranging from 0.2 – 5.0 mA/cm2, reduced polarization, and dense, dendrite-free Li plating at several tested current densities. Furthermore, the ZnO-1 manifested enhanced reversibility in Li|Cu cells and improved rate performance in Li|LCO cells. Therefore, based on the thorough electrochemical testing and post-cycling analysis, the current study highlights the bi-functional role of ZnO-coated separators in enabling stable lithium metal batteries. This results in smoother and denser lithium deposits and reduced risk of internal short circuits. [00130] In-Situ SEI Formation: ZnO undergoes spontaneous electrochemical reduction on contact with lithium to form a Zn-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) composed of Li2O, LiOH, and LixZny alloys. This SEI is chemically and mechanically robust, providing enhanced interfacial stability.
