patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a system and method for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries (LIBs). The method comprising the steps of mixing of one or more spent black mass, natural acid, reducing agent and to accelerate lithium extraction under condition to obtain a black mass dispersion which is separated to form a solution. A base is added to the solution to obtain a pure solution followed by its concentration and crystallization or precipitation with an alkali-phosphate salt to obtain a lithium salt. The solid is subjected to concentrated acid treatment followed by high temperature treatment to get soluble salts of Cobalt, Nickel, Manganese, these are dissolved to get a concentrated solution followed by impurity removal. The impurity free solution containing only Nickel, Manganese & cobalt is converted to high value product used directly Cathode Active Material Manufacturing.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [0001] The present disclosure belongs to the technical field of battery material recycling and specifically relates to a method for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries. The present disclosure also relates to a system for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed invention, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. [0003] Irrespective of the cathode chemistries, i.e. Li(NixMnyCoZAlW)O2 where 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ 1, 0 ≤ w ≤ 1 and w+x+y+z =1 the common denominator is Lithium, the industry is moving towards cheaper Cathode chemistries and safer alternatives, the consumption of Lithium is predicted to exponentially rise in the coming years thanks to EV Revolution. Therefore, sourcing the Lithium is of utmost importance, especially because of its uneven distribution. The exponential demand puts severe strain on the natural resources required for its extraction. It is environmentally feasible and geographically beneficial to preferentially extract lithium first from the spent EV Batteries before extracting other metals to get maximum recovery. [0004] The conventional process requires multiple stages of solvent extraction in series with multiple solvents followed by concentrating them and crystallizing it. It is both CAPEX heavy and energy intensive process when the battery salts further treated to High Value Product. [0005] CN112820974A discloses an impurity removal process for the scrapped positive electrode material leaching solution from lithium batteries involves three main steps: (1) precipitating the leachate to eliminate iron, aluminum, and some copper ions using a first alkaline solution (LiOH), yielding a first filtrate; (2) precipitating the first filtrate to separate lithium ions using a second alkaline solution (LiOH), resulting in a second filtrate with lithium and a target substance precipitate; (3) dissolving the target substance precipitate to create a first solution, then precipitating it to remove calcium, magnesium, and some lead ions using sodium fluoride, producing the target solution, to which a third alkali solution (NaOH) can be added to precipitate the lithium battery precursor. [0006] Choi et al. [Journal of Hazardous Materials, 2022, 424, Part B, 127481] discloses a microwave-assisted green leaching process to leach four strategic metals (Ni, Li, Mn, and Co) from spent NMC batteries. The process comprises leaching spent NMC batteries with 2 M citric acid (leachant) and 5 wt% glucose (reductant), wherein microwave irradiation was performed during the leaching step for 0.5 h. After the leaching process, divalent metal ions, that is, Ni(II), Co(II), and Mn(II), were separated at room temperature using oxalic acid in the form of NiMnCoC2O4⋅nH2O. [0007] Barnwal et al., [Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration, 2024, 41, 3517-3527] discloses a method for selectively recovering lithium (Li), cobalt (Co), and graphite from end-of-life lithium cobalt oxide (LCO)-based lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). The process begins with thermal treatment of the LIB black mass at 800°C for 60 minutes, which dissociates the cathode compound and converts lithium into carbonates, enabling its effective dissolution in distilled water during subsequent processing. Cobalt is leached using 2 M nitric acid with 10 vol.% hydrogen peroxide over 2 hours. Graphite is recovered as a leaching residue after filtration of the acid leachate. Cobalt is precipitated as cobalt oxalate using oxalic acid, which is then thermally treated to produce cobalt oxide (Co₃O₄). [0008] The technical problem associated with the conventional process includes i) lithium ion gets lost during tradition hydrometallurgical, solvent extraction (SX), and precipitation process due to size and identical chemical similarity with sodium ion. For example; both Li and Na-ions hydrodynamic size is almost identical, which compromise with the purity of final Li-salt, ii) strong mineral acid and reducing agents are reported for the lithium recovery with multiple steps processing to recover final products, iii) when treating the extracted black mass by hydrometallurgical processing, lithium is not always enriched in one single product fraction, neither, but can be distributed during the multi-step precipitation series in all filter cakes, iv) reported literature used high temperature pyrolysis process for pretreatment of Blackmass which increases carbon footprint of process, v) flexibility of producing lithium salts including but not limited to LiCl, Li3PO4, Li2C2O4, LiCH3COO, LiOH, Li2CO3. Further, there is no report for the process of getting High Yielding High Value Products from spent LIBs. [0009] Thus, there is a need to overcome the problem associated with the prior arts and to develop a new system and method for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION [0010] An objective of the present invention is to provide a method for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries. [0011] Another objective of the present invention is to provide a system for generating high value products from spent lithium ion batteries. [0012] Another objective of the present invention is to provide a process for high yield industrial scale production of Lithium salts from spent LIBs blackmass. [0013] Still another objective of the present invention is to provide an energy and cost effective process to get high value product with significant reduction in CAPEX. [0014] Yet another objective of the present invention is to obtain a process that is free from secondary pollution generation due to excess chemical use. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0015] This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that are further described below in Detailed Description section. The alkali phosphate salt is added in a stoichiometric amount to get the lithium salts precipitated as lithium phosphate. [0040] In some embodiment of the present disclosure, the inorganic acid in step f) is selected from a group comprising of nitric acid, sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid and combinations thereof and has a weight ratio of 0.5 to 1.0%. Preferably, inorganic acid is nitric acid. [0041] In some embodiment, the condition in step a) includes a temperature in the range of 50 to 100 °C for a period in the range of 1 to 5 hours. Preferably, the temperature is in the range of 50 to 80 °C for a period of 1 to 4 hours. More preferably, the temperature is in the range of 50 to 70 °C for a period of 1 to 3 hours. [0042] In some embodiment, the heat treatment in step f) is carried out at a temperature ranging from 120 to 350 °C. Preferably, the temperature is in the range of 150 to 250 °C. [0043] In an embodiment, the solution in step g) has a pH ranging from 2 to 4. Preferably, the pH is 3. The Impurities I includes Al, Cu, Fe, Mn, Ni, Co and Mg. Al3++3OH-＝Al(OH)3↓ Fe3++3OH-＝Fe(OH)3↓ Mg2++2OH-＝Mg(OH)2↓ Mn2++2OH-＝Mn(OH)2↓ Ni2++2OH-＝Ni(OH)2↓ Co2+ +2OH-＝Co(OH)2↓ Cu2+ +2OH-＝Cu(OH)2↓ [0047] In some embodiment, the impurities I are optionally added to the solid mixture. In one Instance, the impurities I are added to the solid mixture obtained from the filtration unit. In another Instance, it is not added. [0048] The Acid-Heat Treatment primary Reaction can be summarized below: M-Org + HA → MA(s) + CO2 + H2O Wherein, M: Al, Co, Mn and Ni A: Cl, SO4 and NO3. [0049] In some embodiment, the heat treated mixture is dissolved in water in step g) in a ratio ranging from 1:2 to 1:10. This step provides desired concentration of Salts with Concentration of M being 40-100 g/L. [0050] In an embodiment, the purification in step h) includes addition of Fe, Na3PO4 and NaF for removing Cu, Al and Ca/Mg respectively. In a series of steps depending on the concentration wherein the final concentration of all the impurities mentioned is <5 ppm as detected by ICP-OES Analysis. [0051] In an embodiment, the natural salts of Cobalt, Nickel, Manganese precipitates out due to extremely low solubility along with some impurities. an impurity removal unit (102-B) configured to remove soluble impurities within lithium soluble salt solution through precipitation by adding a base from reactor (102-C) to remove soluble impurities I and to obtain a purified lithium salts solution; a collecting unit (103) configured to collect the purified lithium salts solution from the impurity removal unit (102-B) which is transferred to a receiving reactor (103-A) wherein adding a fluoride salt from reactor (103-B) to remove calcium/magnesium impurities and to obtain a purified lithium salts solution; The prepared high value product can be used directly Cathode Active Material Manufacturing. [0057] The process of the present disclosure reduces the number of steps as well as energy because the steps involved in processing Ni, Mn, Co salts and their subsequent processing via solvent extraction for each metal are additional steps, to get battery grade solid Cobalt sulfate, Nickel Sulfate and Manganese Sulfate which involves high evaporation and crystallization costs followed by logistics costs for transporting them followed by their further processing to High value product. Example 1 (A) Method for generating high value products [0060] The Black Mass Powder containing 3-3.5% Li, 5-16% Co, 5-16% Ni, 2-10 % Al, 4-10% Mn was processed by addition of 1-2.5 M citric acid and 1-5% V/V glucose at a temperature of 60-80°C for a period of 2-5 hours. The mixture was filtered in a filtration unit to obtain an extracted solution mixture which was filtered to get the lithium soluble salt solution. A base (Calcium Hydroxide / Sodium Hydroxide) was added to the lithium soluble salt solution to remove soluble impurities (I) by precipitation and to obtain a purified lithium salt solution. The treated solution was concentrated to get crystallized lithium salts and /or Phosphate source was added, namely Tri Ammonium Phosphate/ Tri Sodium Phosphate to precipitate Lithium. 160 grams Lithium Phosphate was recovered / 1 Kg Black Mass Processed. In another Instance 338 grams of Lithium Citrate crystals was recovered / 1 Kg Black Mass Processed. The developed process is suitable for high yield (above 85%) industrial scale production of Lithium salts from spent LIBs blackmass. This process eliminates these steps and directly generates battery grade solution ready to be converted to high value product. Thus, the present method reduces the number of steps involved by 80%, significantly reducing the energy used, capex, Transportation & Logistics while simultaneously the high value getting a premium upto 3x than conventional products. [0064] The method of the present disclosure reduces the number of stages particularly Solvent extraction stages whose end product generated is Sodium Sulfate and Metal sulfates. Total of 6 Stages of these solvent extraction is reduced. Each stage Solvent extraction generate 1X sodium sulfate for each metal salt and final 1X is generated during synthesis of high value product totalling 7X. The method of the present disclosure eliminates the solvent extraction stages, thus only generating 1X Sodium sulfate. patents.abstract: The method for the development of the lithium-ion battery (LIB) production and disposal have increased dramatically as a result of the growing demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which has serious environmental repercussions. In order to recycle LIB cells efficiently and with the least amount of negative environmental impact, this study suggests a deep learning-based green chemical method. The framework increases the accuracy of material separation, lowers the use of hazardous chemicals, and boosts overall recycling efficiency by combining neural network models with green solvent selection, process optimization, and predictive analytics. To optimize extraction parameters and forecast recovery results, the model is trained on large datasets that include battery composition, degradation profiles, and chemical interaction patterns. This creative approach reduces the environmental impact of EV technology while providing a sustainable solution for LIB waste management that is consistent with the ideas of the circular economy. The suggested method shows how integrating environmentally friendly chemical processes with artificial intelligence might revolutionize battery recycling technologies. FIG.1
patents.complete_specification: Description:[0002] As electric vehicles (EVs) gain popularity as a sustainable substitute for fossil fuels, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become essential because of their high energy density, extended cycle life, and portability. But as EV usage has grown exponentially, end-of-life (EoL) LIBs have also increased, which has raised serious concerns regarding waste management, resource depletion, and environmental degradation. Because conventional recycling techniques like pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy are frequently energy-intensive, chemically toxic, and economically inefficient, there is a need for more sustainable, greener processes that are based on the ideas of green chemistry. [0003] The field of green chemistry, which focuses on creating chemical products and procedures that minimize or completely do away with the production of dangerous materials, fits in nicely with the worldwide movement to preserve the environment. Green chemistry places a strong emphasis on the creation of solvent-free or low-toxicity recovery techniques, effective separation procedures, and less waste generation in the context of LIB recycling. However, accurate sorting, material identification, and optimal recovery techniques are extremely difficult due to the complex structure and composition of lithium-ion batteries, which include cathodes, anodes, electrolytes, and binders made from a variety of materials like lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite. [0004] Deep learning, a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) distinguished by multi-layered neural networks, is becoming a game-changing instrument to tackle these issues. Applications in battery diagnostics, materials categorization, process automation, and fault detection are especially well-suited for deep learning algorithms, which learn from big datasets to excel at pattern recognition, prediction, classification, and optimization tasks. [0005] Researchers can greatly improve LIB recycling systems' accuracy, scalability, and efficiency by combining deep learning with green chemistry concepts. For instance, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can model and forecast battery degradation pathways, while convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can be used to evaluate X-ray and hyperspectral pictures of EoL batteries for material identification. By employing eco-friendly reagents and lowering processing temperatures, these discoveries allow for the accurate separation and recovery of valuable components, minimizing environmental damage. Deep learning also makes it easier to monitor and manage chemical processes in real time, which increases yield and selectivity while reducing waste. [0006] Lithium-ion battery recycling is a relatively new yet quickly developing interdisciplinary field that combines deep learning and green chemistry. It presents a viable solution to reduce reliance on mining, conserve vital resources, close the loop in the EV battery lifecycle, and lessen the environmental impact of EV technology. The development of this field of study is expected to be crucial to the establishment of an intelligent, sustainable, and circular energy economy. SUMMARY [0001] In view of the foregoing, an embodiment herein provides a method for deep learning based green chemistry approach for lithium-ion battery cell recycling in electric vehicles. In some embodiments, wherein concerns regarding the environmental effects of battery waste and the shortage of vital raw materials like lithium, cobalt, and nickel have been raised by the explosive growth in demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) brought on by the rapid proliferation of electric vehicles (EVs). [0002] A green chemistry method based on deep learning provides a revolutionary solution to recycle lithium-ion battery cells in a sustainable manner in order to solve these problems. This novel approach maximizes the extraction and reuse of valuable minerals while reducing environmental harm by combining artificial intelligence (AI), more especially deep learning algorithms, with environmentally friendly chemical processes. Conventional recycling techniques, such hydrometallurgy and pyrometallurgy, produce a lot of hazardous byproducts and need a lot of energy. The green chemistry method, on the other hand, places more emphasis on non-toxic solvents, lower reaction temperatures, and less waste generation. This approach improves efficiency and yield by enabling accurate process control, real-time monitoring, and adaptive optimization when paired with deep learning models. For example, depending on battery composition, degradation status, and past recycling data, deep learning can forecast optimal leaching agent, solvent recovery, and purification phase parameters. [0003] In some embodiments, wherein the deep learning models improve the precision and speed of preprocessing steps by enabling automated sorting and categorization of spent battery cells. Visual and sequential data can be analysed using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to identify cathode materials, detect faults, and evaluate the general health of cells. By encouraging closed-loop supply chains and guaranteeing high recovery rates, this capability supports the ideas of the circular economy. [0004] In some embodiments, wherein green chemistry and deep learning combine to support lifecycle assessment (LCA), which allows stakeholders to examine the social, economic, and environmental effects of different recycling techniques. This strategy makes a substantial contribution to the decarbonization of transportation and the sustainable development goals (SDGs) by lowering reliance on the mining of raw materials and encouraging safer recycling alternatives. One of the most important steps toward sustainable EV growth is the deep learning-based green chemistry strategy for LIB recycling. In addition to improving material recovery and minimizing environmental harm, it also encourages data-driven decision-making and technological innovation in recycling. The future of ecologically conscious battery management is best represented by this combination of chemistry and artificial intelligence. [0005] These and other aspects of the embodiments herein will be better appreciated and understood when considered in conjunction with the following description and the accompanying drawings. It should be understood, however, that the following descriptions, while indicating preferred embodiments and numerous specific details thereof, are given by way of illustration and not of limitation. Many changes and modifications may be made within the scope of the embodiments herein without departing from the spirit thereof, and the embodiments herein include all such modifications. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0001] The embodiments herein will be better understood from the following detailed description with reference to the drawings, in which: [0002] FIG. 1 illustrates a method for deep learning based green chemistry approach for lithium-ion battery cell recycling in electric vehicles according to an embodiment herein. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS [0001] The embodiments herein and the various features and advantageous details thereof are explained more fully with reference to the non-limiting embodiments that are illustrated in the accompanying drawings and detailed in the following description. Descriptions of well-known components and processing techniques are omitted so as to not unnecessarily obscure the embodiments herein. The examples used herein are intended merely to facilitate an understanding of ways in which the embodiments herein may be practiced and to further enable those of skill in the art to practice the embodiments herein. Accordingly, the examples should not be construed as limiting the scope of the embodiments herein. [0002] FIG. 1 illustrates a method for deep learning based green chemistry approach for lithium-ion battery cell recycling in electric vehicles according to an embodiment herein. In some embodiments, as electric vehicles (EVs) drive the shift to clean, sustainable transportation, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have emerged as a crucial component. Their growing use, however, presents serious resource and environmental issues, especially with regard to their end-of-life (EoL) management. Although somewhat successful, traditional LIB recycling methods frequently entail energy-intensive and environmentally harmful procedures. Combining the concepts of green chemistry with cutting-edge digital technologies like deep learning presents a revolutionary way ahead as sustainability gains international attention. Green chemistry promotes the creation of goods and procedures that use and produce the fewest possible harmful substances. This entails creating ecologically friendly procedures for the extraction and reuse of materials in the context of LIB recycling. Conversely, deep learning offers a state-of-the-art approach to artificial intelligence (AI) that can examine enormous datasets, find trends, and streamline intricate processes. Together, these domains can improve recovery efficiency, reduce waste, and promote the circular economy, thereby redefining the lifecycle of lithium-ion batteries. This technique explores the steps that must be taken in order to deploy a deep learning-based green chemistry framework for recycling LIBs. It describes how eco-friendly reagents, predictive modeling, smart diagnostics, and real-time decision support systems are all integrated. [0003] In some embodiments, the methodology's initial step focuses on compiling comprehensive data regarding the end-of-life LIBs. The recycling path and reagent selection are influenced by physical, chemical, and electrochemical characteristics. High-dimensional data from battery cells is gathered using a multi-modal sensor suite that includes electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), infrared spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). To determine the morphology and structural integrity of cathode and anode materials, deep learning models in particular, Convolutional Neural Networks, or CNNs are trained to evaluate imaging data from SEM and XRD. The time-series data from EIS is used to evaluate internal degradation trends in conjunction with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention processes. [0004] In some embodiments, the battery removal by hand is dangerous because of residual charge and possible exposure to hazardous materials, in addition to being time-consuming. Therefore, automation is essential. Robotic arms are guided by a visual recognition system based on deep learning to safely remove battery packs. Screws, connectors, and thermal fuses are located using object detection models like YOLO (You Only Look Once) and Faster R-CNN, while semantic segmentation networks assist in real-time identification of various battery components. To avoid short circuits, heat runaways, or unintentional cell punctures, sensor feedback is continuously monitored throughout disassembly. Additionally, the system estimates the state-of-health (SoH) of individual cells using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models to determine if they may be reconditioned or reused, which reduces waste. Electrolyte residue, current collectors, electrode sheets, and separators are among the components that are separated for additional processing. Safer and more scalable recycling operations are made possible by the complete disassembly process, which is optimized for throughput and minimal human interaction. [0001] In some embodiments, sorting the separated components is the next step after disassembly. Because different metals (Li, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu, and Al) require different recovery processes, material separation is essential. Analysis of the elemental and molecular makeup of shredded battery components is done using Raman spectroscopy and hyperspectral imaging. Spectral fingerprints are used by deep learning models to categorize the materials. For example, to differentiate between LiCoO2 and LiFePO4 active materials or between copper current collectors and aluminum foil, a combination of CNNs and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) can be applied to the spectral data. At this stage, selective leaching is accomplished using biodegradable complexing agents and green solvents that were created using cheminformatics and deep generative models. In order to maximize metal recovery and minimize environmental toxicity, the AI models recommend the best combinations of leaching agents and reaction parameters (temperature, pH, and molarity). By modifying machine settings in response to real-time input, reinforcement learning is also incorporated to iteratively refine the sorting and separating process. [0002] In some embodiments, the hazardous waste is produced by conventional hydrometallurgical processes, which frequently depend on strong acids and high temperatures. The use of leachants from green chemistry and bioleaching is a significant breakthrough in this technology. Deep learning models, particularly generative models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), create novel compounds with low environmental effect and great selectivity for key metals using vast datasets of known and speculative leachants. Based on molecular structures, these models forecast solubility, reactivity, toxicity, and biodegradability. These models are trained using simulation data from quantum chemistry tools and suggest the best green reagents for particular LIB chemistries. For example, they might recommend a chelating compound made from plants to remove cobalt from LCO cathodes at room temperature. In-line sensors are used to continuously monitor the reaction kinetics. For the best extraction performance, a feedback loop driven by LSTM forecasting models and Bayesian optimization helps dynamically modify process variables. [0003] In some embodiments, there are dissolved metal ions in the final solution once leaching is finished. Usually, electrochemical deposition, solvent extraction, or precipitation are used in the recovery process. Deep learning models are used here as well to determine the best recovery technique based on redox potentials, pH, and metal concentrations. Deep learning algorithms are also used to construct environmentally friendly flocculants and crystallization agents, guaranteeing that the recovery phase complies with green chemistry guidelines. AI-based spectroscopic interpretation techniques are then used to do a quality study on the recovered metals to make sure they satisfy industry criteria for repurposing in battery production. [0004] Reusing these materials to create fresh battery cells is the next step following the successful recovery and purification of important components such lithium carbonate, cobalt sulfate, nickel hydroxide, manganese oxide, and graphite. In a circular economy, this is an important step in closing the loop. Deep learning models like transformer architectures and graph-based neural networks are used with AI-augmented materials informatics platforms to evaluate the quality and suitability of recovered materials for use with modern cell chemistries. These models forecast the reconstituted materials' electrochemical performance, structural stability, and possible breakdown paths. After that, sophisticated slurry formulation methods directed by neural networks that simulate slurry rheology and homogeneity are used to create the restored cathodes and anodes. Following the tight guidelines of green chemistry, these formulations are adjusted to minimize the amount of binder and get rid of hazardous solvents. AI models that have been taught to choose solvent mixes and lithium salts that maximize conductivity and thermal stability also serve as guides for electrolyte filling. Convolutional neural networks integrated into robotic assembly lines manage visual inspection and fault identification during reassembly to guarantee quality and safety compliance. [0005] The recycling system incorporates predictive maintenance to guarantee continuous operation and great process efficiency. In order to find early indicators of equipment wear or process drift, anomaly detection algorithms that use autoencoders and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) examine sensor data streams, including temperature, vibration, and chemical concentrations. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) models assess the trade-offs between operational risk and downtime to dynamically schedule preventive maintenance tasks. Through an AI-assisted decision interface, these systems communicate continually with human technicians and robotic maintenance units. A closed feedback loop built into the system enables it to learn from both previous and current data. Control strategies for waste neutralization procedures, robotic disassembly sequences, heating cycles, and reagent dose are adaptively improved using reinforcement learning agents. In a variety of recycling circumstances, this real-time modification guarantees optimal performance. [0006] A sophisticated AI-powered decision support system (DSS) sits at the heart of the entire technique. From data collection and disassembly to waste treatment, metal recovery, and reagent selection, this system unifies all of its elements onto a single platform. Explainable AI (XAI) dashboards enable human operators to comprehend the rationale behind the system's choices, such as the selection of a particular bio-leaching agent or the rejection of a batch of cells. Explainable models that assist show feature importance and foster trust in AI-guided processes include SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). [0007] The implementation of a cloud-based deployment architecture is used to spread this methodology across recycling facilities worldwide. The system functions as a cloud-native platform that combines federated learning, edge computing, and real-time analytics. In recycling facilities, edge devices manage sensor calibration, image recognition, and local data processing. The central cloud, which keeps track of a global model trained on dispersed datasets, is constantly synchronized with these devices. With federated learning, several facilities can work together to train models without exchanging raw data. [0008] The methodology's last layer links EV producers, government policy frameworks, and the recycling ecosystem. Recovered materials can be directly reused in battery production lines thanks to AI algorithms that match them with particular manufacturer specifications and certifications. Policy compliance modules produce automated reports for regulatory agencies verifying compliance with hazardous substance limitations, waste management regulations, and circular economy requirements. The system may also simulate the effects of policies, such as how changes to recycling subsidies or e-waste taxes will impact recovery rates and operating costs. This methodology serves as an intermediary between sustainability innovation and industrial implementation by coordinating deep learning predictions with green chemistry principles and policy objectives. The recycling lifecycle is changed into a dynamic, adaptive, and sustainable system by this technology, which makes use of deep neural networks, generative chemistry, robotic disassembly, federated learning, and real-time process monitoring. It facilitates scalable worldwide deployment, supports climate resilience, and is in perfect harmony with the tenets of a circular economy. , Claims:I/We Claim: 1. A method for deep learning based green chemistry approach for lithium-ion battery cell recycling in electric vehicles, wherein the method comprises; using deep learning models to precisely identify the best disassembly and recovery routes in order to increase the recycling efficiency of lithium-ion batteries; minimizing the impact on the environment by combining AI-driven predictive algorithms with green chemistry concepts to reduce waste and choose environmentally friendly solvents; utilizing real-time experimental feedback and extensive chemical datasets to optimize the extraction of vital metals like as nickel, cobalt, and lithium; utilizing convolutional neural networks to understand sensor and computer vision data to automatically classify and sort wasted EV batteries; predicting the physical and chemical characteristics of recycling agents in order to increase recovery yields, lower hazardous emissions, and guarantee safety; utilizing generative deep learning to simulate chemical reactions and degradation patterns in order to expedite the creation of sustainable, scalable recycling methods; enhancing process control decision-making through ongoing learning from actual recycling operations to adjust reaction parameters; and permitting accurate material regeneration quality and lifecycle compatibility forecasts, hence facilitating closed-loop battery material cycles.

patents.abstract: The present invention discloses a liquid cooling battery management system (BMS) for lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles (EVs), designed to enhance thermal stability, safety, and performance. The system comprises temperature sensors, copper tubing, a cooling pad, a radiator, a fluid pump, and a cooling fan integrated into a closed-loop configuration. Real-time thermal data is used to regulate coolant flow around the battery cells, efficiently dissipating heat through copper tubing and radiators. The design ensures uniform temperature distribution, prevents thermal runaway, and supports high-load and fast-charging conditions. The system also integrates with intelligent BMS controls to dynamically adjust cooling parameters based on usage conditions and predictive thermal analysis. By maintaining optimal operating temperatures, the invention improves battery lifespan, operational safety, and energy efficiency, particularly in high-performance and long-range EVs. The compact and scalable solution offers a superior alternative to conventional air-cooling systems for next-generation electric mobility.
patents.complete_specification: Description:The present invention relates to a Liquid Cooling Battery Management System (BMS) designed to thermally stabilize lithium-ion battery packs used in electric vehicles (EVs). It addresses air-cooled battery systems by introducing an efficient and scalable liquid-based thermal regulation system that ensures optimal operating temperatures, improves safety, supports high-performance functions like fast charging, and extends battery life. 1. System Architecture and Components The present invention comprises a closed-loop liquid cooling circuit integrated with the EV battery pack. The key components include: Coolant Tubing and Cooling Plates: Copper tubing and thermally conductive cooling plates are arranged in close proximity and in direct contact with each battery module. These components act as heat absorbers, drawing thermal energy away from the cells during operation. Coolant Pump: A variable-speed electric pump circulates a coolant fluid—typically a water-glycol mixture—through the tubing network. The flow rate is dynamically regulated based on thermal demand. Heat Exchanger (Radiator): The heated coolant is transferred to a heat exchanger where excess thermal energy is dissipated into the environment. The radiator is being fan-assisted to improve heat rejection. Temperature Sensors: Multiple digital thermal sensors are placed across the battery stack to monitor real-time temperature data of individual cells and cell groups. Smart Battery Management Controller: An intelligent control unit collects temperature data and processes it using predefined algorithms. It manages pump speed, coolant routing, and emergency overrides based on temperature thresholds and predictive models. The system ensures consistent and even cooling throughout the battery pack, preventing the formation of localized hotspots, which are one of the primary causes of thermal imbalance and accelerated cell aging. 2. Operational Methodology Upon vehicle startup and battery engagement, the BMS initializes the thermal monitoring routine. If temperature sensors detect that the battery temperature exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g., 30?°C), the controller activates the coolant pump and circulates fluid through the copper tubing embedded between or around the battery cells. The coolant absorbs heat through conduction and carries it to the radiator. During high-load scenarios such as rapid acceleration, uphill driving, or fast charging, the system scales up coolant flow proportionally to the detected heat load. In cold environments, the BMS reduces and delay coolant circulation to allow batteries to reach minimum operational temperatures, thereby optimizing efficiency and protecting battery chemistry from cold-induced damage. Advanced versions of the system utilize machine learning models trained on historical driving and environmental data to predict heat build-up which allows the system to proactively activate cooling before temperature thresholds are reached, thereby reducing thermal lag and extending battery service life. 3. Modular and Scalable Design The present invention is modular in nature, allowing its application across different vehicle types and battery configurations. For example, in smaller EVs with limited thermal load, fewer and smaller cooling plates is being used. In high-capacity battery packs and performance vehicles, the system includes zoned cooling circuits with independent pumps and controls for each zone. The zoned approach ensures thermal uniformity and redundancy in case of component failure. Each battery module is being equipped with a dedicated cooling loop, enabling individualized thermal control which reduces inter-module temperature differentials, which are a key contributor to imbalanced cell aging and safety risks. The modularity also aids in easy maintenance and part replacement without full system disassembly. 4. Integration with EV Systems and Safety Features The Liquid Cooling BMS is fully integrated with the EV’s central control unit (ECU) and other subsystems such as the drive control, power electronics, and climate control. The coordination enables adaptive cooling strategies—for instance, increasing cooling before high-performance driving modes, and using cabin HVAC systems to assist in thermal rejection. In terms of safety, the BMS continuously monitors for anomalies such as: Coolant leakage (via pressure and flow sensors), Flow blockage and pump failure, Excessive localized heating, Sensor malfunction. Upon detecting an issue, the system triggers fail-safe actions such as reducing charging/discharging rates, isolating affected modules, and alerting the user and initiating cooling overrides. 5. Performance Benefits The key performance advantages of the present invention include: Superior heat dissipation efficiency compared to air-cooled systems, especially during fast charging or high-load operation. Improved battery reliability and cycle life, as uniform cooling reduces thermal stress and differential cell aging. Enhanced vehicle safety, minimizing the risk of thermal runaway or related failures. Greater compatibility with advanced driving modes and architectures, including autonomous systems and high-performance EVs. In addition, the intelligent, data-driven BMS allows predictive diagnostics and energy-optimized cooling, thereby reducing the parasitic energy draw from the cooling subsystem and improving the overall driving range. 6. Coolant Selection and Tubing Optimization The coolant used in the system is typically a non-conductive, corrosion-resistant water-glycol blend, selected for its thermal capacity, compatibility with copper tubing, and resistance to freezing and boiling under automotive conditions. In some cases, dielectric fluids are being employed to enable direct-contact liquid cooling without electrical isolation concerns. Copper is chosen for tubing due to its high thermal conductivity, mechanical stability, and ease of fabrication into serpentine and flat plate geometries. Tubing layout is optimized using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to ensure uniform flow, minimal pressure drop, and maximum surface contact with heat-generating zones. Figure 1 illustrates the core concept of the liquid cooling architecture implemented in the present invention, specifically optimized for cylindrical lithium-ion battery cells (such as 18650 cells) arranged in dense modules. The diagram highlights the coolant flow system integrated through a wavy-tube heat exchange mechanism surrounding the battery cells. As the battery cells operate—especially under heavy load conditions such as acceleration, fast charging, and prolonged use—they generate heat. The wavy tube in direct thermal contact with the battery cells conducts this heat into the flowing coolant. Due to its serpentine layout, the wavy tube ensures uniform thermal extraction from all cells, minimizing hotspots and maintaining consistent cell temperatures across the module. The design also supports bi-directional coolant flow, if required, to enhance redundancy and adapt to packaging constraints. The high thermal conductivity of the tubing material and continuous coolant movement enable efficient thermal regulation even during peak usage. The figure 1 reinforces the structural and operational advantages of the liquid cooling system described in the invention, showcasing how strategic coolant routing effectively maintain thermal balance in densely packed lithium-ion battery arrays. Figure 2 depicts a schematic layout of a Liquid Cooling System integrated with lithium-ion battery cells for electric vehicles. The illustration showcases the coolant flow circuit that helps maintain safe and efficient operating temperatures for the battery pack. The liquid-cooled battery system functions by circulating a coolant fluid through a dedicated closed-loop pathway to manage the thermal conditions of lithium-ion battery cells (3). The coolant—typically a water-glycol mixture—enters the system via the inlet fluid vent (1). From there, it flows into copper tubes (2) that are in direct thermal contact with the cylindrical battery cells (3). These copper tubes are specifically selected for their high thermal conductivity, which enables rapid absorption of heat generated during charging and discharging operations. As the coolant travels through the copper tubes (2), it absorbs heat from the surrounding battery cells (3), preventing localized thermal buildup. The now-heated fluid is directed out of the system through the output fluid vent (4) and guided toward the radiator and pump unit (5). Within this unit, the radiator dissipates the accumulated heat into the ambient environment, assisted by airflow and fans, while the pump maintains continuous fluid circulation. Once cooled, the fluid is redirected back to the inlet vent (1) to repeat the cycle, ensuring a stable battery temperature throughout the operation. The present invention incorporates several novel enhancements first and foremost, the use of copper tubes (2) arranged around each lithium-ion cell (3) ensures uniform and efficient heat extraction. Unlike external jacket systems, these tubes enable direct thermal conduction from each individual cell, minimizing temperature differentials and enhancing thermal uniformity across the entire pack. The inlet and outlet fluid vents (1 and 4) are strategically placed to enable smooth directional flow and pressure balancing within the system. The integrated radiator and pump unit (5) not only circulates the coolant but also serves as a heat exchanger that maintains the coolant's thermal capacity during continuous operation. The centralized thermal hub ensures that the battery temperature remains in the optimal range (20°C–40°C) even during fast-charging and high-load discharge events. The system also supports real-time thermal diagnostics through embedded temperature sensors that interface with the BMS to detect abnormal temperature spikes and coolant flow restrictions. The design integrates sensors, a cooling pad, a radiator, a cooling fan (6), and fluid transfer units like connecting pipes (7) and a coolant pump, all working in unison to maintain thermal equilibrium within the battery system. Additionally, the modular design of the copper tube (2) system allows scalability across different vehicle sizes and battery configurations without major redesigns. Combined with the intelligent operation of the radiator-pump module (5), the system ensures maximum energy efficiency and battery longevity. These technical advancements collectively contribute to improved battery safety, cycle life, charging performance, and overall EV reliability, establishing this liquid cooling system as a superior solution for modern electric vehicle thermal management. Figure 3 illustrates an advanced liquid cooling architecture designed for lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles. The layout emphasizes sensor-based control, closed-loop coolant circulation, and modular thermal dissipation. The design integrates sensors, a cooling pad, a radiator, a cooling fan, and fluid transfer units like connecting pipes and a coolant pump, all working in unison to maintain thermal equilibrium within the battery system. The process begins with the sensor, which continuously monitors the temperature of the lithium-ion battery in real time. Once the sensor detects a temperature rise beyond the optimal range (typically above 40°C), it triggers the activation of the cooling system. The cooling pad, placed in direct contact or close proximity to the lithium-ion battery, plays a crucial role in transferring the excess heat from the battery to the circulating coolant. The coolant, driven by the pump, flows through the connecting pipe, absorbing heat from the cooling pad before it is directed to the radiator. In the radiator, the coolant releases the absorbed heat into the atmosphere. The heat dissipation is significantly enhanced by the action of the cooling fan, which forces airflow across the radiator fins, allowing for faster and more efficient cooling. Once the coolant is cooled, it is recirculated back to the cooling pad through the connecting pipe, completing the thermal control loop. The continuous cycle maintains the battery temperature within a safe and efficient operational range. Notably, the system operates in real time, and the integration of sensors allows it to dynamically adjust flow rates and fan speeds as needed, offering intelligent, adaptive thermal regulation. Embodiments of the Invention In one embodiment, the present invention comprises a complete liquid cooling battery management system (BMS) tailored for lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs). The system is built around a network of copper tubes that are in thermal contact with or embedded adjacent to the battery cells. These tubes serve as the primary channel for the circulation of coolant, typically a water-glycol mixture, which is selected for its high thermal conductivity, low freezing point, and chemical stability under automotive conditions. The thermal energy generated during charging, discharging, and vehicular operation is transferred from the battery cells to the coolant, preventing localized overheating and ensuring a uniform temperature distribution across all cells. In another embodiment, real-time temperature sensors are distributed throughout the battery pack to monitor individual cell and system-wide temperatures. These sensors continuously communicate with the Battery Management System (BMS), which acts as a control hub. When temperatures rise beyond a predefined threshold, the BMS activates a coolant pump that circulates the liquid through the copper tubing and into a cooling pad positioned to enhance heat transfer. The heated coolant is then routed to a radiator, where the heat is released into the ambient air. A variable-speed cooling fan is automatically engaged to improve airflow across the radiator surface, thus accelerating the dissipation of thermal energy. In a further embodiment, the copper tubes are arranged in a serpentine or wavy configuration to maximize their surface contact with the battery modules, thereby enhancing thermal conduction efficiency. The design is modular, allowing integration with cylindrical (e.g., 18650 or 21700) and prismatic battery formats. This design flexibility makes the system suitable for various classes of EVs, from two-wheelers and hybrid cars to performance-oriented electric sedans and SUVs. In yet another embodiment, the BMS incorporates machine learning algorithms that analyze historical thermal profiles and usage data to predict peak thermal loads. Based on these predictions, the system dynamically adjusts coolant flow rates, fan speeds, and pump activity to preemptively mitigate temperature spikes. The predictive thermal management not only enhances system responsiveness but also contributes to energy efficiency by minimizing unnecessary coolant circulation during low-demand periods. Additional embodiments include diagnostic capabilities, where the BMS continuously monitors system parameters such as flow rate, temperature gradient, and sensor consistency. In the event of abnormalities—such as air bubbles in the coolant lines, blocked flow paths, or sensor failure—the BMS triggers alerts or modifies system behavior to prevent overheating. The integration of such diagnostic intelligence ensures system reliability and safety, particularly in high-stress conditions such as fast charging or steep hill climbs. , Claims:1. An active liquid cooling system for lithium-ion battery packs used in electric vehicles, comprising: a sensor configured to monitor the temperature of the lithium-ion battery cells inreal time; a cooling pad thermally connected to the battery cells; a network of copper tubes integrated within and adjacent to the battery pack; a fluid pump for circulating coolant through the copper tubes and cooling pad; a radiator for heat dissipation from the coolant; a cooling fan operatively associated with the radiator; and a battery management system (BMS) that dynamically adjusts coolant flow and fan operation based on sensor feedback to maintain battery cell temperature within a pre-defined operational range. 2. The system of claim 1, wherein the coolant comprises a water-glycol mixture with high thermal conductivity and stability across a wide temperature range. 3. The system of claim 1, wherein the copper tubes are configured in a serpentine and wavy arrangement to maximize contact area and heat transfer efficiency. 4. The system of claim 1, wherein the BMS employs machine learning algorithms to predict thermal loads based on historical usage patterns and adjust cooling parameters proactively. 5. The system of claim 1, wherein the cooling fan is variable-speed and controlled automatically in response to temperature thresholds. 6. The system of claim 1, wherein the radiator is integrated with a heat sink for enhanced passive dissipation under low thermal load conditions. 7. A method for thermally regulating lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles using a liquid cooling system, the method comprising: detecting real-time temperature data from sensors associated with the battery cells; activating a pump to circulate coolant through copper tubing in thermal contact with the battery cells; transferring heat from the battery cells to the coolant via a cooling pad; directing heated coolant to a radiator; dissipating heat from the radiator using a cooling fan; and recycling the cooled liquid back into the copper tubing to continuously regulate battery temperature. 8. The method of claim 7, wherein the coolant flow rate is varied dynamically in response to instantaneous battery cell temperatures. 9. The method of claim 7, wherein the system performs diagnostic checks to detect anomalies such as flow obstructions, air pockets, and localized overheating. 10. The method of claim 7, wherein the BMS disables fast charging if the temperature exceeds a critical safety threshold despite maximum cooling effort.

patents.abstract: Embodiments of the present disclosure relates to a system (100) and method for lithium/sodium melting for enhanced electrodes–electrolyte interface engineering. The system features major components including the sealed cylindrical chamber (102) with high-temperature-resistant gaskets, the four-pillar support structure (104) for stability, the force-exerting clamp (110), the integrated force sensor (108) for real-time load monitoring, and the U-shaped resistive heater (106) designed for uniform thermal distribution. patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of advanced electrochemical energy storage systems. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to a system (100) and method for lithium/sodium melting for enhanced electrode–electrolyte interface engineering. Further, the present disclosure addresses challenges in interfacial engineering by enabling precise metal melting and alloying onto electrolyte surfaces within a sealed inert environment, facilitating improved ionic conductivity across the electrolyte, reduced interfacial impedance between electrode and electrolyte, and enhanced cell performance. BACKGROUND [0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present disclosure. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed disclosure, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. [0003] Solid-state batteries (SSBs) represent a next-generation energy storage technology that promises superior safety, higher energy densities, and extended cycle life relative to conventional liquid-electrolyte lithium-ion system (100)s. Central to this technology are ceramic solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) such as garnet-type Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂ (LLZO) and NASICON analogs, which exhibit favourable ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical stability windows, and compatibility with alkali metal anodes. [0004] Despite these advantages, one of the most significant technical barriers to the commercialization of SSBs is the inherently high interfacial resistance at the metal-electrolyte interface. This resistance arises due to poor wettability, the formation of interphases or voids during cycling, and mechanical mismatches between the brittle ceramic electrolyte and ductile metal anode. To overcome this challenge, interlayer coatings (metallic or polymeric) are often employed to improve contact and reduce impedance. [0005] However, existing methods for forming such interfaces including conventional glove box-based thermal melting and swage cell heating are limited by several drawbacks. These include operational complexity, stringent atmosphere requirements, uncontrolled thermal gradients, contamination risks, and mechanical stresses leading to cracking or delamination of the ceramic electrolyte. Moreover, maintaining precise control over both thermal and mechanical parameters simultaneously is challenging in traditional setups, compromising the reproducibility and quality of the interface. There is a need for innovative and efficient solutions to address these challenges and provide scalable manufacturing and widespread deployment of high-performance solid-state battery technologies. [0006] To address these limitations, the present invention provides a novel system (100) and method that overcomes the shortcomings of the prior art. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0007] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies are as listed herein below. [0008] The primary object of the present disclosure is to provide a system (100) for lithium/sodium melting for enhanced electrode–electrolyte interface engineering. [0009] It is an object of the present invention to provide an integrated, cost-effective, and reliable system (100) for forming high-quality, low-resistance interfaces between lithium or sodium metal anodes and ceramic solid-state electrolytes used in advanced battery technologies. [0010] It is an object of the present disclosure to provide a method for lithium/sodium melting for enhanced electrode–electrolyte interface engineering. [0011] Another object of the present disclosure is to address challenges in interfacial engineering by enabling precise metal melting and alloying/fusing onto electrolyte surfaces within a sealed inert environment, facilitating improved ionic conductivity across the electrolyte, reduced interfacial impedance between electrode and electrolyte, and enhanced cell performance. SUMMARY [0012] This section is provided to introduce certain objects and aspects of the present disclosure in a simplified form that are further described below in the detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify the key features or the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0013] The present disclosure relates to the field of advanced electrochemical energy storage systems. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to a system (100) and method for lithium/sodium melting for enhanced electrode–electrolyte interface engineering. Further, the present disclosure addresses challenges in interfacial engineering by enabling precise metal melting and alloying onto electrolyte surfaces within a sealed inert environment, facilitating improved ionic conductivity across the electrolyte, reduced interfacial impedance between electrode and electrolyte, and enhanced cell performance. [0014] In an aspect of the present disclosure, a lithium/sodium melting system (100) for enhanced electrode–electrolyte interface engineering is disclosed. The system (100) comprises a sealed cylindrical chamber (102) made of Stainless Steel 316, equipped with high-temperature-resistant gaskets to maintain an oxygen-and moisture-free argon/nitrogen atmosphere. Further, the system (100) comprises a four-pillar support structure (104) to ensure mechanical stability, alignment and convert the compressive force to shear-less compressive force during operation, while a force-exerting clamp (110) applies uniform compressive pressure to the electrolyte assembly. Further, the system (100) comprises an integrated force sensor (108) to provide real-time pressure monitoring and control up to 5 tons. Furthermore, the chamber (102) is surrounded by a U-shaped resistive heater (106) capable of delivering uniform heating up to 300 °C, with an embedded temperature sensor enabling precise thermal regulation. At last, the integrated configuration supports controlled melting or softening of lithium or sodium metal onto an interlayer-coated ceramic surface, resulting in a uniform, low-impedance, and mechanically stable electrode–electrolyte interface. [0015] In another aspect of the present disclosure, a method for forming enhanced lithium/sodium–electrolyte interfaces through controlled thermal and mechanical processing is disclosed. The clamp (110) design ensures even distribution of force across the ceramic surface. ● Integrated Force sensor (108): Positioned strategically to provide real-time monitoring of applied pressure (up to 2 tons). The heater ensures even melting or softening of lithium/sodium metal layers on the electrolyte surface. ● Temperature Sensor: Continuously monitors internal temperature, feeding back to the control system (100) to maintain stable, programmed heating profiles. Technical Specifications: ● Material: Stainless Steel 316 for corrosion resistance and high-temperature durability. ● Temperature Capacity: Up to 300 °C with uniform heating. ● Pressure Capacity: Up to 5 tons, with precise load monitoring. ● Sealing: High-temperature gaskets maintaining argon atmosphere integrity. [0060] Example 2-Working Principle and Process Steps 1. Preparation and Setup: The ceramic solid-state electrolyte is pre-coated with a metallic or polymeric interlayer to enhance wetting. Sealing and Inert Atmosphere: The chamber (102) is sealed using high-temperature-resistant gaskets, ensuring an argon environment that eliminates oxygen and moisture contamination risks. 3. Mechanical Loading: The sealed chamber (102) is mounted within the four-pillar support structure (104) and clamped using the force-exerting mechanism. The force sensor (108) monitors applied pressure in real time, maintaining constant, uniform load to avoid cracking the fragile ceramic substrate. 4. Heating Process: The U-shaped resistive heater (106) is activated, applying controlled, uniform heat to the chamber (102). The temperature sensor maintains precise thermal conditions, minimizing gradients that could cause uneven melting or thermal stress. 5. Metal Melting/Alloying: Under combined thermal and mechanical control, the lithium or sodium metal softens or melts onto the interlayer-coated ceramic electrolyte, forming an intimate, uniform, low-impedance interface. 6. Real-Time Feedback: Force and temperature sensors provide continuous monitoring, enabling fine adjustments to ensure repeatability and quality of the interface formation. 7. Cooling: Once the desired melting and interfacial formation are complete, the system (100) is gradually cooled under controlled conditions to prevent thermal shocks or microcracking of the ceramic electrolyte. patents.abstract: Lithium ion batteries are the most common type of rechargeable batteries in the market and their demand is escalating with the growth of portable technology and the electric vehicle industry. With a finite lifespan and a loss in capacity with every charge-discharge cycle, huge amounts of waste generation is inevitable as the production increases. A need for efficient recycling techniques is seen. Current recycling techniques are inefficient in repairing used lithium ion batteries back into a workable state directly without undergoing multiple processes like shredding, incineration, dismantling, metal recovery, chemical leaching, thermal treatment, etc. Through the current invention, a device for the safe rejuvenation of a lithium ion battery through the replenishment of electrolyte is produced, which facilitates the process of safely repairing a used lithium ion battery back into a functional battery and extend its lifespan. The invention demonstrates a single step process of electrolyte injection/refilling and simultaneous sealing, which is a facile and scalable method and is much needed considering the growing demand of lithium ion batteries and their waste management.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Object(s) of the invention The main object of the present invention is to provide a device for safe rejuvenation of used lithium ion batteries which obviates the drawbacks of the hitherto known prior art as detailed above. Another objective of the present invention is to develop a novel and safe mechanical setup comprising a battery handling chamber, a vacuum chamber, an electrolyte insertion mechanism, and a sequential sealing system. Still another objective of present invention is to develop a battery holding chamber consisting of an inflatable seal for tightly clasping the battery and is leak-proof. Yet another objective of the present invention is to design a mechanism comprising of a microdrill, a nitrogen purging unit and an electrolyte injection unit, configured to enable safe delivery of electrolyte inside the used batteries. Yet another objective of the present invention is to design a mechanism comprising of a microdrill and a suction system to remove excess gases and electrolyte from inside the battery. Yet another objective of the present invention is to develop a sealing using a UV-sealing gel or heat sealing or kapton tape or gel sealing for battery sealing after the completion of electrolyte refilling process. Brief Description of the Invention The present invention pertains to an electrolyte rejuvenation device designed for the safe reuse of used lithium-ion batteries. The electrolyte rejuvenation device comprises of two vacuum chambers A and B, a battery clasping apparatus with inflatable seal, a spindle containing a microdrill and injection unit, a spindle containing a microdrill and suction unit, automated controls for spindle apparatus movement and a sealing mechanism using a UV-sealing gel or heat sealing or kapton tape or gel sealing. Vacuum chambers A and B are arranged one on top of another and the top chamber, A, has a lid for battery insertion. Chamber A is the inert cap with vacuum inlet which consists of the battery clasping apparatus for holding used lithium ion batteries covering a wide range of sizes from 3*30*40mm to 8*90*105mm of all types of lithium ion batteries through an inflatable seal. The bottom chamber, B, consists of the main assembly of electrolyte rejuvenation. A spindle containing a microdrill and injection unit/ a microdrill with an injection mechanism and a spindle containing a microdrill and suction unit/ a microdrill with a suction mechanism are placed in chamber B, which have hydraulic mechanism for mobility. The spindle/microdrill with injection mechanism is for the replenishment of electrolyte in used lithium ion batteries. And the spindle/ microdrill with a suction mechanism is for the removal of excess gases and electrolyte from inside the battery during the rejuvenation process. Chamber B is provided with a sealing mechanism to seal the drilled holes of the battery using a UV-sealing gel or heat sealing or kapton tape or gel sealing. The two vacuum chambers are connected externally to two separate vacuum pumps. Additionally, a pair of gloves are provided in the chamber B to facilitate manual operations if needed. Through this patent, a semi-automatic, safe electrolyte rejuvenation process for used lithium ion batteries is adopted, where the whole process of injection and sealing is finished within the vacuum chambers. Heterogenous lithium ion battery waste has not been dealt with together through electrolyte rejuvenation to the best knowledge of the inventor's knowledge. The invention is an initiative towards used lithium ion battery reuse. The present invention addresses a critical and unresolved challenge in the field of lithium-ion battery (LIB) repair and reuse—namely, the high risk of explosion due to flammable electrolytes and the formation of internal short circuits in damaged or degraded cells. Existing inventions and patents often overlook these safety hazards or fail to provide comprehensive preventive measures, making their application in real-world settings limited and potentially unsafe. The novelty of this invention lies in the development of an integrated and safe rejuvenation system that enables the reuse of LIBs while actively mitigating explosion risks. The invention incorporates a specially designed mechanical setup comprising a controlled battery handling chamber, a vacuum chamber to minimize ignition risks, a precise electrolyte insertion mechanism, and a sequential sealing system to ensure airtight restoration. These components work in coordination to reduce thermal and chemical hazards during battery rejuvenation—something not evident in prior art. FIG. 2 is a perspective view showing the top chamber, A, of used lithium ion battery electrolyte rejuvenating device shown in FIG. 1. FIG. 3 is a perspective view of the bottom chamber, B, of used lithium ion battery electrolyte injection/ rejuvination apparatus shown in FIG. 1. In the above picture: Bottom chamber, B. Suction apparatus, 111. Glove apparatus, 112. Top chamber, A. Lid for the top chamber, 201. Light interference fit connecting chamber A and lid, 203. Chamber A is a vacuum chamber functioning as the inert cap of chamber B. A light interference fit 204 is designed functioning as a seal between the two chambers A and B, such that there is no leakage of air. Another light interference fit 203 functioning as a seal between chambers A and the top lid is provided. Chamber A has the apparatus for holding a battery 206 in place during the rejuvenation process. A hole 209 is cut in the form of a rectangular slit at the solid-bottom of chamber A capable of fitting batteries of variable sizes. An inflatable seal 210 made of silicone, is fitted in a cavity 205 cut in the slit at the front and the back face of the slit, which on inflation is capable of holding the lithium ion battery 206 tightly without any leakage of air between the two chambers. The microdrill with suction mechanism 102 is also a microdrill with a hollow bit equipped with the function of drilling and simultaneously sucking out the gas and excess electrolyte from inside the battery. When the device is in operation, a lithium ion battery 206 is vertically held at the U-shaped positioning baffle 108 and air is pumped inside the inflatable seal 210 for the seal to inflate. After the inflation process of the seal, the battery is tightly held by the seal and is immovable. The lid 201 of the chamber is fitted and vacuum pumps are turned on with a pressure difference of 10-100 bars for maintaining a differential vacuum between chambers A and B for a uniform circulation of the electrolyte. After the completion of the vacuum process, the microdrills 101 and 102 are switched on and moved upwards from their resting place for battery drilling with the help of clamps 103 and 104. Two holes 0.5-1 mm deep and 0.5-1 mm in diameter are drilled at the bottom side of the battery. After drilling, nitrogen gas is purged through the microdrill with injection mechanism 101 to evacuate any residual oxygen and inert the inside of the battery. The microdrill with suction mechanism 102 is switched on a few seconds after the nitrogen purging starts to eliminate the circulated nitrogen from inside the battery.
