patents.abstract: A system (102) and a method (500) for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122) are disclosed. The system (102) includes a probing module (116) configured to apply a sequence of charge and discharge pulses to the lithium-ion cell (122), a sensing module (118) to capture a voltage response, a memory (106), and a processor (108). The processor (108) executes instructions stored in the memory (106) to extract a plurality of cell-health parameters from the captured voltage response, generate a cell-health vector representing a combined electrochemical state of the lithium-ion cell (122), and classify the lithium-ion cell (122) into one of a plurality of predefined health grades.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of diagnostic testing and monitoring of batteries. In particular, the present disclosure relates to systems and methods for health assessment and grading of lithium-ion cells. BACKGROUND [0002] Lithium-ion cells are widely deployed in consumer electronics, electric mobility, and stationary storage, and large populations of used cells enter end-of-life streams each year. Accurate health assessment and sorting of such cells may be critical to safety, performance, and economic yield, particularly when repurposing cells for second-life applications. Variability in prior usage, storage history, and chemistry may make uniform evaluation challenging, and pack-level risks may be amplified when cells with dissimilar characteristics are binned together. [0003] Conventional diagnostic practices for a lithium-ion cell may include one or more of full charge discharge cycling to determine capacity, Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC) to estimate power capability, open-circuit-voltage rest tests to approximate state of charge, and impedance measurements (for example, AC impedance at 1 kHz). While established, these procedures may require specialized equipment, controlled laboratory settings, substantial test time (ranging from hours to days), significant energy throughput, and changes in a state of charge that complicate downstream handling. Such factors may limit throughput and may make field-level deployment impractical. [0004] A single capacity-based metric such as State of Health (SOH) may not fully capture the multi-faceted, non-linear degradation mechanisms of a lithium-ion cell. Degradation may manifest as increases in direct-current internal resistance (DCIR), losses in energy efficiency, reductions in rate capability and power capability, shifts in Nominal Discharge Voltage (NDV), and changes in voltage hysteresis. Many of these effects may be path-dependent, temperature-sensitive, and history-dependent, so reliance on SOH alone may lead to misclassification of cells and sub-optimal binning outcomes. [0005] Performing separate, sequential tests to estimate each health metric may increase equipment time, operator effort, and total energy processed through the lithium-ion cell. In high-volume environments such as recycling facilities and refurbishing operations, such test burden may create bottlenecks, increase cost, and elevate safety risks. Furthermore, approaches that significantly alter the state of charge during testing may necessitate additional conditioning steps before safe handling, staging, or shipment. [0006] Therefore, it is desired to overcome the drawbacks, shortcomings, and limitations associated with existing solutions. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0007] A general object of the present disclosure is to provide systems and methods for health assessment and grading of lithium-ion cells using pulse-current probing and voltage-response analysis. [0008] Another object of the present disclosure is to enable extraction of a plurality of cell-health parameters from a short-duration diagnostic excitation, so that multiple degradation pathways may be quantified beyond a single capacity-based metric. [0009] Another object of the present disclosure is to classify a lithium-ion cell into predefined health grades using the cell-health vector, thereby supporting end-of-life sorting, reuse decisions, second-life deployment, and recycling workflows. [0010] Another object of the present disclosure is to reduce test time and energy throughput relative to conventional multi-hour protocols by using a time-optimized pulse sequence and data-driven estimation, while maintaining assessment accuracy. SUMMARY [0011] Aspects of the present disclosure relate to the field of diagnostic testing and monitoring of batteries. In particular, the present disclosure relates to systems and methods for health assessment and grading of lithium-ion cells. [0012] In one aspect, a system for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell is disclosed. The system includes a probing module configured to apply a sequence of charge and discharge pulses to the lithium-ion cell. The system also includes a sensing module operatively coupled to the probing module and configured to capture a voltage response of the lithium-ion cell during application of the sequence of charge and discharge pulses. The system also includes a memory and a processor, operatively coupled to the sensing module and the memory. Herein, the memory stores instructions that, when executed by the processor, cause the processor to extract a plurality of cell-health parameters from the captured voltage response. The processor is also configured to generate, based on the plurality of cell-health parameters, a cell-health vector representing a combined electrochemical state of the lithium-ion cell. The processor is also configured to classify the lithium-ion cell into at least one health grade of a plurality of predefined health grades based on the cell-health vector. [0013] In an embodiment, the system further includes a user interface operatively coupled to the processor and configured to display the classified health grade from the plurality of predefined health grades of the lithium-ion cell. [0014] In an embodiment, the sequence of charge and discharge pulses comprises a plurality of pulses having different magnitudes and polarities separated by rest intervals that collectively excite distinct electrochemical kinetics of the lithium-ion cell. [0015] In an embodiment, the plurality of cell-health parameters includes two or more parameters selected from a group comprising: state-of-health (SOH), direct-current internal resistance (DCIR), energy efficiency, rate capability, power capability, voltage hysteresis, and nominal discharge voltage [0016] In an embodiment, the sensing module is configured to sample the voltage response at a defined interval to derive a time-derivative signal, and wherein the processor is configured to extract the plurality of cell-health parameters from the voltage response and the time-derivative signal. [0017] In an embodiment, the processor is configured to perform dimensionality reduction on data representing the sampled voltage response and the voltage-derivative signal using principal component analysis (PCA), and subsequently apply a regression model to the dimensionally reduced data to estimate values of the plurality of cell-health parameters. [0018] In an embodiment, the regression model comprises a ridge regression model having coefficients stored in the memory and updated via firmware updates. [0019] In an embodiment, the processor is configured to transmit the cell-health vector to a remote analytics platform. [0020] In another aspect, a method for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell is disclosed. The method includes applying, by a probing module of a system, a sequence of charge and discharge pulses to the lithium-ion cell. The method also includes capturing, by a sensing module operatively coupled to the probing module, a voltage response of the lithium-ion cell during application of the sequence of charge and discharge pulses. The method also includes extracting, by a processor of the system, a plurality of cell-health parameters from the captured voltage response. The method also includes based on the plurality of cell-health parameters, generating, by the processor, a cell-health vector representing a combined electrochemical state of the lithium-ion cell. The method also includes classifying, by the processor, the lithium-ion cell into one of a plurality of predefined health grades based on the cell-health vector. [0021] Various objects, features, aspects, and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments, along with the accompanying drawing figures in which like numerals represent like components. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [0022] The accompanying drawings, which are incorporated herein, and constitute a part of this disclosure, illustrate exemplary embodiments of the disclosed methods and systems which like reference numerals refer to the same parts throughout the different drawings. Components in the drawings are not necessarily to scale, emphasis instead being placed upon clearly illustrating the principles of the present disclosure. Some drawings may indicate the components using block diagrams and may not represent the internal circuitry of each component. It will be appreciated by those skilled in the art that disclosure of such drawings includes the disclosure of electrical components, electronic components, or circuitry commonly used to implement such components. [0023] FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary block diagram (100) for implementing a system (102) for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0024] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary plot (200) of a current probe applied to a lithium-ion cell (122) and a corresponding voltage response captured over test time, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0025] FIGs. 3A-3G illustrates an exemplary plots (300A-300G) of true vs predicted results on 36 cells for the seven health indicators (7HIs), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0026] FIG. 4 illustrates an exemplary block diagram (400) of the processing unit (104), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0027] FIG. 5 illustrates an exemplary flow diagram of a method (500) for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0028] The foregoing shall be more apparent from the following more detailed description of the disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0029] In the following description, for the purposes of explanation, various specific details are set forth in order to provide a thorough understanding of embodiments of the present disclosure. It will be apparent, however, that embodiments of the present disclosure may be practiced without these specific details. Several features described hereafter can each be used independently of one another or with any combination of other features. An individual feature may not address all of the problems discussed above or might address only some of the problems discussed above. Some of the problems discussed above might not be fully addressed by any of the features described herein. [0030] The ensuing description provides exemplary embodiments only and is not intended to limit the scope, applicability, or configuration of the disclosure. Rather, the ensuing description of the exemplary embodiments will provide those skilled in the art with an enabling description for implementing an exemplary embodiment. It should be understood that various changes may be made in the function and arrangement of elements without departing from the spirit and scope of the disclosure as set forth. [0031] The following is a detailed description of embodiments of the disclosure depicted in the accompanying drawings. The embodiments are in such detail as to clearly communicate the disclosure. If the specification states a component or feature “may”, “can”, “could”, or “might” be included or have a characteristic, that particular component or feature is not required to be included or have the characteristic. [0032] As used in the description herein and throughout the claims that follow, the meaning of “a,” “an,” and “the” includes plural reference unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. Also, as used in the description herein, the meaning of “in” includes “in” and “on” unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. [0033] Conventional health assessment of lithium-ion cells relies on multiple standalone tests, full charge-discharge cycling for capacity, impedance or pulse methods for resistance and power, and extended rest for open-circuit behavior. These procedures are time-consuming, energy-intensive, and difficult to deploy at scale outside controlled laboratories. Further, a single capacity-based metric such as State of Health does not capture distinct degradation pathways such as power fade, increased direct-current internal resistance, voltage hysteresis, and shifts in nominal discharge voltage. As a result, end-of-life sorting is slow, may disturb state of charge, and may misclassify cells, leading to poor bin homogeneity and elevated pack-imbalance risk in second-life deployment. [0034] The present disclosure provides systems and methods that use a time-optimized pulse-current probing sequence with voltage-response analysis to infer a plurality of cell-health parameters in a single short diagnostic pass. A probing module applies charge and discharge pulses separated by rests, a sensing module captures the voltage response, and a processing unit executes a data pipeline that may include feature generation (including a voltage-derivative signal), standardization, dimensionality reduction, and regularized regression. The processing unit estimates multiple indicators, including State of Health, direct-current internal resistance, energy efficiency, rate capability, power capability, voltage hysteresis, and nominal discharge voltage, aggregates them into a cell-health vector, and classifies the cell into predefined health grades. The pulse sequence and grading thresholds may be configurable, safety limits may be enforced during excitation, and temperature may be controlled and/or recorded to stabilize inference. [0035] The proposed approach delivers rapid multi-indicator health assessment with markedly reduced test time and energy throughput, while inducing only a minimal change in state of charge. By extracting a plurality of cell-health parameters from one diagnostic excitation and mapping them to health grades, the method improves sorting accuracy, produces more homogeneous bins for second-life assemblies, and reduces pack-imbalance risk. The architecture is field-deployable, scalable across chemistries and form factors, and amenable to model updates, thereby lowering operational cost and increasing throughput for end-of-life assessment, reuse decisions, and recycling workflows. [0036] Embodiments explained herein relate to the field of diagnostic testing and monitoring of batteries. In particular, the present disclosure relates to systems and methods for health assessment and grading of lithium-ion cells. [0037] The various embodiments throughout the disclosure will be explained in more detail with reference to FIGs. 1-5. [0038] Referring to FIG. 1, an exemplary block diagram (100) for implementing a system (102) for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122) is illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. The system (102) may be implemented as a single enclosure or as multiple housings operatively coupled together. [0039] In one embodiment, the system (102) may include a processing unit (104) and a set of functional modules that include a user interface (114), a probing module (116), and a sensing module (118). The processing unit (104) may include a memory (106), a processor (108), an interface (110), and a communication module (112). The interface (110) may provide electrical and logical connectivity between the processing unit (104) and the user interface (114), the probing module (116), and the sensing module (118). The probing module (116) may be configured to apply a sequence of charge and discharge pulses to the lithium-ion cell (122). The processor (108), using instructions stored in the memory (106), may control parameters of the sequence, such as amplitude, polarity, duration, and timing, via the interface (110) so as to excite distinct electrochemical responses while operating within safe operating limits of the lithium-ion cell (122). The sensing module (118) may be configured to capture a voltage response of the lithium-ion cell (122) during application of the sequence of charge and discharge pulses. The sensing module (118) may provide sampled voltage data to the processing unit (104) at defined intervals, and the processor (108) may generate a time-derivative signal from the sampled voltage data. The processor (108) may execute instructions stored in the memory (106) to extract a plurality of cell-health parameters from the voltage response and the time-derivative signal. Based on the plurality of cell-health parameters, the processor (108) may generate a cell-health vector representing a combined electrochemical state of the lithium-ion cell (122) and may classify the lithium-ion cell (122) into one of a plurality of predefined health grades. In one example, the cell-health vector may hϵR^7 be represented as h = [SOH, DCIR, Energy Efficiency, Rate capability, Power Capability, Voltage hysteresis, nominal discharge voltage]. The user interface (114) may be configured to present one or more outputs generated by the processing unit (104), which may include the health grade of the lithium-ion cell (122) and, in some embodiments, selected elements of the cell-health vector or an indication of a recommended action for reuse, second-life deployment, or recycling. In one embodiment, the plurality of cell-health parameters may include two or more parameters selected from a group including: state-of-health (SOH), direct-current internal resistance (DCIR), energy efficiency, rate capability, power capability, voltage hysteresis, and nominal discharge voltage. The communication module (112) may enable wired or wireless data exchange between the system (102) and external device(s) (120). In some embodiments, the processor (108) may transmit at least one of the cell-health vector and the health grade to the external device(s) (120) for storage, workflow integration, or analytics. While FIG. 1 illustrates one logical arrangement, the functions attributed to the probing module (116) and the sensing module (118) may be implemented using discrete circuitry, integrated circuitry, or firmware executed by the processing unit (104), and the user interface (114) may include one or more of a visual display, a touch input, or other human-machine interface elements, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. In one embodiment, the user interface (114) may be configured to display the classified health grade from the plurality of predefined health grades of the lithium-ion cell (122). In one exemplary embodiment, the term State of Health (SOH) may be defined as a ratio of a maximum current capacity of the lithium-ion cell (122) to an original maximum capacity (rated capacity) of the lithium-ion cell (122). SOH=(current capacity)/(rated capacity)×100 (1) Herein, current capacity is the discharge capacity measured after a standardized charge-discharge cycle and rated capacity is the manufacturer’s specified nominal capacity at beginning of life. However, because a lithium-ion cell is a non-linear electrochemical system, degradation may manifest along multiple pathways that are not fully reflected by capacity alone. For example, capacity fade may be one measurable manifestation of degradation, whereas power fade may arise from kinetic and impedance changes and may not be captured by SOH. Additional operational metrics, such as rate capability, DCIR, and energy efficiency, may further inform an internal state of the lithium-ion cell (122). Internal Resistance (IR) quantifies the battery’s impedance to current flow. It is measured as the average of the Direct Current Internal Resistances measured at 10% increments in state of charge (SOC), from 0% to 100%, under controlled conditions: IR=1/11 ∑_(i=0)^10▒〖DCIR (〖SOC〗_i ) 〗 (2) where measurements are taken at SOC levels of 0%, 10%, 20%, ..., 100%. To increase the quality of cell-sorting and health assessment at end-of-life, the present disclosure introduces a Multi-Dimensional Health Indicator (MDHI). The MDHI may represent an aggregated assessment derived from several health indicators that may encode overlapping or complementary information about electrochemical condition and performance. In various embodiments, the health indicators that populate the MDHI may include SOH, DCIR, energy efficiency, rate capability, power capability, nominal discharge voltage, and an extent of voltage hysteresis. Energy efficiency is a ratio of a total energy discharged to a total energy input during charging, under standard conditions: Energy Efficiency=E_discharge/E_charge ×100 (3) Where: E=∫▒〖V(t)×I(t)dt〗 (4) Herein, the test conditions may include, but not limited to: • Charge rate: 0.5C; • Discharge rate: 0.5C; • Temperature: 25 degrees Celsius; and • Voltage range: 4.2V to 2.5V. [0051] The MDHI may be derived from a short-duration diagnostic excitation (current probe) applied to the lithium-ion cell (122). As described with reference to FIG. 1, a pulse sequence may be selected so that different segments of a voltage response reveal quasi-steady behavior, ohmic response, polarization dynamics, diffusion limits, relaxation, and voltage hysteresis. The diagnostic excitation may be configured to complete within a limited duration and to induce only a minimal change in a state of charge of the lithium-ion cell (122) [0052] The voltage response collected during the diagnostic excitation may be sampled at defined intervals and may be used to generate derived features, such as a voltage-derivative signal and a time index. Using these signals, the system (102) may estimate a plurality of cell-health parameters and may form a cell-health vector that encodes the MDHI for the lithium-ion cell (122). [0053] In a training phase, ground-truth values for each health indicator may be obtained for a sample set of lithium-ion cells using conventional characterization procedures. Using the collected diagnostic voltage responses and derived features, a parameterized estimator may be trained to learn mappings from the voltage response and the derived features to the corresponding health indicators. The resulting model parameters, statistical scaling values, and dimensionality-reduction settings (e.g., principal-component loadings) may be stored in the memory (106) for subsequent inference by the processor (108). [0054] During inference, the system (102) may evaluate a newly presented lithium-ion cell (122) using the diagnostic excitation and may compute the corresponding cell-health vector. The lithium-ion cell (122) may then be assigned to one of a plurality of predefined health grades based on the cell-health vector. By employing the MDHI with the current-probe-based acquisition, the system (102) may reduce characterization time and energy while improving sorting accuracy and promoting similarity among cells grouped for second-life usage, thereby exposing degradation pathways that are not observable through SOH alone. [0055] Referring to FIG. 2, an exemplary plot (200) of a current probe applied to a lithium-ion cell (122) and a corresponding voltage response captured over test time is illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. The solid trace represents cell voltage (left axis, volts) and the dashed trace represents probe current (right axis, amperes). The plot is representative of a cylindrical lithium-ion cell operated under the diagnostic excitation used by the system (102). [0056] In one embodiment, the probing module (116) may apply a sequence of charge and discharge pulses separated by rest intervals to the lithium-ion cell (122), while the sensing module (118) may sample the voltage response of the lithium-ion cell (122) during the sequence. As illustrated in FIG. 2, an initial low-rate charge segment may produce a gradual rise in the voltage trace followed by a rest interval. A subsequent moderate-rate discharge segment may generate an immediate step-like drop in voltage at the current transition and a slower relaxation during the hold. These behaviors may expose quasi-steady open-circuit tendencies and diffusion-related dynamics useful for estimating state-of-health (SOH), energy efficiency, and nominal discharge voltage. [0057] Short, bidirectional pulse segments may follow, in which the probing module (116) may inject brief positive and negative current steps. The instantaneous voltage discontinuities at the onset of these steps may reflect DCIR, while the subsequent short-time settling may encode polarization effects. The relative amplitude of the voltage excursions under different pulse magnitudes may provide observability for power capability and rate capability. [0058] In later high-rate discharge segments, the voltage trace may exhibit deeper, transient sags with rapid recovery during intervening rest periods. These features may indicate transport-limited behavior and electrode overpotential under elevated load, further informing rate capability and power capability. Alternating charge–rest–discharge portions may yield a looped relationship between charge and discharge voltages at comparable states of charge, which may be used by the processing unit (104) to infer an extent of voltage hysteresis. [0059] The processing unit (104) may receive the sampled voltage data from the sensing module (118) and may generate derived features (for example, a voltage-derivative signal and a time index). Using these signals, the processing unit (104) may estimate a plurality of cell-health parameters and may form a cell-health vector for the lithium-ion cell (122). As a result, FIG. 2 visually links distinct pulse blocks of the current probe to corresponding voltage-response segments that carry information for SOH, DCIR, energy efficiency, rate capability, power capability, nominal discharge voltage, and voltage hysteresis, thereby enabling rapid, multi-indicator health assessment within the scope of the present disclosure. [0060] In one embodiment, the sequence of charge and discharge pulses may include a plurality of pulses having different magnitudes and polarities separated by rest intervals that collectively excite distinct electrochemical kinetics of the lithium-ion cell (122). [0061] As used here, nominal discharge voltage is an average operating voltage during discharge under specified standard test conditions such as, but not limited to: • Discharge rate: 0.5C; • Temperature: 25 degrees Celsius; • Upper voltage cut-off: 4.2V; and • Lower voltage cut-off: 2.5V. [0062] The nominal voltage represents a practical voltage value for system design and battery modeling, distinct from maximum or minimum terminal voltages. [0063] Further, the voltage hysteresis quantifies a voltage difference between charging and discharging at the same SOC. Formally: ∆V_hyst (SoC)= V_charge (SoC)-V_discharge (SoC) (5) Key metrics: ∆V_(hyst,max)=■(max@SoC)|V_charge (SoC)-V_discharge (SoC)| (6) ∆V_(hyst,avg)=1/(〖SoC〗_max-〖SoC〗_min ) ∫_(〖SoC〗_min)^(〖SoC〗_max)▒〖|V_charge (SoC)-V_discharge (SoC)| d(SoC) 〗 (7) [0064] Hysteresis reflects energy losses and impacts accuracy in battery modeling and control. [0065] As used herein, rate capability measures the ability of a battery to maintain performance (capacity and voltage) under different charge or discharge rates, typically after a short rest period. Lower rate capability often indicates increased internal resistance or degradation. [0066] As used herein, power capability is the maximum power output during constant current (CC) discharge at a specified C-rate, such as 0.5C (e.g., 2.4A for a 4.8Ah cell): P(t)=V(t)×I (8) [0067] The power capability reflects the battery’s suitability for high-demand applications like electric vehicles or power tools. [0068] Table 1 provides an exemplary test protocol to measure health indicators, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. Further, the parameter values for each step in the testing protocol may be determined using the cell datasheet prepared by the cell manufacturer. Health indicator Test Protocol State of Health (SOH) CCCV charge @ 0.5IC to 4.2V; 15min rest; CC discharge @ 1IC to 2.75V; 15 min rest; CC charge @ 0.5IC to 30%SOC. Average DC internal resistance (IR) From the 0%SOC point, 10s 1IC discharge pulse → 30min rest → 10s 1IC charge pulse at every 10% SOC increment until 100% SOC Voltage hysteresis Slow C/5 galvanostatic scan between 30–80 %SOC: charge → rest 30 min → discharge. Energy efficiency Full CCCV charge @ 0.5IC (cut-off C/20); rest 30 min; CC discharge @ 0.5IC to 2.5 V. Power capability (3.6V limit) Hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC): at 3.6V apply a sequence of 3 10s charge and discharge pulses Rate capability (0.5C/1C) Two back-to-back discharges after a standard charge: (i) CC @ 0.5IC; (ii) CC @ 1IC. Nominal voltage CC discharge @ 0.5IC from 100% to 0%SOC following a full charge. Table 1 [0069] As used herein, terms CCCV means constant-current–constant-voltage and CC is constant-current. IC denotes the rated capacity-based current corresponding to 1 C, also referred to as C-rate. Table 2 provides a list of approximate durations for running each health indicator using the conventional, separate test protocols. For experimental purposes Test protocol for LG M50 is used at the time of inference. The voltage response of this current probe is measured and then supplied to a machine learning (ML) model after processing. Step Number Step Name End condition 1 CC (Constant Current) charge at 0.5 C (2.4 A) 5 minutes 2 Rest 1 minute 3 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 0.5 C (2.4 A) 5 minutes 4 Rest 30 seconds 5 CC (Constant Current) charge at 0.5 C (2.4 A) 5 seconds 6 Rest 10 seconds 7 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 0.5 C (2.4 A) 5 seconds 8 Rest 30 seconds 9 CC (Constant Current) charge at 1 C (4.8 A) 5 seconds 10 Rest 10 seconds 11 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 1.5 C (7.2 A) 5 seconds 12 Rest 30 seconds 13 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 1.5 C (7.2 A) 10 seconds 14 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 1.75 C (8.4 A) 10 seconds 15 Rest 10 seconds 16 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 1.5 C (7.2 A) 10 seconds 17 CC (Constant Current) discharge at 1.75 C (8.4 A) 10 seconds 18 Rest 1 minute Table 3 [0071] In one non-limiting example, the probing module (116) may apply a sequence of constant-current (CC) segments interleaved with rests to a lithium-ion cell (122), while the sensing module (118) records the corresponding voltage response. The sequence may begin with a low-rate CC charge at about 0.5 C for several minutes, followed by a rest interval. A low-rate CC discharge at about 0.5 C for several minutes may follow, after which a short rest may be applied. The sequence may then include short 0.5 C charge and 0.5 C discharge steps (on the order of seconds) separated by rests on the order of seconds, short 1 C charge and 1 C discharge steps with intervening rests, and higher-rate discharge steps (e.g., about 1.5 C and about 1.75 C) repeated with brief rests. As used herein, “1 C charge” refers to charging a cell at a current equal to its rated capacity (in ampere-hours) per hour i.e., Current (A) = C-rate × Capacity (Ah). For example, 0.5C means 2.5A for a 5Ah cell. A final rest may conclude the probe. The specific example above corresponds to a ~15-minute profile in which C-rates and durations are shown for illustration and may be expressed as absolute current values where convenient. The pulse magnitudes, polarities, durations, ordering, repetition count, and rest lengths may be selected or tuned by the processor (108) using parameters stored in the memory (106) so that (i) the probe completes within a limited duration and (ii) a change in state of charge of the lithium-ion cell (122) remains minimal and within safety limits. In various embodiments, safety cut-offs for voltage, current, and temperature may be enforced during execution of the probe. The sensing module (118) may sample the voltage response at defined intervals during each segment and rest. The processing unit (104) may generate derived features, including a voltage-derivative signal and timing markers for current transitions, and may attribute information from different segments to different health indicators as previously described (e.g., low-rate blocks for State of Health, energy efficiency, and nominal discharge voltage; short 0.5 C steps for direct-current internal resistance; 1 C steps for mixed ohmic-polarization dynamics; higher-rate steps for rate capability and power capability; alternating charge-rest-discharge for voltage hysteresis). Although Table 3 lists one representative ordering and set of durations suitable for inference on a cylindrical cell, functionally equivalent pulse patterns that elicit substantially the same underlying electrochemical responses may be used. The current-probe parameters may be scaled to cell capacity, adapted to chemistry, or repeated M times for signal-to-noise improvement, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. In one embodiment, the sensing module (118) may be configured to sample the voltage response at a defined interval to obtain a time-dependent signal and wherein the processor (108) is configured to extract the plurality of cell-health parameters from the voltage response and the time-dependent signal. In one example, a lithium-ion cell may undergo a 15 min (900 sec) test duration using a customized current probe. Measured voltage across the lithium-ion cell may then be sampled e.g., once per second, resulting in a time series of 900 raw voltage values: V={v_1,v_2,v_3,…..,v_900 }. This high-resolution data forms the foundation for time-domain modeling of degradation features. For feature engineering, three key features are derived from the raw voltage series (V): “voltage (v)” – directly recorded at 1 s, “voltage derivative” as dV/dt= v_i-v_(i-1) wherein i={2,3,4 ….900}, and “time (t)” as a simple time vector {1, 2, 3, 4,… .., 900}. [0076] In one embodiment, the processor (108) may be configured to perform dimensionality reduction on data representing the sampled voltage response voltage-derivative signal, and time using principal component analysis (PCA), and subsequently apply a regression model to the dimensionally reduced data to estimate values of the plurality of cell-health parameters. [0077] In one embodiment, the regression model may include a ridge regression model having coefficients stored in the memory (106) and updated via firmware updates. In one exemplary embodiment, the learning system (or the machine learning model) may be an ensemble of seven identical, but separately-tuned, linear pipelines. Each pipeline takes the same 900-time-step, 3-channel voltage trace produced by a single test and predicts one of the seven target variables. Formally, for every sample we reshape the tensor ΧϵR^(900×3) into a flat vector ΧϵR^2700 and pass it through ⏟StandardScaler┬(μ,σ) →⏟PCA┬(U_k ) →⏟Rigde┬(β,b) so that the prediction is y ̂=b+β^T ⏟(〖(U〗_k^T (x-μ)/σ))┬(projected K-dim⁡vector ). The choice of k principal components and the Ridge penalty α is unique to each target (health indicator) and determined via nested cross-validation during model training. In one embodiment, the processing unit (104) may implement a learning pipeline that converts a diagnostic voltage response of a lithium-ion cell (122) into estimates of a plurality of cell-health parameters. The learning pipeline may operate on features derived from sampled voltage data collected by the sensing module (118) during execution of the current probe by the probing module (116). For training, the processor (108) may use labeled datasets in which ground-truth values for each health indicator are obtained by conventional characterization procedures. Parameters learned during training may be stored in the memory (106) for subsequent inference. During training, the Standard Scaler routine may learn a feature-wise mean (μ_j) and a feature-wise standard deviation (σ_j) on the training folds. At the time of inference, the processor may apply the stored scaling coefficients to transform incoming features to zero-mean and unit-variance scale. This ensures that all the 2700 raw features enter PCA with comparable scale without re-learning the coefficients at runtime. During training, the processor (108) may apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the standardized training data to learn an orthonormal basis〖 {U〗_1,U_2,...U_k}that satisfies a target cumulative-variance criterion (for example, ≥ 95 percent) or a fixed component count selected from a predefined set (for example, k ϵ{20, 40, 60, 80, 120}),whichever yields a lower validation error. PCA may reduce the effective dimensionality from 2,700 to k<< nsamples and remove multicollinearity. During inference, the processor (108) may not learn PCA again, instead, the processor (108) may apply the stored PCA loadings U_k (learned during training) to project the standardized input features into the k-dimensional subspace, as a deterministic transformation. A regularized regression stage may then be applied to the principal-component scores. The processor (108) may perform inference using a ridge regressor model on the PCA scores ZϵR^(n×k) by solving ■(min@β,b) |(|y-Zβ-b|)|_2^2+α|(|β|)|_2^2 . .alpha is determined via cross-validation during model training. In various embodiments, one such ridge model may be trained per indicator so that the set of predictions forms a cell-health vector. In one embodiment, the processor (108) may be configured to transmit the cell-health vector to a remote analytics platform such as the external device(s) (120) via the communication module (112). The external device(s) (120) may include, but not limited to, a computer, a laptop, a server system, or a portable communication device such as tablet or smartphone. Referring to FIGs. 3A-3G, an exemplary plots (300A-300G) of true vs predicted results on 36 cells for the seven health indicators (7HIs) using the PCA + Ridge pipelines are illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. In some embodiments, the ambient temperature may be maintained by environmental controls during acquisition; the processor (106) may apply the trained models without requiring cell-temperature measurement. In one exemplary embodiment, the system (102) may categorize each lithium-ion cell (122) into Grade A, Grade B, Grade C, or Grade D, where Grade A may be suited to high-performance reuse, Grade B to mid-range applications, Grade C to low-demand uses, and Grade D to recycle-ready disposition. The grading may be performed after the probing module (116) and the sensing module (118) have produced the diagnostic voltage response and the processor (108) has estimated the plurality of health indicators using the methods described herein. The processing unit (104) may execute diagnostic and learning pipelines for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122), may control excitation provided by the probing module (116), may acquire voltage data from the sensing module (118), and may manage local and external data exchange for the system (102). In one embodiment, the processing unit (104) may include a processor (402). The processor (402) may be implemented using one or more microcontrollers, microprocessors, digital signal processors, application-specific integrated circuits, or system-on-chip devices capable of executing computer-readable instructions. The processor (402) may fetch and execute instructions to: receive sampled voltage data; generate derived features (for example, a voltage-derivative signal and timing markers); perform standardization and Principal Component Analysis (PCA); apply one or more regularized regression models (for example, ridge regression) to estimate a plurality of cell-health parameters; generate a cell-health vector; and assign a health grade using stored grading thresholds. The processing unit (104) may include a main memory (404) that provides volatile storage (for example, DRAM or SRAM) for active program code, voltage traces, intermediate feature tensors, PCA scores, and temporary results during execution. A read-only memory (406) may store boot firmware, secure initialization code, calibration constants, and default configuration parameters for the probe and data-acquisition routines. A mass storage device (408) may provide non-volatile storage for trained model artifacts and configuration data. By way of example, the mass storage device (408) may store standardization statistics, PCA loadings and retained-variance settings, regression coefficients and intercepts for each health indicator, grading thresholds for the plurality of predefined health grades, and operational logs. Parameters and artifacts persisted in the mass storage device (408) may be treated collectively as memory resources of the system (102). One or more communication port(s) (410) may enable bidirectional data exchange between the processing unit (104) and other elements of the system (102) and/or external device(s) (120). The communication port(s) (410) may include, by way of example, Universal Serial Bus, UART, SPI, I²C, Ethernet, or logical endpoints supporting a wireless link provided elsewhere in the system. The communication port(s) (410) may be used to send the cell-health vector, indicator values, and the assigned health grade to external resources for storage or analytics, and to receive configuration updates. An external storage device (414) may be operatively coupled to the processing unit (104) to allow import of probe profiles, model updates, and grading tables, and export of diagnostic logs or datasets for offline analysis. The external storage device (414) may include removable solid-state media or network-attached storage, depending on deployment requirements. A user interface (416) may provide local control and status indication for the processing unit (104). The user interface (416) may include, for example, keys, indicators, or a minimal display to initiate a probe, view connectivity status, or review the assigned health grade. In some embodiments, the user interface (416) may function in coordination with or as a subset of a system-level user interface (114). The elements described above may communicate over a bus (412) that may include one or more internal interconnects for data and control signaling. The bus (412) may couple the processor (402) with the main memory (404), read-only memory (406), mass storage device (408), communication port(s) (410), and user interface (416) to support real-time execution of the health-assessment pipeline. In operation, the processor (402) may retrieve executable instructions and stored parameters from the memories (404, 406, 408), process the voltage response acquired from the sensing module (118), and output the cell-health vector and health grade for the lithium-ion cell (122). Updates to probe parameters, model coefficients, or grading thresholds may be loaded via the communication port(s) (410) or the external storage device (414) and stored in the mass storage device (408) for subsequent use. The block diagram shown in FIG. 4 is illustrative. Elements of the processing unit (104) may be consolidated or distributed across hardware, firmware, or software, and additional components may be included or omitted, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. Referring to FIG. 5, an exemplary flow diagram of a method (500) for health assessment of a lithium-ion cell (122) is illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. The method (500) may be implemented by the system (102). At step (502), the method (500) may include applying, by a probing module (116) of the system (102), a sequence of charge and discharge pulses to the lithium-ion cell (122). At step (504), the method (500) may include capturing, by a sensing module (118) operatively coupled to the probing module (116), a voltage response of the lithium-ion cell (122) during application of the sequence of charge and discharge pulses. At step (506), the method (500) may include extracting, by a processor (108) of the system (102), a plurality of cell-health parameters from the captured voltage response. At step (508), based on the plurality of cell-health parameters, the method (500) may include generating, by the processor (108), a cell-health vector representing a combined electrochemical state of the lithium-ion cell (122). At step (510), the method (500) may include classifying, by the processor (108), the lithium-ion cell (122) into one of a plurality of predefined health grades based on the cell-health vector. One or more steps of the method (500) may be performed in a different order, combined, omitted, or supplemented with additional steps, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. While the foregoing describes various embodiments of the disclosure, other and further embodiments of the disclosure may be devised without departing from the basic scope thereof. The scope of the disclosure is determined by the claims that follow. The disclosure is not limited to the described embodiments, versions, or examples, which are included to enable a person having ordinary skill in the art to make and use the disclosure when combined with information and knowledge available to the person having ordinary skill in the art. ADVANTAGES OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE The present disclosure provides rapid, multi-indicator health assessment of lithium-ion cells using a pulse-current probing sequence and voltage-response analysis, enabling inference of multiple degradation pathways from a single short-duration test. The present disclosure provides reduced test time and energy throughput relative to conventional multi-hour protocols by estimating multiple health indicators from one diagnostic excitation, thereby improving throughput and lowering operational cost. The present disclosure provides minimal disturbance of state of charge during assessment, facilitating safer handling, simplified logistics, and immediate downstream processing of evaluated cells. The present disclosure provides automated classification into predefined health grades, delivering an actionable outcome that supports end-of-life sorting, reuse decisions, second-life deployment, and recycling workflows with consistent, repeatable criteria. , Claims:1. The system (102) as claimed in claim 1, further comprising a user interface (114) operatively coupled to the processor (108) and configured to display the classified health grade from the plurality of predefined health grades of the lithium-ion cell (122). 3. The system (102) as claimed in claim 5, wherein the processor (108) is configured to perform dimensionality reduction on data representing the sampled voltage response and the voltage-derivative signal using principal component analysis (PCA), and subsequently apply a regression model to the dimensionally reduced data to estimate values of the plurality of cell-health parameters. 7. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a multi-agent Edge-AI based predictive safety system (10) for lithium-ion batteries, which enables real-time cell-level detection. The system comprises several cell-level monitoring units (101) that measure voltage, current, and temperature, a CAN bus interface (106) for encrypted telemetry transmission, and a central edge-AI node (800) running a multi-agent safety network module (300). Each cell acts as an independent agent to perform time series anomaly detection, predict the RSOT, and classify safety states. The agents use distributed consensus for fault-tolerant cooperation, eliminating cloud dependencies and allowing real-time decisions. A safety actuator module (400) initiates fire suppression, isolation relays, and thermal control within 10 milliseconds. Additionally, it enables the implementation of federated learning for OTA model updates and ensures the safety of falling back to threshold-based BMS operation logic. It targets multiple markets, such as electric vehicles, drones, grid storage systems, aerospace, and industrial battery platforms.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [001] The present invention generally relates to the field of battery safety and management systems. More specifically, it pertains to a multi-agent Edge-AI based predictive safety system for real-time cell-level detection and prevention of thermal runaway, fire, and explosion events in lithium-ion batteries. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [002] Lithium-ion batteries are the cornerstone of modern energy storage, powering applications ranging from electric vehicles and drones to grid storage systems, aerospace, industrial battery platforms, and consumer electronics. However, they are susceptible to catastrophic failure modes, such as thermal runaway, which can lead to fires and explosions. Ensuring their safety is a critical challenge. Current Battery Management Systems (BMS) face significant limitations in achieving efficient and reliable safety assurance, which are listed herein. [003] Delayed Detection of Thermal Runaway-Traditional BMSs rely on threshold-based detection of parameters like voltage, temperature, and current. They often detect thermal runaway too late, when the damage is already irreversible, that is, only after physical symptoms like extreme heat or smoke are present. Existing systems detect faults only after critical thresholds are exceeded, when damage is often already irreversible. They lack the ability to predict Remaining Safe Operating Time (RSOT) or provide early warnings before physical symptoms manifest. [004] Centralized and Slow Fault Response-Conventional BMS architectures depend on a single, centralized controller to process data from all cells. This creates a single point of failure, leading to delayed or missed responses to local cell anomalies as data is transmitted and processed centrally. [005] Lack of Cross-Cell Coordination-Existing systems lack mechanisms for intelligent collaboration between battery cells. This prevents them from learning complex fault patterns from historical data, adapting to different operating conditions, providing prognostic health assessments and distinguishing between normal variations and genuine safety threat. [006] Absence of Advanced Edge Intelligence-Most BMSs are limited to threshold-based logic and cannot run advanced machine learning inference on the device to predict failures before they occur. They lack the ability to estimate critical metrics like Remaining Safe Operating Time (RSOT). [007] Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities-Many existing systems do not incorporate secure communication and update methods, making them vulnerable to malicious attacks, such as harmful firmware or model injections, which can compromise safety. [008] Ineffective Alerting and Diagnostics-Existing systems primarily operate at the battery pack or module level. They lack the resolution to monitor, diagnose, and act upon conditions at the individual cell level, where faults originate, resulting in vague alerts and limited diagnostic insight. [009] Poor Scalability and Adaptability-Current safety solutions are often designed for specific applications and do not scale well across different platforms, such as electric vehicles, drones, or grid storage systems, leading to inefficient and costly implementations. [0010] The proposed invention provides a technological solution to these challenges, ensuring efficient, precise, and scalable safety for lithium-ion battery systems. As described in the following paragraphs of the present disclosure, various safety methods exist; however, each of them suffers from various disadvantages and limitations. [0011] US11677104B2 discloses functional safety in BMSs, which points out that traditional safety designs in BMSs rely on fixed upper/lower threshold-based detection of individual cell parameters (e.g., cell voltage, temperature, current) and triggers protective actions (shutdown or fault response) when one or more parameters exceed predefined limits. The architecture is primarily centralized, which targets the pack/module level monitoring, lacking predictive or cell-level capability. There is no possibility of predicting and preventing; only to act when it reaches a critical level. Due to the centralized approach, it cannot localize faults at the individual cell level rapidly. Furthermore, there is no mention of AI-driven diagnostics, RSOT, or federated intelligence. [0012] Edge-Cloud Collaborative Machine Learning for Battery Health Prediction by Y. Duan et al., establishes a collaborative machine learning approach between edge devices and the cloud for battery health prediction. The edge collects data, and models are trained or inferred in a cloud-centric fashion. The device requires a permanent cloud connection, which is not feasible for systems where rapid fault intervention is critical. Additionally, machine learning is not yet implemented at the cell/edge level for autonomous fault mitigation. Moreover, centralized analytics can be slow and increase cybersecurity risks since it relies on the cloud. [0013] AI Approaches for Advanced BMS in Electric Vehicle Applications by Shihavuddin and Shakib reviews the applications of AI/ML in battery management. The focus is on the health prediction and centralized models for battery packs. They detect faults only after symptoms exceed thresholds (e.g., overheating, overcurrent), offering no early warning or RSOT prediction. Machine learning inference is not implemented at the edge, and cell-level safety functionalities are not realized. Systems lack multi-agent autonomy, high-precision fault detection latency, and modular scalability. [0014] Empowering the future: a comprehensive review of cutting‐edge battery technologies by Kasniya, B., et al. and Battery safety: Machine learning-based prognostics, Prog. Energy Combust by J. Zhao et al. highlights the need for predictive and AI-based methods in battery health and safety management, but does not address real-time, decentralized multi-agent Edge-AI architectures for cell-level fault mitigation. [0015] Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries by Y. Tang et al. discusses federated learning and a potential future extension but does not implement real-time inference at the edge. [0016] Federated Learning: Challenges, Methods, and Future Directions by A. G. Howard et al. describes over-the-air (OTA) update frameworks but lacks integration with battery-specific predictive safety mechanisms. [0017] ScalOTA: Scalable Secure OTA Software Updates for Vehicles by A. Shoker et al. and US20110093639A1, Secure communications between and verification of authorized Controller Area Network (CAN) devices focus on CAN security and functional safety, respectively, yet none integrate cell-level analytics with real-time autonomous response. [0018] All these limitations highlight the need for a more integrated, precise, and scalable solution. The proposed invention addresses key limitations of prior art by building upon the constraints of conventional BMS architectures, which are mostly threshold-based, centralized, and reactive in nature. It offers a decentralized/distributed multi-agent Edge-AI architecture that introduces cell-level, intelligent agents capable of making independent safety decisions in real time, rather than relying on centralised pack-level controllers. The system performs cell-level predictive analytics, including multi-variable time-series classification (e.g., voltage sag, thermal rise) directly at the edge, eliminating cloud dependency and enabling swift response. It integrates RSOT regression for predictive control, providing a proactive safety margin before critical failure. The invention ensures a real-time autonomous response through its multi-agent safety network framework, which uses consensus for fault validation, significantly improving safety assurance. Furthermore, it incorporates secure OTA updates, allowing the system to evolve its models safely with usage, and implements TLS-encrypted, authenticated CAN bus communication to prevent spoofing and enable fault-tolerant control actions. Designed for large-scale commercial deployment, it is well-suited for electric vehicles, grid storage, drones, and industrial applications. Additionally, the system provides real-time data on cell health and safety status, empowering operators to make informed decisions. Its autonomous operation further reduces reliance on human intervention. The proposed invention therefore bridges critical gaps in responsiveness, resolution, autonomy, and cyber-resilience, which current industry standard BMS frameworks and academic models fail to address comprehensively, making it a robust and efficient solution for modern energy systems. [0019] The advantages of the proposed invention are manifold. The disclosed system ensures proactive safety by anticipating faults before they become hazardous, enabling preventive action. This is a significant improvement over traditional reactive threshold-based BMS systems. It provides cell-level intelligence and local safety enforcement, offering granular diagnostics far superior to broad pack-level alerts found in traditional systems. The architecture delivers real-time inference with ultra-low latency, enabling critical decisions and actions to be made in less than 200 milliseconds to isolate faulty cells in high-energy applications swiftly. Its modular and flexible design ensures cross-platform scalability for diverse applications, including electric vehicles, grid storage, UAVs, renewable systems, and industrial battery platforms. Unlike standard battery systems, this design includes built-in cybersecurity measures, such as secure communication and update protocols to safeguard critical infrastructure. The invention significantly improves the safety of lithium-ion energy systems, lowering the risk of catastrophic battery failures, fires, and explosions in mission-critical applications. It reduces downtime and maintenance costs through early fault detection and condition-based maintenance, thereby decreasing the need for unplanned services. It also enhances overall battery life and reliability by preventing unnoticed cell damage, which helps maintain capacity and health throughout the battery's lifespan. The system is designed to comply with industrial safety standards, meeting the expectations for smart, autonomous battery monitoring in electric mobility and energy storage. Furthermore, it encourages the development of advanced battery safety solutions using affordable open hardware and AI innovation. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION [0020] The primary object of the invention is to present a multi-agent Edge-AI based predictive safety system for real-time cell-level fire and explosion detection in lithium-ion batteries. [0021] Another object of the invention is to enable cell-level fault detection with millisecond-scale response times. [0022] Yet another object of the invention is to implement a multi-agent safety network framework that eliminates single points of failure. [0023] Another object of the invention is to provide real-time data analytics, enabling the monitoring of RSOT estimation for proactive safety management. [0024] Yet another object of the invention is to encrypt CAN bus communication for efficient safety management in lithium-ion energy systems. [0025] Yet another object of the invention is to provide a scalable, modular architecture adaptable to diverse applications, making the system suitable for both small and large-scale energy systems. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0026] The following summary of the present invention is provided to facilitate an understanding of some of the innovative features unique to the present invention. It is intended to be a partial description. A comprehensive understanding of the invention's various aspects can be gained by considering the entire specification, including the claims, drawings, and abstract, as a whole. [0027] The present invention provides an Edge-AI based predictive safety system for lithium-ion batteries. The invention integrates a plurality of cell-level monitoring units that measure voltage, current, and temperature of individual battery cells with real-time sampling rates suitable for detecting rapid fault onset, a CAN bus interface for encrypted telemetry, and a central edge computing device or central edge-AI node, configured with an artificial intelligence inference engine executing a multi-agent framework wherein each cell operates as an autonomous agent performing: real-time anomaly detection mechanism using multivariate time-series classification, prediction of Remaining Safe Operating Time (RSOT) prior to thermal runaway or critical failure, assignment or classification of safety states at the cell level {normal, warning, pre-runaway, critical}. [0028] The disclosed system implements fault-tolerant consensus voting among cell agents to validate critical fault detections before triggering safety actuations, reducing false positives while maintaining high sensitivity. The system’s safety actuator module initiates fire suppression, isolation relays, and thermal control within milliseconds. Additionally, the disclosed system supports on-device federated learning where cell agents are trained locally on proprietary telemetry data and share only differential parameter updates (not raw data) for collaborative model improvement. The system implements cryptographically signed, differential AI model updates over-the-air with automatic rollback and fail-safe mechanisms designed explicitly for safety-critical battery applications. The invention in the present disclosure is scalable and adaptable to various battery applications, making it suitable for electric vehicles, drones, grid storage systems, and industrial platforms. The components of the drawings/figures are illustrated to emphasize the general principles of the present disclosure and are not necessarily drawn to scale. Therefore, reference characters designating corresponding components are repeated as necessary throughout the figures to ensure consistency and clarity.
