[0039] The present invention provides a multi-agent Edge-AI based predictive safety system (10) that fundamentally addresses and solves critical and long-standing technical limitations and safety gaps in current lithium-ion battery systems. The invention is a technological solution to the problems of late thermal runaway detection, slow centralized fault response, lack of cross-cell coordination, absence of advanced edge intelligence, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, ineffective diagnostics, and poor scalability. The system (10) integrates advanced technologies, including a plurality of cell-level monitoring units (101), a fault-resilient, encrypted CAN bus (106) communication interface, a central edge-AI node/Jetson Nano (800) executing a multi-agent safety network framework module (300), a distributed decision-making mechanism, and a safety actuator module (400). This integrated system provides a scalable, efficient, and precise predictive safety framework that operates in real-time, eliminating cloud dependencies for critical decisions. [0040] Figure 1 illustrates a block diagram of the proposed Edge-AI-based predictive safety system (10). The system (10) comprises four primary modules: a sensing and data acquisition module (100) consisting of a plurality of cell-level monitoring units (101), an edge-AI fault prediction module (200) which is centered on an edge-AI node (800), a multi-agent safety network module (300) for distributed, fault-tolerant cooperation consensus, a cloud/SCADA interface module (600), and an OTA module (500) for analytics and secure updates. Each module communicates via a combination of CAN bus (106) and secure Wi-Fi/Ethernet for cloud interfacing, utilising modules like the Jetson Nano (800). [0041] Figure 2 illustrates a cell-level monitoring unit (101), comprising of the embedded microcontroller (102), sensors, and the CAN bus interface (106) responsible for real-time data acquisition and encrypted transmission. Each individual lithium-ion cell, equipped with a cell-level monitoring unit (101), comprises thermal sensors/sensor units (e.g., NTC/PTC thermistors) (103), voltage sensors (104), and current sensors (105). These sensors are interfaced with a low-power microcontroller (102), which samples parameters such as voltage, current, and temperature in real-time and transmits them as encrypted telemetry via a CAN bus (106) transceiver to a central Edge-AI node (800). The use of CAN bus (106) ensures fault-tolerant, real-time data acquisition even under harsh electromagnetic and operational conditions. The telemetry data is transmitted through encrypted CAN bus (106) frames to prevent tampering and ensure cybersecurity. A priority arbitration scheme is employed on the CAN bus (106), where high-risk safety events pre-empt routine telemetry traffic, ensuring critical alerts are never delayed. [0042] The encrypted telemetry data from all cell-level units (acting as agents) is received by a central edge-AI node (such as Jetson Nano) (800) or an equivalent embedded GPU platform. This node is optimized using custom optimized TensorRT pipelines for ultra-low inference latency, below 10 milliseconds. The Jetson Nano (800) executes a distributed edge-AI multi-agent system, wherein each battery cell operates as a virtual autonomous agent. Each agent independently processes the streaming voltage, current, and temperature data from its assigned battery cell. [0043] Figure 3 illustrates a flowchart of the edge-AI fault prediction module (200), showcasing the end-to-end steps from data ingestion and normalization by Jetson Nano (201), edge-AI multi-agent processing (202) to cell-level telemetry (203), real-time evaluation (204), cell-level fault classification (205), and actuation (206). The AI models executed by each agent are trained offline using annotated datasets (e.g., BatteryData_AllC_Rates.csv), which contain over 6,000 cycles across various discharge rates (1C, 2C, 3C) and key fault patterns, such as internal shorts, over-temperature conditions, voltage instability, rapid capacity fade, and early thermal runaway initiation signatures. The models are compressed (INT8 quantized) and optimized to align with the Jetson Nano's (800) memory and GPU constraints for maximum efficiency. Each agent performs three critical functions in real-time: 1. Real-time anomaly detection: Using multivariate time-series classification to identify anomalies like voltage sag and temperature rise. 2. RSOT prediction: Computed via a regression model trained on the slope dynamics of voltage and temperature signals. This prognostic estimate predicts how long a cell can safely operate before a critical failure and enables graded alerts (normal, warning, critical) at the cell level. 3. Safety state classification: Assigns a discrete safety state to the cell, selected from (normal, warning, pre-runaway, critical) based on the anomaly detection and RSOT output. This system achieved 99.85% accuracy and an F1-Score of 1.00 in validation tests. This enables proactive safety by anticipating faults before they become hazardous, enabling preventive action, a key advantage over reactive systems. [0044] Each edge-AI unit along with an independent cell unit is treated as a safety agent in the multi-agent safety network module (300). This introduces a distributed decision-making mechanism wherein the agents reach a consensus on critical fault conditions without reliance on centralized cloud controllers. The agents do not operate in isolation; they: 1. Share their inferred safety states, RSOT estimates and fault metadata via CAN bus (106)/MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport)/HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol. 2. Engage in a consensus voting mechanism to validate critical fault conditions. This cross-referencing of outputs between peer agents drastically reduces false positives and enhances the overall reliability of the system. 3. Can elect a lead agent for global commands in clustered battery systems. 4. Collaborate to reach an agreement on necessary safety actions (isolation, cooling, or shutdown protocols), eliminating reliance on a single, centralized controller and thus removing a critical point of failure. This enables the system to scale seamlessly from a small battery pack to a large grid-scale storage system. [0045] The multi-agent architecture addresses the lack of cross-cell coordination in existing systems, ensuring fault-tolerant cooperation, and eliminating the single point of failure inherent in centralized architectures. The multi-agent safety network module (300) also implements federated learning with incremental model updates, where cell-level agents train locally on their telemetry data and transmit only parameter updates (not raw data) to an aggregator on the edge node i.e., Jetson Nano (800), ensuring data privacy and reducing bandwidth usage and allowing the AI models to adapt and improve continuously across the entire fleet of systems without compromising security. [0046] Figure 4 presents a timeline of the fire and explosion detection process, illustrating how early signs are detected and escalated to actuation (206) within milliseconds, and Figure 5 provides the safety actuator module (400), mapping how relay drivers (401), cooling triggers (402), isolation switches (403), and emergency shutdown (406) protocols are activated via the central edge-AI node (800). Upon detecting pre-critical conditions via multi-agent consensus, the safety actuator module (400) is configured to trigger protective mechanisms within 10 milliseconds, in response to the predictive safety states. These mechanisms include: 1. Isolation relays to disconnect the faulty cell or module electrically. 2. Thermal control devices, such as cooling fans and PCM-based heat sinks, are used to manage temperature. 3. Fire suppression units, such as aerosol injectors or extinguishing gases, are used to contain fires. 4. Emergency alerts to higher-level units, such as vehicle ECUs or building SCADA units. [0047] Actuation decisions are determined by the central edge-AI node (800) and multi-agent consensus with millisecond latency. This ultra-low latency response is crucial for quickly isolating faulty cells in high-energy applications and is a direct result of the edge-based, decentralized architecture. [0048] A parallel data stream of telemetry, fault classifications, and actions is sent to a secure cloud/SCADA interface module (600). Figure 6 displays the SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) & Cloud Analytics Dashboard, illustrating how real-time telemetry is visualized, along with predictive fault alerts, OTA update management, and safety status. Figure 6 provides real-time cell-level health maps, event logs with fault signatures, predictive alerts with time-stamped decisions, and OTA model update management. The visual representation in the form of health maps shows each cell's safety state: Normal (green), Warning (yellow/orange), Pre-Runaway (red), and Critical (dark red). The display also shows real-time graphs showing: voltage time-series for each cell, current flow patterns (charge/discharge cycles), temperature trends with moving averages, and State of Charge (SOC) and State of Health (SOH) indicators. In the present disclosure, the cloud connectivity is for monitoring and updates only—all safety-critical decisions (fault detection, RSOT prediction, and actuation) occur locally at the edge without cloud dependency. This ensures the system continues to protect against thermal runaway even during network outages. [0049] Furthermore, the system includes an OTA module (500) configured with a public-key infrastructure (PKI). This allows for encrypted, signed, and verified updates of both the AI models and the system firmware. The module employs differential updates (transmitting only changed parameters) to reduce size and bandwidth usage. The system periodically checks for these updates, which are verified using digital signatures and applied only when confirmed to be safe, ensuring cybersecurity. [0050] The cybersecurity module (700) highlights the encryption mechanisms, authentication workflows, and secure model update strategies that protect both the cloud and edge nodes. Security is embedded throughout all modules, featuring TLS-encryption module (1000), authenticated CAN bus (106) communication, TLS for cloud communication, secure boot, and device fingerprinting. Secure boot and automatic rollback ensure system stability in case of failure or tampering. The system (10) integrates with these modules to provide real-time alerts, diagnostic logs, and predictive maintenance scheduling, overcoming the problem of ineffective pack-level alerting by enabling cell-specific fault classification, risk scores, and RSOT estimates. Critically, the system (10) supports fail-safe operation. In the unlikely event of an edge hardware or software failure, the system (10) seamlessly reverts to a traditional, proven threshold-based BMS logic with hardware-defined cutoff limits, guaranteeing a continuous baseline level of protection. [0051] Figure 7 details the model lifecycle management for the multi-agent safety network module (300). The AI models are trained and validated using real-world datasets, such as BatteryData_AllC_Rates.csv, which comprises 6000 cycles across 1C, 2C, and 3C discharge rates, along with multivariate features (voltage, current, temperature per cell, and fault labels). The time-series model was evaluated using an 80:20 train-test split, and the achieved performance metrics included 99.85% accuracy, F1-Score of 1.00, and latency of <10 milliseconds per prediction on the Jetson Nano (800). [0052] The system supports federated learning, wherein each cell-level agent can train locally on its own telemetry data. The training (301) involves synthetic and real fault injections (overcharge, forced heating, shorting). The models are then compressed (e.g., INT8 quantization) and optimized (302) via TensorRT pipelines for deployment on the resource-constrained Jetson Nano (303), achieving the critical sub-10ms latency. Only the incremental model parameter updates (not the raw, private data) are transmitted to a central aggregator on the Jetson Nano (800), which orchestrates model improvements. This ensures data privacy, reduces bandwidth usage, and allows the system to adapt to new patterns and battery chemistries over time through transfer learning. [0053] For critical events, the system (10) rapidly escalates to emergency services or triggers module shutdowns, thereby preventing cascade failure and ensuring comprehensive safety. The system's (10) proactive fault management is demonstrated in the following use case scenarios: Application Domain Real-World Scenario Trigger Condition Autonomous System Response Electric Vehicle (EV) Cell 24 overheating during hill climb. Temperature > 60°C with positive thermal gradient. Trigger immediate cell isolation, activate localized cooling system, and send SCADA alert. Grid-Scale Storage Abnormal voltage drift in Cell Group B. Voltage change rate > 0.1 V/sec sustained over 180s. Pre-charge circuit cutoff, predictive fault log, and maintenance scheduling via cloud. Drone Power System Mid-flight current surge from propulsion unit. Instantaneous current > 3C rated threshold. Trigger battery pod ejection and switch to backup power module (if available). Industrial UPS Bank Degradation-induced imbalance. Delta capacity > 15% across parallel strings. Load rebalance + smart module rerouting + alert to maintenance system. Two-Wheeler EV Fleet Sudden thermal hotspot near controller. T_cell > 55°C within 120s of ignition + RSOT < 60s. Stop discharge, activate passive cooling, and push OTA update for fault pattern. UAV Ground Charging Station Persistent voltage sag in fast charging mode. V_drop > 0.2V within 90 seconds of charging start. Adaptive charge profile rollback, push warning to dashboard, and log event in cloud backend. [0054] The invention performs through the following integrated steps: 1. Sensor units collect real-time voltage, current, and temperature data from each cell. 2. Data is transmitted as encrypted telemetry over the CAN bus (106) to the Jetson Nano (800). 3. The Jetson Nano (800) preprocesses the data and performs AI inference using the trained models. 4. Each cell's agent autonomously generates a risk score, fault classification, and RSOT estimate. 5. Agents share their inferences and reach a distributed consensus on critical faults. 6. The safety actuator module (400) triggers protective mechanisms (isolation, cooling) based on the consensus. 7. Data and decisions are logged and sent to the cloud module (600) for analytics. 8. The system periodically checks for and applies secure, signed OTA updates via OTA module (500). 9. Cyber-security module (700) measures are continuously active, and fail-safe fallback is always available. [0055] The functional working prototype was constructed and developed at the Edge Battery Lab, using LiFePO₄ (LFP) cylindrical battery cells (3.2V, 15Ah), integrated with a CAN bus-enabled BMS via MCP2515 CAN-to-SPI interface modules for robust communication, and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano configured as the edge inference unit. The multi-agent architecture was fully realized. The system was rigorously tested under controlled fault injection scenarios, including thermal runaway simulation, voltage sag, forced heating, short circuits, and current spikes. The implementation demonstrated high prediction accuracy (99.85%, F1-Score: 1.00) and sub-10 millisecond latency in triggering protective actuators. The system responded correctly and independently in all situations, confirming the practical feasibility, robustness, and scalability for safety-critical applications in EVs, UAVs, and stationary storage systems. [0056] The system's design aligns with international functional safety and cyber-security standards, including ISO 26262 for automotive functional safety and SAE J3061 for cyber-security best practices. Key safety actions are validated through redundant sensors, encrypted CAN bus communication, and the fail-safe fallback to threshold-based BMS logic. The invention's modular, agent-based design enables easy adaptation across platforms, providing a unified safety framework for various lithium-ion energy applications and addressing the issue of poor scalability and adaptability. It is applicable to one or more domains selected from: electric vehicles (EVs), drones and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), stationary grid storage systems, renewable energy battery systems, military or aerospace power systems, smart factories, and industrial battery banks, while reducing the risk of catastrophic failure, downtime, and maintenance costs. [0057] The present invention offers a first-of-its-kind intelligent, autonomous, and cyber-secure safety framework for modern lithium-ion battery systems. It is a modular, AI-adaptive safety platform tested in real conditions that integrates edge-based intelligence, multi-agent collaboration, secure cloud connectivity, and hardware-level actuation into one scalable solution. It represents one of the first known implementations of a real-time multi-agent Edge-AI battery safety system, delivering predictive prevention rather than reactive mitigation. This enables reliable, scalable, and fault-tolerant deployments in safety-critical environments, thereby bridging critical gaps in responsiveness, resolution, autonomy, and cyber-resilience. patents.abstract: This invention reveals a technique for enhancing the driving range of EV (electric vehicles) through the optimisation of lithium-ion battery attributes. The process takes into account things like energy density (Wh/L), specific energy (Wh/kg), and specific power (W/kg). The Taguchi method uses a L9 orthogonal array to design experimental trials, and ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) is used to see how each factor affects the results. Based on these tests, the best combination of parameters is found to get the most range out of each charge cycle. The suggested method gives a structured way to make EV batteries more reliable and functional, which is good for both manufacturers and users who want to promote sustainable mobility solutions.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Field of Invention [0001] The field of electric vehicles is the focus of the current innovation, namely techniques for improving the performance characteristics of lithium-ion batteries utilised in these vehicles. The innovation specifically emphasises on a systematic technique that employs the Taguchi methodology to find and enhance the optimal combination of battery properties in order to increase the efficiency, dependability, and driving range of electric vehicles. 1.1 Description [0002] As greenhouse gas emissions increase, global warming concerns increase, and fossil fuel availability decreases, EVs have become a viable solution to address global environmental challenges and reduce CO2 emissions. Today, electric vehicles are a focal point for research and development since they reduce atmospheric carbon emissions and play an important role in reducing atmospheric carbon emissions. Components of Electric Vehicles are shown in figure 1.1. Figure 1.1 Component of Electric Vehicle A lithium-ion battery pack is the energy source of an electric vehicle, which stores electricity. The electric motor converts electrical energy from the battery into mechanical energy to drive the vehicle. Optimum performance and efficiency are achieved by controlling the flow of electricity between the battery and the motor. To recharge the battery, the charger converts AC 2 power from the grid into DC power. The DC-DC converter adjusts the voltage of the battery to power auxiliary systems. The DC-DC converter adjusts the voltage of the battery to power auxiliary systems. EVs typically have a single-speed transmission, but some use multi-speed transmissions to maximize performance and efficiency. An effective thermal management system ensures that the battery and electric motor are operated at optimal temperatures for maximum efficiency and longevity. The ECU (Electric Vehicle Control Unit) is the component that controls and manages various aspects of the electric vehicle such as the motor power, the battery state, and the charging process. Airbags, collision avoidance systems, stability control, and other safety features are included in the safety systems of the vehicle. With electric power steering, steering assistance is provided without relying on a hydraulic system. This battery pack is protected from environmental factors as well as collisions by the Traction Battery Housing. The wheels and tires of the vehicle are critical to the contact with the road and to the overall performance of the vehicle. A vehicle's body and frame make up its structural framework. The vehicle's body and frame are designed to maximize aerodynamics and safety. Visibility and safety are ensured by exterior lighting, including headlights, taillights, and indicators. An onboard charger manages charging processes and can be connected to a variety of charging stations in the vehicle. Inverter: Converts DC power from the battery into AC power for the electric motor, Regenerative Braking System: When braking, kinetic energy is captured and converted into electrical energy, which is stored in the battery. High-Voltage Wiring: Connects the battery to various components, such as motors and power electronics. HVAC System: Heat, venting, and air conditioning that provides passenger comfort and efficiency while being environmentally friendly, User Interface: The dashboard, touchscreen, or digital display used by the driver to monitor and control the vehicle. This research study focused on the optimization of Electric vehicle battery parameters by using Taguchi Methodology to determine the performance of EVs. However, the performance of EV mainly depends on the selection of input parameters. Some of these parameters are specific energy, specific power, and energy density are input parameters selected for this study. Taguchi methodology has been used for the optimization of input parameters to obtain the optimal combination of input parameters that gives a high range of EV per charge. In the field of experimental design and statistics, particularly in the context of agricultural sciences, Sir Ronald A Fisher, a renowned British statistician and geneticist, made significant contributions. By developing the Design of Experiments (DOE) method, he revolutionized experimentation and laid the foundation for modern experimental design principles. Typically, DOE is a statistical method of investigating a system or process in which input variables are judged by 3 the significance of their influences, the interactions between input variables, or none of the above. The DOE method can be divided into full factorial design and fractional factorial design. While full factorial design is an important and thorough method of experimental design, it may be time-consuming, especially when a significant n umber of variables and levels are involved. Although fractional factorial design is generally recognized, it is too complicated, with no universal rules for its use. Considering this difficulty, In the late 1940s, Dr. Genichi Taguchi created the Taguchi technique, a completely novel experimental approach that makes use of a simplified and standardized version of DOE. Various steps of the Taguchi Methodology are shown in figure 1.2. Figure 1.2 Steps of Taguchi Methodology 2.1 Working Methodology: Optimization Techniques (Taguchi Methodology) 2.1.1 Selection of Input Parameter [0003] The performance of EVs is based on the selection of input parameters. However, the selection of input parameters in this study is done after having proper brainstorming and 4 literature review. Specific energy (Wh/kg), specific power (W/kg), and Energy Density (Wh/L) are three input parameters that were selected based on the literature review as shown in table 2.1. Observations indicate that when the value of the specific energy (Wh/kg) increases, the range of an electric vehicle increases and then decreases as the value of the specific energy (Wh/kg) increases, indicating a high degree of impedance between the rider and the vehicle. An electric vehicle's range is significantly influenced by the specific energy of its battery, which is measured in watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). Batteries are categorized according to their specific energy, which is the amount of energy they can store relative to their weight. Figure 2.2 Main effect plot for S/N ratio & means [0009] A battery with a higher specific energy can travel longer distances on a single charge, which can reduce the reliance on charging infrastructure, especially in areas with few charging stations. As the specific power of the battery in an electric vehicle (EV) plays a significant role in determining the range of the vehicle and its overall performance, battery-specific power is an important aspect to consider. In batteries, specific power refers to how much power they can deliver relative to their weight or volume. The unit of measurement is typically watts per kilogram (W/kg) or watts per liter (W/L). It is possible to accelerate rapidly and improve performance with batteries that have high specific power due to their ability to discharge energy quickly. For electric vehicles, instant torque is one of their key advantages. With higher specific power batteries, EVs can accelerate faster, making them more appealing to consumers. An electric vehicle's driving range is directly affected by its power. Higher specific power batteries can deliver more power per unit of weight or volume, meaning they provide the energy necessary to propel the vehicle farther. With higher specific power batteries, EVs can travel longer distances on a single charge. The performance, range, and overall usability of an electric vehicle depend on the specific power of its battery. Figure 2.2 indicate that the range of electric vehicle increases with the increase in energy density (W/kg). When it comes to the significance of battery performance in electric vehicles (EVs), energy density, measured in watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg), is an important parameter. A battery's energy density is a measure of how much energy it can store to its weight. A higher energy density battery can reduce EVs' environmental impact over their lifetime. Potential EV buyers benefit from a longer range due to high energy density batteries. Consumer confidence in EVs increases when they know they can cover substantial distances without recharging. Batteries with a high energy density can store more energy than batteries with a low energy density. With high energy density batteries, EVs can travel further on a single charge. They may choose to skip charging if the SOC is relatively high, saving time and energy. Drivers can estimate how far they can travel before they need to recharge by checking their SOC. For battery packs to last longer, it is also crucial to manage the SOC. A battery can degrade faster if it is operated continuously at extremely high or low SOC levels. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a method (100) for sequential recycling of lithium-ion battery waste and synthesis of nano-LiCoO₂ catalysts for biodiesel production. The method (100) involves dismantling spent lithium-ion batteries to separate graphite anodes and LiCoO₂ cathodes, followed by heating, crushing, and treatment of the cathodic material with weak sulphuric acid at 100 °C to obtain purified LiCoO₂ powder. The powder is subjected to thermal stabilization at 800 °C and nanosizing through sequential grinding. An eco-friendly leaching process using citric acid and hydrogen peroxide, followed by nano-filtration and drying, yields high-purity nano-LiCoO₂. The catalyst is then functionalized by mixing with potassium hydroxide, sonication, and drying to produce a reusable basic nano-catalyst. The functionalized catalyst is employed for transesterification of algal oil to produce fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) and glycerol, and subsequently recovered for reuse. < >

patents.abstract: The invention relates to an inverter system (100) integrated with a lithium battery (110) and housed within a slim, vertically oriented enclosure configured for stable installation at a lower-wall height of 1–2 feet or on a ground based on requirement. The disclosed system reorganizes internal components, including the inverter motherboard (106), transformer (108), main socket (102), MCB (104), cooling fan (112), and the lithium battery (110), to achieve balanced weight distribution within a compact enclosure supporting a total mass of 40–48 kilograms. A reinforced mounting hook (114) provides structural stability for long-term wall installation, while the slim profile enables aesthetic integration in residential and commercial environments. The invention offers an improved mounting architecture, enhanced usability, and a space-efficient alternative to traditional bulky inverter systems.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [001] The present invention relates to energy-storage and power-backup systems, and more particularly to an inverter integrated with a lithium battery that is structurally configured for safe, stable, and ergonomic lower-wall-mount installation. BACKGROUND [002] Integrated inverter–battery systems in the 2–3 kVA category are characteristically heavy, with typical operating weights ranging from 40–48 kilograms, and are generally constructed with wide and bulky enclosures. Due to these physical and structural limitations, conventional systems are predominantly designed for either floor placement or high wall-mount installation at 5–8 feet above ground level. However, high-height mounting requires lifting a heavy, bulky enclosure overhead, which introduces significant installation risk, wall-loading challenges, and accessibility issues. User interfaces and protection components positioned at this height become difficult to reach and monitor, reducing overall usability and safety in residential and commercial environments. [003] Floor-placed inverter units similarly present critical constraints. Installing a large integrated inverter–battery unit directly on the floor leads to obstruction of usable living space, reduced airflow and inefficient thermal dissipation, frequent dust accumulation, and cumbersome access for maintenance or operation. As modern architectural layouts trend toward space-efficient and wall-integrated appliances, ground-level placement is increasingly incompatible with user expectations and interior design requirements. [004] Despite the need for placing such systems at an ergonomic lower-wall position of 1–2 feet, conventional inverter architectures cannot be mounted safely at this zone due to factors such as unbalanced weight distribution, top-heavy transformer placement, excessive enclosure thickness, and insufficient structural reinforcement for sustained load support. These configurations lead to front-tilt instability, compromised heat-flow patterns, and mounting risks when positioned close to the floor. Accordingly, there exists a distinct unmet requirement for a slim, structurally optimized, vertically oriented inverter system engineered specifically for safe, stable, and aesthetically aligned lower-wall-mount installation in the 2–3 kVA category. SUMMARY [005] The invention introduces a structurally optimized inverter system engineered specifically for the 2–3 kVA category, integrating a high-capacity lithium battery within a slim, vertically oriented enclosure designed to enable safe and stable lower-wall-mount installation at 1–2 feet above the floor. Conventional inverter–battery systems in this capacity class typically exceed 40 kilograms and rely on wide, bulky enclosures that are unsuitable for ergonomic low-height mounting and impractical for high-level wall installation. The disclosed architecture resolves these constraints through a re-engineered internal component arrangement that balances mass, improves thermal behaviour, and supports long-term structural stability. [006] The inverter system employs a bottom-mounted lithium battery to function as a gravitational anchor, a centrally positioned transformer to stabilize mid-zone mass distribution, and an upper-region inverter motherboard configured for efficient heat dissipation within the enclosure depth of approximately 150–170 millimetres. A dual-fan thermal management assembly, comprising an intake and exhaust fan, is incorporated to establish a consistent airflow path across the transformer and control electronics. This integrated arrangement enables controlled thermal performance while preserving the slim form factor required for close-proximity lower-wall installation. [007] The enclosure is supported by a reinforced mounting hook or multi-point bracket assembly engineered to bear the 40–48 kg system load under long-term operating conditions. A top-inclined front interface enhances visibility and accessibility when the inverter is positioned near floor level, while inclined front-mounted user-interface elements such as the display screen and operation buttons are aligned for convenient interaction By combining structural refinement, ergonomic placement, and efficient spatial organization, the invention creates a new class of compact, aesthetically integrated inverter systems capable of delivering high-capacity performance without the mounting and usability limitations associated with traditional designs. In the drawing, [009] FIG. 1 illustrates the internal structural arrangement of the inverter, showing the overall positioning of the battery section, power-conversion electronics, transformer assembly, airflow components, and the internal layout configured within the vertically oriented slim enclosure; [010] FIG. 2 illustrates the front interface layout of the inverter, depicting the user-facing elements, operational indicators, controls, and external access points presented on the front surface of the enclosure in a clean and compact arrangement suitable for visible installation in residential and commercial environments; [011] FIG. 3 illustrates a side view of the inverter, highlighting the slim enclosure profile and the integrated mounting hook designed to support safe and stable lower-wall installation at a height of 1–2 feet above the floor, while maintaining a modern aesthetic and ergonomic footprint; and, [012] FIG. 4 illustrates the inverter system (100) mounted on a wall, showing the installation distance ‘d’ representing the lower-wall-mount operational zone of 1–2 feet above the ground level, demonstrating the ergonomic viewing and access configuration achieved by the top-inclined front section. [018] The following detailed description sets forth the structural, functional, and ergonomic configuration of the inverter system (100) engineered for the 2–3 kVA category. The system integrates a lithium battery (110), transformer (108), inverter motherboard (106), and a dual-fan thermal-management assembly (112a, 112b) within a vertically oriented slim enclosure designed for stable installation at a lower-wall height of 1–2 feet above the floor. The description is illustrative and should not be construed as limiting, as variations in component geometry, materials, or layout may be implemented without departing from the core principles of the disclosure. [019] The inverter system (100) is housed in a compact enclosure having a depth in the range of 150–170 millimetres, enabling close-proximity wall placement without projecting significantly into the interior space. The total mass of the integrated assembly falls within 40–48 kilograms, consistent with the 2–3 kVA class of inverter-battery systems. To accommodate this load during lower-wall installation, the enclosure incorporates a reinforced mounting hook or multi-point bracket assembly (114) on the rear surface. This mounting structure is fabricated to distribute static and dynamic loads across multiple anchoring points, mitigating torque effects and ensuring long-term structural stability. [020] The internal layout is engineered to deliver optimal weight distribution and thermal behaviour when mounted at 1–2 feet above the floor. The lithium battery (110), being the heaviest component, is positioned in the lower region of the enclosure. This placement establishes a low center of gravity, preventing forward tilt and reducing the moment force acting on the wall-mounted structure. Immediately above the battery (110) is the transformer (108), positioned within a mid-zone that balances mass across the enclosure height while maintaining appropriate separation between high-heat and high-mass components. [021] The inverter motherboard (106) is located in the upper region of the enclosure. This placement supports streamlined cable routing, efficient convection-assisted heat dissipation, and improved accessibility for servicing or diagnostics. The upper zone also accommodates the dual-fan thermal-management assembly (112a, 112b). Both exhaust fans (112a, 112b) are positioned at sides of the motherboard and transformer. Together, these fans establish a controlled airflow path across the motherboard (106) and transformer (108), enabling consistent thermal regulation despite the reduced enclosure depth. [022] The left hand side of the enclosure integrates operational components including the main socket (102) and an MCB (104). These elements are positioned to facilitate comfortable access when the system is installed at lower-wall height. The upper portion of the front face incorporates a top-inclined viewing and interaction surface designed to enhance readability and usability of indicators, displays, and control elements when viewed from a standing position in front of a device mounted 1–2 feet above the floor. [023] The enclosure geometry is designed with vertical orientation to reduce horizontal footprint and improve distribution of mass along the mounting axis. Cable-routing channels are incorporated internally to allow concealed wiring during installation, thereby improving aesthetic integration within residential or commercial interiors. The geometry and internal spacing also allow for controlled airflow channels that maintain separation between high-power components and ventilation paths, ensuring safe thermal operation. [024] The inverter system (100) is architected with a dual-mount deployment framework that enables seamless installation either as a lower-wall-mounted unit positioned at 1–2 feet above the floor or as a ground-placed unit resting on integrated base supports, without requiring any modification to the enclosure geometry or internal component arrangement. The lower-wall configuration leverages the reinforced mounting hook or multi-point bracket assembly (114) to deliver stable load distribution, improved accessibility through the top-inclined interface, and efficient thermal performance via elevated airflow channels. In parallel, the ground-mount option provides a structurally compliant alternative for environments where wall anchoring may be constrained, while retaining full operational integrity, balanced internal mass alignment, and consistent thermal-management behavior. This dual-mount versatility ensures that the inverter system (100) adapts effectively to diverse installation conditions, user preferences, and infrastructural limitations across residential and commercial settings. [025] Through this coordinated arrangement of components, reinforced structural support, dual-fan thermal management, and ergonomic layout, the inverter system (100) delivers a compact, stable, and aesthetically integrated solution for high-capacity power-backup applications. The configuration addresses long-standing limitations associated with floor-placed and high-wall-mounted inverter systems, enabling a new category of slim, safe, and user-centric inverter-battery installations suitable for modern built environments. patents.abstract: The invention discloses a hybrid severe plastic deformation (SPD) processing route for AA2099 aluminium–copper–lithium alloy that integrates multi axial forging, cryorolling, and controlled post annealing. Conventional methods fail to simultaneously achieve refined grain structures, uniform precipitation, and isotropic mechanical properties. The proposed process begins with multi axial forging to impart uniform strain and reduce anisotropy, followed by cryorolling at cryogenic temperatures to suppress recovery and fragment grains, and concludes with post annealing to stabilize microstructure and promote precipitation of strengthening phases. The resulting alloy exhibits ultrafine grains below 1–3 µm, high dislocation density, and dense nanoscale precipitates. Mechanical testing demonstrates yield strength above 470 MPa, tensile strength above 540 MPa, elongation of 8–12%, hardness up to 184 HV, and high cycle fatigue strength of 167 MPa. The process is scalable, cost effective, and industrially feasible, producing AA2099 alloy with superior isotropy, strength, ductility, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability for aerospace and defense applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to metallurgical processing of aluminium–copper–lithium alloys, specifically AA2099. More particularly, it concerns a hybrid severe plastic deformation (SPD) route that integrates multi axial forging, cryorolling, and controlled post annealing to produce ultrafine grained microstructures with enhanced mechanical properties, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability suitable for aerospace and defense applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Among Aluminium–Copper–Lithium (Al–Cu–Li) alloys AA2099 is the main candidate for the advanced structures of the aerospace due to their exceptional specific strength, fatigue resistance and low density. However, with AA2099 there remains a materials engineering challenge for achieving refined grain structure, enhanced damage tolerance and high strength altogether. The old traditional methods such as forging and rolling often produces uneven structures of the grains due to which the material do work differently in different directions and doesn’t form the strengthening phases properly like as θ′ (Al₂Cu) and T1 (Al₂CuLi). The fine grain structures can be created using the Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD) like multi-axial forging ang cyorolling. However, if these methods are used individually and the material is then exposed to heat then each of them have their drawbacks such as lowering process efficiency, lowering microstructural stability and limited strain buildup. The Al-Cu-Li alloys such as AA2099 due to their fatigue resistance and high strength-to-weight ratio are ideal for defense, aerospace and automotive applications. There is requirement of controlled precipitation, refined microstructures and enhanced dislocation structures by the means of advanced thermomechanical processing for achieving their full capability. The SPD methods like HPT, ECAP, cryorolling and multi-axial forging have been studied in Al alloys but their integrated use for AA2099 is highly unexplored. Most of the research emphasizes upon the single routes of SPD, while there remain limitations in using hybrid approaches for manufacturing thermally stable and ultrafine grained (UFG) structures. Multi-axial forging can improve homogeneity and apply large plastic strains provides grain refinement in limited way due to dynamic recovery. Cryorolling supports ultrafine grains and controls recovery, however the amount of the strain per pass in limited and structural stability is challenging during the heat treatment. There is limitation in understanding how together using these techniques makes affect on T1 and θ′ phase precipitation and the mechanical properties of AA2099. Also, there is lack of standard method for boosting parameters of processing like reduction ratio, strain rate, forging sequence, post-annealing and cryogenic temperature due to which the results become unpredictable and also limits the industrial uses. There is strong need of an integrated hybrid SPD strategy which combines cryorolling, multi-axial forging and post annealing is essential for achieving stable ultrafine grains with balanced ductility and strength by enabling AA2099 to meet next-generation defense and aerospace demands. AA2099 aluminium–copper–lithium alloy is widely recognized as a third generation aerospace material due to its high specific strength, fatigue resistance, and low density. However, conventional processing routes such as forging, rolling, and artificial aging often fail to simultaneously achieve refined grain structures, uniform precipitation of strengthening phases, and isotropic mechanical properties. Traditional SPD methods like equal channel angular pressing (ECAP), high pressure torsion (HPT), cryorolling, or multi axial forging, when applied individually, suffer from drawbacks including dynamic recovery, limited strain accumulation, and microstructural instability during subsequent heat treatment. Cryorolling alone can generate ultrafine grains but struggles with structural stability during annealing. Multi axial forging improves homogeneity but is limited by recovery effects. Post annealing stabilizes precipitates but may cause grain coarsening if not carefully controlled. Thus, there exists a gap in integrating these processes into a hybrid SPD route that balances strain accumulation, grain refinement, precipitation strengthening, and isotropy. The proposed invention addresses this gap by combining multi axial forging, cryorolling, and post annealing in a controlled sequence to produce AA2099 alloy with superior strength, ductility, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts, in a simplified format, that are further described in the detailed description of the invention. This summary is neither intended to identify key or essential inventive concepts of the invention and nor is it intended for determining the scope of the invention. The invention provides a hybrid SPD route for AA2099 alloy that integrates multi axial forging, cryorolling, and controlled post annealing. This sequence produces ultrafine grains, suppresses dynamic recovery, and promotes uniform precipitation of strengthening phases such as T1 (Al₂CuLi) and θ′ (Al₂Cu). In the first stage, multi axial forging is applied along perpendicular axes to impart large cumulative strain and reduce anisotropy. This generates shear bands, dislocation cells, and refined grains. In the second stage, cryorolling is performed at cryogenic temperatures using liquid nitrogen cooling, which suppresses recovery, increases dislocation density, and fragments grains into ultrafine structures. In the third stage, controlled post annealing at 150–350°C stabilizes the microstructure, enables precipitation strengthening, and prevents grain coarsening. The hybrid route results in AA2099 alloy with grain sizes below 1–3 µm, high dislocation density, and dense nanoscale precipitates. Mechanical testing demonstrates improved yield strength, tensile strength, ductility, hardness, and fatigue life compared to conventional processing. The process is industrially scalable, cost effective, and suitable for aerospace components requiring isotropic performance. The proposed invention describes a process of advanced hybrid Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD) which is developed specifically for the AA2099 Al-Cu-Li alloy. The goal of this innovation is to made a highly refined UFG microstructure with great thermal and mechanical stability. AA2099 is a 3rd generation alloy of Al-Cu-Li which is known for its high elastic modulus, high strength-to-weight ratio and great corrosion and fatigue resistance. All these properties are made from the combination of precipitation-hardening phases like θ′ (Al₂Cu), T1 (Al₂CuLi) and δ′ (Al₃Li), along with changes in structure made through the thermomechanical processes. The old conventional methods such as ageing, solutionizing and hot rolling do not deal with enough control over uniformity of grain, precipitation distribution and microstructure refinement. As a result, there remains challenge in achieving simultaneous grain refinement, uniform mechanical properties and structural stability. The proposed innovation provides a hybrid SPD process which is a combination of three main steps which are cryorolling, post annealing and multi-axial forging. This provides large cumulative strain, activates cryogenic deformation mechanisms, promotes controlled precipitation and suppresses dynamic recovery which provides improved performance of material. By this combination of these steps makes this process different from single-route SPD methods. The process starts with multi-axial forging of uniform AA2099 billets along with perpendicular axes-X, Y, and Z for providing an overall distortion of 0.9 to 1.8. Supervised distortion rates provide uniform strain and prevent localization of distortion. This provides a compact substructure of shear bands, slender grains and dislocation cells. The crystallographic texture and anisotropy reduce the 3D strain distribution by developing a structurally balanced material for the next SPD step. At next step the billets go with cryorolling at a temperature of 120°C to 196°C using liquid nitrogen spraying. The atomic mobility is reduced by the cold environment which also supress the dynamic recovery with increasing dislocation density. The alloy is rolled to 50 to 80% reduction in thickness which accumulates high strain and fragments grains. Cryrolling increases geometrically necessary boundaries and also forms stable ultrafine grains, which later converts into stable grains during post-annealing. Afte this the alloy is exposed to controlled post heat treatment at 150–350°C for 30 minutes to 240 minutes. This step fixes the microstructure while enabling controlled precipitation of T1 and θ′ phases. The thermal treatment conditions are boosted to prevent excessive grain overaging or growth. When the material is correctly thermal treated it keeps a high number of crystal defect and very fine grains, while there will be even formation of the tiny participates which strengthens the alloy. This process results in AA2099 with grain sizes below 1–3 µm, a high fraction of low and medium-angle boundaries, and dense fine T1 and θ′ precipitates. A remarkable improvement is shown in mechanical testing in tensile strength, ductility, yield strength and fatigue life. These benefits come from the integrated effects of high dislocation density, ultrafine grains and well-distributed precipitates. The thermal stability is also boosted by the process. Coherent nanoscale precipitates and stabilized grain boundaries prevents the growth of grain at high temperatures, making AA2099 suitable for defense and aerospace applications. Multi-axial forging lowers the intensity of the texture while cryorolling evenly distributes the features of deformation. Post-thermal treatment further do the structure stabilization which provides the isotropic mechanical properties essential for aircraft load-bearing components, fuselage skin and wing panels. This method is easy to be implemented in industries as it only requires minor modifications in the rolling and forging equipments. The cryogenic process uses the normal liquid nitrogen systems, hence ensure keeping the results repeatable and quality of the material also remains consistent. While looking overall, this hybrid SPD process combines cryorolling, multi-axial forging and controlled post-thermal treatment produce a strong ultrafine-grained AA2099 alloy with superior isotropy, strength, thermal stability and strength which makes it ideal for next-generation defense and aerospace applications. The goal of this innovation is to made a highly refined UFG microstructure with great thermal and mechanical stability.
