The following specification particularly describes the nature of invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. EXTRACTION OF LITHIUM FROM GEOTHERMAL SOURCE USING A CHEMICALLY MODIFIED LOW COST BIOSORBENT FIELD OF INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of Extractive metallurgy and Material chemistry/Geothermal energy DESCRIPTION OF THE RELATED ART Geothermal Brines are recognized as sustainable and renewable resource enriched with rare earth elements, heavy metals and high salt content. Among these, lithium signifies due to its significant applications such as lithium ion batteries, aluminum and rubber synthesis, glass and ceramics industries etc. Traditionally lithium can be extracted from various resources like salar brines, ores, oil field brines and clays using energy intensive and environmentally harmful processes. Conventional extraction techniques are often costly, involve complex steps, consume high energy and generates hazardous by products. To address these challenges, researchers have focused on developing alternative, green technologies for lithium recovery, especially from geothermal brine, due to its low carbon footprint and eco-friendly potential. A wide range of materials, both natural and synthetic have been developed from lithium recovery which showcasing varying lithium uptake capacities depending on their composition and modification. Among biomass-based materials, phosphorylated hazelnut shells (6.03 mg/g), chemically modified olive branches (6.7 mg/g) and cyanobacterial biomass (1.35 mg/g) demonstrated mechanisms but generally have lower performance compared to synthetic alternative. Synthetic and chemically modified adsorbents showed superior lithium uptake. Crown ether containing polymeric adsorbent reached 2.31 mg/g. Metal-doped LDH (layered double hydroxide) material displayed the highest performance such as Zn+2 doped Li/AI-LDH (13.4 mg/g), cobalt salt doped LDH (10.74 mg/g), and high charge Li/AI-LDH (9.72 mg/g). While PAA/LDH functionalised zeolite composite exhibited lowest capacity at 0.5 mg/g and PAA/LDH composite demonstrated 5.2 mg/g. To enhance the low lithium extraction capacity, a novel methodology should be developed that is cost-effective, easy to process, and more environmentally sustainable. This approach should focus on efficiently extracting lithium from geothermal brine, in the presence of other competing metal ions. The new method must ensure high selectivity for lithium while maintaining eco-friendly practices and economic viability for large-scale applications. To enhance the lower lithium extraction uptake capacity, a novel methodology should be developed that is cost effective, easy to process and more environmentally sustainable. This approach focuses on efficiently extract lithium from geothermal brine in presence of other competing ions. The new process must be ensure high selectivity for lithium while maintaining eco-friendly practices and economic viability for large scale applications. BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION This invention indicates a low cost, biodegradable and scalable method for extraction of lithium from geothermal brine using chemically modified cactus family fruit peel waste. The process includes sorption of Lithium Metal ions followed by extraction of lithium from sorbent surface and its recovery by Crystallization. This invention presents a breakthrough, eco-friendly method for lithium extraction using chemically modified fruit peel waste from cactus family. Designed as a low cost, biodegradable and highly selective adsorbent, this biomass based solution overcomes the limitations of traditional energy intensive techniques. The process follows three three pathways_ adsorption, desorption and crystallization-optimized through batch scale studies to validated via advanced characterization (FTIR, XRD, SEM, BET and XPS) and kinetics study, isotherm study, thermodynamics study, DFT (Density Functional Theory) Study and interference study. Key parameters such as pH, Contact time, Adsorbent dose, Initial lithium concentration, Temperature are turned to maximise lithium uptake from both synthetic and real geothermal water. This method not only ensures high recovery efficiency but also supports scalability via fixed bed column studies and techno-economic analysis. Its versatility extends to lithium recovery from battery waste water and mining effluent, with the added advantages of reinjecting treated water into the environment, fostering a circular and sustainable extraction cycle. Current Challenges: • Poor selectivity in presence of competing ions Geothermal brine contains high concentration of ions such as Na+, Ca+2, Mg+2, K+, Al+3 and Fe+3, making it difficult to selectively extract lithium ions without significant contamination. • High energy and operational cost Conventional methods such as solvent extraction, ion exchange, chemical precipitation techniques requires multiple steps, longer procedure time and significant energy requirements, high operational cost and larger carbon footprints. • Less efficient existing techniques Many of sorbent materials and methods used for lithium extraction offers low sorption capacity, difficult to regenerate and are not sustainable for continuous and scalable operations. • Lack of Environmentally benign methodology Current technologies often rely on non-biodegradable, chemically hazardous material which cannot be economic viable for large scale or remote geothermal applications, posing challenges for suitable lithium recovery. Proposed Solution: • Green synthetic route for biosorbent preparation The process begins with the selection of fruit peel waste from the cactus family, chosen for its inherent biodegradability, porous structure, and natural abundance. The raw biomass undergoes targeted chemical modifications, such as functionalization or surface activation, to optimize its physicochemical properties. These treatments enhance the material's surface area, functional group density, and metal ion-binding affinity, resulting in a novel adsorbent tailored for lithium extraction. • Utilization of chemically modified fruit peel waste for lithium biosorption The chemically modified sorbent derived from fruit peel of cactus family-an abundant, biodegradable and sustainable material for lithium metal extraction. It enhances its selectivity towards lithium ions, allowing it to effectively adsorb lithium even in the presence of high concentrations of competing ions such as Na+, Ca+2, Mg+2, K+, Al+3 and Fe+3'which typically abundant in geothermal brines. • High selectivity and Process efficiency under real world implementation The adsorbent shows high lithium selectivity due to its surface functionalization and optimized interaction mechanism, enabling efficient recovery in brines with complex resources. This system operates under ambient thermal conditions, making it feasible for remote geothermal sites with limited energy resources. • Scientific and technical validification: • The effectiveness of the process is validated through detailed studies including: > Adsorption isotherm, kinetics, thermodynamics study. > Interference study to evaluate performance in multi-ion environment. > Mathematical modeling study to simulate process behavior. > Techno-economic study assess scalability and cost effectiveness. > Density functional theory simulation to understand lithium binding mechanism at the molecular level BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWING Figure 1 shows the drawing for Schematic diagram of Lithium extraction from geothermal brine Figure 1 illustrate a stepwise approach for biosorption based extraction of from geothermal source using a sustainable, low cost and eco-friendly method derived from fruit peel waste of cactus family. Detailed Description of the Invention with Reference to drawing 1. Raw Material Selection and Chemical Modification: The process begins with the selection of fruit peel waste from the cactus family, chosen for its inherent biodegradability, porous structure, and natural abundance. The raw biomass undergoes targeted chemical modifications, such as functionalization or surface activation, to optimize its physicochemical properties. These treatments enhance the material's surface area, functional group density, and metal ion-binding affinity, resulting in a novel adsorbent tailored for lithium extraction. 2. Characterization Studies: The chemically modified biomass is comprehensively characterized using the following analytical techniques to evaluate its surface, chemical, and structural properties: a. FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy): Identifies functional groups responsible for lithium ion binding. b. SEM (Scanning Electron Microscopy): Examines surface morphology and porosity to assess structural modifications. c. EDX (Energy Dispersive X-ray Analysis): Confirms elemental composition and verifies the absence of contaminants. d. XRD (X-ray Diffraction): Analyzes crystallinity and detects structural changes induced by chemical modification. e. TGA (Thermogravimetric Analysis): Evaluates thermal stability and decomposition behavior of the material. f. BET (Brunauer-Emmett-Teller): Quantifies specific surface area and pore size distribution to determine adsorption capacity. 3. Preliminary Adsorption Study Using Synthetic Lithium-Containing Water: The performance of the modified material is first tested on synthetic lithium-containing water, examining the effect of various operational parameters: ♦ pH ♦ Contact time ♦ Adsorbent dose ♦ Initial lithium concentration ♦ Temperature These studies help identify optimum conditions for maximum lithium uptake. 4. Application to Geothermal Water: Under optimised conditions derived from synthetic water tests, the material is further evaluated using geothermal water sample, ensuring real world applicability and selectively towards lithium in presence of competing ions. 5. Experimental studies: ♦> Kinetics study-To understand the rate of the reaction ♦ Isotherm study-To understand adsorption equilibrium and capacity ♦ Thermodynamics study-To determine spontaneity, enthalpy and entropy changes study ♦ DFT (Density Functional Theory) Study: To evaluate the interaction of lithium ions with functional groups at molecular level. 6. Interference study: A detailed examination of co-existing ions (Na+, Ca+2, Mg+2, K+, Al+3 and Fe+3) on lithium sorption ensures selectivity and reliability of the material in complex aqueous matrices. 7. Sorption-desorption-crystallization pathways: After sorption of lithium, the material undergoes for desorption study using a various aqueous medias to recover lithium ions. The eluted lithium is then subjected to crystallization, yielding high purity lithium salts suitable for industrial use. 8. Scale-up and implementation: All the experiment trails conducted at batch scale. For large scale application. A fixed bed column setup is proposed to validate continuous operations and column regeneration. 9. Techno-economic feasibility: A comprehensive techno-economic analysis is performed to evaluate the cost effectiveness, scalability and sustainability and environment impact of the developed lithium extraction process. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention discloses a method for extracting lithium from geothermal water using chemically modified fruit peel waste from the cactus family as an adsorbent. The process begins with the selection of biodegradable and naturally porous cactus fruit peels, which undergo targeted chemical modifications—such as functionalization or surface activation—to enhance their physicochemical properties, including surface area, functional group density, and metal-binding affinity. The modified biomass is then rigorously characterized using advanced analytical techniques such as FTIR (to identify lithium-binding functional groups), SEM (to examine surface morphology), EDX (to confirm elemental composition), XRD (to analyze crystallinity), TGA (to assess thermal stability), and BET (to quantify surface area and pore distribution). Preliminary adsorption studies are conducted using synthetic lithium-containing water to optimize key operational parameters, including pH, contact time, adsorbent dose, initial lithium concentration, and temperature. Once optimal conditions are established, the material is tested on real geothermal water to evaluate its selectivity and efficiency in the presence of competing ions like Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Al3+, and Fe3+. Further experimental studies—kinetic, isotherm, and thermodynamic analyses— are performed to understand adsorption rates, equilibrium capacity, and the spontaneity of the process, supplemented by Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to model lithium-ion interactions at the molecular level. After lithium adsorption, the material undergoes desorption using various aqueous media to recover lithium ions, which are then crystallized into high-purity lithium salts for industrial applications. The process is designed for scalability, with proposed fixed-bed column setups for continuous operation and regeneration. Finally, a comprehensive techno-economic analysis evaluates the cost-effectiveness, environmental sustainability, and feasibility of large-scale implementation, ensuring that the method is both economically viable and environmentally friendly. This innovation offers a green and efficient alternative to conventional lithium extraction methods, leveraging waste biomass to address the growing demand for lithium in renewable energy technologies. ADVANTAGES • Conversion of fruit peel waste to value added material Utilised chemically modified fruit peel from cactus family-an abundant, biodegradable, agricultural by products-as a green and low cost adsorbent for lithium recovery. • High Selectivity Towards Lithium Ions The modified biomass is impregnated with a novel binding agent that ensures superior selectivity for lithium even in the presence of competing metal ions like Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Al+3 and Fe+3. • Eco friendly and green synthetic Process Operates in moderate conditions, without the use of harmful chemicals or high-energy inputs, in accordance with sustainable and environmentally friendly extraction principles. • Applicable for extraction from various lithium sources The technology is widely applicable as it is efficient not only for geothermal brine but also for lithium extraction from mining effluent and battery waste water. • Easy and safe Post disposal with water reusability After lithium removal, the treated water may be safely reinjected into earth, contributing to geothermal reservoirs balance and meeting environment discharge criteria. • Scalable and techno-economically viable Validated at lab size, with possibilities for scaling up utilizing fixed bed column systems and supported by techno-economic analysis and scientific modelling to ensure real world industry applicability. Claim(s) We Claim 1. A method for extraction of lithium from geothermal brine, comprising the steps of: i. preparing a biosorbent from fruit peel waste of cactus family; ii. subjecting the biosorbent to chemical modification with a diketonic compound to enhance lithium ion affinity; iii. contacting the chemically modified biosorbent with geothermal brine under controlled pH, temperature, and contact time to enable lithium adsorption onto the biosorbent surface; iv. performing desorption of lithium ions from the loaded biosorbent using an acidic aqueous medium; and v. recovering lithium in crystalline form through controlled crystallization of the desorbed solution, wherein the process operates under ambient thermal conditions, ensures selective uptake of lithium in the presence of competing ions, and enables regeneration of the biosorbent for multiple adsorption cycles. 2. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the fruit peel waste is obtained from dragon fruit belonging to the cactus family, providing high porosity and surface area suitable for lithium ion adsorption. 3. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the chemical modification of the pretreated fruit peel waste is carried out using an organic diketonic compound that forms active functional sites responsible for lithium ion binding. 4. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the pH at the point of zero charge (pHZPC) of the biosorbent is 6.7, enabling enhanced adsorption of positively charged lithium ions on the negatively charged surface. 5. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the adsorption energy exhibits a negative value, confirming that the interaction between lithium ions and the biosorbent surface is energetically favorable. 6. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area analysis indicates saturation of up to 92% of the active sites by lithium ions during adsorption. 7. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein desorption of lithium ions is achieved effectively in acidic medium with recovery efficiency maintained for up to three adsorption-desorption cycles. 8. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the biosorption process exhibits column adsorption efficiency of 84% under optimized flow rate and residence time in a fixed-bed column configuration. 9. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein the adsorption process parameters such as pH, contact time, adsorbent dose, initial lithium concentration, and temperature are optimized based on kinetic, isotherm, and thermodynamic studies to maximize lithium uptake. 10. The method as claimed in claim 1, wherein treated geothermal water after lithium removal meets environmental discharge standards and is suitable for reinjection into geothermal reservoirs.

patents.abstract: The present invention provides a cobalt-free O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal (TM) oxide cathode material, having a composition of Li₀.₇₄Ni₀.₂₂Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂, which is synthesized via spontaneous chemical ion-exchange. In this process, Na⁺ ions from a high Na-containing P2-structured Na-TM-oxide (Na₀.₈₄Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂) are replaced by Li⁺ ions, as supplied by a Li-containing electrolyte, resulting in the formation of the desired O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material. This composition is achieved without any externally applied potential, and bestows high structural stability, excellent electrochemical reversibility, and enhanced capacity retention upon being subjected to multiple charge/discharge cycles, while eliminating the reliance on cobalt and mitigating issues associated with transition metal migration to the Li-layer (i.e., ‘cation mixing’).
patents.complete_specification: Description: FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to development of a cobalt-free O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal (TM) oxide cathode material for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). The present invention specifically relates to development of a cobalt-free O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal (TM) oxide cathode material via spontaneous chemical ion-exchange process. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION ‘Layered’ Li-transition metal (TM) oxides are among the most studied and commercially viable cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to their high specific capacity, energy density, and design flexibility through compositional tuning. These materials have ‘layered’ or cation-ordered structure, where lithium ions reside between slabs of edge-sharing TMO₆ octahedra (TM = transition metal). Depending on the oxygen stacking sequence and alkali metal ion coordination, these layered oxides can crystallize into various polymorphs such as O3-, O2-, and P2-type structures, as denoted by Delmas’ notation. The O3-structured Li-TM-oxide (space group R3̅m), where Li⁺ ions occupy octahedral sites between ABC-stacked oxygen layers, forms one of the usual class of cathode materials in commercial LIBs. However, cobalt-free Ni/Mn-rich O3-structured cathode materials suffer from structural instability during synthesis as well as delithiation, such as ‘cation mixing’, layer gliding, voltage hysteresis, and irreversible phase transitions to spinel-like phases. These issues result in poor capacity retention, kinetic limitations, and significant impedance growth during electrochemical cycling. Alternatively, O2--structured ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxides, featuring AB CB oxygen stacking, where LiO6 octahedra share faces with TMO6 octahedra in the O2-structure, are not likely to suffer from structural instability due to ‘cation mixing’ and concomitantly exhibit superior structural stability at high states of charge and reduced voltage hysteresis/fading. However, direct synthesis of phase-pure O2-structured Li-TM-oxides is synthetically challenging due to their thermodynamic instability under high temperature annealing conditions, which often lead to undesired phase mixtures or oxygen vacancies. CN117996066A discloses preparation method and application of titanium or zirconium doped cobalt-free nickel-free O2-type lithium-rich oxide positive electrode material. Incorporation of titanium dopants improves the voltage and capacity stability during cycling, while zirconium doping enhances the structural robustness of the electrode, effectively suppressing the formation of cracks and particle fracture during repeated electrochemical cycling. The material was synthesized via conventional solid-state or sol-gel route followed by controlled lithiation. Doping with titanium or zirconium was employed to enhance voltage and capacity stability or mitigating structural degradation. However, such conventional method often involved high-temperature processing, controlled doping strategies, and extended annealing steps. CN119481030A provides secondary spherical lithium-rich manganese-based positive electrode material prepared by an ion exchange method. The material consists of thick, plate-like primary particles aggregated into secondary spherical structures, designed to enhance structural integrity and electrochemical performance. The approach combines particle morphology engineering focusing on macro/microstructural optimization during particle synthesis, along with lattice-level optimization, aiming to mitigate the structural degradation and performance fading commonly observed in lithium-rich manganese-based cathode materials. Experimental results demonstrate that the reduced specific surface area of the thick primary particles contributes to higher mechanical stability, which in turn enhances the energy density, cycling performance, and reduces voltage fade over prolonged cycling. CN118954627A provides O3, O2 and T2-type lithium battery positive electrode material as well as ultrasonic-assisted liquid-phase ion exchange preparation method and application thereof. This approach enables precise control of reaction parameters such as temperature, ion concentration, and duration, facilitating a uniform and efficient Li⁺/Na⁺ exchange. The use of ultrasonic waves introduces mechanical vibrations that enhance ion transport kinetics and improve the homogeneity of the exchange process. By adjusting ultrasonic frequency and treatment time, the method allows for controlled formation of distinct layered structures, including the thermodynamically stable O3 phase, the metastable O2 phase, and the lithium deficient T2 phase. The resulting materials consist of micron-sized oxide particles with good particle size control, structural consistency, and cycling performance. The invention highlights the utility of ultrasonic energy in promoting effective liquid-phase ion exchange and structural tuning in layered lithium transition metal oxides. However, the material compositions remain general, with no specific stoichiometry or doping strategy outlined for optimizing electrochemical or structural performance. The invention emphasizes the ability to access multiple phase types (O3, O2, T2), but lacks focus on eliminating critical transition metals like cobalt or addressing issues like cation mixing in Li layers. CN118479558A discloses a method for producing an O2-type lithium-ion battery positive electrode active material through a two-step lithium incorporation process. The method begins with the preparation of a P2-type Na-containing transition metal oxide, followed by partial Na⁺ → Li⁺ ion exchange to obtain a Li-containing O2-type layered oxide. To further enhance the lithium content and increase the material’s capacity, an additional lithium-doping step is performed that is distinct from the initial ion-exchange process. US2024105921A1 discloses a method for preparing a lithium-ion battery electrode material through a multi-step synthesis and ion-exchange process. The method begins with the synthesis of a microspherical precursor via co-precipitation, followed by calcination with stoichiometric amounts of sodium carbonate, lithium carbonate, and a structural stabilizer to obtain an intermediate product. Subsequently, a molten salt ion-exchange process is carried out using LiNO₃/LiCl as the medium, leading to the formation of the final electrode material in the form of a lumpy residue. The emphasis is on achieving high lithium content and phase stability, but the method employs high-temperature molten salts and does not explicitly address issues like cation disorder, electrochemical integration, or in-situ structural monitoring. Although, in ion-exchange approach P2-structured Na-TM-oxides can be used as templates/precursors which can be subjected to Na⁺ → Li⁺ exchange in the presence of a Li⁺-containing solution, resulting in the formation of the desired O2-structured Li-TM-oxide, the process requires additional lithium containing solution as source of lithium ion for the ion exchange reaction. Further, the process does not guarantee formation of phases in the cathode material and needs to be confirmed prior using in a half cell by using ex-situ characterizations. Accordingly, there is need to provide a facile process for synthesizing high performance O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathodes for lithium-ion battery. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION Accordingly, it is an object of the present invention to overcome the problems associated with the prior art. It is an object of the present invention to provide a high performance O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material. It is further an object of the present invention to provide a direct process for synthesizing O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material. It is also an object of the present invention to provide synthesis of a O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material by ion exchange process. It is another object of the present invention to analyze the development of structural evolution of O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material during its synthesis in ion exchange process by real time monitoring. It is yet another object of the present invention to provide a O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material, having a composition as Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION In an aspect of the present invention there is provided a process for direct synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode material for a lithium-ion battery, which comprises steps of: i. providing a precursor cathode material in a cell comprising an electrolyte and a separator, ii. keeping the cell of step (i) under open circuit condition at room temperature for 11-15 hours, to obtain an in-situ synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide in the cell. It is one of the aspect of the present invention to provide a O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide having a stoichiometry composition comprising Li: 0.74, Mg: 0.02, Ni: 0.22, Mn: 0.66. It is also an of the aspect of the present invention to provide a Li-TM-oxide having a composition of Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. It is further an aspect of the present invention to provide a process for synthesizing a Li-TM-oxide comprising phase conversion reaction between a P2-structured Na-TM-oxide and a lithium containing mixture at room temperature for 11-15 hours. It is another aspect of the present invention to provide a Lithium ‘half’ cell comprising an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode, a lithium metal as anode, a separator, and an electrolyte. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES Figure 1: In-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns recorded over a period of 15 h during the ion-exchange process, showing the gradual transformation of the P2-structure (for the starting Na-TM-oxide) to the O2-structure (for the evolving Li-TM-oxide). (a) In-situ XRD patterns over a 2θ range of 10° to 80°, revealing the structural evolution and phase transformation in real time. (b) Magnified view of the in-situ XRD patterns, focusing on the 2θ range of 10° to 25°, which facilitates a closer look at the peak shifts corresponding to the (002) plane and phase evolution/depletion during the Na⁺/Li⁺ ion-exchange process. Figure 2: Schematic illustrations of the coin cell configurations used: (a) Coin cell based set-up employed for enabling the spontaneous Na⁺/Li⁺ chemical ion-exchange process. The assembly includes the P2-structured Na-TM-oxide powder in the form of an electrode, a glass fiber separator soaked with Li-containing electrolyte as the only Li-source, stainless steel spacer and spring, stainless-steel top and bottom cases as part of the sealed configuration. (b) The modified coin cell configuration, as used for in-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements during the chemical ion-exchange process. This design incorporates a Kapton film window to permit uninterrupted X-ray penetration while maintaining the sealed environment, thereby facilitating real-time structural monitoring throughout the ion-exchange process. Figure 3: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material collected after the completion of the chemical ion-exchange process (for 11 h) and after 24 h of subsequent storage under inert atmosphere (glovebox conditions). The patterns confirm phase purity and absence of secondary/impurity phases in the as-prepared condition, as well as upon storage, thus, confirming the structural stability of the ion-exchanged product (i.e., O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide) at room temperature. Figure 4: Electrochemical performance of the as-prepared cobalt-free O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide cathode material, as depicted by the variations of the reversible Li-storage capacity and Coulombic efficiency with cycle number during galvanostatic charge/discharge cycles in Li ‘half’ cell at a current density equivalent to C/10. In an embodiment there is provided a process for direct synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode material for a lithium-ion battery. The present invention provides an ion-exchange process for synthesizing O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide in a cell. The ion exchange process of the present invention comprises an in-situ phase transformation of a precursor cathode material to an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide. The present invention provides a way by which the in-situ phase transformation of the precursor cathode material to an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide can be analyzed. The inventors of the present invention provide a specially designed XRD compatible coin cell for carrying out an ion exchange process for in-situ phase transformation of a precursor cathode material to an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide. Thus, in an embodiment there is provided a XRD compatible coin cell for real time monitoring of an in situ phase transformation of an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide. The present XRD compatible coin cell comprises a precursor cathode material, a separator and an electrolyte. In an embodiment, there is provided an ion exchange process for synthesizing an O2-structured layered’ lithium transition metal oxide in a XRD compatible coin cell. The ion exchange process comprises: i. providing a precursor cathode material in a cell comprising an electrolyte and a separator, ii. keeping the cell of step (i) under open circuit condition at room temperature for 11-15 hours, to obtain an in-situ synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide in the cell. The process involves providing the precursor cathode material and the electrolyte at a ratio of 1:10 w/v. The precursor cathode material as used in the process is a Na-containing P2-structured ‘layered’ sodium transition metal oxide (Na-TM-oxide) cathode material. In a preferred embodiment, the precursor cathode material is Na₀.₈₄Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. The electrolyte as used in the process is a Lithium containing electrolyte, which comprises a mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC), and a source of Li ion dissolved in the mixture. The electrolyte mixture comprises ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) at 1:1:1 volume ratio. The source of Li ion as used in the process is selected from LiPF6, LiBOB4, ,LiBF4, LiTFSI. In a preferred embodiment the electrolyte mixture comprises 1M LiPF6 in a 1:1:1 mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate. The process involves formation of an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide in a reaction between Na-containing P2-structured ‘layered’ sodium transition metal oxide and the Lithium containing electrolyte. The process involves conversion of Na⁺ → Li⁺ chemical ion-exchange in P2-structured Na-TM-oxide during the conversion to O2-structured Li-TM-oxide oxide. The present invention provides a real time monitoring of the Na+/Li+ exchange process for analyzing the phase transformation of Na-TM-oxide into O2-structured Li-TM-oxide oxide, by an in-situ XRD. The in-situ XRD reveals formation of an XRD patterns instead of characteristic diffraction peaks for the P2-structure of the Na-TM-oxide. The present invention provides synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide without requiring any lithium metal or additional lithium containing solution. In a preferred embodiment the O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as obtained by the process has a stoichiometry composition comprising Li: 0.74, Mg: 0.02, Ni: 0.22, Mn: 0.66. The O2-structured Li-TM-oxide material as obtained exhibits high phase stability and does not show impurity phase formation even after 24 h of storage in inert atmosphere (glovebox conditions), which confirms the long-term structural integrity of the ion-exchanged product. In a preferred embodiment, the present invention provides a Li-TM-oxide having a composition of Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. In a preferred embodiment, the present invention provides an ion exchange process for preparing an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide. The process for preparing an O2--structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide comprises a phase conversion reaction between a P2-structured Na-TM-oxide and a lithium containing mixture at room temperature for 11-15 hours. The P2-structured Na-TM-oxide is Na₀.₈₄Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. The lithium containing mixture comprises a source of Li ion in a 1:1:1 mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC). The source of Li ion present in the lithium containing mixture is selected from LiPF6, LiBOB4, ,LiBF4, LiTFSI. The O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide so obtained by the process is Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. The O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide acts as cathode material for a Lithium ‘half’cell. In another embodiment of the present invention there is provided a lithium ‘half’ cell comprising an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode material. The present invention provides a lithium half-cell comprising: an O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode, a lithium metal as anode, a separator, and an electrolyte. The O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide is Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O2. The electrolyte as used in the lithium ‘half’ cell is the same electrolyte as used for the ion exchange process for synthesizing the O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide as cathode material. The electrochemical charge/discharge studies in Li ‘half’ cell comprising the Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O2 cathode material delivers a high initial reversible capacity of ~187 mAh/g at a current density equivalent to C/10 and retains ~80% of its capacity after 100 cycles within a potential window of 2.0–4.2 V vs. Li/Li⁺. This is highest known capacity of an O2-structured layered Li-TM-O2 obtained from P2-structured layered Na-TM-O2 by chemical ion-exchange. Further embodiments of the present invention are illustrated in Examples and Figures. Example 1: Process for synthesis of O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide The O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide was synthesized in a chemical ion-exchange process in a coin cell configuration. Standard CR2032 coin cells were assembled in an argon-filled glovebox (O₂ and H₂O < 0.1 ppm) using the as-synthesized P2-structured Na-TM-oxide having composition as Na₀.₈₄Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂ powder in the form of a working electrode, Whatman GF/D glass fiber filter as a separator, and 1 M LiPF₆ dissolved in a mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) in 1:1:1 volume ratio as the electrolyte, which solely acts as the source of Li-ions. Li metal was not used and any external bias was not applied. Instead, the cells were allowed to rest under open circuit conditions at room temperature for ~15 h, during which spontaneous ion-exchange (i.e., Li+ for Na⁺ in the cathode material structure) occurred, leading to the transformation from P2-structured Na-TM-oxide to O2-sructured ‘layered’ Li-transition metal oxide (Li-TM-oxide). Example 2: Real time monitoring of ion exchange process in XRD compatible cell To investigate and understand the Na⁺ → Li⁺ chemical ion-exchange mechanism in P2-structured Na-TM-oxide during the conversion to O2-structured Li-TM-oxide oxide, the process was monitored via in-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD), as presented in Fig. 1. The modified CR2032 coin cell designed with a Kapton film window to enable uninterrupted X-ray penetration, while maintaining perfect sealing during the process (see Fig. 2b). The P2-structured Na-TM-oxide powder, along with a glass fiber separator soaked in Li-containing electrolyte, used in the cell for the spontaneous chemical ion-exchange, as illustrated in Fig. 2a. The in-situ XRD patterns collected over 15 h (as in Fig. 1a) clearly reveal the gradual disappearance of the characteristic diffraction peaks for the P2-structure (of the starting Na-TM-oxide) and simultaneous emergence of the reflections corresponding to the O2-structure of the evolving Li-TM-oxide upon Na+/Li+ exchange. The evolution of the (002) reflections were closely monitored in the 2θ region of 10°–25°, as shown in the magnified view in Fig. 1b. The (002) peak corresponding to the disappearing P2-structure maintained a stable peak position, albeit with a progressively decreasing intensity, indicating no notable change in the associated interplanar spacing during the Na+/Li+ exchange process. This is presumably due to Li-ions being unable to directly enter the P2-structure, which would have, otherwise, led to shift in the peak position. By contrast, as the ion-exchange progressed, the new set of diffraction peaks corresponding to the O2-phase which began to emerge and steadily intensify, exhibited shift towards higher 2θ due to Li-incorporation, and then stabilizing after ~11 h. This observation indicates the formation of O2-structured ‘layered’ TM-oxide via the chemical ion-exchange process. Interestingly, a closer look indicates that the P2 to O2 transformation occurred via an O/P intergrowth phase, with the characteristic peak associated with the same emerging in-between those of the fading P2 and growing O2 phases. The shift of the peak corresponding to the O/P intergrowth also towards higher 2θ indicates Li-incorporation in the intergrowth structure with Na-getting removed, unlike for the original P2-structure. Post ion-exchange, the resultant O2-structured Li-TM-oxide material was extracted from the coin cell and stored under inert argon atmosphere for 24 h to evaluate its structure stability. Fig. 3 presents the XRD patterns collected immediately after the 11 h chemical ion-exchange and after 24 h of storage under glovebox conditions (O₂ and H₂O < 0.1 ppm), which shows absolutely no change. The XRD results confirm the development of the desired O2-structure, sans any detectable impurity, and also the stability of the as-prepared material’s structure at room temperature. ICP-AES confirmed the chemical composition (stoichiometry) of the ion-exchanged material to be Li: 0.74, Mg: 0.02, Ni: 0.22, Mn: 0.66, corresponding to the Li-TM-oxide composition of Li₀.₇Ni₀.₂₂Li₀.₀₄Mn₀.₆₆Mg₀.₀₂O₂. Example 3: Process for preparation of Lithium Half Cell The working electrodes for electrochemical cycling were prepared by mixing the as-synthesized O2-structured Li-TM-oxide cathode material with conducting additive (carbon black) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder homogenously in a slurry mixer for 30 min at 1000 rpm. The active material, conducting additive and binder were taken in the ratio of 8:1:1 by mass. The dry mixture was then mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), as solvent, to obtain a viscous slurry. The as-obtained slurry was coated onto Al current collector foils using an automated coating machine, followed by drying overnight (i.e., for 12 h) in a vacuum oven, calendaring and punching out electrode pieces as per the required dimension (viz., 14 mm diameter). The mass loading of the electrodes was 2-2.5 mg/cm2. The electrochemical charge/discharge cycles were conducted in CR2032 coin cells, having the electrode prepared from the O2-structured Li-TM-oxide as the cathode and Li metal foil as the anode (which may also be referred to as Li ‘half’ cell configuration). 1 M LiPF₆ in EC:DEC:DMC (1:1:1) was used as the electrolyte and glass fiber separator was used for preventing contact between the two electrodes. Galvanostatic charge/discharge testing was conducted at a current density equivalent to C/10, within a potential window of 2.0–4.2 V vs. Li/Li⁺, to evaluate the reversible Li-storage capacity and cycling stability. ADVANTAGE OF THE INVENTION The present invention provides development of a cobalt-free O2-structured ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide (Li-TM-oxide) cathode material for Li-ion batteries, by a spontaneous chemical ion-exchange process in a coin cell configuration, but without requiring any externally applied potential or presence of Li metal. The invention demonstrates a cost effective approach for obtaining structurally stable and electrochemically active O2-structured Li-TM-oxide material from a high sodium-containing P2-structured Na-TM-oxide. , Claims: 1. patents.abstract: This invention presents a novel method for early failure detection of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) using a novel factor, Combined Efficiency Factor (CEF), calculated using coulombic and energy efficiency. The study involves a total of 45 lithium-ion battery cells, comprising different chemistries: LiFePO₄ (LFP), LiNiMnCoO₂ (NMC), and LiNiCoAlO₂ (NCA). Among these, 15 cells belong to our laboratory Energy & Environmental Nanomaterials (EEN) Laboratory, while the remaining 30 cells data sourced from the publicly available dataset provided by Sandia National Laboratories (SNL). Analytical behaviour of CEF from early 10 to 50 cycles and studying its statistical features like slope, variance, standard deviation and range exhibited indication of early failure. The X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis of LFP fresh, working and failed cells verified permanent structural damage in degraded cells through observable peak shifts and lattice changes. Among the different machine learning models, the gradient boosting classifier based on slope of CEF classified healthy and degraded cells more accurately than other models. This novel approach of early detection of batteries, validated with electrochemical characterization-based machine learning model, will allows proactive battery health monitoring, high reliability, improving safety and performance in real-world applications of all type of batteries, hence offer inventive technological steps and scalable solution for the betterment of society.
patents.complete_specification: Description:DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention provides a method and system for the early detection and classification of degradation in energy storage devices, particularly LIBs. It combines electrochemical and physical characterization with machine learning to deliver a framework for real-time or offline battery health monitoring. The invention is applicable to various battery chemistries and can be integrated into Battery Management Systems (BMS) for diverse applications including EVs, grid storage, and portable electronics. Example 1: Data Collection and Preparation In one embodiment, the system operates on data collected from LIB cells undergoing cycling tests. The dataset includes 45 cells, with 15 cells tested at EEN Laboratory and 30 cells data sourced from SNL, covering various chemistries including: LFP NMC NCA During cycling, standard battery parameters are recorded, including: Voltage, current, temperature, and time, Charge and discharge capacity, Charge and discharge energy, The CE and EE are obtained from charge capacity, discharge capacity, charge energy and discharge energy. The capacity retention or SOH derived from discharge capacity. These values are tracked cycle-by-cycle and used to compute CEF. Also, the variation of SOH (at maximum cycle life and at 500 cycles), CE, EE, and CEF over 500 cycles is shown in Fig. 1, which indicates CEF and EE are more sensitive indicators of battery degradation. Example 2: Computation of CEF The invention introduces a novel metric, CEF, designed to capture and amplify minor changes in both electrical and energetic performance during the early stages of battery cycling. In a preferred embodiment, the CEF is computed using CE and EE based on charge-discharge cycle through the following equation: CEF= 2/(1/e^((-10(1-CE))) +1/e^((-10(1-EE))) ) Where: CE is calculated as the ratio of discharge capacity to charge capacity, EE is calculated as the ratio of discharge energy to charge energy, EE is often considered more useful because it reflects not only the capacity but also the voltage behaviour of the battery, including internal resistance and other losses, which directly impact the usable energy output. With cycling and calendar aging, increased resistance causes greater voltage loss, making EE a key indicator of battery degradation. However, EE alone cannot capture all degradation phenomena. CE specifically measures the charge capacity retention by comparing charge input and output, detecting irreversible losses such as lithium depletion and side reactions that may occur before noticeable voltage losses. When both CE and EE are near 1, indicating efficient behaviour, the CEF approaches its upper limit. As either CE or EE deviates from 1 due to inefficiencies or emerging degradation, the exponential terms in the denominator grow rapidly, reducing the CEF non-linearly. This makes CEF an ideal candidate for early-life detection of LIB degradation, as it reveals understated trends not easily captured by capacity-dependent parameters such as State of Health (SOH) or State of Charge (SOC). Example 3: Statistical Feature Extraction The statistical features of CEF used in this system are having certain interpretations which are given below: Slope: The linear rate of change in CEF values over time. This feature is important for machine learning algorithm to classify healthy and degraded cells, as demonstrated in Fig. 2. A steep positive slope during the early cycles may indicate early degradation, as shown in Fig. 3. Variance and Standard Deviation: To quantify the fluctuation and spread of CEF values across cycles, variance and standard deviation are used. Increased variability may indicate unstable internal processes or the onset of degradation. Although these features contribute to the machine learning model’s predictions, their importance is lower compared to slope and range, as shown in the feature importance analysis in Fig. 2. Range: The difference between the maximum and minimum CEF values within a given window, may indicate diminished performance or accelerated degradation when large. Consequently, it is one of the most significant predictive features alongside slope, as demonstrated in Fig. 2. Following the computation of the CEF for each cycle, the system performs statistical feature extraction over selected windows of early charge-discharge cycles-typically the first 10, 20, and 50 cycles. To visualize the effectiveness of these features, a heatmap of the CEF slope is plotted for each window size, as shown in Fig. 3. This heatmap reveals a clear distinction between healthy and degraded cells, demonstrating that the CEF slope is a highly sensitive indicator of early degradation across varying cycle ranges as illustrated in Fig. 3. Fig. 3 shows the CEF slope values at the 10th, 20th, and 50th cycles for 45 lithium-ion battery (LIB) cells. The dataset includes Cells 1–15 from EEN-LFP, Cells 16–25 from SNL-LFP, Cells 26–35 from SNL-NCA, and Cells 36–45 from SNL-NMC. Example 4: Machine Learning-Based Classification The invention includes a classification by machine learning algorithms trained on features derived from the CEF. These features, which capture early efficiency behaviour, are extracted from the first 10, 20, or 50 cycles and include statistical descriptors such as slope, standard deviation, variance, and range. Fig. 4 presents a comparative evaluation of various machine learning models used for early battery health classification based on CEF-derived features. Fig. 4a shows the accuracy scores, where the Gradient Boosting Classifier achieved perfect classification with 100% accuracy. In contrast, KNN, Logistic Regression, and SVM models each achieved 80% accuracy, while the Neural Network (MLP) reached 90%. Fig. 4b illustrates the RMSE, further confirming the superior performance of the Gradient Boosting model with an RMSE of 0.00. Other models, including KNN, Logistic Regression, and SVM, showed a higher RMSE of 0.44, while the Neural Network (MLP) exhibited a moderately improved RMSE of 0.31. These results highlight the exceptional predictive accuracy and reliability of the Gradient Boosting approach for early battery degradation classification. To evaluate the classification performance of various machine learning models in detecting early-stage battery degradation, several confusion matrices were analysed. Fig. 5 presents the confusion matrices for five machine learning models. As shown in Fig. 5a the Gradient Boosting Classifier shows perfect classification accuracy, correctly identifying all seven healthy cells and three degraded cells without any false positives. In contrast, the SVM, KNN and Logistic regression models as shown in Fig. 5b, 5c and 5d each misclassify two healthy cells as degraded cells. The Neural Network MLP model performs slightly better than the others (excluding Gradient Boosting), misclassifying one healthy cell as degraded cell as shown in Fig 5e. These results highlight the superior performance and reliability of the Gradient Boosting model for early battery health classification. The complete workflow for early battery degradation prediction is summarized in Fig. 6, which outlines the step-by-step process from raw data acquisition to final degradation monitoring. Initially, voltage (V), current (I), Energy and capacity (Q) data are recorded during charge-discharge cycling. These measurements are then used to calculate CE, EE, and the CEF. Next, statistical features such as slope, variance, and range are extracted from the CEF trajectory over early cycles. Finally, these features are input into machine learning models to classify cells as either healthy or degraded, enabling proactive diagnostics. Example 5: Structural Validation Using XRD To validate the predictive value of the proposed electrochemical diagnostic method, the present invention includes structural validation through XRD analysis. This approach not only enhances diagnostic confidence but also directly correlates observed electrochemical degradation with microstructural changes in electrode materials. In one embodiment, XRD measurements were performed on electrodes extracted from: Fresh cells Working cells Dead cells The structural integrity of both graphite anodes and LFP cathodes was examined to assess degradation over battery life. Anode The X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra of graphite anode extracted from fresh, working, and dead LIB cells are illustrated in Fig. 7a. The prominent peak corresponding to the (002) plane confirms the presence of a graphitic structure. Fig. 7b provides a magnified view of this peak, revealing the structural changes associated with electrochemical aging. In the fresh cell, the (002) reflection appears at 2θ = 26.64°, with a narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.20°, high peak intensity, and a d-spacing of 3.34 Å. These values indicate a well-ordered graphitic structure with minimal lattice strain and high crystallinity. The working cell exhibits a shift of the (002) peak to a lower angle (2θ = 26.59°), an increase in d-spacing to 3.35 Å, and a broader FWHM of 0.21°. These changes are indicative of reversible expansion of the graphite interlayers due to lithium intercalation during cycling. The increase in peak area suggests enhanced structural ordering under (de) intercalation of lithium. In contrast, the dead cell shows a (002) peak at 2θ = 26.63°, with a d-spacing of 3.34 Å and a slightly broader FWHM (0.20°) compared to the fresh cell. Despite the similarity in peak position and width, a noticeable reduction in peak intensity and area is observed, pointing to loss of crystallinity and degradation. These structural transitions are schematically illustrated in Fig. 8, which presents the mechanism of degradation. As shown in Fig. 8a, the fresh cell anode shows well-aligned graphitic layers with regular lithium-ion intercalation. The working cell anode demonstrates expanded layers due to reversible lithium intercalation, maintaining structural integrity as shown in Fig. 8b. The structural degradation in the dead cell is primarily due to irreversible changes caused by prolonged cycling. Repeated lithium (de) intercalation induces mechanical stress and local structural distortion within the graphitic layers. Additionally, side reactions at the anode-electrolyte interface-such as solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) growth, electrolyte decomposition, and lithium plating-contribute to the breakdown of graphite crystallinity. These processes cumulatively lead to the formation of disordered, misaligned, and fragmented graphite as shown in Fig. 8c, which reduce the electrode's ability to reversibly intercalate lithium and ultimately degrade cell performance. Cathode Fig. 9a shows the XRD spectra of LFP electrodes obtained from fresh, working, and dead LIB cells. The prominent peak corresponding to the (200) and (002) planes confirm the presence of an olivine-type LFP structure. Fig. 9b and 9c illustrates a magnified view of XRD spectra of (200) and (002) plane peaks, respectively. These peaks reveal critical structural changes in LFP cathodes. The (200) plane of the fresh, working, and dead cells reveals critical insights into the structural integrity of the cathode during cycling, as shown in Fig. 9b. In the fresh cell, the (200) reflection appears at 2θ = 18.67°, with a FWHM of 0.32°, indicating a well-ordered olivine-type crystalline structure with minimal micro strain and a d-spacing of 4.74 Å. The working cell shows a shift to higher angle for the (200) peak to 2θ = 18.75° showing decrease in d-spacing (4.72 Å). Also, the FWHM narrows significantly to 0.15°, possibly indicating lattice strain relaxation and increased crystallinity. In contrast, the dead cell shows a shift of the (200) peak to a lower angle (2θ = 18.53°) with an increased d-spacing of 4.77 Å, reflecting lattice expansion. The FWHM returns to a broader value (0.32°), indicating a significant increase in lattice disorder, which may be caused by irreversible phase transitions and microcrack formation. The (002) reflection also provides crucial evidence of the cathode’s degradation pathway, as shown in Fig. 9c. In the fresh cell, the (002) peak appears at 2θ = 36.80° with a FWHM of 0.33° and a d-spacing of 2.44 Å, indicating a well-formed layered structure with high crystallinity. In the working cell, the (002) peak slightly shifts to a lower angle (2θ = 36.73°) with a small increase in d-spacing (2.45 Å), consistent with lithium insertion and lattice expansion during cycling. The FWHM narrows to 0.19° related to the mild structural relaxation, which facilitating reversible lithium diffusion. However, in the dead cell, the (002) peak shifts to a higher angle (2θ = 37.07°) with a reduced d-spacing (2.43 Å), indicating lattice contraction. The broadening of the FWHM to 0.37° highlight the onset of significant crystallographic disorder. Whereas, the peak broadening corresponds to increased microstrain and irreversible structural degradation. These structural transitions are schematically illustrated in Fig. 10, which depicts the working mechanism of the LFP cathode. Fig. 10a represents the fresh LFP cathode, exhibiting a well-ordered olivine-type crystal structure with stable lithium diffusion pathways. Fig. 10b shows the structure of working cell cathode after cycling, where slight lattice distortion is observed. This is evidenced by a decrease in d-spacing along the a-axis and an increase along the c-axis, resulting from the (de)intercalation of lithium within the FePO4 matrix. Additionally, a reduction FWHM values for both (200) and (002) planes indicate improved crystallinity due to structural reordering during cycling. In contrast, Fig. 10c illustrates the structural degradation in the dead cell, characterized by significant lattice distortion-marked by a further decrease in d-spacing along the a-axis and an increase along the c-axis. This is accompanied by broadening of FWHM in both planes, signifying a loss of crystallinity and partial amorphization of the LFP framework, due to irreversible lithium loss and structural collapse. The XRD results support the predictions made by the CEF-based analysis. The structural changes seen in XRD, such as lattice distortion and loss of crystallinity, match the early signs of degradation identified by CEF. This shows that CEF is a reliable tool for early failure detection. , C , C , C , Claims:WE CLAIM: 1. A method for the early prediction of lithium-ion battery failure, comprising: Collecting current, voltage, and time data during each charge-discharge cycle; Calculating Charge Energy, Discharge Energy, Charge Capacity and Discharge Capacity from the collected data; Deriving CE and EE from the calculated data. Wherein the method utilizes a CEF that incorporates both CE and EE to provide an early detection signal for battery degradation. 2. The method of claim 1, wherein the CEF is calculated using the equation: CEF= 2/(1/e^((-10(1-CE))) +1/e^((-10(1-EE))) ) In the CEF equation the numerator 2 ensures that the maximum CEF value is 1 when both CE and EE are ideal (equal to 1), effectively keeping the output within a normalized 0–1 range. The number 10 in the exponent controls how sensitive the CEF is to changes in CE and EE. Specifically, it determines how quickly the exponential terms grow as CE or EE drop from 1. A larger value like 10 makes the equation highly sensitive, so even a small reduction in efficiency causes a steep rise in the denominator and a sharp fall in CEF. This makes the CEF a powerful early warning indicator, as it responds quickly to minor inefficiencies that may signal early battery degradation. wherein the equation exponentially combines CE and EE to provide a highly sensitive degradation indicator. 3. The method of claim 2, wherein statistical features of the CEF, the variance, slope, standard deviation, and range are extracted from the early charge-discharge cycles, and wherein: The statistical features are used to detect early degradation trends with higher accuracy than traditional metrics such as charge/discharge capacity. 4. The method of claim 3, wherein the slope of the CEF within the first 10 to 50 charge-discharge cycles is used as a key indicator to detect early degradation trends in the battery cells, and wherein: The slope serves as a novel early detection metric, capable of identifying degradation before capacity fade or other traditional failure signs are apparent. 5. The method of claim 4, wherein a machine learning model, preferably a Gradient Boosting Classifier, is trained on CEF-based statistical features to classify battery cells as either healthy or degrading, and wherein: The machine learning model uses a combination of statistical features (such as slope, variance, range and standard deviation) for high accuracy in predicting early failure, with minimal reliance on traditional performance metrics.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR INTEGRATED PASSIVE THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF LITHIUM‐ION BATTERY PACKS USING A DI WATER-FILLED CYLINDRICAL HEAT PIPE A passive thermal management system is disclosed for lithium‐ion battery packs, comprising a battery pack assembly having a plurality of lithium‐ion cells arranged in series–parallel configuration within a housing with predefined channels and an integrated cylindrical heat pipe. The heat pipe, fabricated from copper with an 8 mm outer diameter and 7.6 mm inner diameter, is segmented into an evaporator section in thermal contact with the cells, an adiabatic section for vapor transport, and a condenser section positioned toward a heat dissipation region. DI water, filled at a 30% volumetric ratio, undergoes phase change, while a single‐layer stainless steel screen mesh wick promotes capillary return of condensate. Temperature sensors may be positioned near the cells to monitor operational heat, ensuring effective cyclic management of thermal energy.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates broadly to thermal management systems and, more specifically, to a compact integrated passive thermal management system employing a DI water-filled cylindrical heat pipe for lithium‐ion battery packs used in electric vehicles, energy storage, and related applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Lithium‐ion batteries are increasingly employed in electric vehicles and energy storage systems, where rapid charging and discharging cycles generate considerable heat. Without effective thermal control, elevated temperatures can trigger thermal runaway, leading to serious safety hazards including potential explosions. The challenges posed by such thermal events necessitate an emphasis on robust thermal management within battery packs. Presently, thermal management of lithium‐ion batteries is achieved through methods such as radiator, fin, liquid, and phase change material based cooling. These approaches typically involve using additional components to dissipate heat, and they have been widely implemented in various systems where cooling is required. The existing solutions, while functionally effective, face notable challenges. In addition to requiring extra space for multiple auxiliary parts, they frequently lead to increased weight, greater system complexity, and additional points of potential failure. These shortcomings complicate the integration process and can adversely affect overall battery performance, safety, and longevity, particularly in compact battery pack configurations. The deficiencies evident in current thermal management techniques highlight the need for a more efficient and compact solution. In light of these limitations, the title, A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR INTEGRATED PASSIVE THERMAL MANAGEMENT OF LITHIUM‐ION BATTERY PACKS USING A DI WATER-FILLED CYLINDRICAL HEAT PIPE, reflects an approach aimed at addressing the critical need for improved thermal control solutions in lithium‐ion battery applications. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION Object of the invention is to provide a compact, integrated lithium-ion battery pack design wherein a series‐parallel arrangement of multiple cells is combined with an internal passive thermal management system that minimizes additional space requirements while ensuring proper electrical balance. Another object of the invention is to provide a battery pack incorporating a custom‐fabricated, copper-based cylindrical heat pipe that is precisely segmented into an evaporator section for rapid heat absorption, an adiabatic section for efficient vapor transport, and a condenser section for effective heat release, thereby maximizing thermal management within the confined battery module. Yet another object of the invention is to provide a thermal management system featuring an integrated, single-layer stainless steel screen mesh wick arranged along the inner wall of the heat pipe. This configuration utilizes capillary action to continuously return condensed de-ionized water—filled at an optimized 30% filling ratio—from the condenser back to the evaporator, ensuring sustained, efficient latent heat transfer. Another object of the invention is to provide a passive cooling mechanism that leverages the latent heat phenomenon during the evaporation and condensation cycles of DI water, thereby lowering the temperature gradient across battery cells and effectively dissipating the heat generated during charging and discharging cycles. A further object of the invention is to provide a thermal management solution that maintains optimal battery performance and longevity under varying electrical loads, including high C-rate operations (e.g., 1.5C) and lower C-rate conditions (e.g., 0.5C), by rapidly redirecting heat away from localized hot spots during intense energy transfer events. Yet another object of the invention is to provide a design that obviates the need for bulky, external cooling components such as radiators or fin arrays, thereby simplifying overall system architecture, reducing energy losses, and enhancing the safety of the battery pack by preventing potential thermal runaway. Another object of the invention is to provide an integrated passive thermal management approach that not only improves the uniformity of temperature distribution across battery cells but also enhances the battery pack’s operational safety and life-cycle performance through rapid, direct, and efficient heat dissipation. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention is described in the following sections by various embodiments. However, it should be understood that the invention can be implemented in various forms and is not limited to the specific embodiment provided herein.In the context of the present disclosure, it should be understood that the described embodiments in this section are put forth for illustrative purposes only. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that various modifications, adaptations, and alternative designs may be employed without departing from the scope and spirit of the invention. Accordingly, the present invention should not be limited to the specific embodiments illustrated herein, but rather should be construed according to the claims and description that follow. Embodiments of the present invention provide an integrated passive thermal management system for lithium‐ion battery packs using a DI water‐filled cylindrical heat pipe. In these embodiments, a battery pack assembly comprises a plurality of lithium‐ion cells arranged in a series–parallel configuration disposed within a housing having predefined channels for receiving the cells. A cylindrical heat pipe fabricated from copper with an 8 mm outer diameter and a 7.6 mm inner diameter is incorporated, the heat pipe being partitioned into an evaporator section, an adiabatic section, and a condenser section. The evaporator section is positioned in thermal contact with the surfaces of the lithium‐ion cells. The adiabatic section serves as a conduit for vapor transport from the evaporator section, while the condenser section is oriented within the housing toward a region configured for effective heat dissipation. A working fluid comprising DI water is filled into the cylindrical heat pipe at a 30% volumetric filling ratio wherein the DI water undergoes phase change via latent heat of vaporization. A single‐layer wick structure constructed from stainless steel screen mesh is arranged along the inner wall of the copper tube to promote capillary return of condensed DI water from the condenser section back to the evaporator section. Advantageously, the close thermal integration achieved by positioning the heat pipe directly in contact with the battery cells ensures rapid heat extraction from areas of high thermal generation. This technical feature results in a lower temperature gradient across the battery pack, effectively reducing risks of overheating and thermal runaway. Furthermore, the compact design enhances thermal efficiency under variable electrical loads, maintains battery performance even at high charging/discharging C‐rates, and eliminates the need for additional bulky or active cooling components, thus preserving a lightweight and space‐efficient battery pack structure. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the battery pack assembly further comprises a staggered arrangement of the lithium‐ion cells disposed within the housing, ensuring a maximized contact area for thermal management and an optimal heat transfer interface with the adjacent cooling components. In addition, the housing is constructed with internal grooves configured to secure the cylindrical heat pipe in a predetermined position, thereby maintaining consistent positioning and effective thermal contact between the battery cells and the integrated cooling device. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the cylindrical heat pipe is fabricated exclusively from copper and includes a single‐layer wick structure constructed from tensioned stainless steel screen mesh that is arranged along the inner wall. Additionally, the tensioned mesh ensures a close and uniform attachment to the inner surface of the copper tube, which is critical for maximizing capillary action and enhancing the return flow of the condensed DI water from the condenser section back to the evaporator section. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the DI water is introduced into the cylindrical heat pipe at a 30% volumetric filling ratio prior to evacuation and sealing. Additionally, this precise filling ratio guarantees that sufficient working fluid is present to absorb the latent heat generated from the battery cells while also providing adequate space for vapor expansion during operation, thus optimizing the overall thermal performance. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, temperature sensors are positioned proximate to the lithium‐ion cells within the battery pack assembly. These sensors are configured to record temperature data during battery pack operation, thereby enabling real-time monitoring of thermal performance and ensuring that operating temperatures remain within safe limits under various charging/discharging C‐rates. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the evaporator section, measuring approximately 333 mm in length, is in intimate thermal contact with the battery cells so as to rapidly absorb generated heat. The subsequent adiabatic section, measuring approximately 167 mm, facilitates the efficient transport of vapor towards the condenser section, which measures approximately 500 mm in length and is oriented toward regions optimized for heat dissipation. Additionally, this sectioning contributes to enhanced heat transfer efficiency across the integrated system. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the battery pack assembly further includes a series–parallel configuration of lithium‐ion cells yielding a battery capacity of approximately 1 kWh. The integration of the passive thermal management system, particularly the DI water‐filled cylindrical heat pipe with its engineered sectioning and wick structure, contributes to improved battery performance, extended cell life, and heightened operational safety by ensuring a uniform temperature distribution throughout the battery pack. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, a method for manufacturing the integrated passive thermal management system is provided. The method includes arranging a plurality of lithium‐ion cells in a predetermined series–parallel configuration within a battery pack housing having predefined channels; machining a copper tube to form a cylindrical heat pipe with distinct evaporator, adiabatic, and condenser sections; inserting a single‐layer wick structure constructed from stainless steel screen mesh along the inner wall of the copper tube; charging the cylindrical heat pipe with DI water at a 30% volumetric filling ratio; evacuating non‐condensable gases from the heat pipe and subsequently sealing it; and integrating the sealed, DI water‐filled cylindrical heat pipe within the battery pack housing such that the evaporator section is positioned in thermal contact with the battery cells and the condenser section is oriented toward a region for ambient heat dissipation. Additionally, temperature sensors are positioned proximate to the lithium‐ion cells prior to integration to monitor operating temperatures during battery pack operation.
