The present invention relates to an integrated passive thermal management system for lithium‐ion battery packs which incorporates a DI water‐filled cylindrical heat pipe within a compact battery assembly. The invention combines an optimized arrangement of a plurality of lithium‐ion cells arranged in a series–parallel configuration with a custom‐fabricated copper heat pipe that is partitioned into an evaporator section, an adiabatic section, and a condenser section. The invention thereby addresses the challenges of heat dissipation generated during battery charging and discharging while maintaining a low-profile configuration and a simplified design. The invention provides a compact battery pack assembly wherein the lithium‐ion cells are arranged in a staggered configuration within a housing having predefined channels. The housing is configured to accommodate both the cells and the integrated thermal management elements so that the battery cells remain in close proximity to the heat receiving surfaces of the heat pipe. The design ensures maximum thermal contact and thereby is able to efficiently disperse heat generated internally by exothermic reactions and internal resistance phenomena in the battery cells. In one embodiment, the battery pack comprises a plurality of lithium‐ion cells arranged in series parallel to yield a capacity of approximately 1 kWh. The cells are mounted within a housing that is structured to include channels for receiving cooling components. The housing is fabricated with sufficient mechanical strength and thermal conductivity to act as an interface between the battery cells and the integrated thermal management device. The cells are positioned so that their outer surfaces abut the evaporator section of the integrated heat pipe. The integrated arrangement may, but is not limited to, include auxiliary safety or temperature sensing elements to provide operational temperature data throughout the cycle of battery operation. An embodiment of the present invention further comprises a cylindrical heat pipe assembly fabricated exclusively from copper. The heat pipe comprises but is not limited to an evaporator section measuring approximately 333 mm, an adiabatic section measuring approximately 167 mm, and a condenser section measuring approximately 500 mm. The cylindrical shape with an 8 mm outer diameter and a 7.6 mm inner diameter is attained through standard machining processes suitable for copper tubing. The heat pipe is integrated within the battery pack such that its evaporator section is positioned into direct thermal contact with surfaces of the lithium‐ion cells, thereby enabling rapid absorption of heat generated during high current operations. The heat pipe further comprises a single‐layer wick structure constructed from stainless steel screen mesh that is inserted along an inner wall of the copper tube. The mesh is tensioned during assembly to ensure uniform contact with the inner surface of the tube, thereby promoting efficient capillary action. The wick structure is configured to return the condensed DI water from the condenser section back to the evaporator section in a continuous cyclic process. Material selection for the wick and the copper tube is made to enhance thermal conductivity as well as to ensure durability over prolonged cycling in thermal management applications. The working fluid in the heat pipe is de‐ionized water, which is introduced at a predetermined 30% volumetric filling ratio into the evacuated copper tube prior to sealing. The use of DI water is predicated on its high latent heat of vaporization and its suitability in sustaining a phase change cycle. Thermal energy is absorbed in the evaporator section because of the heat generated by the battery cells, which causes the DI water to vaporize. The resulting vapor flows through the adiabatic section toward the condenser section, where it releases latent heat and condenses. The resulting condensate is then drawn back through the wick structure into the evaporator section, thereby enabling a self‐sustaining passive cooling mechanism that obviates the need for additional mechanical pumping. An embodiment of the present invention further accommodates a plurality of such heat pipes integrated into a battery pack. In one illustrative example, twelve heat pipes are arranged in predefined positions within the battery pack housing. The positioning is such that the evaporator sections are aligned with the areas of highest thermal load on the battery cells, and the condenser sections are oriented towards regions designed to facilitate ambient heat dissipation. The battery pack housing is engineered to provide grooves or channels which secure the heat pipes in fixed positions while preserving the overall compactness and structural integrity of the assembly. A method embodiment of the present invention comprises preparing the lithium‐ion battery cells for assembly by arranging them in a staggered series–parallel configuration and securing them within a housing that incorporates channels for the integrated cooling device. The method further includes machining a copper tube to produce a cylindrical heat pipe with specified dimensions and subsequently partitioning the tube into an evaporator section, an adiabatic section, and a condenser section. A single‐layer wick made from stainless steel screen mesh is then inserted along an inner wall of the copper tube to ensure that the wick is in intimate contact with the tube surface. De‐ionized water is introduced at a 30% filling ratio into the assembled heat pipe under vacuum conditions to remove non‐condensable gases before the heat pipe is permanently sealed. The sealed heat pipe is then integrated within the battery pack housing so that the evaporator section is in direct thermal contact with the battery cell surfaces and the condenser section is oriented toward an area that enhances heat dissipation. Temperature sensors may be positioned proximate to the battery cells to monitor thermal performance during designated charging and discharging cycles across different C‐rates. An embodiment of the present invention further provides for operational testing methods wherein the battery pack assembly is subjected to cycling at various charging/discharging currents (from 0.5C to 1.5C). During operation, the heat generated by the battery cells is intercepted by the evaporator section of the heat pipe, resulting in vaporization of the DI water which is then transported through the heat pipe and subsequently condensed in the condenser section. The condensed liquid is returned to the evaporator section via the wick structure. This cyclic heat transfer mechanism efficiently dissipates thermal energy and minimizes temperature gradients across the battery pack. Experimental data recorded from temperature sensors validate the robust performance of the integrated passive thermal management system even when the cells are operated under high thermal loads. The invention provides several advantages over conventional battery thermal management systems. The integrated design minimizes the footprint of the overall battery pack assembly by eliminating the need for external cooling components such as radiators, fin systems, or liquid loops that require additional space and power. The passive thermal management approach utilizing the latent heat and capillary-induced return flow of DI water ensures consistent and uniform heat dissipation that enhances the battery life-cycle, safety, and performance. Variations of the present invention may include using alternative materials for the wick structure or adjustments to the dimensions of the heat pipe sections, all of which fall within the purview of the inventive concept. The technical features of the present invention—including the compact integration of a copper heat pipe, a finely engineered single-layer wick, and the precise use of DI water filled at a controlled volumetric filling ratio—enable efficient thermal management under variable electrical loads. The design ensures optimal thermal contact between the battery cells and the passive cooling device, thereby reducing the overall battery surface temperature, mitigating hotspots, and preventing thermal runaway. The inventive arrangement of components not only simplifies thermal management but also contributes to improved battery performance and safety, making the present invention particularly suitable for high-power, densely packed battery configurations. The principles associated with the various embodiments described herein can be applied to additional embodiments. Consequently, the description is not intended to be limited to the embodiments but aims to provide the broadest scope consistent with the principles and the innovative and inventive features disclosed or suggested herein. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a modified high nickel (Ni)-containing ‘layered’ lithium transition metal oxide (Li-TM-oxide) cathode material with enhanced stability upon exposure to air and water, thus, enabling ‘aqueous processing’ of the electrode (i.e., Li-ion battery cathode), while maintaining excellent electrochemical performance. The cathode material has a composition of Li(Ni0.8-xZnxMn0.1Co0.1)O2, where x varies from 0.02 to 0.05. The resulting cathode material not only exhibits excellent air-stability for at least 3 months upon exposure to humid air, but also structural stability even when soaked and stirred in deionized water. Also provided are methods for preparing the said cathode as well as Li-ion batteries comprising the same.
patents.complete_specification: Description: FIELD OF INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Specifically, it relates to the development of modified high nickel (Ni)-containing layered lithium transition metal oxide (Li-TM-oxide) cathode materials with enhanced air and water stability achieved through zinc (Zn)-doping. BACKGROUND AND THE PRIOR ART High Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxides are widely regarded as promising cathode materials for the next-generation lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to their relatively low cobalt content, which addresses supply chain and cost concerns, while facilitating high energy density for LIBs. However, the high Ni-containing Li-TM-oxide based cathodes suffer from several intrinsic challenges that hinder their practical implementation in large-scale applications. One of the critical limitations of the high Ni-containing Li-TM-oxide based cathodes is their poor structural and chemical stability, particularly in ambient air and humid environments. These materials readily absorb moisture and CO₂, leading to the formation of surface lithium carbonate/bicarbonate and lithium hydroxide species [Myung, S. T. et. al., (2017). Nickel-rich layered cathode materials for automotive lithium-ion batteries: achievements and perspectives. ACS Energy Letters, 2(1), 196-223; Zheng, X., et. al., (2023). Nickel-rich layered oxide cathodes for lithium-ion batteries: Failure mechanisms and modification strategies. Journal of Energy Storage, 58, 106405]. This surface degradation results in poor quality of the electrode slurry, an increase in interfacial resistance in Li-ion cells, sluggish Li-ion transport and overall inferior electrochemical performance. Furthermore, moisture exposure induced Li-loss from the Li-layer triggers migration of transition metal ions into the Li-layer. Such ‘cation mixing’ and associated phase/structural instability lead to severe capacity fade during electrochemical cycling in Li-ion cells [Recent progress in cathode materials research for advanced lithium ion batteries. Materials Science and Engineering: R: Reports, 73(5-6), 51-65]. This also leads to enormous challenges with handling/storage of such cathode materials and mandates the usage of toxic/hazardous N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) as the medium, and not water, for preparing the cathode slurry. To overcome these limitations, several strategies have been adopted, including surface coatings, electrolyte additives, and cation doping. Among these, cation doping has proven to be effective in stabilizing the structure and minimizing ‘cation mixing’ [Surface doping vs. bulk doping of cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries: a review. Electrochemical Energy Reviews, 5(4), 2.; Nickel‐rich layered lithium transition‐metal oxide for high‐energy lithium‐ion batteries. Angewandte Chemie International Edition, 54(15), 4440-4457] while coatings help improve the stability at the cathode/electrolyte interface [Comprehensive study of Al-and Zr-modified LiNi0. 8Mn0. 1Co0. 1O2 through synergy of coating and doping. ACS applied energy materials, 3(9), 8978-8987.]. However, the focus has been primarily on improving the structural/interfacial stability during charge/discharge in Li-ion cells, and not on improving the stability upon exposure to air and water. US11658299B2 discloses a lithium secondary battery having a high-nickel cathode and a silicon-based anode. The positive electrode comprises a lithium-nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM)-based active material, where nickel constitutes 80 mol% or greater relative to the other transition metals. The negative electrode utilizes a silicon-based active material. The battery system comprises electrolyte formulation, which comprises lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF₆) and lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) in a highly concentrated non-aqueous solution (1.8 M to 5 M). This high-concentration electrolyte is designed to improve interfacial stability, suppress side reactions, and enhance the overall cycle life of the battery. It focuses on the development of a lithium secondary battery that integrates a high-nickel cathode with a silicon-based anode. However, there is no mention of air and water stability of NCM-based active material. CN114965171B discloses a method for evaluating the compatibility of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) as water-based binders in lithium-ion batteries. Here, the inventors have mentioned the evaluation process which include a contact angle test to assess wettability. However, there is no mention about NCM-based cathode materials. CN117727911A discloses a method to enhance the air stability of high-nickel ternary cathode materials by dispersing the cathode material in an organic solvent containing paraffin and a surfactant, followed by stirring for 1 to 5 hours. The surfactant, selected from fatty alcohol-polyoxyethylene ether, perfluorooctanoic acid, perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, or trimethyl stearyl ammonium chloride, facilitates the formation of a hydrophobic layer, reducing the cathode’s interaction with moisture in the air. This approach focuses primarily on preventing surface degradation caused by environmental exposure. According to CN117727911 the air stability of cathode is enhanced by surface coating method; however, there is no mention of water stability due to coating. Previous studies have demonstrated that Zn-incorporation in Li-NMC cathode materials suppresses anisotropic lattice distortion, maintains structural/mechanical integrity, and enhances interfacial stability, leading to superior electrochemical performance and cycle life [Addressing the high-voltage structural and electrochemical instability of Ni-containing layered transition metal (TM) oxide cathodes by “blocking” the “TM-migration” pathway in the lattice. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 13(22), 25836-25849.]. For instance, Manthiram et al. [Zinc-doped high-nickel, low-cobalt layered oxide cathodes for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 13(13), 15324-15332] showed that 2 mol% Zn²⁺-doping in Li-Ni₀.₉₄Co₀.₀₄Zn₀.₀₂O₁.₉₉ (NCZ) suppressed structural degradation during electrochemical charge/discharge cycles and resulted in improved capacity retention of ~74% after 500 cycles in a Li-ion ‘full’ cell, significantly outperforming the undoped counterpart. In addition to material stability, an equally important aspect of cathode fabrication is the electrode processing technique. Conventionally, Li-ion battery cathodes are prepared using toxic and expensive organic solvents, mainly NMP, as the slurry medium which pose environmental, health and economic challenges. Aqueous processing, which utilizes water instead of NMP, offers a safer, more cost-effective, and eco-friendly alternative. However, high Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide cathode materials suffer from severe degradation in aqueous environments, limiting their compatibility with water-based processing of the cathode slurry or ‘aqueous processing’. The development of a water-stable cathode material is, therefore, crucial for the adoption of ‘aqueous processing’ route. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION It is an objective of the present invention to overcome the drawbacks of the prior or existing inventions. It is an objective of the present invention to provide a lithium-ion battery cathode material that exhibits enhanced air and water stability, enabling aqueous slurry-based electrode processing while maintaining structural integrity and electrochemical performance. SUMMARY Accordingly the present invention provides a lithium-ion battery cathode material comprising a Zn-doped high nickel-containing layered lithium transition metal oxide of the formula Li(Ni₀.₈₋ₓZnₓMn₀.₁Co₀.₁)O₂, where x ranges from 0.02 to 0.05, wherein the cathode material exhibits enhanced air and water stability. According to another aspect of the present invention there is provided an electrode comprising the cathode material and a binder system containing carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). According to a further aspect of the present invention there is provided a method for preparing the Zn-doped high nickel lithium transition metal oxide cathode material, said method comprising: (a) co-precipitating a transition metal hydroxide precursor from an aqueous solution of nickel sulphate, manganese sulphate, cobalt sulphate, and zinc sulphate in a ratio of 7.8: 1: 1: 0.2 to 7.5: 1: 1: 0.5, (b) chemically lithiating the transition metal hydroxide precursor obtained from step (a) using lithium hydroxide monohydrate in a molar ratio of 1:1.05 to 1:1.1, and (c) annealing the mixture under oxygen at 500-540°C for 4-5 hours followed by 780-800°C for 18-20 hours to yield said cathode material. According to a yet another aspect of the present invention there is provided a process of preparing the electrode of the present invention, said process comprising forming a slurry in water with the Zn-doped cathode material of the present invention, carbon black, CMC, and SBR, followed by casting said slurry onto a substrate and drying under vacuum. According to a yet another aspect of the present invention there is provided a lithium-ion battery cell comprising the electrode, a lithium metal anode, a glass fiber separator, and an electrolyte BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS The present invention may be better understood by considering the following descriptions of the embodiments and linking them with the accompanying figures. The figures are intended to be illustrative and shall not be considered limiting to the present inventions' scope. Although the present invention shall be considered to be within the spirit of the present invention. FIG. 1 shows X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) patterns corresponding to the undoped and Zn-doped Li-NMC811, confirming the formation of a well-ordered α-NaFeO₂-type ‘layered’ or cation-ordered structure with a rhombohedral space group (R3̅m). The estimated XRD peak intensity ratio corresponding to the (003) and (104) planes (i.e., I(003):I(104)) indicates minimal ‘cation mixing’, with Zn-doped Li NMC811 maintaining a robust ‘layered’ structure. FIG. 2 shows XRD patterns corresponding to the Li-NMC811 samples exposed to humid air for up to 3 months. (a) XRD patterns corresponding to the undoped Li-NMC811, showing a significant reduction in the I(003):I(104) peak intensity ratio over time, indicating structural degradation or enhanced ‘cation mixing’. (b) XRD patterns corresponding to the Zn-doped Li-NMC811, which maintains a stable I(003):I(104) peak intensity ratio over the entire duration, demonstrating improved air-stability. (c) Bar graph illustrating the variation of the I(003):I(104) peak intensity ratio as a function of air-exposure duration, highlighting the superior resistance of the Zn-doped Li NMC811 to structural instability or ‘cation mixing’ compared to the undoped counterpart. FIG. 3 shows XRD patterns corresponding to the water-soaked undoped Li-NMC811 and Zn-doped Li-NMC811, showing significant structural degradation or ‘cation mixing’ in the case of the undoped Li-NMC811, as compared to the Zn-doped counterpart. XRD pattern corresponding to the Zn-doped Li-NMC811 after 12 h of stirring in deionized water, which confirms its retained ‘layered’ or ‘cation ordered’ structure, maintaining a peak ratio of ~0.9, which is in agreement with the superior water stability. FIG. 4 shows Electrochemical performance of the ‘aqueous processed’ Zn-doped Li-NMC811 cathode, as depicted by the variations of the reversible Li-storage capacity and Coulombic efficiency with cycle number during galvanostatic charge/discharge cycles in Li ‘half’ cell at a current density equivalent to C/10. FIG. 5 shows Li ‘half’ cell configuration for electrochemical cycling of the modified high Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide cathode-active material. FIG. 6 shows X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) patterns corresponding to the 10 mol% Zn-doped Li-NMC811 showing presence of impurity phases of zinc oxide and zinc hydrate, suggesting that it is beyond the solubility limit of Zn2+ in the Li-NMC811 lattice. DETAIL DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention may be embodied in several forms, and the details of embodiments of the present invention will be described in the following content with figures. The embodiments described below with reference to the drawings are merely illustrative of the technical solutions of the present disclosure but are not to be constructed as limited to the technical solutions of the present disclosure. The following detailed description of the invention is provided to aid those skilled in the art in practicing the present invention. Even so, the detailed description should not be construed to unduly limit the present invention as modifications and verifications in the embodiments discussed herein may be made by those of ordinary skill in the art with the help of foregoing description and accompanying figures without departing from the spirit or scope of the present inventive discovery. The contents of all references, patents and published patent applications cited throughout this application are expressly incorporated herein by reference. Unless otherwise defined, all technical and scientific terms used herein have the meaning commonly understood by one of ordinary skill in the art to which this invention belongs. The terminology used herein is for the purpose of describing particular embodiments only and is not intended to be limiting of the invention. The terms and words used in the following description and claims are not limited to the bibliographical meanings, but, are merely used by the inventor to enable a clear and consistent understanding of the invention. Accordingly, it should be apparent to those skilled in the art that the following description of exemplary embodiments of the present invention are provided for illustration purpose only and not for the purpose of limiting the invention as defined by the appended claims and their equivalents. As used in the description of the invention and the appended claims, the singular forms "a", "an" and "the" are intended to include the plural forms as well, unless the context clearly indicates otherwise. The present invention provides a Zn-doped high Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide cathode material with significantly improved stability upon exposure to air and water, enabling the fabrication of ‘aqueous processed’ electrodes without compromising the electrochemical performance. The Zn-doped high-nickel lithium transition metal oxide cathode material in accordance with the present invention demonstrated excellent structural stability upon prolonged exposure to ambient air and water, as confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD). The cathode material of the present invention, Li(Ni₀.₈₋ₓZnₓMn₀.₁Co₀.₁)O₂ (where x = 0.02 to 0.05), incorporates Zn²⁺ as a dopant to mitigate cation-mixing, which in turn preserves structural integrity and electrochemical performance even when exposed to air or processed in water-based systems. The composition of the cathode is crucial as it imparts excellent stability upon exposure to air and water, even facilitating ‘aqueous processing’ of the electrode, while maintaining excellent electrochemical performance. The cathode material of the present invention retains a layered crystal structure with I(003)/I(104) XRD intensity ratio of ≥ 0.9 after being stirred in deionized water for 12 hours. In accordance with the present invention ‘aqueous processing’ of the electrode means preparing the electrode slurry using water as the solvent (medium) for the binder, instead of using the usually used toxic/hazardous and more expensive N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone (NMP) as the solvent. The present modified high-Ni cathode material retains 90% and 82% of its initial capacity after 50 and 100 cycles, respectively, in a Li ‘half’ cell, with a first-cycle specific discharge capacity of ~170 mAh/g at C/10 (2.5–4.5 V). It exhibits excellent structural stability for at least up to 3 months upon exposure to humid air and also when soaked and stirred in de-ionized water for up to at least 12 h. The partial substitution of Ni²⁺ with Zn²⁺ is central to the invention. Zn²⁺ ions, due to their unique electronic configuration (d¹⁰), stabilize the layered structure by hindering cation migration through tetrahedral sites in the Li-layer. This structural effect reduces Li loss during storage or water exposure, thereby preserving the electrochemically active layered phase. The present catalyst comprises 2-5% by weight Zn. Figure 2 and 3 shows the comparative air stability water stability of Zn-doped and undoped cathode material, NMC811. The characteristic (003) and (104) reflections are indicative of layeredness of NMC based cathodes, and when the integrated I(003)/I(104) peak intensity ratio approaches ~1-1.2, it is an indicative of minimal ‘cation mixing’ and a well-preserved ‘layered’ framework. Furthermore, the clear peak splitting of the (006)/(102) and (108)/(110) doublets is a strong indicator of long-range ordering/‘layering’. The XRD of the Zn-doped Li-NMC811 shows that it successfully retained its ‘layered’ structure, with the I(003):I(104) peak intensity ratio stabilizing at ~1.0; thus, confirming its structural stability upon exposure to water, and not just air. By contrast, for the undoped Li-NMC811, significant degradation was observed, with the I(003):I(104)peak intensity ratio dropping to ~0.7 upon water-soaking. Furthermore, even after stirring in water for 12 h, Zn-doped Li-NMC811 maintained its ‘layered’ structure, exhibiting a I(003):I(104)peak intensity ratio of ~0.9 (see Figure. 3), which further confirms its superior structural integrity in aqueous environments. The present invention also provides a process for preparing the cathode material of the present invention, said process comprising the steps of : (a) co-precipitating a transition metal hydroxide precursor from an aqueous solution of nickel sulphate, manganese sulphate, cobalt sulphate, and zinc sulphate in a ratio of 7.8: 1: 1: 0.2 to 7.5: 1: 1: 0.5, (b) chemically lithiating the transition metal hydroxide precursor obtained from step (a) using lithium hydroxide monohydrate in a molar ratio of 1:1.05 to 1:1.1, and (c) annealing the mixture under oxygen at 500-540°C for 4-5 hours followed by 780-800°C for 18-20 hours to yield said cathode material of Li(Ni₀.₈₋ₓZnₓMn₀.₁Co₀.₁)O₂ wherein x = 0.02–0.05. The transition metal co-precipitation can be performed in a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) at 50-55°C, pH ~10.8-11, and includes a complexing agent. The complexing agent can be selected from commonly used ammonia or other agents like citric acid, Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA). According to a further aspect of the present invention there is provided an electrode comprising a substrate coated with a slurry comprising the cathode material of the present invention, carbon black or carbon filler and a binder system containing carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). The electrode comprises 92-96 wt% cathode active material of the present invention, 2-5 wt% carbon black or carbon filler, 0.5-2 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose CMC and 0.5-2 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). The cathode active material : carbon black : CMC: SBR are combined in a preferred mass ratio of 94.4 : 4 : 0.6 : 1.0. The substrate can be selected from aluminum current collector foil or carbon-coated aluminum current collector foil. The electrode has an initial specific discharge capacity of approximately 170 mAh/g at C/10, retained up to ~90% after 50 cycles and ~82% after 100 cycles in a lithium half-cell. The electrode of the present invention can be prepared by forming a slurry in water with the present Zn-doped cathode material, carbon black, CMC, and SBR, followed by casting onto a carbon-coated aluminum foil and drying under vacuum. According to a further aspect of the present invention there is provided a lithium-ion battery cell comprising the electrode of the present invention, a lithium metal anode, a glass fiber separator, and an electrolyte. The electrolyte can be selected from 1 M LiPF₆ in a 1:1:1 mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) or 1 M LiPF6 in a 3:7 mixture of EC: EMC 3:7 can be used. In a preferred embodiment the lithium-ion battery cell is a Li ‘half’ cell comprising a bottom stainless steel case (1), followed by a first layer of cathode-active material coated cathode current collector (2), a second layer of glass fiber separator soaked in an electrolyte (3), third layer of Li metal foil as anode active material (4), fourth layer of stainless steel spacer (5) and fifth layer of stainless steel spring (6), with the entire assembly packed by the top stainless steel case (7). Furthermore, the ‘aqueous processed’ electrodes of the present invention prepared using carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) as binders in water-based slurry exhibited a high reversible specific capacity of ~170 mAh/g and excellent cyclic stability. The Zn-doped, ‘aqueous processed’ high Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide based cathodes in accordance with the present invention provides a viable cost-effective cathode class for the next-generation high-energy LIBs, with a health and environment friendly manufacturing approach. Advantages of the Invention • Enables NMP-free aqueous processing using water-based binders. • Achieves excellent air and water stability, improving handling and storage. • Delivers high specific capacity and cycling stability. • Supports sustainable and scalable high energy density LIB for various applications, including electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy storage, and portable electronic devices. The present invention is now illustrated by way of non-limiting examples. Example 1 The synthesis of modified high Ni-containing ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide cathode material was initiated with the preparation of the transition metal solution. Precursor Preparation The synthesis began with the preparation of a 2 M aqueous solution containing stoichiometric amounts of: • Nickel (II) sulphate hexahydrate (NiSO₄·6H₂O) • Zinc sulphate heptahydrate (ZnSO₄·7H₂O) • Manganese (II) sulphate monohydrate (MnSO₄·H₂O) • Cobalt (II) sulphate heptahydrate (CoSO₄·7H₂O) All precursors were sourced from Sisco Research Laboratories (SRL), India. The solution was stirred continuously at room temperature until clear and homogeneous. Co-precipitation Process A 4 M NaOH solution and a 1 M ammonia solution (prepared using deionized water) were simultaneously prepared. These three solutions—transition metal, NaOH, and ammonia—were continuously introduced into a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor (CSTR) under the following conditions: • Transition metal solution flow rate: 300 mL/h • Ammonia solution flow rate: 30 mL/h • Stirring speed: 1100 rpm • Temperature: 50°C • pH: Maintained at 11 • Reaction duration: 12 hours The resulting precipitate was a transition metal hydroxide precursor, which was then washed thoroughly, filtered, and dried at 60°C to eliminate residual moisture and impurities. Chemical Lithiation and Annealing The dried hydroxide precursor was mixed with lithium hydroxide monohydrate (LiOH·H₂O) in a molar ratio of 1:1.05 and ground uniformly. The mixture was then subjected to a two-stage high-temperature annealing process in a tube furnace under an oxygen-rich atmosphere (99.99% purity): • Stage 1: 540°C for 4 hours • Stage 2: 780°C for 18 hours Post-annealing, the product was cooled in an oxygen atmosphere to obtain the final Zn-doped high-Ni ‘layered’ Li-TM-oxide cathode active material. Example 2 Electrode preparation for a Li ‘half’ cell The electrode preparation for the Li ‘half’ cell involved an initial dry mixing process, where the cathode active material prepared by Example 1 was uniformly mixed with carbon black (Super P; from Alfa Aesar) as the conducting additive at 1000 rpm for 25 min to achieve a homogeneous mixture. Following this, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC; from Sigma Aldrich) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR; from Sigma Aldrich) were introduced as binders, and deionized water was used as the solvent. The components were mixed in a mass ratio of 94.4 : 4.0 : 0.6:1.0 (cathode active material : carbon black : CMC:SBR), ensuring uniform dispersion. After binder addition, the electrode slurry was mixed at 400 rpm to ensure uniform distribution. The slurries were tape casted onto a carbon-coated aluminum foil (Batsol). The coated electrodes were then dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 12 h. The dried foil was then calendared at 50 °C. The mass of the active electrode material was ~2.5 mg/cm2. Standard CR2032 coin cells were assembled in an Ar-filled glove box (having H2O and O2 levels < 0.1 ppm) with the as-prepared working electrode, metallic Li as the counter-cum-reference electrode, Whatman glass fiber filter (GF/D) as separator and 1 M LiPF6 in EC:DEC:DMC (1:1:1 by volume) as the electrolyte. Galvanostatic cycling runs were performed at a current density equivalent to C/10 (C-rate estimated considering theoretical cathode capacity as 200 mAh g-1) within a cell voltage window of 2.5–4.5 V. Example 3 Structural and Electrochemical studies X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis Both the undoped and Zn-doped Li-NMC811 showed well-ordered α-NaFeO₂-type layered structures with a rhombohedral space group (R3̅m). The intensity ratio of the (003) and (104) XRD peaks (I₍₀₀₃₎/I₍₁₀₄₎) was ~1.17 for the Zn-doped sample, confirming minimal cation mixing. Stability Under Air and Water Exposure • Air Stability: Zn-doped samples retained I₍₀₀₃₎/I₍₁₀₄₎ ~1.2 after 90 days; undoped samples degraded to ~0.84 within 7 days. • Water Stability: Zn-doped samples maintained a peak ratio of ~0.9 even after 12 hours of stirring in water; undoped samples dropped to ~0.7. Electrochemical Performance • First-cycle discharge capacity: ~170 mAh/g at C/10 • Capacity retention: o ~90% after 50 cycles o ~82% after 100 cycles These results confirmed that Zn-doping significantly improved moisture resistance and allowed for the successful use of aqueous electrode processing without compromising performance. Example 4 Doping Zn in NMC811 X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis Zn²⁺ was introduced as a dopant to reduce nickel migration in high-nickel layered Li-transition metal oxides (Li-NMC 811) and found to be air-stable for up to 90 days, as well as water-stable for 12 h. Zn-doping in Li-NMC811 is expected to play a critical role in determining the structural and electrochemical behavior, i.e., the effectiveness or detrimental aspect of Zn-doping. While optimized Zn-doping in the right lattice site may improve the structural stability, excessive Zn-incorporation may adversely affect the Li-ion mobility and the overall performance. When Zn-content is 2-5 mol%, I(003)/I(104) 1-1.2, which is indicative of reduced ‘cation mixing’ for this higher Zn2+-content when replacing Ni2+ in the Li-NMC811 lattice. By contrast, the mol% of Zn is increased to 10 in Li-NMC811 leads to a much lower I(003)/I(104) ~0.75, along with the introduction of impurity peaks corresponding to zinc oxalate hydrate and zinc oxide. Higher Zn doping level resulted in a lowering of this peak ratio and broadening of the reflections, indicating accrued ‘cation mixing’ and possible structural distortions. The XRD pattern of the 10 mol% Zn-doped Li-NMC811 also revealed the presence of impurity phases of zinc oxide and zinc hydrate, suggesting that it is beyond the solubility limit of Zn2+ in the Li-NMC811 lattice (see Figure 6). , Claims: 1. A lithium-ion battery cathode material comprising a Zn-doped high nickel-containing layered lithium transition metal oxide of the formula Li(Ni₀.₈₋ₓZnₓMn₀.₁Co₀.₁)O₂, where x ranges from 0.02 to 0.05, wherein the cathode material exhibits enhanced air and water stability. 2. The cathode material as claimed in claim 1, wherein the material retains a layered crystal structure with I(003)/I(104) XRD intensity ratio of ≥ 0.9 after being stirred in deionized water for 12 hours. 3. The electrode as claimed in claim 3, wherein said electrode comprises 92-96 wt% said cathode active material, 2-5 wt% carbon black or carbon filler, 0.5-2 wt% carboxymethyl cellulose CMC and 0.5-2 wt% styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). 5. The electrode as claimed in claim 3, said electrode having an initial specific discharge capacity of approximately 170 mAh/g at C/10, retained up to ~90% after 50 cycles and ~82% after 100 cycles. 6. A method for preparing the Zn-doped high nickel lithium transition metal oxide cathode material as claimed in claim 1, said method comprising: (a) co-precipitating a transition metal hydroxide precursor from an aqueous solution of nickel sulphate, manganese sulphate, cobalt sulphate, and zinc sulphate in a ratio of 7.8: 1: 1: 0.2 to 7.5: 1: 1: 0.5, (b) chemically lithiating the transition metal hydroxide precursor obtained from step (a) using lithium hydroxide monohydrate in a molar ratio of 1:1.05 to 1:1.1, and (c) annealing the mixture under oxygen at 500-540°C for 4-5 hours followed by 780-800°C for 18-20 hours to yield said cathode material. 7. The method as claimed in claim 6, wherein the transition metal co-precipitation occurs in a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) at 50-55°C, pH ~10.8-11, and includes a complexing agent. 8. The method as claimed in claim 7, wherein said complexing agent is selected from ammonia, citric acid, Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA). 9. A process of preparing the electrode as claimed in claim 3, said process comprising forming a slurry in water with the Zn-doped cathode material as claimed in claim 1, carbon black, CMC, and SBR, followed by casting said slurry onto a substrate and drying under vacuum. 10. The process as claimed in claim 9, wherein said substrate is selected from aluminum current collector foil or carbon-coated aluminum current collector foil. 11. The process as claimed in claim 9, wherein said cathode active material : carbon black : CMC: SBR are combined in a mass ratio of 94.4 : 4 : 0.6:1.0. 12. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT Extraction of Lithium and Cobalt Salts from Waste Lithium-Ion Batteries An eco-friendly hydrometallurgical process recovers lithium and cobalt salts from black mass derived from spent lithium-ion batteries. Following a mechanical black mass separation, lithium salts are recovered by water leaching and CO₂ or ammonium carbonate carbonation, while cobalt is extracted via DL-malic and succinic acid leaching followed by oxalic acid precipitation. The method achieves >90% recovery yields and ≥99% product purities using mild, biodegradable reagents and reduced environmental impact. Reference Fig 1
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of recycling or processing waste materials, in particular to a method for recycling waste lithium-ion batteries. More particularly it relates to hydrometallurgical recycling of spent lithium-ion battery. More particularly relates to extraction of cobalt and lithium salts from lithium-ion batteries. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Lithium batteries are energy storage devices that utilize electrochemical reactions involving lithium. These batteries are widely used due to their ability to efficiently store electrical energy, enabling power generation when and where it is needed. Among them, secondary (rechargeable) lithium batteries are of particular importance for energy storage applications. They offer high energy density, primarily due to lithium’s low atomic weight and high ionization energy. As a result, they have become the preferred power source for a wide range of portable electronic devices such as mobile phones, laptop computers, and digital cameras, as well as for electric vehicles (EVs). However, the increasing global demand for critical raw materials like lithium, cobalt, and nickel poses significant challenges for the future, particularly in terms of resource availability and sustainable sourcing. Industrial battery recycling processes are primarily classified into pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical methods. Pyrometallurgical processes typically aim to recover lithium, cobalt, and nickel from the cathode active materials. The process generally begins with the removal of non-metallic components such as polymer binders, electrolytes, and aluminum current collectors. Two major thermal routes include incineration and pyrolysis. Following thermal treatment, the remaining cathode material may be subjected to roasting or smelting. Smelting processes can also directly treat whole battery cells; however, this requires preconditioning to prevent hazardous reactions from volatile components. These pyrometallurgical methods are energy-intensive, produce hazardous effluents, and face challenges such as high capital investment, equipment corrosion, and substantial CO₂ emissions. In contrast, hydrometallurgical processes involve leaching the active materials using aqueous solutions, typically mineral acids like sulfuric acid in combination with reducing agents such as hydrogen peroxide. For example, US20170077564A1 discloses leaching with sulfuric acid and H₂O₂ for metal extraction from cathodes. These methods are generally characterized by lower energy consumption and minimal toxic gas emissions. However, they rely on corrosive reagents, pose occupational safety risks, and require complex multi-step purification protocols to selectively recover individual metals. Recent patent disclosures—such as US2025219177A1, US20220274841A1, WO2024171161A1, and WO2024059051A2—describe mineral acid-based leaching, organic acids, or deep eutectic solvents followed by solvent extraction or precipitation. European patents such as EP3517641A1 and EP3202929A1 propose modular mechanical pretreatment followed by acid leaching systems. While these methods achieve high metal recovery rates, they often involve strong acids, hazardous by-products (e.g., SO₂, HF), and costly neutralization and corrosion control measures. Accordingly, there is a need in the art for an improved recovery method that integrates mechanical black mass separation with mild organic acid leaching and CO₂ carbonation or ammonium carbonate crystallization. The invention disclosed herein provides such a continuous process, enabling the recovery of high-purity lithium and cobalt salts while minimizing environmental impact, operational hazards, and downstream purification challenges. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION The objective of the present invention is to provide a safe, efficient hydrometallurgical process to recover lithium and cobalt salts from spent lithium-ion battery black mass using biodegradable organic acids. It is another objective of the present invention to minimize environmental hazards and equipment corrosion compared to mineral acid processes. It is another objective of the present invention to achieve high recovery yields (>90%) and high product purities (>99%). Another objective of the present invention provides a process to recover lithium and cobalt salts using an economical effective method. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION This summary is provided to disclose the concepts related to a process for extraction of lithium and cobalt salts from lithium-ion batteries. This summary is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter nor is it intended for use in determining or limiting the scope of the claimed subject matter. In an embodiment, leaching is carried out for 45-90 minutes. In an embodiment, the leaching solution obtained is filtered to obtain the filtrate. In an aspect, leaching reactions with DL-malic acid are initially controlled by surface chemical reactions, leading to rapid dissolution within the first 10–15 minutes. After this, diffusion controls the process, providing stable and predictable kinetics, with moderate activation energies that balance process speed and selectivity. DL-malic acid forms stable complexes with transition metals, sometimes allowing better control of metal separation and purity compared to the broader solubility of metals in mineral acids In an aspect, the filtrate of cobalt malate is precipitated with aqueous oxalic acid to form the salt of cobalt; i.e. cobalt oxalate represented by the formula IIB: Reaction of Cobalt malate with Oxalic acid :-IIB In one aspect, the entire precipitation takes 3-4 hours. The present invention relates to an eco-friendly hydrometallurgy process to obtain cobalt and lithium with a purity of more than 99% and a recovery yield of more than 90%. The method employs leaching with a weak organic acid, specifically DL-malic acid, which enables the dissolution of critical metals while minimizing environmental hazards. Compared to conventional mineral acids, DL-malic acid offers the advantages of reduced toxicity, easier waste treatment, and a lower risk of harmful gas emissions. Experimental results demonstrate that DL-malic acid can achieve high leaching efficiencies, with cobalt recovery up to 94.3% and lithium recovery up to 98.9% under optimized conditions. • Li: ~98.9% • Co: ~94.3% • Ni: ~95.1% • Mn: ~96.4% These leaching efficiencies match or exceed those achieved using conventional mineral acids such as sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid, as demonstrated in various comparative studies. Furthermore, the ability to operate at lower acid concentrations not only minimizes reagent consumption but also extends equipment lifespan by mitigating corrosion-related degradation. After separating the black mass from Aluminium, steel and Copper, the mixture is dissolved in water by froth floating separation, where plastic is separated out. Then the mixture of Aluminium Steel and copper is dissolved into NaOH solution, where Aluminium is dissolved with evolution of hydrogen gas. The residual mixture contains Copper and Steel which is separated out by Magnetic roller. Lithium recovery reached 92% under similar conditions with a cobalt salt purity of 99.3% and lithium salt purity of more than 99%.
