patents.abstract: ABSTRACT SMART THERMAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERY MODULES The disclosed smart thermal management system comprises a cold plate thermally coupled between two lithium-ion pouch cells, containing a coolant channel filled with liquid coolant. A variable flow rate coolant circulation pump connected to the channel adjusts coolant flow based on battery conditions. Temperature sensors embedded on or near the cell surfaces provide real-time surface temperature data. A processor-based control module stores a trained model generated from thermofluidic simulations over parameters including C-rate, State-of-Charge, and heat generation, and uses a dynamic mapping model to predict future electrochemical load profiles. The control module receives real-time or forecast vehicle velocity data and generates time-resolved profiles of C-rate, State-of-Charge, and heat generation. Using these profiles, it computes a time-varying coolant velocity profile to keep battery surface temperatures under a predefined thermal safety threshold. The command interface dynamically adjusts coolant flow, minimizing auxiliary power consumption and mitigating thermal runaway risk throughout the operational period. FIGURE 2
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION: This invention relates to the field of electronics engineering and thermal engineering. Particularly, this invention relates to battery management systems and methods. Particularly, this invention relates to smart thermal management system for lithium-ion battery modules, capable of dynamically controlling coolant flow during both discharging and charging operations, including fast and ultra-fast charging conditions. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTON: Shift towards electric vehicles (EVs) from conventional internal combustion (IC) engine vehicles is due to tightening environmental regulations addressing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Rechargeable lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries have emerged as a preferred energy storage solution for EVs. However, Li-ion batteries’ performance, longevity, and safety are highly susceptible to variations in their operating temperatures. Inevitable temperature fluctuations in cells, influenced by environmental conditions and heat generation during charging and discharging processes, underscore a need for an effective Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS). This BTMS is crucial for maintaining optimal operating temperatures within a prescribed range to mitigate adverse effects including declination of cell performance and risk of thermal runaway. According to prior arts, various thermal management techniques are in practice, namely, air cooling, liquid cooling, hybrid cooling, phase change material-based heat sinks, heat pipes, spray, and immersion cooling to deal with the temperature excursions of the cell beyond a maximum permissible limit (Set Point Temperature, TSPT). Liquid cooling systems stand out among other cooling techniques due to their ability to enhance heat transfer effectively and adapt well to varying environmental and operational conditions. This effectiveness gradually established them as the prevailing choice for BTMS applications. Thermal performance of liquid cooled BTMS depends on inlet velocity and temperature of the coolant. Heat generation from any Li-ion cell depends on C-rate (rate at which the current is extracted from or supplied to the cell) and percentage of charge left in the cell (State of charge (SoC). At a constant C-rate, the heat generation from Li-ion cell increases non-linearly with increase in SoC. Similarly, at a constant SoC, the heat generation is a positive non-linear function of C-rate. As operating conditions of any electric vehicle varies continuously, either due to traffic or path of travel or charging protocol, heat generation from its Li-ion cell is also subject to change continuously in a non-linear trend. BTMS, with a constant flow rate of coolant, is capable of removing heat at a constant rate. However, supplying coolant to BTMS with a constant flow rate either overcools (consumes extra power than required) or undercools (may lead to thermal runaway of the cell) the battery pack. This issue becomes particularly critical during fast or ultra-fast charging, where high charging currents lead to elevated heat generation that can quickly exceed safe thermal limits. Given this, it is essential to identify minimum velocity of the coolant for every operating condition of the cell-whether under discharge or charging-such that the problems of thermal runaway and unnecessary consumption of power to run the pump can be solved, simultaneously. In prior art systems, coolant is typically circulated at a fixed or threshold-based flow rate, determined empirically or based on coarse thermal feedback. This static approach introduces several limitations: overcooling during low-demand phases, leading to unnecessary auxiliary power draw. undercooling during transient thermal surges in both driving and charging, risking safety violations. lack of adaptivity to real-world driving dynamics such as traffic variability, which affects power demand and heat generation non-linearly. Furthermore, heat generation in Li-ion cells is governed by complex electrochemical-thermal interactions, where power dissipation increases non-linearly with both C-rate and SoC. Prior art systems do not explicitly model or account for this non-linearity in their control logic, especially under high-current charging conditions. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a thermal management system that dynamically adjusts coolant flow in real time, with foresight into vehicle speed, charging / discharging C-rate, and SoC variations, to maintain thermal safety with minimal energy overhead. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION: An object of the invention is to provide a thermal management system which identifies minimum velocity of a coolant, for every operating condition of an associated battery / cell, such that problems of thermal runaway and unnecessary consumption of power (from the battery / cell) to run an associated coolant pump can be solved, simultaneously. Another object of the invention is to provide a thermal management system that dynamically adjusts coolant flow in real time, with foresight into vehicle speed, C-rate, and SoC variations, to maintain thermal safety with minimal energy overhead. A further object of the invention is to ensure safe and efficient thermal management during charging operations, including fast and ultra-fast charging, by predicting charge-induced C-rate trajectories and adjusting coolant velocity to prevent thermal overshoot while minimizing pump energy consumption. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION: According to this invention, there is provided a smart thermal management system for lithium-ion battery modules. Typically, this invention teaches an intelligent, predictive, and dynamically controlled liquid cooling system for Li-ion cells, which adapts coolant flow rates based on real-time and forecasted operating conditions, such as vehicular velocity, state-of-charge (SoC), and C-rate, to ensure thermal safety and improve energy efficiency during both discharging and charging operations. The present invention provides a Smart Thermal Management System (STMS) that adaptively controls the coolant flow rate within a liquid-cooled battery thermal management system based on predictive modeling of real-time and future vehicle dynamics vehicle dynamics and charging power input. The invention leverages: real-time and forecasted vehicular speed (e.g., via Google Maps traffic data), charging power and protocol information (e.g., CC–CV phases from the charging station) a computational model translating speed or charging power into C-rate and SoC variations, a pre-trained machine learning model, thermal simulations of a cold-plate-based BTMS (via Ansys CFD), and a control algorithm for computing minimum viable coolant velocity that ensures that cell surface temperature remains below a predefined safety threshold. The system outputs: a time-varying velocity profile for intelligent pump actuation, an optimized constant velocity value for fixed-flow systems, and an energy savings’ estimate comparing variable vs. constant flow. This results in: enhanced thermal safety, reduced power draw from the auxiliary cooling system, adaptability to diverse driving cycles and charging conditions, and improved safety during fast and ultra-fast charging by preventing thermal overshoot. According to this invention, there is provided a smart thermal management system for lithium-ion battery modules, said system comprising: a cold plate sandwiched, and thermally coupled, between two Li-ion pouch cells; a coolant channel, disposed within the cold plate, filled with a liquid coolant; a coolant circulation pump with variable flow rate capability connected to the coolant channel; temperature sensors embedded on or near the cell surface to measure surface temperature of said sells; a processor-based control module that computes flow rate commands to be delivered to said coolant circulation pump, said processor-based control module consisting, essentially, of: a non-transitory memory storing: a trained model generated from thermofluidic simulations over a multidimensional design space consisting of a group of parameters selected from a group consisting of C-rate, State-of-Charge (SoC), heat generation values, coolant inlet temperature, initial battery temperature, and maximum permissible battery surface temperature; a dynamic mapping model configured to convert operational data to corresponding future time-varying C-rate and SoC profiles; a predictive logic configured to: receive real-time or forecasted vehicle velocity data from a vehicle having said battery modules and having a navigation module; generate a time-resolved electrochemical load profile consisting of parameters being C-rate corelative to time, State-of-Charge correlative to time, and heat generation correlative to time; compute, via a model, a time-varying velocity profile of said coolant fluid required to ensure that predicted cell surface temperature remains below a predefined thermal safety threshold throughout an operational period; a command interface operatively connected to said coolant circulation pump and configured to transmit control signals that dynamically adjust coolant flow rate according to said velocity profile, wherein, velocity profile is a minimum viable velocity profile that ensures mitigation of thermal runaway while minimizing auxiliary power draw by said circulation pump under all operating conditions in the defined operational period within the defined parameter space. In at least an embodiment, said operational data consisting a parameter selected from a group consisting of vehicle velocity data, traffic prediction data, charging power profile, or charging protocol data. In at least an embodiment, said predictive logic for control of said coolant through said coolant channel, consisting of the steps of: acquiring a time series of predicted vehicle velocities from a navigation or traffic prediction system; computing a corresponding time series of electrochemical load parameters consisting of C-rate and State-of-Charge (SoC) by mapping said time series to electrical power demand-based drive dynamics and battery parameters; retrieve initial cell temperature, coolant inlet temperature, and a predefined maximum permissible surface temperature; applying said inputs to a trained model generated from thermal-fluid simulations to determine a mapping between said electrochemical load parameters and thermal response; determining predicted minimum coolant velocity profile such that the maximum cell surface temperature remains below said maximum permissible surface temperature; controlling said coolant circulation pump to track said predicted minimum coolant velocity profile; wherein said predictive logic mitigates overcooling and undercooling by accounting for non-linear thermal behavior of lithium-ion cells as a function of state-of-charge and C-rate. In at least an embodiment, the processor-based control module consists of a predictive logic configured to acquire predicted vehicle velocity data, convert said velocity data into corresponding electrochemical load parameters including C-rate and state-of-charge, retrieve coolant inlet temperature and permissible surface temperature limits, apply said inputs to a predictive thermal model, and determine a minimum coolant velocity profile required to maintain cell surface temperature below said permissible limit. In at least an embodiment, the processor-based control module consists of a C-rate computation sub-module configured to convert predicted current demand during operation of the battery into a time-resolved C-rate profile. In at least an embodiment, the processor-based control module consists of a C-rate computation sub-module configured to convert predicted current demand during operation of the battery into a time-resolved C-rate profile, in that, said C-rate computation sub-module consists of a discharging unit configured to determine vehicle tractive power demand from vehicle dynamics, convert said tractive power demand into corresponding battery power, determine battery current from said battery power and cell voltage, and compute a discharge C-rate value from said battery current and nominal cell capacity. In at least an embodiment, said processor-based control module consists of a C-rate computation sub-module configured to convert predicted current demand during operation of the battery into a time-resolved C-rate profile, in that, said C-rate computation sub-module consists of a charging unit configured to determine charging power from pack voltage and charging current, compute charge current from said charging power and pack voltage, and compute a charging C-rate value from said charge current and nominal cell capacity. In at least an embodiment, said processor-based control module consists of a C-rate computation sub-module configured with a unified C-rate profile encompassing charging and discharging conditions, said predictive logic being operable to seamlessly transitions between charging and discharging modes and to supply the resulting unified C-rate profile to said predictive logic of said processor-based control module. In at least an embodiment, said trained model is derived from a response surface trained on heat transfer simulations of a cold plate battery module, performed across C-rates ranging from 0.1C to 5C and coolant inlet temperatures from 15 °C to 35 °C, with maximum limit of the cells ranging from 20 °C to 40°C. According to this invention, there is provided a method for smart thermal management of lithium-ion battery modules, the method comprising: thermally coupling at least one lithium-ion battery cell to a cold plate having an internal coolant channel filled with a liquid coolant; circulating the liquid coolant through the coolant channel using a variable-speed coolant circulation pump; sensing cell surface temperature using one or more temperature sensors disposed on or near the battery cell; acquiring operational data including at least one of vehicle velocity, traffic prediction data, charging protocol, charging power profile, state-of-charge, coolant inlet temperature, initial cell temperature, and a predefined maximum permissible surface temperature; generating, from said operational data, a time-resolved electrochemical load profile including C-rate, state-of-charge, and heat generation correlated to time; applying said electrochemical load profile to a predictive thermal model trained on thermofluidic simulations over a multidimensional design space; computing, from said predictive thermal model, a minimum coolant velocity profile required to maintain the maximum cell surface temperature below said maximum permissible surface temperature throughout an operational period; and controlling said coolant circulation pump according to said minimum coolant velocity profile, wherein said method mitigates thermal runaway while minimizing auxiliary pump power draw relative to constant-flow cooling systems. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS: The invention will now be described in relation to the accompanying drawings, in which: FIGURE 1 illustrates variation of C-rate with State-of-Charge (SOC); FIGURE 2 illustrates design of this invention’s battery thermal management system; FIGURE 3 illustrates prediction of velocity profile for a given C-rate variation; FIGURE 4 illustrates prediction of constant velocity for a given C-rate variation; and FIGURE 5 illustrates percentage of energy saved in every cycle with variable velocity profile over constant velocity profile. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS: According to this invention, there is provided a smart thermal management system for lithium-ion battery modules. The present proposed technology identifies a time-varying velocity profile for a given time-varying operating set of conditions. In at least an embodiment, this invention’s Smart Thermal Management System (STMS) is designed, typically, for lithium-ion battery modules, particularly those used in electric vehicles. The system dynamically determines and applies a minimum coolant velocity profile required to maintain cell surface temperature below a predefined safety threshold (SPT), while minimizing auxiliary energy consumption by a coolant circulation pump. The Smart Thermal Management System (STMS) functions during both discharge and charging operations, ensuring effective thermal control under traction loads and during grid-connected or fast-charging conditions. The Smart Thermal Management System (STMS) consists of: Battery Module: One or more lithium-ion cells (pouch or cylindrical) arranged within a module, each equipped with embedded or surface-mounted temperature sensors. Cold Plate Assembly: Fabricated from a thermally conductive metal (e.g., aluminum alloy, thermal conductivity ≥ 200 W/m•K). Contains a serpentine or other optimized coolant channel geometry to maximize heat transfer uniformity. Positioned between adjacent cells to extract heat from both sides. Coolant Circulation System: Variable-speed pump capable of delivering coolant velocities between ~0.05 m/s and 0.3 m/s. Inlet and outlet ports connected to the cold plate channels. Coolant is typically water or a water-glycol mixture, selected for thermal performance and freeze protection. Processor-based Control Module: Embedded microcontroller or industrial computer. Interfaces with vehicle CAN bus and sensor inputs. Executes the prediction and control algorithms. Communicates with external navigation/traffic APIs (e.g., Google Maps) for speed forecasts, and with charging infrastructure for charging power data. In at least an embodiment, this invention’s Smart Thermal Management System (STMS) comprises a Data Acquisition and Pre-processing module coupled to the Processor-based Control Module. The processor-based control module receives and processes the following inputs: Discharge-related: Real-Time Vehicle Speed: From onboard sensors or navigation systems. Predicted Vehicle Speed Profile: Derived from traffic and route data over a specified prediction horizon. Charging-related: Charging Power Input: Measured from the charging station (slow, fast, or ultra-fast charging). Charging Protocol: Constant Current (CC), Constant Voltage (CV), or pulse charging profiles. Common inputs: State of Charge (SoC): From the BMS. Coolant Inlet Temperature: From thermistor/RTD at cold plate inlet. Initial Cell Temperature: From surface-mounted temperature sensors. Ambient Temperature: From environmental sensors. In at least an embodiment, this invention’s control module comprises a C-rate computation sub-module. The predicted current demand (discharge or charge) is converted into a C-rate profile as follows: In at least an embodiment, the C-rate computation submodule comprises a discharging unit configured for computations relating to discharging cycles. For Discharge: Tractive power demand: P_traction (t)= v(t)×F_total (t) Where, F_total (t)= m×g×C_r+1/2 ρ×C_d×A×v(t)^2+ m×g×sin(θ)+ m×a(t) Here, m is vehicle mass, g gravitational acceleration, Cr rolling resistance coefficient, ρ air density, Cd aerodynamic drag coefficient, A frontal area, θ road grade angle, and a(t) instantaneous acceleration. Battery power: P_battery (t)=(P_traction (t))/η_drive Where, η_drive is drive-train efficiency. Battery current: I(t)=(P_battery (t))/(V_cell (t)⋅N_s ) Where, V_cell (t) instantaneous cell voltage and N_s is the number of cells in series. C-rate: C-rate (t)=I(t)/Q_cell Where, Q_cell is nominal cell capacity in Ah. In at least an embodiment, the C-rate computation submodule comprises a charging unit configured for computations relating to charging cycles. For Charging: Charging power: P_charge (t)=V_pack (t)×I_charge (t) Where, V_pack (t) is pack voltage Charge current: I_charge (t)=(P_charge (t))/(V_pack (t) ) C-rate: C-rate (t)=(I_charge (t))/Q_cell This unified framework yields a future C-rate profile during both charging and discharging, which is supplied to the predictive thermal model. In at least an embodiment, this invention’s control module comprises a predictive thermal modeling sub-module. The STMS employs a hybrid approach combining precomputed CFD thermal simulations and machine learning. The model captures heat generation due to both discharge resistive losses and charge-induced side reactions, predicting the minimum coolant velocity to keep cell temperature below SPT. In at least an embodiment, this invention’s control module comprises a control algorithm. The control logic operates as follows: Acquire real-time and predicted operational data. Convert discharge/charge profiles into C-rate trajectories. Pass the C-rate profile and thermal parameters to the trained regression model. Predict the minimum required coolant velocity profile. Adjust pump speed accordingly. Update predictions periodically. This applies in driving (discharge) and charging (grid or fast charging) modes. In at least an embodiment, the control module, vide its control algorithm, is configured to be communicably coupled to a pump control mechanism for controlling pump operations in order to control coolant fluid flow. Typically, the control module, vide control algorithm, operates as follows: Data Acquisition and Pre-processing module: Collect real-time and predicted operational data (vehicle speed, charging power, SoC, temperatures). C-rate computation sub-module: Convert discharge or charge profiles into C-rate trajectories using the equations above. predictive thermal modeling sub-module: Pass the C-rate profile and thermal parameters to the trained regression model to predict the minimum coolant velocity profile. Pump control mechanism: Adjust the variable-speed pump to deliver the predicted velocity profile. Continuous Update: Periodically update predictions based on new sensor data and external inputs (e.g., traffic updates or charging protocol changes). This algorithm operates seamlessly during both driving (discharge) and charging (grid-connected or fast charging) modes, ensuring adaptability to diverse operational scenarios. FIGURE 1 illustrates variation of C-rate with State-of-Charge (SOC). According to a non-limiting exemplary embodiment, consider an electric vehicle is running on the road. Any maps’ application predicts future velocity of the vehicle depending on traffic on the path chosen by the maps’ application. The current invention uses this information about time varying vehicle speed (indirectly, variation of C-rate with SoC) and predicts a minimum velocity of the coolant that needs to be adjusted in future. The model also takes the information of inlet temperature of the coolant and the maximum allowable temperature (SPT) of the cell to identify the velocity profile that keeps the maximum cell temperature below SPT throughout the operation. As C-rate decides the power input to the electric vehicle, the future velocity of the vehicle is converted into the future C-rate variation with SoC based on the traffic data collected from maps associated with the vehicle. In this instance, please assume that the blue colour line in Fig 1 is the variation of future C-rate obtained from traffic data. Now, the aim is to predict the velocity of the coolant such that the maximum temperature of the cell should not reach the maximum allowable temperature limit (SPT). Please assume that the SPT for this demonstration is equal to 35 ˚C. In another non-limiting exemplary embodiment, consider the vehicle undergoing charging, such as fast or ultra-fast charging at a public charging station. The charging station provides information about charging power and protocol (for example, CC–CV profile). This information is used to compute a future C-rate trajectory during charging, in combination with SoC and pack voltage. The model then predicts the minimum coolant velocity required during the charging process to ensure that the cell temperature remains below the SPT. For instance, during the high-current CC phase, the coolant velocity is predicted to increase to prevent rapid thermal rise, while during the CV phase, the coolant velocity requirement decreases as the current tapers, thereby minimizing auxiliary pump energy consumption. FIGURE 2 illustrates design of this invention’s battery thermal management system. In at least at embodiment, the thermal management system comprises: a cold plate sandwiched between two Li-ion pouch cells, a serpentine coolant channel filled with a liquid coolant, a coolant circulation pump with variable flow rate capability, one or more temperature sensors embedded on or near the cell surface, a control module (hardware or software) that computes flow rate commands. The design depicted in Figure 2 shows a battery thermal management system (BTMS) considered in association with this invention in order to achieve cooling of a battery surface. The BTMS is comprised of cold plate/s (21) placed between two pouch cells (22a, 22b) and a serpentine coolant channel (23) filled with water. Reference numeral 24a refers to inlet of coolant and reference numeral 24b refers to outlet of coolant. Identification of the minimum velocity profile of the coolant for the given C-rate profile is the new innovation in this research. The control module receives inputs including: real-time or predicted vehicular speed, inlet coolant temperature, maximum allowable cell surface temperature, initial battery temperature, ambient temperature, battery pack state-of-charge. From this data, the C-rate profile is computed using a model that maps vehicle power demand (derived from speed and resistance characteristics) to the corresponding cell discharge current during driving, and maps charger power input (from the applied charging protocol, e.g., CC–CV) to the corresponding cell charging current during plug-in events.. This mapping is influenced by SoC-dependent internal resistance and voltage profile in both discharge and charging modes. The invention outputs: variable flow rate profile, constant flow rate, predicted maximum surface temperature, estimated pump energy savings (%) for variable vs. constant flow. FIGURE 3 illustrates prediction of velocity profile for a given C-rate variation. Figure 3 shows a velocity profile predicted by the current invention’s system to mitigate thermal runaway and overcooling, simultaneously. Figure 3 also depicts variation of temperature on the surface of the battery / cell for the predicted velocity of the coolant. It is clear from Figure 3 that the temperature on the surface of the cell is confined below 35 ˚C with the predicted minimum velocity of the coolant. FIGURE 4 illustrates prediction of constant velocity for a given C-rate variation. Figure 4 shows calculated constant velocity for the same given profile of C-rate mentioned in Figure 1. From Figure 4, it is clear that the model suggests to maintain constant velocity of 0.15 m/s throughout the operation to confine the surface of temperature of the cell below 35 ˚C. FIGURE 5 illustrates percentage of energy saved in every cycle with variable velocity profile over constant velocity profile. Figure 5 shows percentage of energy saved in each cycle. The final bar chart (Cycle-6) gives the average energy that can be saved in the entire operation by using the variable velocity over constant velocity of the coolant. This system’s invention predicts variable velocity profile, constant velocity, and percentage of energy saved for any combination of input parameter values in the ranges mentioned below. Input parameter Range C-rate 0.1 – 5 C Inlet temperature of the coolant 15 – 35 ˚C Initial temperature of the system 15 – 35 ˚C Maximum limit of the cell 20 – 40 ˚C Table 1: The possible range of input parameters for prediction of velocity profile. The electrochemical-thermal behavior of Li-ion batteries dictates that: at high SoC, the overpotential and internal resistance are higher, increasing Joule heating. C-rate determines current draw, which quadratically affects I2R losses. therefore, heat generation is highly non-linear and time-varying during both charging and discharging operations. By correlating real-time traffic and terrain conditions with expected vehicle speed, we forecast the future C-rate profile for discharging, and by correlating charging protocol data (e.g., CC–CV charging current, fast-charging events, and ambient inlet coolant conditions), we forecast the future C-rate profile for charging.. A trained regression model to predict just enough coolant flow to maintain thermal equilibrium. Unlike prior art, which either assumes fixed thermal loads or uses reactive temperature feedback, our system preemptively calculates the precise flow needed using predictive data and thermal models for both charging and discharging scenarios. Example Operational Scenarios Discharge case: An EV in mixed urban traffic (20–80 km/h). C-rate peaks during accelerations. STMS dynamically adjusts coolant velocity and keeps temperature below 35 °C. Charging case: Fast charging at 100 kW. C-rate ~2–3C depending on SoC and pack size. STMS increases coolant velocity during the high-current CC phase, then relaxes flow during CV taper, maintaining temperature below the SPT with lower pump energy than a fixed-flow system. Combined use case (charging + discharging): When an EV transitions directly from highway driving to a fast-charging session, STMS seamlessly switches from discharge-based C-rate prediction (traffic/terrain-driven) to charge-based prediction (protocol-driven). This dual-mode operation ensures safe cooling continuity across both energy delivery modes. According to a non-limiting exemplary embodiment, there is disclosed, further below, a demonstration for a drive profile. FIGURE 6 illustrates variation of C-rate against SoC. The smart and constant coolant velocity profiles and their respective maximum temperature variation of the cell corresponding to the above variation of C-rate against SoC are shown in Figure 7. The initial (Tint), inlet (Tinlet), and set point temperatures (TSPT) are fixed at 25, 20, and 35 °C, respectively. FIGURE 7 illustrate smart and constant coolant velocity profiles and their resulting cell temperature variations against SoC for C-rate profile shown in Figure 6. The smart and constant coolant velocity profiles (Figure 8a) and their respective maximum temperature variation (Figure 8b) of the cell corresponding to the C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 for different initial temperatures (Tint = 20, 25, 30 °C) are presented in Figure 8. The inlet (Tinlet) and set point temperatures (TSPT) are fixed at 20 and 35 °C, respectively. FIGURE 8 shows: a) smart and constant coolant velocity profiles, and b) resulting cell temperature variations against SoC for a C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 at initial temperatures (Tinitial) equal to 20, 25, and 35 °C. The smart and constant coolant velocity profiles (Figure 9a) and their respective maximum temperature variation (Figure 9b) of the cell corresponding to the C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 for different inlet temperatures (Tinlet = 16, 20, 24 °C) are presented in Figure 9. The initial (Tint) and set point temperatures (TSPT) are fixed at 24 and 35 °C, respectively. FIGURE 9 shows: a) smart and constant coolant velocity profiles and b) resulting cell temperature variations against SoC for a C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 at inlet temperatures equal to 16, 20, and 24 °C. The smart and constant coolant velocity profiles (Figure 10a) and their respective maximum temperature variation (Figure 10b) of the cell corresponding to the C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 for different inlet temperatures (Tspt = 30, 33, 38 °C) are presented in Figure 10. The initial (Tint) and inlet temperature of the coolant (Tinlet) are fixed at 18 and 18 °C, respectively. FIGURE 10 shows: a) smart and constant coolant velocity profiles and b) resulting cell temperature variations against SoC for a C-rate profile shown in Figure 6 with set point temperatures equal to 30, 33, and 38 °C. The percentage of energy being saved with a smart velocity profile over a constant velocity profile, for the above-considered variations in initial (Tint), inlet (Tinlet), and set point temperatures (TSPT), is shown in Figures 11a, 11b, and 11c, respectively. FIGURE 11 shows the percentage of energy being saved with a smart velocity profile over a constant velocity profile for a) different initial temperatures (20, 25, and 30 °C) at a fixed inlet and set point temperatures equal to 20 and 35 °C, respectively, b) different inlet temperatures (16, 20, and 24 °C) at a fixed initial and set point temperatures equal to 24 and 35 °C, respectively, and c) different set point temperatures (30, 33, and 38 °C) at a fixed initial and inlet temperatures equal to 18 °C. The proposed invention solves the dual technical problems of: preventing thermal runaway due to inadequate cooling during transient high-load periods in both charging and discharging conditions; avoiding energy waste due to unnecessary overcooling when thermal demands are low. This is accomplished by leveraging predictive modeling and real-time traffic integration for discharge and predictive charging protocol analysis for charge, to determine a coolant flow rate profile that is minimal yet sufficient, which is not obvious from existing BTMS techniques that rely on threshold-based cooling logic or empirical tuning. TECHNICAL ADVANTAGES: the proposed invention is simple and quick. this invention can be used to identify the velocity profile of the coolant for any custom driving cycle and popular European, Australian, Canadian, Indian, and US driving cycles. one more salient feature of this model is that it also calculates minimum constant velocity of the coolant for the given profile of C-rate, if one does not want to change the velocity of the coolant continuously as per prediction. this invention also calculates the percentage of energy saving by using variable velocity profile over constant velocity. this invention works seamlessly for both charging and discharging. this invention prevents thermal overshoot in high-power fast charging. this invention reduces auxiliary pump power in both modes. this invention improves battery safety and longevity by keeping cells below SPT. this invention is scalable to different applications beyond EVs. The TECHNICAL ADVANCEMENT, of this invention, mainly lies in the dynamic and predictive adjustment of coolant velocity in a Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) for Li-ion batteries, under both charging and discharging conditions, based on real-time and forecasted operating conditions, such as vehicular speed, C-rate, and state-of-charge (SoC). Unlike traditional liquid cooling systems that employ a static or threshold-based flow rate, the proposed system integrates data-driven modeling, thermal simulations, and machine learning to determine the minimum required coolant flow rate that maintains cell surface temperature within a safe and optimal operating range, while simultaneously minimizing auxiliary power consumption by the coolant circulation system. No known prior art in the domain of electric vehicle thermal management integrates forecasted vehicular telemetry, non-linear heat generation modeling, and machine learning-based flow rate prediction into a single, deployable system that works seamlessly for both high-load discharging and high-power fast charging. Therefore, the system embodies a significant technical advancement in terms of intelligence, efficiency, scalability, and thermal safety assurance in BTMS design. The system, of this invention, accounts for non-linear interdependence of SoC, C-rate, and heat generation rate during both charging and discharging; an electrochemical-thermal coupling that is often oversimplified in prior art systems. The system, of this invention, provides a multi-constraint optimization framework, where the primary constraint is the thermal safety limit and the objective is to minimize pump power while maintaining safe thermal operation. Unlike prior approaches that either overcool (excess power consumption) or undercool (leading to unsafe operation), this system computes a minimum viable coolant velocity profile across charging and discharging events that meets thermal criteria with minimal energy overhead. Inventive Step: The invention advances beyond prior art by combining predictive telemetry (traffic data, charging power), non-linear thermal modeling, and dynamic flow control into a unified system. Prior art systems rely on static or threshold-based cooling, which cannot adapt to real-time variations or anticipate future thermal demands. The energy efficiency achieved through variable velocity profiles addresses a critical gap in prior art, where constant-flow systems either overcool (wasting energy) or undercool (risking safety). The unified framework for charging and discharging ensures versatility, making the STMS applicable to diverse EV and stationary storage scenarios. The machine learning integration enables the system to generalize across different operating conditions, unlike empirical or rule-based approaches in prior art. The non-linear heat generation in Li-ion cells, driven by Joule heating and side reactions, was explained using electrochemical-thermal principles. This justifies the need for predictive modeling to handle dynamic C-rate and SoC variations. The hybrid machine learning approach ensures accurate prediction of coolant velocity, balancing computational efficiency with thermal precision. The integration of external data (e.g., traffic forecasts, charging protocols for grid-or fast-charging scenarios) enables proactive thermal management, reducing latency compared to reactive systems. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT "Tissue-Equivalent Dysprosium-Doped Lithium Calcium Silicate Thermoluminescent Phosphor and Method for Ultraviolet-C Radiation Dosimetry" The present invention relates to a thermoluminescent phosphor comprising lithium calcium silicate (Li₂CaSiO₄) doped with trivalent dysprosium (Dy³⁺), optimized for ultraviolet (UV) radiation dosimetry, particularly in the UV-C spectrum (200–280 nm). The phosphor, distinguished by a tetragonal crystalline structure, micron-sized irregular particles, and an effective atomic number (Zeff ≈ 14) for enhanced tissue equivalence, exhibits high thermoluminescent sensitivity, a stable glow peak at 180–200°C, and a linear dose response. It is synthesized via a solid-state reaction method involving mixing stoichiometric amounts of lithium carbonate, calcium carbonate, silicon dioxide, and dysprosium oxide in a 1:1 acetone-water medium, followed by calcination at 850°C. This process ensures high phase purity, compositional homogeneity, and scalability. The invention overcomes limitations in tissue equivalence, signal stability, and UV-C sensitivity, providing a robust, reproducible phosphor for precise dose quantification in personal dosimetry, environmental monitoring, and industrial UV sterilization.

[0037] The present invention discloses a process of synthesizing a novel thermoluminescent (TL) phosphor with the chemical formula Li₂CaSiO₄:Dy³⁺, abbreviated as LCS:Dy for dysprosium-doped lithium calcium silicate samples, specifically designed for ultraviolet (UV) radiation dosimetry, particularly in the UV-C spectrum (254 nm). The process is explained in detail with reference to the experimental setup, data, and tables. [0038] In an embodiment of the present invention, the process of synthesizing the thermoluminescent phosphor involves a solid-state reaction method using high-purity precursors, including lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃), calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), silicon dioxide (SiO₂), and dysprosium oxide (Dy₂O₃), to form the Li₂CaSiO₄:Dy³⁺ composition. [0039] In an embodiment of the present invention, the precursors may be selected from the group consisting of Li₂CO₃ (>99% purity), CaCO₃ (>99% purity), SiO₂ (>99.5% purity), and Dy₂O₃ (>99.9% purity), ensuring stoichiometric accuracy and optimal TL performance. [0040] In an embodiment of the present invention, synthesis aids, such as fluxes (e.g., boric acid), may be employed to enhance phase formation or reduce calcination temperature, without compromising the material’s dosimetric properties. [0041] In an embodiment of the present invention, the reaction medium is a wet mixing solution of 1:1 acetone-water, which facilitates uniform precursor distribution and homogeneity during mixing. [0042] In an embodiment of the present invention, X-ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis revealed that the compound crystallizes in the tetragonal structure, matching the standard Li₂CaSiO₄ phase (JCPDS 27-0290) with lattice parameters a = b = 5.05 Å, c = 6.64 Å, and crystallite sizes of ~50 nm for LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺, as shown in Table 1. [0043] In an embodiment of the present invention, the structure features micron-sized irregular particles (~1–10 μm) with high phase purity, as confirmed by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM) and Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX), as detailed in Table 2. [0044] In an embodiment of the present invention, the compound exhibits a prominent thermoluminescent response under UV-C irradiation (254 nm), characterized by a single, well-defined TL glow peak centered at ~190°C (±10°C), with high sensitivity and a quantum yield of ~80%, as detailed in Tables 4 and 6. [0045] In an embodiment of the present invention, the enhanced TL response is attributed to the incorporation of Dy³⁺ ions, which create stable trapping centers within the Li₂CaSiO₄ bandgap, as shown in Table 4. [0046] In an embodiment of the present invention, significant improvements in TL intensity (~1.5–2 times higher than CaSO₄:Dy), effective atomic number (Zeff ≈ 14, closer to human tissue Zeff ≈ 7.4), and signal stability (<5% fading over 30 days) provide evidence for superior dosimetric performance, as shown in Tables 4, 5, and 7. [0047] In an embodiment of the present invention, to demonstrate the potential application of the compound in dosimetry, a LCS:Dy-based personal dosimeter badge was fabricated, showing high sensitivity, reproducibility, and accuracy for UV-C dose quantification, as depicted in FIG. 3. [0048] Additionally, in an embodiment of the present invention, the material showed excellent linearity (~95% R²) in TL response across UV exposure times (5–60 min), suitable for personal and environmental monitoring, as detailed in paragraph [0089]. [0049] In an embodiment of the present invention, the material was synthesized across multiple batches, and phase purity was confirmed by XRD measurements, as shown in FIG. 1 and Table 1. [0050] In an embodiment of the present invention, ambient stability was investigated by performing TL measurements after exposure to room temperature conditions for 30 days, showing negligible fading (<5%), as detailed in Table 4. [0051] In an embodiment of the present invention, the prominent TL glow peak was observed under 254 nm UV irradiation, with LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺ exhibiting ~1.5–2 times higher intensity compared to undoped LCS or CaSO₄:Dy, as shown in FIG. 3 and Table 4. [0052] In an embodiment of the present invention, irradiation at 254 nm resulted in a strong TL signal with a sensitivity of ~1.5x that of CaSO₄:Dy, as detailed in Table 4. [0053] In an embodiment of the present invention, FESEM and EDX studies provided strong evidence of uniform particle morphology and homogeneous elemental distribution (Ca, Si, O, Dy), as shown in FIG. 2 and Table 3. Lithium was not detected due to its low Kα energy. [0054] In an embodiment of the present invention, application prototypes, such as UV dosimeter badges, were fabricated and tested, demonstrating superior TL properties for occupational safety and environmental monitoring, as shown in FIG. 3. [0055] In an embodiment of the present invention, synthesis of the Li₂CaSiO₄:Dy³⁺ phosphors was carried out using a solid-state reaction process. Stoichiometric amounts of precursors (Li₂CO₃, CaCO₃, SiO₂, Dy₂O₃) were weighed, mixed in a 1:1 acetone-water solution using an agate mortar and pestle for 1 hour, and calcined in an alumina crucible at 850°C for 10 hours in an air atmosphere. [0056] In an embodiment of the present invention, the calcined product was cooled slowly to room temperature and ground into a fine powder for further characterizations, ensuring consistency across batches. [0057] In an embodiment of the present invention, FIG. 1 displays the XRD patterns comparing the crystallinity of undoped LCS and LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺, showing sharper peaks for LCS:Dy, indicating high phase purity, as detailed in Table 1. [0058] In an embodiment of the present invention, FIG. 2(a–b) displays FESEM images of LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺ at 100 μm magnification, demonstrating irregular micron-sized particle morphology (~1–10 μm), as detailed in Table 2. [0059] In an embodiment of the present invention, FIG. 2(c) displays elemental mapping of LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺, confirming uniform distribution of Ca, Si, O, and Dy, as detailed in Table 3. [0060] In an embodiment of the present invention, FIG. 2(d) displays the EDX spectrum of LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺, verifying the presence of Ca (25 wt%), Si (15 wt%), O (50 wt%), and Dy (1–2 wt%), as detailed in Table 3. [0061] In an embodiment of the present invention, FIG. 3 displays the TL glow curves of LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺ under varying UV-C (254 nm) exposure times (5–60 min), showing a single peak at ~190°C with intensity increasing linearly (R² ≈ 0.99), as detailed in Table 4. [0062] In an embodiment of the present invention, the synthesis process was optimized by testing Dy³⁺ concentrations (0.5–5 mol%), with 1 mol% yielding the highest TL intensity, as shown in Table 4. [0063] In an embodiment of the present invention, the collected phosphors were ground into fine powder for characterizations, including phase purity analysis, morphological analysis, and TL measurements. The bulk phase purity was confirmed by XRD analysis, where the experimental XRD pattern for LCS:Dy matched well with the tetragonal Li₂CaSiO₄ structure (JCPDS 27-0290), as shown in FIG. 1 and Table 1. The material was synthesized on a lab scale (~5–10 g per batch) and is easily scalable for industrial production. [0064] In an embodiment of the present invention, the TL glow curves show a narrow, symmetrical peak at ~190°C, indicating well-defined trap depths, as detailed in Table 7. The peak position ensures low fading at room temperature. [0065] In an embodiment of the present invention, the linear dose response was validated by irradiating samples for 5, 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 minutes, with TL intensity increasing proportionally, as shown in Table 4 and FIG. 3. [0066] In an embodiment of the present invention, the material’s Zeff ≈ 14 was calculated using the Mayneord formula, significantly closer to human tissue (Zeff ≈ 7.4) than CaSO₄:Dy (Zeff ≈ 15.3), as detailed in Table 5. [0067] In an embodiment of the present invention, reproducibility was confirmed by synthesizing five batches, consistently yielding ~50 nm crystallite sizes and identical TL peak positions, as shown in Tables 1 and 4. [0068] In an embodiment of the present invention, environmental stability was assessed by performing TL measurements after exposure to room temperature conditions, showing negligible fading (<5%), as detailed in Table 4. [0069] In an embodiment of the present invention, the material’s TL sensitivity was ~1.5–2 times higher than CaSO₄:Dy under identical UV-C conditions, as shown in Table 4. R² (Linearity) 5 200 0.99 10 400 0.99 20 800 0.99 30 1200 0.99 45 1800 0.99 60 2400 0.99 [0076] Table 7 displays the TL kinetic parameters for LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺, showing stable traps with activation energy ~0.7 eV. | Table 7: TL Kinetic Parameters for LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺ | T₁ (°C) Tₘ (°C) T₂ (°C) τ δ ω μ = δ/ω Activation Energy (eV) Frequency Factor (s⁻¹) 170 190 210 20 20 40 0.50 0.70 2.0 × 10⁹ [0077] In an embodiment of the present invention, XRD patterns confirm the tetragonal structure of Li₂CaSiO₄:Dy³⁺, with LCS:Dy showing sharper peaks than undoped LCS, indicating higher phase purity due to effective Dy³⁺ incorporation, as shown in Table 1 and FIG. 1. [0078] In an embodiment of the present invention, FESEM images reveal that LCS:Dy phosphors consist of irregular micron-sized particles (~1–10 μm), with consistent morphology across batches, as shown in Table 2 and FIG. 2(a–b). Elemental mapping and EDX confirm uniform distribution of Ca, Si, O, and Dy, as shown in Table 3 and FIG. 2(c–d). The linearity (R² ≈ 0.99) ensures accurate dose quantification. [0080] In an embodiment of the present invention, the material’s Zeff ≈ 14 provides superior tissue equivalence compared to CaSO₄:Dy (Zeff ≈ 15.3), enabling accurate biological dose correlation, as shown in Table 5. [0083] In an embodiment of the present invention, the synthesis process reduces energy consumption by ~30% compared to alternative methods (e.g., sol-gel), measured at ~0.6 kWh/g vs. 0.9 kWh/g, as measured by energy meters during calcination at 850°C. [0084] In an embodiment of the present invention, comparative performance: LCS:1 mol% Dy³⁺ outperforms CaSO₄:Dy by ~1.5–2 times in TL intensity and offers better tissue equivalence, validated by XRD, FESEM, and TL data, as shown in Tables 1, 4, and 5. [0085] In an embodiment of the present invention, reproducibility: The process was repeated five times, consistently yielding LCS:Dy phosphors with ~50 nm crystallite size and ~80% TL efficiency, as shown in Table 1 and Table 4. [0086] In an embodiment of the present invention, environmental impact: The process reduces carbon footprint by using earth-abundant, non-toxic precursors, promoting sustainable production. [0088] Technical Advancements The invention is distinguished over prior art by integrating Dy³⁺-doped Li₂CaSiO₄ as a novel thermoluminescent phosphor for UV-C dosimetry, achieving: 1. Enhanced TL properties, including superior sensitivity (~1.5–2x CaSO₄:Dy), linear dose response (R² ≈ 0.99), and stable glow peak at ~190°C, surpassing conventional silicate-based phosphors. 2. Improved tissue equivalence through Zeff ≈ 14, closer to human tissue (Zeff ≈ 7.4) than CaSO₄:Dy (Zeff ≈ 15.3), enabling accurate biological dose assessment. 3. Uniform particle morphology and high phase purity through solid-state synthesis, ensuring scalable production. 4. Elimination of signal fading (<5% over 30 days) and high thermal stability (m.p. ~1700°C), promoting reliability in harsh environments. 5. Optimized performance for personal dosimeters, environmental sensors, and UV sterilization monitoring, addressing occupational safety and public health needs. , Claims:WE CLAIM 1. A thermoluminescent phosphor material for ultraviolet (UV) radiation dosimetry, comprising: a lithium calcium silicate (Li₂CaSiO₄) host lattice doped with trivalent dysprosium (Dy³⁺) ions at a concentration of approximately 1 mol% relative to calcium ions; characterized in that; the material exhibits an effective atomic number (Zeff) of approximately 14, providing improved tissue equivalence compared to conventional dosimeters; the material exhibits a thermoluminescence glow peak centered in the temperature range of 180°C to 200°C upon exposure to UV-C radiation at 254 nm; and The material is synthesized by a solid-state reaction method involving calcination of stoichiometric precursors at approximately 850°C for about 10 hours, yielding a high-purity tetragonal phase. 2. The thermoluminescent phosphor as claimed in claim 1, wherein the phosphor exhibits a tetragonal crystalline structure and micron-sized irregular particles for improved phase purity and compositional homogeneity. 3. The thermoluminescent phosphor as claimed in claim 1, wherein the phosphor is optimized for UV-C radiation detection in the wavelength range of 200-280 nm, providing reliable dose quantification for applications in personal dosimetry, environmental monitoring, and industrial safety. 4. A method for synthesizing the thermoluminescent phosphor as claimed in claim 1, characterized in that the method comprises: mixing stoichiometric amounts of precursors comprising lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃), calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), silicon dioxide (SiO₂), and dysprosium oxide (Dy₂O₃) in a wet medium to form a homogeneous mixture; calcining the mixture in an air atmosphere at a temperature and duration effective to form a crystalline phosphor with high phase purity; and cooling and grinding the calcined product into a fine powder; wherein the produces a high-purity, tissue-equivalent Li₂CaSiO₄:Dy³⁺ phosphor with reproducible thermoluminescent properties suitable for UV-C dosimetry, enhanced sensitivity, and reduced signal fading compared to conventional dosimeters. 5. The method as claimed in claim 4, wherein the wet medium is a solution of acetone and water in a ratio effective for uniform precursor distribution. 6. The method as claimed in claim 4, wherein the calcination is performed at a temperature range of 800-900°C for a duration of 8-12 hours to achieve reproducible synthesis and scalability. 7. The thermoluminescent phosphor as claimed in claim 1, wherein the phosphor provides a thermoluminescent glow peak in a temperature range suitable for signal stability and minimal fading, enabling accurate UV-C dose measurement. 8. A dosimeter device comprising the thermoluminescent phosphor as claimed in claim 1, wherein the device is configured for personal or environmental UV-C radiation monitoring, offering improved tissue equivalence and linear response for biologically relevant dose assessment.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT The Si-Cell is a high-density portable energy storage module built using a compact array of 21700 lithium-ion cells and an intelligent management system to overcome the capacity and durability limits of common portable power devices. The system’s electrical, thermal, and structural behavior was evaluated through detailed multidomain analysis, helping identify the most influential design factors such as cell layout, airflow pathways, and power distribution characteristics. An optimization framework was applied to refine these parameters, yielding a configuration that delivers higher energy output with reduced heat buildup and lower internal losses. The most effective design included a staggered cell arrangement paired with an improved cooling structure and a high-efficiency power conversion stage, resulting in better stability and longer operating life. A predictive soft-computing model was also used to verify performance trends, showing minimal deviation from simulated results. Overall, the refined Si-Cell design supports sustained high-power operation and offers a robust, portable alternative to traditional backup systems

PREAMBLE TO THE DESCRIPTION COMPLETE SPECIFICATION The proposed product is a portable solar generator designed to deliver high 2 energy density, multi-source charging flexibility, and compact form factor for household and outdoor power applications. It features a 3S configuration using high-performance 21700 lithium-ion cells, providing a total capacity of 150 Ah (≈1.7 kWh) while weighing only 12 kg, nearly 80% lighter than a traditional 150 Ah lead-acid inverter setup. The generator supports four charging methods — 1. Solar charging through an integrated MPPT controller, 2. USB Type-C (PD/Tach) input for fast charging, and 3. Car cigarette-lighter port charging using CCCV control. 4. AC outlet charging with appropriate adapter. A smart BMS (Battery Management System) ensures safe operation by monitoring voltage, temperature, and current, enabling balanced charging and discharging. The system also includes voltage regulators to maintain stable 5 V, 12 V, and 24 V outputs regardless of load fluctuations. For thermal safety, the generator uses an active trigger-based air-cooling system that automatically activates when temperature thresholds are reached, improving efficiency and extending lifespan. The design also supports battery expansion beyond the original capacity without restriction to proprietary modules, providing flexibility for users. With a mass-production manufacturing cost of around ₹25,000, the system offers a return on investment nearly 2.5× higher than traditional inverter systems due to its longer lifespan, faster charging, and higher energy efficiency. 3 Title Portable Multi-Source Lithium-Ion Energy Storage and Power Delivery System (Si-Cell) TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present invention relates to the field of portable renewable energy systems, specifically to a multi-source solar generator capable of serving as a complete household inverter replacement as well as a portable off-grid power supply. The system integrates solar, AC wall, and automotive charging inputs within a compact energy storage unit, featuring a high-frequency inverter that delivers 230 V AC output while maintaining low overall weight. It employs an ESP32 microcontroller for intelligent control of relays, MOSFETs, and userinteractive display functions. The energy storage module utilizes 21700 lithium-ion cells and an integrated radiator-assisted fan cooling system with non-conductive liquid thermal transfer, which activates automatically when required. The invention allows open battery expansion between 12 V and 30 V with independent BMS protection, offering a lightweight, high-efficiency, small-footprint solution characterized by multiple charging modes and high return on investment (ROI) compared to traditional inverter systems. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] The majority of existing household backup solutions rely on lead-acid batteries combined with transformer-based inverters, which are typically bulky, heavy, and inefficient, limiting portability and ease of use. Such systems often occupy significant space, impose high installation requirements, and suffer from reduced energy conversion efficiency, leading to higher operational costs over their lifespan. [0003] While some companies have introduced portable lithium-ion solar generators with multi-source charging capabilities, these products are often prohibitively expensive, especially for consumers in developing countries. In 4 addition, many commercially available systems lack USB Type-C input support, universal battery expansion options, and integration of smart BMS technologies, limiting flexibility, adaptability, and ease of maintenance. [0004] The motivation for the present invention is to promote the adoption of lithium-ion technology in India, thereby creating opportunities for high-density energy storage solutions within a compact and portable footprint. The invention aims to provide a cost-effective, lightweight, and efficient alternative to traditional inverter-based systems, without compromising performance or safety. Key technological gaps addressed by this invention include the limited research and development infrastructure in India for advanced portable lithium-ion generators, as well as challenges associated with importing or locally manufacturing high-quality components necessary for reliable operation. [0005] The proposed system provides approximately 80% weight reduction, multiple charging inputs, and smart battery management, while delivering a 2.5× higher return on investment compared to conventional lead-acid inverter systems. Furthermore, it achieves a similar retail cost to traditional inverters, making high-performance, portable energy storage more accessible to a broader range of consumers. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION [0006] The primary object of the present invention is to provide a portable lithium-ion solar generator that delivers high energy density while maintaining a lightweight and compact form factor, suitable for household, off-grid, and emergency power applications. [0007] Another object of the present invention is to offer a multi-source charging system, allowing energy replenishment via solar panels, AC wall input, Type-C PD and automotive cigarette-lighter ports, thereby ensuring flexibility and universal applicability. [0008] A further object of the present invention is to incorporate a smart Battery Management System (BMS) integrated with ESP32-based control, 5 enabling safe and efficient charging and discharging, voltage regulation across multiple outputs (5 V, 12 V, 24 V, 230 V AC), and interactive user monitoring. [0009] An additional object of the present invention is to provide battery expansion flexibility, supporting the integration of external lithium-ion modules with voltages between 12–30 V, given that the external battery has its own BMS for overdischarge protection. [00010] A further object of the present invention is to employ an adaptive active cooling system, using a radiator and non-conductive liquid with a temperature-triggered fan, which operates only when necessary, enhancing safety, efficiency, and lifespan. [0011] Another object of the present invention is to create a cost-effective and high-return energy solution, achieving approximately 80% weight reduction and 2.5× higher ROI compared to conventional lead-acid inverter systems, while remaining affordable and accessible for developing countries. SUMMARY [0012] The proposed portable lithium-ion solar generator integrates a high-energydensity 3-series 21700 battery pack providing approximately 150 Ah (≈1.7 kWh) capacity while maintaining a total system weight of around 12 kg, achieving an 80% reduction compared to conventional lead-acid inverter setups. The system supports multi-source charging, including solar input through an MPPT controller, AC wall input, and USB Type-C PD or automotive cigarette-lighter ports, enabling flexible and convenient energy replenishment. A smart Battery Management System (BMS) monitors voltage, current, temperature, and cell balance to ensure safe and efficient operation, while voltage regulators maintain stable outputs at 5 V, 12 V, 24 V, and 230 V AC. Thermal management is achieved using an active radiator-assisted fan and non-conductive liquid cooling, which activates only when required, improving lifespan and efficiency. The modular battery architecture allows expansion between 12–30 V with BMS protection, and the lightweight, small-footprint design, combined with high efficiency and multiple charging modes, results in approximately 2.5× higher ROI compared to traditional systems, making it an affordable and portable energy solution for household, off-grid, and emergency applications. 6 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS Figure 1. Final Product. 8 BRIE F DESCRIPTION OF THE TABLES 9 DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0013] The present invention relates to a portable lithium-ion solar generator capable of delivering high-density electrical power in a lightweight, compact, and modular form. The system integrates a 3-series 21700 lithium-ion battery pack of approximately 150 Ah capacity, providing a total energy output of about 1.7 kWh, with an overall system weight of around 8.3 kg. This configuration achieves nearly 80% weight reduction compared to traditional lead-acid inverter systems of equivalent capacity. The design emphasizes portability, expandability, and energy efficiency, enabling the unit to function as both a household inverter and an outdoor power source for off-grid or mobile use. [0003] The system employs a multi-source charging mechanism, allowing energy replenishment through solar panels (via MPPT controller), AC mains input, automotive cigarette-lighter port, and USB Type-C Power Delivery (PD) interface supporting up to 240 W programmable input. The inclusion of USB Type-C PD technology enables flexible charging from modern adapters and laptops, significantly improving mobility. The intelligent Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithm ensures optimum solar energy utilization, while the Constant Current–Constant Voltage (CCCV) charging protocol maintains cell safety and efficiency across all input sources. 10 [0004] At the core of the invention lies a Smart Battery Management System (BMS) equipped with ESP32-based microcontroller architecture for intelligent monitoring and control. This BMS manages cell voltage, current, temperature, and balancing, while simultaneously controlling solid-state relays and MOSFET arrays for precise load switching. The integrated digital display provides real-time data such as power input/output, temperature, battery health, and estimated runtime. This enhances user interaction and safety, reducing the risks of overcharge, deep discharge, or thermal runaway. The system incorporates a hybrid cooling structure comprising a liquidassisted radiator and an active fan that automatically activates only under elevated thermal conditions. The liquid used is non-conductive, ensuring electrical safety while efficiently dissipating heat from the battery modules and power electronics. This temperature-triggered cooling mechanism maintains operational stability and extends battery lifespan. The generator’s modular architecture supports universal battery expansion, allowing users to connect external lithium-ion modules rated between 12–30 V, provided they feature internal BMS protection. This flexibility permits scalability for diverse applications, ranging from small portable energy banks to full household power backup systems. The power regulation network utilizes high-frequency DC-DC converters and an inverter stage, generating stable 5 V, 12 V, 24 V, and 230 V AC outputs suitable for consumer electronics, appliances, and industrial tools. [0014] The entire power conversion process is optimized for efficiency, with high-frequency switching elements reducing transformer size and weight. The system achieves an energy conversion efficiency exceeding 92%, enabling longer operation per charge. The design’s compactness and reduced mechanical mass result in significant savings in material and transport costs, while maintaining high output performance. 11 [0015] Comparative analysis with conventional inverter systems demonstrates a 2.5× higher return on investment (ROI), due to lower maintenance, longer lifecycle, and improved portability. The total estimated manufacturing cost remains around ₹25,000, making it accessible for developing nations transitioning from lead-acid to lithium technology. This cost efficiency, combined with open expansion and smart control, positions the invention as a sustainable and scalable solution for distributed energy systems. [0016] The integration of ESP32 IoT connectivity further allows optional wireless monitoring, firmware upgrades, and fault diagnostics. This enables predictive maintenance and real-time analytics on battery health and power consumption. The modular software design supports integration with renewable energy microgrids, allowing it to act as both a standalone generator and a node in smart energy networks. [0017] The invention, therefore, introduces a next-generation portable energy solution, combining high-density lithium technology, adaptive cooling, multisource charging, and universal battery compatibility within a single lightweight system. It aims to replace bulky lead-acid inverter systems with a more efficient, intelligent, and eco-friendly power generator, promoting sustainable energy independence for homes and remote regions alike.
