patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR FABRICATING A MULTI-LAYERED BINDER-FREE ANODE ARCHITECTURE FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES A binder-free multilayer electrode for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries is disclosed, comprising a pre-cleaned copper current collector on which an active tin oxide (SnO₂) layer (A) is deposited via radio-frequency magnetron sputtering, to a thickness below 100 nm, followed by a controlled post deposition heat treatment, which includes calcination process, followed by a surface coating of an ultra-thin ZnO protective artificial SEI layer (T) of thickness less than 20 nm via thermal atomic layer deposition . A series of repeating composite layers (L), each consisting of an SnO₂ film immediately succeeded by an ALD ZnO layer, are sequentially added to form a multi-layered structure represented as ((A+T) + n·L) with n being the number of composite layers. The present invention relates to the field of energy storage systems, providing a system and method for fabricating a light-weight multi-layered binder-free anode architecture with high reversible specific capacity and volumetric capacity, along with scalable areal capacity via scalable active mass loading capability for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FORM 2 THE PATENTS ACT 1970 (39 of 1970) & THE PATENTS RULES, 2003 COMPLETE SPECIFICATION [See section 10 and rule 13] Title: A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR FABRICATING A MULTI-LAYERED BINDER-FREE ANODE ARCHITECTURE FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES APPLICANT DETAILS: (a) NAME: INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY INDORE (b) NATIONALITY: Indian (c) ADDRESS: Khandwa Road, Simrol, Indore – 453552, Madhya Pradesh, India PREAMBLE TO THE DESCRIPTION: The following specification particularly describes the nature of this invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. A SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR FABRICATING A MULTI-LAYERED BINDER-FREE ANODE ARCHITECTURE FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention generally relates to the field of energy storage systems, and more particularly to a system and method for fabricating a light-weight multi-layered binder-free anode architecture with high reversible specific capacity and volumetric capacity along with scalable areal capacity (via scalable active mass loading capability) for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries aimed at enhancing electrode stability, and reducing charge-transfer resistance, for a wide range of applications including flexible and portable electronics, wearable health monitors, implantable medical devices, smart cards, and IoT sensors, portable consumer devices (e.g., digital cameras, smartwatches, laptops), automotive cells, and integrated micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) based technologies. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Energy storage devices play a crucial role in integrated electronic systems. With the increasing demand for flexible and portable electronics—such as wearable health monitors, implanted medical devices, electronic skins, smart cards, and IoT sensors—the need for miniaturized energy storage solutions has become more significant. In this regard, thin-film Li-ion micro-batteries have attracted considerable research interest due to their potential to enhance energy density (and power density for a given energy density), as well as to offer high-rate capability in various applications. Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have revolutionized energy storage, enabling the widespread adoption of portable electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and renewable energy storage systems. However, despite their high energy density and efficiency, LIBs face significant challenges that hinder their long-term performance. The significant challenges which remain in the fabrication process of LIB electrodes, needs to be addressed. Firstly, typical fabrication techniques in the art incorporate binders, conductive additives (like for the case of typical pasted electrode preparation method) to secure active materials to current collectors. The presence of such inactive materials causes adverse effect in performance of the battery by reducing the energy density. Furthermore, the existence of binders or other inactive components emerges issues like weak interaction and interface problem between binder and electrode material causing self-aggregation of active materials and hence reduced battery performance. Secondly, one critical issue that arises in the conventional electrodes of rechargeable LIBs is the instability of the electrode-electrolyte interface, because of repeated charge and discharge cycles, parasitic side reactions, and structural degradation that contribute to significant capacity fading and reduced cycle life. The gradual degradation of the electrode–electrolyte interface, combined with the presence of inactive mass from additives, further diminishes overall energy density. To achieve longer cycle-life of active electrode (delivering high specific capacity), these challenges are required to be resolved. In this regard, possibility of introduction of beneficial artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer (or protective layer/buffer layer) on electrodes towards formation of a stable interface that suppresses continuous electrolyte decomposition and buffers the volume changes during cycling thereby maintaining structural integrity and longer cycle life have been explored in various literature. Further complicating the situation, experiments and practical implementations have revealed several drawbacks associated with established methods. In view of the above, another approach involving the fabrication process for typical “binder-free” electrodes, where no binders, conductive agents, or other additional inactive components are used results in improved energy density by reducing the effective weight of the LIB. This method also offers distinct advantages such as safe operation over a wide temperature range, compatibility with flexible substrates, and ease of integration into microdevices. Moreover, the drive for eco-friendly and sustainable green technology has underscored the significance of binder-free thin-film batteries employing safer materials for superior recyclability and reduced environmental impact. However, attempts to increase electrode thickness without binders frequently result in poor adhesion to current collectors, reduced electrical connectivity, and increased susceptibility to mechanical failure. Thus, despite several advantages, significant challenges remain in the fabrication of binder-free electrodes. These include achieving compatibility between the electrode and current collector materials (with a focus on electrode thickness and interfacial structure), which is essential for ensuring proper adhesion and forming a stable wetting layer of entire electrode material on the current collector hence a good electrical conductivity at the electrode-current collector interface. Good electrical conductivity at the electrode–current collector interface is paramount. To achieve a longer cycle life for the active electrode while delivering high specific capacity, it is necessary to resolve these challenges. In this regard, the introduction of an artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) or protective buffer layer has been posited as a promising solution. Such a layer would help form a stable interface that suppresses continuous electrolyte decomposition and buffers the volume changes during cycling, thereby maintaining structural integrity and extending cycle life. This approach is particularly critical for achieving both high energy density and long-term battery performance in next-generation portable and miniaturized electronic devices. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION Object of the invention is to provide a binder‐free, multi-layered anode architecture for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries that maximizes the effective active material loading by eliminating binders, conductive additives, and other inactive components, thereby enhancing both the specific capacity and overall energy density along with good stability/cycle life, rate performance and coulombic efficiency. An object of the invention is to provide a binder-free, multilayered anode architecture for lithium-ion batteries that maximizes effective active material loading by eliminating binders, conductive additives, and other inactive components. The anode employs high–mass-density active materials, thereby significantly enhancing volumetric capacity in addition to improving specific capacity and overall energy density. The architecture further delivers good electrochemical stability, long cycle life, high rate performance, and excellent coulombic efficiency. Another object of the invention is to offer an innovative multi-layered electrode design comprising an initial active SnO₂ layer (A) with a controlled post-deposition heat treatment, followed by an ultra-thin ZnO protective layer (T) deposited via atomic layer deposition, and further repeating units (L) with interfacial ZnO buffers that enables increased mass loading while preserving strong adhesion with the current collector (i.e., each layer, L, consists of one SnO2 layer along with a ZnO buffer-layer coating). Yet another object of the invention is to provide an electrode featuring engineered interfacial layers where the insertion of ultra-thin ZnO layers acts as both an artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and a mechanical buffer, improving the interfacial contact between the successive SnO₂ layers and the Cu current collector, thereby reducing Li-ion diffusion resistance and charge-transfer resistance. A further object of the invention is to deliver a novel thin-film deposition approach utilizing RF magnetron sputtering for SnO₂ and thermal ALD for ZnO that affords nanometer-scale precision in controlling the film thickness and morphology ensuring that each layer contributes optimally to overall capacity without compromising electrical conductivity or mechanical integrity. Another object of the invention is to enable significant reduction in interfacial resistances by engineering graded interfaces that not only facilitate rapid Li-ion transport but also sustain high-rate electrochemical performance during prolonged cycling. Yet another object of the invention is to achieve a scalable electrode design wherein the overall capacity (or the scalable areal capacity) can be enhanced by increasing the number of multi-layer units without leading to deleterious effects on adhesion or structural stability. A further object of the invention is to ensure robust mechanical stability and long cycle life by mitigating the stresses associated with volume changes in conversion-type and alloying-type anode materials through an alternating layering approach that distributes mechanical stress uniformly across the electrode. Finally, another object of the invention is to provide a high-performance anode design particularly suited for advanced portable and miniaturized electronic applications by combining the benefits of binder-free architecture, precise interfacial engineering, and optimized nano-scale thin-film deposition techniques to overcome the inherent limitations of conventional lithium-ion battery electrodes. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention is described in the following sections by various embodiments. However, it should be understood that the invention can be implemented in various forms and is not limited to the specific embodiment provided herein. In the context of the present disclosure, it should be understood that the described embodiments in this section are put forth for illustrative purposes only. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that various modifications, adaptations, and alternative designs may be employed without departing from the scope and spirit of the invention. Accordingly, the present invention should not be limited to the specific embodiments illustrated herein, but rather should be construed according to the claims and description that follow. Embodiments of the present invention provide a binder-free multilayer electrode for a rechargeable lithium-ion battery that comprises a copper current collector; an active layer of tin oxide (SnO₂) deposited directly on the copper (Cu) current collector by radio-frequency (RF) magnetron sputtering wherein the active layer is maintained at a thickness below 100 nm after optimization of the growth parameters via RF magnetron sputtering system; employing consecutive controlled post-deposition heat treatment, which includes calcination process as well (denoted as system A); an ultra-thin protective layer of zinc oxide (ZnO) deposited on the active layer by atomic layer deposition (ALD) wherein the protective layer is maintained at a thickness below 20 nm (ultra-thin optimized ALD grown layer has been denoted as T), hence, the ultra-thin protective/buffer layer coated A system (SnO2 based system on Cu current collector) has been denoted as system (A+T); and a plurality of repeating composite layers sequentially deposited on the base structure, each composite layer comprising a SnO₂ film immediately followed by an ALD-deposited ZnO layer, and each such layer denoted as L, so that the overall multilayered structure is represented as ((A+T) + n·L), with n, being an integer denoting the number of layers (L) employed on top of (A+T) system . The technical advantages of this structure include the maximization of the effective active material mass, an increase in specific capacity and areal capacity, and a reduction in electrode weight by eliminating binders and other inactive additives which leads to enhanced energy density. Additionally, the interleaved multilayer design overcomes the poor adhesion issues inherent in simply thickening the SnO₂ film; by partitioning the active material into multiple layers with ultra-thin interfacial ZnO buffers, the design ensures robust adhesion, reduced Li-ion diffusion resistance, and enhanced charge-transfer kinetics critical for high-rate performance and cycling stability. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, a pre-cleaned copper current collector is employed to form a smooth substrate, and deposition parameters such as RF sputtering power, gas composition, and process pressure are precisely controlled to deposit a tin oxide active layer with a thickness maintained below 100 nm. Immediately thereafter, a post-deposition heat treatment, including calcination, is applied to optimize the nano-crystallinity and surface morphology of the SnO₂ layer, thereby enhancing its adhesion to the substrate (the system denoted as A). Additionally, an ultra-thin ZnO protective layer (T) is conformally deposited on the SnO₂ layer by ALD, and further the ZnO layer acts as an artificial solid electrolyte interface (SEI) that both minimizes parasitic reactions with the electrolyte and serves as an interfacial buffer to aid the adhesion of subsequently deposited layers. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, improvement in areal capacity (or in enhanced active mass loading) is achieved by sequentially depositing a plurality of repeating composite layers (L), each comprising a SnO₂ film followed immediately by an ultra-thin ALD-deposited ZnO layer, so that the overall multilayer design, designated as ((A+T) + n·L), where n being the number of layers. Additionally, the ZnO layers between successive SnO₂ films serve as interfacial buffers that not only improve adhesion between the active layers but also contribute their own theoretical capacity to the overall electrode. The repeating multilayer design, ((A+T) + n·L), allows the overall electrode thickness to reach beyond the critical threshold while maintaining structural integrity and ensuring significantly reduced Li-ion diffusion and charge-transfer resistances. This engineering approach effectively addresses the conventional degradation and delamination issues encountered during high active mass loading. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the precise thin-film deposition techniques using RF magnetron sputtering for SnO₂ and ALD for ZnO enable nanoscale control over the film thickness and morphology. Furthermore, maintaining each SnO₂ layer below 100 nm and each ZnO layer below 20 nm ensures that the multi-layered composite electrode displays high specific capacity (Approximately 1650 mAh g-1 at 50 cycles, for the total electrode of thickness exceeding 300 nm, with n<5), high volumetric capacity (exceeding 10,000 mAh cm-³), and enhanced areal capacity (about 0.36 mAh cm-2) with high coulombic efficiency (about 98-99%), reasonably good rate-performance (300 mA g-1), capacity retention (exceeding 90%) and thus stability/cycle life (Figures 1 and 2). Additionally, the engineered interfaces lower the SEI resistance from approximately 10 Ω to about 4.5 Ω and reduce the charge-transfer resistance by over 40% (as compared for A and A+T electrode systems in Figure 3). Similarly for the multilayered electrode, ((A+T) + n·L), of thickness exceeding 300 nm, the SEI resistance and overall charge transfer resistance are reduced by over 50% and 70% respectively compared to uncoated single-layer thick SnO₂ films, thereby enhancing the overall electrochemical kinetics and stability during high-rate charge-discharge cycles. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the multi-layered electrode is further integrated into a complete battery configuration, such as a coin cell assembly. In this embodiment, the fabricated binder-free electrode is combined with a lithium metal counter/reference electrode, a LiPF₆-based electrolyte, and a PP/PE/PP separator. Additionally, the carefully engineered interfacial design leads to improved cycling stability where the assembled cell exhibits capacity retention of more than 90% after 50 cycles at a current density of 300 mA g-1, with a high specific capacity of 1650 mAh g-1. The holistic design, which includes precise substrate preparation, controlled thin-film deposition, and sequential layer assembly, effectively overcomes conventional limitations by optimizing active mass loading, reducing electrode resistance, and ensuring uniform and robust adhesion throughout the multilayer structure. Thus, the embodiments of the present invention collectively disclose a novel binder-free, multilayer electrode architecture that not only provides an increased energy density and improved specific capacity along with layer-number dependent scalable areal capacity, but also ensures long-term cycle stability and high-rate performance in lithium-ion batteries. The disclosed structure, fabrication process, and integrated assembly present significant technical advancements over conventional electrode designs and offer a versatile and scalable approach for future high-performance energy storage systems. (b) Cycle performance along with the coulombic efficiency plot of the multilayered electrode system at a current density of 300 mA g-1. The electrode shows significantly high electrochemical performance exhibiting high specific capacity of about 1650 mAhg-1 at 50 cycle (equivalent volumetric capacity is more than 10,000 mAhcm-3) and about 1442 mAhg-1 at 100 cycle (equivalent volumetric capacity is more than 9,500 mAhcm-3) and above, at a reasonably good rate capability (300 mAg-1) in LIB application. (c) Cross-sectional FESEM image of the multilayered electrode system with scale bar, indicating thickness of the electrode on the current collector. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention is subsequently described herein using various embodiments. Throughout this description, the term 'may' is used in a permissive sense, indicating the potential to, rather than in a mandatory sense, indicating a requirement. Additionally, the words 'a' or 'an' signify at least one, and the word 'plurality' signifies 'one or more' unless otherwise specified. Moreover, the terminology and phraseology employed herein are solely for descriptive purposes and should not be construed as limiting in scope. Terms such as 'including', 'comprising', 'having', 'containing', or 'involving', and their variations, are intended to be broad and encompass the listed subject matter thereafter, as well as equivalents and additional subject matter not explicitly mentioned, and should not be interpreted as excluding other additives, components, integers, or steps. Similarly, the term 'comprising' is considered synonymous with the terms 'including' or 'containing' for applicable legal purposes. The present invention relates to a binder‐free multilayer electrode architecture for rechargeable lithium‐ion batteries. The invention employs precise thin‐film deposition techniques and interfacial engineering to create an electrode that comprises an active tin oxide (SnO₂) material deposited on a copper current collector, followed by post deposition heat treatment, coupled with a conformally grown ultra-thin zinc oxide (ZnO) protective layer, and further sequential deposition of a plurality of repeating composite layers, each comprising a SnO₂ film followed immediately by an ultra-thin ALD-deposited ZnO layer, delivering multilayer design ((A+T) + n·L). The ZnO layer acts as an artificial solid electrolyte interface (SEI) that both minimizes parasitic reactions with the electrolyte and serves as an interfacial buffer to aid the adhesion of subsequently deposited layers. The electrode is designed to overcome limitations associated with conventional binder‐based electrodes by eliminating inactive additives and by implementing a multi-layered structure that maintains strong adhesion between active layers and the current collector while enabling enhanced active mass loading. An embodiment of the present invention further increases the specific, volumetric and areal capacities of the battery by utilizing a repeating composite structure represented as ((A+T) + n·L), where n is the number of layers. The present invention relies on fabrication of high-performance light-weight, binder-free multi-layered electrode (act as anode in full cell) with better stability/longer cycle-life for rechargeable LIBs, introducing compatible electrode system involving ultra-thin artificial SEI layer and simultaneously the incorporation of intermediate ultrathin protective buffer layer. Specifically, our invention relies on the strategy, by developing multi-layered electrode system introducing ultra-thin buffer layers (in between two consecutive layers of active electrode materials) in addition to protective ultra-thin artificial SEI layer at the electrode surface, to increase the active mass loading of high specific capacity material without using any binders, conductive polymers or any other additional inactive components in developing light-weight, high specific capacity, high and scalable areal capacity (by increasing layer-number, in the multilayered electrode), stable electrode with long cycle-life, high energy density and rate performance for rechargeable LIB. Furthermore, while the multi-layered binder-free electrode, has high specific capacity (as mentioned above), the constituents of the electrode material also have a high mass-density (SnO2 based system with ultra-thin ZnO buffer layer) and thus exhibits a high volumetric capacity, which overall leads to a light-weight, smallest size electrode to provide a given total capacity (or areal capacity) in LIB applications. The process and the resulting product both are protected under the present invention. In one embodiment, an active layer (A) comprising tin oxide is deposited onto a pre cleaned and polished copper current collector by radio-frequency magnetron sputtering. The deposition parameters, including sputtering power, gas composition, working pressure, deposition time and substrate temperature, are carefully controlled so that the active SnO₂ layer exhibits a thickness maintained below 100 nm. The thin active layer not only ensures high specific capacity due to the direct deposition of SnO₂ (without any binders, conductive polymers or any other additional inactive components) in lithium storage but also guarantees proper adhesion to the current collector. The thin film formation is further supported by a controlled post-deposition heat treatment, including a calcination step, which optimizes the crystallinity and surface morphology of the SnO₂ film (A). Subsequent to the formation of the active SnO₂ layer, an ultra-thin protective layer (T) comprising zinc oxide is conformally deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD). In one embodiment, the ZnO layer is deposited using thermal ALD with conditions optimized to achieve a conformal coating that uniformly covers the SnO₂ surface. The thickness of this ZnO layer is maintained below 20 nm to function as both an artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and an interfacial buffer. In this manner, the ultra-thin ZnO layer serves to reduce the Li-ion diffusion resistance and the charge-transfer resistance while simultaneously enhancing the mechanical adhesion between the active material and successive layers. In another embodiment, a plurality of repeating composite layers (L) is sequentially deposited on the (A+T) base, thereby providing a highly scalable multilayer architecture. Each composite layer (L) comprises a fresh SnO₂ deposition immediately followed by an ALD-deposited ZnO coating. The repeating layering of SnO₂ and ZnO not only ensures that the overall electrode thickness can be reliably increased, exceeding 300 nm in total but also maintains the inherent specific capacity of the active material by preserving optimal film adhesion even at higher thicknesses. The present design thereby eliminates the need for binders and conductive additives, resulting in an electrode with a higher effective mass fraction of the active material and improved energy density while reducing overall electrode weight. Importantly, the scalability of this multilayer approach is a key advantage: it allows for systematic augmentation of the active mass loading by simply increasing the number of multilayer units (n), without compromising the electrode's mechanical integrity or electrochemical performance. Each ZnO buffer layer in the repeating composite sequence plays a dual role by mediating interfacial stress and contributing its own theoretical capacity, which further supports the achievement of scalable areal capacity. This design strategy ensures that the electrode system may be easily tailored to meet the capacity requirements of various applications, ranging from portable electronics to electric vehicles while maintaining high performance and reliability throughout the scaling process. An embodiment of the present invention also contemplates the integration of the fabricated multilayer electrode into a complete battery configuration. In one such embodiment, the electrode may be assembled in a coin cell along with a lithium counter/reference electrode, a standard LiPF₆-based electrolyte and a separator composed of a polypropylene-polyethylene-polypropylene (PP/PE/PP) trilayer. This integration allows the electrode to deliver high reversible capacity and cycle stability over prolonged cycling. The designed interfaces within the multilayer structure further minimize the lithium-ion diffusion resistance and contribute to lowering the charge-transfer resistance, which ensures improved battery performance at high current densities. Collectively, these advantages result in an electrode system that delivers exceptionally high electrochemical performance while maintaining long-term structural and interfacial stability, thereby addressing several critical limitations of conventional lithium-ion battery electrodes. The binder-free configuration ensures that nearly the entire electrode mass actively participates in lithium storage, leading to substantially higher specific, volumetric, and areal capacities than slurry-cast electrodes that contain electrochemically inactive binders and conductive additives. Direct thin-film contact between the active material and the current collector along with the desired morphology further minimize ohmic losses and promotes efficient electron transport, which is particularly beneficial under high-rate charging and discharging conditions. In addition, the incorporation of ultra-thin ZnO interlayers enhances electrode durability and cycle life by stabilizing the electrode–electrolyte interface and accommodating the large volume changes associated with tin oxide during repeated lithiation and delithiation. These ZnO layers act as artificial SEI components that suppress continuous electrolyte decomposition, reduce irreversible capacity loss during initial cycles, and prevent mechanical delamination of the active material. As a result, the electrode maintains strong interfacial adhesion and consistent electrochemical performance over extended cycling, even at increased active mass loadings. The multilayer architecture further contributes to improved safety and thermal reliability. Uniformly deposited, conformal layers minimize localized current density hotspots and reduce the likelihood of mechanical fracture or short-circuit formation. The stable interfacial chemistry promoted by the ZnO buffer layers also lowers the risk of uncontrolled side reactions, thereby enhancing operational safety across a broad temperature range. Moreover, the ability to systematically scale the electrode thickness and active mass loading through a controlled repetition of the composite layer sequence enables superior performance at high current densities without compromising mechanical integrity. Short lithium-ion diffusion paths within each thin active layer, combined with reduced charge-transfer resistance at engineered interfaces, allow for rapid lithium transport and efficient kinetics. This makes the electrode particularly well suited for high-power applications that require fast charging and high-rate capability. Taken together, these features position the present invention as a robust, versatile, and technologically advanced electrode platform capable of meeting the demanding requirements of next-generation rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. The invention offers a compelling combination of high energy density, long cycle life, scalable manufacturability, and enhanced safety, making it adaptable to a wide range of applications, from miniaturized and flexible electronics to large-format energy storage and electric mobility systems. In an alternative embodiment, the method of fabricating the multi-layered electrode further comprises sequential steps starting with substrate preparation, followed by RF magnetron sputtering of the SnO₂ layer, a post-deposition heat treatment to enhance crystallinity and adhesion, and subsequent ALD of the ZnO layer to obtain the (A+T) system. Following these steps, additional multilayer stacks (each comprising an SnO₂ film deposited under controlled conditions and an immediate ZnO buffer layer deposited by ALD) may be applied to build up the overall active mass loading. Each deposition step is monitored using characterization techniques such as field emission scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive X-ray analysis so that the layer thickness, morphology and interfacial integrity comply with the required parameters. In another embodiment of the invention, variations in deposition parameters may be implemented to fine-tune the structure and properties of the electrode. For instance, varying the sputtering power and gas flow rates during the SnO₂ deposition or altering the ALD precursor pulse durations may be used to optimize film thicknesses and surface uniformity. Such variations are contemplated to ensure that the final electrode structure not only exhibits high capacity (with a specific capacity approaching 1650 mAh per gram and a volumetric capacity exceeding 10,000 mAh per cubic centimeter) but also demonstrates reduced Li-ion diffusion resistance and lowered charge-transfer resistance, thereby enabling enhanced battery performance even under high current demands. An embodiment of the present invention provides significant benefits over existing electrode technologies. The integration of binder-free designs with a multilayered configuration permits higher active mass loading while eliminating the drawbacks associated with inactive binder and conductive additives. Additionally, the ultra-thin ZnO layers confer both artificial SEI protection and interfacial buffering, which mitigate mechanical stress and minimize the degradation of electrode–current collector adhesion during extended cycling. This layered architecture, combined with the precise thin-film techniques, yields an electrode structure that is capable of high-rate performance, extended cycle life and improved safety across a wide operating temperature range, thereby rendering it suitable for next-generation portable and miniaturized electronic devices. A key advantage of the present invention is its inherent scalability, enabled by the modular and repeatable multilayer electrode architecture. The electrode design allows the active mass loading to be increased in a controlled and predictable manner by simply varying the number of repeating composite units (n) in the ((A+T) + n·L) structure, without altering the fundamental material system or deposition methodology. Each additional multilayer unit contributes incrementally to the overall capacity while preserving strong interfacial adhesion and mechanical integrity. This layer-by-layer scalability ensures uniform thickness control, reproducibility, and structural robustness even as the total electrode thickness exceeds several hundred nanometers. Consequently, the architecture can be readily adapted for a wide range of applications, from thin-film microbatteries requiring low thickness to higher-capacity cells demanding increased active material loading, all while maintaining consistent electrochemical performance. The present invention further provides a significant enhancement in volumetric capacity compared to conventional binder-based electrodes. By eliminating inactive components such as polymer binders and conductive carbon additives, the electrode volume is almost entirely occupied by electrochemically active materials. Furthermore, the use of densely packed SnO₂ (the material, which is inherently having high mass density of about 6.95 gcm-3) layers deposited directly onto the current collector showing high specific capacity (approximately, 1650 mAh g-1at 50 cycle) ensures efficient utilization of the available volume for lithium storage. In addition, the conformal ZnO interlayers introduce minimal volumetric penalty while contributing both interfacial stabilization and supplementary lithium storage capability. The resulting SnO2 active mass based dense, multilayer thin-film architecture enables volumetric capacities substantially exceeding those achievable with slurry-cast electrodes, making the invention particularly advantageous for space-constrained energy storage applications. The electrode architecture of the present invention also exhibits enhanced mechanical, interfacial, and electrochemical stability during repeated charge–discharge cycling. The ultra-thin ZnO layers function as interfacial buffer layers that accommodate the volume changes of tin oxide associated with lithiation and delithiation, thereby reducing stress accumulation and preventing cracking, delamination, or pulverization of the active material. Furthermore, the ZnO layers act as artificial solid electrolyte interphase layers that stabilize the electrode–electrolyte interface, suppress continuous electrolyte decomposition, and minimize irreversible capacity loss. The strong adhesion between successive layers and the current collector ensures long-term structural integrity, leading to improved capacity retention, reduced impedance growth, and sustained electrochemical performance over extended cycling, even at high current densities and elevated active mass loadings. The Invention is further described with the help of non-limiting examples: Example 1: Utilizing tin-oxide (SnO2) based multi-layered electrode system involving ALD grown buffer layer in between i.e., ((A+T) + n.L), where n, is the number of layers employed on top of (A+T) system, and each layer (L) consists of one SnO2 layer along with a ZnO buffer-layer coating. In this way, the total electrode thickness was achieved of above 300 nm (which is more than the threshold thickness of SnO2 layer (which is about 100 nm or less) on Cu current collector), which enable to achieve simultaneously high active electrode mass loading along with high specific capacity and thus high areal capacity, in addition to the stability or high-capacity retention at larger cycle. It should be noted that the areal capacity of the electrode may be increased further, by increasing the layer number of the multi-layered electrode, following the process established in this invention. This methodology (involving designed multi-layer electrode on Cu current collector) itself, and followed by the product development of high-performance binder-free electrode for rechargeable LIBs (which has potential to be applicable for other metal-ion batteries also), has not been reported earlier to the best of our knowledge. The novelty of the developed product lies in its overall superior performance, which has resulted from the novel process established under this invention, involving the incorporation of the ultra-thin artificial SEI layer (or protective layer) of thermal ALD grown zinc-oxide (ZnO) onto the interface designed post deposition heat treated SnO2 based electrode on Cu current collector. Furthermore, such ALD grown ZnO layer act also as an efficient conformal buffer coating between consecutive layers of active SnO2 materials, in formation of a plurality of repeating composite layers (L), which was sequentially deposited on the (A+T) base, in developing stable binder-free multi-layered efficient electrode with high active mass loading. While this efficient protective layer provides a beneficial interface for the electrode with the electrolyte, and simultaneously plays an important role in interface designing for developed multi-layered electrode (i.e., binder-free thicker system with desired high mass loading via designed multi-layer formation), yielding a largely reduced Li-ion-diffusion-resistance in the SEI layer, RSEI (more than 50% reduction) and charge transfer resistance, Rct (more than 70% reduction) in comparison to the uncoated thick binder-free single layered SnO2 based system on Cu current collector, the combination of these resistance values is also lower in comparison to the reported study in the literature. The thoughtful choice of the compatible ultrathin coating material as artificial SEI at the surface of the electrode or as interfacial layers in the multilayered SnO2 based electrode (on Cu current collector), ensures that it also contributes to the overall capacity /areal capacity (as ZnO itself has a theoretical capacity of about 987 mAh g-1) of the electrode (instead of increasing weight of the overall electrode as inactive material) (instead of enhancing weight of the electrode only as inactive component, causing poorer energy density). The designed process via optimization of the composition of the compatible artificial protective SEI layer/buffer layer coating on to the active electrode layer, layers’ thicknesses, suitable interfaces, desired nano-crystallinity/structural properties, surface morphology, compositional configuration through thoughtful selections, control and engineering of deposition technique, growth parameters (including deposition temperature), and choice of current collector, helps to increase the active electrode mass loading with stability, and thus enhances the areal capacity with high specific capacity, rate capability and cycle-life, by producing a high-performance light-weight, binder-free multilayered stable nano-structured SnO2 composite based electrode with designed interfaces along with Cu current collector. This optimization process was achieved through extensive research towards the fabrication of a multilayered binder-free electrode system in achieving the high stable total capacity with long cycle life for practical applications. Example 2: The design and fabrication of the novel electrode were conducted following the steps below: (I). Active tin-oxide (SnO2) based system for the binder-free electrode with the desired interface and surface morphology was formed by deposition of SnO2 film on Cu current collectors (denoted as system A), after optimization of the growth parameters via RF magnetron sputtering system and employing consecutive controlled post-deposition heat treatment, which includes calcination process as well. A series of systems were prepared within the range of 10 to few hundred nm of SnO2 film thickness, by varying the growth parameters, in achieving the optimum thickness (below 100 nm, as obtained) along with the desired morphology and interfacial structure of the deposited film on Cu current collector ensuring the requisite proper adhesion, thus exhibiting the consistent promising electrochemical performance (via GCD, CV) (as discussed in the previous sections about the issues related to the threshold thickness of the deposited film on the current collector, based on the material properties and interfaces). (Different current collectors were also tested for the similar system). (II) In next step, ultra-thin protective layer coating of zinc-oxide (ZnO) of optimal thickness (below 20 nm, as obtained), with appropriate structure, interface and morphology was employed via thermal atomic layer deposition (ALD) technique using optimized growth parameters (ultra-thin optimized ALD grown layer has been denoted as T), onto the developed SnO2 based system on Cu current collector (A). Hence, the ultra-thin protective/buffer layer coated A system (SnO2 based system on Cu current collector) has been denoted as system A+T. The next step details the development of desired multi-layered electrode system. We employed the similar ALD-grown optimized ZnO coatings as an efficient conformal buffer layer in fabrication of stable binder-free multi-layered SnO2 based efficient electrode system with high active mass loading, as described below in step-III. (III) The multilayered thin film systems were thoughtfully designed and fabricated utilizing the findings and outcomes of the electrochemical performance of the artificial SEI layer coated SnO2 based high specific capacity stable electrode on Cu current collector. Our multi-layered electrode system was developed by growing sets of designed ZnO buffer-layer coated SnO2 layer (where each such layer denoted as L), on base A+T system. Thus, overall multi-layered electrode system has been represented as ((A+T) + n.L), where n, is the number of layers (L) employed on top of A+T system. (Just to be precise, each layer, L, consists of one SnO2 layer along with a ZnO buffer-layer coating). In this way, in multi-layered system, more than 300 nm electrode (binder-free) thickness was achieved (where for direct single-layer deposition, the threshold thickness of SnO2 layer on Cu current collector is below 100 nm, to achieve the consistent high specific capacity, as that of the thinner films), which enable to achieve simultaneously high active electrode mass loading along with high specific capacity and thus high areal capacity, in addition to the stability or high-capacity retention at larger cycle. It should be noted that the invention also established the process for scalable high areal capacity (or total capacity) of the electrode which can be increased further, by increasing the layer number of the multi-layered electrode, following the process established in this invention. In this light-weight binder-free multi-layered electrode system, the ALD grown ultra-thin ZnO coating plays role as compatible protective artificial SEI layer on top surface of the electrode providing beneficial interface for the electrode with the electrolyte, and also was employed as efficient interfacial buffer layer coating between two consecutive layers (of high specific capacity SnO2 active material) in developing stable multi-layered electrode system for enhanced active mass loading, and thus the enhanced areal capacity along with high energy density and long cycle life (as mentioned above) [It should be noted that (A+T) and L are different since the interface for (A+T) system is with Cu current collector (with appropriate designed interface and morphology), whereas L (which involves ultrathin ZnO coated thin SnO2 layer, i.e., each layer (L) consists of one SnO2 layer along with a ZnO buffer-layer coating) has the interface with consecutive SnO2 layer only. The ion-transport mechanism and electrical conductivity are very much dependent on the requisite interface, so these two systems have been defined separately as (A+T) and L.] This methodology (involving designed multi-layer electrode on Cu current collector) itself, and followed by the product development of high-performance binder-free electrode for rechargeable LIBs (which has potential to be applicable for other metal-ion batteries also), has not been reported earlier to the best of our knowledge. (IV) At each step, mentioned above, the developed electrodes were characterized in-depth with relevant techniques (such as Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM) with Energy Dispersive Analysis of X-rays (EDAX) and elemental mapping, X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), UV-Vis spectroscopy etc.) and examined for their electrochemical performances using GCD, CV and EIS (for rechargeable LIB application). Electrochemical performance of the fabricated working electrode was studied in coin-cell (CR2032 coin-type cells) battery, where Li is used as reference and counter electrode (in full cell configuration the novel electrode work as anode in rechargeable LIB). We used standard LiPF6 based electrolyte and polypropylene (PP) separators in these rechargeable Li-ion batteries. The CR2032 coin-type cells were assembled in argon-filled glovebox (MBRAUN UNIlab Plus, Germany). The galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) cycling tests of these coin-cells were conducted using CH Instrument, battery testing systems (CHI423B and 8-channel NEWARE BTS4000 Battery Testing System were also utilized for this purpose), at current densities of 300 mA g-1, at room temperature. Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) was conducted using electrochemical workstations at a scan rate of 0.05 mV sec-1. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted using electrochemical workstation (CHI423B), applying a sine wave with an amplitude of 5.0 mV over the frequencies from 105 Hz to 0.05 Hz. The performances of these coin-cells with the fabricated novel binder-free working electrodes for rechargeable Li-ion batteries were analysed and systematically correlated with their combined effect of film thickness (for SnO2 layer and ZnO buffer-layer or artificial SEI layer coating), structure, nano-crystallinity, surface-morphology, compositional configuration (through elemental analysis) and suitable designed interface. Such characteristics/properties of the electrodes are largely dependent on overall synthesis process/parameters, and material selection (including compatibility of the coating material) based on their intrinsic physical, electronic and electrochemical properties. Such extensive research helped to tune the system for optimization and controlling these key features/properties to achieve the most promising binder-free electrode which exhibit the best performance. Example 3: While simultaneous enhancement in areal capacity of the electrode system is achieved (about 0.36 mAh cm-2 for multi-layered electrode ((A+T) + n.L) at 50 cycle for n<5) without compromising the high specific capacity, based on the enhanced active electrode mass loading through development of stable multi-layered electrode. This indicates the formation of stable multi-layered electrode, through its holistic participation (as active mass) to contribute to the overall electrochemical performance, in rechargeable LIB application. It should be noted that simply by increasing the film thickness (indefinitely) of the deposited electrode material on the current collector may not help to increase the active electrode mass loading (i.e., the mass which will be able to actively contribute to the total electrochemical capacity of the electrode system), due to the fact that higher the thickness of the deposited film, lower the average attractive van der Waals interactions between entire thicker film and the current collector, which results in decreased adhesion of the electrode material with the current collector and thus introduces poor electrical conductivity at the electrode-current collector interface. As a result, the overall electrochemical performance gets compromised. Thus to grow an efficient binder-free thin-film batteries where active electrode material grows directly on a current collector, it is crucial to ensure excellent adhesion capability of the entire electrode material on current collector, hence a good electrical conductivity at the electrode-current collector interface. In view of the above discussion, it is shown in Figure 4 that simply enhancing the thickness of electrode material, cannot fulfil the purpose of enhancing active mass loading, thus will not allow to achieve the same specific capacity and thus will not provide the higher areal capacity. Even such electrode system, with low level of stability, with similarly grown single SnO2 layer of about 150 nm (i.e., larger than the observed threshold SnO2 thickness on Cu current collector) causes low cycle life of the battery along with the low specific capacity, in comparison to the novel multi-layered SnO2 based electrode (involving intermediate ultrathin buffer-layer coating) under this invention, which holds even much higher thickness of SnO2 (more than 300 nm altogether), as discussed above and is evident from Figure 4 for the results. There are several applications for our binder free, light weight multi-layered electrode with high specific capacity and higher active mass loading capability, thus capable of delivering high total capacity along with high energy density in rechargeable Li ion battery, such as implanted devices in the medical field like pacemakers, digital cameras, smartwatches, laptops, electric vehicles, and many more. Some of them are as mentioned below: i) Implantable and wearable medical devices, such as pacemakers, biosensors, neurological stimulators, and drug delivery systems, require compact, long-lasting power sources. The designed artificial SEI coated stable light-weight binder-free multi-layered electrode system, under this invention, provide high specific capacity and high volumetric capacity, along with high scalable areal capacity (or total capacity), mechanical stability, and precise layer control, allowing for safe, long-term energy delivery in restricted geometries (light-weight and small-size electrode system). ii) The rechargeable metal-ion batteries with such designed artificial SEI coated stable multi-layered electrode system (as established under this invention), well suited for space applications where high energy density, light-weight, restricted size construction and flexibility are required. The multilayer design enhances the mechanical robustness during battery cycling, improving long term operation in space conditions. iii) The LIBs with the designed artificial SEI coated stable binder-free, light-weight multi-layered electrode system, under this invention, providing high specific capacity and high volumetric capacity, along with high scalable areal capacity, mechanical stability, have the potential have the potential to be utilized in high-performance electric vehicle (EV) cells, enhancing energy density, cycle life, and safety through sophisticated electrode designs. Furthermore, the multilayer structures improve lithium storage capacity while lessening the stress caused by volume changes during cycling. These beneficial configurations, established under our invention, can be incorporated into layered electrodes for electric vehicle cells, resulting in better energy density and rate capabilities. iv) Modern electronics are becoming progressively smaller and more power intensive. Devices such as smart watches, wireless earphones, health monitors, IoT sensors, and integrated micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) need miniaturized batteries with high areal capacities, fast charge–discharge rates, and excellent cycling stability. The stable light-weight binder-free electrode system, under this invention, delivering high specific capacity, high volumetric capacity, along with high scalable areal capacity (or scalable total capacity) via suitable multilayered architecture with appropriate compatible protective coating, provides benefits such as high scalable areal capacity, mechanical integrity, design flexibility (including benefits of light-weight and small-size electrode) and safety, can serve as excellent candidates for powering portable microelectronic devices. Comparison of the present Invention over the existing technologies: Numerous efforts have been made to investigate novel high-capacity electrode materials in order to replace the standard graphite electrodes, which has a de-lithiation potential of approximately 0.3 V (vs. Li/Li+) [Ref.1] and a low theoretical specific capacity of 372 mAh g-1. Several materials have been studied as high-capacity anodes over the last two decades, including alloying-type metals like Sn, Al, Si, and Ge that can deliver capacities greater than 1000 mAh g-1 at potentials of about 0.5 V, and conversion-type transition metal oxides (MOx) like Co3O4, Fe2O3, and CuO that have capacities of about 800 mAh g-1 when de-lithiated at potentials > 2.0 V. [Ref.2] Among these, tin oxide (SnO2) has garnered a lot of interest because of its high gravimetric capacities at moderate operating potentials.[Ref.3] However, the following problems mostly prevent SnO2 from reaching its full potential. Commonly observed pulverization issues associated with the SnO2 based electrodes, [Ref.4] leading to a sharp capacity loss, compromising the stability of the electrode, and thus performance of the overall battery. The low conductivity of SnO2 is also one of the reasons for the pulverization problem. In this regard, it should be noted that most of the published report with general SnO2 based electrode in LIB, presented the specific capacity only up to 100cycles (based on the sharp fall in the specific capacity with increasing cycle number or low-capacity retention). [Ref.5-8] In the field of light-weight binder-free electrodes having higher side of theoretical specific capacity (i.e., above 1000 mAh g-1), most of the reported systems suffer either from low capacity retention (i.e., below 85% retention at 50 cycles in comparison to the stable capacity at the initial cycles, i.e, low stability, causing capacity fading with increasing cycle number, which leads to short cycle-life) [Ref.9-12] or low active mass loading (i.e., less electrode film thickness, about 100nm or lesser, which leads to a low areal capacity of the electrode, which limits the use of such electrodes for the practical purpose) [Ref.13-15]. Another issue with some of these systems is the low-rate capability (about 50 mA g-1) [Ref.9,16-19]. Details of the references are provided below: [1] M. N. Obrovac and V. L. Chevrier, Chem. patents.abstract: The disclosure relates to a composite solid electrolyte (CSE) for a battery in various formats including a freestanding CSE separator, electrode-CSE laminate, current collector-CSE laminate, or CSE-based mixed ionic-electronic conductor (MIEC) electrode. The disclosure also relates to the methods of making composite solid electrolytes and batteries therewith. A CSE is disclosed having at least one polymer; at least one lithium salt; a solvent plasticizer; at least one inorganic additive particle; a substrate; and one or more liquid or solid additives. A method of making a CSE is disclosed as providing, as a liquid slurry, at least one polymer, at least one lithium salt, a solvent plasticizer, at least one inorganic additive particle, and one or more liquid or solid additives and coating a substrate with the liquid slurry.
patents.complete_specification: INTERNATIONAL APPLICATION FOR COMPOSITE SOLID-STATE ELECTROLYTE AND LITHIUM BATTERIES USING THE SAME Inventors: ALEXANDER KOSYAKOV SOHEIL MALEKPOUR DIPOBRATO SARBAPALLI DAH-SHYANG TSAI DUKE PO-CHEN SHIH DILLON GRANT GAVIN DEPEW BRUCE KRAAY Docket no. 072379.P4WO2 (11010) Sheets of Drawings: 33 Attorneys Robert Keeler IceMiller LLP 1500 Broadway Suite 2900 New York, NY 10036 212-824-4982 CROSS REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS [0001] This patent application claims priority to United States Provisional Patent Application 63/380,889 filed on October 25, 2022 and United States Patent Application 18/492,229 filed on October 23, 2023, the entireties of which are hereby incorporated herein by reference. GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE [0002] In accordance with 35 U.S.C. §202(c)(6), Applicant hereby states that the invention disclosed in this specification was made with United States of America Federal Government support (the Department of Defense, contract number N6893622C00180) and the United States of America FederalGovernment has certain rights in the invention. TECHNICAL FIELD [0003] The present disclosure is directed to improved battery structures. Specifically, the disclosure is related to lithium rechargeable batteries assembled using a hybrid solid-state electrolyte that is composed of a combination of one or more polymers, lithium salts, non-lithium salts, solvent plasticizers, active inorganic additives, inactive inorganic additives, and reinforcement phases. The hybrid solid-state electrolyte may be used as a freestanding separator film inside of cells or directly laminated with battery electrodes. BACKGROUND [0004] Current state-of-the-art rechargeable Li-ion battery (LIB) cells employed in consumer electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and numerous other applications are comprised of three primary components: i.) a positive electrode (cathode) that is the original source of lithium and charge within a cell, ii.) a negative electrode (anode) where lithium is temporarily stored when a cell is in a charged state, and iii.) an electrolyte that sits in the middle of a cell and facilitates the transfer of lithium between the electrodes. [0005] Since their conception about 30 years ago, LIBs have seen the most innovation take place in their cathode materials. Until recently, LIB cathodes were the primary bottleneck with regards to cell cycle life (that is, the number of charge/discharge cycles a cell can deliver), charging speed, and energy density (that is, the amount of energy stored by a cell per unit of volume or mass). However, significant advances in cathode development have helped reverse these trends. Most LIBs are now built with either high-nickel layered-oxide cathodes like LiNio.8Mno.1Coo.1O2 (NMC811), which deliver excellent charging speeds and energy densities, or olivine-type electrodes based on LiFePO4 (LFP), which possess less impressive power and energy capability but extremely high stability and cycle life. [0006] The attention of academic and industrial development has now shifted to address new roadblocks to LIB capability originating from the anode and the electrolyte. For most of their history, LIBs have utilized graphite-based anodes. Li+ intercalates into graphite and occupies free space that exists in between the layers of one-dimensional graphene that comprises graphite. Graphite anodes have been a technological mainstay for many reasons, but their main advantage is the efficiency with which Li+ can be intercalated and de-intercalated into graphite. When paired with the right electrolyte, lithium can be shuttled in and out of graphite with virtually no loss. This type of efficiency of the reversibility of the intercalation process is referred to as coulombic efficiency (CE) and is why state-of-the-art LIBs can, under the right conditions, achieve thousands of charge/discharge cycles of cycle life with minimal capacity degradation. [0007] The new challenge with graphite anodes, however, is their limited specific capacity of-370 milliamp-hours (mAh) per gram. This is imposed by the fact that six carbon atoms within the graphite structure must be allocated for the storage of each Li+ ion. The use of novel materials is required if any improvement is to be seen on the anode side that would contribute to enhanced overall LIB cell energy density. Intercalation also stands in the way of increasing the speeds at which LIBs can charge as it is an intrinsically thermodynamically slow, surface-limited process. [0008] Liquid electrolytes, meanwhile, are the source of current LIBs’ fire safety risks. LIBs are produced by sandwiching a porous separator membrane between the anode and cathode. The separator is typically made from a blend of polypropylene (PP) or polyethylene (PE), and its primary purpose is to keep the electrodes from touching. The cathode and anode are also porous, and the pore network of the cathode/separator/anode stack is subsequently infiltrated with liquid electrolyte. Liquid electrolytes are typically a solution of Lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPFe) or other types of lithium salt in a mixture of carbonate solvents like ethylene carbonate (EC) and diethyl carbonate (DEC). The potential safety issues of such systems are obvious, as carbonates are volatile and highly flammable — liquid electrolytes possess a flash point of ~0°C, above which their vapors form a combustible mix with air. In a thermal runaway event, heating of an LIB cell can initiate rapid conversion of the electrolyte into gas products coupled with melting of the separator. Eventually, even the cathode and anode become fuel sources that drive ever-increasing self-heating of the cell and certain fire and/or explosion. [0009] Manufacturers of LIBs have made significant progress towards mitigating external and internal short circuits with improved quality control and cell design which reduces the likelihood of a thermal runaway being started. However, few improvements have been made to ameliorate the severity of the fire and heat release of a thermal runway if one does occur. Moreover, studies of electrification of the automotive industry have found that EVs are less likely to catch fire than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, but the consequences of an EV fire are significantly more dangerous for its passengers. [00010] Overall, mass-market consumer sentiment demands that EVs improve in terms of five key criteria that all depend on the battery cells with which they are manufactured: i.) affordability (the battery pack is-75% of the total cost of an EV), ii.) charging speed, iii.) driving range on a single charge (a function of battery energy density), iv.) lifespan, and v.) safety. The technological need has led many in the industry to seek to commercialize solid-state batteries (SSBs). SSBs are broadly analogous to conventional LIBs but reduce or eliminate the use of liquid electrolyte via substitution with solid-state electrolyte (SSE) materials. The goal behind using SSEs is to reduce the combustibility of the materials comprising a cell and to enable the use of next-generation anode materials that boost cell energy density and charging speed. [00011] SSEs generally fall under two classifications: inorganic SSEs (ceramics) and organic SSEs (polymers). Inorganic SSEs include oxidic materials such as lithium-lanthanum-zirconate (LLZO) and sulfidic materials like argyrodites. In these SSEs, defects in the ceramic crystal lattice facilitate lithium-ion transport wherein Li+ “hops” from defect site to defect site across the material. Organic SSEs are synthesized by dissolving lithium salts in polymer systems such as polyethylene glycol (PEG); ion transport is subsequently mediated by Arrhenius-dependent motion of polymer chain segments above the glass-transition temperature of the polymer. Such segmental chain motion continuously disassociates and associates Li+ with anions to move it across the material. [00012] Both organic and inorganic SSEs tend to be significantly more electrochemically and thermally resilient than liquid electrolytes and can be utilized to construct cells that remain benign even when short-circuited or subjected to other forms of abuse. Inorganic SSEs tend to provide more wide-ranging safety improvement in this regard. Inorganic SSEs also possess distinctly higher ionic conductivity — usually at least an order of magnitude higher than organic SSEs. This ion transport performance discrepancy is made more severe by the fact that only a fraction of the ion transference in an organic SSE constitutes Li+ due to simultaneous mobility of the anions of the lithium salt in the polymer; in an inorganic SSE, meanwhile, all the ion transference that takes place is Li+. Moreover, the combination of higher ionic conductivity and Li+ transference in inorganic electrolytes facilitates high flux densities that can pave the way to ultra-fast charging whereas organic SSEs lack such capability and will underperform state-of-the-art liquid electrolytes. [00013] However, inorganic SSEs have seen limited commercial success so far as a result of their poor manufacturability. LLZO, for example, is produced using common ceramic calcination and sintering processes at high temperatures (>1200°C). The process is energy and resource intensive — due to lithium evaporation at such elevated temperatures, additional lithium must be constantly introduced into LLZO furnaces. [00014] LLZO must often be made with multiple heat treatment/annealing steps to stabilize the material’s crystallinity and grain boundary interfaces and minimize its susceptibility to cracking. Even so, LLZO and related inorganic SSE materials suffer from unfavorable mechanical properties such as limited flexibility and high brittleness. To replace polyolefin separator in an LIB cell construction, a continuous inorganic SSE phase must be produced and stacked between the anode and cathode. Ceramic SSEs’ propensity to crack means that they must be made thicker (50pm-70pm) than regular separators (8pm-25pm). This compromises energy density and nullifies the extents to which charging speed can be improved as ionic conductance is dependent on material thickness. [00015] Another major issue plaguing inorganic SSEs is the high resistance of their surfaces. While ion transport in the bulk of an inorganic SSE may be rapid, this is not the case at its interfaces. It is especially difficult to establish sufficient contact between an SSE separator and electrodes. Indeed, most commercial examples of inorganic SSE-using batteries have resorted to retaining liquid electrolyte within the porosity of their anodes and cathodes so that it may “grease” the interfaces with the SSE. [00016] Recently, sulfidic SSEs have garnered academic and industrial attention. Sulfides are mechanically softer and more conformal at the electrode interfaces than LLZO. Sulfidic SSEs, however, possess their own manufacturing and handling challenges. They are unstable in air and made using toxic hydrogen sulfide gas. [00017] Another drawback of sulfide is its instability against Li-metal anode (LMA). LMA is used in Li-metal batteries (LMBs), which have the potential to deliver greatly improved energy density performance characteristics as compared to state-of-the-art LIBs as LMA has a theoretical specific capacity of over 3000 mAh g'1. LMBs have seen limited successful commercial introduction, though, because of the high reactivity of metallic lithium. Liquid electrolytes are rapidly reduced by LMA into inactive solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) products, resulting in poor cyclability. SSEs, with their enhanced electrochemical stability, are often considered to be an enabling technology for LMBs. However, sulfidic SSEs are plagued with a similar interaction with LMA as liquid electrolyte. [00018] “Hybrid” or “composite” electrolytes that blend ceramic and polymer SSE phases are viewed as a way to combine the ion transport performance of the former with the favorable mechanical traits, processability, and electrochemical stability of the latter. A well-described hybrid system is LLZO-in-polyethylene oxide (PEO) or polyethylene glycol (PEG). In such a system, LLZO particles are dispersed in a lithium salt-containing PEO/PEG continuous matrix. Ion transport occurs in both phases, though there are synergistic effects. For instance, the presence of LLZO lowers the glass-transition temperature of the surrounding PEO/PEG matrix and provides mechanical reinforcement. Still, the ion transport capability of such a system can be generally described as a volume fraction average of the phases: a larger proportion of polymer to ceramic will mean more ion movement through organic phase and lower overall ionic conductivity. [00020] The present disclosure provides lithium rechargeable batteries that integrate a novel composite solid electrolyte (CSE). [00021] The CSE is comprised of one or multiple polymers, lithium salts, solvent plasticizers, active (intrinsically Li-ion conductive) inorganic additive particles, inactive (not intrinsically Li-ion conductive) inorganic additive particles, continuous or discontinuous reinforcement phases, and other liquid or solid additives. [00022] The addition of solvent plasticizers allows the CSE to be processed in a liquid slurry form. The slurry may be applied as a coating to substrates through various methods including but not limited to slot-die coating, spray coating, immersion coating, blade coating, etc. [00023] The substrate to which the CSE slurry is applied may be a reinforcement phase such as a porous continuous webbing. This porous continuous webbing may be a conventional commercial LIB PE, PP, or PE/PP separator or another suitable continuous webbing. The plasticizer may be fully or partially removed from the slurry to solidify the CSE phase on and within the webbing to produce freestanding CSE separator film. This film may be densified using methods such calendering. A CSE slurry of one composition may be used on one side of the webbing while a slurry of a different composition may be used on the other side of the webbing, with the compositions optimized for the electrodes that each side of the separator will face. [00024] The substrate to which the CSE slurry is applied may be a battery electrode, such as a tape composed of electrode active material, binder, and conductive additive coated onto a metal foil. The slurry may flow and infiltrate into the pore network of the electrode and/or establish a distinct coating on top of the electrode. A reinforcement webbing may be added to the distinct slurry coating on top of the electrode to support a discrete CSE separator layer. The plasticizer may be fully or partially removed from the slurry to solidify the composite solid electrolyte on and within the electrode and webbing. The electrode-CSE laminate may be densified using methods such as calendering. The electrode-CSE laminate may also be treated with a vacuum bagging technique to help facilitate thorough intrusion of CSE slurry into the electrode pore network as well as sufficient plasticizer removal. [00025] The substrate to which the CSE slurry is applied may also be a current collector. A reinforcement webbing may be added to support the formation of a distinct CSE separator layer. The current collector may be a metal foil such as copper, aluminum, zinc, tin, nickel, magnesium, etc., or a non-metal material such as carbon textile. The current collector may be lithiophilic or lithiophobic or be coated with lithiophilic material such as zinc-oxide nanoparticles. The current collector may be two-dimensional or have a three-dimensional surface morphology or microstructure. Plasticizer may be fully or partially removed from the slurry to solidify it on the current collector. The current collector-CSE laminate may be densified using methods such as calendering. [00026] The substrate to which the CSE slurry is applied may be a current collector with a metallic lithium coating. The metallic lithium coating may be produced through melt-infusion, vapor deposition, electrodeposition, or other methods. Electrodeposition may be accomplished in situ inside of a lithium battery cell. The substrate itself may also be a pure lithium metal foil. A reinforcement webbing may be added to support the formation of a discrete CSE separator layer. The current collector-CSE laminate may be densified using methods such as calendering. [00027] Electrode active material particles and electronically conductive additives such as amorphous carbon particles may be added to the CSE slurry to form a mixed ionic-electronic conductor (MIEC) slurry. The MIEC slurry may be coated onto current collector materials and the plasticizer fully or partially removed to solidify the CSE matrix and produce a battery electrode. The CSE matrix serves the combined role of binder for the electrode active material and electronically conductive additive as well as Li+-conducting phase network for the electrode as a whole. A reinforcement webbing may be added to support the formation of a discrete CSE separator layer. The CSE-based MIEC electrode may be densified using methods such as calendering. [00028] A densified or non-densified freestanding CSE separator, electrode-CSE laminate, current collector-CSE laminate, or CSE-based MIEC electrode may additionally have their surfaces coated with lithiophilic material such as magnesium nanoparticles or metallic lithium. This may be accomplished using vapor deposition, electrodeposition, or other methods. Electrodeposition may be accomplished in situ inside of a lithium battery cell. [00029] Rechargeable lithium batteries may be assembled by layering freestanding CSE separator film between cathode and anode. Liquid electrolyte may be added to improve ion transport at the interfaces between the electrodes and the separator and/or if the electrodes are porous and their pore network is not accessible to the separator. A different liquid electrolyte may be used on the cathode side than on the anode side. Functional interphase stabilizers (FISs) may also be added to the surfaces of the cathode and/or anode, respectively. [00030] Rechargeable lithium batteries may also be assembled by using electrode-CSE laminate, current collector-CSE laminate, or CSE-based MIEC electrode in the place of an electrode and electrolyte.
