patents.abstract: The present invention relates to the technical field of secondary battery materials. Disclosed are a safety coating and the use thereof, an electrode sheet and a lithium-ion battery. By limiting the particle size of an inorganic filler in the safety coating, particle size grading is achieved, which enables the safety coating to have a compact structure, thereby reducing the probability of contact between positive and negative electrodes and thus improving the safety performance of a battery cell. Moreover, the amount of the binder in the safety coating is optimized to promote the electrolyte absorption of the safety coating, which can improve the rate capability, the low-temperature discharge performance and the cycle performance of a battery cell. Ultimately, in the present invention, by limiting the particle size of the inorganic filler and selecting the binder, the rate capability, low-temperature discharge performance and cycle performance of a battery cell can be improved while the safety performance of the battery cell is enhanced.
patents.complete_specification: TECHNICAL FIELD The present disclosure relates to the technical field of secondary battery materials, and in particular relates to a safety coating and use thereof, an electrode sheet, and a lithium-ion battery. 5 BACKGROUND Lithium-ion batteries are widely used in products such as 3C electronics (computer, communication and consumer), electric vehicles, and electric tools due to their advantages of high energy density, no memory effect, long cycle life, environmental friendliness, and adaptability to various environments. 10 In practical applications, the requirements for the safety performance and cycling performance of the lithium-ion batteries are also becoming increasingly stringent. To improve the safety performance of the batteries, introducing safety coatings into the electrode sheets is one of the commonly used measures in the industry. These safety coatings typically comprise a certain proportion of inorganic 15 fillers, conductive agents, and binders. However, conventional safety coating structures are relatively porous, unable to effectively improve the safety performance of the battery cells, and may increase the internal resistance of the cells, resulting in increased polarization, deteriorated low-temperature performance, deteriorated rate performance, and deteriorated cycling performance of the battery 20 cells. However, the lithium-ion battery is subject to kinetic limitations, making it prone to lithium plating, which results in decreased cycling performance and rate performance of the battery cell. When lithium plating occurs, increased side reactions lead to electrolytic solution consumption, meanwhile, the formation of new solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) during cycling further consumes the 25 electrolytic solution, accelerating deterioration of cycling performance. In addition, during mechanical abuse tests of the battery cell, such as nail penetration, the positive electrode and negative electrode of the battery may also experience short circuit and thermal runaway, ultimately causing the fail of tests. Therefore, it is of great significance to solve the current problems of safety 30 coatings being unable to effectively improve the rate performance and cycling 3 performance of the battery cell, and to provide a safety coating that can improve the safety performance of the battery cell while enhancing its rate performance, lowtemperature discharge performance, and cycling performance. SUMMARY 5 The present disclosure aims to solve at least one of the technical problems existing in the prior art. To this end, the present disclosure provides a safety coating and use thereof, an electrode sheet, and a lithium-ion battery, which aim to solve the current problems of safety coatings being unable to effectively improve the lowtemperature performance, rate performance, and cycling performance of the battery 10 cell. A first aspect of the present disclosure provides a safety coating, wherein raw materials of the safety coating comprise an inorganic filler and a first binder; a coefficient of nonuniformity Cu of the inorganic filler satisfies 2 ≤ Cu ≤ 18, a curvature coefficient Cc of the inorganic filler satisfies 0.5 ≤ Cc ≤ 3.1; a mass fraction w of the first binder in the safety coating satisfies w = k×(Cu) 0.5 15 /Dv50, where 0.2 ≤ k ≤ 2, and k is a constant; wherein a formula for calculating the coefficient of nonuniformity Cu is as follows: Cu = Dv90/Dv10, and a formula for calculating the curvature coefficient Cc is as follows: Cc = Dv50×Dv50/(Dv10×Dv90); and 20 Dv10, Dv50, and Dv90 refer to particle sizes corresponding to volume distribution cumulative values of the inorganic filler reaching 10%, 50%, and 90%, respectively. The safety coating according to an embodiment of the present disclosure has at least the following beneficial effects: The safety coating provided by the present disclosure comprises an inorganic filler and a binder. By limiting the particle size 25 of the inorganic filler and selecting the binder, the safety performance of the battery cell can be improved while enhancing its rate performance, low-temperature discharge performance, and cycling performance. Wherein, the particle sizes Dv10, Dv50, and Dv90 of the inorganic filler should satisfy: 2≤Cu=Dv90/Dv10≤18, 0.5≤Cc=Dv50×Dv50/(Dv10×Dv90) ≤3.1, where Cu and Cc represent the coefficient of 30 nonuniformity and curvature coefficient of the inorganic filler, respectively; Dv10, 4 Dv50, and Dv90 represent particle sizes corresponding to volume distribution cumulative values of the inorganic filler reaching 10%, 50%, and 90%, respectively. When the particle size of the inorganic filler satisfies the above relationship, the gradation curve exhibits good continuity, and the fine particles and coarse particles 5 are well graded, thereby enabling the safety coating to have a relatively dense structure, reducing the probability of short circuits between the positive electrode and the negative electrode, and enhancing the safety performance of the battery cell. The mass fraction w of the first binder should satisfy w=k×(Cu) 0.5/Dv50, where 0.2≤k≤2. When k falls within this range, the binder not only provides sufficient 10 adhesion and minimized polarization of the battery cell, but also promotes the electrolytic solution absorption by the safety coating, thereby improving the rate performance, low-temperature discharge performance, and cycling performance of the battery cell. Ultimately, the safety coating provided by the present disclosure achieves a well-graded distribution of large and small particles by limiting the 15 particle size of the inorganic filler, resulting in a relatively dense structure for the safety coating. This in turn reduces the probability of contact between the positive electrode and the negative electrode, thereby enhancing the safety performance of the battery cell. Meanwhile, by optimizing the binder content in the safety coating, the electrolytic solution absorption by the safety coating is promoted, which can 20 improve the rate performance, low-temperature discharge performance, and cycling performance of the battery cell. In the present disclosure, the coefficient of nonuniformity of the particle size of the inorganic filler, defined as Cu=Dv90/Dv10, should satisfy: 2≤Cu=Dv90/Dv10≤18. The coefficient of nonuniformity (Cu) is an important parameter for describing the 25 particle size distribution of the inorganic filler, reflecting the degree of nonuniformity in the particle size of the inorganic filler. When Cu is greater than 18, it indicates a wide distribution range of the particle sizes of the inorganic filler particles, with the presence of some particles with exceptionally large sizes. During coating of the safety coating, instances of coating skips may occur, which may 30 adversely affect the safety performance of the battery cell. When Cu is less than 2, the distribution range of the particle sizes of the inorganic filler particles is narrow, 5 with most particles having similar sizes. In this case, there are insufficient fine particles to fill the gaps between larger particles, resulting in poor particle grading. Consequently, the safety coating has lower density, which negatively impacts the safety performance and energy density of the battery cell. When Cu falls within the 5 aforementioned range, the safety coating can achieve a relatively dense structure while also minimizing the risk of coating skips during coating of the safety coating, resulting in superior overall performances. In the present disclosure, the curvature coefficient of the inorganic filler, defined as Cc=Dv50×Dv50/(Dv10×Dv90), should satisfy: 0.5≤Cc=Dv50×Dv50/(Dv10×Dv90) 10 ≤3.1. The curvature coefficient (Cc) is a parameter describing the shape of the particle size distribution curve. When Cc equals 1, the particle size distribution of the inorganic filler is in an ideal state, with a continuous particle size distribution without significant gaps or jumps in size. The shape of the particle size distribution curve is uniform, indicating a smooth transition from fine to coarse particles. When 15 Cc deviates from 1, it indicates that the particle size distribution of the inorganic filler deviates from the ideal state. When Cc is greater than 1, it indicates that the particle size distribution curve is convex on a logarithmic plot of particle size, meaning that the particle size distribution of the fine particle fraction is more concentrated than that of the coarse particle fraction. Conversely, when Cc is less 20 than 1, it indicates that the particle size distribution curve is concave, meaning that the particle size distribution of the coarse particle fraction is more concentrated than that of the fine particle fraction. However, the particle size distribution of the inorganic filler often deviates from the ideal state, with the inorganic filler predominantly consisting of either fine particles or coarse particles, resulting in a 25 discontinuous overall shape of the gradation curve. This leads to a higher porosity and lower density of the safety coating. In the present disclosure, by limiting the Cc value within the aforementioned range, the better continuity of the gradation curve can be ensured, thereby facilitating an improvement in the density of the safety coating. 30 In the present disclosure, a content of the first binder, w, should satisfy w=k×(Cu) 0.5/D v50, where 0.2≤k≤2, and k is a constant related to the density of the 6 inorganic filler. Generally, when the particle shape and pore structure are determined, a smaller Dv50 of the particles indicates a larger specific surface area of the particles, resulting a greater contact area with the binder. Accordingly, the binder content needs to be increased. Cu reflects the particle distribution, and a smaller Cu 5 value means that all particle sizes tend to concentrate toward Dv50, resulting in fewer fine particles in the system and a smaller overall specific surface area, thereby allowing for a reduced binder content. The k value indicates the level of binder content in the safety coating. When k < 0.2, the adhesion between the safety coating and the current collector is poor, posing a risk of peeling off; when k > 2, it leads to 10 increased polarization of the battery cell, thereby deteriorating the rate performance, low-temperature discharge performance, and cycling performance of the battery cell. When the k value is within the range of 0.2-2, not only is the adhesion sufficient and the polarization of the battery cell minimized, but the electrolytic solution absorption by the safety coating is also promoted, the rate performance, low15 temperature discharge performance, and cycling performance of the battery cell are improved. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, a median particle size Dv50 of the inorganic filler ranges from 0.2 μm to 4 μm, and the specific surface area is 5 m2 /g to 50 m2 /g. When the Dv50 of the inorganic filler is less than 0.2 μm and the specific surface area is greater than 50 m2 20 /g, the inorganic filler tends to agglomerate and is difficult to disperse; when the Dv50 of the inorganic filler is greater than 4 μm and the specific surface area is less than 5 m2 /g, due to the larger particle size, it will be challenging to obtain a thin safety coating, thereby affecting energy density of the battery cell. Additionally, during the coating of the safety 25 coating, primer coating skips may occur, which affects the safety of the battery cell. When the median particle size and specific surface area of the inorganic filler fall within the aforementioned ranges, a good balance can be achieved between the processability of the safety coating and the energy density of the battery cell. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, the inorganic filler comprises 30 one or more of aluminum oxide, boehmite, aluminum hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, silicon dioxide, titanium dioxide, lithium iron phosphate, lithium 7 manganese iron phosphate, lithium aluminum titanium phosphate, lithium lanthanum titanate, or lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide; preferably, the inorganic filler is boehmite. The inorganic filler used in the present disclosure may be an inert inorganic filler, such as aluminum oxide, boehmite, aluminum hydroxide, 5 magnesium hydroxide, silicon dioxide, and titanium dioxide; or an active material exhibiting certain capacity and good thermal stability, such as lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese iron phosphate; or a solid electrolyte such as lithium aluminum titanium phosphate (LATP), lithium lanthanum titanate (LLTO), and lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide (LLZO). Preferably, the inorganic filler is 10 boehmite. Compared to other inorganic fillers, boehmite is not only cost-effective but also has a lower Rockwell hardness, which results in less wear on the gravure rolls and thereby reducing manufacturing costs. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, a mass fraction of the inorganic filler in the safety coating is 73.8% to 98.5%. 15 In some embodiments of the present disclosure, the first binder comprises one or more of a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder, a sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) binder, or a polyacrylate (PAA)-based binder. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, a mass fraction of the first binder in the safety coating is 1 wt% to 21.2 wt%, preferably 5 wt% to 15 wt%. 20 When the binder content in the safety coating is less than 1%, the adhesion of the safety coating is insufficient, making it prone to peeling off during subsequent use; when the binder content is greater than 21.2%, it may cause difficulties in processing during gravure printing of the safety coating and also deteriorate the internal resistance of the battery cell. Additionally, the binder content within the 25 range of 1% to 21.2% helps to adjust a pH value of slurry to below 8.5, thereby mitigating corrosion of the aluminum foil current collector caused by alkaline aqueous solution of the active material. In some preferred embodiments of the present disclosure, the first binder is a polyacrylate-based binder, which can reduce corrosion of the aluminum foil by the 30 active material, exhibits excellent adhesion performance, is cost-effective, and uses 8 deionized water as a solvent, making it environmentally friendly. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, a structural formula of the polyacrylate-based binder is as follows: ; 5 wherein, R1 is H, Li, or Na; R2 is substituted or unsubstituted C1-C10 alkyl; and 5 ≤ (x+z)/y ≤ 20, 1.2 ≤ z/x ≤ 2, where x, y, and z are all non-zero. The polyacrylate-based binder provided by the present disclosure achieves excellent adhesion performance by defining the contents of cyano groups (-CN), 10 ester groups (-COOR2), and carboxylate groups (-COOR1) in the molecular chain of the binder. The binder is water-soluble, and uses water as a solvent, which eliminates the need for harmful organic solvents such as NMP, and makes it harmless to human and environmentally friendly. Moreover, the polyacrylate-based is abundant in supply, cost-effective, and widely applicable for industrial production. 15 When the aforementioned binder is introduced into an electrode sheet as a raw material for water-based safety coating, based on its superior adhesion performance, the water-based safe coating can firmly adhere to the surface of current collector of the electrode sheet, which not only reduces surface contact resistance, but also minimizes the generation of current collector burrs during safety testing of the 20 battery cell, thereby reducing contact short circuits between the current collector burrs and unstable active materials in the charged state, and enhancing safety of the battery cell. Furthermore, by defining the molecular weight of the binder and the content of the cyano groups, ester groups, and carboxylate groups in the molecular chain, the electrolytic solution absorption rate of the binder may be adjusted, which 25 significantly improves the rate performance, high-temperature discharge performance and low-temperature discharge performance of the battery cell, and enhances the safety performance and cycling performance of the battery. In the binder provided by the present disclosure, the molecular chain contains 9 cyano groups (-CN, accounting for a fraction of n1 among all side chain groups, and n1=z/(x+y+z)), carboxylate groups(-COOR1, wherein R1 is H, Li, or Na, accounting for a fraction of n2 among all side chain groups, and n2=x/(x+y+z)), and ester groups (-COOR2, wherein R2 is substituted or unsubstituted C1-C10 alkyl, accounting for a 5 fraction of n3 among all side chain groups, and n3=y/(x+y+z)), with n1+n2+n3=1. Wherein,-CN is a highly polar group with good electrolytic solution affinity and electrochemical stability, providing strong adhesion. However, due to rigid nature of this group, it cannot accommodate the significant volume changes that occur during the intercalation/deintercalation of lithium ions in the active materials. 10 Wherein,-COOR1 carries a negative charge, causing mutual repulsion between the groups, which facilitates the extension of binder molecules and promotes uniform dispersion of conductive agents, while also regulating swelling degree of the binder in the electrolytic solution, reducing erosion of the binder caused by electrolytic solution dissolution and better maintaining the adhesion 15 capacity and adhesion performance of the binder. Wherein,-COOR2 has polarity and solubility parameters that are similar to those of carbonate-based solvents in the electrolytic solution, which facilitates moderate absorption of the electrolytic solution by the binder. The absorption of electrolytic solution in turn plasticizesthe binder, imparting elasticity and flexibility 20 to adapt to the periodic volume changes of the electrode active materials during lithium-ion intercalation/deintercalation in the process of charging and discharging. Meanwhile, the absorption of electrolytic solution enhances the ionic conductivity of the water-based safety coating, promoting improvement of the low-temperature discharge performance of the battery cell. 25 The binder is an indispensable component for maintaining the integrity of an electrode sheet and play a crucial role in improving battery performance, such as specific capacity and cycling stability. Polyacrylic acid has been used as a binder for both positive electrode and negative electrode of lithium-ion batteries due to its high content of polar functional groups, water solubility, and good adhesion. 30 However, the polar groups in polyacrylic acid form hydrogen bonds between 10 molecular chains, resulting in high chain rigidity, which is detrimental to maintaining the integrity of electrode sheet during charging and discharging. Therefore, controlling the number of functional groups in polyacrylic acid, altering the types of functional groups, and modifying the molecular chain structure of 5 polyacrylic acid are imperative for improving the electrical performance of lithiumion batteries. In the present disclosure, the contents of cyano groups, ester groups, and carboxylate groups in the molecular chain of the binder are limited as follows: (1) 1.2 ≤ z/x ≤ 2 i.e., n1 and n2 satisfy 1.2≤n1/n2≤2; when n1/n2<1.2, it is easy to cause insufficient adhesion of the binder; when n1/n2>2, the molecular chain 10 presents a coiled conformation, which hinders the dispersion of conductive agents, and the binder is more susceptible to swelling by the electrolytic solution; (2) 5≤(x+z)/y≤20, i.e., n1, n2, and n3 satisfy 5≤(n1+n2)/n3≤20; when (n1+n2)/n3<5, the binder contains an excessive amount of-COOR2, leading to the binder to absorb an excessive amount of electrolytic solution, causing rapid decrease in adhesion, 15 reduced elasticity, and deterioration of battery cell performance; and when (n1+n2)/n3>20, the content of-COOR2 in the binder is too low, resulting in insufficient elasticity of the binder, low ionic conductivity of the water-based safety coating, and significant reduction in the low-temperature discharge performance and rate discharge performance of the battery cell. Ultimately, by adjusting the 20 contents of cyano groups, ester groups, and carboxylate groups in the molecular chain of the binder, the present disclosure achieves optimal adhesion of the binder, and adjusted electrolytic solution absorption by the binder, thereby enhancing the rate performance, high-temperature discharge performance and low-temperature discharge performance of the battery cell. 25 In some embodiments of the present disclosure, R2 is C1-C10 linear alkyl, C1-C10 branched alkyl, or C1-C10 cycloalkyl; preferably C1-C10 linear alkyl; more preferably C1-C4 alkyl. In some embodiments of the present disclosure, an electrolytic solution absorption rate c of the polyacrylate-based binder at 80 °C is 10% to 50%, e.g., it 30 may be 10% to 20%, 20% to 30%, 30% to 40%, or 40% to 50%. 11 In the present disclosure, the adjustment of the electrolytic solution absorption rate of the binder is achieved by defining the contents of cyano groups, ester groups, and carboxylate groups in the molecular chain of the binder. The electrolytic solution absorption rate c of the binder at 80 °C satisfies 10%≤c≤50%; when c<10%, 5 the binder absorbs insufficient electrolytic solution, resulting in poor elasticity and an inability to buffer the periodic volume changes during lithium-ion intercalation/deintercalation in the active materials. Example 1 The present example provided a lithium-ion battery, which comprised a positive electrode sheet comprising a safety coating, wherein the safety coating 10 comprised a first binder, a first conductive agent Super P Li, and an inorganic filler boehmite; wherein the structural formula of the first binder was as follows: (1) Preparation of the first binder: 15 a) Calculated in parts by weight, 1000 parts of distilled water was added to a reaction vessel, stirring was initiated, and high-purity nitrogen gas was introduced to remove oxygen for 1 hour; then 50 parts of acrylonitrile, 35 parts lithium acrylate, and 15 parts of methyl acrylate were added, a resulting mixture was heated to 65 °C under an inert atmosphere and maintained at that temperature. 20 b) Calculated in parts by weight, 5 parts by weight of an ammonium persulfate solution with a mass concentration of 20% was then added as an initiator to initiate a reaction, and the reaction lasted for 5 hours. c) After the reaction was completed, a resulting product was subjected to filtering, drying, crushing, and sieving to obtain the binder. For the binder, the-CN 25 group content n1 was 50%, the-COOLi group content n2 was 35%, and the-COOCH3 group content n3 was 15%; the weight-average molecular weight (Mw) was 3.6×105 , the number-average molecular weight (Mn) was 2.0×105 , a Mw/Mn 36 ratio was 1.8, and the electrolytic solution absorption rate c was equal to 22.7%. (2) Preparation of a positive electrode current collector comprising the safety coating: By using deionized water as a solvent, calculated in parts by weight, 10 parts 5 of the aforementioned binder were added, dissolving and mixing were performed, and the amount of the deionized water was adjusted until a binder solution with a solid content of 15% and a viscosity of 2.2×104 mPa·s was obtained; then, 88 parts of the inorganic filler boehmite (with Dv10, Dv50, and Dv90 of 0.2 μm, 0.4 μm, and 0.9 μm, respectively, Cu=4.5, Cc=0.89, and a specific surface area of 9.5 m2 /g) and 10 2 parts of the first conductive agent Super P Li were uniformly mixed to obtain a safety coating slurry with a solid content of 20% and a viscosity of 750 mPa·s. The safety coating slurry was coated on both side surfaces of an aluminum foil by gravure printing. During coating, LA2 and LB2 were both set to 0, i.e., LA1=LB1=LA=LB=L, Z=Y=1, and X=4. Additionally, a temperature of the oven 15 during printing was set to 95 °C, and the printing speed was set to 30 m/min. Finally, a positive electrode current collector with a double-sided safety coating was obtained. The double-sided areal density of the safety coating was 10.3 mg/1540.25 mm2 , the double-sided thickness was 5.3 μm, the double-sided film resistance was 3.1 Ω @0.4T, and the adhesion between the safety coating and the current collector 20 was 1356 N/m. (3) Preparation of a positive electrode sheet: A positive electrode active material, a conductive agent (a mixture of conductive carbon black and carbon nanotubes in a mass ratio of 6:5), a PVDF binder, and NMP were uniformly mixed according to a mass ratio of 97.6:1.1:1.3:35 25 to produce a positive electrode slurry with a solid content of 75% and a viscosity of 7000 mPa·s. The positive electrode slurry was coated on one side of the aforementioned aluminum foil current collector comprising the safety coating, dried at 85 °C and winded. Then, the other side of the aluminum foil current collector comprising the safety coating was coated with the positive electrode slurry 30 and dried using the same method, followed by cold pressing. Subsequently, edges 37 were trimmed, and the sheet was cut to obtain the positive electrode sheet of lithium-ion battery (film resistance: 0.8 Ω @0.4T). (4) Preparation of the negative electrode sheet: By using water as a solvent, graphite, a thickening agent, and a SBR binder 5 were uniformly mixed according to a mass ratio of 97.7:1.1:1.2 to produce an negative electrode slurry for lithium-ion battery with a solid content of 50% and a viscosity of 5000 mPa·s. The negative electrode slurry was coated on one side surface of a copper foil current collector, dried at 80 °C and winded. The other side of the copper foil was then coated with the negative electrode slurry and dried using 10 the same method, to obtain a negative electrode sheet coated with an active material on both sides. (5) Preparation of electrolytic solution: Lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) was dissolved in a mixed solvent of dimethyl carbonate (DMC), ethylene carbonate (EC), and ethyl methyl carbonate 15 (EMC) with a mass ratio of 3:5:2 to obtain the electrolytic solution. (6) Assembly of battery: The prepared positive electrode sheet, negative electrode sheet, and a separator were wound to form a battery cell with a capacity of approximately 5 Ah. The separator was arranged between the adjacent positive electrode and negative 20 electrode sheet. The positive electrode was connected by spot-welding an aluminum tab, and the negative electrode was connected by spot-welding a nickel tab. The battery cell was then placed in an aluminum-plastic pouch, baked, and introduced with the aforementioned electrolytic solution. After being subjected to sealing, formation, and capacity grading processes, the lithium-ion battery was finally 25 obtained. Test examples To verify the impact of introducing the safety coating of the present disclosure on the performance of battery cell, tests were conducted on the particle size of the 20 inorganic filler, the electrolytic solution absorption rate c of the binder, the doublesided film resistance of the safety coating, as well as nail penetration, lowtemperature discharge performance, rate performance, and cycling performance of the battery cell. Method for testing particle size: dispersing the inorganic filler in water which 25 was used as a dispersing agent, and measuring the particle size of the inorganic filler by using a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern, Mastersizer 3000). Method for testing electrolytic solution absorption rate c: pouring a binder solution into a polytetrafluoroethylene dish and then baking to evaporate deionized water, so as to form a binder polymer film with a thickness controlled at 100 μm; 44 cutting the film into pieces, to obtain film sheets with a length of 50 mm and a width of 50 mm; after vacuum drying the film sheets for 24 hours, weighing the dried film sheets; immersing the dried film sheets in an electrolytic solution at 80 °C for 12 hours and then taking the film sheets out of the electrolytic solution, wiping off the 5 electrolytic solution adhering to the surfaces of film sheets, and weighing the film sheets again to obtain the weight of the film sheets after absorbing the electrolytic solution; and a percentage increase in weight (%) of the film sheets after being immersed in the electrolytic solution is the electrolytic solution absorption rate of the binder at 80 °C. 10 Method for testing film resistance: testing the film resistance by using the ACCFILM film resistance testing system (Model TT-ACCF-G2A) from Hangzhou Chuanyuan Technology Co., Ltd, China, wherein the pressure for testing was 0.4 t, and the pressure holding time was 10 s. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a system (100) and method (400) for estimating the State of Charge (SOC) of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with high precision. The system (100) employs a Fractional-Order Model (FOM) (103) to capture the dynamic behaviour of the battery using fractional-order derivative theory. The captured parameters are processed by a hybrid Manta Ray Foraging Optimization with Differential Evolution (MRFODE) (102), combining Manta Ray Foraging Optimization (MRFO) for broad exploration of parameter values and Differential Evolution (DE) for refinement and convergence. The fine-tuned parameters are further utilized by a FO-ARICKF algorithm, which dynamically analyzes real-time data and compensates for errors using an adaptive noise covariance matrix. This comprehensive approach ensures accurate SOC estimation by addressing challenges such as measurement noise, sensor drift, and initialization errors, enabling enhanced performance and reliability under diverse operating conditions. The method (400) is particularly suited for real-world battery management applications. (to be published with Figure 1)
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION: [0001] The present invention relates to a system and method for estimating the State of Charge (SOC) of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). The system leverages a Fractional-Order Model (FOM) to capture battery dynamics, a hybrid optimization framework to fine-tune model parameters, and an adaptive filtering technique to process real-time data, ensuring accurate and robust SOC estimation under varying conditions. BACKGROUND AND PRIOR ART: [0002] The subject matter discussed in the background section should not be assumed to be prior art merely because of its mention in the background section. Similarly, a problem mentioned in the background section or associated with the subject matter of the background section should not be assumed to have been previously recognized in the prior art. [0003] State-of-Charge (SOC) estimation is a critical aspect of lithium-ion battery management. Numerous techniques and equipment have been developed, each with its advantages and limitations. Below is an overview of the closest existing methods and their respective challenges, followed by how the current invention addresses these issues: [0004] “Ampere-Hour Integration (AHI)” methods for State-of-Charge (SOC) estimation calculates SOC by integrating the charge or discharge current over time. This technique, while straightforward, suffers from significant limitations such as cumulative errors arising from inaccurate current measurements or sensor drift, a dependency on accurate initial SOC values, and an inability to account for dynamic conditions like battery ageing or temperature effects. Therefore, this method is impractical for real-time or adaptive battery management systems. [0005] “Open-Circuit Voltage (OCV)” Method estimates SOC based on the correlation between open-circuit voltage and SOC. However, it requires extended rest periods to achieve equilibrium, limiting its application in real-time systems. Additionally, the non-linear OCSOC relationship varies with battery chemistry, temperature, and ageing, resulting in lower accuracy in intermediate SOC ranges where voltage changes minimally. [0006] “Battery Impedance Technique” involves measuring the impedance of a battery to infer SOC, given the variation of impedance with SOC and operating conditions. Despite its advantages, this method requires sophisticated equipment, is highly dependent on operating conditions like temperature and state-of-health (SOH), and faces challenges in real-time applications due to its computational complexity. [0007] “Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)” method employs a non-linear state-space model for SOC estimation by fusing voltage and current measurements. However, it suffers from drawbacks such as model dependency, linearisation errors under dynamic conditions, and assumptions of white Gaussian noise, which may not hold true in practical scenarios, leading to inaccuracies. [0008] “Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)” improves upon EKF by avoiding linearisation and propagating a set of sample points through the non-linear model. However, UKF is computationally intensive, making it less suitable for embedded systems. Like EKF, it also assumes white Gaussian noise, limiting its effectiveness in real-world conditions. [0009] “Fuzzy Logic-based Methods” relies on rule-based systems that use input features like voltage, current, and temperature for SOC estimation. Despite their simplicity, these methods are heavily dependent on the quality of the rule set, face scalability issues for complex systems or diverse battery chemistries, and lack adaptability to dynamic conditions such as ageing or environmental changes. [0010] “Machine Learning Methods (SVM, ANN)” utilizes extensive training datasets to model SOC estimation. While effective in certain scenarios, these methods are data-dependent and prone to overfitting when training data does not represent all operating conditions. Additionally, their computational demand limits real-time applications. [0011] Furthermore, the Fractional Order Model (FOM) has gained attention as a preferred approach for SOC estimation in LIBs due to its ability to capture the complex electrochemical dynamics of the batteries. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by the challenge of accurately determining the numerous model parameters, which increases the complexity of the estimation process. Traditional optimization techniques often struggle with these challenges, as they are prone to getting trapped in local minima, preventing the achievement of globally optimal solutions. Overcoming these limitations in parameter identification is essential to improve the reliability and accuracy of SOC estimation using FOM, particularly in applications requiring high precision under diverse operating conditions. [0012] In non-linear systems, the estimation accuracy of the state can degrade because the system’s behaviour does not follow a simple linear relationship, which makes it difficult to predict accurately. [0013] The conventional EKF addresses this challenge by linearizing the non-linear system. This is done by using a first-order approximation of the system (a first-order Taylor series expansion) at the point of estimation. However, this approximation discards higher-order terms, which introduces linearization errors. [0014] Conventional optimization techniques, such as the Manta Ray Foraging Optimization (MRFO) algorithm, often face challenges like premature convergence and getting trapped in local minima. These issues arise due to the algorithm's reliance on random processes, limiting its ability to effectively explore the entire solution space and reach the global optimum, especially in complex and multimodal optimization scenarios. [0015] Conventional SOC estimation techniques, such as the Iterative Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF) and Cubature Kalman Filter (CKF), have been widely used for lithium-ion battery modeling. However, these methods often struggle with the inherent nonlinearity of battery dynamics, leading to degraded estimation accuracy under varying operating conditions. Additionally, traditional approaches lack the adaptability needed to handle noise, disturbances, and inaccuracies in initial parameter values, limiting their reliability in practical applications. [0016] Traditional Kalman Filter (KF) algorithms operate under the assumption that measurement noise and process noise levels remain constant. However, in practical applications, these noise levels are closely tied to the sensor's measurement accuracy and often fluctuate in real time. Typically, the initial parameters for process and measurement noise are determined based on experience and require iterative fine-tuning to achieve optimal filtering performance. [0017] Therefore, there is a need for an advanced SOC estimation system that overcomes the limitations of existing methods by providing high accuracy, robustness to noise, computational efficiency, and adaptability to dynamic conditions such as battery ageing, temperature variations, and diverse chemistries. [0018] The present invention addresses these challenges through a novel approach combining fractional-order dynamics with advanced optimization (MRFODE) and adaptive noise handling. The FO-ARICKF algorithm incorporates a fractional-order model to dynamically represent battery behaviour, compensating for inaccuracies due to sensor drift, initialization errors, and ageing. It achieves real-time SOC estimation with high accuracy, robustness to non-Gaussian noise, and computational efficiency, establishing itself as a comprehensive solution to the challenges in lithium-ion battery management systems. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION: [0019] The primary object of the present invention is to provide an advanced system and method for precise and real-time estimation of the State of Charge (SOC) of lithium-ion batteries (LIB), ensuring reliability across various operating conditions. [0020] Another object of the present invention is to leverage innovative modeling and optimization techniques to accurately capture and refine battery parameters for improved SOC estimation. [0021] Another object of the present invention is to enable dynamic adaptability in SOC estimation by minimizing the impact of real-time measurement errors and process variations. [0022] Another object of the present invention is to enhance the performance and robustness of battery management systems through the integration of advanced algorithms and adaptive techniques tailored for diverse battery conditions. [0023] Overall, the present invention aims to address the limitations of conventional SOC estimation methods by providing a precise, adaptive, and efficient solution, contributing to the optimization of lithium-ion battery performance and management. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION: [0024] This summary introduces concepts related to a system and method for the accurate and real-time estimation of the State of Charge (SOC) of lithium-ion batteries (LIB). It is not intended to define essential features or limit the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0025] The present invention pertains to an innovative system and method for estimating the SOC of lithium-ion batteries with high precision and adaptability. The system integrates advanced fractional-order modeling, optimization techniques, and real-time data analysis to ensure reliable SOC estimation under varying conditions. [0026] In one aspect, the system includes a processor, a memory communicatively coupled to the processor and a plurality of modules such as a Fractional-Order Model (FOM) (103), a Hybrid Manta-Ray Foraging Optimisation with Differential Evolution (MRFODE) (102), a Fractional-Order Adaptive Root Integrated Cubature Kalman Filter (FO-ARICKF), wherein the processor is configured to execute instructions from the plurality of modules. [0027] In one aspect, the system includes the Fractional-Order Model (FOM) configured to capture the dynamic behaviour of the battery with high precision by applying fractional-order derivative theory. The captured parameters are sent to the Hybrid MRFODE module for further processing. The Hybrid MRFODE combines Manta Ray Foraging Optimization (MRFO) for exploring a wide range of potential parameter values and Differential Evolution (DE) for refining and converging these parameters, ensuring accurate and fine-tuned estimation. [0028] The system also includes the Fractional-Order Adaptive Recursive Inverse Covariance Kalman Filter (FO-ARICKF), which receives the optimized parameters from the MRFODE module. The FO-ARICKF dynamically analyzes real-time data and compensates for measurement errors and process variations by utilizing an adaptive noise covariance matrix. This ensures precise SOC estimation, even in complex and changing battery conditions. [0029] In another aspect, the invention includes a method for SOC estimation of lithium-ion batteries. The method involves capturing the battery's dynamics using the FOM, optimizing the parameters through the Hybrid MRFODE, and dynamically analyzing real-time data with the FO-ARICKF to adjust for errors and variations. The method ensures reliable and adaptive SOC estimation through a stepwise integration of modeling, optimization, and filtering techniques. [0030] Overall, the present invention provides a robust, scalable, and efficient solution for SOC estimation in lithium-ion batteries. The combination of fractional-order modeling, hybrid optimization, and adaptive filtering techniques enhances the accuracy and adaptability of SOC estimation, ensuring reliable battery management in diverse applications. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION: [0031] The invention has other advantages and features which will be more readily apparent from the following detailed description of the invention and the appended claims, when taken in conjunction with the accompanying drawings, in which: [0032] The invention is described herein in detail with the help of figures appended at the end of the specification. A cubature Kalman filter (CKF) is a filter that estimates the uncertainty of a state and how that uncertainty propagates through non-linear measurement and state equations. It uses a fixed number of cubature points to approximate a Gaussian distribution up to the third moment even in the presence of additional Gaussian noise. This technique avoids truncation errors that arise from linearising non-linear functions. in the Iterated Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF), offering superior precision. Nonetheless, during the CP transformation process, it becomes imperative to derive the square root of the CM. This operation inevitably escalates the computational complication of the process as well as potentially introduces non-positive definiteness in the resultant matrix. To address this issue, square root filtering is presented into the CKF, & RICKF is implemented on FO model. The RICKF circumvents potential filter divergence arising from the several square root decompositions of t positive definite CMs. Instead, it directly operates with the covariance square root matrix (SRM) between successive time instances. The recursive update approach significantly mitigates the process's computational complication, thereby enhancing its numerical stability and computational efficiency. In Step 1, the battery is allowed to remain at 25 °C for 2 hours before being charged to a desired threshold voltage at a current rate of 0.5C. It is then allowed to rest for 1 hour. Step 2 involves pulse tests conducted at four different current rates (0.5C, 1C, 1.5C, and 2C), each corresponding to a 10% SOC level of the battery. The process continues with a 1C continuous current rate for an hour. Step 3 involves repeating Step 2 until the LIB is fully discharged. patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to Lithium doped magnesium molybdate (Mg1-xLix) MoO4 of the general formula I with enhanced crystallinity, stabilization to its parent phase and with improved optical properties. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO4) is a widely studied material for its luminescent and catalytic properties. An article titled “Structural and optical properties of MgМоO4 prepared by mechanochemical technique” by M. Gancheva et.al published in Ceramics International, Volume 48, Issue 12, 15 June 2022, Pages 17149-17156 discloses MgMoO4 with hexagonal particles prepared by combining high energy ball milling with heat treatment technique. The MgMoO4 exhibits energy band gap value of 2.03eV and photoluminescence emission above 600 nm. The preparation of MgMoO4 by combustion method or mechanochemical methods have failed to produce pure and single phase MgМоO4. The Indian patent IN567531 discloses the single phase molybdenum based (MgMoO4) nano-materials prepared by green Sol Gel method using aloe-vera gel as a chelating agent. MgMoO4 though are known for its use in optical and electronic applications its use is limited due to due to intrinsic defects and suboptimal charge transport properties. Doping of nanomaterials involves introducing impurities (dopants) into the crystal lattice of a nanomaterial to modify its properties. Doping can increase conductivity, improve luminescence, or alter magnetic behavior. The introduction of lithium (Li) as a dopant has been found to improve the structural stability and optical properties of the nanomaterial significantly. Article titled “Thermal behavior of ammonium molybdate-basic magnesium carbonate system doped with lithium nitrate” by Nagi R. E. Radwan et.al published in Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry, Vol. 71 (2003) 977–986 discloses Li2O-doping of ammonium molybdate supported on basic magnesium carbonate with small amount of lithium nitrate. The article discloses that solid–solid interaction between molybdenum and lithium oxides occur at temperatures starting from 400°C to yield Li2MoO4 phase. The article however does not mention the structural stability and crystallinity of the doped magnesium molybdate in pure parent phase. Further, the article does not mention the optical performance of the Lithium doped magnesium molybdate stabilized to the parent phase. A need in the art persists to provide the doped magnesium molybdate, wherein, the doped magnesium molybdate retains the crystallinity and structural stability of its parent phase and yet improves its optical performance. The present inventors found that doping magnesium molybdate with lithium in appropriate concentration could yield lithium doped magnesium molybdate with crystallinity and structural stability to its parent phase and with improved optical performance with reduced band gap. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION The primary objective of the present invention is to provide novel lithium doped magnesium molybdate with crystallinity and structural stability to its parent phase and with improved optical performance with reduced band gap. The other objective is to synthesize the lithium doped magnesium molybdate by the sol gel process using aloe vera as a chelating agent such that the lithium doped magnesium molybdate obtained has the crystallinity and structural stability to its parent phase. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION In accordance with the above, the present invention provides Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO4) of the general formula (I) comprising; (Mg1-xLix)MoO4-------(I) wherein ‘x’ =0.05-0.20; wherein said Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO4) retains the crystallinity and structural stability to the parent phase; and wherein the said Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO4) exhibits the reduced energy band gap. In an aspect, the present invention discloses the sol-gel process for preparation of single phase Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO4) of the general formula (I); (Mg1-xLix)MoO4 (I) wherein ‘x’ =0.05-0.20. comprising; Preparing the solutions of the precursors ammonium heptamolybdate ((NH4)6Mo7O24.4H2O), magnesium nitrate (Mg(NO3)2∙6H2O) and lithium nitrate (LiNO3) separately in deionized water; Adding aloe vera extract to the mixed solution of step (i) and maintaining the pH of the solution about to 7.0 with ammonia solution; Stirring the mixture of step (ii) at a temperature ranging between 65-70ᵒC until gel is formed; Drying the gel of step (iii) at a temperature ranging between 230-245ᵒC followed by grinding to powder form; and Heating the powder of step (iv) at a temperature ranging between 550-650ᵒC to obtain the desired product. In an aspect, the X-ray diffraction pattern of Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) of the present invention reveals single phase formation of oxide materials up to x = 0.20. The maximum intensity peak at Bragg’s angle 2θ (degree) = 26.3246 was observed which corresponds to 220 plane of the monoclinic phase, similar to the parent MgMoO4 phase. For x = 0.30, impurity/secondary phases were observed. Thus, the parent phase was found to be stabilized up to lithium with doping (x) = 0.20 (Fig 1). In another aspect, the Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) of the present invention crystallizes in a monoclinic structure with space group C2/m as confirmed by Rietveld refined-cum-diffraction patterns in Fig 2. The structure comprises isolated [MoO4]2-tetrahedra and Mg ions coordinated by oxygen. In an aspect, the Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of the formula Mg0.95Li0.05MoO4 has the unit cell lattice parameters comprising; a =10.2807Å, b = 9.2896Å, c = 7.0286Å, angles: α = 90º β = 106.916º γ = 90º space group C2/m In another aspect, the Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of the formula Mg 0.9Li0.10MoO4 has the unit cell lattice parameters comprising; a =10.2569Å, b = 9.2721Å, c = 7.0124Å, angles: α = 90º β = 106.897º γ = 90º space group C2/m. In yet another aspect, the Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of the formula Mg0.8Li0.20MoO4 has the unit cell lattice parameters comprising;; a =10.2826Å, b = 9.2955Å, c = 7.0301Å, angles: α = 90º β = 106.888º γ = 90º space group C2/m The lattice parameters for the Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of the present invention given above indicates the formation of pure and single phase of lithium (x) doped (Mg1-xLix)MoO4 oxides up to x= 0.20. In another aspect, the unit cell of the present Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) contains multiple formula units, leading to a complex vibrational spectrum. The Raman spectrum of Mg1-xLixMoO4 (x = 0.05 to 0.20) reveals well-defined vibrational bands at specific frequencies, confirming the presence of characteristic modes of the [MoO4]2-tetrahedral as depicted in Fig 3. The distinct Raman bands were observed at ~ 969, 958, 911, 906, 875, 856, 425, 385, 372, 350, 335, 325, 277, 205, 180, 156, and 122 cm-1 which reflect the contributions from both internal MoO4 modes and lattice dynamics. The spectrum was observed to be clearly dominated by strong high-frequency modes corresponding to the internal vibrations of the [MoO4]2-group. The presence of multiple peaks in the 850–970 cm-1 region indicated slight distortions or splitting of vibrational levels due to crystalline anisotropy. Mid-and low-frequency bands reflected bending modes and lattice phonons, demonstrating the structural stability and bonding interactions within the framework. In an aspect, the increase in bond length of Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) with increase in the doping of the lithium ions from x=0.05 to 0.20. Accordingly, the bond length values increased as ~ 2.0848, 2.1987 and 2.3300Å for x = 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20, respectively. The bond angle of Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) also increased with increase in the doping of the lithium ions from x=0.05 to 0.20 as shown in table below. In yet another embodiment, the UV-visible absorption spectra of Lithium (Li) doped Magnesium molybdate of formula (I) exhibited shifting towards higher wavelength with increase in doping of the lithium ions. In another embodiment, the optical band gaps were observed at 4.22, 3.65, 3.63, 3.59 and 3.57eV for Li doped Mg1-xLixMoO4 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 respectively). The gradual decrease in the band gap with increasing Li content is attributed to lattice distortion due to ionic size mismatch between Mg²⁺ (0.72 Å) and Li⁺ (0.76 Å), creation of localized states and modified electronic interactions and enhanced defect levels and changes in orbital hybridization. This distortion facilitates band tailing, leading to a reduction in the energy required for electronic transitions. In yet another aspect, the present invention provides an optoelectronic device comprising lithium doped magnesium molybdate of formula (I) as a conducting material. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A PROCESS FOR EFFICIENT EXTRACTION OF LITHIUM FROM LITHIUM CONTAINING MATERIAL The present invention discloses a process for extracting valuable lithium metals, preferably lithium, from lithium containing material. The process involves mechanical separation of cathode materials followed by bioleaching using a specialized bacterial strain under optimized conditions, achieving high-purity metal extraction without harsh chemicals. The process combines mechanical processing, microbial treatment, and analytical modules to enable efficient, eco-friendly metal extraction. Key innovations include strain-specific selectivity, one cycle, and complete exclusion of thermal/chemical treatments with sustainability.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TITLE OF THE INVENTION A Process for Efficient Extraction of lithium from Lithium Containing Material. FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of metallurgy and the recycling of lithium from lithium containing material. It specifically concerns the extraction of lithium from lithium containing material using microbial processes. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The widespread adoption of lithium containing material, particularly lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in electronics, electric vehicles, and energy storage processes has resulted in a growing volume of spent batteries, creating both environmental hazards and opportunities for critical material extraction. Lithium, categorized as a strategic resource, is in high demand; however, its extraction from primary sources is limited and resource intensive. Conventional recycling processes such as pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy, though effective, are energy-intensive, rely on toxic reagents, and generate secondary pollutants, making them environmentally and economically unsustainable. However, existing bioleaching processes are often inefficient for lithium extraction. Most are optimized for cobalt or nickel and involve multiple stages, harsh pre-treatments, or extended incubation times. For example, CN100499252C utilizes acidophilic bacteria but requires prolonged leaching (>15 days) and low pH conditions.US20220352570A1 and EP4112757A1 focus on multi-metal extraction, treating lithium as secondary. Therefore, there is a clear unmet need for a simplified, efficient, and lithium-specific bioleaching process that eliminates chemical pre-treatment, operates under mild conditions, and supports Eco-friendly and scalable application. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION An object of the invention is to develop a process for microbial extraction of lithium from lithium containing material. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention provides a single-step process for extraction lithium from lithium containing material batteries using a bioleaching approach. The process involves mechanically processing waste lithium containing material to recover cathode materials without the use of thermal or chemical treatment. The recovered cathode material, typically referred to as black mass, is inoculated with a specific lithium-solubilizing bacterial strain, Acinetobacter schindleri, which facilitates the bioleaching process. The inoculated material is incubated under controlled conditions suitable for bacterial activity and lithium solubilization. These conditions may include incubation at 37 ◦C, with aeration and agitation at about 100-200 rpm, for a period of about 4-6 days. The pH of the medium is maintained within a range conducive to bacterial growth and metal solubilization. Following incubation, the bioleached material is subjected to analytical process to assess lithium extraction. Techniques such as Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FE-SEM) are employed to quantify and characterize the solubilized lithium and morphological changes in the black mass. The invention also encompasses mechanical processing, bacterial inoculation, incubation, and analysis for executing the process described. This process is cost-effective and eco-friendly alternative to pre-existing traditional processes such as pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy. This process allows for an effective solution for lithium extraction, eliminating the need for toxic chemicals, complex processing steps and minimizing input of energy. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES Figure 1 depicts a flow chart of the bioleaching process for lithium extraction. Figure 2 illustrates (a) Breaking of lithium containing material and (b) Scraping of black Mass. Figure 3 depicts (a) Control (b) inoculated culture without black mass(c) Complete bioleaching experiment. Figure 4 depicts FE-SEM images of (a) Raw black mass; (b) Control black mass; and (c) Bioleached residue. Figure 5 depicts FTIR Spectra of black mass after bioleaching. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to a process for extraction lithium metal from lithium containing material using a bioleaching process. The invention provides an eco-friendly and cost-effective alternative to conventional pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical process by employing a specific metal solubilizing bacterium in a controlled incubation environment to enable selective extraction of lithium from black mass, the active cathode material of lithium-ion batteries. In an embodiment, the invention discloses a process for extracting lithium from lithium containing material, comprising: screening, selecting and identification of an isolated bacterial strain from the lithium containing material, using 16S rRNA sequencing; processing the lithium containing material by mechanical method excluding chemical or thermal pre-treatment, to obtain cathode material in form of black mass; inoculating the black mass in a nutrient broth medium and incubating under bioleaching conditions at 37 ◦C, agitation 100-200 revolutions per minute (rpm), aeration, and a pH suitable for bacterial growth; and analyzing the solubilized lithium using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), wherein the process achieves metal extraction, excluding mineral acids/chelators/thermal energy, and completes extraction in one step using metal solubilizing bacterial strain from the lithium containing material in 4-6 days. The bacterial inoculation and incubation are configured to receive the pre-treated black mass, inoculate it with the bacterial culture, and maintain incubation conditions at 37◦C, 100-200 rpm and appropriate pH in a range of 6 to 8 and aeration for a duration of five days at 100 to 200rpm speed. The analytical characterization and accurate elemental quantification were done by instrumentation for Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FE-SEM), enabling comprehensive assessment of lithium extraction and material characterization. In accordance with the present Invention, microbial strain, A. schindleri is obtained from lithium containing material and identified via 16S rRNA sequencing, which provided the sequence to show a 99.36% match to known sequences and assigned GenBank accession number PV453749(Table 1). This naturally occurring strain was selected due to its high lithium solubilization efficiency and eco-friendly bio-metabolic properties. The strain is cultivated in nutrient broth to obtain an active culture for inoculation into the black mass slurry. GenBank Accession Number Microbe Name Sequence PV453749 A. schindleri TTATCGCGTTAGCTGCGCCACTAAAGCCTCAAAGGCCCCAACGGCTAGTAGAC ATCGTTTACGGCATGGACTACCAGGGTATCTAATCCTGTTTGCTCCCCATGCTT TCGTACCTCAGCGTCAGTATTAGGCCAGATGGCTGCCTTCGCCATCGGTATTCC TCCAGATCTCTACGCATTTCACCGCTACACCTGGAATTCTACCATCCTCTCCCAT ACTCTAGCTTTCCAGTATCGAATGCAATTCCTAAGTTAAGCTCAGGGATTTCAC ATCCGACTTAAAAAGCCGCCTACGCACGCTTTACGCCCAGTAAATCCGATTAA CGCTCGCACCCTCTGTATTACCGCGGCTGCTGGCACAGAGTTAGCCGGTGCTTA TTCTGCGAGTAACGTCCACTCACTTTAGGTATTAACTAAAGGAGCCTCCTCCTC GCTTAAAGTGCTTTACAACCAAAAGGCCTTCTTCACACACGCGGCATGGCTGG ATCAGGCTTGCGCCCATTGTCCAATATTCCCCACTGCTGCCTCCCGTAGGAGTC TGGGCCGTGTCTCAGTCCCAGTGTGGCGGATCATCCTCTCAGACCCGCTACAGA TCGTCGCCTTGGTAGGCCTTTACCCCACCAACTAGCTAATCCGACTTAGGCTCA TCTATTAGCGCAAGGTCCGAAGATCCCCTGCTTTCCCCCGTAGGACGTATGCGG TATTAGCATTCCTTTCGGAATGTTGTCCCCCACTAATAGGCAGATTCCTAAGCA TTACTCACCCGTCCGCCGCTAGG Table 1: Details of Microbe In accordance with the present invention, the lithium containing material, preferably spent lithium-ion batteries, is subjected to mechanical processing to extract cathode material in the form of black mass by scrapping without using thermal or chemical pre-treatment. Mechanical processing includes disassembly of the outer casing using tools such as a hammer or chisel, followed by sorting and scrapping of the internal components. The cathode material is air-dried and physically scraped off from the aluminum substrate to yield fine black powder. This black mass serves as the substrate for bioleaching and contains the target lithium component in a solid matrix form. Importantly, this pre-treatment does not involve heating or acid digestion, thereby minimizing energy input and avoiding the production of hazardous spent lithium-ion batteries. A comparison of treated and control samples confirms that A. schindleri plays a direct role in lithium extraction, achieving a lithium extraction efficiency of approximately 78.93% under the specified incubation conditions. The minimal requirement for energy or chemicals, combined with a short processing time, renders this process both scalable and environmentally sustainable. After incubation, the leachate and biomass are subjected to analysis to determine lithium content and to assess the efficiency of the bioleaching process. Lithium concentration is quantified using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES). Prior to ICP-OES, microbial biomass is digested using microwave-assisted acid digestion according to USEPA Process 3052, ensuring complete breakdown of organic and inorganic components. Further chemical and structural analysis are conducted using FTIR and FE-SEM. The FTIR results reveal distinct changes in functional group vibrations indicative of chemical transformations in the black mass. Notable peaks are observed at 2348 cm⁻¹ (C–H stretching), 1720 cm⁻¹ (C=O stretching), 1092 cm⁻¹ (C–F stretching), 670 cm⁻¹ (metal-ligand interaction), and 470 cm⁻¹ (metal-carbon vibrations), validating microbial interaction with the black mass matrix. Meanwhile, FE-SEM images at magnifications ranging from 5,000× to 50,000× show clear morphological differences between raw black mass, control samples, and bioleached residues. The bioleached samples exhibit surface pitting, erosion, and structural disintegration consistent with microbial solubilization activity. Visual evidence of this process is provided in associated figures. Figure 1 outlines the stepwise flow of the bioleaching process; figure 2 shows mechanical processing and black mass extraction. Figure 3 presents incubation samples and control conditions, where the figure 3 includes FE-SEM images at various magnifications comparing raw, control, and treated black mass. Figure 4 depicts the FTIR spectra highlighting chemical changes. Overall, this invention provides a low-cost, and eco-friendly bioleaching-based process for lithium extraction that avoids secondary pollution and toxic chemical usage. Its simplicity, efficiency, and sustainability position as a viable solution for circular economy-based lithium recycling from lithium containing material. EXAMPLES Example 1: Obtaining A. schindleri Strain and Its Identification-A bacterial strain capable of lithium solubilization was isolated from e waste contaminated soil and identified as A. schindleri using 16S rRNA sequencing (table 1). This strain was used as the bioleaching agent in subsequent experiments. Example 2: Mechanical pre-treatment of spent lithium-ion batteries were manually opened (Figure 2a), and cathode materials (black mass) were physically scraped from internal layers (Figure 2b). No chemicals or heat were used in this pre-treatment step. Figure 2 illustrates the entirely mechanical pre-treatment process for spent lithium-ion batteries, where (a) battery casings are carefully opened using manual tools (hammer and chisel) under ambient temperature conditions without employing any thermal or chemical methods, followed by (b) air-drying of inner components at and subsequent physical scraping of the active black mass from aluminum current collectors using non-reactive Teflon-coated tools to prevent contamination. The recovered black mass is then stored in argon-filled containers to maintain material integrity before bioleaching. This process ensures purity of recovered cathode material while completely avoiding the use of hazardous chemicals, high temperatures, or complex equipment, making it both environmentally benign and economically viable for industrial-scale battery recycling. Figure 3 demonstrates the bioleaching process using A. schindleri with GenBank accession number is (Pv453749), where: (a) a control setup containing only nutrient broth and black mass (5 g/L) was maintained to assess abiotic leaching, (b) an inoculated culture without black mass served to monitor background bacterial growth, and (c) the complete bioleaching system combined nutrient broth, pre-treated black mass (5 g/L), and A. schindleri inoculum under controlled conditions (37°C), 150 rpm agitation, aerobic environment) for 120 hours (5 days). The experimental design enabled precise evaluation of microbial leaching efficiency by comparing lithium solubilization against controls, with the complete system (Fig. 3c) showing 78.93 lithium extraction via ICP-OES analysis while maintaining pH through automated regulation. This configuration validated the strain's specific lithium-extraction capability, excluding chemical leaching artifacts or non-target metal extraction. Example 3: For the determination of the quantification of lithium recovered in the bioleaching process, ICP-OES was utilized (Model: Optima 2100 DV, Perkin, USA). The bioleached samples were first centrifuged to efficiently separate the supernatant and bacterial biomass. The biomass fraction was then assessed to measure the total leaching efficiency. The solid biomass fraction was digested according to the USEPA 3052 microwave-assisted digestion procedure (USEPA, 1996) so that all cellular and particulate material was broken down for effective elemental analysis. ICP-OES was then used to analyze the digested biomass solution to determine the extraction and distribution of lithium.
