patents.abstract: ABSTRACT TITLE: Ultra-high Nickel-rich, Manganese and Cobalt-free cathode integration with PVDF-HFP nanofiber polypropylene separator in lithium-ion batteries and method of manufacture Ultrahigh nickel-rich layered oxide cathodes are attractive for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) owing to their high specific capacity. However, conventional LiNi0.95Mn0.025Co0.025O2 (NMC95) suffers from structural degradation, Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing, oxygen release, and transition-metal dissolution, resulting in poor cycling stability and thermal safety, particularly under high-voltage operation. Moreover, cobalt’s scarcity, toxicity, and price volatility, along with Mn3+ instability from Jahn–Teller distortion and disproportionation, limit large-scale viability. Herein, we develop manganese-and cobalt-free ultrahigh-Ni-rich LiNi0.95Zr0.025Mg0.025O2 (NZM95) cathode as a sustainable alternative. Structural analyses via XRD, Rietveld refinement, and HR-TEM reveal improved crystallinity, reduced cation disorder, and enlarged interlayer spacing. Zr4+ and Mg2+co-substitution strengthens Ni–O bonding and suppresses antisite and oxygen defects, as confirmed by synchrotron EXAFS, XPS, and wavelet transform analyses. DSC indicates superior thermal stability with a higher exothermic peak (~226 °C) and lower heat release of NZM95. To further enhance the performance, a polarized β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber (NF) coating was electrospun onto a polypropylene (PP) separator (NF@PP). The strong ferroelectric polarization of the β-phase PVDF-HFP regulates ion flux by repelling PF6− anions, enriching Li+ near the interface and scavenging detrimental HF, mitigating interfacial degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirm the β-phase-induced ion redistribution, revealing significantly stronger interaction energies of NF@PP with Li+ and HF compared to pristine PP. This theoretical insight supports uniform Li+ transport, suppressed anion aggregation, and enhanced interfacial ion stability. NZM95 paired with NF@PP delivers ~215 mAh g−1 with 86% retention over 200 cycles, surpassing PP (~207 mAh g−1, 78%). The synergistic effect of the cathode-separator approach affords a scalable route toward energy-dense and long-life cathodes in LIBs. Figure 1
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to the development of Mn-and Co-free ultrahigh-Ni-rich LiNi0.95Zr0.025Mg0.025O2 (NZM95) cathode with acceptable electrochemical performance, compared to Co-and Mn-containing LiNi0.95Mn0.025Co0.025O2 (NMC95) cathode. The incorporation of stabilizing ions such as magnesium and zirconium effectively suppresses undesirable side reactions with the electrolyte, reduces structural degradation and transition-metal dissolution, and minimizes active lithium loss. This study provides a comprehensive assessment of surface characteristics, structural stability, and bulk properties to understand the underlying mechanisms driving performance enhancement in NZM95. Additionally, the present invention relates to the design and application of a composite separator comprising an electrospun β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber (NF) coating on a commercial Celgard® 2400 polypropylene (PP) membrane (NF@PP). This composite separator is integrated with NZM95 during cell fabrication to enhance the electrochemical performance. The NF@PP separator demonstrates significantly improved wettability, porosity, electrolyte uptake, and ionic conductivity compared to bare PP. Moreover, the ferroelectric PVDF-HFP nanofibers facilitate PF6− anion immobilization, promotes uniform lithium-ion transport and suppresses dendrite formation on the lithium metal anode. The intrinsic adsorption ability of β-phase PVDF-HFP also contributes to HF scavenging and impurity removal, thereby enhancing the cycling stability of Ni-rich cathodes. Additionally, crystallinity control and electrostatic field polarization of the β-phase PVDF-HFP further promote uniform interfacial lithium transport, minimize anion-related side reactions, and reduce CEI growth and cathode surface degradation. Collectively, this work presents a promising strategy to enhance the safety, efficiency, and longevity of high-energy lithium-ion batteries by integrating a functionalized separator and a transition-metal-free cathode. BACKGROUND ART: Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have emerged as the leading energy storage solution for the rapidly growing electric vehicle industry, owing to their high energy density and long cycle life [1]. Among the various cathode materials, Ni-rich layered transition metal oxides, particularly LiNixMnyCozO2 (NMC), offer high practical capacities exceeding 200 mAh g−1 along with high discharge voltages, making them attractive for high-energy density energy storage applications [2]. However, the continued use of cobalt and manganese in these materials presents significant challenges, including cost volatility, manganese dissolution, and undesired side reactions with the electrolyte, all of which contribute to capacity loss and structural degradation [3]. In conventional low-Co or Co-free ultra-high Ni-rich cathodes, Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing and structural disorder typically occur during cycling. This results in irreversible phase transitions and surface reconstructions, ultimately compromising both cyclic performance and thermal stability [4]. Consequently, minimizing Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing is crucial for enhancing the electrochemical performance and structural integrity of these cathode materials. Further efforts are essential to enhance the voltage window, specific capacity, and capacity retention of ultrahigh Ni-rich cathode materials, particularly with low Co or Co-free utilization. Among the numerous cations, Co and Mn are normally considered the essential in ultrahigh Ni-rich cathode chemistry to maintain the thermal and structural stability. However, Mn ions, particularly on the outer surface, often undergo a reduction to Mn3+ due to the Jahn-Teller distortion [5]. The Mn3+ state is highly unstable and prone to disproportionation into soluble Mn2+, leading to active material loss and gradual capacity fading [6]. The dissolution of Mn significantly impacts the coulombic efficiency and long-term cycling stability of Mn-based cathodes. In addition, high-voltage operation accelerates cathode degradation by promoting electrolyte decomposition and the formation of an unstable cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) layer [7]. There are two possible mechanisms for manganese dissolution, i.e., HF attack and anion dissolution due to structural disorder during cycling. The HF molecules formed when residual surface water molecules react with LiPF6, as shown in equations 1-3 [8]. LiPF6 ↔ LiF(s) + PF5 (1) LiPF6 + H2O ↔ LiF(s) + 2HF + POF3 (2) PF5 + H2O ↔ 2HF + POF3 (3) The presence of HF rationalises the migration of manganese to form MnF2 due to the decomposition of the irreversible Li1-xMn2O4 cathode material, as shown in equation 4 [9]. Li1-xMn2O4 + 2(1-x)HF ↔ ((3+x)/4)Mn2O4 + (1-x)LiF + (1-x)H2O + (1-x/2)MnF2 (4) The reduction of PF6 to PF5 anion during the charged state leads to the reduction of Mn4+ to Mn3+ occurring through the acceptance of electrons [10]. Therefore, the disproportionation reaction of Mn3+ occurs on the surface of the cathode particle (2Mn3+ (solid) → Mn4+ (solid) + Mn2+ (solution)). Here, the Mn2+ ions are readily dissolved in the electrolyte and could migrate to the anode, leading to capacity fading during charge/discharge [11]. Furthermore, Co while contributing to structural stability, has its own limitations, i.e., it reduces lithium utilization in the layered structure, thereby lowering the reversible capacity [12]. Moreover, the limited availability, toxicity, and volatile pricing of Co pose major challenges for its sustainable use in the global supply chain [13]. These drawbacks, particularly the instability of Mn and the associated cost and supply risks of Co, have spurred an increasing interest in developing Mn-and Co-free cathode materials to overcome these limitations [14]. Among various substituents such as Al, Nb, Fe, Cu, Zn, Mg, Ti, and Zr, several elements have shown promise as alternative dopants in electrode materials due to their favourable electrochemical performance, controlled synthesis, tunable morphology, wide availability, and low cost [15]. Although the large-scale commercial application of these high-voltage nickel-rich ternary oxide cathodes is still hindered by parasitic surface reactions, particle cracking, and continuous phase transitions, which degrade cycling and rate performance. Furthermore, cathode–electrolyte interfacial instability leads to excessive electrolyte decomposition and the formation of a resistive cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI), resulting in sluggish Li+-ion transfer kinetics and incremental electrochemical polarization [16]. Meanwhile, the electrolyte by-products, such as hydrofluoric acid (HF), can further destroy the cathode surface, accelerating transition-metal dissolution and promoting a layered-to-rock-salt phase transition [17]. To mitigate these challenges, considerable effort has been devoted to understanding the origin of cathode-electrolyte interfacial instability and addressing it to achieve higher cell performance, improved safety, and lower costs. A critical component influencing interfacial behaviour is the separator, a microporous membrane placed between the electrodes that prevents electrical shorting while allowing ionic transport and serving as an electrolyte reservoir [18]. Commercial separators are typically made of polyolefin materials, such as polypropylene (PP), valued for their mechanical robustness, chemical stability, and low cost [19]. However, PP separators suffer from poor thermal stability, limited electrolyte wettability, and uneven lithium deposition, which can lead to dendrite formation and compromised solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) stability [20]. In various modification methods, surface coating has been widely employed to enhance the properties of PP separators [21]. Among these, surface coatings using materials such as SiO2, Al2O3, and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) have shown significant advancement [22]. In particular, poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) has attracted attention due to its superior electrolyte wettability and electrochemical stability. PVDF-HFP is a semi-crystalline fluoropolymer capable of crystallizing in multiple polymorphic forms (α, β, γ, δ, ε) [23]. The α-phase is the most stable but non-ferroelectric due to its antiparallel dipole arrangement (fluorine and hydrogen atoms alternately appear on the carbon chain), whereas the β-phase exhibits ferroelectric behavior, owing to its all-trans planar conformation that all fluorine atoms are arranged on the same side of the carbon chain, resulting in strong spontaneous polarization. A well-polarized ferroelectric β-phase PVDF-HFP as a separator coating introduces unique interfacial effects [24]. The oriented dipoles within the ferroelectric domains can modulate the local electrolyte structure at the cathode surface by repelling anions and enriching Li+ concentration, thereby enhancing (de)lithiation kinetics and suppressing parasitic reactions [25]. However, the electrospinning has emerged as an efficient approach to prepare nanofibrous coatings, offering high porosity, enhanced electrolyte uptake, and improved ionic conductivity due to the interconnected one-dimensional fibre network [26]. OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION: The primary objective of the present invention is to develop a manganese-and cobalt-free, ultrahigh nickel-rich cathode with excellent electrochemical properties, which could serve as the best possible alternative to the problem of transition metal dissolution in next-generation lithium-ion batteries and the battery industry. Another objective of the present invention is to develop a cobalt and manganese-free ultrahigh nickel-rich (≥95 mol% Ni) layered oxide cathode that eliminates the dependency on cobalt, which has become an issue for battery suppliers and industries worldwide due to limited global reserves and rapid price escalation constraining the global supply chain. Another objective of the present invention is to develop a cobalt and manganese-free, ultrahigh nickel-rich (≥95 mol% Ni) layered oxide cathode that exhibits better cation ordering and provides a higher Ni3+ ratio due to low Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing. Another objective of the present invention is to stabilize the layered oxide structure and ensure that specific capacity is not compromised during cycling at higher voltage (3-4.5V). Another objective of the present invention is to design a composite separator comprising an electrospun β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber (NF) coating on a commercial Celgard® 2400 PP membrane (NF@PP). Another objective of the present invention is to investigate the role of ferroelectric β-phase PVDF-HFP in anion immobilization, uniform Li+ transport, dendrite suppression, HF scavenging, and impurity removal for improved electrochemical stability of NZM95. Another objective of the present invention is to fabricate a separator that is integrated with a manganese and cobalt-free ultrahigh-Ni cathode (NZM95) with enhanced wettability, porosity, electrolyte uptake, and ionic conductivity for high-energy lithium-ion batteries. Another objective of the present invention is to perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to uncover the atomistic mechanisms governing ion–separator interactions and Li+ transport within the separators. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION As discussed hereinbefore, the present invention provides for a manganese-and cobalt-free ultrahigh nickel-rich cathode-LiNi0.95Zr0.025Mg0.025O2 (NZM95), exhibiting attractive electrochemical performance benchmarked against the LiNi0.95Mn0.025Co0.025O2 (NMC95) cathode in lithium-ion batteries. The impact of Zr and Mg substitution on the structural and electrochemical properties of Ni-rich NZM95 layered oxides was comprehensively evaluated with respect to the NMC95 reference cathode. The NZM95 (R m space group) exhibits minimal Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing (~9.1%) compared to the Co and Mn-bearing NMC95 (11.1%) as verified by XRD, and therefore offers improved electrochemical and structural stability during cycling at a higher voltage window (3-4.5 V). Importantly, the I(003) diffraction peak was slightly shifted towards a lower angle due to the incorporation of Zr and Mg, leading to an enlarged interlayer spacing (~0.378 nm). The wavelet transformation of XANES data pertaining to NZM95 reveals intense Ni-O bonding, indicating the stability and reversibility of the local coordination environment, contributing to enhanced structural stability. Electrochemical properties of the NZM95 cathode exhibit a stable rate capability at different C rates and enhanced cycling performance-specific capacity of ~207 mAh g−1 and ~94% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 0.1C compared to specific capacity of ~216 mAh g−1 and capacity retention of ~70% for NMC95. The substantial dissolution and migration of transition metals (particularly Mn) from the NMC95 cathode contribute to the pronounced capacity degradation during cycling, as revealed by TOF-SIMS analysis. Overall, Ni-rich and Co/Mn-free NZM95 may be a revolutionary cathode in resolving the battery industry's long-standing issues with the cost and availability of cobalt, as well as transition-metal dissolution to break the monopoly. To further enhance the cell performance, a polarized β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber (NF) coating was electrospun onto a polypropylene (PP) separator (NF@PP). The electrospun β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber layer significantly improves separator wettability, porosity, and electrolyte uptake, while its intrinsic anion-immobilization ability enhances Li+ mobility. This ferroelectric layer modulates the local solvation structure, repels electrolyte anions, and promotes Li+ aggregation as examined by chronoamperometric and galvanostatic plating/stripping analysis, improving (de) lithiation kinetics. These combined effects promote homogeneous Li⁺ flux and effectively inhibit dendrite nucleation and growth. To gain deeper atomistic insights into the interfacial behaviour, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to investigate the interaction energies between LiPF6 and PVDF-HFP. The simulations reveal the time-dependent interaction energies of NF@PP–Li+, PP–Li+, NF@PP–PF6−, PP–PF6−, NF@PP–HF, and PP–HF systems, as well as the time-dependent minimum distance between the HF and separator surfaces. NF@PP exhibits significantly stronger Li+ interaction energies (–150 to –200 kJ mol−1) compared to PP (0 to –30 kJ mol−1), indicating higher Li+ affinity due to its enhanced polarity and fluorine-rich surface. Similarly, NF@PP demonstrates stronger interaction energies with PF6−, (–350 to –400 kJ mol−1) and HF (–30 to –70 kJ mol−1) than PP, demonstrating effective anion trapping and HF scavenging. Solvation sheath analysis within a 5 Å radius shows that β-phase PVDF-HFP restructures the local solvation environment of Li+, favoring coordination with linear carbonates such as EMC for improved ion mobility. Moreover, radial distribution function (RDF) analysis reveals that NF@PP suppresses contact ion-pair formation between Li+ and PF6−, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity and interfacial ion stability. Collectively, β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofibers provide a multifunctional strategy for separator modification, simultaneously enhancing ion transport, suppressing parasitic reactions, scavenging HF, and stabilizing the cathode–electrolyte interface. NZM95 paired with NF@PP delivers a specific capacity of ~215 mAh g−1 with 86% capacity retention over 200 cycles, surpassing PP (~207 mAh g−1, 78%). This synergistic cathode–separator approach offers a scalable route toward high-energy-density, thermally stable, and long-life LIBs. In one embodiment, the layered oxide LiNi0.95M'0.025M''0.025O2, wherein M' = Co and/or Mg and M'' = Mn and/or Zr, cathode materials were synthesized using the modified citrate-nitrate route (see Figure 1a). In solution 1, citric acid (Fisher Scientific) and deionized water were dissolved in the appropriate molar ratios of 1.06 mol lithium hydroxide (Fisher Scientific), with the ratio of citric acid to transition metals maintained at 1:1. Simultaneously, the appropriate molar ratios of 0.95 mol nickel nitrate (Fisher Scientific), 0.025 mol cobalt nitrate (Fisher Scientific), 0.025 mol zirconyl Nitrate (Oxford lab), 0.025 mol magnesium nitrate (Fisher Scientific), and 0.025 mol manganese acetate (Fisher Scientific) were dissolved in a solution 2 of deionized water. The solutions were vigorously stirred for 45 min and maintained at 45 °C. Solution 1 was then added dropwise into solution 2, followed by continuously stirring and allowing the excess water to evaporate at ~45°C. The dropwise addition of citric acid to form a homogeneous precursor solution containing metal-citrate chelating complexes leads to esterification (forms a covalent network). The pH of the solution was modified by the addition of ammonia until it reached 6.5, facilitating gel formation. As the viscous gel formed, the temperature was gradually increased to ~90 °C until spontaneous combustion occurred, yielding a porous, foamy intermediate powder. The obtained precursor was ground using an agate mortar and subsequently preheated at 450 °C for 5 h in air, followed by calcination at 850 °C for 12 h in a muffle furnace. The as-prepared LiNi0.95Mn0.025Co0.02O2 and LiNi0.95Zr0.025Mg0.025O2 were named as NMC95 and NZM95, respectively. In another embodiment, the PVDF-HFP (Sigma-Aldrich) coated microporous polypropylene membrane Celgard® 2400 (PP) was prepared using dip coating (DC) and nanofiber (NF) coating by the electrospinning technique (see Figure 1(b, c)). The 12 w/v.% of PVDF-HFP was dissolved completely in DMF after stirring for 12 h. For dip coating, the PP membrane was gently immersed into PVDF-HFP solution for 10 min and then dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C. During nanofiber coating, the PVDF-HFP solution was electrospun onto a PP membrane attached to an aluminium foil-covered rotating drum collector. The viscous PVDF-HFP solution was evenly coated on one side of the PP membrane until the desired thickness was achieved. The electrostatic force increased and became greater than the surface tension of the drop (PVDF-HFP solution), which then led to splitting into fibres. The following electrospinning conditions were maintained during the process: applied voltage: 7.5 kV; relative humidity: 50-60%; rotating drum collector speed: ~1200 rpm; tip to collector distance: 15 cm; feed rate: ~0.5 mL h−1; temperature: ~22 °C. The dip and nanofiber-coated PP membranes, named as DC@PP and NF@PP, respectively, were punched out into 18 mm diameter discs and used as separators. In another embodiment, the cathode consists of prepared powder samples (active material), conductive carbon additive, and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) as a binder, mixed in a weight ratio of 80:10:10, and formed into a slurry with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent. The resulting homogeneous slurry was tape-cast onto aluminum foil using a doctor blade and subsequently dried in a vacuum oven at 90 °C for 12 h. Electrodes were punched into 14 mm diameter discs with an active material loading of approximately 5.5–6.5 mg/cm2, and dried further under vacuum at 60 °C for 24 h. The prepared electrodes were transferred to an argon-filled glove box (mBraun UniLab Pro, O2& H2O < 0.1 ppm) for storage. CR-2032-type coin cells were assembled using the prepared electrodes as cathode, lithium metal foil (~50 μm thickness, ~15 mm diameter) as the anode, followed by microporous polypropylene (PP) Celgard® 2400, DC@PP, or NF@PP separators. The electrolyte consisted of approximately 14 wt.% LiPF6 dissolved in a solvent mixture of 36.6 wt.% ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), 19.2 wt.% ethylene carbonate (EC), 19.3 wt.% dimethyl carbonate (DMC), 8 wt.% propylene carbonate (PC), and 1.8 wt.% vinylene carbonate (VC), procured from BASF, Germany. EXAMPLE 1 In the present invention, structural and morphological analyses of the as-prepared NMC95 and NZM95 cathode materials, synthesized via the citrate–nitrate method, were examined using XRD, FESEM, XPS, and HRTEM. XRD analysis: The XRD pattern was recorded to identify the structure of the NMC95 and NZM95 materials (see Figure 2a). It can be clearly seen that the diffraction peaks are sharp, indicating good crystallinity and a well-defined hexagonal α-NaFeO2 lattice structure belonging to R m space group (ICDD No. 98-011-1904). The diffraction peak at I(003) is slightly shifted (~0.28º) toward a low angle as shown in Figure 2b, indicating an expansion in the unit cell volume, which may be due to the substitution of Zr4+ (~0.79 Å) and Mg2+ (~0.72 Å) in Mn4+ (~0.53 Å) and Co3+ (~0.55 Å) sites, respectively. The high-valence cation Zr4+, substituted into the transition-metal sites, enlarges the interplanar spacing between the Li and TM layers owing to its larger ionic radius, thereby facilitating Li+ diffusion. In contrast, the low-valence cation Mg2+ can occupy either the Li layer (3a site) or the TM layer (3b site), influencing cation mixing and lattice stability depending on its distribution. To elucidate the role of Zr and Mg incorporation in the Mn-and Co-free NZM95 lattice, Rietveld refinement was performed under three structural scenarios: (i) Mg occupying only the 3b (transition metal) sites, (ii) Mg distributed across both 3a (lithium) and 3b sites, and (iii) Mg confined to the 3a sites, with NMC95 serving as a reference. The refined lattice parameters, atomic coordinates, and site occupancies are summarized in Table 1. Considering the degree of Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing and the corresponding goodness-of-fit (χ2), Mg substitution at the transition-metal sites (9.1% cation mixing, χ2 ~4.71) emerges as the most favorable configuration. In contrast, hypotheses with Mg occupying both TM/Li sites (9.7% mixing, χ2 ~4.94) or only Li sites (13.4% mixing, χ2 ~6.31) exhibit poorer fits and higher disorder. The clear splits of the I(006)/I(102) and I(108)/I(110) doublets observed in NZM95 corroborate that a well-ordered layered structure was formed, diminished in NMC95. Nonetheless, Zr4+ and Mg2+ were considered to occupy the transition metal site (3b sites); better goodness of fit in NZM95 was achieved with the crystal structure and experimental data (see Table 1). The lattice parameters, site positions, and site occupancies of the samples are calculated and presented in Table 1. Generally, the c/a value is employed to examine a layered structure, i.e., a higher c/a value (should be higher than ~4.899), indicating better ordering [27]. In our work, the c/a values of the NMC95 and NZM95 were 4.938 and 4.944, respectively, indicating the ideal hexagonal structure of the samples. The cationic disordering between Li+/Ni2+ leads to a partial destructive interference of the (003) plane’s constructive interference at a Bragg angle of θd(003), causing a decrease in the intensity of the (003) plane. On the contrary, the intensity of the (104) plane increases owing to the movement of TM-ions (especially Ni2+) in the lithium layer (3a sites), leading to an increase in the constructive interference of the θd(104) plane. Therefore, the relative intensity ratio of I(003)/I(104) should be higher for less-disordered samples [28]. In Table 1, the I(003)/I(104) ratio of NZM95 (~1.029) was higher than NMC95 (~1.011), indicating better cation ordering. The Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing in NMC95 and NZM95 was estimated to be ~11.1% and ~9.1%, respectively. Notably, Co-and Mn-free NZM95 show lesser Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing and steadily increases the unit cell volume compared to the Co-and Mn-bearing NMC95 cathode. Furthermore, the antisite defect concentration (Cantisite), which represents the proportion of NiLi and LiNi mutual defects, was calculated following the method proposed by Yin et al. [29], Cantisite = (0.2423 × [amount of Ni2+] + 0.01808) × [total amount of Ni]. The Cantisite of NMC95and NZM95 was found to be 0.043 and 0.038, respectively. EXAMPLE 4 In the present invention, PVDF-HFP is employed as a functional coating wherein the β-phase in PVDF-HFP, owing to its strong ferroelectric properties, provides the highest spontaneous polarization. The ordered dipoles within the ferroelectric domains induce a redistribution of electrolyte ions at the cathode interface, repelling anions and enriching Li+ cations near the surface. This ferroelectric-induced ion regulation facilitates uniform and rapid lithium transport across the interface while suppressing anion-related parasitic reactions, cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) growth, and surface degradation. Moreover, the electrospun β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber layer significantly improves separator wettability, porosity, and electrolyte uptake, while its intrinsic anion-immobilization ability enhances Li+ mobility. These combined effects promote homogeneous Li⁺ flux and effectively inhibit dendrite nucleation. In contrast, in conventional PP separator, Li⁺ ions accumulate within the micropores while anions released from LiPF6, obstruct Li⁺ transport, leading to heterogeneous ion distribution and dendrite growth. Furthermore, the β-phase in PVDF-HFP nanofibers acts as HF scavenger, thereby mitigating Mn3+ dissolution from NMC-based cathodes and enhancing long-term cycling stability. Collectively, β-phase in PVDF-HFP nanofibers provides a multifunctional strategy for separator modification, simultaneously enhancing ionic transport, suppressing parasitic reactions, scavenging HF, and stabilizing the cathode–electrolyte interface. Molecular dynamics simulations: In atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, the interaction energy represents the non-bonded potential energy between two defined groups of atoms or molecules, providing insight into their mutual attraction or repulsion. It comprises electrostatic (Coulombic) interactions arising from charge–charge forces, and van der Waals (Lennard-Jones) interactions, which include dispersion and short-range repulsion. Figure 7a shows the time-dependent interaction energies of NF@PP and PP separators with Li+-ions. Since the ordered mobility of Li+ plays a crucial role in battery performance, these interaction energy plots were computed to evaluate the extent of Li+ interaction with NF@PP and PP. The results indicate a significantly stronger interaction of NF@PP with Li⁺ than with PP in the presence of HF. The time-dependent interaction energy of NF@PP with Li+ varies between –150 and –200 kJ mol−1, whereas PP exhibits much weaker binding, ranging from ~0 to –30 kJ mol−1, likely due to its lower polarity. Invention qualifying aspects: The present invention introduces a dual-pronged approach that combines cation-engineered Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes with ferroelectric-functionalized separators to enhance lithium-ion battery performance and safety. The Mn-and Co-free LiNi0.95M’0.025M’’0.025O2 (where M' = Mg, and M'' = Zr) cathode synthesized via a modified citrate–nitrate route demonstrates superior crystallinity, reduced Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing, higher defect formation energy, and improved structural stability compared to conventional NMC-based cathode. Simultaneously, β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber-coated polypropylene (NF@PP) separator, fabricated by electrospinning, provide enhanced wettability, electrolyte uptake, ionic conductivity, and thermal stability. The strong ferroelectric polarization of β-phase PVDF-HFP regulates ion flux by repelling PF6− anions, enriching Li+ at the interface, and scavenging HF, thereby mitigating interfacial degradation. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed stronger interaction energies of NF@PP with Li+, PF6−, and HF than with pristine PP, confirming β-phase-induced ion redistribution that promotes uniform Li⁺ transport, and suppresses anion accumulation. This synergistic integration of transition metal site doping in ultrahigh Ni-rich and Mn, Co-free cathode and ferroelectric separator modification affords a multifunctional strategy to suppress parasitic reactions, inhibit dendrite growth, and extend cycling stability in energy-dense lithium-ion batteries. Advantages: This invention lies in its integrated strategy that simultaneously improves both the cathode and the separator performances, addressing key limitations of ultra-high-Ni-rich cathodes in lithium-ion batteries. The developed Mn-and Co-free ultrahigh-Ni layered oxide (NZM95) cathode exhibits superior structural stability due to suppressed Li+/Ni2+ cation mixing, stronger Ni–O bonding, and larger interplanar spacing, leading to faster Li+ transport and higher capacity retention compared to conventional NMC95. Notably, the β-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber-coated PP separator (NF@PP) provides multifunctional benefits, including enhanced porosity, wettability, and ionic conductivity, as well as ferroelectric polarization that enriches Li+, suppresses PF6− aggregation, and mitigates dendrite formation. patents.abstract: A METHOD FOR RECOVERING LITHIUM SALTS FROM SPENT LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES AND SYNTHESIZING LITHIUM-FORM ZEOLITE ADSORBENT The present invention provides a method for recovering lithium from spent lithium-ion batteries and converting the recovered lithium into high-performance lithium zeolite adsorbents. The method includes pretreating discharged cells to isolate the active cathode material, followed by organic-acid leaching in the presence of an oxidizing agent to dissolve lithium and associated metals. Selective pH-controlled precipitation using ammonium hydroxide and lithium hydroxide removes aluminum and transition-metal impurities while retaining lithium in solution. The purified lithium-rich solution is acidified crystallized and evaporated to obtain high-purity lithium chloride, which is directly used in a multi-stage ion-exchange process to convert sodium-form zeolite into a lithium-form zeolite. The two-stage exchange significantly reduces processing time and yields a LiX adsorbent with enhanced surface area and nitrogen adsorption capacity. The invention enables circular-economy valorisation of battery waste, integrates reagent and solvent recycling, and produces medical-grade adsorbents suitable for oxygen concentrators and gas-separation applications. patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present invention relates to the field of waste valorisation, hydrometallurgical extraction, and advanced adsorbent synthesis, and more particularly to processes for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and converting the recovered lithium into lithium-exchanged zeolite adsorbents suitable for gas separation applications. BACKGROUND [0002] As the shift towards green energy increases, the widespread electrification of traditional equipment and vehicles will significantly increase the number of lithium-ion batteries spent. Spent lithium-ion batteries are primarily recycled through two main processes: pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy. The hydrometallurgical approach has garnered substantial research interest, particularly for lithium recovery. Lithium salts can be effectively recovered from spent cathode materials using a leaching solution that consists of formic acid (HCOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) (W.Gao et al.,2017, [Gao, W., Zhang, X., Zheng, X., Lin, X., Cao, H., Zhang, Y. and Sun, Z.H.I., 2017. Lithium carbonate recovery from cathode scrap of spent lithium-ion battery: a closed-loop process. Environmental science & technology, 51(3), pp.1662-1669]), achieving up to 99% lithium leaching efficiency. Such process allows for the selective removal of other metal constituents, such as cobalt, nickel, manganese, and aluminum, from the leachate. Most studies concentrate on the leaching properties of inorganic acids, which usually lack selectivity towards lithium. This has led to growing interest in organic acids such as formic acid, citric acid, and lactic acid – for their promising potential in selectively leaching lithium. In the study by Haiyang et al. (2013), a mixture of lithium-ion battery cathode materials-LCO (lithium cobalt oxide), NMC (lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide), and LFP (lithium iron phosphate) – was subjected to leaching using a solution of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The research highlighted that the overall metal recovery efficiency tends to be lower when processing mixed cathode materials. [0003] Additionally, multiple metals can lead to competitive reactions during leaching, further complicating the recovery process. The use of sodium-based compounds for pH adjustment and selective precipitation of lithium and other transition metals is well established; however, the issue of residual sodium removal from the solution is seldom addressed. Given the high solubility of both sodium and lithium salts, conventional separation based on solubility differences is ineffective, presenting a significant challenge in achieving high-purity lithium recovery. Ion exchange is the most effective method for synthesizing lithium zeolite (LiX) from commercial sodium zeolite (NaX). In this process, NaX powder is mixed with a specific volume of 2.5 M LiCl and agitated on a turntable for 24 hours, followed by washing with deionized water to obtain LiX (Trivelpiece et al., 2024; [Trivelpiece, C.L., Shukla, P.K., Rasmussen, C., Sykes, K. and Angelette, L.M., 2024. Synthesis of Zeolites LiX and LiAgX (No. SRNL-STI-2024-00281). Savannah River National Laboratory (SRNL), Aiken, SC (United States)]). However, direct ion exchange with LiCl alone may not fully replace sodium with lithium due to lithium's lower cationic strength than sodium. [0004] Consequently, research gaps are identified in the extraction of lithium salts from spent lithium-ion battery active cathode material and proposes a recovery method that combines selective precipitation with specialized purification, while avoiding the use of sodium salts. The production of lithium zeolite is done via a two-stage ion exchange instead of a single stage ion exchange with LiCl which aims to convert the sodium form to ammonium form with first ion-exchange with NH4Cl and followed by LiCl ion exchange to convert the ammonium form to lithium form. The present disclosure is directed to overcome one or more limitations stated above, and any other limitation associated with the prior arts. SUMMARY [0005] One or more shortcomings of the prior art are overcome, and additional advantages are provided through the present disclosure. Additional features and advantages are realized through the techniques of the present disclosure. Other embodiments and aspects of the disclosure are described in detail herein and are considered a part of the claimed disclosure. [0006] The present disclosure relates to a method for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and synthesizing a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent. The method comprises pretreating spent lithium-ion batteries to isolate an active cathode material, leaching the active cathode material using an organic-acid-based leaching system in the presence of an oxidizing agent to obtain a leachate containing lithium and other metal ions. The method further comprises the steps of selectively removing impurities from the leachate by adjusting solution conditions to sequentially precipitate non-lithium metal species while retaining lithium in solution, and converting the lithium-containing solution into a lithium salt through acid treatment and solidification. The method includes purifying the lithium salt to obtain a purified lithium chloride; and producing a lithium-form zeolite by performing a multi-stage ion-exchange process on a sodium-form zeolite, including exchanging sodium ions with ammonium ions followed by exchanging ammonium ions with lithium ions using the purified lithium chloride. [0007] The foregoing summary in illustrative only and is not intended to be in any way limiting. In addition to the illustrative aspects, embodiments, and features described above, further aspects, embodiments, and features will become apparent by reference to the drawings and the following detailed description. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS [0008] The novel features and characteristics of the disclosure are set forth in the appended claims. The disclosure itself, however, as well as a preferred mode of use, further objectives, and advantages thereof, will best be understood by reference to the following detailed description of an illustrative embodiment when read in conjunction with the accompanying figures. One or more embodiments are now described, by way of example only, with reference to the accompanying figures wherein like reference numerals represent like elements and in which: Figure 1 (a – b) illustrate the steps involved in pretreatment of spent lithium-ion batteries, in accordance with embodiments of the present disclosure; Figure 2 illustrates a process flow for extracting lithium salts through leaching, in accordance with embodiments of the present disclosure; Figure 2(a) illustrates a method for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and synthesizing a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent, in accordance with embodiments of the present disclosure; Figure 3 (a – b) illustrate an experimental setup for ion exchange to produce lithium zeolites, in accordance to an embodiment of the present invention; Figure 4 (a – b) illustrates the experimental effect of vol% of H2O2 and HCOOH concentration on the lithium leached in L1, in accordance to an embodiment of the present invention; Figure 5 illustrates the N2 adsorption isotherm obtained from doing BET analysis for the lithium zeolites synthesized using the LiCl recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries with different ion exchange conditions, in accordance to an embodiment of the present invention; and Figure 6 illustrates a flow sheet for lithium salt extraction and LiX zeolite synthesis, in accordance to an embodiment of the present invention. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0009] In the present document, the word "exemplary" is used herein to mean "serving as an example, instance, or illustration." Any embodiment or implementation of the present subject matter described herein as "exemplary" is not necessarily to be construed as preferred or advantageous over other embodiments. [0010] While the disclosure is susceptible to various modifications and alternative forms, specific embodiment thereof has been shown by way of example in the drawings and will be described in detail below. It should be understood, however, that it is not intended to limit the disclosure to the forms disclosed, but on the contrary, the disclosure is to cover all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives falling within the spirit and the scope of the disclosure. [0011] The terms “comprises”, “comprising”, or any other variations thereof, are intended to cover a non-exclusive inclusion, such that a setup, device, or process that comprises a list of components or steps does not include only those components or steps but may include other components or steps not expressly listed or inherent to such setup or device or process. In other words, one or more elements in a system or apparatus proceeded by “comprises… a” does not, without more constraints, preclude the existence of other elements or additional elements in the system or apparatus. [0012] In the following detailed description of the embodiments of the disclosure, reference is made to the accompanying drawings that form a part hereof, and which are shown by way of illustration-specific embodiments in which the disclosure may be practiced. These embodiments are described in sufficient detail to enable those skilled in the art to practice the disclosure, and it is to be understood that other embodiments may be utilized and that changes may be made without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. The following description is, therefore, not to be taken in a limiting sense. [0013] The present invention aims to provide a method for recovering lithium from spent lithium-ion batteries through an environmentally benign and efficient hydrometallurgical route that avoids the use of strong mineral acids and sodium-based reagents contributing to downstream contamination. The proposed invention further develops a selective leaching system based on organic acids and oxidizing agents capable of dissolving lithium and transition metals from diverse cathode chemistries including LCO, NMC, LFP, and NCA. The proposed invention achieves sequential impurity removal by employing controlled pH adjustments using ammonium hydroxide and lithium hydroxide to selectively precipitate aluminum and transition-metal hydroxides while retaining lithium in solution with minimal co-precipitation losses. Further, the object of the present invention is to obtain high-purity lithium chloride by acid treatment, evaporation, and washing, enabling its direct utilization in subsequent ion-exchange processes without dependence on commercially sourced lithium salts, and to provide a closed-loop lithium reagent cycle wherein recovered lithium chloride is electrochemically converted to lithium hydroxide for reuse, and optionally to lithium fluoride as a higher-value by-product, thereby improving material efficiency and process economics. The method of the proposed invention synthesizes a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent (LiX) through a rapid multi-stage ion-exchange process involving ammonium exchange followed by lithium exchange, significantly reducing ion-exchange duration compared to conventional methods. Thus, the present invention produces a medical-grade lithium zeolite having enhanced surface area, high nitrogen adsorption capacity, and superior performance relative to sodium zeolite 13X, making it suitable for oxygen generation and gas-separation applications, and enables closed-loop solvent management, including recovery and recycling of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) utilized during cathode pretreatment. [0014] The proposed invention further minimizes environmental impact through effluent treatment strategies that recover residual lithium, reduce dissolved solids, and facilitate safe discharge or process-water reuse, and provides a holistic waste-valorisation pathway that converts end-of-life lithium-ion batteries into high-value functional materials, thereby strengthening circular-economy practices and reducing dependency on virgin lithium resources. [0015] Several variations to eliminate the use of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and the use of any bases which tend to introduce external contaminates into the system have been tried. All the previous studies have extensively used NaOH for pH adjustments and selectively removing aluminum and transition metals in their hydroxide form. However, they lack a method to eradicate the sodium impurities. [0016] To address this issue in our proposed method, employed NH4OH to selectively remove aluminum from the solution, followed by LiOH to remove transition metal hydroxides. Such approach is practical since large portion of the bases is utilized to remove aluminum hydroxides, thereby minimizing the risk of sodium ion contamination in the solution. Furthermore, once the transition metals, such as cobalt, manganese, and nickel, are eliminated in their hydroxide form, the resulting filtrate is treated with concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl). This treatment converts all metal ions in the solution to their respective chlorides. The solution is then evaporated, yielding a solid chloride residue comprising of both ammonium and lithium chlorides. Separation is achieved through crystallization, step in where LiCl is retained in the mother liquor due to high solubility, while NH4Cl selectively crystalizes which can be reused and on further evaporation of the mother liquor will produce pure lithium chloride. [0017] The second objective is synthesizing a medical-grade adsorbent through ion exchange of sodium-based zeolite. In prior studies, the approach typically involved direct ion exchange with LiCl without fully addressing the limited effectiveness of replacing sodium ions with lithium ions, given that sodium ions possess higher cationic strength than lithium ions, making complete exchange less efficient. To tackle this limitation, a two-stage ion exchange process was developed. In the first stage, sodium ions are exchanged for ammonium ions using ammonium chloride. This is followed by a second exchange with lithium chloride, which replaces ammonium with lithium ions. Unlike previous studies, the proposed method is conducted over a shorter duration and utilizes intact pellets instead of powdered samples. [0018] Extraction of lithium salts from the active cathode material from spent lithium-ion batteries is a multistage process. This study specifically focuses on lithium cobalt oxide (LCO)-based spent lithium-ion batteries. The spent lithium-ion batteries can’t be dismantled into its constituents directly. This is due to the fact that these batteries are prone to short circuiting and thermal run of, hence a proper pretreatment step is necessary. [0019] Figure 1 (a – b) illustrate the steps involved in pretreatment of spent lithium-ion batteries, in accordance with embodiments of the present disclosure. In one embodiment, the batteries are first discharged using resistors and the discharged cells are then carefully opened in a glove box to prevent reactions between internal components and atmospheric gases. The cathode is separated from other cell components and dried overnight in a vacuum oven to remove residual electrolytes. The cathode is then sonicated in NMP (N-Methyl pyrrolidone), which dissolves the PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) binder that attaches the active material to the aluminum current collector. The resulting slurry is vacuum filtered, and the solid residue active cathode material is washed with double-distilled water to eliminate any remaining PVDF. Such process is followed by drying at 60-65°C in a vacuum oven overnight. Finally, the material is ground to finer particles to increase surface area and improve leaching efficiency. [0020] Figure 2 illustrates a process flow for extracting lithium salts through leaching, in accordance with embodiments of the present disclosure. In one embodiment, the active cathode material is introduced into a reactor containing a leaching solution of 6 M formic acid (HCOOH) and 20 vol% hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The leaching reaction is performed at a temperature of 60-65 °C for 30-35 minutes, using a solid-to-liquid (S/L) ratio of 1:1000. After the reaction, the mixture is filtered to obtain the leachate (L1), which contains key constituents such as lithium, cobalt, and aluminum from the cathode scrap. The primary objective is to selectively remove other elements from the leachate, allowing for lithium's efficient separation and recovery. The pH of L1 is measured and found to be 1.8. The pH has to be increased to 6.45 to precipitate out aluminum hydroxide and this can be done by the addition of ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) into L1. The resulting filtrate primarily contains transition metal impurities—cobalt, manganese, and nickel. These can be selectively removed by gradually increasing the pH from 6.45 to 10 using ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH) is used to further vary the pH from 10 to 11. Maintaining the solution at pH 11 for 24 hours facilitates the complete precipitation of these transition metals, leaving lithium in the solution. The solution is neutralized and acidified to pH 2 using concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl), converting all dissolved metals to their respective chlorides. Upon evaporation, a mixed metal chloride residue comprising of lithium chloride and ammonium chloride is obtained. Purification is achieved by crystallization, utilizing the differing solubilities of the chlorides, leaving LiCl in the mother liquor and NH4Cl selectively crystallizes. Lithium chloride is then recovered by evaporating the mother liquor, followed by washing with deionized water and dried to obtain purified lithium chloride. [0021] The preparation of lithium zeolite from sodium zeolite was carried out through a two-step ion exchange process using zeolite 13X as the starting material. In the first stage, sodium ions within the zeolite framework were replaced with ammonium (NH₄⁺) ions through ion exchange with a 1 M NH₄Cl solution. The second stage involved replacing the NH₄⁺ ions with lithium (Li⁺) ions using a 1 M LiCl solution. The procedure involves performing two consecutive ion exchange steps at temperatures between 85°C and 90°C; each sustained for one hour. NaX + NH4Cl → NH4X + NaCl (1st exchange) NH4X + LiCl → LiX + NH4Cl (2nd exchange) [0022] After each ion exchange step, the zeolite samples were thoroughly washed with double distilled water for 30 minutes to completely remove surface-bound salts and residual salt solutions. Following the washing process, the samples were dried under high vacuum at 70°C for a duration of 12 hours to eliminate any remaining moisture. Figure 3 (a-b) illustrates the ion exchange schematics. [0023] As illustrated in Figure 2(a), the method (200) comprises one or more blocks for providing method for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and synthesizing a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent. The order in which the method (200) is described is not intended to be construed as a limitation, and any number of the described method blocks can be combined in any order to implement the method. [0024] At block (202), the spent lithium-ion cells are safely discharged, opened in an inert environment, and the cathode material is separated. The PVDF binder is removed by sonication in NMP, followed by filtration, washing, vacuum-drying, and grinding to obtain a clean, high-surface-area active material suitable for leaching. [0025] At block (204), the prepared cathode material is leached using a mixture of an organic acid and an oxidizing agent – exemplified by formic acid and hydrogen peroxide – to dissolve lithium and associated metals into solution under controlled temperature and solid-to-liquid conditions. This enables efficient lithium extraction with reduced environmental impact. [0026] At block (206), impurities are removed in a sequential pH-controlled manner. Ammonium hydroxide is first used to precipitate aluminum, after which ammonium hydroxide and lithium hydroxide are applied to precipitate transition-metal hydroxides such as cobalt, nickel, and manganese. Lithium remains in solution throughout the purification process. [0027] At block (208), the purified lithium-rich solution is acidified, typically with hydrochloric acid, to convert dissolved species to their chloride forms. Subsequent evaporation or crystallization produces a solid lithium chloride and ammonium chloride-containing residue. [0028] At block (210), purification by crystallization and the solid lithium chloride is washed with deionized water and dried to remove residual contaminants, yielding high-purity LiCl suitable for ion-exchange synthesis. A portion of this LiCl may be electrochemically converted to LiOH for reuse or reacted to form LiF as a value-added product. [0029] At block (212), a lithium-form zeolite (LiX) is synthesized by sequentially exchanging sodium ions in a base zeolite with ammonium ions and then replacing the ammonium ions with lithium ions using the recovered LiCl solution. This two-stage exchange, conducted under elevated temperature, produces a high-performance LiX adsorbent suitable for gas-separation applications. [0030] In an experiment, initially the optimal blend of the leaching solution was estimated with varying concentrations of formic acid (HCOOH) and vol % of hydrogen peroxide(H2O2). This study demonstrates that a leaching solution containing 6 M formic acid (HCOOH) and 20 vol % hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is highly effective in extracting lithium from the cathode material of spent Li-ion batteries. Typically, lithium accounts for approximately 5–6% of the total mass of the cathode material, and experimental results confirm that this leaching combination enables the dissolution of nearly all the lithium content into the solution, validating the efficiency and selectivity of the proposed leaching process. Figure 4 (a – b) illustrates the experimental effect of vol% of H2O2 and HCOOH concentration on the lithium leached in L1, in accordance to an embodiment of the present invention. [0031] Further, Table 1 shows the concentration of impurities in the LiCl recovered from the active cathode material of spent lithium-ion batteries. Li (mg/g) Al (mg/g) Mn (mg/g) Co (mg/g) Ni (mg/g) 8 0.626 0.302 0.6 0.834 Table 1 [0032] The table presents the composition of LiCl obtained from 50 mg of active cathode material sourced from spent Li-ion batteries, using a leaching solution of 6 M formic acid (HCOOH) and 20 vol% hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The pH was initially adjusted from 1.8 to 6.45 using NH₄OH to precipitate aluminum, followed by further pH adjustment to 10 using NH₄OH and then to 11 with LiOH to remove transition metals from the leachate. [0033] Further, Table 2 shows the mass of various elements recovered during the entire lithium recovery process from active cathode material. Li (mg/g) Al (mg/g) Mn (mg/g) Co (mg/g) Ni (mg/g) 80 420 260 179.4 60 Table 2 [0034] Figure 5 illustrates the N2 adsorption isotherm obtained from doing BET analysis for the lithium zeolites synthesized using the LiCl recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries with different ion exchange conditions. [0035] Among the various LiX samples synthesized via ion exchange, the variant treated with 1 hr 1M NH₄Cl followed by 1 hr 1M LiCl exhibits the highest N₂ adsorption capacity, surpassing sodium zeolite 13X. This enhanced adsorption behavior corresponds to a significantly higher surface area of 595 m²/g compared to 330 m²/g for zeolite 13X. Table 3 illustrates comparison the surface areas of 13 X with LiX produced. Sample Surface Area Sodium Zeolite (13 X) 330 m2/g LiX (1hr 1M NH4Cl +1hr 1M LiCl) 595 m2/g LiX (1hr 1M NH4Cl +2hr 1M LiCl) 490 m2/g LiX (2hr 1M NH4Cl +1hr 1M LiCl) 291 m2/g LiX (2hr 1M NH4Cl +2hr 1M LiCl) 288 m2/g LiX (24hr 1M NH4Cl +24hr 1M LiCl) 213 m2/g LiX (24hr 1M NH4Cl +24hr 6M LiCl) 114 m2/g LiX (24hr 1M NH4Cl +24hr (1M LiCl + 6M LiCl) 81 m2/g Table 3 [0036] The residual liquid generated post-ion exchange and washing primarily constitutes the process effluent. For every 1 kg of lithium zeolite produced, approximately 10 liters of effluent is generated. This waste stream is mildly alkaline (pH ~7.8–8.0) with a total dissolved solids (TDS) concentration of approximately 60.7 ppt (60700 ppm). While this TDS level is relatively high for general industrial effluents, it falls within the expected range for ion exchange processes (generally between 40000-70000ppm) due to the presence of concentrated salts like Li⁺, NH₄⁺, and Cl⁻ from the reagents. However, it exceeds permissible limits for direct environmental discharge and necessitates further treatment. Strategies such as closed-loop water recycling, recovery of residual lithium through selective adsorption or membrane separation, and integration of effluent treatment systems can be adopted to enhance the overall process viability. These measures minimize environmental impact, improve resource efficiency, and support the sustainability and commercial feasibility of the overall process. [0037] Further, an economic assessment was carried out, with laboratory-scale expenditure serving as the baseline, to estimate the cost of producing 1 kg of LiX. As shown in Figure 6, LiOH addition is necessary for effective lithium recovery, indicating that a portion of the produced LiCl must be recycled to maintain process viability. LiCl can be converted back to LiOH via electrolysis, during which valuable by-products such as chlorine and hydrogen gases are also generated, enhancing the overall economic feasibility. It is proposed that LiOH can be recycled for up to five cycles. Beyond this, LiOH is converted to high-purity LiF through a reaction with NaF, as LiF possesses a higher commercial value than LiOH, thereby helping to recover the initial capital invested in LiOH which was utilized for pH adjustment. [0038] The study primarily focuses on recovering lithium from spent lithium-ion batteries using lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) as the representative cathode chemistry. All experimental conditions, including leaching, and precipitation have been optimized based on LCO-type cells, which are commonly used in portable electronics. However, the overall methodology particularly the mild leaching system and subsequent lithium recovery steps – is versatile and can be extended to other lithiumion battery chemistries such as NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt), LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate), or NCA (Nickel Cobalt Aluminum) with minor adjustments in process parameters. This adaptability enhances the invention's broader applicability and commercial relevance across various battery waste streams. Advantages of the proposed invention [0039] The proposed analyzer offers multiple advantages over existing methods used for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and synthesizing a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent: 1. Environmentally benign lithium recovery: The invention utilizes organic acids such as formic acid along with hydrogen peroxide as the leaching system, avoiding strong mineral acids and significantly reducing environmental and corrosion-related hazards during lithium extraction. 2. Elimination of sodium contamination: By replacing conventional NaOH-based precipitation with ammonium hydroxide and lithium hydroxide, the process prevents sodium ion contamination and enables the production of high-purity lithium chloride suitable for advanced applications. 3. Highly selective multi-stage purification: The sequential pH-controlled precipitation of aluminum and transition-metal hydroxides ensures effective removal of impurities while retaining lithium in solution, leading to improved purity and higher lithium recovery efficiency. 4. Direct utilization of recovered lithium salts: The lithium chloride obtained from spent batteries is directly used in the ion-exchange step to synthesize lithium zeolite, thereby eliminating the need for commercially sourced lithium salts and lowering material costs. 5. Accelerated ion-exchange process: The two-stage ion-exchange (Na⁺→NH₄⁺→Li⁺) at elevated temperature drastically reduces exchange duration compared to conventional single-stage approaches, improving process throughput and scalability. 6. Production of high-performance lithium zeolite: The produced LiX exhibits significantly enhanced surface area and nitrogen adsorption capacity compared to sodium zeolite 13X, enabling its use as a medical-grade adsorbent in oxygen concentrators and other gas-separation systems. 7. Effective circular-economy implementation: The process converts end-of-life lithium-ion batteries into high-value functional materials, thereby promoting waste valorisation and reducing dependence on virgin lithium resources. 8. Integrated chemical recycling loops: The ability to convert recovered LiCl into LiOH for reuse, and subsequently to LiF as a higher-value product, improves overall lithium utilization and enhances the economic viability of the process. 9. Reduced process waste and environmental load: Recycling of NMP solvent, recovery of residual lithium from effluents, and reduction of total dissolved solids support sustainable waste management and minimize environmental discharge. 10. Applicability to multiple battery chemistries: While optimized for LCO cathodes, the method is adaptable to NMC, LFP, and NCA chemistries with minor adjustments, expanding its industrial applicability across diverse waste streams. The description is, therefore, not to be taken in a limiting sense. , Claims:We Claim: 1) A method (200) for recovering lithium salts from spent lithium-ion batteries and synthesizing a lithium-form zeolite adsorbent, the method comprising: pre-treating (202) spent lithium-ion batteries to isolate an active cathode material; leaching (204) the active cathode material using an organic-acid-based leaching system in the presence of an oxidizing agent to obtain a leachate containing lithium and other metal ions; selectively removing (206) impurities from the leachate by adjusting solution conditions to sequentially precipitate non-lithium metal species while retaining lithium in solution; converting (208) the lithium-containing solution into a lithium salt through acid treatment and solidification; purifying (210) the lithium salt to obtain a purified lithium chloride; and producing (212) a lithium-form zeolite by performing a multi-stage ion-exchange process on a sodium-form zeolite, including exchanging sodium ions with ammonium ions followed by exchanging ammonium ions with lithium ions using the purified lithium chloride. 2) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein pre-treatment comprises discharging the batteries, opening them in an inert atmosphere, removing cathode components, dissolving a binder using N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone under sonication, filtering, washing, drying at 60-65°C under vacuum overnight, and grinding the cathode material. 3) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the leaching system comprises formic acid and hydrogen peroxide in concentrations of 6 M and 20 vol% respectively, operated at 60-65°C for 30-35 minutes and a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:1000. 4) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein selective removal of impurities comprises the steps of: adjusting the leachate pH using ammonium hydroxide to precipitate aluminium hydroxide; and increasing the pH sequentially using ammonium hydroxide and lithium hydroxide to precipitate cobalt, nickel, and manganese hydroxides, with the solution maintained under alkaline conditions for at least 12 hours. 5) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein acid treatment comprises adding hydrochloric acid to convert metal ions into chloride forms, evaporating the solution to obtain a solid chloride mass, and washing the mass with deionized water to yield purified lithium chloride. 6) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the purified lithium chloride contains less than 1 mg/g of aluminium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese impurities. 7) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1 further comprising converting a portion of the purified lithium chloride to lithium hydroxide via electrolysis and optionally reacting the lithium hydroxide with sodium fluoride to produce lithium fluoride as a value-added product. 8) The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the sodium-form zeolite comprises zeolite 13X in pelletized form, and the ion-exchange steps are performed using 1 M ammonium chloride and lithium chloride solutions at temperatures of 85 – 90°C.
