patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a novel method for extraction of lithium oxide from Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks, which are bauxite mining waste materials generated during bauxite extraction operations. Specifically, the invention provides an economical, environmentally sustainable, and scalable process for recovering valuable lithium oxide from PLK rock waste through a controlled leaching process using organic, inorganic, or synergetic acid treatment. The PLK rocks containing approximately 0.07-0.2% lithium oxide (LiO₂) are ground to fine particles below 45 microns and subjected to optimized leaching under controlled conditions including acid concentration, stirring speed, temperature, and reaction time. The extracted lithium oxide is purified and characterized to meet BIS standards for application in rechargeable lithium battery manufacturing. This waste-to-wealth approach simultaneously addresses environmental pollution caused by extensive dumping of mining waste while providing a potential resource for the rapidly growing battery industry. The method demonstrates commercial viability with extracted lithium reaching 0.2324 ppm concentration in the leachate, offering significant economic and environmental benefits for the aluminum and battery sectors.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION: [0001] The present invention belongs to the technical domain of Chemical Engineering, specifically focusing on hydrometallurgical processes and mineral extraction methodologies. The invention relates to the recovery of rare-earth elements, particularly lithium oxide, from industrial mining waste materials through leaching and purification techniques. The field encompasses the development of environmentally sustainable extraction processes that convert waste materials into valuable products, thereby contributing to circular economy principles and reduction of landfill volumes. This technical domain intersects with materials science, as it deals with the characterization and processing of mineral ores to obtain high-purity lithium compounds suitable for advanced battery applications. Furthermore, the invention falls within the scope of waste management and environmental remediation technologies that address the ecological challenges posed by large-scale mining operations and their byproducts. The technical applications extend to battery technology, renewable energy storage systems, and industrial chemistry sectors requiring high-purity lithium oxide as a raw material. [0002] The specific technical aspect of this invention addresses the challenge of processing Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks, which are generated as waste products during bauxite mining operations at large-scale facilities such as NALCO's Damanjodi mining site. The invention involves detailed process engineering, including particle size optimization, leaching chemistry optimization, and purification methodologies to recover lithium oxide that would otherwise remain unutilized in mining waste. The chemical engineering principles employed include acid-base chemistry, leaching kinetics, separation techniques, and product purification methods that fall under hydrometallurgical engineering practices. The invention represents an advancement in sustainable mining practices by demonstrating the technical feasibility of recovering valuable minerals from what is conventionally considered waste material. The technical domain also encompasses quality control and standardization aspects, including characterization of raw materials, intermediate products, and final lithium oxide products according to Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and international specifications. [0003] This invention contributes significantly to the emerging field of green chemistry and sustainable mineral processing by demonstrating how industrial waste streams can be effectively utilized for resource recovery. The technical innovation involves optimization of leaching parameters through experimental design of experiments (DOE) and mathematical modeling using computational tools such as MATLAB, enabling industrial-scale deployment of the technology. The field extends to the development of scalable processes that can handle large volumes of PLK rock waste generated annually, approximately in line with the 63.4 lakh tonnes of bauxite mined annually by NALCO at the Damanjodi mining site. This invention bridges the gap between traditional mining waste management practices and modern sustainable industrial chemistry, providing a technically sound and economically viable solution for lithium recovery from previously unutilized ore sources. BACKGROUND: [0004] The Panchapatmalli plateau region is renowned for its extensive bauxite reserves, which constitute a significant portion of India's mineral wealth and support the country's aluminum production industry. Large-scale mining operations, particularly those conducted by the National Aluminum Company Limited (NALCO) at Damanjodi, extract approximately 63.4 lakh tonnes of bauxite annually to meet the demands of the aluminum industry. During the extraction of bauxite ore, substantial quantities of rock material are excavated along with the primary ore body, resulting in the generation of Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks as a byproduct. These PLK rocks are either excavated and dumped at mining sites, creating man-made mountains of waste material, or used for backfilling of abandoned mines. The volume of PLK rock waste generated is proportional to the mining intensity and has become a significant environmental concern, requiring large land areas for storage and management. The management of this mining waste represents a major challenge for mining companies and environmental authorities, as improper handling can lead to land degradation, water pollution, and ecological disruption. [0005] PLK rocks possess a unique mineralogical composition containing various valuable mineral phases that have not been adequately exploited in conventional mining operations focused primarily on alumina extraction. The average composition of PLK rocks includes iron oxide (Fe₂O₃) ranging from 0.3-30%, aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) constituting 40-56%, silicon dioxide (SiO₂) present in 20-30%, titanium oxide (TiO₂) comprising 0.97-3%, loss on ignition (LOI) accounting for 20-30%, and importantly, lithium oxide (LiO₂) in concentrations of 0.07-0.2%. The presence of reactive silica in PLK rocks prevents their utilization in metallurgical applications for alumina extraction, as the reactive silica interferes with conventional Bayer's process chemistry. This compositional characteristic has rendered PLK rocks unsuitable for direct integration into standard aluminum production workflows, leaving them as waste material despite their substantial mineral content. However, the presence of lithium oxide in these rocks represents an untapped resource opportunity, particularly given the growing global demand for lithium and lithium compounds in energy storage applications. [0006] The lithium battery industry has experienced unprecedented growth in recent years, driven by the global shift toward renewable energy, electric vehicles, and portable electronic devices requiring rechargeable power storage solutions. Lithium is recognized as a critical material for battery manufacturing, and its global demand continues to increase exponentially as battery technology becomes central to energy transitions worldwide. Currently, lithium oxide is primarily extracted from dedicated lithium ore deposits and brine reservoirs, which are geographically concentrated and subject to supply chain vulnerabilities. The development of alternative lithium sources from mining byproducts and waste materials would significantly enhance resource security and reduce dependency on conventional lithium mining operations. The recovery of lithium from PLK rocks represents a novel and potentially significant contribution to meeting global lithium demand while simultaneously addressing waste management and environmental pollution concerns in mining regions. [0007] The conventional approaches to managing PLK rock waste have primarily focused on physical containment and disposal rather than resource recovery and value addition. Environmental pollution resulting from extensive dumping of mining waste at mining sites has led to habitat destruction, erosion, and contamination of soil and groundwater in affected regions. The creation of artificial mountains of waste material consumes valuable land that could otherwise be utilized for productive purposes, and the environmental impact extends beyond the immediate mining site through dust generation, water runoff, and potential leaching of mineral constituents into surrounding ecosystems. Previous attempts to extract alumina from PLK rocks have been unsuccessful due to the interference of reactive silica, which prevents application of conventional metallurgical extraction methodologies. There has been no systematic investigation into recovering other valuable mineral components, particularly lithium oxide, from PLK rocks through dedicated extraction processes adapted to the unique characteristics of this waste material. [0008] The present invention addresses this gap by developing a scientifically rigorous, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable method for extracting lithium oxide from PLK rocks through carefully optimized leaching processes. The innovation recognizes that PLK rocks, despite their unsuitability for conventional aluminum extraction pathways, contain valuable lithium oxide that can be recovered through specialized hydrometallurgical techniques. By converting waste material into a valuable product, the invention contributes to the circular economy model and provides mining companies with an additional revenue stream while simultaneously reducing environmental pollution and land consumption associated with waste dumping. The technology is designed to be scalable and compatible with existing mining infrastructure, enabling integration into current mining operations with minimal disruption to established workflows. OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION: [0009] The primary objective of the present invention is to develop and provide a commercially viable, scalable, and environmentally sustainable method for extracting high-purity lithium oxide from Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks that are currently treated as waste byproducts of bauxite mining operations. The invention aims to transform what is conventionally considered mining waste into a valuable resource, thereby implementing waste-to-wealth principles in the mining and materials processing industries. By establishing a technically sound extraction process, the invention seeks to provide an alternative and supplementary source of lithium oxide for battery manufacturing industries, contributing to energy security and supporting the global transition toward renewable energy and electric vehicle technologies. The successful achievement of this objective would demonstrate that PLK rocks represent an economically recoverable lithium resource while simultaneously addressing environmental challenges associated with large-scale mining operations. [0010] The secondary objective is to minimize environmental pollution and waste generation at bauxite mining sites by providing a practical utilization pathway for PLK rock waste material. Rather than accumulating vast quantities of waste material that create environmental hazards and consume valuable land resources, the invention enables the conversion of this material into a marketable product. This approach reduces the volume of waste requiring long-term management and storage, alleviates the environmental burden on mining regions, and prevents potential contamination of soil and water resources from waste material leaching. The invention thereby contributes to sustainable mining practices and supports regulatory compliance with environmental protection standards. By addressing waste management concerns, the invention enhances the social license to operate for mining companies and promotes environmentally responsible industrial development. [0011] A tertiary objective of the invention is to develop a process that is technically simple, economically affordable, and capable of implementation at various scales ranging from pilot operations to full commercial production. The invented extraction methodology employs wellestablished chemical engineering principles and leaching techniques, avoiding reliance on complex or proprietary equipment that would limit accessibility and scalability. The use of common organic or inorganic acids for leaching, combined with standard equipment for grinding, filtering, and purification, ensures that the technology can be deployed by mining companies with existing infrastructure and technical capabilities. The process optimization through controlled parameter adjustment (acid concentration, stirring speed, temperature, and reaction time) enables customization for specific operational conditions and material characteristics, ensuring broad applicability across different mining sites and operational scales. [0012] The quaternary objective is to contribute to battery technology advancement and support the growing demand for lithium oxide in the renewable energy and electric vehicle sectors by establishing a new lithium supply source. As lithium demand continues to escalate globally, diversifying lithium sources through recovery from mining waste and other secondary sources becomes strategically important for energy security and economic sustainability. The successful implementation of the invented process would add lithium oxide production capacity without requiring the development of new primary mining operations in ecologically sensitive regions. This objective aligns with national and international sustainability targets, supports the development of a circular economy in materials processing, and contributes to building resilient and secure supply chains for battery manufacturing industries critical to global energy transitions. SUMMARY: [0013] The present invention provides a comprehensive and innovative methodology for recovering lithium oxide (LiO₂) from Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks, which are generated as substantial byproducts during large-scale bauxite mining operations, particularly in regions such as the Panchapatmalli plateau where the National Aluminum Company Limited operates major extraction facilities. The PLK rocks, containing approximately 0.07-0.2% lithium oxide along with iron oxide, aluminum oxide, silicon dioxide, and other mineral constituents, have previously been unutilized and disposed of as waste material creating environmental and land management challenges. The invented process transforms these mining waste rocks into a valuable source of lithium oxide through a series of carefully controlled steps including sample collection, characterization, particle size optimization, leaching, filtration, purification, and quality assessment according to established industrial standards. The methodology represents a significant advancement in sustainable mining and materials recovery practices by demonstrating the technical and economic feasibility of extracting valuable minerals from previously discarded waste streams. [0014] The extraction process according to the invention begins with sample collection from active mining sites and comprehensive characterization including mineralogical analysis and size distribution assessment to identify optimal processing conditions for maximum mineral liberation. The PLK rock samples are then ground to fine particles with a maximum size of below 45 microns through mechanical grinding operations, enabling liberation of valuable mineral phases and increasing the surface area available for subsequent leaching reactions. This size optimization is critical for process efficiency and is determined through careful experimental analysis and mathematical optimization using design of experiments (DOE) methodology or computational modeling through MATLAB software. The ground particles are then subjected to a controlled leaching process wherein the material is treated with carefully selected and optimized concentrations of organic, inorganic, or synergistic combinations of acids in a specially designed leaching reactor under controlled conditions. [0015] The leaching process according to the invention is performed in a leaching reactor with controlled parameters including acid or alkaline concentration, stirring speed, temperature, and reaction time, all of which are systematically optimized to maximize lithium oxide extraction while minimizing undesired side reactions and impurity dissolution. Following completion of the leaching reaction, the liquor containing dissolved lithium oxide and other soluble components is separated from solid residue through filtration, yielding both a filtrate containing dissolved lithium oxide and a residue containing undissolved mineral phases. Comprehensive analytical characterization is conducted on both the filtrate and residue fractions to determine lithium oxide content, purity, and the distribution of other mineral components. The filtrate is then processed through purification and concentration steps to obtain lithium oxide in a form and purity meeting Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications and requirements suitable for application in lithium battery manufacturing, with demonstrated recovery achieving lithium concentrations of approximately 0.2324 ppm in the final product. [0016] The invention represents a practical implementation of waste-to-wealth principles that simultaneously addresses three critical challenges: providing an alternative lithium source for the growing battery industry, eliminating environmental pollution from mining waste accumulation, and creating economic value from currently discarded materials. The technology is designed for scalability and compatibility with existing mining infrastructure, enabling integration into current operations without requiring substantial capital investment or infrastructure development. By establishing the technical feasibility and economic viability of lithium recovery from PLK rocks through this innovative extraction methodology, the invention opens new opportunities for sustainable resource development and demonstrates how industrial waste streams can be effectively utilized for resource recovery in support of circular economy principles and environmental sustainability objectives. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EMBODIMENTS: [0017] The present invention will be more fully understood with reference to the following detailed description of various embodiments and the accompanying technical specifications demonstrating the implementation of the invented extraction process. The Panchapatmalli plateau region, where extensive bauxite mining occurs, contains significant PLK rock deposits generated as byproducts of aluminum ore extraction. The NALCO mining operation at Damanjodi extracts approximately 63.4 lakh tonnes of bauxite annually, generating proportionally large volumes of PLK rock waste material. This waste material, previously managed through dumping at mining sites or limited use in mine backfilling, is identified in the invention as a valuable source of lithium oxide recovery. [0018] The characterization phase represents the initial embodiment of the invention and involves comprehensive analysis of PLK rock samples collected from active mining sites to establish baseline mineralogical composition and identify optimal processing parameters. Representative samples are subjected to X-ray diffraction analysis to determine mineralogical phases, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to quantify elemental composition, and granulometric analysis to assess particle size distribution of run-of-mine material. The characterization data, demonstrating PLK rock composition with lithium oxide content of 0.07-0.2%, aluminum oxide of 40-56%, silicon dioxide of 20-30%, iron oxide of 0.3-30%, and titanium oxide of 0.97-3%, provides essential information for process design. Detailed characterization establishes that maximum liberation of lithium oxide and valuable mineral phases occurs within specific particle size ranges, typically below 45 microns, guiding subsequent grinding operations and optimization studies. [0019] The sample preparation embodiment involves mechanical comminution of run-of-mine (ROM) PLK rock samples through grinding operations to achieve fine particle sizes below 45 microns, thereby increasing surface area and facilitating liberation of lithium oxide mineral phases. Grinding is performed using standard mineral processing equipment including ball mills or other comminution devices commonly available in mining and materials processing facilities. The particle size is optimized through experimental testing and design of experiments methodology to identify the specific size fraction yielding maximum lithium oxide recovery during subsequent leaching operations. The optimization process systematically varies grinding time and mill parameters to achieve target particle size distributions, with results documented and analyzed to establish optimal conditions balancing mineral liberation with energy consumption and operational efficiency. The finely ground material produced in this embodiment provides the feedstock for the leaching process described in subsequent embodiments. [0020] The leaching process embodiment represents the core innovative component of the invention and involves treatment of finely ground PLK rock material with carefully selected and optimized combinations of organic, inorganic, or synergetic acids in a dedicated leaching reactor maintained under controlled conditions. The leaching reactor is equipped with precise temperature control capabilities, mechanical stirring systems, acid dosing mechanisms, and sampling ports for monitoring reaction progress. The process parameters including acid type, acid concentration, stirring speed, reaction temperature, and reaction time are systematically optimized through experimental design to maximize lithium oxide extraction while minimizing extraction of undesired impurities and side reactions. Common acids employed include sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, or combinations thereof, with concentrations ranging typically from 0.5 to 3 M depending on specific process optimization results. [0021] The optimization embodiment employs design of experiments (DOE) methodology or computational modeling through MATLAB software to systematically establish optimal leaching parameters without requiring prohibitive numbers of experimental trials. The optimization process evaluates the individual effects and interactive effects of key process variables including acid concentration, temperature, stirring speed, and reaction time on lithium oxide recovery, impurity dissolution, and overall process efficiency. Response surface methodology (RSM) or other statistical techniques are employed to develop predictive mathematical models relating process parameters to extraction outcomes, enabling rapid identification of optimal operating windows. The optimization results are documented in comprehensive process parameter tables establishing the conditions required to achieve maximum lithium oxide recovery and product quality standards for various raw material characteristics and operational scenarios. [0022] The filtration and separation embodiment follows completion of the leaching reaction and involves separation of the leachate containing dissolved lithium oxide from solid residue material through mechanical filtration using standard industrial filtration equipment such as vacuum filters, pressure filters, or membrane filtration systems. The filtration process yields a filtrate containing dissolved lithium oxide and other soluble components, and a solid residue containing minerals that did not dissolve during the leaching reaction. Both the filtrate and residue are subjected to comprehensive analytical characterization including chemical composition analysis, impurity quantification, and lithium oxide concentration determination using analytical techniques such as atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), or X-ray fluorescence (XRF). [0023] The purification embodiment addresses the removal of impurities from the lithium oxidecontaining filtrate and involves selective precipitation, crystallization, or chromatographic techniques to concentrate lithium oxide and eliminate associated impurities that could compromise product quality for battery applications. The purification process may employ techniques such as selective precipitation of iron compounds using pH adjustment and oxidizing agents, removal of aluminum through selective complexation or precipitation, and concentration of lithium oxide through evaporation or crystallization. The purification steps are optimized to achieve lithium oxide product purity meeting Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications and international battery industry requirements for lithium oxide chemical composition, moisture content, and trace element levels. [0024] The quality assessment embodiment involves comprehensive analytical characterization and testing of the final lithium oxide product to verify compliance with BIS standards and suitability for application in lithium battery manufacturing. Quality assessment encompasses determination of lithium oxide assay through titration or spectroscopic methods, evaluation of trace elemental impurities through ICP analysis, assessment of moisture content through thermogravimetric analysis, and evaluation of particle size and morphology through microscopic examination. The quality assessment results are documented in comprehensive test reports providing verification that the extracted lithium oxide meets all specifications required for battery application. The demonstrated recovery of lithium reaching concentrations of approximately 0.2324 ppm in the final product confirms the technical feasibility and effectiveness of the invented extraction process. [0025] The scale-up and commercialization embodiment addresses the expansion of the invented process from laboratory or pilot scale to full commercial production capable of processing large volumes of PLK rock material generated at mining sites. The scale-up process involves detailed engineering design of leaching reactors and support equipment capable of handling throughputs of multiple tonnes of ground material per day, installation of automated process control systems for monitoring and optimization of leaching parameters, and development of material handling systems for efficient feedstock preparation and product recovery. The commercialization embodiment considers integration of the lithium extraction process with existing mining operations, utilization of available infrastructure, and optimization of capital and operational costs to achieve economic viability and profitability at commercial production scales. [0026] The waste minimization embodiment demonstrates how the invented process contributes to environmental sustainability through minimization of mining waste requiring long-term storage and management while simultaneously reducing environmental pollution from waste material dumping. By converting PLK rock waste into a valuable lithium oxide product, the invention eliminates the need for continued accumulation of mining waste at mining sites and reduces the environmental footprint of mining operations. The residue material remaining after lithium extraction may be evaluated for further applications including use in road construction, cement manufacturing, or other industrial applications, further enhancing waste utilization and environmental sustainability of the overall mining operation. [0027] The application embodiment describes the utilization of the extracted lithium oxide product in lithium battery manufacturing and other industrial applications requiring high-purity lithium compounds. The lithium oxide product meeting BIS standards can be directly incorporated into lithium battery manufacturing processes or further processed into other lithium compounds such as lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide through conventional chemical conversion steps. The battery industry represents the primary market for lithium oxide products, particularly given the growing demand for rechargeable lithium batteries in electric vehicles, portable electronics, and renewable energy storage applications. The successful implementation of the invented process thus provides a sustainable and economically viable source of lithium for supporting the rapidly expanding battery manufacturing industry and contributing to global energy security and sustainability objectives. ABSTRACT: The present invention relates to a novel method for extraction of lithium oxide from Partially Laterised Khondalite (PLK) rocks, which are bauxite mining waste materials generated during bauxite extraction operations. Specifically, the invention provides an economical, environmentally sustainable, and scalable process for recovering valuable lithium oxide from PLK rock waste through a controlled leaching process using organic, inorganic, or synergetic acid treatment. The PLK rocks containing approximately 0.07-0.2% lithium oxide (LiO₂) are ground to fine particles below 45 microns and subjected to optimized leaching under controlled conditions including acid concentration, stirring speed, temperature, and reaction time. The extracted lithium oxide is purified and characterized to meet BIS standards for application in rechargeable lithium battery manufacturing. This waste-to-wealth approach simultaneously addresses environmental pollution caused by extensive dumping of mining waste while providing a potential resource for the rapidly growing battery industry. patents.abstract: A battery management system (BMS) having a printed circuit board (PCB) with a diagonal arrangement for use in a Li-ion battery, a Li-ion battery having a battery management system (BMS) having a printed circuit board (PCB) with a diagonal arrangement, and a BMS having a printed circuit board with diagonal arrangement method.
patents.complete_specification: BACKGROUND 25 [0004] Lithium ion batteries differ from other battery technologies in that they require a Battery Management System (BMS) in order to provide protection. The BMS is typically integrated into the battery and is designed to disconnect the internal battery cells from the external battery terminals in case of over-charge, over-discharge, over-current, short-circuit, and over-temperature. 30 [0005] Since the BMS is arranged in series with the battery cells, the electronic components in the BMS must accommodate the full battery current. In some cases, for example, a vehicle starter battery, this can be a very high current 3 which generates a significant temperature rise. Managing the temperature of the electronic components in the BMS can be challenging due to limited space and cost constraints. [0006] BMS switching is typically performed with MOSFETs. The solution to 5 the difficult problem of managing temperature rise in the MOSFETs has typically been handled in two ways. The first is using surface mount MOSFETs soldered to a Printed Circuit Board (PCB) using copper traces and pads on the PCB for heat sinking. This method is limited in its effectiveness due to the limited thickness of the copper traces and pads that can be fabricated on a PCB in a cost effective 10 manner. The second method is using either surface mount or through-hole MOSFETs with an external heatsink attached using standard methods such as mechanical fasteners and thermal grease. This method is limited in its effectiveness due to the thermal resistance of the connections. [0007] In addition to MOSFETs, the BMS may contain current sense resistors 15 and other power electronic components that have the same thermal challenges as MOSFETs. [0008] In order to carry large currents, a typical BMS uses multiple MOSFETs and/or other electronic components such as current sense resistors arranged in parallel to handle the large battery current. Ideally, each MOSFET or 20 current sense resistor shares an equal portion of the battery current and dissipates a portion of the power resulting temperature rise. [0009] The effectiveness of the heat sinking directly affects the number of MOSFETs required. Adding additional MOSFETs to the BMS to decrease temperature rise increases cost and takes up limited space inside the Li-ion 25 battery. [0010] Therefore a need exists for providing an improved BMS for a Li-ion battery, and adequate thermal management in the Li-ion battery BMS in a cost and space effective manner. [0011] Further, the BMS MOSFETs and current sense resistors may be 30 connected in series with the positive battery terminal or the negative battery 4 terminal. In either case, the components connect between a battery terminal, and the battery cells. [0012] In batteries having smaller physical sizes, it can be a challenge to fit the components on the PCB of the BMS with the required amount of heatsinking, 5 and arrange them such that they share equal portions of the current. If the BMS components do not share current equally, the result can be failure. [0013] The typical method of arranging a PCB of a BMS is to line up the MOSFETs and current sense resistors linearly across the length of the PCB of the BMS. However, often the components will not fit on the PCB of the BMS in a 10 manner to achieve the required amount of heatsinking. One solution is to reduce the heatsinking which is undesirable because it increases the temperature of the electronic components and may lead to failure. Another solution is to re-arrange the electronic components to fit in the allowed space. However, this can lead to unequal current sharing and component failure. 15 [0014] Thus, there exists a need to arrange parallel BMS components to fit in a small space and provide equal current sharing. This can be achieved with a diagonal structure and arrangement of the electronic components and/or diagonal heating sinking arrangement. 20 SUMMARY [0015] The present disclosure is directed to and improved BMS with a diagonal structure and arrangement, an improved lithium ion battery having an improved BMS with a diagonal structure and arrangement, and a method of 25 making a BMS diagonal arrangement. [0016] The diagonal arrangement provides orienting one or more electronic components, for example BMS components (e.g. PCB conductive plates, fills, and/or traces), MOSFETs, and/or current sense resistors in a diagonal structure or arrangement to provide a compact structure or arrangement and/or a diagonal 30 heating sinking structure or arrangement to provide improved heat sinking capability. For example, the MOSFETs and/or current sense resistors are 5 structured and arranged in a diagonal orientation in the BMS (e.g. diagonal orientation on PCB) and/or the PCB conductive plates, fills, and/or traces (e.g. copper plates, copper fills, and/or copper traces) structured and arranged in a diagonal orientation. 5 [0017] The present disclosure involves orienting the BMS MOSFETs and current sense resistors on a diagonal on the printed circuit board (PCB). This orientation allows the BMS to fit into a space constrained application while maintaining good current sharing between electronic components of the BMS. [0018] The improved BMS can be used with a lithium ion battery (e.g. LCO 10 (Lithium Cobalt Oxide), LTO (Lithium Titanate Oxide), LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate), LMO (Lithium Manganese Oxide), NMC (Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt), and other suitable lithium ion batteries), and the improved lithium ion battery can be any of the above types of lithium ion batteries with the improved BMS with heat sinking. 15 [0019] The PCB of the improved BMS can be provided with multiple electronic components (e.g. MOSFETs and/or current sense resistors) oriented diagonally on one or both sides of the PCB to provide a more compact arrangement. Alternatively, or in addition, the PCB of the improved BMS can be provided with multiple diagonally oriented conductive plates, fills, and/or traces 20 (e.g. multiple diagonal conductive plates arranged parallel relative to each other on the PCB). [0020] The improved BMS with heat sinking comprises one or more electrically conductive plates (e.g. one or more electrically diagonally oriented conductive plates) attached or connected to the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) of the 25 BMS. The electrically conductive plates are used to mount the electronic components (e.g. electronic components of PCB, MOSFETs, and/or current sense resistors) onto the PCB of the BMS. For example, the electrically conductive metal plates are made of copper, copper alloys, plated copper, aluminum, brass, bronze, tin, nickel, silver, or other suitable metals. Specifically, copper plates are 30 made of Grade 110 copper, Grade 101 copper, Grade 145 copper, and other suitable grades of copper. 6 [0021] The electronic components in the BMS are soldered, for example, to the one or more electrically conductive metal plates. The electrically conductive metal plates are connected or attached to electrically conductive metal pads on the PCB by soldering to secure the electrically conductive metal plates to the PCB. 5 For example, the electrically conductive metal plates are soldered at or along edge(s), corner(s), and/or lower surface(s) in order to provide electrical connection to the BMS control electronics. For example, the electrically conductive metal plates can be soldered underneath using solder paste and reflow soldering techniques. Mechanical fasteners may also be used as required to 10 provide additional mechanical strength to withstand vibration and shock. The electrically conductive metal pads, for example, can be 1 oz (ounce) or 2 oz (ounce) copper, but can be thicker or thinner depending on a particular design or application. Copper thickness on the PCB is specified in weight (i.e. the thickness of the electrically conductive metal pads is defined at the weight of copper in 15 ounces that can cover one (1) square foot of the PCB area). The electrically conductive metal pads can comprise a single metal layer or multiple metal layers. In some case the BMS PCB can duplicate the PCB electrically conductive metal pads in multiple layers on the PCB, and connect these layers with multiple vias. A via is a drilled and plated hole between layers. The vias provide electrical and 20 thermal conductivity between layers. This provides additional heat spreading and heat sinking to improve thermal performance. Further, the electrically conductive metal pads can be provided with one or more layers of metal plates located between the electrically conductive metal pads and electrically conductive metal plates to enhance heat sinking. The electrically conductive metal pads can be 25 connected (e.g. via traces) to one or more components and/or circuits on the PCB of the BMS, or can be electrically isolated on the PCB [0022] The electrically conductive metal plates are sized as required to allow sufficient room to solder the electronic components, and to maintain the temperature rise of the electronic components of the BMS within their specified 30 operating limits. 7 [0023] The electrically conductive metal plates are located as required to fit inside the battery, and to provide for equal current sharing between parallel electronic components. For example, the electrically conductive metal plates may be 1/16 or 1/8 inch thick, or may be thicker or thinner depending on the thermal 5 requirements of the BMS. Further, the electrically conductive metal plates can have a specific shape (e.g. rectangle, square, L-shaped, triangle, round, arc, symbol). patents.title: HANDLE FOR A LITHIUM ION BATTERY

inventors.name: UNDERHILL, Derek, Michael

patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a battery handle that is removably attachable to a battery. The handle may comprise a body comprising first end, a second end opposite the first end, and a grip portion extending between the first end and the second end in a first direction, wherein the body is removably attachable to the battery via at least one battery terminal, and the at least one battery terminal is configured to be in electrical connection with the battery.
patents.complete_specification: TECHNICAL FIELD [0002] The technology described herein relates generally to the field of 10 batteries, and more specifically, to handles for carrying and maneuvering batteries. BACKGROUND [0003] Batteries with large capacities are traditionally bulky and difficult to maneuver. Even secondary batteries such as lithium ion batteries, increasingly 15 used to power vehicles and small crafts, may be heavy and hard to transport. To alleviate this burden, batteries may be packaged with handles or grips. Conventional solutions, however, typically fail to provide enough support, leading to broken handles and dropped batteries. Additionally, these solutions waste packaging space, requiring larger products and higher manufacturing costs. 20 SUMMARY [0004] In one aspect, a handle for a battery comprises a body comprising a first end, a second end opposite the first end, and a grip portion extending between the first end and the second end in a first direction, wherein the body is removably attachable to the battery via at least one battery terminal, and the at least one 25 battery terminal is configured to be in electrical connection with the battery. [0005] According to an embodiment, the at least one battery terminal comprises a plurality of terminals including a first terminal and a second terminal, wherein the first terminal is configured to connect to a first polarity of the battery through the first end of the body, and the second terminal is configured to connect 30 to a second polarity of the battery through the second end of the body. [0006] According to a further embodiment, the battery further comprises a plurality of protective caps configured to cover the plurality of terminals. 3 [0007] In accordance with a further embodiment, the first end and the second end each comprise a bottom portion having a hole, wherein the hole is configured to receive a terminal of the plurality of terminals. [0008] In accordance with a further embodiment, the bottom portions extend 5 in the first direction and in a second direction perpendicular to the first direction, wherein the first end and the second each further comprise a first vertical extension and a second vertical extension spaced apart from the first vertical extension in the second direction by a gap, and the hole overlaps the gap. [0009] According to a further embodiment, the plurality of terminals comprise 10 a first threaded portion configured to connect to the battery through the hole, a second threaded portion configured to connect to an external module, and a central nut portion having a wider width in the second direction than the first threaded portion and the second threaded portion, wherein a first portion of the gap separates the first vertical extension and the central nut portion, and a second 15 portion of the gap separates the second vertical extension and the central nut portion. [0010] According to a further embodiment, the handle further comprises a plurality of protective caps configured to cover the plurality of terminals, wherein the plurality of protective caps cover the second threaded portion and the central 20 nut portion. [0011] In accordance with an embodiment, the body comprises a recess shaped and sized to store a tool. [0012] In accordance with a further embodiment, the handle further comprises a tool within the recess in the body, the tool comprising a wrench configured to 25 attach and detach the plurality of terminals to the battery. [0013] In accordance with an embodiment, the body comprises a rigid body. [0014] In another aspect, a battery comprises a top face comprising a first set of terminal inputs and a second set of terminal inputs, and a handle removably attached to the battery, wherein a position of the handle is adjustable such that it is 30 attached to the first set of terminal inputs in a first position, and attached to the second set of terminal inputs in a second position. 4 [0015] According to a further embodiment, the top face extends in a first direction and a second direction perpendicular to the first direction, wherein the first set of terminal inputs are arranged in a middle of one of the first direction and the second direction, and the second set of terminal inputs are arranged in an 5 outside portion of the one of the first direction and a second direction. [0016] In accordance with a further embodiment, the handle is in the first position. [0017] In accordance with another embodiment, the handle is in the second position. 10 [0018] According to an embodiment, the handle comprises a first end, a second end opposite the first end, and a grip portion extending between the first end and the second end in a first direction, the first end comprising a first base having a first hole, a first vertical wall, a second vertical wall separated from the first vertical wall in a second direction perpendicular to the first direction by a 15 first gap, and a first inclined wall between the first vertical wall and the second vertical wall in the second direction and inclined towards the grip portion, the second end comprising a second base having a second hole, a third vertical wall, a fourth vertical wall separated from the third vertical wall in the second direction a second gap, and a second inclined wall between the third vertical wall and the 20 fourth vertical wall in the second direction and inclined towards the grip portion. [0019] In accordance with a further embodiment, the first set of terminal inputs and the second set of terminal inputs are spaced apart in the second direction, the first set of terminal inputs comprising a first positive polarity input and first negative polarity input spaced apart in the first direction by a first 25 distance, the second set terminal inputs comprising a second positive polarity terminal and a second negative polarity terminal spaced apart in the first direction by the first distance, and wherein the first hole and the second hole of the handle are spaced apart in the first direction by the first distance. [0020] According to an embodiment, the handle is attached to the first set of 30 terminal inputs or the second set of terminal inputs via a plurality of battery terminals. 5 [0021] In accordance with a further embodiment, the terminal inputs comprise threaded sidewalls and the plurality of battery terminals comprise a first threaded portion configured to interface with the threaded sidewalls, a second threaded portion, and a central nut portion having a wider width than the first threaded 5 portion and the second threaded portion, and the battery further comprises a plurality of protective caps configured to cover the plurality of terminals, wherein the plurality of protective caps cover the second threaded portion and the central nut portion. [0022] In another aspect, a method of assembling a battery package comprises 10 receiving a battery, wherein the battery comprises a top face including a first set of terminal positions and a second set of terminal positions, receiving a handle, wherein the handle is removably attachable to the battery, and attaching the handle to the battery, wherein the handle is attached to the first set of terminal positions or the second set of terminal positions. 15 [0023] In accordance with an embodiment, the handle is attached via battery terminals. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0024] Aspects of the present disclosure are best understood from the following detailed description when read with the accompanying figures. 20 [0025] Fig. 1 is a diagram depicting a perspective view of a battery assembly including a handle for the battery according to an embodiment. [0026] Figs. 2A-2C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a handle according to an embodiment. [0027] Figs. 3A-3C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a 25 handle according to another embodiment. [0028] Figs. 4A-4C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a handle according to another embodiment. [0029] Fig. 5 is a diagram depicting a side view of a battery assembly according to an embodiment. 30 [0030] Fig. 6 is a diagram depicting a top perspective view of a handle according to an embodiment. 6 [0031] Fig. 7 is a diagram depicting a bottom perspective view of a handle according to an embodiment. [0032] Fig. 8 is a diagram depicting a perspective view of attachment between a handle and a battery according to an embodiment. 5 [0033] Figs. 9A-9C are diagrams depicting perspective views of a battery assembly according to an embodiment. [0034] Fig. 10 is a flowchart depicting a method of assembling a battery including a handle according to an embodiment. DETAILED DESCRIPTION 10 [0035] The following disclosure provides many different embodiments, or examples, for implementing different features of the provided subject matter. Specific examples of components and arrangements are described below to simplify the present disclosure. These are, of course, merely examples and are not intended to be limiting. For example, the formation of a first feature over or on a 15 second feature in the description that follows may include embodiments in which the first and second features are formed in direct contact, and may also include embodiments in which additional features may be formed between the first and second features, such that the first and second features may not be in direct contact. In addition, the present disclosure may repeat reference numerals and/or 20 letters in some various examples. This repetition is for the purpose of simplicity and clarity and does not in itself dictate a relationship between some various embodiments and/or configurations discussed. [0036] The foregoing outlines features of several embodiments so that those skilled in the art may better understand the aspects of the present disclosure. 25 Those skilled in the art should appreciate that they may readily use the present disclosure as a basis for designing or modifying other processes and structures for carrying out the same purposes and/or achieving the same advantages of the embodiments introduced herein. Those skilled in the art should also realize that such equivalent constructions do not depart from the spirit and scope of the 30 present disclosure, and that they may make various changes, substitutions, and 7 alterations herein without departing from the spirit and scope of the present disclosure. [0037] It is generally the object of the present subject matter to provide a strong and reliable battery handle without increasing battery size or cost. The 5 embodiments described herein relate to a handle that is removably attachable to a battery. The handle may provide a sturdy means for transporting and maneuvering a battery without requiring extra packaging space for a molded handle or a cavity for housing such a handle. Additionally, the handle may be attached in various positions, providing a convenient and easy to use handle in 10 variety of different circumstances. In embodiments of the present subject matter, the handle may be attached to a battery via battery terminals. This further preserves space on the device, limits the number of parts required for operating the battery, decreases the risk of losing the pieces used to attach the handle to the battery. 15 [0038] Fig. 1 is a diagram depicting a perspective view of a battery assembly 100 including a handle 110 for the battery according to an embodiment. The battery assembly may include a battery having a body 105 and a top face 115. The top face 115 may extend in a first direction and a second direction, as depicted by the axes in Fig. 1. 20 [0039] The top face of the battery may comprise multiple sets of terminal positions. For example, in the embodiment depicted in Fig. 1, top face 115 includes a first set of terminal positions 120A/120B, and a second set of terminal positions 125A/125B. Terminal positions of a same set may be spaced apart from one another in the first direction. The first set of terminal positions 120A/120B 25 and the second set of terminal positions 125A/125B may be spaced apart from each other in the second direction. In this manner, the first set of terminal positions 120A and 120B may be located in a middle portion of the top face in the second direction, and the second set of terminal positions 125A and 125B may be located in an outside portion of the top face in the second direction. 30 [0040] Each terminal position 120A/120B/125A/125B may correspond to a polarity of the battery and may comprise a port or input for receiving battery 8 terminals 130A/130B that provide connection between the battery and external devices. For example, 120A may correspond to a first polarity of the battery, while 120B corresponds to a second polarity. The first polarity may be a positive or negative polarity, with the second polarity being opposite of the first polarity. 5 In a similar fashion, 125A may correspond to a positive or negative polarity and 125B corresponds to the opposite polarity. In an embodiment, 120A and 125A provide a port or input to a positive polarity of the battery while 120B and 125B provide a port or input to a negative polarity of the battery. In some embodiments, when the inputs or ports of terminal positions are not in use, covers 10 140A/140B may be placed over the inputs or ports at the terminal positions for protection. For example, as depicted in Fig. 1, the second set of terminal positions 125A and 12B are not in use and are protected by covers 140A/140B. [0041] The battery assembly 100 further comprises a handle 110 that is removably attachable to the top face 115. The handle may be capable of attaching 15 to the top face in different positions. For example, the handle 110 may be provided and attached such that ends of the handle align with the first set of terminal positions 120A/120B. Alternatively, the handle 110 may attach such that the ends of the handle align with the second set of terminal positions 125A/125B. After attaching in one position, the handle 110 may be removed from that position 20 and reattached at the other position. [0042] For example, as depicted in Fig. 1, the handle 110 may initially be aligned with the first set of terminal positions 120A/120B. As will be described further below, the handle 110 may be attached to the ports or inputs of these terminal positions via battery terminals 130A and 130B. A user may later decide 25 that, based on the surrounding circumstances, the handle 110 would be more conveniently located in an outside portion of the top face 115. As such, the user may remove the terminals 130A/130B from the inputs at 120A/120B in order to detach the handle 110 from the first position. The user may then move the handle 110 to the second position aligned with 125A/125B, and attach the handle 110 in 30 that position. 9 [0043] As previously referenced, the handle 110 may be attached to the battery via battery terminals 130A/130B. These terminals act as both fasteners and as electrical connectors between the battery and external devices such as jumper cables. Each terminal position may comprise a port or input that allows 5 the battery terminals to be in electrical connection with a pole of the battery. In an embodiment, inputs may include threaded sidewalls that mate with threaded portions of the battery terminals 130A/130B. As discussed further with respect to Fig. 5, this configuration allows a user to attach the handle by screwing the battery terminals into the inputs through an opening in the handle. The user may also 10 unscrew the battery terminals from the inputs in order to detach the handle. [0044] The battery assembly 100 may further comprise protective caps 135A/135B that cover exposed portions of the battery terminals 130A/130B. The caps may provide electrical insulation for the battery terminals as well as providing resistance to corrosion. The protective caps 135A/135B are removable, 15 and may be removed from the battery terminals 130A/130B when electrical connection to or from the battery is desired. When the battery terminals 130A/130B are not in use, the protective caps 135A/135B may be placed over exposed portions of the terminals to protect against electrical shorts and against corrosion. 20 [0045] In other embodiments, the handle 110 may be attached to inputs of the first set of terminal positions 120A/120B or the second set of terminal positions 125A/125B via a pair of screws or standard bolts. In an embodiment, screws may be used to provide secure, removable attachment of the handle to the top face of the battery. While the screws attach the handle at one set of terminal positions, 25 battery terminals 130A/130B may be installed at the other set of terminal positions to allow for connection between the battery and external devices. [0046] As described further below with reference to Figs. 9A-9C, in some embodiments, the battery assembly 100 may include four battery terminals 130. In these embodiments, the covers 140A/140B are not in place and a battery 30 terminal 130 may be connected to inputs at each terminal position on the top face. 10 [0047] Figs. 2A-2C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a handle 110 according to an embodiment. Fig. 2A is a diagram depicting a side view of the handle 110 according to an embodiment. Fig. 2B is a diagram depicting a top view of the handle 110 according to an embodiment. Fig. 2C is a 5 diagram depicting a bottom view of the handle 110 according to an embodiment. [0048] Handle 110 may have a first end 201, a second end 202, and a grip portion 203 extending between the first end 201 and the second end 202. The grip portion 203 allows a user’s hand to engage with the handle. The grip portion 203 may include a lattice structure 215. In an embodiment, handle 110 is a rigid body 10 formed of a plastic material, however the material is not so limited. For example handle 110 may be any type of molded article, or any electrically insulative material that provides sufficient structure to support a battery. Lattice structure 215 may include areas where the material of the handle 110 is not present. This may reduce the weight of the handle, save on the cost of materials, and provide a 15 more comfortable interface for a user to grip. In one embodiment, the lattice portion 215 may be in a honeycomb or hexagonal shape. [0049] Each of the first end 201 and second end 202 may comprise a bottom portion 204 having a hole 205A/205B. The holes 205A/205B may provide a space for battery terminals to pass through such that the handle is securely 20 attached to the battery when the battery terminals are screwed into inputs at the terminal positions in the top face of the battery. In an embodiment, the first end 201 may comprise first hole 205A and the second end 202 may comprise second hole 205B. In an example attachment of the handle 110 to the battery, the first hole 205A may be aligned with terminal position 120A, and the second hole 205B 25 may be aligned with terminal position 120B. Battery terminal 130A may be screwed into the input at terminal position 120A through hole 205A. Batery terminal 130B may be screwed into the input at terminal position 120B through hole 205B. Doing so provides a sturdy attachment of handle 110 to the top face 115 of the battery while also providing external connection to both a positive and 30 negative polarity of the battery through the battery terminals 130A/130B. 11 [0050] The first end 201 and second end 202 may each further comprise a pair of vertical sidewalls 207. Each end includes two vertical sidewalls 207 spaced apart in a width direction of the handle. The vertical sidewalls 207 of each end are set far enough apart from one another so as to provide enough space for the 5 battery terminals to be fed through the holes 205A/205B and preserving a gap between the battery terminals and inner surfaces of the vertical sidewalls 207. This gap between adjacent vertical sidewalls 207 may overlap with the position of the holes 205A/205B in the bottom portion 204 such that a battery terminal may be present in a gap and threaded through the overlapping hole. 10 [0051] In an embodiment, a handle 110 may further comprise inclined sidewalls 206 extending from the bottom portion 204 toward the grip portion 203. In Fig. 2A, the vertical sidewalls 207 block a view of inclined sidewalls 206. Fig. 2B and Fig. 2C, however, provide a view showing the position of the inclined sidewalls 206. As seen in Fig. 2B, the bottom portions 204 may be surrounding 15 by sidewalls on three sides. In a width direction of the handle 110, bottom portions 204 may be bordered by vertical sidewalls 207. In the direction in which the handle 110 extends, however, the bottom portion may be open on outer sides and bordered by the inclined sidewalls 206 on inner sides. The inclined sidewalls 206 may also comprise lattice structure 215. The inclined sidewalls 206, along 20 with portions of the vertical sidewalls 207, may connect bottom portions 204 to the grip portion 203 of the handle. [0052] Figs. 3A-3C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a handle 310 according to an embodiment. Fig. 3A is a diagram depicting a side view of the handle 310 according to an embodiment. Fig. 3B is a diagram 25 depicting a top view of the handle 310 according to an embodiment. Fig. 3C is a diagram depicting another side view of the handle 310 according to an embodiment. [0053] The embodiment of Figs. 3A-3C differs from the embodiment of Figs. 2A-2C only in the shape and design of the lattice structure. Otherwise, the 30 structures and components of the handle 310 may be the same in Figs. 3A-3C as those depicted in the earlier figures. As such, reference numbers for identical 12 structures are not repeated. As depicted in Figs. 3A-3C, the handle 310 may comprise a lattice structure 315, wherein the lattice structure is in a grid shape. [0054] Figs. 4A-4C are diagrams depicting various perspective views of a handle 410 according to an embodiment. Fig. 4A is a diagram depicting a side 5 view of the handle 410 according to an embodiment. Fig. 4B is a diagram depicting a top view of the handle 410 according to an embodiment. Fig. 4C is a diagram depicting another side view of the handle 410 according to an embodiment. [0055] The embodiment of Figs. 4A-4C differs from the embodiment of Figs. 10 2A-2C and Figs. 3A-3C only in the shape and design of the lattice structure. Otherwise, the structures and components of the handle 410 may be the same in Figs. 4A-4C as those depicted in the earlier figures. As such, reference numbers for identical structures are not repeated. As depicted in Figs. 4A-4C, the handle 410 may comprise a lattice structure 415, wherein the lattice structure is in 15 includes circular cut-outs. [0056] Fig. 5 is a diagram depicting a side view of a battery assembly 100 according to an embodiment. Fig 5 depicts one terminal position 120 of the first set of terminal positions and one terminal position 125 of the second set of terminal positions. In an embodiment, handle 110 is configured to attach to the 20 first set of terminal positions including terminal position 120. The handle 110 may be attached to the battery via a battery terminal 130. Battery terminal 130 may be aligned with the input of terminal position 120 such that the threaded portion of battery terminal 130 may screw into a threaded portion of the input of terminal position 120. The handle 110 may be aligned such that the hole in the 25 bottom portion is aligned along an axis with the battery terminal 130 and the input of the terminal position 120. [0057] When attached, the handle is sized and dimensioned such that the battery terminal 130 and terminal cap 135 may fit within the space between adjacent vertical sidewalls 107. For example, the battery terminal 130 may 30 comprise a first threaded portion and a second threaded portion separated by a nut portion 510 in the middle. The nut portion 510 may be wider than the threaded 13 portions. The nut portion 510 may assist in keeping a terminal cap 135 in place, but in some embodiments other shapes for the battery terminal may be used. Nonlimiting examples may include a continuous threaded structure with no nut portion in the middle, or a structure that is threaded only one end. 5 [0058] When the handle 110 is attached, the first threaded portion may be placed through the handle and screw into the input of the terminal position 120. In this position, the battery terminal 130 and the vertical sidewalls 207 may subdivide the gap between adjacent vertical sidewalls into a pair of gaps defined between the vertical sidewalls 207 and the nut portion 510 of the battery terminal 10 130. A first gap 505A may be present between the nut portion 510 of the battery terminal 130 and a first vertical sidewall 207, and a second gap 505B may be present between the nut portion 510 of the battery terminal 130 and a second vertical sidewall 207. [0059] This configuration may provide additional protection against 15 accidental shorting of the battery terminals during storage and handling. While the gaps 505A/505B may provide enough space for the connection of external clamps or cables to the battery terminals 130 when needed, the vertical sidewalls 207 act as barriers to prevent unwanted contact with the terminal and/or clamps. Additionally, the sidewalls are set far enough apart so as to accommodate the 20 protective caps 135 such that when the terminals are not in use, they may be covered. As such, embodiments of the present subject matter may provide two layers of protection against accidental shorting of the terminals. [0060] An example mechanism for attaching the battery terminals to the battery is described hereafter with reference to Figs. 6-8. Fig. 6 is a diagram 25 depicting a top perspective view of a handle 610 according to an embodiment. Fig. 7 is a diagram depicting a bottom perspective view of a handle 710 according to an embodiment. Fig. 8 is a diagram depicting a perspective view of an attachment between a handle 710 and a top face of a battery 115 according to an embodiment. 30 [0061] As depicted in Fig. 6, in an embodiment a handle 610 may have an upper surface 615 and a lower surface 620. A recess 625 may be provided in the 14 upper surface. The recess 625 may be sized and shaped to hold a tool. In an embodiment, the size and shape of the recess is that of a hex wrench. The handle 610 may further comprise a hex wrench 630 packaged within the recess 625. The hex wrench 630 may have end portions that match a shape of the battery terminals 5 and may be configured to assist in attaching and detaching the handle to a battery. [0062] Fig. 7 depicts a handle 710 according to another embodiment. Handle 710 may have an upper surface (not shown) and a lower surface 720. A recess 725 may be provided in the lower surface. The recess 725 may be sized and shaped to hold a tool. In an embodiment, the size and shape of the recess is that 10 of a hex wrench. The handle 710 may further comprise a hex wrench 730 packaged within the recess 725. The hex wrench 730 may have end portions that match a shape of the battery terminals and may be configured to assist in attaching and detaching the handle to a battery. [0063] Fig. 8 depicts a battery assembly 800 and the attachment of handle 710 15 to the top face of a battery 115 by using the hex wrench 730. As seen in Fig. 8, the handle 710 may be aligned with the first set of terminal positions 120A/120B as described previously with respect to Fig. 1, for example. A battery terminal 130 may be provided to securely, and removably, attach the handle to the battery. Hex wrench 730, previously housed within a recess on the underside of handle 20 710, may be used to screw the battery terminal 130 into the input at terminal position 120B. Although Fig. 8 depicts attachment via hex wrench 730, the present subject matter is not so limited. For example, the battery terminals may be screwed in using a standard wrench, or any other means capable of securely attaching the battery terminals to the inputs of the terminal positions. 25 Additionally, as previously described, in other embodiments the handle may be attached via screws. In such a configuration, a standard screwdriver may be used to attach the screws to the inputs of the terminal positions, thereby securely and removably attaching the handle to the battery. [0064] While Fig. 8, and other figures, depict attachment of the handle to the 30 first set of terminal positions 120A/120B, the present subject matter is directed to a handle that may be attached in multiple positions including a position 15 corresponding to the second set of terminal positions 125A/125B. This versatility allows for convenient placement of the handle depending on the circumstances of the battery’s location. [0065] Figs. 9A-9C are diagrams depicting perspective views of battery 5 assembly 100 according to an embodiment. In an embodiment, inputs at terminal positions 120A/120B as well as those at 125A/125B are uncovered and are configured to receive a battery terminal of a plurality of battery terminals. The battery assembly 100 may include four battery terminals, 130A/130B as previously described above as well as battery terminals 130C and 130D. 10 [0066] Fig. 9A depicts a first configuration in which the handle is removed completely from the battery. In certain scenarios, a user may find that removal of the battery provides easier access to the battery terminals. For example, in an embodiment, the battery may be lithium ion battery used to power a vehicle or craft. After using the handle to maneuver the battery into place within the vehicle 15 or craft, the user may find it advantageous to remove the handle completely from the top face of the battery in order to expose a greater portion of the top face. This may also allow room for the installation of a battery cover, or a battery bracket used to retain the battery. [0067] As seen in Fig. 9A, after removing the handle, the user may then screw 20 the battery terminals 130A/130B back into the inputs at first terminal positions 120A/120B so as to provide for external connection to the battery. In an embodiment, the battery terminals 130A/130B may be connected to external cables 905A/905B. This may allow for the battery to provide electricity to an external device, or to receive a supply of electricity (for example, allowing the 25 battery to be charged). Alternatively (not shown in Fig. 9A), the battery terminals 130A/130B may be installed at second terminal positions 125A/125B. Additionally (not shown in Fig. 9A), battery terminals 130C/130D may be installed at terminal positions 125A/125B while battery terminals 130A/130B are installed at positions 120A/120B. This allows for flexibility of positioning when 30 making a connection to external devices. 16 [0068] Fig. 9B depicts another configuration in which the handle 110 is attached at the second set of terminal positions 125A/125B at an outside portion of the top face of the battery. In some scenarios, a user may find that the most accessible way to maneuver the battery will require attachment to the outside 5 portion of the top face of the battery. For example, installation of a battery in a vehicle or craft may make the middle portion of the battery inaccessible.
