patents.abstract: A battery configured to have improved thermal management and structural stability. The battery including a battery pack construction with at least one battery cell spacer having a first surface contacting substantially all of the bottom surface of a first battery cell and a second surface contacting substantially all of the top surface of a second battery cell, the battery cell spacer including an adhesive component. Additionally, the battery may include a battery management system (BMS) in electrical communication with the first and second battery cells, the BMS having one or more thermal components configured to disperse heat from the BMS, and a thermal epoxy contacting the one or more thermal components and a battery housing. The battery further including a stability cage at least partially enclosing the battery pack construction and positioned between the battery cells and the battery housing.
patents.complete_specification: FIELD 10 [0002] The present disclosure relates to batteries. Specifically, the present disclosure relates to lithium-ion batteries having features to promote durability. BACKGROUND [0003] Lithium-ion batteries are the predominant type of rechargeable 15 batteries used in many commercial applications today. Given their wide usage, lithium-ion batteries are often required to have different sizes, shapes, arrangements, and chemistries depending on the intended application. Unfortunately, lithium-ion batteries can be safety hazards when they are not properly designed, are improperly charged, or undergo severe mechanical forces 20 (e.g. vibrations). [0004] One way for a lithium-ion battery to become compromised is through thermal abuse due to insufficient cooling. When lithium-ion cells become overheated, they can suffer thermal runaway that can lead to cell rupture. Because 25 many lithium-ion batteries include flammable electrolytes, a compromised lithium-ion cell can produce an explosion or fire. In order to address this issue, some lithium-ion battery designs include heat sinks associated with a battery management system (BMS), which typically includes a printed circuit board (PCB) and electronic circuitry. The heat generated by the circuitry is transferred to 30 the heatsink, which then relies on convection through air contained within the battery housing to further dissipate the heat. 3 [0005] Another common way for a lithium-ion battery to become compromised is through mechanical stresses resulting from movement of the battery (e.g. a vehicle containing the battery hitting a bump in the road, a boat containing the battery going over a wave, etc.). In order to physically protect 5 batteries, larger lithium-ion batteries are typically stored within a polymer shell, sometimes referred to as a battery housing, which can help alleviate some of the mechanical forces that the lithium-ion cells ultimately experience during usage. SUMMARY 10 [0006] The present disclosure is directed to systems and methods for improving the thermal and mechanical stability of batteries, such as lithium-ion batteries. In one aspect, battery management systems having improved thermal cooling through conduction are provided. By utilizing conductive heat transfer away from a battery management system, such as by transferring energy through a 15 thermal resin in contact with a battery housing, cooling improvements can be realized over existing convection-based designs. Furthermore, structural improvements through the use of specialized battery spacers, specific battery cell adhesive restraints, and a battery stability cage can help ensure that battery cells do not become compromised due to forces imposed on a battery during use. 20 [0007] In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a battery configured to have improved stability. The battery may include a battery pack construction including a first battery cell having a top surface and a bottom surface, a second battery cell having a top surface and a bottom surface, and a battery cell spacer 25 having a first surface contacting substantially all of the bottom surface of the first battery cell and a second surface contacting substantially all of the top surface of the second battery cell, wherein the first and the second surfaces each include an adhesive component. The battery may further include a battery management system (BMS) in electrical communication with the first and second battery cells, 30 the BMS having one or more thermal components configured to disperse heat from the BMS, a battery housing enclosing the battery pack construction and the 4 BMS, and a thermal epoxy contacting the one or more thermal components and the battery housing. The battery may also include a stability cage at least partially enclosing the battery pack construction and positioned between the battery cells and the battery housing. The stability cage may include a polymer frame having 5 four sidewalls positioned in a rectangular form, wherein each sidewall includes a plurality of apertures forming a mesh pattern. [0008] In another aspect, the present disclosure provides a battery configured to have improved stability, the battery may include a battery management system 10 (BMS) in electrical communication with a plurality of battery cells, the BMS having one or more thermal components configured to disperse heat from the BMS, a battery housing enclosing the battery cells and the BMS, and a thermal epoxy contacting the one or more thermal components and the battery housing. 15 [0009] In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a method of manufacturing a battery configured to have improved stability. The method may include: providing a battery management system (BMS) in electrical communication with a plurality of battery cells, the BMS having one or more thermal components configured to disperse heat from the BMS, arranging a 20 battery housing to enclose the battery cells and the BMS, and applying a thermal epoxy between the BMS and the battery housing, wherein the thermal epoxy contacts the one or more thermal components and the battery housing. [0010] In another aspect, the present disclosure provides a battery configured 25 to have improved stability, the battery may include a first battery cell having a top surface and a bottom surface, a second battery cell having a top surface and a bottom surface, a battery cell spacer having a first surface contacting substantially all of the bottom surface of the first battery cell and a second surface contacting substantially all of the top surface of the second battery cell, wherein the first and 30 the second surfaces of the battery cell spacer each include an adhesive component. 5 [0011] In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a method of manufacturing a battery configured to have improved stability. The method may include: arranging a plurality of battery cell spacers between a plurality of battery cells to form a battery pack, wrapping the battery pack in a first layer of adhesive 5 tape, wherein the first layer of adhesive tape contacts substantially all of a top surface of the battery pack, arranging a plurality of protective plates along the multiple geometric sides of the battery pack, wherein the protective plates are configured to substantially cover the multiple geometric sides, and wrapping the battery pack, the first layer of adhesive tape, and the protective plates in a second 10 layer of adhesive tape. [0012] In yet another aspect, the present disclosure provides a battery configured to have improved stability, the battery may include a plurality of battery cells, a battery housing configured to enclose the battery cells, the battery 15 housing having a main body and a cover, and a stability cage at least partially enclosing the battery cells and positioned between the battery cells and the battery housing. The stability cage may include a polymer frame having four sidewalls positioned in a rectangular form, wherein each sidewall includes a plurality of apertures forming a mesh pattern. 20 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0013] FIG. 1 illustrates a side view of a battery having a thermal resin layer positioned along substantially the entire length of a bottom surface of a cover of a housing of the battery; an associated battery management system includes several 25 metal plates contacting the thermal resin layer, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0014] FIG. 2 illustrates a side view of a battery having a thermal resin layer positioned along select sections of a bottom surface of a cover of a housing of the 30 battery; an associated battery management system includes several metal plates contacting the thermal resin layer sections, which does not extend in a lateral 6 direction beyond the edges of the metal plates, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0015] FIG. 3 illustrates a side view of a battery having a thermal resin layer 5 positioned along a section of a bottom surface of a cover of a housing of the battery; an associated battery management system includes a printed circuit board (PCB) contacting the thermal resin layer, which extends in a lateral direction beyond the edges of the PCB but does not cover the entire length of the bottom surface of the battery housing cover, in accordance with one aspect of the present 10 disclosure. [0016] FIG. 4 illustrates a side view of a battery having a thermal resin layer positioned along a section of a bottom surface of a cover of a housing of the battery; an associated battery management system includes a printed circuit board 15 and multiple field-effect transistors (FETs) both in contact with the thermal resin, which extends in a lateral direction beyond the edges of the PCB but does not cover the entire length of the bottom surface of the battery housing cover, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 20 [0017] FIG. 5A illustrates a bottom view of a battery housing cover having a thermal resin layer positioned along a large portion of its bottom surface; an associated battery management system includes several metal plates contacting the thermal resin layer, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 25 [0018] FIG. 5B illustrates a perspective view of the battery housing cover of FIG. 5A. [0019] FIG. 6 is a process flowchart for a method of manufacturing a battery configured to have improved stability, in accordance with one aspect of the 30 present disclosure. 7 [0020] FIG. 7A illustrates a partial exploded view of a battery housing and an associated battery stability cage, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 5 [0021] FIG. 7B illustrates a partial cutaway view of the battery housing and the battery stability cage of FIG. 7A, along with an associated battery management system and thermal epoxy layer, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 10 [0022] FIG. 7C illustrates an isometric view of the battery stability cage of FIGs. 7A-7B, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0023] FIG. 7D illustrates a front view of the battery stability cage of FIGs. 7A-7C, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 15 [0024] FIG. 7E illustrates a side view of the battery stability cage of FIG. 7A7D, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0025] FIG. 8 illustrates a side view of a battery pack construction having 20 multiple battery cell spacers positioned at three points between each battery cell, with two adhesive tape sections wrapped around the battery pack in-between the battery cell spacers, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0026] FIG. 9 is a process flowchart for a method of manufacturing a battery 25 configured to have improved stability, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. [0027] FIG. 10 illustrates a perspective view of a battery cell having a pouch form, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 30 [0028] FIG. 11 illustrates a perspective view of a battery pack formed of several battery cells with interconnects providing electrical communication pathways between the battery cells, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 8 [0029] FIG. 12 illustrates a side view of a battery pack construction having multiple battery cell spacers extending along substantially the entire length of the battery cells, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 5 [0030] FIG. 13 illustrates a perspective view of a battery pack construction formed of several battery cells with a layer of adhesive taping enclosing the entire battery pack, including the battery cells and the battery cell spacers, if any, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 10 [0031] FIG. 14 illustrates a perspective view of the battery pack construction of FIG. 13 further enclosed in protective plates positioned along several geometric sides of the battery pack construction, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 15 [0032] FIG. 15 illustrates a perspective view of the battery pack construction of FIG. 14 further enclosed in a second layer of adhesive tape, which may help to further secure the protective plates to the first layer of adhesive tape and ensure the stability of the battery pack, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 20 [0033] FIG. 16 illustrates a perspective view of the battery pack construction of FIG. 15 at least partially enclosed in a shrink-wrapped polymeric film, in accordance with one aspect of the present disclosure. 25 [0034] The current subject matter will be better understood by reference to the following detailed description when considered in combination with the accompanying drawings which form part of the present specification. DETAILED DESCRIPTION 30 [0035] Unless specifically stated or apparent from context, as used herein, the terms “a”, “an”, and “the” are understood to be singular or plural. The terms “include(s)” or “such as,” and the like are intended to convey inclusion without 9 limitation, unless otherwise specifically indicated. The terms “or” and “and” can be used interchangeably and can be understood to mean “and/or.” [0036] As used herein, the term “substantially” refers to the qualitative 5 condition of exhibiting total or near-total extent or degree. Substantially may refer to a minimum degree understood in the art. For example, substantially all of a value (e.g. an area of a surface) may refer to at least 80%, at least 85%, at least 90%, at least 95%, or specifically at least 99% of that value. 10 [0037] As used herein “battery management system” (BMS) may refer to a group of battery components that manage a rechargeable battery, often by preventing the battery from operating outside of its safe operating area. Various constructions of battery management systems are disclosed, for example, in U.S. Pat. App. Pub. 2022/0209307 entitled “Lithium-Ion Battery Management System 15 (BMS) Having Diagonal Arrangement,” the contents of which are incorporated herein by reference in their entirety. [0038] As used herein “thermal epoxy” may refer to a polymer resin that has a viscosity that allows it to be poured and has a high thermal conductivity. Thermal 20 epoxy may be used as a generic term herein, and does not necessarily indicate the composition of the product unless context specifically indicates otherwise. For instance, a thermal epoxy, as used herein, need not necessarily be formed from polyepoxides, but may instead comprise alternative or additional polymer resins, such as urethanes. 25 Battery Management System Heat Transfer [0039] The battery management system in a lithium-ion battery requires electronic circuitry to disconnect the internal battery pack from the external battery terminals in case of a fault condition. This circuitry can dissipate a 30 significant amount of power which generates heat that needs to be dissipated to the exterior of the battery housing. Due to exposure concerns, such BMS systems are often enclosed in a battery housing that contains limited, if any, external 10 venting to provide airflow. Since the removal of heat through the limited natural convection occurring within a battery housing can be slow, such constructions can result in stagnant hot air within battery housings. This stagnant hot air can accumulate near the BMS until the heat eventually transfers from the internal air 5 to the battery housing cover and then to the external environment. [0040] The present disclosure provides battery systems that allow for the direct and efficient transfer of heat from the heat generating components of a BMS to the battery housing via a thermal resin conduction pathway, such as 10 through an applied thermal epoxy layer. By providing a direct conduction pathway instead of relying on the limited natural convection typically available within a battery housing, a more efficient heat removal construction can be achieved. Furthermore, by relying on a thermally conductive viscous liquid that can be poured or injected to take the shape of the surfaces it covers, thermal 15 contact over large areas of a BMS can be achieved, even for irregularly shaped components. Because of the improved heat transfer, battery systems incorporating the teachings of the present disclosure may be able to operate at higher currents for similarly sized constructions. 20 [0041] Accordingly, a battery configured to have improved stability may be provided, wherein the battery has a battery management system in electrical communication with a plurality of battery cells, a battery housing enclosing the battery cells and the BMS, and a thermal epoxy contacting one or more thermal components and the battery housing. The thermal components of the BMS may be 25 specifically configured to disperse heat from the BMS. For example, the one or more thermal components in contact with the thermal epoxy may include an electrical component configured to generate heat when subjected to an electric current, such as a field-effect transistor (FET), or more specifically, a metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET). Alternatively, the one or more 30 thermal components in contact with the thermal epoxy may include a conductive component, such as a metal (e.g. copper) plate. Such a metal plate may be in contact with an electrical component (e.g. MOSFET) configured to generate heat 11 when subjected to an electric current. FIGs. 1-5B illustrate various battery arrangements that allow for conductive heat transfer from a BMS in an enclosed battery system. 5 [0042] FIG. 1 illustrates a battery 100 configured to have improved stability. The battery 100 may have a positive battery terminal 102 and a negative battery terminal 104. The battery 100 may include a battery management system 110 in electrical communication with multiple battery cells 120. The BMS 110 may have a printed circuit board 112 and one or more thermal components configured to 10 disperse heat from the BMS 110, such as the depicted MOSFETs 114A, 114B and metal plates 116A, 116B, 116C. A battery housing 130 may enclose the battery cells 120 and the BMS 110. A thermal epoxy layer 140 may be at least partially interposed between and contacting the metal plates 116A, 116B, 116C and the battery housing 130. As shown, the thermal resin layer 140 may substantially 15 cover an entire bottom surface of a cover of the battery housing 130, which may allow for sufficient dispersion of energy away from the metal plates 116A, 116B, 116C and the BMS 110. [0043] FIG. 2 illustrates a battery 200 also configured to have improved 20 stability with an alternative thermal epoxy arrangement compared to the battery 100 of FIG. 1, which shares many of the same components with the battery 200. For instance, the battery 200 also may include a positive battery terminal 202, a negative battery terminal 204, multiple battery cells 220, a battery housing 230, a thermal epoxy layer 240, and a BMS 210 having a printed circuit board 212, 25 multiple MOSFETS 214A, 214B, and metal plates 216A, 216B, 216C. However, unlike the thermal epoxy layer 140 in battery 100 of FIG. 1, the thermal epoxy 240 of the battery 200 may not extend in a lateral direction beyond the edges of the metal plates 216A, 216B, 216C of the BMS. Rather, the thermal epoxy 240 may be substantially restricted to the area of the metal plates 216A, 216B, 216C, 30 which may allow for adequate thermal transfer from the metal plates 216A, 216B, 216C without excess thermal resin being included. 12 [0044] FIG. 3 illustrates a battery 300 also configured to have improved stability with an alternative thermal epoxy arrangement compared to the batteries 100, 200 of FIGs. 1, 2, which share many of the same components with the battery 300. For instance, the battery 300 also may include a positive battery terminal 5 302, a negative battery terminal 304, multiple battery cells 320, a battery housing 330, a thermal epoxy layer 340, and a BMS 310 having a printed circuit board 312 and multiple MOSFETs 314A, 314B. However, unlike in prior depictions, the BMS 310 may not include metal plates, but may instead rely on heat transfer from the MOSFETs 314A, 314B to the thermal resin layer 340 through the PCB 312, 10 on the bottom side of which the MOSFETs 314A, 314B are positioned. Furthermore, as shown, the thermal epoxy layer 340 may extend in a lateral direction beyond the edges of the PCB 312, but may not take up an entire bottom surface of a cover of the battery housing 330. 15 [0045] FIG. 4 illustrates a battery 400 also configured to have improved stability with an alternative thermal epoxy arrangement compared to the battery 300 of FIG. 3, which shares many of the same components with the battery 400. For instance, the battery 400 also may include a positive battery terminal 402, a negative battery terminal 404, multiple battery cells 420, a battery housing 430, a 20 thermal epoxy layer 440, and a BMS 410 having a printed circuit board 412 and multiple MOSFETs 414A, 414B. However, unlike in prior depictions, the MOSFETs 414A, 414B and the PCB 412 may be in direct contact with the thermal resin layer 440. Because the thermal epoxy layer may have direct contact with the heat generating MOSFETs 414A, 414B, thermal energy may be more 25 easily transferred outside of the battery 400. [0046] The application of the thermal epoxy layers 140, 240, 340, 440 can be important to the performance and durability of the respective batteries 100, 200, 300, 400. Generally, the thermal epoxy layer may be constructed to avoid air gaps, 30 thereby providing direct contact between the BMS and the battery housing. As described, the thermal epoxy layer may cover the entire underside of the battery housing cover, may be placed only underneath the copper plates or PCB, or may 13 be limited to smaller areas where the most heat is generated. Rather than include polyepoxides, the thermal epoxy layer may be instead formed of urethane or another thermally conductive resin that has a viscosity that allows it to be poured into the area between the BMS and the battery housing in order to provide a 5 thermal conduction pathway. In order to provide sufficient heat transfer, the thermal epoxy may have a thermal conductivity of at least 0.8 W/mK, at least 1 W/mK, or more specifically about 1.2 W/mK. [0047] In order to provide improved structural stability and prevent movement 10 during shock and vibration, it has been recognized that the use of a rigid epoxy may prevent damage to the BMS system when the battery is subjected to exterior forces. In this manner, the introduction of a rigid thermal epoxy provides both structural stability and thermal stability to the battery system. Specifically, a rigid thermal epoxy may be used that has a cured hardness of at least 70 Shore A, at 15 least 75 Shore A, at least 80 Shore A, or more specifically between 85 and 90 Shore A. Furthermore, the rigid thermal epoxy may have a tensile strength of at least 15 N/mm2 , at least 20 N/mm2 , or specifically about 23 15 N/mm2 . [0048] When the MOSFETs are embedded into a rigid thermal epoxy, it has 20 been recognized through experimentation that they may become damaged over time due to thermal cycling. The MOSFETs, metal plates, and thermal epoxy may all have different coefficients of thermal expansion, which can cause stresses on the MOSFETs and crack their leads. As a result, when a rigid thermal epoxy is used, it may specifically be arranged so as to contact only the metal plates of the 25 BMS, but not the MOSFETS themselves. Conversely, a soft thermal epoxy may be specifically used in constructions where the thermal epoxy layer contacts the MOSFETs in order to avoid damage to the BMS, and the thermal epoxy layer may even substantially cover the entire BMS. A soft thermal epoxy may be a thermal epoxy that has a cured hardness of less than 60 Shore A, less than 50 Shore A, or 30 more specifically less than 40 Shore A. In this manner, depending on the properties of the epoxy used, the heat generating components (e.g. MOSFETs) of 14 the BMS may be mounted facing downward away from the thermal epoxy, or they may be mounted facing upward into the thermal epoxy. [0049] FIGs. 5A-5B illustrates a battery housing cover arrangement 500 and 5 select components of a BMS 510 in contact with a thermal epoxy layer 540. The battery housing cover arrangement 500 is similar to the arrangements in the batteries 100-400 of FIGs. 1-4, which share many of the same components. For instance, the battery housing cover arrangement 500 may include positive battery terminals 502, negative battery terminals 504, a battery housing cover body 530, 10 which may or may not be configured to be easily removed, and a thermal epoxy layer 540. The BMS 510 may include multiple MOSFETs 514 (two groupings of eight MOSFETs) and multiple metal plates 516A, 516B, 516C, 516D. As shown, the thermal resin layer 540 may contact a large portion of the battery housing cover 530 and be in direct contact with all four metal plates 516A, 516B, 516C, 15 516D, but not in contact with the MOSFETs 514. In this manner, the thermal epoxy layer 540 may not be in contact with the electrical components configured to generate heat, which are the MOSFETs 514 in this depiction. Generally, the MOSFETs 514 may generate heat from electrical current passing through them, which is first transferred to the series of metal plates 516A, 516B, 516C, 516D, 20 then to the thermal resin layer 540 through the metal plates 516A, 516B, 516C, 516D, and then finally to the battery housing cover 530. [0050] FIG. 6 depicts a method 600 of manufacturing a battery configured to have improved stability, consistent with the battery arrangements depicted in 25 FIGs. 1-5B. At 602, a battery management system in electrical communication with a plurality of battery cells may be provided. The BMS may have one or more thermal components configured to disperse heat from the BMS. At 604, a battery housing may be arranged to enclose the battery cells and the BMS. At 606, a thermal epoxy may be applied between the BMS and the battery housing. The 30 thermal epoxy may contact the one or more thermal components and the battery housing. 15 Battery Stability Cage [0051] In order to improve the mechanical stability of battery pack within an enclosed battery system, a battery stability cage is provided herein. An example configuration of the battery stability cage is depicted in FIGs. 7A-7E. The stability 5 cage may include features and may be positioned between a battery housing and a battery pack in such a manner that external forces on the exterior of the battery are less likely to damage the battery cells of the battery pack. [0052] As shown in the partial exploded view of various components 700 of a 10 battery of FIG. 7A, as well as in FIGs. 7B-7D, a battery stability cage 710 may partially enclose an interior area for a battery pack containing a plurality of battery cells, which may be connected to a positive battery terminal 702 and a negative battery terminal 704. The stability cage 710 may be positioned between the area for the battery cells and the battery housing, including the battery housing body 15 720 and a battery housing cover 722. [0053] As shown, the battery stability cage 710 may be polymer frame having four sidewalls positioned in a rectangular form with a variety of specific structural features that allow the battery stability cage 710 to protect the battery cells and 20 connect to the other components of the battery. For instance, as shown, each sidewall of the battery stability cage 710 may include a plurality of apertures 716 forming a mesh pattern, which provides adequate structural stability without adding excess material and weight to the battery. The apertures 716 may specifically include hexagonal shaped apertures, or alternatively include 25 comparable structurally cutouts. The polymer frame may include a plurality of horizontal supports 712 positioned along each corner of the polymer frame. As shown, the horizontal supports 712 may at least partially protrude outward from the surface of at least one of the sidewalls immediately adjacent to the corner. 30 [0054] The battery stability cage 710 may also include one or more cover attachment mechanisms 714 configured to connect the stability cage to the battery housing cover 722. In embodiments, the cover attachment mechanisms 714 may 16 connect with the battery housing cover 722 using a tongue and groove configuration. In order to secure the battery stability cage 710 to the housing body 720, body attachment mechanisms 715 may be included near the bottom of the stability cage, as shown. In embodiments, the body attachment mechanisms 5 715 may connect with the housing body 720 using a tongue and groove configuration. In order to further secure the battery stability cage 710 in place, an adhesive may be further applied to the attachment mechanisms 714, 715 in order to secure their connection to the respective housing components. Furthermore, additional adhesive or mechanical attachment forms may be provided along the 10 sides of the battery stability cage 710 in order to further ensure a solid connection to the housing body 720. [0055] FIG. 7B illustrates a partial cutaway view of the battery housing and the battery stability cage 710 of FIG. 7A, along with an associated battery 15 management system 730 and thermal epoxy layer 740. Battery Pack Construction 5 [0057] Because battery packs are formed of multiple battery cells, the specific arrangement and connections between battery cells is important for preventing battery failures resulting from external forces. In particular, when a battery pack is formed of stacked pouch-type battery cells, it has been recognized through experimentation that movement (e.g. sliding due to vibration) or inconstant forces 10 on the battery pouches can lead to failure. Accordingly, the present disclosure provides a battery pack construction and method of forming the same that has improved structural integrity. In particular, the battery pack construction may restrain the battery cells and prevent movement by providing even pressure across the surfaces of the battery pack. Additionally, spacers with adhesive components 15 may further help to limit the movement of the battery cells. [0058] FIG. 8 depicts a wrapped battery pack construction 800 with three sets of spacers 802 positioned in left, center, and right columns, the spacers 802 are generally included to separate the battery cells 810 and promote thermal 20 dissipation. The battery pack construction 800 also includes two adhesive tape sections 804 located between the columns of spacers 802 and configured to secure the battery cells 810 together in a rigid construction. It has been recognized through experimentation that the battery pack 800, with the inconsistent forces provided by the battery cells spacers 802 and the adhesive tape sections 804, can 25 produce movement and deformation of the cells during vibration, which can eventually cause internal damage and rupturing of the cells. Specifically, if has been recognized through experimentation that the battery cells 810 remain together along the adhesive tape sections 804, but can become deformed in between the tape sections 804 where the spacers 802 are located. Accordingly, the 30 present disclosure addresses these drawbacks by providing a battery pack 18 construction that produces more consistent forces during vibration and prevents internal movement of battery cells. patents.title: INVESTIGATION OF OPTICAL AND ELECTROCHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF DY3+ DOPED LITHIUM BORO-PHOSPHATE GLASS FOR LED AND SUPERCAPACITOR APPLICATIONS

inventors.name: VINOTHKUMAR PANJANATHAN
inventors.address: Assistant Professor,Department of Physics,Saveetha Engineering College,Saveetha Nagar, Thandalam, Chennai-602105, TamilNadu·, India.

patents.abstract: Dy3+-doped B,O,-P,Os-Ta,Os-Li,CO,-Al,O,-NaF-Dy,O, (BPTLAND) glass was synthesized using the melt-quenching method. The amorphous nature of the Dy'+-doped BPTLAND glass was confirmed through powder X-ray diffraction analysis. The chemical composition and surface morphology were examined using energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy confirmed the presence of borate and phosphate functional groups. '!'he optical properties of the glass were investigated using absorption spectroscopy, revealing a refractive index of 1.4 at 2 eV. The optical band gap was determined to be an indirect band gap, with an estimated value of 2.80 eV, derived from the tangent intercept on the x-axis. Photoluminescence analysis indicated prominent emission peaks at a wavelength of 573 nm. The CIE chromaticity coordinates (x = 0.3647, y = 0.4762) suggested daylight-like emission, with a correlated color temperature (CCT) of 4823 K. The ferromagnetic properties of the synthesized glass were confirmed through vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), which evaluated the hysteresis loop to determine retentivity and coercivity. Electrochemical properties were assessed through galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and cyclic voltammetry (CV) in a 5 M KOH electrolyte. The Dy'+-doped BPTLAND glass electrode exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 258.12 F g-• after 2000 cycles, as detem1ined by GCD analysis. The material demonstrated redox behavior, with an increase in anodic-cathodic peak separation and peak intensity as the scan rate increased, suggesting quasi-reversible charge storage behavior. The CV curves exhibited a near-rectangular shape, confirming the ideal double-layer capacitance characteristics of the Dy'+-doped BPTLAND glass. Charge transfer resistance was measured at 34.53 n cm2, while ohmic resistance was determined to be 14.21 n em'. The electrode exhibited stable cycling performance, with consistent CV curves maintained even after 5000 cycles, indicating excellent structural and electrochemical stability. These findings contirm that Dy'+-doped lithium borophosphate (BPTLAND) glass holds significant potential for application as an electrode material in LEOs and supercapacitors.
patents.complete_specification: DESCRIPTION 4.1 BACKGROUND OF INVENTION The advancement of energy storage and lighting technologies has led to extensive research into novel materials with superior optical and electrochemical properties. Among the various materials explored, rare-earth-doped glass systems have gained significant attention due to their remarkable luminescence characteristics and enhanced electrical conductivity. These materials offer promising applications in optoelectronic devices and energy storage systems such as light-emitting diodes (LEOs) and supercapacitors. In this context, the development of dysprosium (Dy'+)-doped lithium borophosphate (BPTLAND) glass presents an innovative approach to enhancing the performance of these devices. Borophosphate-based glasses have attracted considerable research interest due to their excellent chemical durability, thermal stability, and high transparency. The incorporation of lithium carbonate (Li,CO,), tantalum pentoxide (Ta,Os), aluminum oxide (AhO,), and sodium fluoride (NaF) into the glass matrix significantly influences its structural and functional properties. The inclusion of Dy'' ions further modifies the optical and electrochemical behavior, making the glass suitable for multifunctional applications. The unique characteristics ofDy>+doped BPTLAND glass result from the interaction between rare-earth ions and the borophosphate network, which governs its light emission and charge storage capabilities. lighting. Rare-earth-doped glasses exhibit sharp emission lines due to their 4f-4f electronic transitions, which are minimally affected by the host lattice. The luminescence of Dy'+ ions produces strong emissions in the visible spectrum, particularly in the yellow region, making the material suitable for LED applications. The measured chromaticity coordinates suggest that the emitted light closely resembles daylight, making it ideal for indoor lighting applications. Furthermore, the high refractive index and optical band gap contribute to efficient light transmission and absorption, enhancing the overall performance of the glass as an optical material.-Q) C) Ill D.. In addition to optical applications, Dy'+-doped BPTLAND glass exhibits promising electrochemical properties for use in supercapacitors. The increasing demand for highperformance energy storage devices necessitates the development of materials with superior charge storage capabilities, fast charge-discharge cycles, and long-term stability. Electrochemical investigations of Dy>+-doped glass reveal excellent capacitive behavior with high specific capacitance, making it a potential candidate for energy storage applications. The glass matrix provides a stable framework for redox-active Dy>+ ions, facilitating charge transfer and ion diffusion. The near-rectangular cyclic voltammetry (CV) profiles confirm the presence of ideal double-layer capacitance behavior, while galvanostatic· charge-discharge (GCD) analysis demonstrates _consistent cycling performance, even after thousands of cycles. The stability and efficiency of energy storage devices are critical for their widespread implementation in portable electronics, renewable energy systems, and electric vehicles. The low charge transfer resistance and excellent cycling stability of Dy>+-doped BPTLAND glass make it a viable electrode material for next-generation supercapacitors. Furthermore, the quasireversible redox behavior observed in electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis indicates that the material can efficiently store and release charge, ensuring prolonged operational performance. The glass structure also provides superior mechanical strength and c.:hemical resilience, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of electrodes during repeated charge-discharge cycles. The versatility of DyH-doped lithium borophosphMe glass arises from its unique combination of optical and electrochemical properties. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A System for Fabricating a Cost-Effective Lithium Oxide (Li₂O) Photodetector and Method thereof The present invention relates to a system and method for fabricating a cost-effective lithium oxide (Li₂O) photodetector using nebulizer spray pyrolysis. Conventional photodetector fabrication methods are expensive and energy-intensive, limiting their commercial scalability. This invention overcomes these limitations by employing a nebulizer-assisted spray pyrolysis technique, which enables uniform thin-film deposition with enhanced optical and electrical properties. The system comprises a Li₂O-based photodetector with a high responsivity, detectivity, and external quantum efficiency. The method involves preparing a lithium-based precursor solution, atomizing it into fine aerosols, directing the aerosolized solution onto a heated substrate, and initiating a chemical reaction to form a uniform Li₂O thin film. This approach reduces material waste, minimizes production costs, and supports large-scale manufacturing. The resulting photodetector finds applications in medical diagnostics, environmental sensing, optical communication, and defense systems, making it a viable and sustainable alternative to existing photodetection technologies.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of optoelectronic engineering, particularly to the development of an affordable and novel lithium oxide (Li2O) photodetector for commercial applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Optoelectronic devices, including light-emitting diodes (LEDs), photovoltaic cells, and photodetectors, have become integral to modern technology, playing a crucial role in telecommunications, medical diagnostics, defense, automation, and renewable energy systems. The conventional state of the art in photodetectors predominantly relies on semiconductor materials such as silicon and compound semiconductors, which, although effective, often present significant cost and fabrication challenges. Traditional fabrication techniques, such as molecular beam epitaxy, sputtering, and chemical vapor deposition, are resource-intensive and expensive, thereby limiting widespread accessibility, particularly in cost-sensitive applications. Despite advancements in photodetector technologies, existing models still face several shortcomings. Many currently available photodetectors suffer from high production costs, limited scalability, and energy-intensive manufacturing processes. Additionally, the performance parameters, such as external quantum efficiency, detectivity, and responsivity, vary significantly based on material limitations. These constraints hinder the feasibility of deploying photodetectors in broader applications, including budget-constrained industries and emerging markets. The present invention overcomes these limitations by disclosing a cost-effective and environmentally friendly Li2O photodetector fabricated using a low-cost nebulizer spray pyrolysis technique. This method ensures the uniform deposition of thin films, enhancing film consistency and improving optical and electrical properties. The novel fabrication technique enables large-scale production, making it commercially viable and reducing material waste compared to conventional methods. The Li2O photodetector developed through this approach demonstrates superior responsivity, detectivity, and external quantum efficiency, thereby outperforming conventional materials. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION The primary object of the present invention is to provide an affordable and efficient Li2O-based photodetector for optoelectronic applications. Another object of the present invention is to introduce a low-cost fabrication technique that ensures high uniformity in film deposition while maintaining superior optical and electrical properties. Yet another object of the present invention is to enhance photodetector performance parameters, including responsivity, detectivity, and quantum efficiency, through optimized material composition and deposition techniques. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION To overcome the shortcomings of the prior arts and to meet the objects of the instant invention it is disclosed herein a system for fabricating a lithium oxide (Li₂O) photodetector, comprising: a nebulizer spray pyrolysis unit configured to convert a lithium-based precursor solution into fine aerosol droplets; a precursor solution reservoir containing a lithium-based compound dissolved in a solvent; a spray nozzle operatively connected to the nebulizer for directing the aerosolized precursor solution toward a substrate; a heated substrate holder configured to maintain the substrate at a controlled temperature for thin-film formation; a deposition chamber housing the nebulizer spray pyrolysis unit and the substrate to facilitate controlled deposition; a temperature control unit configured to regulate the temperature of the substrate to ensure uniform film formation; an exhaust system configured to remove gaseous byproducts during the deposition process; and a photodetector system comprising a lithium oxide (Li₂O) thin film deposited on the substrate, wherein the Li₂O thin film exhibits enhanced responsivity, detectivity, and external quantum efficiency by optimizing the nebulizer spray pyrolysis parameters, ensuring uniform film deposition, minimizing material waste. The lithium oxide thin film is deposited with optimized process parameters to achieve high uniformity and electrical performance. The photodetector exhibits a rapid response and recovery time suitable for high-speed optoelectronic applications. It is also disclosed herein a method for fabricating a lithium oxide (Li₂O) photodetector, comprising the steps of: preparing a lithium-based precursor solution by dissolving a lithium compound in a suitable solvent to achieve a predefined concentration; atomizing the precursor solution using a nebulizer spray system to generate fine aerosol droplets; directing the aerosolized solution onto a heated substrate using a controlled spray nozzle to initiate thin-film deposition; maintaining the substrate at an optimized temperature to facilitate a chemical reaction, resulting in the formation of a uniform lithium oxide (Li₂O) thin film; evaporating residual byproducts during deposition to obtain a high-purity Li₂O film; and annealing the deposited thin film at a predetermined temperature to enhance its optical and electrical properties, wherein the nebulizer spray pyrolysis technique provides a cost-effective, scalable, and energy-efficient deposition process that ensures improved film uniformity, minimizes material wastage, and enables large-area fabrication for commercial applications. The deposition process parameters, including temperature and precursor concentration, are optimized to achieve high responsivity and detectivity. The fabricated photodetector is integrated into commercial optoelectronic applications. The lithium oxide photodetector is incorporated into a system for real-time light detection and measurement. The nebulizer spray pyrolysis technique allows deposition on flexible substrates, enabling potential applications in wearable optoelectronics. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE FIGURES Figure 1(a): Depicts schematic representation of Li2O photo detector using Nebulizer spray pyrolysis technique Figure 1(b): Depicts schematic representation of Li2O photo detector sensing mechanism using Keithley source meter Figure 2(a): Depicts prototype model of the sensor with sample Figure 2(b): Depicts experimental prototype module of Li2O photo detector system DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to a system and method for fabricating a cost-effective lithium oxide (Li₂O) photodetector using nebulizer spray pyrolysis. The instant invention provides a novel approach to optoelectronic photodetector fabrication by employing an efficient, low-cost deposition method that ensures superior optical and electrical properties while reducing manufacturing expenses. The system of the present invention comprises a Li2O-based photodetector fabricated using the nebulizer spray pyrolysis technique. This technique involves atomizing a precursor solution into fine aerosols, which are then directed onto a heated substrate to form a thin film of lithium oxide. The deposition process ensures uniform film formation, leading to improved optoelectronic properties. The photodetector system integrates a sensing mechanism where incident photons generate electron-hole pairs within the Li2O thin film, leading to a measurable photocurrent. This system is characterized by high sensitivity and rapid response times, making it suitable for commercial applications. The process of fabricating the Li2O photodetector involves preparing a precursor solution containing lithium-based compounds, which is then nebulized into fine droplets. These droplets undergo a chemical reaction upon reaching the heated substrate, resulting in the formation of a Li2O thin film. The byproducts of this reaction evaporate into the atmosphere, leaving behind a highly pure and uniform film. The resulting photodetector is tested for its electrical and optical characteristics, demonstrating significantly improved detectivity, responsivity, and external quantum efficiency compared to existing models. The system of the present invention comprises the following key components: Lithium Oxide (Li₂O) Photodetector: The core of the system is a Li₂O-based thin-film photodetector that exhibits enhanced optical absorption and charge carrier mobility. Nebulizer Spray Pyrolysis Deposition System: This deposition mechanism consists of: Nebulizer: Converts the precursor solution into fine aerosol droplets. Heated Substrate: Provides a surface for the thin-film formation. Spray Nozzle: Ensures controlled and uniform deposition of the aerosolized precursor solution. Photodetector Sensing Mechanism: The system includes an optoelectronic circuit that enables real-time light detection by measuring the photocurrent generated in response to incident photons. Power and Measurement Unit: A Keithley source meter or equivalent device is integrated to measure responsivity, detectivity, and other key parameters. Mechanism and Working Principle The Li₂O photodetector operates on the principle of photoconductivity, where incident light excites electrons, leading to the generation of electron-hole pairs. The increased charge carrier density enhances conductivity, resulting in a measurable photocurrent. The following steps illustrate the operation of the photodetector: Photon Absorption: Incident photons strike the Li₂O thin film, exciting electrons from the valence band to the conduction band. Charge Carrier Generation: Electron-hole pairs are generated, increasing the free carrier density. Charge Transport and Detection: The generated carriers move under an applied bias, creating a photocurrent, which is measured to determine the intensity and wavelength of the incident light. Method of Fabrication The method for fabricating the Li₂O photodetector using nebulizer spray pyrolysis involves the following steps: Preparation of the Precursor Solution A lithium-based precursor, such as lithium nitrate (LiNO₃) or lithium acetate (LiCH₃COO), is dissolved in a suitable solvent. The solution concentration and pH are carefully controlled to ensure optimized film deposition. Atomization of Precursor Solution The precursor solution is fed into a nebulizer, which converts it into fine aerosol droplets. The aerosolized solution is directed towards the heated substrate using a controlled airflow. Deposition on Heated Substrate The substrate (such as glass, silicon, or flexible polymer) is heated to a pre-determined temperature. The fine aerosol droplets undergo a chemical reaction upon contact with the heated surface, leading to the formation of a uniform lithium oxide thin film. Evaporation of Byproducts Unwanted byproducts from the reaction evaporate into the atmosphere, ensuring a high-purity Li₂O film. Annealing and Post-Processing The deposited thin film is subjected to annealing at an optimized temperature to enhance its crystallinity and improve optoelectronic properties. Characterization and Testing The fabricated photodetector is tested for electrical and optical performance, including responsivity, detectivity, and external quantum efficiency. The best mode of performing the invention involves optimizing key process parameters: Substrate Temperature: Maintaining an optimal temperature range (e.g., 250°C – 400°C) ensures uniform film formation. Precursor Concentration: The molar concentration of lithium-based compounds is controlled to achieve desired film thickness. Spray Rate and Nozzle Pressure: Adjusting the aerosol spray rate enhances uniform deposition. Annealing Conditions: Post-deposition annealing improves crystallinity and enhances electrical properties. The optimal combination of these factors ensures that the Li₂O photodetector exhibits high responsivity, fast response time, and superior detectivity, making it suitable for real-world applications. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT This invention provides a lithium-ion battery (100) with an anode (101) on a copper foil (101a) and a cathode (102) on an aluminum foil (102a). The battery employs water-based and organic-based slurries, each containing amorphous and graphitic carbon. A separator (103) is placed between the electrodes, while an electrolyte (104) supports lithium-ion transport. By integrating ball milling, tip sonication, and centrifugation, carbon dispersion is optimized in both electrodes, enhancing conductivity and cycle life. The battery (100) can reach 90% capacity in about 15 minutes at a 4C charge rate and retain over 80% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles, even at elevated temperatures. This approach yields low internal resistance and stable operation over many cycles, addressing demanding battery requirements and reducing thermal hotspots for high-power applications such as electric vehicles and grid storage. patents.complete_specification: Description:DESCRIPTION Technical Field of the invention The present invention relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage devices, specifically to lithium-ion batteries. More particularly, the invention pertains to a modified electrode slurry solution for enhancing the fast-charging capabilities and improving the cycle life of lithium-ion batteries. Background of the invention Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become the dominant energy storage technology for countless applications, including electric vehicles (EVs), portable electronics, and stationary power systems. Their relatively high energy density, good power delivery, and acceptable cycle life have driven widespread adoption over competing chemistries such as lead-acid and nickel-metal hydride. However, despite these advantages, lithium-ion batteries still present obstacles that limit their broad applicability and commercial viability. One of the most pressing problems is the need for faster charging capabilities to reduce downtime. Consumers and industries alike require battery packs that can be recharged within minutes, rather than hours, to approximate the convenience of refilling gasoline or diesel. This demand is especially evident in the electric vehicle market, where fast charging can address range anxiety and reduce the requirement for extensive charging infrastructure. Yet, accelerating charge times introduces multiple technical challenges—chief among them is the accelerated degradation of battery cells over repeated quick-charge cycles. Historically, lithium-ion battery development has centered on improving energy density, cycle life, and safety. While significant progress has been made, the mainstream adoption of electric vehicles and expansion of grid-level energy storage now highlight the urgent need for faster and more reliable charging. Conventional lithium-ion batteries typically take several hours to fully charge when using standard charge rates (e.g., 0.5C to 1C). Although specialized high-power lithium-ion cells can accept higher rates (2C or more), these cells often incur thermal management issues and capacity fade. Thus, any gains in charging speed can be undercut by safety risks and the fundamental limits imposed by the electrode materials’ capability to handle high current. Moreover, most rapid-charging solutions rely on robust external cooling systems, which add weight, cost, and complexity. This mismatch between consumer expectations for refueling (minutes for gasoline vehicles) and real-world charging times for lithium-ion systems continues to pose a major barrier to EV adoption. Over the past few decades, a variety of prior-art solutions have attempted to mitigate these challenges. One avenue has been the use of advanced electrode materials, such as lithium titanate (LTO) anodes, which exhibit excellent rate capabilities and minimal lithium plating. However, LTO-based cells often suffer from lower energy density and higher cost, limiting their appeal for mainstream automotive applications. Another line of research has focused on specialized binders, conductive additives, or coatings to improve the electronic and ionic conductivity within electrodes. For instance, some prior art proposes incorporating high-load carbon black or carbon nanotubes to enhance conductivity and reduce polarization under fast-charge conditions. Yet, these additions can create processing difficulties, such as agglomeration in slurry preparations, which can compromise electrode uniformity. Other solutions in the prior art emphasize electrode architecture—using thinner electrodes, for example, to shorten ion diffusion pathways. Thinner electrodes can indeed facilitate faster charging, but at the expense of the battery’s overall energy density, because more current collector material becomes necessary relative to the active material. In addition, manufacturing extremely thin electrodes on a large scale raises production costs, complicates calendaring (mechanical compression of electrodes for optimal porosity), and increases handling challenges. Similarly, some researchers have experimented with three-dimensional or “structured” electrodes, incorporating porous metal foams or hierarchical designs. While potentially effective, these methods can be difficult and expensive to implement at commercial scale. An alternative strategy in prior art revolves around modifying the electrolyte composition to improve ionic conductivity or reduce lithium plating at high charge rates. Additives such as fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) or vinylene carbonate (VC) are sometimes introduced to stabilize the solid-electrolyte interface (SEI), enabling better cycle life under stressful charging. However, these additives do not fully address conductivity limitations in the active material layers or at the electrode-electrolyte boundary. Similarly, some designs include higher salt concentrations or use ionic liquid electrolytes. While these can raise conductivity and reduce flammability, they often present new challenges, such as increased viscosity, cost, or complicated manufacturing requirements. Because temperature is also a significant factor during rapid charging, many prior-art approaches introduce active thermal management systems. These solutions may involve liquid cooling plates, forced air, or phase-change materials integrated into a battery pack. Although such systems help mitigate the heat generated by high current flow, they increase complexity, cost, weight, and volume. They also do not intrinsically improve the intrinsic charge acceptance of the electrode materials themselves. As a result, even with robust cooling, the electrodes can degrade if they are not structurally optimized. High current densities accelerate side reactions, degrade the SEI, and lead to morphological changes that reduce usable capacity over time. Despite all these incremental improvements, a recurring bottleneck is often found at the electrode level—specifically, how the conductive additives and active materials are dispersed within the electrode slurry before coating onto the current collector. Traditional electrode slurry preparation typically involves mixing solid, powder-based conductive additives (e.g., carbon black) with binders, solvents (e.g., NMP for cathodes or water-based systems for certain anodes), and active material powders. If the carbon particles are not well-dispersed, the resulting electrode may have regions of high resistance, poor adhesion, or heterogeneous porosity. Non-uniform or agglomerated carbon clusters can likewise reduce ionic pathways, generate local hot spots under fast charging, and accelerate capacity fade. This shortcoming becomes even more pronounced under higher C-rates, where uniform current distribution is critical for battery health and longevity. Additionally, many prior arts do not systematically account for the differences between anode and cathode slurry requirements. Anodes, especially graphite-based anodes, are often produced in aqueous slurries using water-soluble binders (like carboxymethyl cellulose), while cathodes—containing layered oxide active materials such as NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt)—commonly rely on organic solvents like N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). Prior references frequently treat these two electrode preparations as separate processes without considering how a carefully optimized synergy between them might address the overarching goal of fast charging. Consequently, attempts to unify the entire cell assembly strategy—matching an anode’s fast-charge capability with a cathode that can also accept large currents without significant polarization—remain insufficient. The disadvantages of existing approaches are manifold. High carbon-loading electrodes or complicated electrode architectures can be prohibitively expensive and difficult to mass-produce, hindering large-scale commercialization. Specialized materials, like lithium titanate for anodes, help with charging speed but reduce overall energy density and raise costs. Innovative high-temperature or high-salt electrolytes introduce safety concerns or manufacturing complexity. Even when modest improvements are made in charging speed, cycle life can be severely compromised, particularly if the electrode surfaces or microstructures are not robust under the strain of large-scale lithium intercalation. In real-world use cases—like EVs that need to charge frequently and quickly—these disadvantages limit the practicality of prior-art designs. Another vital consideration is environmental and safety regulation. Some prior-art solutions rely on volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or toxic solvents, complicating manufacturing and introducing health hazards. Although some attempt to shift to entirely aqueous systems, the mismatch between water-based anode processes and typical organic-based cathode slurries poses a barrier to consistent, large-scale production lines. Meanwhile, demands for greener manufacturing methods, such as lowering the use of NMP, are becoming more pronounced due to stricter regulations in many countries. Therefore, while many partial solutions exist, a truly comprehensive approach—covering high-rate capability, safety, reliability, simpler manufacturing, and good environmental compliance—remains elusive. Given this context, there is a dire need for innovative yet practical solutions that bridge the gap between incremental improvements in lab-scale fast-charging batteries and a commercially viable product ready for electric vehicles and other high-demand applications. The limitations in conventional electrode slurry techniques persist: carbon particles that either remain agglomerated or fail to disperse uniformly lead to underwhelming performance gains. At high charge rates, any electrode non-uniformity can result in localized heating, lithium plating, or microstructural damage. Simultaneously, there must be a balance between power density (how quickly the battery can be charged or discharged) and energy density (how much total capacity is available). Strictly focusing on fast charging often means using thicker conductive networks or sacrificing energy density; focusing solely on high energy density can hinder charging speeds. It is in view of these hurdles that the present inventors recognized the necessity of a comprehensive electrode design paradigm—one that specifically addresses the challenges associated with dispersing conductive carbon in both the anode and cathode slurries without resorting to overly complex or costly materials. By combining amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon in carefully controlled ratios, a new level of conductive network homogeneity can be achieved, thereby improving electron and ion transport simultaneously. These improvements are further enhanced by deliberate process steps, like ball milling, tip sonication at high amplitude, and subsequent centrifugation, all tailored to eliminate particle aggregates. The practical result is an electrode layer free from large clusters of carbon, which can otherwise create local sites of voltage drop or elevated temperature during high current flow. In addition to addressing dispersion challenges, the inventors aimed to enhance the thermal stability of lithium-ion batteries under fast-charging conditions. Extended cycling at elevated temperatures can accelerate side reactions and degrade the battery’s useful life, a problem that is amplified when recharging occurs rapidly. The synergy of combining an aqueous anode slurry with an organic-based cathode slurry, each of which has been specially formulated to incorporate a mixture of amorphous and graphitic carbon, yields surprising robustness at temperatures such as 40–45°C. The simplified yet high-performance approach avoids requiring purely exotic electrolyte formulations or thick, specialized electrode coatings. By focusing on a universal solution—refining the electrode slurry and the carbon distribution—this invention demonstrates that it is possible to reduce standard charging times from multiple hours to as little as 15 minutes for 90% state of charge. Moreover, the design can maintain capacity retention figures above 80% even after thousands of cycles in real-world operational temperatures. Crucially, none of the prior-art references known to the inventors fully teach or suggest the meticulous interplay of water-based and organic-solvent-based processing, combined with a distinctive blend of amorphous and graphitic carbon, followed by intensive dispersion and cleaning procedures. While older patents and publications have outlined partial solutions, such as using conductive carbon in electrode formulations or employing ultrasonic agitation, they generally do not converge on an integrated approach that ensures uniform carbon dispersion in both the anode and cathode slurries, each optimized for high-rate capability. Nor do they adequately resolve the mounting concern about thermal stability under fast-charge conditions without resorting to external cooling systems. The present invention seeks to fill this gap, offering a balanced improvement of charge speed, cycle longevity, and manufacturing feasibility. Therefore, there remains a pressing demand for an electrode slurry solution that seamlessly incorporates advanced carbon dispersions in both an anode and a cathode. Such a solution must be scalable for large-volume production, ensure the safety and reliability demanded by automotive and consumer electronics markets, and deliver uniform performance characteristics across thousands of cycles and high C-rates. Addressing this need would propel electric vehicles toward more rapid public acceptance, alleviating concerns related to range anxiety, long charging sessions, and shortened battery lifespans. Similarly, industries reliant on lithium-ion packs—ranging from drones to portable power tools—could benefit from systems that recharge in minutes and maintain consistent output over extended operational periods. The social and economic impact of such a leap forward in lithium-ion battery technology cannot be overstated. Recognizing these interlinked problems—degradation under fast charging, non-uniform electrode architecture, limitations of prior-art materials and processes, and the difficulty in balancing cost and performance—the inventors have devised a novel electrode slurry solution. This new approach is predicated on mixing a precisely formulated blend of amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon in separate dispersions: one for the anode (water-based) and one for the cathode (organic-based). By carefully selecting dispersants, employing high-amplitude tip sonication, and performing centrifugation, the inventors ensure a level of uniformity that was not previously achieved. This uniformity directly impacts the battery’s electrical conductivity and mitigates local current hotspots. Additionally, the design accounts for real-world usage scenarios, allowing the cells to tolerate repeated fast-charge cycles without dramatic losses in capacity or heightened safety risks. In an exemplary embodiment of the present invention, a lithium-ion battery is constructed using two specially formulated electrode slurries: one for the anode electrode and another for the cathode electrode. The invention focuses on achieving rapid charging, improved cycle life, and high thermal stability through a unique combination of amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon in both electrodes. Unlike conventional cells where solid conductive additives can clump and create uneven current flow, this invention employs specific dispersants, sonication parameters, and centrifugation steps to achieve a uniform carbon network. As a result, the battery can be charged at a rate of at least 4C, thereby reaching around 90% of its rated capacity in roughly 15 minutes, while also sustaining more than 80% capacity retention after extended cycling. The anode electrode in this exemplary embodiment is prepared from a water-based slurry. To begin, deionized water is mixed with one or more water-soluble dispersants—such as polyacrylic acid (PAA), carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), or sodium alginate—in a concentration sufficient to keep carbon particles uniformly dispersed (typically 0.1–5 wt% relative to the slurry). Next, a mixture of amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon is added. The ratio of these carbons can vary according to performance requirements, but in a preferred embodiment the weight ratio ranges from about 1:1 to 1:4 (amorphous to graphitic). This blend leverages the high conductivity of graphitic carbon while retaining amorphous carbon’s disordered structure, which can enhance ion transport. The slurry then undergoes high-amplitude tip sonication, typically at 20–30 kHz, to break up any remaining agglomerates. Afterwards, a centrifugation step (e.g., 2,000–5,000 rpm for 5–15 minutes) removes larger particulates, leading to a stable dispersion with an average particle size optimized for efficient electrode coating. Once the anode slurry is thoroughly mixed and cleaned of large agglomerates, it is coated onto a copper foil current collector via standard manufacturing methods such as doctor blade coating or slot-die coating. The wet coating is then dried under controlled temperature conditions—commonly at 60–80°C in a convection oven—until all residual water or volatile components have evaporated. In certain embodiments, the anode is further calendered to reach a target thickness and porosity, thus balancing mechanical integrity with ion transport pathways. The resulting anode electrode possesses a uniform distribution of amorphous and graphitic carbon, which lowers both ohmic and polarization resistances during high-rate charge and discharge cycles. Similarly, the cathode electrode employs an organic-based slurry formulated to improve conductivity and minimize degradation at high temperatures. In one preferred embodiment, a solvent such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), ethanol, or glycol is first combined with an organic dispersant to form a homogeneous solution. A similar mixture of amorphous and graphitic carbon is added, typically in a ratio of about 1:2 to 1:6, depending on the target capacity and structural integrity. This mixture is subjected to ball milling to reduce the particle size and then tip sonication to disperse the particles thoroughly. Centrifugation may again be employed to filter out any large clusters that could compromise electrode uniformity. By adopting this two-step dispersion process—ball milling followed by sonication—the cathode slurry attains a fine and stable consistency. Subsequent to slurry preparation, the cathode mixture is coated onto an aluminum foil current collector, again using a method such as doctor blade coating. Temperature-controlled drying removes organic solvents, ensuring that a solid cathode film remains on the aluminum substrate. Calendering can be performed to fine-tune the electrode’s thickness and porosity. In exemplary embodiments, the cathode coating thickness ranges from about 50 to 100 micrometers, striking an optimal balance between capacity density and high-rate capability. This electrode architecture synergizes with the anode’s design by offering similarly uniform dispersion of conductive carbon. As a result, the lithium-ion battery can handle high current flows on both electrodes without localized hotspots or accelerated degradation. The two electrodes— anode and cathode— are assembled with a separator sandwiched between them. In many embodiments, this separator is a microporous polymer film made of polyolefin materials (e.g., polyethylene or polypropylene) that can withstand the mechanical and thermal stresses of repeated fast charging. An appropriate electrolyte is introduced into the cell, typically lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF₆) dissolved in a mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC), with optional additives like fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) to stabilize the interface. After electrolyte filling, the cell is sealed, forming the complete lithium-ion battery. The synergy between a water-based anode slurry and an organic-based cathode slurry addresses not only performance but also certain environmental and production concerns, as it reduces reliance on any single class of solvents. Testing indicates that, under a charging rate of 4C, the battery can reach 90% state of charge within about 15 minutes, while retaining at least 80% of its original capacity after 1,000 or more cycles. Higher or lower C-rates may be used as desired, but the cohesive carbon network in both electrodes stands out under demanding conditions. Moreover, experiments suggest that the invention maintains robust performance at temperatures of 40–45°C, a crucial advantage for electric vehicles and outdoor power systems. This improved thermal stability stems from the well-dispersed carbon, which discourages localized thermal build-ups and stabilizes internal resistance. Consequently, the battery requires less external cooling than many commercially available fast-charging cells, minimizing overall system weight and cost. In certain exemplary embodiments, the amorphous carbon fraction is fine-tuned to enhance specific properties such as rate capability or cycle life, whereas adjusting graphitic carbon content may further improve overall conductivity and mechanical integrity. The tip sonication and centrifugation steps are particularly beneficial, as they lead to substantially uniform dispersion of carbon particles, thereby reducing the probability of localized current density peaks. Such localized peaks often accelerate electrode degradation, especially during high C-rate charging. By centering on the fundamental issue of electrode slurry preparation and ensuring that both the anode and cathode undergo carefully orchestrated dispersion steps, the invention addresses a root cause of uneven battery aging. The final product is a lithium-ion cell with extended life, faster charging, and reliable performance across a broad temperature range.
