Method of Manufacturing In one exemplary manufacturing process, the anode electrode (101) is prepared by first dissolving or dispersing a water-soluble binder and dispersant (e.g., polyacrylic acid, carboxymethyl cellulose, or sodium alginate) in deionized water at a controlled concentration. A carefully selected mixture of amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon is gradually introduced into this aqueous solution, after which the slurry undergoes high-amplitude tip sonication. Subsequently, the mixture is centrifuged to eliminate large carbon agglomerates, resulting in a uniform, stable dispersion. The homogenized slurry is then coated onto a copper foil current collector (101a) via standard methods such as doctor blade coating or slot-die coating. After thorough drying at moderate temperatures (e.g., 60–80°C), the anode electrode (101) is calendered to achieve a desired thickness and porosity conducive to high-rate capability. The cathode electrode (102) is produced using a similar approach but in an organic-solvent medium. An organic binder/dispersant (e.g., N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, ethanol, glycol, or a mixture thereof) is first stirred to form a homogeneous solution. A blend of amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon is then added, followed by ball milling to reduce particle size. After milling, tip sonication is applied to break up any residual clumps, and a centrifugation step ensures removal of large particles or settled debris. The refined cathode slurry is coated onto an aluminum foil current collector (102a) and dried at appropriate temperatures (often 80–100°C) to eliminate residual solvent. The dried cathode electrode (102) is thereafter subjected to calendaring for uniform thickness. Both electrodes are stacked or wound around a separator (103), typically a microporous polymer film, and an electrolyte (104) such as LiPF₆ in a mixture of carbonate solvents is then infused. Finally, the battery (100) is sealed in its chosen cell format (e.g., pouch or cylindrical) and undergoes initial formation cycles to stabilize the solid-electrolyte interface on the electrodes. Method of Use/Operation In operation, the lithium-ion battery (100) is placed in a device or application (e.g., an electric vehicle, consumer electronics, or energy storage system) where it provides DC power during discharge. During the discharge phase, lithium ions move from the anode (101) through the separator (103) and into the cathode (102), driving electrons through an external circuit to power a load. The user or system controller typically monitors key parameters such as voltage, current, and cell temperature to ensure safe operation. Because the electrode formulation is optimized for uniform carbon dispersion, the battery (100) can sustain moderate to high discharge rates without significant polarization or localized heating issues. To recharge, a DC power source or specialized fast-charging station applies a controlled voltage and current. The lithium ions migrate back to the anode (101), embedding themselves in the carbon matrix. The innovative slurry compositions, which incorporate both amorphous and graphitic carbon, enable high C-rate charging—often up to 4C or more—thereby reducing recharge times to as little as 15 minutes for 90% state of charge. Various battery management systems can be integrated to regulate parameters such as charge current, cut-off voltage, or temperature thresholds, ensuring the battery safely achieves rapid charging while minimizing capacity fade and heat generation. Enhanced Features and Benefits A core benefit of this invention lies in its fast-charging capability, which allows the battery (100) to substantially reduce conventional recharge times (e.g., from multiple hours down to 15 minutes for most of the rated capacity). This feature particularly appeals to users of electric vehicles and portable devices, where downtime must be minimized. Additionally, by carefully balancing amorphous and graphitic carbon in both the anode (101) and cathode (102), the electrodes maintain low internal resistance, reducing localized temperature spikes under high current flow. Another notable advantage is improved cycle life. Traditional lithium-ion cells exposed to repeated fast charging may suffer early capacity loss due to uneven lithium plating or severe electrode degradation. By contrast, the optimized electrode slurry described here ensures uniform ion and electron pathways, preventing excessive stress on any single region of the electrode. As a result, the battery (100) sustains a high capacity retention above 80% even after 1,000 or more cycles at elevated temperatures. This enhanced reliability translates into longer warranties, reduced maintenance, and higher consumer confidence, all while minimizing the need for complex external cooling systems. A method of manufacturing the lithium-ion battery (100) according to claim 1, the method comprising: preparing an anode slurry by mixing deionized water, a water-soluble dispersant, and a carbon mixture comprising amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon, subjecting the mixture to high-amplitude tip sonication, and then centrifuging to remove agglomerates; coating the anode slurry onto a copper foil current collector (101a) to form an anode electrode (101), followed by drying and calendaring; preparing a cathode slurry by mixing an organic solvent, an organic dispersant, and a carbon mixture comprising amorphous carbon and graphitic carbon, ball milling the mixture, and then performing tip sonication to achieve a stable dispersion; coating the cathode slurry onto an aluminum foil current collector (102a) to form a cathode electrode (102), followed by drying and calendaring; assembling the battery cell by stacking or winding the anode electrode (101), the separator (103), and the cathode electrode (102); and introducing the lithium-ion conducting electrolyte (104) into the assembled cell and sealing the cell enclosure, whereby the resultant lithium-ion battery (100) attains at least 90% of its rated capacity within about 15 minutes of charging and maintains a high capacity retention over extended cycling.

patents.abstract: Title: Hybrid Cell Balancing-Based Thermal Management System for Lithium-Ion Battery Packs in Electric Vehicles, System and Method Thereof The present invention provides a smart hybrid thermal management and cell balancing system for lithium-ion battery packs, particularly designed for application in electric vehicles (EVs). The system integrates a dual-layer balancing approach comprising passive balancing at the individual cell level and active balancing at the module level. Passive balancing is achieved using resistive elements of approximately 10 ohms, which safely dissipate small voltage differences across cells, maintaining voltage uniformity and minimizing thermal stress. At the module level, active balancing is performed through galvanically isolated bidirectional DC-DC converters that facilitate high-current energy transfer between modules with uneven load distribution. This isolation prevents fault propagation and ensures system-wide electrical safety. The system continuously monitors voltage, current, and temperature using Hall effect sensors embedded within microcontroller-based Cell Monitoring Units (CMUs), which communicate with a central Battery Management System (BMS) to dynamically manage balancing operations. Additionally, a temperature-activated fire suppression mechanism is integrated into or adjacent to the battery pack; it is automatically triggered by the BMS when abnormal thermal thresholds are detected, preventing thermal runaway and ensuring rider safety. The invention eliminates the need for complex mechanical cooling systems, improves energy efficiency, reduces current leakage, and enables uniform cell aging and degradation. This intelligent hybrid design offers a cost-effective, scalable, and fault-tolerant solution for enhancing the thermal stability, safety, and lifecycle performance of high-density lithium-ion battery systems in electric mobility platforms.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE DISCLOSURE [0001] The present invention relates to the field of electric vehicle (EV) battery systems and, more specifically, to thermal management in lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery packs. The invention provides a hybrid cell balancing system integrating passive cell-level and active 5 module-level balancing to prevent thermal runaway, enhance battery life, and improve safety and efficiency. BACKGROUND [0002] Lithium-ion batteries have become the dominant energy source for electric vehicles (EVs) due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and efficiency. However, their 10 safety remains a major concern, particularly under high-stress conditions such as high-rate discharging (>5C), overcharging, and mechanical abuse. EV battery packs contain hundreds to thousands of interconnected cells, making them vulnerable to thermal runaway—a hazardous phenomenon that can result in fire or explosion. [0003] Traditional thermal management approaches involve mechanical systems such 15 as liquid cooling and heat sinks. While effective to some extent, these methods add considerable cost, complexity, and weight. Similarly, conventional balancing strategies are either purely passive—dissipating excess energy through resistors—or purely active—transferring charge using non-isolated DC-DC converters. Passive methods are inefficient and unsuitable for large-scale or dynamic balancing, while non-isolated active approaches pose 20 safety risks due to the potential for fault propagation through shared ground paths. [0004] There remains a need for a safe, cost-effective, and scalable thermal management system that can dynamically balance energy across the battery pack while preventing thermal failures. SUMMARY 25 [0005] The present invention provides a smart hybrid thermal management and cell balancing system for lithium-ion battery packs, specifically designed for electric vehicles. The system integrates dual-level balancing: passive balancing at the cell level and active balancing at the module level. Passive balancing is achieved using fine-grained resistive elements (approximately 10 ohms) that allow safe dissipation of excess energy from overcharged cells, 30 enabling voltage equalization and reducing thermal stress. At the module level, high-current balancing is conducted through galvanically isolated bidirectional DC-DC converters, allowing 3 efficient energy redistribution between modules while preventing cross-module fault propagation due to electrical isolation. [0006] To enhance reliability and responsiveness, the system incorporates real-time voltage, current, and temperature monitoring using Hall effect sensors embedded in microcontroller-based Cell Monitoring Units (CMUs). These CMUs communicate with a 5 central Battery Management System (BMS), which dynamically triggers the appropriate balancing mechanism based on sensor data. Furthermore, the system includes a built-in fire suppression mechanism integrated with the battery pack. A temperature sensor monitors critical thresholds, and upon detecting unsafe heat levels, the BMS activates a canister to release suppressant, ensuring thermal safety. This hybrid approach eliminates the need for 10 mechanical cooling systems, enhances battery lifespan, and delivers a fault-tolerant, cost-effective solution for next-generation electric vehicle power systems. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0007] The above and still further features and advantages of aspects of the present disclosure become apparent upon consideration of the following detailed description of aspects thereof, especially when taken in conjunction with the accompanying drawings, and wherein: 15 [0008] Figure 1 displays a flowchart of the hybrid cell balancing-based thermal management process in lithium-ion battery packs for electric vehicles, outlining fault detection, sensor feedback, and activation of passive and active balancing. [0009] Figure 2 shows a system block diagram illustrating the hybrid balancing architecture, including passive cell-level and active module-level balancing integrated with 20 Hall effect sensors, temperature sensing, and smart BMS control. [00010] Figure 3 illustrates the modular cell balancing approach for thermal management in battery packs, depicting the integration of cell groups, resistive elements, and DC-DC converters for uniform balancing. [00011] Figure 4 presents experimental waveforms for Case 1 (VC1 > VC2 and VC3), 25 where 4(a) shows VGS1, IL1(A), VDS1, and VDS2, and 4(b) shows VGS1, IC1(A), and IC2(A). [00012] Figure 5 shows experimental results of voltage equalization under various test conditions, where 5(a) illustrates module balancing for Case 1 (VM1 > VM2), 5(b) shows Case 2 (VM2 > VM1), 5(c) to 5(h) illustrate six different cell balancing cases, and 5(i) summarizes 30 module and cell balancing performance. [00013] Figure 6 illustrates cell voltage versus balancing time for fifteen series-connected cells, where 6(a) shows results with cell balancing and 6(b) shows results without 4 cell balancing. [00014] Figure 7 shows module voltage versus balancing time for a battery pack consisting of five modules, each formed by three series-connected cells, where 7(a) presents results with module balancing and 7(b) without module balancing. [00015] Figure 8 presents voltage behaviour of fifteen series-connected cells under 5 various operating conditions, where 8(a) shows charging, 8(b) shows discharging, 8(c) shows static conditions, and 8(d) shows module balancing performance. [00016] Figure 9 illustrates dynamic charge-discharge behaviour of the battery pack over time, where 9(a) shows cell voltage without any balancing, 9(b) shows results with cell-level balancing only, and 9(c) shows results with both cell and module-level balancing. 10 DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS [00017] The following description provides specific details of certain aspects of the disclosure illustrated in the drawings to provide a thorough understanding of those aspects. It should be recognized, however, that the present disclosure can be reflected in additional aspects and the disclosure may be practiced without some of the details in the following description. 15 [00018] The various aspects including the example aspects are now described more fully with reference to the accompanying drawings, in which the various aspects of the disclosure are shown. The disclosure may, however, be embodied in different forms and should not be construed as limited to the aspects set forth herein. Rather, these aspects are provided so that this disclosure is thorough and complete, and fully conveys the scope of the disclosure to those 20 skilled in the art. In the drawings, the sizes of components may be exaggerated for clarity. [00019] Spatially relative terms, such as “top,” “bottom,” and the like, may be used herein for ease of description to describe one element or feature's relationship to another element(s) or feature(s) as illustrated in the figures. It is to be understood that the spatially relative terms are intended to encompass different orientations of the structure in use or 25 operation in addition to the orientation depicted in the figures. [00020] Modification of example aspects as illustrated herein is done with specificity that aims at meeting the legal requirements that the law demands. The expositional part, which deals with the invention, is not, however, designed to be a limitation of the patent's applicability. Quite to the contrary, the inventor/inventors have taken into consideration the 30 argument that the present subject matter can be also realized in other different forms, i.e. other kinds of lovely features, besides those described in this document, along with other technologies. [00021] The present invention relates to a thermal management and cell balancing 5 system for lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery packs (201) used in electric vehicles (EVs), particularly designed for two-wheeler and four-wheeler EV applications. The proposed system addresses the persistent issue of thermal runaway by introducing a smart hybrid cell balancing approach that integrates passive cell-level balancing and active module-level balancing. Thermal runaway, which has become a major concern in high-energy-density Li-ion batteries, often 5 results from electrical, mechanical, or heat abuse. These abuse conditions—such as overcharging, internal short circuits, and high environmental temperatures—can lead to uncontrolled temperature rise, exothermic reactions, gas generation, and ultimately fire or explosion. The invention aims to prevent such incidents through intelligent charge equalization, thermal regulation, and real-time anomaly detection, thereby enhancing both 10 operational safety and battery life. [00022] The battery pack structure is modularized and consists of fifteen lithium-ion cells of type 18650. Each cell has a nominal voltage of 3.6 volts, a minimum threshold of 2.7 volts, and a maximum capacity of 4.2 volts. These cells are organized into five modules, with each module comprising three series-connected cells, and the system is adaptable to both series 15 and parallel configurations depending on the application. In one tested configuration (101), initial voltage values across the fifteen cells before balancing were measured as follows: 3.8 V, 3.5 V, 3.59 V, 3.55 V, 3.6 V, 3.79 V, 3.7 V, 3.68 V, 3.62 V, 3.741 V, 3.695 V, 3.78 V, 3.62 V, 3.645 V, and 3.65 V, respectively. These values reflect inherent voltage deviations due to differences in internal resistance, self-discharge rates, and aging effects. If left uncorrected, 20 such imbalances can lead to uneven current flow, localized heating, increased self-discharge, and premature cell degradation, ultimately affecting battery life and performance. [00023] To address such imbalance, each individual cell is equipped with a passive balancing circuit that includes a resistor of approximately 10 ohms. This circuit allows excess energy in higher-voltage cells to be safely dissipated as heat, thereby reducing voltage 25 disparities among cells. Passive balancing is particularly suitable for low-current equalization tasks, operating in the background to maintain consistent voltages without imposing significant thermal stress. For example, if one cell registers 3.7 V while another shows 3.6 V, the higher-voltage cell discharges a small current through the resistor (202) until both cells reach a common voltage. This strategy minimizes leakage current, prevents internal short circuits, and 30 promotes uniform coulombic efficiency across the battery pack. However, passive balancing alone is insufficient for larger imbalances that arise during high-rate charging or discharging (e.g., >5C), where significant current differentials can generate heat and stress specific cells disproportionately. 6 [00024] To handle such high-energy imbalances, an active balancing circuit is implemented at the module level. Each module is connected to an isolated bidirectional DC-DC converter capable of safely transferring energy between modules without a shared electrical ground. Unlike non-isolated balancing systems that rely on a common ground, increasing the risk of cascading failures, the proposed galvanically isolated topology ensures that faults in one 5 module do not propagate across the entire battery pack. This feature significantly improves fault tolerance and system reliability. During operation, if one module is discharging at a high current (e.g., 25 A) while another is underloaded, the active balancing controller redistributes energy from the heavily loaded module to the underutilized one. This mechanism reduces thermal buildup in specific areas, balances the energy load across modules, and enhances 10 overall efficiency without the need for mechanical cooling systems. [00025] Monitoring and control (102) of the hybrid balancing process are handled by microcontroller-based Cell Monitoring Units (CMUs). Each CMU integrates Hall effect sensors for precise current detection, as well as voltage and temperature sensors to monitor the real-time health of each cell and module. The CMUs communicate with a centralized or 15 distributed Battery Management System (BMS), which dynamically adapts balancing strategies based on real-time charge and discharge conditions. Under normal operation, the BMS prioritizes passive balancing, activating active balancing only when voltage or current thresholds exceed predefined limits. Additionally, the BMS plays a critical safety role by interpreting temperature data and initiating emergency responses when abnormal heating 20 patterns are detected. By continuously tracking self-discharge rates, inrush currents, and voltage drift, the system prevents premature capacity loss and enhances battery longevity. [00026] A key safety feature of the invention is the inclusion of a fire suppression mechanism within or near the battery pack. A canister filled with a suitable extinguishing agent is connected via a passage tube to the interior of the battery housing. When a thermal sensor 25 embedded in the pack detects a temperature rise beyond the critical threshold, it signals the BMS to open a valve on the canister, releasing the suppressant into the pack and suppressing potential combustion. This automated fire suppression system adds another layer of protection and is especially critical in compact two-wheeler EV platforms where space constraints often preclude complex cooling systems (105). 30 [00027] The system was experimentally validated using the fifteen-cell prototype. During the balancing process, the voltages of all fifteen cells converged to approximately 3.66 V within 1080 seconds, demonstrating the effectiveness of the hybrid approach in equalizing cell voltages rapidly and uniformly. Various tests were conducted to analyze the thermal and 7 electrical behaviour of the system under different operational conditions. Data plots illustrate the relationship between state-of-charge (SOC) and temperature during charging, discharging, and during balanced operation. These test confirms that the temperature of the battery pack remains within safe limits throughout all operational modes, even during balancing, which is traditionally associated with heat generation. 5 [00028] Additional evaluations were conducted to compare voltage behaviour under both balanced and unbalanced scenarios. When hybrid balancing was applied, voltage deviation was quickly corrected, and self-balancing behaviour was observed as voltages naturally converged. In contrast, when balancing was not applied, significant voltage deviations persisted, leading to increased risk of thermal instability and uneven cell 10 degradation. The presence of fewer temperature variations between adjacent cells indicated that the hybrid balancing system promotes uniform degradation and improves battery longevity. [00029] Unlike conventional battery packs that rely on mechanical cooling systems or unidirectional balancing methods, the proposed system achieves cost-effective, software-15 controlled, and fault-tolerant energy management using purely electronic methods. The modular architecture not only facilitates thermal uniformity but also allows nearby cells to operate under similar thermal and electrical conditions, further reducing stress-induced failures. The isolated DC-DC topology, in particular, ensures safe energy transfer and galvanic protection across modules, which is a critical improvement over non-isolated active balancing 20 systems known to propagate failures. [00030] In conclusion, the hybrid balancing approach disclosed in this invention successfully manages both minor and major energy imbalances through passive and active balancing layers, respectively. It maintains uniform self-discharge rates, prevents voltage drift, minimizes the effects of entropy-driven temperature elevation, and mitigates internal short 25 circuits. By avoiding mechanical cooling, incorporating real-time thermal response, and enabling uniform degradation across the pack, the invention ensures safe, efficient, and cost-effective battery operation for EV platforms. [00031] Figure 1 displays the hybrid cell balancing-based thermal management system for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles. 30 [00032] The process begins with the initialization of the battery pack (101), where lithium-ion cells are configured in series or parallel and organized into functional modules. This modular structure provides the foundation for hierarchical energy management, allowing both localized cell-level balancing and inter-module energy coordination. 8 [00033] Next, the smart Battery Management System (BMS) continuously monitors key parameters across the battery system (102). This includes the voltage, current, and temperature of each cell and module, using data collected from Hall effect current sensors (206) and embedded temperature sensors (206). The BMS evaluates this data in real time to identify any developing faults or imbalances. 5 [00034] A decision point follows where the system determines whether a voltage, current, or thermal imbalance or fault condition has been detected (103). If no issues are identified, the monitoring loop continues uninterrupted. However, if an anomaly is detected, the system proceeds to corrective action through a balancing operation. [00035] Once an imbalance is confirmed, the hybrid balancing mechanism is activated 10 (104). At the cell level, passive balancing is carried out using resistors (202) of approximately 10 ohms to safely dissipate excess charge from overcharged cells. At the module level, active balancing is performed through isolated DC-DC converters (204) that redistribute energy across modules without compromising electrical isolation. [00036] Finally, a temperature feedback mechanism ensures thermal safety of the 15 battery pack (105). The BMS monitors thermal signals during and after the balancing operation. If the temperature crosses a critical threshold, a suppression system is triggered—such as a canister-based cooling or extinguishing mechanism—to prevent thermal runaway and ensure overall system stability. [00037] Figure 2 illustrates the system block diagram of the proposed hybrid thermal 20 management and cell balancing architecture for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles. [00038] The lithium-ion battery pack (201) comprises multiple rechargeable cells connected in series and/or parallel and grouped into modules. These cells serve as the primary source of energy storage and are subject to voltage and current imbalances during charging, discharging, and load variation, necessitating real-time monitoring and correction. 25 [00039] The resistors (202) are employed for passive balancing at the cell level. When a cell voltage exceeds a predetermined threshold, these resistive paths allow controlled dissipation of excess charge as heat, helping to equalize voltage across the cells within a module. This approach provides a low-complexity means of trimming voltage differences under moderate current levels. 30 [00040] The cell-level passive balancing unit (203) manages these resistors based on input from the sensors. It selectively routes current through resistive paths to balance cell voltages, thereby preventing overcharging of individual cells and reducing the likelihood of cell degradation and thermal hotspots. 9 [00041] The isolated DC-DC converter (204) enables active balancing at the module level. It transfers charge between modules that exhibit voltage imbalances, ensuring efficient energy distribution across the battery pack. The galvanic isolation of this converter prevents fault propagation between modules and enhances safety during high-current operation. [00042] The module-level active balancing unit (205) controls the energy redistribution 5 among modules using the isolated DC-DC converters. It plays a key role in maintaining system-level voltage uniformity, reducing stress on cells, and prolonging the operational lifespan of the battery pack, especially under heavy load or repeated cycling conditions. [00043] The sensors and control unit (206) oversees the entire system. It receives input from Hall effect sensors, temperature sensors, and voltage sensing circuits, enabling it to detect 10 imbalances, thermal events, or faults. Based on this data, the control unit triggers either passive or active balancing operations as needed, ensuring safe and efficient energy management. Additionally, if the system detects critical thermal thresholds, it activates a temperature feedback mechanism that triggers a canister-based cooling or fire suppression unit integrated within the battery pack, providing an added layer of safety against thermal runaway. 15 [00044] Figure 3 illustrates the modular cell balancing approach proposed for thermal management in lithium-ion battery packs used in electric vehicles. In this configuration, the cells within the battery pack are connected either in series or parallel to form modules. Each module is monitored by a dedicated battery monitoring integrated circuit (IC), which tracks cell voltages, currents, and potential imbalance conditions. The architecture incorporates both 20 passive and active balancing layers. At the cell level, conventional passive balancing is implemented using resistors that dissipate excess energy in overcharged cells. At the module level, active balancing is achieved through isolated DC-DC converters, which enable energy transfer between modules while maintaining electrical isolation. [00045] The schematic shows that the battery monitoring ICs interact with the BMS 25 controller, which processes data from current sensors and initiates balancing actions based on real-time conditions. In parallel-connected modules, inrush currents and voltage mismatches can result in internal short circuits or thermal runaway. The system prevents these failures through early detection and coordinated balancing. Isolated DC-DC converters allow controlled transfer of energy between high-voltage (HV) and low-voltage (LV) buses, and also 30 facilitate energy redistribution between modules, preventing hotspots or localized overcharging. [00046] Furthermore, the modular balancing configuration addresses uneven degradation in large battery packs—a common cause of performance decline. By organizing 10 physically adjacent cells into modules, and managing them uniformly, the design ensures reduced temperature variance and more consistent aging across the pack. This approach not only minimizes thermal stress but also extends the overall life of the battery system. Each module operates with both passive dissipations for fine-tuned voltage trimming and active redistribution for high-energy balance, resulting in a robust, fault-tolerant, and thermally stable 5 system optimized for electric mobility. [00047] Figure 4(a) presents the experimental waveforms for Case 1, where the voltage of Cell 1 (VC1) is greater than that of Cell 2 (VC2) and Cell 3 (VC3). The captured signals include VGS1 (gate-source voltage), IL1(A) (inductor current), and the drain-source voltages VDS1 and VDS2. These waveforms illustrate the switching behaviour of the balancing circuit 10 when a voltage imbalance is detected. VGS1 initiates the switching operation, causing IL1 to ramp up as energy is transferred through the inductor. VDS1 and VDS2 show complementary switching cycles, verifying the controlled redirection of current through the energy path. This real-time switching response confirms the system’s ability to detect and address voltage disparities using the designed active balancing architecture. 15 [00048] Figure 4(b) shows the current distribution behaviour during the same Case 1 condition. It includes the waveform of VGS1 along with IC1(A) and IC2(A), which represent the charging currents flowing toward the lower-voltage cells. The synchronized pulsing of these currents in response to the gate signal indicates precise control of energy transfer from the overcharged cell to the undercharged ones. This validates that the balancing mechanism 20 effectively redistributes charge across the cells, thereby reducing voltage differentials and supporting the thermal management objective of the system under dynamic operating conditions. [00049] Figure 5(a) illustrates module voltage behaviour for Case 1, where Module M1 initially has a higher voltage than Module M2 (VM1 > VM2). The X-axis represents time in 25 seconds, and the Y-axis represents module voltage in volts (V). Over time, the system detects this imbalance and activates module-level active balancing using isolated DC-DC converters. The energy from M1 is redistributed to M2, reducing the voltage difference (ΔV) and stabilizing both modules to a uniform voltage level. This confirms the system’s capability to correct asymmetry in energy distribution at the module level, a key contributor to thermal stress 30 in conventional packs. [00050] Figure 5(b) shows Case 2, where Module M2 has a higher voltage than Module M1 (VM2 > VM1). The X-axis represents time in seconds, and the Y-axis represents module voltage (V). The system effectively reverses the energy transfer using its bidirectional 11 capability, demonstrating symmetrical handling of voltage deviation. Once again, isolated active balancing ensures that the two modules converge toward a common voltage without risk of fault propagation between modules. [00051] Figure 5(c) presents Case 1 of cell-level balancing, where Cell C1 has a higher voltage than Cells C2 and C3 (VC1 > VC2 & VC3). The X-axis denotes time (sec), and the Y-5 axis represents cell voltage (V). Through passive balancing using resistors (~10 ohms), excess energy from C1 is dissipated safely until voltage uniformity is achieved across all three cells. This prevents localized overheating and eliminates thermal propagation due to voltage imbalance. [00052] Figure 5(d) depicts Case 2, where Cells C2 and C3 have higher voltages than 10 C1 (VC2 & VC3 > VC1). The graph confirms the passive balancing system’s ability to discharge multiple higher-voltage cells simultaneously until equilibrium is reached, preventing energy accumulation in specific cells that could otherwise cause thermal runaway. [00053] Figure 5(e) corresponds to Case 3, where Cells C1 and C2 have higher voltages than C3 (VC1 & VC2 > VC3). Here, the system selectively discharges C1 and C2 through the 15 resistive balancing path, again demonstrating efficient simultaneous multi-cell equalization that maintains cell health and pack reliability. [00054] Figure 5(f) shows Case 4, where Cell C3 has the highest voltage among the three (VC3 > VC1 & VC2). The balancing system isolates C3 for discharge while preserving the stability of the other cells, ensuring that no cell enters a dangerously overcharged state. 20 [00055] Figure 5(g) represents Case 5, where Cell C2 is higher than both C1 and C3 (VC2 > VC1 & VC3). The passive resistor across C2 gradually dissipates the excess voltage, and the cells achieve uniform potential, preventing internal current loops caused by voltage mismatch. [00056] Figure 5(h) presents Case 6, where Cells C1 and C3 are both higher than C2 25 (VC1 & VC3 > VC2). The balancing algorithm concurrently addresses C1 and C3, showing the system's distributed passive balancing capability. This kind of correction is vital in dynamic EV conditions, where uneven cell usage is common. [00057] Figure 5(i) provides a comprehensive view of both module-level and cell-level balancing under a hybrid balancing operation. The X-axis represents Time (sec), the left Y-30 axis represents Module Voltage (V), and the right Y-axis indicates Cell Voltage (V). The graph illustrates how the hybrid strategy—passive balancing at the cell level and active balancing at the module level—works together to reduce voltage deviation across both scales. This comprehensive balancing action prevents uneven aging, mitigates thermal gradients, and 12 enhances the overall safety and efficiency of the lithium-ion battery pack. [00058] Figure 6(a) illustrates the behaviour of fifteen series-connected lithium-ion cells under the influence of the proposed cell-level passive balancing mechanism. The X-axis represents Time (sec), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). Initially, each cell has a distinct voltage ranging between approximately 3.5 V and 3.8 V, due to manufacturing 5 inconsistencies and varying internal resistances. As balancing begins, the system utilizes 10-ohm resistive elements to safely dissipate excess energy from higher-voltage cells. Over time—within approximately 1080 seconds—all cell voltages converge to a uniform level near 3.66 V, demonstrating the effectiveness of the passive balancing strategy in minimizing cell-to-cell voltage deviation. This convergence ensures that no individual cell overcharges or 10 undercharges, reducing the likelihood of thermal runaway and improving overall pack reliability. [00059] Figure 6(b) presents the same cell configuration and initial voltage disparity, but with no balancing mechanism applied. The X-axis again represents Time (sec), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). Unlike in Figure 6(a), the voltage differences between cells 15 persist throughout the 1250-second observation period. Some cells continue to diverge from the average trend, indicating that, without passive balancing, the system allows imbalance to grow. This sustained mismatch can lead to inefficient operation, premature aging, and a higher risk of localized overheating. The comparative results between 6(a) and 6(b) highlight the critical role of the proposed hybrid thermal management system, particularly the cell-level 20 passive balancing layer, in maintaining voltage uniformity and thermal stability across the pack. [00060] Figure 7(a) shows the relationship between module voltage and balancing time for a battery pack consisting of five modules, each formed by three series-connected lithium-ion cells. The X-axis represents Time (seconds), and the Y-axis represents Module Voltage 25 (V). In this case, active module-level balancing using galvanically isolated bidirectional DC-DC converters is enabled. Initially, the five modules exhibit noticeable voltage differences due to varying cell conditions and state-of-charge levels. As the balancing system activates, energy is transferred from higher-voltage modules to lower-voltage ones. Over a period of 600 seconds, the voltage levels across all modules converge toward a common value. This 30 demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed active balancing system in achieving uniform energy distribution across modules, which helps minimize thermal gradients and optimize overall battery pack performance. [00061] Figure 7(b) presents the module voltage profile over time for the same battery 13 configuration, but without any active balancing applied. The X-axis again represents Time (seconds), and the Y-axis represents Module Voltage (V). Without balancing, the voltage discrepancies between the five modules persist and fluctuate throughout the observed period. This divergence can lead to inefficient charge utilization, accelerated cell degradation, and potential safety risks during high-rate operations. The contrast between Figures 7(a) and 7(b) 5 highlights the critical role of active module-level balancing in maintaining system uniformity, preventing overcharge or under-discharge of specific modules, and ensuring safe, long-lasting battery operation in electric vehicle environments. [00062] Figure 8(a) presents the charging behaviour of fifteen series-connected lithium-ion cells over a 60-minute period. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis 10 represents Cell Voltage (V). The system initiates charging from a baseline of approximately 3.4–3.6 V. As current is injected, all cell voltages rise uniformly, approaching the cutoff voltage limit (CVL) of 4.2 V without any individual cell exceeding it. This behaviour confirms that the proposed hybrid thermal management system, through both monitoring and balancing, effectively maintains voltage symmetry across cells, preventing overvoltage risks and 15 contributing to safer energy intake and thermal regulation. [00063] Figure 8(b) illustrates the discharging behaviour of the same fifteen-cell configuration under load. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). Cell voltages decline uniformly over the course of 60 minutes, approaching but not breaching the deep voltage limit (DVL) set around 3.4 V. The even slope across all cell 20 voltage curves confirms controlled discharge coordination, demonstrating that the balancing mechanism prevents any single cell from under-voltage stress. This uniformity helps avoid energy inefficiencies and uneven degradation, both of which are critical concerns in large EV battery packs. [00064] Figure 8(c) shows the system’s performance under static (idle) conditions over 25 a 135-minute duration. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). The plot starts with a wide cell voltage spread of approximately 560 mV, which narrows to just 25 mV over time. This indicates that cell-level passive balancing continues to operate even during idle phases, equalizing residual charge levels and reducing long-term imbalance. The effectiveness of this function helps preserve battery health by ensuring all cells 30 settle near nominal values even when the vehicle or battery pack is not actively charging or discharging. [00065] Figure 8(d) demonstrates module-level active balancing performance across a battery pack composed of five modules, each consisting of three series-connected cells. The 14 X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Module Voltage (V). The system begins with a voltage disparity of approximately 500 mV between the highest and lowest modules. Over the course of 49 minutes, the active balancing system reduces this gap to 18 mV. This balancing action is achieved using galvanically isolated DC-DC converters that redistribute charge between modules. The outcome validates that module-level energy 5 asymmetry is effectively resolved, minimizing temperature differentials and enhancing safety during high-rate operations. [00066] Figure 9(a) illustrates the behaviour of fifteen lithium-ion cells under dynamic charging and discharging conditions without any balancing mechanism applied. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). The test spans four 10 operating phases—charging, discharging, charging, and discharging—over a total duration of 240 minutes. Without balancing, cell voltages begin to diverge significantly during the charging phases, with some approaching the cutoff voltage limit (CVL ≈ 4.0 V) while others remain below. During discharging, a similar mismatch is observed as some cells drop closer to the deep voltage limit (DVL ≈ 3.4 V). This voltage spread grows over repeated cycles, leading 15 to non-uniform aging, reduced usable capacity, and higher thermal risk—especially in high-current EV applications. [00067] Figure 9(b) presents the same dynamic charge-discharge scenario, but with cell-level passive balancing enabled. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). The balancing system uses resistive elements to dissipate excess 20 energy from higher-voltage cells during rest and charge phases. As a result, the voltage spread between cells is reduced compared to Figure 9(a). While minor voltage differences still persist, especially during transitions between charging and discharging, the performance is notably improved. This confirms that passive cell balancing alone helps maintain moderate voltage alignment, extending cell life and reducing imbalance-induced stress. 25 [00068] Figure 9(c) shows the cell voltage response during the same test, but with the full hybrid balancing strategy in effect—combining cell-level passive balancing and module-level active balancing. The X-axis represents Time (minutes), and the Y-axis represents Cell Voltage (V). Throughout the charging and discharging cycles, the cell voltages remain highly synchronized, maintaining consistent alignment close to the nominal range. The voltage 30 deviations are minimal and well-contained within safe margins. This demonstrates that the hybrid approach provides optimal balancing performance, effectively managing dynamic conditions, preventing overcharge or deep discharge of individual cells, and enhancing both safety and efficiency of the battery pack in real-time EV operation. 15 [00069] While various embodiments of the present disclosure have been described above, it should be understood that they have been presented by way of example only, and not limitation. Thus, the breadth and scope of the present disclosure should not be limited by any of the above-discussed embodiments but should be defined only in accordance with the following claims and their equivalents. , Claims:We claim: 1. A thermal management system for lithium-ion battery packs (201) comprising a passive cell-level balancing circuit including resistive elements across individual cells for voltage equalization; an active module-level balancing circuit comprising galvanically isolated bidirectional DC-DC converters (204) configured to transfer energy between modules; microcontroller-based Cell Monitoring Units (CMUs) equipped with Hall effect sensors (206) for real-time voltage, current, and temperature monitoring (102); a Battery Management System (BMS) communicatively coupled to the CMUs, configured to trigger passive or active balancing operations based on detected imbalances; and a thermally responsive fire suppression mechanism integrated into or adjacent to the battery pack, activated by the BMS upon detection of abnormal temperature rise (105). 2. The system for thermal Management of Li-ion battery pack claimed in claim 1, wherein each resistive element used in the passive balancing circuit has a resistance of approximately 10 ohms, configured to dissipate excess energy from overcharged cells in a safe and controlled manner. 3. The system for thermal Management of Li-ion battery pack claimed in claim 1, wherein the isolated DC-DC converters (104) are configured to maintain electrical isolation between modules and prevent fault propagation, while allowing bidirectional energy transfer to balance current distribution during high-rate discharging or charging events. 4. The system for thermal Management of Li-ion battery pack claimed in claim 1, wherein the fire suppression mechanism comprises a pressurized canister connected to a discharge passage inserted into the battery pack, wherein a thermally activated valve is triggered by temperature data from the CMUs relayed to the BMS. 5. A method for thermal management and voltage equalization in a lithium-ion battery pack, the method comprising detecting real-time voltage, current, and temperature conditions through Hall effect sensors embedded in CMUs (102); initiating passive balancing by discharging higher-voltage cells through resistors; and activating active module-level balancing using isolated DC-DC converters to redistribute energy between modules when imbalance thresholds are exceeded. 17 6. The method for thermal management and voltage equalization in a lithium-ion battery pack claimed in claim 5, wherein the passive balancing operation is triggered when the voltage difference between adjacent cells exceeds a threshold of 0.1 volts and active balancing is triggered when discharge current exceeds 25 amperes in any module. 7. The method for thermal management and voltage equalization in a lithium-ion battery pack claimed in claim 5, further comprising activating a fire suppression system when thermal data received by the BMS from the CMUs exceeds a predefined safety limit, wherein the suppression canister discharges suppressant into the battery pack through a connected tube (105). 8. An energy-optimized hybrid balancing system for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles, comprising a dual-mode balancing architecture configured to minimize energy loss by combining low-current passive balancing with high-current active balancing; a smart control algorithm that selectively engages the appropriate balancing mode based on real-time sensor input; and a modular design that ensures uniform degradation, thermal distribution, and improved operational efficiency of the overall battery system. 9. A method, system, and apparatus with one or more features as described in the Specifications and drawings

patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage, specifically disclosing eco-friendly, high-voltage, and thermally stable solid-state electrolytes. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to the impregnation of lithium salt of anacardic acid on a polymer matrix, wherein the anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL).
patents.complete_specification: DESC:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present disclosure relates to field of electrochemical energy storage. In particular, the present disclosure pertains to solid-state electrolytes for use in electrochemical devices including lithium-ion batteries. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to eco-friendly, high-voltage, and thermally stable solid-state electrolytes comprising a polymer matrix impregnated with lithium salt of anacardic acid, wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). The use of CNSL-derived anacardic acid enables the formulation of environmentally benign and sustainable electrolyte systems while maintaining or enhancing electrochemical performance, thermal stability, and safety characteristics. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The global transition toward renewable energy and sustainable technologies has intensified the demand for advanced energy storage systems. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and reliable performance, have become the cornerstone for powering consumer electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and stationary grid storage. However, conventional lithium-ion batteries rely on liquid electrolytes, which are often flammable, volatile, and prone to leakage, thereby posing safety hazards such as thermal runaway and battery fires. Furthermore, these liquid electrolytes exhibit limited electrochemical stability windows and are incompatible with lithium metal anodes, constraining the development of next-generation high-voltage and high-capacity battery chemistries. Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) have emerged as promising alternatives to liquid electrolytes, addressing many of the safety and performance limitations. SSEs offer intrinsic safety due to their non-flammable nature and provide mechanical rigidity that can potentially suppress lithium dendrite formation which is a key factor in prolonging battery life and preventing short-circuits. Despite these advantages, existing SSE technologies suffer from several inherent limitations that hinder their widespread commercial adoption. Polymer-based solid-state electrolytes, such as those comprising polyethylene oxide (PEO), are known to exhibit low ionic conductivity at ambient temperatures due to their semi-crystalline nature, which restricts ion transport. Additionally, such polymer systems often lack sufficient mechanical strength and thermal stability, thereby limiting their applicability in high-performance and high-voltage devices. On the other hand, inorganic or ceramic solid-state electrolytes, while offering relatively higher ionic conductivity, are associated with significant drawbacks including brittleness, poor interfacial contact with electrodes, and complex fabrication processes. These materials typically require high-temperature sintering and stringent processing conditions, which increase manufacturing cost and reduce scalability. Moreover, issues such as interfacial resistance and mechanical fragility further limit their practical implementation. In addition to the above, many conventional electrolyte systems rely on synthetic, petroleum-derived components that may pose environmental and toxicity concerns. The increasing demand for sustainable and environmentally benign energy storage technologies has therefore highlighted the need for electrolyte materials derived from renewable resources, without compromising electrochemical performance. Accordingly, there exists a need for solid-state electrolytes that simultaneously exhibit high ionic conductivity, improved thermal and mechanical stability, reduced toxicity, cost-effectiveness, and compatibility with scalable manufacturing processes. There is also a growing demand for such systems to incorporate sustainable, bio-derived materials to align with green chemistry principles and circular economy practices. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION This summary is intended to introduce, in simplified form, a selection of concepts that are further described in the detailed description. This summary is merely presented as a brief overview of the subject matter described and claimed herein and does not aid in determining the scope of the claimed subject matter. In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix; and • a lithium salt of anacardic acid; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix; • a lithium salt of anacardic acid, and • an ionic liquid; wherein anacardic acid employed for preparation of lithium salt of anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In another aspect, the present disclosure process for preparing solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving a polymer matrix in a solvent to obtain a polymer solution; b) adding a lithium salt of anacardic acid to the polymer solution of step a) to form an electrolyte composition; c) casting the electrolyte composition obtained in step b) onto a substrate to form a film; and d) drying the cast film of step c) to obtain a solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a process for preparing the solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving a polymer matrix in a solvent to form a polymer solution; b) adding an ionic liquid to the polymer solution of step a); c) adding a lithium salt of anacardic acid to the solution of step b) to form an electrolyte composition; d) casting the electrolyte composition onto a substrate to form a film; and e) drying the film of step d) to obtain a solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In yet another aspect, the present disclosure provides an electrochemical cell comprising an anode; a cathode; and a solid-state electrolyte disposed between the anode and cathode, wherein the solid-state electrolyte comprises a polymer matrix and lithium salt of anacardic acid, and optionally an ionic liquid wherein anacardic acid employed for preparation of lithium salt of anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES Figure 1 is a schematic representation of membrane preparation, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 2 illustrates the electrochemical performance of the LiAn10 electrolyte at room temperature (RT): (a) Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) Nyquist plot of LiAn10 at RT; (b) Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) of Li/LiAn10/SS at a scan rate of 1 mV s?¹; (c) Chronoamperometry (CA) response of the Li/LiAn10/Li cell at an applied potential of 10 mV at 25 °C, with the inset showing Nyquist plots before and after polarization; and (d) Voltage profile of a symmetric Li/LiAn10/Li cell exhibiting an overpotential of approximately 150 mV. Figure 3 illustrates the electrochemical performance of a Li/LiAn10/LiFePO4 cell: (a) charge–discharge profiles and (b) long-term cycling performance at a rate of 0.1 C, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 4 illustrates (a) EIS plots of SS/0LiAn/SS and SS/10LiAn/SS cell at 25 °C (b) LSV of Li/0LiAn/SS and Li/10LiAn/SS at a scan rate of 1 mV s–1, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 5 illustrates Galvanostatic lithium plating/stripping plots of Li/10LiAn/Li cells at a current density of (a) 0.1 mA cm–2 for 1600 h and (b) Galvanostatic lithium plating/stripping plot of Li/ 10LiAn/Li at different current densities (each cycle correspond to 1h plating and 1 h stripping), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Figure 6 illustrates Li/10LiAn/LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 cell performances: (a and b) charge-discharge curves and long-term cycle performance at 1 C, (c and d) charge-discharge curves at different C rate, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION An object of the present disclosure is to provide a sustainable, and high-performance solid-state electrolyte comprising lithium salt of anacardic acid derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL), which exhibits improved ionic conductivity, mechanical properties, and safety characteristics compared to conventional electrolyte systems. As used herein, the term “anacardic acid” refers to a class of naturally occurring phenolic compounds obtained from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL), which is a renewable byproduct of cashew nut processing and “ancardate” refers to the salt form of anacardic acid, wherein the acidic proton of the carboxyl group is replaced by a cation, such as lithium, sodium, or potassium.
