In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix; and • a lithium salt of anacardic acid; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In certain embodiments, the lithium salt of anacardic acid is dispersed within a polymer matrix to facilitate lithium-ion transport. In certain embodiments, the lithium salt of anacardic acid is lithium anacardate (LiAn). In certain embodiments, the polymer matrix functions as the structural framework, offering mechanical stability and flexibility, while also serving as a medium that supports the dispersion of the lithium salt. The polymer matrix maybe selected from a group comprising poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP), polyethylene oxide (PEO), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), blend of PEO/PVDF-HFP, blend of PVDF-HFP/PMMA, poly(acrylonitrile) (PAN), poly(ethylene carbonate) (PEC), poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), polycarbonate-based polymers, polyurethanes (PU), poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based polymers, and polyimides (PI) and the like or combinations thereof. In preferred embodiment, the polymer matrix is PVDF-HFP. In certain embodiments, the lithium salt of anacardic acid is present in an amount of 5 wt.% to 15 wt.%, or from 5 to 10 wt% with respect to the total weight of the solid state electrolyte including all intermediate values and sub-ranges therein. In certain preferred embodiments, the lithium salt is present at or about 10 wt.% with respect to the total weight of the solid state electrolyte. In a specific embodiment, the solid-state electrolyte comprises lithium anacardate incorporated within the polymer matrix in an amount ranging from about 5 wt.% to about 10 wt.% with respect to the total weight of the solid state electrolyte exhibiting enhanced ionic conductivity and improved interfacial performance, attributable to increased lithium-ion availability and more efficient ion transport pathways within the polymer matrix. At concentrations lower than 5 wt.%, the improvement in electrochemical performance is comparatively limited, while incorporation beyond about 10 wt.% is constrained due to solubility limitations, resulting in phase separation and formation of non-uniform electrolyte membranes. In certain embodiments, lithium anacardate is uniformly dispersed in the polymer matrix to create continuous pathways for lithium-ion migration. The aromatic structure of anacardic acid contributes chemical stability, while the lithium salt provides mobile lithium ions that dissociate and move through the polymer under an applied electric field. This arrangement ensures efficient ionic conductivity, reduces interfacial resistance, and enhances electrochemical performance. The immobilization of the salt within the polymer prevents crystallization, maintaining a favorable amorphous phase that supports ion mobility. CNSL is a renewable byproduct of cashew processing, and therefore is a sustainable and eco-friendly source. Compared to conventional lithium salts such as LiPF6, lithium anacardate provides improved dissociation and conductivity, while the solid-state nature of the electrolyte reduces risks of leakage and flammability associated with liquid electrolytes. In an embodiment, the solid state electrolyte of the preceding embodiment further comprises an ionic liquid. Accordingly, in an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix; • a lithium salt of anacardic acid, and • an ionic liquid; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In certain embodiments, the polymer matrix, the lithium salt of anacardic acid, and the respective quantities thereof are as defined in the preceding embodiments. In certain embodiment, the ionic liquid comprises one or more imidazolium-based ionic liquids. In further embodiments, the ionic liquid is selected from 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate [BMIM][BF4], 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate [EMIM][BF4], 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide [BMIM][TFSI], 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide [EMIM][TFSI], 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate [BMIM][PF6], or 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate [EMIM][PF6]. In certain embodiments, the ionic liquid is present in an amount ranging from about 30 wt.% to about 60 wt.% relative to the total weight of the solid state electrolyte, including all intermediate values and sub-ranges therein, such as from about 35 wt.% to about 55 wt.%, from about 40 wt.% to about 50 wt.%, or from about 45 wt.% to about 60 wt.%. In certain embodiments, the solid-state electrolyte comprises a polymer matrix, lithium salt of anacardic acid and an ionic liquid, wherein the ionic liquid is incorporated into the polymer matrix to enhance ionic conductivity and electrochemical performance. In a preferred embodiment, the ionic liquid is incorporated at about 50 wt.% relative to the polymer matrix, corresponding to an approximate about 1:1 weight ratio between the polymer matrix and the ionic liquid. In an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix; • 5 to 10 wt% of lithium salt of anacardic acid, and • 30 to 60 wt% of an ionic liquid; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL), and wt% is based on the total weight of the solid state electrolyte. In a specific embodiment, the ionic liquid comprises 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([BMIM][BF4]). The solid-state electrolyte membrane comprising the ionic liquid is configured to enhance ionic conductivity and to provide compatibility with high-voltage cathode materials, including LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4. In a further specific embodiment, the present disclosure provides a solid-state electrolyte comprising: • a polymer matrix comprising PVDF-HFP; • 5 to 10 wt% of lithium salt of anacardic acid, and • 30 to 60 wt% of an ionic liquid comprising 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([BMIM][BF4]); wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL), and wt% is based on the total weight of the solid state electrolyte. In certain embodiments, the ionic liquid comprising 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([BMIM][BF4]) is incorporated within the PVDF-HFP/LiAn matrix. This facilitates improved ion transport by increasing the amorphous phase of the polymer matrix and by providing additional pathways for lithium-ion migration. Further, the ionic liquid enhances electrochemical stability and improves interfacial contact between the electrolyte and electrode materials, thereby improving the overall electrochemical performance of a lithium-ion battery. The presence of [BMIM][BF4] in the electrolyte membrane results in increased ionic conductivity of the solid-state electrolyte and contributes to improved charge–discharge characteristics and enhanced cycling stability of battery cells comprising the same. In certain embodiments, the solid-state electrolyte of the present disclosure exhibits an oxidative stability window in the range of about 3.5 V to 6.0 V vs. Li?/Li, preferably from 4.0 V to 5.5 V vs. Li?/Li, and more preferably at least 4.5 V vs. Li?/Li. In certain embodiments, the solid state electrolyte of the present dislcoure has an ionic conductivity of at least about 0.5 × 10?4 S/cm at room temperature and an oxidative stability window of at least 4.5 V vs. Li?/Li. In another aspect, the present disclosure provides a process for preparing solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving a polymer matrix in a solvent to obtain a polymer solution; b) adding a lithium salt of anacardic acid to the polymer solution of step a) to form an electrolyte composition; c) casting the electrolyte composition obtained in step b) onto a substrate to form a film; and d) drying the cast film of step c) to obtain a solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In certain embodiments, the polymer matrix, lithium salt of anacardic acid and their quantities are the same as defined in the previous embodiments. In certain embodiments, solvents which can be employed in step a) for dissolving the polymer matrix are selected from a group comprising polar solvent such as N,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF), N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), Acetone, Toluene, Tetrahydrofuran (THF), Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), Propylene carbonate (PC), Ethylene carbonate (EC), and Dimethyl carbonate (DMC) and the like. In preferred embodiment, the solvent is DMF. The ratio of solvent is 1:2 to 1:5, preferably 1:4. In certain embodiments, the polymer matrix is dissolved in a solvent at a temperature in the range of 25 °C to about 100 °C. In some embodiments, the temperature ranges from about 25 °C to about 60 °C, or from about 30 °C to about 50 °C. In certain preferred embodiments, the temperature ranges from about 25 °C to about 35 °C. In certain embodiments, anacardic acid for the preparing lithium salt of anacardic acid is obtained from cashew nut shell liquid (CNSL), a renewable resource rich in phenolic compounds. The extraction of anacardic acid may be carried out using one or more conventional or advanced extraction techniques suitable for isolating the acid in high purity. In one embodiment, anacardic acid is extracted using supercritical carbon dioxide as a solvent under controlled temperature and pressure conditions, thereby enabling selective extraction and yielding high-purity anacardic acid without the use of harsh chemicals. In another embodiment, CNSL is subjected to solvent extraction using organic solvents such as ethyl acetate, acetone, ethanol, hexane, or combinations thereof, followed by purification steps to isolate anacardic acid. In a specific embodiment, CNSL is converted into a metal anacardate, including calcium anacardate, by treatment with a suitable calcium base in a solvent such as acetone, followed by acidification to obtain anacardic acid. The extracted anacardic acid is further purified by techniques including distillation, recrystallization, or chromatographic methods to obtain anacardic acid suitable for use in solid-state electrolyte applications. In a specific embodiment, anacardic acid is obtained from a calcium salt of anacardic acid. The calcium salt is suspended in an organic solvent and subjected to stirring to remove impurities, followed by phase separation and decantation. The washing step may be repeated one or more times until the supernatant becomes substantially free of colored impurities. The resulting solid is then isolated, for example by filtration. Suitable organic solvents for the washing and/or extraction steps include, but are not limited to, esters such as ethyl acetate, ketones such as acetone, alcohols such as ethanol, and hydrocarbons such as hexane, or combinations thereof. The isolated calcium salt is subsequently acidified using an acid to regenerate anacardic acid. In certain embodiments, the acid comprises a mineral acid, including but not limited to hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, or nitric acid. The acidification is carried out under stirring for a suitable duration to ensure completion of the reaction. The resulting mixture is subjected to liquid–liquid extraction using an organic solvent to separate the organic phase containing anacardic acid. The organic phase is optionally washed with aqueous solutions, including water and/or brine, and dried using a suitable drying agent. The solvent is thereafter removed, for example under reduced pressure, to obtain anacardic acid, which may be in the form of a mixture. Anacardic acid can be further purified by catalytic hydrogenation of an unsaturated anacardic acid mixture. The crude anacardic acid is dissolved in a suitable organic solvent and contacted with a hydrogenation catalyst under an inert atmosphere. The catalyst may comprise a supported noble metal catalyst, including but not limited to palladium on carbon (Pd/C), platinum, or nickel-based catalysts. Hydrogenation is carried out in the presence of hydrogen gas for a duration sufficient to achieve the desired level of saturation. Upon completion of the reaction, the catalyst is removed, for example by filtration through a suitable filtration aid. The resulting filtrate is concentrated, for example under reduced pressure, to obtain a residue. The residue is further purified, for example by chromatographic techniques, including column chromatography using an appropriate solvent system, to obtain purified anacardic acid. In certain embodiments, the purified anacardic acid comprises a saturated form of anacardic acid. In certain embodiments, lithium anacardate is prepared by reacting anacardic acid with a lithium base. The anacardic acid, which may be in a saturated or unsaturated form, is dissolved in a suitable organic solvent and heated to an elevated temperature, typically in the range of about 50 °C to about 100 °C, under stirring. Preferred solvents include alcohols such as ethanol and methanol, and polar aprotic solvents such as tetrahydrofuran (THF), dimethylformamide (DMF), or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), or combinations thereof. A lithium base is dissolved in an aqueous medium to form a solution, which is subsequently added, for example dropwise, to the anacardic acid solution under continuous stirring. Preferred lithium bases include lithium hydroxide (including hydrates thereof), lithium carbonate, and lithium alkoxides, with lithium hydroxide being particularly preferred. In certain embodiments, the reaction mixture containing the lithium base and anacardic acid solution is maintained at an elevated temperature, typically in the range of about 60 °C to about 110 °C, for a duration sufficient to facilitate formation of lithium anacardate. In certain embodiments, the reaction is continued under heating to remove water formed during the reaction, thereby promoting salt formation. The resulting mixture is further maintained at a temperature in the range of about 60 °C to about 90 °C under reduced or ambient pressure conditions to obtain a dried lithium anacardate product. Step b) of adding a lithium salt of anacardic acid to the polymer solution of step a) to form electrolyte composition is carried out by stirring at temperature in the range of 25 °C to about 100 °C. In some embodiments, the temperature ranges from about 25 °C to about 60 °C, or from about 30 °C to about 50 °C. In certain preferred embodiments, the temperature ranges from about 25 °C to about 35 °C. This results in a homogeneous electrolyte composition. Step c) involves casting the electrolyte composition onto a substrate. In certain embodiments, a polymer electrolyte membrane is prepared by a solution casting. Electrolyte composition obtained in step b) is cast onto a substrate using a film-forming technique, including but not limited to doctor blade casting, dip coating, or spin coating, to obtain a film of desired thickness. Optionally, the electrolyte composition may be first dissolved in a suitable solvent under continuous stirring to obtain a clear and homogeneous solution before casting. In certain embodiments, the electrolyte composition is cast onto a substrate to form a film. Suitable substrates include glass, metal, or polymeric substrates. Non-limiting examples of metal substrates include stainless steel, aluminum, or copper, while polymeric substrates may include polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polypropylene (PP), or polyimide (PI). In certain embodiments, the substrate comprises glass. The use of a glass substrate due to its smooth surface, chemical inertness, and ease of film removal after drying facilitates formation of uniform films with controlled thickness and minimal surface defects. In some embodiments, the substrate surface may be pre-treated, for example by cleaning or surface modification, to improve film adhesion and uniformity during the casting process. In certain embodiments, the thickness of the cast film is controlled in the range of about 10 µm to about 500 µm, including all intermediate values and sub-ranges therein, such as from about 20 µm to about 400 µm, from about 50 µm to about 300 µm, or from about 100 µm to about 200 µm. Step d) involves drying the cast film under vacuum to obtain a solid-state electrolyte. The cast film is subsequently dried to remove residual solvent. Drying may be carried out under ambient or reduced pressure conditions at a temperature typically ranging from about 40 °C to about 100 °C, or from 50 °C to 80 °C for a duration sufficient to achieve solvent removal, for example from about 6 hours to about 48 hours, or from 10 to 15 hours. In certain embodiments, drying is performed under vacuum to facilitate efficient solvent removal to form a solid polymer electrolyte membrane. After drying, the resulting polymer electrolyte membrane is separated from the substrate to obtain a free-standing film. The electrolyte membrane is flexible, free-standing, and suitable for cell assembly. The membrane may be flexible and is optionally stored under controlled conditions, including in a low-humidity environment or desiccator, prior to further characterization or use in electrochemical devices. In a specific embodiment, the present disclosure provides a process for preparing solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving PVDF-HFP in DMF to obtain a polymer solution; b) adding a 5 to 10 wt% of lithium anacardate to the polymer solution of step a) to form an electrolyte composition; c) casting the electrolyte composition onto a glass substrate using doctor blade technique to form a thin film; and d) drying the cast film under vacuum at 60°C for 12 h to obtain a solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In an embodiment, the present disclosure provides a process for preparing the solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving a polymer matrix in a solvent to form a polymer solution; b) adding an ionic liquid to the polymer solution of step a); c) adding a lithium salt of anacardic acid to the solution of step b) to form an electrolyte composition; d) casting the electrolyte composition onto a substrate to form a film; and e) drying the film of step d) to obtain a solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In certain embodiments, the conditions for steps a), c), d) and e) are the same as described for the corresponding steps in preceding embodiments. Step (b) involves incorporating an ionic liquid into the polymer solution. In certain embodiments, the ionic liquid is added in an amount ranging from about 30 wt.% to about 60 wt.% relative to the polymer matrix, including all intermediate values and sub-ranges therein, such as from about 35 wt.% to about 55 wt.%, from about 40 wt.% to about 50 wt.%, or from about 45 wt.% to about 60 wt.%. In certain preferred embodiments, the ionic liquid is present in an amount ranging from about 40 wt.% to about 50 wt.% relative to the polymer matrix. The incorporation of the ionic liquid is carried out at a temperature ranging from about 25 °C to about 100 °C. In some embodiments, the temperature ranges from about 25 °C to about 60 °C, or from about 30 °C to about 50 °C, with a preferred temperature range of about 25 °C to about 35 °C. The mixture is stirred for a duration sufficient to achieve a substantially homogeneous dispersion of the ionic liquid within the polymer solution. Step b) involves incorporating an ionic liquid into the polymer solution. In certain embodiments, the ionic liquid is added in an amount of 30 wt.% to 60 wt.% relative to the polymer matrix. In a preferred embodiment, the ionic liquid is incorporated at about 50 wt% relative to the polymer matrix, corresponding to an approximate 1:1 weight ratio between the polymer matrix and the ionic liquid. In certain embodiments, when the ionic liquid content is below about 30 wt.%, the resulting solid-state electrolyte exhibits comparatively lower ionic conductivity due to insufficient ion transport pathways. In certain embodiments, when the ionic liquid content exceeds about 60 wt.%, excessive plasticization of the polymer matrix occurs, leading to deterioration of mechanical integrity and structural stability of the electrolyte membrane. In certain embodiments, the ionic liquid enhances amorphous phase formation within the polymer matrix, thereby improving lithium-ion mobility and interfacial compatibility with electrode materials. In certain embodiments, an ionic liquid is incorporated into the polymer solution and the resulting mixture is stirred to ensure uniform dispersion within the polymer matrix. Thereafter, a lithium anacardate, is added to the solution, and the mixture is further stirred until a substantially homogeneous electrolyte composition is obtained. In a specific embodiment, the present disclosure provides a process for preparing solid-state electrolyte comprising: a) dissolving a polymer matrix in a solvent to form a polymer solution; b) adding 30 to 60 wt% of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([BMIM][BF4]) into the polymer solution of step a); c) adding a 5 to 10 wt% of lithium salt of anacardic acid to the solution obtained in step b) to form an electrolyte composition; d) casting the electrolyte composition obtained in step c) onto a glass substrate to form a film; and e) drying the film under vacuum at 60°C for 12 h to obtain the solid-state electrolyte; wherein anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). In yet another aspect, the present disclosure provides an electrochemical cell comprising: an anode; a cathode; and a solid-state electrolyte disposed between the anode and cathode, wherein the solid-state electrolyte, wherein the solid-state electrolyte comprises a polymer matrix impregnated with a lithium salt of anacardic acid, and optionally an ionic liquid wherein the anacardic acid is derived from cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL). This invention is particularly suited for applications in lithium-ion batteries used in consumer electronics, electric vehicles, large-scale energy storage systems, and flexible or wearable devices. By combining renewable chemistry with advanced electrochemical performance, the disclosed solid-state electrolyte represents a sustainable and high-performance alternative to existing electrolyte technologies. In an another embodiment, the solid state electrolyte of the present disclosure is compatible with lithium metal anode as confirmed by galvanostatic lithium plating/stripping experiments. In a specific embodiment, the anode comprises lithium metal and the cathode comprises lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) or lithium nickel manganese oxide (LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4). In certain embodiment, the electrochemical cell operates at a voltage of at least 4.0 V and the electrochemical cell exhibits a coulombic efficiency of at least 95%. In a specific embodiment, the present disclosure provides a full cell comprising Li metal anode, LiFePO4 cathode, and LiAn10 membrane as the electrolyte. The cell exhibits an initial discharge capacity of 160 mAh/g and retains ~140 mAh/g after 100 cycles, indicating a capacity retention of 87.5% and a coulombic efficiency of 99.8%. The examples used herein are intended merely to facilitate an understanding of ways in which the embodiments herein may be practiced and to further enable those of skill in the art to practice the embodiments herein. Accordingly, the examples should not be construed as limiting the scope of the embodiments herein. Examples: Example 1: Anacardic Acid modulated Solid State Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Preparation: Step a) Extraction of anacardic acid (unsaturated) Calcium salt of anacardic acid mixture was commercially procured and used for the extraction of anacardic acid. Calcium anacardate (43 g, 125 mmols) is suspended in ethyl acetate (200 mL) in a beaker and stirred for 1 h. After that the suspension is allowed to settle and dark brown ethyl acetate layer decanted and the same process was repeated until the ethyl acetate layer is free of colour. At the end the suspension is filtered under a vacuum through the Buchner funnel. The obtained calcium salt acidified with 6N HCl (500 mL, 3000 mmols) by continuously stirring for 5-6 hrs. Then the obtained organic layer was extracted with ethyl acetate and washed with water and brine. Finally, the obtained organic layer is dried over anhydrous Na2SO4 and concentrated to dryness to afford the unsaturated anacardic acid ene-mixture as a dark brown viscous oil (~18-20 g, 47%). 1H NMR (CDCl3, 25 °C, 500 MHz): d 1.17-1.33 (6H, (tt)) 1.43 (2H, (tt)), 1.59 (2H, (tt)), 1.98 (2H, (q)), 2.58-2.72 (6H, 2.65 (dd)), 4.76-4.91 (2H, 4.84 (dd)), 5.30-5.48 (4H, 5.38 (dt)), 5.62 (1H, (ddt)), 6.88 (1H, (dd)), 7.12 (1H, (dd)), 7.30 (1H, (dd)). Step b) Synthesis of saturated anacardic acid by hydrogenation reaction To a stirred solution of THF (10 mL) containing the crude unsaturated anacardic acid mixtures (5 g, 14.6 mmol) was added 10% Pd/C (0.8 g, 7.5 mmol) slowly under an inert atmosphere into a round bottom flask. Hydrogenation was carried out with hydrogen gas for 48 h. The contents were filtered through a pad of celite to remove the catalyst, collected the clear filtrate, concentrated under the reduced pressure, and the crude residue was purified by silica gel column chromatography (EtOAc/hexanes, (1:9)) affording the pure saturated anacardic acid (4.5 g, 90% yield). 1H NMR (DMSO-d6, 25 °C, 500 MHz): d 0.86 (3H, (t)), 1.16-1.34 (24H, 1.23 (tt)), 1.59 (2H, (tt)), 2.65 (2H, (t)), 6.88 (1H, (dd)), 7.12 (1H, (dd)), 7.30 (1H, (dd)). Step c) Synthesis of lithium anacardate: Saturated anacardic acid obtained in step b) was dissolved in ethanol and heated at 80oC. A solution of LiOH. H2O (2.5 eq.) were prepared by dissolving into distilled water and subsequently added dropwise into the above solution with continuous stirring at 80 o C. Then the mixture was heated and maintained at 100 o C for 1 h. After the reaction the mixture was kept for another 1 h at 100 o C to remove the formed water until the solution turned brown. The brown colour solution was kept at 65 o C for 24 h to obtain completely dried product. Step d): The polymer electrolyte membrane was prepared by first dissolving poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) in N,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF) under continuous stirring until a clear solution was obtained. The cast film was subsequently dried under vacuum at 60 °C for 12 hours to ensure complete removal of the residual solvent. After drying, the flexible polymer electrolyte membrane was carefully peeled from the glass substrate. The obtained membrane, designated as 10LiAn, was stored in a desiccator prior to further physicochemical characterization and electrochemical evaluation. Example 2: Preparation of Solid State Electrolyte Membrane of PVDF-HFP and lithium anacardate and ionic liquid ([BMIM][BF4]): The polymer electrolyte membrane was prepared by dissolving PVDF-HFP in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) under continuous stirring until a clear and homogeneous solution was obtained. Subsequently, the ionic liquid ([BMIM][BF4]) was incorporated into the polymer solution in a 1:1 weight ratio with PVDF-HFP, as illustrated in Fig. 1, followed by further stirring to ensure uniform dispersion of the ionic liquid throughout the polymer matrix. Thereafter the steps of casting and drying the electrolyte membrane is carried out in the same procedure as provided in Example 1. Example 3: Electrochemical studies of solid state electrolytes prepared in Examples 1 and 2: 3a) A polymer electrolyte membrane (LiAn10) is prepared containing 10% lithium anacardate by weight with respect to PVDF-HFP. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) reveals that this membrane exhibits ionic conductivity of approximately 0.5 × 10?4 S cm?¹ at room temperature. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) demonstrates a stable electrochemical window up to 4.6 V vs. Li?/Li, and lithium transference number (tLi?) is determined to be 0.5 using the Bruce-Vincent method. As shown in Fig. 2b, the oxidative decomposition potential of LiAn10 is about ~ 4.6 V vs. Li+/Li, indicating its suitability for lithium battery application. A higher lithium-ion transference number (tLi?) offers several advantages, such as minimizing electrode polarization, promoting uniform lithium deposition, and reducing the risk of lithium dendrite formation. Fig. 2c presents the chronoamperometry profile obtained by applying a 10mV bias, while the inset depicts the EIS spectra of the Li/LiAn10/Li symmetric cell recorded before and after polarization. Using the Bruce–Vincent equation, the tLi? value for LiAn10 was determined to be 0.5. To predict the compatibility of LiAn10 with a lithium metal anode, a galvanostatic plating/stripping experiment was carried out using a Li/ LiAn10/Li symmetric cell. The symmetric cells were cycled at a current density of 0.1 mA cm–2 with 60 min of charging/discharging at RT, as shown in Fig. 2d. The symmetric Li/ LiAn10/Li cell demonstrated an overpotential of approximately 150 mV. Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b, illustrates the galvanostatic charge-discharge profile of the Li/LiAn10/Li/LiFePO4 cell, cycled within a voltage range of 2.8 to 4.2 V at a 0.1 C rate. The cell exhibited an initial discharge capacity of 160 mAh g?¹. After 100 cycles, it retained a capacity of approximately 140 mAh g?¹, corresponding to a capacity retention of 87.5% and a coulombic efficiency of 99.8%, indicating excellent cycling stability. 3b) Three sets of membranes were prepared, varying the percentage of lithium anacardate content to 5%, 10%, and 20% (labeled LiAn5, LiAn10, LiAn20). The ionic conductivity measurements of the as-prepared membrane were carried out via AC electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) using stainless steel symmetric cells (SS/LiAn/SS) over a frequency range of 1 MHz to 1 Hz, with an amplitude of 10 mV at room temperature (RT) Fig.4a. Among the three compositions, the SS/10LiAn/SS cell with 1M LiPF6 in EC/DCE resulted in an improved conductivity of 8.8 × 10-4 S cm-1. The electrochemical stability window of the 0LiAn and 10LiAn membranes was evaluated using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV). The measurements were performed using a Li/LiAn/stainless steel (SS) cell configuration at a scan rate of 1 mV s?¹ over a voltage range from the open-circuit voltage (OCV) to 6 V. As shown in Fig. 4b, the 0LiAn membrane exhibits an oxidative decomposition potential of approximately 5.5 V vs. Li?/Li. In contrast, the 10LiAn membrane shows no noticeable oxidative decomposition within the investigated voltage range, demonstrating its superior electrochemical stability. This enhanced stability indicates the suitability of the 10LiAn membrane for application in high-voltage lithium battery systems. 3c) The electrochemical stability of the 10LiAn membrane was evaluated using a Li/10LiAn/Li symmetric cell through a lithium plating-stripping experiment. The measurements were carried out at a constant current density of 0.1 mA cm-2 with a fixed areal capacity of 0.1 mAh cm-2 to assess the interfacial stability and lithium-ion transport behavior of the 10LiAn membrane. As shown in Fig. 5a, the Li/10LiAn/Li symmetric cell exhibits stable and highly reversible lithium plating-stripping behavior over an extended cycling period of ~1600 hours. The voltage profile remains nearly constant throughout the entire cycling duration, displaying a low polarization of ~30 mV, which indicates stable lithium plating-stripping at the electrode-electrolyte interface. The non-appearance of significant voltage fluctuations or short-circuit behavior during prolonged cycling suggests that the 10LiAn membrane effectively maintains a stable interface with the lithium anode and may contribute to suppressing lithium dendrite formation. To further investigate the interfacial stability under different operating conditions, lithium plating-stripping experiments were also performed at various current densities ranging from 0.05 to 0.8 mA cm-2. As illustrated in Fig. 5b, the Li/10LiAn/Li symmetric cell demonstrates stable voltage profiles across the entire current density range. As expected, a gradual increase in polarization voltage was observed with increasing current density due to the higher lithium-ion flux during the plating-stripping process. Nevertheless, the cell maintained stable cycling behavior without any indication of short-circuiting, highlighting the robust electrochemical stability of the 10LiAn electrolyte membrane even under increased current density conditions. The long-term cycling stability and consistent performance across a wide current density range demonstrate that the 10LiAn membrane is capable of supporting stable lithium plating-stripping processes. These results indicate that the developed 10LiAn membrane is a promising candidate for solid-state lithium-ion battery applications, particularly in systems requiring enhanced safety, and improved electrochemical performance. 3d) Fig. 6(a) and 6(b) present the galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles and cycling performance of the Li/10LiAn/ LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 cell operated within a voltage window of 3.8-5.0 V at a rate of 1 C. The cell maintained stable discharge capacities across the tested current rates for 10 cycles at each rate, demonstrating the ability of the 10LiAn membrane to support efficient lithium-ion transport even at high current densities. When the current rate was returned to a lower value, the capacity was largely recovered, further confirming the electrochemical stability of the 10LiAn electrolyte. These results collectively highlight the promising electrochemical performance of the 10LiAn membrane for high-voltage lithium battery applications. patents.abstract: INNOVATIVE SOH ESTIMATION APPROACH FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES USING DIFFERENTIAL THERMAL VOLTAMMETRY AND SSA-ELMAN NEURAL NETWORK The present invention discloses an innovative method for estimating the State of Health (SOH) of lithium-ion batteries by integrating Differential Thermal Voltammetry (DTV), Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA), and Elman Neural Network (Elman NN). Unlike conventional techniques relying solely on electrical parameters, the proposed method utilizes thermal-voltage behavior to extract deeper insights into battery degradation. SSA is employed to optimize feature selection, reducing computational load while enhancing accuracy. The selected features are then processed using an Elman Neural Network, which retains memory of previous battery states, enabling adaptive and real-time SOH prediction. This novel approach significantly improves prediction precision, lowers computational expense, and offers scalability for deployment in Battery Management Systems (BMS) of electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to an innovative method for estimating the State of Health (SOH) of lithium-ion batteries by integrating Differential Thermal Voltammetry (DTV) with a Self-Structure Adjusting Elman Neural Network (SSA-Elman NN). This approach enhances SOH prediction accuracy and battery performance monitoring. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Lithium-ion batteries are essential for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESS), but they wear out over time due to repeated charging and discharging, temperature changes, and internal chemical reactions. This aging process reduces their capacity, efficiency, and safety. To keep batteries reliable and working well, it is important to accurately estimate their State of Health (SOH). Traditional methods rely on measuring voltage, current, and impedance, but these techniques can be expensive, less accurate, or difficult to use in real-time conditions. Incorrect SOH predictions can lead to unexpected battery failures, shorter lifespan, and poor energy management. Therefore, there is a need for a more precise, flexible, and cost-effective SOH estimation method that can provide real-time data, helping with timely maintenance and better performance. State of Health (SOH) estimation is currently done using Battery Management Systems (BMS) from companies like Tesla, LG Chem, and Panasonic, as well as AI-based tools such as AVL, Battelle, and Bosch Battery in the Cloud. Some methods also use high-precision devices like Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) from Gamry and Solartron. Most commercial approaches rely on voltage, current, and machine learning models, but Differential Thermal Voltammetry (DTV) is rarely used. This opens the door for innovation by combining DTV with an Sparrow Search Algorithm-Elman Neural Network, which could provide a faster, more accurate, and adaptable way to estimate SOH. Existing State of Health (SOH) estimation methods lack accuracy, require extensive data, and often need battery-specific calibration, making real-time prediction challenging. Additionally, advanced techniques like Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) are costly and impractical. OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION Main objective of the present invention is to develop a novel SOH estimation technique for lithium-ion batteries using Differential Thermal Voltammetry (DTV). Another objective of the present invention is to integrate a Self-Structure Adjusting Elman Neural Network (SSA-Elman NN) for enhanced prediction accuracy. Another objective of the present invention is to improve real-time battery health diagnostics through temperature and voltage-based data interpretation. patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to novel electrodes for lithium-based electrochemical energy storage devices, specifically Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) and Lithium-ion Capacitors (LICs), utilizing silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic panels as a key component of the negative electrode (anode). The disclosure discloses a composite anode material comprising commercial graphite and recovered solar silicon (CG-rSi), fabricated through mechanical synthesis. The CG-rSi composite anode, after electrochemical pre-treatment, is paired with a suitable cathode (activated carbon for LICs or LiMn2O4 for LIBs) and a lithium-ion conducting electrolyte containing fluoroethylene carbonate additive. The resulting energy storage devices exhibit enhanced specific capacity, high energy and power density, and excellent cycling stability. The disclosure provides a sustainable approach to valorize photovoltaic waste by transforming recovered silicon into a high-performance anode material, thereby contributing to the development of next-generation, environmentally conscious energy storage solutions.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure pertains broadly to the technical domain of electrochemical energy storage systems, and more particularly, to advanced materials and configurations for high-energy and high-power density electrochemical energy storage devices. Specifically, the disclosure relates to novel electrode compositions, their fabrication methodologies, and their application within Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) and Lithium-ion Capacitors (LICs), with a salient focus on the valorization and reutilization of silicon material recovered from end-of-life photovoltaic (solar) panels as a constituent component of the negative electrode (anode). The disclosure further encompasses the integration of said recovered silicon-based anodes with appropriate cathode materials., separators and electrolytes to construct functional and high-performance LIBs and LICs, thereby addressing critical aspects of sustainable materials management and next-generation energy storage technology. BACKGROUND [0002] The escalating global demand for sustainable energy solutions necessitates commensurate advancements in energy storage technologies. Electrochemical energy storage devices, such as Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) and supercapacitors, are pivotal in facilitating widespread adoption of renewable energy sources and enabling the electrification of transportation and portable electronics. LIBs are widely recognized for their high energy density, rendering them suitable for applications requiring extended operational periods. Supercapacitors, conversely, excel in power density and cycle life, making them ideal for applications demanding rapid charge-discharge capabilities. Notwithstanding their respective merits, a performance gap exists between LIBs and supercapacitors concerning the simultaneous delivery of high energy and high power, a gap that Lithium-ion Capacitors (LICs), as hybrid devices, endeavour to bridge by combining characteristics of both battery-type and capacitive-type electrodes. [0003] Traditional LIBs predominantly utilize graphite as the anode material due to its stable intercalation properties and relatively low cost. However, the theoretical specific capacity of graphite (approximately 372 mAh g-1) represents a limiting factor for achieving higher energy densities required for future applications. Silicon, with its significantly higher theoretical specific capacity (approximately 4200 mAh g-1), is considered a highly promising alternative or additive anode material. Nevertheless, the practical implementation of silicon anodes is hampered by significant volume expansion (up to ~ 300%) during lithium insertion (alloying), leading to the mechanical degradation, pulverization, loss of electrical contact, and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation, collectively resulting in rapid capacity fading and poor life cycle. [0004] Concurrently, the proliferation of photovoltaic technology has led to a growing concern regarding the management of end-of-life solar panels. These panels contain valuable materials, including silicon, but also pose environmental challenges if not properly recycled. Conventional recycling processes for solar panels can be complex and energy-intensive, and the recovered silicon often requires extensive purification to meet the stringent requirements for re-use in new solar cells. There exists a compelling need for innovative approaches to effectively and sustainably reutilize materials from discarded solar panels, particularly the silicon component, in high-value addition applications. [0005] The present disclosure addresses these challenges by providing a novel approach to incorporate silicon recovered from discarded solar panels into composite anode materials for LIBs and LICs. This approach not only offers a sustainable pathway for managing photovoltaic waste but also leverages the high theoretical capacity of silicon to enhance the performance of electrochemical energy storage devices., thereby contributing to the development of more energy-dense, powerful and environmentally conscious battery and capacitor technologies. OBJECTIVE [0006] The primary objective of the present disclosure is to provide a sustainable and economically viable method for fabricating high-performance electrodes for lithium-based electrochemical energy storage devices by effectively utilizing silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic panels. A further objective is to develop a composite anode material comprising commercial graphite and recovered solar silicon that exhibits enhanced specific capacity, improved life cycle, and stable electrochemical performance when incorporated into Lithium-ion Batteries and Lithium-ion Capacitors. [0007] Another objective is to provide a fabrication process for such composite anodes that is amenable to scaling or industrial production and integrates seamlessly with existing battery and capacitor manufacturing technologies. Yet another objective is to demonstrate the efficacy of the disclosed recovered silicon-based anodes in both Lithium-ion Battery and Lithium-ion Capacitor configurations, showcasing their potential to bridge the performance gap between conventional energy storage technologies. A still further objective is to contribute to the circular economy by transforming waste materials from the solar sector into valuable components for the energy storage sector, thereby reducing environmental impact and promoting resource efficiency. SUMMARY [0008] The present disclosure presents a novel electrochemical energy storage device and methods for its fabrication, characterized by the incorporation of negative electrode (anode) material comprising a composite of commercial graphite and silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic panels. In one aspect, the disclosure provides a Lithium-ion Capacitor (LIC) configuration utilizing the aforesaid commercial graphite-recovered-solar silicon (CG-rSi) composite as the anode and commercially available activated carbon (AC) as the positive electrode (cathode). In another aspect, the disclosure provides a Lithium-ion Based (LIB) configuration employing the same CG-rSi composite as the anode and a lithium manganese oxide, specifically LiMn2O4 (LMO), as the positive electrode (cathode). Both device configurations utilize a non-aqueous electrolyte comprising 1 M lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) dissolved in a solvent mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) in a 1:1 volume ratio, with the addition of 10 volume percent of fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) as an additive. The anode and cathode are spatially separated by a porous membrane, preferably a Whatman glass microfibre separator. [0009] A key feature of the disclosure involves the electrochemical pre-treatment of the CG-rSi anode prior to its assembly into a full cell. This pre-treatment is conducted in a half cell configuration utilizing lithium metal as the counter and reference electrode and involves subjecting the CG-rSi electrode to a few charge-discharge cycles within a specified potential window (e.g., 0.005 to 2 V) at controlled current rates. This electrochemical conditioning is critical for mitigating the initial irreversible capacity loss commonly associated with silicon-containing anodes and for forming a stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, thereby enhancing the subsequent cycling stability and performance in the full cell. [0010] The CG-rSi composite anode material is presented by mechanically synthesizing varying compositions of commercial graphite and recovered solar silicon, such as CG(100)-rSi(0), CG(95)-rSi(5), CG(90)-rSi(10), CG(85)-rSi(15), CG(80)-rSi(20) and CG(0)-rSi(100). The electrodes are fabricated by preparing a slurry comprising the active material (CG-rSi, AC, or LMO), a conductive additive (e.g., acetylene black), and a binder (e.g., carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) or Teflonized Acetylene Black (TAB-2)) in a specific weight ratio (e.g., 8:1:1), and casting this slurry onto a suitable current collector (e.g., copper foil for the anode, aluminium foil or stainless steel for the cathode). [0011] The assembled full cells (AC//CG-rSi LIC and LMO//CG-rSi LIB) are evaluated for their electrochemical performance through techniques such as galvanostatic charge-discharge cycling and cyclic voltammetry within defined voltage windows (e.g., 1.3 to 4.3 V for LICs and 3.4 to 4.15 V for LIBs) at various current rates and under different temperature conditions. The electrochemical characterization demonstrates that the CG-rSi composite anodes, particularly those with a judicious proportion of recovered silicon (e.g., CG(95)-rSi(5)), exhibit superior specific capacity compared to pure graphite anodes and maintain stable cycling performance over extended periods, thereby enabling the fabrication of high-energy, high-power, and long life-cycle electrochemical energy storage devices. The disclosure thus provides a sustainable and high-performance solution for next-generation energy storage by effectively leveraging materials recovered from photovoltaic waste streams. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [0012] FIG.1 illustrates the schematic of recovery of spent solar silicon and synthesis of its composite with graphite as electrode material for LIB/LIC. FIG.2 illustrates the Cyclic voltammogram of CG-rSi composites in half-cell configuration with Li metal tested in the potential window of 0.005 to 2 V. FIG.3 illustrates the Galvanostatic charge-discharge of Li/CG-rSi metal batteries at a current density of 0.1 A g–1. FIG.4 illustrates the long-term cycling profile of Li/CG-rSi metal batteries at a current density of 0.1 A g–1. FIG.5 illustrates the Ecell vs. time plot of AC//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIC at room temperature conditions FIG.6 illustrates the Ragone plot comparing energy and power densities of AC//CG-rSi LICs at room temperature conditions. FIG.7 illustrates the Ragone plot comparing energy and power densities of AC//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIC at different temperature conditions. FIG.8 illustrates the galvanostatic charge-discharge of LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB at 0.1 A g–1 current density. FIG.9 illustrates the long-term cycling profile of LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB at 0.1 A g–1 current density. FIG.10 illustrates the long-term cycling profile of LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB at different temperatures at 0.5 A g–1 current density. DETAILED DECRIPTION [0013] The present disclosure provides a comprehensive method for the design, fabrication and implementation of advanced electrodes for Lithium-based electrochemical energy storage devices, specifically Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) and Lithium-ion Capacitors (LICs), by strategically incorporating silicon material recovered from discarded photovoltaic (PV) panels into the anode composition. This approach represents a significant step towards enhancing the sustainability and performance characteristics of energy storage technologies. Figure 1 of the accompanying drawings provides a schematic illustration depicting the overall process flow, commencing with the recovery of silicon from end-of-life solar panels and culminating in the synthesis of the commercial graphite-recovered solar silicon (CG-rSi) composite material which forms the cornerstone of the disclosed anode technology. The recovery process for solar silicon from discarded panels, while not the primary focus of the instant disclosure’s novelty in terms of the recovery technique itself, is understood to involve various known methods in the art for dismantling and separating the constituent materials of PV modules, including but nor limited to mechanical, thermal and chemical processes aimed at isolating the silicon wafers. The silicon recovered through such processes, herein referred to as “recovered solar silicon” or “rSi”, may undergo initial processing steps such as crushing, grinding, and potentially preliminary purification to render it suitable for subsequent composite synthesis. The core of the anode material innovation lies in the synergistic combination of this recovered silicon with commercial graphite (CG) to form CG-rSi composite. The synthesis of the CG-rSi composite is achieved through high-energy mixing techniques like ball milling which facilitate the intimate mixing and particle size reduction of the constituent materials. Various weight ratios of commercial graphite to recovered solar silicon are contemplated and evaluated within the scope of this disclosure to optimize electrochemical performance. Exemplary compositions investigated include CG(100)-rSi(0), CG(95)-rSi(5), CG(90)-rSi(10), CG(85)-rSi(15), CG(80)-rSi(20) and CG(0)-rSi(100). The mechanical synthesis process is controlled to achieve a desired particle size distribution and homogeneity of the composite material, which are crucial factors influencing the electrochemical performance, particularly the rate capability and cycling stability. The resulting CG-rSi composite powder serves as the active material for the negative electrode. The detailed methodology for the recovery of solar silicon and the mechanical synthesis of the CG-rSi composite is schematically presented in FIG.1, illustrating the transformation of waste material into a high-value component for energy storage applications. The disclosure recognizes that while higher silicon content theoretically offers greater capacity, it also exacerbates the volume expansion issue. Therefore, the investigation of various CG-rSi ratios is essential to identify compositions that balance high capacity with acceptable cycling stability, leveraging the buffering effect of graphite to mitigate the detrimental effects of silicon’s volume changes during lithiation and de-lithiation. The use of recovered silicon, which might have different morphological or structural characteristics compared to pristine battery-grade silicon, is specifically addresses by demonstrating its efficacy when combined with graphite in the disclosed composite structure. [0014] Following the synthesis of active materials, the electrodes for the electrochemical energy storage devices are fabricated. This involves preparing a slurry by combining the active material (either the CG-rSi composite for the anode or activated carbon (AC)) or LiMn2O4 (LMO) for the cathode), a conductive additive, and a binder in a specific weight ratio. A preferred ratio for the active material, Conductive carbon (such as acetylene black) and binder (such as carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) for the anode and teflonized acetylene black (TAB-2) for the cathode is 8:1:1 by weight, respectively. The conductive additive is crucial for ensuring good electrical conductivity throughout the electrode structure, facilitating efficient electron transport to and from the active material particles. The binder provides mechanical integrity to the electrode, holding the active material and conductive additive particles together and adhering the layer to the current collector. The choice of the binder and conductive additive may be optimized based on the specific active material and desired electrode properties. The prepared slurry is cast into a suitable current collector. For the anode, copper foil is typically used as the current collector due to its excellent electrical conductivity and stability in the potential range of the anode. For the cathode, aluminium foil or stainless steel may be employed. The casting process can be performed using various techniques known in the art, such as doctor blading, tape casting or slot die coating, to achieve a uniform electrode layer thickness and mass loading. After casting, the electrodes are dried to remove the solvent from the slurry and then typically calendered to compress the electrode layer, improving its density and electrical contact between particles and with the current collector. The dried and calendered electrodes are then cut into appropriate shapes and sizes for cell assembly. [0015] A critical step in the fabrication process particularly for silicon containing anodes, is the electrochemical pre-treatment of the CG-rSi electrode. This pre-treatment is performed in a half cell configuration, where the CG-rSi electrode serves as the working electrode and a Lithium metal foil acts as both the counter and reference electrode. The half-cell utilizes the same electrolyte composition intended for the full cell, which is a 1 M solution of lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) in a 1:1 volume mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC), with the addition of 10 volume percent of fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). The FEC additive is particularly important as it is known to improve the stability of the SEI layer formed on silicon-containing anodes, mitigating the effects of volume expansion and enhancing cycling performance. The half-cell is assembled in an inert atmosphere, typically within a glove box filled with high purity argon, to prevent contamination of the Lithium metal and electrolyte by moisture and oxygen. The electrochemical pre-treatment involves subjecting the CG-rSi half-cell to a few charge-discharge cycles within the potential window of 0.005 to 2 V versus Li/Li+ at a low current density. This initial cycling facilitates the formation of a stable SEI layer on the surface of the CG-rSi particles and helps to accommodate the initial irreversible capacity loss associate with the first lithiation cycle of silicon. Figure 2 presents representative cyclic voltammetry (CV) traces obtained from the Li/CG-rSi half-cell studies. The CV curves provide valuable insights into the electrochemical reactions occurring at the CG-rSi electrode during lithium insertion and extraction. For CG-rSi composites containing graphite, reduction peaks near 0.06 V versus Li/Li+ are observed during the cathodic sweep, corresponding to the intercalation of Li+ ions into the graphite structure. Corresponding oxidation peaks near 0.22 V Versus Li/Li+ are observed during the anodic sweep, indicating the deintercalation of Li+ ions from the graphite. For CG-rSi composites containing silicon, additional reduction peaks near 0.16 V versus Li/Li+ are present, attributable to the alloying reaction of Lithium with silicon. During the anodic sweep, oxidation peaks near 0.49 V versus Li/Li+ are observed, corresponding to the de-alloying of Lithium from silicon. The presence and intensity of the peaks vary depending on the ratio of graphite to silicon in the composite, as illustrated in FIG.2. [0016] FIG.3 shows the galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) profiles of the Li/CG-rSi half-cells at a current density of 0.1 A/g within the potential window of 0.005 to 2 V versus Li/Li+. These profiles demonstrate the specific discharge capacity achieved by different CG-rSi compositions. As shown in the figure, the specific discharge capacity generally increases with increasing silicon content, reflecting the higher theoretical capacity of silicon compared to graphite. For example, in the second cycle, the specific discharge capacities for CG(100)-rSi(0), CG(95)-rSi(5), CG(90)-rSi(10), CG(85)-rSi(15), CG(80)-rSi(20) and CG(0)-rSi(100) were measured to be approximately 319, 496, 693, 861, 1098 and 2807 mAhg-1 respectively. While higher silicon content yields higher initial capacity, FIG.4, which depicts the cycling performance of the Li/CG-rSi half-cells over 95 cycles at 0.1 Ag-1, reveals the trade-off between capacity and cycling stability. Composites with higher silicon content, such as CG(85)-rSi(15), CG(80)-rSi(20) and CG(0)-rSi(100), exhibit significant capacity fading over cycling, primarily due to the severe volume expansion of silicon. In contrast, the CG(100)-rSi(0) and CG(95)-rSi(5) composites demonstrate better capacity retention. Notably, the CG(95)-rSi(5) composite maintains a specific capacity of approximately 422 mAhg-1 after 95 cycles, which is higher than that of pure graphite while exhibiting comparable stability, highlighting the beneficial effect of incorporating a small amount of recovered silicon into the graphite matrix. This pre-treatment step, by stabilizing the SEI and activating the silicon component, is crucial for the successful operation of the CG-rSi anode in full cell configurations and represents a key aspect of the present disclosure. Upon completion of the electrochemical pre-treatment, the electrochemically conditioned CG-rSi electrode is integrated into a full cell configuration. The disclosure contemplate two primary full cell types: Lithium-ion Capacitors (LICs) and Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs). For the fabrication of LICs, the electrochemically pre-treated CG-rSi anode is paired with a mass-balance activated carbon (AC) cathode. Mass balancing between the anode and cathode is performed to optimize the cell performance and ensure efficient utilization of both electrode materials within the desired operating voltage window. The AC cathode is prepared using the same slurry casting method described previously, with AC as the active material. The assembled LIC cell comprises the pre-treated CG-rSi anode, an electrolyte-soaked separator, and the AC cathode, typically in a lab-scale coin cell setup assembled under inert conditions. The electrolyte used is the aforementioned 1 M LiPF6 in EC:DMC (1:1 v/v) with 10% vol.% FEC. The separator, preferably a Whatman glass microfibre separator, is positioned between the anode and cathode to prevent electronic contact while allowing ionic transport through its porous structure when saturated with the electrolyte. The assembled LIC cells are then subjected to galvanostatic charge-discharge studies at various current rates within the voltage window of 1.3 to 4.3 V to evaluate their energy and power density characteristics. FIG.5 presents the galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles of the AC//CG-rSi LIC full cells at different current rates under mass balanced conditions. These profiles illustrate the voltage-capacity/time response of the LICs during charging and discharging cycles. FIG.6 shows the Ragone plot derived from the GCD data, which plots the energy density versus the power density of the LICs fabricated with different CG-rSi composite anodes. As anticipated, the energy density generally increases with an increase in the silicon percentage in the CG-rSi composite reflecting the higher capacity contribution from silicon. The Ragone plot provides a comprehensive overview of the performance capabilities of the LICs., demonstrating their ability to deliver both high energy and high power. The full cell performance is also evaluated under different temperature conditions to assess the operational range and stability of the LICs. FIG. 7 illustrates the performance of the AC//CG-rSi full cell when tested at different temperatures. It is observed from the Ragone plot presented in the said figure, that the LIC full cell delivers a maximum energy density of approximately 196 Wh kg–1 and maximum power density of approximately 5.9 kW kg–1 at 250C, demonstrating excellent performance metrics for a hybrid energy storage device. The ability of the LICs to operate effectively across a range of temperatures is crucial for practical applications. The combination of the high-capacity CG-rSi anode and the high-power AC cathode, facilitated by the optimized electrolyte and separator, results in the LICs that bridge the performance gap between traditional batteries and supercapacitors, offering a promising solution for applications requiring both high energy and high power delivery. The use of recovered silicon contributes to the sustainability aspect of these high-performance LICs. [0017] In parallel to the LIC development, the disclosure also encompasses the fabrication and characterization of Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) utilizing the electrochemically pre-treated CG-rSi composite as the anode. For the LIB configuration, the pre-treated CG-rSi anode is paired with a mass balanced LiMn2O4 (LMO) cathode. LMO is a well-established cathode material for LIBs, known for its good rate capability and thermal stability. The LMO cathode is prepared using the same slurry casting method as described for the AC cathode, with LMO as the active material. The LIB cell is assembled in a similar manner to the LIC, comprising the pre-treated CG-rSi anode, an electrolyte-soaked separator, and the LMO cathode, typically in a coin cell setup assembled under inert conditions. The electrolyte composition remains the same: 1 M LiPF6 in EC:DMC (1:1 v/v) with 10% vol. FEC. The assembled LIB cells are evaluated for their electrochemical performance through galvanostatic charge-discharge studies within the voltage window of 3.4 to 4.15 V at various current rates. FIG.8 presents the galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles for LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB full cell under mass-balanced conditions. The CG(95)-rSi(5) composition was selected for detailed LIB testing based on its promising balance of capacity and stability observed in the half cell studies. The GCD profiles in FIG. 8 demonstrate the typical charge and discharge plateaus characteristic of LMO and the CG-rSi anode within the specified voltage range. The LIB exhibits an initial specific capacity of approximately 47 mAh g–1 based on the total weight of the active materials in both electrodes. A key performance indicator for the LIBs is their cycling stability over extended periods. FIG. 9 illustrates the long-term cycling performance of the LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB at a current density of 0.1 A g–1. The LIB demonstrates stable cycling performance for more than 750 cycles, the LIB exhibits a specific capacity of approximately 29.4 mAh g–1 with a high coulombic efficiency of 99.5 %. The high coulombic efficiency indicates that the charge and discharge processes are highly reversible, which is essential for long cycle life. The performance of the LIB full cell is also assessed under different temperature conditions and at higher current rates to evaluate its robustness and power capability. FIG. 10 depicts the long-term cycling performance of the LMO//CG(95)-rSi(5) LIB at a higher current rate of 0.5 A g–1 under different temperature conditions (10 0C, 25 0C, and 50 0C). The LIB demonstrates remarkable long-term cycling stability, enduring more than 2500 charge-discharge cycles. At 10 0C, 25 0C, and 500C, the LIB retains approximately 85 %, 96 % and 65 % of its initial capacity after 2500 cycles, respectively. The excellent capacity retention, particularly at 25 0C and even at elevated temperatures, highlights the robustness and stability of the CG(95)-rSi(5) anode for practical LIB applications requiring long cycle life and reliable performance across varying environmental conditions. The successful integration of recovered solar silicon into high-performance LIBs, as demonstrated by these results, underscores the potential of this disclosure to contribute to both sustainable materials management and the advancement of battery technology. The capacity values reported for the full cells are based on the total mass of active materials in both the anode and cathode, as is common practice in evaluating full cell performance. The disclosure thus provides a versatile and sustainable platform for developing high-performance lithium-based energy storage devices by effectively utilizing a valuable resource from the photovoltaic waste stream. The detailed embodiments presented herein, including the specific materials used, ratios investigated, fabrication steps, and electrochemical characterization results, serve to illustrate the technical feasibility and advantageous properties of the disclosed disclosure, without limiting the scope of the disclosure to these specific examples. Variations and modifications within the spirit and scope of the disclosure will be apparent to those skilled in the art. ADVANTAGES [0018] The present disclosure offers several significant advantages: 1. Sustainability: effectively utilizes silicon recovered from discarded solar panels, diverting waste and promoting a circular economy for photovoltaic materials. 2. Enhanced anode performance: the CG-rSi composite anode leverages the high theoretical capacity of silicon while mitigating its inherent volume expansion issues through combination with graphite, resulting in higher specific capacity compared to pure graphite. 3. Improved Energy and Power density: The use of high-capacity CG-rSi anode enables the fabrication of LIBs and LICs with enhanced energy density and power density. 4. Extended life cycle: the electrochemical pre-treatment and the synergistic effect of the CG-rSi composite structure contribute to the formation of stable SEI layer and improved mechanical integrity, leading to significantly enhanced cycling stability and longer operational life for the energy storage devices. 5. Versatility: The disclosed CG-rSi anode material is applicable to both Lithium-ion Battery and Lithium-ion Capacitor configurations, offering flexibility in designing energy storage solutions for diverse applications. 6. Cost Effectiveness: utilizing recovered silicon from a waste stream potentially reduces the material cost of anode fabrication compared to using pristine battery-grade silicon. , Claims: 1. An electrode for a Lithium-based electrochemical energy storage device comprising: I. a composite material comprising commercial graphite and silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic panels; II. a conductive additive; and III. a binder, coated on a current collector. 2. The electrode of claim 1, wherein the composite material comprises commercial graphite and recovered solar silicon in a weight ratio selected from the group consisting of CG(95)-rSi(5), CG(90)-rSi(10), CG(85)-rSi(15), and CG(80)-rSi(20). 3. The electrode of claim 2 wherein the weight ratio of commercial graphite to recovered silicon is approximately 95:5. 4. The electrode of claim 1, wherein the conductive additive is acetylene black. 5. The electrode of claim 1, wherein the binder is selected from the group consisting of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and teflonized acetylene black (TAB-2). 6. A lithium-based electrochemical storage device comprising: I. a negative electrode as claimed in claim 1 ; II. a positive electrode selected from the group consisting of activated carbon and LiMn2O4; III. a separator positioned between the negative electrode and positive electrode; and IV. a non-aqueous electrolyte comprising a Lithium salt dissolved in organic solvent mixture. 7. The device as claimed in claim 6, wherein the device is a Lithium-ion Capacitor, and the positive electrode in activated carbon. 8. The device as claimed in claim 6, wherein the device is a Lithium-ion Battery, and the positive electrode in LiMn2O4. 9. The device as claimed in claim 6, wherein the electrolyte comprises 1 M lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) in a 1:1 volume mixture of ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC), with the addition of 10 volume percent of fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). 10. A method for fabricating an electrode for a lithium-based electrochemical energy storage device, comprising the steps of: I. obtaining silicon from discarded photovoltaic panels; II. mechanically synthesizing a composite material comprising commercial graphite and the recovered silicon; III. preparing a slurry comprising the composite material, a conductive additive, and a binder; IV. casting the slurry onto a current collector to form an electrode layer; and V. electrochemically pre-treating the electrode layer in a lithium-containing environment.
