patents.abstract: ABSTRACT Power bank with programmable power delivery and lithium titanate energy storage. The invention utilizes a 1S4P configuration of LTO cells, enabling ultra-fast charging and extended cycle life. It incorporates a microcontroller-managed control system, a USB Power Delivery controller (STUSB4500), a Battery Management System (BMS) with active cell balancing, and integrated thermal protection. The power bank includes dual output ports such as USB-A (Quick Charge 3.0) and USB-C (Power Delivery) with support for dynamic voltage profiles. The system is designed for safe, efficient operation in demanding consumer and industrial applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION The present invention relates to portable energy storage systems. Specifically, the present invention relates to power bank using lithium titanate (LTO) batteries. More particularly, the present invention relates to Power Bank with Programmable Power Delivery and Lithium Titanate Energy Storage. BACKGROUND Traditional lithium-ion power banks degrade quickly with frequent use, provide limited fast-charging flexibility, and are prone to thermal issues. Most commercial power banks lack programmability and do not support dynamic charge/discharge profiles or battery life extension. Moreover, USB-C Power Delivery systems are often implemented without intelligent coordination between firmware and hardware. A known patent US10498274B2 describes a multi-port charging system with battery status indication but does not disclose integration of LTO chemistry with programmable USB Power Delivery (PD) and real-time active balancing using a smart Battery Management System (BMS). Therefore, there is a need for a rugged, intelligent power bank system integrating programmable USB-PD, thermal control, and a long-life LTO battery configuration. The present invention solves the above problem by offering a smart power bank built on LTO chemistry with active protection and power optimization through microcontroller logic and advanced circuitry. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION The main object of the present invention is to provide power bank with programmable power delivery and lithium titanate energy storage. It is one object of the present invention, wherein the power bank comprises dual output ports (USB-C PD and USB-A QC) controlled via firmware logic., and an advanced battery management system (BMS) for rapid charging, extended cycle life, and improved safety. It is one object of the present invention, wherein the said power bank provides a combination of a high-endurance battery system with advanced programmable control and safety features. It is another object of the present invention, wherein a smart BMS enables active cell balancing and thermal protection. It is one another object of the present invention, wherein dual output ports (USB-C PD and USB-A QC) controlled via firmware logic. It is yet another object of the present invention, wherein the said power bank utilize the STUSB4500 controller to dynamically negotiate USB power delivery voltages. It is one object of the present invention, wherein the said power bank uses a BQ25792 IC for charge control and power path management. It is one object of the present invention, wherein utilizes microcontroller to coordinate charging, discharging, safety logic, and display functions. It is one object of the present invention, wherein the said power bank system is safe, efficient, compact, and long-lasting, suitable for both consumer and industrial use. SUMMARY The main aspect of the present invention is to provide power bank with programmable power delivery and lithium titanate energy storage characterized in that lithium titanate battery pack connected to microcontroller, the said microcontroller is further connected to power delivery controller, PLOC converter and BLPCV converter, the said PLOC converter is connected to battery charging IC at one end and USB A and C output at another end, the display is connected to the BLPCV converter and the PLOC converter is further connected to boost converter. It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the said power bank further comprises a battery management system that is integrated with a thermal sensor for safety management and cell longevity; It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the said power bank further comprise ventilation slots and thermal pathways for passive cooling during high current discharge operations; It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the microcontroller firmware includes fault handling routines to trigger shutdown or throttle operations based on overheat or overload conditions; It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the USB Power Delivery is connected to an integrated circuit, enabling programmable voltage profiles for both input and output operations; and It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the charging of the battery cells are controlled by another integrated circuit supporting programmable charging rates, battery detection, and I2C communication with the microcontroller. It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein a boost converter to elevate the battery voltage to 5V for output supply through USB interfaces. It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the microcontroller monitors the battery parameters, controls input/output logic, displays status indicators, and communicates with power and charging ICs over I2C. It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein the output comprises a USB-A port with Quick Charge 3.0 support and a USB-C port supporting Power Delivery up to 12V. It is one aspect of the present invention, wherein all components are mechanically arranged to ensure compact enclosure with separate power and signal routing to reduce EMI. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS Figure 1 illustrates the block diagram of the connections of components in the power bank, according to the present invention. Figure 2 illustrates the schematic diagram of circuit displaying electrical interconnection of the power bank, according to the present invention. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF INVENTION WITH REFERENCE TO ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS With reference to the figures 1 and 2, the present invention comprises Lithium Titanate battery pack connected to microcontroller. The said microcontroller is further connected to power delivery controller, PLOC converter and BLPCV converter. The said PLOC converter is connected to battery charging IC at one end and USB A and C output at another end. The display output is given to BLPCV converter. The PLOC converter is further connected to boost converter. Specification of components of the present invention LTO Battery Pack (1S4P): Four cylindrical 2.4V LTO cells (Model 23680, 2.4V each) connected in parallel to provide high durability, ultra-fast charge, and long cycle life. The cells are placed on the rear side of the PCB with thermal sensors for precise temperature tracking. Battery Management System (JBD-HP01S001): Monitors cell balancing, temperature, overcharge, and short-circuit protection. It is thermally linked to the microcontroller for safety shutdowns. Power Management ICs • STUSB4500 (PD Controller): Manages dynamic power negotiation over USB-C input/output, with programmable voltage profiles (e.g., 5V, 9V, 12V). It controls input/output power negotiation via USB PD protocol. It enables the system to dynamically request or provide voltages from 5V to 12V. • BQ25792 (Battery Charging IC): Supports programmable charging logic, thermal monitoring, and power path switching. Interfaces with the MCU via I2C. It controls charging with thermal monitoring, programmable charging current, and dynamic power path control. • TPS61088 (Boost Converter): Converts battery voltage to 5V for output. Microcontroller Control : STM32 Microcontroller: Governs logic control, monitors thermal and power signals, communicates with STUSB4500 and BQ25792, updates display, and executes safety protocols. Displaying charge/discharge state on a digital screen. It monitors battery voltage, current, and temperature via I2C communication. Managing current limits and initiating protective shutdowns in case of faults. Output Interfaces: USB-A (QC 3.0) and USB-C (PD), routed through appropriate control ICs. USB-A port provides QC 3.0 output.USB-C port supports PD output and charging input. PD voltage profiles and limits are programmed via STUSB4500 registers Display/Indicators: LED/LCD shows battery level, temperature warnings, and status. Firmware Logic initializes and configures PD and charger ICs, monitors battery voltage and temperature, executes charging logic, displays status and shuts down system in case of fault. Battery management system: The smart BMS with active balancing ensures all LTO cells are maintained uniformly. Overcharge, overdischarge, thermal faults, and short circuits are monitored continuously. Mechanical and PCB Layout: PCB dimension: 12.5 cm × 8 cm, 2-layer FR4 with HASL/ENIG finish, Heat dissipation achieved using ventilation slots and copper traces, Enclosure designed with 0.5 cm clearance on all sides, mounting holes provided for casing and module fixation. Working of the invention: • Fast Recharge in 10-15 Minutes: A delivery person plugs the power bank in during a coffee break. The LTO battery rapidly charges to 80% in ~10 minutes due to high C-rate tolerance. • Extreme Weather Use: A trekker in the Himalayas uses the Neon Power Bank in sub-zero conditions. Traditional Li-ion cells degrade in cold, but LTO cells perform reliably even at-30°C. • Extended Lifespan: A heavy smartphone user uses the power bank every day. Unlike typical banks that last ~500 cycles, Neon delivers over 5000 charge cycles, lasting years longer. Advantages: A. Technical Edge • 10x Lifespan: >5000 charge cycles compared to 300–500 of Li-ion. • 10–15 Min Recharge: Drastically faster than standard power banks. • High Safety: Non-flammable, thermally stable at high and low temperatures. • Low Self-Discharge: LTO retains charge better over time. B. Market Differentiation • First-in-India: LTO-based smart power bank. • Premium durability positioning: Ideal for logistics, field operations, defense, and premium tech users. • Dual Output + Smart Display: USB PD + QC3.0 with live battery stats. C. Revenue Model Fit • Targeting 1 million units @ ₹2,500 = ₹250 crore topline. • Long life and premium features justify higher price → 50% gross margins possible. • Great fit for offline channels where feature demos influence purchase. , Claims:WE CLAIM 1. Power bank with programmable power delivery and lithium titanate energy storage characterized in that: a. a lithium titanate battery pack configured in a parallel cell arrangement; b. a microcontroller operatively connected to: a USB power delivery controller, a battery charging integrated circuit (IC), a boost converter, and a display interface; c. a battery management system comprising active cell balancing and an integrated thermal sensor; d. at least one USB-C port configured for programmable power delivery and at least one USB-A port supporting quick charge; e. firmware configured to monitor battery parameters, control charging and discharging logic, implement safety shutdowns, and dynamically adjust output profiles. Wherein the said battery management system is integrated with a thermal sensor for safety management and cell longevity; wherein the said power bank further comprises ventilation slots and thermal pathways for passive cooling during high current discharge operations; wherein the USB Power Delivery is connected to an integrated circuit, enabling programmable voltage profiles for both input and output operations; and wherein the charging of the battery cells are controlled by another integrated circuit supporting programmable charging rates, battery detection, and I2C communication with the microcontroller. 2. Power bank as claimed in claim 1, wherein the said microcontroller monitors the battery parameters, controls input or output logic, displays status indicators, and communicates with power and charging ICs over I2C. 3. Power bank as claimed in claim 1, wherein the USB Power Delivery controller is a configured to negotiate input and output voltages dynamically between 5V and 12V. 4. Power bank as claimed in claim 1, wherein all components are mechanically arranged to ensure compact enclosure with separate power and signal routing to reduce EMI. 5. Power bank as claimed in claim 1, wherein the microcontroller firmware includes fault handling routines to trigger shutdown or throttle operations based on overheat or overload conditions.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A METHOD FOR ELECTROLYTE FILLING AND LITHIUM-ION BATTERY CELL THEREOF The present disclosure provides a method for electrolyte filling for a lithium-ion battery cell, the method comprising: (i) degassing the battery c 5 ell at a pressure in a range of 0 kPa to 5 kPa; (ii) applying a high pressure at a range of 20 kPa to 50 kPa to fill the electrolyte into the battery cell; (iii) applying a low vacuum step at a range of-40 kPa to-90 kPa to create an internal vacuum in the battery-cell; (iv) optionally, applying high vacuum at a pressure in a range of-70 kPa to-90 kPa and (v) applying pressure in a range of 15 kPa to 10 30 kPa for complete electrolyte filling into the cell. The present disclosure further provides a lithium-ion battery cell filled with electrolyte using the method as disclosed herein.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [001] The subject matter of the present disclosure broadly relates to the field of battery, preferably lithium-ion battery. Particularly, the present disclosure relates to electrolyte filling methods for lithium-ion battery cells. 5 BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [002] Lithium-ion batteries have revolutionized portable electronics by providing a lightweight, high-capacity power source, largely owing to their exceptional energy density, extensive cycle life, and minimal self-discharge. The movement of lithium ions, which shuttle back and forth between the cathode and anode during charging and discharging cycles is the 10 most crucial functionality. This ion migration occurs through an electrolyte medium, which acts as a conductive pathway while simultaneously ensuring the electrochemical stability of the entire system. The electrolyte's composition, which is a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent must allow for efficient ion conduction, prevent electronic conductivity that could cause short circuits, and remain stable over a wide voltage range and temperature spectrum. 15 The quality and properties of the electrolyte are therefore pivotal in determining the battery's performance, safety, and longevity, making it a critical component in the design and optimization of lithium-ion battery technology. [003] The process of filling lithium-ion battery cells with electrolyte is a critical yet intricate step in manufacturing that significantly impacts the overall performance and reliability of the 20 battery. Traditional methods typically involve multiple filling cycles, each followed by a soaking period designed to ensure thorough permeation of the electrolyte into the porous electrode materials and separator layers. This multi-step approach aims to achieve complete wetting, which is essential for optimal ionic conductivity and uniform electrochemical behaviour across the cell. However, the extended duration of these repeated cycles can hinder 25 large-scale production efficiency, reducing throughput and increasing manufacturing costs. Moreover, the repeated handling increases the risk of electrolyte spillage, contamination, and material wastage, all of which can compromise product quality and safety. [004] In addition to time and safety concerns, conventional filling techniques often struggle to ensure uniform electrolyte distribution, especially in larger-format cells or those with 30 densely packed electrodes. Non-uniform wetting can lead to regions within the cell that have insufficient ionic pathways, resulting in decreased capacity, higher internal resistance, and accelerated capacity fade over time. Another significant challenge is the formation of trapped air pockets or voids within the cell structure during filling, which can create localized areas of 2 poor ion conductivity. These air pockets not only impair initial performance but can also cause long-term degradation, as they promote uneven current distribution and mechanical stress. [005] Hence, there is a need in the art for advanced filling economically significant methods capable of achieving full, uniform electrolyte saturation while minimizing defects, thereby enhancing t 5 he longevity and safety of lithium-ion batteries. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [006] In a first aspect of the present disclosure, there is provided a method for electrolyte filling for a lithium-ion battery cell, the method comprising: (i) degassing the battery cell at a pressure in a range of 0 kPa to 5 kPa; (ii) applying a high pressure at a range of 20 kPa to 50 10 kPa to fill the electrolyte into the battery cell; (iii) applying a low vacuum step at a range of-40 kPa to-90 kPa to create an internal vacuum in the battery-cell; (iv) optionally, applying high vacuum at a pressure in a range of-70 kPa to-90 kPa; and (v) applying pressure in a range of 15 kPa to 30 kPa for complete electrolyte filling into the cell. [007] In a second aspect of the present disclosure, there is provided a lithium-ion battery cell 15 filled with electrolyte using the method as disclosed herein. [008] These and other features, aspects, advantages of the present subject matter will be better understood with reference to the following description and appended claims. This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to 20 be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [009] The following drawings form a part of the present specification and are included to further illustrate aspects of the present disclosure. The disclosure may be better understood by reference to the drawings in combination with the detailed description of the specific 25 embodiments presented herein. [010] Figure 1 depicts computed tomography (CT) scan results for (a) multi-shot electrolyte filling process; (b) two-shot electrolyte filling process; and (c) single-shot electrolyte filling process, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION 30 [011] Those skilled in the art will be aware that the present disclosure is subject to variations and modifications other than those specifically described. It is to be understood that the present 3 disclosure includes all such variations and modifications. The disclosure also includes all such steps, features, compositions, and compounds referred to or indicated in this specification, individually or collectively, and any and all combinations of any or more of such steps or features. 5 Definitions [012] For convenience, before further description of the present disclosure, certain terms employed in the specification, and examples are delineated here. These definitions should be read in the light of the remainder of the disclosure and understood as by a person of skill in the art. The terms used herein have the meanings recognized and known to those of skill in the art, 10 however, for convenience and completeness, particular terms and their meanings are set forth below. [013] The articles “a”, “an” and “the” are used to refer to one or to more than one (i.e., to at least one) of the grammatical object of the article. [014] The terms “comprise” and “comprising” are used in the inclusive, open sense, meaning 15 that additional elements may be included. It is not intended to be construed as “consists of only”. [015] Throughout this specification, unless the context requires otherwise the word “comprise”, and variations such as “comprises” and “comprising”, will be understood to imply the inclusion of a stated element or step or group of elements or steps but not the exclusion of 20 any other element or step or group of elements or steps. [016] The term “including” is used to mean “including but not limited to”. “Including” and “including but not limited to” are used interchangeably. [017] The term “electrolyte filling” refers to the process of introducing the conductive medium into the cell to facilitate the movement of lithium ions between the cathode and anode 25 during charge and discharge cycles.. This step is crucial for enabling efficient ion transport, which directly impacts the battery’s performance, capacity, and lifespan. [018] The term "degassing" refers to the process of removing gases from the battery cell, typically performed under low pressure conditions to extract trapped air or other gaseous components from within the cell structure. In an aspect of the present disclosure, degassing of 30 the battery cell is carried out at a pressure in a range of 0 kPa to 5 kPa, where 0 kPa corresponds to atmospheric pressure. [019] The term "high pressure" in the context of electrolyte filling refers to the application of pressure significantly above atmospheric pressure to force electrolyte into the porous structures 4 of the battery cell components. In an aspect of the present disclosure, to fill the electrolyte into the battery cell, high pressure is applied at a range of 20 kPa to 50 kPa. [020] The term "low vacuum" describes a state of reduced pressure that is moderately below atmospheric pressure, used to create a partial vacuum within the battery cell to facilitate electrolyte penetration. In an aspect of the present 5 disclosure, to create an internal vacuum in the battery-cell, low vacuum is applied at a range of-40 kPa to-90 kPa. [021] The term "high vacuum" refers to a state of very low pressure, approaching a nearcomplete vacuum, used to remove residual gases and ensure thorough electrolyte distribution. In an aspect of the present disclosure, high vacuum is applied at a pressure in a range of-70 10 kPa to-90 kPa. [022] The term “single filling” refers to the process of introducing the electrolyte into a battery cell in one continuous and complete step, rather than multiple partial fills or iterative injections. It ensures that the electrolyte is uniformly distributed throughout the cell's internal components in a single operation, which helps to minimize the risk of air entrapment, uneven 15 wetting, or contamination. [023] The term "injection cycles" refer to the discrete instances of introducing electrolyte into the battery cell during the filling process. In an aspect of the present disclosure, the electrolyte is injected into the lithium-ion battery cell in 15 to 16 injection cycles during the single filling cycle. 20 [024] The term "electrolyte" refers to the ionically conductive medium in a lithium-ion battery that facilitates the movement of lithium ions between the cathode and anode during charge and discharge cycles. [025] The term "lithium-ion battery cell" refers to an electrochemical cell or a combination of electrochemical cells wherein the cell undergoes chemical reactions that get converted and 25 stored as electrical energy. [026] The term "cylindrical cell" refers to a type of lithium-ion battery cell that has a cylindrical shape, typically characterized by a tubular metal casing that houses the electrode assembly and electrolyte. It is a specific geometry of lithium-ion battery where the electrodes and separator are rolled into a cylindrical shape and enclosed in a cylindrical casing. In an 30 aspect the present disclosure, cylindrical cell is selected from wet NMC, dry NMC, wet LiFePO4 without core tube.. [027] The term “cathode” refers to the positive terminal where ions gain electrons (are reduced) during discharge. In an aspect of the present disclosure, cathode is selected from layered metal oxides, spinel metal oxides or olivine phosphates. 5 [028] The term "layered metal oxides" refers to a class of cathode materials with a layered crystal structure, typically including compounds such as lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2) or lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC). [029] The term "spinel metal oxides" refers to a cathode material with a three-dimensional cubic crystal structure, known as 5 the spinel structure, which follows the general formula AB₂O₄, such as lithium manganese oxide (LiMn2O4). In this structure, metal cations occupy specific sites within an oxygen anion framework, resulting in a highly stable and conductive material. [030] The term "olivine phosphates" refers to cathode materials with an olivine crystal 10 structure, which has the general formula LiMPO₄, where M typically represents transition metals such as iron, manganese, or cobalt, the most common being lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4). [031] The term “anode” refers to the electrode where lithium or other ions are released (oxidized) during discharge, and it typically serves as the negative terminal. In an aspect of the 15 present disclosure, anode is selected from graphite, silicon, silicon-carbon composites, or Lithium Titanate Oxide (LTO). [032] Ratios, concentrations, amounts, and other numerical data may be presented herein in a range format. It is to be understood that such range format is used merely for convenience and brevity and should be interpreted flexibly to include not only the numerical values 20 explicitly recited as the limits of the range, but also to include all the individual numerical values or sub-ranges encompassed within that range as if each numerical value and sub-range is explicitly recited. [033] Unless defined otherwise, all technical and scientific terms used herein have the same meaning as commonly understood by one of ordinary skills in the art to which this disclosure 25 belongs. Although any methods and materials similar or equivalent to those described herein can be used in the practice or testing of the disclosure, the preferred methods, and materials are now described. All publications mentioned herein are incorporated herein by reference. [034] The present disclosure is not to be limited in scope by the specific embodiments described herein, which are intended for the purposes of exemplification only. Functionally 30 equivalent products, and methods are clearly within the scope of the disclosure, as described herein. [035] As discussed in the background, conventional methods for electrolyte filling in lithiumion battery cells often involve multi-shot or two-shot processes, which are time-consuming and may lead to inconsistent electrolyte distribution. These methods typically require multiple 6 filling cycles and extended soaking periods, resulting in low production rates and potential electrolyte wastage. Additionally, the prolonged exposure of battery components to air during these processes may introduce impurities and affect cell performance. Therefore, the present disclosure addresses these limitations by introducing a single-shot electrolyte filling process for lithium-ion battery cells. patents.abstract: The present invention discloses a highly integrated and programmable quantum simulation platform utilizing ultracold fermionic Lithium-6 atoms confined in a two-dimensional optical lattice, combined with atom-resolved quantum gas microscopy and a chip-scale control architecture. The system enables the real-time emulation of strongly correlated quantum systems, condensed matter phenomena, and quantum information dynamics with unprecedented precision. In this method, Lithium-6 atoms are first cooled to quantum degeneracy using a synergistic combination of evaporative cooling, Raman sideband cooling, and magneto-optical trapping. These atoms are then loaded into a dynamically configurable 2D optical lattice formed by interference of precisely phase-locked laser beams. The lattice potential depth, geometry, and inter-site spacing are tunable in situ, supporting multiple topologies including square, triangular, and honeycomb lattices. A quantum gas microscope with a high numerical aperture objective lens is employ
patents.complete_specification: Description:Field of the Invention: The present invention lies at the intersection of quantum technologies, atomic physics, and condensed matter simulation, with a focus on the site-resolved control and observation of ultracold fermionic atoms, specifically Lithium-6, confined in two-dimensional optical lattice traps. It encompasses the design and implementation of atom-resolved microscopy techniques integrated with quantum simulator chip architectures to realize programmable quantum systems at the single-particle level. This invention enables the direct investigation of emergent quantum phases, spin-ordering phenomena, and correlated fermionic behavior in engineered low-dimensional geometries, offering a scalable platform for next-generation quantum computation, simulation of many-body physics, and precision quantum metrology. patents.abstract: Abstract A novel Li-Ni-Co-Mg-Al-0 (LNCMAO) layered oxide cathode was developed to achieve ultra-long cycle life and high-power output in lithium-ion batteries. The material exhibits a high initial discharge capacity of205 mAh'g-1 at 0.1 C. After I ,000 charge-discharge cycles at I C, the capacity retention remains above 90%, confinning excellent stmctural stability. The rate capability is outstanding, maintaining 155 mAh g-1 at 5 C, suitable for fast-. charging applications. XRD analysis reveals a well-maintained layered a-NaFeO, structure with reduced cation mixing due to Mg and AI co-doping. SEM images show unifom1 particle morphology with minimal surface degradation after cycling. TEM confinns homogeneous elemental distribution and suppression ofmicrocr01ck formation. The addition ofMg stabilizes the lattice, while AI improves thermal stability and reduces phase transitions. The cathode also shows improved them1al decomposition onset temperature, increasing safety margins above 250 °C. Overall, LNCMAO offers a promising pathway toward next-generation electric vehicle and grid-scale energy storage batteries.
patents.complete_specification: 4.1 BACKGROUND OF INVENTION The increasing global demand for high-perfom1ance energy storage systems has driven extensive research and development efforts toward· improving lithium-ion battery (LIB) technology. Over the past few decades, LIBs have become the dominant power source for portable electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and stationary energy storage applications due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and reliable safety profile. However, the accelerating shift toward large-scale electrification, including-electric mobility and renewable energy integration, demands further enhancements in cycle llfe, power density, thermal stability, and overall safety. Among the critical components of a lithium-ion battery, the cathode material plays a pivotal role in detem1ining its capacity, rate capability, energy density, and long-term stability. Conventional layered transition metal oxides such as LiCo02, LiNio-xCo,02, and their derivatives have been widely u·sed due to their high voltage operation and acceptable specific capacities. Nevertheless, these materials still face significant limitations, including capacity fading, structural instability under high-voltage operation, and thennal degradation during prolonged cycling [ 1-5]. In recent years, nickel-rich layered oxides, specifically LiNio .• Coo.,sAio.os02 (commonly known as NCA) and LiNio.,Mno.,Coo.,O, (NMC), have gained considerable attention due to their higher specific capacities (up to-200 mAh g-') and lower cobalt content, thereby reducing cost and addressing ethical sourcing issues. However, nickel-rich cathodes are prone to surface microcracking, severe cation mixing, and lattice oxygen release at elevated voltages, which compromise cycling stability and safety. These ·challenges are exacerbated under high-rate operation and high-temperature conditions commonly encountered in electric vehicle applications. As a result, there is an urgent need to develop advanced cathode materials with improved structural integrity, reduced degradation mechanisms, and enhanced thermal properties to meet stringent perfom1ance requirements [6-8]. Recent strategies to overcome these challenges include elemental doping and surface modification. Doping with suitable elements can effectively stabilize the crystal lattice, suppress detrimental phase transitions, and mitigate capacity loss over extended cycling. Magnesium and aluminum have emerged as promising dopants owing to their ability to improve the structural stability of layered cathode materials. Magnesium ions (Mg>+) occupy transition metal sites, effectively reducing cation mixing between lithium and nickel and enhancing lattice rigidity. Moreover, aluminum doping has been shown to enhance-thcm1al stability and inhibit oxygen evolution reactions, thereby improving the overall safety profile of the cathode material. The incorporation of aluminum also reduces lattice distortion and enhances the mechanical strength of the pmticles, which is crucial for minimizing particle pulverization and maintaining electrochemical performance over a large number of cycles. The concept of multi-element doping introduces synergistic effects that go beyond the individual benefits of single-clement doping. In _the context of Li-Ni-Co-Mg-AI-0 systems, magnesium and aluminum work cooperatively to stabilize .the layered structure, suppress microcrack propagation, and improve high-temperature perfonnance. The resulting cathode material denionstrates superior stmctural robustness and electrochemical reversibility, addressing key shortcomings associated with traditional nickel-rich oxides. Furth.ermore, the introduction of Mg and AI can help reduce the fom1ation of detrimental rock-salt or spinel phases. during repeated charge-discharge cycles. This phase stability is critical in maintaining high capacity retention and rninimizing impedance growth, which directly impacts the battery's Electrochemical studies on Li-Ni-Co-Mg-Al-0 cathodes have revealed promising data.--For instance, cells assembled with these advanced catl1odes exhibit initial discharge capacities exceeding 200 mAh g-1 .at low cun-ent rates (0.1 C) and maintain more than 90% capacity retention after I ,000 cycles at I C. Such performance metrics highlight the exceptional cycling stability and suitability for high-energy applications. Additionally, high-rate capability tests demonstrate that these cathodes can deliver over 150 mAh g-1 even at 5 C rates, ·contim1ing r-their potential for fast-charging and high-power scenarios. These remarkable improvements are attributed to the combined effects of improved lattice stability, reduced interfacial side reactions, and enhanced lithium-ion diffusion kinetics facilitated by Mg and AI doping [ 15-18). Beyond performance improvements, the Li-Ni-Co-Mg-Al-0 cathode system als.o addresses safety conceros, a critical consideration for commercial applicatiQns. Thermal stability studies using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thennogravimetric analysis (TGA) have shown that these cathodes exhibit higher decomposition onset temperatures, often above 250 °C, which reduces the risk of thennal nmaway and improves battery safety under abusive conditions. This enhanced them1al rohustness makes the Li-Ni-Co-Mg-Al-0 system particularly attractive for automotive and aerospace applications, where stringent safety standards are essential. Moreover, the environmental and economic aspects of battery manufacturing are becoming increasingly important. The reduced cobalt content in Li-Ni-Co-Mg-Al-0 cathodes not only alleviates reliance on a critical raw material with fluctuating supply and ethical concerns but also contributes to lowering overall material costs. By partially substituting cobalt with magnesium and aluminum, the cathode maintains high electrochemical perfom1ance without compromising sustainability objectives. This is in line with global initiatives to develop eco-friendly and ethically sourced battery technologies, further supporting the commercial viability of this advanced cathode system [19-21]. In addition to doping strategies, particle morphology and surface design also play a crucial role in the performance of cathode materials. Spherical secondary particle structures composed of natw-sized primary particles· help mitigate internal stress and suppress surface reactivity, thus minimizing side reactions with the electrolyte. The Li-Ni-Co-Mg-AI-0 cathodes often exhibit such well-controlled microstructures, contributing to their excellent cycling durability and rate capability. Advanced characterization techniques such os X-ray ditli-action (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy. (TEM) have been employed to confim1 the uniform distribution of dopant elements, the preservation of layered structures, and the suppression of undesired secondary phases throughout cycling. Over the past two decades, significant research efforts have focused on the development of advanced cathode materials to nleet the rapidly increasing demands for higher energy flensity, longer lifespan, and improved safety. Conventional cathode materials, such as LiCoO,, were among the earliest widely commercialized layered oxides. While LiCoO, delivers a stable voltage and relatively good capacity (-140 mAh g-1), it suffers from high material costs, safety concerns at high voltages, and structural instability during prolonged cycling. To address these issues, nickel-rich layered oxides, such as LiNio.sCoo.lSAiocosO, (NCA) and LiNio.sMno.,Coo .• O, (NMC), were introduced. Nevertheless, nickel-rich oxides present challenges related to structural degradation, microcrack formation, and them1al instability, particularly when charged to high voltages above 4.2 V. These issues stem from increased cation mixing between . . lithium and nickel ions, oxygen release from the lattice at high states of charge, and fom1ation of microcracks that propagate during cycling, .leading to rapid capacity fade and safety risks. Numerous studies have focused on doping strategies to stabilize nickel-rich cathodes. For instance, aluminum doping has been employed to reinforce the crystal lattice, enhancing thcm1al stability and suppressing detrimental phase transfom1ations. Aluminum's strong bonding with oxygen improves lattice cohesion, t~ereby reducing oxygen release and minimizing surface degradation. However, aluminum alone does not sufficiently address cation mixing or microcrack propagation, particularly under aggressive cycling and high-temperature conditions. Similarly, magnesium has been investigated as a dopant to reduce cation mixing and improve structural stability by occupying transition metal sites and reinforcing the lattice. While magnesium doping enhances certain structural properties, it may slightly compromise initial capaci.ty if not carefully optimized. Other approaches in the related art include surface coatings to protect cathode materials. Metal oxide coatings such as AbO,, TiO,, and ZrO, have been shown to mitigate electrolyte decomposition and transition metal dissolution, thereby improving cycle life and high-voltage perfonnance. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a lithium-ion battery module (100) featuring a cell assembly (102) comprising a plurality of cylindrical lithium-ion cells arranged in a predetermined configuration within a flame-retardant housing. An optimized bus bar assembly (104) having wide surface areas and streamlined current pathways is secured in designated slots of the housing using integrated snap-lock mechanisms. Electrical connections between the cell assembly (102) and the bus bar assembly (104) are established using a plurality of ultrasonic wire bonds, wherein each cell terminal is bonded with at least two aluminum wires through an ultrasonic bonding process, minimizing thermal damage and ensuring low-resistance, vibration-resistant connections. A temperature sensor (106) monitors internal thermal conditions and interfaces with an integrated power control board assembly (IPCBA) (108), which manages AC grid charging, solar charging via MPPT, and DC to AC conversion. A battery management system (BMS) interface (110) continuously monitors voltage levels across each series segment.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [001] The present invention pertains to the field of advanced energy storage systems. More particularly, the present invention relates to a lithium-ion battery module architecture that employs an optimized configuration of an innovative bus bar arrangement for enhanced electrical conductivity and thermal performance. BACKGROUND OF INVENTION [002] Lithium-ion battery modules have become essential components in electric vehicles, portable electronics and stationary energy storage systems, owing to their superior energy density, rechargeability, and cycle life. In the prior art, various configurations of lithium-ion cell arrangements and electrical interconnection techniques have been developed to improve energy output and safety. However, most conventional battery modules still rely on spot welding or laser welding techniques to connect individual battery cells to bus bars or interconnect plates. These bonding techniques, while widely adopted, present several challenges. [003] Firstly, spot welding and laser welding generate significant heat during the bonding process, which can cause localized damage to battery cells, degrading their electrochemical performance and longevity. Secondly, these methods often result in inconsistent bonding strength and varying contact resistance, leading to uneven current distribution across the cells. This non-uniformity not only reduces the energy efficiency of the battery module but also causes the formation of thermal hotspots, posing safety hazards such as cell venting or thermal runaway. [004] Moreover, conventional bus bar designs in battery modules are often bulky and inadequately optimized for even current flow. The lack of streamlined current pathways increases resistive losses and contributes to unnecessary heat generation. Additionally, existing battery module housings and structural designs do not sufficiently address the thermal management challenges associated with high-density energy storage applications, such as electric vehicles and grid energy storage systems. [005] There remains a critical need for a battery module design that minimizes internal resistance, optimizes current flow, and enhances thermal management without introducing the detrimental effects associated with traditional bonding processes. A solution that addresses these deficiencies would improve the safety, efficiency, and durability of lithium-ion battery modules and enable their broader application in demanding energy storage environments. SUMMARY OF INVENTION [006] The present invention provides an advanced lithium-ion battery module designed to overcome the limitations associated with conventional battery module architectures. The invention introduces a novel integration of optimized electrical, mechanical, and thermal management features to enhance the safety, performance, and longevity of the battery module in demanding energy storage applications. [007] At the heart of the invention is a cell assembly comprising a plurality of cylindrical lithium-ion cells arranged in a predetermined configuration, such as a series-parallel arrangement, to achieve a specific voltage and capacity output. These cells are housed within a flame-retardant enclosure fabricated from a high-grade thermoplastic material. The housing not only imparts structural rigidity but also provides thermal insulation and flame resistance, thereby safeguarding the cells against mechanical stresses and thermal events. [008] An innovative bus bar assembly, formed from conductive metals such as aluminum or copper, is positioned within the battery module housing. The bus bar assembly is engineered with wide surface areas and streamlined pathways, ensuring optimized current flow, minimized resistive losses, and even distribution of electrical load across the cells. The bus bars are mechanically secured using integrated snap-lock mechanisms that align and retain the bus bars within the housing, ensuring precision and structural stability. [009] A key feature of the invention lies in the method of forming electrical connections between the battery cells and the bus bar assembly. Unlike conventional spot welding or laser welding techniques, the present invention employs ultrasonic wire bonding. In this process, each cell terminal is bonded to the bus bar using at least two aluminum wires. The ultrasonic bonding process is characterized by the absence of localized heat, thereby preserving the electrochemical integrity of the cells and preventing thermal damage during assembly. This technique results in consistent, low-resistance, and vibration-resistant electrical connections, improving overall module reliability. [010] The invention further incorporates a temperature sensing mechanism strategically positioned within the cell assembly. This temperature sensor enables real-time thermal monitoring of the battery module, providing critical data for thermal management. The sensor is electrically interfaced with an integrated power control board assembly, which serves as the central energy management system for the module. [011] The integrated power control board assembly facilitates advanced energy management functionalities, including managing the charging and discharging operations of the battery module. It supports AC grid charging, solar charging through a maximum power point tracking (MPPT) mechanism, and DC to AC power conversion, making the battery module compatible with a variety of power sources and load profiles. The board assembly may further integrate smart features such as wireless communication for remote monitoring and firmware updates. [012] Voltage monitoring is achieved through a battery management system interface electrically coupled to the bus bar assembly. This interface continuously monitors the voltage levels of each series segment of the cell assembly, ensuring balanced charging and preventing overvoltage or undervoltage conditions across the module. [013] The synergy between the ultrasonic bonding process, the optimized bus bar architecture, and the integrated power and thermal management components yields significant improvements in electrical conductivity, thermal performance, and safety compared to conventional lithium-ion battery modules. These technical enhancements make the battery module particularly well-suited for use in electric vehicles, residential and industrial energy storage systems, portable power applications, and renewable energy grid balancing. [014] The invention may further include variations in the cell configuration, housing materials, and bus bar geometry to tailor the module's performance to specific applications. Additional enhancements may involve integrating heat dissipation pathways into the bus bars and customizing ultrasonic bonding parameters to accommodate different lithium-ion cell chemistries. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [015] The accompanying drawings, which are incorporated in and constitute a part of this specification, show certain aspects of the subject matter disclosed herein and together with the description, help explain some of the principles associated with the disclosed implementations. In the drawing, [016] Figure 1 illustrates a perspective view of the lithium-ion battery module showing the overall arrangement of the housing; [017] Figure 2 depicts an exploded view of the battery module, highlighting the housing components; [018] Figure 3 illustrates a top view of the bus bar arrangement, showing the streamlined current pathways and wide surface area design; [019] Figure 4 shows a sectional view of the battery module housing along with the brass inserts used to secure the components within the housing; [020] Figure 5 depicts the positive end bus bar, the negative end bus bar, the arrangement of the lithium-ion cells, and the aluminum wires connecting the cells to the bus bar assembly; [021] Figure 6 illustrates various views of the battery module, including side, front view highlighting the external structure and positioning of key components; [022] Figure 7 shows the bottom cover plate of the battery module, highlighting its design features and attachment mechanism; [023] Figure 8 illustrates the top cover plate of the battery module, highlighting its structural design; [024] Figure 9 depicts the negative busbar cover, showing its arrangement and how it provides insulation and mechanical protection for the negative end bus bar; [025] Figure 10 illustrates the positive busbar cover, showing its arrangement and how it provides insulation and mechanical protection for the positive end bus bar; [026] Figure 11 depicts the positive end bus bar, showing its design and how it is mounted relative to the battery cells within the battery module enclosure; [027] Figure 12 illustrates the series bus bar, showing its configuration and electrical connection across multiple lithium-ion cells to facilitate series connection within the battery module; [028] Figure 13 depicts the negative end bus bar, showing its design and how it is mounted relative to the battery cells within the battery module enclosure; [029] Figure 14 illustrates the assembled battery module showing the interconnection of sub-components; [030] Figure 15 shows the top and bottom cover plates and their attachment using bolts; [031] Figure 16 illustrates the assembled battery module showing the interconnection of sub-components; [032] Finally, figure 17 illustrates the process flow diagram for assembling the battery module. [036] The following detailed description provides an in-depth understanding of the advanced lithium-ion battery module, its construction, and operation. The invention integrates advanced electrical and mechanical engineering principles to create a robust, thermally efficient, and energy-dense battery module suitable for a wide range of energy storage applications. The detailed embodiments described herein aim to overcome the deficiencies of conventional battery module designs, offering an optimized solution that balances electrical conductivity, structural integrity, and thermal management. The invention will now be described with reference to its various components, assembly processes, and alternative configurations without limiting its scope to the embodiments disclosed herein. [037] The present invention discloses a lithium-ion battery module (1) designed to deliver enhanced electrical performance, mechanical stability, and thermal management through an optimized configuration of components and assembly methods. [038] Referring to Figure 1, the lithium-ion battery module (1) is shown in a perspective view, illustrating the complete assembly of the housing, top cover plate (10), and bottom cover plate (7). The housing securely encloses the lithium-ion cells (6) and the internal bus bar arrangement, providing an overview of how the individual components fit together to form a compact and integrated module. [039] In Figure 2, an exploded view of the battery module (1) is presented. This figure highlights the sequential arrangement of components during assembly, including the positioning of the brass inserts (2) within the housing to receive the series bus bar (3), positive end bus bar (4), and negative end bus bar (5). The lithium-ion cells (6) are centrally aligned, and the interconnecting aluminum wires (9) demonstrate the pathways for ultrasonic bonding. The relationship between the structural components and electrical pathways becomes clear in this view. [040] Figure 3 provides a top view of the bus bar assembly. The optimized geometry of the series bus bar (3), positive end bus bar (4), and negative end bus bar (5) is evident, showing their wide surface areas and streamlined current pathways designed to minimize resistive losses. This view complements Figures 2 and 5 by showing how the bus bars interface with the terminals of the lithium-ion cells (6). [041] As shown in Figure 4, a sectional view of the battery module (1) housing displays the strategic placement of the brass inserts (2) within the molded housing channels. These inserts provide mechanical rigidity and electrical isolation, ensuring secure mounting of the bus bar assembly as previously indicated in Figure 2. The section also shows the containment provided by the housing for the lithium-ion cells (6). [042] Figure 5 depicts the internal electrical layout, detailing how the positive end bus bar (4) and negative end bus bar (5) are positioned relative to the lithium-ion cells (6). This figure highlights the ultrasonic bonding of aluminum wires (9) connecting the cells to the bus bars. It directly relates to Figures 2 and 3, emphasizing the critical function of secure, low-resistance electrical connections. [043] In Figure 6, various external views of the battery module (1) are illustrated, including side and front views. These perspectives show the robust design of the housing and demonstrate how the top cover plate (10) and bottom cover plate (7) protect the internal components described in Figures 1 through 5. [044] Figure 7 shows the design of the bottom cover plate (7), illustrating how it fits onto the housing. The attachment mechanism using bottom cover plate bolts (8) ensures the structural integrity of the module, enclosing the components shown in Figure 2. [045] Figure 8 details the top cover plate (10), illustrating its mounting provision using M4 top cover plate bolts (11). This cover plate seals the battery module from above, providing protection for the bus bar assembly and lithium-ion cells shown in Figures 3 and 5. [046] Figure 9 shows the negative busbar cover (14), demonstrating how it fits over the negative end bus bar (5) to provide electrical insulation and mechanical protection. This cover is positioned as shown in the assembly sequence of Figure 2 and complements the internal arrangement seen in Figure 5. [047] In Figure 10, the positive busbar cover (12) is illustrated. Similar to the negative busbar cover (14), this component shields the positive end bus bar (4), ensuring safe operation of the electrical assembly depicted in Figures 3 and 5. [048] Figure 11 isolates the positive end bus bar (4), highlighting its structural features such as connection tabs and mounting holes. This figure correlates with Figures 3, 5, and 10, providing a clear understanding of the bus bar’s role in the electrical interconnection scheme. [049] Figure 12 details the series bus bar (3), showing how it connects adjacent lithium-ion cells (6) in series to form the required voltage configuration of the battery module (1). This complements the electrical layout shown in Figures 3 and 5. [050] Figure 13 depicts the negative end bus bar (5), showing its pathways for connecting the negative terminals of the lithium-ion cells (6). It works in conjunction with the series bus bar (3) and positive end bus bar (4) as seen in Figures 3, 5, and 9. [051] Figure 14 illustrates a partially assembled battery module (1), demonstrating the interconnection of internal components, including the bus bars, lithium-ion cells (6), and protective covers. This figure visually bridges the assembly progression from Figure 2 to the final product shown in Figure 16. [052] In Figure 15, the assembly of the top cover plate (10) and bottom cover plate (7) using bolts (11, 13) is shown, enclosing the components identified in Figures 2, 5, and 6. This step secures the entire assembly, preparing the battery module for operational use. [053] Figure 16 presents the fully assembled lithium-ion battery module (1). All sub-components, including the housing, electrical connections, bus bars, and cover plates, are integrated into a compact, operationally ready unit. This figure represents the culmination of the assembly process outlined in the previous figures. [054] Finally figure 17 illustrated the process flow diagram for assembly of the Battery module. [055] The design of the lithium-ion battery module (1) ensures ease of assembly and maintenance while providing secure electrical connections, effective heat dissipation, and robust mechanical protection. This configuration is suitable for electric vehicles, stationary energy storage systems, and renewable energy grid balancing, offering enhanced safety and reliability. [056] The following detailed description describes various embodiments of the lithium-ion battery module (1) and methods of its assembly. While specific configurations and materials are discussed, these are illustrative and do not limit the scope of the invention. [057] The lithium-ion battery module (1) comprises a cell assembly that includes a plurality of cylindrical lithium-ion cells (6) arranged in a predefined configuration, such as a 6S-20P arrangement, designed to achieve desired voltage and capacity characteristics. The cell assembly is housed within a flame-retardant plastic enclosure that provides structural rigidity and thermal insulation, ensuring the safety and integrity of the battery module (1) during operation. [058] The module further includes a bus bar assembly formed from conductive metals like aluminum or copper. This includes a series bus bar (3), a positive end bus bar (4), and a negative end bus bar (5). The bus bar assembly is designed with streamlined current pathways and a wide surface area to optimize current flow and minimize resistive losses. The bus bars are secured within the housing using brass inserts (2) and integrated snap-lock mechanisms for ease of assembly and mechanical stability. Electrical connections between the lithium-ion cells (6) and the bus bar assembly are established using ultrasonic wire bonding. Each cell terminal is bonded with at least two aluminum wires (9) through an ultrasonic bonding process, creating robust, low-resistance connections without introducing thermal stress to the cells (6). This bonding technique results in vibration-resistant and highly reliable electrical interconnections. [059] A temperature sensor (200) is positioned within the cell assembly and is configured to monitor the internal thermal conditions of the battery module (1). The sensor interfaces with a power control board (17), which is responsible for managing the charging and discharging operations. The power control board (17) supports various charging options including AC grid charging, solar charging via a maximum power point tracking (MPPT) mechanism, and DC to AC conversion for load supply. [060] Additionally, a battery management system (BMS) interface is electrically coupled to the bus bar assembly. The BMS interface continuously monitors the voltage levels across each series segment of the cell assembly, enabling precise battery management and enhancing the safety and performance of the module. [061] The housing components include a top cover plate (10), a bottom cover plate (7), positive busbar cover (12), negative busbar cover (14), and brass inserts (2). These components collectively provide mechanical protection and electrical insulation for the internal components. The top and bottom cover plates are attached using bolts (11, 13), studs (15), and nuts (17), ensuring secure enclosure of the battery module components. Bushes (16) are provided for mechanical isolation and alignment. [062] The assembled battery module (1) is well-suited for applications in electric vehicles, stationary energy storage systems, and renewable energy grid balancing. It offers improved electrical conductivity, thermal performance, and operational safety over conventional lithium-ion battery modules. [063] Referring to the figure 1, the lithium-ion battery module (1) of the present invention consists of several integrated assemblies and processes. A Cell Assembly comprises multiple cylindrical lithium-ion cells (6) arranged in a 6S-20P configuration, where six groups of twenty parallel cells are connected in series to achieve the required voltage and capacity characteristics. These cells are housed in the module enclosure (1) casing fabricated from ABS fire-retardant grade plastic which providing structural rigidity and flame resistance. [064] A Bus Bar Assembly comprises a series bus bar (3), positive bus bar (4) and negative bus bar (5) constructed from aluminum or copper is strategically positioned within the module (1) housing. These bus bars are inserted into designated slots and secured using snap-lock mechanisms molded into the ABS casing. The bus bars assembly are designed with wide surface areas and streamlined pathways to ensure optimal current distribution and minimal electrical resistance. The design further incorporates features to facilitate heat dissipation, thereby mitigating the formation of hotspots during operation. [065] Electrical interconnections between the cell’s assembly (2) and the bus bars (4, 5) are formed using Ultrasonic Wire (9) Bonding. This process employs two aluminum wires per cell terminal, bonded ultrasonically to the bus bar surface. Ultrasonic bonding eliminates the need for localized heating during the bonding process, preserving the electrochemical integrity of the battery cells. This results in low-resistance, reliable, and vibration-resistant connections that enhance overall module safety and performance. [066] A Temperature Sensor (200) is embedded within the cell array to monitor internal temperatures. This sensor (200) is connected to the Integrated Power Control Board Assembly hereinafter referred as IPCBA (17), enabling real-time thermal management and preventing overheating. A Battery Management System hereinafter referred as BMS Interface (110) includes voltage sensing wires connected to the bus bars (3, 4, 5) to continuously monitor the voltage of each series segment. The IPCBA (17) facilitates system-level power management. It includes provisions for AC grid charging, solar charging via a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) mechanism, and DC to AC conversion to supply power to household or industrial loads. The IPCBA (17) is directly connected to the module’s positive and negative terminals, integrating the battery pack into a smart energy management system. The assembly process involves arranging lithium-ion cells (6) in the prescribed configuration, installing the bus bars, performing ultrasonic bonding, inserting thermal and voltage sensors, and connecting power terminals to the IPCBA. Once assembled, the system is ready for integration into smart home energy storage solutions, electric vehicles, or other energy storage applications. [067] Alternative embodiments may include variations in the cell configuration, such as 4S, 5S, 6S (20P-10P), depending on specific application requirements. The bus bar design may incorporate integrated current and temperature sensors to enable more granular monitoring. The module housing may be fabricated from advanced polymer composites to further improve thermal conductivity. Additionally, ultrasonic bonding parameters such as power, frequency, and bonding time can be customized for compatibility with different lithium-ion chemistries, such as NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) and LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate). The advanced battery module described herein is ideally suited for applications including electric vehicle drivetrains, residential and industrial energy storage systems, portable power stations, and renewable energy grid balancing system. [068] In a further embodiment of the present invention, referring to the figure 17, there is provided a method for assembling the advanced lithium-ion battery module (100), wherein the method is executed in a sequential and systematic manner to ensure structural integrity, electrical reliability, and operational safety of the module. [069] At step (300), the method commences with arranging a plurality of cylindrical lithium-ion cells referred as cell assembly (2) at step (302) in a 6S-20P configuration, wherein the cell assembly (2) are securely positioned within a module (100) casing fabricated from ABS fire-retardant grade plastic. This casing serves the dual purpose of providing a structurally stable enclosure while also delivering flame-retardant properties essential for safety compliance. [070] At step (304), a bus bar assembly (3, 4, 5), preferably composed of aluminum or copper, is positioned within the designated slots of the module casing. The bus bars (3, 4, 5) are affixed in place by means of snap-lock mechanisms integrally formed in the ABS housing, thereby ensuring accurate alignment and secure retention of the bus bars within the assembly. [071] At step (306) and (308), the method involves the connection of the battery management system referred as BMS (110) sensing wires to the bus bars (3, 4, 5). These wires are meticulously routed through the module and coupled to the Integrated Power Control Board Assembly (IPCBA) (17), thus facilitating continuous voltage monitoring across each series-connected segment of the cell assembly. [072] Following the establishment of preliminary electrical connections, ultrasonic wire bonding is performed. In this step, each lithium-ion cell terminal is bonded to the corresponding bus bar using two aluminum wires per cell, where the bonding process is accomplished through an ultrasonic wire bonding machine. This technique establishes uniform, low-resistance electrical junctions without introducing thermal stresses to the cells, thereby preserving their electrochemical integrity. [073] At step (310) and (312), a temperature sensor (200) is inserted strategically within the cell array to enable accurate thermal monitoring. This sensor (200) is electrically interfaced with the IPCBA (17), allowing for real-time detection and management of temperature variations within the battery module (1). [074] At step (314), the main positive and negative terminals of the fully assembled battery module are then connected to the corresponding DC input terminals of the IPCBA (17), thereby establishing the primary power pathways between the battery cells and the power management circuitry. [075] Subsequently, the IPCBA (17) is configured to manage multiple power flow scenarios. These include AC input charging from an external power grid, solar charging facilitated by a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) mechanism, and DC to AC conversion to provide alternating current to external loads. [076] At step (316), the assembly method concludes with the connection of the AC output from the IPCBA to residential or industrial loads, and optionally, the connection of a solar panel directly to the IPCBA to facilitate solar charging without the requirement of an external inverter. patents.abstract: Simulation-driven design of an intelligent battery management system for 24v lithium-ion packs in electric vehicles is the proposed invention. As the electric vehicle (EV) industry expands, efficient battery management systems (BMS) are essential for optimizing lithium-ion battery performance and safety. This project focuses on designing and simulating a BMS for 24v lithium-ion packs in EVS, emphasizing thermal management and protective circuitry. Existing BMS solutions struggle with temperature regulation and battery protection, risking thermal runaway, overcharging, and over-discharging. To address these issues, the project includes comprehensive charging and discharging circuits, plus advanced mechanisms for overcharge, over-discharge, undercharge, and undervoltage protection. The simulation framework enables real-time monitoring of battery parameters and assessments of state-of-charge (soc) and state-of-health (soh). This approach enhances reliability and safety, contributing to safer, more efficient energy storage and promoting sustainable transportation.

The BMS continuously tracks these metrics and compares them with historical benchmarks to detect shifts in battery health. By monitoring resistance changes and response under load, SoH predictions offer insights into the remaining useful life of the pack, enabling timely maintenance and preventing unexpected failures. Integrating these estimations supports battery longevity and reliability, as well as safe power management, by adjusting current limits and optimizing charging cycles for the best performance under diverse operating conditions. patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a hybrid cooling system for thermal management of lithium-ion battery packs, particularly suitable for electric vehicles. The system comprises a battery pack with multiple battery cells, a plurality of capillary tubes thermally coupled to the cells, a sump positioned above the battery pack, and a heat transfer fluid contained within the sump and capillary tubes. The lower end of each capillary tube is sealed, and the upper end is open and connected to the sump. Heat generated by the battery cells is transferred to the fluid via thermal conduction and transported upward to the sump via natural convection. One or more fans are positioned over the sump to actively dissipate heat from the fluid by forced convection. This integrated passive-active system effectively regulates the battery temperature within safe operating limits, thereby enhancing the performance, lifespan, and safety of lithium-ion batteries under high-demand thermal conditions.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [0001] The present disclosure relates generally to the field of thermal management systems for energy storage devices, and more particularly, the present disclosure pertains to a Hybrid cooling system for lithium-ion battery packs, especially suitable for electric vehicle applications. BACKGROUND [0002] Lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries are the core power source in electric vehicles (EVs) due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and efficient energy output. However, their performance and safety are highly sensitive to temperature fluctuations. During high-rate charging and discharging operations, Li-ion battery cells generate substantial heat from electrochemical reactions and internal resistances. Without efficient heat dissipation, battery temperatures can rise above the safe threshold of 45°C, leading to accelerated degradation, reduced performance, shortened lifespan, or in severe cases, thermal runaway that may cause fires or explosions. [0003] Conventional EV battery thermal management systems fall under two major categories-active cooling systems and passive cooling systems. Passive systems, such as those using phase change materials (PCMs), heat sinks, and metal matrices, operate without external power and offer simpler designs. However, they typically exhibit poor thermal conductivity and limited heat transfer rates, making them inadequate during high thermal loads. Active systems, including forced air or liquid cooling mechanisms using fans, pumps, or compressors, are more efficient in heat removal but come with drawbacks like increased power consumption, system complexity, added weight, and the risk of coolant leakage. [0004] KR20230009158 (A) discloses a battery cooling apparatus employing upper and lower cooling passages to circulate cooling fluid around battery cells via forced convection. While effective in enhancing cooling efficiency, this approach is energy-dependent and adds mechanical bulk, which is undesirable in lightweight EV architectures. [0005] KR102440189 (B1) discloses an air-based cooling and heating system using compressed air and a vortex generator to thermally regulate EV battery packs. The system suffers from low thermal conductivity of air and inefficiency at higher temperatures. Moreover, reliance on moving parts and compressed air infrastructure introduces maintenance challenges and energy inefficiency. [0006] KR20110090491 (A) discloses a cooling and heating apparatus utilizing oscillating heat pipes filled with working fluid in a closed-loop structure. Though semi-passive, the system still requires external heating or cooling components to sustain fluid motion. Furthermore, such systems are sensitive to installation orientation and are prone to performance variability under dynamic operational conditions. [0007] Hence, there is an urgent need for an effective, compact, and energy-efficient cooling system that overcomes the limitations of purely active or passive approaches. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0008] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies are as listed herein below. [0009] An object of the present disclosure is to provide a hybrid cooling system for thermal management of lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles. [0010] Another object of the present disclosure is to combine passive cooling by natural convection with active cooling by forced convection to enhance thermal regulation of EV battery packs. [0011] Yet another object of the present disclosure is to maintain battery surface temperature within the safe operating range of 20°C to 45°C during high-load operations such as fast charging or discharging. [0012] Still another object of the present disclosure is to increase the efficiency and lifespan of lithium-ion batteries by preventing overheating and thermal runaway. [0013] A further object of the present disclosure is to provide a system that minimizes external power consumption while still delivering effective cooling performance. [0014] Yet a further object of the present disclosure is to offer a scalable and adaptable thermal management solution that is compact and suitable for integration into various EV battery architectures. [0015] Another object of the present disclosure is to utilize thermally conductive capillary tubes and high-performance heat transfer fluids to enhance thermal dissipation efficiency. [0016] Still another object of the present disclosure is to simplify the battery thermal management system by reducing the dependency on bulky liquid cooling circuits or complex refrigerant systems. [0017] A still further object of the present disclosure is to provide a reliable cooling system that is less prone to mechanical failure and fluid leakage. SUMMARY [0018] This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that is further described below in the detailed description section. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used as an aid in determining the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0019] Aspects of the present disclosure relate to a hybrid cooling system for thermal management of a lithium-ion battery pack, particularly for electric vehicle (EV) applications. The system integrates passive cooling using thermally conductive capillary tubes and a sump containing heat transfer fluid, with active cooling via one or more fans mounted above the sump. Heat generated by the battery cells is first transferred to the fluid through conduction and then transported upwards through natural convection into the sump. The fans facilitate forced convection to cool the heat transfer fluid within the sump, thereby maintaining the battery temperature within optimal safety limits. This hybrid approach enhances thermal performance while reducing reliance on complex or bulky cooling mechanisms. [0020] Accordingly, in an aspect, the present disclosure provides a hybrid cooling system for thermal management of a lithium-ion battery pack, the system comprising: a) a battery pack comprising a plurality of battery cells; b) a plurality of capillary tubes thermally coupled to the battery cells, each capillary tube having a sealed lower end and an open upper end; c) a sump disposed above the battery pack and connected to the upper ends of the capillary tubes; d) a heat transfer fluid filled within the sump and the capillary tubes; and e) a single or plurality of fans positioned over the sump, wherein heat generated by the battery cells is transferred to the heat transfer fluid within the capillary tubes through thermal conduction, and transported to the sump via natural convection, and further fans actively cool the heat transfer fluid in the sump, thereby enabling hybrid thermal regulation by combining passive and active cooling mechanisms. [0021] In some embodiments, four capillary tubes are thermally coupled to four lateral surfaces of each battery cell. [0022] In some embodiments, the capillary tubes are made of a thermally conductive material selected from copper or aluminium. [0023] In some embodiments, the inner surface of each capillary tube comprises a plurality of micro-grooves. [0024] In some embodiments, the micro-grooves have geometries selected from U-shaped, V-shaped, sinusoidal, circular, triangular, or rectangular profiles. [0025] In some embodiments, the heat transfer fluid has high thermal conductivity, high specific heat capacity, low viscosity, and a high boiling point. [0026] In some embodiments, the sump is vertically located above the battery pack to facilitate natural convection flow of the heat transfer fluid. [0027] In some embodiments, the fans are configured to dissipate heat from the heat transfer fluid in the sump by forced convection, maintaining the battery surface temperature within a range of 20°C to 45°C. [0028] In some embodiments, the battery pack has a length ranging from 5 to 200 cm, width ranging from 5 to 200 cm, and height ranging from 3 to 20 cm. [0029] In some embodiments, each battery cell has a diameter ranging from 0.5 to 5 cm and a height ranging from 2 to 15 cm; each capillary tube has a diameter ranging from 0.01 to 0.1 cm and a height ranging from 1 to 20 cm; and the sump has a length ranging from 5 to 200 cm, a width ranging from 5 to 200 cm, and a height ranging from 1 to 10 cm. [0030] Various objects, features, aspects and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [0031] The accompanying drawings are included to provide a further understanding of the present disclosure and are incorporated in and constitute a part of this specification. The drawings illustrate exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure and, together with the description, serve to explain the principles of the present disclosure.
