[0060] Aspects of present disclosure relates to a hybrid cooling system for thermal management of lithium-ion battery packs, particularly suitable for electric vehicles. The system comprises a battery pack with multiple battery cells, a plurality of capillary tubes thermally coupled to the cells, a sump positioned above the battery pack, and a heat transfer fluid contained within the sump and capillary tubes. The lower end of each capillary tube is sealed, and the upper end is open and connected to the sump. Heat generated by the battery cells is transferred to the fluid via thermal conduction and transported upward to the sump via natural convection. One or more fans are positioned over the sump to actively dissipate heat from the fluid by forced convection. This integrated passive-active system effectively regulates the battery temperature within safe operating limits, thereby enhancing the performance, lifespan, and safety of lithium-ion batteries under high-demand thermal conditions. [0070] In some embodiments, the heat transfer fluid has high thermal conductivity, high specific heat capacity, low viscosity, and a high boiling point. [0071] In some embodiments, the sump is vertically located above the battery pack to facilitate natural convection flow of the heat transfer fluid. patents.abstract: Disclosed herein is a composition (200) and method (300) for formulating lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors. The composition comprises manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate (202) as a precursor material to form hausmannite through thermal decomposition, lithium chloride anhydrous (204) as a dopant material to enhance electrochemical performance, ethanediol (206) as a solvent additive to stabilize the precursor solution, graphite felt (208) as a flexible substrate providing structural integrity and conductivity, sodium sulphate anhydrous (210) as an electrolyte component, ethanol (212) as a processing solvent, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) (214) as a binder agent, and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) (216) as a solvent. The method involves spray pyrolysis at 380°C (224) to achieve uniform deposition and optimal phase formation, resulting in flexible supercapacitor electrodes with superior specific capacitance, energy density, power density, and cycling stability.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF DISCLOSURE [0001] The present disclosure generally relates to energy storage devices, more specifically, relates to composition and method for formulating lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors based on a combination of precursor materials, thermal decomposition techniques, and flexible substrates for enhanced electrochemical performance. BACKGROUND OF THE DISCLOSURE [0002] Energy storage devices play a crucial role in modern technology applications, particularly with the growing demand for portable electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems. Supercapacitors, also known as electrochemical capacitors, have emerged as promising energy storage devices due to their unique combination of high-power density, rapid charge-discharge capability, and exceptional cycling stability compared to conventional batteries. [0003] The global community faces several challenges concerning energy storage devices. Traditional batteries, while offering high energy density, suffer from slow charging rates, limited cycle life, and performance degradation over time. Supercapacitors bridge the gap between conventional capacitors and batteries by providing rapid energy storage and release capabilities, making them ideal for applications requiring quick bursts of power. [0004] With the increasing focus on flexible electronics and wearable technology, including flexible displays, implantable healthcare devices, and smartwatches, there is a growing demand for flexible energy storage solutions. Flexible supercapacitors play an important role in this expanding field of electronics, offering consistent and reliable power delivery over extended periods while maintaining mechanical flexibility and structural integrity. [0005] Among various electrode materials for supercapacitors, transition metal oxides have gained significant attention due to their high theoretical capacitance values and pseudocapacitive behavior. Hausmannite (Mn3O4), a mixed-valence manganese oxide, exhibits excellent electrochemical properties including high specific capacitance, good electrical conductivity, and stable cycling performance. However, the electrochemical performance of hausmannite can be further enhanced through strategic modifications. [0006] Lithium incorporation into metal oxide structures has been recognized as an effective strategy to improve electrochemical performance. Lithium ions can enhance ionic conductivity, increase specific capacitance, and improve cycling stability of electrode materials. However, conventional synthesis methods often involve complex processes, expensive materials, and limited scalability. [0007] Current fabrication methods for flexible supercapacitor electrodes typically employ expensive substrates such as thin films, nickel foam, or fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) coated substrates. These approaches present significant challenges in terms of cost-effectiveness, scalability, and manufacturing complexity. Additionally, many existing methods fail to achieve uniform deposition of active materials, leading to inconsistent electrochemical performance. [0008] The spray pyrolysis technique offers several advantages for depositing metal oxides, including low cost, high throughput, scalability, and the ability to control morphology and composition. However, the application of spray pyrolysis for synthesizing lithium-incorporated hausmannite on flexible substrates for supercapacitor applications has not been extensively explored. [0009] Graphite felt, as a flexible and conductive substrate, offers unique advantages including excellent electrical conductivity, mechanical flexibility, chemical stability, and cost-effectiveness. The combination of lithium-incorporated hausmannite with graphite felt substrate through spray pyrolysis presents an opportunity to develop high-performance flexible supercapacitor electrodes with superior electrochemical properties. [0010] Existing formulations and methods for flexible supercapacitor electrodes face significant limitations in achieving optimal balance between flexibility, conductivity, and electrochemical performance. Many conventional approaches result in poor adhesion between active materials and substrates, limited mechanical stability, and suboptimal electrochemical characteristics. [0011] The present invention overcomes the limitations of prior art by providing a novel composition and method for formulating lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode that enhances specific capacitance, energy density, power density, and cycling stability while maintaining excellent mechanical flexibility and cost-effectiveness. [0012] Thus, in light of the above-stated discussion, there exists a need for a composition and method for formulating lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors. SUMMARY OF THE DISCLOSURE [0013] The following is a summary description of illustrative embodiments of the invention. It is provided as a preface to assist those skilled in the art to more rapidly assimilate the detailed design discussion which ensues and is not intended in any way to limit the scope of the claims which are appended hereto in order to particularly point out the invention. [0014] According to illustrative embodiments, the present disclosure focuses on a composition and method for formulating lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors which overcomes the above-mentioned disadvantages and provides users with a useful and commercial choice. [0015] The present invention overcomes all the above major limitations of existing compositions and methods for flexible supercapacitor electrode fabrication. [0016] An objective of the present disclosure is to develop a novel lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode composition for flexible supercapacitors that enhances specific capacitance, energy density, and power density through strategic material selection and processing techniques. [0017] Another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a cost-effective and scalable method for synthesizing lithium incorporated hausmannite on flexible graphite felt substrates using spray pyrolysis technique. [0018] Another objective of the present disclosure is to improve the electrochemical performance of hausmannite-based electrodes by incorporating lithium ions to enhance ionic conductivity and pseudocapacitive effects. [0019] Another objective of the present disclosure is to develop flexible supercapacitor electrodes with superior cycling stability and mechanical durability while maintaining excellent electrochemical properties. [0020] Another objective of the present disclosure is to provide a composition that combines optimal concentrations of precursor materials, dopants, and processing aids to achieve uniform deposition and enhanced electrochemical performance. [0021] Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to offer a method that utilizes precise temperature control and solution preparation techniques to ensure consistent formation of desired hausmannite phase with proper morphology. [0022] Yet another objective of the present disclosure is to develop a scalable and environmentally friendly synthesis approach that can be easily manufactured and commercially produced for widespread use in flexible energy storage applications. [0023] In light of the above, in one aspect of the present disclosure, a composition for a lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors is disclosed herein. The composition comprises manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate in a pre-defined quantity with thermal decomposition properties. The composition also includes lithium chloride anhydrous in a pre-defined quantity with lithium incorporation properties. The composition also includes ethanediol in a pre-defined quantity with solvent and stabilizing properties. The composition also includes graphite felt with a thickness of 2.8(+/-0.5) mm as a substrate with conductive and flexible support properties. The composition also includes sodium sulphate anhydrous in a pre-defined quantity with ionic conductivity properties. The composition also includes ethanol in a pre-defined quantity with cleaning and processing properties. The composition also includes polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) in a pre-defined quantity with binding properties. The composition also includes N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) in a pre-defined quantity with solvent properties. [0024] In light of the above, in another aspect of the present disclosure, a lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode composition for high-performance flexible supercapacitors is disclosed herein. The composition comprises manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate as a precursor material to form hausmannite through thermal decomposition and provide electrochemical activity. The composition also includes lithium chloride anhydrous as a dopant material to enhance the electrochemical performance and specific capacitance of the hausmannite electrode. The composition also includes ethanediol as a solvent additive to stabilize the precursor solution and facilitate uniform deposition during spray pyrolysis. The composition also includes graphite felt as a flexible substrate to provide structural integrity, electrical conductivity, and mechanical flexibility for the electrode. The composition also includes sodium sulphate anhydrous as an electrolyte component to enhance ionic conductivity and electrochemical performance. The composition also includes ethanol as a processing solvent to ensure proper cleaning and preparation of the electrode surface. The composition also includes polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) as a binder agent to ensure mechanical stability and adhesion of active materials to the substrate. The composition also includes N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) as a solvent to dissolve PVDF and maintain the desired consistency of the electrode formulation, ensuring even dispersion of all components. [0025] In one embodiment, the composition includes a concentration of 0.2M of manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate, different weight percentages of lithium chloride anhydrous, 2ml of ethanediol, graphite felt with dimensions of 1×1 cm², a sufficient quantity of sodium sulphate anhydrous, ethanol, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). [0026] In one embodiment, the manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate and ethanediol form a precursor solution to enhance the thermal decomposition and uniform deposition of the hausmannite on the graphite felt substrate. [0027] In one embodiment, the composition further comprises a three-electrode system to facilitate the electrochemical characterization of the flexible supercapacitor electrode. [0028] In one embodiment, the composition further comprises precise temperature control at 380°C as a thermal processing parameter to maintain optimal thermal decomposition conditions and enhance the formation of desired hausmannite phase with proper morphology. [0029] In light of the above, in another aspect of the present disclosure, a method for formulating a lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors is disclosed herein. The method comprises preparing a precursor solution by dissolving manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate in a solvent in a pre-defined quantity. The method also includes adding ethanediol to the precursor solution with continuous stirring. The method also includes incorporating lithium chloride anhydrous in different weight percentages into the precursor solution. The method also includes subjecting the mixture to continuous stirring for 20 minutes to ensure uniform distribution and stability. The method also includes transferring the solution to a 20ml syringe for spray pyrolysis equipment. The method also includes preheating the graphite felt substrate to a precise temperature of 380°C. The method also includes spraying the precursor solution onto the heated substrate through spray pyrolysis to form lithium incorporated hausmannite. The method also includes allowing thermal decomposition to occur on the substrate to form the flexible supercapacitor electrode. [0030] In one embodiment, the hausmannite formed has enhanced electrochemical properties in the range suitable for high-performance flexible supercapacitors, facilitating superior specific capacitance, energy and power density. [0031] In one embodiment, the hausmannite is lithium-incorporated with variable weight percentages selected to optimize electrochemical performance, to selectively enhance the pseudocapacitive effects and cycling stability of the electrode. [0032] In one embodiment, the method further comprises adding sodium sulphate anhydrous, ethanol, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) to improve the electrochemical performance, mechanical stability, and processing properties of the flexible supercapacitor electrode. [0033] These and other advantages will be apparent from the present application of the embodiments described herein. [0034] The preceding is a simplified summary to provide an understanding of some embodiments of the present invention. This summary is neither an extensive nor exhaustive overview of the present invention and its various embodiments. The summary presents selected concepts of the embodiments of the present invention in a simplified form as an introduction to the more detailed description presented below. As will be appreciated, other embodiments of the present invention are possible utilizing, alone or in combination, one or more of the features set forth above or described in detail below. [0035] These elements, together with the other aspects of the present disclosure and various features are pointed out with particularity in the claims annexed hereto and form a part of the present disclosure. For a better understanding of the present disclosure, its operating advantages, and the specified object attained by its uses, reference should be made to the accompanying drawings and descriptive matter in which there are illustrated exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0036] To describe the technical solutions in the embodiments of the present disclosure or in the prior art more clearly, the following briefly describes the accompanying drawings required for describing the embodiments or the prior art. [0049] The composition 100 may include manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 102 in a pre-defined quantity with thermal decomposition properties. The composition 100 may also include lithium chloride anhydrous 104 in a pre-defined quantity with lithium incorporation properties. The composition 100 may also include ethanediol 106 in a pre-defined quantity with solvent and stabilizing properties. [0050] FIG. 2 illustrates a block diagram of a lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode composition 200 for high-performance flexible supercapacitors, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure. [0051] The lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode composition 200 may include manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202, lithium chloride anhydrous 204, ethanediol 206, graphite felt 208, sodium sulphate anhydrous 210, ethanol 212, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) 214, and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 216. [0052] In one embodiment of the present invention, the composition 200 includes a concentration of 0.2M of manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202, different weight percentages of lithium chloride anhydrous 204, 2ml of ethanediol 206, graphite felt 208 with dimensions of 1×1 cm², a sufficient quantity of sodium sulphate anhydrous 210, ethanol 212, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) 214, and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 216. [0053] Manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202 serves as the primary precursor material in the composition 200. This compound undergoes thermal decomposition during the spray pyrolysis process at 380°C to form hausmannite (Mn₃O₄) on the substrate surface. The tetrahydrate form provides controlled decomposition kinetics and uniform phase formation, where the acetate groups are oxidized and removed as volatile products, leaving behind manganese oxide in the desired hausmannite phase. The specific concentration of 0.2M has been optimized to ensure complete decomposition while maintaining uniform deposition on the graphite felt substrate 208. [0054] Lithium chloride anhydrous 204 functions as a dopant material that significantly enhances the electrochemical performance and specific capacitance of the hausmannite electrode. The incorporation of lithium ions into the hausmannite structure increases ionic conductivity and enhances pseudocapacitive effects. Different weight percentages of lithium chloride anhydrous 204 can be used to optimize the electrochemical performance, with the lithium ions becoming incorporated into the crystal lattice during the thermal decomposition process. The anhydrous form is preferred to prevent unwanted moisture-related reactions during the synthesis process. [0055] Ethanediol 206 serves multiple crucial functions in the composition 200 as a solvent additive that stabilizes the precursor solution and facilitates uniform deposition during spray pyrolysis. It acts as a co-solvent that improves the solubility of the precursor materials and facilitates uniform distribution in the solution. During spray pyrolysis, ethanediol 206 helps maintain solution stability and promotes uniform droplet formation, leading to consistent deposition on the substrate. The addition of 2ml of ethanediol 206 has been optimized to provide the right balance between solution stability and proper atomization during the spraying process. [0056] Graphite felt 208 serves as the flexible substrate that provides structural integrity, electrical conductivity, and mechanical flexibility for the electrode. The specific dimensions of 1×1 cm² offer optimal surface area for electrochemical characterization while maintaining practical handling properties. Graphite felt 208 offers several advantages including excellent electrical conductivity, mechanical flexibility, chemical stability, and three-dimensional porous structure that enhances electrolyte access and ion transport. The precise thickness specification of 2.8(+/-0.5) mm ensures consistent performance and reproducible results. [0057] Sodium sulphate anhydrous 210 functions as an electrolyte component that enhances ionic conductivity and overall electrochemical performance of the system. It provides additional ionic species that facilitate charge transport during electrochemical testing and operation. The anhydrous form prevents unwanted water content that could interfere with the thermal decomposition process. [0058] Ethanol 212 serves as a processing solvent for cleaning and preparation procedures. It ensures proper cleaning of the graphite felt substrate 208 before deposition and helps in maintaining the cleanliness of the system during processing. Ethanol's volatility and cleaning properties make it ideal for removing contaminants without leaving residues that could affect electrode performance. [0059] Polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) 214 acts as a binder agent that ensures mechanical stability and strong adhesion of the active materials to the substrate. PVDF 214 provides excellent chemical stability, mechanical strength, and electrochemical compatibility, making it ideal for supercapacitor applications. The binder helps maintain the structural integrity of the electrode during cycling operations. [0060] N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 216 functions as a solvent for dissolving PVDF 214 and maintaining the desired consistency of the electrode formulation. NMP 216 ensures even dispersion of all components and provides the appropriate viscosity for processing. Its high boiling point and excellent solvating properties make it ideal for electrode slurry preparation. [0061] In one embodiment of the present invention, the manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202 and ethanediol 206 form a precursor solution to enhance the thermal decomposition and uniform deposition of the hausmannite on the graphite felt substrate 208. The coordination between ethanediol 206 and manganese ions creates a homogeneous solution that prevents phase separation during storage and provides controlled decomposition kinetics during the spray pyrolysis process. [0062] In one embodiment of the present invention, the composition 200 further comprises a three-electrode system 222 to facilitate the electrochemical characterization of the flexible supercapacitor electrode. This system consists of the fabricated lithium incorporated hausmannite on graphite felt 208 as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl with saturated KCl as the reference electrode, and platinum wire as the counter electrode. [0063] In one embodiment of the present invention, the composition 200 further comprises precise temperature control at 380°C 224 as a thermal processing parameter to maintain optimal thermal decomposition conditions and enhance the formation of desired hausmannite phase with proper morphology. This temperature has been optimized to ensure complete decomposition of the acetate precursor while promoting the formation of pure hausmannite phase without secondary phases. [0064] FIG. 3 illustrates a flowchart of a method 300, outlining the sequential steps for formulating a lithium incorporated hausmannite electrode for high-performance flexible supercapacitors, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure. [0065] The method 300 may include, at step 302, preparing a precursor solution by dissolving manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202 in a solvent in a pre-defined quantity, at step 304, adding ethanediol 206 to the precursor solution with continuous stirring, at step 306, incorporating lithium chloride anhydrous 204 in different weight percentages into the precursor solution, at step 308, subjecting the mixture to continuous stirring for 20 minutes to ensure uniform distribution and stability, at step 310, transferring the solution to a 20ml syringe for spray pyrolysis equipment, at step 312, preheating the graphite felt substrate 208 to a precise temperature of 380°C, at step 314, spraying the precursor solution onto the heated substrate through spray pyrolysis to form lithium incorporated hausmannite, and at step 316, allowing thermal decomposition to occur on the substrate to form the flexible supercapacitor electrode. [0066] At step 302, the method involves preparing a precursor solution by dissolving manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202 in a solvent in a pre-defined quantity. The 0.2M concentration of manganese (II) acetate tetrahydrate 202 provides the optimal precursor availability for thermal decomposition while ensuring complete dissolution and uniform distribution in the solution. This step is critical for creating a homogeneous precursor solution that will later form the hausmannite phase on the substrate. [0067] At step 304, adding ethanediol 206 to the precursor solution with continuous stirring. The addition of 2ml of ethanediol 206 serves multiple functions including acting as a co-solvent to improve precursor solubility, providing solution stability during spray pyrolysis, and facilitating uniform droplet formation during the spraying process. The continuous stirring ensures complete mixing and prevents phase separation. [0068] At step 306, incorporating lithium chloride anhydrous 204 in different weight percentages into the precursor solution. The lithium chloride anhydrous 204 acts as a dopant material that will be incorporated into the hausmannite structure during thermal decomposition. Different weight percentages can be used to optimize the electrochemical performance based on specific application requirements, with the lithium ions enhancing ionic conductivity and pseudocapacitive effects. [0069] At step 308, subjecting the mixture to continuous stirring for 20 minutes to ensure uniform distribution and stability. This stirring duration has been optimized to achieve complete homogenization of all components including the manganese precursor, ethanediol 206, and lithium chloride anhydrous 204, while preventing precipitation or phase separation that could lead to non-uniform deposition. [0070] At step 310, transferring the solution to a 20ml syringe for spray pyrolysis equipment. The 20ml syringe volume provides adequate solution volume for uniform spraying while maintaining solution homogeneity throughout the deposition process. The syringe format is compatible with standard spray pyrolysis equipment and allows for controlled solution delivery. [0071] At step 312, preheating the graphite felt substrate 208 to a precise temperature of 380°C. This temperature is critical for proper thermal decomposition of the manganese acetate precursor and ensures complete conversion to the hausmannite phase. The precise temperature control promotes optimal crystallinity, phase purity, and morphology of the deposited hausmannite while enabling lithium incorporation into the crystal structure. [0072] At step 314, spraying the precursor solution onto the heated substrate through spray pyrolysis to form lithium incorporated hausmannite. During this step, the precursor solution undergoes immediate thermal decomposition upon contact with the heated graphite felt substrate 208, resulting in the formation of lithium incorporated hausmannite directly on the flexible substrate surface. The spray pyrolysis technique ensures uniform coverage and controlled deposition thickness. [0073] At step 316, allowing thermal decomposition to occur on the substrate to form the flexible supercapacitor electrode. This final step completes the electrode fabrication process, where the thermal energy drives the complete conversion of precursor materials to the desired lithium incorporated hausmannite phase with optimal electrochemical properties for supercapacitor applications. [0074] In one embodiment of the present invention, the hausmannite formed has enhanced electrochemical properties in the range suitable for high-performance flexible supercapacitors, facilitating superior specific capacitance, energy and power density. The lithium incorporation enhances the electrochemical performance by increasing ionic conductivity and providing additional charge storage sites through pseudocapacitive mechanisms. [0075] In one embodiment of the present invention, the hausmannite is lithium-incorporated with variable weight percentages selected to optimize electrochemical performance, to selectively enhance the pseudocapacitive effects and cycling stability of the electrode. The variable lithium content allows for fine-tuning of the electrochemical properties based on specific performance requirements. [0076] In one embodiment of the present invention, the method 300 further comprises adding sodium sulphate anhydrous 210, ethanol 212, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) 214, and N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 216 to improve the electrochemical performance, mechanical stability, and processing properties of the flexible supercapacitor electrode. [0077] In a preferred embodiment, the method 300 may utilize apparatus including magnetic stirrer, spray pyrolysis equipment, and electrochemical workstation operated on a three-electrode system for comprehensive characterization and performance evaluation. [0078] The present invention offers several key advantages, including enhanced electrochemical performance through strategic lithium incorporation, cost-effective and scalable synthesis method, excellent mechanical flexibility while maintaining high conductivity, superior cycling stability and long-term performance, and compatibility with various flexible electronics applications. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT CHARGING AND DISCHARGING CYCLE FOR FORMATION OF LITHIUM-ION CELLS The present subject matter discloses a method and system (100) for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle. For example, the method includes charging the secondary cell in a predefined number of charging cycles at a constant current with a current-rate (C-rate) between 0.025C and 0.1C to a predefined voltage value. Upon charging the secondary cell to a first voltage value, the cell is discharged to a second voltage value, wherein the second voltage value is less than the first voltage value. Further, a pulse charge cycle is applied to the cell, wherein the pulse charge cycle comprises a predefined number of alternating cycles of charging to the first voltage value and discharging to the second voltage value.
patents.complete_specification: Description:BACKGROUND [0001] Lithium-ion (Li-ion) cells (hereinafter referred to as (“cells”) have emerged as the dominant energy storage technology across a broad range of applications, including portable electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and stationary grid storage systems. The widespread adoption of the Li-ion cells is attributed to favorable characteristics such as high energy density, long-cycle life, and relatively low self-discharge rates. In a typical Li-ion cell, energy storage and release are facilitated by the reversible movement of lithium ions between cathode and anode during charge and discharge cycles. However, as the demand for higher capacity and faster charging cells continues to grow, ways to enhance the performance of lithium-ion cells are required. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES [0002] Systems and/or methods, in accordance with examples of the present subject matter are described and with reference to the accompanying figures, in which: [0003] FIG. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a charging and discharging system, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; [0004] FIG. 2 illustrates a graphical representation of voltage variations over time at various stages of charging and discharging of cell during cell formation process, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; [0005] FIG. 3 illustrates a graphical representation depicting charge retention in the cell during charging and discharging of secondary cells during formation cycle, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; 3 [0006] FIG. 4 illustrates a method for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle of the secondary cell, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; [0007] FIG. 5 illustrates another method 500 for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle of the secondary cell, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; [0008] FIG. 6 illustrates another method for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle of the secondary cell, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter; and [0009] FIG. 7 illustrates a graphical representation depicting a comparative analysis of effectiveness of charging and discharging methods of the present subject matter, in accordance with an example of the present subject matter. [0010] It may be noted that throughout the drawings, identical reference numbers designate similar, but not necessarily identical, elements. The figures are not necessarily to scale, and the size of some parts may be exaggerated to more clearly illustrate the example shown. Moreover, the drawings provide examples and/or implementations consistent with the description; however, the description is not limited to the examples and/or implementations provided in the drawings. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0011] Traditionally, graphite has served as the anode material of choice due to its structural stability and consistent electrochemical performance. However, its theoretical specific capacity is limited to approximately 372 Milliampere-hour per gram (mAh/g), thereby constraining the energy density of Li-ion cells employing graphite anodes. This limitation is particularly critical in applications where high energy and power densities are required. [0012] In recent years, silicon and silicon/graphite composite anodes have garnered significant attention as potential replacement for graphite anodes, owing to silicon’s considerably higher theoretical specific capacity, 4 which is up to 3579 mAh/g. These anodes offer the advantage of tunable capacity, which can be engineered to meet specific performance requirements. Moreover, they are widely used cathode chemistries, such as nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC), and nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (NCA), enhancing the sustainability for next-generation high-performance batteries. [0013] However, the practical implementation of silicon and silicon-based composite anodes remains challenged by several material and electrochemical limitations. A formation cycle, which is the initial charge-discharge cycle of a newly manufactured lithium-ion battery, plays a role in establishing a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer and determining the long-term performance of the battery. However, there is a substantial consumption of lithium during the initial formation cycles. This over-consumption of lithium results in lithium loss. Lithium loss arises due to irreversible reactions between lithium and silicon, as well as the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer. The irreversible nature of these reactions results in a significantly reduced initial coulombic efficiency (ICE), which may be as low as 60%, thereby directly impacting the discharge capacity and overall energy density of the cell. [0014] For silicon-containing anodes, the formation cycle can be particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the silicon surface during lithiation and delithiation. The expansion and contraction of silicon particles can lead to continuous exposure of fresh surfaces, resulting in ongoing SEI formation and lithium consumption. This phenomenon can contribute to lower ICE values compared to traditional graphite anodes. [0015] The lithium loss observed during the formation cycle may be classified into reversible and irreversible components. The reversible loss is associated with the alloying and dealloying of lithium with silicon during charge and discharge cycles. In contrast, the irreversible loss is primarily due to lithium consumed in non-reversible reactions, including irregular SEI 5 layer formation and other parasitic side reactions. This irreversible consumption reduces the amount of active lithium available for subsequent cycling, adversely affecting long-term battery performance. [0016] Example approaches for providing improved formation methodologies for batteries are described. The present subject matter relates to approaches for mitigating irreversible lithium losses and enhance the initial coulombic efficiency of silicon-based anodes by extracting the residual capacity from silicon/graphite blend anodes. [0017] For example, a method for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle of the secondary cell (hereinafter referred to as a cell) is described. The cell may be a lithium-ion (Li-ion) cell having a positive electrode and a negative electrode. In an example, the negative electrode of the cell comprises up to 25% silicon by weight, i.e., 25% of a total weight of the negative electrode may comprise of silicon. In an aspect, the positive electrode of the cell may comprise a material selected from the group consisting of nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC), nickel cobalt aluminium oxide (NCA), and combinations thereof. [0018] The method is performed during the formation cycle of the cell. The cell undergoes a formation cycle to activate one or more electrochemical components of the cell, such as lithium-ion, nickel-cadmium, or lead-acid batteries. The method for charging and discharging the cell during the formation cycle includes charging the secondary cell in a predefined number of charging cycles at a constant current with a current-rate (C-rate) between 0.025C and 0.1C to a predefined voltage value. In the predefined number of charging cycles, each successive cycle has a voltage value greater than the voltage value of a previous cycle. The method further includes, upon charging the cell to a first voltage value, discharging the cell to a second voltage value, wherein the second voltage value is less than the first voltage value, and wherein the first voltage value is selected from a range of 4.05 V to 4.25 V and the second voltage value is selected from a 6 range of 3.6 V to 4.24 V. Continuing further, the method includes causing to apply a pulse charge cycle to the cell at a C-rate between 0.1C and 1C, wherein the pulse charge cycle comprises a predefined number of alternating cycles of charging to the first voltage value and discharging to the second voltage value. [0019] In another example, a system for charging and discharging a secondary cell during a formation cycle of the secondary cell is described. The system may include a control engine to perform charging and discharging during the formation cycle of the cell. The system may be configured to perform the method for charging and discharging the secondary cell during formation cycle of the cell. [0020] The system and method for charging and discharging the secondary cell during the formation cycle of the cell, of the present subject matter offers several advantages over existing approaches by improving solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) uniformity on the electrode surfaces. The controlled voltage steps and pulse charging cycles allow for consistent SEI formation, thereby reducing unwanted side reactions between the electrolyte and electrode materials. In this manner, the aforementioned approaches for charging and discharging the cell during formation cycle may enhance the cycle life of secondary cells by up to 5% due to the optimized SEI layer formed during the initial cycles. [0021] Further, the tailored voltage profiles and current rates in the present approaches may lead to an increase in initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) of the secondary cell by 0.5% to 2%. This enhanced efficiency in the first cycle improves the overall cell performance. Additionally, the controlled charging and discharging also enhances electrode stability by managing voltage levels and charge/discharge rates, thereby mitigating structural changes in the electrode materials during initial cycling. This improved stability may lead to consistent performance over the cell's lifetime. 7 [0022] The above aspects are further described in conjunction with the figures, and in the associated description below. It should be noted that the description and figures merely illustrate principles of the present subject matter. Therefore, various assemblies that encompass the principles of the present subject matter, although not explicitly described or shown herein, may be devised from the description, and are included within its scope. [0023] FIG. 1 illustrates a block diagram of a charging and discharging system 100 (hereinafter referred to as system 100), in accordance with an example of the present subject matter. The system 100 may be coupled with one or more secondary cells (not shown in the figure) to perform the formation process of the cell. The formation process may refer to the initial charging and discharging of the cell after assembly of the cell. Upon assembly, every cell undergoes the formation process to activate the chemical material of the cell to allow the cell to become rechargeable. In an example, the system 100 may enable charging and discharging cycles to be performed during the formation process of the cell. [0024] As depicted in FIG. 1, the system 100 includes a control engine 102. The Control engine 102, amongst other capabilities, may be configured to fetch and execute computer-readable instructions to perform charging and discharging of one or more secondary cells. In an example, the control engine 102 may be implemented as one or more processing units, microprocessors, microcomputers, microcontrollers, digital signal processors, central processing units, state machines, logic circuitries, and/or any devices that manipulate signals based on operational instructions. The functions of the various elements shown in the figure may be provided through the use of dedicated hardware as well as hardware capable of executing machine readable instructions. Although depicted in the form of functional module, the control engine 102 may be implemented in the form of electronic circuitry, which amongst other capabilities, may 8 specifically be configured to charge and discharge one or more secondary cells. The invention is designed for embedded deployment with low computational requirements, making it suitable for applications in electric vehicles, portable electronics, renewable energy storage, and industrial power systems. patents.abstract: The present invention discloses a biodegradable solid polymer electrolyte membrane made from natural guar gum blended with polyvinyl alcohol and doped with lithium chloride, designed for lithium battery applications. This eco-friendly electrolyte demonstrates a high ionic conductivity of 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ S/cm at room temperature, combined with excellent thermal stability and mechanical strength. Structural and electrochemical characterizations, including X-ray diffraction, FTIR, impedance spectroscopy, and thermal analysis confirm the membrane’s durability and efficient lithium-ion transport. By eliminating the need for hazardous liquid electrolytes, this biodegradable membrane offers a safer alternative that reduces environmental impact in battery manufacturing, usage, and disposal. This innovation advances the development of sustainable lithium battery technologies, providing an effective and environmentally responsible solution for next-generation energy storage systems.

patents.abstract: This development introduces an electrochemical process designed for the efficient recycling of lithium from spent battery waste, aiming to address the growing challenge of sustainable resource management in the energy storage industry.Conventional recycling methods, such as pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy, often involve high energy consumption, complex chemical treatments, and environmental hazards. Our process overcomes these drawbacks by employing a cost-effective electrochemical technique that selectively extracts lithium ions from waste streams while minimizing secondary pollution. The system incorporates advanced electrode materials and optimized electrolytes to enhance recovery efficiency, reduce operational costs, and ensure high purity of the recovered lithium. With a modular and scalable design, the process can be adapted to various battery chemistries, including lithium-ion and lithium-polymer batteries. Early experimental results indicate that this method achieves higher recovery rates compared to traditional approaches, with significant reductions in chemical waste generation. This project contributes to the circular economy by promoting the reuse of critical raw materials, supporting greener energy technologies, and providing a sustainable model for large-scale battery recycling.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a novel and efficient Solution-derived gel technique for synthesizing lithiated transition metal molybdate-based ternary inetal oxides (LXMO). The invention further aims to utilize the synthesized coin pounds· in multi-domain applications, including antimicrobial activity and as electrocatalysts for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in environmental and energy-related applications. The synthesized materials. crystallize ·in orthorhombic and monoclinic phases as confirmed by X-ray diffraction with Rietveld refinement, and their structures were further visualized using VESTA software. Raman spectroscopy established the vibrational characteristics, while FESEM analysis revealed sheet-like and rod-like intercomiected morphologies favorable. for electrochemical applications. Furthermore, the compounds exhibited . notable antibacterial activity against Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus) and Gram-negative (Escherichia coli, Salmonella typhi, Pseudomonas aeroginosa) bacteria on Mueller-Hinton Agar (MHA) with Cu-LXMO exhibiting the highest antibacterial activity. The electrocatalytic evaluation demonstrated that Co-LXMO exhibits superior hydrogen evolution reaCtion (HERY activity with a low overpotential of 60 m V at I 0 rnA cm·2 and reduced Tafel slope, alongside efficient oxygen evolution reaction (OER) behavior. Thus, the multifunctional properties of LXMO materials render them as promising candidates for antibacterial ·coatings and electrocatalytic applications.
patents.complete_specification: Field of the invention (0001] The present disclosure relates to the development of lithiated transition metal molybdatebased ternary metal oxides synthesized via a solution-derived gel technique. The sequential synthesis yields multifunctional materials that exhibit antimicrobial activity and electrocatalytic behavior. The resulting ternary compounds demonstrate an effective antimicrobial performance towards Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus) and Gram-negative (Escherichia coli. Salmonella typhi. Pseudomonas aeroginosa) under dark conditions, thereby functioning as longlasting. self-cleaning agents. In addition, the compounds serve as efficient electrocatalysts for hydrogen evolution (HER) and oxygen evolution (OER) reactions in water splitting systems. The disclosed approach offers advantages over conventional synthetic routes in terms of composition, functionality, and application potential. The developed ternary compounds are particularly suited for biomedical protection against pathogenic microbes responsible for various infectious diseases, as well as for use in sustainable energy conversion and storage applications. Background of the invention (0002] Public spaces such as hospitals, healthcare facilities, food-processing plants, hotels, dormitories, and public transport systems are highly vulnerable to microbial contamination and the spread of infectious diseases. The increasing emergence of drug-resistant and pathogenic microbes has created a pressing need for advanced antimicrobial solutions that can effectively reduce bio-burden levels in such environments. It has been discovered that the antimicrobial performance of a single oxidation-state metal oxide can be significantly improved by combining it with a mixed oxidation-state metal oxide. When the two oxides are in ionic contact, the resulting material exhibits a synergistic effect that surpasses the antimicrobial activity of the individual components. Even the incorporation of a small amount {less than 10 wt.%) of the mixed oxidation-state oxide is sufficient to generate a notable enhancement in antimicrobial efficiency. Inorganic antibacterial agents such as silver, copper, and zinc have been widely investigated as alternatives to organic agents due to their long-lasting activity, broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties, and superior heat stability. However, silver-based systems face limitations such as high cost and discoloration. In contrast, zinc-based oxides are cost-effective, thermally and colour stable, and exhibit reliable antibacterial performance, while rare-earth ions have long been utilized in medicine owing to their safety and broad-spectrum antimicrobial action. Thus, the development of new composite oxide-based antimicrobial agents offers a promising pathway toward sustainable, low-cost, and efficient antimicrobial materials. Brief description of prior art [0003) CN115058732B (2024) discloses a method for preparing a magnesium-doped nickel-iron oxide and its use as a hydrogen evolution electrocatalyst. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT An Interpretable Battery Modeling System For Lithium-Ion Batteries And A Method Of Operating The Same The present disclosure relates to an interpretable battery modeling system for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data. The system includes a physics-based equivalent circuit model (ECM) including at least a two-RC network, integrated with a hybrid neural network module (618) in a fusion framework. The hybrid neural network module (618) includes a recurrent neural network (620) configured to estimate SOC from sequential current measurements and one or more feedforward neural networks (622) configured to predict selected equivalent-circuit parameters, the parameters including open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1). A computation unit (614) implements the fusion framework by combining estimated SOC and predicted parameters with the ECM under physical constraints to generate terminal-voltage predictions in real time, wherein remaining equivalent-circuit parameters are maintained at fixed values. (FIG. 2)
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION [001] The present invention relates to battery management technologies for energy storage systems, and in particular, to an interpretable system and method for modeling lithium-ion batteries through a fusion of physics-based equivalent circuit models (ECMs) and neural network architectures, enabling accurate estimation of state of charge (SOC) and prediction of terminal voltage in real time. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present invention. [003] Lithium-ion batteries are the preferred energy storage devices for electric vehicles (EVs), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), portable electronics, and grid-scale energy storage systems due to their high energy density, low self-discharge rate, and efficiency across varying environmental conditions. Accurate estimation of state of charge (SOC) and terminal voltage is critical for ensuring battery safety, operational efficiency, and long-term reliability. In real-world usage, the batteries are subjected to dynamically varying current loads, temperature fluctuations, and progressive aging. This operational complexity makes precise estimation of SOC and voltage prediction particularly challenging. [004] Conventional physics-based Equivalent Circuit Models (ECMs) require extensive and time-consuming parameter identification, typically conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, which makes them less adaptable to field applications. Such ECMs, although interpretable, often fail to generalize across different operational conditions, requiring frequent recalibration when load profiles, temperatures, or cell chemistries vary. Full electrochemical models, while capable of high accuracy, impose high computational burdens that render them impractical for real-time deployment on embedded battery management system (BMS) hardware such as microcontrollers or digital signal processors. [005] Purely data-driven machine learning and deep learning models, such as fully connected neural networks, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and long short-term memory (LSTM)-based SOC estimators, have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities. However, they suffer from a fundamental drawback of being “black box” models, providing predictions without physical interpretability. This lack of interpretability prevents compliance with safety certifications and reduces trustworthiness in safety-critical applications such as electric vehicles, aerospace, and defense systems, where predictions must remain consistent with established physical laws. [006] Hybrid and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as alternatives that combine physics-based equations with data-driven learning. Some PINN approaches have been applied to battery capacity estimation and SOC estimation. However, these existing methods often use physics only for error modeling or require large numbers of known physical parameters as prior inputs, thereby limiting applicability when parameter values are uncertain or vary with battery usage and aging. Many prior methods also accumulate errors over long prediction horizons, leading to unreliable SOC and voltage estimates during prolonged use. [007] Battery modeling and state estimation approaches therefore generally fall into three broad categories. First, physics-based models, such as Rint, Thevenin, 1-RC, 2-RC, higher-order ECMs, and pseudo-2D electrochemical models, explicitly represent internal battery processes but require laborious parameter estimation for each operating condition and battery type. Electrochemical models, while highly accurate, remain computationally intensive and unsuitable for real-time embedded deployment. Second, data-driven machine learning and deep learning models can capture non-linear mappings and adapt to varying conditions but fail to embed inherent physical constraints, often yielding unrealistic predictions under unseen operating conditions. Third, hybrid or physics-informed neural networks combine data-driven methods with physical models. However, as noted, many PINN approaches either focus narrowly on error correction or demand extensive prior characterization of physical constants, limiting their scalability for practical deployment. [008] Several prior art disclosures illustrate these limitations. For example, U.S. Patent No. US10598712B2 describes a method for estimating the state of charge of a battery using neural networks, but this disclosure relies entirely on data-driven approaches without embedding a full physics-based ECM, thereby raising potential safety and interpretability issues. U.S. Patent Application Publication No. US20190234477A1 discloses a battery state estimation device and method using equivalent circuit models in combination with Kalman filtering; however, it requires extensive offline parameter identification and lacks adaptability under rapidly changing operating conditions. U.S. Patent Application Publication No. US20220245959A1 describes a physics-informed neural network for battery modeling, but this approach applies only partial physics constraints for SOC estimation and does not integrate a learnable ECM structure capable of dynamically adapting critical parameters such as resistance (R1) and open-circuit voltage (Vb). [009] Related academic literature further demonstrates the shortcomings of existing conventional approaches. Nascimento et al. (Journal of Power Sources, 2021) proposed hybrid physics-informed neural networks for lithium-ion battery modeling and prognosis, employing reduced-order physics models combined with multi-layer perceptron (MLP) estimation; however, this work primarily modeled error terms and required extensive prior parameter knowledge. Tian et al. (Energy Storage Materials, 2022) applied physics-informed deep learning for SOC estimation by decomposing voltage into open-circuit voltage, ohmic, and polarization components, but this approach required pre-characterization of physical elements, restricting its broader applicability. [0010] Thus, existing solutions to battery state estimation are constrained by one or more limitations: (i) lack of generalization across variable load and temperature conditions, (ii) computational complexity preventing real-time deployment on embedded hardware, (iii) black-box behavior that undermines interpretability and safety assurance, (iv) partial or incomplete integration of physics-based models into neural architectures, and (v) error accumulation over long prediction horizons. [0011] Thus, there is a need for an interpretable, computationally efficient, and practically deployable battery modeling framework that integrates physics-based modeling with neural-network adaptability, enabling accurate and physically consistent estimation of SOC and terminal voltage under diverse and dynamic operating conditions without requiring exhaustive parameter identification or calibration. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION: [0012] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies, are listed herein below. [0013] The primary object of the present invention is to provide an interpretable battery modeling system and method for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data, through integration of a physics-based equivalent circuit model (ECM) and a hybrid neural network module within a fusion framework. [0014] Another object of the present invention is to provide a system and method that employs a recurrent neural network, preferably a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, for sequential processing of current measurements to estimate SOC in real time. [0015] Another object of the present invention is to provide a system and method that employ one or more feedforward neural networks, preferably Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks, configured to predict selected equivalent circuit parameters including open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1), while maintaining remaining equivalent circuit parameters such as internal resistance (R0), secondary resistance (R2), and capacitances (C1, C2) at empirically determined fixed values to reduce computational complexity. [0016] Another object of the present invention is to provide a resistance prediction mechanism wherein the neural network is configured to predict reciprocal resistance (1/R1) instead of R1, thereby mitigating exploding gradient issues and improving numerical stability and convergence during training. [0017] Another object of the present invention is to provide a system and method for training the hybrid neural network module using a custom loss framework combining a weighted smooth mean absolute error (wMAE) loss prioritizing early-stage prediction accuracy and a boundary loss penalizing predicted voltages outside predefined safe charge and discharge limits. [0018] Another object of the present invention is to provide a training optimization framework including application of an Adam optimizer with task-specific learning rates for recurrent and feedforward networks, including a learning rate of about 0.00015 for the LSTM, a learning rate of about 0.02 with a step scheduler reducing the rate by about 0.05 for the MLPs, and a training duration of about 100 epochs. [0019] Another object of the present invention is to provide a hybrid neural network module trainable using reduced datasets including fewer than 100 samples per discharge cycle, while maintaining generalization capability across varying load conditions without requiring recalibration. [0020] Another object of the present invention is to provide a computation unit that implements the fusion framework by combining the estimated SOC, the predicted ECM parameters, and the ECM under physical constraints to generate terminal-voltage predictions in real time, thereby ensuring interpretability and compliance with physical battery dynamics. [0021] Another object of the present invention is to provide an embedded hardware implementation of the system on platforms such as microcontrollers, digital signal processors (DSPs), or field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), thereby enabling practical real-time deployment without requiring extensive offline parameter identification or calibration sweeps. [0022] These and other objects and advantages will become more apparent when reference is made to the following description and accompanying drawings. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0023] This summary is provided to introduce concepts related to battery management technologies for energy storage systems, and in particular, to an interpretable system and method for modeling lithium-ion batteries through a fusion of physics-based equivalent circuit models (ECMs) and neural network architectures, enabling accurate estimation of state of charge (SOC) and prediction of terminal voltage in real time. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0024] In an aspect of the present invention, an interpretable battery modeling system for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data, is described. The system includes a physics-based equivalent circuit model (ECM) of the battery, a hybrid neural network module, and a computation unit. The physics-based ECM of the battery includes at least a two-RC network. The hybrid neural network module is integrated with the ECM in a fusion framework. The hybrid neural network module includes a recurrent neural network configured to estimate SOC from sequential current measurements, and one or more feedforward neural networks configured to predict selected equivalent circuit parameters. The selected parameters include an open-circuit voltage (Vb) and a resistance (R1). The computation unit is configured to implement the fusion framework by combining the estimated SOC, and the predicted selected parameters with the ECM under physical constraints, to generate terminal-voltage predictions in real time. The remaining equivalent-circuit parameters are maintained at fixed values to reduce computational complexity. The integrated fusion framework of neural networks with equivalent circuit physics enables accurate, and interpretable estimation without requiring extensive datasets or exhaustive experimental calibration. [0025] In at least one embodiment, the recurrent neural network includes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network having four layers with 128 hidden units, configured to process at least current and time-step inputs to output an SOC estimate at each time step. [0026] In at least one embodiment, the feedforward neural networks include Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks. The MLP includes a first MLP and a second MLP. The first MLP is configured to predict open-circuit voltage (Vb) from SOC and current, the first MLP includes three layers with ReLU and Sigmoid activations. The second MLP is configured to predict a reciprocal resistance value (1/R1), wherein reciprocal resistance prediction mitigates exploding gradient issues and improves numerical stability during training. [0027] In at least one embodiment, remaining fixed equivalent-circuit parameters include internal resistance (R0), secondary resistance (R2), and capacitances (C1, C2). [0028] In at least one embodiment, the training of the neural-network submodules employs a custom loss framework combining a weighted smooth mean absolute error (wMAE) loss prioritizing early-stage prediction accuracy to reduce cumulative error drift, and a boundary loss penalizing predicted voltages outside predefined safe charge and discharge limits. [0029] In at least one embodiment, the training optimization includes applying an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of about 0.00015 for the recurrent neural network, a learning rate of about 0.02 with a step scheduler reducing the rate by a factor of about 0.05 for the feedforward neural networks, and a training duration of about 100 epochs. [0030] In at least one embodiment, the hybrid neural network module is trainable using reduced datasets including fewer than 100 samples per discharge cycle, and is configured to generalize across varying load conditions without requiring recalibration. [0031] In at least one embodiment, the computation unit is implemented on an embedded hardware platform selected from a microcontroller, a digital signal processor (DSP), or a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), and is configured for real-time operation without requiring extensive offline parameter sweeps. [0032] In yet another aspect of the present invention, a method of operating a battery modeling system for a lithium-ion battery, to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage of the battery, is described. The method includes the step of receiving sequential current measurements from the battery. The method further includes the step of estimating SOC using a recurrent neural network applied to the sequential current measurements. The method further includes the step of predicting selected equivalent-circuit parameters using one or more feedforward neural networks. The selected parameters include at least open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1), while maintaining remaining equivalent-circuit parameters at fixed values. The method further includes the step of generating a terminal-voltage prediction by applying a fusion framework that integrates the estimated SOC, and the predicted parameters with the equivalent-circuit model under physical constraints. The fusion of neural networks with equivalent-circuit physics yields accurate and interpretable predictions using limited training data and without requiring exhaustive offline calibration. [0033] In at least one embodiment, the predicting resistance includes predicting a reciprocal resistance value (1/R1) to improve training stability and convergence. Further, the training of the recurrent and feedforward neural networks includes applying an Adam optimizer with task-specific learning rates, employing fewer than 100 samples per discharge cycle, and minimizing a custom loss function that combines a weighted smooth mean absolute error loss with a boundary loss enforcing safe operational voltage limits. [0034] Various objects, features, aspects, and advantages of the inventive subject matter will become more apparent from the following detailed description of preferred embodiments, along with the accompanying drawing figures in which like numerals represent like components. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS: [0035] The illustrated embodiments of the subject matter will be understood by reference to the drawings, wherein like parts are designated by like numerals throughout. The accompanying drawings, which are incorporated in and constitute a part of this disclosure, illustrate exemplary embodiments and, together with the description, serve to explain the disclosed principles. In the figures, the left-most digit(s) of a reference number identifies the figure in which the reference number first appears. The same numbers are used throughout the figures to reference like features and components. The following description is intended only by way of example and simply illustrates certain selected embodiments of devices, apparatus, systems, and methods that are consistent with the subject matter as claimed herein, wherein: [0036] FIG. 1 illustrates a schematic diagram of a two-RC equivalent circuit model (ECM) of a lithium-ion battery, showing internal resistance (R0), resistor–capacitor networks (R1–C1 and R2–C2), and bulk capacitance (Cb) configured to represent dynamic electrical behavior of the battery, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; [0037] FIG. 2 illustrates a block diagram of an interpretable battery modeling system configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data, showing the fusion of a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for SOC estimation and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks for open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1) prediction within a physics-informed framework, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; [0038] FIG. 3 illustrates a workflow diagram of the proposed modeling process of the interpretable battery modeling system, depicting data collection, feature extraction, neural network processing, and integration of physics-based constraints, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; [0039] FIG. 4 illustrates experimental voltage and current profiles for five discharge cycles of an LG 18650 lithium-ion cell, demonstrating variations in load conditions, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; [0040] FIG. 5 illustrates comparison plots of predicted versus actual state of charge (SOC) and terminal voltage for five randomly selected discharge cycles, demonstrating the accuracy and robustness of the interpretable battery modeling system, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; [0041] FIG. 6 illustrates a system architecture diagram of the hybrid neural network module and computation unit of the interpretable battery modeling system for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate SOC and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure; and [0042] FIG. 7 illustrates a method flow diagram of operating the interpretable battery modeling system for estimating state of charge (SOC) and predicting terminal voltage in real time under physical constraints, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure. [0043] The figures depict embodiments of the present subject matter for the purposes of illustration only. A person skilled in the art will easily recognize from the following description that alternative embodiments of the structures and methods illustrated herein may be employed without departing from the principles of the disclosure described herein. DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION: [0044] The following is a detailed description of embodiments of the disclosure depicted in the accompanying drawings. The embodiments are in such detail as to clearly communicate the disclosure. However, the amount of detail offered is not intended to limit the anticipated variations of embodiments; on the contrary, the intention is to cover all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives falling within the spirit and scope of the present disclosure as defined by the appended claims. [0045] While the embodiments of the disclosure are subject to various modifications and alternative forms, specific embodiments thereof have been shown by way of example in the figures and will be described below. It should be understood, however, that it is not intended to limit the disclosure to the particular forms disclosed, but on the contrary, the disclosure is to cover all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives falling within the scope of the disclosure. [0046] The terms “comprises”, “comprising”, or any other variations thereof used in the disclosure, are intended to cover a non-exclusive inclusion, such that a device, apparatus, system, or assembly that comprises a list of components does not include only those components but may include other components not expressly listed or inherent to such system, or apparatus, or assembly, or device. In other words, one or more elements in a system or apparatus or device proceeded by “comprises… a” does not, without more constraints, preclude the existence of other elements or additional elements in the system or apparatus or device. [0047] The present disclosure provides an interpretable battery modeling system for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data. The system implements a fusion framework that integrates a physics-based equivalent circuit model (ECM) with data-driven learning mechanisms including neural networks, thereby addressing the deficiencies of conventional modeling approaches. [0048] In various embodiments, the system includes: (i) a physics-based ECM of the battery including at least a two-RC network; (ii) a hybrid neural network module integrated with the ECM in the fusion framework, wherein the hybrid neural network module includes a recurrent neural network for SOC estimation and one or more feedforward neural networks for predicting selected ECM parameters; and (iii) a computation unit configured to implement the fusion framework by combining the estimated SOC and the predicted parameters with the ECM under physical constraints to generate terminal-voltage predictions in real time. [0049] In one embodiment, the two-RC ECM includes, internal resistance (R0), a first resistor–capacitor pair (R1–C1), a second resistor–capacitor pair (R2–C2), and bulk capacitance (Cb), thereby modeling short-term, long-term, and bulk storage effects within the lithium-ion battery. In the disclosed system, only selected ECM parameters, including open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1), are adaptively predicted, while remaining ECM parameters including R0, R2, C1, and C2 are maintained at fixed empirically determined values to reduce computational complexity. [0050] In some embodiments, the recurrent neural network employed in the system is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network configured to estimate SOC from sequential current measurements. The LSTM network may include four layers with 128 hidden units and is configured to process at least current and time-step inputs to output an SOC estimate at each time step. This configuration enables the system to capture temporal dependencies and dynamic responses of the battery SOC under varying current loads without requiring manual Coulomb counting or numerical integration. [0051] The feedforward neural networks are implemented as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks. In one embodiment, a first MLP is configured to predict the open-circuit voltage (Vb) from SOC and current, and includes three layers with ReLU and Sigmoid activations to ensure nonlinear learning capability while maintaining physically plausible outputs. A second MLP is configured to predict a reciprocal resistance value (1/R1) instead of R1, wherein reciprocal resistance prediction mitigates exploding gradient issues, improves training stability, and ensures numerical robustness of the hybrid modeling framework. [0052] In one embodiment, training of the hybrid neural network module employs a custom loss framework that integrates physics-based constraints. The framework includes a weighted smooth mean absolute error (wMAE) loss configured to prioritize early-stage prediction accuracy and reduce cumulative error drift over long prediction horizons, and a boundary loss configured to penalize voltage predictions outside predefined safe charge and discharge limits, thereby ensuring physical validity and operational safety of the predictions. [0053] The training optimization may further include applying an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of about 0.00015 for the recurrent neural network, a learning rate of about 0.02 with a step scheduler reducing the rate by a factor of about 0.05 for the feedforward neural networks, and a training duration of about 100 epochs. The hybrid neural network module is further configured to be trainable using reduced datasets including fewer than 100 samples per discharge cycle, while retaining the capability to generalize across varying load conditions without requiring recalibration. [0054] The computation unit of the system is implemented on an embedded hardware platform selected from a microcontroller, a digital signal processor (DSP), or a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). The computation unit executes the fusion framework to combine SOC estimates, predicted ECM parameters, and fixed ECM values under physical constraints to compute real-time terminal-voltage predictions without requiring extensive offline parameter sweeps, thereby enabling practical deployment in embedded battery management systems (BMS). [0055] For better understanding, one or more embodiments of the present invention shall be described with respect to the earlier-mentioned drawings. [0056] FIG. 1 illustrates a schematic diagram (100) of a two-RC equivalent circuit model (ECM) of a lithium-ion battery, showing internal resistance (R0), resistor–capacitor networks (R1–C1 and R2–C2), and bulk capacitance (Cb) configured to represent dynamic electrical behavior of the battery, in accordance with an exemplary embodiment of the present disclosure. [0057] In an embodiment, the ECM provides the physics-based framework within which neural-network predictions operate, thereby enabling a hybrid approach that integrates physics-constrained models with data-driven learning modules. In an embodiment, the ECM includes internal resistance (R0), two resistor–capacitor networks (R1–C1 and R2–C2), and a bulk capacitance (Cb). The internal resistance (R0) accounts for the instantaneous voltage drop associated with current flow through the battery. The bulk capacitance (Cb) models the main charge storage capability of the battery, wherein the voltage across the bulk capacitance, denoted as Vb, represents the open-circuit voltage (OCV). The bulk current flowing through this component is denoted as I, and the OCV is directly associated with the State of Charge (SOC) of the battery. [0058] The first RC network (R1–C1) models short-term transient dynamics of the battery, including charge transfer effects and double-layer capacitance phenomena. The current through this branch is denoted as I1, while the voltage across the branch is denoted as V1.
