An interpretable battery modeling system for lithium-ion batteries, configured to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage with high accuracy using limited experimental data, the system comprising: • a physics-based equivalent circuit model (ECM) of the battery including at least a two-RC network; • a hybrid neural network module integrated with the ECM in a fusion framework, wherein the hybrid neural network module comprises: o a recurrent neural network configured to estimate SOC from sequential current measurements; and o one or more feedforward neural networks configured to predict selected equivalent circuit parameters, the selected parameters comprising open-circuit voltage (Vb) and a resistance (R1); and • a computation unit configured to implement the fusion framework by combining the estimated SOC, and the predicted selected parameters with the ECM under physical constraints to generate terminal-voltage predictions in real time, wherein remaining equivalent-circuit parameters are maintained at fixed values to reduce computational complexity, the integrated fusion framework of neural networks with equivalent circuit physics enables accurate, and interpretable estimation without requiring extensive datasets or exhaustive experimental calibration. 2. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the recurrent neural network comprises a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network having four layers with 128 hidden units, configured to process at least current and time-step inputs to output an SOC estimate at each time step. 3. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the feedforward neural networks comprise Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks, including: • a first MLP configured to predict open-circuit voltage (Vb) from SOC and current, the first MLP comprising three layers with ReLU and Sigmoid activations; and • a second MLP configured to predict a reciprocal resistance value (1/R1), wherein reciprocal resistance prediction mitigates exploding gradient issues and improves numerical stability during training. 4. A method of operating a battery modeling system for a lithium-ion battery, to estimate state of charge (SOC) and predict terminal voltage of the battery, the method comprising: • receiving sequential current measurements from the battery; • estimating SOC using a recurrent neural network applied to the sequential current measurements; • predicting selected equivalent-circuit parameters using one or more feedforward neural networks, the selected parameters comprising at least open-circuit voltage (Vb) and resistance (R1), while maintaining remaining equivalent-circuit parameters at fixed values; and • generating a terminal-voltage prediction by applying a fusion framework that integrates the estimated SOC, the predicted parameters with the equivalent-circuit model under physical constraints, wherein the fusion of neural networks with equivalent-circuit physics yields accurate and interpretable predictions using limited training data and without requiring exhaustive offline calibration. 10. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR ESTIMATING INTERNAL PARAMETERS OF A LITHIUM-ION CELL UNDER SELECTABLE THERMAL ENVIRONMENTS The present discloses relates to method (100) and system (200) for estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell (101) under selectable thermal environments (102), including immersion cooling (102a) with dielectric coolant (104a) in an immersion bath (104) coupled to a temperature control unit (106) and fluid circulation subsystem (118), and natural convection (102b). A multi-channel test platform (103) executes OCV (108a) and HPPC (108b) protocols at multiple C-rates. Sensors (110) comprising voltage (110a), current (110b), and temperature (110c) record signals to form dataset (D), which is processed by an estimation module (112) to generate initial parameters for an equivalent circuit model simulated by ECM simulator (113). A processor (114) computes fit metric (E), and an optimizer module (116) refines parameters iteratively to obtain optimized set (P*). Results are stored (118) or transmitted via output interface (120) and communication module (126) to a battery management system (117) or digital twin (124).
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD [0001] The present disclosure relates to battery parameter estimation and optimization techniques. More specifically it relates generally to battery parameter estimation and optimization techniques. DEFINITIONS [0002] As used in the present disclosure, the following terms are generally intended to have the meaning as set forth below, except to the extent that the context in which they are used indicates otherwise. [0003] The term “Thermal environments” refers to configurable operating conditions under which a lithium-ion cell is tested. These include Immersion cooling environment that is a setup in which the cell is submerged in a dielectric coolant within a thermally controlled bath and natural convection environment that is an ambient air environment in which the cell dissipates heat passively without immersion. [0004] The term “Dielectric coolant” refers to an electrically insulating fluid, which may include hydrocarbon-or fluorocarbon-based liquids, used to extract heat from the cell in immersion cooling conditions. [0005] The term “Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) protocol” refers a diagnostic procedure used to measure the equilibrium voltage of the cell as a function of state-of-charge. [0006] The term “Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC) protocol” refers to a diagnostic procedure in which the cell is subjected to charge and discharge pulses at varying current levels, thereby enabling assessment of internal resistance, dynamic response, and available power capability. [0007] The term “Equivalent Circuit Model (ECM)” refers to a mathematical representation of the lithium-ion cell using electrical circuit elements, typically including an ohmic resistance in series with one or more resistor-capacitor branches. In the present context, a second-order ECM is employed with two parallel RC branches, which capture both short-term and medium-term electrochemical dynamics. [0008] The term “Fit metric” refers to a quantitative error function used to assess the similarity between simulated voltage waveforms produced by the equivalent circuit model and the measured waveforms in the experimental dataset. Examples of fit metrics include root mean square error, mean absolute error, and maximum error. [0009] The term “Battery Management System (BMS)” refers to an external electronic control system that monitors, protects, and manages the operation of a battery pack, and may receive optimized parameter sets to improve state-of-charge and state-of-health estimation. [0010] The term “Digital twin” refers to a virtual replica of a physical battery system, which can accept optimized parameter sets to enable predictive analytics, lifecycle forecasting, and large-scale fleet performance monitoring. BACKGROUND [0011] The background information herein below relates to the present disclosure but is not necessarily prior art. [0012] Accurate estimation of internal parameters of lithium-ion batteries is fundamental for predicting performance, ensuring safety, and prolonging the life of battery-powered systems. Conventional estimation approaches, including electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and simplified parameter fitting, often suffer from limited accuracy under varying load and temperature conditions. Moreover, conventional air cooling or indirect liquid cooling techniques are insufficient in mitigating localized thermal hotspots, particularly at high charge/discharge rates. [0013] Additionally, immersion cooling has emerged as a promising thermal management technique, where the battery cell is directly submerged in a dielectric coolant. This approach enhances heat dissipation, improves thermal uniformity, and suppresses parameter drift caused by temperature gradients. However, existing methods do not systematically integrate immersion cooling effects into parameter estimation frameworks. [0014] Furthermore, while optimization algorithms such as genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization have been applied to battery modelling, they often converge slowly or yield sub-optimal solutions when fitting nonlinear battery dynamics. There exists a need for a robust, adaptive, and computationally efficient framework that can accurately extract lithium-ion battery model parameters under varying cooling conditions and operational loads. [0015] Therefore, there exists a need to address these limitations by providing a system and method for estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments. OBJECTS [0016] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies, are as follows: [0017] It is an object of the present disclosure to provide a method for accurate estimation of internal parameters of lithium-ion cells under different thermal environments. [0018] The main object of the present disclosure is to integrate immersion cooling as a thermal management approach in parameter estimation experiments. [0019] An object of the present disclosure is to generate robust experimental datasets using OCV and HPPC protocols at multiple C-rates. [0020] Another object of the present disclosure is to develop a second-order equivalent circuit model capturing short-and medium-term battery dynamics. [0021] Yet another object of the present disclosure is to employ a population-based optimization algorithm, preferably Harris Hawks Optimization, for parameter refinement. [0022] Still another object of the present disclosure is to minimize the error between simulated and measured terminal voltage responses. [0023] Yet another object of the present disclosure is to validate parameter accuracy using error metrics including RMSE, MAE, and maximum error. [0024] Another object of the present disclosure is to enhance safety, reliability, and performance of lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles and energy storage systems. [0025] Yet another object of the present disclosure is to integrate optimized models into digital twin platforms for predictive battery analytics. [0026] Still another object of the present disclosure is to enable storage and transmission of optimized parameter sets for further use in battery management systems. [0027] Other objects and advantages of the present disclosure will be more apparent from the following description, which is not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure. SUMMARY [0028] This summary is provided to introduce concepts related to estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments. The concepts are further described below in the following detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter nor is it intended for use in determining or limiting the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0029] The present disclosure estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments comprises a lithium-ion cell, a plurality of thermal environments, an immersion cooling environment, a multi-channel battery test platform, an immersion bath, a dielectric coolant, a temperature control unit, a set of diagnostic protocols, an open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol, a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) protocol, sensors, a voltage sensor, a current sensor, a temperature sensor, an estimation module, an ECM simulator, a processor, an optimizer module, a battery management system, a fluid circulation subsystem, a pump, a heat-exchanger, an output interface, a data acquisition module, a digital twin module and a communication module. [0030] The multi-channel battery test platform is configured to apply open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol and a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) test profiles to a cell. [0031] Further, the immersion bath is configured to receive the cell and to contain a dielectric coolant and the immersion bath is being coupled to a temperature control unit and a fluid circulation subsystem. [0032] In an aspect, the plurality of sensors including at least a voltage sensor, a current sensor and temperature sensors that are arranged to sense terminal and thermal signals from the cell and the immersion bath. [0033] Further, the data acquisition module is communicatively coupled to the sensors and the test platform and is configured to produce a labelled experimental dataset (D) from the sensed signals that is simulated by the simulation module/estimation module that is configured to accept the dataset (D) and to derive an initial ECM parameter vector (P0) and to compute simulated terminal voltages (Vsim) from any supplied parameter vector (Pn). [0034] Furthermore, the optimizer module comprising a processor is configured to implement an iterative population-based optimisation routine which receives as inputs the fit metric (E) and the parameter vectors (Pn) and produces updated parameter vectors (Pn+1), each updated parameter vector being provided as input to the simulation module for re-evaluation. [0035] Thereafter, the output interface is configured to present or transmit an optimized parameter set (P*) and associated validation reports to external systems including a battery management system (BMS). [0036] In an embodiment, said iterative population-based optimizer is a Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) or a functionally equivalent optimizer. [0037] In an embodiment, the test platform is a multi-channel battery test system including a BTS-4000 or equivalent, the BTS-4000 being an example of the multi-channel battery test platform used to generate OCV and HPPC data. [0038] In an embodiment, the immersion bath further comprises an electrically insulating containment structure, a fluid inlet and outlet coupled to the fluid circulation subsystem, and external ports for connecting the test platform and the sensors and the dielectric coolant being chosen from non-conductive hydrocarbon or fluorocarbon dielectric liquids. [0039] In an embodiment, the optimizer module is configured to accept temperature measurements from the sensors and to adapt optimization weights or candidate selection in response to measured local temperature or thermal gradients so that parameter updates account for thermal state when evaluating fit metric (E). [0040] In an embodiment, the output interface is configured to deliver the optimized parameter set (P*) to a vehicle battery management system (BMS) and to the digital twin module for use in state-of-charge (SOC) and state-of-health (SOH) estimation, and wherein the system includes the communication module to transmit the optimized parameter set (P*) over wired or wireless links. [0041] In an embodiment, the data acquisition module time-stamps and stores raw waveforms and related metadata in a memory. [0042] In an embodiment, the ECM comprises a second-order RC network defined by ohmic resistance (R0) in series with two parallel resistances and capacitances (RC) branches (R1//C1 and R2//C2), each branch time constant chosen to capture short and medium time-scale dynamics, and wherein the estimation and optimization explicitly fit those resistances and capacitances. [0043] In an embodiment, the system is configured to execute test sequences representative of electric-vehicle driving cycles and wherein the optimizer module is configured to update the optimized parameter set (P*) adaptively in response to changes in load profile and cooling modality [0044] The present disclosure further envisages a method for estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments. The method includes the following steps:  mounting the lithium-ion cell on a multi-channel battery test platform;  placing the mounted lithium-ion cell selectively into one of a plurality of thermal environments including: o (i) an immersion cooling environment provided by an immersion bath containing a dielectric coolant, the immersion bath being coupled to a temperature control unit; and o (ii) a natural convection environment;  executing on the test platform a set of diagnostic protocols comprising at least an open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol and a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) protocol at a plurality of charge/discharge C-rates, wherein the test platform drives current profiles into and out of the cell and causes the cell to produce terminal voltage and current responses;  measuring, with sensors including at least a voltage sensor, a current sensor, and a temperature sensor, the terminal voltage, current and temperature waveforms produced by the cell during said execution of the set of diagnostic protocols to obtain experimental dataset (D);  providing the experimental dataset (D) as input to an estimation module and, using said experimental dataset (D), generating an initial set of electrical parameter values (P0) for a second-order equivalent circuit model (ECM) of the cell comprising an ohmic resistance (R0), polarization resistances (R1, R2), and capacitances (C1, C2);  providing the initial set of electrical parameter values (P0) as input to an ECM simulator to compute a simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) corresponding to the test current waveform in the experimental dataset (D);  computing, by a processor, a fit metric (E) between the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) and the measured test current waveform in the experimental dataset (D);  providing the fit metric (E) and the parameter set (P0) as inputs to an optimizer module configured to implement an iterative population-based optimizer, the optimizer module iteratively updating the parameter set (Pn) to produce updated parameter sets (Pn+1) such that each updated parameter set (Pn+1) is provided as an input to the ECM simulator to regenerate the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) for subsequent fitness evaluation, and repeating said iterations until a convergence criterion is met being an optimized parameter set (P*); and  outputting the optimized parameter set (P*) for storage, transmission to a battery management system, or for user in further predictive models. [0045] In an embodiment, said iterative population-based optimizer is a Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) or a functionally equivalent optimizer. [0046] In an embodiment, the immersion bath comprises a fluid circulation subsystem including a pump and a heat-exchanger coupled to the temperature control unit to maintain the dielectric coolant within a target temperature band, and wherein the temperature measurements from sensors are used as part of dataset (D) to control the temperature control unit and to weight the fit metric E during optimization. [0047] In an embodiment, plurality of charge/discharge C-rates comprises at least a low C-rate, a medium C-rate, and a high C-rate, and the HPPC pulses include charge and discharge pulses sized to excite the ohmic resistance (R0), the polarization resistances (R1, R2), and the capacitances (C1, C2) time-constants of the ECM, and wherein in the measurement step, time-stamps and labels dataset (D) with test metadata including cooling mode, C-rate, pulse timing and ambient temperature. [0048] In an embodiment, the estimation module extracts the initial parameter set (P0) by fitting the ECM to the transient segments of dataset (D) using time-domain fitting of the measured voltage/current pulses, the resulting parameter set (P0) being provided as input to the ECM simulator in the step of providing the initial set. [0049] In an embodiment, optimizer module executes an HHO routine comprising at least the operations of: (i) population initialization with candidate parameter vectors derived from the parameter set (P0); (ii) fitness evaluation of each candidate by invoking the ECM simulator to compute the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) and evaluating the fit metric (E); (iii) candidate update rules corresponding to the HHO hawk escape/attack operators; and (iv) termination when change in the fit metric (E) is below a predefined threshold or upon reaching a maximum iteration count; each candidate update (iii) producing an updated parameter vector that is provided as input, for re-evaluation, to step of providing the initial set. [0050] In an embodiment, the termination criterion is selected to achieve a root mean square error (RMSE) less than or equal to 0.06 V for the simulated versus measured terminal voltage under specified test conditions, the RMSE being calculated from the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) and the measured waveform in the dataset (D). [0051] In an embodiment, the method further comprising generating a validation report that includes error histograms, RMSE, mean absolute error (MAE) and maximum error (ME) before and after optimization, and storing the report together with the optimized parameter set (P*) in a non-volatile memory or transmitting the report via an output interface. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS [0052] A system and a method of the present disclosure will now be described with the help of the accompanying drawing, in which: [0053] Figures 1A-1C illustrate a method for estimation and iterative optimization of internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; [0054] Figure 2 illustrates a block diagram of a system estimation and iterative optimization of internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; [0055] Figure 3A illustrates OCV-SOC curves with and without coolant, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; [0056] Figure 3B illustrates Ohmic resistance variation in immersion coolant and without coolant concerning SOC, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; [0057] Figures 4A-4D illustrate impact of coolant and without coolant on ECM parameters under three C rates corresponding to SOC, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; [0058] Figures 5A-5F illustrate simulated and measured terminal voltage under coolant and non-coolant conditions at low C rate with error histograms, before and after HHO: Plots A and B represents voltage pulses. Subplots C and E show results before HHO, and Subplots D and F show results after HHO, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure; and [0059] Figures 6A-6F illustrate simulated and measured terminal voltage under coolant and non-coolant conditions at high C rate with error histograms, before and after HHO: Plots A and B represent voltage pulses. Subplots C and E show results before HHO, and Subplots D and F show results after HHO, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0061] Embodiments are provided so as to thoroughly and fully convey the scope of the present disclosure to the person skilled in the art. Numerous details are set forth, relating to specific components, and methods, to provide a complete understanding of embodiments of the present disclosure. As used in the present disclosure, the forms "a,” "an," and "the" may be intended to include the plural forms as well, unless the context clearly suggests otherwise. The terms “including,” and “having,” are open-ended transitional phrases and therefore specify the presence of stated features, integers, steps, operations, elements, and/or components, but do not forbid the presence or addition of one or more other features, integers, steps, operations, elements, components, and/or groups thereof. [0064] To address the issues of estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell, the present disclosure envisages a method for estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments, (hereinafter referred to as “method 100”) and a system (hereinafter referred to as “system 200”). The estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell under selectable thermal environments method 100 will now be described with reference to Figure 1 and the system 200 will be described with reference to Figure 2. Further, illustrations in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure will be described with reference to Figures 2-6F. [0065] Figure 1 and Figure 2 illustrates a lithium-ion cell 101 under selectable thermal environments 102 comprises a lithium-ion cell 101, a plurality of thermal environments 102, an immersion cooling environment 102a, a multi-channel battery test platform 103, an immersion bath 104, a dielectric coolant 104a, a temperature control unit 106, a set of diagnostic protocols 108, an open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol 108a, a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) protocol 108b, sensors 110, a voltage sensor 110a, a current sensor 110b, a temperature sensor 110c, an estimation module 112, an ECM simulator 113, a processor 114, an optimizer module 116, a battery management system 117, a fluid circulation subsystem 118, a pump 118a, a heat-exchanger 118b, an output interface 120, a data acquisition module 122, a digital twin module 124 and a communication module 126. [0066] Figures 1A-1C outline the method for estimating internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell (101) under selectable thermal environments. The order in which method 100 is described is not intended to be construed as a limitation, and any number of the described method steps may be combined in any order to implement method 100, or an alternative method. Furthermore, method 100 may be implemented by processing resource or computing device(s) through any suitable hardware. The method 100 comprises the following steps: [0067] In method step 102, the method 100 includes, mounting the lithium-ion cell 101 on a multi-channel battery test platform 103. [0068] In method step 104, the method 100 includes, placing the mounted lithium-ion cell 101 selectively into one of a plurality of thermal environments 102 including: o (i) an immersion cooling environment (102a) provided by an immersion bath (104) containing a dielectric coolant (104a), the immersion bath (104) being coupled to a temperature control unit (106); and o (ii) a natural convection environment 102b. [0069] In method step 106, the method 100 includes, executing on the test platform 103 a set of diagnostic protocols 108 comprising at least an open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol 108a and a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) protocol 108b at a plurality of charge/discharge C-rates, wherein the test platform 103 drives current profiles into and out of the cell and causes the cell to produce terminal voltage and current responses. [0070] In method step 108, the method 100 includes, measuring, with sensors 110 including at least a voltage sensor 110a, a current sensor 110b, and a temperature sensor 110c, the terminal voltage, current and temperature waveforms produced by the cell during said execution of the set of diagnostic protocols to obtain experimental dataset (D). [0071] In method step 110, the method 100 includes, providing the experimental dataset (D) as input to an estimation module 112 and, using said experimental dataset (D), generating an initial set of electrical parameter values (P0) for a second-order equivalent circuit model (ECM) of the cell comprising an ohmic resistance (R0), polarization resistances (R1, R2), and capacitances (C1, C2). [0072] In method step 112, the method 100 includes, providing the initial set of electrical parameter values (P0) as input to an ECM simulator 113 to compute a simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) corresponding to the test current waveform in the experimental dataset (D). [0073] In method step 114, the method 100 includes, computing, by a processor 114, a fit metric (E) between the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) and the measured test current waveform in the experimental dataset (D). [0074] In method step 116, the method 100 includes, providing the fit metric (E) and the parameter set (P0) as inputs to an optimizer module 116 configured to implement an iterative population-based optimizer, the optimizer module 116 iteratively updating the parameter set (Pn) to produce updated parameter sets (Pn+1) such that each updated parameter set (Pn+1) is provided as an input to the ECM simulator 113 to regenerate the simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) for subsequent fitness evaluation, and repeating said iterations until a convergence criterion is met being an optimized parameter set (P*). [0075] In method step 118, the method 100 includes, outputting the optimized parameter set (P*) for storage, transmission to a battery management system 117, or for user in further predictive models. [0076] Figure 2 illustrates a system 200 for estimation and iterative optimization of internal parameters of a lithium-ion cell 101. The lithium-ion cell 101 is selectively placed into one of a plurality of thermal environments 102. In a first configuration, the cell is placed into an immersion cooling environment 102a comprising an immersion bath 104 containing a dielectric coolant 104a, further the immersion bath is thermally coupled to a temperature control unit 106. [0077] In an embodiment, the system 200 includes a multi-channel battery test platform 103 upon which the lithium-ion cell 101 is mounted. The test platform is configured to execute diagnostic protocols, including an open circuit voltage (OCV) protocol 108a and a hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) protocol 108b, at multiple charge/discharge C-rates. By applying controlled current pulses to the cell and recording corresponding voltage responses, the test platform initiates the collection of experimental data. [0078] The system 200 further includes a plurality of sensors 110 arranged to measure terminal and thermal signals from the lithium-ion cell. The sensors include at least a voltage sensor 110a, a current sensor 110b, and one or more temperature sensors 110c. The signals from the sensors are collected by a data acquisition module 122, which records time-stamped waveforms and labels the dataset (D) with metadata including cooling condition, C-rate, and pulse timing. [0079] The experimental dataset (D) is supplied to an estimation module 112 configured to derive an initial set of electrical parameters (P0) of the cell by fitting a second-order equivalent circuit model (ECM). The ECM comprises an ohmic resistance, two polarization resistances, and two capacitances corresponding to short-and medium-term electrochemical dynamics. [0080] In an embodiment, the initial parameter set (P0) is provided as input to an ECM simulator 113, which generates a simulated terminal voltage waveform (Vsim) corresponding to the applied test current waveform in the dataset (D). A processor 114 computes a fit metric (E) by comparing the simulated voltage waveform with the measured waveform in the dataset (D). [0081] The fit metric (E) and parameter vectors are then provided to an optimizer module 116, which implements an iterative population-based optimization algorithm, preferably a Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) routine. The optimizer iteratively updates the parameter sets (Pn) to produce refined sets (Pn+1), each of which is re-evaluated through the ECM simulator (113). The iterations continue until a convergence criterion is met, yielding an optimized parameter set (P*). [0082] The optimized parameter set (P*) is output for storage in non-volatile memory 118 or for transmission to external systems. In one embodiment, the output interface 120 communicates the optimized parameter set to a battery management system 117 for use in real-time state-of-charge (SOC) and state-of-health (SOH) estimation. In another embodiment, the parameter set is transmitted to a digital twin module 124 for predictive analytics and lifecycle management. [0083] The immersion bath is thermally coupled to a temperature control unit 106 and to a fluid circulation subsystem 118 comprising a pump 118a and a heat exchanger 118b. These subsystems cooperate to regulate the coolant temperature within a defined target band, thereby maintaining thermal uniformity around the immersed cell. In a second configuration, the lithium-ion cell operates under a natural convection environment 102b in which it is exposed to ambient conditions without coolant. [0084] Additionally, the system includes the communication module 126 configured to transmit the optimized parameter set and validation reports over wired or wireless communication links to external platforms. The communication module enables integration of the optimized parameters into vehicle systems, cloud-based monitoring infrastructures, or fleet management solutions. [0086] Figures 4A to 4D show the validation results for low C-rate operating conditions under immersion cooling and natural convection environments. Before optimization, the simulated voltage waveforms derived from the initial parameter set show visible discrepancies compared to measured responses, and the corresponding error histograms indicate relatively high deviations. After optimization using the Harris Hawks algorithm, the simulated waveforms align more closely with measured voltages, and error histograms show substantial reduction in deviation, with convergence achieved at root mean square error values near 0.06 V. These results demonstrate that immersion cooling stabilizes the electrochemical dynamics of the cell by reducing thermal gradients, thereby improving the reproducibility and accuracy of parameter extraction even at low current rates. [0087] Figures 5A and 5F illustrate simulated and measured terminal voltages under coolant and non-coolant conditions at low C-rate, with accompanying error histograms before and after optimization using the Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) algorithm, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. Plots A and B represent voltage pulse responses, subplots C and E show simulation versus measurement results prior to optimization, and subplots D and F show the corresponding results after optimization. Plots A and B represent voltage pulse responses, subplots C and E show results before optimization, while subplots D and F show results after optimization. At high C-rates, the optimization step yields substantial improvement in accuracy, with error values reduced to within the targeted convergence thresholds, and immersion cooling shown to suppress resistance growth and stabilize dynamic response parameters. [0089] The system 100 operates in real time where lithium-ion cell 101 is mounted on the multi-channel battery test platform 103. The platform executes diagnostic protocols including the open circuit voltage protocol 108a and the hybrid pulse power characterization protocol 108b at different charge or discharge C-rates. By applying programmed current profiles into and out of the cell, the platform drives the cell to generate terminal voltage and current responses. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to an advanced energy storage device comprising a lithium-ion battery that integrates a nano-silicon anode structure to significantly enhance energy density, charge-discharge efficiency, and lifecycle performance. The nano-engineered silicon anode, combined with optimized binder composition and protective coatings, mitigates the volumetric expansion typically associated with silicon, thereby improving mechanical stability and cycling performance. This innovation is suitable for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and grid-scale energy storage applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Field of the Invention: The invention falls under the domain of electrochemical energy storage, particularly lithium-ion battery technologies. It pertains to the development of a high-efficiency lithium-ion battery using nano-silicon based anodes, which improves energy storage capacity and battery lifespan. Background of the Invention: Conventional lithium-ion batteries typically employ graphite anodes, which have a theoretical capacity of approximately 372 mAh/g. This capacity is insufficient to meet the increasing energy demands of next-generation technologies such as electric vehicles, renewable energy storage systems, and high-performance portable electronics. Silicon has emerged as a promising alternative due to its high theoretical capacity of ~4,200 mAh/g, nearly ten times higher than graphite. However, silicon anodes face significant challenges, including large volume expansion (~300%) during lithiation, which leads to structural degradation, electrode pulverization, and unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers. Existing solutions using micro-silicon or silicon composites only partially address these issues and often suffer from poor conductivity and limited cycle life. There is a need for a robust nano-structured silicon anode system integrated with effective binder and coating technologies to enable high-performance lithium-ion batteries. Summary of the Invention: The invention provides an energy storage device comprising a lithium-ion battery with a nano-silicon anode, designed to maximize capacity and maintain structural integrity over repeated cycles. Key innovations include:  Nano-silicon particles with controlled size distribution (10–150 nm) to accommodate volumetric expansion without mechanical failure.  Hybrid conductive network using carbon nanofibers or graphene layers to improve electron transport.  Elastic polymeric binder system with self-healing properties to maintain electrode integrity.  Surface coating of nano-silicon using oxide or carbon shells to stabilize SEI formation.  Optimized electrolyte additives (e.g., fluoroethylene carbonate) to improve interfacial stability. The integration of these components results in a battery with higher energy density, faster charge–discharge rates, reduced capacity fading, and extended cycle life. Detailed Description of the Invention: 1. Nano-Silicon Anode Structure  Material: Nano-silicon particles are synthesized through chemical vapor deposition or ball milling techniques to achieve a particle size distribution between 10–150 nm.  Coating: Each nano-silicon particle is coated with a thin carbon or silicon oxide layer (thickness: 2–10 nm) to buffer volume expansion and enhance surface conductivity.  Porous Structure: The nano-silicon layer is deposited on a porous copper current collector to provide mechanical flexibility and ion transport pathways. 2. Conductive Network  A network of graphene nanosheets or carbon nanotubes is embedded throughout the anode to create efficient electron conduction pathways, reducing internal resistance. 3. Binder Composition  A hybrid polymer binder (e.g., carboxymethyl cellulose + styrene-butadiene rubber + self-healing polymer segments) is used to maintain electrode cohesion despite silicon expansion.  The binder exhibits stretchability > 300%, ensuring mechanical stability through multiple charge–discharge cycles. 4. Electrolyte System  A standard carbonate-based electrolyte is enhanced with fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) and other film-forming additives to promote stable SEI formation on silicon surfaces.  Optional use of solid-state or gel polymer electrolytes for advanced battery safety. 5. Cell Configuration  The nano-silicon anode is paired with a conventional cathode material such as LiCoO₂, NMC, or LFP, depending on the application.  The entire cell is assembled in a pouch or cylindrical format, ensuring compatibility with existing manufacturing lines. 6. Performance Characteristics  Specific Capacity: > 1,000 mAh/g anode capacity after 100 cycles.  Coulombic Efficiency: > 99% after initial cycles.  Cycle Life: > 500 cycles with minimal capacity fade.  Energy Density: Increase of 30–50% compared to graphite-based cells. Advantages of the Invention: 1. Significantly higher energy storage capacity compared to conventional anodes. 2. Improved structural stability through nano-engineering and hybrid binders. 3. Enhanced cycling performance and lifetime. 4. Compatibility with existing battery production technologies. 5. Applicability across multiple sectors (EVs, grid storage, consumer electronics). , Claims:An energy storage device comprising a lithium-ion battery with a nano-silicon based anode, wherein the nano-silicon particles are coated with carbon or silicon oxide layers to improve structural and electrochemical stability. 2. The device of claim 1, wherein the nano-silicon particles have a size range between 10–150 nm, enabling accommodation of volumetric changes during lithiation and delithiation. 3. The device of claim 1, wherein the anode comprises a hybrid conductive network formed from carbon nanotubes, graphene nanosheets, or carbon nanofibers. 4. The device of claim 1, wherein the binder comprises elastic and self-healing polymers to maintain electrode integrity over repeated cycles. 5. The device of claim 1, wherein the electrolyte includes fluoroethylene carbonate additives to stabilize SEI formation on the silicon surface. 6. The device of claim 1, wherein the lithium-ion battery demonstrates a specific capacity greater than 1,000 mAh/g after 100 cycles with a coulombic efficiency greater than 99%. 7. The device of claim 1, wherein the cell format is selected from pouch, cylindrical, or prismatic types suitable for high-volume manufacturing.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT BATTERY CHARGING DEVICE AND METHOD FOR CHARGING LITHIUM-ION AND LEAD-ACID BATTERIES A battery charging device (100) and method (300) include an input terminal (I1) to receive a variable input alternating current connected to a bridge rectifier (D1) for converting alternating current to direct current output. A multi-mode controller (U1) connected to a primary side of transformer (T1) receives direct current and stores energy in transformer (T1) primary during ON-time and transfers it to transformer (T1) secondary during OFF-time creating galvanic isolated direct current output. An isolated feedback loop (L1) is connected to the multi-mode controller (U1), and the transformer (T1) output provides voltage and current regulation that generates a target output voltage (O1). A current control element (R5) is connected to output of transformer (T1) naturally limits initial current flow and progressively tapers as output voltage approaches the target output voltage (O1) for charging both lithium-ion battery (B1) or a lead-acid battery (B2). patents.complete_specification: DESC:BATTERY CHARGING DEVICE AND METHOD FOR CHARGING LITHIUM-ION AND LEAD-ACID BATTERIES TECHNICAL FIELD OF THE INVENTION [0001] The present invention relates to a battery charging device and more particularly relates to a stable, simple battery charging device for efficiently charging various battery types with wide input compatibility, robust, and reliable performance. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] A battery charging device typically includes a battery charging circuit which is connectable to a power source and to a rechargeable battery and is operable to charge the battery. Conventional battery chargers support charging single battery chemistry such as either a lithium-ion battery or a lead-acid battery and are designed for specific constant voltage (CV) endpoint and charging profiles. However, battery charging systems capable of charging multiple chemistries are increasingly required in various applications. [0003] Majority of prior battery charging devices for charging multiple battery types typically require a detection circuit configured to identify the battery characteristics and charging parameters. Additionally, such prior art battery charging devices require complex on-board temperature compensation and microcontroller-based circuits and do not provide charge current to the batteries as efficiently as possible. The inclusion of microcontroller-based detection and supporting circuit increases the overall cost complexity and design overhead of the battery charging devices thereby increasing cost effectiveness particularly in low cost or compact applications. This becomes particularly disadvantageous in agricultural applications where cost sensitivity, robustness and ease of use are critical factors especially in rural or resource constrained environment. Also, the prior art charging devices require dedicated current-control elements or microcontrollers to actively regulate current with complex feedback loops. Such microcontroller unit increases cost, complexity, and component count and results in firmware-related failure modes and update requirements. Additionally, prior art battery charging devices delivers unstable damages, leading to overcharging or undercharging which reduces battery lifespan, causes performance degradation and damage the battery permanently. Furthermore, the problem associated with some existing battery chargers is that they have a limited input voltage range and the battery charging circuit does not operate continuously on different sources of AC power. [0004] Hence, there is a need in that art to provide a solution to address all the above-mentioned problems. [0026] The battery charging device (100) further includes the multi-mode controller (U1) with integrated protection connected to the primary side of the transformer (T1) for isolation and voltage conversion. In a preferred embodiment, the multi-mode controller (U1) comprises a flyback controller with a plurality of terminals for integrated protection that creates the galvanic isolated DC output that flows through the reverse polarity protection diode (D4) to charge the battery (B1, B2). The multi-mode controller (U1) switches ON and the current flows through the transformer (T1) primary winding and the energy stores in the magnetic field (like compressing a spring). The fly-back type multi-mode controller (U1) is designed with high integration CMOS circuit, and includes protection functions for short circuits, secondary side open circuit, over temperature, over voltage and so on. With built-in HV power transistor and self-power supply circuit, the multi-mode controller (U1) has the characteristics of saving external components. [0027] The rectified AC mains feed the multi-mode controller (U1) and stores energy in the transformer primary during ON-time and transfers it to the secondary during OFF-time, creating galvanic isolated DC output. The transformer (T1) provides both electrical isolation and voltage conversion. The multi-mode controller (U1) switches OFF so that the magnetic field collapses (spring releases) and the energy jumps to the secondary winding and flows through the diode (D4) to charge the battery (B1, B2). The protection network (P1) comprises an RCD snubber network having the resistor (R1), the capacitor (C4), and the diode (D2). The RCD snubber network is used for suppressing the voltage spike and high-frequency ringing that occur during fast switching of the multi-mode controller (U1) caused by the collapsing magnetic field in the transformer primary protecting the battery (B1, B2). [0028] The diode (D2) connected in reverse polarity to the multi-mode controller (U1) turns on when the drain voltage exceeds the clamp capacitor voltage, allowing current to flow into the protection network (P1). The capacitor (C4) charges up to provide a stable voltage during transient events and the resistor (R1) connected in parallel to the capacitor (C4) discharges the stored energy. The isolated feedback loop (L1) comprises a Zener-optocoupler analog loop having the Zener diode (Z1), the resistor network (R2, R3) and the optocoupler LED (U2). The Zener diode (Z1), the resistor (R2, R3), and the optocoupler infrared LED (U2) are connected in series, across the voltage source. The Zener-optocoupler analog loop works by combining the Zener diode's precise voltage breakdown characteristic with the optocoupler's ability to maintain electrical isolation between two circuits. The Zener diode (Z1) with the resistor network (R2, R3) creates a stable voltage reference and biases the optocoupler LED (U2) when output voltage rises and an increased opto-transistor current lowers a feedback pin (FB) voltage of the multi-mode controller (U1) thereby reducing the output voltage (O1) to the end-of-charge voltage of the battery (B1, B2). patents.abstract: A process for recycling lithium-ion battery production scrap to recover battery-grade cathode active materials without harsh chemicals. The process applies low-temperature thermal treatment at 100°C to 180°C to soften binder materials, followed by mechanical separation to obtain virgin black mass containing cathode active materials. The virgin black mass undergoes thermal regeneration at elevated temperatures in controlled atmospheric conditions to remove polymer binders and impurities. Relithiation using lithium carbonate restores stoichiometric composition to regenerate battery-grade cathode active materials. The process handles slurry waste through vacuum drying, while coated electrode materials undergo low-temperature delamination. Defective cells are mechanically dismantled to obtain coated foils for processing. The process achieves material recovery rates exceeding 90% for LiFePO4 chemistry production scrap, providing an environmentally sustainable and cost-effective approach to battery material recycling with reduced carbon emissions.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [0001] The present invention relates to recycling techniques for lithium-ion battery production scrap, particularly to processes for recovering valuable materials from battery manufacturing waste including slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells. More particularly, the invention relates to direct recycling processes that utilize low-temperature treatment and thermal regeneration to recover battery-grade cathode active materials from production scrap without the use of harsh chemicals or acids. The invention provides an economically feasible and environmentally sustainable approach to material recovery with reduced carbon emissions. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] The global shift toward electrification, particularly in electric vehicles and energy storage systems, has led to unprecedented demand for lithium-ion batteries. This surge in battery production has resulted in significant manufacturing waste, including slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells, which contain valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. With battery manufacturing facilities generating approximately 15-30% production scrap during initial operations, the recovery of these critical materials has become increasingly important for both economic and environmental sustainability. [0003] The need for effective recycling of lithium-ion battery production scrap has become more pressing as raw material costs continue to rise and supply chain constraints limit access to virgin materials. Current estimates suggest that by 2030, manufacturing scrap will play a central role in material recovery efforts, as end-of-life batteries typically take about a decade to become available for recycling. The quality of materials obtained from production scrap is often similar to virgin materials, making direct recycling approaches particularly attractive for maintaining material performance while reducing environmental impact. [0004] Conventional recycling approaches primarily rely on pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes that involve high-temperature smelting or aggressive chemical leaching using strong acids. These methods often result in significant material losses, high energy consumption, and the generation of hazardous waste streams. Pyrometallurgical processes typically achieve recovery rates below 80% and often lose valuable materials like lithium and aluminum to slag. Hydrometallurgical approaches, while more selective, require extensive use of corrosive acids and generate toxic waste streams that require costly treatment. [0005] One US Patent No. 12,431,553 describes methods for scalable direct recycling of battery waste through multiple heat treatment steps to decompose binders and separate electrode materials from current collectors. The process involves applying first and second heat treatments at temperatures between 100-1200°C, followed by separation and surface treatment operations. However, this approach may require multiple high-temperature processing steps and complex separation procedures, potentially increasing energy consumption and processing costs while limiting applicability to certain battery chemistries. [0006] Similarly, another Australian Patent Application no. AU2023250215A1 discloses a lithium-ion battery recycling process involving disassembly, dismantling, and hydrometallurgical processing using organic acids for material recovery. The process includes sequential chemical separation procedures to obtain individual metal elements from pregnant leach liquor through solvent extraction and precipitation steps. Nevertheless, this approach still relies on chemical processing and multiple separation steps, which may increase complexity and processing time while requiring careful handling of chemical reagents and waste streams. [0007] Keeping in view the challenges associated with the state of art, there is a need for a simplified direct recycling process that can efficiently recover battery-grade cathode active materials from lithium-ion battery production scrap using low-temperature thermal treatment without harsh chemicals. The present invention provides an economically viable and environmentally sustainable solution that achieves high material recovery rates while minimizing energy consumption and eliminating the need for acid-based processing, thereby reducing carbon emissions and operational costs. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION [0008] The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a direct recycling process for lithium-ion battery production scrap that recovers battery-grade cathode active materials without the use of harsh chemicals or acids. [0009] Another objective of the present invention is to achieve high material recovery rates exceeding 90% while minimizing energy consumption through low-temperature thermal treatment processes. [0010] Another objective of the present invention is to eliminate the generation of hazardous waste streams and toxic emissions commonly associated with conventional pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical recycling methods. [0011] Another objective of the present invention is to provide an economically viable recycling solution that reduces operational costs and dependency on virgin raw materials from mining operations. [0012] Another objective of the present invention is to develop a scalable processing system suitable for industrial implementation that can accommodate varying production volumes and scrap generation rates typical of gigafactory operations. [0013] Another objective of the present invention is to preserve the quality and performance characteristics of recovered cathode active materials to enable direct reuse in battery manufacturing applications without extensive purification requirements. [0014] Another objective of the present invention is to reduce carbon emissions and environmental impact compared to conventional recycling approaches while providing an environmentally sustainable solution for battery material recovery. [0015] Yet another objective of the present invention is to handle multiple types of production scrap including slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells through a unified processing approach that maintains material purity and separation requirements. [0016] Other objectives and advantages of the present invention will become apparent from the following description taken in connection with the accompanying drawings, wherein, by way of illustration and example, the aspects of the present invention are disclosed. SUMMARY OF THE PRESENT INVENTION [0017] The present invention provides a process for recycling lithium-ion battery production scrap comprising slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells to recover battery-grade cathode active materials. The process includes applying low-temperature thermal treatment to the production scrap at temperatures between approximately one hundred to one hundred eighty degrees Celsius to soften binder materials without decomposition, followed by mechanical separation to obtain virgin black mass containing cathode active materials. The virgin black mass undergoes thermal regeneration at elevated temperatures in controlled atmospheric conditions to remove polymer binders and impurities, followed by relithiation using lithium carbonate to restore stoichiometric composition and regenerate battery-grade cathode active materials suitable for reuse in battery manufacturing. [0018] In another embodiment, the process include pre-treatment steps for different types of production scrap, wherein slurry waste undergoes vacuum drying to form solid black mass, while coated electrode materials are processed through low-temperature delamination to separate active materials from current collectors. The process further include mechanical processing such as shredding and sieving to achieve clean separation, followed by calcination in inert atmosphere with controlled heating programs to ensure complete regeneration. The process also incorporate quality control measures including compositional analysis and electrochemical testing to verify the recovered materials meet battery-grade specifications. A key advantage of the invention is the elimination of harsh chemical processing while achieving high material recovery rates exceeding ninety percent, thereby providing an environmentally sustainable and cost-effective approach to battery material recycling. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES [0019] The present invention will be better understood after reading the following detailed description of the presently preferred aspects thereof with reference to the appended drawings, in which the features, other aspects, and advantages of certain exemplary embodiments of the invention will be more apparent from the accompanying drawing in which: [0020] Figure 1 illustrates the production scrap categorization system showing the three main types of battery manufacturing waste including slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells. [0021] Figure 2 illustrates the low-temperature roasting system for coated foil delamination operating at roasting temperature 150°C to soften binder materials without decomposition. [0022] Figure 3 shows images of various production scrap materials obtained from battery manufacturing facilities including cathode slurry, anode slurry, coated foils, and defective cells. [0023] Figure 4 demonstrates the slurry pre-treatment process flow showing the transformation of viscous slurry waste into solid virgin black mass through vacuum drying operations. [0024] Figure 5 presents the vacuum tray furnace prototype configuration with Teflon trays used for large-scale industrial processing of slurry waste materials. [0025] Figure 6 illustrates the low-temperature delamination method showing the roll-to-roll process integration for continuous processing of coated electrode materials. [0026] Figure 7 illustrates the low-temperature roasting drum system designed for scalable delamination processing of coated foils with industrial automation compatibility. [0027] Figure 8 illustrates the TGA/DSC analysis plot for LiFePO4 heated to 800°C demonstrating the thermal decomposition behavior and weight loss characteristics. [0028] Figure 9 illustrates furnace heating program for calcination. [0029] Figure 10 illustrates the relithiation process flow showing the solid-state synthesis method for regenerating battery-grade LFP cathode material using lithium carbonate. [0030] Common reference numerals are used throughout the figures to indicate similar features. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0031] The following description describes various features and functions of the disclosed system. The illustrative aspects described herein are not meant to be limiting. It may be readily understood that certain aspects of the disclosed system can be arranged and combined in a wide variety of different configurations, all of which have not been contemplated herein. [0032] Accordingly, those of ordinary skill in the art will recognize that various changes and modifications of the embodiments described herein can be made without departing from the scope of the invention. In addition, descriptions of well-known functions and constructions are omitted for clarity and conciseness. [0033] Features that are described and/or illustrated with respect to one embodiment may be used in the same way or in a similar way in one or more other embodiments and/or in combination with or instead of the features of the other embodiments. [0034] The terms and words used in the following description are not limited to the bibliographical meanings but are merely used to enable a clear and consistent understanding of the invention. Accordingly, it should be apparent to those skilled in the art that the following description of exemplary embodiments of the present invention is provided for illustrative purposes only and not for the purpose of limiting the invention. [0035] It is to be understood that the singular forms “a”, “an”, and “the” include plural referents unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. [0036] It should be emphasized that the term “comprises/comprising” when used in this specification is taken to specify the presence of stated features, steps, or components but does not preclude the presence or addition of one or more other features, steps, components, or groups thereof. [0037] Accordingly, the present invention relates to recycling techniques for lithium-ion battery production scrap, particularly to processes for recovering valuable materials from battery manufacturing waste including slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells. The invention provides a direct recycling process utilizing low-temperature treatment and thermal regeneration to recover battery-grade cathode active materials from production scrap without the use of harsh chemicals or acids. [0038] The present invention comprises a vacuum tray furnace for slurry pre-treatment, a low-temperature roasting system for coated foil delamination, mechanical dismantling equipment for cell scrap processing, thermal regeneration furnaces operating at controlled atmospheric conditions, and relithiation systems using lithium carbonate. The invention provides an economically feasible and environmentally sustainable approach to material recovery with reduced carbon emissions while achieving material recovery rates exceeding ninety percent. [0039] In the present invention, the recycling process begins with the categorization and pre-treatment of different types of production scrap generated during lithium-ion battery manufacturing. As shown in Figure 1, the production scrap includes three main categories: slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells from the assembly line. The slurry waste comprises cathode slurry containing LiFePO4 (LFP) mixed with N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and super P carbon, along with anode slurry containing graphite, super P carbon, styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC). The coated electrode scrap includes both single-sided and double-sided coated aluminum and copper foils, while defective cells encompass various stages of cell assembly including jelly rolls, semi-finished goods, and finished cells with or without electrolyte. [0040] Table 1 provides a detailed breakdown of the types and volume of production scrap generated in the production of lithium-ion battery cells for a 6GWh manufacturing facility. The production scrap includes cathode slurry for both NMC (144 kg/day) and LFP (1278.1 kg/day) chemistries, anode slurry for NMC (142.6 kg/day) and LFP (611.8 kg/day) chemistries, coated aluminum foil for NMC (14.8 kg/day) and LFP (42.7 kg/day), coated copper foil for NMC (32.3 kg/day) and LFP (72.2 kg/day), non-coated aluminum foil (592.8 kg/day), non-coated copper foil (1057.5 kg/day), and defective cells for NMC (1564 kg/day) and LFP (3693.6 kg/day). This data demonstrates the significant volume of recoverable materials available from battery manufacturing operations. Battery chemical waste includes cathode slurry waste [LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) +NMP (N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone) +PVDF (Polyvinylidene Fluoride) +SPC (Super P Carbon)], anode slurry waste (Gr (Graphite)+SPC (Super P Carbon)+SBR (styrene–butadiene rubber )+CMC (carboxymethyl cellulose)], and mixed slurry compositions, typically resulting from viscosity issues, composition variations, or environmental factors such as temperature and humidity. Powder waste encompasses excess materials from dedusting operations and cannot be refined through the direct recycling process. Coated electrode scrap includes both aluminum and copper foils with single-sided or double-sided coatings, often rejected due to coating uniformity, thickness, porosity, adhesion, or surface integrity issues, and are processed through binder removal using solvent-based methods. Semi-finished goods and defective cells from various assembly stages undergo mechanical dismantling followed by processing as coated samples. Types of Cell Production Scrap, Reason for Failure, and Process Used for Recycling [0042] The slurry pre-treatment process addresses the viscous nature of the slurry waste through vacuum drying operations. As illustrated in Figure 4 and Figure 5, the slurry undergoes processing in a vacuum tray furnace where Teflon trays are loaded with the viscous slurry material. The vacuum tray furnace operates at temperatures between 130°C to 150°C under vacuum conditions to remove solvents and form solid virgin black mass. The composition of the slurry varies depending on the chemistry, with LFP cathode slurry containing Li-2.60%, Fe-20.8%, P-11.58%, O4-23.93%, Carbon-0.92%, PVP-0.08%, PVDF-1.10%, and NMP-38.92%, while NMC cathode slurry contains Li-5.18%, Ni-39.40%, Mn-2.05%, Co-2.20%, O2-23.87%, Carbon-0.72%, PVP-0.12%, PVDF-0.97%, and NMP-25.50%. [0043] Table 3 details the composition and chemistry of different slurry types processed in the recycling operation. For LFP chemistry, the anode slurry comprises graphite, super P carbon, styrene-butadiene rubber, and carboxymethyl cellulose, while for NMC chemistry, the anode contains 46.97% carbon, 2.56% SiO, 0.68% CMC, 0.97% SBR, and 48.82% deionized water. The cathode slurry compositions vary significantly between chemistries: LFP cathode slurry contains 2.60% Li, 20.8% Fe, 11.58% P, 23.93% O₄, 0.92% carbon, 0.08% PVP, 1.10% PVDF, and 38.92% NMP, while NMC cathode slurry comprises 5.18% Li, 39.40% Ni, 2.05% Mn, 2.20% Co, 23.87% O₂, 0.72% carbon, 0.12% PVP, 0.97% PVDF, and 25.50% NMP. These compositional differences require tailored processing parameters for optimal material recovery. Component Chemistry Compositions Anode LFP Gr+SPC+SBR+CMC NMC Carbon-46.97%,SiO-2.56%,CMC-0.68%,SBR-0.97%,DIW-48.82% Cathode LFP Li-2.60%;Fe-20.8%;P-11.58%;O4-23.93%;Carbon-0.92%;PVP-0.08%;PVDF-1.10%NMP-38.92% NMC Li-5.18%,Ni-39.40%,Mn-2.05%,Co-2.20%,O2-23.87%,Carbon-0.72%,PVP-0.12%,PVDF-0.97%,NMP-25.50% [0044] In an exemplary embodiment, the vacuum tray furnace prototype operates with precise temperature control to ensure complete solvent removal while preserving the integrity of the active materials. The process transforms the liquid slurry into a solid black mass suitable for subsequent thermal regeneration steps. [0045] The low-temperature delamination method processes coated foils derived from lithium-ion battery production scrap through a specialized thermal treatment approach. As depicted in Figure 6 and Figure 7, the process utilizes a sub-decomposition temperature range of 120°C to 180°C to soften the binder without decomposing the active material or damaging the current collector foil. The low-temperature roasting system includes a roll-to-roll process integration designed for continuous delamination processing, making the system scalable and compatible with industrial automation. The roasting drum operates at controlled temperatures to achieve binder softening without generating hazardous emissions such as hydrogen fluoride commonly associated with conventional pyrolysis processes above 400°C. [0046] Following binder softening, mechanical processing including pulverizing, shredding, and sieving enables clean separation of coatings with minimal physical damage to the active materials. The separated components include functional active materials and intact foils suitable for reuse, representing a significant advantage over existing thermal or chemical processes. The delamination process preserves material properties while avoiding the environmental and safety concerns associated with harsh chemical treatments. [0047] In an exemplary embodiment, the low-temperature roasting process operates at 150°C for 40 minutes, effectively delaminates cathode coatings from aluminum foil substrates while maintaining the structural integrity of both the active material and the current collector. [0048] The cell scrap processing addresses semi-finished goods, defective cells, and finished goods from the battery assembly line through mechanical dismantling operations. The process involves systematic disassembly of various cell configurations to obtain coated foils for subsequent processing. The dismantling process handles different cell formats including cylindrical, pouch, and prismatic cells, extracting the electrode materials while preserving their structural characteristics. The mechanical dismantling approach avoids the material losses and contamination associated with shredding-based methods commonly used in conventional recycling processes. [0049] The dismantled components undergo sorting and classification to separate cathode materials, anode materials, separators, and current collectors. The coated foils obtained from the dismantling process are then processed through the low-temperature delamination method described previously to recover the cathode active materials. [0050] In an exemplary embodiment, the mechanical dismantling process achieves complete separation of cell components while maintaining material purity levels suitable for direct recycling without additional purification steps. [0051] The thermal regeneration process represents the core technology for converting virgin black mass into battery-grade cathode active materials. The virgin black mass collected from dried mixed slurry, coated foils, and dismantled cells undergoes a two-stage thermal treatment process. The first stage involves heating the virgin black mass at temperatures between 800°C to 850°C in an oxygen atmosphere for approximately 3 hours. The process triggers the decomposition of LiFePO4 according to the reaction: 4 LiFePO4 + O2 → 2 Fe2O3 + 2 Li3PO4 + P2O5↑ (gas), resulting in the formation of lithium-deficient black mass. [0052] The thermal analysis data presented in Figure 8 demonstrates the decomposition behavior of LiFePO4 during heating, showing gradual weight loss beginning around 500°C due to initial decomposition, with sharper decline occurring around 700-800°C corresponding to crystal structure breakdown and loss of lithium and phosphorus. The differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) curve shows exothermic activity around 700-800°C due to structural collapse and oxidation, with endothermic signals beyond 800°C indicating volatilization and decomposition product formation. [0053] In an exemplary embodiment, the thermal regeneration process achieves complete removal of polymer binders and organic impurities while maintaining the fundamental crystal structure necessary for subsequent relithiation. [0054] The relithiation process restores the stoichiometric lithium content in the lithium-deficient black mass through solid-state synthesis. As shown in Figure 9, the process involves mixing the lithium-deficient black mass with lithium carbonate in stoichiometric ratios using either an agate mortar and pestle or a planetary ball mill with zirconium oxide components. The mixture undergoes calcination in an alumina crucible at 850°C in an argon atmosphere with a flow rate of 300 ml/min following a controlled heating program with a heating rate of 5°C per minute. [0055] The solid-state chemical reaction proceeds according to: Li2CO3 + 1/2 Fe2O3 + Li3PO4 → 2 LiFePO4 + CO2↑, regenerating battery-grade LFP cathode material. The controlled heating program ensures uniform temperature distribution and complete reaction conversion while preventing thermal shock and maintaining crystal structure integrity. [0056] Table 4 provides the composition and weight percentage of different materials throughout the recycling process. The virgin black mass contains 90% LiFePO₄, 4% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), 5% carbon, and 1% traces of aluminum. Following thermal regeneration, the lithium-deficient black mass comprises 50% Fe₂O₃ (iron III oxide) and 50% Li₃PO₄ (lithium phosphate). The final regenerated battery-grade LFP cathode material achieves a composition of 90% LiFePO₄, 5% PVDF, and 5% carbon, demonstrating successful restoration of the active material while maintaining the necessary conductive additives and binder components for battery manufacturing applications. Composition and weight percentage of different materials [0057] In an exemplary embodiment, the relithiation process produces regenerated battery-grade LFP cathode material with composition of 90% LiFePO4, 5% PVDF, and 5% carbon, suitable for direct reuse in battery manufacturing applications. [0058] The process incorporates quality control measures including compositional analysis and electrochemical testing to verify recovered materials meet battery-grade specifications. The material characterization involves X-ray diffraction analysis to confirm crystal structure, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for elemental composition, and electrochemical performance testing in coin cell configurations. The quality control protocols ensure consistent material properties and performance characteristics comparable to virgin materials. [0059] The invention addresses different battery chemistries including LFP (Lithium iron phosphate) and NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) systems, with specific processing parameters optimized for each chemistry type. The process handles mixed production scrap streams while maintaining separation and purity requirements for different active material types. The scalable design accommodates varying production volumes and scrap generation rates typical of gigafactory operations. [0060] In an embodiment, as shown in Figure 1, the present invention also relates to a method for recycling lithium-ion battery production scrap to recover battery-grade cathode active materials. The method comprises the following steps: • categorizing production scrap into slurry waste, coated electrode scrap, and defective cells; • pre-treating slurry waste by vacuum drying at temperatures between 130°C to 150°C to form solid virgin black mass; • processing coated electrode materials through low-temperature delamination at temperatures between 120°C to 180°C; • mechanically dismantling defective cells to obtain coated foils; • applying mechanical processing including pulverizing, shredding, and sieving for clean separation; • collecting virgin black mass from all processing streams; • applying thermal regeneration at temperatures between 800°C to 850°C in oxygen atmosphere; • performing relithiation using lithium carbonate at 850°C in argon atmosphere; • implementing controlled heating programs with heating rates of 5°C per minute; • conducting quality control testing including compositional analysis and electrochemical testing; • producing battery-grade cathode active materials suitable for reuse in battery manufacturing. [0061] The present invention provides the following advantages: 1. The present invention provides elimination of harsh chemical processing while maintaining high material recovery rates. 2. The present invention provides material recovery rates exceeding 90% for LiFePO4 chemistry production scrap. 3. The present invention provides reduced carbon emissions compared to conventional recycling methods. 4. The present invention provides cost-effective processing through simplified operations and reduced energy consumption. 5. The present invention provides environmentally sustainable approach to battery material recycling. 6. The present invention provides preservation of material quality comparable to virgin materials. 7. The present invention provides scalable processing suitable for industrial implementation. 8. The present invention provides direct reuse capability without extensive purification requirements 9. The present invention provides reduced dependency on virgin raw materials and mining operations. 10. The present invention provides versatility in handling different types of production scrap. It should be understood that the description of an embodiment or example provided above is by way of example only, and various modifications could be made by one skilled in the art.
