patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a high-performance lithium-ion battery incorporating a nano-silicon anode for enhanced energy storage efficiency. The battery addresses the limitations of conventional graphite anodes by utilizing nano-silicon particles embedded within a conductive carbon matrix, combined with optimized binder systems and protective surface coatings. This design accommodates the volumetric expansion of silicon during lithiation and delithiation, ensuring structural integrity, improved cycle life, and high coulombic efficiency. Advanced electrolyte formulations with specific additives are employed to stabilize the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and minimize capacity loss during repeated charge-discharge cycles. Fabrication techniques ensure uniform particle distribution, high porosity, and enhanced lithium-ion diffusion, resulting in faster charging rates, superior energy density, and mechanical stability. The invention is suitable for portable electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy storage systems, providing a scalable, cost-effective, and environmentally sustainable solution. Overall, the invention delivers reliable, high-capacity, and long-lasting lithium-ion energy storage with improved performance and safety.
patents.complete_specification: Description:The present invention relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage systems, particularly to advanced lithium-ion batteries designed for high-performance applications. More specifically, the invention pertains to lithium-ion batteries incorporating nano-silicon-based anode materials to achieve superior energy storage efficiency, higher specific capacity, and improved cycle life. This invention addresses the limitations of conventional graphite anodes, which exhibit lower capacity and faster degradation during repeated charge-discharge cycles. By integrating nano-silicon anodes, the battery demonstrates enhanced lithium-ion intercalation, reduced volume expansion, and improved electrochemical stability. The proposed system is applicable in portable electronic devices, electric vehicles, renewable energy storage, and other high-demand energy storage applications. Moreover, it emphasizes improved charge retention, faster charging rates, and safety under extreme operating conditions. The invention also covers the method of fabricating the nano-silicon anode and optimizing the electrode architecture to maximize energy density and mechanical durability. This field encompasses innovations in materials science, nanotechnology, and battery engineering aimed at next-generation energy storage solutions. Background of the invention: The development of lithium-ion batteries has been one of the most significant advancements in energy storage technology over the past few decades. Lithium-ion batteries have become the preferred choice for portable electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy storage due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and relatively low self-discharge. Traditional lithium-ion batteries primarily utilize graphite as the anode material, which provides stable electrochemical performance but suffers from limited specific capacity. Graphite anodes typically achieve a theoretical capacity of around 372 mAh/g, which restricts the overall energy density of lithium-ion cells. The growing demand for high-energy-density batteries for electric vehicles and grid-scale energy storage has necessitated the exploration of alternative anode materials with higher capacity and better performance. Among the various materials studied, silicon has emerged as a promising candidate due to its extremely high theoretical specific capacity of approximately 3579 mAh/g, which is nearly ten times that of graphite. Silicon, when used as an anode, can significantly enhance the energy density of lithium-ion batteries, making it a key material for next-generation energy storage systems. However, silicon anodes face major challenges, primarily due to their significant volume expansion during lithiation, which can reach up to 300%. This expansion leads to mechanical stress, pulverization of the active material, and rapid capacity fading over repeated charge-discharge cycles. In addition, the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the silicon surface is unstable during cycling, further reducing the battery's lifespan. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored the use of nano-sized silicon particles, which offer better structural stability and accommodate volume changes more effectively than bulk silicon. Nano-silicon anodes exhibit shorter lithium-ion diffusion paths, higher surface area for electrochemical reactions, and reduced mechanical stress, all of which contribute to enhanced battery performance. integration of nano-silicon into composite anodes with conductive carbon matrices or flexible binders has shown promising results in mitigating the issues of volume expansion and capacity loss. Various fabrication techniques, including chemical vapor deposition, ball milling, and electrospinning, have been employed to synthesize nano-silicon structures with controlled morphology, particle size, and porosity. These techniques aim to optimize the electrochemical performance while maintaining mechanical integrity during repeated cycling. Furthermore, surface modification of nano-silicon particles with protective coatings, such as carbon layers or metal oxides, has been investigated to improve SEI stability and enhance the overall cycle life of the battery. The electrolyte formulation also plays a crucial role in the performance of silicon-based anodes. Advanced electrolytes with additives that form stable SEI layers on silicon surfaces have been developed to reduce capacity fading and improve coulombic efficiency. Alongside material innovations, the design and architecture of the electrode have been optimized to maximize energy density while ensuring mechanical stability. Porous structures, binder selection, and electrode thickness are carefully engineered to balance the trade-offs between capacity, conductivity, and cycle life. High-performance lithium-ion batteries with nano-silicon anodes have demonstrated remarkable improvements in specific capacity, energy density, and rate capability compared to conventional graphite-based batteries. These batteries can achieve higher charge storage, faster charging rates, and extended cycle life, making them suitable for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and renewable energy storage systems. The implementation of nano-silicon anodes aligns with the global push toward sustainable energy solutions, as higher-capacity batteries can reduce the frequency of charging, extend the operational lifespan of devices, and lower the environmental impact associated with battery production and disposal. Moreover, the development of high-performance lithium-ion batteries supports the transition from fossil fuel-based energy systems to electrified transportation and smart grid technologies, enabling a cleaner and more efficient energy ecosystem. Despite the significant progress, challenges remain in scaling up nano-silicon anode technology for commercial applications. Issues related to cost-effective synthesis, uniform particle distribution, and long-term stability under high-rate cycling must be addressed to achieve widespread adoption. Continuous research is being conducted to optimize the composition, structure, and fabrication techniques of nano-silicon anodes to meet the rigorous requirements of commercial batteries. Advances in computational modeling, in situ characterization techniques, and materials engineering are providing deeper insights into the behavior of silicon anodes during lithiation and delithiation, guiding the design of more robust and efficient electrode architectures. The development of high-performance lithium-ion batteries incorporating nano-silicon anodes represents a multidisciplinary effort, combining expertise in materials science, nanotechnology, electrochemistry, and battery engineering. Collaborative efforts between academia, industry, and research institutions are accelerating the innovation and commercialization of these next-generation batteries. By addressing the limitations of conventional graphite anodes and harnessing the advantages of nano-silicon, this technology offers a transformative solution for high-energy-density storage applications. The proposed invention focuses on leveraging these advancements to create a lithium-ion battery with enhanced energy storage efficiency, superior cycle life, and high-rate performance. Through careful selection of nano-silicon particle size, optimized electrode architecture, protective coatings, and advanced electrolytes, the battery achieves remarkable improvements in specific capacity and overall energy density. This technology has the potential to redefine energy storage standards and enable the development of more powerful, reliable, and sustainable electronic devices, electric vehicles, and renewable energy storage systems. The proposed system addresses the critical challenge of volume expansion in silicon anodes by integrating nano-silicon particles within a conductive carbon matrix, ensuring structural integrity during repeated cycling. Additionally, the use of advanced binders and surface coatings enhances SEI stability, reducing capacity fading and improving coulombic efficiency. The invention also emphasizes scalable fabrication methods, enabling the production of high-performance batteries suitable for commercial deployment. The synergy of material innovation, electrode design, and electrolyte optimization in this invention creates a lithium-ion battery capable of meeting the increasing demands of modern energy storage applications. The development of this battery not only contributes to the advancement of portable electronics and electric vehicles but also supports renewable energy integration by providing reliable and efficient energy storage solutions. Furthermore, the adoption of nano-silicon anode technology is expected to drive further research in hybrid materials, multi-functional electrodes, and next-generation battery chemistries, paving the way for even higher energy densities and improved performance metrics in the future. The proposed invention ultimately seeks to overcome the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, providing a robust, high-capacity, and long-lasting energy storage solution that aligns with global sustainability goals and emerging technological trends. The development of high-performance lithium-ion batteries has been driven by the increasing demand for portable electronics, electric vehicles, and large-scale renewable energy storage systems. Conventional lithium-ion batteries primarily employ graphite as the anode material, which provides relatively stable cycling performance but suffers from limited energy density. Graphite’s theoretical capacity of approximately 372 mAh/g restricts the energy storage capability of conventional lithium-ion cells, creating the need for alternative high-capacity anode materials. Among potential candidates, silicon has emerged as a highly promising material due to its exceptional theoretical capacity of nearly 3579 mAh/g, which is almost ten times that of graphite. Silicon can accommodate a higher number of lithium ions during the lithiation process, significantly increasing the specific capacity and energy density of the battery. However, silicon-based anodes face major challenges, particularly due to their substantial volumetric expansion of up to 300% during lithiation. This expansion leads to mechanical stress, particle pulverization, electrode cracking, and instability of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), resulting in rapid capacity fading during repeated cycling. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored the use of nano-silicon, which exhibits improved structural stability, reduced stress-induced degradation, and enhanced lithium-ion diffusion kinetics compared to bulk silicon. Nano-silicon particles possess a high surface area and reduced diffusion length for lithium ions, enabling faster intercalation and deintercalation, which improves the battery’s rate capability and cycle life. Various fabrication techniques, including chemical vapor deposition, ball milling, solution-based synthesis, and electrospinning, have been developed to produce nano-silicon particles with controlled size, morphology, and porosity. Surface coatings, such as carbon layers, metal oxides, or polymer films, are applied to stabilize the SEI and prevent continuous electrolyte decomposition, thereby improving coulombic efficiency and overall electrochemical performance. Conductive carbon matrices are employed to enhance electron transport and buffer the volumetric expansion of the silicon particles, ensuring mechanical integrity and maintaining electrical contact within the electrode. The selection of binder materials is equally important, as flexible and conductive binders help accommodate silicon’s expansion while preserving structural cohesion of the anode. Electrolyte optimization is another key aspect of enhancing the performance of nano-silicon anodes. Electrolytes with suitable lithium salts and functional additives form stable interfacial layers on the anode surface, minimizing capacity loss and ensuring long-term cycling stability. Advanced electrolyte formulations reduce side reactions, suppress dendrite formation, and enhance ionic conductivity, contributing to the battery’s high efficiency and safety. The integration of nano-silicon anodes with optimized electrode architecture, conductive matrices, surface coatings, and advanced electrolytes results in lithium-ion batteries that deliver superior energy density, higher specific capacity, faster charging rates, and improved cycle stability. High-performance lithium-ion batteries with nano-silicon anodes are particularly beneficial for electric vehicles, as they allow for extended driving ranges, reduced charging times, and longer battery lifespan, addressing key challenges in electric mobility adoption. In addition, these batteries are well-suited for portable electronics, including smartphones, laptops, and wearable devices, where higher energy density and compact form factors are critical requirements. Renewable energy storage systems also benefit from the enhanced energy storage efficiency and cycle life of nano-silicon-based lithium-ion batteries, enabling more reliable integration of solar and wind power into the electrical grid. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in scaling up nano-silicon anode technology for commercial applications. Uniform particle distribution, controlled porosity, reproducible synthesis, and cost-effective production methods are essential for ensuring consistent battery performance at large scale. Advanced characterization techniques, such as in situ electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, provide insights into the lithiation process, structural changes, and interfacial phenomena, guiding optimization of nano-silicon anode design. Hybrid electrode strategies, combining nano-silicon with graphite or other carbon-based materials, have been explored to balance high capacity, mechanical stability, and cost-effectiveness. Optimized electrode thickness, porosity, and active material loading are critical parameters in achieving high energy density while maintaining mechanical robustness. Thermal management and safety are also important considerations for high-energy-density batteries. High-performance batteries must operate safely under extreme temperatures and high-rate charge-discharge conditions. By selecting thermally stable materials and optimizing electrode configuration, overheating and thermal runaway risks are mitigated. The proposed high-performance lithium-ion battery technology represents a comprehensive approach to overcoming the limitations of conventional graphite-based systems. Through the integration of nano-silicon anodes, conductive carbon matrices, flexible binders, surface coatings, and advanced electrolytes, the battery achieves superior electrochemical performance, longer cycle life, and enhanced energy density. Scalability, reproducibility, and commercial viability are key features of the invention, making it suitable for a wide range of applications, including electric vehicles, portable electronics, industrial energy storage, and renewable energy systems. The invention also provides a foundation for future innovations in battery technology, including hybrid anode materials, advanced electrolyte formulations, and next-generation cell architectures with higher energy density and improved performance metrics. By addressing the challenges of silicon anodes and optimizing battery components, the proposed technology offers a reliable, efficient, and sustainable energy storage solution. The continued development and implementation of nano-silicon-based lithium-ion batteries will contribute significantly to the advancement of energy storage systems worldwide, supporting electric mobility, portable electronics, and renewable energy integration. Overall, the background of this invention highlights the evolution of lithium-ion battery technology, the critical role of nano-silicon anodes, and the engineering innovations required to realize high-performance, scalable, and sustainable energy storage systems capable of meeting the demands of modern applications. Brief description of the proposed invention: The proposed invention provides a high-performance lithium-ion battery that incorporates a nano-silicon anode to achieve enhanced energy storage efficiency and superior electrochemical performance compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries. These methods ensure uniform particle distribution, optimal electrode porosity, and enhanced lithium-ion transport, which contribute to improved electrochemical performance. The design of the electrode architecture is carefully optimized to balance high energy storage capacity with mechanical stability, ensuring that the battery can withstand repeated cycling without significant degradation. The nano-silicon particles are integrated within a three-dimensional porous network, allowing for volume expansion without causing mechanical failure or loss of electrical contact. The conductive carbon matrix facilitates electron transport throughout the electrode, ensuring efficient charge transfer and minimizing internal resistance. The proposed lithium-ion battery also incorporates safety mechanisms to prevent overheating, short-circuiting, and other potential hazards associated with high-energy-density batteries. These safety features include optimized electrode thickness, thermal management systems, and selection of stable electrolyte compositions that reduce the risk of thermal runaway. The integration of these insights into the fabrication process results in a battery that maintains structural integrity, electrochemical stability, and high energy density over prolonged use. The invention also considers the interaction between the anode, cathode, and electrolyte to ensure compatibility, minimize side reactions, and enhance overall battery efficiency. The nano-silicon anode technology can be combined with various cathode materials, including lithium cobalt oxide, lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide, and lithium iron phosphate, to tailor the battery performance for specific applications. To mitigate these challenges, the invention employs a combination of nano-engineered silicon particles and a flexible, conductive binder system. This ensures that the anode maintains structural integrity while allowing for the dynamic expansion and contraction of the silicon particles. The conductive binder network facilitates electron transport across the electrode, ensuring that even if minor cracks occur, the overall electrode remains electrically connected and continues to function effectively. Moreover, the invention incorporates advanced carbon-based conductive matrices that serve multiple functions: they provide mechanical reinforcement, enhance electrical conductivity, and buffer volume changes. Carbon matrices, including porous carbon, graphene, and carbon nanotubes, are integrated with the nano-silicon particles to create a composite anode that exhibits superior structural stability. The porous structure allows lithium ions to diffuse rapidly throughout the electrode, reducing concentration polarization and improving rate capability. This design results in a battery that can be charged and discharged at higher current densities without significant degradation in performance, making it suitable for applications requiring rapid energy delivery. Surface modification of nano-silicon particles is another critical aspect of the invention. The SEI layer is crucial for preventing continuous electrolyte decomposition, minimizing irreversible capacity loss, and ensuring high coulombic efficiency over long-term cycling. The formation of a stable SEI also contributes to improved safety, as it reduces the risk of dendrite formation and thermal instability. Electrolyte optimization is equally essential for the performance of nano-silicon anodes. These additives may include fluorinated compounds, lithium salts, or other organic molecules that interact favorably with the silicon surface. By integrating thermally stable materials, optimizing electrode thickness, and employing suitable separators, the battery maintains safe operating temperatures and prevents thermal runaway. This makes the system reliable for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and industrial applications where safety is paramount. In addition to performance and safety, the invention addresses environmental and economic considerations. Furthermore, the proposed system enables rapid innovation in electric mobility. This advancement addresses key challenges in the adoption of electric vehicles, making them more practical and convenient for daily use. The proposed lithium-ion battery also offers potential for integration with smart energy management systems. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT MULTI-STEP CHARGING PROTOCOLS FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERY CELLS The present subject matter discloses a battery management system (BMS) (106) for managing a lithium-ion battery pack (102). The 5 system (106) comprises a processor (202) coupled to a data acquisition module (210) configured to obtain real-time sensor data, including cell voltage, current, and temperature. An analysis module (212) determines the state of charge (SOC) of the cells based on the sensor data. A charging profile selection module (214) selects a predefined multi-step constant 10 current (MSCC) charging profile from multiple profiles, each specifying capacity rate (C-rate) values for different SOC ranges. The C-rate values are selected such that higher rates correspond to SOC ranges with stable direct current internal resistance (DCIR). A control module (216) applies a charging voltage to the battery pack (102) at a constant current (CC), based 15 on the selected C-rate and cell temperature, thereby optimizing charging efficiency and maintaining cell safety. < > 41
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present invention relates, in general, to battery management systems for lithium-ion batteries, and particularly to a multi-step charging protocol optimized for fast charging of lithium-ion battery cells. 5 BACKGROUND [0002] Lithium-ion batteries have become the predominant energy storage technology for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and grid-scale applications due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and low self-discharge rates. As the demand for faster charging capabilities continues to 10 grow, especially in electric vehicle applications, there is an increasing need for charging protocols that reduce charging times while maintaining battery safety and longevity. The development of larger format cylindrical cells, such as the 4680-form factor, reflects a shift toward higher energy density and improved manufacturing efficiency. These cells incorporate design 15 innovations, including tabless electrode architectures and advanced active materials. However, the larger size and modified construction introduces challenges in optimizing charging performance. Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries requires a careful balance between multiple competing factors. These factors include, but not limited to charging speed, thermal 20 management, and long-term capacity retention. Battery management systems (BMSs) plays a role in implementing and controlling charging protocols, monitor cell conditions in real time, and ensure safe operation during high rate charging. SUMMARY 25 [0003] Various embodiments of systems and methods for managing a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells are described herein. [0004] The details of some embodiments of the invention described in this specification are set forth in the accompanying drawings and the description below. Other features, aspects, and advantages of the invention 30 will become apparent from the description, the drawings, and the claims. 2 [0005] This summary is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter nor is it intended for use in determining or limiting the scope of the claimed subject matter. [0006] In accordance with an example embodiment of the present subject matter, a battery management system (BMS) for managing a battery 5 pack comprising lithium-ion cells is provided. The BMS comprises a processor and a data acquisition module. The data acquisition module is coupled to the processor and is configured to obtain sensor data from a plurality of sensors associated with the battery pack. The sensor data comprises real-time values of at least cell voltage, cell current, and the cell 10 temperature of the lithium-ion cells. The BMS further comprises an analysis module coupled to the processor and is configured to determine a real-time state of charge (SOC) of the lithium-ion cells based on the sensor data. A charging profile selection module coupled to the processor is configured to select a predefined multi-step constant current (MSCC) charging profile 15 from among a plurality of MSCC charging profiles. Each of the plurality of predefined MSCC charging profiles specifies at least one capacity rate (C-rate) value corresponding to each of a plurality of SOC ranges, such that the at least one C-rate value corresponding to a SOC range in which the direct current internal resistance (DCIR) of the lithium-ion cells remains 20 substantially constant is higher than a SOC range in which the DCIR of the lithium-ion cells varies. The BMS further comprises a control module coupled to the processor and is configured to select from the predefined MSCC charging profile, a C-rate value corresponding to the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the lithium-ion cells. The control module 25 is to further apply, to the battery pack, a charging voltage corresponding to the selected C-rate value from the predefined MSCC charging profile at a constant charging current (CC). [0007] In accordance with another embodiment of the present subject matter, a method for fast charging a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells 30 is provided. The method comprises receiving sensor data from a plurality of 3 sensors associated with the battery pack, the sensor data comprising at least real-time temperature, cell voltage, and cell current of the lithium-ion cells. A current state of charge (SOC) of the battery pack is determined using the received sensor data. The method further comprises selecting a predefined multi-step constant current (MSCC) charging profile from among 5 a plurality of MSCC charging profiles based on the determined SOC. Each of the plurality of predefined MSCC charging profiles specifies at least one capacity rate (C-rate) value corresponding to each of a plurality of SOC ranges, such that the at least one C-rate value corresponding to a SOC range in which the direct current internal resistance (DCIR) of the lithium-10 ion cells remains substantially constant is higher than a SOC range in which the DCIR of the lithium-ion cells varies. A charging voltage is applied to the battery pack corresponding to the C-rate value defined for the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the lithium-ion cells in the selected MSCC charging profile at a constant charging current (CC). 15 [0008] The techniques for managing battery packs enables adaptive and efficient charging of lithium-ion battery packs by dynamically selecting a suitable charging current based on the real-time SOC and temperature conditions. By employing a predefined MSCC charging strategy that correlates each SOC range with a C-rate determined from the DCIR 20 characteristics of the cells, the BMS ensures that higher charging rates are applied only when internal resistance is minimal and cell stress is low. This results in reduced charging time without compromising safety or battery health. Overall, the technique achieves an optimal balance between charging speed, energy efficiency, and long-term durability of the battery 25 pack. [0009] Additional features and advantages are realized through the concepts of the present invention. Other embodiments and aspects of the invention are described in detail herein and are considered a part of the claimed invention. 30 4 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [0010] The detailed description is described with reference to the accompanying figures. In the figures, the left-most digit(s) of a reference number identifies the figure in which the reference number first appears. The same numbers are used throughout the drawings to reference features 5 and components. [0011] Figure 1 illustrates a system implementing example techniques for managing battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter; [0012] Figure 2 illustrates a battery management system (BMS) for 10 managing battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter; [0013] Figure 3 illustrates a method for fast charging a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter; 15 [0014] Figure 4A illustrates exemplary graph depicting the variation of temperature of the 4680-lithium-ion cell with respect to charging cycles in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter; [0015] Figure 4B illustrates an exemplary graph depicting the variation of capacity retention percentage with respect to charging cycles of the 4680-20 lithium-ion cell, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter; and [0016] Figure 4C illustrates another exemplary graph depicting the variation of differential capacity of the 4680-lithium-ion cell with respect to the state-of-charge in accordance with an example implementation of the 25 present subject matter. [0017] In the figures, the left-most digits of a reference number identify the figure in which the reference number first appears. The same numbers are used throughout the drawings to reference like features and components. 30 5 DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0018] The present subject matter relates to techniques for managing a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells. These techniques may have various applications, including but are not limited to electric vehicles (EVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), energy storage systems (ESS), portable 5 electronic devices, and renewable energy integration systems. [0019] Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a complex challenge because it involves managing several factors at the same time. The goal is to deliver high charging currents, often several times greater than the battery’s normal capacity rate (C-rate), so the battery can be charged in a 10 short time, sometimes under 30 minutes for large cells. However, pushing so much current into the battery can create problems. If not controlled properly, it may cause unwanted chemical reactions, mechanical stress in the electrode materials, and uneven temperature rise, all of which can damage the battery and shorten its life. 15 [0020] To make fast charging safe and effective, the battery management systems must constantly balance key parameters such as the applied current, the voltage response of the cell, its temperature, and internal resistance. These factors do not stay constant, they change as the battery charges and as the battery ages over time. For example, as the state 20 of charge (SOC) increases, the battery’s internal resistance and heat generation may rise, making it harder to maintain stability. This means fast charging is not just about applying more power; it requires smart control strategies that adapt to the battery’s condition in real time. [0021] The ability of a lithium-ion battery to charge quickly is mainly 25 limited by charging polarization, which is the difference between the battery’s ideal voltage and its actual voltage during charging. Polarization becomes worse at high charging currents and changes with factors like state of charge (SOC), temperature, and current density. If polarization gets too high, it can create local voltage spikes at the electrode surfaces, leading 30 to harmful side reactions such as solvent breakdown, lithium plating, or 6 unstable layer formation. To prevent these issues, fast-charging systems need accurate ways to measure and control polarization using smart, adaptive algorithms. [0022] Polarization in lithium-ion batteries during fast charging is caused by three main factors: slow ion movement through the liquid electrolyte, 5 resistance at the electrode-electrolyte interface, and limited diffusion inside the solid electrode materials. In the electrolyte, lithium ions travel through complex porous pathways, and at high C-rates, steep concentration gradients form, creating depletion zones that increase resistance. At the interface, charge transfer resistance rises when electron exchange slows 10 under high currents, influenced by particle surface characteristics, SEI layer composition, and temperature effects. Finally, once ions enter the electrode, they must diffuse through the solid lattice, a process that becomes slower with larger particle sizes or high state of charge, leading to stress and microcracks. Together, these limitations make polarization a critical 15 challenge for safe and efficient fast charging. [0023] During fast charging, especially at moderate to high temperatures, the movement of lithium ions through the electrolyte often becomes the main bottleneck. At high C-rates, ion concentration near the anode drops sharply, creating uneven distribution and increasing cell 20 overpotential. This leads to higher internal heat generation. While heat can improve ion mobility by reducing viscosity, it also raises the risk of thermal runaway if cooling is inadequate. Effective thermal management using liquid cooling, phase-change materials, or predictive algorithms is essential to maintain uniform temperature and prevent hotspots that can damage the 25 SEI layer or trigger side reactions. If polarization becomes excessive, the anode potential can fall below 0 V versus Li/Li⁺, making lithium plating thermodynamically favorable. Instead of intercalating into graphite, lithium deposits as metal on the anode surface. This typically occurs when local current density exceeds the exchange current density of the intercalation 30 7 reaction and can happen suddenly or progressively, causing irreversible chemical changes and reliability issues. [0024] Lithium plating introduces serious safety and performance risks. Deposited lithium does not participate in future cycles, causing permanent capacity loss. Over time, these deposits can grow into dendrites that 5 puncture the separator, creating internal short circuits that may lead to localized heating, gas evolution, or even thermal runaway. Lithium plating also disrupts the SEI layer, increasing resistance and reducing efficiency, and tends to accelerate once it begins due to uneven current distribution. [0025] Accordingly, there exists a need for a battery management 10 system (BMS) capable of implementing adaptive fast-charging protocols tailored to the electrochemical and thermal characteristics of dry-processed 4680 lithium-ion cells. Such a system must dynamically regulate charging currents based on parameters such as direct current internal resistance (DCIR), temperature rise, and SOC-dependent polarization behavior. 15 [0026] In accordance with the present subject matter, a battery management system (BMS) for managing a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells is provided. In example implementations, the battery management system provides to solve the above-mentioned problems. [0027] In accordance with an example embodiment of the present 20 subject matter, the BMS comprises a processor and a data acquisition module. The data acquisition module is coupled to the processor and is configured to obtain sensor data from a plurality of sensors associated with the battery pack. The sensor data comprises real-time values of at least cell voltage, cell current, and the cell temperature of the lithium-ion cells. The 25 BMS further comprises an analysis module coupled to the processor and is configured to determine a real-time state of charge (SOC) of the lithium-ion cells based on the sensor data. A charging profile selection module coupled to the processor is configured to select a predefined multi-step constant current (MSCC) charging profile from among a plurality of MSCC charging 30 profiles. Each of the plurality of predefined MSCC charging profiles specifies 8 at least one capacity rate (C-rate) value corresponding to each of a plurality of SOC ranges, such that the at least one C-rate value corresponding to a SOC range in which the direct current internal resistance (DCIR) of the lithium-ion cells remains substantially constant is higher than a SOC range in which the DCIR of the lithium-ion cells varies. The BMS further comprises 5 a control module coupled to the processor and is configured to select from the predefined MSCC charging profile, a C-rate value corresponding to the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the lithium-ion cells. The control module is to further apply, to the battery pack, a charging voltage corresponding to the selected C-rate value from the predefined MSCC 10 charging profile at a constant charging current (CC). [0028] By providing a system that enables adaptive selection of charging currents based on real-time SOC and temperature of lithium-ion cells, the present invention ensures efficient and safe charging across varying operating conditions. The system employs a predefined MSCC charging 15 strategy that correlates specific capacity rate (C-rate) values with SOC ranges determined using DCIR characteristics. As a result, higher charging rates are applied only within SOC ranges exhibiting minimal internal resistance, thereby improving charging efficiency while minimizing stress on the battery cells. This controlled charging approach reduces charging time, 20 enhances energy utilization, and prolongs the overall lifespan and reliability of the battery pack. [0029] The above-mentioned implementations are further described herein with reference to the accompanying figures. It should be noted that the description and figures relate to exemplary implementations and should 25 not be construed as a limitation to the present subject matter. It is also to be understood that various arrangements may be devised that, although not explicitly described or shown herein, embody the principles of the present subject matter. Moreover, all statements herein reciting principles, aspects, and embodiments of the present subject matter, as well as specific 30 examples, are intended to encompass equivalents thereof. 9 [0030] Figure 1 illustrates a system for implementing example techniques for managing a battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter. [0031] Efficient and safe fast charging of lithium-ion battery packs is increasingly critical in modern electric vehicles and high-performance 5 portable energy systems. For users, faster charging reduces downtime and enhances the overall convenience and usability of battery-powered applications. For the batteries themselves, controlled fast charging is essential to maintain thermal stability, prevent lithium plating, and minimize degradation of electrode materials, thereby preserving capacity and 10 extending service life. Moreover, intelligently managing charging currents based on real-time battery conditions ensures that high charging speeds do not compromise safety, efficiency, or long-term reliability. This combination of speed and safety contributes to improved user experience and promotes wider adoption of battery-powered technologies. 15 [0032] In accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter, the system 100 comprises a battery pack 102. The battery pack 102 may be composed of a plurality of lithium-ion cells connected in series and/or parallel configurations to achieve a desired voltage and capacity. In certain implementations, the battery pack 102 may comprise 20 dry 4680 lithium-ion cells having a nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC)-based cathode and a graphite-based anode, encapsulated within a thermal management housing. [0033] In an example, the battery pack 102 may be installed in a vehicle 104 that is configured for either hybrid or fully electric operation. Examples 25 of the vehicle 104 may include, but are not limited to, two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers, and heavy-duty vehicles such as buses, trucks, tractors, and construction equipment. In some implementations, the vehicle 104 may comprise an electric powertrain coupled to one or more electric drive motors powered by the battery pack 102. The battery pack 102 may 30 10 supply electrical energy to the drive system as well as to auxiliary electrical systems such as lighting, infotainment, or control electronics. [0034] In an example embodiment, the vehicle 104 may further comprise a battery management system (BMS) 106 configured to monitor and control the operation of a battery pack 102, the battery pack comprising a plurality 5 of lithium-ion cells. The BMS 106 may be configured to perform a range of functions, including monitoring the electrical and thermal behavior of the cells, balancing cell voltages, and regulating charging and discharging operations. These functions may be facilitated by a plurality of sensors installed within the battery pack 102. 10 [0035] In an example, the sensors may include, but not limited to voltage sensing circuits, current sensors such as Hall effect or shunt-based sensors, and temperature sensors such as thermistors or resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) positioned at various locations within the battery pack. [0036] In an example, the BMS 106 is configured to obtain sensor data 15 from the plurality of sensors associated with the battery pack 102. The sensor data may include real-time measurements of cell voltage, cell current, and cell temperature corresponding to each of the lithium-ion cells in the pack. This data may be utilized by the BMS 106 to assess the operational status of individual cells and to execute control functions that 20 ensure the battery pack operates within predefined safety and performance thresholds. [0037] The BMS 106 may comprise a processor for executing the process of managing battery pack comprising lithium-ion cells. In an example, the processor may be implemented as microprocessors, 25 microcomputers, microcontrollers, digital signal processors, central processing units, state machines, logic circuitries, and/or any devices that manipulate signals based on operational instructions. The BMS 106 may comprise a memory for storing the instructions executable by the one or more processors. The memory may include any computer-readable medium 30 known in the art including, for example, volatile memory (e.g., RAM), and/or 11 non-volatile memory (e.g., EPROM, flash memory, etc.). The memory may also be an external memory unit, such as a flash drive, a compact disk drive, an external hard disk drive, or the like. [0038] In an example, the BMS 106 and the battery pack 102 may communicate, enabling the BMS 106 to continuously receive real-time 5 information regarding the operational state of the battery pack and to transmit control commands for charging, discharging, and other management functions. In some embodiments, the communication may be facilitated by standard communication protocols that may include but are not limited to a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, and a Local 10 Interconnect Network (LIN), utilizing a high-speed data interface to access the sensor data, for subsequent data analysis. [0039] In an example, the battery pack 102 may comprise a charging interface or port configured to connect with an external power supply 108 to enable the BMS 106 to implement a fast-charging protocol, such as a multi-15 step constant current (MSCC) strategy, which allows for higher charging currents to be applied selectively based on the real-time SOC and thermal conditions of the cells. The charging interface may include necessary circuitry and safety components, such as fuses, contactors, or communication interfaces, to ensure reliable energy transfer, monitor 20 charge parameters, and prevent overcurrent or overvoltage conditions. The BMS 106 may continuously monitor the charging process through this interface, adjusting current levels in accordance with the MSCC profile to optimize charging speed while maintaining cell safety, efficiency, and longevity. 25 [0040] In an example, the BMS 106 is configured to determine a real-time SOC of the lithium-ion cells. In an example, the SOC estimation may be carried out using a combination of coulomb counting (based on integrated charge and discharge currents) and voltage correlation methods employing pre-calibrated open-circuit voltage (OCV)-to-SOC maps. 30 Accurate real-time SOC determination enables the BMS 106 to implement 12 optimized charging strategies, manage cell balancing, and ensure safe operation of the battery pack while maintaining high performance and longevity of the lithium-ion cells. [0041] In an example, the BMS 106 may comprise a charging profile selection module 110, coupled to the processor, that is configured to select 5 a predefined multi-step constant current (MSCC) charging profile from among a plurality of MSCC charging profiles stored in a memory component couple to the processor. Each of the predefined MSCC charging profiles may define a set of charging parameters corresponding to different state of charge (SOC) ranges of the lithium-ion cells. Each MSCC charging profile 10 may specify at least one capacity rate (C-rate) value for each SOC range, wherein the C-rate value determines the rate at which charging current is to be applied relative to the nominal capacity of the battery pack. In an example, the plurality of predefined MSCC charging profiles may be formulated based on empirical characterization data of the lithium-ion cells, 15 including variations in direct current internal resistance (DCIR) observed across different SOC levels. [0042] In an example, once a predefined MSCC charging profile is selected from among the plurality of MSCC charging profiles, the BMS 106 may be configured to identify, from the selected MSCC charging profile, a 20 C-rate value corresponding to the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the lithium-ion cells. [0043] In an example, the selection of the C-rate value may be dynamically adjusted in response to the instantaneous operating conditions of the battery pack, such as variations in cell temperature, voltage balance, 25 and aging characteristics. By taking into account both the SOC and temperature parameters, the BMS ensures that the applied charging current remains within an optimal range to enhance charge acceptance, minimize lithium plating, and maintain the longevity of the battery cells. Once the appropriate C-rate value is determined, the BMS may control a charging 30 module or power conversion unit to apply, to the battery pack, a 13 corresponding charging voltage at a constant charging current (CC) in accordance with the selected C-rate value. The specific details of the MSCC charging profile selection process are further described in reference to Figure 2. [0044] Figure 2 illustrates a BMS 106 for managing battery pack 5 comprising lithium-ion cells, in accordance with an example implementation of the present subject matter. The BMS 106 implements a technical process for optimizing fast charging of lithium-ion battery cells by dynamically selecting C-rates based on real-time SOC and temperature conditions, while ensuring safe and efficient operation of the battery pack. The BMS 10 106 as described herein addresses the technical limitations of conventional battery management approaches, which are often unable to apply high charging currents safely, resulting in longer charging times. [0045] In an example implementation, the BMS 106 may include at least one processor 202 and a memory 204 coupled to the processor 202. In an 15 example, the processor 202 may be implemented as microprocessors, microcomputers, microcontrollers, digital signal processors, central processing units, state machines, logic circuitries, and/or any devices that manipulate signals based on operational instructions. The memory 204 may include any computer-readable medium known in the art including, for 20 example, volatile memory (e.g., RAM), and/or non-volatile memory (e.g., EPROM, flash memory, etc.). The memory 204 may also be an external memory unit, such as a flash drive, a compact disk drive, an external hard disk drive, or the like. [0046] As also depicted in Figure 2, in an example implementation, 25 interface(s) 206 may be coupled to the processor 202. The interfaces 206 may include hardware and software components that enable the BMS 106 to communicate with external devices, such as charging stations, vehicle control units, network servers, and data storage systems, and the vehicle dashboard, as well as with peripheral sensors and actuators associated with 30 the battery pack. The interfaces 206 further facilitate data exchange among 14 the modules within the BMS 106, allowing real-time monitoring of cell voltage, current, temperature, and SOC, and supporting coordinated execution of charging strategies, cell balancing, and safety management functions. [0047] The BMS 106 may comprise module(s) 208 and data 220 coupled 5 to the processor 202. In one example, the module(s) 208 and data 220 may reside in the memory 204. [0048] In an example, the data 220 may comprise a sensor data 222, and charging profile data 224 and other data 226. The module(s) 208 may include routines, programs, objects, components, data structures, and the 10 like, which perform particular tasks or implement particular abstract data types. The module(s) 306 further includes modules that supplement applications on the BMS 106, for example, modules of an operating system. The data 220 serves, amongst other things, as a repository for storing data that may be fetched, processed, received, or generated by one or more of 15 the module(s) 208. The module(s) 208 may include a data acquisition module 210, an analysis module 212, a charging profile selection module 214, a control module 216, and other module(s) 218. The other module(s) 218 may include programs or coded instructions that supplement applications and functions, for example, programs in the operating system 20 of the BMS 106. [0049] The data acquisition module 210 of the BMS 106 is configured to obtain sensor data from a plurality of sensors integrated within or associated with the battery pack 102. The sensor data may include real-time measurements of individual cell voltages, cell currents, and cell 25 temperatures across the battery pack. [0050] In an example, the voltage sensors may detect the potential difference across each cell to monitor for over-voltage or under-voltage conditions, while current sensors, such as Hall effect or shunt-based sensors, may measure instantaneous charge and discharge currents of the 30 cells to enable accurate monitoring of energy flow and for SOC calculations. 15 Temperature sensors, such as thermistors or resistance temperature detectors (RTDs), may be positioned at multiple locations within the battery pack to track thermal variations and hotspots that may occur during charging or discharging. This real-time data acquisition enables the BMS 106 to implement charging strategies, monitor cell safety, and provide timely 5 feedback to the vehicle dashboard or other connected systems, thereby ensuring efficient, safe, and optimized operation of the battery pack. [0051] The analysis module 212 of the BMS 106 determines a real-time SOC of the lithium-ion cells based on the sensor data. The SOC represents the available capacity of a battery relative to its nominal full capacity, 10 typically expressed as a percentage, and provides an indication of how much energy remains in the battery for use. Accurate determination of SOC is critical for safe and efficient charging, discharging, and overall battery management. [0052] In an example, the BMS 106 may calculate SOC using various 15 techniques, including but not limited to: coulomb counting, which involves integrating the current flowing into and out of the cells over time; voltage-based methods, which compare the measured cell voltage to pre-calibrated open-circuit voltage (OCV) versus SOC curves; and model-based estimation methods, such as equivalent circuit models, Kalman filters, or 20 observer algorithms, which can account for effects of temperature, aging, and internal resistance variations. By leveraging these techniques, the analysis module 212 can provide an accurate, real-time SOC measurement that enables the BMS 106 to optimize fast-charging operations, thereby enhancing both safety and battery longevity. 25 [0053] The charging profile selection module 214 of the BMS 106 is to select a predefined MSCC charging profile from among a plurality of MSCC charging profiles. In an example, the charging profile selection module 214 is similar to the charging profile selection module 100 as mentioned in Figure 1. Each profile comprises a sequence of charging steps that define 30 the C-rate to be applied at different SOC ranges of the lithium-ion cells. The 16 selection of a specific MSCC profile is based on the real-time SOC and temperature conditions of the battery cells as determined by the analysis module, ensuring that the applied charging strategy is optimized for the current operating state of the battery pack. [0054] In an example, each of the plurality of predefined MSCC charging 5 profiles specifies at least one C-rate value corresponding to each SOC range, allowing the BMS 106 to modulate charging current dynamically as the cells progress through different SOC bands. In an example, the C-rate values within each profile are determined based on the electrochemical characteristics of the lithium-ion cells, including direct current internal 10 resistance (DCIR), thermal behavior, and historical performance data. DCIR refers to the resistance offered by a cell to the flow of direct current, which influences voltage response, heat generation, and overall energy efficiency during charging and discharging. In SOC ranges where the DCIR of the cells remains substantially constant, the corresponding C-rate values are 15 configured to be higher, allowing faster charging while maintaining safe operating conditions. Conversely, in SOC ranges where DCIR exhibits significant variation, lower C-rate values may be applied to minimize stress, prevent overheating, and avoid lithium plating, thereby protecting battery life and performance. 20 [0055] In an example, the plurality of MSCC charging profiles may be developed and validated by subject matter experts using extensive experimental testing and characterization of the lithium-ion cells. Such experiments may include cycling the battery cells under controlled conditions to measure parameters such as voltage response, current flow, 25 temperature rise, and DCIR at various SOC. The experimental data may be used to identify SOC ranges in which the DCIR remains substantially constant as well as ranges where the internal resistance exhibits significant variation. The preparation of these profiles ensures that the BMS can implement optimized, safe, and efficient fast charging strategies across a 30 wide range of operating conditions. 17 [0056] In an example implementation, the plurality of MSCC charging profiles may be stored as charging profile data 222 within data 220 of the BMS 106, making them readily accessible to the charging profile selection module 214 for real-time application based on the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the battery pack. 5 [0057] The control module 216 of the BMS 106 is configured to select a C-rate value from the predefined MSCC charging profile based on the determined real-time SOC and temperature of the lithium-ion cells. The control module 216 continuously monitors the SOC and temperature data provided by the analysis module 212 and dynamically identifies the 10 appropriate SOC band within the MSCC profile. By selecting the C-rate corresponding to the current SOC and temperature, the control module 216 ensures that the applied charging current is optimized for safe and efficient charging, applying higher currents in SOC ranges with low or stable DCIR and lower currents in ranges where DCIR varies significantly or where 15 thermal limits may be approached. [0058] The control module 216 is further configured to apply, to the battery pack, a charging voltage corresponding to the selected C-rate value from the predefined MSCC charging profile while maintaining a constant charging current (CC) during the charging step. The control module 216 20 may adjust the applied voltage in real time to maintain the desired current despite variations in cell impedance, temperature, and SOC. This operation ensures that each cell in the battery pack receives a uniform and controlled charging current, minimizing voltage imbalances, reducing thermal stress, and preventing conditions such as lithium plating or overcharging. 25 [0059] In an example, the control module 216 of the BMS 106 is configured to apply a first C-rate in a first SOC region between 0% and 10% SOC. The first C-rate may be in a range of 0.1C to 0.5C, providing a gentle initial charging current that reduces stress on the lithium-ion cells when they are at very low charge levels. By limiting the current in this SOC region, the 30 BMS 106 mitigates risks of excessive heat generation, local lithium plating, 18 and early-stage capacity loss while preparing the battery for subsequent higher-current charging steps. In an example, the control module 216 is further configured to sequentially apply higher C-rate values as the battery progresses through subsequent SOC regions. For example, a second C-rate may be applied between 10% and 20% SOC, in the range of 1C to 2C, 5 followed by a third C-rate in the 20% to 50% SOC region at 2C to 3C, and a fourth C-rate in the 50% to 80% SOC region at 1.5C to 2C. The BMS 106 modulates the charging current dynamically according to these predefined C-rate steps. [0060] As the battery approaches full charge, the control module 216 10 may apply a fifth C-rate in the 80% to 85% SOC region ranging from 0.5C to 1C, and then return to the first C-rate in the 85% to 100% SOC region. This staged reduction in charging current at higher SOC levels allows the BMS 106 to minimize overvoltage, thermal stress, and risk of lithium plating, while ensuring that the battery achieves full charge efficiently. By executing 15 this MSCC strategy, the BMS 106 balances fast charging performance with safety and longevity, adapting the applied current at each SOC range based on real-time battery conditions and the predefined MSCC profile. [0061] In an example, the analysis module 212 of the BMS 106 is further configured to continuously monitor the real-time temperature of each 20 lithium-ion cell during charging. The monitored temperature data is communicated to the control module 216, which ensures safe charging based on thermal conditions. Upon detecting that the real-time temperature exceeds a predefined threshold, the control module 216 is configured to reduce the applied charging voltage to a baseline charging voltage, 25 corresponding to a lower C-rate. This adaptive response prevents excessive heat generation, mitigates the risk of thermal runaway, overcharging, or lithium plating, and maintains the overall safety and longevity of the battery pack. By dynamically adjusting the charging voltage in response to real-time temperature feedback, the BMS 106 ensures that fast charging is performed 30 19 safely under varying thermal conditions, while still optimizing efficiency whenever the battery remains within safe operating limits. [0062] In an example, the BMS is further configured to perform active cell balancing during both charging and discharging operations. The control module utilizes MOSFET-based circuitry to selectively shunt or redirect 5 current among the individual cells of the battery pack, thereby maintaining minimal voltage variation across the pack. By equalizing the cell voltages in real time, the BMS enhances the overall energy utilization, improves cycle life, and maintains the safety and reliability of the battery pack. This cell balancing operation works in conjunction with the MSCC charging strategy, 10 ensuring that fast charging is achieved without compromising thermal management, electrochemical stability, or long-term performance of the lithium-ion cells. [0063] Thus, by providing a battery management system that dynamically selects a MSCC charging profile based on the real-time SOC 15 and temperature of lithium-ion cells, the present subject matter enables fast and efficient charging while maintaining battery safety and longevity. [00106] As shown in Figure 4C, the NMC/graphite cell exhibits four distinct SOC regions, each corresponding to characteristic phase transformations within the NMC cathode material. In the 0-~20% SOC 5 region, the cell operates primarily in the intercalation region, where lithium ions are inserted into the graphite layers without significant structural changes, ensuring high reversibility and minimal internal resistance. In the ~20-60% SOC region, the cell undergoes the H1 (hexagonal) to M (monoclinic) phase transition, indicating a structural rearrangement within 10 the NMC lattice associated with rapid lithium-ion diffusion and moderate voltage variation. [00107] Further, in the ~60-80% SOC region, a M (monoclinic) to H2 (hexagonal-2) phase transition occurs, representing a more pronounced structural transformation accompanied by increased internal resistance and 15 potential heat generation during high C-rate charging. Finally, in the ~80–100% SOC region, the H2 (hexagonal-2) to H3 (hexagonal-3) phase transition is observed, typically characterized by lattice contraction and mechanical strain within the NMC cathode. This region is highly sensitive to overcharging and is often associated with accelerated degradation and 20 capacity fade. Accordingly, the understanding of these SOC-dependent phase transitions enables the development of optimized multi-stage constant current (MSCC) charging profiles that apply suitable C-rate values within each SOC band, thereby minimizing stress on the electrode materials and enhancing cycle life. The predefined MSCC charging profiles are 25 therefore prepared based on the precise identification of these SOC-dependent phase transitions, ensuring that the charging strategy is aligned with the electrochemical behavior of the lithium-ion cells. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A PROCESS FOR SEPARATION AND PURIFICATION OF RECYCLED LITHIUM CARBONATE The present invention relates to a filed of chemical engineering. More particularly the present invention provides an efficient and effective process for separation and purification of Recycled Lithium Carbonate. The process comprises various process involving dissolution, separation and purification resulting in obtaining high purity Lithium Carbonate with less than 50 ppb impurity necessary for high-value applications, such as battery-grade lithium compounds. The present process involves dissolution of Low purity Lithium Carbonate in demineralized (DM) water, alkali treatment and Organophosphorous complexing treatment subjected to heating, shear agitation and pressure filtration process followed by beneficiation and selective adsorption of impurity from solution and high-pressure CO₂-assisted lithium carbonate precipitation from purified lithium solutions resulting in obtaining a high purity Lithium Carbonate with less than 50 ppb impurity.
