patents.abstract: Anti-site defects, Li-ion diffusion, electronic and ionic conductivity, structural instability, and phase changes are key challenges in lithium metal orthosilicates. The present invention discloses an innovative and sustainable protocol for the elaboration of anti-site defects, Li-ion diffusion, and enhancement of ionic and electronic conductivity in lithium metal orthosilicates. A viable and sustainable protocol for the synthesis of LMCS/C, LFCS/C, and LNCS/C rod-shaped nanoparticles by supercritical fluid hydrothermal method. LMS/C, LFS/C, and LNS/C compounds are prepared by the solid-state reaction method. The high-angle annular darkfield scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM) analysis discloses the anti-site defect in LMS/C, LFS/C, and LNS/C. Co-doping at the 4c site of Mn, Fe, Ni in Li2MxCo1-xSiO4 (M = Mn, Fe, Ni, x = 0.5) prevents the anti-site defect formation.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to a novel solution for anti-site defects in lithium metal orthosilicates, more particularly related to a process of synthesis of nano-rods of three dissimilar compositions including L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LMCS/C), L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LFCS/C) and L2Ni0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LNCS/C) by employing hydrothermal and calcination technique. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) are dominating the transportation market around the globe due to the greenhouse effect. The large-scale use of Li-ion batteries (LIBs) is in the stationary energy storage of intermittent solar, wind, and tidal power technologies [1-4]. LIBs are the best energy storage systems due to their high energy and power densities, longer cyclic life [1-4]. The high capacity, voltage, energy, and power densities are prime requirements for next-generation LIBs to fulfil the growing energy demand [1-5]. The anode and cathode materials are the main components of LIBs. Different types of carbon-based anode materials such as graphite, carbon nanofibers, and two-dimensional (2D) graphene are thoroughly investigated, and they reveal that carbon nano fibers (CNF) exhibit ultra-high capacity and performance [5]. The layered, spinel, olivine, and polyanion-based compounds are different kinds of positive electrode materials [1-3]. In case of olivine compounds, LiFePO4 is already commercialised [6]even though the olivine compounds (LiMPO4, M= Fe, Mn, Co, Ni) exhibit poor electronic and ionic conductivity, low discharge capacity and potential, and a one-electron reaction. These drawbacks of the olivine compounds are a barrier to their application [6]. Silicates-based polyanion compounds with (SiO4)n− assemblies have been chosen as better replacements for olivine cathodes owing to their excellent safety and cost-effectiveness [7,8]. The lithium metal orthosilicates (Li2MSiO4, M = Fe, Mn, Co, Ni) are appealing electrode materials among the various polyanion-based cathodes. The high theoretical capacity (331 mA h g-1), voltage range (3-5.4 V), and two-electron reaction, environmental benignancy, and low cost of lithium metal orthosilicates (Li2MSiO4, M = Fe, Mn, Co, Ni) are attracting lots of attention from the research community [7-9]. However, the lithium metal orthosilicates exhibit poor electrochemical activity due to sluggish electron and ion transport capability [9]. Earlier experimental investigations divulge those numerous approaches, including multivalent transition metal substitution/doping, and heteroatom doping, were implemented for the improvement of electronic conductivity [9-13]. The reduction of particle size and conductive carbon coating are key techniques for enhancing the ionic conductivity [10]. These approaches will augment the electrochemical performance via the decrease of charge transfer resistance, and augmentation of Li-ion diffusion coefficient [10,13]. The doping of the high redox transition metals (TM) and the conversion of two Li-ions per redox reactionare numerous probable methods to lift up the operating voltage window, theoretical capacity, energy, and power densities [10-14]. Previous experimental studies have disclosed that the Li atom occupies the TM site and forms the anti-site defect during the charge-discharge process in Li2FeSiO4 /C (LFS/C) [14-16]. It also disclosed that anti-site defect formation leads to a significant phase change, and it becomes a key barrier to better cyclic stability [16]. There is no experimental evidence of Li-ion diffusion and anti-site defect formation in LFS/C [15,16]. The atomic-level understanding of lithium metal orthosilicates is essential for elucidating anti-site defect formation, structure-property correlations, and the Li-ion diffusion mechanism. The lithium orthosilicates exhibit three dissimilar crystal structures. Li2MSiO4 (M = Fe, Mn, Co, Ni) consists of an orthorhombic structure with Pmn21, Pmnb two phases [15,16]. The third one is a monoclinic structure with a space group of P21/n [16]. Li2FeSiO4 with space group P21/n, Pmn21 shows a dual-phase reaction under a continuous charge-discharge process. Their intercalation/de-intercalation during charge-discharge, Li-ion diffusion, phase transformation mechanism, and structure-property correlations are key challenges [13-16]. For the first time, the present invention sheds light on experimental evidence of the Li-ion diffusion mechanism as well as addresses a unique and innovative solution for anti-site defects, enhancement of electronic and ionic conductivity, structural stability, and prevention of phase change. OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a lithium metal orthosilicate-based electrode material (Li₂MSiO₄, where M = Fe, Mn, Co, or Ni) with improved electrochemical performance for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Another objective of the present invention is to enhance both electronic and ionic conductivity of lithium metal orthosilicate cathodes. Yet another objective of the present invention is to mitigate or eliminate anti-site defect formation during the charge-discharge cycling process, thereby improving the structural stability and cyclic life of the cathode material. Still another objective of the present invention is to experimentally investigate and provide evidence for the lithium-ion diffusion mechanism within Li₂MSiO₄ compounds, particularly in various crystal structures such as Pmn2₁, Pmnb, and P2₁/n. Yet another objective of the present invention is to develop a cathode material capable of supporting a two-lithium-ion redox process, thereby increasing theoretical capacity and expanding the operating voltage window. Still another objective of the present invention is to provide a cost-effective, environmentally benign, and scalable solution for next-generation LIB cathodes, suitable for applications in electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION According to one of the embodiments, the present invention discloses a novel solution for curing the anti-site defects in lithium metal orthosilicates, more particularly related to a process of synthesis of nano-rods of three dissimilar compositions including L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LMCS/C), L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LFCS/C) and L2Ni0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LNCS/C) by employing hydrothermal and calcination technique. According to another embodiment, the present invention discloses a process of synthesis of L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4 (LFCS/C) rod-shaped nanoparticles by supercritical fluid hydrothermal method comprising the steps of: a. Adding 40 ml of tetra ethylene orthosilicate to beaker A, containing 60 ml of ethylene glycol and subjecting it to constant magnetic stirring, and adding 1.2 g of LiOH.H2O to the beaker A to obtain Solution A; b. Adding 1g of FeCl2.H2O to 40 ml of ethylene glycol in 100 ml of beaker B under constant magnetic stirring, and mixing 1.2 g of CoCl2.6H2O to the beaker B to obtain Solution B; c. Pouring the Solution B into Solution A for 1 h in an organ (Ar2) gas-filled glove box; d. Shifting and holding the homogeneous mixture of Solution A and B to a 100 ml Teflon-lined autoclave at 150° C for 48 h; e. Repeatedly washing the obtained light grey colour solution of L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4 with distilled water and acetone and drying overnight at 100° C in a vacuum oven; f. Mixing 1 g of as-prepared LFCS powder with 0.4g of sugar in 40 ml of ethanol and drying at room temperature and calcinated at 700° C in N2 atmosphere for 5 hours towards carbon coating; and g. Washing the obtained black colour powder of L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LFCS/C) rod-like nanoparticles multiple times with distilled water and acetone and then drying overnight at 100° C. According to yet another embodiment, the present invention discloses a process of synthesis of L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4 (LMCS/C) rod-shaped nanoparticles by supercritical fluid hydrothermal method comprising the steps of: a. Adding 40 ml of tetra ethylene orthosilicate to beaker A, containing 60 ml of ethylene glycol and subjecting it to constant magnetic stirring, and adding 1.2 g of LiOH.H2O to the beaker A to obtain Solution A; b. Adding 1g of MnCl2.H2O to 40 ml of ethylene glycol in 100 ml of beaker B under constant magnetic stirring, and mixing 1.2 g of CoCl2.6H2O to the beaker B to obtain Solution B; c. Pouring the Solution B into Solution A for 1 h in an organ (Ar2) gas-filled glove box; d. Shifting and holding the homogeneous mixture of Solution A and B to a 100 ml Teflon-lined autoclave at 180° C for 48 h; e. Repeatedly washing the obtained light pink colour solution of L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4 with distilled water and acetone and drying overnight at 100° C in a vacuum oven; f. Mixing 1 g of as-prepared LMCS powder with 0.4g of sugar in 40 ml of ethanol and drying at room temperature and calcinated at 700°C in N2 atmosphere for 5 hours towards carbon coating; and g. Computational studies DFT-based calculations were implemented to disclose the electronic properties such as band structure (BS), density of states (DOS), and projected density of states (PDOS) of the LMCS, LFCS, and LNCS structures. The generalised gradient approximation (GGA+ U) with Hubbard term was adopted as an exchange correlation [17]. DFT-dependent spin-polarised calculations were executed using projected augmented wave potentials within the pseudo-potential plane-wave method in the ABINIT package [17,18]. The Li2MxCo1-xSiO4 (M = Fe, Mn, Ni) (36 atoms/unit cell) with P21 space group was represented inside the supercell, and it was isolated by 22 Å to prevent inter-cell interactions [10,11]. With the help of the Monkhorst-pack grid, k-point sampling within the Brillouin zone in a, b, c-axis was 8 x 8 x 8, respectively. The selected crystal structures were optimised through GGA+U exchange-correlation. The Kohn-Sham equation was resolved by using a plane wave basis set. The density mesh cut-off energy of the elongated wave function and a force acceptance were set to 230 Ha and 0.04 eV Å-1, respectively. The fast Fourier transform was assigned as the Poisson solver for density calculation. Considered geometry was optimised based on 390 iterations using the limited Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (LBFGS) technique and the Pulay mixer algorithm [11]. Each section comprises 10 points per segment. A total band (59) on either side of the Fermi level were considered for BS calculations. The spin components in DOS, PDOS were investigated through a smearing technique in regards to 0.016 Ha occupation value, 8 x 8 x 8 grid points, and a potential range of-4 to +4 eV [10-13]. Experimental Section Synthesis of LMS/C, LFS/C, LNS/C: Li2MnSiO4 (LMS) was prepared using the solid-state reaction aided through the refluxing technique. Lithium acetate (CH3COOLi), manganese oxalate, and tetraethyl orthosilicate at a molar ratio of 2:1.05:1 was taken in ethanol under constant magnetic stirring [19]. The homogeneous mixture was shifted to the reflux system. The obtained blend was held at 80° C for 22 h, followed by vacuum drying. The achieved dehydrated 1g gel of LMS was blended with 0.4 g sucrose in acetone by ball-milling for 1 h and calcinated at 600 °C in an argon atmosphere for 5 h to obtain LMS/C. Li2FeSiO4 (LFS) was prepared using the solid-state reaction aided through the refluxing technique. Lithium acetate (CH3COOLi), ferrous oxalate, and tetraethyl orthosilicate at a molar ratio of 2:1:1 were taken in ethanol under constant magnetic stirring. The homogeneous mixture was shifted to the reflux system. The obtained blend was held at 90° C for 22 h, followed by vacuum drying [19]. The obtained 1g gel of LFS was blended with 0.4 g sucrose in acetone by ball-milling and calcinated at 650 °C in an argon atmosphere for 4 h to obtain LFS/C. Li2NiSiO4 (LNS) was prepared using the solid-state reaction aided through the refluxing technique. Lithium acetate (CH3COOLi), nickel oxalate, and tetraethyl orthosilicate at a molar ratio of 2:0.96:1 were taken in ethanol under constant magnetic stirring. The homogeneous mixture was shifted to the reflux system. The obtained LNS was overnight vacuum dried at 80° C [19]. The attained 1g gel of LNS was blended with 0.4 g sucrose in acetone by ball-milling and calcinated at 700 °C in an argon atmosphere for 5 h to obtain LNS/C. Synthesis of nanocrystalline of LFCS/C, LMCS/C, LNCS/C rod like nano particles: The nano-rods of three dissimilar compositions are synthesised by employing the hydrothermal and solvothermal lithiation technique (Figure 1). For L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4 (LFCS) rod-like nanoparticles, 40 ml of tetra ethylene orthosilicate was added to beaker A, which contained 60 ml of ethylene glycol and subjected to constant magnetic stirring and 1.2 g of LiOH.H2O was added to above beaker A. 1g of FeCl2.H2O added to 40 ml of ethylene glycol in 100 ml of beaker B under constant magnetic stirring. 1.2 g of CoCl2.6H2O mixed to beaker B. Finally, the solution of beaker B was poured into beaker A for 1 h in an organ (Ar2) gas-filled glove box. The homogeneous mixture of solution A and B was shifted to a 100 ml Teflon-lined autoclave and held at 150° C for 48 h. The obtained light grey colour solution of L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4 was repeatedly washed with DI water and acetone and dried overnight at 100° C in a vacuum oven. For carbon coating, 1 g of as-prepared LFCS powder was mixed with 0.4g of sugar in 40 ml of ethanol and dried at room temperature and calcinated at 700° C in N2 atmosphere for 5 h. The obtained black colour powder of L2Fe0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LFCS/C) rod-like nanoparticles was washed multiple times with DI water and acetone and then overnight dried at 100° C. For L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4 (LMCS) rod-like nanoparticles, 40 ml of tetra ethylene orthosilicate was added to beaker A, which contain in 60 ml of ethylene glycol and subjected to constant magnetic stirring and 1.2 g of LiOH.H2O added to above beaker A. 1g of MnCl2.H2O added to 40 ml of ethylene glycol in 100 ml of beaker B under constant magnetic stirring. 1.2 g of CoCl2.6H2O mixed into beaker B. Finally, the solution of beaker B was poured into beaker A for 1 h in an organ gas-filled glove box. The homogeneous mixture of solution A and B was shifted to a 100 ml of Teflon-lined autoclave and held at 180° C for 48 h. The obtained light pink colour solution of L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4 was repeatedly washed with DI water and acetone and dried overnight at 100° C in a vacuum oven. For carbon coating, 1 g of as-prepared LMCS powder was mixed with 0.4g of sugar taken in 40 ml of ethanol and dried at room temperature and calcinated at 700°C in N2 atmosphere for 5h. The obtained black colour solution of L2Mn0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LMCS/C) rod-like nanoparticles was washed multiple times with DI water and acetone and dried overnight at 100° C. For L2Ni0.5Co0.5SiO4 (LNCS) rod-like nanoparticles, 40 ml of tetra ethylene orthosilicate was added to beaker A, which contained 60 ml of ethylene glycol and subjected to constant magnetic stirring and 1.2 g of LiOH.H2O was added to the above beaker A. 1g of NiCl2.H2O added to 40 ml of ethylene glycol in 100 ml of beaker B under constant magnetic stirring. 1.2 g of CoCl2.6H2O mixed into beaker B. Finally, the solution of beaker B was poured into beaker A for 1 h in an organ gas-filled glove box. The homogeneous mixture of solution A and B was shifted to a 100 ml Teflon-lined autoclave and held at 200 °C for 48 h. The obtained light yellow colour solution of L2Ni0.5Co0.5SiO4 was repeatedly washed with DI water and acetone and dried overnight at 100° C in a vacuum oven. For carbon coating, 1 g of as-prepared LNCS powder was mixed with 0.4 g of sugar taken in 40 ml of ethanol and dried at room temperature and calcinated at 700° C in N2 atmosphere for 5h. The obtained black colour powder of L2Ni0.5Co0.5SiO4/C (LNCS/C) rod-like nanoparticles was washed multiple times with DI water and acetone and dried overnight at 100°C. The charge density and distribution (CDD) analysis and Li-ion diffusion and subsequent line profiles are obtained from observed XRD data and respective details are included in the supplementary information (SI). Li-ion diffusion and its pathways play a crucial role in determining the ionic conductivity, charge-discharge mechanism, and the evolution of electrochemical properties. Li-ion diffusion analysis was carried out using CDD analysis, and respective details are given in the SI. The three-dimensional (3D) view of CDD, along with the atomic position iso-surface of LFCS is shown in Figure 5a. The Li-ion diffusion is quite different in directions that normally hinge on migration pathways, and the diffusivity is described as D = a2 υ-----------eq [1] where a is the diffusion distance, υ is the attempt frequency, Eact is the activation energy, T is the temperature, and KB is the Boltzmann constant [16,17]. The charge distribution of LFCS along the a-axis (Figure 5b) reveals that there is no diffusion of Li-ion pathways. The charge distribution along the b-axis (Figure 5c) discloses that no Li-ions are diffused along the b-axis of the LFCS crystal structure. Figure 5d demonstrates that Li-ion migrated along the negative c-axis and shows wavelike pathways. Li-ions transmission (Figure 5e, g) along the positive c-axis from one octahedral position to another octahedral position through a tetrahedral at a distance of 1.69 Å, and the subsequent line profile is illustrated in Figure 5f. It also discloses that Li-ion follow the wavelike transmission pathways along both positive and negative c-axis. Therefore, CDD analysis from the observed XRD pattern can conclude that two Li-ions migration take place per reaction in LFCS (Figure 5e, g). These results are well matched with our experimental HAADF-STEM outcomes, which boost the electrochemical performance and offer enhanced ionic conductivity. The specific surface area, pore size and distribution are addressed by employing nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherm conducted at-195.8 °C for LFCS/C, LMCS/C, and LNCS/C rod-like nanoparticles. The corresponding surface area and pore size distribution plots are depicted in Figure 6a-f. According to IUPAC classification attained physisorption isotherms are type Ⅳ isotherms, and it elaborates the three well-defined pressure regions and their mechanism were discussed in our previous studies [4]. Figure 6a suggests the type Ⅳ isotherm with H1 hysteresis loop, clustered rod-like nano particles, active and reversible pore filling step with considerable uptake is positioned at P/P0 = 0.27. The comparative pressure of 0.27 is treated as the superior boundary for monolayer adsorption and bottom point for multilayers, hysteresis loop connected to the capillary condensation of nitrogen at-195.8 °C. The lengthy mesa of nitrogen adsorption at P/P0 > 0.27 and heterogeneous pore size distribution curve (Figure 6b) disclose the homogeneous mesopore (3-40 nm) and macro-pores (> 52 nm) sealing and it undergoes until P/P0 = 1.0, primary-order change in physisorption. As per Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) technique, each nitrogen molecule occupies 0.162 nm2 in the adsorbed single layer and monolayer capacities (nm) of LFCS/C, LMCS/C, and LNCS/C nanorods are 2.4, 5.3, 3.6 cm3 g−1, respectively. The corresponding BET specific surface area are 13.6, 28.97 and 74.38 m2 g-1, respectively. High specific surface area of LNCS/C nanorods offer better electrochemical properties. Barett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) pore size distribution heterogeneous curves (Figure 6b, 6d, 6f) centred at 7.8, 1.3, 24.4 Å. Therefore, BET analysis concludes that meso, micro-pore together filling during adsorption, and extreme pore size distribution of ~50 nm. A mixture of micro, meso-porous assembly of LFCS/C, LMCS/C, and LNCS/C nanorods are extremely advantageous for offering tremendous Li-ion diffusion and transportation via the electrolyte while intercalation/deintercalation phenomenon. Calculation of electronic properties: The electronic properties of LFCS, LMCS, and LNCS, such as band structure (BS), density of states (DOS), and projected density of states (PDOS) are calculated using density functional theory (DFT). The Co-doped at 4c position of Fe, Mn, Ni in LFCS, LMCS, and LNCS (14 atoms/unit cell) with P21 space group was represented inside the supercell and the subsequent crystal structure is shown in Figure S1. BS of LFCS is shown in Figure 6g, and it demonstrates the energy levels across the Fermi level. Co-doping induces the electrons into the conduction band (CB) and offers the channels for conduction of electrons from valence band (VB) to CB, energy gap of LFCS vanishes as a result (Eg). DOS of LFCS (Figure 6h) exhibits the highly degenerated energy, their symmetric nature and equal contribution of electrons for spin up and down energy levels in both VB, CB. PDOS (Figure 6i) reveals the spin-dependent energy states that are favourably confined across the Fermi state in both the VB and the CB. Similar results are noticed from PDOS analysis, and these results are well consistent with BS and DOS findings. Figure 6j shows the BS profile for LMCS, and it discloses that the energy states across the Fermi level are fully degenerated and shows the curved dispersion near to , -points. These energy states offer the channels for electron tunnelling from VB to CB, and the subsequent bandgap vanishes (Eg = 0) and LMCS is metallic as a result. DOS of LMCS (Figure 6k) depicts the high intensity peaks near to the Fermi level and indicating that the equilibrium exists among the fully degenerated spin up and down states across the Fermi state are mirror image of each other. The unpaired electron in the Co-3dyz orbital is accessible for conduction from VB to CB, and there are no free accessible electrons of Mn for conduction. Therefore, LMCS is metallic in nature. PDOS of LMCS is shown in Figure 6l and it demonstrates the similar result as obtained from BS, DOS. BS of LNCS (Figure 6m) demonstrates the completely disintegrated energy states over the Fermi level. Co-doping introduce the electrons into CB and their energy pathways acts as the channels for conduction of electrons from VB to CB that results in vanishes the energy gap (Eg) of LNCS. DOS of LNCS is depicted in Figure 6n and it exhibits the highly degenerated energy levels, their equilibrium nature and equal contribution of electrons for spin up and down energy levels in both VB, CB. PDOS (Figure 6o) reveals the spin dependent energy states that are favourably confined across the Fermi state in both the VB and the CB. Similar results are noticed from PDOS analysis and these results well consistent with BS and DOS findings. Electrochemical properties of a half-cell: The electrochemical performance of Li/LFCS/C, LMCS/C, and LNCS/C nanorods in conventional Li-ion batteries (LIBs) was studied using a two-electrode cell assembly. The subsequent fabrication details of conventional LIBs were included in the SI. The cyclic voltammetry (CV), gravimetric charge-discharge (GCD) and cyclic performance of Li/LFCS/C were carried out in the potential range of 1.6-4.8 V. The similar characteristics of Li/LMCS/C, Li/LNCS/C were performed in the potential range of 1.8-5 V and 2-5.2 V, respectively. CV of Li/LMCS/C is demonstrated in Figure 7a, and it divulges the dual oxidation and reduction nature of Mn, Co. The initial oxidation peak of Mn/Co lies within the range of 1.68-2.3 V, second oxidation peak of Mn/Co present in the range of 2.5-3.5 V. The first reduction peak of Mn/Co is located within the range of 4.4-3.5 V, and the second reduction peak of Mn/Co is situated in the span of 1.7-2.6 V. The mean peak values in the oxidation/reduction area disclose the Mn2+/Co2+  Mn3+/Co3+ and second peak values elaborate the Mn3+/Co3+  Mn4+/Co4+. CV of Li/LFCS/C is shown in Figure 7b, and it discloses the two oxidation and reduction peaks of Fe, Co. The first oxidation peak of Fe/Co lies within the range of 1.8-2.52 V, second oxidation peak of Fe/Co present in the range of 2.7-3.8 V. The first reduction peak of Fe/Co is located within the range of 4.8-3.7 V, and the second reduction peak of Fe/Co is situated in the span of 1.9-2.9 V. The mean peak values in the oxidation/reduction area disclose the Fe2+/Co2+  Fe3+/Co3+ and second peak values elaborate the Fe3+/Co3+  Fe4+/Co4+. Figure 7c demonstrates the CV of Li/LNCS/C, and it reveals the binary oxidation and reduction states of Ni, Co. The first oxidation curve of Ni/Co lies inside the span of 1.97-2.5 V, and the next oxidation point of Ni/Co is situated in the domain of 2.9-3.7 V. The first reduction peak of Ni/Co is located within the range of 4.3-5 V, and the second reduction peak of Ni/Co is situated in the span of 2.1-3 V. The mean peak values in the oxidation/reduction area disclose the Ni2+/Co2+  Ni3+/Co3+ and second peak values elaborate the Ni3+/Co3+  Ni4+/Co4+. Therefore, CV analyses conclude that the two Li-ion per reaction is due to the dual oxidation and reduction nature. The discharge capacities of Li/LFCS/C at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 C-rates are 310.249, 301.47, 292.397, 285.435, 275.193, 260.698, 238.98, 198.939, 179.789 mA h g-1. The preliminary discharge capacity of Li/LNCS/C is 322.937 mA h g-1, which is 96.97% of the theoretical capacity. The discharge capacity decreases as the current rate increases due to the polarisation of the electrode material. The discharge capacities of Li/LNCS/C at 1-100 C-rate lie within the range of 316.288-185.989 mA h g-1. These high-capacity cathodes are extremely suitable for Li-ion EVs and HEVs battery applications, and discharge capacities are much higher than the previously reported results [19, 20]. The highest value was obtained at a 0.1 C-rate for each considered one. The Li-insertion capacities of Li/LMCS/C, LFCS/C, and LNCS/C at different scan rates from 0.1 C to 100 C and then return to 0.1 C after 50 cycles and there is no capacity fading. Therefore, it concludes that these Li-ion batteries can withstand various loading conditions in real-life applications. The cyclic stabilities of Li/LMCS/C, LFCS/C, and LNCS/C are performed at 0.1 C-rate, and compared with theoretical capacities. The subsequent plot is demonstrated in Figure 7k and it discloses that the initial discharge capacities of Li/LMCS/C, LFCS/C, and LNCS/C are 317.397, 319.104 and 322.937 mA h g-1, respectively. The subsequent capacity retentions are 99.5, 98.53, 99.7 % respectively. The capacity loss rate of 0.25, 0.15, 0.16 was found in the Li/LMCS/C, LFCS/C, and LNCS/C, respectively. The capacities fading for 63 cycles are 2.3, 1.5, 1.4 % per cycle. At 120th cycle, discharge capacities are 314.827, 317.174, 321.956 mA h g-1, respectively. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT METHOD FOR REMOVING A PHARMACEUTICAL COMPOUND FROM AQUEOUS SOLUTIONS USING RECYCLED GRAPHITE FROM SPENT LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES The present disclosure provides a method (100) for removing pharmaceutical compounds from aqueous solutions using recycled graphite from spent lithium-ion batteries. The method (100) includes obtaining and completely discharging spent lithium-ion batteries (102), submerging copper sheets coated with graphite in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solution (104), heating the solution for approximately 2 hours to dissolve polyvinylidene fluoride binder (106), scraping the graphite from copper sheets (108), washing and drying the scraped graphite to obtain raw graphite powder (110), adding the raw graphite powder to an aqueous solution containing pharmaceutical compounds (118), and removing the pharmaceutical compound through adsorption onto the raw graphite powder (120). The method (100) may further include immersing the raw graphite powder in 0.25 M hydrogen peroxide solution overnight (114) and centrifuging and drying the treated graphite to obtain modified graphite powder (116) for enhanced adsorption performance. (FIG. 1)

PREAMBLE [0002] The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. FIELD OF INVENTION [0003] The present disclosure relates to water treatment and environmental remediation technologies, and more particularly to a method for removing pharmaceutical compounds from aqueous solutions using recycled graphite adsorbent material recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries. BACKGROUND [0004] The following text of background art is provided for purposes of understanding and is not an admission that any cited document or technique forms part of the prior art under applicable law. [0005] Water contamination by pharmaceutical compounds has emerged as a growing environmental concern due to the widespread use of antibiotics and other medicinal substances. Oxytetracycline (OTC), a broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic, is commonly detected in wastewater streams from healthcare facilities and pharmaceutical manufacturing operations. The presence of such compounds in aquatic environments poses risks including the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and ecotoxicological effects on aquatic organisms. Various treatment methods have been employed for pharmaceutical compound removal, including chemical oxidation, biological degradation, membrane filtration, and adsorption processes. Among these approaches, adsorption has gained attention due to its effectiveness and relatively simple implementation. [0006] Concurrently, the rapid growth of the electric vehicle industry has led to increased production and subsequent disposal of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). These batteries contain valuable materials including graphite, which serves as the anode material due to its high electrical conductivity and stable structure. As reported by J.C.S. Aguilar et al. (2021), graphene-OH synthesized from spent batteries demonstrated sheet-like morphology with a surface area of 182.1 m2/g and achieved adsorption capacity of 59.5 mg/g for amoxicillin removal. W.T. Tee et al. (2011) showed that thermally processed expanded graphite exhibited surface area of about 47 m2/g with adsorption capacity values of approximately 400 mg/g. M. Cuccarese et al. (2021) reported that 3D-BGO formed strong porous frameworks with maximum predicted adsorption capacities ranging from 658.3 to 737.4 mg/g for amitriptyline removal. [0007] Current pharmaceutical wastewater treatment methods face limitations including high operational costs, complex infrastructure requirements, and generation of secondary pollutants. Conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon, while effective, are expensive and require energy-intensive production processes. Additionally, the growing accumulation of spent lithium-ion battery waste presents environmental challenges, as these materials contain both valuable recoverable components and potentially hazardous substances that require proper management. [0008] Existing approaches for pharmaceutical compound removal often lack cost-effectiveness and sustainability. The disposal of spent lithium-ion batteries represents a missed opportunity for material recovery and reuse. Furthermore, many current treatment technologies do not adequately address the dual challenge of waste management and environmental remediation in an integrated approach that supports circular economy principles. [0009] It has been appreciated that a method is needed that overcomes one or more of these problems. [0010] The present invention addresses the above shortcomings of the prior art. However, the invention is entirely different from the prior art in terms of novelty and technological advancements. [0012] In an aspect, the invention provides a method for removing pharmaceutical compounds from aqueous solutions using recycled graphite from spent lithium-ion batteries. The process involves fully discharging the batteries, submerging copper sheets coated with graphite in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solution, heating to dissolve the polyvinylidene fluoride binder, and scraping off the graphite. The graphite is then washed, dried, and used to adsorb pharmaceutical compounds, such as oxytetracycline hydrochloride, from water. [0035] FIG. 3 illustrates the molecular structure of Oxytetracycline Hydrochloride (OTC) according to various embodiments. The OTC molecule exhibits a complex polycyclic aromatic system consisting of four fused rings with multiple functional groups attached. The structural formula reveals several hydroxyl groups (-OH) positioned at various locations on the ring system, which contribute to the hydrophilic character of the molecule. The structure contains multiple carbonyl groups (C=O) integrated into the ring framework, providing sites for potential hydrogen bonding interactions. An amide group (-NH₂) is present as a substituent, along with a dimethylamino group (-N(CH₃)₂) that introduces basic character to the molecule. The molecule further comprises a hydroperoxide group (-OOH) and additional hydroxyl functionalities that enhance the polar nature of the compound. The stereochemistry of the molecule is defined by specific three-dimensional arrangements of substituents, as indicated by the wedged and dashed bond representations in the structural formula. [0036] The presence of multiple polar functional groups in the OTC structure influences the molecule's behavior in aqueous solution and affects the adsorption interactions with carbon-based adsorbent materials. The hydroxyl and carbonyl groups provide sites for hydrogen bonding, while the aromatic ring system enables π-π interactions with graphitic surfaces. The dimethylamino group contributes to the overall charge distribution of the molecule, affecting electrostatic interactions during the adsorption process. [0037] The CRL molecule displays a different structural arrangement compared to OTC, featuring a simpler aromatic system with distinct functional group positioning. The structure contains multiple hydroxyl groups (-OH) that provide hydrophilic character and hydrogen bonding capability. An amino group (-NH) is present as a substituent, contributing to the basic properties of the molecule. The structure includes a dichloroacetamide side chain (-NHCOCH₂Cl₂) that introduces both polar and halogenated characteristics to the compound. Several carbonyl functionalities (C=O) are integrated into the molecular framework, offering additional sites for intermolecular interactions. [0038] The molecular architecture of CRL combines both hydrophilic regions, primarily through the hydroxyl and amino groups, and hydrophobic aromatic areas that can participate in various adsorption mechanisms. The dichloroacetamide side chain provides a unique structural feature that distinguishes CRL from other pharmaceutical compounds and influences the specific interaction patterns with adsorbent surfaces. The combination of polar functional groups and aromatic character in the CRL structure determines the compound's affinity for graphite-based adsorbents through mechanisms including hydrogen bonding, π-π interactions, and electrostatic forces. [0039] FIG. 1 illustrates a flowchart for a pharmaceutical compound removal method 100 using recycled graphite from spent lithium-ion batteries according to various embodiments. The method 100 provides a systematic approach for converting waste battery materials into functional adsorbents for water treatment applications. [0040] FIG. 5 illustrates a systematic process flow for graphite recovery from spent lithium-ion batteries according to various embodiments. The process is presented as a sequence of five stages labeled (a) through (e), demonstrating the complete extraction and purification methodology for recovering graphite adsorbent material from end-of-life battery waste. [0041] The method 100 begins with a step 102, where spent lithium-ion batteries are discharged completely. Stage (a) in FIG. 5 shows multiple cylindrical discharged lithium-ion battery cells arranged in rows within a container, representing the starting material for the graphite extraction process. Complete discharge of the batteries ensures safe handling and processing of the battery components during subsequent extraction steps. [0042] The method 100 proceeds to a step 104, where copper sheets are submerged in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solution. Stage (b) in FIG. 5 depicts a close-up view of the battery cell components, specifically showing the copper sheets with graphite coating that serve as the anode material. The copper sheets lined with graphite are submerged in a solution of N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone to initiate the separation process between the graphite coating and the copper substrate. [0043] Following the submersion step, the method 100 continues to a step 106, where the solution is heated for 2 hours to dissolve the PVDF binder. The graphite extraction process involves heating the copper sheets submerged in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solution for about 2 hours in an oil bath to dissolve the polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder. The oil bath heating provides controlled temperature conditions that facilitate the dissolution of the PVDF binder material, which acts as an adhesive layer between the graphite particles and the copper substrate. The heating duration of approximately 2 hours ensures complete dissolution of the binder material, enabling effective separation of the graphite from the copper sheets. [0044] The method 100 then advances to a step 108, where graphite is scraped from the copper sheets. The graphite is manually scraped off the copper sheets after the binder is dissolved. The manual scraping process involves physical removal of the loosened graphite material from the copper substrate surface. Stage (d) in FIG. 5 displays copper sheets that have been separated from the anode, appearing as thin metallic foils stacked together, while the upper path (c) shows stacked separated cathode materials. [0045] The method 100 concludes the extraction phase with a step 110, where the graphite is washed and dried to obtain raw powder. The scraped graphite material is then dried in an oven to obtain raw graphite powder. The drying procedures remove residual solvent and moisture from the graphite material, resulting in a dry, powdered form suitable for subsequent processing or modification steps. Stage (e) in FIG. 4 presents the final product—pure graphite in fine powdered form, appearing as a dark, granular material. The washing and drying procedures ensure the removal of any remaining N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solvent and other impurities, producing clean graphite powder with suitable characteristics for adsorption applications. [0046] The method 100 includes a step 112, which presents a decision point determining whether graphite modification is required. The decision point at step 112 evaluates whether enhanced adsorption characteristics are desired for the specific application. If modification is required, the process proceeds along a modification pathway to improve the adsorption capacity of the raw graphite material. If modification is not required, the process bypasses the modification steps and proceeds directly to the adsorption application phase. [0047] When modification is required, the method 100 proceeds to a step 114, where graphite is immersed in 0.25M H₂O₂ solution overnight. A 10 ml solution of 0.25 M hydrogen peroxide is prepared for the immersion of 2.5 g of graphite. The graphite material is placed in the hydrogen peroxide solution and then positioned in an orbital shaker overnight. The overnight immersion period allows sufficient time for the hydrogen peroxide to interact with the graphite surface, introducing oxygen-containing functional groups that enhance the adsorption properties of the material. The orbital shaker provides continuous agitation during the immersion process, ensuring uniform contact between the hydrogen peroxide solution and all graphite particles. [0048] Following the overnight immersion, the method 100 continues to a step 116, where the graphite is centrifuged and dried to obtain modified graphite. The graphite material is removed from the hydrogen peroxide solution and washed with distilled water to remove residual hydrogen peroxide and reaction byproducts. The washing process involves multiple rinses with distilled water to ensure complete removal of the modifying agent. The modified graphite is separated into precipitate via centrifugation after washing with distilled water. The centrifugation process applies centrifugal force to separate the solid graphite particles from the liquid phase, concentrating the modified graphite material into a precipitate form. [0049] The thus obtained slurry form of modified graphite is placed in an oven for drying and processed into fine powder form. The modified graphite slurry is placed in an oven for drying and processed into fine powder form. The oven drying process removes residual moisture and water from the centrifuged material, transforming the wet precipitate into a dry, powdered form suitable for adsorption applications. The drying temperature and duration are controlled to prevent thermal degradation of the modified surface functional groups while ensuring complete moisture removal. [0050] If modification is not required at the decision point in step 112, the process bypasses steps 114 and 116 and proceeds directly to a step 118. At step 118, the graphite material, whether raw or modified, is added to OTC contaminated aqueous solution. The method 100 concludes with a step 120, where pharmaceutical compounds are removed through the adsorption process. The adsorption process involves contact between the graphite adsorbent and the pharmaceutical contaminants in the aqueous solution, resulting in the transfer of the contaminant molecules from the liquid phase to the solid adsorbent surface. [0051] FIG. 2 illustrates a flowchart for an optimization and analysis method 200 for OTC removal using graphite materials according to various embodiments. The method 200 provides a systematic approach for parameter optimization and analytical verification to achieve optimal OTC removal efficiency in pharmaceutical compound removal processes. [0052] The method 200 begins with a step 202, where an OTC stock solution is prepared at 1000 ppm concentration. The preparation of the OTC stock solution involves measuring 250 mg of industrial grade powdered OTC for dissolution in 250 ml of distilled water. The industrial grade powdered OTC provides the pharmaceutical contaminant material for subsequent adsorption experiments and optimization studies. The specific quantity of 250 mg OTC powder dissolved in 250 ml distilled water establishes the 1000 ppm stock solution concentration that serves as the basis for preparing various test concentrations during the experimental procedures. [0053] The dissolution process employs magnetic stirring to dissolve the powdered OTC in distilled water. The magnetic stirring dissolution technique involves placing a magnetic stir bar in the solution container and applying continuous rotational motion to facilitate complete dissolution of the OTC powder particles. The magnetic stirring action creates fluid motion within the distilled water, promoting uniform distribution and dissolution of the industrial grade powdered OTC throughout the solution volume. The stirring process continues until complete dissolution of the OTC powder is achieved, resulting in a homogeneous 1000 ppm stock solution. [0054] The magnetic stirring dissolution method ensures uniform concentration distribution throughout the stock solution and prevents localized concentration gradients that could affect subsequent experimental measurements. The continuous agitation provided by the magnetic stirring system promotes efficient mass transfer between the solid OTC particles and the liquid phase, accelerating the dissolution process and ensuring complete solubilization of the pharmaceutical compound. The resulting 1000 ppm OTC stock solution serves as the primary source material for preparing various test concentrations used in the adsorption optimization experiments described in the subsequent steps of method 200. [0055] The method 200 then proceeds to a step 204, which involves conducting preliminary batch experiments with varying parameters. The preliminary batch experiments are designed to evaluate the adsorption performance of both raw and modified graphite materials under different operational conditions. The preliminary studies establish baseline performance data and identify parameter ranges for subsequent optimization procedures. [0056] The preliminary batch experiments involve preparing 50 ml solutions of 10 ppm, 50 ppm and 100 ppm concentrations using the stock solution and distilled water in 250 ml conical flasks. The required volume of stock solution is calculated using the relationship between the volume of the solution, required concentration, and concentration of the stock solution. The solutions are tested at multiple pH conditions including 4 pH, 7.5 pH and 11 pH to evaluate the effect of solution acidity on adsorption performance. [0057] Different dosages of graphite are tested in the preliminary studies, including 25 mg/L, 50 mg/L, 100 mg/L, 150 mg/L and 200 mg/L concentrations. The varying adsorbent dosages allow for evaluation of the relationship between adsorbent quantity and removal efficiency across different concentration ranges. The batch adsorption experiments are conducted in an orbital shaker at 120 rpm, providing consistent agitation conditions that promote uniform contact between the adsorbent particles and the pharmaceutical contaminants in solution. [0058] The pH is controlled using 1 M NaOH and 1 M HCl solutions during the experiments. The pH control solutions enable precise adjustment and maintenance of the desired pH conditions throughout the experimental duration. The 1 M sodium hydroxide solution provides alkaline pH adjustment capability, while the 1 M hydrochloric acid solution enables acidic pH adjustment as required for the different pH testing conditions. [0059] Samples are taken at specific time intervals including 0 mins, 30 mins, 60 mins, 90 mins, 120 mins, 150 mins and 180 mins. The systematic sampling protocol enables evaluation of adsorption kinetics and determination of equilibrium contact times for the different experimental conditions. The initial sample at 0 minutes establishes the baseline concentration before adsorption begins, while the subsequent samples track the progression of pharmaceutical compound removal over time. [0060] Following the preliminary studies, the method 200 moves to a step 206, where a Box-Behnken Design is applied for experimental optimization. The Box-Behnken Design provides a statistical experimental framework for understanding parameter interactions and their effects on adsorption efficiency results. The Box-Behnken Design refers to a statistical experimental design used in Response Surface Methodology to systematically evaluate how multiple parameters interact with each other and influence the overall adsorption performance. [0061] The method 200 continues to a step 208, where 54 trials each are performed for raw and modified graphite. The Box-Behnken model suggests a set of 27 experimental conditions for systematic evaluation of parameter combinations. All adsorption tests are carried out in duplicate to ensure consistency and replicability of data, resulting in a total of 54 trials for each adsorbent type. The duplicate testing protocol provides statistical reliability and enables identification of experimental variability in the adsorption measurements. [0062] The 54 trials for both raw and modified graphite encompass systematic variations in adsorbent concentration, adsorbate concentration, pH conditions, and contact time parameters. The comprehensive experimental matrix generated by the Box-Behnken Design ensures adequate coverage of the parameter space while minimizing the total number of experiments required for optimization. The duplicate measurements for each experimental condition provide statistical confidence in the results and enable calculation of experimental uncertainty for the adsorption efficiency determinations. [0063] Subsequently, the method 200 advances to a step 210, where samples are filtered using Whatman No. 1 filter paper. The filtration process involves passing the sampled solutions through a Whatman No. 1 filter paper to remove suspended graphite particles and other solid materials from the liquid phase. The Whatman No. 1 filter paper provides standardized filtration characteristics with defined pore size and retention properties suitable for separating fine graphite particles from the aqueous solution containing dissolved pharmaceutical compounds. [0064] The filtration step ensures that the analytical measurements are performed on clear solutions free from particulate matter that could interfere with spectrophotometric analysis. The filtered samples contain the dissolved pharmaceutical compounds remaining in solution after the adsorption process, enabling accurate determination of the residual contaminant concentration. The filtration process using the Whatman No. 1 filter paper provides consistent separation performance across all experimental samples, ensuring reliable and reproducible analytical results. [0065] The method 200 then proceeds to a step 212, where samples are analyzed using UV-Spectrophotometer at 275 nm. The spectrophotometric analysis employs a Jasco V-700 Version UV-visible Spectrophotometer for measuring the absorbance of light by the sample solutions. The Jasco V-700 spectrophotometer operates across a wavelength range of 200 nm to 800 nm, providing comprehensive spectral analysis capabilities for pharmaceutical compound detection and quantification. [0066] The specific wavelength of 275 nm is selected for OTC analysis based on the characteristic absorption properties of the pharmaceutical compound at this wavelength. The UV-Spectrophotometer measures the absorbance of light by the sample solution at the 275 nm wavelength, generating optical density data that correlates with the concentration of OTC remaining in solution after the adsorption process. The spectrophotometric measurements provide quantitative data for calculating the concentration of pharmaceutical compounds in the filtered samples. [0067] The analytical procedure includes preparation of standard solutions for calibration purposes. Standard solutions are prepared at concentrations of 1 ppm, 2 ppm, 5 ppm, 10 ppm, 20 ppm, 30 ppm, 40 ppm, 50 ppm, 60 ppm, 70 ppm, 80 ppm, 90 ppm and 100 ppm using the 1000 ppm stock solution and distilled water. The comprehensive range of standard concentrations enables construction of a calibration curve that covers the expected concentration range of the experimental samples. [0068] The standard solutions provide reference points for establishing the relationship between optical density measurements and pharmaceutical compound concentration. The calibration procedure involves measuring the absorbance of each standard solution at 275 nm using the Jasco V-700 spectrophotometer, generating a series of optical density values corresponding to known concentrations. The calibration data establishes a mathematical relationship between measured absorbance and concentration, enabling calculation of unknown sample concentrations from their optical density measurements. [0069] The concentration of sampled solutions is calculated using the optical density data obtained from the UV-Spectrophotometer based on the calibration relationship established by the standard solutions. The calculation involves applying the mathematical relationship between optical density and concentration, typically expressed as a linear equation derived from the calibration curve. The formula for concentration determination utilizes the measured optical density, the intercept of the standard calibration curve, and the slope of the standard calibration curve. [0070] The adsorption efficiency is determined by comparing the final concentration of the solution with the concentration of the control solution. Control samples are prepared with identical parameters to the experimental samples but without the addition of adsorbent material. The control samples establish the baseline concentration of pharmaceutical compounds in the absence of adsorption, providing a reference point for calculating removal efficiency. The comparison between experimental sample concentrations and control sample concentrations enables quantification of the pharmaceutical compound removal achieved through the adsorption process. [0071] The method 200 includes a step 214, which represents a decision point where determination is made whether optimal conditions are achieved. The decision point at step 214 evaluates the adsorption performance results obtained from the experimental trials to determine if the removal efficiency meets the desired optimization criteria. The evaluation process involves analyzing the experimental data to identify parameter combinations that produce maximum pharmaceutical compound removal efficiency. [0072] When optimal conditions are achieved, the method 200 proceeds to a step 216, where maximum 73.1% removal efficiency is achieved with modified graphite. The optimization results demonstrate that the modified graphite adsorbent achieves superior performance compared to raw graphite under the identified optimal conditions. The 73.1% removal efficiency represents the maximum pharmaceutical compound removal achieved with the modified graphite material under the optimized parameter combinations determined through the Box-Behnken Design analysis. [0073] The optimal conditions for achieving maximum OTC removal efficiency include specific combinations of adsorbent concentration, pharmaceutical compound concentration, pH conditions, and contact time parameters. The optimization analysis identifies the parameter values that maximize the adsorption performance while considering the interactions between different variables that influence the overall removal efficiency. [0074] If optimal conditions are not achieved at the decision point in step 214, the method 200 moves to a step 218, where parameters are adjusted and the optimization process is repeated. The parameter adjustment step involves modifying the experimental conditions based on the analysis of previous results to explore different regions of the parameter space. The iterative optimization approach enables systematic refinement of the experimental conditions to achieve improved adsorption performance. [0075] The parameter adjustment process considers the relationships between different variables and their effects on pharmaceutical compound removal efficiency. The adjustments are guided by the statistical analysis results from the Box-Behnken Design, which identifies parameter combinations that show potential for improved performance. The iterative nature of the optimization process allows for progressive improvement in adsorption efficiency through systematic parameter refinement and experimental validation. A sharp peak appears around 2668 cm⁻¹, which corresponds to C-H stretch vibrations in the graphite structure. The C-H stretching vibration indicates the presence of hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon atoms within the graphitic framework. [0079] The spectrum displays a prominent peak near 1646 cm⁻¹, which is attributed to C=C stretch vibrations characteristic of the aromatic carbon-carbon double bonds present in the graphitic structure. The C=C stretching vibration confirms the presence of the conjugated aromatic system that defines the fundamental structure of graphite materials. Additional peaks appear at lower wavenumbers, including a notable absorption around 1416 cm⁻¹ that corresponds to C-C in ring vibrations, indicating the presence of carbon-carbon bonds within the aromatic ring structures of the graphite. [0080] The FTIR spectrum reveals an absorption peak at approximately 869 cm⁻¹, which is assigned to C-H out of plane bending vibrations. The out-of-plane C-H bending vibration provides information about the orientation and bonding environment of hydrogen atoms attached to the aromatic carbon framework. A distinct peak appears around 533 cm⁻¹, which corresponds to CF₂ bending vibrations, indicating the presence of residual polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder material on the graphite surface. The CF₂ bending vibration confirms that traces of the PVDF binder remain associated with the graphite material despite the extraction and purification procedures. [0081] The spectrum exhibits an absorption feature at approximately 420 cm⁻¹, which is attributed to C-C bond vibrations within the graphitic structure. The intensity variations in the C-H stretch region around 2668 cm⁻¹ indicate changes in the hydrogen bonding environment resulting from OTC adsorption onto the graphite surface. [0084] The C=C stretch peak at 1646 cm⁻¹ shows modified intensity in the post-adsorption spectrum, suggesting that the aromatic system of the graphite participates in π-π interactions with the aromatic components of the OTC molecule. Panel (b) shows that the modified graphite retains fundamental morphological features similar to raw graphite but with improved surface characteristics due to hydrogen peroxide treatment. [0093] Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping confirms the chemical composition of the modified graphite, showing high carbon content (93.40%) and oxygen (5.57%), with trace amounts of copper, nickel, aluminum, manganese, and cobalt. The high carbon purity ensures effective interaction with pharmaceutical compounds through π-π stacking mechanisms, while the oxygen content indicates additional binding sites for polar molecules. The trace metals do not significantly impact adsorption performance. The combined SEM and EDX analyses demonstrate that hydrogen peroxide modification creates an enhanced adsorbent material with improved surface characteristics and suitable chemical composition for pharmaceutical compound removal. [0094] FIG 9 illustrates X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns for raw graphite materials from spent lithium-ion batteries, providing detailed characterization of their crystalline structure and phase composition. The XRD analysis, performed using a Bruker D8 Advanced Power X-Ray Diffractometer, covers a 2θ range from approximately 10 to 80 degrees, identifying crystalline phases and structural characteristics. The patterns display intensity versus 2θ, with sharp, well-defined peaks indicating a crystalline graphitic structure. Pattern (a) shows the XRD pattern before adsorption, with prominent peaks around 26-27 2θ and additional peaks at 43, 54, and 77 2θ, confirming the preservation of the graphitic structure during extraction and purification. [0095] Pattern (b) shows the XRD pattern after adsorption of OTC, with reduced peak intensities compared to pattern (a), indicating adsorption of OTC molecules onto the graphite surface. The primary peak remains at 26-27 2θ, and the reduction in intensity signifies disruption of the crystalline structure due to surface interactions with OTC. The consistent peak positions between pre-and post-adsorption patterns confirm that the fundamental graphitic structure remains intact, demonstrating the graphite material's structural integrity while effectively binding pharmaceutical compounds to its surface. [0096] FIG 10 illustrates X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns for raw graphite (RG) samples before and after oxytetracycline (OTC) adsorption, providing a detailed crystallographic analysis of structural changes during the adsorption process. Figure (a) shows the XRD pattern of raw graphite before adsorption, with a prominent sharp peak at approximately 26° 2θ, corresponding to the (002) crystallographic plane characteristic of graphitic carbon materials. This peak indicates a well-ordered crystalline structure with minimal defects, confirming that the graphite recovery process from spent lithium-ion batteries preserves the crystalline quality of the original anode material. [0097] Figure (b) displays the XRD pattern of the same graphite material after OTC adsorption, showing the (002) peak at approximately 26° 2θ with noticeably reduced intensity. The decrease in peak intensity suggests structural changes or surface interactions due to the presence of adsorbed pharmaceutical molecules on the graphite surface. This intensity reduction provides direct evidence of successful interaction between OTC and the graphite adsorbent, creating local disorder within the crystalline structure. Despite these changes, the retention of the (002) reflection at the same angular position indicates that the interlayer spacing remains unchanged, confirming that the graphite material maintains its fundamental properties while effectively removing pharmaceutical contaminants. The XRD analysis demonstrates that the recovered graphite possesses suitable crystalline characteristics for pharmaceutical adsorption applications, ensuring long-term stability and reusability of the adsorbent material. [0098] FIG 11 illustrates X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns for modified graphite materials, providing a comprehensive characterization of the crystalline structure and phase composition of hydrogen peroxide-treated graphite. The XRD analysis, conducted using a Bruker D8 Advanced Power X-Ray Diffractometer, ensures consistent analytical conditions for comparative evaluation between raw and modified materials. The diffractometer operates across a 2θ range from approximately 20 to 80, covering the angular range where characteristic diffraction peaks of graphitic materials appear. Panel (a) shows the XRD pattern labeled "MG" (Modified Graphite) before pharmaceutical compound adsorption, exhibiting prominent crystalline peaks with the most intense peak at approximately 26 2θ corresponding to the (002) reflection. This confirms that the hydrogen peroxide modification preserves the fundamental crystalline architecture of the graphite material. A secondary peak labeled (103) at approximately 55 2θ indicates similarity to natural graphite, confirming that the modification process maintains essential structural features while introducing surface enhancements for improved adsorption performance. [0099] Panel (b) shows the XRD pattern labeled "MG_OTC" (Modified Graphite after Oxytetracycline adsorption), indicating crystallographic characteristics after pharmaceutical compound adsorption. The post-adsorption pattern maintains the same characteristic peaks as the pre-adsorption pattern, with the (002) and (103) reflections at their respective positions. However, a noticeable reduction in peak intensity, particularly for the (002) reflection, suggests structural changes or surface interactions during adsorption. This intensity reduction indicates successful adsorption of the pharmaceutical compound onto the modified graphite surface, creating local disorder without significant changes in peak positions, thus preserving the fundamental graphitic structure. The XRD data confirms that the hydrogen peroxide treatment creates an adsorbent material with excellent crystalline quality and enhanced binding sites for pharmaceutical compounds, ensuring structural stability and successful compound removal from aqueous solutions. [0100] FIG 12 illustrates an optimization analysis display for Response Surface Methodology (RSM) using a Box-Behnken Design to optimize the removal of pharmaceutical compounds with graphite adsorbents from spent lithium-ion batteries. This design provides a statistical framework to systematically evaluate multiple process parameters and their interactions, minimizing the number of experimental trials required. JMP software processes the experimental data, enabling comprehensive statistical analysis and optimization. The display includes five panels: a line graph showing response values versus principal components, a desirability metric plot, and distribution plots for adsorbent concentration, adsorbate concentration, pH, and contact time. The desirability function identifies optimal conditions for maximum pharmaceutical compound removal efficiency. [0101] Statistical validation of the RSM model employs Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and lack-of-fit tests, confirming model significance with p-values less than 0.0001 for both raw and modified graphite materials, indicating significant effects on OTC adsorption performance. The lack-of-fit test results, with p-values of 0.0300 for raw graphite and 0.0184 for modified graphite, validate the model's predictive accuracy. Actual-by-predicted plots further confirm the model's reliability. The analysis identifies adsorbent concentration and pH as significant factors, with higher adsorbent dosages and pH influencing adsorption performance due to electrostatic interactions. This comprehensive statistical analysis demonstrates the Box-Behnken Design's effectiveness in optimizing pharmaceutical compound removal using graphite adsorbents. [0102] FIG 13 illustrates a comprehensive analytical display for prediction profiler results and optimal parameter combinations using the Response Surface Methodology framework. The display comprises two sections: a top panel with four overlapping line graphs (X1 to X4) showing concentration measurements against different parameters, and a lower panel with peak distribution plots. The line graphs reveal complex interactions between process variables influencing pharmaceutical compound removal efficiency, with X1 showing an optimal adsorbent concentration of 867.7 mg/L, X2 an optimal pharmaceutical compound concentration of 32.22 mg/L, X3 an optimal pH condition of 4.12, and X4 an optimal contact time of 180 minutes. The lower panel's desirability measurements exhibit sharp, uniform peaks, indicating precise parameter combinations that maximize adsorption efficiency. [0103] The prediction profiler results highlight dual efficiency outcomes for raw and modified graphite materials under different optimization scenarios. Raw graphite achieves 59% removal efficiency with 550 mg/L adsorbent concentration, 10 mg/L OTC concentration, pH 4, and 90 minutes contact time, demonstrating substantial pharmaceutical compound removal capability. Modified graphite, under the same conditions, achieves 731% removal efficiency, showcasing the significant enhancement achieved through hydrogen peroxide modification. This 14.1 percentage point increase in removal efficiency underscores the improved binding capacity for pharmaceutical compounds due to the surface modification process, providing quantitative evidence of the adsorption capacity enhancement. [0104] The desirability function predictions reveal that raw graphite can achieve a maximum 95% removal efficiency under optimal conditions, which include 1000 mg/L adsorbent concentration, 27.19 mg/L OTC concentration, pH 4, and 180 minutes contact time. This high efficiency indicates that raw graphite has substantial adsorption potential when operated under these optimized conditions. On the other hand, modified graphite achieves a maximum 99% removal efficiency under optimal conditions of 867.7 mg/L adsorbent concentration, 32 mg/L OTC concentration, pH 4, and 180 minutes contact time. The near-complete removal efficiency of 99% demonstrates the superior performance of hydrogen peroxide-modified graphite, indicating that it can provide nearly complete pharmaceutical compound removal from aqueous solutions under optimized conditions. [0105] The comparison between the two materials shows that modified graphite achieves a 4 percentage point improvement in maximum performance capability over raw graphite. Both materials perform best under acidic pH conditions of 4, extended contact times of approximately 180 minutes, and specific adsorbent-to-contaminant concentration ratios. The consistent pH optimum of 4 enhances electrostatic interactions between the graphite surfaces and OTC molecules, while the extended contact time ensures complete mass transfer and maximum utilization of binding sites. The lower adsorbent concentration requirement for modified graphite (867.7 mg/L) compared to raw graphite (1000 mg/L) indicates improved binding efficiency per unit mass due to the hydrogen peroxide modification. The slightly higher optimal contaminant concentration for modified graphite (32 .22mg/L) suggests it can handle higher pharmaceutical compound loadings while maintaining maximum efficiency. These results validate the technical effectiveness of the hydrogen peroxide modification process in enhancing the adsorption capacity of graphite materials, confirming that the surface modification creates enhanced binding sites and improved surface chemistry for superior pharmaceutical compound removal. , Claims:WE CLAIM: 1. A method (100) for removing pharmaceutical compounds from aqueous solutions using recycled graphite from spent lithium-ion batteries, the method (100) comprising: obtaining spent lithium-ion batteries and discharging them completely (102); submerging copper sheets coated with graphite from the spent lithium-ion batteries in N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone solution (104); heating the solution for approximately 2 hours to dissolve polyvinylidene fluoride binder (106); scraping the graphite from the copper sheets after dissolution of the binder (108); washing and drying the scraped graphite to obtain raw graphite powder (110); adding the raw graphite powder to an aqueous solution containing pharmaceutical compounds (118); and removing the pharmaceutical compounds from the aqueous solution through adsorption onto the raw graphite powder (120). 2. The method (100) of any of claims 1 to 2, wherein the adsorption process is conducted under conditions comprising an adsorbent concentration of 550 mg/L, a pharmaceutical compound concentration of 10 mg/L, a pH of 4, and a contact time of 90 minutes. 4. The method (100) of any of claims 1 to 3, further comprising characterizing the graphite materials before and after adsorption using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy, and X-ray Diffraction analysis to confirm structural properties and adsorption mechanisms. 5. The method (100) of any of claims 1 to 4, wherein the pharmaceutical compounds comprise oxytetracycline hydrochloride prepared by dissolving 250 mg of oxytetracycline hydrochloride powder in 250 ml of distilled water to create a 1000 ppm stock solution (202). 6. The method (100) of any of claims 1 to 5, wherein the method achieves a maximum removal efficiency of 95% for raw graphite and 99% for modified graphite under optimal conditions comprising 1000 mg/L adsorbent concentration for raw graphite, 867 mg/L adsorbent concentration for modified graphite, pH 4, and 180 minutes contact time. 7. A graphite adsorbent material recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries according to the method (100) of any of claims 1 to 6, the graphite adsorbent material having surface characteristics suitable for pharmaceutical compound adsorption and being capable of removing pharmaceutical compounds from aqueous solutions with a removal efficiency of 59%. 8. The graphite adsorbent material of claim 7, wherein the graphite adsorbent material is modified with hydrogen peroxide treatment and achieves a maximum removal efficiency of 73.1% (216) for oxytetracycline hydrochloride under optimized conditions. 9.
