patents.abstract: ABSTRACT MULTI-SCALE COMPUTATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERY ELECTRODE THERMAL ANALYSIS The present disclosure provides a computer-implemented method (100) for multi-scale computational framework analysis of lithium-ion battery electrodes. The method (100) performs density functional theory calculations on cathode materials including lithium iron phosphate, lithium manganese oxide, and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide to determine electronic structure parameters including HOMO-LUMO energy gaps, bond lengths, and charge distributions. The method (100) generates electrochemical polarization curves using Butler-Volmer modeling incorporating activation overpotential, ohmic resistance, and mass transfer limitations. The method (100) performs thermal simulations using Multi-Scale Multi-Domain modeling to predict temperature distributions during battery operation. The method (100) correlates density functional theory-derived parameters with electrochemical model parameters including exchange current density and area-specific resistance. The method (100) integrates density functional theory calculations, polarization modeling, and thermal simulations to enable prediction of electrochemical performance and thermal stability across multiple length scales. (FIG. 1)
patents.complete_specification: Description:CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS AND PRIORITY The present application does not claim priority from any patent application. PREAMBLE The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. FIELD OF INVENTION The present disclosure relates to computational modeling and simulation frameworks for lithium-ion battery systems, and more particularly to a multi-scale computational framework that integrates density functional theory, electrochemical polarization modeling, and finite volume method thermal analysis for predicting thermal behavior and electrochemical performance of lithium-ion battery electrodes. BACKGROUND The following text of background art is provided for purposes of understanding and is not an admission that any cited document or technique forms part of the prior art under applicable law. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) serve as the primary energy storage technology for electric vehicles and portable electronics, operating through electrochemical reactions wherein lithium ions transfer between graphite anodes and cathode materials such as lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, LFP), lithium manganese oxide (LiMn2O4, LMO), and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) through an electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) dissolved in organic solvents. The performance and safety of these systems depend on the structural stability and thermal behavior of the electrode materials during charge-discharge cycling. Different cathode chemistries exhibit distinct structural frameworks: LFP possesses an olivine structure with corner-sharing FeO6 octahedra and PO4 tetrahedra, LMO features a spinel structure with edge-sharing MnO6 octahedra, and NMC adopts a layered oxide configuration. These structural differences result in varying electrochemical properties, thermal stability characteristics, and operational voltage windows. Understanding the relationship between atomic-scale material properties and macroscopic battery performance has become a focus of research efforts aimed at improving energy density, cycle life, and thermal management strategies for next-generation battery systems. Existing approaches to battery electrode analysis face limitations in connecting atomic-level material properties with macroscopic thermal and electrochemical behavior. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations can predict electronic structure, bond lengths, HOMO-LUMO energy gaps, and charge distributions of cathode materials, but these atomic-scale insights remain disconnected from practical performance metrics. Electrochemical modeling techniques, including Butler-Volmer equation-based polarization analysis, can characterize activation overpotential, ohmic resistance, and mass transfer limitations, yet these models typically lack direct correlation with underlying atomic properties such as bond strength and electronic configuration. Thermal runaway simulations using finite volume methods (FVM) can predict temperature distributions and heat generation patterns during high-rate discharge, but these macroscopic thermal models do not incorporate the fundamental material properties that govern thermal stability at the molecular level. The absence of an integrated framework that bridges quantum-mechanical calculations, electrochemical performance modeling, and thermal behavior prediction limits the ability to systematically optimize cathode materials and predict failure modes across multiple length scales. It has been appreciated that a computational framework is needed that overcomes one or more of these problems. The present invention addresses the above shortcomings of the prior art. However, the invention is entirely different from the prior art in terms of novelty and technological advancements. SUMMARY The following summary is intended to introduce aspects of the present invention in a simplified form and does not identify all the features or the scope of the claimed invention. The summary is provided to assist in understanding the invention and is to be read in conjunction with the detailed description and accompanying drawings, claims, and abstract. One or more embodiments of the present disclosure are set forth below solely for illustrative purposes and should not be construed as limiting. The invention presents a multi-scale computational framework for lithium-ion battery electrode thermal analysis, integrating quantum-mechanical atomic properties with macroscopic electrochemical and thermal behavior. The framework involves obtaining crystallographic structural data for cathode materials such as lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium manganese oxide (LiMn2O4), and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) from a materials database. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations using a B3LYP functional and LANL2DZ basis set determine electronic structure parameters, including HOMO-LUMO energy gaps, optimized bond lengths, bond angles, Mulliken charge distributions, and dipole moments. Geometry optimization and frequency simulations verify structural stability and thermodynamic properties. Electrochemical polarization curves are generated using a Butler-Volmer equation-based analytical model, correlating activation overpotential, ohmic resistance, and mass transfer limitations with DFT-derived electronic structure parameters. Finite volume method (FVM) thermal simulations using a Multi-Scale Multi-Domain (MSMD) model coupled with NTGK methodology predict temperature distributions, thermal gradients, and depth of discharge relationships during battery operation. This integration establishes structure-property-performance relationships, enabling the prediction of thermal stability, electrochemical performance degradation, and failure modes across multiple length scales. The framework further correlates HOMO-LUMO energy gaps with exchange current density parameters, optimized bond lengths with temperature-dependent material properties, and Mulliken charge distributions with ionic transport parameters. Advanced computational techniques like Self-Consistent Field (SCF) methodology ensure accurate determination of ground-state molecular structures and electronic properties. Comprehensive polarization analysis captures voltage loss mechanisms, while thermal simulations incorporate energy conservation equations, capturing heat generation and transfer mechanisms. Specific applications, such as lithium iron phosphate cathodes under high-rate discharge, demonstrate thermal resilience, validating their suitability for high-power applications. Comparative analysis of cathode materials based on thermal stability and structural stability through DFT-calculated bond dissociation energies provides insights into degradation mechanisms. The framework predicts thermal runaway behavior by correlating DFT-derived dipole moments with thermal decomposition temperatures and estimates atomic properties of new cathode materials through comparative polarization curve characteristics. Validation through finite volume method simulations confirms the accuracy of the multi-scale integration approach, establishing confidence in using atomic-level calculations to predict macroscopic battery performance and safety characteristics. Material selection guidelines based on integrated DFT, polarization, and thermal analysis results optimize battery performance for diverse applications. The foregoing general description of the illustrative embodiments and the following detailed description thereof are merely exemplary aspects of the teachings of this disclosure and are not restrictive. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES The drawings appended herein illustrate exemplary embodiments of the present invention and are provided to enhance understanding of the inventive features disclosed. These figures, when read in conjunction with the detailed description, depict the operational flow, component architecture, and other mechanisms. FIG. 1 illustrates a flowchart of a multi-scale computational framework for lithium-ion battery electrode analysis, according to aspects of the present disclosure. FIG. 2 depicts a computational workflow diagram showing the integration of materials database retrieval, electronic structure analysis, structure modification, and optimization simulation phases, according to an embodiment. FIG. 3 illustrates a systematic computational workflow for lithium-ion battery modeling and simulation including geometry creation, meshing, and thermal analysis, according to aspects of the present disclosure. FIG. 4 shows molecular orbital visualizations from density functional theory calculations displaying current surface and optimized molecular geometry representations, according to an embodiment. FIG. 5 depicts control surface representations of molecular orbital structures for LiFePO4 and LiMn2O4 cathode materials with corresponding energy scale parameters, according to aspects of the present disclosure. FIG. 6 illustrates polarization curves for a lithium iron phosphate cathode at different operating temperatures showing current density versus electrode potential relationships, according to an embodiment. FIG. 7 shows polarization curves for a lithium manganese oxide cathode at various temperatures demonstrating electrochemical performance characteristics, according to aspects of the present disclosure. FIG. 8 depicts polarization curves for a nickel manganese cobalt oxide cathode comparing performance at different temperature conditions, according to an embodiment. FIG. 9 illustrates three-dimensional thermal contour visualizations of a lithium-ion battery cell wall zone showing temperature distribution patterns, according to aspects of the present disclosure. FIG. 10 shows a graph of temperature versus depth of discharge curves for different initial temperature conditions during battery operation, according to an embodiment. DETAILED DESCRIPTION The following detailed description is intended to provide an in-depth understanding of the invention and its various components, configurations, and operational aspects. While specific embodiments are described with reference to the accompanying drawings, the invention is not limited to the particular forms disclosed herein. The scope of the invention shall be interpreted broadly and in accordance with the claims appended hereto. The terms “comprises,” “comprising,” “includes,” “including,” and similar expressions used in this description are intended to be open-ended and should be interpreted to include, but not be limited to, the mentioned elements. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, singular terms may include their plural equivalents and vice versa, depending on the context in which they appear. Reference is now made to the accompanying figures, which illustrate example embodiments of the present invention. It should be appreciated that the figures are intended for illustration and explanatory purposes only and do not limit the scope of the invention. Similar reference numerals have been used to denote functionally similar components throughout the figures. The embodiments described herein are presented for illustrative purposes and are subject to variations, modifications, and adaptations by those skilled in the art. Any equivalent implementations that perform substantially the same function in substantially the same manner are intended to fall within the scope of this disclosure and the claims appended hereto. The present invention will now be described in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings illustrating exemplary embodiments. FIG. 1 illustrates a method 100 for multi-scale framework analysis of lithium-ion battery electrodes according to various embodiments. The method 100 provides an integrated computational approach that connects atomic-scale density functional theory analysis with macroscopic electrochemical polarization modeling and thermal behavior simulation to enable comprehensive electrode performance evaluation. A method 100 encompasses three distinct computational domains that operate synergistically to characterize lithium-ion battery cathode materials across multiple length scales. The method 100 integrates quantum mechanical property determination, electrochemical kinetics assessment, and thermal runaway prediction within a unified analytical framework. The method 100 enables correlation of atomic-scale electronic structure parameters with macroscopic battery performance metrics through systematic computational modeling approaches. The method 100 incorporates density functional theory calculations to determine fundamental atomic properties of cathode materials including bond lengths, electronic energy states, charge distributions, and molecular orbital configurations. The density functional theory component of the method 100 utilizes Gaussian-based computational algorithms to optimize geometric structures and calculate HOMO-LUMO energy gaps that correlate with electrochemical stability and thermal decomposition resistance. The method 100 applies Kohn-Sham equations to evaluate electron density distributions and predict structural stability under thermal stress conditions. The method 100 further includes empirical electrochemical modeling to generate polarization curves that characterize charge transfer kinetics and overpotential behavior of cathode materials. The electrochemical modeling component of the method 100 employs Butler-Volmer equations to quantify activation overpotential, ohmic resistance, and mass transfer limitations across varying current densities and operating temperatures. The method 100 correlates exchange current density parameters with atomic-scale electronic properties derived from density functional theory calculations to establish structure-performance relationships. The method 100 additionally incorporates finite volume method thermal simulations to predict temperature distributions and thermal runaway behavior during battery operation. The thermal modeling component of the method 100 utilizes Multi-Scale Multi-Domain models coupled with NTGK electrochemical-thermal methods to simulate heat generation, conduction, and dissipation within battery cells under high-rate discharge conditions. The method 100 applies energy conservation equations and charge conservation principles to determine temperature evolution as a function of depth of discharge and operating parameters. The method 100 establishes correlations between the three computational domains through systematic parameter mapping and validation procedures. The method 100 utilizes atomic bond lengths and electronic energy gaps from density functional theory calculations to inform electrochemical model parameters including area-specific resistance and exchange current density values. The method 100 further correlates polarization curve data with thermal simulation boundary conditions to predict thermal stability limits and thermal runaway thresholds for different cathode chemistries. The method 100 enables comparative analysis of multiple cathode materials including lithium iron phosphate, lithium manganese oxide, and nickel manganese cobalt oxide through standardized computational protocols. The method 100 provides quantitative metrics for evaluating structural stability, electrochemical performance, and thermal safety characteristics across different operating conditions and temperature ranges. The method 100 generates predictive models that correlate atomic-scale material properties with macroscopic battery performance parameters to guide cathode material selection and optimization strategies. FIG. 2 illustrates a density functional theory computational workflow for lithium-ion battery electrode analysis according to various embodiments. The workflow establishes a systematic approach for atomic-scale characterization of cathode materials through quantum mechanical calculations and structural optimization procedures. The method 100 incorporates density functional theory simulation using Gaussian-based calculations with B3LYP theory and LANL2DZ basis set to analyze atomic-scale properties of lithium-ion battery electrodes. The density functional theory workflow begins with crystallographic data retrieval from a Materials Project Legacy database that provides initial structural coordinates and unit cell parameters for cathode materials. The method 100 uses crystallographic data from Material Project Legacy database as initial structural input for DFT calculations. The database provides three-dimensional crystal structure information including atomic positions, lattice parameters, and space group symmetries for lithium iron phosphate, lithium manganese oxide, and related cathode chemistries. The computational workflow proceeds through unit cell selection and Gaussian input file generation procedures that establish calculation parameters and molecular geometry specifications. The method 100 applies B3LYP hybrid density functional theory with LANL2DZ effective core potential basis set to balance computational efficiency with accuracy for transition metal-containing cathode systems. The B3LYP functional incorporates exact Hartree-Fock exchange with gradient-corrected correlation terms to provide reliable predictions of electronic structure and geometric properties. The method 100 includes geometry optimization using Self-Consistent Field method with Berny algorithm and GEDIIS techniques to determine equilibrium molecular structures. The geometry optimization process applies the Berny algorithm for coordinate transformation and step size control during structural relaxation procedures. The GEDIIS technique accelerates convergence through direct inversion of iterative subspace methods that extrapolate optimal geometric configurations from previous calculation cycles. The density functional theory calculations implement Kohn-Sham equation formulation according to-0.5∇^2+v_eff (r)·ϕ_i (r), where ϕ_i (r) represents single-particle wave functions, ε_i corresponds to energy eigenvalues, and v_eff (r) denotes the effective potential incorporating external and exchange-correlation contributions. The Kohn-Sham formulation reduces the many-body electron problem to a system of coupled single-particle equations that enable practical calculation of electronic properties for complex cathode materials. The computational approach utilizes Hohenberg-Kohn ground state energy relationship expressed as E=E_0·p_0 (r), where E represents the ground state energy and p_0 (r) denotes the electron density functional. The Hohenberg-Kohn theorems establish that the ground state electron density uniquely determines all electronic properties of the system and that variational principles govern energy minimization procedures. The method 100 performs frequency simulation to verify structural stability and obtain thermodynamic properties of cathode materials. The frequency calculations evaluate vibrational modes and harmonic frequencies to confirm that optimized structures correspond to local minima on the potential energy surface. The frequency analysis provides thermodynamic corrections including zero-point energy, thermal energy, and entropy contributions that enable calculation of formation energies and phase stability parameters. The optimization convergence criteria include RMS gradient norms that quantify the accuracy of structural relaxation procedures. The method 100 achieves convergence when RMS gradient norms reach values below specified thresholds, typically in the range of 10-5 to 10-4 Hartree per Bohr, indicating that atomic forces have been minimized and equilibrium geometric configurations have been obtained. The converged structures provide optimized bond lengths, bond angles, and charge distributions that serve as input parameters for subsequent electrochemical and thermal modeling components of the multi-scale framework. FIG. 4 illustrates molecular orbital structures obtained from Gaussian-based density functional theory simulations according to various embodiments. The computational visualization panels display current surface representations and optimized molecular geometries with three-dimensional renderings of atomic orbitals featuring distinct color-coded lobes representing electron density distributions in space. The method 100 analyzes HOMO-LUMO energy gaps to determine electronic stability and oxidation-reduction tendencies of electrode materials. The HOMO-LUMO energy gap calculations provide quantitative measures of electronic stability and charge transfer characteristics for cathode materials under electrochemical cycling conditions. The energy gap analysis enables prediction of oxidation susceptibility and reduction tendency through evaluation of frontier molecular orbital energies and electron density distributions. FIG. 5 illustrates HOMO atomic structures for lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide cathode materials according to various embodiments. The computational visualizations present three-dimensional molecular orbital renderings showing electron density distributions as colored lobed structures superimposed on ball-and-stick atomic models with spheres representing different elements including lithium, iron, manganese, phosphorus, and oxygen atoms. The method 100 specifically analyzes lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide cathode materials with comparison to nickel manganese cobalt oxide. The lithium iron phosphate analysis reveals a HOMO-LUMO energy gap of 0.02554 eV that indicates moderate electronic stability and controlled charge transfer kinetics during electrochemical operation. The lithium manganese oxide evaluation demonstrates a narrower HOMO-LUMO energy gap of 0.00208 eV that facilitates rapid electron transfer but increases susceptibility to structural degradation under thermal stress. The optimized bond length calculations provide structural parameters that correlate with electrochemical stability and thermal resistance properties. The lithium iron phosphate structure exhibits optimized Fe-O₂ bond lengths of 1.821 Å that reflect strong covalent bonding interactions within the olivine framework structure. The lithium manganese oxide configuration displays Li-Mn bond lengths of 1.919 Å that correspond to the spinel lattice arrangement with edge-sharing octahedral coordination environments. The method 100 calculates Mulliken charge distributions to assess charge distribution symmetry and lattice strain effects. The Mulliken charge analysis for lithium iron phosphate reveals iron atoms carrying +1.2e charge and oxygen atoms bearing-0.8e charge, indicating balanced charge distribution that minimizes lattice strain during lithium intercalation and deintercalation processes. The lithium manganese oxide charge distribution analysis shows manganese atoms with +0.7e charge and oxygen atoms with-0.35e charge, demonstrating asymmetric charge localization that contributes to structural instability under electrochemical cycling. The dipole moment calculations quantify charge separation and molecular polarity characteristics that influence thermal stability and electrolyte interactions. The lithium iron phosphate structure exhibits a dipole moment of 5.28163 Debye that reflects symmetric charge distribution and enhanced ionic interactions that suppress oxygen release until elevated temperatures. The lithium manganese oxide configuration displays a dipole moment of 2.38545 Debye that indicates weaker lattice cohesion and reduced thermal stability compared to the olivine structure. The method 100 identifies Jahn-Teller distortions in manganese-based cathodes through electronic configuration analysis of Mn³⁺ ions with d⁴ configuration. The Mn³⁺ ions in lithium manganese oxide undergo Jahn-Teller distortions to relieve electronic degeneracy in the e_g orbital set, resulting in elongated Mn-O bond lengths and destabilization of the spinel lattice structure. The d⁴ electronic configuration creates orbital degeneracy that drives cooperative distortions throughout the crystal lattice, leading to structural collapse and capacity fade during electrochemical cycling. The electronic structure analysis correlates HOMO localization patterns with charge transfer mechanisms and structural stability characteristics. The HOMO orbitals in lithium iron phosphate localize on Fe-O bonds with octahedral symmetry due to Fe 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization, creating covalent bonding networks that resist lattice strain and maintain structural coherence. The HOMO orbitals in lithium manganese oxide exhibit delocalization across Mn-O bonds that enhances redox activity but increases susceptibility to Mn³⁺/Mn⁴⁺ charge imbalance and subsequent structural degradation. The correlation between electronic structure parameters and thermal decomposition resistance establishes predictive relationships for cathode material selection and optimization. The wider HOMO-LUMO gap in lithium iron phosphate correlates with higher thermal stability and delayed oxygen release compared to lithium manganese oxide systems. The symmetric charge distribution and strong covalent bonding in the olivine structure provide thermal decomposition resistance that extends operational temperature ranges and enhances safety characteristics under high-rate discharge conditions. FIG. 3 illustrates a finite volume method computational workflow for lithium-ion battery modeling and simulation according to various embodiments. The workflow establishes a systematic approach for electrochemical-thermal analysis through coupled physics-based modeling that incorporates lumped-parameter electrochemical equations and thermal boundary conditions. The method 100 employs lumped-parameter electrochemical modeling using Butler-Volmer equations to generate polarization curves for cathode performance evaluation. The lumped-parameter approach simplifies complex electrochemical phenomena into manageable mathematical relationships that correlate current density with electrode potential across three distinct overpotential regions. The Butler-Volmer formulation provides the theoretical foundation for quantifying charge transfer kinetics at electrode-electrolyte interfaces through activation overpotential calculations. The method 100 incorporates three distinct overpotential regions: activation overpotential using modified Butler-Volmer equation, ohmic overpotential through area-specific resistance, and mass transfer overpotential using logarithmic functions. The activation overpotential component quantifies the energy barrier for electrochemical reactions and applies the modified Butler-Volmer relationship expressed as η_activation=(R·T)/(α·F)·sinh^(-1) (j/(2·i_oc )), where R represents the universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K), T denotes absolute temperature, α corresponds to the charge transfer coefficient (0.5 for symmetrical charge transfer), F represents Faraday's constant (96485 C/mol), j indicates current density, and i_oc denotes exchange current density. The ohmic overpotential calculation incorporates area-specific resistance effects through the relationship η_Ohmic=j·ASR, where ASR represents the cumulative area-specific resistance including electrode-electrolyte resistance, electrolyte ionic resistance, solid electrolyte interface layer resistance, and contact resistance normalized to unit area. The area-specific resistance parameter encompasses multiple resistance contributions that affect voltage efficiency and power delivery characteristics during battery operation. The mass transfer overpotential component addresses concentration gradient effects using the logarithmic function η_MassTransfer=-0.1·log((1-j)/(10^5·i_L )), where i_L represents the limiting current density corresponding to the maximum sustainable current before rapid capacity degradation. The mass transfer overpotential becomes significant when diffusion rates become slower than electrochemical reaction rates, particularly at high current densities and elevated temperatures. The method 100 correlates DFT-derived bond lengths, electronic energies, and charge distributions with empirical electrochemical parameters including exchange current density and area-specific resistance. The correlation methodology establishes quantitative relationships between atomic-scale properties calculated through density functional theory and macroscopic electrochemical performance parameters measured through polarization curve analysis. The exchange current density for lithium iron phosphate reaches 29.96 A/m² based on correlation with HOMO-LUMO energy gap values and charge transfer coefficient calculations derived from electronic structure analysis. The area-specific resistance correlation for lithium iron phosphate yields 0.00033 Ω·m² through systematic mapping of optimized bond lengths and charge distribution symmetry parameters to ionic transport resistance characteristics. The strong Fe-O covalent bonds with lengths of 1.821 Å provide structural stability that minimizes interfacial resistance and maintains coherent lithium-ion diffusion pathways throughout electrochemical cycling. The symmetric charge distribution with balanced Mulliken charges reduces lattice strain effects that contribute to resistance increases during battery operation. The charge distribution symmetry analysis correlates Mulliken charge calculations with ionic transport characteristics and electrochemical kinetics parameters. The balanced charge distribution in lithium iron phosphate with iron atoms carrying +1.2e charge and oxygen atoms bearing-0.8e charge creates uniform electric field gradients that facilitate lithium-ion migration through one-dimensional channels within the olivine structure. The symmetric charge arrangement minimizes activation energy barriers for lithium intercalation and deintercalation processes, resulting in lower activation overpotential and higher exchange current density values. The bond strength correlation methodology links optimized bond lengths and binding energies to thermal decomposition thresholds and structural stability limits. The strong Fe-O bonds in lithium iron phosphate with binding energies derived from density functional theory calculations correlate with elevated thermal decomposition temperatures exceeding 270°C and enhanced resistance to oxygen release under thermal stress conditions. The covalent bonding network provides structural coherence that maintains electrochemical performance at elevated operating temperatures and prevents thermal runaway initiation. The correlation framework enables prediction of electrochemical parameters for cathode materials through atomic-scale property calculations without extensive experimental characterization. The systematic mapping of HOMO-LUMO energy gaps to exchange current density values provides predictive capability for evaluating charge transfer kinetics of new cathode chemistries. The correlation of optimized bond lengths and charge distributions to area-specific resistance parameters enables assessment of power delivery characteristics and voltage efficiency for different cathode materials. The lumped-parameter model validation incorporates experimental polarization curve data to verify correlation accuracy and refine parameter relationships. The model validation process compares calculated overpotential values with measured electrode potential data across varying current densities and operating temperatures. The correlation methodology achieves quantitative agreement between density functional theory predictions and experimental electrochemical measurements, establishing the multi-scale framework as a reliable tool for cathode material evaluation and optimization. FIG. 6 illustrates polarization curves for a lithium iron phosphate cathode half-cell displaying the relationship between current density and electrode potential versus the reversible hydrogen electrode according to various embodiments. The polarization curves demonstrate electrochemical performance characteristics across three distinct operating temperatures: 30.0°C, 40.0°C, and 170.0°C, with electrode potential ranges spanning approximately 1.1 V to 1.7 V vs RHE and current densities reaching 0.12 A/cm². The method 100 analyzes temperature ranges from 303K to 313K for ambient conditions and up to 333K for thermal stress evaluation through systematic polarization curve characterization. The ambient temperature analysis encompasses the 30.0°C and 40.0°C operating conditions that correspond to normal battery operation ranges, while the elevated temperature evaluation at 170.0°C represents thermal stress conditions that approach the upper limits of safe battery operation. The temperature range analysis enables quantification of thermal stability margins and identification of performance degradation thresholds for lithium iron phosphate cathode materials. The polarization curves at 30.0°C and 40.0°C demonstrate nearly identical electrochemical behavior with overlapping current density profiles across the entire potential range. The thermal stability between these ambient operating conditions reflects the structural robustness of the olivine framework and the resistance to temperature-induced performance variations. The current density values at both temperatures reach approximately 0.12 A/cm² at electrode potentials near 1.7 V, indicating consistent charge transfer kinetics and minimal activation energy changes within the moderate temperature range. The elevated temperature polarization curve at 170.0°C exhibits marginal performance reduction compared to the ambient temperature conditions while maintaining the characteristic sigmoidal shape and reaching similar maximum current densities. The slight performance reduction manifests as a delayed onset of current density rise and marginally lower current values across the mid-potential range, yet the overall electrochemical behavior remains stable and predictable. The thermal resilience at 170.0°C demonstrates the structural integrity of the lithium iron phosphate cathode under extreme thermal stress conditions. The method 100 evaluates thermal runaway thresholds with lithium iron phosphate maintaining stability up to 270°C through correlation of polarization curve performance with atomic-scale structural parameters. The thermal stability analysis establishes that lithium iron phosphate cathodes retain electrochemical functionality at temperatures approaching 270°C before oxygen release and thermal decomposition initiate. The elevated thermal runaway threshold results from the strong Fe-O covalent bonds with optimized lengths of 1.821 Å that provide structural coherence and resist thermal degradation processes. The wide HOMO-LUMO energy gap of 0.02554 eV contributes to thermal stability by creating electronic configurations that resist thermally activated charge transfer processes and structural rearrangements. The electronic energy gap provides a barrier against thermal excitation of electrons that could initiate decomposition reactions or structural instabilities. The moderate energy gap enables controlled electrochemical reactions while preventing uncontrolled thermal processes that lead to capacity fade and safety hazards. The symmetric charge distribution with balanced Mulliken charges enhances thermal resilience through uniform electric field gradients that maintain structural stability under thermal stress. The balanced charge arrangement with iron atoms carrying +1.2e charge and oxygen atoms bearing-0.8e charge creates electrostatic interactions that stabilize the olivine lattice against thermal expansion and contraction effects. The symmetric charge distribution minimizes local stress concentrations that could initiate crack formation or structural collapse at elevated temperatures. The correlation between atomic-scale properties and macroscopic thermal performance establishes predictive relationships for thermal safety assessment. The strong Fe-O covalent bonding network provides thermal decomposition resistance that extends operational temperature ranges beyond conventional lithium-ion cathode materials. The olivine structure maintains crystallographic integrity and electrochemical functionality at temperatures where other cathode chemistries experience rapid degradation and thermal runaway initiation. The polarization curve analysis demonstrates that lithium iron phosphate cathodes provide reliable electrochemical performance across wide temperature ranges with minimal degradation effects. The thermal stability characteristics enable safe operation in high-temperature environments and provide safety margins against thermal runaway events during battery abuse conditions. The combination of strong covalent bonding, wide electronic energy gaps, and symmetric charge distributions creates a cathode material with exceptional thermal resilience and electrochemical stability for demanding battery applications. FIG. 7 illustrates polarization curves for a lithium manganese oxide cathode in a lithium-ion battery half-cell configuration according to various embodiments. The polarization curves plot current density on the y-axis against electrode potential versus the reversible hydrogen electrode in volts on the x-axis, displaying electrochemical performance characteristics at operating temperatures of 30.0°C, 40.0°C, and 120.0°C with voltage operating window extending to approximately 1.9 V vs RHE. The method 100 analyzes lithium manganese oxide electrochemical behavior across three distinct temperature conditions that reveal temperature sensitivity characteristics and structural degradation effects. The polarization curves demonstrate sigmoidal shapes initiating near zero current density at approximately 1.1 V and rising progressively as electrode potential increases toward 1.9 V. The voltage operating window for lithium manganese oxide extends from approximately 1.1 V to 1.9 V, providing a marginally wider potential range compared to lithium iron phosphate cathodes and offering advantages for applications requiring higher voltage operation. The polarization curves at 30.0°C and 40.0°C exhibit nearly overlapping behavior across the lower and mid-potential ranges from 1.1 V to 1.7 V, indicating minimal temperature sensitivity in the activation and ohmic polarization regions. The overlapping performance characteristics reflect the structural stability of the spinel lattice under moderate temperature conditions and demonstrate consistent charge transfer kinetics within the ambient operating range. The current density profiles at both temperatures follow similar trajectories through the activation-dominated region and the ohmic resistance region, reaching comparable values across the majority of the potential window. The method 100 identifies divergence at higher potentials approaching 1.9 V where the curves begin to separate, with the 120.0°C curve showing marginally reduced current density compared to the 30.0°C and 40.0°C curves. The performance divergence at elevated potentials suggests the onset of mass transfer limitations and structural degradation effects that become pronounced at higher temperatures and current densities. The reduced current density at 120.0°C indicates compromised electrochemical kinetics resulting from structural instabilities within the spinel lattice framework. The relatively steep initial slope of the polarization curves reflects the three-dimensional spinel structure of lithium manganese oxide that facilitates rapid lithium-ion diffusion through interconnected tetrahedral and octahedral sites. The spinel framework provides multiple pathways for lithium-ion transport, enabling higher exchange current density compared to the one-dimensional olivine pathways in lithium iron phosphate cathodes. The enhanced ionic transport characteristics manifest as rapid current density rise in the activation polarization region and superior initial electrochemical response. The method 100 evaluates thermal runaway thresholds with lithium manganese oxide showing degradation above 120°C through correlation with atomic-scale structural parameters and electronic configuration analysis. The thermal degradation threshold at 120°C corresponds to the initiation of manganese dissolution processes and structural collapse mechanisms that compromise electrochemical performance and safety characteristics. The reduced thermal stability compared to lithium iron phosphate results from weaker Mn-O bonds and electronic instabilities within the spinel lattice structure. The weaker Mn-O bonds with optimized lengths of 1.919 Å contribute to structural vulnerability under thermal stress conditions and facilitate manganese dissolution at elevated temperatures. The Mn-O bond lengths in the spinel structure exhibit greater susceptibility to thermal expansion and contraction effects compared to the stronger Fe-O bonds in olivine frameworks. The bond length analysis correlates with reduced thermal decomposition thresholds and accelerated degradation kinetics above 120°C operating conditions. The narrower HOMO-LUMO energy gap of 0.00208 eV facilitates rapid electron transfer kinetics but increases susceptibility to thermally activated structural degradation processes. The reduced energy gap enables faster electrochemical reactions through lower activation energy barriers but creates electronic configurations that become unstable under thermal stress. The narrow energy gap allows thermal excitation of electrons that initiate unwanted side reactions and structural rearrangements leading to capacity fade and performance degradation. The method 100 identifies Jahn-Teller distortions in Mn³⁺ ions with d⁴ electronic configuration as the primary mechanism for structural degradation above 120°C. The Mn³⁺ ions undergo Jahn-Teller distortions to relieve electronic degeneracy in the e_g orbital set, resulting in elongated Mn-O bond lengths and destabilization of the spinel lattice structure. The cooperative distortions propagate throughout the crystal lattice, creating structural collapse mechanisms that manifest as voltage fading and capacity loss during electrochemical cycling at elevated temperatures. The asymmetric charge distribution with manganese atoms carrying +0.7e charge and oxygen atoms bearing-0.35e charge creates localized stress concentrations that amplify under thermal conditions. The charge distribution asymmetry generates non-uniform electric field gradients that contribute to lattice strain and facilitate crack initiation at grain boundaries and defect sites. The unbalanced charge arrangement reduces structural coherence and accelerates degradation processes compared to the symmetric charge distributions observed in lithium iron phosphate systems. The manganese dissolution mechanism becomes thermally activated above 120°C through disproportionation reactions that convert Mn³⁺ ions into Mn²⁺ and Mn⁴⁺ species. The disproportionation process leads to manganese migration from the cathode structure into the electrolyte, resulting in active material loss and impedance increases that degrade electrochemical performance. The manganese dissolution correlates with the reduced current density observed in polarization curves at 120.0°C and establishes the thermal stability limit for lithium manganese oxide cathodes. The correlation between atomic-scale electronic structure and macroscopic thermal degradation establishes predictive relationships for thermal safety assessment of spinel cathode materials. The combination of weak Mn-O bonds, narrow HOMO-LUMO energy gaps, and asymmetric charge distributions creates vulnerability to thermal stress that limits operational temperature ranges and safety margins. The structural degradation mechanisms identified through density functional theory analysis provide fundamental understanding of thermal runaway initiation and progression in lithium manganese oxide cathode systems. FIG. 8 illustrates polarization curves for a nickel manganese cobalt oxide cathode half-cell according to various embodiments. The polarization curves plot current density on the vertical axis against electrode potential on the horizontal axis, displaying electrochemical performance characteristics at operating temperatures of 30.0°C and 147.0°C with electrode potential ranges spanning approximately 1.4 V to 2.4 V and current densities reaching up to 0.12 A/cm². The method 100 analyzes nickel manganese cobalt oxide electrochemical behavior across two distinct temperature conditions that reveal thermal sensitivity characteristics and performance degradation mechanisms under elevated temperature operation. The polarization curves demonstrate characteristic three-region behavior encompassing activation-dominated regions at low current densities, ohmic resistance regions with relatively linear voltage drop characteristics, and mass transfer-limited regions at higher current densities. The electrode potential operating window extends from approximately 1.4 V to 2.4 V, providing higher voltage operation compared to lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide cathode systems. The polarization curve at 30.0°C demonstrates stable electrochemical performance with steady current density output across the potential range, reflecting the structural integrity of the layered oxide lattice under ambient operating conditions. The ambient temperature performance exhibits smooth lithium-ion transport characteristics through the layered structure with minimal resistance effects in the activation and ohmic polarization regions. The current density profile at 30.0°C follows predictable electrochemical behavior patterns with gradual increases corresponding to applied potential changes and reaches maximum values approaching 0.12 A/cm² at elevated potentials. The method 100 identifies thermal vulnerability at 147.0°C through analysis of polarization curve degradation that manifests as reduced current density output and earlier onset of mass transfer limitations compared to ambient temperature conditions. The elevated temperature polarization curve exhibits pronounced performance degradation with lower limiting current density values and shifted overpotential characteristics that indicate compromised electrochemical kinetics. The thermal sensitivity contrasts with the more thermally stable behavior observed in lithium iron phosphate cathodes and demonstrates nickel manganese cobalt oxide vulnerability to performance degradation under elevated operating temperatures. The earlier onset of mass transfer limitations at 147.0°C results from structural instabilities within the layered oxide lattice that impede lithium-ion diffusion and create concentration gradient effects at lower current densities. The mass transfer limitations manifest as rapid voltage increases and current density plateaus that occur at reduced potential values compared to ambient temperature operation. The degraded mass transport characteristics correlate with lattice expansion, interlayer spacing changes, and transition metal migration that disrupt lithium-ion pathways within the layered structure. The method 100 estimates atomic properties of nickel manganese cobalt oxide through correlation with lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide polarization data and density functional theory analysis. The correlation methodology utilizes systematic comparison of polarization curve characteristics including exchange current density, area-specific resistance, and limiting current density parameters to predict atomic-scale structural properties. The transition metal bond lengths for nickel manganese cobalt oxide are estimated within the range of 1.95-2.05 Å based on correlation with electrochemical performance parameters and structural stability characteristics observed in polarization curve analysis. The estimated HOMO-LUMO energy gap for nickel manganese cobalt oxide falls within the range of 0.008-0.015 eV based on correlation with charge transfer kinetics and thermal stability characteristics derived from polarization curve behavior. The narrow energy gap facilitates rapid electron transfer processes that enable high power density operation but creates electronic configurations susceptible to thermal instability and structural degradation. The energy gap estimation correlates with the observed thermal sensitivity at 147.0°C and provides insight into the electronic structure factors that contribute to performance degradation under elevated temperature conditions. The correlation analysis establishes that nickel manganese cobalt oxide exhibits intermediate thermal stability characteristics between lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide systems. The estimated bond lengths of 1.95-2.05 Å provide structural stability sufficient for ambient temperature operation while remaining vulnerable to thermal stress effects that compromise performance at elevated temperatures. The bond length range reflects the mixed transition metal composition that creates structural complexity and variable bonding characteristics within the layered oxide framework. The method 100 identifies structural instabilities in the layered oxide lattice as the primary mechanism for thermal vulnerability and performance degradation at 147.0°C. The layered structure consists of transition metal oxide layers separated by lithium-containing interlayer spaces that facilitate lithium-ion intercalation and deintercalation processes. The structural arrangement becomes unstable under thermal stress through thermal expansion effects, transition metal migration, and oxygen loss mechanisms that disrupt the layered architecture and compromise electrochemical functionality. The transition metal bond weakening at elevated temperatures contributes to structural collapse and performance degradation through reduced lattice cohesion and increased defect formation. The mixed transition metal composition creates variable bonding strengths and thermal expansion coefficients that generate internal stress concentrations during temperature cycling. The bond weakening manifests as increased resistance, reduced current density output, and shifted polarization characteristics that correlate with the degraded performance observed at 147.0°C. The thermal instability mechanisms include oxygen release from the layered structure that creates structural defects and reduces electrochemical activity through active material loss. The oxygen evolution becomes thermally activated at temperatures approaching 147.0°C and leads to irreversible structural changes that compromise long-term cycling stability. The oxygen loss correlates with the reduced limiting current density and earlier onset of mass transfer limitations observed in the elevated temperature polarization curve. The method 100 establishes that nickel manganese cobalt oxide provides high energy density operation under ambient conditions while exhibiting thermal vulnerability that limits high-temperature applications and safety margins. The electrochemical performance characteristics enable power tool applications and high-rate discharge scenarios under controlled thermal conditions. The thermal sensitivity requires active thermal management systems to prevent performance degradation and maintain operational safety during high-power operation or elevated ambient temperature conditions. The correlation framework enables prediction of nickel manganese cobalt oxide performance characteristics through systematic comparison with lithium iron phosphate and lithium manganese oxide reference materials. The predictive capability provides guidance for cathode material selection based on application requirements including operating temperature ranges, power density specifications, and thermal safety considerations. The multi-scale analysis approach establishes quantitative relationships between atomic-scale properties and macroscopic electrochemical performance that enable optimization of cathode material compositions and operating parameters. The method 100 utilizes finite volume method with Multi-Scale Multi-Domain model coupled with NTGK method for thermal runaway simulation of lithium-ion battery cells under high-rate discharge conditions. The finite volume method provides computational efficiency for large-scale thermal analysis while maintaining accuracy through discretization of conservation equations across multiple physical domains. The Multi-Scale Multi-Domain approach enables coupling of electrochemical phenomena with thermal transport processes through systematic integration of particle-scale, electrode-scale, and cell-scale physics within a unified computational framework. The method 100 applies energy conservation equations incorporating transient heat accumulation, conduction heat transfer, ohmic heating from electrode phases, electrochemical reaction heat, and short-circuit heat generation. The comprehensive energy conservation equation is expressed as (∂(ρⓜ┤c_pⓜT))/∂t-∇·(kⓜ┤∇ⓜT)=σ_+ |∇ϕ_+ |^2+σ_-|∇ϕ_-|^2+q┴˙_ECh+q┴˙_short, where the transient term (∂(ρⓜ┤c_pⓜT))/∂t represents temperature change over time, the conduction term ∇·(kⓜ┤∇ⓜT) accounts for heat transfer through materials, and the right-side terms encompass heat generation sources including ohmic heating from positive and negative electrode phases, electrochemical reaction heat, and potential short-circuit heat contributions. The material properties including density ρ, specific heat capacity c_p, and thermal conductivity k determine the thermal response characteristics of each cell component during discharge operations. The density and specific heat capacity terms govern thermal inertia and heat storage capacity, while thermal conductivity parameters control heat transfer rates through electrode materials, current collectors, and electrolyte regions. The ohmic heating terms σ_+ |∇ϕ_+ |^2 and σ_-|∇ϕ_-|^2 quantify resistive losses in positive and negative electrode phases based on conductivity values and potential gradients during current flow. The method 100 implements charge conservation equations governing current distribution in positive and negative electrode phases with intercalation current density calculations. The charge conservation formulation includes ∇·σ_-∇ϕ_-=j_ECh-j_short for the negative electrode phase and ∇·σ_+ ∇ϕ_+=-(j_EChⓜ┤-ⓜj_short ) for the positive electrode phase, where σ_+ and σ_-represent phase conductivities, φ_+ and φ_-denote phase potentials, and j_ECh represents intercalation current density. The total heat generation incorporates three distinct mechanisms: irreversible joule heating, reversible entropic heating, and side reaction heat through the comprehensive relationship q┴˙=I(U_OCVⓜ┤-ⓜV_batt )+IT (dU_OCV)/dT+q_sidereaction. The irreversible joule heating term I(U_OCVⓜ┤-ⓜV_batt ) quantifies energy dissipation due to overpotential losses during discharge, while the reversible entropic heating term IT (dU_OCV)/dT accounts for temperature-dependent changes in open-circuit voltage. The side reaction heat term q_side reaction encompasses additional heat generation from parasitic reactions and electrolyte decomposition processes that become significant at elevated temperatures. The NTGK method implements temperature-dependent parameters through polynomial relationships that correlate equilibrium potential and reaction rate parameters with depth of discharge and temperature variations. The equilibrium potential relationship is expressed as U=(∑_(n=0)^5ⓜ┤a_nⓜ(Dⓜ┤OⓜDⓜ〖^〗ⓜn) ┤exp[-ⓜ┤c_1ⓜ(1/Tⓜ┤-ⓜ1/T_ref ) ], where a_n represents empirical coefficients determined from battery characterization and c_1 denotes temperature sensitivity factors. The electrochemical reaction rate parameter follows Y=(∑_(n=0)^5ⓜ┤b_nⓜ(Dⓜ┤OⓜDⓜ〖^〗ⓜn) ┤-c_2 (Tⓜ┤-ⓜT_ref ), where b_n corresponds to empirical coefficients and c_2 represents temperature sensitivity for reaction kinetics. The method 100 operates at discharge rates of 3C with voltage cutoffs between 1.4V minimum and 5V maximum for thermal analysis under high-rate conditions. The 3C discharge rate corresponds to complete battery discharge within 20 minutes and represents demanding operational conditions that generate substantial heat through resistive losses and electrochemical polarization effects. The voltage cutoff parameters establish operational boundaries that prevent over-discharge conditions while enabling comprehensive thermal characterization across the full capacity range of the battery cell. The method 100 analyzes temperature ranges from 303K to 313K for ambient conditions and up to 333K for thermal stress evaluation during high-rate discharge operations. The ambient temperature analysis encompasses initial conditions of 303K (30°C) and 313K (40°C) that represent typical battery operating environments, while the thermal stress evaluation extends to 333K (60°C) to characterize performance under elevated temperature conditions. The temperature range analysis enables quantification of thermal gradients, heat accumulation rates, and thermal management requirements for safe battery operation. The method 100 applies convective heat transfer coefficient of 20 W/m²K representing forced air-cooling conditions in thermal simulations. The convective heat transfer coefficient establishes boundary conditions for heat dissipation from battery surfaces to the surrounding environment and represents moderate cooling effectiveness typical of forced air-cooling systems. The heat transfer coefficient value enables realistic simulation of thermal management scenarios and provides practical guidance for cooling system design and thermal safety assessment. The method 100 employs 1-second time-step size with 1200 time-steps for thermal simulation stability and convergence monitoring throughout the discharge cycle. The temporal discretization parameters ensure numerical stability while providing sufficient resolution to capture transient thermal phenomena and temperature evolution during battery operation. The 1200 time-step simulation duration corresponds to the complete 3C discharge cycle and enables comprehensive analysis of thermal behavior from initial conditions through full capacity utilization. FIG. 9 illustrates thermal contour visualizations of a lithium-ion battery cell wall zone displaying temperature distributions under different initial temperature conditions according to various embodiments. The thermal contours employ color-coded temperature scales ranging from 303 K (blue) at the lower end to 333 K (yellow) at the upper end, with intermediate temperatures represented by cyan, green, and orange hues that provide visual representation of spatial temperature variations within the battery cell structure. The method 100 generates depth of discharge curves correlating temperature evolution with battery capacity utilization during discharge cycles. The depth of discharge evolution follows the relationship DOD=1/Q_c ∫_0^t Jdt, where Q_c represents the cell capacity and J denotes the applied current. The depth of discharge calculation provides quantitative correlation between capacity utilization and thermal state evolution throughout the discharge process. The thermal contours demonstrate non-uniform heat distribution within the battery cell during operation, with temperature gradients visible across different regions of the cell structure. The left thermal contour displays predominantly green coloration with localized cyan regions at the base and small yellow zones at the top edges, indicating temperature distributions approximately between 310 K and 325 K across most of the cell surface. The spatial temperature variation reflects heat generation patterns within the electrode regions and heat dissipation characteristics through current collectors and terminal connections. The right thermal contour exhibits a warmer thermal profile with extensive orange and yellow regions dominating the upper two-thirds of the structure, while green and cyan zones persist at the lower portion. The elevated temperature distribution suggests thermal accumulation reaching 330-333 K in the upper electrode sections, consistent with high-rate discharge conditions and elevated initial operating temperatures. The temperature gradients demonstrate the importance of thermal management strategies to prevent localized overheating and maintain uniform temperature distributions. The geometric configurations include stepped rectangular protrusions at the top representing battery terminals and connection tabs that facilitate heat dissipation through metallic current collectors. The terminal regions remain 10-15 K cooler than the main cell body due to enhanced thermal conductivity of current collector materials and direct thermal contact with external cooling systems. The temperature differential between terminals and cell body demonstrates the effectiveness of current collectors as thermal pathways for heat removal during battery operation. FIG. 10 illustrates temperature versus depth of discharge curves displaying thermal behavior of a lithium-ion battery under different initial temperature conditions according to various embodiments. The depth of discharge curves demonstrate characteristic three-phase thermal evolution patterns that correlate with electrochemical phenomena and heat generation mechanisms throughout the discharge cycle. The method 100 identifies characteristic three-phase thermal patterns including rapid initial rise from 0-0.2 DOD, quasi-linear mid-discharge behavior from 0.2-0.8 DOD, and accelerated climb near full discharge from 0.8-1.0 DOD. The initial rapid temperature increase corresponds to activation polarization effects and initial heat generation as electrochemical reactions initiate and current flow establishes through the electrode structure. The activation-dominated region generates substantial heat through charge transfer resistance and interfacial phenomena that create temperature rises within the first 20% of discharge capacity. The quasi-linear mid-discharge region from 0.2 to 0.8 DOD exhibits steady temperature increases that correlate with ohmic heating and consistent electrochemical activity during the main discharge plateau. The linear temperature rise reflects stable heat generation rates through resistive losses and electrochemical polarization that remain relatively constant during the middle portion of the discharge cycle. The steady thermal behavior corresponds to the flat voltage plateau characteristic of lithium iron phosphate cathodes during the Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ redox transition. The accelerated temperature climb from 0.8 to 1.0 DOD demonstrates increased heat generation as concentration polarization effects become pronounced and electrochemical resistance increases near full discharge. The accelerated thermal rise results from mass transfer limitations, increased overpotential losses, and elevated current densities required to maintain discharge rates as lithium concentrations become depleted within the electrode structure. The final discharge phase generates substantial heat through concentration gradient effects and transport limitations. The temperature evolution curves demonstrate that cells starting at 30°C reach maximum temperatures of approximately 52°C by complete discharge, while cells starting at 40°C reach peak temperatures of approximately 59°C. The temperature increases of 22 K and 19 K respectively demonstrate the thermal impact of high-rate 3C discharge conditions and the influence of initial temperature on final thermal state. The vertical separation between the curves remains relatively consistent throughout the discharge cycle, indicating that initial temperature offsets are largely preserved during thermal evolution. The thermal behavior analysis establishes that convective cooling with heat transfer coefficient of 20 W/m²K provides sufficient heat dissipation to prevent dangerous temperature escalation and maintain battery temperatures well below thermal runaway thresholds. The maximum temperatures of 52°C and 59°C remain substantially below the thermal runaway threshold of approximately 170°C for lithium iron phosphate cathodes, demonstrating adequate thermal safety margins under the applied cooling conditions. The thermal management effectiveness enables safe high-rate operation while highlighting the importance of cooling system design for sustained high-power applications. The correlation between finite volume method thermal simulations and electrochemical polarization analysis demonstrates consistent thermal stability characteristics for lithium iron phosphate cathodes across multiple analytical approaches. The thermal resilience observed in finite volume method simulations aligns with the stable polarization behavior at elevated temperatures, confirming the structural integrity and thermal safety characteristics of the olivine cathode framework. The multi-scale analysis approach provides comprehensive understanding of thermal behavior from atomic-scale bonding characteristics through macroscopic heat transfer and thermal management requirements. patents.abstract: Novel cost effective methods of removing circulating currents in Lithium batteries of a BESS are given to avoid PCB burnouts and Fire. To provide 100% stop of circulating currents in the Rack batteries, in the BESS, the charging path and discharging path of the inverter must be separated and diodes are to be used to enfoce current in one direction of each path. Three methods are given first for a case where the inside of the Inverter/PCS can be modified to separate the charging and discharging paths, second for a case of when the inside circuits of Inverter/PCS can not be modified and third for a case of using a Stack BMS to combine the outputs of several Rack BMSs. The proposed methods are simple and very cost effective that can help in constructing future BESS systems with out failures, PCB burn outs and Fire and also can help in increasing the life time of batteries due to the removal of circulating currents.
patents.complete_specification: Field of Invention The invention is in the field of Battery Energy Storage Systems that deploy a number of Lithium batteries connected in series to obtain a high voltage controlled by a Rack BMS and several racks of batteries connected in parallel to achieve a high storage capacity in the range of 2 MWh to 5 MWh assembled in a 20 feet container. Use of Innovation When one of the applicant was trying to buy the BESS from abroad few vendors who had supplied the BESS systems earlier were reluctant to offer further supplies. It appeared that their BESS systems were having issues of burnouts of BMS PCBs. Further studies showed that many countries who installed BESS systems were having fire, explosion and PCB burnouts. The fire problem was mostly due to surge currents (infinite) when connecting the high voltage battery racks in parallel that created hidden circulating currents from one rack to another when the de rack ·voltages were different at the time of paralleling. The other reason was due to communication link failure between the battery BMS and the inverter along with a high ambient temperature. A closer study revealed that the fire and failures can be stopped if the large circulating currents in the battery racks are stopped. A simple solution was found to stop the battery circulating currents and that is the topic of this patent application. Prior Art Details Background When we parallel two voltage sources with different voltages, it is equivalent to a sl)ort circuit and the circulating current is equal to the voltage difference divided by the internal series resistances of the batteries. In a BESS, several cells (say 16 cells) are connected in series to build a "module" or "Pack" with an output voltage of n * 3.2 V (ie 16*3.2 = 51.2 V). A BMS is used by the pack for "cell balancing" that tries to make all the cell voltages almost equal. This BMS also monitors all cell voltages and cell temperatures. Then several Packs of batteries of 51.2 V are connected in series to build the required high voltage to drive the inverter of the BESS. If we connect 12 packs in series that will result in an output voltage of 12 x 51.2 = 614.4 V. High power BESS systems use upto a high voltage of 1500 V. The Rack of the 51.2 V batteries is controlled by a High Voltage Box or a Rack BMS. In small power BESS systems, the de path of the RACK BMS connects to the Inverter . The RACK BMS is connected to all the PACK batteries in the RACK via an optically isolated CAN signaling connection. The CAN signaling also connects the Rack BMS to the Inverter. In higher capacity BESS systems, several Racks of batteries are connected via a Stack BMS to increase the current capacity. If each rack has a 1500 V with current capacity of 314 Ah, the stack BMS will have 1500 V de with a current capacity of m*314 Ah. If m = 4, the stack BMS current capacity will become 4 * 314 = 1256 A. The Stack BMS de path will now connect to the Inverter or PCS and also will have a CAN signaling link to the Inverter as well as to each of the RACK BMSs. The stack BMS or simple parallel connection of the de paths of RACK BMS PCBs pose a danger of Fire in the BESS (or burn out of components in the RACK BMS PCBs) due to the circulating currents poosible. Switching OFF and ON of the circuit breaker in each RACK BMS will do the harm over a period of time. Prior Art Patents and research on stopping circulating currents when paralleling high-voltage lithium battery racks focus on methods such as voltage matching before connection, the use of DC/DC converters or current-limiting circuits, and advanced control algorithms (like adaptive droop control) within the Battery Management System (BMS). Key Patented and Technical Solutions Solutions for managing circulating currents primarily involve either preventing the voltage imbalance that causes the current flow or actively managing the current once the packs are connected. Voltage Matching and Connection Algorithms The most basic approach to minimize circulating current during "hot-swap" (connecting a new pack to an existing parallel system).is to ensure the new battery pack's State of Charge (SOC) and voltage closely match those ot the existing system before the connection is fully made. Sequential Connection: One patented method [1] (e.g., EP3985781Al *)involves a charging control operation that sequentially closes switches of battery packs based on their voltage levels, starting with the lowest, to manage the inrush and circulating currents during parallel charging. Hardware-Based Current Limitation Various hardware circuits are used to physically limit current flow between parallel branches. Current Limiting Circuits: Patents [2] like US7872443B2 describe using a currentlimiting circuit (e.g., a simple resistor or more complex active circuit) to prevent excessive current flow during charging or discharging, which helps manage heat and current surges. PTC Elements: Another method [3] described in CN104577015A involves using Positive Temperature Coefficient (PTC) elements to. connect groups of batteries in parallel, which provides inherent current-limiting properties in case of a short circuit or high current event. Resistive Elements and Switching: The patent US9024585B2 [ 4] details a battery parallel-operation circuit that incorporates a resistive element and a switching element in different lines to manage current flow and prevent large inter-unit currents Objects of the Invention Objects which the Invention has in view: The principal object of the invention is to invent a simple method to stop completely the circulating currents in the RACK batteries when several RACK batteries are paralleld either directly or via STACK BMS. The method used must be economical as well as rugged to avoid failures and Fire in the BESS. To stop the circulating currents, it will require us to separate the charging and discharging DC paths starting from the Inverter. The invention will have 3 cases: Case 1) where the de charging path from inside the inverter is separated from the DC discharging path. In this case the Inverter should have a de output port for charging the batteries and one de input port for discharging the batteries. Case 2) where no modification is done inside the inverter (as that is often difficult). In this case the Inverter will have only one de port to connect to the batteries for both charging and discharging. Case 3) where the de path to inverter is via a Stack BMS connecting to multiple Rack BMSs. 4. Detailed Description of the Invention Methodl: The trick to stop circulating currents is to first separate the charging path and the discharging path and use diodes in series both in the de charging path and the de discharging path of the BESS. For 100% stoppage of the circulating currents in the battery, the solution is given in Fig.l. The inside of the Inverter/PCS is modified to separate the de charging path (output) and the de Discharging Path (Input). Diodes D1, D2, D3, D4 are series connected to the outputs of 4 (or any number of) Rack BMS's and then connected in parallel forming the Discharge path that is connected to the Inverter input port. This allows the batteries to send current in to the inverter for de to ac conversion. Diodes D5, D6, D7, DB are again series connected in the reverse direction to allow charging current from the Inverter/PCS to the Rack BMS's to charge the batteries . From first principles verify that the battery current from one rack can not pass to any other rack, avoiding 100% stoppage of circulating currents. Some manufacturers use 2 or more parallelconnected cells in stead of one cell. This must be avoided to stop circulating currents at cell level. Fig.1 shows that inside a Pack Battery only single cells must be series connected. Method 2: Often the Inverter manufacturers may not agree to make the separation of the charging and discharging circuits and in that case (Case 2), Fig.2 shows the circuit diagram to be used to avoid circulating currents. This works as long as the voltage difference between any two racks is less than 1.4 V (that will not make two diodes say D1 and DS) to forward bias from one rack to another). If the cell balancing in the PACK batteries are controlled (with the help of CAN signaling) from the Rack BMS's to the Pack BMS's, the voltage difference between any two rack voltages can be made less than 1.4 V. If we need the maximum voltage differences to be above 1.4 V for any reason, one can use instead of single diodes in the charging path DS, D6, D7 and DB) we can use N number of diodes in series in stead of a single diode and the circulaing current will not flow if voltage difference between any two racks is less than (N+1)* 0.7V where N is number of diodes used instead of a sigle diode and 0. 7 Vis the nominal forward bias voltage of a Si diode. Method 3: For the circuits in Fig.1 and Fig.2 the the high voltage boxes (Rack BMSs) outputs were feeding the Inverter directly with out any Stack BMS. In case 3, if a stack BMS is used that combines the de outputs of several Rack BMSs and then connect to the Inverter's DC port, the stack BMS will provide additional intelligent control and protection features. Fig 3 shows the circuit diagram for avoiding circulating currents from one Rack BMS to another Rack BMS via the Stack BMS. The diodes used in series in the charging path (DS, Do, D7, DB) can be either a single silicon diode or multiple diodes in series depending on the effectiveness of the Rack BMSs in cell balancing. The 3 circuit diagrams given as inventions will reduce major failures and Fires in BESSs of future as there will be no circulating currents in the BESS batteries. In the 3 circuit diagrams only 4 racks of batteries were shown but we can use any number of racks as per the need of the BESS storage capacity. In each rack, the cells are always series connected. Manufacturers must not parallel more cells to any one cell, to avoid ciculating current from cell to cell and to increase the effectiveness of the "cell balancing" of the Pack BMS. So the design uses only series connections of single cells in each rack by avoiding circulating currents from cell to cell and the patent suggested how to parallel connect the RACK BMSs to avoid any circulating current from one rack to another rack. The proposed invention will increase the life time of batteries (20 years expected) and will also avoid PCB burn outs and .Fires in the BESS. The proposed invention is very cost effecive just needing the use of few diodes . REFERENCES [1] XIAO, Rui, HUANG, Ying, WU, Donglei, PARALLEL BATTERY MANAGEMENT METHOD, Microvast Power Systems Co., Ltd, Pattent Application: EP 3 9B5 7B1 A1, EUROPEAN PATENT APPLICATION published in accordance with Art. 153(4) EPC, 20.04.2022 Bulletin 2022/16 We claim 1. A method as shown in Figure 1 of avoiding circulating currents in any high voltage BESS by separating the de charging ciruits and discharging circuits inside the Inverter/PCS box by providing separate de ports for Charging the batteries and for discharging the batteries and by using diodes in the charging path and discharging path of each Rack BMS (High Voltage Box). 2. A method as shown in Figure 2 by using diodes to avoid circulating currents in the BESS batteries when multiple Racks of Batteries are paralleled via High Voltage Boxes (Rack BMSs), when the Inverter/PCS can not be modified by the manufacurer to provide separate de ports for charging and discharging. · 3. A method as shown in Figure 3 by using diodes to avoid circulating currents in the BESS batteries when multiple Racks of Batteries are paralleled via High Voltage Boxes (Rack BMSs) connecting to a stack BMS for combining the de currents towards the Inverter and for splitting the charging currents from the Inverter/PCS to the Rack batteries, if a Stack BMS is used to connect the multiple RACK BMSs to th Inverter/PCS for the DC current flow.
