patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a process for recovering valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using a clean and selective hydrometallurgical approach. The process comprises complete discharge of spent lithium-ion batteries using a hybrid conducting material in the presence of graphite, followed by removal of electrolyte components by shredding and heating at about 150°C under reduced pressure. The resultant battery material is subjected to hydrometallurgical treatment at low temperatures to obtain an aqueous metal-ion containing solution. Manganese ions are selectively separated using an aminophosphine oxide reagent at a pH of 2.0 to 4.5, cobalt ions are separated using an ion-imprinted polymer at a pH of 5.0 to 6.5, and nickel ions are recovered by electroless plating at a pH of 7.5 to 9.0. Lithium ions are recovered as lithium carbonate by heating at 80°C to 100°C. The process is acid-fume free, energy-efficient, enables multi-metal recovery with high selectivity, and is suitable for sustainable recycling of lithium-ion batteries.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [0001] The present invention relates to the field of battery recycling and metal recovery, and more particularly to a process for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using selective hydrometallurgical treatment methods. BACKGROUND OF INVENTION [0002] The recovery of valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries has become increasingly important due to the growing demand for these materials and environmental concerns associated with battery waste disposal. Lithium-ion batteries contain significant quantities of valuable metals including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which can be recovered and reused in new battery production. Various approaches have been developed to extract these metals from spent batteries, with hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processes being the primary methods employed in the industry. [0003] The recovery of valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries has become increasingly important due to the growing demand for these materials and environmental concerns associated with battery waste disposal. Lithium-ion batteries contain significant quantities of valuable metals including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which can be recovered and reused in new battery production. Various approaches have been developed to extract these metals from spent batteries, with hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processes being the primary methods employed in the industry. [0004] Hydrometallurgical approaches have been developed as alternatives to high-temperature processing methods. US patent application US20230080556A1 discloses a hydrometallurgical method for recovering lithium and transition metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using alkaline and acid leaching steps. US patent application US12218322B2 describes a manganese-lithium separation process for comprehensive recovery of cobalt, nickel, manganese and lithium elements from ternary battery wastes using hydrolysis and extraction methods. US patent application US12412940B1 presents systems and methods for metal recovery from lithium-ion batteries where components are leached into solution and non-lithium components are adsorbed to ion exchange resins. These hydrometallurgical processes typically employ strong mineral acids such as sulfuric acid or hydrochloric acid to dissolve the metal oxides present in battery materials. [0005] Existing hydrometallurgical processes face several technical challenges including limited selectivity in metal separation, generation of acidic waste streams, and difficulties in achieving high purity recovery of individual metals. US patent application US11710857B2 describes a process for recovering nickel cobalt manganese hydroxide from recycled lithium-ion battery material using acidic leaching with sulfuric acid or hydrochloric acid at pH less than 2, followed by precipitation with sodium hydroxide. Many current processes rely on precipitation methods that can result in co-precipitation of multiple metals, reducing the purity of recovered materials. The use of strong acids also creates environmental concerns related to acid waste management and potential emissions of acid fumes during processing operations. [0006] The selective separation and recovery of individual metals in high purity forms remains a significant technical challenge in lithium-ion battery recycling. Current methods often struggle to achieve complete recovery of all valuable metals while maintaining the purity levels required for direct reuse in new battery manufacturing. The development of more selective separation techniques and environmentally sustainable processing conditions continues to be an active area of research and development in the battery recycling industry. OBJECT OF INVENTION [0007] Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies, are as follows: [0008] The primary object of the present invention is to provide a process for recovering valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries in an environmentally benign and energy-efficient manner. [0009] Another object of the present invention is to provide a clean hydrometallurgical process that avoids pyrometallurgical smelting, operates at relatively low temperatures, and eliminates the generation of hazardous gaseous emissions. [0010] Another object of the present invention is to provide a process that enables sequential and selective recovery of manganese, cobalt, nickel and lithium from spent lithium-ion batteries under controlled pH conditions. [0011] Another object of the present invention is to provide a process that ensures safe handling of spent lithium-ion batteries by complete discharge prior to mechanical processing and controlled removal of electrolyte components. [0012] Another object of the present invention is to provide a process that achieves high metal recovery efficiency with improved selectivity compared to conventional recycling methods. [0013] Another object of the present invention is to provide a process that is compatible with different lithium-ion battery chemistries, including NMC, NCA, LFP and mixed-chemistry batteries. [0014] Another object of the present invention is to provide a process that is industrially viable, modular and scalable, enabling deployment in decentralized or semi-urban recycling facilities. [0015] Other objects and advantages of the present disclosure will be more apparent from the following description, which is not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0016] The present invention relates to a process for recovering valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, which overcomes the environmental, energy and recovery inefficiencies associated with conventional battery recycling technologies. Existing pyrometallurgical processes are characterized by high energy consumption, hazardous gaseous emissions and high capital and maintenance costs, while conventional hydrometallurgical processes rely on strong acids, exhibit poor selectivity and result in incomplete metal recovery and secondary environmental contamination. The present invention addresses these drawbacks by providing a clean, selective and low-temperature hydrometallurgical process capable of sequentially recovering multiple metals with high efficiency. [0017] In accordance with the invention, spent lithium-ion batteries are first completely discharged using a hybrid conducting material in the presence of graphite to ensure safe handling prior to mechanical processing. Electrolyte components are removed by shredding followed by heating at about 150°C under reduced pressure, after which the resultant battery material is subjected to hydrometallurgical treatment at temperatures ranging from room temperature to about 70°C to obtain an aqueous metal-ion containing solution. From this solution, manganese ions are selectively separated using an aminophosphine oxide reagent at a pH of 2.0 to 4.5, cobalt ions are selectively separated using an ion-imprinted polymer at a pH of 5.0 to 6.5, nickel ions are recovered by electroless plating at a pH of 7.5 to 9.0, and lithium ions are recovered as lithium carbonate by heating at a temperature in the range of 80°C to 100°C. [0018] The process of the present invention operates under clean hydrometallurgical conditions with selective polymer-based metal capture, is acid-fume free, does not involve pyrometallurgical smelting, and eliminates the generation of toxic gaseous emissions, including dioxins and fluorinated compounds. The invention enables overall metal recovery efficiencies greater than 90% for lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, and is compatible with NMC, NCA, LFP and mixed-chemistry lithium-ion batteries. The process is modular and scalable, suitable for decentralized deployment, and supports sustainable recycling through closed-loop reuse of process water and leachates, thereby providing an environmentally benign and industrially viable solution for lithium-ion battery recycling. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWINGS [0019] The other objects, features and advantages will occur to those skilled in the art from the following description of the preferred embodiment and the accompanying drawings in which: [0020] Figure 1 illustrates a schematic representation of the proposed hybrid system for efficient metal recovery from spent lithium-ion batteries, depicting the integration of hydrometallurgical, electro-hydrometallurgical and polymer-based selective separation techniques employed in the process of the present invention. [0021] Figure 2 illustrates a schematic representation of the synthesis and working principle of a molecularly ion-imprinted polymer, showing selective complexation of specific metal ions and formation of metal-specific cavities within a polymer matrix, followed by removal of the metal ion to generate selective binding sites for subsequent metal recovery. [0022] Figure 3 illustrates a process flow diagram of the overall metal recovery process according to the present invention, showing sequential steps including discharging of spent lithium-ion batteries, comminution, hydrometallurgical leaching, selective separation of manganese, cobalt and nickel, and recovery of lithium as lithium carbonate. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [0023] The present invention may be embodied in several forms, and the details of embodiments of the present invention will be described in the following content with figures. The embodiments described below with reference to the drawings are merely illustrative of the technical solutions of the present disclosure but are not to be construed as limited to the technical solutions of the present disclosure. [0024] The terms and words used in the following description and claims are not limited to the bibliographical meanings but are merely used by the inventor to enable a clear and consistent understanding of the invention. Accordingly, it should be apparent to those skilled in the art that the following description of the present invention is provided for illustration purposes only and not for the purpose of limiting the invention as defined by the appended claims. As used in the description of the invention and the appended claims, the singular forms "a", "an" and "the" are intended to include the plural forms as well, unless the context clearly indicates otherwise. [0025] Unless otherwise defined, all terms (including technical and scientific terms) used herein have the same meaning as commonly understood by one of ordinary skill in the art to which this disclosure pertains. It will be further understood that terms, such as those defined in commonly used dictionaries, should be interpreted as having a meaning that is consistent with their meaning in the context of the relevant art and will not be interpreted in an idealized or overly formal sense unless expressly so defined herein. [0026] The present invention relates to a process for recovering valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using a clean and selective hydrometallurgical approach. The process overcomes the environmental, energy and recovery limitations associated with conventional pyrometallurgical and strong acid-based hydrometallurgical recycling processes by enabling sequential recovery of manganese, cobalt, nickel and lithium under controlled pH and temperature conditions with high selectivity and recovery efficiency.. [0027] In an embodiment of the present invention, spent lithium-ion batteries are completely discharged prior to mechanical processing to ensure safe handling and to prevent electrical hazards. The complete discharge is carried out using a hybrid conducting material in the presence of graphite, wherein the hybrid conducting material enables controlled dissipation of residual electrical energy and the graphite provides conductive pathways to facilitate uniform and complete discharge of the batteries. [0028] In another embodiment of the present invention, following complete discharge, the spent batteries are mechanically processed to obtain battery residues. Electrolyte components are removed from the battery residues by shredding followed by heating at a temperature of about 150°C under reduced pressure. The reduced pressure is maintained at approximately 1 bar to facilitate efficient removal of volatile electrolyte solvents while preventing solvent degradation and suppressing emission of hazardous or fluorinated fumes. [0029] In another embodiment of the present invention, the electrolyte-free battery residues are subjected to hydrometallurgical treatment to dissolve metal values into an aqueous phase. The hydrometallurgical treatment is carried out using aqueous chemistry at temperatures ranging from room temperature to about 70°C, thereby reducing energy consumption and avoiding high-temperature smelting. This treatment results in an aqueous metal-ion containing solution comprising lithium, manganese, cobalt and nickel ions. [0030] In another embodiment of the present invention, manganese ions are selectively separated from the aqueous metal-ion containing solution prior to recovery of other metals. The separation of manganese is carried out using an aminophosphine oxide reagent at a pH in the range of 2.0 to 4.5. The aminophosphine oxide reagent selectively complexes manganese ions through hard donor P=O coordination chemistry, enabling preferential separation of manganese over cobalt and nickel ions and producing a manganese-depleted solution. [0031] In another embodiment of the present invention, cobalt ions are selectively separated from the manganese-depleted solution. The cobalt separation is carried out using an ion-imprinted polymer at a pH in the range of 5.0 to 6.5. The ion-imprinted polymer is structurally templated for cobalt ions, thereby enabling selective adsorption of cobalt ions over nickel and residual manganese ions and facilitating recovery of cobalt with high purity. [0032] In another embodiment of the present invention, nickel ions are selectively recovered from the cobalt-depleted solution. The recovery of nickel is performed using an electroless plating process at a pH in the range of 7.5 to 9.0. The electroless plating process results in deposition of nickel in metallic form without the application of external electrical energy, thereby reducing energy consumption and operational complexity. [0033] In another embodiment of the present invention, lithium ions are recovered from the nickel-depleted solution. The lithium recovery is carried out by heating the solution at a temperature in the range of 80°C to 100°C, resulting in precipitation of lithium carbonate. The lithium carbonate obtained is of battery-grade quality and is suitable for reuse in lithium-ion battery manufacturing. [0034] In another embodiment of the present invention, the process is monitored using an in-house portable colorimeter for real-time analysis of metal-ion concentrations during various stages of the process. This enables effective process control while avoiding reliance on expensive laboratory instrumentation. [0035] In another embodiment of the present invention, process water and leachates generated during the hydrometallurgical treatment and separation steps are recovered and reused in a closed-loop manner, thereby reducing water consumption and minimizing liquid waste generation. [0036] In another embodiment of the present invention, the process is applicable to spent lithium-ion batteries selected from NMC, NCA, LFP or mixed-chemistry batteries and can be operated on a common processing line. The process is modular and scalable, enabling deployment in decentralized or semi-urban recycling facilities with relatively low capital expenditure. [0037] In another embodiment of the present invention, the process operates under clean hydrometallurgical conditions and is acid-fume free, does not involve pyrometallurgical smelting, and eliminates the generation of toxic gaseous emissions, including dioxins and fluorinated compounds. The overall metal recovery efficiency achieved by the process is greater than 90% for lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese. [0038] According to the present invention, the overall process is configured as a sequential, pH-controlled hydrometallurgical recovery system in which spent lithium-ion batteries are safely discharged, pretreated, and subjected to selective metal recovery using reagent-based separation, polymer-based selective adsorption and electroless metal recovery techniques. The integrated configuration enables efficient multi-metal recovery with reduced environmental impact, low energy consumption and high product purity. [0039] The invention will now be described in detail with reference to the accompanying drawings. These embodiments are provided to explain the working of the invention and should not be interpreted as limiting the scope of the claims. [0040] With reference to Figure 1, the present invention provides a hybrid and integrated system for efficient recovery of valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, wherein hydrometallurgical processing is combined with electro-hydrometallurgical techniques and selective polymer-based metal separation. The overall configuration enables sequential, selective and high-efficiency recovery of manganese, cobalt, nickel and lithium under controlled chemical conditions while operating at relatively low temperatures and without the use of pyrometallurgical smelting. [0041] With reference to Figures 1 and 3, spent lithium-ion batteries, including batteries selected from NMC, NCA, LFP and mixed-chemistry lithium-ion batteries, are first subjected to complete electrical discharge prior to mechanical processing. The discharge is carried out using a hybrid conducting material in the presence of graphite, which facilitates controlled dissipation of residual electrical energy and ensures safe handling of the batteries during subsequent processing. The discharged batteries are then mechanically processed, such as by shredding or comminution, to obtain battery residues comprising active materials, current collectors and residual electrolyte components. [0042] With reference to Figure 3, electrolyte components are removed from the battery residues by heating at a temperature of about 150°C under reduced pressure. The reduced pressure, maintained at approximately 1 bar, enables efficient removal of volatile electrolyte solvents while preventing solvent degradation and suppressing emission of hazardous or fluorinated fumes. This pretreatment step produces electrolyte-free battery material suitable for downstream hydrometallurgical processing. [0043] The electrolyte-free battery material is then subjected to hydrometallurgical treatment, as shown in Figures 1 and 3, to dissolve metal values into an aqueous phase. The hydrometallurgical treatment is carried out using aqueous chemistry at temperatures ranging from room temperature to about 70°C, thereby significantly reducing energy consumption compared to conventional high-temperature processes. The treatment results in an aqueous metal-ion containing solution comprising lithium, manganese, cobalt and nickel ions. [0044] With reference to Figures 2 and 3, manganese ions are selectively separated from the aqueous metal-ion containing solution prior to recovery of other metals. The separation is carried out using an aminophosphine oxide reagent at a pH in the range of 2.0 to 4.5. The aminophosphine oxide reagent selectively complexes manganese ions through hard donor P=O coordination chemistry, enabling preferential capture of Mn(II) ions while leaving cobalt, nickel and lithium ions substantially in solution. The separated manganese may be recovered in the form of a manganese salt, and the remaining solution is rendered manganese-depleted. [0045] Subsequently, cobalt ions are selectively separated from the manganese-depleted solution, as illustrated in Figures 2 and 3. The cobalt separation is performed using an ion-imprinted polymer at a pH in the range of 5.0 to 6.5. As shown in Figure 2, the ion-imprinted polymer comprises molecular recognition sites that are structurally templated for cobalt ions, enabling selective adsorption of cobalt ions over nickel and residual manganese ions. Following adsorption, cobalt is recovered by suitable desorption or regeneration of the polymer. [0046] Thereafter, nickel ions are selectively recovered from the cobalt-depleted solution, as shown in Figure 3, using an electroless plating process conducted at a pH in the range of 7.5 to 9.0. The electroless plating process results in deposition of nickel in metallic form without the application of external electrical energy, thereby reducing energy consumption and enabling efficient recovery of high-purity metallic nickel. [0047] Finally, lithium ions are recovered from the nickel-depleted solution, as illustrated in Figure 3, by heating the solution at a temperature in the range of 80°C to 100°C, resulting in precipitation of lithium carbonate. The lithium carbonate obtained is of battery-grade quality and is suitable for reuse in lithium-ion battery manufacturing, thereby completing the sequential metal recovery process. [0048] Throughout the process, as depicted in Figures 1 and 3, monitoring of metal-ion concentrations may be carried out using an in-house portable colorimeter, enabling real-time process control and optimization of separation conditions. Process water and leachates generated during the hydrometallurgical and separation steps are recovered and reused in a closed-loop manner, thereby minimizing water consumption and reducing environmental impact. [0049] According to the present invention, the overall process operates under clean hydrometallurgical conditions with selective polymer-based metal capture, is acid-fume free, does not involve pyrometallurgical smelting, and eliminates the generation of toxic gaseous emissions, including dioxins and fluorinated compounds. The integrated and modular configuration enables overall metal recovery efficiencies greater than 90% for lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, and allows scalable deployment in decentralized or semi-urban recycling facilities. [0050] The present invention may take many forms and modifications, and the specific embodiments thereof have been shown by way of example in the drawings and are herein described in detail. It should be understood, however, that the invention is not to be limited to the particular forms set forth in the detailed description, but rather to include all modifications and equivalents within the scope of the invention as defined. , Claims:I / We Claim: 1. A process for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, comprising: completely discharging spent lithium-ion batteries using a hybrid conducting material in the presence of graphite; removing electrolyte components by shredding battery residues followed by heating at about 150°C under reduced pressure; subjecting the resultant battery material to hydrometallurgical treatment to obtain an aqueous metal-ion containing solution; selectively separating manganese ions from the aqueous solution using an aminophosphine oxide reagent at a pH in the range of 2.0 to 4.5; selectively separating cobalt ions from the manganese-depleted solution using an ion-imprinted polymer at a pH in the range of 5.0 to 6.5; selectively recovering nickel ions from the cobalt-depleted solution by an electroless plating process at a pH in the range of 7.5 to 9.0; and recovering lithium ions from the nickel-depleted solution as lithium carbonate by heating at a temperature in the range of 80°C to 100°C. 2. The process as claimed in claim 1, wherein the process operates under clean hydrometallurgical conditions with selective polymer-based metal capture and enables recovery of multiple metals with high selectivity. 3. The process as claimed in claim 1, wherein the hybrid conducting material facilitates safe and complete electrical discharge prior to mechanical processing. 5. The process as claimed in claim 1, wherein the aminophosphine oxide reagent selectively complexes manganese ions due to hard donor P=O coordination chemistry. 7. patents.abstract: The titled invention discloses a compact energy storage device to deliver efficient and reliable charging for modern electronic devices. The device incorporates an optimized lithium-ion cell (1) arrangement to achieve high energy density in a compact and 10 lightweight form factor. It includes a battery management system (2) for monitoring voltage, current, and temperature, ensuring safe operation through features such as overcharge, over-discharge, and short-circuit protection. A charging control circuit (3) regulates input power and supports fast-charging protocols, while a DC-DC converter (4) provides stable output voltage for multiple USB and Type-C ports (5). Additional is features include a smart display module (6) for real-time status updates and integrated protection circuitry for enhanced safety. The modular design and advanced thermal management ensure long lifespan, efficient energy conversion, and user convenience, making it suitable for portable applications and adaptable to various power requirements.
patents.complete_specification: This invention relates to portable energy storage technology, specifically to the design and development of a compact energy storage device (power bank) with an enhanced lithium-ion cell configuration. It focuses on optimizing battery arrangement, thermal management, and charging efficiency to provide a lightweight, high-capacity, and reliable power source for electronic devices. DESCRIPTION OF THE RELATED ART In the rapidly evolving field of portable energy storage, power banks have become indispensable accessories for modem lifestyles. With the proliferation of smartphones, tablets, wearable gadgets, and other portable electronics, users increasingly rely on external energy storage devices to maintain u oductivity. Most traditional power banks employ standard lithium-ion cell arrangements combined with basic charging and discharging circuits. Although these designs provide a means of storing and delivering electrical energy, they frequently suffer from inefficient space utilization, which leads to bulkier devices that compromise portability. Thermal management is typically limited, resulting in overheating during high-load charging or discharging conditions. This not only reduces user safety but also accelerates cell degradation, shortening the overall lifespan of the device. Furthermore, charging speeds in conventional designs are often slower, as they lack support for advanced fast-charging protocols that modem devices demand. The present invention solves the issues in the prior art by providing compact energy storage device with enhanced lithium-ion cell design that maximizes energy density while maintaining a small size. It integrates a Battery Management System to ensure safe operation, thermal protection, and balanced charging across cells. Furthermore, it includes support for advanced fast-charging protocols, efficient power conversion through a DC-DC converter, and multiple output ports for simultaneous charging of devices. The device is designed to provide reliable, safe, and efficient charging while remaining portable and cost-effective. 5 BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention is compact energy storage device with enhanced lithium-ion cell design. This invention focuses on the design and development of a compact and 10 efficient power bank using an optimized lithium-ion cell configuration to provide high energy density and reliable charging performance. The device integrates advanced components such as a battery management system for monitoring and safety, a charging control circuit for controlled power input, and a DC-DC converter for stable output voltage. It supports multiple fast-charging protocols and includes smart features is like real-time status display and multi-level protection circuitry. The design ensures portability, cost-effectiveness, and enhanced safety, making it suitable for various portable electronic devices and adaptable for different power requirements. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCOMPANYING DRAWING Figurel shows the block diagram of “Compact Energy Storage Device with 20 Enhanced Lithium-ion Cell Design” LITHIUM-ION CELL PACK The lithium-ion cell pack serves as the primary energy storage unit of the power bank, composed of multiple high-capacity cells arranged in an optimized series­parallel configuration to achieve the desired voltage and overall capacity. This arrangement provides high energy density in a compact form factor, making the device lightweight and portable. The cell pack is designed to deliver stable power output while ensuring safety through proper insulation and robust housing. Integrated thermal management features help prevent overheating, while the Battery Management System (BMS) ensures balanced charging, overcharge and discharge protection, and extended battery life. This component is essential for providing efficient, reliable, and long-lasting power for various electronic devices. 2. BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (BMS) The Battery Management System (BMS) is an essential component of the power bank, responsible for monitoring and controlling the performance of the lithium-ion cells to ensure safe and efficient operation. It manages critical parameters such as voltage, current, and temperature of each cell to prevent conditions like overcharging, over-discharging, and short circuits. The BMS includes cell balancing functions that maintain equal charge levels across all cells, improving battery health and extending overall lifespan. Additionally, it incorporates protection features against thermal runaway, overload, and reverse polarity to enhance safety. The BMS also controls the power flow between the charging circuit and the output ports, ensuring stable voltage delivery for connected devices. Its intelligent design supports advanced charging protocols like fast charging and optimizes energy usage to improve efficiency. Overall, the BMS plays a crucial role in maintaining battery safety, maximizing performance, and increasing the durability of the energy storage device. CHARGING CONTROL CIRCUIT 5 The charging control circuit is an important component in the power bank that manages the safe and efficient transfer of energy from the input source to the lithium-ion cell pack. Its main function is to regulate the incoming voltage and current to match the charging requirements of the battery and prevent overcharging while ensuring optimal energy storage. The circuit contains a power regulation 10 module that converts varying input power such as from USB or wall adapters into a stable and controlled output suitable for charging the cells. Advanced versions of this circuit include support for fast charging protocols like Quick Charge and USB Power Delivery and adjust the charging current based on the connected source and device requirements. The charging control circuit also monitors temperature is and current flow in real time to prevent overheating or excessive load during the charging process. Safety features like over voltage over current and short circuit protection are built into the circuit to ensure long term battery health and operational safety. It also works with the Battery Management System to balance charging across multiple cells which improves battery performance and lifespan. 20 By efficiently managing energy conversion and protecting the system from electrical faults the charging control circuit plays a crucial role in maintaining the reliability and durability of the compact energy storage device. DC-DC CONVERTER 25 The DC-DC converter is an essential component of the power bank that converts the direct current voltage from the lithium-ion battery pack to the required output voltage suitable for charging external devices. Since the lithium-ion cells provide a variable voltage depending on the charge level the converter ensures a constant and stable output voltage for connected devices. This conversion process is highly 30 efficient and helps in delivering the appropriate power for different electronic devices such as smartphones tablets and laptops. The converter operates using high frequency switching techniques and includes inductors and capacitors to regulate voltage with minimal energy loss. It can perform step up or step-down conversion depending on whether the device requires a higher or lower voltage than the battery output. Advanced converters also support multiple output levels and fast charging protocols to meet modern charging standards. Safety features are incorporated to protect against over voltage short circuit and thermal overload ensuring reliable performance. By maintaining consistent voltage and efficient energy transfer the DC-DC converter plays a crucial role in the overall functionality of the compact energy storage device. OUTPUT PORTS (USB / TYPE-C) The output ports of the power bank serve as the primary interface for delivering stored electrical energy from the battery to external devices. These ports are designed to provide stable and regulated power through standard connections such as USB Type A and USB Type C which are widely compatible with smartphones tablets laptops and other electronic devices. The output section works in coordination with the DC-to-DC converter to maintain a constant voltage level even when the battery charge decreases ensuring consistent performance throughout the discharge cycle. Modern output ports support multiple charging protocols including fast charging standards that allow higher current delivery for rapid charging of compatible devices. Some advanced designs include Power Delivery support through Type C ports which can handle higher power levels for charging larger devices such as laptops. The output ports are equipped with built in protection against over current short circuits and voltage fluctuations to safeguard both the power bank and the connected devices. Multiple output options allow simultaneous charging of more than one device making the power bank versatile and user friendly. The smart display module provides a user-friendly interface that enhances transparency and usability of the compact energy storage device. It continuously shows the real-time battery percentage, allowing users to monitor the remaining charge capacity with precision. The module also indicates the charging status, including whether the device is actively charging, discharging, or in standby mode, and displays the progress of fast-charging protocols such as USB Power Delivery or Quick Charge. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention compact energy storage device with enhanced lithium-ion cell design to provide efficient and reliable charging for modem electronic devices. The device is implemented using high-energy-density lithium-ion cells arranged in an optimized series-parallel configuration to achieve maximum capacity within a small size. The design ensures portability without compromising on power output. The system begins with an input power source such as a USB adapter or solar panel connected to a charging control circuit. This circuit regulates the incoming voltage and current to ensure safe and controlled charging of the battery cells. It also supports advanced fast-charging protocols like USB Power Delivery and Quick Charge to reduce charging time. Once the energy is stored, the DC-DC converter (4) converts the variable battery voltage into a stable output voltage suitable for different devices. Multiple output ports including USB Type-A and Type-C(5) are provided to allow simultaneous charging of multiple gadgets. The converter ensures high efficiency in power transfer and supports different voltage levels as required by the connected device. To improve usability, the power bank includes a smart display module (6) that shows real-time battery percentage, charging status, and alerts for any faults. Additionally, a multi-layer protection circuitry adds an extra level of safety against thermal overload and sudden voltage fluctuations. The compact and lightweight design makes this power bank easy to carry while its modular approach allows customization for different capacities and applications. By combining optimized lithium-ion cell configuration, intelligent power management, fast charging support, and advanced safety features, this invention provides a cost-effective and efficient solution for portable energy storage. The invention works by storing electrical energy in an optimized lithium-ion cell pack (1) and delivering it efficiently to charge multiple electronic devices. The process begins when an external power source such as a USB charger or solar panel is connected to the power bank. The charging control circuit regulates the incoming voltage and current to ensure safe charging of the battery cells. The Battery Management System(2) monitors each cell’s voltage, current, and temperature to prevent overcharging, deep discharge, or short circuits and also ensures cell balancing for longer battery life. Once charged, the stored energy is converted into a stable output voltage using a DC-DC converter (4), which maintains efficiency and supports various fast-charging standards. The device includes multiple output ports such as USB Type-A and USB Type-C (5) for charging different gadgets simultaneously. A smart display module (6) shows real-time battery percentage, charging status, and safety alerts. Protection 4 circuitry adds additional safety by preventing thermal overload, overcurrent, and voltage fluctuations. Overall, the system works seamlessly to provide safe, fast, and reliable charging in a compact and portable design. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT LITHIUM-CARBON DIOXIDE BATTERY USING ELECTROLYTE ADDITIVE AND CATHODE COMBINATION OPERABLE IN SIMULATED MARTIAN GASEOUS ATMOSPHERE A low overpotential, long cycle-life lithium-carbon dioxide battery system (100) operable in a simulated Martian gaseous atmosphere (Li-CO2Mars) (112) is disclosed. The battery system (100) includes an anode (102) made of lithium. The battery system (100) further includes a porous cathode (106) having nitrogen-doped carbon. The porous cathode (106) is made of nitrogen‑doped carbon and is obtained by pyrolysis of melamine foam. The porous cathode (106) is configured as a freestanding integrated catalyst electrode. Further, the battery system (100) includes a separator (104) between the anode (102) and the porous cathode (106). The battery system (100) further includes a non-aqueous electrolyte comprising a glyme-based solvent, at least one lithium salt, and an additive combination (110) of 2,5-di-tert-butyl-1,4-benzoquinone (DBBQ) and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO). patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a high-performance lithium-ion capacitor (LIC) employing sustainable, heteroatom-doped carbon nanofibers derived from biomass as electrochemically compatible dual electrodes. The invention discloses a scalable process for converting biomass into high-surface-area, nitrogen-and sulfur-doped porous carbon materials exhibiting interconnected micro-and mesoporous structures and enhanced electrical conductivity. The derived carbon materials are configured for use as both anode and cathode, thereby reducing kinetic mismatch, suppressing lithium plating, and improving device safety and stability. The cathode exhibits superior capacitive behavior compared to commercial activated carbon cathodes, while the anode delivers high specific capacity. An asymmetric LIC assembled with an optimized electrode mass ratio and a lithium salt based organic electrolyte operates within an extended voltage window of up to about 0-4 V, achieving an energy density of up to about 150 Wh kg⁻¹ and high-power density. The device maintains substantially full capacity over at least 100,000 charge-discharge cycles, providing a low-cost, sustainable solution for long-life, high-rate energy storage applications. (Figure-3 shall be the abstract figure)
patents.complete_specification: Description: FIELD OF INVENTION [0001] The present invention relates to carbon-based electrodes and dual-carbon lithium-ion capacitors, particularly to sustainable, heteroatom-doped porous carbon materials derived from biomass for high-performance energy storage applications. BACKGROUND [0002] The rising demand for advanced energy storage driven by renewable energy, portable electronics, and electric vehicles has exposed the limitations of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and supercapacitors (SCs). LIBs provide high energy density but poor cycle life, while SCs offer high power density but limited energy storage. Lithium-ion capacitors (LICs) bridge this gap by combining a battery-type anode and capacitive cathode, enabling improved energy and power performance. However, conventional LICs face challenges such as kinetic mismatch, polarization, and Li plating due to differing charge-storage mechanisms, which compromise their stability and long-term performance in practical applications. [0003] To address the limitations associated with conventional lithium-ion capacitors, increasing research efforts have been directed toward the development of advanced all-carbon lithium-ion capacitors (ACLICs), wherein carbon-based materials are employed as both the anode and the cathode. Carbon is an attractive electrode material due to its low cost, chemical stability, ease of processing, and high electrical conductivity. Furthermore, carbon materials offer exceptional tunability in terms of structure, morphology, and surface chemistry, which can be effectively tailored to enhance electrochemical performance. Unlike conventional battery-type anode materials, carbon can support multiple charge storage mechanisms, including lithium-ion intercalation within the bulk structure, adsorption at defect sites and pores, and surface-controlled pseudocapacitive reactions. Simultaneously, high-surface-area carbon with hierarchical porosity enables efficient charge storage at the cathode through electric double-layer formation. Further engineering of such carbon materials facilitates the realization of ACLIC systems with reduced kinetic mismatch, lower polarization, and intrinsic resistance to lithium plating, thereby significantly improving device stability, safety, and cycle life. [0004] The prior art document EP1942510A1 discloses a lithium-ion capacitor with a hard carbon negative electrode, activated carbon positive electrode, and a non protonic organic solvent electrolyte with a lithium salt. The key feature is that the negative electrode is pre-doped with lithium so that, when discharged to half the charging voltage, its potential is ≤0.15V vs Li/Li⁺. However, EP1942510A1 only functionally defines pre doping (negative potential ≤0.15V at half voltage) and does not specify fixed pre lithiation protocol or 1:2 anode: cathode mass ratio combined with the biomass derived N, S doped carbon system. It discloses a non-graphitizable (hard) carbon for the negative electrode, defined by H/C ratio, not necessarily does not teach from biomass. [0005] WO2021154332A1 discloses methods for preparing high-surface-area nitrogen-doped activated carbon from biomass sources such as agricultural residues and wood, primarily for use in supercapacitors. The carbon is produced via chemical activation and nitrogen incorporation, resulting in enhanced conductivity and charge storage. Unlike the present invention, this disclosure lacks teaching on fiber morphology control, sulfur co-doping, and direct application in LICs, which are critical for ultralong cycle life and high capacitance retention. [0006] Despite progress, LICs still suffer from kinetic mismatch between the slow anode intercalation and fast cathode surface processes, leading to polarization, Li plating, and capacity decay. Existing carbon-based electrodes are often expensive, have low surface area, or lack sufficient active sites. Biomass-derived carbons offer cost and porosity benefits but underperform without functionalization. Most studies focus on single electrodes or heterogeneous carbons, failing to optimize all-carbon LICs. The present invention overcomes these issues by employing biomass-derived, N, S co-doped carbon with high surface area and abundant heteroatom content for both anode and cathode, combined with pre-lithiation and 1:2 mass balancing, thereby reducing kinetic mismatch and enhancing stability, capacity, and cycle life. [0007] The present invention discloses an ACLIC utilising carbon derived from biomass with high surface area and abundant heteroatom content at both anode and cathode sides. The highlight of the present invention lies in the reduced kinetic mismatch between the anode and cathode, which effectively suppresses lithium plating and substantially enhances the cycle stability of the device. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION [0008] An object of the present invention is to provide a sustainable and low-cost method for producing high-performance carbon electrode materials from biomass for energy storage applications. [0009] Another object of the present invention is to develop heteroatom-doped porous carbon materials with high surface area, controlled micro-and mesoporosity, and abundant electrochemically active sites suitable for use as both anode and cathode in lithium-ion capacitors. [0010] Another object of the present invention is to overcome kinetic mismatch between anode and cathode materials in conventional lithium-ion capacitors by employing chemically and structurally similar carbon materials on both electrode sides. [0011] Another object of the present invention is to suppress lithium plating and reduce irreversible capacity loss through optimized electrode design and controlled anode prelithiation. [0012] Another object of the present invention is to provide a dual-carbon lithium-ion capacitor capable of delivering high energy density and high-power density within an extended operating voltage window. [0013] Yet another object of the present invention is to achieve ultra-long cycle stability with minimal capacity fade, enabling stable operation over extended charge discharge cycles for practical and safe energy storage applications. SUMMARY [0014] In an aspect of the present invention, a method is disclosed for preparing heteroatom-doped porous carbon materials derived from biomass, addressing the challenge of achieving simultaneously high surface area, controlled porosity, and abundant heteroatom content required for advanced lithium-ion capacitor (LIC) electrodes. The method comprises washing and drying the biomass, followed by precarbonization under an inert atmosphere and chemical activation using an alkaline activator in combination with nitrogen and sulfur-containing precursors in predetermined ratios to obtain functionally distinct carbon materials. [0015] In another aspect of the present invention, the invention addresses the challenge of limited cathode capacity and kinetic mismatch between anode and cathode materials in conventional LICs. The as-prepared carbon materials exhibit high specific capacity when optimized for cathode application, enabling improved charge balance and higher energy density in the full-cell device. [0016] In a further aspect of the present invention, an electrode fabrication process is provided, wherein the prepared carbon materials are formulated into slurries with conductive additives and polymeric binders, coated onto current collectors, and dried to form stable electrodes. A controlled prelithiation step is applied to the anode to mitigate initial irreversible capacity loss and to enable stable operation over an extended voltage window. [0017] In yet another aspect of the present invention, a dual-carbon lithium-ion capacitor is assembled using biomass-derived carbon materials at both anode and cathode sides with an optimized mass ratio. The reduced kinetic mismatch between the electrodes decreases lithium plating during cycling, thereby significantly enhancing cycle life while delivering high energy density and long-term electrochemical stability. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0018] The accompanying drawings are included to provide a further understanding of the present disclosure and are incorporated in and constitute a part of this specification. The drawings illustrate exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure and, together with the description, serve to explain the principles of the present disclosure. [0019] Figure 1 is the Flowchart illustrating the method for synthesizing heteroatom-doped carbon material from agro-industrial waste. [0020] Figure 2 is the Flowchart illustrating the method for Electrode Fabrication. [0021] Figure 3 is the Schematic diagram of LIC with CNS based cathode and anodes. [0022] Figure 4 is the Morphological Characterizations of As-synthesized Carbon. [0023] Figure 5 is the Structural, Surface, and Porosity Characterization. [0024] Figure 6 shows the Performance comparison of CNS-based anodes in voltage range of 0.01-3V: (a) GCD curves for first 2 consecutive cycles at a current density of 0.1 A/g and (b) Rate capability tests at different current densities; performance comparison of CNS-based samples and commercial activated carbon (AC) when employed as cathode materials within a voltage range of 2-4V; (c) GCD curves at a current density of 0.1 A/g; (d) Rate capability tests at different current densities. [0025] Figure 7 illustrates the electrochemical performance of a CNS-2//CNS-4 dual-carbon lithium-ion capacitor, including charge-discharge behavior, capacitive response, energy-power characteristics, and cycling stability. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [0026] Method for synthesizing heteroatom-doped carbon material from agro-industrial waste In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure-1 presents a method for synthesizing heteroatom-doped carbon material derived from agro-industrial waste, more particularly nitrogen-and sulfur-doped carbon obtained from biomass suitable for electrochemical, adsorption, catalytic, or energy-storage applications. According to an embodiment of the invention (101), raw biomass obtained from a textile or industrial source is initially subjected to a cleaning step to remove surface impurities, dust, and soluble contaminants. The biomass is thoroughly washed with deionized (DI) water (102) and subsequently dried at a temperature of about 80°C for a duration sufficient to remove residual moisture (103), preferably overnight. The dried biomass is then subjected to a precarbonization step to convert the organic material into a carbonaceous char (104). Precarbonization is carried out in an inert atmosphere, preferably argon, at a temperature of about 550°C for approximately 1 hour. The temperature is increased at a controlled ramp rate of about 5°C per minute to prevent structural collapse and to ensure uniform thermal decomposition. The resulting product is a porous char material. In a subsequent activation and doping step, the obtained char is intimately mixed with a chemical activating agent and heteroatom precursor compounds. In one preferred embodiment, potassium hydroxide (KOH) is used as the activating agent, while thiourea is employed as a nitrogen and sulfur dopant precursor. The char, KOH, and thiourea are mixed in predetermined weight ratios, such as 1:1:2, 1:1:4, and 1:1:6, to produce compositions referred to herein as CNS-2, CNS-4, and CNS-6, respectively (105). The resulting mixtures are dried at approximately 110°C, preferably overnight, to remove moisture and promote uniform impregnation. The dried mixtures are then subjected to a high-temperature pyrolysis step to induce carbon activation, pore formation, and heteroatom incorporation. Pyrolysis is carried out in an inert argon atmosphere at a temperature of about 800°C for approximately 1 hour, with a heating ramp rate of about 5°C per minute (106). During this step, chemical activation by KOH generates a hierarchical porous structure, while thermal decomposition of thiourea results in the incorporation of nitrogen and sulfur atoms into the carbon lattice. Following pyrolysis, the resulting nitrogen-and sulfur-doped biomass-derived carbon materials are subjected to a purification step to remove residual inorganic species and metallic impurities. The carbonized product is washed with an aqueous acid solution, preferably 3M hydrochloric acid (107), followed by repeated washing with deionized water (108) until a neutral pH is achieved. The purified material is then dried (109), preferably overnight, to obtain the final N,S-doped carbon product. The resulting carbon material exhibits enhanced surface area, porosity, and heteroatom functionalization, making it particularly suitable for use in electrochemical energy storage devices, catalysis, adsorption processes, and environmental remediation applications. In an embodiment of the present invention, the biomass material used for the preparation of nanofibers or carbonaceous materials may include cotton or one or more alternative biomass sources. Suitable biomass sources include, but are not limited to, natural plant fibers such as jute, hemp, flax, ramie, kenaf, bamboo, sisal, and coir; agricultural and food residues such as corn stover, banana pseudostem, orange peel, pomegranate peel, and coconut shell; as well as polymeric biopolymers including bacterial cellulose, lignin, cellulose acetate, chitosan, alginate, silk fibroin, gelatin, and starch. The selected biomass may be used individually or in combination, and may undergo suitable pre-treatment, carbonization, chemical activation, or electrospinning processes to yield nanofibrous or porous carbon structures suitable for electrode, adsorption, or catalytic applications. This flexibility in biomass selection ensures broad applicability and allows the tailoring of the material properties for specific performance requirements. [0027] Method for Electrode Fabrication In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure 2, a method for fabricating carbon nanostructure (CNS)-based electrodes suitable for electrochemical testing is disclosed. The method comprises preparing a homogeneous slurry (201) by combining an electrochemically active CNS material, a conductive carbon additive, and a polymeric binder in a predetermined weight ratio. In one embodiment, the active material, Super P conductive carbon, and poly-vinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder are mixed in a weight ratio of 8:1:1, respectively. The mixture is dispersed in an organic solvent, preferably 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), under continuous stirring to obtain a uniform and stable slurry. The obtained slurry is subsequently applied onto a metallic current collector selected from copper foil for anode fabrication and aluminium foil for cathode fabrication (202). Coating is carried out using a slurry casting or doctor-blade coating technique to ensure uniform thickness and surface coverage. Following coating, the electrodes are subjected to a drying step at a temperature of about 80°C for an extended duration, preferably overnight, to remove residual solvent and to promote adhesion between the active layer and the current collector (203). After drying, the electrodes are cooled to ambient temperature and optionally cut into desired dimensions (204). The active material loading density of each electrode is determined by measuring the mass difference of the current collector before and after slurry coating and drying. The resulting electrodes are thereby rendered suitable for subsequent electrochemical characterization and performance evaluation. WORKING EXAMPLES [0028] Synthesis of Carbon Nanofibers from Cotton Waste i) Materials Requirement: • Cotton waste (CW) from textile industry • Deionized (DI) water • Nitrogen and sulfur precursors (e.g., urea, thiourea) for heteroatom doping • Argon gas for inert atmosphere • Lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) electrolyte (for LIC testing) ii) Procedure: Preparation of Cotton Waste: The cotton waste was thoroughly washed with DI water to remove impurities and dried at 80°C overnight. Pre-carbonization: The dried cotton was placed in a tubular furnace and heated to 550°C at a ramp rate of 5°C/min under argon flow for 1 h to obtain a carbonized char. Activation and Doping: The carbonized char was mixed with urea and thiourea in a 1:1:1 weight ratio and transferred to a furnace. The mixture was heated to 800°C at 5°C/min under argon for 2 h to produce nitrogen-and sulfur-doped porous carbon nanofibers. Cooling and Collection: The furnace was allowed to cool to room temperature under argon, and the carbon nanofibers (CNFs) were collected as a black powder. Characterization: The CNFs exhibited a high surface area (~800 m²/g), interconnected micro-and mesoporous structure, and uniform N and S doping, as confirmed by BET, SEM, TEM, and XPS analyses. [0029] Assembly and Electrochemical Evaluation of CNS-Based Lithium-Ion Capacitor CR2032-type coin cells were assembled to evaluate the electrochemical performance of the CNS-based electrodes prepared according to the method described herein. In this example, the CNS-based anode and cathode were employed as working electrodes. A microporous polypropylene separator (Celgard® 2400) was positioned between the electrodes. Lithium metal foil was used as both counter electrode and reference electrode. The electrolyte comprised a 1.0 mol/L solution of lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) dissolved in a mixed carbonate solvent system containing ethylene carbonate (EC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and dimethyl carbonate (DMC) in a volume ratio of 1:1:1. All cell assembly steps were carried out in an argon-filled glove box, wherein the oxygen and moisture contents were each maintained below 0.2ppm to prevent electrolyte degradation and electrode contamination. Electrochemical characterization of the assembled coin cells was performed using galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), cyclic voltammetry (CV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques. GCD measurements were conducted on a Neware battery testing system over a potential window of 0.01 V to 3.0 V versus Li/Li⁺. CV and EIS analyses were carried out using an electrochemical workstation (CHI760E) under standard testing conditions. Prior to full-cell assembly, the anode electrode was subjected to a pre-lithiation process by cycling for five charge-discharge cycles at a current density of 0.1 A g⁻¹ within a potential range of 0.01 V to 3.0 V versus Li/Li⁺. The pre-lithiation process was terminated at a lithiated end potential of approximately 0.3V versus Li/Li⁺. Subsequently, the pre-lithiated anode and the cathode were combined at an optimized anode-to-cathode mass ratio of 1:2 to assemble a full-cell lithium-ion capacitor (LIC) device, which was then subjected to further electrochemical performance evaluation. This working example demonstrates the practical implementation of the disclosed electrode materials and methods in a full-cell configuration suitable for energy storage applications. [0030] Schematic diagram of LIC with CNS based cathode and anodes In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure 3 presents Schematic diagram of LIC with CNS based cathode and anodes. The schematic diagram illustrates a lithium-ion capacitor comprising CNS-based carbon electrodes, wherein nitrogen-and sulfur-doped porous carbon materials are employed as both cathode and prelithiated anode, separated by a separator and an electrolyte containing LiPF6, enabling reversible PF₆⁻ anion adsorption at the cathode and Li⁺ ion intercalation or adsorption at the anode during charge-discharge operation. CHARACTERIZATION [0031] Morphological Characterizations In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure 4 presents morphological features of the as-synthesized carbon samples. The sample exhibits a well-defined long fibrous morphology with a highly rough and wrinkled surface, as observed from FESEM and TEM analyses. Such a fibrous and interconnected architecture is advantageous for LIC applications, as it facilitates continuous electron transport pathways and enhances electrode integrity during repeated charge-discharge cycles. High-resolution TEM images further reveal the presence of abundant micro and mesopores distributed throughout the fibrous carbon matrix, providing a large accessible surface area and shortened ion-diffusion pathways. Additionally, the largely amorphous carbon structure, confirmed by SAED patterns, contributes to improved lithium-ion accommodation and fast charge storage kinetics. The uniform distribution of heteroatoms (N and S) within the porous fibrous framework further enhances electrochemical activity, making it particularly suitable for high-performance LIC electrodes. [0032] Structural, Surface, and Porosity Characterization In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure 5, the prepared carbon sample exhibits structural and surface characteristics optimized for lithium-ion capacitor applications. Comparative X-ray diffraction (5a) and Raman analyses (5b) confirm a predominantly amorphous, defect-rich graphene framework with an I_D/I_G ratio of about 1.1, arising from controlled chemical activation and heteroatom precursor concentration. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy ((5c-e) verifies the incorporation of nitrogen and sulfur within the carbon matrix in graphitic, pyridinic, pyrrolic, and sulfur-bonded configurations. Nitrogen adsorption-desorption studies (5f) show type-IV isotherms with combined micro-and mesoporosity and high specific surface area, collectively providing abundant electrochemically active sites and facilitating efficient, reversible lithium-ion storage. [0033] Electrochemical performance evaluation of CNS-based samples in LIC Device In an embodiment of the present disclosure, Figure 6 demonstrates the results for anode and cathode half cell tests for the CNS-based samples. The optimized CNS-4 based anode shows highest specific capacity of 1328.2 and 635.1 mAh g-1 during 1st and 2nd discharge cycles, respectively, at 0.1 A g-1, a good capacity retention at higher current densities, and an excellent reversibility regaining around 90% of the initial capacity when coming back to 0.1 A g-1. Besides, the CNS-2 based cathode presents a much better specific capacity (~71 mAh g-1 at 0.1 A g-1) and rate reversibility in comparison to not only other CNS samples but also commercial activated carbon (AC) based cathode. Further, Figure 7 illustrates the electrochemical performance evaluation of a full-cell dual-carbon lithium-ion capacitor (LIC) device constructed using CNS-4 as the anode and CNS-2 as the cathode. The carbon materials are derived from washed and dried biomass, precarbonized at 550°C under argon, followed by chemical activation with KOH and thiourea at ratios of 1:1:2 (CNS-2) and 1:1:4 (CNS-4). Prior to full-cell assembly, the CNS-4 anode is prelithiated to minimize irreversible capacity loss. Charge balance is optimized by controlling the anode-to-cathode mass ratio between 1:1 and 1:3, with an optimal ratio of 1:2 identified. Cyclic voltammetry exhibits quasi-rectangular profiles over scan rates of 5-100 mV s⁻¹, indicating dominant capacitive behavior with good reversibility. Galvanostatic charge-discharge studies demonstrate high rate capability and stable symmetric profiles. The optimized LIC achieves a maximum energy density of 152 Wh kg⁻¹ and power density of 4041 W kg⁻¹, outperforming activated-carbon-based devices. Notably, the LIC maintains 100% capacity retention over 100,000 cycles within a 0-4V window, demonstrating exceptional cycling stability and practical applicability.
