patents.abstract: A system (102) for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass is provided. The system (102) includes a feeder (104) configured to supply untreated black mass to a rotary kiln reactor (106). The rotary kiln reactor (106) includes an inlet for receiving black mass, an outlet for discharging treated material, a rotating shell, and heating elements configured to maintain a predetermined temperature. An acid dosing unit (108) injects sulfuric acid vapor into the rotary kiln reactor (106). A nitrogen purge unit (118) supplies nitrogen gas to maintain an inert atmosphere and transport gaseous products. An off-gas treatment unit (110) is connected to the rotary kiln reactor (106) and includes a cyclone separator (112), a condenser (114), and a scrubber tower (116) for sequential removal of particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and hydrogen fluoride. A control unit (120) monitors and regulates temperature, pressure, and flow conditions throughout the system (102). FIG. 1
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD The present disclosure relates to a field of battery recycling. Moreover, the present disclosure relates to a system and a method for pre-treating a lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities. BACKGROUND In recent years, the growing adoption of lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and energy storage systems has led to an increased focus on recycling and recovery of valuable materials from spent batteries. The valuable materials include lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. The recycling domain broadly employs hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical techniques to extract these metals from processed battery waste known as black mass. The black mass comprises cathode and anode material residues, binders, electrolytes, and various organic solvents, that must undergo several pre-treatment steps before metal recovery to achieve product purity levels exceeding 99%, maintain workplace hydrogen fluoride concentrations below 3 parts per million, and reduce processing time by 15 to 25 percent. However, existing pre-treatment techniques remain limited in eliminating organic and inorganic contaminants to concentrations below 500 parts per million, thus impacting downstream performance. Conventional battery recycling methods often involve direct feeding of untreated black mass into the leaching or extraction stages. The presence of ethylene carbonate (EC), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and fluoride compounds in untreated black mass leads to operational challenges that increase capital expenditures by 15 to 25 percent and operational expenditures by 15 to 25 percent. The operational challenges include excessive off-gassing at rates exceeding 10 normal cubic meters per ton of processed black mass, corrosion of processing equipment that reduces equipment service life by 30 to 50 percent, and environmental hazards due to volatile organic compound emissions exceeding 1,000 parts per million in off-gas streams. Furthermore, the contamination carried into downstream hydrometallurgical circuits results in reduced metal recovery efficiency, increased reagent consumption, and higher operational expenditures. Existing filtration or solvent-based pre-treatments only partially remove volatile and fluorinated compounds and often require capital investments exceeding USD 2 million per ton of daily processing capacity, making industrial implementation cost-prohibitive. Therefore, in light of the foregoing discussion, there exists a need to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks associated with the conventional method for extracting the rare earth metals from the black mass of the spent lithium-ion batteries. SUMMARY The present disclosure provides a system and a method for pre-treating a lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities. The present disclosure provides a solution to a technical problem of removal of volatile organic compounds, organic carbon compounds, and fluoride-containing compounds present in untreated lithium-ion battery black mass. An aim of the present disclosure is to provide a solution that overcomes at least partially the problems encountered in the prior art and provide an improved system and a method for pre-treating a lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities. The present disclosure aims to provide a controlled pre-treatment approach that stabilizes the black mass by reducing organic content to concentrations below 500 parts per million and fluoride content to concentrations below 400 parts per million for downstream extraction of lithium and transition metals. One or more objectives of the present disclosure are achieved by the solutions provided in the enclosed independent claims. Advantageous implementations of the present disclosure are further defined in the dependent claims. In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a method for pre-treating a lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities. The method includes feeding untreated black mass containing volatile organic compounds, total organic carbon, and fluorides into a rotary kiln reactor. The method includes heating the black mass in the rotary kiln reactor to a predetermined temperature while rotating the rotary kiln reactor. The method includes injecting sulfuric acid vapor into the rotary kiln reactor to react with fluoride-containing compounds in the black mass. The method includes purging the rotary kiln reactor with nitrogen gas to facilitate removal of volatile decomposition products. The method includes separating off-gases from the rotary kiln reactor through a cyclone separator. The method includes condensing volatile organic compounds from the off-gases. The method includes scrubbing remaining gaseous contaminants including hydrogen fluoride using an alkaline solution in a scrubber tower. The method presents a systematic process for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction by using controlled thermal processing, sulfuric acid vapor injection, nitrogen purging, and off-gas treatment. The predetermined temperature and rotational movement promote uniform removal of organic compounds across all black mass particles. The sulfuric acid vapor converts fluoride-containing compounds into forms that remain stable during further processing. The nitrogen purge maintains an inert atmosphere inside the rotary kiln reactor and transports gaseous products toward the off-gas treatment unit. The sequence of cyclone separation, condensation, and alkaline scrubbing removes particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and hydrogen fluoride from the off-gases. The combined operation of thermal processing, chemical conversion, gas transport, and off-gas cleaning produces treated black mass with reduced organic content and reduced fluoride content suitable for leaching operations, while maintaining stable process conditions and supporting consistent downstream extraction performance. In another aspect, the present disclosure provides a system for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities, comprising a rotary kiln reactor having an inlet for receiving untreated black mass, an outlet for discharging treated black mass, and a rotating shell configured to operate at a predetermined temperature. The system comprising an acid dosing unit operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor and configured to inject sulfuric acid vapor into the rotary kiln reactor. The system comprising a nitrogen purge unit configured to supply nitrogen gas to the rotary kiln reactor. The system comprising an off-gas treatment unit comprising a cyclone separator operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor for separating particulate matter from off-gases, a condenser operatively connected to the cyclone separator for condensing volatile organic compounds, and a scrubber tower operatively connected to the condenser and configured to capture hydrogen fluoride and remaining volatile organic compounds using an alkaline solution. The system achieves all the advantages and technical effects of the method for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction formed in the present disclosure. It is to be appreciated that all the aforementioned implementation forms can be combined. All steps which are performed by the various entities described in the present application as well as the functionalities described to be performed by the various entities are intended to mean that the respective entity is adapted to or configured to perform the respective steps and functionalities. FIG. 1 is a diagram illustrating a block diagram of a system for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. The system 102 includes a feeder 104 connected to a rotary kiln reactor 106. The rotary kiln reactor 106 is connected to an acid dosing unit 108 and an off-gas treatment unit 110. Further, the off-gas treatment unit 110 includes a cyclone separator 112 connected to a condenser 114, and the condenser 114 is connected to a scrubber tower 116. The system 102 further includes a nitrogen purge unit 118 connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106. The system 102 includes a control unit 120 communicatively coupled to the feeder 104, the rotary kiln reactor 106, the acid dosing unit 108, the off-gas treatment unit 110, and the nitrogen purge unit 118 to regulate process parameters. The lithium-ion battery black mass may be referred to as a powdered material obtained from mechanical shredding and separation of lithium-ion batteries that have reached the end of usable life. The black mass contains metals including lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper along with graphite. Furthermore, the black mass contains various impurities originating from battery components. The various impurities include organic binders, electrolyte residues, volatile organic compounds (VOC), fluoride-containing compounds, and residual carbonate solvents. The VOC originate from residual electrolyte solvents, in particular ethylene carbonate (EC) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC), which remain absorbed in the black mass. Additionally, polyvinylidene fluoride binders exist within the black mass. Total organic carbon (TOC) content in the black mass ranges from 12,000 parts per million to 15,000 parts per million. Moreover, fluoride content in the material ranges from 4,000 parts per million to 5,000 parts per million. Direct feeding of the black mass into hydrometallurgical extraction process introduces the VOC and fluorides into extraction reactors. Consequently, the VOC cause off-gassing during hydrometallurgical extraction process. Furthermore, the fluorides decompose to release hydrogen fluoride gas during extraction process. The hydrogen fluoride gas causes corrosion of extraction equipment. Additionally, the organic compounds require extensive purification of extracted metal solutions in downstream stages. Therefore, pre-treatment of the black mass removes the organic compounds and fluorides before extraction process. Low-temperature thermal processing combined with chemical treatment decomposes the VOC. Moreover, the chemical treatment converts the fluorides into removable forms. The pre-treatment reduces the number of purification steps required to remove organic compounds and fluoride-containing compounds from the black mass. Furthermore, the pre-treatment increases the purity of lithium-bearing and transition-metal-bearing solutions generated during hydrometallurgical extraction and reduces the energy consumed by dissolution, neutralization, and filtration units within the hydrometallurgical extraction process. The feeder 104 may be referred to as a sealed input delivery unit configured to transfer untreated black mass into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The feeder 104 transfers the untreated black mass into the rotary kiln reactor 106 at controlled feed rates. The feeder 104 regulates the flow of the black mass to maintain consistent processing rates within the rotary kiln reactor 106. The rotary kiln reactor 106 may be referred to as a thermal processing vessel configured to remove volatile organic compounds and fluoride-containing compounds from the untreated black mass. The rotary kiln reactor 106 includes an inlet for receiving the untreated black mass from the feeder 104 and an outlet for discharging treated black mass. Further, the rotary kiln reactor 106 includes a rotating shell configured to operate at a predetermined temperature. In an implementation, the rotating shell measures 3 meters in length and 0.5 meters in internal diameter. The rotating shell includes stainless steel 316 construction with silicon carbide lining to withstand corrosive environments and elevated temperatures. The dimensional configuration supports continuous processing of untreated black mass at feed rates ranging from 50 kilograms per hour to 4,000 kilograms per hour . The rotating shell receives indirect heat from external heaters positioned around an outer surface of the rotating shell to maintain the predetermined temperature inside the rotary kiln reactor 106. The rotating shell rotates at a controlled rotational speed to mix the untreated black mass and expose particle surfaces uniformly to the applied temperature. The rotational speed and feed rate together determine a residence time of the untreated black mass inside the rotating shell. In an implementation, the rotary kiln reactor 106 operates at the predetermined temperature ranging from 200 degrees Celsius to 300 degrees Celsius. The temperature sensors positioned along the rotating shell measure temperature continuously and transmit readings to the control unit 120. The control unit 120 adjusts heating power supplied to external heaters to maintain temperatures within the predetermined temperature range. The temperatures around 200 degrees Celsius initiate decomposition of ethylene carbonate, and the temperatures between 250 degrees Celsius and 300 degrees Celsius decompose dimethyl carbonate and release hydrogen fluoride from polyvinylidene fluoride. The temperatures below 200 degrees Celsius do not provide enough thermal energy for decomposition of VOC. Further, the temperatures above 300 degrees Celsius cause oxidation and sintering of black mass. The predetermined temperature decomposes organic compounds while preserving metal components in oxide and metallic forms that dissolve in sulfuric acid solutions during hydrometallurgical extraction. In an implementation, the rotary kiln reactor 106 includes a lining formed of stainless steel and silicon carbide material. The rotating shell includes an outer structural layer and an inner lining layer configured to withstand the thermal and chemical conditions present during black mass processing. The inner lining layer includes stainless steel 316 to provide structural support and resistance to acidic environments. A silicon carbide layer is applied over the stainless steel 316 to form a chemically resistant surface exposed to the black mass and off-gases. The silicon carbide layer is applied through coating or bonding techniques suitable for high-temperature operation. The combined stainless steel and silicon carbide lining protects the rotating shell from corrosive species generated during processing and maintains reactor integrity during prolonged operation. In an implementation, the rotary kiln reactor 106 provides rotational speed ranging from 0.5 revolutions per minute to 2 revolutions per minute. In such implementations, a motor connects to the rotating shell through a gear reduction system or a direct-drive mechanism configured to deliver controlled rotational movement. The motor receives speed control signals from the control unit 120 to set rotational speed within the specified range. Rotational speeds near 0.5 revolutions per minute produce slower tumbling motion of the black mass, and rotational speeds near 2 revolutions per minute produce faster mixing within the rotating shell. Rotational speeds below 0.5 revolutions per minute do not generate adequate mixing, and rotational speeds above 2 revolutions per minute produce centrifugal forces that prevent tumbling. The rotational speed range maintains continuous movement of black mass particles and supports uniform exposure to thermal and chemical conditions during processing. The acid dosing unit 108 may be referred to as a chemical injection unit configured to inject acid vapours into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The acid dosing unit 108 is operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106. The acid dosing unit 108 includes a liquid sulfuric acid storage tank, a transfer pump, and a vaporization chamber configured to convert liquid sulfuric acid into vapor phase. In an implementation, the vaporization chamber employs electric heating elements or steam coils to heat the liquid sulfuric acid to temperatures sufficient for vapor generation. In an implementation, the acid dosing unit 108 is connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106 through injection ports positioned along the rotating shell. The sulfuric acid vapor contacts fluoride-containing compounds present in the untreated black mass, including lithium fluoride, and converts the fluoride-containing compounds into sulphate compounds and hydrogen fluoride gas. The hydrogen fluoride gas enters the off-gas stream directed toward the off-gas treatment unit 110, and the sulphate compounds remain within the treated black mass as lithium sulphate that dissolves in water and dilute acid solutions during subsequent extraction process. In an implementation, the acid dosing unit 108 maintains sulfuric acid vapor injection rates within predetermined minimum and maximum limits to achieve conversion of fluoride-containing compounds while preventing excessive acid consumption. The vapor phase injection promotes uniform penetration into porous black mass particles and supports conversion efficiencies achieving fluoride reduction from approximately 4,000 parts per million to less than 400 parts per million. Update-In an implementation, the acid dosing unit (108) maintains sulfuric acid vapor injection rates within predetermined minimum and maximum limits, typically ranging from 6 kg to 18 kg of H₂SO₄ per metric ton of black mass, with a nominal operating range of 8–12 kg per ton, to achieve effective conversion of fluoride-containing compounds while preventing excessive acid consumption. The vapor-phase injection promotes uniform penetration into porous black mass particles and supports fluoride conversion efficiencies exceeding 90 percent, resulting in reduction of fluoride content from approximately 4,000–5,000 ppm to less than 400 ppm. The off-gas treatment unit 110 may be referred to as a treatment unit configured to clean off-gases generated within the rotary kiln reactor 106. The off-gas treatment unit 110 is operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106. In an implementation, the off-gas treatment unit 110 is operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106 through a high-temperature exhaust duct configured to direct off-gases containing particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and hydrogen fluoride into the cyclone separator 112. The off-gas treatment unit 110 processes the off-gases through sequential stages including particle separation removing 95 percent of particulates larger than 10 micrometres, condensation removing 90 percent of volatile organic compounds, and chemical scrubbing removing 99 percent of hydrogen fluoride before atmospheric discharge. The cyclone separator 112 may be referred to as a centrifugal separation device configured to remove entrained particulate matter from the off-gases. The cyclone separator 112 connects to the rotary kiln reactor 106 through the exhaust duct and receives the off-gases tangentially to generate centrifugal force inside the separation chamber. The centrifugal force drives entrained particulate matter toward the cyclone walls, and the particles descend into a discharge hopper. The cyclone separator 112 transfers particle-reduced off-gases to the condenser 114 through connecting piping. The condenser 114 may be referred to as a heat exchange unit configured to convert volatile organic compounds in the off-gases from gaseous phase to liquid phase. The condenser 114 receives particle-reduced off-gases from the cyclone separator 112 and reduces the temperature of the off-gases below dew points of volatile organic compounds by passing the gas stream over cooled heat-exchange surfaces. The condenser 114 employs cooling water or refrigerant as a cooling medium to achieve the required temperature reduction and collects condensed organic liquids in a receiver vessel. Non-condensable off-gases exit the condenser 114 and flow to the scrubber tower 116. The scrubber tower 116 may be referred to as a chemical absorption column configured to capture hydrogen fluoride and remaining volatile organic compounds from the off-gases. The scrubber tower 116 receives non-condensable off-gases from the condenser 114 and circulates an alkaline solution through internal packing material to promote gas-liquid contact. The alkaline solution neutralizes hydrogen fluoride through acid–base reactions and absorbs remaining volatile organic compounds before discharging treated off-gases to atmosphere. The nitrogen purge unit 118 may be referred to as an inert gas supply unit configured to supply nitrogen gas to the rotary kiln reactor 106. The nitrogen purge unit 118 is operatively connected to the rotary kiln reactor 106 through inlet ports positioned to distribute nitrogen gas uniformly within the rotating shell. The nitrogen purge unit 118 includes a nitrogen gas source, pressure regulators, and flow control valves for delivering nitrogen gas at controlled operating pressure and flow rate. The nitrogen gas source includes compressed nitrogen cylinders, liquid nitrogen storage systems with vaporizers, or nitrogen generators based on air separation. The pressure regulators reduce nitrogen pressure to an operating level suitable for introduction into the rotary kiln reactor 106, and the flow control valves regulate nitrogen flow based on signals from the control unit 120. The nitrogen purge unit 118 introduces nitrogen gas into the rotary kiln reactor 106 to maintain controlled atmospheric conditions and displace oxygen within the processing environment. The nitrogen gas flow facilitates removal of volatile decomposition products including carbon dioxide, water vapor, and hydrogen fluoride and carries off-gases toward the off-gas treatment unit 110. In an implementation, the nitrogen purge unit 118 maintains nitrogen flow rates around 2 normal cubic meters per hour, monitored by flow meters that transmit measured values to the control unit 120. The nitrogen flow maintains positive pressure within the rotary kiln reactor 106 to prevent air ingress during processing. In an implementation, the nitrogen purge unit (118) maintains nitrogen flow rates within predetermined limits, typically ranging from 2 to 10 normal cubic meters per hour, depending on black mass feed rate and kiln operating conditions. The nitrogen flow is monitored by flow meters that transmit measured values to the control unit (120). The controlled nitrogen purge maintains a slight positive pressure within the rotary kiln reactor (106), thereby preventing air ingress, limiting oxygen concentration, and facilitating continuous removal of volatile decomposition products during processing. The control unit 120 may be referred to as an automation unit configured to monitor and regulate operating parameters throughout the system 102. The control unit 120 is operatively connected to the feeder 104, the rotary kiln reactor 106, the acid dosing unit 108, the off-gas treatment unit 110, and the nitrogen purge unit 118. The control unit 120 receives sensor inputs including temperature measurements, pressure measurements, and flow measurements, and adjusts process conditions to maintain predetermined setpoints for stable and consistent working of the system 102. In an implementation, the control unit 120 includes a plurality of sensors including temperature sensors, pressure sensors, and flow sensors configured to maintain the predetermined temperature within the rotary kiln reactor 106. The temperature sensors mount at multiple positions along the rotating shell and measure temperatures continuously. The pressure sensors connect to the rotary kiln reactor 106 to measure internal pressure during working of the system 102. The flow sensors measure nitrogen gas flow from the nitrogen purge unit 118, sulfuric acid vapor flow from the acid dosing unit 108, and black mass feed rate from the feeder 104. The plurality of sensors transmit measurement signals to the control unit 120 through communication connections suitable for industrial monitoring systems. The control unit 120 processes the measurement signals and adjusts heating power supplied to external heaters to maintain the predetermined temperature within the rotary kiln reactor 106. In an implementation, the control unit 120 automatically shuts off heating when temperature exceeds 320 degrees Celsius. The temperature sensors mounted on the rotating shell of the rotary kiln reactor 106 transmit temperature measurements continuously to the control unit 120. The control unit 120 compares each temperature measurement against a safety threshold of 320 degrees Celsius. When any temperature measurement exceeds 320 degrees Celsius, the control unit 120 sends shutdown signals to heating elements supplying heat to the rotary kiln reactor 106, de-energizing external heaters or closing fuel supply valves for gas-fired burners. The shutdown of the external heaters prevents further heating until temperature decreases below a defined safe limit and restart conditions are satisfied. The safety threshold of 320 degrees Celsius limits exposure of the rotary kiln reactor 106 and the black mass to temperatures that cause oxidation of metal components and degradation of the lining formed of stainless steel and silicon carbide material. In an implementation, the rotary kiln reactor 106 reduces total organic carbon content in the black mass from 12,000 parts per million to 500 parts per million. The untreated black mass entering the rotary kiln reactor 106 contains TOC originating from EC, DMC, and polyvinylidene fluoride binders. The rotary kiln reactor 106 operates at the predetermined temperature and rotational conditions that decompose the organic compounds into carbon dioxide and water vapor. The nitrogen purge unit 118 supplies nitrogen gas that transports the gaseous decomposition products from the rotary kiln reactor 106 toward the off-gas treatment unit 110. The treated black mass discharging through the outlet contains TOC reduced to levels below 500 parts per million. Further, analytical instruments measure TOC content in the treated black mass samples to verify removal performance. In an implementation, the rotary kiln reactor 106 reduces fluoride content in the black mass from between 4,000 parts per million and 5,000 parts per million to less than 400 parts per million. Untreated black mass entering the rotary kiln reactor 106 contains fluoride compounds including lithium fluoride and residual polyvinylidene fluoride. The acid dosing unit 108 injects sulfuric acid vapor into the rotary kiln reactor 106, and the sulfuric acid vapor contacts the black mass particles to convert lithium fluoride into lithium sulphate and hydrogen fluoride gas. Polyvinylidene fluoride decomposes under the operating temperature conditions of the rotary kiln reactor 106 and releases additional hydrogen fluoride gas. The nitrogen purge unit 118 supplies nitrogen gas that transports the hydrogen fluoride gas from the rotary kiln reactor 106 toward the off-gas treatment unit 110. The treated black mass discharging from the outlet contains fluoride content reduced to concentrations below 400 parts per million. Analytical instruments measure fluoride content in treated black mass samples to verify removal performance. The system 102 achieves operational and economic advantages compared to direct feeding of untreated black mass into hydrometallurgical extraction facilities. Direct feeding of untreated black mass introduces volatile organic compounds and fluorides that increase capital expenditures by 15 to 25 percent and operational expenditures by 15 to 25 percent due to requirements for additional purification equipment, increased reagent consumption, and extended processing times. The pre-treatment system 102 reduces operational expenditures by 22 percent through elimination of organic extraction stages, reduction of acid consumption in leaching reactors by 30 to 40 percent, and decrease in filtration requirements by 40 percent. The system 102 reduces energy consumption by 19 percent compared to combined energy requirements of untreated black mass processing and downstream purification operations. The pre-treatment approach increases lithium carbonate purity in final products from 99.5 percent to 99.9 percent, representing a purity improvement of 0.4 percentage points. The capital expenditure increase of 12 percent for pre-treatment equipment installation is offset by operational expenditure savings within 6 months of continuous operation at processing rates exceeding 500 kilograms per hour. FIG. 2 is a flowchart illustrating a method for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 2 is described in conjunction with the elements of the FIG. 1. With reference to FIG. 2, there is shown a method 200 that includes steps 202 to 214. At step 202, the method 200 includes feeding the untreated black mass containing the VOC, TOC, and fluorides into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The feeder 104 transfers the untreated black mass through the inlet into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The untreated black mass contains ethylene carbonate ranging from 2.5 percent to 3.2 percent by weight, dimethyl carbonate, polyvinylidene fluoride binders, and fluoride compounds including lithium fluoride. Further, the feeder 104 regulates the feed rate to maintain consistent material flow into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The rotating shell receives the untreated black mass and initiates a tumbling motion that distributes particles across 60 to 80 percent of the internal cross-sectional area within the thermal processing environment. At step 204, the method 200 includes heating the black mass in the rotary kiln reactor 106 to the predetermined temperature while rotating the rotary kiln reactor 106. The external heaters positioned around the outer surface of the rotating shell supply thermal energy to raise the temperature of the black mass to levels within the predetermined temperature range. The rotating shell rotates at speeds between 0.5 revolutions per minute and 2 revolutions per minute to mix the black mass continuously. The rotation exposes particle surfaces uniformly to thermal energy supplied by the external heaters. The predetermined temperature initiates thermal decomposition of organic compounds present in the black mass. The elevated temperature promotes decomposition reactions of ethylene carbonate and dimethyl carbonate molecules. Ethylene carbonate undergoes thermal decomposition in the presence of oxygen according to the following reaction: (CH₂O)₂CO + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O The ethylene carbonate molecules absorb thermal energy and break down into carbon dioxide and water vapor. Dimethyl carbonate undergoes similar decomposition at temperatures between 250 degrees Celsius and 300 degrees Celsius. The decomposition reaction of dimethyl carbonate can be represented as follows: C₃H₆O₃ + O₂ → 3CO₂ + 3H₂O The dimethyl carbonate molecules decompose to produce carbon dioxide and water vapor, which exit the rotary kiln reactor 106 in gaseous form. Polyvinylidene fluoride chains degrade under thermal exposure according to the following reaction: PVDF → HF + C(s) The polyvinylidene fluoride releases hydrogen fluoride gas and solid carbon residue during thermal decomposition. The temperature sensors mounted along the rotating shell measure temperature continuously and transmit readings to the control unit 120 to maintain thermal conditions within the predetermined range. At step 206, the method 200 includes injecting sulfuric acid vapor into the rotary kiln reactor 106 to react with fluoride-containing compounds in the black mass. The acid dosing unit 108 vaporizes liquid sulfuric acid in the vaporization chamber and introduces sulfuric acid vapor through injection ports positioned along the rotating shell. The sulfuric acid vapor penetrates into porous black mass particles and contacts lithium fluoride compounds distributed within the material. The elevated temperature and presence of sulfuric acid vapor promote the chemical reaction between lithium fluoride and sulfuric acid molecules. The reaction can be represented as follows: 2LiF + H₂SO₄ → Li₂SO₄ + 2HF Lithium fluoride reacts with sulfuric acid to form lithium sulphate and hydrogen fluoride gas. The lithium sulphate formed during the conversion reaction remains in solid phase within the black mass and dissolves in water and dilute sulfuric acid solutions at concentrations ranging from 10 grams per liter to 100 grams per liter during subsequent hydrometallurgical extraction operations. The hydrogen fluoride gas generated from both the acid reaction and polyvinylidene fluoride decomposition enters the gas phase and mixes with other gaseous products within the rotary kiln reactor 106. The acid dosing unit 108 maintains controlled injection rates to achieve fluoride conversion while preventing excessive acid consumption that would increase operating costs without improving fluoride removal performance. At step 208, the method 200 includes purging the rotary kiln reactor 106 with nitrogen gas to facilitate removal of volatile decomposition products. The nitrogen purge unit 118 supplies nitrogen gas through the inlet distributed along the rotating shell. The nitrogen gas enters the rotary kiln reactor 106 and displaces oxygen present in the processing environment, that creates an inert atmosphere that prevents oxidation of metal components in the black mass. The nitrogen gas flow sweeps volatile decomposition products including carbon dioxide, water vapor, and hydrogen fluoride toward the outlet connected to the off-gas treatment unit 110. The nitrogen gas maintains positive pressure within the rotary kiln reactor 106 to prevent air ingress during processing operations. The flow meters measure nitrogen flow rate and transmit values to the control unit 120 for monitoring and adjustment. The nitrogen purge removes gaseous products continuously throughout processing and prevents accumulation of volatile compounds within the rotary kiln reactor 106. At step 210, the method 200 includes separating off-gases from the rotary kiln reactor 106 through the cyclone separator 112. The off-gases exit the rotary kiln reactor 106 through the exhaust duct and enter the cyclone separator 112 tangentially. The tangential entry generates centrifugal force that drives entrained particulate matter toward the cyclone walls. The particulate matter includes fine black mass particles carried by the gas stream during processing operations. The black mass particles descend along the cyclone walls under combined effects of centrifugal force and gravity and collect in the discharge hopper positioned at the bottom of the cyclone separator 112. The particle-reduced off-gases exit through a central outlet at the top of the cyclone separator 112 and flow toward the condenser 114. The cyclone separator 112 removes particulate matter with separation efficiency exceeding 95 percent for particles larger than 10 micrometres to prevent fouling of downstream heat-exchange surfaces in the condenser 114 and packing material in the scrubber tower 116. At step 212, the method 200 includes condensing the volatile organic compounds from the off-gases. The particle-reduced off-gases enter the condenser 114 and contact cooled heat-exchange surfaces maintained at temperatures below dew points of ethylene carbonate and dimethyl carbonate vapours. The cooling medium circulating through the heat-exchange surfaces extracts thermal energy from the off-gases and reduces gas temperature. Ethylene carbonate and dimethyl carbonate vapors undergo phase transition from gaseous state to liquid state when temperature decreases below respective condensation temperatures. The condensed organic liquids accumulate on heat-exchange surfaces and drain into the receiver vessel connected to the condenser 114. The receiver vessel collects condensed organic compounds for disposal or further processing. Non-condensable gases including carbon dioxide, water vapor, hydrogen fluoride, and residual nitrogen pass through the condenser 114 without phase change and exit toward the scrubber tower 116. At step 214, the method 200 includes scrubbing remaining gaseous contaminants including hydrogen fluoride using an alkaline solution in a scrubber tower. The non-condensable off-gases enter the scrubber tower 116 at a lower inlet and flow upward through internal packing material. The alkaline solution circulates from a storage reservoir through distribution nozzles positioned above the packing material. The distribution nozzles spray the alkaline solution over the packing material to create wetted surfaces for gas-liquid contact. The off-gases flowing upward through the packing material contact the alkaline solution flowing downward. Further, hydrogen fluoride molecules dissolve into the alkaline solution and undergo neutralization reactions with alkaline compounds including sodium hydroxide or calcium hydroxide. The neutralization reaction between hydrogen fluoride and sodium hydroxide can be represented as follows: HF + NaOH → NaF + H₂O Hydrogen fluoride reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium fluoride and water. The sodium fluoride remains dissolved in the alkaline solution, and the solution recirculates through the scrubber tower 116 until fluoride concentration reaches predetermined maximum levels requiring solution replacement or regeneration. Remaining volatile organic compounds not captured during condensation also absorb into the alkaline solution through physical dissolution. The treated off-gases exit the scrubber tower 116 through a top outlet and discharge to atmosphere with hydrogen fluoride concentrations reduced to levels below 50 parts per million and volatile organic compound concentrations meeting regulatory emission standards. The method 200 reduces volatile organic compound emissions from the rotary kiln reactor 106 by 95 percent compared to direct feeding approaches. Untreated black mass fed directly into extraction reactors generates off-gas streams containing volatile organic compound concentrations exceeding 1,000 parts per million during leaching operations. The pre-treatment method 200 reduces volatile organic compound concentrations in off-gases to levels below 50 parts per million after treatment through the off-gas treatment unit 110, representing emission reductions of 95 percent or greater. The method 200 reduces hydrogen fluoride emissions from downstream extraction operations by 90 percent through conversion of fluoride-containing compounds into stable sulphate forms during pre-treatment. The emission reductions eliminate requirements for secondary off-gas treatment systems at downstream extraction facilities and reduce atmospheric discharge of hazardous air pollutants. The method 200 presents a systematic process for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction by using controlled thermal processing, sulfuric acid vapor injection, nitrogen purging, and off-gas treatment. The predetermined temperature and rotational movement promote uniform removal of organic compounds across all black mass particles. The sulfuric acid vapor converts fluoride-containing compounds into forms that remain stable during further processing. The nitrogen purge maintains an inert atmosphere inside the rotary kiln reactor 106 and transports gaseous products toward the off-gas treatment unit 110. The sequence of cyclone separation, condensation, and alkaline scrubbing removes particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and hydrogen fluoride from the off-gases. The combined operation of thermal processing, chemical conversion, gas transport, and off-gas cleaning produces treated black mass with reduced organic content and reduced fluoride content suitable for leaching operations, while maintaining stable process conditions and supporting consistent downstream extraction performance. FIG. 3 is a flowchart illustrating operations of the method, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. FIG. 3 is described in conjunction with the elements of the FIGs. 1 and 2. The flowchart 300 depicts sequential operations required for pre-treating lithium-ion battery black mass to remove impurities before hydrometallurgical extraction. At operation 302, loading includes transferring the untreated black mass from storage containers into the feeder 104. The untreated black mass is loaded in batches or continuously depending on processing capacity requirements. At operation 304, feeding includes delivering the untreated black mass from the feeder 104 through the inlet into the rotary kiln reactor 106. The feeder 104 controls flow rate to maintain consistent processing throughput. At operation 306, processing includes heating and rotating the black mass within the rotary kiln reactor 106 while injecting sulfuric acid vapor and purging with nitrogen gas. The processing operation decomposes volatile organic compounds and converts fluoride-containing compounds into removable forms. At operation 308, separating includes removing entrained particulate matter from off-gases using the cyclone separator 112. The cyclone separator 112 uses centrifugal force to drive particles toward walls for collection in the discharge hopper. At operation 310, condensing includes reducing the temperature of particle-reduced off-gases in the condenser 114 to convert volatile organic compounds from gaseous phase to liquid phase. The condensed organic liquids collect in the receiver vessel for disposal. At operation 312, scrubbing includes contacting non-condensable off-gases with alkaline solution in the scrubber tower 116 to neutralize hydrogen fluoride and absorb remaining volatile organic compounds. The treated off-gases exit through the top outlet. At operation 314, venting includes discharging treated off-gases to atmosphere after hydrogen fluoride and volatile organic compound concentrations meet regulatory emission standards. The venting operation completes off-gas treatment. At operation 316, transferring includes moving treated black mass from the outlet of the rotary kiln reactor 106 through cooling equipment to reduce material temperature before storage. The cooling prevents thermal damage to collection containers. At operation 318, collecting includes accumulating cooled treated black mass in discharge hoppers or collection bins for transport to hydrometallurgical extraction facilities. The collected material contains reduced levels of volatile organic compounds, total organic carbon, and fluorides suitable for subsequent processing. patents.abstract: An automated system (102) for recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese from spent lithium-ion batteries comprising a thermal pretreatment unit (104) configured to decompose electrolyte salts at a first temperature and to perform carbothermic reduction at a second temperature in a reducing atmosphere, a leaching reactor (106) equipped with oxidation-reduction potential sensors and pH sensors, configured to perform acid-reductive leaching using sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide, a staged impurity precipitation unit (110) configured to remove iron, aluminum and copper, a first solvent extraction circuit (112) employing saponified D2EHPA configured to selectively extract manganese, a second solvent extraction circuit (114) employing a saponified organophosphorus extractant configured to selectively extract cobalt, a crystallization unit (116) configured to recover metal salts; and a controller (108) configured to regulate hydrogen peroxide dosing, reagent addition rates and solvent circulation rates based on sensor feedback from the oxidation-reduction potential sensors and pH sensors. patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD The present disclosure relates to a field of battery recycling technology. Moreover, the present disclosure relates to an automated system and method for recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from spent lithium-ion batteries using hybrid thermo-hydrometallurgical processing along with solvent extraction and crystallisation. BACKGROUND Lithium-ion batteries have wide range of applications including electric vehicles, portable electronics, energy storage systems, and the like, due to various characteristics, such as high energy density, long cycle life, and high specific capacity. Due to the rapid growth in electric vehicle adoption and consumer electronics usage, large volumes of spent lithium-ion batteries are generated annually, creating an urgent need for efficient recycling technologies. However, the recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries raises environmental and technical concerns, such as low metal recovery efficiency, high energy consumption, incomplete separation of valuable metals, environmental pollution from improper disposal, and limited scalability of existing processes. Conventional recycling technologies for lithium-ion batteries rely primarily on pyrometallurgical smelting or batch-mode hydrometallurgical processing. Pyrometallurgical processes consume excessive energy, generate hazardous emissions, and result in loss of lithium due to slag formation. Batch hydrometallurgical processes, while offering better selectivity, suffer from several limitations including manual reagent dosing, fixed residence times regardless of feed variability, incomplete metal dissolution, co-precipitation of metals during purification, inconsistent product quality, and limited process control. Moreover, such conventional methods lack integration between thermal pretreatment and chemical leaching stages, resulting in inefficient processing. Additionally, conventional solvent extraction systems operate in open-loop configurations with significant reagent losses and environmental concerns. Furthermore, existing recycling processes are not adaptable to variable battery chemistries such as NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt), LCO (lithium-cobalt oxide), and LFP (lithium-iron phosphate), which have different cathode compositions and leaching characteristics. The lack of automated feedback control in conventional systems results in excessive reagent consumption, suboptimal metal recovery rates, and the inability to achieve battery-grade product purity required for cathode material remanufacturing. Thus, there exists a technical problem of how to recover lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from the spent lithium-ion batteries with high recovery efficiency, battery-grade product purity, reduced reagent consumption, and adaptability to variable feed compositions. Therefore, in light of the foregoing discussion, there exists a need to overcome the aforementioned drawbacks associated with the conventional systems and conventional methods for recovering metals from the spent lithium-ion batteries. SUMMARY The present disclosure provides an automated system and method for recovery of metals from spent lithium-ion batteries. The present disclosure provides a solution to a technical problem of how to recover lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from spent lithium-ion batteries with high recovery efficiency, battery-grade product purity, reduced reagent consumption, and adaptability to variable feed compositions. In accordance with an embodiment, the predetermined range of oxidation-reduction potential is 400 mV to 600 mV. The specific oxidation-reduction potential range of 400 mV to 600 mV is provided to address the problem of identifying optimal redox conditions that simultaneously achieve complete dissolution of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from pretreated battery material while preventing undesired side reactions, excessive reagent consumption, or precipitation of dissolved metals. The oxidation-reduction potential range operates by establishing electrochemical conditions wherein metal oxides and reduced metal species from carbothermic reduction undergo efficient dissolution in sulfuric acid solution, wherein oxidation-reduction potential values below 400 mV indicate overly reducing conditions that result in incomplete dissolution of manganese dioxide and higher oxidation state manganese compounds which require moderately oxidizing conditions to convert to soluble manganeseII ions, while oxidation-reduction potential values above 600 mV indicate excessively oxidizing conditions that cause unnecessary hydrogen peroxide consumption without significant improvement in metal dissolution rates and may lead to oxidation of dissolved metal ions to higher oxidation states that could precipitate or form undesired complexes. The range of 400 mV to 600 mV provides balanced redox conditions wherein hydrogen peroxide addition maintains sufficient oxidizing potential to facilitate reduction of higher oxidation state manganese compounds to soluble Mn²⁺ ions while simultaneously keeping cobalt and nickel in their soluble divalent oxidation states, and lithium remains as Li⁺ ions throughout the leaching process regardless of oxidation-reduction potential due to its highly electropositive nature. The predetermined range enables achievement of metal extraction efficiency exceeding 95% for all target metals by maintaining electrochemical conditions favorable for simultaneous dissolution of multiple metal species with different redox characteristics, minimizes formation of elemental sulfur or other sulfur species that can occur at very low oxidation-reduction potential values and would contaminate the leach solution, prevents excessive oxidation that would increase hydrogen peroxide consumption and operating costs without proportional benefit to metal recovery, and provides a sufficiently wide control range to accommodate minor process variations while maintaining optimal leaching performance, thereby ensuring efficient and consistent metal dissolution with minimal reagent waste through precise electrochemical control. In accordance with an embodiment, the staged impurity precipitation unit 110 is configured to precipitate iron and aluminum using calcium hydroxide and to precipitate copper using sodium hydroxide in sequential stages. The use of different precipitating agents in sequential stages is provided to address the problem of achieving selective removal of each impurity metal group while minimizing co-precipitation of valuable metals and avoiding formation of mixed precipitates that are difficult to separate and handle. The sequential precipitation operates by first adjusting the pH of the purified leach solution to a range where iron and aluminum preferentially precipitate through addition of calcium hydroxide, wherein iron forms insoluble iron oxyhydroxide species such as FeOOH and aluminum forms aluminum hydroxide or aluminum oxide according to reactions: Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2FeOOH + 3CaSO₄ + 2H₂O Al₂(SO₄)₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → Al₂O₃ + 3CaSO₄ + 3H₂O CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄ while at this pH range lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and copper remain predominantly in solution due to their higher solubility at the controlled pH conditions. Following solid-liquid separation to remove the iron and aluminum precipitate, the solution undergoes a second precipitation stage wherein pH is further adjusted through addition of sodium hydroxide to a higher pH range where copper selectively precipitates as copper hydroxide according to the reaction CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → CuOH₂ + Na₂SO₄, while lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese remain soluble due to their higher precipitation pH thresholds. The use of calcium hydroxide in the first stage exploits the distinct precipitation behavior of iron and aluminum which form insoluble hydroxides at lower pH compared to other metals, while the use of sodium hydroxide in the second stage enables precise pH control for selective copper removal without excessive calcium sulfate formation that would occur if calcium hydroxide were used throughout. The sequential staged approach enables removal of iron and aluminum with efficiency exceeding 99% in the first stage while maintaining losses of valuable metals below 1%, followed by copper removal with efficiency exceeding 98% in the second stage, prevents formation of mixed metal precipitates containing multiple impurity species that would be difficult to filter and handle, minimizes co-precipitation and occlusion of valuable metals by conducting precipitation in separate controlled stages rather than simultaneous precipitation of all impurities, and produces distinct precipitate streams that can be separately processed or disposed based on their composition, thereby achieving high selectivity impurity removal with minimal losses of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese to the precipitate phase. In accordance with an embodiment, the automated system 102 further comprises a closed-loop solvent regeneration circuit 120 configured to strip extracted metals from the D2EHPA and the organophosphorus extractant using sulfuric acid and to recycle regenerated extractants back to the respective solvent extraction circuits. The stripping and recycling operation functions by contacting the metal-loaded organic phase from the first solvent extraction circuit 112 containing manganese complexed with D2EHPA with concentrated sulfuric acid in a stripping contactor, wherein the acid reverses the extraction equilibrium and releases manganese ions from the organic phase back into aqueous phase as concentrated manganese sulfate solution according to the reaction (D2EHPA)₂Mn + H₂SO₄ → 2D2EHPA + MnSO₄, thereby regenerating the D2EHPA extractant to its free acid form that can be re-saponified and reused for extraction. Similarly, the metal-loaded organic phase from the second solvent extraction circuit 114 containing cobalt complexed with organophosphorus extractant undergoes stripping with sulfuric acid to release cobalt ions as concentrated cobalt sulfate solution according to analogous stripping reactions, thereby regenerating the organophosphorus extractant for reuse. The regenerated extractants are returned to their respective solvent extraction circuits through recycle piping wherein the D2EHPA is pumped back to the first solvent extraction circuit 112 after re-saponification and the organophosphorus extractant is returned to the second solvent extraction circuit 114 after re-saponification, establishing continuous closed-loop flow of organic extractants through extraction, stripping, and recycling stages. The closed-loop solvent regeneration circuit 120 enables continuous operation of solvent extraction circuits with minimal fresh extractant makeup requirements typically below 5% of total circulating extractant volume to compensate for mechanical losses and degradation, reduces operating costs by eliminating need for continuous fresh extractant procurement and minimizing spent extractant disposal, prevents environmental pollution by containing organic extractants within the closed system rather than discharging them as waste, produces concentrated metal sulfate solutions suitable for direct crystallization through efficient stripping that transfers metals from organic phase to small volumes of aqueous acid, and improves overall process sustainability by enabling multiple reuse cycles of valuable organic extractants, thereby achieving economically viable and environmentally responsible solvent extraction operation with minimal reagent consumption and waste generation. FIG. 2 is a flowchart depicting a method for recovering lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese from spent lithium-ion batteries, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. With reference to FIG. 2, there is shown a flowchart of a method 200 that includes the steps 202 to 216. There is provided the method 200 for recovering lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese from spent lithium-ion batteries. The method 200 provides an automated integrated process combining thermal pretreatment, acid-reductive leaching, staged impurity removal, sequential solvent extraction, and crystallization. The method 200 enables high metal recovery efficiency with battery-grade product purity while minimizing reagent consumption through automated feedback control. As a result, the method 200 helps in achieving efficient recycling of diverse battery types with reduced environmental impact and lower chemical consumption. At step 202, the method 200 includes performing thermal pretreatment of shredded battery material, including electrolyte decomposition and carbothermic reduction of metal oxides. At step 204, the method 200 further includes performing acid-reductive leaching of thermally pretreated material using sulfuric acid and a reductant under automated oxidation-reduction potential control and pH control to dissolve lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese into solution. At step 206, the method 200 further includes removing impurities from the leach solution by staged precipitation. At step 208, the method 200 further includes selectively extracting manganese from purified leach solution using a first solvent extraction circuit. At step 210, the method 200 further includes selectively extracting cobalt from manganese-depleted solution using a second solvent extraction circuit. At step 212, the method 200 further includes recovering manganese and cobalt as crystallized sulfate salts. At step 214, the method 200 further includes recovering nickel as carbonate. At step 216, the method 200 further includes recovering lithium as carbonate. In accordance with an embodiment, the step of performing acid-reductive leaching comprises continuously monitoring oxidation-reduction potential and regulating reductant addition to maintain oxidation-reduction potential within a predetermined range. The continuous monitoring and regulation of oxidation-reduction potential is provided to address the problem of achieving consistent and complete metal dissolution during leaching operations where fixed reductant dosing rates cannot accommodate variations in feed composition, metal concentrations, and leaching kinetics that occur during processing of diverse battery types. The continuous monitoring operates by employing oxidation-reduction potential sensors that measure the redox state of the leaching solution in real-time and transmit measurement signals continuously throughout the leaching process, wherein the oxidation-reduction potential values indicate whether the solution maintains appropriate electrochemical conditions for efficient dissolution of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese from pretreated battery material. The regulation of reductant addition functions by automatically adjusting the dosing rate of reductant such as hydrogen peroxide in response to measured oxidation-reduction potential values, wherein the reductant addition rate is increased when oxidation-reduction potential falls below the predetermined range indicating insufficient oxidizing conditions that would result in incomplete dissolution of higher oxidation state metals such as manganese, and the reductant addition rate is decreased when oxidation-reduction potential exceeds the predetermined range indicating excessive oxidizing conditions that would cause unnecessary reagent consumption without proportional improvement in metal dissolution. The continuous monitoring and regulation enables achievement of metal extraction efficiency exceeding 95% for all target metals by maintaining optimal electrochemical conditions throughout the leaching process, minimizes reductant consumption by dosing only the amount required to maintain target oxidation-reduction potential rather than applying fixed stoichiometric ratios that do not account for actual process conditions, prevents incomplete leaching that would reduce overall metal recovery and require reprocessing of incompletely leached residues, adapts automatically to variations in battery feed composition including different cathode materials and metal ratios without requiring manual process adjustments, and ensures consistent leaching performance across variable feed stocks, thereby achieving efficient and economical metal extraction with optimal reagent utilization through real-time adaptive process control. In accordance with an embodiment, the step of recovering lithium as carbonate comprises converting lithium sulfate to lithium hydroxide by reaction with calcium hydroxide and reacting the lithium hydroxide with carbon dioxide to precipitate lithium carbonate. The two-step conversion process is provided to address the problem of producing battery-grade lithium carbonate from lithium sulfate solution obtained after extraction of other metals, wherein direct precipitation of lithium carbonate from sulfate solution is inefficient due to high solubility of lithium sulfate and difficulty in achieving complete conversion and high purity. The conversion to lithium hydroxide operates by reacting lithium sulfate solution with calcium hydroxide according to the reaction Li₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2LiOH + CaSO₄, wherein calcium hydroxide provides hydroxide ions that displace sulfate from lithium forming soluble lithium hydroxide while simultaneously precipitating calcium as insoluble calcium sulfate that can be removed by filtration, thereby converting lithium from sulfate form to hydroxide form which is more reactive toward carbonation. Following separation of calcium sulfate precipitate, the lithium hydroxide solution undergoes carbonation by reaction with carbon dioxide according to the reaction 2LiOH + CO₂ → Li₂CO₃ + H₂O, wherein carbon dioxide gas is bubbled through or otherwise contacted with the lithium hydroxide solution causing precipitation of lithium carbonate crystals while forming water as byproduct, and the precipitation is controlled by regulating carbon dioxide flow rate, temperature, and residence time to achieve desired crystal morphology and purity. The two-step conversion process enables production of lithium carbonate with purity in the range of 99% to 99.9% suitable for direct use in battery cathode manufacturing, achieves high lithium recovery efficiency exceeding 95% by employing sequential conversion reactions that drive lithium through different chemical forms, produces crystalline lithium carbonate with controlled particle size distribution appropriate for dissolution and use in cathode precursor synthesis, removes sulfate ions completely through precipitation as insoluble calcium sulfate thereby preventing sulfate contamination of the final lithium carbonate product, and enables closed-loop material recovery by producing battery-grade lithium carbonate that can be directly recycled into new battery production, thereby completing the lithium recovery process and enabling circular economy for this critical battery material. Advantageously, the method 200 is configured to enable integrated hybrid thermo-hydrometallurgical processing with real-time feedback control, thereby achieving high metal recovery efficiency while maintaining controlled chemical conditions throughout thermal pretreatment, leaching, extraction, and crystallization stages. As a result, the method 200 reduces reagent consumption, minimizes processing time, and produces battery-grade metal products suitable for cathode remanufacturing. Further, the method 200 enables adaptive operation for variable battery feed compositions by automatically adjusting process parameters in response to changing metal concentrations and leaching kinetics, thereby ensuring consistent performance and enabling scalable industrial deployment for recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries. patents.abstract: The invention relates to a battery pack structure for lithium iron phosphate prismatic cells incorporating a dual-sided cooling arrangement. The battery pack includes a lower cooling plate positioned beneath the cells and an upper cooling plate arranged above electrical interconnections, with thermally conductive interface layers disposed between the cooling plates and the battery components. The interface layers conform to surface variations to promote effective heat transfer. Heat generated within the battery cells and electrical connections is removed through both cooling plates, enabling improved temperature control and reduced thermal gradients across the cell assembly. The disclosed configuration enhances thermal uniformity and operational reliability of the battery pack during charging and discharging conditions.Industrial Applicability The invention is applicable to systems requiring reliable thermal management of lithium iron phosphate battery packs and is suitable for use in various industrial and commercial applications. Electric Vehicle Applications In electric vehicle systems, effective temperature control of battery packs is essential for maintaining performance, safety, and service life. The disclosed dual-sided cooling arrangement supports stable operation of battery cells under varying load conditions, including rapid charging and high-power discharge. By improving temperature uniformity within the battery pack, the invention contributes to consistent vehicle performance across different ambient conditions and operating profiles. The enhanced thermal control also assists in limiting thermal stress on battery components, thereby supporting longer operational life and improved safety margins during demanding driving conditions. Energy Storage System Applications For stationary energy storage installations, including grid-connected storage, renewable energy integration, and commercial or industrial energy systems, the invention provides improved thermal regulation during repeated charge and discharge cycles. Maintaining battery cells within a controlled temperature range reduces degradation and supports reliable long-term operation. The disclosed configuration enables effective heat removal during high-power operation while allowing compact system design, making it suitable for applications where efficiency, durability, and space utilization are important considerations.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Description : Field and Background of the Invention Field: The present invention relates to thermal management systems for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs, and more particularly to a dual cooling plate configuration with specialized thermal gap filler interfaces positioned at both top and bottom surfaces of prismatic battery cells for enhanced thermal management efficiency. Background: Technical Field Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have gained significant adoption in electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and various industrial applications due to their inherent safety characteristics, long cycle life, and cost-effectiveness. However, effective thermal management remains critical for optimizing performance, extending battery lifespan, and ensuring safe operation under various load conditions. Description of Related Art Existing battery pack thermal management solutions commonly rely on cooling arrangements applied to only one side of the battery module, typically from the bottom. While such systems offer basic temperature control, they often result in uneven heat distribution along the height of the cells. Heat generated at the upper regions, particularly near electrical interconnections, is not efficiently removed, leading to localized temperature rise. Additionally, the use of rigid interface materials or reliance on mechanical compression alone can create inconsistent thermal contact and air gaps, reducing heat transfer efficiency. These limitations become more pronounced during high-current charging and discharge conditions. Summary of the Invention The invention relates to an improved thermal management arrangement for lithium iron phosphate battery packs, wherein cooling is provided from both the lower and upper regions of prismatic battery cells. By employing cooling plates on opposite sides of the cell stack in combination with conformable thermal interface materials, the system enables more effective heat removal and improved temperature uniformity during battery operation. Key aspects of the invention include: • Provision of a dual-sided cooling architecture that enhances overall heat dissipation compared to conventional single-surface cooling approaches. • Control of cell operating temperature within a safe and efficient range during normal use and high-load conditions such as fast charging. • Reduction of temperature gradients along the height of the battery cells to limit thermal stress and degradation. • Dedicated thermal management of electrical interconnection regions, including busbar zones, where localized heat generation is significant. • A layered battery pack structure comprising a bottom cooling plate, lower thermal interface material, battery module, busbar assembly, upper thermal interface material, and a top cooling plate, arranged to maintain manufacturability and system simplicity. Key Benefits of the Invention The dual cooling configuration with specialized thermal gap filler interfaces provides multiple synergistic advantages: 1. The dual-sided cooling arrangement enables heat removal from both the lower and upper regions of the battery cells, thereby improving overall thermal dissipation compared to single-surface cooling systems. 2. Heat flow is distributed in two directions across the cell structure, which helps in reducing temperature gradients along the height of the cells and improves thermal balance within the battery pack. 3. Localized heating at electrical interconnection areas, including busbar regions, is effectively managed by the upper cooling plate, reducing the likelihood of hotspot formation and long-term connection degradation. 4. The use of conformable thermal interface materials allows consistent thermal contact despite surface irregularities, manufacturing tolerances, and thermal expansion during operation. 5. Operating cell temperatures are maintained within an efficient range under normal and high-load conditions, contributing to improved battery performance and extended service life. 6. The modular layered configuration supports easy adaptation to different battery pack sizes and layouts, making the system suitable for electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and similar applications. 7. The overall design achieves improved thermal performance without introducing the complexity, cost, or reliability concerns typically associated with fully liquid-immersed cooling systems. Detailed Description of the Invention The present invention relates to a thermal management arrangement for a battery pack comprising lithium iron phosphate prismatic cells. The invention provides a cooling configuration in which heat generated during battery operation is removed from both lower and upper regions of the cell assembly. In one embodiment, a cooling structure is positioned beneath the battery cells to extract heat from the lower portion of the cells. A thermally conductive interface material is arranged between the cooling structure and the cells to maintain effective thermal contact while providing electrical insulation. The battery cells are arranged above the interface material in a selected electrical configuration. An electrical interconnection structure is provided at the upper region of the cells to establish current flow between individual cells. A second thermally conductive interface material is positioned above the electrical interconnection structure. An additional cooling structure is arranged above this interface material to remove heat from the upper portion of the cells and the electrical interconnection region. During operation, heat generated within the battery pack is transferred toward both cooling structures through the respective interface materials, enabling bidirectional heat removal. This arrangement reduces temperature variations across the battery cells and improves overall thermal control. The cooling structures may operate with a circulating cooling medium and may be controlled according to operating conditions of the battery pack. The described configuration is suitable for use in electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and similar applications requiring effective battery thermal management. , Claims:Claims Independent Claims Claim 1 (Apparatus Claim): A battery pack assembly comprising: a lower cooling plate arranged beneath a plurality of lithium iron phosphate prismatic battery cells; a first thermally conductive interface layer disposed between the lower cooling plate and the battery cells; an electrical interconnection assembly positioned at an upper region of the battery cells; a second thermally conductive interface layer disposed above the electrical interconnection assembly; and an upper cooling plate positioned above the second interface layer, wherein the lower cooling plate and the upper cooling plate are configured to remove heat from opposite regions of the battery cells during operation. Claim 2 (System Claim): A thermal management system for a battery pack comprising: a lower cooling structure positioned adjacent to a lower portion of battery cells; an upper cooling structure positioned adjacent to an upper portion of the battery cells and associated electrical interconnections; thermally conductive interface materials arranged between the battery cells and the respective cooling structures; and a cooling medium circulation arrangement configured to transfer heat away from the battery pack through the cooling structures. Claim 3 (Method Claim): A method of managing temperature in a battery pack, the method comprising: positioning a lower cooling element beneath battery cells; establishing thermal contact between the battery cells and the lower cooling element using a conformable interface material; providing electrical interconnections at an upper region of the battery cells; establishing thermal contact between the electrical interconnections and an upper cooling element using a second interface material; and removing heat from the battery cells through both the lower and upper cooling elements during operation. Dependent Claims Claim 4: The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein the first and second interface layers comprise thermally conductive and electrically insulating materials. Claim 5: The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein the lower cooling plate and the upper cooling plate include internal passages for circulation of a cooling medium. Claim 6: The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein the interface layers are compressible to accommodate surface irregularities of the battery cells and electrical interconnections. Claim 7: The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein the electrical interconnection assembly includes busbar elements arranged to connect the battery cells in series or parallel configurations. Claim 8: The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein the lower and upper cooling plates are formed from thermally conductive metal materials. Claim 9: The thermal management system as claimed in Claim 2, wherein the cooling medium circulation arrangement is configured to operate based on detected battery temperature. Claim 10: The thermal management system as claimed in Claim 2, wherein temperature sensing elements are provided to monitor at least one of battery cell temperature or electrical interconnection temperature. The thermal management system as claimed in Claim 2, wherein the cooling structures are arranged to enable simultaneous heat removal from lower and upper regions of the battery pack. The method as claimed in Claim 3, wherein the interface materials are applied by dispensing, placement, or similar conforming processes. The method as claimed in Claim 3, further comprising applying a compressive force to the battery pack to maintain thermal contact between adjacent layers. The method as claimed in Claim 3, further comprising circulating a cooling medium through the lower and upper cooling elements during charging or discharging of the battery pack. The battery pack assembly as claimed in Claim 1, wherein heat generated within the battery cells is transferred toward both the lower and upper cooling plates to reduce temperature gradients across the cells.
