[00044] In an embodiment, the term “integrated process” as used herein refers to a process configuration wherein two or more-unit operations are functionally interconnected such that outputs from one operation serve as inputs to one or more subsequent operations, including through intermediate streams and recycle loops. [00045] In an embodiment, the term “closed-loop system” refers to a process in which process streams are internally recycled and reagents are regenerated and reused within the system. [00046] The term “substantially zero liquid discharge” refers to a condition wherein aqueous effluents generated during the process are substantially reused, recycled, or treated such that no significant liquid waste is discharged outside the process boundary. [00047] In an embodiment, the term “black mass” refers to a material obtained from spent lithium-ion batteries comprising a mixture of electrode materials including lithium-containing compounds, transition metal oxides, conductive carbon, and metallic constituents. [00048] In an embodiment, the term “solvent extraction” refers to a liquid-liquid extraction process wherein one or more metal species are selectively transferred from an aqueous phase to an immiscible organic phase containing an extractant, followed by recovery of the metal through a stripping step. [00049] In an embodiment, the term “solid-to-liquid ratio” refers to the ratio of mass of solid material to volume of liquid used in a given process. [00050] In an embodiment, the term “O/A ratio” or “organic-to-aqueous ratio” refers to the ratio of volume of organic phase to volume of aqueous phase used in solvent extraction (SX). [00051] In an embodiment, the term “reagent regeneration” refers to recovery of chemical reagents from spent process streams in a form suitable for reuse within the process. [00052] The present invention addresses challenges associated with recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries, particularly black mass derived therefrom, which contains a complex mixture of valuable metals including lithium, cobalt, manganese, copper and zinc along with impurities such as iron, aluminium and graphite. [00053] Conventional hydrometallurgical processes for recovery of such metals typically rely on acid leaching followed by precipitation or solvent extraction. However, these known processes suffer from several limitations including high consumption of chemical reagents, generation of significant volumes of secondary effluents, poor selectivity in separation of closely associated metals such as cobalt and manganese, and inefficient recovery of lithium from downstream streams. Additionally, existing processes generally lack integration between unit operations and do not provide for effective regeneration and reuse of reagents, thereby increasing operational costs and environmental burden. [00054] Accordingly, there exists a need for an integrated and closed-loop hydrometallurgical process capable of selectively recovering multiple metals from black mass while minimizing reagent consumption, improving separation efficiency, enabling recovery of high-purity products, and substantially reducing or eliminating liquid effluent discharge. [00055] In an aspect, the present invention provides an integrated hydrometallurgical process for recovery of metals from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. [00056] In an embodiment, the process comprises: • a pre-treatment stage for removal of interfering species; • a leaching stage using an acidic lixiviant system to solubilize metal values; • a solid-liquid separation stage to remove insoluble fractions including carbonaceous material; • an electrochemical recovery stage for selective recovery of one or more metals; • a controlled precipitation stage for removal of impurity metals; • one or more liquid-liquid extraction stages employing selective extractants for separation of target metals; • one or more conversion stages to obtain value-added products; • one or more metal recovery stages including precipitation, electrochemical deposition and/or reduction; and • a reagent regeneration stage configured to recover and recycle process chemicals. [00057] In another embodiment, the process is configured such that: • separation of metals is achieved in a sequential and selective manner; • intermediate streams are internally recycled; • reagents are regenerated and reused within the process; and • the overall system operates under a closed-loop configuration with minimal or zero liquid discharge. [00058] In a further embodiment, the process integrates multiple unit operations including leaching, solvent extraction, precipitation, electrowinning, and membrane-based separation into a unified process architecture. [00059] In an embodiment, the process comprises subjecting the black mass to a washing step configured to remove soluble and interfering species. In a further embodiment, the washing step facilitates separation of magnesium into an aqueous phase, thereby improving downstream selectivity and reducing interference during subsequent metal recovery stages. [00060] In a specific embodiment, the washing is carried out in an aqueous medium under controlled pH conditions, with a solid-to-liquid ratio selected to enable effective dissolution of magnesium species, and at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures. [00061] In a further embodiment, magnesium is recovered from the washing solution via precipitation using a carbonate source, followed by separation and optional drying of the precipitated magnesium compound. [00062] In a specific embodiment, the washing is conducted at a pH of 6–8, a temperature of 25–60°C, and a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:4–1:8, and magnesium is precipitated using sodium carbonate to obtain magnesium carbonate. [00063] In an embodiment, the washed solid residue is subjected to an acidic leaching step to dissolve metal values. In a further embodiment, the leaching is performed using an inorganic acid-based lixiviant system (for example one or more mineral acids selected from sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, and mixtures thereof), optionally in the presence of a reducing environment to enhance dissolution of transition metals. [00064] In a specific embodiment, the leaching is conducted under controlled temperature and agitation, with the pH maintained in an acidic range to ensure effective dissolution of metal species. [00065] In a specific embodiment, the acid i.e. sulfuric acid is used at a concentration of 1–3 M, the temperature is maintained at 60–90°C, the leaching time is 1–4 hours, and an optional reducing agent selected from hydrogen peroxide or glucose is employed. [00066] In an embodiment, the resulting leach slurry is subjected to a solid-liquid separation step. [00067] In a further embodiment, an insoluble carbonaceous fraction is separated as a solid residue, while the liquid phase comprises dissolved metal species. [00068] In a specific embodiment, graphite is recovered by filtration from the leach slurry. [00069] In an embodiment, the metal-bearing solution obtained after separation is subjected to an electrochemical recovery step for selective recovery of copper. In a further embodiment, copper is deposited on a cathode under controlled electrochemical conditions. [00070] In a specific embodiment, the electrowinning is carried out at a current density of 150–350 A/m² and a temperature of 30–50°C, resulting in recovery of copper as metallic plates. [00071] In an embodiment, the copper-depleted solution is subjected to a controlled precipitation step to remove impurity metals. In a further embodiment, the pH of the solution is adjusted using an alkaline reagent to precipitate impurity hydroxides. [00072] In a specific embodiment, iron and aluminium are precipitated at a pH of 3.5–4.5 using sodium hydroxide, resulting in an impurity-depleted solution. [00073] In an embodiment, the impurity-depleted solution is subjected to a first liquid-liquid extraction stage for selective separation of manganese. In a further embodiment, manganese is selectively extracted into an organic phase using an organophosphorus-based extractant system. [00074] In a specific embodiment, extraction is carried out under controlled pH and phase ratio conditions to achieve selective loading of manganese into the organic phase. [00075] In a specific embodiment, the extractant comprises Di(2-ethylhexyl)phosphoric acid (D2EHPA) at a concentration of 10–25% in a hydrocarbon diluent (for e.g. kerosene), the extraction is conducted at a pH of 4–5 with an organic-to-aqueous ratio of 1:1–3:1, and the loaded organic phase is subjected to stripping using an acidic solution to obtain a manganese-containing aqueous solution. [00076] In an embodiment, the manganese-containing solution obtained after stripping is subjected to a conversion step to obtain a value-added manganese product. [00077] In a further embodiment, the conversion step comprises oxidation of manganese to a higher oxidation state. [00078] In a specific embodiment, oxidation is carried out using sodium persulfate at a temperature of 70–95°C and a pH of 1–2 to obtain manganese dioxide. [00079] In an embodiment, the raffinate obtained from the first solvent extraction stage is subjected to a second liquid-liquid extraction stage for selective separation of cobalt. [00080] In a further embodiment, cobalt is selectively extracted using a phosphinic acid-based extractant system. [00081] In a specific embodiment, extraction is carried out at a higher pH relative to the manganese extraction stage to enable selective separation of cobalt. [00082] In a specific embodiment, the extractant comprises Bis(2,4,4-trimethylpentyl)phosphinic acid (Cyanex 272), the extraction is conducted at a pH of 5–6 and a temperature of 30–60°C, and the loaded organic phase is subjected to stripping using an acidic solution to obtain a cobalt-containing aqueous solution. [00083] In an embodiment, cobalt is recovered from the cobalt-containing solution through a precipitation step. In a further embodiment, cobalt is precipitated as an intermediate compound, which is subsequently converted to metallic cobalt. [00084] In a specific embodiment, cobalt is precipitated as cobalt oxalate using oxalic acid, followed by reduction at a temperature of 400–650°C in a hydrogen-containing atmosphere to obtain cobalt metal powder. [00085] In an embodiment, lithium is recovered from the raffinate obtained after cobalt extraction. In a further embodiment, lithium is precipitated using a carbonate source under controlled temperature and pH conditions. [00086] In an embodiment, the carbonate source comprises one or more compounds selected from sodium carbonate, potassium carbonate, ammonium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate and mixtures thereof. [00087] In a specific embodiment, the carbonate source is sodium carbonate and is used at a temperature of 80–95°C and a pH of 10–11 to obtain lithium carbonate. [00088] In an embodiment, zinc is recovered from one or more process streams. In a further embodiment, zinc is subjected to a separation step followed by electrochemical recovery. [00089] In a specific embodiment, zinc is recovered by solvent extraction followed by electrowinning to obtain metallic zinc. [00090] In an embodiment, one or more spent process streams generated during the process are subjected to a reagent regeneration step. In a further embodiment, the regeneration step comprises treatment using a membrane-based electro-separation system to recover reusable chemical species. [00091] In a specific embodiment, bipolar membrane electrodialysis is employed to regenerate sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide, which are recycled to upstream process steps including leaching and precipitation, thereby enabling closed-loop operation and reduction of liquid effluent discharge. [00092] Referring to the accompanying drawing (FIG. 1), the integrated hydrometallurgical process is configured as a continuous and closed-loop system comprising sequential processing units, intermediate stream transfers, and internal reagent regeneration pathways. [00093] In an embodiment, the process begins with a Magnesium Washing unit, wherein the black mass feed is contacted with an aqueous medium to selectively solubilize magnesium values, thereby generating (i) a washed solid stream enriched in lithium, cobalt, manganese, copper and zinc, and (ii) a magnesium-containing solution stream. The magnesium-containing solution is directed to a precipitation unit, wherein a carbonate source is introduced to form a magnesium carbonate (MgCO3) precipitate, followed by a filtration unit to recover solid MgCO3 as a product stream and a filtrate stream which may be recycled or directed to downstream treatment. [00094] The washed solid stream from the magnesium washing unit is transferred to a Leaching unit, wherein the solids are contacted with an acidic lixiviant to dissolve metal values, thereby producing a leach slurry comprising dissolved metal ions (Li⁺, Co²⁺, Mn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺) and an undissolved solid fraction. The leach slurry is subsequently directed to a Filtration unit, resulting in separation into (i) a graphite-rich solid residue stream recovered as a product, and (ii) a metal-bearing leach solution stream. [00095] The metal-bearing leach solution is fed to a Copper Electrowinning (EMEW, Electrometals Electrowinning) unit, wherein copper ions are selectively reduced and deposited as metallic copper plates at the cathode, thereby producing (i) a copper metal product stream, and (ii) a copper-depleted solution stream. [00096] The copper-depleted solution is then introduced into a Neutralization / Impurity Precipitation unit, wherein the pH is adjusted using an alkaline stream, preferably dilute sodium hydroxide regenerated from the effluent treatment unit, to precipitate impurity metals. This step generates (i) a precipitated impurity stream comprising iron hydroxide (Fe(OH)3) and aluminium hydroxide (Al(OH)3), which is removed via filtration, and (ii) a clarified solution stream substantially depleted of iron and aluminium. [00097] The clarified solution stream is subsequently directed to a Manganese Solvent Extraction circuit (Na-D2EHPA system), comprising one or more extraction stages. In this unit, manganese is selectively transferred from the aqueous phase into an organic phase containing D2EHPA, resulting in (i) a loaded organic phase containing manganese (Mn-loaded D2EHPA) and (ii) a raffinate stream containing cobalt, lithium and residual zinc. The loaded organic phase may optionally pass through a scrubbing stage and is then subjected to a stripping stage, wherein manganese is transferred back into an aqueous phase to generate a manganese sulfate (MnSO4) solution stream, while regenerating the stripped organic phase (regenerated D2EHPA) for recycling back to the extraction stage. [00098] The manganese sulfate solution stream is then directed to a Manganese Oxidation unit, wherein manganese is oxidized to produce electrolytic manganese dioxide (EMD) as a solid product stream, along with a residual solution stream that may be recycled or treated. [00099] In an embodiment, the manganese extraction employs an organic phase comprising an extractant and kerosene is used as diluent. [000100] The raffinate stream from the manganese extraction circuit is transferred to a Cobalt Solvent Extraction circuit (Cyanex 272 system). In this unit, cobalt is selectively extracted into an organic phase, producing (i) a cobalt-loaded organic phase (Co-loaded Cyanex 272) and (ii) a raffinate stream enriched in lithium and zinc. The cobalt-loaded organic phase is subjected to a stripping stage to generate a cobalt sulfate (CoSO4) solution stream and a regenerated Cyanex 272 organic phase, which is recycled back to the extraction stage. [000101] The cobalt sulfate solution is directed to a Cobalt Oxalate Precipitation unit, wherein cobalt is precipitated as cobalt oxalate (CoC2O4). The precipitated cobalt oxalate is separated and transferred to a Reduction unit, wherein it is reduced under a hydrogen-containing atmosphere to form cobalt metal powder as a final product stream. [000102] The raffinate stream from the cobalt extraction circuit is directed to a Lithium Precipitation unit, wherein lithium is precipitated using a carbonate source to form lithium carbonate (Li2CO3). The lithium carbonate is recovered as a solid product stream, while the remaining solution stream is directed to further processing. [000103] In parallel or downstream, zinc present in one or more process streams is directed to a Zinc Solvent Extraction and Electrowinning unit, wherein zinc is selectively extracted into an organic phase and subsequently stripped to obtain a zinc-containing electrolyte, followed by electrowinning to produce metallic zinc plates. This step generates (i) a zinc metal product stream, and (ii) one or more spent solution streams. [000104] Multiple spent solution streams, including those identified in the drawing as Spent Solution streams (e.g., Spent Sol. 4, Spent Sol. 5, and other raffinate streams), are collectively directed to an Effluent Treatment unit comprising Bipolar Membrane Electrodialysis (BMED). In this unit, the spent solutions are processed to regenerate (i) an acid stream (e.g., sulfuric acid) and (ii) a base stream (e.g., sodium hydroxide). [000105] The regenerated acid stream is recycled to upstream units including the Leaching unit and solvent extraction stripping stages, while the regenerated base stream is recycled to units requiring pH adjustment, including the Neutralization / Impurity Precipitation unit and other precipitation stages. This internal recycling of reagents enables reduction in fresh chemical consumption and minimizes discharge of liquid effluents. [000106] Thus, the process as illustrated in the drawing establishes an integrated flow architecture wherein: • magnesium is recovered as MgCO3; • graphite is recovered as a solid fraction; • copper is recovered as metallic plates; • iron and aluminium are removed as hydroxide precipitates; • manganese is recovered as EMD via D2EHPA loading and regeneration; • cobalt is recovered as metal powder via Cyanex 272 extraction, oxalate precipitation and reduction; • lithium is recovered as Li2CO3; • zinc is recovered as metallic zinc via solvent extraction and electrowinning; and • process reagents including acid and base are regenerated and reused through the BMED unit. [000107] In this manner, all major process streams are either converted into value-added products or internally recycled, thereby enabling a closed-loop hydrometallurgical process with substantially zero liquid discharge. [000108] In an embodiment, the solvent extraction stages employed in the process are carried out in a multi-stage configuration, comprising two or more extraction stages, optionally followed by scrubbing and stripping stages, to enhance selectivity and phase transfer efficiency. In a further embodiment, the number of stages is selected based on the concentration of metal species and desired purity levels. [000109] In an embodiment, the organic phases used in solvent extraction comprise extractant-diluent systems, wherein the diluent is selected from hydrocarbon-based solvents, and the extractant concentration is adjusted to optimize loading capacity and phase separation characteristics. [000110] In an embodiment, the extraction and stripping operations are conducted at controlled organic-to-aqueous phase ratios, enabling selective transfer of target metals while minimizing co-extraction of impurities. [000111] In an embodiment, the pH adjustment steps employed for impurity precipitation and solvent extraction are carried out using alkaline streams generated internally within the process, thereby reducing dependence on external reagents. [000112] In an embodiment, the regenerated acid streams obtained from the reagent regeneration unit are reintroduced into the leaching stage and/or stripping stages, thereby maintaining process continuity and reducing fresh acid consumption. [000113] In an embodiment, the regenerated base streams are reused in one or more of: • impurity precipitation steps, • lithium precipitation, • and intermediate pH adjustment stages. [000114] In an embodiment, the precipitation steps for lithium, cobalt, and magnesium are carried out under controlled supersaturation conditions to enable formation of filterable and high-purity precipitates. [000115] In an embodiment, the electrochemical recovery steps for copper and zinc are conducted using inert or dimensionally stable electrodes, enabling efficient metal deposition and long operational life. [000116] In an embodiment, the process is configured such that intermediate raffinate streams are not discarded, but are instead routed to subsequent recovery stages or to the reagent regeneration unit, thereby improving overall metal recovery. [000117] In an embodiment, the process achieves metal recovery efficiencies exceeding 90% for lithium and manganese, and exceeding 95% for cobalt and copper, under optimized operating conditions. [000118] In an embodiment, the process operates as a closed-loop hydrometallurgical system, wherein substantially all aqueous streams are either recycled within the process or subjected to reagent regeneration, thereby minimizing or eliminating liquid effluent discharge. [000119] In an alternative embodiment, the order of solvent extraction stages may be modified such that cobalt extraction is performed prior to manganese extraction, provided that appropriate control of pH and extractant selectivity is maintained to enable selective separation. This variation may be employed depending on feed composition and desired product purity. [000120] In another alternative embodiment, the manganese conversion step may be configured to produce manganese salts or other manganese compounds, instead of manganese dioxide, by employing alternative downstream processing conditions. [000121] In an alternative embodiment, cobalt recovery may be carried out without intermediate oxalate precipitation, by directly recovering cobalt from the stripped solution through electrochemical deposition or other reduction techniques. [000122] In another alternative embodiment, lithium recovery may be performed using alternative precipitation agents or crystallization techniques, enabling production of lithium compounds other than lithium carbonate. [000123] In an alternative embodiment, zinc recovery may be performed directly from the leach solution or intermediate streams, bypassing one or more solvent extraction stages, depending on zinc concentration and process requirements. [000124] In an alternative embodiment, the reagent regeneration unit may comprise other electrochemical or membrane-based separation systems capable of generating reusable acid and base streams, while maintaining the integrated and closed-loop nature of the process. [000125] In another alternative embodiment, the magnesium removal step may be integrated with or performed after the leaching stage, wherein magnesium is selectively precipitated from the leach solution. [000126] In an embodiment, the sequence of steps described herein is configured to achieve progressive separation of metals based on their chemical behavior, including differences in solubility, redox potential, and extractant affinity, thereby enabling selective recovery. [000127] In an embodiment, the removal of magnesium prior to leaching enhances downstream process efficiency by: • reducing consumption of leaching reagents, • minimizing interference in solvent extraction stages, and • improving selectivity of metal separation. [000128] In an embodiment, the integration of electrowinning, solvent extraction, precipitation, and reduction steps within a single process framework provides synergistic advantages, including improved recovery efficiency, reduced process complexity, and enhanced product purity. [000129] In an embodiment, the reagent regeneration step using bipolar membrane electrodialysis enables simultaneous generation of acid and base streams, which are directly reusable in upstream steps, thereby establishing a circular reagent economy within the process. [000130] In an embodiment, the routing of multiple spent solution streams to a centralized regeneration unit enables consolidated treatment of process effluents, simplifying plant design and improving sustainability. [000131] In an embodiment, the process is adaptable to variations in feed composition, including differences in metal content and impurity levels, by adjusting operating parameters such as pH, phase ratios, and reagent concentrations. [000132] In an embodiment, the process enables production of battery-grade metal compounds and metallic products, suitable for reuse in battery manufacturing or other industrial applications. TECHNICAL ADVANCEMENTS AND NON-LIMITING ADVANTAGES OF THE INVENTION [000133] The present invention provides significant technical advancements over conventional hydrometallurgical processes for recovery of metals from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. These advancements arise from the integrated configuration of unit operations, the selective sequencing of separation stages, and the closed-loop reagent regeneration architecture, resulting in improved recovery efficiency, product quality, process sustainability, and economic viability. [000134] In an important aspect, the invention incorporates a pre-leaching magnesium removal step, which reduces the presence of interfering species prior to acid leaching. This results in reduced consumption of leaching reagents, minimizes formation of competing salts, and enhances the efficiency and selectivity of downstream solvent extraction stages. Additionally, recovery of magnesium as a separate product stream contributes to improved resource utilization. [000135] In another aspect, the invention employs a controlled and sequential separation strategy, wherein copper is first recovered by electrowinning, followed by precipitation of iron and aluminium impurities, and thereafter sequential solvent extraction of manganese and cobalt. This ordered arrangement enables progressive enrichment and selective isolation of metals, reduces co-extraction, and improves purity of individual product streams. In particular, selective extraction of manganese prior to cobalt enhances separation efficiency between these chemically similar metals. [000136] In a further aspect, the invention integrates multiple recovery pathways, including electrowinning, solvent extraction, controlled precipitation, oxidation, and reduction, within a single process framework. This enables conversion of dissolved metal species into high-value products, including electrolytic manganese dioxide, cobalt metal powder, lithium carbonate, metallic copper, metallic zinc, and magnesium carbonate. The ability to recover metals in value-added forms significantly enhances the overall economic potential of the process. [000137] In another important aspect, the invention provides a dedicated cobalt recovery pathway involving intermediate oxalate formation followed by reduction to metallic cobalt. This approach enables improved control over purity and morphology of cobalt product compared to conventional precipitation-based methods. [000138] In a further aspect, the process enables efficient recovery of lithium from downstream raffinate streams, thereby minimizing lithium losses and improving overall lithium recovery efficiency, which is often a limitation in conventional processes. [000139] In a significant advancement, the invention incorporates a reagent regeneration system based on bipolar membrane electrodialysis, which enables simultaneous recovery of acid and base streams from multiple spent process solutions. The regenerated acid is reused in leaching and stripping stages, while the regenerated base is reused in precipitation and neutralization steps. This establishes a circular reagent economy, significantly reducing fresh chemical consumption. [000140] In another aspect, the integration of reagent regeneration with upstream and downstream process units enables a closed-loop hydrometallurgical system, wherein process streams are internally recycled and reused. This configuration minimizes generation of secondary effluents and enables operation with substantially zero liquid discharge, thereby reducing environmental impact. [000141] In a further aspect, the process provides enhanced selectivity and separation efficiency through the use of differentiated extractant systems and controlled pH conditions, enabling effective separation of closely associated metals such as manganese and cobalt. [000142] In an additional aspect, the process enables consolidated handling of multiple spent solution streams, which are directed to a centralized regeneration unit, thereby simplifying process flow, reducing plant complexity, and improving operational efficiency. [000143] In another aspect, the process demonstrates high overall metal recovery efficiencies, including lithium recovery of greater than 90%, cobalt and copper recovery of greater than 95%, and manganese and zinc recovery at similarly high levels, achieved through the synergistic interaction of multiple integrated unit operations. [000144] In a further aspect, the process provides operational flexibility, allowing adaptation to variations in feed composition by adjusting process parameters without altering the overall process configuration. [000145] In addition, the integrated process design results in reduced sludge generation, lower waste handling requirements, and improved environmental compliance, further contributing to the sustainability of the process. [000146] From an economic standpoint, the invention enables higher revenue generation through recovery of metals in high-value forms, while simultaneously reducing operational costs through reagent regeneration, minimized fresh chemical input, and reduced effluent treatment requirements. [000147] Accordingly, the present invention provides a technically advanced, integrated, and sustainable hydrometallurgical process that overcomes limitations of conventional processes and enables efficient, selective, and environmentally responsible recovery of multiple metals from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. EXAMPLES [000148] The present invention is further explained in the form of the following examples. However, it is to be understood that the foregoing examples are merely illustrative and are not to be taken as limitations upon the scope of the invention. Various changes and modifications to the disclosed embodiments will be apparent to those skilled in the art. Such changes and modifications may be made without departing from the scope of the invention. The washing solution is treated with 10% excess sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) to precipitate magnesium. • Product: Magnesium carbonate (MgCO3) • Separation: Filtration and drying [000152] Step 2: Acid Leaching • Leaching agent: 1.8-2.2 M sulfuric acid (H2SO4) • Reducing agent: 1.5-2.5 wt% hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) • Temperature: 60-80°C • Time: 3-4 hours • Solid-to-liquid ratio: 1:7-1:9 [000153] Metals are dissolved to form sulfate salts in solution. [000154] Step 3: Solid-Liquid Separation • Method: Pressure filtration • Solid product: Graphite (~340–350 kg recovered) • Filtrate: Metal-bearing solution [000155] Step 4: Copper Electrowinning • Current density: 250±2.5 A/m² • Temperature: 40±5°C • Cathode: Stainless steel • Anode: Pb–Sn alloy • Product: ~78-80 kg copper metal plates [000156] Step 5: Iron and Aluminium Precipitation • Reagent: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH); O/A ratio: 1:1-2:1; pH: 4.2-4.6; Stages: 3-4 • Stripping: Stripping agent: 1.5-2 M H2SO4; Output: MnSO4 solution; Organic phase: Regenerated and recycled [000158] Step 7: Manganese Oxidation • Oxidant: Sodium persulfate (Na2S2O8); Temperature: 70-90°C; pH: 1.0-1.5 • Product: ~205-210 kg electrolytic manganese dioxide (EMD) [000159] Step 8: Cobalt Solvent Extraction • Extractant: 12-17% Cyanex 272 in kerosene • O/A ratio: 1.3-1.6:1.0 • pH: 5-6 • Temperature: 30-40°C [000160] Stripping: • Stripping agent: 1.5-2 M H2SO4 • Output: CoSO4 solution [000161] Step 9: Cobalt Oxalate Precipitation • Reagent: Oxalic acid (5–10% excess) • Temperature: 55-70°C • pH: 1.9-2.1 • Product: Cobalt oxalate (CoC2O4) [000162] Step 10: Reduction to Cobalt Metal • Temperature: 540-560°C • Atmosphere: H2 / Ar (reducing) • Time: 2-4 hours • Product: ~118-120 kg cobalt metal powder [000163] Step 11: Lithium Carbonate Precipitation • Reagent: Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) • Temperature: 80-90°C • pH: 10-11 • Product: ~300-320 kg lithium carbonate (Li2CO3) [000164] Step 12: Zinc Recovery • Method: Solvent extraction followed by electrowinning [000165] Electrowinning conditions: • Current density: 500±5 A/m² • Temperature: 35±5°C • Product: ~19-20 kg zinc metal [000166] Step 13: Reagent Regeneration (BMED) • Feed: Combined spent solutions (raffinates and wash streams) • Process: Bipolar membrane electrodialysis • Outputs: i. Regenerated sulfuric acid (recycled to leaching and stripping) ii. Regenerated sodium hydroxide (recycled to precipitation steps) [000167] Recovery Efficiency: Metal Feed (kg) Recovered Product Recovery (%) Lithium 60±6 320±16 kg Li₂CO₃ 92–95% Cobalt 120±12 118±5 kg Co metal 96–98% Manganese 150±15 210±10 kg MnO₂ 90–94% Copper 80±8 78±4 kg Cu metal 97–99% Zinc 20±2 19±2 kg Zn metal 95–98% [000168] The above example demonstrates that the integrated hydrometallurgical process enables efficient and selective recovery of multiple metals from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. [000169] The pre-removal of magnesium improves downstream processing efficiency, while the sequential separation strategy ensures minimal interference between metals and high purity of recovered products. patents.abstract: The invention relates to a scalable sol–gel process for fabricating LiMn1–xFexPO4 cathode materials that combines precise reaction control and uniform composition. A reaction vessel equipped with a magnetic stirrer and integrated heating element maintains a glycol solvent (e.g., a 1:1 mixture of ethylene glycol and propylene glycol) at about 50°C. Sequential addition of stoichiometric precursor salts including a lithium precursor (e.g., lithium hydroxide or carbonate), manganese precursor (e.g., manganese acetate or oxide), and iron precursor (e.g., iron oxalate or sulfate), as well as a phosphorus source (e.g., phosphoric acid or ammonium dihydrogen phosphate) added dropwise which forms a homogeneous sol. Continuous stirring promotes hydrolysis and polycondensation, followed by drying at 100°C under reduced pressure and calcining at 700°C under inert gas to crystallize the cathode phase, optionally followed by post-calcination grinding.
patents.complete_specification: Description:A METHOD FOR SCALABLE SOL–GEL SYNTHESIS OF LITHIUM MANGANESE IRON PHOSPHATE CATHODE MATERIALS FIELD OF THE INVENTION The invention relates generally to energy storage and battery technologies, and more particularly to a scalable one-step sol–gel synthesis process for high-purity lithium manganese iron phosphate cathode materials for advanced lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles, grid storage, and other high-energy applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The current state of the art in energy storage devices highlights the pressing need for electrode materials that combine high energy density with long-term durability, especially for demanding applications such as electric vehicles and grid energy storage. Traditional cathode materials, such as those based on nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM), are capable of delivering high capacities, often exceeding 180 mAh/g, but they tend to fall short in several critical areas. For instance, NCM electrodes generally offer only moderate electrochemical stability (approximately 1500 to 2000 cycles), which limits their overall longevity. Additionally, these materials typically operate at voltages below 4.2 V and display less-than-optimal thermal performance, factors that can lead to safety concerns and reduced energy efficiency under high-demand conditions. In contrast, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathodes are renowned for their excellent thermal and electrochemical stability, often exceeding 3000 cycles. However, LFP cathodes are hampered by low operating voltages, generally below 3.7 V, which restricts the overall energy density and limits their use in applications demanding high power output. To bridge the gap between these two approaches, multi-transition metal cathodes such as lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) have emerged as a promising alternative. LMFP cathode materials aim to harness the thermal and cycle life advantages of LFP while also achieving higher operating voltages, sometimes exceeding 4.5 V and enhanced rate capabilities (greater than 4C). This balance makes LMFP particularly attractive for next-generation high-performance batteries. Despite their potential, the synthesis of multi-transition metal cathodes like LMFP has posed significant challenges. Traditional techniques used for synthesizing these materials including sol–gel processing, ball milling, and extended autoclave heat treatments, each come with inherent drawbacks: 1. Energy Intensity: Ball milling and prolonged heat treatments require substantial energy input. The high-energy processing conditions translate into increased production costs and environmental concerns, as these processes demand significant power and often result in elevated operating temperatures. 2. Prolonged Processing Times: Methods such as autoclave heat treatments and certain multi-stage sol–gel processes can have lengthy durations. The extended processing times reduce throughput and make it difficult to scale production efficiently for industrial applications. 3. Complex Multi-Stage Procedures: Many existing synthesis methods involve intricate, stepwise processes that require careful control over precursor selection, solvent choices, and reaction conditions. This multi-stage complexity not only increases the likelihood of processing inconsistencies but also creates challenges in ensuring uniformity and reproducibility in the final electrode material. 4. Strict Precursor and Solvent Requirements: The success of these traditional methods often hinges on the precise use of specific precursor salts and solvents. The narrow range of acceptable materials restricts the adaptability of the synthesis process, limiting its versatility and driving up production costs in large-scale manufacturing contexts. These challenges together impede the ability to consistently produce high-yield, high-purity LMFP materials suitable for next-generation energy storage devices. The need for an improved synthesis method is therefore required which can deliver the benefits of high energy density, robust thermal and electrochemical stability, and scalability while addressing the drawbacks of energy intensity, time consumption, process complexity, and rigidity in precursor selection inherent in prior art methods. In summary, while multi-transition metal cathodes like LMFP hold significant promise for high-performance battery applications, there remains a critical need for a synthesis approach that overcomes the limitations of prior art techniques. The invention addressed herein seeks to resolve these issues by introducing a streamlined, scalable sol–gel process that minimizes energy consumption, simplifies the synthesis steps, and enhances the overall adaptability and environmental compatibility of the production method. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION Object of the invention is to provide a simplified, two‐step synthesis process based on a modified sol–gel method that eliminates the need for energy‐intensive ball milling and autoclave treatments, thereby streamlining the production of LiMn1–xFexPO4 cathode materials. Another object of the invention is to provide molecular-level homogeneous mixing of metal precursors including those for lithium, manganese, iron, and phosphorus ensuring a uniform dispersion through controlled mixing and stirring, which leads to a high-purity three-dimensional gel network prior to thermal treatment. Yet another object of the invention is to provide precursor flexibility by accommodating a wide range of lithium, manganese, and iron salts (such as hydroxides, carbonates, nitrates, acetates, sulphates, oxalates, and chlorides), thereby enabling fine-tuning of reaction conditions without compromising yield or purity. Another object of the invention is to provide an environmentally compatible and economically advantageous process through the utilization of non-toxic, eco-friendly solvents such as propylene glycol in combination with ethylene glycol, thus reducing hazardous impacts and production costs. A further object of the invention is to provide low energy consumption and time-efficient processing by employing moderate mixing temperatures (approximately 50°C for 4 hours), a rapid drying stage (at 100°C for 5 hours), and a single-step calcination process (700°C for 12 hours) under a controlled inert gas environment. Yet another object of the invention is to provide controlled thermal treatment and crystallization that, under a continuous inert gas flow, promotes nucleation and growth of the LiMn1–xFexPO4 phase, resulting in a cathode material with excellent electrochemical performance and stability. Another object of the invention is to provide a scalable and robust synthesis method that consistently achieves high yields (exceeding 95%) and high purity (greater than 99%), making the process adaptable for industrial manufacturing of next-generation energy storage devices. Embodiments of the present invention provide a method for scalable sol–gel synthesis of lithium manganese iron phosphate cathode materials. The method comprises providing a reaction vessel with a magnetic stirrer and an integrated heating element that is maintained at an elevated temperature of approximately 50°C, and introducing into the reaction vessel a glycol solvent selected from the group comprising ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, or a mixture thereof. The method further comprises sequentially adding stoichiometrically measured precursor salts comprising a lithium precursor, a manganese precursor, an iron precursor, and a phosphorus source, wherein the lithium precursor is added first, followed by the manganese and iron precursors, and the phosphorus source is added dropwise to yield a homogeneous sol; the resultant sol is then continuously stirred to promote hydrolysis and polycondensation reactions that form a three-dimensional metal phosphate gel network. The process proceeds by transferring the formed gel to a drying unit where it is dried at approximately 100°C at atmospheric pressure for about 5 hours to effect solvent removal; thereafter, the dried gel is calcined at approximately 700°C for about 12 hours in a calcination furnace to crystallize the lithium manganese iron phosphate phase, with an optional further step of processing the calcined material in a post-calcination grinding module to produce a fine powder suitable for use as a cathode material. The process requires a continuous flow only until the calcination temperature stabilizes at 700 °C (initial period). The technical advantages conferred by the present invention primarily reside in the uniform molecular-level mixing enabled by the sol–gel process, which ensures that the reactive metal ions are precisely combined to yield a pure and crystalline LiMn1–xFexPO4 phase with high yield and purity. Additionally, the method provides significant improvements in energy efficiency and processing time, using moderate temperature conditions during mixing, drying, and calcination; the flexible selection of precursor salts and environmentally compatible glycol solvents contributes to enhanced economic viability and industrial scalability. The controlled inert atmosphere during the calcination step further prevents oxidation, thus ensuring the production of a thermally and chemically stable cathode material ideal for lithium-ion battery applications. The present invention relates to a novel sol–gel synthesis method for the production of lithium manganese iron phosphate cathode materials. The invention involves a simplified synthesis technique based on molecular-level chemical reactions resulting in a homogeneous metal phosphate network and further crystallization by controlled thermal treatments. The process allows the use of a variety of precursor salts and environmentally safe glycol solvents, thereby providing high purity and yield in a time‐ and energy‐efficient manner while being adaptable to industrial scale production. The Invention provides a scalable, high yield, high purity process to synthesize LMFP electrodes via a one-pot, two-step process. The method is precursor and solvent flexible, environmental and energy efficient. The process can be readily scaled to industrial synthesis of high energy density cathode for LIB applications. In an embodiment, the invention provides an economical and scalable synthesis methodology to produce high energy density cathode material, for lithium-ion batteries. The process uses a one pot sol-gel technique, involving a non-toxic and environment friendly solvent. The method is independent of the anionic composition of the precursor cation (Li, Fe, Mn) material. The method produces high yield (> 95%, gravimetric) and high purity (> 99%, via XRD). The invention can yield different combination of LiMn1-xFexPO4 (LMFP) cathode compositions via a two-step scalable methodology for high energy density batteries with EV and grid energy storage applications. The present invention addresses the synthesis of cathode material for lithium-ion batteries, particularly synthesis of LiMn1-xFexPO4 (LMFP) through modified sol-gel technique. The reported technique involves only one mixing-drying step prior to calcination. A wide variety of precursors can be employed in the synthesis of cathode electrode material. The method produces LiMn1-xFexPO4 with high yield (> 95%, gravimetric) and high purity (> 99%, via XRD). This makes it viable technique for industrial adoption, without the requirement of specialized apparatus. The method is environmental, requiring non-toxic precursors. The invention achieves a high degree of uniformity by dissolving stoichiometrically measured precursor salts of lithium, manganese, and iron together with a phosphorus source in a glycol solvent. This homogeneous mixing is accomplished by initially preheating the glycol solvent, selected from ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, or their 1:1 mixture, to approximately 50°C while continuously stirring in a reaction vessel equipped with a magnetic stirrer and integrated heating element. The sequential addition of precursors, wherein the lithium precursor is added first followed by the manganese and iron precursors and finally the phosphorus source is introduced dropwise, ensures that hydrolysis and polycondensation reactions occur uniformly, thus forming a three-dimensional gel network. This controlled mixing and reaction condition constitutes an important aspect of the invention. In one embodiment, the process initiates with a solvent and mixing assembly. A reaction vessel is arranged with a heating element to maintain the glycol solvent at an elevated temperature of around 50°C. The stirring action provided by a magnetic stirrer facilitates uniform distribution of metal ions once the lithium precursor, such as lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate, is introduced into the solvent. The precursor feed system is then engaged when manganese and iron precursors, for example manganese acetate or manganese oxide and iron oxalate or iron sulfate, are added sequentially to the solution. The phosphorus source, chosen from phosphoric acid or ammonium dihydrogen phosphate, is carefully administered dropwise over a period to ensure that no localized concentration imbalances occur, thereby promoting complete interaction and formation of the sol. The sol formation stage occurs within the same reaction vessel, where continuous stirring for approximately 4 hours leads to hydrolysis and polycondensation reactions. These reactions cause the formation of a uniform three-dimensional metal phosphate network (gel) that exhibits the desired stoichiometric ratio of Li:Mn:Fe:P. The uniform molecular dispersion attained in this stage is critical to obtaining a high-purity intermediate phase, which is then subjected to subsequent processing. The described embodiment of the sol formation is intimately connected with the precursor feed system, in that the order and timing of precursor addition are essential to achieving the homogeneous sol. Following formation of the homogeneous sol, the process further comprises a drying unit wherein the gel is transferred into a vacuum oven. The drying unit is configured to operate at a temperature of about 100°C at atmospheric condition for approximately 5 hours. Such conditions are selected to rapidly remove solvent molecules while preventing any re-aggregation or segregation of the distributed metal ions. The drying step is designed to protect the integrity of the gel structure such that the uniform distribution of metal constituents is retained, thereby facilitating subsequent high-temperature treatments. The dried gel is subsequently moved into a high-temperature calcination furnace which, in an embodiment, comprises an alumina crucible placed within a tube furnace designed with multiple inlets for inert gases. In an embodiment, the process may be carried out using any conventional tube furnace, and no specialized or custom-designed furnace is required. The tube furnace may include a single inlet or a plurality of inlets, and the process can be effectively performed irrespective of the number or configuration of inlets. The furnace is ramped to a temperature of approximately 700°C and maintained at this temperature for around 12 hours under a continuous flow of an inert gas (such as nitrogen or a predetermined argon–hydrogen mixture) till stable 700 degree Celsius calcination temperature is achieved. The inert gas delivery and control system serves to create an oxygen-deficient environment which is vital for preventing unwanted oxidation during crystallization. This thermal treatment initiates the nucleation and growth of crystalline LiMn1–xFexPO4, wherein x may vary from 0 to 1 according to the desired material properties. The calcination step results in a product exhibiting high purity (greater than 99%) with a yield exceeding 95%, thus underscoring the efficacy of the method. After completion of the calcination, the invention further contemplates a post-calcination grinding module. In this embodiment, the calcined material, still maintained in an inert atmosphere until cooled, is transferred to a grinding apparatus. The grinding module is configured to gently reduce the material into a fine powder while preserving the crystalline integrity attained during calcination. The resulting cathode material exhibits a particle size distribution suitable for use in lithium-ion battery applications. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the lithium precursor is selected from the group comprising lithium hydroxide, lithium carbonate, and mixtures thereof, thereby providing flexibility in precursor selection without compromising the stoichiometry or quality of the final product. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the manganese precursor is selected from the group comprising manganese acetate, manganese oxide, and mixtures thereof, which facilitates the formation of intermediate complexes essential for homogeneous mixing. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the iron precursor is selected from the group comprising iron oxalate, iron sulfate, and mixtures thereof, thereby ensuring that the iron ions are uniformly distributed within the sol. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the phosphorus source is selected from the group comprising phosphoric acid and ammonium dihydrogen phosphate, providing a controlled source for phosphate ions during gel network formation. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the glycol solvent comprises a 1:1 mixture of ethylene glycol and propylene glycol, which not only acts as an effective reaction medium but also enhances the environmental and economic viability of the process. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the dropwise addition of the phosphorus source is carried out over a period ranging from 30 minutes to 2 hours to promote uniform sol formation; additionally, this controlled addition ensures that local concentration imbalances are minimized during the reaction. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the stoichiometric ratios of the lithium, manganese, and iron precursors are adjusted to yield a final composition of LiMn1–xFexPO4, wherein x ranges from 0 to 1, thus allowing the tailoring of the cathode material’s properties as required. In an embodiment, the lithium precursor is supplied in an amount 10% greater than the stoichiometric requirement. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the calcination step is performed under a continuous flow of inert gas till stable 700 degree Celsius calcination temperature is achieved. The inert gas is selected from the group comprising nitrogen and an argon–hydrogen mixture; additionally, the inert gas flow maintains an oxygen-deficient environment to suppress unwanted oxidation during the high-temperature treatment. In accordance with an embodiment of the present invention, the stirring of the sol is maintained for a period of approximately 4 hours to ensure molecular-level homogeneous mixing of the metal ions prior to gel formation; additionally, this extended stirring period fosters the optimal progression of hydrolysis and polycondensation reactions that are critical for forming a uniformly distributed gel network poised for subsequent processing. Alternative embodiments of the invention include variations in the precursor salt selections, allowing for salts such as carbonates, nitrates, acetates, sulphates, oxalates, and chlorides, so that the process is adaptable for different industrial needs without sacrificing product quality. In another embodiment, the solvent system may comprise either ethylene glycol or propylene glycol individually, or their mixtures, with propylene glycol imparting environmentally compatible features which are beneficial for reducing ecological impact. The invention also allows modifications to the duration and order of addition of the precursors which may be optimized according to specific industrial requirements. An embodiment of the present invention further contemplates the integration of the aforementioned components into a process line where the output of one processing unit serves as the input to the next, thereby streamlining the synthesis and reducing both processing time and energy demand. Variation in the process parameters, such as the stirring duration, temperature profiles, and drying times, may be adjusted without deviating from the core inventive concept of achieving uniform molecular mixing and high-purity crystallization. Similarly, the choice of inert gas and its flow rate during the calcination process are subject to optimization based on the available equipment and desired material properties. The technical advantages of the invention arise from the synergistic interaction among the components and processing steps wherein the simplified two-step process involving mixing with controlled stirring at moderate temperature followed by vacuum drying and a single-step calcination – eliminates the need for more complex and energy-intensive procedures such as ball milling or prolonged autoclave treatments. The process versatility in terms of precursor flexibility, solvent selection, and process timing not only enhances the reproducibility of the final cathode material but also renders the invention highly adaptable for large-scale industrial applications. This leads to a substantially reduced synthesis time and lower energy consumption while concurrently achieving high-quality lithium manganese iron phosphate materials suitable for next-generation battery technologies. patents.abstract: A split metallic casing for a lithium-ion battery pack is disclosed, comprising diagonally separable base sections and a removable top cover secured using countersunk screws. The configuration enables non-destructive disassembly and removal of a battery cell pack encapsulated with silicone based potting material. The design improves serviceability, safety, and reusability of the battery enclosure while eliminating the need for mechanical cutting.

patents.abstract: The present invention discloses an electro-optically tunable ultrashort pulse shaping system configured as an integrated device for precision laser-assisted neurosurgical applications. The system comprises an ultrafast laser source, a beam conditioning unit, and a Lithium Niobate crystal-based electro-optic modulation arrangement coupled with a programmable voltage control unit. By applying controlled electric fields across the crystal, the system induces refractive index variations that enable dynamic modulation of pulse duration, phase, chirp, and peak intensity in real time. A pulse shaping processor executes a control technique to generate adaptive voltage waveforms based on desired pulse characteristics and feedback from tissue interaction. The shaped pulses are delivered through a beam delivery unit integrated with a neurosurgical probe to achieve highly localized and controlled energy deposition. The invention enables enhanced surgical precision, reduced thermal damage, and improved safety, thereby advancing minimally invasive neurosurgical procedures through real-time adaptive laser pulse control.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of laser-based biomedical engineering and, more particularly, to electro-optic control systems for ultrafast laser pulse modulation. Specifically, the invention pertains to a Lithium Niobate crystal-based electro-optically tunable ultrashort pulse shaping device configured for integration with laser-assisted neurosurgical instruments. The invention further relates to precision optical systems capable of dynamically controlling temporal and spectral characteristics of femtosecond laser pulses for applications involving high-resolution tissue interaction, including minimally invasive neurosurgery, neural tissue ablation, and microsurgical procedures requiring real-time adaptive laser modulation. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The present invention pertains to advanced laser pulse engineering systems designed for biomedical and neurosurgical applications, wherein ultrashort laser pulses are employed to achieve highly localized tissue interaction with minimal collateral damage. Neural tissues exhibit extreme sensitivity to thermal diffusion and mechanical perturbations, thereby necessitating surgical tools capable of delivering energy with sub-micron spatial confinement and ultrafast temporal precision. Femtosecond laser systems have emerged as promising tools in this domain; however, conventional systems are typically configured with fixed pulse characteristics, limiting adaptability in dynamic surgical environments characterized by heterogeneous tissue properties such as varying refractive indices, densities, and vascular structures. Existing pulse shaping and compression techniques rely on static nonlinear optical components, including fibers and diffraction gratings, which lack real-time tunability and are unsuitable for responsive surgical modulation. Lithium Niobate (LiNbO₃), a nonlinear optical crystal exhibiting strong electro-optic coefficients, high optical transparency, and high damage thresholds, has been utilized in optical modulation applications, but its integration into dynamically tunable neurosurgical pulse shaping systems remains underdeveloped. Accordingly, there exists a technical need for an electro optically controllable ultrashort pulse shaping system capable of real-time modulation of pulse duration, phase, and intensity to enhance surgical precision and safety. Laser-assisted neurosurgery has evolved significantly with the advent of ultrafast laser systems, particularly femtosecond pulse lasers, which enable highly localized energy deposition and precise tissue ablation with minimal thermal diffusion. These systems are widely used in delicate neurological procedures such as tumor resection, neural pathway dissection, and minimally invasive microsurgery. Conventional femtosecond laser platforms typically rely on fixed pulse durations and pre-configured temporal profiles, which are optimized for general use but lack adaptability to the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of neural tissues. Biological tissues in the brain exhibit significant variability in optical properties, including refractive index, absorption coefficients, and scattering behavior, which change depending on tissue type, vascularization, and physiological conditions. As a result, fixed-parameter laser systems often fail to deliver optimal performance across varying intraoperative scenarios, leading to suboptimal precision and potential collateral damage. To address pulse control requirements, existing solutions have employed passive pulse shaping and compression techniques using nonlinear optical elements such as diffraction gratings, prism pairs, chirped mirrors, and optical fibers. While these components can manipulate pulse duration and dispersion characteristics, they are inherently static in nature and require manual calibration prior to operation. Once configured, these systems do not allow real-time adjustment of pulse characteristics, making them unsuitable for responsive surgical environments where tissue interaction conditions continuously evolve. Furthermore, fiber-based nonlinear compression techniques are susceptible to optical losses, nonlinear distortions, and limited damage thresholds, which can degrade pulse quality and reduce system efficiency. Similarly, grating-based systems are bulky, alignment-sensitive, and prone to mechanical instability, thereby limiting their integration into compact surgical instruments. Another class of existing solutions involves acousto-optic and liquid crystal-based modulators for pulse shaping. Although these technologies provide a degree of programmability, they suffer from limited modulation speeds, restricted bandwidth, and relatively low damage thresholds when subjected to high-intensity ultrashort pulses. Additionally, these systems introduce insertion losses and complexity in optical alignment, which can adversely affect overall system reliability in clinical settings. The latency associated with such modulation techniques further restricts their applicability in real-time surgical feedback systems, where rapid adaptation of laser parameters is critical. Lithium Niobate (LiNbO₃) has been extensively studied as a nonlinear optical material due to its strong electro-optic (Pockels) effect, high transparency in the near-infrared region, and robust physical properties. It has been utilized in telecommunications for phase modulation and signal processing; however, its application in dynamic ultrashort pulse shaping for biomedical systems remains limited. Existing implementations of LiNbO₃-based modulators are primarily designed for continuous-wave or long-pulse regimes and are not optimized for high-peak-power femtosecond pulses required in neurosurgery. Moreover, conventional electro-optic modulators lack integration with surgical delivery systems and do not provide synchronized control between optical modulation and surgical operation. A further limitation in current technologies is the absence of closed-loop or adaptive control mechanisms that can modify pulse characteristics based on real-time feedback from tissue interaction. Most systems operate in an open-loop configuration, where parameters are predefined and remain unchanged during the procedure. This restricts the surgeon’s ability to respond to variations in tissue response, increasing the risk of unintended thermal damage, shockwave effects, and imprecise ablation. Accordingly, despite advancements in ultrafast laser technology, existing pulse shaping solutions suffer from limitations including lack of real-time tunability, bulky and complex optical configurations, susceptibility to optical losses and damage, and poor integration with surgical devices. These drawbacks highlight the need for a dynamically controllable, compact, and integrated electro-optic pulse shaping system capable of delivering precise, adaptive, and high-speed modulation of ultrashort laser pulses for advanced neurosurgical applications. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention discloses a device-integrated electro-optically tunable ultrashort pulse shaping system configured for incorporation into a laser-assisted neurosurgical apparatus. The system comprises a femtosecond laser source operatively coupled with a Lithium Niobate crystal-based electro-optic modulation unit, wherein dynamic control of pulse characteristics is achieved through externally applied electric fields. The device architecture enables modulation of refractive indices within the LiNbO₃ crystal, thereby inducing controlled phase shifts and nonlinear interactions that facilitate pulse compression, temporal reshaping, and chirp regulation. The invention further provides a high-voltage control subsystem configured to generate programmable electric fields across electrode structures associated with the crystal, enabling real-time adjustment of pulse parameters in response to intraoperative conditions. The system is structurally integrated with beam conditioning optics and a neurosurgical probe assembly, forming a cohesive machine/device capable of delivering precisely shaped ultrashort pulses to targeted neural regions. This configuration allows surgeons to dynamically tailor laser-tissue interaction based on procedural requirements, thereby minimizing thermal damage, improving accuracy, and enabling minimally invasive neurosurgical interventions. Yet another object is to improve overall clinical outcomes by delivering highly controlled, reproducible, and precise laser energy deposition at sub-micron spatial scales, thereby advancing the field of laser-assisted neurosurgery through enhanced accuracy, efficiency, and patient safety.
