To achieve this with high precision, the processor relies on a calibrated mapping between applied voltage and induced phase shift, taking into account the electro-optic coefficients of the Lithium Niobate crystal and the effective interaction length. Additionally, synchronization mechanisms ensure that the timing of the applied electric field aligns with the arrival of corresponding spectral components, which is particularly important when dealing with complex or higher-order phase profiles. Fine adjustments may also be introduced iteratively based on feedback measurements to correct residual phase errors. In a representative scenario, a pulse that has been intentionally stretched to several hundred femtoseconds using a dispersive grating pair can be recompressed within the crystal by applying a complementary electro-optic phase profile. As the pulse exits the crystal, the spectral components converge temporally to produce a significantly shorter pulse with increased peak intensity. This controlled recombination enables restoration of near-transform-limited pulse duration without requiring additional bulk optical compressors, thereby reducing system complexity and insertion losses. The overall result is a coordinated interaction between passive spectral conditioning and active electro-optic modulation, enabling precise control over spectral phase and temporal structure of ultrafast pulses. This approach allows efficient correction of complex dispersion profiles and supports applications requiring high peak intensities and temporal precision, such as deep-tissue optical stimulation, nonlinear imaging, and ultrafast spectroscopy, while maintaining stability and repeatability across varying operational conditions. In an embodiment, the pulse shaping processor regulates the voltage control unit to generate voltage waveforms having transition intervals shorter than a transit time of the laser pulse through the Lithium Niobate crystal, and wherein multiple voltage transitions are applied during propagation of a single pulse through the crystal, such that different longitudinal segments of the pulse encounter different electric field magnitudes at different spatial positions within the crystal, producing a distributed modulation of instantaneous frequency across the pulse duration, and wherein the beam delivery unit directs the shaped ultrashort pulses through the focusing optics to produce a focal region within neural tissue, and wherein the pulse shaping processor coordinates the applied electric field with a focal depth parameter by adjusting the temporal compression profile of the pulses through modulation of the voltage waveform, such that pulses intended for deeper focal regions are subjected to a different temporal compression sequence relative to pulses intended for shallower regions, based on optical path variation through the tissue. In this embodiment, the pulse shaping processor drives the voltage control unit in a manner that deliberately introduces multiple rapid transitions in the applied electric field within a time window shorter than the transit duration of a single femtosecond pulse through the Lithium Niobate crystal. In practice, the crystal length and group velocity of light define a finite transit time—for example, a few picoseconds for millimeter-scale propagation—while the voltage waveform is engineered with transition intervals in the sub-picosecond regime. This ensures that as the optical pulse propagates longitudinally through the crystal, the electrical field experienced by the pulse is not static but evolves dynamically during traversal. Consequently, different temporal portions of the same pulse encounter different electric field magnitudes at different spatial positions inside the crystal, effectively coupling temporal segmentation with spatial propagation. To implement this, the processor generates a high-speed waveform in which voltage transitions—such as rapid increases, decreases, or shaped ramps—are scheduled at intervals shorter than the optical transit time. These transitions are synchronized with the expected arrival of specific temporal slices of the pulse at corresponding positions within the crystal. Because the electro-optic effect directly links electric field strength to refractive index variation, each transition alters the instantaneous phase velocity experienced by the pulse at that moment and location. As a result, the pulse undergoes a distributed modulation of its instantaneous frequency, where the frequency chirp is not applied uniformly but varies continuously along the pulse duration as it propagates. This enables fine control over intra-pulse frequency structure, allowing selective stretching or compression of different temporal regions within a single pulse. The beam delivery unit subsequently directs the modulated pulse through a focusing optical system, such as a high numerical aperture lens assembly, to generate a localized focal region within neural tissue. At this stage, the temporal profile of the pulse directly influences the spatial distribution of optical energy due to dispersion and scattering effects within the tissue. Recognizing this, the pulse shaping processor incorporates a focal depth parameter into its control logic. This parameter represents the intended depth of the focal region and is associated with known optical path variations, refractive index heterogeneity, and dispersion characteristics of the intervening tissue. Based on the selected focal depth, the processor adjusts the temporal compression profile of the pulse by modifying the timing, amplitude, and density of voltage transitions within the waveform. For deeper focal regions, where pulses experience greater dispersion and temporal broadening during propagation through tissue, the processor configures a waveform that induces stronger or more prolonged phase compensation, such as introducing additional high-amplitude transitions or extending modulation over a longer portion of the pulse. Conversely, for shallower focal regions with minimal dispersion effects, a reduced or simplified modulation sequence is applied to preserve pulse integrity without overcompensation. This depth-dependent modulation strategy allows the system to deliver pulses that arrive at the focal region with a controlled temporal width and peak intensity tailored to the specific interaction depth. For example, a pulse intended for a deeper neural layer may be pre-conditioned with a complex multi-transition waveform that compresses the pulse at the target depth despite intermediate dispersion, whereas a pulse for a superficial layer may require only minimal shaping to maintain optimal focus. By enabling multiple voltage transitions within a single pulse transit and coordinating these transitions with spatial targeting parameters, the system achieves a tightly coupled control over both temporal and spatial energy distribution. This leads to improved confinement of optical energy at the intended focal region, enhances interaction precision within neural structures, and reduces unintended spread to surrounding, thereby supporting highly selective and efficient photonic stimulation or intervention. The electro-optically tunable ultrashort pulse shaping system is constituted entirely of physically realizable hardware elements arranged to perform deterministic electro-optical interactions without reliance on abstract or non-physical constructs. The ultrafast laser source is implemented using a gain medium, resonant cavity structure, and optical pumping arrangement configured to emit femtosecond pulses. The beam conditioning unit comprises discrete optical components including collimating lenses, optical isolators with polarization-dependent transmission characteristics, and mechanically adjustable alignment optics mounted on rigid supports to maintain spatial beam stability. The Lithium Niobate crystal is a solid-state electro-optic medium having a defined crystallographic orientation and electrode-coated surfaces forming a capacitive structure across which an external electric field is physically established. The electrode arrangement consists of conductive layers deposited with controlled thickness and spacing to generate a uniform electric field distribution through direct electrical excitation. The voltage control unit includes a high-voltage generation stage comprising power electronic switching elements, energy storage components, and analog drive circuitry configured to produce time-resolved electrical waveforms that are physically applied to the electrodes. The pulse shaping processor is realized as a dedicated electronic control circuit comprising timing generators, signal conditioning circuitry, and hardware logic configured to produce synchronized electrical control signals governing the voltage application sequence. The beam delivery unit incorporates focusing optics fabricated from optical-grade materials and a mechanically rigid neurosurgical probe structure including alignment fixtures and damping elements to physically direct and stabilize the shaped laser beam onto neural tissue. Referring to Figure 3, a flow chart of method for electro-optically shaping ultrashort laser pulses for neurosurgical applications is illustrated. The method 300 comprising: At step 302, the method 300 includes generating, by an ultrafast laser source, a sequence of femtosecond laser pulses having initial temporal characteristics; At step 304, the method 300 conditioning, by a beam conditioning unit, the generated laser pulses to achieve spatial coherence and stable propagation; At step 306, the method 300 directing the conditioned pulses through a Lithium Niobate crystal positioned along an optical path; At step 308, the method 300 applying, by an electrode arrangement and a voltage control unit, a controlled electric field across the Lithium Niobate crystal to induce refractive index modulation; At step 310, the method 300 modulating, by a pulse shaping processor, the electric field in a programmable manner to alter temporal characteristics of the pulses including duration, phase, chirp, and peak intensity; At step 312, the method 300 compressing or reshaping the pulses through electro-optic interaction within the Lithium Niobate crystal; and At step 314, the method 300 delivering, by a beam delivery unit including a neurosurgical probe, the shaped ultrashort pulses onto targeted neural tissue to achieve precise and minimally invasive surgical effects. Referring to Figure 1, the present invention provides a structurally integrated electro-optic pulse shaping device embodied as a neurosurgical laser delivery machine comprising a housing structure enclosing an ultrafast laser generation module, an electro-optic modulation module, a control electronics subsystem, and a beam delivery assembly. The ultrafast laser generation module is configured to produce femtosecond pulses, typically of approximately 150 femtoseconds duration, which are directed through a beam conditioning unit comprising collimators, optical isolators, and alignment optics to ensure stable propagation and spatial coherence. The conditioned beam is subsequently introduced into a nonlinear optical medium constituted by a Lithium Niobate crystal mounted within an electro-optic modulation chamber. The Lithium Niobate crystal is provided with electrode interfaces disposed along predefined crystallographic orientations, enabling application of an external electric field across the crystal lattice. The electrodes are electrically coupled to a programmable high-voltage control unit capable of delivering rapid voltage variations over a defined operational range, thereby inducing refractive index modulation via the Pockels effect. This electro-optic interaction alters the phase velocity of propagating optical pulses, resulting in controllable chirp and temporal reshaping of the pulse envelope. The induced refractive index variation is governed by the electro-optic coefficient of the crystal and the magnitude of the applied electric field, enabling precise manipulation of pulse characteristics. The device further comprises a pulse compression and shaping subsystem wherein cascaded second-order nonlinear interactions within the Lithium Niobate crystal facilitate reduction of pulse duration from approximately 150 femtoseconds to sub-50 femtosecond regimes, thereby enhancing peak intensity without increasing total energy exposure. This temporal compression is dynamically adjustable in real time through modulation of the applied electric field, allowing adaptive control during surgical procedures. The shaped optical pulses are subsequently transmitted through a beam delivery assembly comprising focusing optics, waveguides, and protective optical interfaces, all structurally integrated within a neurosurgical probe. The probe is configured as a handheld or robotic-assisted surgical instrument capable of directing the modulated laser pulses onto targeted neural tissue with high spatial precision. The mechanical structure of the probe ensures vibration isolation, thermal stability, and ergonomic handling, thereby enabling consistent and reproducible surgical performance. The device architecture operates as a closed-loop system wherein pulse shaping parameters may be adjusted based on intraoperative feedback, including tissue response, depth of penetration, and procedural requirements. The electro-optic control eliminates the need for mechanical adjustment mechanisms, thereby enhancing system responsiveness and reliability. The integration of optical, electrical, and mechanical subsystems within a unified device structure allows seamless incorporation into existing neurosurgical platforms without substantial modification. In operation, the system enables selective ablation of neural tissues, precise dissection of neural pathways, and bloodless microsurgical interventions by confining energy deposition to sub-micron volumes. The dynamically tunable pulse shaping capability minimizes thermal diffusion, reduces shockwave-induced damage, and preserves surrounding healthy tissue. The invention thus provides a significant advancement in neurosurgical instrumentation by combining electro-optic modulation with ultrafast laser technology in a structurally integrated device capable of real-time adaptive control, thereby improving surgical precision, safety, and clinical outcomes. Referring to the claimed system, the present invention provides an electro-optically tunable ultrashort pulse shaping device in which optical propagation, electrical actuation, and computational control are co-operatively integrated to achieve real-time modulation of femtosecond laser pulses for neurosurgical applications. In operation, the ultrafast laser source generates a temporally stable train of input pulses which are first conditioned by the beam conditioning unit to ensure collimation, phase uniformity, and suppression of back reflections. The conditioned optical signal is directed into the Lithium Niobate crystal unit, wherein electro-optic interaction is induced through an externally applied electric field generated by the voltage control unit via the electrode arrangement. The pulse shaping processor governs the entire modulation process through a closed-loop control technique that dynamically determines the required electrical excitation profile based on predefined pulse shaping objectives and, where available, real-time feedback derived from tissue interaction. The control technique implemented within the pulse shaping processor begins by acquiring an initial pulse characterization dataset, which includes temporal width, spectral bandwidth, phase distribution, and peak intensity of the incoming laser pulse. This dataset may be obtained through calibration measurements or through integrated optical sensing elements positioned along the beam path. Based on the acquired parameters, the processor computes a target pulse profile corresponding to a desired surgical mode, such as high-precision ablation or controlled dissection. The processor then executes a transformation routine in which the difference between the initial pulse characteristics and the target pulse characteristics is mapped into a required refractive index modulation profile within the Lithium Niobate crystal. This mapping is achieved through a deterministic control function that correlates electric field strength, polarity, and temporal variation with induced phase shift and chirp modulation. Subsequently, the processor generates a time-dependent voltage control signal, which is transmitted to the voltage control unit. The voltage control unit, in turn, produces high-voltage electrical waveforms that are applied across the electrode arrangement, thereby establishing a spatially uniform yet temporally varying electric field across the Lithium Niobate crystal. The electro-optic effect within the crystal results in a controlled variation of refractive index, which introduces a phase modulation across the propagating optical pulse. This phase modulation is engineered such that spectral components of the pulse experience differential delays, thereby enabling compression, stretching, or reshaping of the pulse in accordance with the computed target profile. The technique further incorporates an iterative refinement routine, particularly in embodiments where feedback signals are available. Optical or opto-acoustic sensors positioned proximate to the beam delivery unit capture signals indicative of tissue response, including scattering intensity, absorption characteristics, or ablation thresholds. These signals are digitized and transmitted back to the pulse shaping processor, where a feedback analysis routine evaluates deviations between expected and actual interaction outcomes. Based on this evaluation, the processor updates the control function parameters and recalculates the voltage waveform required to achieve improved conformity to the desired pulse profile. This iterative adjustment occurs in real time, enabling continuous adaptation of pulse characteristics during surgical procedures. Additionally, the technique incorporates safety and stability constraints to prevent excessive electric field application or unintended pulse distortion. Threshold conditions are defined within the processor to limit voltage amplitude, rate of change, and pulse energy, thereby ensuring safe operation within the damage tolerance of both the Lithium Niobate crystal and biological tissue. The processor also compensates for dispersion effects introduced by preceding optical components by pre-adjusting the phase modulation profile, thereby ensuring that the output pulse achieves the intended temporal compression at the target site. The shaped pulse exiting the Lithium Niobate crystal is then transmitted through the beam delivery unit, where focusing optics and structural alignment elements ensure precise targeting onto neural tissue via the neurosurgical probe. Due to the techniqueically controlled electro-optic modulation, the delivered pulse exhibits optimized temporal duration, peak intensity, and phase coherence, resulting in highly localized energy deposition. This enables selective ablation, reduced thermal diffusion, and minimal collateral damage. The integrated technique thus provides a high-speed, adaptive control mechanism that transforms static ultrafast laser sources into dynamically tunable surgical tools, significantly enhancing precision, repeatability, and clinical effectiveness in neurosurgical interventions. patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a system (100) and a method (800) for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell. The system (100) includes one or more processors (104) and a memory (106) storing instructions that cause the one or more processors (104) to control, via an equipment interface (108), test equipment (110) to apply a partial charge/discharge protocol and acquire snippet test data including voltage measurements and time information. The one or more processors (104) normalize the snippet test data by interpolation and resampling into a fixed set of points, generate a feature vector including a voltage-drift feature computed based on comparison to a reference curve (230), select a capacity-estimation model based on an initial voltage and/or a data-quality condition, and generate an estimated usable capacity or a capacity class.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure generally relates to the field of battery diagnostics. In particular, the present disclosure relates to a system and a method for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell. BACKGROUND [0002] In lithium-ion battery applications, an ability to estimate usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell is important for screening, grading, and deployment of lithium-ion cells in battery packs and energy storage systems. Usable capacity estimation may support decision-making for quality control, refurbishment, and second-life utilization of lithium-ion cells, where large volumes of lithium-ion cells may need to be evaluated efficiently. [0003] Conventional usable capacity estimation commonly relies on full charge and full discharge testing to obtain discharge capacity under controlled conditions. However, such testing may require long test durations per lithium-ion cell, which may limit throughput and increase operational cost when processing a large population of lithium-ion cells. [0004] Furthermore, practical test environments may involve test equipment that logs voltage measurements at low frequency, resulting in snippet test data having non-uniform sampling, missing data, and other data-quality conditions. Lithium-ion cells may also begin testing at different initial voltage values, which may affect partial charge/discharge behavior and may introduce variability in data processing and feature extraction used for capacity estimation. [0005] Therefore, there is a need for an improved approach that overcomes at least the above-mentioned drawbacks. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0006] A general object of the present disclosure is to provide a system and a method for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell using snippet test data acquired during a partial charge/discharge protocol. [0007] Another object of the present disclosure is to reduce per-cell testing time and improve throughput by enabling usable capacity estimation without requiring full charge and full discharge characterization of each lithium-ion cell. [0008] Another object of the present disclosure is to improve robustness of usable capacity estimation when voltage measurements are logged at low frequency by normalizing snippet test data using interpolation and resampling into a fixed set of points. [0009] Another object of the present disclosure is to improve prediction reliability by generating a feature vector that includes a voltage-drift feature computed based on a comparison of normalized snippet test data to a reference curve. [0010] Another object of the present disclosure is to increase coverage across lithium-ion cells having different initial voltage values by selecting a capacity-estimation model from a plurality of capacity-estimation models based on an initial voltage derived from snippet test data. [0011] Another object of the present disclosure is to reduce sensitivity to data-quality conditions by detecting at least one of non-monotonicity, missing-data, or interpolation-error conditions and selecting an alternate capacity-estimation model based on the detected data-quality condition. SUMMARY [0012] Aspects of the present disclosure pertain to the field of battery diagnostics. In particular, the present disclosure relates to a system and a method for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell. [0013] An aspect of the present disclosure pertains to a system for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell. The system may include one or more processors and a memory storing instructions executable by the one or more processors. The one or more processors is be configured to control, via an equipment interface, test equipment to apply a partial charge/discharge protocol to the lithium-ion cell. The one or more processors is be configured to acquire, from the test equipment, snippet test data including at least voltage measurements and time information. The one or more processors is be configured to normalize the snippet test data by interpolating and resampling, based on the time information, the snippet test data into a fixed set of points. The one or more processors is be configured to generate, using the normalized snippet test data, a feature vector including at least one voltage-drift feature computed based on a comparison to a reference curve. The one or more processors is be configured to select, based on an initial voltage derived from the snippet test data and/or a data-quality condition detected from the snippet test data, a capacity-estimation model from a plurality of capacity-estimation models. The one or more processors is be configured to generate, using the feature vector and the selected capacity-estimation model, an estimated usable capacity or a capacity class for the lithium-ion cell. [0014] In one embodiment, the system is configured to control the partial charge/discharge protocol such that, upon completion of the partial charge/discharge protocol, the lithium-ion cell is at an end voltage corresponding to a storage-safe state-of-charge. [0015] In one embodiment, the end voltage corresponds to a state-of-charge (SoC) substantially between 10% and 20%. [0016] In one embodiment, the one or more processors are configured to select the capacity-estimation model by determining, based on an initial voltage value derived from the snippet test data, whether the initial voltage value is below a threshold voltage or above the threshold voltage. The one or more processors are further configured to select, based on the determining, a first capacity-estimation model for a below-threshold category or a second capacity-estimation model for an above-threshold category. [0017] In one embodiment, the threshold voltage corresponds to a state-of-charge (SoC) substantially between 40% and 50%. [0018] In one embodiment, the one or more processors are configured to resample the snippet test data into the fixed set of points by generating, using interpolation, resampled voltage values at substantially equidistant time intervals to compensate for low-frequency logging of the test equipment. [0019] In one embodiment, the one or more processors are configured to generate the feature vector by generating, based on the normalized snippet test data, a voltage-derivative feature. The one or more processors are further configured to compute the voltage-drift feature using a derivative-difference operation between a derivative of the normalized snippet test data and a derivative of the reference curve over a common voltage range. [0020] In one embodiment, the reference curve is obtained from historical snippet test data received from the test equipment for a set of reference lithium-ion cells having a known usable capacity or a known capacity class. [0021] In one embodiment, the data-quality condition includes at least one of a non-monotonicity condition in voltage versus time, a missing-data condition, or an interpolation-error condition detected based on the snippet test data. In one embodiment, selecting the capacity-estimation model includes selecting, based on the data-quality condition, an alternate capacity-estimation model from the plurality of capacity-estimation models. [0022] Another aspect of the present disclosure pertains to a method for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell. The method includes controlling, by one or more processors and via an equipment interface, test equipment to apply a partial charge/discharge protocol to the lithium-ion cell. The method includes acquiring, by the one or more processors from the test equipment, snippet test data including at least voltage measurements and time information. The method includes normalizing, by the one or more processors, the snippet test data by interpolating and resampling, based on the time information, the snippet test data into a fixed set of points. The method includes generating, by the one or more processors and using the normalized snippet test data, a feature vector including at least one voltage-drift feature computed based on a comparison to a reference curve. The includes selecting, by the one or more processors, based on an initial voltage derived from the snippet test data and/or a data-quality condition detected from the snippet test data, a capacity-estimation model from a plurality of capacity-estimation models. The method includes generating, by the one or more processors and using the feature vector and the selected capacity-estimation model, an estimated usable capacity or a capacity class for the lithium-ion cell. [0027] FIG. 4 illustrates an exemplary plot (400) of a testing protocol during model training, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0028] FIG. 5 illustrates an exemplary plot (500) of model evaluation accuracy against lithium-ion cell batches, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0029] FIG. 6 illustrates an exemplary block diagram of the processing module (102), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0030] FIG. 7 illustrates an exemplary block diagram of a server system (700), in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0031] FIG. 8 illustrates an exemplary flow chart of a method (800) for rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0032] In the following description, for the purposes of explanation, various specific details are set forth in order to provide a thorough understanding of embodiments of the present disclosure. It will be apparent, however, that embodiments of the present disclosure may be practiced without these specific details. [0036] Rapid estimation of usable capacity of a lithium-ion cell is difficult in high-throughput testing because conventional capacity characterization relies on full charge and full discharge testing, which is time-intensive. Practical test environments may further log voltage measurements at low frequency, resulting in snippet test data with non-uniform sampling, missing data, and non-monotonicity, and lithium-ion cells may enter testing with different initial voltage values, which introduces variability that reduces reliability of capacity estimation. [0037] The present disclosure uses a partial charge/discharge protocol to acquire snippet test data including voltage measurements and time information, and then normalizes the snippet test data by interpolation and resampling into a fixed set of points. The present disclosure generates a feature vector that includes at least one voltage-drift feature computed based on a comparison of normalized snippet test data to a reference curve. The present disclosure further selects a capacity-estimation model from a plurality of capacity-estimation models based on an initial voltage derived from the snippet test data and/or a detected data-quality condition, and generates an estimated usable capacity or a capacity class using the selected capacity-estimation model. [0038] The present disclosure enables faster usable capacity estimation with improved throughput relative to full-cycle testing, while maintaining consistent model inputs despite low-frequency logging. The present disclosure improves robustness and coverage by adapting capacity-estimation model selection to initial voltage variability and to data-quality conditions such as missing data, non-monotonicity, or interpolation errors. The present disclosure thereby supports reliable usable capacity estimation or capacity classification across a large population of lithium-ion cells processed under practical test constraints. In one embodiment, the one or more step parameters may include one or more constant-current values, one or more constant-voltage values, one or more rest durations, and one or more end conditions including voltage thresholds and current cut-off thresholds, but not limited thereto. In one embodiment, the plurality of sequential steps may include one or more constant-current charge steps, one or more constant-current discharge steps, one or more rest steps, and one or more constant-voltage charge steps. In one embodiment, the one or more processors (104) may derive the initial voltage from the snippet test data acquired from the test equipment (110). [00115] In one embodiment, the one or more processors (104) may categorize the snippet test data into a plurality of categories based on the initial voltage and/or one or more data-quality conditions detected from the snippet test data. In one embodiment, the plurality of categories may include a BELOW category, an ABOVE category, a DISCARD_BELOW category, and a DISCARD_ABOVE category. In one embodiment, the plurality of categories may further include an ELIMINATED_DATA category corresponding to an absence of data points during testing, but not limited thereto. [00116] In one embodiment, an output of the one or more processors (104) may be provided as an output report and/or a data structure suitable for downstream processing. In one exemplary embodiment, the one or more processors (104) may generate a mapping in which keys correspond to channel identifiers of the test equipment (110) and values correspond to an estimated usable capacity or a capacity class generated for a lithium-ion cell associated with a corresponding channel identifier, but not limited thereto. [00117] In one embodiment, the estimated usable capacity or the capacity class generated by the one or more processors (104) may be represented as a capacity-class bin. In one exemplary embodiment, the capacity-class bin may include a first class corresponding to a usable capacity below about 3000 mAh, a second class corresponding to a usable capacity between about 3000 mAh and about 4400 mAh, and a third class corresponding to a usable capacity above about 4400 mAh, but not limited thereto. In one embodiment, the capacity-class bin may be used for grading a lithium-ion cell as a bad category, an okay category, or a good category, but not limited thereto. [00118] In one embodiment, the plurality of capacity-estimation models may include a plurality of gradient-boosted decision-tree models. In one exemplary embodiment, the plurality of capacity-estimation models may include a plurality of XGBoost models (314) corresponding to a plurality of categories including the BELOW category, the ABOVE category, the DISCARD_BELOW category, and the DISCARD_ABOVE category. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A RECONFIGURABLE BUCK-BOOST BASED ACTIVE CELL BALANCING SYSTEM FOR LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES The present invention discloses a reconfigurable buck-boost based active cell balancing topology for a plurality of series-connected electrochemical cells (101, 102, 115, 116). The topology comprises a first limb and a second limb interconnected through an inductor (110) and a plurality of switching elements (103–108, 111–114) configured to selectively connect, isolate, or bypass individual electrochemical cells. The switching elements are configured to establish a charging current path from a selected source electrochemical cell to the inductor (110) and a discharging current path from the inductor (110) to a selected target electrochemical cell. Intrinsic body diodes of the switching elements provide conduction paths without requiring external diode networks or balancing capacitors. The topology enables controlled energy transfer between non-adjacent electrochemical cells using a single inductor (110) with reduced switching complexity and minimized component count.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [0001] The present invention generally relates to electrical engineering and battery management systems. More particularly, the invention relates to power electronic converter topologies for active cell balancing in lithium-ion battery packs, especially suitable for applications such as electric vehicles and large-scale energy storage systems BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Lithium-ion battery packs, particularly in electric vehicles and energy storage systems, require effective cell balancing to ensure uniform state of charge (SoC), improved lifespan, and safe operation. Conventional balancing approaches are broadly categorized into passive and active methods. Passive balancing dissipates excess energy through resistive elements, leading to energy loss and thermal inefficiencies, whereas active balancing enables energy transfer between cells, thereby improving efficiency. However, existing active balancing techniques suffer from increased circuit complexity, higher component count, and longer balancing time. [0003] For instance, prior art such as United States patent application US2018226808A1 discloses a balancing topology utilizing multiple bidirectional switches and inductors arranged in an H-bridge configuration. While functional, this approach requires a high number of switches (approximately 4n+8), resulting in increased cost, switching losses, and control complexity. [0004] Similarly, a European patent EP2400622A describes a switch-matrix-based balancing system employing multiple inductors and external diodes to manage current flow. This system is limited by its inability to support non-adjacent cell balancing and lacks provisions for bypassing faulty cells, thereby reducing reliability and flexibility. [0005] Additionally, many known topologies rely on multiple inductors (typically n−1 for n cells) or require additional passive components such as capacitors and diodes, which increase system size and losses. Another critical limitation observed in existing solutions is the lack of effective control over circulating currents during charging and discharging, which may lead to cell degradation or safety concerns. [0006] Hence, there exists a need for an improved active cell balancing system that reduces component count, minimizes switching losses, enables efficient energy transfer between any cells in a battery string, and provides fault tolerance through selective cell bypassing. The present invention addresses these challenges by introducing a reconfigurable buck-boost based topology utilizing a single inductor and reduced switch configuration. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION [0007] The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a reconfigurable buck-boost based active cell balancing system capable of efficiently equalizing the state of charge (SoC) among lithium-ion cells using a reduced number of components, thereby enhancing system efficiency and reliability. The invention seeks to overcome the limitations of existing balancing systems, which typically require multiple inductors, a high number of switches, and additional passive components such as diodes and capacitors, resulting in increased cost, complexity, and energy losses. [0008] Another objective of the invention is to implement a single-inductor-based energy transfer mechanism that facilitates bidirectional energy exchange between cells through controlled switching actions, thereby minimizing switching losses and simplifying circuit architecture. This approach reduces the dependency on multiple energy storage elements while maintaining effective balancing performance. [0009] A further objective of the invention is to provide a fault-tolerant cell balancing system capable of selectively bypassing defective or unhealthy cells through reconfigurable switching arrangements, thereby ensuring uninterrupted operation of the battery pack and enhancing overall system robustness. [0010] The invention also has the objective of eliminating the need for external diodes and capacitors by utilizing intrinsic body diodes of semiconductor switches, thereby reducing component count, simplifying hardware implementation, and lowering system cost while maintaining efficient current flow control. [0011] Another objective is to enable controlled energy transfer between any arbitrary cells within the battery string, including non-adjacent cells, thereby improving balancing flexibility and reducing balancing time compared to conventional topologies that are limited to adjacent cell energy transfer. [0012] An additional objective of the invention is to provide a control strategy based on pulse-width modulation (PWM) that allows dynamic adjustment between maximum efficiency mode and maximum power mode, thereby offering flexibility in operation depending on application requirements and available idle time of the battery system. [0013] The invention further aims to reduce sensing complexity by utilizing a minimal number of sensors, including a single current sensing mechanism for the entire battery string, thereby simplifying system integration and reducing overall system cost. [0014] Another objective is to mitigate circulating currents during charging and discharging operations through controlled switching and inherent circuit design, thereby preventing potential damage to cells and improving operational safety and longevity. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0015] In one aspect, the present invention provides a reconfigurable active cell balancing system for lithium-ion battery packs, wherein energy transfer between cells is achieved using a buck-boost converter-derived topology incorporating a single inductor and a reduced switch configuration. [0016] In one aspect, the system comprises a plurality of lithium-ion cells arranged in a series configuration and divided into at least two limbs, each cell being associated with a pair of semiconductor switches configured to selectively connect, isolate, or bypass the respective cell during balancing and operational modes. [0017] In one aspect, the invention includes an energy transfer module comprising a single inductor positioned between the limbs of the battery string and a set of control switches configured to regulate charging and discharging of the inductor, thereby enabling controlled transfer of energy from a higher SoC cell to a lower SoC cell. [0018] In one aspect, the system further comprises a switching control module configured to generate pulse-width modulation (PWM) signals for operating the switches, wherein the duty cycle of the PWM signals determines the charging and discharging intervals of the inductor and governs the efficiency and speed of the balancing process. [0019] In one aspect, the invention utilizes intrinsic body diodes of the semiconductor switches to establish current paths during balancing, charging, and discharging operations, thereby eliminating the requirement for external diodes and reducing the number of passive components in the system. [0020] In one aspect, the system includes a state-of-charge determination module configured to measure and arrange SoC values of individual cells, identify maximum and minimum SoC cells across the limbs, and dynamically select source and target cells for energy transfer based on the identified SoC difference. [0021] In one aspect, the invention comprises a reconfiguration mechanism configured to bypass one or more faulty or degraded cells through selective switching, thereby maintaining continuity of the battery string and ensuring fault-tolerant operation without interruption. [0022] In one aspect, the present invention addresses the objective technical problem of reducing component count, switching losses, and circuit complexity in active cell balancing systems while enabling efficient energy transfer between arbitrary cells, by introducing a single-inductor, reduced-switch, reconfigurable buck-boost topology with inherent current path control. [0023] In one aspect, the invention provides the technical advantage of improved efficiency, reduced hardware complexity, lower cost, enhanced scalability for large battery packs, and improved operational safety through controlled current flow and elimination of circulating currents. [0024] In one aspect, the invention enables flexible operation between maximum efficiency mode and maximum power mode by varying the PWM duty cycle, thereby allowing optimization of balancing speed and energy efficiency based on application requirements, making it suitable for electric vehicles and large-scale battery energy storage systems. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [0025] The foregoing summary, as well as the following detailed description of the invention will be better understood when read in conjunction with the appended drawings. For the purpose of assisting in the explanation of the invention, they are shown in the drawings, embodiments which are presently preferred and considered illustrative. It should be understood, however, that the invention is not limited to the precise arrangements and instrumentalities shown therein. In the drawings: Figure 1 illustrates the overall topology of the present inventionbuck-boost based active cell balancing system, Figure 2 illustrates the charging and discharging current paths for series-connected cells, Figure 3 illustrates the bypassing of an unhealthy or faulty cell using selective switching, Figure 4 illustrates the equivalent circuit model of the present invention topology, Figure 5 illustrates the equivalent circuit diagram depicting two modes of operation, Figure 6 illustrates the first mode of operation of the present invention topology Figure 7 illustrates the second mode of operation of the present invention topology Figure 8 illustrates the control logic flowchart for selection of source and target cells Figure 9 illustrates input and output voltage and current waveforms corresponding to different duty cycles Figure 10 illustrates simulation results showing the convergence of state-of-charge levels. REFERENCE NUMERALS 101-First electrochemical cell in first limb 102-Second electrochemical cell in first limb 103-First switching element associated with first limb 104-Second switching element associated with first limb 105-Third switching element associated with first limb 106-Fourth switching element associated with first limb 107-First inductor-side switching element 108-Second inductor-side switching element 109-Resistance associated with inductor 110-Inductor 111-First switching element associated with second limb 112-Second switching element associated with second limb 113-Third switching element associated with second limb 114-Fourth switching element associated with second limb 115-First electrochemical cell in second limb 116-Second electrochemical cell in second limb 401-Input source 402-Switching element in equivalent circuit 403-Diode element in equivalent circuit 404-Inductor in equivalent circuit 405-Output node in equivalent circuit DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [0026] The present invention will now be described more fully herein after. For the purposes of the following detailed description, it is to be understood that the invention may assume various alternative variations and step sequences, except where expressly specified to the contrary. Thus, before describing the present invention in detail, it is to be understood that this invention is not limited to particularly exemplified systems or embodiments that may of course, vary. The use of examples anywhere in this specification including examples of any terms discussed herein is illustrative only, and in no way limits the scope and meaning of the invention or of any exemplified term. Likewise, the invention is not limited to various embodiments given in this specification. [0027] As used herein, the singular forms "a," "an," and "the" include plural reference unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. The term "and/or" means one or all of the listed elements or a combination of any two or more of the listed elements. [0028] The terms “preferred” and “preferably” refer to embodiments of the invention that may afford certain benefits, under certain circumstances. However, other embodiments may also be preferred, under the same or other circumstances. Furthermore, the recitation of one or more preferred embodiments does not imply that other embodiments are not useful and is not intended to exclude other embodiments from the scope of the invention. [0029] When the term “about” is used in describing a value or an endpoint of a range, the disclosure should be understood to include both the specific value and endpoint referred to. [0030] As used herein the terms “comprises”, “comprising”, “includes”, “including”, “containing”, “characterized by”, “having” or any other variation thereof, are intended to cover a non-exclusive inclusion. [0031] The present invention discloses a reconfigurable buck-boost based active cell balancing topology for lithium-ion battery packs, configured to enable efficient transfer of energy between cells having unequal states of charge. The topology comprises a plurality of series-connected cells (101, 102, 115, 116) arranged into at least two limbs and interconnected through an inductor (110) acting as an energy transfer element. Each cell is associated with controlled switching elements (103–108, 111–114) configured to selectively connect, isolate, or bypass the respective cell. During operation, the topology identifies a source cell having a relatively higher state of charge and a target cell having a relatively lower state of charge, and facilitates controlled energy transfer between them using a pulse-width modulation based switching mechanism. The buck-boost derived configuration eliminates the requirement for external diodes and capacitors by utilizing intrinsic conduction paths within the switching elements, thereby reducing component count and improving efficiency. [0032] In an operational cycle, the topology functions in two distinct operating states which together complete one balancing cycle. In a first operating state, a selected higher state-of-charge cell, such as cell (101), is connected to the inductor (110) through switching elements (103, 107), enabling the inductor (110) to store energy. The switching sequence is configured such that current flows from the selected source cell into the inductor (110) while bypassing other cells through corresponding switching elements, thereby ensuring targeted energy extraction without affecting the remaining cells in the string. The duration of this operating state is governed by a controlled duty cycle, allowing precise regulation of energy stored in the inductor (110). [0033] Subsequently, in a second operating state, the energy stored in the inductor (110) is transferred to a selected lower state-of-charge cell, such as cell (115) or cell (116). The switching configuration is altered through switching elements (108, 111–114) to establish a discharge path from the inductor (110) to the target cell, enabling controlled release of stored energy. This transfer process ensures that the target cell receives the required charge while maintaining directional current flow and preventing reverse or circulating currents within the topology. The coordinated execution of the charging and discharging operating states enables continuous redistribution of energy among cells until equilibrium in state of charge is achieved across the battery pack. [0034] The topology further supports reconfigurability by enabling selective bypassing of any faulty or degraded cell through appropriate switching combinations using switching elements (103–108, 111–114), thereby maintaining operational continuity of the battery pack. Additionally, the duty cycle of the switching signals may be dynamically varied to operate the topology either in a maximum efficiency mode or a maximum power mode, thereby providing flexibility in balancing speed and energy utilization based on operational requirements. The architecture, characterized by the use of a single inductor (110) and reduced number of switching elements, ensures scalability for large battery strings while minimizing switching losses, circuit complexity, and overall system cost. [0035] Figure 1 illustrates the overall topology of the present invention, wherein a plurality of lithium-ion cells (101, 102, 115, 116) are connected in series and arranged into two distinct limbs. The limbs are electrically coupled through an inductor (110) having an associated resistance (109), which acts as the primary energy transfer element. Each cell is associated with switching elements (103–108, 111–114) configured across the cell terminals to selectively connect, isolate, or bypass the cell from the balancing path. The topology further includes controlled switching paths established through switching elements (107, 108) to enable routing of current from one limb to another through the inductor (110). The topology is derived from a buck-boost converter configuration, wherein the inductor (110) facilitates energy storage and release between cells. The arrangement eliminates the requirement for external diodes and capacitors by utilizing intrinsic conduction paths of the switching elements. The structure allows any selected cell in one limb to transfer energy to any selected cell in the opposite limb, thereby enabling non-adjacent cell balancing with reduced component count and improved efficiency. [0036] Figure 2 illustrates the charging and discharging current paths within the topology when the cells (101, 102, 115, 116) are connected in series for normal battery operation. During the charging phase, current flows from an external source through predefined conduction paths established via intrinsic diode conduction of switching elements (103–108, 111–114), allowing all cells to be charged without requiring active switching. During the discharging phase, controlled switching elements are activated to allow current flow from the battery pack to the load. The figure clearly distinguishes the current paths using directional indicators, demonstrating seamless transition between charging and discharging modes without disturbing the balancing configuration. This arrangement ensures reduced switching complexity during standard operation and improves reliability by utilizing inherent conduction paths for current flow. [0037] Figure 3 illustrates the fault-tolerant feature of the topology, wherein a defective or unhealthy cell, such as cell (102), can be selectively bypassed using appropriate switching configurations through switching elements (105, 106). The bypassing mechanism isolates the faulty cell from the main current path while maintaining continuity of the remaining battery string. The figure shows how the current is rerouted around the faulty cell through alternate switching paths, ensuring uninterrupted operation of the battery pack. This capability is particularly critical in large battery systems, as it prevents performance degradation and enhances safety by avoiding the influence of malfunctioning cells. The reconfigurable nature of the topology enables dynamic adaptation based on cell health conditions. [0038] Figure 4 illustrates the equivalent circuit model representing the functional behavior of the topology in a simplified buck-boost converter form. The equivalent circuit includes an input source (401), a switching element (402), a diode element (403), an inductor (404), and an output node (405). This abstraction is used to analyze operational characteristics including energy transfer, voltage conversion, and current flow dynamics. The equivalent model assists in understanding the operation during charging and discharging intervals and is utilized for deriving performance parameters including efficiency and duty-cycle-dependent behavior. [0039] Figure 5 illustrates the two fundamental operating states of the topology using an equivalent circuit representation. In a first operating state, the current path is established such that the inductor (404) is charged by the input source (401) through switching element (402). In a second operating state, the stored energy in the inductor (404) is discharged to the output node (405) through diode element (403). The figure uses distinct path indications to differentiate between the two operating states, clearly showing switching transitions and energy flow directions. These operating states together constitute one complete balancing cycle enabling controlled energy redistribution among cells. [0040] Figure 6 illustrates the charging operating state of the topology, wherein a selected higher state-of-charge cell, such as cell (101), is connected to the inductor (110). During this operating state, controlled switching through switching elements (103, 107) establishes a current path that allows energy to flow from the source cell into the inductor (110). Other cells in the string are bypassed through intrinsic conduction paths to ensure that only the selected cell contributes to the inductor charging process. The current path is clearly indicated, demonstrating how the inductor (110) accumulates energy during this interval. The duration of this operating state is governed by the duty cycle of the switching signals, enabling precise control over the amount of energy stored in the inductor (110). [0041] Figure 7 illustrates the discharging operating state of the topology, wherein the energy stored in the inductor (110) during the charging operating state is transferred to a selected lower state-of-charge cell, such as cell (115) or cell (116). The switching configuration is modified through switching elements (108, 111–114) to create a discharge path from the inductor (110) to the target cell. The current flows through the established path, delivering stored energy to the target cell while maintaining controlled and unidirectional flow. This operating state ensures efficient energy redistribution and prevents undesired current circulation within the topology. The coordinated operation of the charging and discharging operating states ensures effective balancing across the battery string. [0042] Figure 8 illustrates the control logic implemented for selecting source and target cells during the balancing process. The logic begins with measurement of the state of charge of all cells, followed by arrangement of cells based on their SoC values. The topology identifies the cells with maximum and minimum SoC across the limbs and pairs them for energy transfer. If required, subsequent pairing is performed iteratively until the SoC difference among all cells falls within a predefined threshold. The control mechanism ensures systematic balancing by dynamically selecting cells and controlling switching actions based on real-time SoC data. [0043] In an alternative embodiment, the present invention may be implemented for any number of lithium-ion cells connected in series, wherein the overall topology is scalable beyond the illustrated configuration. The arrangement of cells into two limbs can be extended to accommodate larger battery strings, while maintaining the single inductor-based energy transfer mechanism through inductor (110). The number of switching elements (103–108, 111–114) increases proportionally with the number of cells, following a configuration requiring only (2n + 2) switches for n cells, thereby preserving reduced component count even in large-scale implementations. [0044] In another embodiment, the topology may operate with different state-of-charge estimation techniques ranging from basic voltage-based estimation to advanced algorithmic methods, without altering the core balancing structure. The selection of source and target cells may be dynamically controlled using various computational approaches, including matrix-based SoC mapping of cells in each limb, enabling flexible integration with different battery management systems. [0045] In yet another embodiment, the duty cycle of the switching signals applied to switching elements (103–108, 111–114) may be adaptively varied to operate the topology either in a maximum efficiency mode or a maximum power mode. At lower duty cycles, the topology emphasizes energy efficiency with slower balancing, whereas at higher duty cycles, the topology prioritizes faster balancing with increased power transfer. This adaptive control enables the topology to be tailored based on operational requirements, such as available idle time or load conditions. [0046] In a further embodiment, the reconfigurable architecture allows selective bypassing of one or more faulty or degraded cells through appropriate switching combinations using switching elements (103–108, 111–114). This embodiment ensures fault-tolerant operation of the battery pack by maintaining continuity of the series connection even in the presence of defective cells. The bypassing mechanism may be activated dynamically based on cell health monitoring, thereby improving reliability and extending battery life. [0047] In another embodiment, the topology may utilize intrinsic conduction paths of switching elements (103–108, 111–114) to perform charging operations without requiring active switching, wherein current flows through inherent diode paths during charging and controlled switching during discharging. This embodiment reduces control complexity and improves robustness by minimizing active switching requirements during certain operating conditions. [0048] In an additional embodiment, the topology may be implemented with a minimal sensing configuration, wherein a single current sensing element is used to estimate and monitor the state of charge of multiple cells, thereby reducing sensor count and simplifying system integration. This embodiment is particularly advantageous for cost-sensitive and large-scale battery systems. [0049] In yet another embodiment, the topology may be configured to prevent circulating currents during both charging and discharging operations through controlled switching and inherent circuit design. This embodiment enhances safety and efficiency by mitigating undesired current loops that may otherwise lead to energy loss or cell degradation. [0050] The present invention provides a significant advancement in active cell balancing technology by introducing a reconfigurable buck-boost based topology that achieves efficient energy transfer using a single inductor (110) and a reduced number of switching elements (103–108, 111–114). This results in a substantial reduction in component count, circuit complexity, and overall system cost when compared to conventional topologies that rely on multiple inductors, additional diodes, and complex switching arrangements. The elimination of external diodes and capacitors further simplifies the hardware design while maintaining effective current control and energy transfer. [0051] Additionally, the invention offers enhanced operational flexibility and reliability through its ability to transfer energy between arbitrary cells, including non-adjacent cells, and its capability to bypass faulty cells without interrupting system operation. The charging and discharging operating states enable optimization between efficiency and balancing speed, making the topology adaptable to various operational requirements. Furthermore, the reduction in switching losses, mitigation of circulating currents, and simplified sensing requirements contribute to improved efficiency, safety, and scalability for large battery systems. [0052] Experimental validation [0053] The performance of the present invention was evaluated through simulation studies carried out on the proposed buck-boost based active cell balancing topology, wherein the operational characteristics, efficiency, and balancing capability were analyzed under varying conditions. The simulation environment was configured to replicate practical operating conditions of lithium-ion battery strings, including variations in initial state of charge among cells and different duty cycle settings for the switching control. [0054] Referring to Figure 9, the input and output voltage and current waveforms are illustrated for different duty cycle conditions, demonstrating the operational behavior of the topology during energy transfer. The waveforms correspond to the charging and discharging operating states which together form a complete balancing cycle. During the charging operating state, the inductor (110) is charged from a selected higher state-of-charge cell, resulting in a rise in inductor current corresponding to the applied duty cycle interval. During the discharging operating state, the stored energy in the inductor (110) is discharged to a selected lower state-of-charge cell, producing a corresponding current waveform indicative of energy transfer. [0055] The results demonstrate that the duty cycle plays a critical role in determining the efficiency and speed of the balancing process. At a lower duty cycle of approximately 10%, the topology operates in a maximum efficiency mode, achieving an efficiency of about 95.9%, with relatively slower balancing action. In contrast, at a higher duty cycle of approximately 71%, the topology operates in a maximum power mode, wherein the rate of energy transfer between cells is significantly increased, resulting in faster balancing at the expense of reduced efficiency. [0056] Further, the equivalent circuit representation comprising the input source (401), switching element (402), diode element (403), inductor (404), and output node (405) reflects the same operational principles as the actual topology, wherein the inductor charging and discharging phases are governed by the switching duty cycle. One complete switching cycle consists of the charging operating state during which energy is stored in the inductor (404), followed by the discharging operating state during which the stored energy is transferred to the output node (405). [0057] Referring to Figure 10, the simulation results illustrate the balancing performance for a battery string with an initial state-of-charge variation of approximately 13% among the cells. The graph demonstrates the convergence of state-of-charge levels over time, wherein cells with higher initial state of charge gradually transfer energy to cells with lower state of charge through repeated charging and discharging operating states. The results clearly indicate that the topology is capable of achieving uniform state-of-charge distribution across all cells in a stable and controlled manner. , Claims:We Claim: 1. patents.abstract: The present invention discloses a method (100) for preparing the self-healable and sustainable polymer electrolyte for lithium-ion battery applications, comprising steps of: dissolving a cellulose-derived biopolymer matrix in the solvent system, wherein the cellulose-derived biopolymer matrix comprises methyl cellulose and cellulose acetate butyrate respectively, at step (102); incorporating the lithium perchlorate (LiClO₄) as a lithium salt dopant into the biopolymer matrix, wherein the lithium perchlorate is incorporated in an amount of about 20 wt.% with respect to the polymer matrix, at step (104); adding the 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIm-TFSI) as an ionic liquid plasticizer, wherein the EMIm-TFSI ionic liquid is incorporated in an amount of about 50 wt.% with respect to the cellulose-derived biopolymer matrix, at step (106); casting the resulting composition into a film, at step (108); and drying the film to obtain a solid self-healable polymer electrolyte membrane, at step (110). < >

patents.abstract: An adaptive cell balancing controller for lithium battery packs is disclosed. The controller includes a cell voltage sensing network, pack current sensor, temperature and impedance estimator, balancing switch matrix, bidirectional energy transfer converter, controller core, state calculation module, balancing scheduler, protection interlock, communication interface, and parameter memory. The controller evaluates cell deviation, charge relation, thermal margin, impedance tendency, and stored response history to generate supervised balancing commands. Energy transfer is selectively enabled only when protection conditions permit, thereby improving usable pack capacity and balancing efficiency.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Title: “AN ADAPTIVE CELL BALANCING CONTROLLER FOR LITHIUM BATTERY PACKS” FIELD OF THE INVENTION: The present invention relates to battery management electronics, and more particularly to an adaptive cell balancing controller for lithium battery packs using sensed cell conditions, computed imbalance parameters, controlled energy transfer paths, and protective coordination for improving pack reliability in electric, stationary, and portable power applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION: Lithium battery packs are widely used in electric mobility platforms, renewable energy storage assemblies, industrial backup supplies, robotics, medical equipment, telecom power banks, and portable electronic systems because they offer relatively high energy density, scalable voltage formation, and repeatable charge and discharge capability. A pack generally includes a plurality of electrochemical cells connected in series, parallel, or a combination thereof. During use, the individual cells may not remain electrically identical, even when the cells originate from the same production batch. Manufacturing variation, aging rate differences, temperature gradients, unequal contact resistance, leakage currents, and nonuniform loading can cause cell-to-cell divergence in voltage, available capacity, internal resistance, and state of charge. When such divergence is not managed effectively, the usable capacity of the entire pack may be constrained by the weakest or most charged cell, because charging and discharging must remain within safe cell limits. Existing battery management systems commonly rely on passive balancing arrangements in which excess charge from selected cells is dissipated through resistive elements. Such arrangements are comparatively simple and may be acceptable for small packs or low current applications. However, passive dissipation can convert useful stored energy into heat, thereby increasing thermal stress inside a battery enclosure. In dense lithium battery packs, localized heating around bleed resistors may complicate thermal design, reduce balancing speed when conservative resistor ratings are used, and lower overall energy efficiency. Passive balancing may also be scheduled only near the upper end of charge, which can leave useful correction opportunities unused during rest, partial charge, or discharge periods. A controller that merely responds to fixed voltage thresholds may therefore fail to address hidden imbalance related to capacity drift or impedance mismatch. Active balancing techniques attempt to transfer energy from relatively higher charged cells to relatively lower charged cells or to a pack bus. Known active solutions may employ capacitor shuttling, inductor transfer, transformer coupling, or modular converter stages. While these techniques can improve energy utilization, many implementations require complex hardware, numerous switches, bulky magnetic parts, or rigid balancing sequences. A predetermined sequence may not reflect the real operating condition of a lithium pack in a vehicle or storage plant, where temperature, load demand, regenerative charging, cell impedance, and available dwell time continuously change. Some systems estimate state of charge from pack current integration alone, but accumulated measurement error may reduce confidence over extended operation. Others use open circuit voltage lookup during rest, but such conditions are not always available in service. A further difficulty in existing controllers is coordination between balancing and protection. Balancing commands may need to be suspended when a cell is near an overvoltage limit, undervoltage limit, excessive temperature condition, communication fault, sensor inconsistency, or current transient. If the balancing circuit is controlled independently from the protection logic, the system may enter a conservative disable state too frequently or may continue balancing at unsuitable moments. In multi-module packs, uneven communication latency between local monitoring boards and a supervisory controller can also delay corrective action. This limitation can become more pronounced as pack voltage increases and as modules are replaced or serviced at different times. Conventional cell balancing controllers are often calibrated using fixed parameters selected for a nominal cell chemistry and capacity. Lithium cell chemistries, however, exhibit different voltage curves, temperature coefficients, aging characteristics, and recommended balancing currents. A fixed calibration may be insufficient when the pack includes cells that age differently or when operating profiles alternate between high power events and low current storage periods. There remains a practical need for a controller capable of adapting balancing priority and balancing intensity according to measured electrical and thermal behavior, while maintaining hardware compatibility with modular battery pack designs. Such a controller may reduce avoidable energy loss, improve balancing accuracy, and support safer long term operation without requiring excessive user intervention or frequent manual recalibration. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION: The prime object of the invention is to provide an adaptive cell balancing controller for lithium battery packs that determines balancing priority from live cell condition data rather than a permanently fixed threshold table. Another object of the invention is to provide a controller architecture capable of selecting a suitable balancing path for each cell group by considering voltage deviation, estimated charge availability, impedance tendency, temperature exposure, and permitted current. Yet another object of the invention is to provide coordinated control between energy transfer elements and battery protection functions so that corrective balancing is carried out without compromising cell safety limits. Still another object of the invention is to provide a modular balancing controller that can be incorporated in series connected lithium battery modules and can communicate pack health information to a host battery management unit. A further object of the invention is to provide adaptive scheduling logic that updates balancing commands during charge, discharge, rest, and partial state conditions. Another further object of the invention is to reduce avoidable heat generation by preferring controlled energy transfer whenever the measured imbalance and pack condition justify active correction. Yet another further object of the invention is to provide stored calibration and learning parameters so that the controller remains suitable for different lithium cell capacities, chemistries, and aging stages. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION: The invention provides an adaptive cell balancing controller for lithium battery packs in which cell measurement inputs, pack current information, thermal information, stored pack parameters, and diagnostic status are processed together to generate controlled balancing commands. The controller includes a cell voltage sensing network, a current sensing input, a temperature acquisition interface, a parameter memory, a computational controller core, a balancing scheduler, a balancing switch matrix, and an energy transfer converter arranged for selective coupling to selected cells or cell groups. The system classifies imbalance by comparing measured values with calculated pack references and by assigning a correction priority that changes according to operating mode and safety margin. An inventive aspect of the invention is to provide a balancing decision process that combines voltage spread with an estimated charge relation, thereby avoiding selection based solely on instantaneous cell voltage. Another inventive aspect of the invention is to provide a dynamically adjustable balancing current command that is reduced or increased in accordance with temperature margin, cell impedance indication, converter capacity, and pack operating state. Yet another inventive aspect of the invention is to provide a protection interlock that supervises each balancing command before the balancing switch matrix is energized. Still another inventive aspect of the invention is to provide a memory assisted adaptation mechanism in which previous balancing duration, convergence rate, and cell response are used to refine later balancing intervals. The controller may operate during charging, during discharge, or during nonloaded storage when the sensed condition allows, and may suspend balancing when protective conditions, connector irregularities, sensor disagreement, or communication faults are detected. The controller may be implemented as a module level board connected to a local group of cells, or as a pack level controller supervising plural module boards through an isolated communication link. By using adaptive prioritization, controlled transfer hardware, and safety coordination in a single control arrangement, the invention provides a practical system for improving useful pack capacity and maintaining cell uniformity over repeated cycling. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS: The accompanying drawing is provided for illustrative purposes and forms a part of the specification, and the same shall not be construed as limiting the scope of the invention, since structural variations and functional equivalents may be adopted without departing from the inventive concept. FIG. 1 depicts a block diagram of an adaptive cell balancing controller for lithium battery packs, wherein a lithium battery pack (101) is coupled to a cell voltage sensing network (102), a temperature and impedance estimator (103), a balancing switch matrix (104), a bidirectional energy transfer converter (105), a controller core (106), a state calculation module (107), a balancing scheduler (108), a protection interlock (109), a communication interface (110), a pack current sensor (111), and a parameter memory (112), such that the controller core (106) receives condition data from the sensing elements, determines balancing commands through the state calculation module (107) and balancing scheduler (108), and enables controlled energy movement through the switch matrix (104) and converter (105) under supervision of the protection interlock (109).
