With reference to FIG. 1, the adaptive cell balancing controller is configured around a lithium battery pack (101) having a plurality of series connected cells or cell groups arranged between pack terminals (114). The cells may be physically organized in module trays, prismatic stacks, cylindrical holders, or pouch cell frames, while the electrical connection points are made available to a monitoring harness. Each cell tap is routed through guarded conductors to reduce coupling of switching noise into measurement paths. The pack terminals (114) provide the positive and negative pack references for load delivery, charger connection, and converter reference alignment. Mechanical spacing, insulation barriers, and connector orientation are selected so that the balancing controller can be positioned near the pack without requiring a redesign of the electrochemical cell assembly. The cell voltage sensing network (102) comprises a plurality of differential input channels connected to the respective cell taps through input protection elements, sampling filters, and isolation compliant routing. The network (102) may include resistor dividers, analog multiplexers, precision reference elements, and analog to digital conversion circuitry suitable for measuring each cell potential relative to adjacent nodes. Channel spacing and creepage separation are selected according to the maximum module voltage. The sensing network (102) is arranged to provide cell-specific measurement data to the controller core (106), while limiting input current under abnormal wiring conditions. In embodiments, calibration coefficients stored in the parameter memory (112) are associated with corresponding sensing channels to compensate for tolerance and offset variation. The pack current sensor (111) is structurally positioned in series with a pack conductor or in magnetic relation with the conductor, and may be formed by a shunt element, Hall effect transducer, fluxgate sensor, or isolated current measurement module. The sensor (111) includes signal conditioning circuitry arranged to deliver a scaled current representation to the controller core (106). A bidirectional current sign reference may be defined so that charge direction and discharge direction are electrically distinguishable. The current sensor (111) is connected to the same timing domain as the cell voltage sensing network (102) or to a synchronized acquisition interface, thereby allowing current data to be correlated with cell measurement sets without relying upon a separate supervisory device. The temperature and impedance estimator (103) includes temperature sensing inputs distributed near thermally significant regions of the battery pack (101), including regions adjacent to high current interconnects, cell surfaces, and balancing power components. The estimator (103) is further coupled to measured voltage and current data for generating an impedance indication for each cell group or for selected representative groups. The temperature inputs may be thermistors, resistance temperature detectors, semiconductor sensors, or digital temperature devices. The estimator (103) is not limited to a single physical sensor board and may be distributed across module sections. Signal paths from the estimator (103) are filtered and mapped to pack locations so that the controller core (106) can associate thermal margins with specific balancing channels. The balancing switch matrix (104) is electrically interposed between selected cell terminals of the battery pack (101) and the bidirectional energy transfer converter (105). The switch matrix (104) includes semiconductor switching devices, gate drivers, current limiting elements, reverse conduction management elements, and channel selection conductors. The semiconductor devices may comprise field effect transistors, solid state relays, or other controllable switching arrangements selected for the applicable cell voltage and balancing current. The topology of the matrix (104) permits selective coupling of a chosen cell or cell group without permanently loading nonselected cells. Isolation clearances and driver references are arranged so that high side and low side switching portions remain electrically stable across the module voltage span. The bidirectional energy transfer converter (105) is configured as a controlled power stage capable of receiving energy from a selected higher energy cell path and delivering the same toward a lower energy cell path, an intermediate balancing bus, or a pack level storage node. The converter (105) may include an inductor, transformer, coupled inductor, flying capacitor arrangement, resonant element, or hybrid transfer circuit, together with switching transistors and current sensing components. The converter (105) is dimensioned for balancing current rather than propulsion or main load current, thereby allowing compact construction. Its power terminals interface with the balancing switch matrix (104), while its control terminals receive gating signals that are supervised by the protection interlock (109). The controller core (106) comprises a programmable processing unit, mixed signal controller, microcontroller, digital signal processor, field programmable gate array, or application specific control circuit mounted on a controller substrate. The controller core (106) is electrically coupled to the state calculation module (107), the balancing scheduler (108), the protection interlock (109), the communication interface (110), and the parameter memory (112). The controller substrate may also carry power regulation circuits, clock circuits, watchdog circuitry, and diagnostic test points. A galvanic isolation barrier may be provided between the controller core (106) and a host system when pack voltage or installation regulations require separated communication domains. The state calculation module (107) is arranged as a computational block implemented in firmware, hardware logic, or a combination thereof. The module (107) receives cell voltage data, pack current data, temperature location data, and stored calibration parameters, and provides calculated cell status descriptors to the balancing scheduler (108). The descriptors may include a voltage deviation value, a relative charge estimate, a temperature margin value, an impedance trend value, and a confidence indicator. The state calculation module (107) is structurally associated with the parameter memory (112) so that cell chemistry tables, capacity settings, balancing current limits, and aging coefficients remain available to the controller core (106) without dependence on a remote server. The balancing scheduler (108) is configured as a command generation block that stores channel priority data, converter availability data, switching constraints, and channel exclusion flags. The scheduler (108) interfaces with the balancing switch matrix (104) through gate command lines and with the bidirectional energy transfer converter (105) through converter command lines. Its internal registers or memory locations may define permitted channel combinations, maximum channel dwell settings, and mandatory separation intervals between adjacent cell selections. The scheduler (108) is also linked with the communication interface (110) so that pack level coordination messages can alter scheduler limits while leaving local protection authority within the controller. The protection interlock (109) is provided as a hardware or firmware supervised safety gate between the command generating portions and the power switching portions. The interlock (109) receives overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, undertemperature, overcurrent, measurement plausibility, gate driver fault, and converter fault signals. Its output enable lines are connected to the balancing switch matrix (104) and converter driver circuits so that a balancing path cannot be energized unless the required permissive conditions are present. A fail safe default state may disconnect the matrix (104) and deenergize converter control signals when supply voltage, clock integrity, or watchdog status is outside a valid range. The communication interface (110) comprises a wired or isolated communication circuit for exchange of diagnostic and coordination data with a host battery management unit, charger, vehicle controller, inverter, or external service tool. The interface (110) may support controller area network, serial peripheral communication, isolated universal asynchronous communication, differential serial communication, or another industrial protocol. The parameter memory (112) is accessible through the controller core (106) for storing identification data, calibration records, balancing history, fault counters, and configuration limits. The physical housing of the controller may include connector seals, thermal conduction paths, electromagnetic shielding, and mounting features suited to installation in a lithium battery pack enclosure. The working of the invention, during an initial energization phase, the controller core (106) receives regulated operating power and establishes an internal reference for the lithium battery pack (101). The parameter memory (112) is read to obtain cell count, permitted voltage range, balancing current limits, temperature limits, chemistry data, and channel mapping. The protection interlock (109) remains in a disabled command state while the cell voltage sensing network (102), pack current sensor (111), and temperature and impedance estimator (103) complete plausibility checks. When the channel map matches the sensed pack configuration, the controller core (106) records a valid initialization status and prepares the measurement timing sequence. During the measurement acquisition phase, the cell voltage sensing network (102) samples the individual cell or cell group voltages according to a timed acquisition pattern. The pack current sensor (111) supplies a contemporaneous current value, and the estimator (103) supplies localized thermal readings. The controller core (106) rejects readings that fall outside plausibility windows or that are inconsistent with adjacent channel relationships. Accepted readings are time stamped and transferred to the state calculation module (107). A short settling delay may be inserted after large current changes so that transient measurement artifacts are not treated as stable imbalance evidence. During the state computation phase, the state calculation module (107) derives a pack reference from the valid cell measurement set and determines a deviation value for each monitored cell group. The module (107) combines the deviation value with current direction, temperature margin, stored capacity information, and impedance tendency to form a balancing need indicator. The confidence of the indicator is adjusted when sensor noise, rest duration, or recent load transition affects the reliability of the computed condition. The resulting indicators are supplied to the balancing scheduler (108) as ranked channel candidates rather than as simple pass or fail threshold events. During the priority scheduling phase, the balancing scheduler (108) evaluates the ranked channel candidates against converter availability, allowed dwell time, channel adjacency restrictions, and pack operating mode. The scheduler (108) selects a channel pair, balancing bus relation, or pack node relation depending upon the imbalance pattern recognized by the state calculation module (107). If the pack is being charged, the scheduler (108) may limit correction intensity near the upper cell boundary. If the pack is discharging, the scheduler (108) may reserve correction commands for cells having adequate safety margin. A pending command is then submitted to the protection interlock (109). During the permissive verification phase, the protection interlock (109) compares the pending command with instantaneous safety inputs. The interlock (109) blocks the command when any involved cell is outside a safe voltage window, when a related temperature input exceeds an authorized range, when the current sensor (111) reports an unsuitable transient, or when a gate driver diagnostic signal indicates an irregularity. When permissive conditions are present, the interlock (109) releases an enable signal to the balancing switch matrix (104) and the bidirectional energy transfer converter (105). The release signal is maintained only for the approved balancing interval. During the energy correction phase, the balancing switch matrix (104) connects the selected cell path to the bidirectional energy transfer converter (105). The converter (105) establishes a controlled balancing current and moves energy according to the command supplied by the scheduler (108). The controller core (106) monitors converter current, involved cell voltages, and temperature data while the interval proceeds. If convergence is detected before the scheduled interval expires, the scheduler (108) shortens the active duration. If a monitored variable approaches a limit, the protection interlock (109) withdraws the enable signal and the matrix (104) returns to a nonconductive condition. During the update and communication phase, the controller core (106) stores balancing duration, channel response, convergence behavior, and any interruption reason in the parameter memory (112). The balancing scheduler (108) revises later priority calculations using the newly stored response information. The communication interface (110) transmits pack status, cell spread, balancing activity, and diagnostic flags to a host device. When no channel requires correction, the controller enters a reduced activity monitoring condition while retaining periodic measurement, protection supervision, and readiness for a subsequent balancing request. The experimental validation of the invention, a prototype controller was evaluated on a twelve cell lithium battery module having nominally identical cells intentionally prepared with different initial charge levels. The module was charged and rested before testing, and the cell voltage sensing network (102) was compared against a calibrated laboratory voltmeter at each cell tap. The average channel deviation was within 3 millivolts after calibration coefficients from the parameter memory (112) were applied. When the adaptive algorithm was enabled, the cell voltage spread reduced from 86 millivolts to 14 millivolts within the selected balancing window, while a fixed threshold passive reference board under the same cell preparation left a wider residual spread at the end of the observation period. A thermal validation experiment was conducted in an environmental chamber at 15 C, 25 C, and 45 C to determine whether balancing commands remained responsive to temperature margin. Thermistors associated with the temperature and impedance estimator (103) were placed near cell surfaces and near the balancing power stage. At 25 C, the controller permitted the rated balancing current for most of the correction interval. At 45 C, the balancing scheduler (108) reduced command intensity and increased rest intervals between channel selections. The measured surface temperature rise near the balancing circuit was lower than the passive reference configuration operated at an equivalent correction target, indicating reduced localized heat accumulation. A dynamic load experiment was performed using a programmable bidirectional supply and electronic load to simulate charge pulses, discharge pulses, and rest intervals. The pack current sensor (111) was monitored together with the cell measurement set so that correction decisions could be assessed under changing operating states. During high current transitions, the controller core (106) delayed balancing selection until the measurement values stabilized. During moderate discharge, the state calculation module (107) avoided selecting cells with narrow undervoltage margin. The recorded logs showed that balancing commands were issued during stable parts of the profile and that channel selection changed when load direction altered the confidence value associated with the charge estimate. A fault response experiment was carried out by introducing open sense line conditions, artificial overtemperature input, simulated gate driver fault, and converter current irregularity. In each test condition, the protection interlock (109) was observed through diagnostic outputs and gate enable monitoring. The balancing switch matrix (104) remained disabled during open sense line simulation, and the bidirectional energy transfer converter (105) was not commanded when the overtemperature signal exceeded the configured limit. When the gate driver fault line was asserted during an active interval, the enable signal was removed within the measured protection response window and the controller stored the interruption reason in the parameter memory (112). A repeated cycling experiment was conducted over one hundred charge and discharge cycles using a controlled battery cycler and periodic rest measurements. The adaptive cell balancing controller was compared with a nonadaptive balancing schedule using the same module type and similar starting imbalance. The adaptive controller reduced the average end of charge spread more consistently across later cycles and required fewer total balancing minutes after the first adaptation period. Stored convergence data showed that certain channels required shorter dwell commands as their response history became available. Capacity delivered to a defined cutoff voltage showed improved usable pack energy relative to the comparison schedule under the tested conditions. ADVANTAGES OF THE INVENTION: The prime advantage of the invention is to provide improved cell uniformity by selecting balancing action from combined electrical, thermal, and historical response information rather than from a single voltage trigger. Another advantage of the invention is to provide reduced energy wastage because controlled transfer hardware can redirect useful charge between selected pack locations instead of dissipating the entire correction amount as heat. Yet another advantage of the invention is to provide enhanced pack safety by placing balancing commands under protection interlock supervision before any switch matrix or converter path is energized. Still another advantage of the invention is to provide better service adaptability because stored parameters and response history support different lithium chemistries, module layouts, and aging conditions. patents.abstract: A process for producing lithium hydroxide monohydrate from lithium chloride, the process comprising (a) adding an aqueous sodium hydroxide-containing solution to a first aqueous lithium chloride-containing solution, thereby obtaining a mixture comprising lithium hydroxide, sodium chloride and water, (b) cooling the mixture to selectively precipitate lithium hydroxide monohydrate, (c) separating the lithium hydroxide monohydrate precipitate from the first mother liquor solution, (d) adding a second aqueous lithium chloride-containing solution to the separated first mother liquor solution, thereby obtaining a lithium chloride-enriched first mother liquor solution, and (e) removing, preferably evaporating, water from the lithium chloride-enriched first mother liquor solution to selectively precipitate sodium chloride.

patents.abstract: Provided in the present application are a preparation method for a lithium iron phosphate positive electrode material, a positive electrode material and a battery. The preparation method comprises: (I) mixing an iron phosphate precursor, a lithium source, a dopant, a carbon source and a solvent, so as to obtain a dispersion; (II) subjecting the dispersion to wet grinding, so as to obtain an intermediate material; and (III) sequentially calcining and crushing the intermediate material, so as to obtain a lithium iron phosphate positive electrode material. patents.abstract: A battery cell, a battery, an electrical apparatus, and a battery cell core, belonging to the technical field of batteries. When the length-width ratio m of a positive electrode sheet satisfies 1 =m=6 and the compaction density ? of a positive electrode active material layer satisfies 3.3 g/cm3=?=3.7 g/cm3, the mass ratio of single-crystal particles of the positive electrode active material is controlled to be no less than 50%, and the porosity of the positive electrode active material layer is controlled to be 23% to 33%. Since single-crystal particles are less prone to fracture during cold pressing and long-term charging/discharging processes, excessive active specific surface area is not exposed compared to polycrystalline particles, thereby reducing side reactions with an electrolyte and reducing the increase of positive electrode impedance in a battery. Moreover, the occurrence of the situation in which an effective conductive network cannot be established at a new interface due to material particle fracture is reduced, so that the phenomenon of local potential increase caused by a particle "island" formed by the positive electrode active material is prevented, thereby achieving mitigation of the DCR in a battery cell core and mitigation of the electrode sheet resistance of a high-energy-density battery cell core.

patents.complete_specification: FORM 2 THE PATENTS ACT 1970 [39 OF 1970] & THE PATENTS (AMENDMENT) RULES, 2006 COMPLETE SPECIFICATION [See Section 10; rule 13] “A NOVEL ALKALINE LEACHING PROCESS OF LITHIUM CONCENTRATES” METSO FINLAND OY, of Rauhalanpuisto 9, 02230 Espoo, Finland, (Nationality: Finland), The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed: WO 2025/120254 1 PCT/FI2024/050654 A NOVEL ALKALINE LEACHING PROCESS OF LITHIUM CONCENTRATES FIELD [0001] The present invention relates to a process for recovering lithium from a 5 lithium-containing mineral in a process utilizing a leaching step, wherein non carbonates are required. BACKGROUND 10 15 20 25 [0002] Lithium is an element forming compounds with several industrial applications. The lithium for these purposes is mainly obtained from lithium brines and ores using a hydrometallurgical extraction process. The conventional lithium processing from ores contains a calcination or roasting process at high temperatures, followed by hydrometallurgical treatment such as pressure leaching. [0003] For example, US 9255012 B2 and US 11292725 B2 describe the leaching of calcined lithium-containing mineral materials in relatively mild leaching condition with leach solutions containing a carbonate. In US 9255012 B2, the solution obtained from the leaching step contains bicarbonate, which is then crystallized into a lithium carbonate product. In US 11292725 B2, the lithium in the leach slurry is reacted further into the hydroxide. However, both publications describe processes, wherein a calcination of the raw material, combined with a leaching using carbonate-based leach solution, has been used to provide the desired lithium extraction rates. [0004] One of the main issues of existing processes using known leaching conditions is that they require the material to have been carried via a calcination with optimum calcination conditions, which are difficult to maintain in an industrial scale. Therefore, there is a need for new processes, wherein lithium can be effectively leached also from uncalcined mineral raw materials and materials calcined under non-optimal conditions. Likewise, the leaching in the presence of carbonates is not optimal in view of extraction rates. WO 2025/120254 2 PCT/FI2024/050654 10 SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0005] The invention is defined by the features of the independent claims. Some specific embodiments are defined in the dependent claims. [0006] According to a first aspect of the invention, there is provided a process for 5 separating lithium from lithium-containing mineral raw-materials, using leaching conditions that are capable of solubilising even uncalcined minerals. 15 20 25 [0007] According to a second aspect, there is provided a process for leaching lithium-containing mineral raw-materials, without the need for leaching chemicals, such as carbonates. [0008] According to a third aspect, there is provided a process, wherein at least one of the solid and solution phases of the leach slurry obtained from the leaching step is treated further to decrease the contents of by-products and impurities in the process streams. [0009] According to a further aspect, there is provided a process that desilicates a process stream and utilizes the desilicated stream in recycle streams. [0010] The present invention thus relates to a process for recovering lithium from a lithium-containing mineral, comprising a) a leaching step, carried out in an aqueous leaching solution having a pH of ≥ 11.5, at a temperature of 120-240 °C, these leaching conditions providing a silicate product, b) a step for desilicating the leach solution obtained from the leaching step, and recirculating the remaining solution to one or more other steps of the process, and c) one or more steps for recovering lithium as a solid lithium compound from the lithium-containing leach residue obtained from the leaching step. [0011] The invention is based on the discovery that lithium can be recovered from lithium-containing minerals without utilizing leaching chemicals, particularly carbonate reagents, and even without requiring the calcination of the mineral. These factors have both been considered essential in past processes. WO 2025/120254 3 PCT/FI2024/050654 5 [0012] Significant advantages are achieved using the invention. Among others, the invention makes it possible to leach lithium concentrates without calcination pretreatment and without the related expensive equipment, whereby significant savings can be achieved in both cost and energy, the emissions of gases, such as CO2, can be reduced, and more sustainable and environmentally friendly lithium products can be obtained. [0013] Further, it has been surprisingly discovered that at least for some lithiumcontaining minerals, also better extraction rates can be achieved for lithium, when using concentrates of uncalcined mineral in the leaching step of the process. [0014] An advantage of the desilication step in the process is that the recycling 10 options in the process are improved, and the silicates carried to the process from the mineral, still being present in high contents in the leach solution, can be removed. 15 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0015] FIGURE 1 illustrates the process configuration in accordance with at least some embodiments of the present invention, with block 1 representing the leaching step of the process, block 2 representing a desilication step, and blocks 3 and 4 representing one or more steps for recovering lithium, or converting the lithium in a slurry or solution into a form that can easily be precipitated. The dotted arrows represent the possible recycling options. 20 [0016] FIGURE 2 illustrates a process configuration of an advantageous embodiment, with additional block 0 representing an optional pulping step, block 1 representing an optional solid/liquid separation step, and block 2' representing an optional further solid/liquid separation step. Further, block 3 herein represents a carbonization step and block 4 represents a lithium recovery step. The solution obtained from separation step 2' can be recycled back to the pulping step 0 or carried further to the carbonization step 3 (as shown with the dotted arrows). 25 CLAIMS: 1. A process for recovering lithium from a lithium-containing mineral, comprising a) a leaching step (1) carried out in an aqueous leaching solution having a pH of 11.5, at a temperature of 120-240 oC, after which a leach slurry is obtained, which contains lithium in the form of its silicate, and from which a lithium-containing leach residue and a leach solution can be separated, b) a step for desilicating (2) the leach solution obtained from the leaching step (1), and recirculating the remaining solution to one or more other steps of the process, and c) one or more steps (3,4) for recovering lithium as a solid lithium compound from the lithium-containing leach residue obtained from the leaching step. 2. The process of claim 1, wherein the lithium-containing mineral is selected from spodumene, petalite, lepidolite, zinnwaldite and intermediate minerals between petalite and spodumene (e.g. LiAISi3Og), or any combination thereof. 3. The process of claim 1, wherein the lithium-containing mineral is selected from calcined spodumene, petalite, lepidolite and zinnwaldite or any combination thereof, preferably being calcined spodumene. 4. The process of claim 1, wherein the lithium-containing mineral is selected from uncalcined spodumene, petalite, lepidolite and zinnwaldite or any combination thereof, preferably being uncalcined petalite. 5. The process of claim 1, wherein the lithium-containing mineral is selected from a combination of calcined and uncalcined minerals selected from spodumene, petalite, lepidolite and zinnwaldite or any combination thereof, preferably a combination of uncalcined petalite and calcined spodumene. 6. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the pH level of the leaching solution is adjusted to 12-14. 7. The process of any preceding claims, wherein the pH is adjusted before the leaching step using a hydroxide reagent, such as an alkali metal hydroxide, which preferably is selected from sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH), or a mixture thereof, preferably being sodium hydroxide. 8. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the leaching step (1) is carried out at the hydroxide content of preferably 1-6 mol∕L. 9. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the leaching step (1) is carried out at a temperature of at a temperature of 150-220 oC. 10. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the leaching step (1) is carried out at a pressure of 3-30 bar, preferably 5-25 bar, more preferably 10-25 bar. 11. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the leaching step (1) is carried out for a period of 30 min-4 h. 12. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the leaching step (1) is carried out without carbonate reagent, in a leaching solution containing no added carbonate. 13. The process of any of claims 1 to 3 and 5 to 10, wherein the leaching solution further contains a carbonate reagent, such as sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) or potassium carbonate (K2CO3), preferably in a stoichiometry of up to 3 related to the lithium content in the mineral, most suitably in a stoichiometry of >0-2.5 related to the lithium content in the mineral. 14. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the recovery step(s) (3,4) include a carbonization step (3), wherein the obtained leach slurry is reacted with a carbon dioxide (CO2), preferably the carbon dioxide is used in an excess amount. 15. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the desilication step (2) is carried out by adding a calcium reagent to the leach slurry or a solution separated therefrom, the calcium reagent preferably being calcium oxide (CaO) or calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2), and separating the formed solid silicate from a filtrate. 16. The process of any preceding claim, wherein the solution obtained from the desilication step (2) is recycled, either to be reused in the leaching step (1), or preferably in a preceding optional pulping step (0), or it may be carried to a subsequent processing step, such as a bicarbonization step (3). 17. The process of any preceding claim, wherein recovery steps (3,4) includes a precipitation (4) to obtain a solid lithium compound. 18. The process of claim 12, wherein the solid lithium compound is lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide. ABSTRACT A NOVEL ALKALINE LEACHING PROCESS OF LITHIUM CONCENTRATES According to the present invention, there is provided a process for recovering lithium from a lithium-containing mineral in a process utilizing a leaching step, wherein no carbonates are required, the obtained leach slurry thus containing silicates. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to: a lithium secondary battery having improved safety when high heat is applied from an external heat source, since the relationship among the size of the secondary battery, the content of remaining ethylene carbonate, and the reaction area of a negative electrode satisfies specific conditions; and to a method for evaluating thermal safety of a lithium secondary battery, whereby, through the information, thermal safety of a cylindrical lithium secondary battery can be evaluated.
patents.complete_specification: FORM 2 THE PATENTS ACT, 1970 (39 of 1970) & THE PATENTS RULES, 2003 COMPLETE SPECIFICATION (See section 10, rule 13) “LITHIUM SECONDARY BATTERY AND METHOD FOR EVALUATING THERMAL SAFETY OF LITHIUM SECONDARY BATTERY” LG ENERGY SOLUTION, LTD., a Korean company of Tower 1, 108, Yeoui-daero Yeongdeungpo-gu Seoul 07335, Republic of Korea; The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. 1 2 TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present invention relates to a lithium secondary battery and a method of evaluating thermal safety of a lithium 5 secondary battery. BACKGROUND ART [0002] A lithium secondary battery is generally prepared by a method in which electrode active material slurries are applied onto a positive electrode collector and a negative 10 electrode collector to prepare a positive electrode and a negative electrode, respectively, and, after the positive electrode and the negative electrode are stacked on both sides of a separator to form an electrode assembly having a predetermined shape, the electrode assembly is accommodated in 15 a pouch and an electrolyte is injected. [0003] Secondary batteries are classified into a pouch type, a can type, and the like, according to a material of a case for accommodating the electrode assembly. Among them, the pouch type secondary battery is prepared by a method of press 20 working a flexible pouch film laminate to form a cup portion, accommodating the electrode assembly in the cup portion, injecting an electrolyte, and then sealing a sealing portion, and the can type secondary battery is prepared by a method of accommodating the electrode assembly in a can formed of a 25 metallic material, injecting an electrolyte, and then 3 assembling a top cap on an upper portion of the can to seal the can. [0004] A 4680 cylindrical type secondary battery, which has emerged as a next-generation secondary battery among the can 5 type secondary batteries, is a cylindrical type secondary battery with a diameter of 46 mm and a height of 80 mm, wherein it has an advantage of high energy density and output because the diameter and the height are increased in comparison to those of a conventional cylindrical type secondary battery, 10 but since heat generation increases due to the high energy density and output, internal heat dissipation is not easy. As described above, as the increase of the diameter and height of the cylindrical type secondary battery increases an internal volume thereof, ensuring safety in high-temperature 15 environments becomes a more important issue. DISCLOSURE OF THE INVENTION TECHNICAL PROBLEM [0005] An aspect of the present invention provides a lithium secondary battery in which safety is ensured when high heat is 20 applied from an external heat source. [0006] Another aspect of the present invention provides a method of evaluating thermal safety of a lithium secondary battery which may evaluate whether safety of the lithium secondary battery is ensured when high heat is applied from an 25 external heat source. 4 TECHNICAL SOLUTION [0007] In order to solve the above-described task, the present invention provides a lithium secondary battery. [0008] [1] The present invention provides a lithium secondary 5 battery including: an electrode assembly including a positive electrode, a negative electrode, and a separator disposed between the positive electrode and the negative electrode; an electrolyte including ethylene carbonate as a solvent; and a cylindrical battery case accommodating the electrode assembly 10 and the electrolyte, wherein the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1: [0009] [Equation 1] [0010] In Equation 1, R is a diameter (mm) of the battery, H is a height (mm) of the battery, dEC is an amount (g) of the 15 ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium secondary battery after formation, AA is an area(cm2) of the negative electrode, LA is a loading amount(g/cm2) of the negative electrode, RA is a ratio of a negative electrode active material, and BA is Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area (m2/g) of 20 the negative electrode active material, wherein R is in a range of 45 to 47, and H is in a range of 78 to 130. [0011] [2] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of [1] above, wherein R and H are a diameter and a height of a 4680 lithium secondary battery, a 4695 5 lithium secondary battery, a 46120 lithium secondary battery, or a 46125 lithium secondary battery, respectively. [0012] [3] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of [1] or [2] above, wherein dEC is in a 5 range of 2.0 to 10.0. [0013] [4] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [3] above, wherein AA is in a range of 2,800 to 2,900. [0014] [5] The present invention provides the lithium 10 secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [4] above, wherein LA is in a range of 0.1000 to 0.2000. [0015] [6] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [5] above, wherein RA is in a range of 0.80 to 0.99. 15 [0016] [7] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [6] above, wherein BA is in a range of 0.01 to 100. [0017] [8] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [7] above, wherein 20 the electrolyte further includes an organic solvent other than the ethylene carbonate, wherein the organic solvent includes at least one selected from the group consisting of an esterbased solvent, an ether-based solvent, a ketone-based solvent, an aromatic hydrocarbon-based solvent, a carbonate-based 25 solvent other than the ethylene carbonate, an alcohol-based 6 solvent, nitriles, amides, dioxolanes, and sulfolanes. [0018] [9] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [8] above, wherein the electrolyte further includes an electrolyte additive, 5 wherein the electrolyte additive includes at least one selected from the group consisting of a cyclic carbonate-based compound, a halogen-substituted carbonate-based compound, a sultone-based compound, a sulfate-based compound, a phosphatebased compound, a borate-based compound, a nitrile-based 10 compound, a benzene-based compound, an amine-based compound, a silane-based compound, and a lithium salt-based compound. [0019] [10] The present invention provides the lithium secondary battery of at least one of [1] to [9] above, wherein the positive electrode includes a positive electrode active 15 material, wherein the positive electrode active material includes a lithium transition metal oxide containing 60 mol% or more of nickel (Ni) among total metals excluding lithium. [0020] Also, in order to solve the other tasks, the present invention provides a method of evaluating thermal safety of a 20 lithium secondary battery. [0021] [11] The present invention provides a method of evaluating thermal safety of a cylindrical type lithium secondary battery which includes the steps of: (s1) measuring a diameter and a height of the lithium secondary battery; (s2) 25 measuring an amount of ethylene carbonate (EC) remaining in 7 the lithium secondary battery after formation; (s3) measuring a reaction area of a negative electrode active material layer of a negative electrode included in the lithium secondary battery; and (s4) determining that the lithium secondary 5 battery has thermal safety when Equation 1 is satisfied: [0022] [Equation 1] [0023] In Equation 1, R is the diameter (mm)of the battery, H is the height (mm)of the battery, dEC is the amount (g)of the ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium secondary 10 battery after formation, AA is an area (cm2) of the negative electrode, LA is a loading amount (g/cm2) of the negative electrode, RA is a ratio of a negative electrode active material, BA is Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area (m2/g) of the negative electrode active material, and the 15 reaction area of the negative active material layer is calculated as AA×LA×RA×BA, wherein R is in a range of 45 to 47, and H is in a range of 78 to 130. [0024] [12] The present invention provides the method of [11] above, wherein R and H are a diameter and a height of a 4680 20 lithium secondary battery, a 4695 lithium secondary battery, a 46120 lithium secondary battery, or a 46125 lithium secondary battery, respectively. ADVANTAGEOUS EFFECTS [0025] As in a lithium secondary battery according to the 8 present invention, in a case in which a relationship among a size of the battery, an amount of ethylene carbonate remaining after formation, and a reaction area of a negative electrode satisfies a specific condition, safety may be improved when 5 high heat is applied from an external heat source, and accordingly, a lithium secondary battery with improved thermal safety may be provided. Also, according to a method of evaluating thermal safety of a lithium secondary battery of the present invention, the thermal safety of the lithium 10 secondary battery may be predicted and evaluated from the size of the battery, the amount of the ethylene carbonate remaining after formation, and the reaction area of the negative electrode. MODE FOR CARRYING OUT THE INVENTION 15 [0026] It will be understood that words or terms used in the specification and claims shall not be interpreted as the meaning defined in commonly used dictionaries, and it will be further understood that the words or terms should be interpreted as having a meaning that is consistent with their 20 meaning in the context of the relevant art and the technical idea of the invention, based on the principle that an inventor may properly define the meaning of the words or terms to best explain the invention. 25 [0027] Hereinafter, the present invention will be described 9 in more detail. [0028] A lithium secondary battery according to the present invention includes an electrode assembly including a positive 5 electrode, a negative electrode, and a separator disposed between the positive electrode and the negative electrode; an electrolyte including ethylene carbonate as a solvent; and a cylindrical battery case accommodating the electrode assembly and the electrolyte, wherein the lithium secondary battery 10 satisfies Equation 1 below. [0029] [Equation 1] [0030] In Equation 1, R is a diameter (mm) of the battery, H is a height (mm) of the battery, dEC is an amount (g) of the 15 ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium secondary battery after formation, AA is an area(cm2) of the negative electrode, LA is a loading amount(g/cm2) of the negative electrode, RA is a ratio of a negative electrode active material, and BA is Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area (m2/g) of 20 the negative electrode active material, wherein R is in a range of 45 to 47, and H is in a range of 78 to 130. [0031] Recently, as the demand for high-capacity batteries, such as batteries for electric vehicles, increases, rated capacity of a secondary battery cell is increasing, and 10 accordingly, size and weight of an electrode assembly have tended to increase. As the size and weight of the electrode assembly increase, there is an advantage of high energy density and output, but since heat generation increases due to the 5 high energy density and output, internal heat dissipation is not easy, and accordingly, influence of heat transfer by an external heat source further affects thermal stability of the battery. [0032] Factors affecting thermal stability and safety of a 10 cylindrical type secondary battery with larger diameter and height than a conventional cylindrical type secondary battery may include internal space and electrolyte solution injection amount of the cylindrical type secondary battery, and may also include influence due to formation of a solid electrolyte 15 interphase (SEI) layer caused by an electrolyte solution additive. Among the above factors, the influence of the SEI layer is greater than that of the electrolyte solution injection amount, and thus, a decrease in the SEI layer due to a decrease in absolute amount of the electrolyte solution 20 additive rather than an increase in the internal space due to a decrease in the electrolyte solution injection amount further affects the thermal stability and safety of the secondary battery. Therefore, in order to sufficiently form the SEI layer for ensuring the thermal stability and safety of the 4680 25 cylindrical secondary battery, a certain amount or more of the 11 electrolyte solution additive must be included in the cylindrical type secondary battery. [0033] In the lithium secondary battery, an SEI layer is formed as Li ions diffused from the positive electrode during 5 initial formation are deposited on a surface of the negative electrode. In a process of forming the SEI layer, since the electrolyte solution additive reacts first and then the ethylene carbonate (EC), as the electrolyte solution solvent, reacts, a degree of SEI layer formation may be confirmed by a 10 degree of decomposition of the ethylene carbonate included in the lithium secondary battery. That is, based on the fact that sufficient formation of the SEI layer significantly affects the thermal stability and safety of the lithium secondary battery, whether or not the SEI layer is sufficiently formed 15 in the lithium secondary battery is confirmed by confirming the degree of decomposition of the ethylene carbonate included in the lithium secondary battery in a formation process, and thus, the thermal stability and safety of the lithium secondary battery may be confirmed. 20 [0034] Since a size of the lithium secondary battery, an amount of the ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium secondary battery after formation, and a reaction area of the negative electrode satisfy Equation 1 below, the lithium secondary battery according to the present invention includes 25 a sufficiently formed SEI layer. 12 [0035] [Equation 1] [0036] In Equation 1, R is a diameter (mm) of the battery, H is a height (mm) of the battery, dEC is the amount (g) of the 5 ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium secondary battery after formation, AA is an area (cm2) of the negative electrode, LA is a loading amount (g/cm2) of the negative electrode, RA is a ratio of a negative electrode active material, and BA is BET specific surface area (m2/g) of the negative electrode 10 active material. Also, AA×LA×RA×BA in Equation 1 refers to the reaction area of the negative electrode. [0037] The lithium secondary battery satisfying Equation 1 is a lithium secondary battery after formation. [0038] In an embodiment of the present invention, Equation 1 15 may specifically be represented by Equation 1-1 below, and may more specifically be represented by Equation 1-2 below. [0039] [Equation 1-1] [0040] [Equation 1-2] 20 [0041] In Equations 1-1 and 1-2, R is the diameter (mm) of the battery, H is the height (mm) of the battery, dEC is the amount (g)of the ethylene carbonate remaining in the lithium 13 secondary battery after formation, AA is the area (cm2) of the negative electrode, LA is the loading amount (g/cm2) of the negative electrode, RA is the ratio of the negative electrode active material, and BA is the BET specific surface area (m2/g) 5 of the negative electrode active material. [0042] Also, in an embodiment of the present invention, a value of Equation 1 may satisfy 5.00 to 10.00, the value of Equation 1 may specifically satisfy 5.00 to 8.00, and the value of Equation 1 may more specifically satisfy 5.00 to 6.00. 10 [0043] In a case in which the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1-1, it may exhibit better battery performance and thermal safety, and in a case in which the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1-2, it may exhibit even better battery performance and thermal safety. 15 [0044] In an embodiment of the present invention, R is the diameter (mm) of the battery, wherein it may be a diameter of the lithium secondary battery or a diameter of the cylindrical battery case. R may be in a range of 45 to 47, R may specifically be in a range of 45.5 to 46.5, and R may more 20 specifically be 46. [0045] Furthermore, in an embodiment of the present invention, H is the height (mm) of the battery, wherein it may be a height (length) of the lithium secondary battery or a height (length) of the cylindrical battery case. H may be in a range of 78 to 25 130, H may specifically be in a range of 79.0 to 126.0, 79.0 14 to 121.0, 79.0 to 82.0, 94.0 to 96.0, 119.0 to 121.0, or 124.0 to 126.0, and H may more specifically be in a range of 79.5 to 80.5, 94.5 to 95.5, 119.5 to 120.5, or 124.5 to 125.5. [0046] R (the diameter of the battery) and H (the height of 5 the battery) may be the diameter and the height which are measured from an outer surface of the lithium secondary battery or the cylindrical battery case. [0047] Also, in an embodiment of the present invention, R (the diameter of the battery) and H (the height of the battery) 10 may specifically represent a diameter and a height of a cylindrical type lithium secondary battery, and may more specifically represent a diameter and a height of a 4680 lithium secondary battery, a 4695 lithium secondary battery, a 46120 lithium secondary battery, or a 46125 lithium secondary 15 battery. [0048] In an embodiment of the present invention, dEC is the amount (g) of the remaining ethylene carbonate, wherein it represents the amount of the ethylene carbonate included in 20 the lithium secondary battery. Also, it may refer to a weight (g) of the ethylene carbonate remaining after the formation of the lithium secondary battery in the electrolyte solution injected into the lithium secondary battery. [0049] In an embodiment of the present invention, while the 25 lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1, dEC may be in 15 a range of2.0 to 10.0, may specifically be in a range of 2.4 to 7.5, and may more specifically be in a range of 4.95 to 5.83. [0050] In an embodiment of the present invention, AA is the 5 area (cm2) of the negative electrode, and may be a total area of one surface of the negative electrode included in the lithium secondary battery. [0051] In an embodiment of the present invention, while the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1, AA may be in 10 a range of 2,800 to 2,900, may specifically be in a range of 2,820 to 2,880, and may more specifically be in a range of 2841.3 to 2855.3. [0052] In an embodiment of the present invention, LA is the loading amount (g/cm2) of the negative electrode, wherein it 15 is available capacity of the negative electrode per unit area. [0053] In an embodiment of the present invention, while the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1, LA may be in a range of 0.1000 to 0.2000, may specifically be in a range of 0.1400 to 0.1600, and may more specifically be in a range of 20 0.1468 to 0.1512. [0054] In an embodiment of the present invention, RA is the ratio of the negative electrode active material, wherein it represents a weight ratio of the negative electrode active material to a total weight of a negative electrode active 25 material layer. 16 [0055] In an embodiment of the present invention, while the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1, RA may be in a range of 0.80 to 0.99, may specifically be in a range of 0.82 to 0.99, and may more specifically be in a range of 0.84 5 to 0.99. [0056] In an embodiment of the present invention, BA is a Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area (m2/g) of the negative electrode active material, and the “BET specific surface area” is measured by a BET method, wherein, 10 specifically, the BET specific surface area may be calculated from a nitrogen gas adsorption amount at a liquid nitrogen temperature (77K) using BELSORP-mino II by Bell Japan Inc. [0057] In an embodiment of the present invention, while the lithium secondary battery satisfies Equation 1, BA may be in 15 a range of 0.01 to 100, may specifically be in a range of 0.01 to 50, and may more specifically be in a range of 0.5 to 3.0. [0058] A lithium secondary battery satisfying Equation 1 may exhibit excellent thermal stability and thermal safety because the SEI layer is sufficiently formed during initial formation. 20 [0059] In an embodiment of the present invention, the electrolyte may further include an organic solvent other than the ethylene carbonate while including the ethylene carbonate as a solvent. 25 [0060] The organic solvent may include at least one selected 17 from the group consisting of an ester-based solvent, an etherbased solvent, a ketone-based solvent, an aromatic hydrocarbon-based solvent, a carbonate-based solvent other than the ethylene carbonate, an alcohol-based solvent, 5 nitriles, amides, dioxolanes, and sulfolanes. Specifically, the ester-based solvent such as methyl acetate, ethyl acetate, γ-butyrolactone, and ε-caprolactone; the ether-based solvent such as dibutyl ether or tetrahydrofuran; the ketone-based solvent such as cyclohexanone; the aromatic hydrocarbon-based 10 solvent such as benzene and fluorobenzene; the carbonate-based solvent such as dimethyl carbonate (DMC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), ethylmethyl carbonate (EMC), and propylene carbonate (PC); the alcohol-based solvent such as ethyl alcohol and isopropyl alcohol; the nitriles such as R-CN (where R is a 15 linear, branched, or cyclic C2-C20 hydrocarbon group and may include a double-bond aromatic ring or ether bond); the amides such as dimethylformamide; the dioxolanes such as 1,3-dioxolane; or the sulfolanes may be used as the organic solvent. More specifically, the carbonate-based solvent may be used, 20 and a solvent capable of forming a mixture of a cyclic carbonate having high ionic conductivity and high dielectric constant, which may increase charge/discharge performance of the battery, and a low-viscosity linear carbonate-based compound (e.g., ethylmethyl carbonate, dimethyl carbonate, or 25 diethyl carbonate) may be used. 18 [0061] Also, in an embodiment of the present invention, the electrolyte may further include a known electrolyte additive in the non-aqueous electrolyte, if necessary, in order to 5 prevent the occurrence of collapse of the negative electrode due to the decomposition of the non-aqueous electrolyte in a high power environment or to further improve low-temperature high rate discharge characteristics, high-temperature stability, overcharge prevention, and an effect of suppressing 10 battery swelling at high temperature. [0062] The electrolyte additive may be an additive for forming an SEI layer, and, for example, may be at least one selected from the group consisting of a cyclic carbonate-based compound, a halogen-substituted carbonate-based compound, a sultone15 based compound, a sulfate-based compound, a phosphate-based compound, a borate-based compound, a nitrile-based compound, a benzene-based compound, an amine-based compound, a silanebased compound, and a lithium salt-based compound. [0063] In a case in which the electrolyte additive is included, 20 since the electrolyte additive participates in the formation of the SEI layer while being decomposed earlier than the ethylene carbonate during the initial formation of the lithium secondary battery, it may improve thermal stability of the SEI layer by forming the more uniform and sufficient SEI layer. 25 [0064] The cyclic carbonate-based compound may be vinylene 19 carbonate (VC) or vinyl ethylene carbonate. [0065] The halogen-substituted carbonate-based compound may be fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). patents.abstract: The disclosure relates to a method for manufacturing a piezoelectric transducer (1) comprising a front electrode (10a), a rear electrode (10b) and a piezoelectric ceramic (50) made from lithium niobate. The method comprises: a step (a) of depositing a layer (40a, 40b) of metal bonding primer on each opposing face of the ceramic (50); a step (b) of depositing, on each electrode (10a, 10b), a compliance layer (20a, 20b) made from an electrically conductive material with Tfusion > 700°C and drupture > 20%; a step (c) of placing a strip (30a, 30b) based on an Ag-Cu alloy on each layer (40a, 40b) of bonding primer; a step (d) of forming an assembly (60) by stacking the elements in this order (10a, 20a, 30a, 40a, 50, 40b, 30b, 20b, 10b); a step (e) of compression-brazing the assembly (60) in a furnace at more than 450°C in a non-oxidizing atmosphere.

patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a current collector, an electrode comprising same, and a secondary battery, the current collector comprising a primer layer that includes a conductive material, a binder and a thickener, wherein the conductive material is a multi-walled carbon nanotubes having a BET specific surface area of at least 170 m2/g, and thus the present invention has excellent adhesion with an electrode active material layer, low interfacial resistance, and excellent scratch resistance.
patents.complete_specification: [Technical Field] 5 [1] CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION [2] The present application claims priority to Korean Patent Application No. 10-2023-0174768, filed on December 05, 2023, the entire content of which is incorporated herein for all purposes by reference. [3] 10 [4] Technical Field [5] The present invention relates to a current collector including a primer layer, and an electrode and a lithium secondary battery including the same. [6] [Background Art] 15 [7] Recently, as the application area of lithium secondary batteries has rapidly expanded to not only power supply for electronic devices such as electric, electronic, communication, and computers, but also power storage supply for large-area devices such as automobiles and power storage devices, the demand for high-capacity, high-output, and high-stability lithium secondary batteries is 20 increasing. [8] The lithium secondary batteries are generally manufactured as follows: A slurry is prepared by mixing a positive electrode active material capable of intercalating and deintercalating lithium ions or a negative electrode active material capable of absorbing and releasing lithium ions, and optionally a binder 25 and a conductive material. The slurries are applied to a positive electrode current 3 collector and a negative electrode current collector, respectively, and the solvent is removed by heat, etc., thereby manufacturing a positive electrode and a negative electrode. The positive and negative electrodes are stacked on both sides of a separator to form an electrode assembly with a predetermined shape. 5 Then, the electrode assembly and a non-aqueous electrolyte are inserted into a battery case to manufacture a lithium secondary battery. However, when manufacturing the positive electrode and negative electrode in this way, there is a problem that the solvent contained in the slurry needs to be removed through an additional process, and as a result, the cost of the manufacturing process 10 increases and productivity is low. Therefore, a dry manufacturing method has been proposed in which each active material is positioned on a current collector in the form of a film and passed through a rolling roll. [9] Meanwhile, since the electrode manufactured by the dry manufacturing method of coating the electrode active material on the current collector without a solvent 15 has weak adhesive strength between the current collector and the electrode active material layer, there is a problem that the electrode active material layer is detached from the current collector due to shrinkage and expansion of the electrode that occurs during charging and discharging of the secondary battery. Accordingly, a method has been proposed to provide a primer layer on the 20 surface of the current collector to strengthen the adhesive strength between the current collector and the electrode active material layer. [10] The primer layer is usually composed of a binder and a conductive material, wherein the binder melts during high-temperature rolling to secure adhesive strength, and the conductive material can serve to lower the interfacial resistance 25 with the electrode active material layer. However, since the conventional primer 4 layer composed only of a binder and a conductive material has poor scratch resistance, there is a problem that scratches easily occur during rolling. Accordingly, there is a need for the development of a current collector coated with a primer layer that has excellent adhesive strength, low interfacial 5 resistance, and excellent scratch resistance. [11] [Disclosure] [Technical Problem] [12] The present invention has been devised to solve the problems of the above10 mentioned prior art, and aims to provide a current collector having excellent scratch resistance along with excellent adhesive strength and low interfacial resistance characteristics. [13] In addition, the present invention aims to provide an electrode having an electrode active material layer on the above current collector. 15 [14] Furthermore, the present invention aims to provide a lithium secondary battery including the above electrode. [15] [Technical Solution] [16] In order to solve the above-mentioned problems, the present invention provides 20 current collector, electrode, and lithium secondary battery. [17] (1) The present invention provides a current collector comprising: a metal layer and a primer layer coated on at least one surface of the metal layer, wherein the primer layer includes a conductive material, a binder, and a thickener, wherein the conductive material is a multi-walled carbon nanotube having a BET specific 5 surface area of 170 m2 /g or more, and a weight ratio of the conductive material to the binder is 1:1 or more and 10 or less. [18] (2) The present invention provides the current collector according to (1) above, wherein a content of the thickener is 5 parts by weight or more and 20 parts by 5 weight or less, based on 100 parts by weight of the total weight of the conductive material, binder, and thickener. [19] (3) The present invention provides the current collector according to (1) or (2) above, wherein a content of the conductive material is 10 parts by weight or more and 50 parts by weight or less, based on 100 parts by weight of the total 10 weight of the conductive material, binder, and thickener. [20] (4) The present invention provides the current collector according to any one of (1) to (3) above, wherein a content of the binder is 35 parts by weight or more and 75 parts by weight or less, based on 100 parts by weight of the total weight of the conductive material, binder, and thickener. 15 [21] (5) The present invention provides the current collector according to any one of (1) to (4) above, wherein the binder is at least one selected from the group consisting of polyvinylidene fluoride, vinylidene fluoride-hexafluoropropylene copolymer, hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber, styrene butadiene rubber, polyacrylonitrile, polymethyl methacrylate, polyethylene, 20 polytetrafluoroethylene, and polyacrylic acid. [22] (6) The present invention provides the current collector according to any one of (1) to (5) above, wherein the thickener is at least one selected from the group consisting of carboxymethylcellulose, polyvinylpyrrolidone, and polyvinyl alcohol. 6 [23] (7) The present invention provides the current collector according to any one of (1) to (6) above, wherein a thickness of the primer layer is 0.2 μm or more and 2 μm or less. [24] (8) The present invention provides the current collector according to any one of 5 (1) to (7) above, wherein a surface roughness of the primer layer is 1.1 μm or less. [25] (9) The present invention provides an electrode comprising: the current collector of any one of (1) to (8) above; and an electrode active material layer, wherein the electrode active material layer is attached on the primer layer of the current 10 collector. [26] (10) The present invention provides the electrode according to (9) above, wherein an adhesive strength between the electrode active material layer and the primer layer is 40 gf/2cm or more as measured at a peeling speed of 100 mm/min in a 90° peel test. 15 [27] (11) The present invention provides the electrode according to (9) or (10) above, wherein an interfacial resistance between the electrode active material layer and the current collector is 0.6 Ω·cm2 or less. [28] (12) The present invention provides a lithium secondary battery comprising the electrode according to any one of (9) to (11) above. 20 [29] [Advantageous Effects] [30] The current collector of the present invention comprises a primer layer including a conductive material, a binder, and a thickener, wherein the conductive material is a multi-walled carbon nanotube having a BET specific surface area of 170 7 m2 /g or more, thereby exhibiting excellent adhesive strength with the electrode active material layer, low interfacial resistance, and excellent scratch resistance. [31] In addition, the electrode of the present invention has an electrode active material layer attached to the primer layer of the current collector, thereby 5 exhibiting excellent battery characteristics due to excellent adhesive strength and low interfacial resistance. [32] Further, the lithium secondary battery of the present invention comprises the above electrode, thereby preventing the problem of the electrode active material layer being peeled off during charging and discharging, which enables the 10 secondary battery to be operated stably. [33] [Description of Drawings] [34] FIG. 1 is a scanning electron microscope (SEM) photograph of a primer layer of a current collector manufactured in Example 1 of the present invention. 15 [35] FIG. 2 is a scanning electron microscope (SEM) photograph of a primer layer of a current collector manufactured in Comparative Example 3 of the present invention. [36] FIG. 3 is a photograph of current collectors manufactured in Example 1 and Comparative Example 3 of the present invention after a friction test in a scratch 20 resistance evaluation. The current collector of Comparative Example 3 is shown on the left, and the current collector of Example 1 is shown on the right. [37] [Best Modes of the Invention] [38] Hereinafter, the present invention will be described in more detail to help 25 understand the present invention. 8 [39] The terms or words used in the specification should not be construed as being limited to their ordinary or dictionary meanings, but should be interpreted as meanings and concepts consistent with the technical spirit of the present invention, based on the principle that the inventor may adequately define the 5 concepts of terms to best describe his invention. [40] The terms used in the specification are used only to describe exemplary embodiments, and are not intended to limit the present invention. Singular expressions include plural expressions unless the context clearly implies otherwise. 10 [41] It should be understood that terms such as “comprise”, “include”, and “have” as used herein are intended to designate the presence of implemented features, numbers, steps, components, or combinations thereof, but not to preclude a possibility of existence or addition of one or more other features, numbers, steps, components, or combinations thereof. 15 [42] [43] Current Collector [44] The present invention provides a current collector in which a primer layer is coated on at least one surface of a metal layer. [45] According to one embodiment of the present invention, the current collector may 20 comprise: a metal layer and a primer layer coated on at least one surface of the metal layer, wherein the primer layer may include a conductive material, a binder, and a thickener, wherein the conductive material may be a multi-walled carbon nanotube having a BET specific surface area of 170 m2 /g or more, and the weight ratio of the conductive material to the binder may be 1:1 or more and 25 10 or less. 9 [46] The current collector may have the primer layer coated on at least one surface of the metal layer, and for example, the primer layer may be coated on both surfaces of the metal layer. In addition, the metal layer may comprise copper, stainless steel, aluminum, nickel, titanium, fired carbon, copper or stainless steel 5 surface-treated with carbon, nickel, titanium, silver, or the like, or an aluminumcadmium alloy, and for example, may be at least one selected from the group consisting of aluminum foil, aluminum mesh, stainless steel foil, and copper foil. [47] The primer layer of the current collector includes multi-walled carbon nanotubes as a conductive material, and thus can have significantly high peeling resistance 10 and low interfacial resistance. Specifically, the multi-walled carbon nanotubes have high strength compared to conductive materials such as carbon black, and thus can significantly improve the peeling resistance of the primer layer, and as a result, the primer layer including the multi-walled carbon nanotubes can have excellent scratch resistance. In addition, the multi-walled carbon nanotubes have 15 excellent electrical conductivity, and thus can also reduce the interfacial resistance of the current collector. [48] In addition, the multi-walled carbon nanotube may have a specific surface area of 170 m2 /g or more. Specifically, the specific surface area of the multi-walled carbon nanotube may be 170 m2 /g or more, 180 m2 /g or more, 190 m2 /g or more, 200 m2 /g or more, 210 m2 /g or more, 220 m2 /g or more, or 230 m2 20 /g or more, and may also be 300 m2 /g or less, 290 m2 /g or less, 280 m2 /g or less, 270 m2 /g or less, 260 m2 /g or less, or 250 m2 /g or less. When the specific surface area of the multi-walled carbon nanotube satisfies the above range, the dispersibility of the multi-walled carbon nanotube as a conductive material can be excellent, and 25 the conductive material can be evenly distributed within the primer layer and 10 strongly bonded with the binder, and accordingly, the adhesive strength and peeling resistance of the primer layer can be significantly increased. [49] In addition, the multi-walled carbon nanotube may have an average diameter of 5 nm or more and 20 nm or less. Specifically, the average diameter may be 5 nm 5 or more, 6 nm or more, 7 nm or more, 8 nm or more, 9 nm or more, or 10 nm or more, and may also be 20 nm or less, 19 nm or less, 18 nm or less, 17 nm or less, 16 nm or less, or 15 nm or less. [50] In the conventional primer layer composed of only a conductive material and a binder, since the conductive material and the binder are weakly bonded, there 10 was a problem that the peeling resistance of the primer layer was poor, and the layer separation of the conductive material and the binder occurred due to friction. Accordingly, the primer layer of the current collector of the present invention includes a thickener, so that the binder and the conductive material can be strongly bonded to each other by the thickener, and as a result, the layer 15 separation of the conductive material and the binder can be suppressed, thereby improving the peeling resistance of the primer layer and the adhesive strength with the electrode active material layer, and also reducing the interfacial resistance.
