Optionally, the reaction product gas-solid mixture can be delivered into a gas-solid separator (e.g., a gas-solid separator 328) to separate and obtain final solid product particles and a gaseous side product. In addition, one or more flows of cooling fluids (e.g., gases or liquids) may be used to cool the temperature of the reaction products. The final solid product particles can be delivered out of the system 300 for further analysis on their properties (e.g., specific capacity, power performance, battery charging cycle performance, etc.), particle sizes, morphology, crystal structure, etc., to be used as a material in a battery cell. Finally, the final particles are packed into a component of a battery cell. [00105] Figure 3 is a schematic of the system 300, which is one example of an integrated tool/apparatus that can be used to carry out a fast, simple, continuous and low cost manufacturing process for preparing a material for a battery electrochemical cell. The system 300 is connected to a liquid mixer 304, which in turn is connected to two or more reactant sources 302A, 302B. The reactant sources 302A, 302B are provided to store various precursor compounds and liquid solvents. Desired amounts of precursor compounds (in solid or liquid form) and solvents are dosed and delivered from the reactant sources 302A, 302B to the liquid mixer 304 so that the precursor compounds can be dissolved and/or dispersed in the solvent and mix well into a liquid mixture. If necessary, the liquid mixer 304 is heated to a temperature, such as between 30 °C and 90 °C to help uniformly dissolve, disperse, and/or mix the precursors. The liquid mixer 304 is optionally connected to a pump 305, which pumps the liquid mixture from the liquid mixer 304 into the mist generator 306 of the system 300 to generate a mist. [00106] The mist generator 306 converts the liquid mixture into a mist with desired droplet size and size distribution. In addition, the mist generator 306 is coupled to the drying chamber 310 in order to dry and remove moisture from the mist and obtain thoroughly-mixed solid precursor particles. In one embodiment, the mist generator 306 is positioned near the top of the drying chamber 310 that is positioned vertically (e.g., a dome-type drying chamber, etc.) to inject the mist into the drying chamber 310 and pass through the drying chamber vertically downward. Alternatively, the mist generator can be positioned near the bottom of the drying chamber 310 that is vertically positioned to inject the mist upward into the drying chamber to increase the residence time of the mist generated therein. In another embodiment, when the drying chamber 310 is positioned horizontally (e.g., a tube drying chamber, etc.) and the mist generator 306 is positioned near one end of the drying chamber 310 such that a flow of the mist, being delivered from the one end through another end of the drying chamber 310, can pass through a path within the drying chamber 310 for the length of its residence time. [00107] The drying chamber 310 generally includes a chamber inlet 315, a chamber body 312, and a chamber outlet 317. In one configuration, the mist generator 306 is positioned inside the drying chamber 310 near the chamber inlet 315 and connected to a liquid line 303 adapted to flow the liquid mixture therein from the liquid mixer 304. For example, the liquid mixture within the liquid mixer 304 can be pumped by the pump 305 through the liquid line 303 connected to the chamber inlet 315 into the internal volume of the drying chamber 310. Pumping of the liquid mixture by the pump 305 can be configured, for example, continuously at a desired delivery rate (e.g., adjusted by a metered valve or other means) to achieve good process throughput of system 300. In another configuration, the mist generator 306 is positioned outside the drying chamber 310 and the mist generated therefrom is delivered to the drying chamber 310 via the chamber inlet 315. [00108] One or more gas lines (e.g., gas lines 331 A, 331 B, 331 C, 331 D, etc.) can be coupled to various portions of the drying chamber 310 and adapted to flow a gas from a gas source 332 into the drying chamber 310. A flow of the gas stored in the gas source 332 can be delivered, concurrently with the formation of the mist inside drying chamber 310, into the drying chamber 310 to carry the mist through the drying chamber 310, remove moisture from the mist, and form a gas-solid mixture containing the precursors. Also, the flow of the gas can be delivered into the drying chamber 310 prior to the formation of the mist to fill and preheat an internal volume of the drying chamber 310 prior to generating the mist inside the drying chamber 310. [00109] In one example, the gas line 331 A is connected to the top portion of the drying chamber 310 to deliver the gas into the mist generator 306 positioned near the chamber inlet 315 to be mixed with the mist generated by the mist generator 306 inside the drying chamber 310. In one embodiment, the gas is preheated to a temperature of between 70 °C and 600 °C to mix with and remove moisture from the mist. As another example, the gas line 331 B delivering the gas therein is connected to the chamber inlet 315 of the drying chamber 310, in close proximity with the liquid line 303 having the liquid mixture therein. Accordingly, the gas can thoroughly mix with the mist of the liquid mixture inside the drying chamber 310. [001 0] In another example, the gas line 331 C is connected to the chamber body 312 of the drying chamber 310 to deliver the gas therein and mix the gas with the mist generated from the mist generator 306. [00111] The flow of the gas may be pumped through an air filter to remove any particles, droplets, or contaminants, and the flow rate of the gas can be adjusted by a valve or other means. In one embodiment, the gas is heated to a drying temperature to mix with the mist and remove moisture from the mist. It is designed to obtain spherical solid particles from a thoroughly-mixed liquid mixture of two or more precursors after drying the mist of the liquid mixture. In contrast, conventional solid-state manufacturing processes involve mixing or milling a solid mixture of precursor compounds, resulting in uneven mixing of precursors. [00112] Once the mist of the liquid mixture is dried and formed into a gas-solid mixture with the gas, the gas-solid mixture is delivered out of the drying chamber 310 via the chamber outlet 317. The drying chamber 310 is coupled to the gas-solid separator 320 of the system 300. Accordingly, the system 300 is designed to mix the two or more precursors uniformly, dry the two or more precursors, separate the dried two or more precursors, and react the two or more precursors into final solid product particles of the crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials in a continuous manner. [00116] Suitable gas-solid separators include cyclones, electrostatic separators, electrostatic precipitators, gravity separators, inertia separators, membrane separators, fluidized beds, classifiers, electric sieves, impactors, particles collectors, leaching separators, elutriators, air classifiers, leaching classifiers, and combinations thereof, among others. [00117] Once the one or more solid particles of a lithium cobalt oxide material are separated and obtained, it is delivered into the reactor 340 for further reaction. Optionally, a vessel 325 is adapted to store the solid particles prior to adjusting the amounts of the solid particles delivered into the reactor 340. [00118] The gas inlet 333 of the reactor 340 is coupled to a heating mechanism 380 to heat a gas from a gas source 334 to an annealing temperature of between 400 °C and 1200 °C. The heating mechanism 380 can be, for example, an electric heater, a gas-fueled heater, a burner, among other heaters. Additional gas lines can be used to deliver heated air or gas into the reactor 340, if needed. The pre-heated gas can fill the reactor 340 and maintained the internal temperature of the reactor 340, much better and energy efficient than conventional heating of the chamber body of a reactor. [00119] The gas flown inside the reactor 340 is designed to be mixed with the one or more solid particles of a lithium cobalt oxide material and form an oxidized reaction product inside the reactor 340. Thermal energy from the pre-heated gas is used as the energy source for reacting the one or more solid particles of a lithium cobalt oxide material within the reactor 340. The reaction process includes, but not limited to, reduction, decomposition, combination reaction, phase-transformation, re-crystallization, single displacement reaction, double displacement reaction, combustion, isomerization, and combinations thereof. The oxidized reaction product is then going through annealing process for a residence time of between 1 second and ten hours, or longer, depending on the annealing temperature and the type of the precursors initially delivered into the system 300. One embodiment of the invention provides the control of the temperature of the reactor 340 by the temperature of the heated gas. The use of the heated gas as the energy source inside the reactor 340 provides the benefits of fast heat transfer, precise temperature control, uniform temperature distribution therein, and/or easy to scale up, among others. [00120] Once the reactions inside the reactor 340 are complete, for example, upon the formation of desired crystal structure, particle morphology, and particle size, oxidized reaction products are delivered out of the reactor 340 via the reactor outlet 347 and/or a reactor outlet 348. The cooled reaction products include final solid product particles of the crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials containing, for example, oxidized reaction product particles of the precursor compounds which are suitable as a material of a battery cell. The gaseous side products may be delivered into a gas abatement device 326B to be treated and released out of the system 300. [00126] Accordingly, a continuous process for producing a material of a battery cell using a system having a mist generator, a drying chamber, one or more gas-solid separators and a reactor is provided. A mist generated from a liquid mixture of one or more metal precursor compounds in desired ratio is mixed with air and dried inside the drying chamber, thereby forming gas-solid mixtures. One or more gas-solid separators are used in the system to separate the gas-solid mixtures from the drying chamber into solid particles packed with the one or more metal precursors and continuously deliver the solid particles into the reactor for further reaction to obtain final solid material particles with desired ratio of two or more intercalated metals. [00127] In one embodiment, preparation and manufacturing of a metal oxide material is provided. Depending on the details and ratios of the metal precursor compounds that are delivered into the system 300, the resulting final solid material particles obtained from the system 300 may be a metal oxide material, a doped metal oxide material, an inorganic metal salts, among others. In addition, the metal oxide materials can exhibit a crystal structure of metals in the shape of layered, spinel, olivine, etc. In addition, the morphology of the final solid product particles (such as the oxidized reaction product prepared using the method 100 and the system 300 as described herein) exists as desired solid powders. The particle sizes of the solid powders range between 10 nm and 100 μm. [00128] In operation, a mist is mixed with a gas flow of a gas inside a mist generator to form a gas-liquid mixture, where the liquid mixture includes a lithium-containing salt compound, a cobalt-containing salt compound, and one or more metal-dopant-containing salts compounds. In addition, the liquid mixture is mixed with a gas flow of another gas inside a drying chamber. It is contemplated that these gas flows are provided to thoroughly mix the liquid mixture to uniformly form into the gas-liquid mixture and assist in carrying the gas-liquid mixture inside the drying chamber. The liquid mixture can be adjusted digitally or manually prepared in a desirable molar ratio of the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salts compounds at a ratio of around x : y : a : b: ...:n inside reactant sources and delivered into one or more liquid mixers. [00129] In one embodiment, the adjusting of the molar ratio of the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salt compounds is performed prior to the forming the mist of the liquid mixture inside a liquid mixer. Desired molar ratio of the lithium-containing salt, the cobalt-containing salt, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salts are digitally or manually measured and delivered from reactant sources to the liquid mixer so that the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salts compounds can be dissolved and/or dispersed in the solvent and mix well into the liquid mixture inside the liquid mixer. The lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-containing salts compounds are all soluble in a suitable solvent within the liquid mixture. [00130] In another embodiment, the adjusting of the molar ratio of the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salt compounds is performed simultaneously with the forming the mist of the liquid mixture. The desirable molar ratio of the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-dopant-containing salt compounds can be adjusted digitally or manually from each reactant source and delivered into the mist generator to generate the mist of the liquid mixture inside the mist generator. [00131] The liquid mixture comprising the lithium-containing salt compound, the cobalt-containing salt compound, and the one or more metal-containing salts compounds is mixed with a gas flow to form a gas-liquid mixture inside a drying chamber. Then, the gas-liquid mixture is dried at a drying temperature inside the drying chamber to form a gas-solid mixture of solid particles of an oxide material. The gas-solid mixture is continuously delivered into the gas-solid separator which separates the gas-solid mixture into one or more solid particles of the oxide material and waste products. [00132] The one or more solid particles of the oxide material are then delivered into an annealing chamber to be mixed with a flow of a gas. The one or more solid particles of the oxide material are reacted and annealed at an annealing temperature inside the annealing chamber to obtain high quality lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants at desired size, morphology and crystal structure. Table 5: Exemplary LCO materials doped with one or more metal dopants compositions [00153] PREPARATION: Lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants were prepared in the following steps: (a) mixing 1 M solutions of forming a liquid mixture having a lithium-containing salt at a molarity of MLisalt, a cobalt-containing salt at a molarity of Mcosalt, a first metal salt at a molarity of MMe1salt, a second metal salt at a molarity of MMe2salt, and a third metal salt at a molarity of MMe3salt wherein the liquid mixture achieves a molar ratio of MLisalt : Mcosalt : MMe1salt : MMe2Salt : MMe3salt; (b) generating a mist of the liquid mixture inside a mist generator of the drying chamber. The mist of the liquid mixture is mixed with a gas flow of a gas inside a mist generator to form a gas-liquid mixture. In addition, the liquid mixture is mixed with a gas flow of another gas inside a drying chamber; (c) mixing the mist of the liquid mixture with a gas flow to form a gas-liquid mixture inside the drying chamber; (d) dry the gas-liquid mixture at a drying temperature for a time period and form a gas-solid mixture inside the drying chamber; (e) separate the gas-solid mixture into one or more solid particles of a an oxide material and a waste product; (f) deliver the solid particles of the lithium cobalt oxide material into an annealing chamber to react and anneal the solid particles of the lithium cobalt oxide material in the presence of a flow of a gas at an annealing temperature to obtain crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants, and anneal the crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants inside the annealing chamber for a time period to obtain crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials; (g) cool the crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants and obtain final solid product particles of crystalized lithium cobalt oxide materials doped with one or more metal dopants at desired size, morphology and crystal structure. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT DEEP EUTECTIC SOLVENTS FOR SELECTIVE RECOVERY OF METALS FROM LITHIUM-ION BATTERY BLACK MASS The present invention discloses novel Deep Eutectic Solvent (DES) compositions and methods for selective dissolution and recovery of critical metals—cobalt, lithium, and nickel—from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. Forty-eight DES formulations were prepared by combining three quaternary ammonium salts—tetramethylammonium chloride, tetrabutylammonium bromide, and benzyltrimethylammonium chloride—as hydrogen bond acceptors with four organic acids—citric acid, malic acid, oxalic acid, and lactic acid—as hydrogen bond donors in various molar ratios. Preparation involves thermal mixing at 110°C with stirring for 45–60 minutes, followed by addition of 40% distilled water by weight. Thirty-three formulations yield stable liquid DES at room temperature. Leaching efficiency, quantified by ICP-OES, is highest for the DES of benzyltrimethylammonium chloride and citric acid in a 1:3 molar ratio, dissolving 462.86 mg cobalt, 125.67 mg lithium, and 279.53 mg nickel per 100 g DES. The invention offers an eco-friendly alternative to conventional corrosive acid-based recycling. [to be published with fig.1]
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of green chemistry and sustainable hydrometallurgy, specifically concerning the recycling of critical metals from spent lithium-ion batteries. More particularly, the invention pertains to novel Deep Eutectic Solvent (DES) compositions prepared in the laboratory using unique combinations of quaternary ammonium salts and organic acids, and their application as efficient leaching media for the selective dissolution and recovery of cobalt, lithium, and nickel from lithium-ion battery black mass. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The exponential growth in the adoption of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) for electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and grid-scale energy storage systems has created an urgent need for efficient and sustainable recycling technologies. With the global stock of electric vehicles growing exponentially from 2013 to 2023, the volume of spent LIBs reaching end-of-life is increasing proportionally. These batteries typically serve for five to ten years in electric vehicles and approximately three years in mobile phones and smaller devices, after which they must be either discarded or recycled. However, less than five percent of spent LIBs are currently recovered through scientific recycling methods, while the remainder are subjected to non-scientific reuse, exportation, incineration, or landfilling. The cathode materials of spent LIBs contain substantial quantities of high-value metals such as cobalt, lithium, nickel, and manganese. Approximately eighty percent of the minerals commonly used in lithium-ion battery production originate from a limited number of countries, including Australia, China, Chile, Canada, and Argentina. This geographic concentration of supply makes recycling essential to maintaining a stable supply chain for critical minerals and ensuring the continued manufacture and deployment of new batteries. Existing methods for recovering metals from spent LIBs include hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, and mechano-chemical or direct recycling processes. Pyrometallurgical methods involve high temperatures and significant energy consumption, while also generating toxic gases. Conventional hydrometallurgy relies on highly corrosive inorganic acids such as hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, and nitric acid for metal leaching and recovery, which inevitably leads to the generation of large volumes of corrosive and hazardous wastewaters. Even weak organic acids, though less ecotoxic individually, require reducing agents like hydrogen peroxide for effective leaching, resulting in abrasive waste streams. Furthermore, secondary raw materials produced through current industrial recycling processes are often not directly reusable in new battery manufacturing due to limited process efficiency. Deep Eutectic Solvents (DESs) have emerged as promising green alternatives for hydrometallurgical processing. A DES is formed by combining a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) to produce a eutectic mixture with a melting point significantly lower than those of the individual components. DESs offer advantages including biodegradability, low toxicity, ease of preparation, and tunability of physicochemical properties. Prior research has primarily focused on choline chloride-based DES systems combined with organic acids or glycols for battery recycling applications. However, there remains a significant gap in exploring novel combinations of quaternary ammonium salts beyond choline chloride, particularly tetramethylammonium chloride, tetrabutylammonium bromide, and benzyltrimethylammonium chloride, with organic acids such as citric acid, malic acid, oxalic acid, and lactic acid for the selective leaching of critical metals from LIB black mass. The following prior art references are reported: US 20200399737: This patent application discloses a process for extracting, recovering, and recycling metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using deep eutectic solvents comprising choline chloride as the hydrogen bond acceptor and ethylene glycol as the hydrogen bond donor. The method involves leaching metals with heat and agitation, followed by recovery via precipitation and electrodeposition. However, this prior art is limited to choline chloride-based DES systems and does not explore quaternary ammonium salts such as tetramethylammonium chloride, tetrabutylammonium bromide, or benzyltrimethylammonium chloride. US 11664542 B2 This patent describes a method for recycling spent lithium-ion batteries using triethyl phosphate as a green solvent for delaminating electrode materials from current collectors. While the patent addresses green chemistry principles, it does not employ deep eutectic solvents for metal leaching and focuses on physical separation rather than chemical dissolution of critical metals. CA 3076688 C : This patent discloses a comprehensive lithium-ion battery recycling process involving shredding, organic solvent immersion, drying, magnetic separation, grinding, acid leaching, sulfide precipitation, solvent extraction, and lithium carbonate crystallization. The process employs conventional acid-based hydrometallurgy and does not utilize deep eutectic solvents as the primary leaching medium. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies, are as follows. An objective of the present invention is to provide novel Deep Eutectic Solvent compositions using previously unexplored combinations of quaternary ammonium salts, namely tetramethylammonium chloride (TMACl), tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr), and benzyltrimethylammonium chloride (BTMAC), with organic acids including citric acid, malic acid, oxalic acid, and lactic acid, for the selective dissolution and recovery of critical metals from lithium-ion battery black mass, thereby offering a sustainable and environmentally benign alternative to conventional corrosive acid-based hydrometallurgical processes. Another objective of the present invention is to develop and optimize a method for preparing stable ternary Deep Eutectic Solvents by thermal mixing of the hydrogen bond acceptor and hydrogen bond donor components at controlled temperatures, followed by the addition of a controlled quantity of distilled water to achieve a fluid consistency suitable for efficient leaching of metals from solid battery waste materials. Still another objective of the present invention is to provide a systematic comparative analysis of the leaching efficiencies of forty-eight different DES formulations for the extraction of cobalt, lithium, and nickel from lithium-ion battery black mass, thereby establishing the most efficient solvent composition and optimal molar ratio for maximum metal recovery. Yet another objective of the present invention is to identify and establish that the DES comprising benzyltrimethylammonium chloride and citric acid in a molar ratio of 1:3 demonstrates the highest leaching efficiency among all tested compositions, leaching 462.86 mg of cobalt, 125.67 mg of lithium, and 279.53 mg of nickel per 100 grams of DES from the black mass. A further objective of the present invention is to provide a green and cost-effective recycling process that utilizes biodegradable, easily available, and non-corrosive chemical components, thereby reducing environmental contamination, eliminating the generation of hazardous wastewater, and supporting the circular economy for critical battery materials. Other objects and advantages of the present disclosure will be more apparent from the following description, which is not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The following presents a simplified summary of the invention in order to provide a basic understanding of some aspects of the invention. This summary is not an extensive overview of the present invention. It is not intended to identify the key or critical elements of the invention or to delineate the scope of the invention. Its sole purpose is to present some concepts of the invention in a simplified form as a prelude to a more detailed description of the invention presented later. The present invention provides a process for preparing forty-eight different novel Deep Eutectic Solvents (DESs) using unique, previously unexplored combinations of three quaternary ammonium salts, namely tetramethylammonium chloride (TMACl), tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr), and benzyltrimethylammonium chloride (BTMAC), as hydrogen bond acceptors, with four organic acids, namely citric acid, malic acid, oxalic acid, and lactic acid, as hydrogen bond donors. The DES compositions are prepared by thermal mixing of the components at a temperature of 110 degrees Celsius with continuous mechanical stirring for 45 to 60 minutes, followed by the addition of 40 percent distilled water by weight to produce ternary DES formulations with a fluid consistency suitable for leaching operations. The invention systematically investigates the leaching efficiencies of all thirty-three successfully formed DES compositions for the extraction of cobalt, lithium, and nickel from lithium-ion battery black mass, utilizing ICP-OES analysis to quantify the leached metal concentrations. The comparative analysis establishes that the DES comprising benzyltrimethylammonium chloride and citric acid in a 1:3 molar ratio exhibits the highest leaching performance, dissolving 462.86 mg cobalt, 125.67 mg lithium, and 279.53 mg nickel per 100 grams of DES. The invention contributes to sustainable hydrometallurgy by replacing conventional corrosive solvents with green, biodegradable, and economical alternatives, thereby reducing environmental impact and supporting the circular economy for critical battery materials. The disclosed process is scalable and compatible with downstream metal recovery processes including electrochemical methods. The present invention discloses novel Deep Eutectic Solvent (DES) compositions and a method for their preparation and use in the selective dissolution and recovery of critical metals, specifically cobalt, lithium, and nickel, from lithium-ion battery (LIB) black mass. The invention addresses the growing need for sustainable and environmentally friendly recycling technologies for spent lithium-ion batteries, which contain valuable metals that are essential for the continued manufacture of new energy storage devices. The method disclosed herein replaces conventional corrosive solvents, such as hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, and various organic solvents, with novel green DES formulations composed of biodegradable, readily available, and economical components. A Deep Eutectic Solvent is formed by combining a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) in specific molar ratios to produce a eutectic mixture whose melting point is significantly lower than those of the individual components. In the present study, three quaternary ammonium salts (QASs) have been selected as hydrogen bond acceptors, namely Tetramethylammonium Chloride (TMACl) having a molar mass of 109.596 g/mol, Tetrabutylammonium Bromide (TBABr) having a molar mass of 322.358 g/mol, and Benzyltrimethylammonium Chloride (BTMAC) having a molar mass of 185.688 g/mol. These QASs were selected based on various parameters including ease of availability, cost-effectiveness, recyclability, and biodegradability. To combine with these QASs and produce competent DES formulations, four organic acids have been selected as hydrogen bond donors, namely Citric Acid (CA) having a molar mass of 192.12 g/mol, Malic Acid (MA) having a molar mass of 134.09 g/mol, Oxalic Acid (OA) having a molar mass of 90.036 g/mol, and Lactic Acid (LA) having a molar mass of 74.506 g/mol. These specific combinations of QASs and organic acids have not been previously reported in any existing literature for the preparation of DES or for the leaching of critical metals from battery black mass, making the disclosed combinations novel. Table 1: Concentration range for acids used in the past Sr. No. Acid Concentration Range 1 Citric Acid 0.4-0.6 mol/L 2 Malic Acid 0.0005-0.025 mol/L 3 Oxalic Acid 0.0005-0.5 mol/L 4 Lactic Acid 0.05-0.521 mol/L The use of various organic acids as hydrogen bond donors in Deep Eutectic Solvent (DES) formulations for metal recovery. Citric acid was employed in a concentration range of 0.4 to 0.6 mol/L, while malic acid was used at much lower concentrations ranging from 0.0005 to 0.025 mol/L. Oxalic acid was tested within a broad range of 0.0005 to 0.5 mol/L, and lactic acid was utilized at concentrations between 0.05 and 0.521 mol/L. These concentration ranges were optimized to evaluate the formation of stable DES and their efficiency in selectively dissolving critical metals from lithium-ion battery black mass. Based on the literature survey, the ratios in which HBAs and HBDs have been typically used in past experiments to produce DESs are documented. For TMACl, the ratio range is 1:2 to 1:8; for TBABr, the range is 1:2 to 1:5; and for BTMAC, a ratio of 1:3 has been reported. In the present study, the QASs and acids are combined in specific ratios as detailed in Table 2. Table 2: Ratios of QASs and Acids used in the present study Sr. No. Quaternary Ammonium Salt (QAS) Ratio of QAS to Acid 1 Tetramethylammonium Chloride (TMACl) 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:8 2 Tetrabutylammonium Bromide (TBABr) 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5 3 Benzyltrimethylammonium Chloride (BTMAC) 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5 A total of forty-eight combinations are prepared and their effectiveness as DESs is analysed. Each combination of QAS and acid at a given ratio constitutes one sample. Since the amounts of chemicals calculated directly from the molar masses are too large for laboratory-scale experimentation, all quantities have been reduced by a scale factor of twenty. Additionally, 40 percent distilled water by weight of the total QAS and acid mass is added to each sample to achieve a fluid consistency suitable for leaching. Adding water in excess of ten percent by weight converts the binary DES into a ternary DES system. EXAMPLE 1: Preparation of Deep Eutectic Solvents The DES preparation process involves the following procedure. The QAS and organic acid are weighed according to the calculated quantities for the desired molar ratio (reduced by a factor of twenty for laboratory scale) and placed together into a glass beaker. The beaker is placed on a hot plate maintained at a temperature of 110 degrees Celsius. The beakers containing the mixtures of hydrogen bond donors and hydrogen bond acceptors, along with glass stirrers for continuous agitation, placed on the hot plate maintained at 110 degrees Celsius as shown in Figure 2. It is observed during the study that temperatures below 110 degrees Celsius are ineffective in melting and mixing the components adequately. Once placed on the hot plate, the powdered masses slowly melt into semi-liquid forms. The solution is mechanically stirred continuously with the help of glass stirrers throughout the heating process. After heating for approximately 30 minutes, a thick, translucent paste is obtained with a consistency similar to petroleum jelly. This paste-like consistency is incompetent to leach or even dissolve substances into itself efficiently. Furthermore, upon cooling to room temperature, the mass completely solidifies and becomes hard. To impart a leachable fluid consistency to the mixture, 40 percent by weight of distilled water is added, calculated as the product of the combined weight of QAS and acid multiplied by 0.4. The mixture requires continuous heating and rigorous agitation for an additional 15 minutes after the addition of water to achieve thorough dissolution. The liquid is then allowed to cool to room temperature. Out of the forty-eight prepared combinations, thirty-three produce successful DESs that remain as perfectly clear watery liquids at room temperature. The remaining fifteen combinations do not produce successful DESs due to various anomalies detailed subsequently. EXAMPLE 2: Mixing of Black Mass with DES and Leaching Process Once the DES has completely cooled to room temperature, 15 ml of the DES is extracted using a pipette and transferred into a sample bottle containing 1 gram of LIB black mass. The entire mass is shaken vigorously to achieve proper mixing. The sample is then kept undisturbed for 24 hours to ensure thorough leaching of the critical metals from the black mass into the DES. After 24 hours of non-disturbance, the solids are observed to settle down to the bottom of the sample bottle. These settled solids get dispersed throughout the DES again upon mixing. With the solution well agitated, it is filtered using a Buchner funnel under vacuum filtration. Whatman filter paper size 41 is used for the filtration. The filtered liquid, referred to as the leachate, and further analytical work is carried out on this filtered leachate. The colours of different leachates are visibly different, as observed in, suggesting different levels of leaching by different DES compositions. EXAMPLE 3: ICP-OES Analysis for Metal Quantification Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES) is conducted on each filtered leachate using a Thermo Scientific ICAP PRO model instrument. The primary objective of this analysis is to determine the quantity of cobalt, lithium, and nickel present in each sample leachate. A higher quantity of metal in the leachate indicates better leaching efficiency of the corresponding DES formulation. EXAMPLE 4: Anomalies Observed During DES Preparation During the course of experimentation, certain anomalies are observed that result in the rejection of specific combinations as viable DES formulations. These anomalies are systematically documented as follows. Samples 14, 15, and 16, comprising TMACl with Malic Acid in ratios of 1:4, 1:6, and 1:8 respectively, show the formation of very fine particles on cooling to room temperature. The solvents prepared with tetramethylammonium chloride and higher concentrations of malic acid in ratios exceeding 1:2 form crystals on cooling and are therefore not suitable for use as DES. This crystallization behaviour is attributed to the limited solubility of TMACl in higher concentrations of malic acid. Samples 25 through 36, comprising all combinations of TMACl, TBABr, and BTMAC with Oxalic Acid in all tested ratios, solidify completely upon coming down to room temperature and cannot be used to prepare stable liquid DES formulations. This behaviour is observed to be consistent across all three QASs when combined with oxalic acid, indicating that oxalic acid is fundamentally unsuitable as an HBD for preparing room-temperature stable DES with the selected QASs. The solidification of the mixtures. Table 6: Anomalies observed leading to rejection of certain DES combinations Sample No. Combinations Ratios Observation / Summary 14, 15, 16 TMACl + MA 1:4, 1:6, 1:8 Fine particles formed on cooling; crystals form at higher malic acid concentrations; not suitable for DES 25-28 TMACl + OA 1:2 to 1:8 Solidified at room temperature; not suitable for DES 29-32 TBABr + OA 1:2 to 1:5 Solidified at room temperature; not suitable for DES 33-36 BTMAC + OA 1:2 to 1:5 Solidified at room temperature; not suitable for DES EXAMPLE 5: Comparative Analysis and Identification of the Most Efficient DES The comparative analysis of leaching efficiencies across all thirty-three successful DES formulations reveals distinct patterns in the effectiveness of different QAS-acid combinations. The citric acid-based DES formulations consistently outperform malic acid and lactic acid-based formulations in terms of cobalt, lithium, and nickel extraction. Among the three QASs tested, benzyltrimethylammonium chloride demonstrates superior performance as a hydrogen bond acceptor when combined with citric acid, followed by tetrabutylammonium bromide. Tetramethylammonium chloride shows comparatively lower leaching efficiencies for all three metals when combined with any of the tested organic acids. The optimal DES composition identified through this systematic study is Sample number 10, comprising benzyltrimethylammonium chloride and citric acid in a molar ratio of 1:3, which achieves leaching of 462.86 mg of cobalt, 125.67 mg of lithium, and 279.53 mg of nickel per 100 grams of DES. This superior performance is attributed to the combined effect of the benzyl group in BTMAC providing enhanced solvation characteristics and the chelating ability of citric acid with its three carboxyl groups facilitating stronger coordination with the metal ions present in the black mass. The 1:3 molar ratio represents the optimal balance between sufficient hydrogen bond donor availability for effective eutectic formation and adequate hydrogen bonding capacity for metal ion complexation. The mechanism of metal dissolution in the DES can be understood as follows. The organic acid component, acting as the hydrogen bond donor, participates in hydrogen bonding with the metal oxides in the black mass, weakening the metal-oxygen bonds. Simultaneously, the chloride or bromide ions from the quaternary ammonium salt attack the metal centre to form chlorometalate or bromometalate complexes, facilitating the dissolution of the metals into the DES medium. The water component of the ternary DES assists in reducing the viscosity of the solvent, thereby enhancing mass transfer and improving the kinetics of the leaching process. The results demonstrate that the disclosed DES formulations offer a viable, green, and efficient alternative to conventional acid-based leaching systems for the recovery of critical metals from spent lithium-ion battery black mass. The process is carried out under mild conditions of temperature and pressure, utilises readily available and biodegradable chemicals, generates no hazardous waste, and produces leachates that are compatible with downstream metal recovery processes including electrochemical methods. The scalability of the process from laboratory to industrial scale is facilitated by the straightforward preparation protocol and the use of commonly available equipment such as hot plates, stirrers, and standard filtration apparatus. patents.abstract: [037] The present invention relates to modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites exhibiting tunable structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical properties. The nanocomposite is formed by integrating lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles within a silica matrix using controlled chemical synthesis techniques such as sol-gel or co-precipitation methods, resulting in a uniform hybrid structure with enhanced stability and reduced particle agglomeration. The silica matrix acts as a stabilizing framework that regulates grain growth and improves dispersion of ferrite nanoparticles, thereby enhancing the overall performance of the material. The resulting hybrid nanocomposite demonstrates adjustable electrical conductivity, dielectric behavior, magnetic permeability, and optical band gap depending on compositional variation and nanoscale interactions. These tunable properties make the material highly suitable for advanced applications including electromagnetic interference shielding, microwave absorption, sensors, optoelectronic devices, and energy storage systems, thereby providing a multifunctional nanomaterial platform for next-generation technological applications. Accompanied Drawing [FIGS. 1-2]
patents.complete_specification: Description:[001] The present invention relates generally to the field of advanced functional nanomaterials and, more particularly, to modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites exhibiting tunable structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical characteristics. The invention specifically concerns the design, synthesis, and engineering of nanoscale composite materials in which lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles are integrated within a silica-based matrix to achieve enhanced stability, controlled morphology, and multifunctional performance. The invention further pertains to the manipulation of crystal structure, particle size distribution, and interfacial interactions within the hybrid system to enable precise tuning of dielectric behavior, electrical conductivity, magnetic permeability, and optical band gap. Additionally, the invention finds relevance in the development of next-generation materials for use in optoelectronic devices, microwave absorption systems, energy storage technologies, electromagnetic interference shielding, sensing applications, and other advanced electronic and photonic applications requiring highly stable and customizable nanocomposite materials. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [002] Spinel ferrite materials have been extensively studied due to their unique combination of magnetic, electrical, and dielectric properties, which make them suitable for a wide range of technological applications such as microwave devices, magnetic storage systems, sensors, and electronic components. Among various ferrites, lithium zinc ferrite has attracted considerable attention owing to its low coercivity, high resistivity, and stable magnetic behavior, which are essential for high-frequency and low-loss applications. [003] Despite these advantages, conventional lithium zinc ferrites often suffer from certain limitations, including uncontrolled grain growth, non-uniform particle size distribution, and structural instability at the nanoscale. These drawbacks significantly affect their functional efficiency, particularly in applications requiring precise control over electromagnetic and optical properties. [004] In recent years, nanostructuring of ferrite materials has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance their performance. Nanoscale ferrites exhibit improved surface area, enhanced reactivity, and modified magnetic and electrical behavior compared to their bulk counterparts. However, maintaining structural stability and preventing particle agglomeration remain major challenges in nanoparticle-based ferrite systems. [005] Silica-based materials have been widely employed as stabilizing matrices in composite systems due to their excellent thermal stability, chemical inertness, and ability to act as a barrier against particle agglomeration. Incorporating silica into ferrite systems has been shown to improve dispersion and structural integrity, thereby enhancing overall material performance. [006] Although ferrite-silica composites have been explored, most existing systems lack precise control over the interfacial interactions between ferrite nanoparticles and silica matrix. This results in limited tunability of key properties such as dielectric constant, conductivity, and optical absorption, thereby restricting their application scope. [007] Conventional synthesis techniques such as solid-state reactions often require high processing temperatures, which can lead to particle coarsening, phase impurities, and poor control over nanoscale morphology. These issues further reduce the efficiency and reproducibility of ferrite-based composite materials. [008] Moreover, existing approaches do not adequately address the need for multifunctional materials that simultaneously exhibit tunable structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical properties. This limitation restricts their integration into advanced multifunctional devices such as smart sensors, photonic systems, and energy-efficient electronic components. [009] There is therefore a growing demand for hybrid nanocomposite systems that combine the advantageous properties of lithium zinc ferrites with the stabilizing and tuning capabilities of silica matrices, enabling controlled modification of physical properties through compositional and structural engineering. [010] Accordingly, there exists a need for an improved synthesis approach and material system that provides enhanced control over particle morphology, phase stability, and interfacial interactions, while enabling tunability of electrical conductivity, optical band gap, and magnetic response for next-generation technological applications. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [011] The present invention provides modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites designed to overcome the limitations of conventional ferrite materials by offering enhanced structural stability and tunable multifunctional properties. The hybrid nanocomposite integrates lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles within a silica matrix in a controlled manner to achieve improved dispersion, reduced agglomeration, and optimized nanoscale interactions. [012] In an embodiment of the invention, the lithium zinc ferrite phase is synthesized using controlled chemical routes such as sol-gel, co-precipitation, or hydrothermal techniques, enabling precise control over particle size, crystallinity, and phase purity. This ensures the formation of uniform spinel-structured ferrite nanoparticles suitable for integration into composite systems. [013] The silica component of the hybrid system is introduced as a stabilizing and functional matrix, typically derived from precursors such as tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), which undergo controlled hydrolysis and condensation reactions. The silica network acts as a structural scaffold that prevents particle agglomeration and enhances thermal and chemical stability. [014] The invention enables controlled tuning of electrical properties by varying the relative proportion of lithium zinc ferrite to silica. This compositional modulation allows adjustment of conductivity and dielectric behavior, making the material suitable for high-frequency electronic and microwave applications. [015] The optical properties of the nanocomposite are also tunable, wherein variations in particle size, composition, and interfacial structure result in adjustable band gap energy. This characteristic enables the material to be used in optoelectronic devices, UV shielding systems, and photonic applications. [016] The hybrid nanocomposite further exhibits improved magnetic properties, including controlled coercivity and permeability, due to the modified spinel structure and silica-mediated particle separation. This makes the material suitable for electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding and magnetic core applications. [017] The invention also provides enhanced structural integrity and thermal stability by preventing grain growth and maintaining nanoscale dispersion of ferrite particles within the silica matrix, thereby improving long-term material reliability under operational conditions. [018] Overall, the present invention offers a multifunctional nanocomposite system that combines structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical tunability within a single material platform, making it highly suitable for advanced applications in sensors, energy storage systems, microwave absorption devices, and next-generation electronic and photonic technologies. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [019] The accompanying drawings illustrate exemplary embodiments of the modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites and are intended to provide a better understanding of the structure, synthesis process, and functional behavior of the present invention. The drawings are schematic in nature and are not necessarily drawn to scale, but they clearly depict the essential components, interactions, and configuration of the hybrid nanocomposite system for ease of interpretation and implementation. [020] Figure 1 illustrates a schematic representation of the synthesis process of the modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposite, showing the formation of lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles through a controlled chemical route and their subsequent incorporation into a silica matrix to form a uniform hybrid structure. The figure further depicts the role of precursor materials, reaction conditions, and thermal treatment steps in achieving a stable and homogeneously dispersed nanocomposite. [021] Figure 2 illustrates the structural configuration and functional behavior of the synthesized hybrid nanocomposite at the nanoscale level, showing the dispersion of lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles within the silica network. The figure also highlights the interaction between ferrite and silica phases and demonstrates the tunable electrical, magnetic, and optical properties arising from compositional variation and interfacial engineering within the composite system. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION Overview of the Hybrid Nanocomposite System [022] The present invention relates to modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites engineered to exhibit tunable structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical properties. The nanocomposite system is designed by integrating lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles within a silica matrix, thereby forming a hybrid structure that combines the functional advantages of ferrite materials with the stabilizing and tunable characteristics of silica. The resulting material exhibits improved homogeneity, reduced particle agglomeration, and enhanced physicochemical stability at the nanoscale. Synthesis of Lithium Zinc Ferrite Nanoparticles [023] In one embodiment of the invention, lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles are synthesized using a controlled chemical method such as sol-gel, co-precipitation, or hydrothermal processing. Metal nitrate precursors of lithium, zinc, and iron are dissolved in an appropriate solvent under continuous stirring to ensure complete homogenization. The pH of the solution is carefully regulated to facilitate controlled nucleation and growth of ferrite nanoparticles. The obtained precursor gel or precipitate is subsequently subjected to drying and calcination at optimized temperatures to obtain phase-pure spinel structured lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles with controlled crystallite size. Preparation of Silica Matrix [024] The silica matrix is prepared using a silica precursor such as tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) through hydrolysis and condensation reactions under acidic or basic conditions. The controlled hydrolysis process leads to the formation of a three-dimensional silica network, which serves as a host matrix for ferrite nanoparticles. The silica sol is maintained under continuous stirring to ensure uniform polymerization and gel formation, resulting in a stable and porous silica framework. Formation of Hybrid Nanocomposite [025] The lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles are subsequently introduced into the silica sol under controlled stirring conditions to ensure uniform dispersion throughout the matrix. The interaction between ferrite nanoparticles and silica network facilitates the formation of a homogeneous hybrid gel. This gel is then subjected to controlled drying to remove residual solvents, followed by thermal treatment to enhance structural stability and achieve the final hybrid nanocomposite form. Structural Characteristics [026] The resulting hybrid nanocomposite exhibits a modified spinel crystal structure in which lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles are embedded within the silica matrix. The silica phase acts as a barrier that restricts grain growth and prevents agglomeration of ferrite particles. This leads to improved crystallinity, enhanced surface area, and refined nanoscale morphology. The interfacial interaction between ferrite and silica phases plays a critical role in determining the overall structural stability of the composite. Electrical Properties and Tunability [027] The electrical properties of the nanocomposite are significantly influenced by the ratio of lithium zinc ferrite to silica. An increase in ferrite content enhances electrical conductivity, while higher silica content increases resistivity and dielectric stability. This tunability enables the material to be optimized for specific electronic applications such as capacitors, sensors, and microwave devices. The controlled distribution of ferrite particles within the silica matrix ensures stable dielectric behavior and reduced energy loss. Magnetic Behavior [028] The hybrid nanocomposite retains the soft magnetic characteristics of lithium zinc ferrite while exhibiting modified magnetic parameters due to silica incorporation. The silica matrix reduces magnetic interaction between adjacent ferrite nanoparticles, resulting in controlled coercivity and improved magnetic stability. This behavior makes the material suitable for electromagnetic interference shielding and magnetic core applications in high-frequency devices. Optical Properties [029] The optical properties of the nanocomposite are tunable based on particle size, composition, and interfacial structure. The presence of silica modifies the electronic structure of ferrite nanoparticles, leading to variation in band gap energy. This allows the material to exhibit adjustable optical absorption behavior, making it suitable for applications in photodetectors, UV shielding coatings, and optoelectronic devices. Thermal Stability and Morphology Control [030] The silica matrix enhances the thermal stability of the hybrid nanocomposite by preventing particle coalescence and inhibiting phase degradation at elevated temperatures. The controlled synthesis process ensures uniform particle distribution and minimizes structural defects. This results in improved mechanical integrity and long-term stability under operational conditions. Industrial Applicability [031] The modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposites of the present invention are highly suitable for advanced technological applications including microwave absorption systems, energy storage devices, biosensors, optical coatings, and electromagnetic shielding materials. The multifunctional nature of the composite allows its integration into next-generation electronic and photonic systems requiring high performance and material adaptability. [032] The present invention provides a modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposite system that successfully integrates structural stability with tunable electrical, magnetic, and optical properties. The incorporation of lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles within a silica matrix enables controlled modification of nanoscale interactions, resulting in enhanced dispersion, reduced agglomeration, and improved functional performance compared to conventional ferrite-based materials. The invention therefore offers a versatile material platform suitable for a wide range of advanced technological applications. [033] The developed hybrid nanocomposite demonstrates significant improvements in dielectric behavior, magnetic stability, and optical band gap tunability, making it highly suitable for integration into high-frequency electronic devices, electromagnetic shielding systems, optoelectronic components, and energy-related applications. The ability to tailor material properties through compositional and structural adjustments further enhances its adaptability for application-specific requirements. [034] From a future perspective, the present invention opens avenues for further enhancement through doping with rare-earth or transition metal ions to achieve improved magnetic anisotropy, higher conductivity control, and broader optical response ranges. Additionally, surface functionalization strategies may be employed to expand its applicability in biomedical sensing, catalytic systems, and environmental remediation technologies. [035] The scalability of the synthesis process also provides strong industrial potential, enabling large-scale production of the hybrid nanocomposite with consistent quality and reproducible properties. Further research may focus on integrating this material into flexible electronics, smart coatings, and next-generation energy storage systems such as supercapacitors and advanced battery electrodes. [036] In conclusion, the modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposite represents a promising multifunctional material platform with wide-ranging applicability and significant scope for future development in emerging fields of nanotechnology, electronics, photonics, and advanced functional materials engineering. , Claims:A modified spinel lithium zinc ferrite-silica hybrid nanocomposite comprising lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles uniformly embedded within a silica matrix, wherein the nanocomposite exhibits tunable structural, electrical, magnetic, and optical properties. 2. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the lithium zinc ferrite nanoparticles are synthesized using sol-gel, co-precipitation, or hydrothermal methods. 3. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the silica matrix is formed using a precursor selected from tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) through hydrolysis and condensation reactions. 4. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the silica matrix functions as a stabilizing medium that prevents agglomeration and controls grain growth of ferrite nanoparticles. 5. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the electrical conductivity and dielectric properties are tunable by varying the ratio of lithium zinc ferrite to silica. 6. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the optical band gap is adjustable based on particle size, composition, and interfacial interaction between ferrite and silica phases. 7. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the material exhibits controlled magnetic properties including modified coercivity and magnetic permeability due to silica incorporation. 8. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein thermal treatment is employed to enhance crystallinity and structural stability of the hybrid system. 9. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the hybrid structure exhibits a modified spinel crystalline phase with improved nanoscale uniformity. 10. The nanocomposite as claimed in claim 1, wherein the material is applicable in electromagnetic interference shielding, sensors, optoelectronic devices, microwave absorption, and energy storage systems.
