patents.complete_specification: Description:“HIGH-PERFORMANCE LITHIUM-BASED BATTERY WITH ENHANCED THERMAL MANAGEMENT AND CYCLE LIFE FOR ELECTRIC VEHICLES” TECHNICAL FIELD The present invention pertains to the domain of electrochemical energy storage technologies and, in particular, to rechargeable lithium-based battery systems. More specifically, the invention is directed to lithium-ion battery cells, battery modules, and battery pack assemblies developed for application in electric vehicles and related electrified transportation systems. The invention focuses on battery configurations and system architectures that enhance thermal regulation during operation, thereby mitigating excessive heat generation and improving temperature uniformity across the battery pack. Additionally, the disclosed technology addresses safety-related aspects such as thermal stability, operational reliability, and protection against failure modes that may arise during high-rate charging, discharging, or prolonged cycling. Furthermore, the invention relates to design and material innovations aimed at improving electrochemical durability and cycling efficiency, resulting in extended service life and consistent performance over repeated charge–discharge cycles. Collectively, these advancements enable robust, safe, and high-performance lithium-ion battery solutions suitable for next-generation electric vehicle applications. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION Electrical vehicles rely on lithium-based battery systems for propulsion. Conventional lithium-ion battery packs face challenges such as capacity fade, thermal runaway, limited cycle life, and insufficient power density. There is a need for improved lithium-based battery cells and modular battery pack designs that address heat dissipation, electrode stability, and safety for EV applications. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION The present invention provides a next-generation lithium-based battery system for electric vehicles that incorporates optimized thermal management and improved cycling stability. The battery system includes a plurality of electrochemical cells configured with enhanced electrode materials and an integrated thermal regulation structure to control heat generation and dissipation during operation. The optimized thermal management arrangement ensures uniform temperature distribution throughout the battery assembly, thereby reducing thermal stress and minimizing degradation mechanisms. By maintaining the cells within a controlled temperature range, the invention improves electrochemical stability, reduces capacity fading, and extends overall cycle life. The disclosed battery system is capable of supporting high-power operation and rapid charging while maintaining safety and durability. The combination of improved material selection and effective thermal control results in enhanced energy efficiency, prolonged service life, and reliable performance, making the invention well suited for advanced electric vehicle energy storage applications. The present invention discloses a next-generation lithium-based battery system for electric vehicles that integrates optimized thermal management with enhanced long-term cycling stability. The invention focuses on improving heat regulation, electrochemical durability, and operational safety during high-power and fast-charging conditions. Structural Description The battery system comprises a plurality of lithium-based electrochemical cells assembled in a modular configuration. Each cell includes a positive electrode, a negative electrode, a separator positioned between the electrodes, and a lithium-ion conductive electrolyte. The electrodes are fabricated using optimized active materials that exhibit improved thermal tolerance and electrochemical stability. A thermal management structure is integrated within the battery pack. This structure may include thermally conductive layers, heat dissipation channels, and temperature-regulating interfaces positioned adjacent to the cell surfaces. The thermal components are arranged to promote uniform heat transfer and prevent localized temperature rise during battery operation. Operational Description During charging and discharging, electrochemical reactions within the cells generate heat. The integrated thermal management system efficiently absorbs and redistributes this heat across the battery assembly. Excess heat is dissipated through designated thermal pathways, maintaining the cells within a predefined safe temperature range. By ensuring uniform temperature distribution, the system reduces thermal stress on electrode materials and minimizes side reactions such as electrolyte decomposition and lithium plating. This controlled thermal environment significantly improves capacity retention and cycling stability over prolonged usage. , C , Claims:CLAIMS: We Claim: 1. A lithium-based battery cell comprising: • a cathode comprising a lithium metal oxide active material; • an anode comprising a composite of graphite and silicon nanoparticles; • a separator positioned between the cathode and the anode; • an electrolyte comprising a lithium salt dissolved in a solvent mixture; • a thermal interface layer in contact with at least one of the cathode and the anode, the thermal interface layer configured to facilitate heat dissipation during charge and discharge cycles. 2. The battery cell of claim 1, wherein the electrolyte further comprises one or more electrolyte additives selected from the group consisting of fluoroethylene carbonate, vinylene carbonate, and lithium bismite (fluor sulfonyl). 3. The battery cell of claim 1, wherein the separator comprises a multilayer ceramic-coated polymer film configured to suppress lithium dendrite penetration. 4. The battery cell of claim 1, further comprising a reinforced current collector having a micro-channel cooling structure integrated therein, the micro-channel cooling structure configured to circulate a coolant during operation. 5. The battery cell of claim 1, wherein the composite anode comprises 5–20 weight percent silicon nanoparticles dispersed in a porous graphite matrix. 6. A battery pack for an electric vehicle comprising: • a plurality of battery modules, each comprising a plurality of battery cells according to claim 1; • a thermal management system comprising at least one coolant loop thermally coupled to the thermal interface layer of each battery cell; • a battery control unit configured to adjust charging and discharging based on temperature data received from sensors positioned adjacent to the battery cells. 7. The battery pack of claim 6, wherein the thermal management system comprises a phase-change material thermally interfaced with the battery modules to absorb and redistribute heat during high-power operation. 8. The battery pack of claim 6, further comprising a structural support frame fabricated from a lightweight composite material to reduce overall pack weight. 9. The battery pack of claim 6, wherein the battery control unit is configured to implement a balancing algorithm that selectively adjusts current flow through individual battery cells based on real-time state-of-health metrics. 10. A method for operating a lithium-based battery pack in an electric vehicle, comprising: • monitoring temperature and voltage data from a plurality of battery cells as recited in claim 1. • adjusting a coolant flow rate through a thermal management system in response to the monitored temperature data. • executing a charge-balancing procedure to mitigate cell imbalance based on the monitored voltage data.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT Title: High Ionic Conductive Gel-Polymer Electrolytes for Sodium-ion and Lithium-ion Batteries A coated gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation and electrolytic composite scaffolds/ membranes thereof configured to operate in both sodium-ion and lithium-ion based alkali metal batteries/ cells is provided. The membrane uses a PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix that is in-situ plasticized with EC/PC and the relevant alkali salt, yielding a mechanically robust film with enhanced ionic conductivity, cation transference and electrochemical stability. It can be prepared as a free-standing film or supported on a porous non-woven, depending on the handling and mechanical requirements of the target cell format. Figure 1
patents.complete_specification: Description:Field of the invention: The present invention provides coated gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation and electrolytic composite scaffolds/ membranes thereof configured to operate in both sodium-ion and lithium-ion based alkali metal batteries/ cells. The membrane uses a PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix that is in-situ plasticized with EC/PC and the relevant alkali salt, yielding a mechanically robust film with enhanced ionic conductivity, cation transference and electrochemical stability. It can be prepared as a free-standing film or supported on a porous non-woven, depending on the handling and mechanical requirements of the target cell format. Background Art: Rechargeable Li-ion and Na-ion batteries commonly use organic liquid electrolytes because of their high room-temperature ionic conductivity (typically 12-15 mS/cm). However, these liquids are associated with flammability, leakage, and struggle with interfacial stability at metallic anodes. Gel-polymer electrolytes (GPEs) aim to capture the best of both solid and liquid electrolytes, offering liquid-like ion transport within a solid/gel matrix, utilising polymer hosts, plasticisers, and compatible salts (LiPF6/LiTFSI or NaPF6/NaClO4). Polymers such as PVDF-HFP, PEO, PAN, and PMMA are widely used as hosts for gel polymer electrolytes. PVDF-HFP is the dominant choice due to its high dielectric constant, mechanical and chemical stability, and ability to retain substantial liquid electrolyte; phase-inverted PVDF-HFP membranes typically achieve 0.1–1 mS/cm at room temperature and can reach ~1.9 mS/cm through ionic-liquid plasticization or composite engineering (e.g., PVDF-HFP/PEO/SiO₂ ≈1.12 mS/cm; PVDF-HFP–succinonitrile ≈1.35 mS/cm, t⁺ ≈0.69). PEO, while highly effective at solvating alkali salts, exhibits excessive crystallinity and correspondingly low room-temperature conductivity ((~10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸ S/cm). Although plasticization, cross-linking, and inorganic or MOF fillers can raise conductivity (e.g., cross-linked PEO ≈0.2 mS/cm at ~20 °C), these approaches often compromise mechanical integrity. Gelled PEO systems and PEO-based composites (e.g., electrospun PEO/PVDF with LiTFSI, t⁺ ≈0.64) demonstrate improved performance, but face limitations in stability and ambient-temperature ion transport. These contrasting characteristics create a well-recognized need to blend PVDF-HFP with PEO: the former provides mechanical robustness, dielectric salt dissociation, and electrolyte retention, while the latter provides strong ion coordination and continuous ion-transport pathways. Together, the two polymers can address deficiencies that each exhibits alone. Prior work on PVDF-HFP/PEO blends shows that incorporating PEO disrupts crystalline domains and increases the amorphous fraction available for ion conduction, while the PVDF-HFP matrix reinforces mechanical stability and enhances electrolyte uptake. Such blends have demonstrated measurable improvements in ionic conductivity, transference number, and cycling stability compared with unmodified PVDF-HFP or PEO systems. Literature search: Prior art on polymer and gel electrolytes spans a wide spectrum of hosts including fluoropolymers (PVDF variants), polyethers (PEO and copolymers), acrylates (PMMA), nitriles (PAN/succinonitrile systems), polycarbonates, polyurethanes, polysiloxanes, polyimides, and hybrid/ceramic-filled matrices, often combined with plasticizers, ionic liquids, cross-linkers, or fillers to tune transport and stability. Within this landscape, PVDF-HFP and PEO remain widely reported reference systems because they offer complementary strengths: PVDF-HFP provides film-forming ability, chemical/thermal robustness, and helpful dielectric properties but has weak cation solvation and limited segmental mobility (so RT conductivity relies on plasticization and risks over-swelling); PEO strongly solvates Li+/Na+ and supports continuous ion pathways but is semicrystalline and mechanically soft at room temperature, leading to low intrinsic conductivity and crystallization-driven aging. The literature explores blends and composites to balance conductivity, cation transference, mechanics, and scalability. In sodium-based gel polymer electrolytes, reported room-temperature conductivities span approximately 0.2-3.5 mS/cm with wide variability in ion transference number. PEO-rich systems generally occupy the lower end of this range; for example, cross-linked PEO/NaTf plasticized with TEGDME delivers ≈ 0.2 mS/cm with modest transference numbers (t+ ≈ 0.26-0.36; Lehmann et al., 2019). PVDF-HFP matrices provide higher conductivity when paired with suitable liquid phases or fillers, as demonstrated by PVDF-HFP/NaAlO2 in EC:PC (≈0.68 mS/cm; t+ ≈ 0.45; Chauhan et al., 2021) and PVDF-HFP swollen with 1 M NaTFSI in EMIM-TFSI (≈1.9 mS/cm; t+ ≈0.27; Mishra et al., 2021). Hybrid composite systems can further increase performance: a UV-cured PEO/MOF-supported electrolyte reaches ≈3.48 mS/cm with t+ ≈0.60 (Z. Zhang et al., 2021), while a single-ion PEGMEM electrolyte confined in ZIF-8 trades conductivity for very high cation selectivity (≈0.40 mS/cm; t+ ≈0.87; J. Zhang et al., 2024). A ternary PEO/PMMA/PVDF-HFP blend incorporating SiO2 reports ≈ 0.88 mS/cm with t+ ≈ 0.86 (Shi et al., 2018), illustrating the benefit of multi-component matrices for balancing conductivity and cation transference. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that while PVDF-HFP and PEO frameworks can achieve competitive conductivity and transport metrics, there remains no single polymer system that simultaneously maximizes σ, t+, mechanical robustness, and long-term stability in sodium-ion environments. In lithium-based gel polymer electrolytes, room-temperature conductivities are generally in the mS/cm range with mid-to-high cation transference numbers, but trade-offs persist. UV-polymerized PEO with LiPF6 in EC-DEC-DMC reaches ≈3.3 mS/cm with t+ ≈0.76 (Li et al., 2017). Ternary blends can push selectivity higher: a PEO/PMMA/PVDF-HFP + SiO2 matrix reports ≈2.02 mS/cm with t+ ≈ 0.84 (Shi et al., 2018). Other PVDF-HFP composites show balanced but lower t+, e.g., PVDF-HFP-PEO-SiO2 (1 M LiTFSI in EC/DMC) at ≈1.12 mS/cm, t+ ≈ 0.48 (P. Zhang et al., 2021), and PVDF-HFP-succinonitrile at ≈ 1.35 mS/cm, t+ ≈ 0.69 (Huang et al., 2023). A MOF-supported, UV-cured PEO composite attains higher σ (≈4.99 mS/cm) with moderate t+ ≈0.61 (Z. Zhang et al., 2021), whereas an electrospun PEO/PVDF solid polymer sacrifices σ (≈0.0618 mS/cm) despite t+ ≈0.64 (Gao et al., 2025). Across both chemistries, literature demonstrates (i) σ typically 0.2-2 mS/cm, with select UV-cured/MOF or ionic-liquid systems pushing 3–5 mS/cm; (ii) t+ spans ~0.27-0.87, where single-ion concepts raise t⁺ at the expense of σ; and (iii) most exemplars are soak-in gels or cast films. A dual-chemistry membrane that simultaneously achieves liquid-like σ and high t+ at RT remains uncommon in the surveyed reports. Patent search: There are multiple patents with respect to using PVDF-HFP or PEO as a polymer matrix for gel-polymer electrolytes. A few notable patents which included composite engineering of PVDF-HFP are included here for our prior art. KR101677537B1 (KIST, 2016) discloses a gel polymer electrolyte formed from poly (sodium 4-styrene sulfonate) blended with PVDF-HFP and coated on a substrate, then swollen with 1 M NaClO₄ in PC + FEC; it attains a maximum ~0.797 mS/cm at very high solvent uptake (~194%), but is Na-only and relies on high liquid content. CN111628213B (Hunan Agricultural Univ., 2021) teaches an organic/inorganic solid composite using PVDF-HFP + ceramic powders (β-Al₂O₃, Na₃PS₄, NASICON) that is coated and then soaked in a pre-polymerized electrolyte, reporting ~0.2–0.4 mS/cm at room temperature, solid-state focused with lower conductivity and no gel matrix. WO2018183771A1 (Univ. of Maryland, 2018) describes hybrid solid-state electrolytes in which a polymer layer is applied on the exterior of a solid electrolyte to improve interfacial contact; in Li systems the conductivity is ~0.25 mS/cm, and the approach is laminate/solid rather than a gel on a porous scaffold. Finally, US20230253676A1 (Blue Solutions, 2023) presents a composite GPE comprising PVDF-HFP + PEO + PC + LiTFSI with a Li₂ZrSi₆O₁₅ additive, achieving ~0.3 mS/cm (Li-only) without disclosing a dip-coated non-woven architecture or high cation transference. Our group patent IN202231056106 (IIT Kharagpur, 2022), where we disclosed a PVDF-HFP (~15 wt%) film solution-cast onto a non-woven textile, roll-pressed to ~170–250 μm, and post-soaked to gel using 1 M NaPF₆ in PC:TMP:FEC (Na) or 1 M LiPF₆ in MP:TMP:FEC (Li). At room temperature we reported σ ≈ 1.16×10⁻4 S/cm (Na; t⁺ ≈ 0.68; ESW ~4.7 V) and σ ≈ 4.92×10⁻⁵ S/cm (Li; t⁺ ≈ 0.85; ESW ~5.0 V), with non-flammability and durable cycling (e.g., ~98.4% retention after 2500 cycles with NVP). That filing centered on a textile-supported, soak-swollen GPE. The present invention departs from the earlier report that does not provide any in-situ-plasticized PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix engineered to deliver multi-mS conductivities and high cation transference across both Na and Li in a single membrane. However, significant gaps remain in the art: the conductivity–mechanical-strength trade-off persists, particularly in thin membranes required for high-energy cells; interfacial impedance growth during long-term cycling, especially against alkali-metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes, remains insufficiently controlled; and scalable, uniform, roll-to-roll-compatible fabrication processes for PVDF-HFP/PEO composites are not yet well established. These limitations underscore the continued need for improved polymer architectures, molecular-level compatibilization strategies, and multifunctional additives that can enable PVDF-HFP/PEO blends to achieve simultaneously high conductivity, structural durability, and manufacturability suitable for commercial deployment. Objects of the invention: It is thus the primary object of the present invention to provide for gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) and scaffolds based thereon, suitable for both sodium-ion and lithium-ion cells, which would reveal conductivity, mechanical strength, and thermal stability. It is another object of the present invention to provide for said gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) and scaffolds based thereon that would display liquid-like electrolytic performance to attain high ionic conductivity at room temperature exceeding those for typical PVDF-HFP gels and solid/composite electrolytes. It is yet another object of the present invention to provide for said gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) that would have high cation transference, cycling with reduced concentration polarization. It is still another object of the present invention to provide for said gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) and scaffolds based thereon that would be a conformal, low-R interface to promote intimate electrode contact, lowering interfacial resistance versus brittle solids or soak-swollen gels. It is yet another object of the present invention to provide for said gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) and scaffolds based thereon that would prohibit post-soak swelling to improve dimensional stability and leakage resistance. It is another object of the present invention to provide for said gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) and scaffolds based thereon that would be enabled by simple and low-temperature processing-based manufacture, yielding consistent scaffolds/ films and properties displaying reproducibility, thereby easing tech transfer from lab to pilot coating lines. Summary of the invention: Thus according to the basic aspect of the present invention there is provided Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds comprising Poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP)/PEO (polyethylene oxide) co-matrix of polymers plasticized in-situ with carbonate solvent based plasticizer blend including Ethylene carbonate (EC)/ propylene carbonate (PC) and alkali salts. A gel polymer electrolyte (GPE) membrane or electrolytic composite scaffold comprising said GPE formulation is provided wherein the GPE is configured as either (i) a free-standing membrane directly cast or coated from the formulation, or (ii) a conformal coating on a porous substrate to form a composite scaffold; wherein the porous substrate comprises a non-woven fabric or other porous support; wherein the composite scaffold comprises a thin, conformal, and robust membrane formed by casting or dip-coating of the said GPE formulation, thereby promoting conformal wettability of electrodes; wherein the GPE comprises PVDF-HFP to impart mechanical and thermal stability and PEO to provide solvating domains and facilitate fast ion transport, thereby forming continuous ion-conduction pathways with low interfacial resistance and enabling solid-like handling; and wherein the GPE membrane or composite scaffold is fabricated by a process selected from casting, dip-coating, or doctor-blade coating on a substrate, including coating on a rigid support substrate followed by optional removal to obtain a free-standing membrane. Preferably said Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds is provided wherein said formulation works for Na+ and Li+ transport based cells with suitable alkali salt free of any re-formulation or post-treatments. More preferably said Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds is provided wherein said membrane delivers an unexpected combination of attributes at room temperature as a single formulation: liquid-like ionic conductivity (~12.1 mS/cm for Na; ~6.2 mS/cm for Li), high cation transference (t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85), long-hour symmetric-cell stability (~2000 h at 0.1 mA/cm2), and mechanical/thermal integrity with said membrane composite displaying thermal stability up to 200 °C, when said formulation of PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix plasticized in-situ with EC/PC + alkali salt is formed into a thin, conformal solution-casted/dip-coated film preferably on a porous non-woven free of any soak-in swelling, and arising out of co-action based on PVDF-HFP imparting mechanical structural stability/ thermal retention and solvent management of the composite scaffold in association with PEO that furnishes dense ion solvating domains while reducing PEO crystallinity leading to enhanced ionic conductivity and mechanical flexibility, and with EC/PC together with alkali salts therein lowering Tg to unlock segmental motion while the thickness conformity of the composite ensuring low interfacial resistance thereby breaking the expected trade-off between higher plasticizer → higher σ but lower t+. According to another preferred aspect of the present invention there is provided said Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds wherein said plasticized co-matrix of polymers include: said PVDF based fluoropolymers selected from PVDF; PVDF copolymers including PVDF-HFP, PVDF-CTFE, PVDF-TrFE, PVDF-TrFE-CFE; PTFE/ePTFE; PVF; PCTFE), polyimides, aramids, polyetherimides, or combinations thereof; said polyether based polymers including (PEO, PPO, PEO-PPO-PEO), polycarbonates (poly(ethylene carbonate), poly(trimethylene carbonate)), polyesters (e.g., PCL), nitrile polymers (PAN), acrylates (PMMA, PVAc), vinyl lactams (PVP), polysiloxanes, polyurethanes, poly(ionic liquid)s, or combinations thereof; said plasticizer phase comprises at least one carbonate solvents (EC, PC, DMC, EMC, DEC), nitriles (succinonitrile, adiponitrile), sulfones (DMS, EMS), and/or ionic liquids (e.g., EMIM-TFSI, PYR₁₃-TFSI). said alkali-metal salt dissolved in said matrix and/or a liquid phase, said salt selected from LiFSI, NaFSI, LiTFSI, NaTFSI, LiPF6, NaPF6, LiClO4, NaClO4, LiBF4, NaBF4, LiBOB, NaBOB; Preferably said Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds is provided wherein said porous substrate comprises non-woven or microporous films including of polypropylene PP, polyethylene PE, PET, PI, aramid, glass fiber, cellulose or cellulose nanofiber, or combinations thereof having porosity in the range of 40% to 80% to enhance ionic conductivity, with said polymer matrix being solution-processed onto the substrate by dip-coating, slot-die, doctor-blade, bar-coat, or spray-coat and dried to form GPE composite scaffold. According to another preferred aspect of the present invention there is provided said gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds wherein said PVDF-HFP to PEO is in ratio range of 20:80 to 80:20 by weight, said EC: PC in the plasticizer blend is in ratio range from 2:1 to 1:2, said alkali metal salt is present in a concentration range of 0.375 M to 2.0 M. Preferably said Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds is provided with said scaffolds integrate able into flexible alkali metal batteries for wearable or portable electronic devices. According got another aspect of the present invention there is provided a method of manufacturing Gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds comprising steps of: Dissolving PVDF-HFP and PEO in solvents separately to prepare separate polymer solution that was stirred continuously at 60°C to ensure complete dissolution and homogeneity that were then combined; Adding an alkali metal salt and a plasticizer blend of EC and PC to the combined polymer solution to form a homogeneous electrolyte formulation; Either simple casting or the formulation or Immersing/coating non-woven substrate into/with the electrolyte formulation to coat the substrate; and Drying the thus coated substrate to remove the solvent, forming the composite electrolyte membrane. Preferably said method is provided wherein the solvent is selected from acetone, N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), acetonitrile, or a combination thereof. More preferably said method is provided wherein the drying of the coated substrate is performed at a temperature of 25 °C to 70 °C for a duration of 12 to 24 hours, and wherein the non-woven substrate prior to coating is freed of impurities, with said coating performed by dip-coating, slot-die, doctor-blade, bar-coat, or spray-coat. According to another aspect of the present invention there is provided an alkali metal battery, comprising: a cathode; an anode; and the gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) formulation based electrolytic composite scaffolds as claimed in anyone of claims 1 to 8 positioned between the cathode and anode. Preferably said alkali metal battery is provided wherein said battery delivers unexpected combination of attributes of high ionic conductivity, improved cycling stability, at room temperature and enhanced thermal safety whereby: liquid-like ionic conductivity is (~12.1 mS/cm for Na; ~6.2 mS/cm for Li), high cation transference (t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85), long-hour symmetric-cell stability (~2000 h at 0.1 mA/cm2), and mechanical/thermal integrity and thermal stability up to 200 °C More preferably said alkali metal battery is provided wherein said battery demonstrates improved safety by mitigating the risk of electrolyte leakage and thermal runaway compared to other liquid electrolytes, wherein said cathode comprises a material selected from the group including Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃, NaFePO₄, NaMnO₂, layered sodium oxide materials, LiFePO₄, LiCoO₂, LiNiMnCoO₂, and layered lithium transition-metal oxides, and wherein said anode comprises material selected from the group including hard carbon, soft carbon, sodium titanate-based materials, graphite, lithium titanate, and metals like Sn, Zn, SnO. Brief description of figures: Figure 1: gives the FESEM images of the polymer solution dip-coated on a non-woven cloth. The image shows irregular, porous structures with interconnected particles and voids. These porous regions suggest good electrolyte uptake potential, which is critical for gel polymer electrolytes in battery applications. Figure 2: gives the Nyquist plot of the polymer dip-coated on a non-woven sample. The Nyquist plot showed a straight line representing a series circuit of a resistor and a constant phase element. The circuit fitting using EC-view software will give the bulk resistance which can be used for the estimation of ionic conductivity. Figure 3: Chronoamperometry of Li symmetric cells for transference number calculations, gives the chronoamperometry profile of the Li || Li symmetric cell with PVDF-HFP/PEO-LiClO4 gel polymer electrolyte under a potential step of 10 mV. The initial current (~8.5×10-4 A) decays to a steady-state value (~4.6×10-4 A) over ~4500 s, used for the transference number calculation via the Bruce–Vincent–Evans method. Figure 4: Galvanostatic cycling of Li || Li symmetric cells with PVDF-HFP/PEO–LiClO4 gel polymer electrolyte at 0.1 mA/cm2, gives the galvanostatic cycling of Li || Li symmetric cells with PVDF-HFP/PEO–LiClO4 gel polymer electrolyte at 0.1 mA/cm2. The cell sustains stable cycling for nearly 2000 h, with early-stage voltage fluctuations giving way to a long stable regime (~400-1100 h) of low overpotentials. Sporadic noise after ~1200 h reflects interfacial instability at extended times. Figure 5: Enlarged view of the stable cycling region (580–740 h) at 0.1 mA/cm2, gives the enlarged view of the stable cycling region (580–740 h) at 0.1 mA/cm2, showing nearly constant and symmetric polarization (~±36 mV), indicative of efficient Li plating/stripping and good electrolyte–electrode compatibility. Figure 6: Rate performance of Na3V2(PO4)3 || gel-polymer electrolyte || Na half cell cycled between 2.2 to 4.2 V vs Na+/Na at current rates from 0.1C to 1C followed by recovery at 0.1C. The cell delivers ~113-115 mAh/g at 0.1C, with progressive capacity decrease at higher C-rates and good recovery when the rate is returned to 0.1C, indicating reversible sodium storage and stable electrolyte-electrode compatibility. Detailed description of the invention: As discussed hereinbefore, the present invention provides for a dual-chemistry gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) for both sodium-ion and lithium-ion cells. It uses a PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix plasticized in situ with EC/PC and alkali salts, then dip-coated onto a porous non-woven scaffold and dried at RT–70 °C. The scaffolded gel wets electrodes conformally, while PVDF-HFP gives mechanical/thermal stability, and PEO provides solvating, fast ion-transport domains yielding continuous pathways with low interfacial resistance and solid-like handling. At room temperature, the membrane achieves σ ~12.1 mS/cm (Na) and ~6.2 mS/cm (Li) with t⁺ ≈ 0.82–0.85, and supports Li∥Li cycling ~2000 h at 0.1 mA/cm2; it remains intact to ~200 °C. The novelty is the co-matrix + in-situ plasticization + porous non-woven dip-coat that is roll-to-roll ready and delivers liquid-like conductivity with high t⁺ across both chemistries. Materials are commodities, and the process maps to existing separator-coating lines, targeting safer Na-ion storage and improved safety in Li-ion markets; remaining work focuses on long-term solvent retention/flammability tuning and high-loading full-cell validation. Mechanistically, PVDF-HFP provides the mechanical/thermal backbone and helps manage solvent retention, while PEO contributes to solvating, ion-transport microdomains. The EC/PC plasticizer lowers the glass-transition temperature to enhance segmental mobility, so Na+/Li+ moves via coordinated hopping along PEO ether oxygens. This co-matrix architecture establishes continuous ion pathways and promotes intimate, low-resistance contact at the electrode–electrolyte interface without resorting to high-uptake, soak-swollen gels. At room temperature, the membrane demonstrates liquid-like ionic conductivity up to ~12.1 mS/cm for Na systems and ~6.2 mS/cm for Li systems together with high cation transference numbers (t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85, Bruce-Vincent). Symmetric Li || Li cells show ~2000 h of stable plating/stripping at 0.1 mA/cm2 with low over potential, and the composite maintains structural integrity to ~200 °C. These metrics address the field’s usual trade-off between conductivity, cation selectivity, and interfacial stability in ambient conditions. From a manufacturing standpoint, the process relies on solution mixing, dip-coating, and low-temperature drying (RT–70 °C) using commodity polymers, salts, and solvents. Film thickness and electrolyte uptake are tuned via solids content and withdrawal speed, and quality can be controlled with standard separator-coating metrology (basis weight, thickness, impedance). Relative to ceramic solid electrolytes or ionic-liquid-heavy gels, expected CAPEX/COGS are lower, and line integration is simpler. Commercially, the technology is relevant for sodium-ion stationary storage (cost/safety driven) and for lithium-ion applications that need safer handling and strong room-temperature performance without free liquid electrolyte. A single formulation serving both Na and Li simplifies supply chains and portfolio management for manufacturers and integrators. Uniqueness of the present invention: This invention introduces a dip-coated gel-polymer electrolyte (GPE) that uniquely combines a PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix with in-situ EC/PC plasticization and salt addition, deposited onto a porous non-woven to form thin, conformal, mechanically reinforced films. The same formulation operates in both sodium-and lithium-ion cells and, unlike prior PVDF-HFP gels, PEO-only systems, or solid composites, simultaneously achieves liquid-like room-temperature conductivity and high cation transference, together with long-hour interfacial stability. Key distinguishing features: • Single formulation, dual chemistry: Works for Na+ and Li+ without re-formulation or post-treatments. • Co-matrix with in-situ plasticization: PVDF-HFP/PEO + EC/PC + salt added in-situ (no soak-in), maximizing solvating domains while limiting excess solvent uptake. • Dip-coated architecture: Solution dip-coated on porous non-woven and low-temperature dried (RT–70 °C) into thin (~100–150 µm) conformal, robust membranes. • Liquid-like RT performance: σ up to ~12.1 mS/cm (NaClO4) and ~6.2 mS/cm (LiClO4) in handleable films. • High cation transference: t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85 (Bruce–Vincent), reducing polarization versus typical gels. • Interfacial robustness: Li || Li plating/stripping stable for ~2000 h at 0.1 mA/cm2 with low overpotential. • Thermal integrity & handling: Retains structure to ~200 °C; easy cutting/lamination like standard separators. • Process control & practicality: Thickness/porosity tunable via withdrawal speed and solids content; uses commodity polymers, salts, and solvents. • Distinct from prior art: First to integrate co-matrix chemistry, in-situ plasticization, porous-scaffold dip-coating, and dual-chemistry operation to deliver high σ and high t+ at room temperature. Invention qualifying aspects of the present invention: Relative to the closest patents (e.g., PVDF-HFP gels that reach ≤~0.8 mS/cm only at very high solvent uptake; PVDF-HFP/ceramic solid composites ~0.2–0.4 mS/cm; hybrid solid-polymer laminates ~0.25-0.3 mS/cm, typically Li-only) and the literature (PEO or PVDF-HFP based GPEs that either show high σ but moderate t⁺, or high t⁺ with sub-mS σ, and are usually single-chemistry), our membrane delivers an unexpected combination at room temperature in one formulation: liquid-like ionic conductivity (~12.1 mS/cm Na; ~6.2 mS/cm Li), high cation transference (t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85), long-hour symmetric-cell stability (~2000 h at 0.1 mA/cm2), and mechanical/thermal integrity achieved via a PVDF-HFP/PEO co-matrix with in-situ EC/PC + salt, formed as a thin, conformal solution-cast/dip-coated film (optionally on a porous non-woven) without soak-in swelling. Notably, our group’s earlier textile-supported, soak-swollen PVDF-HFP GPE (IN202231056106) reported σ ≈ 1.16×10⁻4 S/cm (Na; t⁺≈0.68; ESW ~4.7 V) and σ ≈ 4.92×10⁻⁵ S/cm (Li; t⁺≈0.85; ESW ~5.0 V) with non-flammability and ~98.4% retention after 2500 cycles (NVP), underscoring how the present co-matrix/in-situ design surpasses our own prior approach by orders of magnitude in σ while maintaining high t⁺ and stability. • Different from PVDF-HFP gels: We obtain high σ and high t+ without extreme solvent uptake, preserving film strength and safety. • Different from PEO-centric routes: We keep PEO’s solvating pathways but avoid its RT σ limitation by co-matrix design and plasticizer tuning. • Different from ceramic/MOF/single-ion approaches: We avoid the typical σ penalty (sub-mS) while still achieving high t+ and stable interfaces. • Dual-chemistry, single recipe: Performing strongly on both Na and Li without re-formulation is non-obvious given the different ion size/solvation demands. The technical effect arises from a synergy not taught by the prior art: PVDF-HFP supplies mechanical/thermal retention and solvent management; PEO furnishes dense solvating domains; EC/PC lowers Tg to unlock segmental motion; and the thin, conformal film ensures low interfacial resistance together breaking the field’s expected trade-off (higher plasticizer → higher σ but lower t+) and thus constituting a non-obvious advance over the prevailing state of the art. Advantages: The present invention offers several key advantages over existing GPEs: • Liquid-like RT performance: Achieves high ionic conductivity at room temperature (≈12.1 mS/cm (Na); ≈6.2 mS/cm (Li)), exceeding typical PVDF-HFP gels and solid/composite electrolytes. • High cation selectivity: t+ ≈ 0.82–0.85 reduces concentration polarization and improves rate capability versus common GPEs (often ≤0.6–0.7). • Dual-chemistry, one recipe: Same membrane works for both Na+ and Li+, unlike most Na-only or Li-only disclosures, simplifies development and supply chain. • Stable metal-anode interface: Long, low-noise Li || Li cycling (~2000 h @ 0.1 mA/cm2) indicates durable SEI/contact and mitigates dendrite-induced shorts. • Conformal, low-R interface: Co-matrix plus porous support promotes intimate electrode contact, lowering interfacial resistance versus brittle solids or soak-swollen gels. • Mechanical & thermal integrity: Maintains structure up to ~200 °C, with robust handling in thin films (≈100–150 µm). • No post-soak swelling: In-situ salt/EC-PC plasticization avoids excessive solvent uptake, improving dimensional stability and leakage resistance. • Simple, low-temperature processing: Solution casting/dip-coating with RT–70 °C drying; thickness/porosity tunable by solids content and withdrawal speed; uses commodity polymers/salts/solvents. • Fire-safety via textile: Compatible with flame-retardant/self-extinguishing non-woven substrates, which limit flame propagation and improve abuse tolerance compared with standard polyolefin separators. • Reproducibility: Architecture/process yields consistent films and properties, easing tech transfer from lab to pilot coating lines. Net effect: The invention overcomes the field’s usual trade-off by combining high σ at RT with high t⁺ and durable interfaces in a single, dip-coated flame-retardant membrane for both Na and Li systems, capabilities not collectively demonstrated by the cited prior art. patents.abstract: Abstract The present invention discloses a highly homogeneous hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte for solid-state lithium batteries. The composite electrolyte comprises a multi-component matrix consisting of an organic polymer matrix (40–70 wt%), a highly dissociable lithium conductive salt (10–25 wt%), and nano-sized inorganic ceramic filler particles (10–40 wt%) that are uniformly dispersed within the polymer structure. The ceramic nanoparticles are optionally treated with a surface modification agent, such as graphene or a silane coupling agent, to eliminate particle agglomeration and enhance phase compatibility. The resulting integrated configuration establishes continuous, three-dimensional lithium-ion transport pathways that provide an exceptional room-temperature ionic conductivity greater than 10^{-4} S/cm, while simultaneously enhancing mechanical shear modulus to suppress lithium dendrite penetration and ensuring thermal stability up to 300°C. A low-temperature, roll-to-roll compatible solution-casting and hot-pressing fabrication methodology is also disclosed. The invention is ideally suited for high-safety, high-energy-density applications in electric vehicles, aerospace systems, and grid energy storage.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Detailed Description The following detailed description of example embodiments is provided to illustrate the technical principles, structural configurations, material formulations, and manufacturing steps of the hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte of the present invention. This description is not to be construed in a limiting sense, but rather as an enabling disclosure of the preferred embodiments designed to convey the core inventive features to a person skilled in the relevant art. In accordance with a preferred embodiment of the present invention, the hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte is formulated to comprise a precisely balanced composition of an organic polymer matrix, a lithium conductive salt, nano-sized inorganic ceramic fillers, and a specialized surface modification agent. The polymer matrix constitutes the continuous structural phase of the composite and comprises between 40 wt% and 70 wt% of the total electrolyte mass. The polymer matrix is selected from high-molecular-weight polymers capable of coordinating with lithium ions and providing flexible mechanical properties, such as polyethylene oxide (PEO), poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP), polyacrylonitrile (PAN), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), or structural combinations and copolymers thereof. In a highly preferred iteration, poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) is utilized at a concentration of approximately 50 wt%. The inclusion of PVDF-HFP ensures a high dielectric constant, which facilitates efficient salt dissociation, while its semi-crystalline nature provides a matrix of amorphous domains that accelerate polymer chain mobility and segment-mediated ion transport alongside mechanically robust crystalline domains. To introduce mobile charge carriers into the polymer matrix, a lithium conductive salt is incorporated within a weight percentage range of 10 wt% to 25 wt%. The lithium salt is selected based on its high dissociation constant, large anionic radius, and superior electrochemical stability, and may include lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), lithium hexafluorophosphate ({LiPF}_6), lithium perchlorate ({LiClO}_4), or mixtures thereof. In the preferred embodiment, lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) is employed at a concentration of approximately 20 wt%. The {TFSI}^-anions act as plasticizing agents within the PVDF-HFP polymer network, effectively lowering the glass transition temperature (T_g) of the polymer matrix, disrupting localized polymer crystallinity, and expanding the free volume available for rapid lithium-ion hopping mechanisms. The inorganic phase of the hybrid composite electrolyte comprises nano-sized ceramic fillers incorporated within a weight percentage range of 10 wt% to 40 wt%. The ceramic fillers are selected from active lithium-ion conducting ceramics or passive insulating metal oxides, including lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide ({Li}_7{La}_3{Zr}_2{O}_{12}, commonly referred to as LLZO), lithium aluminum titanium phosphate ({Li}_{1+x}{Al}_x{Ti}_{2-x}({PO}_4)_3, commonly referred to as LATP), aluminum oxide ({Al}_2{O}_3), silicon dioxide ({SiO}_2), titanium dioxide ({TiO}_2), or combinations thereof. In the preferred embodiment, LLZO nanoparticles are deployed at a concentration of approximately 25 wt%. The LLZO nanoparticles possess high intrinsic bulk ionic conductivity and excellent electrochemical stability against metallic lithium anodes. When distributed uniformly at the nanoscale, these ceramic fillers alter the local coordination chemistry of the polymer matrix, creating highly conducting space-charge regions along the polymer-ceramic phase boundaries. These boundaries serve as low-activation-energy express routes for rapid lithium-ion migration, bypassing the slower, tortuous paths typical of pure polymer segments. To mitigate the high surface energy inherent to nano-sized ceramic particles and prevent detrimental agglomeration during processing, a surface modification agent is incorporated at a concentration of 1 wt% to 5 wt%. The surface modifier is selected from functional nanomaterials or chemical coupling agents, such as graphene, reduced graphene oxide, or silane coupling agents. In the preferred configuration, a graphene coating or functionalization layer is applied to the LLZO nanoparticles at a concentration of approximately 5 wt%. This surface modification layer drastically reduces the interfacial tension between the inorganic LLZO crystals and the organic PVDF-HFP chains. The modification promotes a highly uniform, monodisperse distribution of the ceramic particles, optimizing the interfacial contact area and preventing the formation of structural voids or pinholes that could otherwise lead to localized current concentration and subsequent cell failure. The operational mechanism of the hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte depends on the synergy of its components during the charging and discharging cycles of a solid-state lithium battery. During a typical charging phase, lithium ions undergo de-intercalation from the active host material of the cathode (such as lithium iron phosphate, lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide, or lithium cobalt oxide) and enter the hybrid composite electrolyte. Driven by the electric field, the lithium ions migrate rapidly through the electrolyte film via two parallel transport mechanisms. The first mechanism involves coordinated hopping along the segments of the flexible polymer matrix, where the motion of the polymer chains assists the migration of ions through coordinating sites. The second, dominant mechanism occurs via the continuous, three-dimensional, interconnected network formed by the surface-modified LLZO ceramic nanoparticles, which provide continuous, low-resistance pathways for rapid ion conduction. Upon traversing the bulk of the composite electrolyte, the lithium ions arrive at the interface of the lithium metal anode, where they accept electrons and deposit uniformly as metallic lithium. During the discharging phase, this ionic flux is reversed; lithium ions de-intercalate from the anode, pass back through the hybrid composite matrix along the ceramic-polymer interfaces, and re-intercalate into the cathode host framework, while electrical energy is delivered to an external load. Crucially, the presence of the uniformly dispersed, surface-modified LLZO nanoparticles elevates the mechanical shear modulus of the overall composite membrane to a level that satisfies the Monroe-Newman criterion for dendrite suppression. When microscopic lithium dendrites begin to nucleate at the anode surface during rapid charging, they encounter the rigid, high-modulus ceramic nanoparticles embedded within the polymer matrix. These particles act as physical obstacles that arrest the propagation of the dendrite tip, forcing the lithium deposition to distribute laterally and maintain a flat, uniform morphology. This mechanical blockage eliminates the risk of internal short-circuits and thermal runaway. Furthermore, the lack of volatile liquid components ensures that the membrane retains its structural integrity and chemical stability up to temperatures of 300°C, providing an unprecedented safety margin. The manufacturing process for the hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte membrane is executed via a highly controlled, sequence-specific, scalable solution-casting and thermal-densification methodology. In the initial stage, a predefined mass of the polymer matrix (e.g., PVDF-HFP) is dissolved completely in an anhydrous organic solvent, such as N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) or dimethylformamide (DMF), under continuous magnetic stirring at an elevated temperature of approximately 60°C until a perfectly transparent, homogeneous polymer solution is achieved. Following complete polymer dissolution, the selected lithium conductive salt (e.g., LiTFSI) is added gradually into the heated polymer solution. Stirring is maintained continuously until the lithium salt undergoes complete dissociation into its constituent cations and anions, establishing a uniform ion-complexed polymer phase. In a parallel or sequential operation, the nano-sized ceramic fillers (e.g., LLZO nanoparticles) are subjected to a high-energy ultrasonic dispersion process within a portion of the organic solvent. This ultrasonic treatment applies intense localized shear forces that break up any pre-existing particle clusters or agglomerates, ensuring the ceramic particles are entirely isolated at the nanoscale. Prior to or during this dispersion stage, the ceramic particles are treated with the surface modification agent (such as a graphene coating or a silane coupling agent) to chemically modify their surfaces and enhance their chemical affinity for the polymer matrix. Once dispersed, the surface-modified ceramic nanoparticle suspension is transferred into the ion-complexed polymer solution. The combined mixture is subjected to high-shear mechanical blending and continuous mixing for a duration ranging from 6 to 8 hours, yielding a highly stable, uniform, and viscous composite slurry free of phase separation. The fully homogenized composite slurry is subsequently degassed under vacuum to remove any entrapped micro-bubbles and is cast onto a flat, clean substrate, such as a highly polished glass plates or a continuous moving polymeric carrier web. The casting operation is precisely metered utilizing a precision doctor blade coating apparatus set to a wet gap thickness calibrated to yield a final dry membrane thickness between 20 µm and 100 µm. The cast wet film is immediately transferred into a specialized vacuum drying oven, where it is dried under a deep vacuum at a temperature of approximately 80°C for a continuous duration of 12 hours. This controlled thermal evaporation process ensures the complete extraction of volatile solvent molecules without causing surface skinning or internal microscopic blistering. Following the vacuum drying step, the solid composite electrolyte film is peeled from the substrate and subjected to a mechanical hot-pressing operation executed at a controlled temperature of approximately 100°C under a predefined linear pressure. The hot-pressing step acts to consolidate the internal structure of the film, eliminating any remaining microscopic voids, reducing internal porosity, and driving the polymer chains into intimate, continuous contact with the surface-modified ceramic nanoparticles. The resulting self-supporting, pinhole-free hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte membrane possesses optimal mechanical flexibility, isotropic ionic conductivity, and superior interfacial matching characteristics, rendering it ready for direct integration into roll-to-roll solid-state battery assembly lines. Advantages of the Invention The hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte of the present invention offers a multitude of technical, operational, and commercial advantages over conventional liquid and solid-state electrolytes. Chief among these advantages is the simultaneous realization of high mechanical flexibility and exceptional room-temperature ionic conductivity. By establishing an interconnected, three-dimensional nanoscale ceramic network within a flexible polymer matrix, the electrolyte avoids the brittleness typical of pure ceramics while completely overcoming the low ambient conductivity associated with pure polymer systems. This combination allows the electrolyte to deliver an ionic conductivity greater than 10^{-4} S/cm at room temperature, ensuring high-rate capability and efficient operation under normal environmental conditions. From a safety perspective, the present invention provides unprecedented resistance to thermal and mechanical failure modes. The total elimination of volatile organic solvents inherent to liquid systems completely removes the risks of electrolyte leakage, internal pressure buildup, and catastrophic fire or explosion due to thermal runaway. The hybrid electrolyte membrane demonstrates exceptional thermal stability up to temperatures of at least 300°C, preserving its chemical structure and preventing internal short-circuits even under extreme overheating conditions. Furthermore, the exceptionally high shear modulus achieved via the uniform dispersion of surface-modified nano-ceramic fillers provides an effective mechanical barrier that suppresses the growth of lithium dendrites, extending the operational lifespan of high-capacity lithium-metal batteries. From a manufacturing standpoint, the invention offers significant commercial advantages due to its straightforward chemistry and processing compatibility. The low-temperature fabrication process relies on scalable solution-casting and hot-pressing techniques that easily integrate into standard roll-to-roll battery manufacturing infrastructure. The surface modification of the ceramic nanoparticles ensures long-term slurry stability and prevents clogging or uneven deposition during continuous high-throughput coating operations. The resulting membranes, with a tightly controlled thickness profile between 20 µm and 100 µm, exhibit excellent interfacial wetting and lower charge-transfer resistance against solid electrodes. This eliminates the need for extreme assembly pressures and accelerates the mass-market commercialization of safe, high-energy-density solid-state batteries. , Claims:Claims 1. A hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte for solid-state lithium batteries, comprising: an organic polymer matrix present in an amount ranging from 40 wt% to 70 wt% based on the total weight of the composite electrolyte; a lithium conductive salt present in an amount ranging from 10 wt% to 25 wt% based on the total weight of the composite electrolyte, wherein said lithium conductive salt is substantially dissociated within said organic polymer matrix; and inorganic nano-sized ceramic filler particles present in an amount ranging from 10 wt% to 40 wt% based on the total weight of the composite electrolyte, wherein said ceramic filler particles are uniformly distributed at the nanoscale within said organic polymer matrix to form continuous, interconnected three-dimensional lithium-ion transport pathways, characterized in that the composite electrolyte exhibits a room-temperature ionic conductivity greater than 10^{-4} S/cm, structural thermal stability up to at least 300°C, and mechanical resistance adapted to suppress lithium dendrite propagation. 2. The hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte according to claim 1, wherein the organic polymer matrix is selected from the group consisting of polyethylene oxide (PEO), poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP), polyacrylonitrile (PAN), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), and combinations or copolymers thereof. 3. The hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte according to claim 1, wherein the lithium conductive salt is selected from the group consisting of lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), lithium hexafluorophosphate ({LiPF}_6), lithium perchlorate ({LiClO}_4), and combinations thereof. 4. The hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte according to claim 1, wherein the inorganic nano-sized ceramic filler particles are selected from the group consisting of lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide ({Li}_7{La}_3{Zr}_2{O}_{12}, LLZO), lithium aluminum titanium phosphate (LATP), aluminum oxide ({Al}_2{O}_3), silicon dioxide ({SiO}_2), titanium dioxide ({TiO}_2), and combinations thereof. 5. The hybrid ceramic–polymer composite electrolyte according to claim 1, comprising a preferred composition of approximately 50 wt% of poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) as the organic polymer matrix, approximately 20 wt% of lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) as the lithium conductive salt, death-weight-adjusted approximately 25 wt% of LLZO nanoparticles as the inorganic nano-sized ceramic filler particles, and approximately 5 wt% of a graphene coating as the surface modification agent. 8. patents.complete_specification: Description: FORM 2 THE PATENTS ACT, 1970 (39 of 1970) & THE PATENTS RULES, 2003 COMPLETE SPECIFICATION (See section 10 and rule 13) A DEEP EUTECTIC SOLVENT FOR RECOVERING METALS FROM SPENT LITHIUM-ION BATTERIES AND A METHOD THEREOF TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION IN EXPLORATION & MINING FOUNDATION a company incorporated in India, having address at 3rd Floor, i2h Tower (Institute Innovation Hub), IIT(ISM) Dhanbad, Jharkhand-826004 The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. FIELD OF THE INVENTION The embodiments of the subject matter described in this specification relate to deep eutectic solvent (DES) for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and a method thereof. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The demand for efficient energy storage systems has increased significantly due to growing global energy requirements and the increasing adoption of renewable energy technologies. Renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind energy, are intermittent in nature and therefore require reliable energy storage systems for effective utilization. In addition to renewable energy applications, efficient and reliable power sources are also required for vehicles, electronic devices, and other energy storage applications. Among various energy storage devices, lithium-ion batteries have gained wide acceptance owing to their high energy density, long cycle life, fast charging capability, excellent cyclic stability, and comparatively lower environmental impact than certain conventional rechargeable batteries. Consequently, the production and consumption of lithium-ion batteries have increased substantially. A large quantity of spent lithium-ion batteries is being generated after completion of their life. Spent lithium-ion batteries contain valuable metals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and other metals depending on the battery chemistry. The limited availability of primary sources of these metals, increasing cost of battery materials, and environmental concerns associated with mining and disposal have created a strong need for recovering valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries. Recycling of spent lithium-ion batteries can provide a secondary source of battery-grade materials, reduce environmental burden, and support sustainable battery production. Conventionally, spent lithium-ion batteries are recycled mainly by pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes. Pyrometallurgical processes involve high-temperature treatment, such as roasting, incineration, calcination, and smelting, for extraction and recovery of metals. Although pyrometallurgical processes are capable of treating different types of battery waste and provide relatively rapid processing, such processes generally require high energy input and may result in significant carbon emissions. Further, recovery of certain metals, particularly lithium, may be inefficient in pyrometallurgical processes. Hydrometallurgical processes involve leaching of metals from spent lithium-ion batteries using suitable solvents or leaching agents, followed by separation and recovery of the dissolved metals. Hydrometallurgical processes are generally preferred for selective recovery of metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese due to their relatively lower operating temperature and better metal recovery efficiency. However, the performance of hydrometallurgical processes depends significantly on the nature of the solvent or leaching agent used. Conventional solvents or leaching agents used in hydrometallurgical recycling include inorganic acids such as hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, sulfuric acid, and phosphoric acid, and organic acids such as oxalic acid, citric acid, tartaric acid, ascorbic acid, and DL-malic acid. Inorganic acids, although effective for metal leaching, are highly corrosive and may damage process equipment. They may also generate toxic or harmful gases and corrosive effluents, thereby increasing environmental and safety concerns. Organic acids are comparatively less corrosive, but often require large quantities, may increase processing cost, and may complicate subsequent metal separation and solvent recovery. In addition, conventional solvent-based recovery processes may suffer from one or more drawbacks, such as high solvent consumption, solvent loss due to volatility, difficulty in recycling or reusing the solvent, generation of liquid waste, poor selectivity toward target metals, and limited suitability for industrial-scale operation. These limitations adversely affect the economic viability, environmental sustainability, and scalability of existing processes for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries. Therefore, there remains a need for a solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries that reduces or overcomes one or more limitations associated with conventional leaching solvents. There is also a need for a method that enables efficient recovery of valuable metals from spent lithium-ion batteries in an economical, scalable, and environmentally sustainable manner. The present invention seeks to address one or more of the aforementioned needs. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION Deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries and a method thereof are disclosed. In some embodiments, the deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, comprising ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA). In some embodiments, the method of preparing a deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, comprising ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA), wherein the said method comprises steps of drying, ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) to remove moisture; mixing, the dried EAC and MA in the range of molar ratio of (2.8-3.2) : (1.8-2.2); and heating and stirring, the mixture at a temperature in the range of 60–80 °C, at a stirring speed in the range of 400–600 rpm, for a duration in the range of 1–6 hours until a clear, homogeneous and transparent deep eutectic solvent (EM6) is obtained. In some embodiments, the method for recovering metals from cathode material of spent lithium-ion batteries, using the deep eutectic solvent (EM6) as claimed in any one of claims 1 to 9, the method comprising contacting the cathode material with said deep eutectic solvent to form a mixture; heating and stirring the mixture to dissolve metals into the deep eutectic solvent; and separating the resulting mixture by centrifugation to obtain a deep eutectic solvent solution containing dissolved metals separated from undissolved residue, wherein the cathode material comprises at least one of (i) lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) cathode material, or (ii) lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) cathode material from spent lithium-ion batteries. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION Embodiments of the present disclosure relate to deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries and a method thereof. The following is a detailed description of embodiments of the disclosure. The embodiments are in such detail as to clearly communicate the disclosure. However, the amount of detail offered is not intended to limit the anticipated variations of embodiments; on the contrary, the intention is to cover all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives falling within the spirit and scope of the present disclosure as defined by the appended claims. As used in the description herein and throughout the claims that follow, the meaning of “a,” “an,” and “the” includes plural reference unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. Also, as used in the description herein, the meaning of “in” includes “in” and “on” unless the context clearly dictates otherwise. In some embodiments, deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, comprising ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA), wherein said deep eutectic solvent is obtained by a process comprises drying ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) to remove moisture, mixing the dried EAC and MA, and heating and stirring the mixture at a temperature in the range of 60–80 °C, at a stirring speed in the range of 400–600 rpm, for a duration in the range of 1 to 6 hours until a clear, homogeneous and transparent deep eutectic solvent is obtained. In some embodiments, the deep eutectic solvent consists of ethylammonium chloride (EAC) as a hydrogen bond acceptor and malonic acid (MA) as a hydrogen bond donor, and the molar ratio of EAC to MA is about (2.8–3.2):(1.8–2.2). In some embodiments, the step of drying is carried out at a temperature of about 80 °C and a vacuum pressure of about 400 mmHg for about 12 hours in the vacuum dryer until a constant mass is obtained to ensure complete removal of residual moisture. In some embodiments, the heating is carried out using a silicon oil bath, and the heating and stirring is carried out in a condenser-fitted vessel with a magnetic stirrer hot plate. The deep eutectic solvent as claimed in claim 1, wherein the deep eutectic solvent recovers more than 90% of constituent metals in the cathode material, including lithium, nickel, manganese, and cobalt, under the applied conditions. The deep eutectic solvent is named as EM6, and the deep eutectic solvent (EM6) has a melting point of about −37 °C, is thermally stable up to about 126 °C with a weight retention of about 95%, and is a clear, homogeneous and transparent liquid at ambient conditions. The disclosed deep eutectic solvent (EM6) exhibits defined thermophysical properties. The density and viscosity of the solvent were measured at different temperatures using an Anton Paar SVM3001 viscometer/densitometer system. The results indicate temperature-dependent variation in density and dynamic viscosity, as shown in Figure 1. The thermal characterization of deep eutectic solvent (EM6) was carried out using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The DSC analysis indicates that the solvent has a melting point of approximately −37 °C, confirming its liquid nature at ambient conditions. The TGA analysis demonstrates that the solvent is thermally stable up to approximately 126 °C with about 95% weight retention, as shown in Figures 2(a) and 2(b). In some embodiments, the method of preparing a deep eutectic solvent for recovering metals from spent lithium-ion batteries, comprising ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) comprises steps of: a) drying, ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) to remove moisture; b) mixing, the dried EAC and MA; and c) heating and stirring, the mixture at a temperature in the range of 60–80 °C, at a stirring speed in the range of 400–600 rpm, for a duration in the range of 1–6 hours until a clear, homogeneous and transparent deep eutectic solvent is obtained. In some embodiments, the method for recovering metals from cathode material of spent lithium-ion batteries, using the deep eutectic solvent as disclosed herein comprises: a) contacting the cathode material with said deep eutectic solvent to form a mixture; b) heating and stirring the mixture to dissolve metals into the deep eutectic solvent; and c) separating the resulting mixture by centrifugation to obtain a deep eutectic solvent solution containing dissolved metals separated from undissolved residue, wherein the cathode material comprises at least one of: (i) lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) cathode material, or (ii) lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) cathode material from spent lithium-ion batteries. In some embodiments, the cathode material comprises lithium cobalt (III) oxide (LCO) powder, and the solid–liquid ratio in the range of 15–30 g/L, and heating is at the temperature in the range of 50–80 °C. In some embodiments, the stirring speed is in the range of 400–800 rpm, the leaching duration is in the range of 1 to 12 hours, and the centrifuging is carried out for about 10 to 30 minutes. In some embodiments, after centrifuging, a supernatant comprising the deep eutectic solvent solution containing dissolved lithium and cobalt is separated from a precipitate comprising undissolved residue. In some embodiments, further comprising determining dissolved lithium concentration and dissolved cobalt concentration in the deep eutectic solvent solution using microwave plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (MP-AES). In some embodiments, wherein, at a temperature of about 80 °C and a duration of about 12 hours, the dissolution efficiency is about 99.08% for cobalt and about 98.65% for lithium. In some embodiments, the cathode material comprises lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) cathode powder obtained from spent lithium-ion batteries after peeling. In some embodiments, the solid (g)–liquid (L) ratio is 20 g/L , the heating is carried out at a temperature of about 80 °C, the stirring is carried out at about 600 rpm, the leaching duration is about 12 hours, centrifugation is carried out at about 10,000 rpm, and the centrifugation is carried out for about 30 minutes. In some embodiments, the dissolved metals comprise lithium, nickel, manganese, and cobalt, and more than 90% of constituent metals in the cathode material, including lithium, nickel, manganese, and cobalt, are dissolved into the deep eutectic solvent under the applied conditions. In some embodiments, the cathode material is obtained from the spent lithium-ion batteries and comprises cathode active material supported on aluminium foil with binder. In some embodiments, method further comprises a pre-treatment step of separating the cathode active material from the aluminium foil prior to contacting with the deep eutectic solvent. The disclosed deep eutectic solvent (EM6) and method are further described with reference to the following examples: Example 1 1. Preparation of deep eutectic solvent (EM6): EM6 is produced by using ethylammonium chloride (EAC) as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and malonic acid (MA) as a hydrogen bond donor (HBD). EAC and MA are then mixed in a (2.8 – 3.2): (1.8 – 2.2) molar ratio. The synthesis process is carried out on a condenser-fitted magnetic stirrer hot plate, using a silicon oil bath set at 50 – 80 °C and stirred at 400 – 600 rpm for a duration of not more than 6 hours. A clear and transparent deep eutectic solvent (EM6) is obtained. Example 2 1. Preparation of deep eutectic solvent (EM6) is disclosed in Example 1. 2. Leaching of Lithium and Cobalt metals from lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) powder using EM6 as deep eutectic solvent: In the leaching process, cobalt (Co) and lithium (Li) metals are extracted from LCO powder using EM6. For metal extraction, LCO powder is dissolved in EM6 at a 15 g/L solid-liquid ratio. This mixture is then placed in a closed-cap bottle on a hot plate magnetic stirrer, where it is stirred at 800 rpm for an 8h duration at various 80 °C temperatures. 3. Then, the sample is centrifuged for 10 – 30 minutes. The precipitate settles at the bottom of the centrifuge tube, while lithium and cobalt ions are dissolved in EM6. 4. The dissolved Li and Co solution is collected carefully using a dropper and diluted with 5% HNO3 for analysis using MP-AES to measure the concentration of lithium and cobalt present in EM6. For metal extraction, LCO powder is dissolved in EM6 at a 20 g/L solid-liquid ratio. This mixture is then placed in a closed-cap bottle on a hot plate magnetic stirrer, where it is stirred at 800 rpm for a 4h duration at various 80 °C temperatures. 3. The dissolved Li and Co solution is collected carefully using a dropper and diluted with 5% HNO3 for analysis using MP-AES to measure the concentration of lithium and cobalt present in EM6. The leaching efficiency is 74.86 % for cobalt ions and 84.68 % for lithium ions. Example 5 1. Preparation of deep eutectic solvent (EM6) is disclosed in Example 1. 2. Leaching of Lithium and Cobalt metals from LCO powder using EM6: In the leaching process, cobalt (Co) and lithium (Li) metals are extracted from LCO powder using EM6. For metal extraction, LCO powder is dissolved in EM6 DES at a 20 g/L solid-liquid ratio. This mixture is then placed in a closed-cap bottle on a hot plate magnetic stirrer, where it is stirred at 800 rpm for a 12h duration at various 80 °C temperatures. 3. Then, the sample is centrifuged for 10 – 30 minutes. The precipitate settles at the bottom of the centrifuge tube, while lithium and cobalt ions are dissolved in EM6. 4. The dissolved Li and Co solution is collected carefully using a dropper and diluted with 5% HNO3 for analysis using MP-AES to measure the concentration of lithium and cobalt present in EM6. The leaching efficiency is 99.08 % for cobalt ions and 98.65 % for lithium ions. The microwave plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (MP-AES) analysis was carried out using an Agilent 4200 MP-AES instrument. The samples were diluted 250 times using 5% HNO₃.Cobalt and Lithium standard solutions, each having a concentration of 1,000 µg/mL in 5% HNO₃ and obtained from Agilent, were used for calibration. The concentration of dissolved metals in the EM6 deep eutectic solvent (DES) was determined using the following MP-AES operating parameters: pump speed of 10 rpm, sample uptake time of 15 s, stabilization time of 15 s, nebulizer flow rate of 0.75 L/min, and three replicates. Reference will be made to embodiments of the invention, example of which may be illustrated in the accompanying figure(s). These figure(s) are intended to be illustrative, not limiting. Although the invention is generally described in the context of these embodiments, it should be understood that it is not intended to limit the scope of the invention to these particular embodiments. Referring to Figure 3, an experimental setup and a method for recovering metals is shown according to an embodiment of the present invention. Referring to Figure 4, physical appearance and experimental data of ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) mixtures prepared at different molar ratios is shown according to an embodiment of the present invention. As shown in figure, ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) mixtures were observed at 25 °C at different molar percentages of EAC (40, 50, 55, 60 (χeut), 65, 70, 75 mol% EAC). The lowest observed melting point for the mixture occurs at an EAC:MA ratio of 3:2 and is about-37 °C, making the mixture liquid at room temperature. The ratio at which the lowest melting point occurs is defined as the eutectic composition (χeut). Referring Figure 5, a 1H-NMR analysis of malonic acid (MA), ethylammonium chloride (EAC), deep eutectic solvent (EM6), and dissolved lithium and cobalt in deep eutectic solvent (EM6) showing the bond formation between ethylammonium chloride (EAC) and malonic acid (MA) is shown according to an embodiment of the present invention. As shown in the figure, pure MA exhibits two peaks at 11.5 ppm and 2.43 ppm, corresponding to the –OH and –CH2 groups, respectively. In contrast, EAC shows a single peak for hydrogen at 8.069 ppm, associated with the –CH2 group, along with two additional peaks at 3.41 and 7.745 ppm from the CH2 groups, and another peak at 1.12 ppm corresponding to the NH3 group. The 1H NMR spectrum of EM6 displays five peaks at 8.069, 3.14, 2.7, 1.78, and 1.069 ppm. Further, there is a significant shift of the peak at 2.43 in MA to 1.78 ppm in EM6, which is observed for the H5 peak. This observation suggests an intermolecular hydrogen bonding interaction between MA and EAC, leading to the formation of a deep eutectic solvent, which is liquid at room temperature (RT).
