patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition and a process for preparation thereof. The composition, represented by the formula Mg0.80(Ni/Li)0.20MoO4, is prepared by an Aloe vera-assisted sol-gel method that facilitates uniform incorporation of nickel and lithium into the magnesium molybdate lattice. The synthesized composition exhibits a single-phase crystalline structure with retained crystallinity and structural stability, without significant phase separation. The co-doping modifies the lattice vibrations and reduces the optical band gap compared to undoped magnesium molybdate. The combination of improved structural characteristics and reduced band gap makes the composition suitable for optoelectronic applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF INVENTION [1] The present invention relates to inorganic metal oxide materials. More particularly, the present invention relates to a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition, a process for preparation thereof, and its application in optoelectronic devices. BACKGROUND AND PRIOR ART [2] Magnesium molybdate (MgMoO₄) is an important inorganic oxide material that has attracted considerable research interest owing to its favourable structural stability, thermal stability, dielectric behaviour, and optical properties. These characteristics make MgMoO₄ suitable for applications including phosphors, photocatalysts, optical devices, sensors, and other optoelectronic systems. The performance of MgMoO₄ is largely governed by its crystal structure and electronic configuration, and therefore various approaches have been explored to tailor its properties for advanced functional applications. [3] Among these approaches, doping and co-doping have emerged as effective strategies for modifying the structural, optical, electrical, catalytic, and electrochemical properties of inorganic materials. The incorporation of suitable dopant ions into a host lattice can influence crystal growth, lattice distortion, defect concentration, electronic interactions, and band structure, thereby improving the functional characteristics of the material. Consequently, transition metals, alkali metals, and rare-earth elements have been extensively investigated as dopants in oxide-based materials. [4] Several researchers have reported the synthesis and modification of magnesium molybdate and related molybdate materials. For example, Xavier et al. (2014) investigated the structural and optical properties of MgMoO₄, demonstrating its potential as a functional optical material. Other studies have likewise shown that the synthesis route and processing conditions significantly influence the crystallinity, phase formation, microstructure, and optical behaviour of magnesium molybdate, thereby highlighting the importance of controlled synthesis techniques. [5] Co-doping has also been widely investigated as an effective approach for achieving synergistic improvements in material performance. For instance, Al-Naggar et al. (2025) reported manganese and sulfur co-doped nickel molybdate/nickel molybdate hydrate microstructures for supercapacitor applications, demonstrating that simultaneous incorporation of multiple dopants can modify the crystal structure and significantly enhance the functional performance of molybdate-based materials. Similarly, Chinese Patent Application CN120581550A discloses a molybdenum-magnesium co-doped Li₂MoO₄-coated high-nickel ternary positive electrode material, wherein co-doping is employed to improve structural stability and electrochemical performance. Further, Chinese Patent CN113036119B describes a doped nickel-cobalt-lithium manganate precursor incorporating aluminium and tungsten dopants to improve the electrochemical characteristics of cathode materials through atomic-scale compositional modification. [6] These developments collectively demonstrate that doping and co-doping have become widely adopted approaches for tailoring the structural, optical, electrical, catalytic, and electrochemical properties of inorganic materials. However, the reported studies are largely directed towards specific applications or material systems, and the influence of different dopant combinations on magnesium molybdate continues to be an active area of research. Furthermore, the relationship between co-doping, crystal structure, lattice vibrations, and optical properties has not yet been comprehensively explored for all dopant combinations. OBJECTS OF THE INVENTION [7] It is an object of the present invention is to provide a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition having improved structural stability. [8] It is another object of the present invention to provide a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition exhibiting a reduced optical band gap, thereby improving its suitability for optoelectronic applications. [9] It is yet another object of the present invention to provide a simple, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly Aloe vera-assisted sol-gel process for preparing the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [10] The present invention provides a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate with improved structural stability and optical properties. [11] In an aspect, the invention provides a nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate having a general formula (I): Mg0.80Nix Liy MoO4 (I) wherein x + y = 0.20, and x ranges from 0.05 to 0.20, wherein the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate retains the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase; and wherein the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate exhibits a reduced optical energy band gap. [12] In an aspect the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition exhibits a monoclinic crystal structure belonging to the C2/m space group. The composition is further characterized by distinct Raman bands at 964, 954, 906, 875, 846, 788, 424, 381, 368, 343, 333, 320, 275, 202, 177, and 152 cm⁻¹, indicative of the characteristic vibrational modes of the co-doped crystal lattice. The composition further exhibits optical band gap values of 4.09 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.20MoO4, 3.93 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.15Li0.05MoO4, 3.94 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.10Li0.10MoO4, and 3.90 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4. [13] In another aspect the invention provides a process of preparation of nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate. The process comprises the steps of; a) preparing the solutions of the precursors ammonium heptamolybdate ((NH4)6Mo7O24.4H2O), magnesium nitrate (Mg(NO3)2∙6H2O), lithium nitrate (LiNO3), and nickel (II) nitrate hexahydrate (Ni(NO3)2.6H2O) separately in deionized water; b) mixing the precursor solutions; c) adding aloe vera extract as a chelating agent to the mixed solution and maintaining the pH of the solution to 7.0 with ammonia solution; d) stirring the mixture at a temperature ranging between 70-90°C until gel is formed; e) drying the gel followed by grinding to powder form; and f) heating the powder to obtain nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate. [14] The nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition of the present invention provides homogeneous incorporation of nickel and lithium into the magnesium molybdate lattice through a simple and cost-effective Aloe vera-assisted sol-gel process to obtain a single-phase crystalline composition while retaining the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase. The co-doped composition exhibits a reduced optical band gap and modified lattice vibrations, making it suitable for use in optoelectronic devices, optical sensors, photocatalytic systems, phosphor materials, and other functional electronic and photonic applications. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF DRAWINGS [15] The figures below show an exemplary embodiment: Figure 1 shows X-ray diffraction pattern of Nickel and lithium co-doped Mg0.80(Ni Li)0.20MoO4 oxides. Figure 2 shows Raman spectra of nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate Mg0.80(Ni Li)0.20MoO4 oxides. Figure 3 shows UV-visible absorption spectra for co-doped Mg0.80(Ni Li)0.20MoO4 oxides Figure 4 Tauc plot depicts the band gap calculation with Ni/Li co-doping in composition Mg0.80(Ni Li)0.20MoO4 Figure 5 shows Band gap variation with nickel and lithium co-doped Mg0.80(Ni Li)0.20MoO4 oxides DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [16] The present invention will now be described in detail with reference to optional and preferred embodiments, so that various aspects of the invention may be more clearly understood. However, this description should not be construed as limiting the scope of the invention. The following embodiments describe various technical features and advantages of the present invention in a clear and complete manner. Apparently, the described embodiments are some but not all of the embodiments of the present invention. The examples used herein are intended merely to facilitate an understanding of the ways in which the embodiments herein may be practiced and to further enable those of skill in the art to practice the embodiments herein. [17] The terms "nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate", "Ni/Li co-doped magnesium molybdate", "co-doped magnesium molybdate", or "composition" used interchangeably throughout the specification mean and refer to a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition having the general formula Mg0.80Nix Liy MoO4, wherein x + y = 0.20 and x ranges from 0.05 to 0.20, wherein nickel and lithium are incorporated into the magnesium molybdate crystal lattice to form a single-phase crystalline composition that retains the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase, exhibits modified lattice vibrations, and possesses a reduced optical band gap, thereby rendering the composition suitable for optoelectronic and related functional material applications. [18] The present invention discloses a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition and a process for preparation thereof. [19] In an embodiment, the invention provides a nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate having a general formula (I): Mg0.80Nix Liy MoO4 (I) wherein x + y = 0.20, and x ranges from 0.05 to 0.20, wherein the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate retains the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase; and wherein the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate exhibits a reduced optical energy band gap. [20] In a preferred embodiment the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate is selected from; Mg0.80Ni0.20MoO4, Mg0.80 Ni0.15Li0.05MoO4, Mg0.80 Ni0.10Li0.10MoO4, and Mg0.80 Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4. [21] In another embodiment, the invention provides a process of preparation of nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate. The process comprises preparing separate aqueous solutions of the precursors ammonium heptamolybdate ((NH4)6Mo7O24.4H2O), magnesium nitrate (Mg(NO3)2∙6H2O), lithium nitrate (LiNO3), and nickel (II) nitrate hexahydrate (Ni(NO3)2.6H2O), followed by mixing the precursor solutions. Aloe vera extract is added as a chelating agent, and the pH of the resulting mixture is adjusted to 7.0 using ammonia solution. The mixture is stirred at 70-90°C until a gel is formed, after which the gel is dried, ground into a fine powder, and heated to obtain the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate. [22] In a preferred embodiment, the gel is dried at about 150-200°C for about 2 hours, and the resulting powder is heated at about 600°C-650°C for about 3 hours to obtain the desired crystalline composition. [23] In a same preferred embodiment, the aloe vera gel extract is prepared by washing the big piece of home-grown aloe vera (C16H13NO3) with water to remove dust and other impurities. Then it is cut into small pieces, chopped and heated with distilled water at 80⁰C for 30 min. Allowed it to cool to room temperature and filtered to get the extract. [24] In an embodiment, the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition forms a single-phase crystalline material while retaining the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase. The composition exhibits a monoclinic crystal structure belonging to the C2/m space group, characteristic Raman bands corresponding to the vibrational modes of the crystal lattice, and a reduced optical band gap relative to the parent magnesium molybdate. The combination of these structural and optical characteristics renders the composition suitable for optoelectronic and related functional material applications. [25] With reference to the figures, the detailed explanation of the present invention is as follows: [26] Referring to Figure 1, the X-ray diffraction pattern of the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions demonstrates the formation of a single-phase crystalline material. The diffraction peaks are indexed to the monoclinic magnesium molybdate phase having the C2/m space group, thereby confirming that the nickel and lithium co-doping does not alter the parent crystal structure. The Bragg peak positions, corresponding diffraction intensities, and Miller indices (hkl) of the co-doped compositions are summarized in Table 2. The diffraction patterns of Mg0.80Ni0.20 MoO4, Mg0.80Ni0.15Li0.05 MoO4, Mg0.80Ni0.10Li0.10MoO4, and Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4 confirm retention of the crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase, consistent with the claimed composition. [27] Referring to Figure 2, the Raman spectra of the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions exhibit characteristic vibrational bands corresponding to the monoclinic magnesium molybdate crystal structure. The Raman spectra are characterized by distinct bands at 964, 954, 906, 875, 846, 788, 424, 381, 368, 343, 333, 320, 275, 202, 177, and 152 cm⁻¹, which are associated with the vibrational modes of the MoO₄ tetrahedra and lattice framework. The observed Raman bands confirm the retention of the crystal structure upon nickel and lithium co-doping and are indicative of the structural integrity and phase purity of the co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions. [28] Referring to Figure 3, the UV-visible absorption spectra of the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions demonstrate a shift in the absorption edge with variation in the nickel and lithium co-doping ratio, indicating modification of the optical properties of the compositions. [29] Referring to Figures 4 and 5, the optical band gaps of the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions are determined from the corresponding Tauc plots. The compositions exhibit optical band gap values of 4.09 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.20MoO4, 3.93 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.15 Li0.05MoO4, 3.94 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.10Li0.10 MoO4, and 3.90 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4. The reduction in the optical band gap relative to the parent magnesium molybdate demonstrates that nickel and lithium co-doping modifies the electronic properties of the composition, thereby rendering the composition suitable for optoelectronic applications. [30] Advantages of the invention include: • Provides a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition exhibiting a single-phase crystalline structure with retained crystallinity and structural stability of the parent magnesium molybdate phase. • Exhibits a monoclinic crystal structure belonging to the C2/m space group, characteristic Raman bands, and a reduced optical band gap, thereby confirming improved structural integrity and optical properties of the co-doped magnesium molybdate composition. • Provides a simple and cost-effective Aloe vera-assisted sol-gel process for preparing the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition. • Provides a nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate composition suitable for use in optoelectronic devices, optical sensors, photocatalytic systems, phosphor materials, and other functional electronic and photonic applications. The invention will now be described with reference to the following examples, which are provided for illustrative purposes and should not be construed as limiting the scope of the invention. Example 1: Preparation of nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions [31] Nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions having the general formula Mg0.80NixLiyMoO₄, wherein x + y = 0.20, were prepared by an Aloe vera-assisted sol-gel process. [32] The precursor materials used for preparing the different co-doped compositions, namely Mg0.80Ni0.20 MoO4, Mg0.80Ni0.15Li0.05 MoO4, Mg0.80Ni0.10Li0.10MoO4, and Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4, together with their respective quantities, molecular weights, sources, and purity, are provided in Table 1. The mixture was allowed to cool to room temperature and filtered to obtain an Aloe vera extract, which was used as a natural chelating agent during the synthesis. The powder was subsequently heated at 600°C for 3 hours to obtain the corresponding nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions. [40] The Raman spectra exhibit different bands corresponding to bending, stretching, and lattice vibrations, thereby providing a comprehensive representation of the vibrational properties of the co-doped compositions. Distinct Raman bands were observed at approximately 964, 954, 906, 875, 846, 788, 424, 381, 368, 343, 333, 320, 275, 202, 177, and 152 cm⁻¹, reflecting the contributions from both the internal vibrational modes of the MoO₄ tetrahedra and the lattice dynamics. The spectra are dominated by strong high-frequency modes corresponding to the internal vibrations of the [MoO₄]²⁻ group. The presence of multiple peaks in the 846–964 cm⁻¹ region indicates slight distortions or splitting of the vibrational levels due to crystalline anisotropy. The mid-and low-frequency bands correspond to bending modes and lattice phonons, demonstrating the structural stability and bonding interactions within the crystal framework. [41] The nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions crystallize in a monoclinic structure with space group C2/m. The structure comprises isolated [MoO₄]²⁻ tetrahedra and Mg ions coordinated by oxygen. The unit cell contains multiple formula units, resulting in a complex vibrational spectrum. The Raman spectra reveal well-defined vibrational bands at specific frequencies, confirming the presence of characteristic vibrational modes of the [MoO₄]²⁻ tetrahedra. [42] The observed Raman-active frequencies and their corresponding assignments are as follows: (i) 964 cm⁻¹: Symmetric stretching mode (ν₁) of Mo=O in [MoO₄]²⁻. (ii) 954 cm⁻¹ and 911 cm⁻¹: Asymmetric stretching modes (ν₃). (iii) 906 cm⁻¹, 875 cm⁻¹, and 846 cm⁻¹: Additional stretching components and potential mode splitting due to crystal field effects. (iv) 424 cm⁻¹ and 381 cm⁻¹: Bending vibrations (ν₄). (v) 368 cm⁻¹ and 343 cm⁻¹: Internal bending of MoO₄ units. (vi) 333 cm⁻¹ and 320 cm⁻¹: Combined bending and lattice vibrations. (vii) 275 cm⁻¹: Lattice vibration involving the Mg/Li and O framework. (viii) 202 cm⁻¹, 177 cm⁻¹, and 152 cm⁻¹: External modes and translational vibrations of Mg/Li/Ni and Mo atoms within the crystal. The Raman spectroscopic analysis confirms the structural integrity and phase purity of the monoclinic nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions. iii) Optical Absorbance Spectra: [43] The optical absorption characteristics of the prepared nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions were investigated using UV-visible spectroscopy. The optical absorption spectra of the co-doped compositions are shown in Figure 3. [44] The optical absorption spectra exhibit an intense absorption peak at approximately 257 nm for the Mg0.80Ni0.20MoO4 composition. With increasing lithium co-doping, the absorption peak shifts towards a higher wavelength, reaching approximately 277 nm for the Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4 composition. The observed shift in the absorption edge indicates a modification of the optical properties of the nickel and lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate compositions. [45] The optical band gaps of the prepared compositions were determined by plotting (αhν)² versus photon energy (Tauc plot), assuming a direct electronic transition, as shown in Figure 4. The calculated optical band gap values were 4.09 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.20MoO4, 3.93 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.15 Li0.05MoO4, 3.94 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.10Li0.10 MoO4, and 3.90 eV for Mg0.80Ni0.05Li0.15MoO4. [46] The variation in the optical band gap of the prepared compositions is illustrated in Figure 5. The reduction in the band gap of the co-doped compositions indicates a red shift in the absorption edge. The narrowing of the band gap is attributed to lattice distortion arising from the ionic size mismatch between Mg²⁺ (0.72 Å), Ni²⁺ (0.69 Å), and Li⁺ (0.76 Å), resulting in the creation of localized states, modified electronic interactions, enhanced defect levels, and changes in orbital hybridization. The Ni²⁺/Li⁺ co-doping induces lattice disorder by altering the bond lengths and bond angles within the Mg–O and Mo–O framework, thereby facilitating band tailing and reducing the energy required for electronic transitions. The extent of this effect increases with the co-doping concentration, as evidenced by the systematic variation in the optical band gap values. , Claims:1. The nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate as claimed in claim 1 wherein the nickel/lithium co-doped magnesium molybdate exhibits a monoclinic structure with space group C2/m. 3. patents.abstract: Thermal Management System for Lithium-Ion Battery Pack Using Rings The present invention introduces a novel air-cooled battery thermal management system (100, 200, 300) employing various arrangements of curved strips (3a) or rings (3b) or rings with fins (3c), tubes (4), and plates (5, 5A) to enhance the cooling of cells (1) inside the box (2, 2A) by conductive and convective heat transfer. Curved strips (3a) and tubes (4) help to maintain the uniformity of temperature inside the battery pack. Plates (5, 5A) positioned at the top of the top busbar (6) and at the bottom of the bottom busbar (6) accelerate heat dissipation from the busbar (6) by conductive heat transfer. Cool air is introduced into the battery pack through a single inlet port or plurality of inlet ports on the inlet face (7), which removes heat from the cells (1), curved strips (3a) or rings (3b) or rings with fins (3c) and tubes (4) via convective heat transfer, and finally dissipates this heat in the environment via a single outlet port or plurality of outlet ports on the outlet face (8) to reduce the temperature of the cells (1) in the battery pack and improve the performance, safety, and life of the battery pack. Additional inlet port (9) of air at the bottom of the box (2A) helps to improve the cooling of the cells further. [figures 5]
patents.complete_specification: Description:According to the invention, Fig. 1 shows the different parts of an air-cooled Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) (100). Fig. 2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 are the assembled view of type-1, type-2 and type-3, respectively, of the air-cooled BTMS (100). First embodiment In first embodiment, the present invention discloses an air-cooled Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) (100) comprising the following components: cells (1), a rectangular box (2 and 2A), plurality of curved strips (3a) being inserted between the cells (1) conforming to the contour of the cells (1) and thereby maintaining an intimate contact with the surfaces of the cells (1), plurality of tubes (4) implemented in the centre row, and plates (5 and 5A) positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). Plurality of curved strips (3a) are connected together with the help of a straight strip, as shown in Fig. 1. Further, the contact areas of the curved strips (3a), tubes (4), and the plates (5) with the cells (1) are coated with a layer of electrically insulating and thermally conductive material to prevent short circuit in the battery pack. This invention of an air-cooled battery thermal management system enables improved temperature uniformity and a reduction in maximum temperature of the battery pack by the utilization of plurality of curved strips (3a), tubes (4) and plates (5 and 5A). Type 1 In type-1 (Fig. 2) of the present invention, plurality of cells (1) is arranged inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack in a row and connected electrically in series. Also, plurality of rows of cells (1) are arranged and connected electrically in parallel inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack. Plurality of curved strips (3a) are strategically placed between the cells (1) in every row. The curved strips (3a) wrap around the cells (1) over a significant contact area, which helps in heat transfer from the cells (1) by conduction. Significant amount of heat generated in the cells (1) is transported to the busbar (6), thereby raising the temperature of the busbar (6). Plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Inlet face (7) contains single inlet port or plurality of inlet ports for the intake of cold air inside the battery pack. Outlet face (8) contains a single outlet port or plurality of outlet ports for the outflow of hot air from the battery pack. The inlet ports on the inlet face (7) and the outlet ports on the outlet face (8) are arranged in various positions for enhanced efficiency of the BTMS (100). Cold air flows through the inlet ports located on the inlet face (7) into the battery pack. Inside the battery pack, the air flows along the curved strips (3a) and the cells (1). The cold intake air extracts heat from the cells (1) and the curved strips (3a) by convection, while the tight fit of the curved strips (3a) with the surfaces of the cells (1) ensures uniform temperature distribution inside the battery pack by conductive heat transfer. The stream of cool air extracts heat from the cells (1) and the curved strips (3a) and dissipates it into the environment via the outlet ports located on the outlet face (8). Type 2 In type-2 (Fig. 3) of the present invention, plurality of curved strips (3a) is strategically placed between the cells (1) in every row, except in the centre row, and plurality of tubes (4) are implemented only in the central row. In a battery pack, maximum heat is accumulated in the central region. So, plurality of tubes (4) is used in the centre row to transport heat from the central region of the battery pack. Cool air stream passes through these tubes (4) and absorbs the heat from the cells (1) in the central region of the battery pack and removes the heat to the environment. Furthermore, plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Type 3 Type-3 (Fig. 4) of the present invention comprises of plurality of cells (1), box (2A), plurality of curved strips (3a), plurality of tubes (4), plate (5) at the top of the top bus-bar (6), plate (5A) at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6), the regular inlet ports at the inlet face (7), as well as additional inlet port (9), which is located at the bottom side of the battery pack. In order to flow the air inside the battery pack via the additional inlet port (9), hole is made at the bottom face of the box (2A) and at the plate (5A) located at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). Inclusion of the additional inlet port (9) at the bottom of the battery pack results in a significant enhancement in the uniformity of temperature distribution and reduction of the maximum temperature of the battery pack. Second embodiment In second embodiment, an air-cooled Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) (200) as illustrated in figure 5 comprises the following components: cells (1), a rectangular box (2 and 2A), plurality of rings (3b), plurality of tubes (4) implemented in the centre row, and plates (5 and 5A) positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). Each cell (1) passes through plurality of rings (3b) maintaining tight fit, thereby removing the heat generated in the cell (1) via conduction. Plurality of rings (3b) are connected together with the help of a straight strip, as shown in Fig. 1. However, connection of plurality of rings with a straight strip is optional. The contact areas of the rings (3b), tubes (4), and plates (5) with the cells are coated with a layer of electrically insulating and thermally conductive material to prevent short circuit in the battery pack. This invention of an air-cooled battery thermal management system enables improved temperature uniformity and a reduction in the maximum temperature of the battery pack by the utilization of a plurality of rings (3b), tubes (4), and plates (5 and 5A). Type 1 In type-1 (Fig. 6), plurality of cells (1) is arranged inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack in a row and connected electrically in series. Also, plurality of rows of cells (1) are arranged and connected electrically in parallel inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack. Each cell (1) passes through plurality of rings (3b) maintaining tight fit. Significant amount of heat generated in the cells (1) is transported to the busbar (6), thereby raising the temperature of the busbar (6). Plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Inlet face (7) contains single inlet port or plurality of inlet ports for the intake of cold air inside the battery pack. Outlet face (8) contains a single outlet port or plurality of outlet ports for the outflow of hot air from the battery pack. The inlet ports on the inlet face (7) and the outlet ports on the outlet face (8) are arranged in various positions for enhanced efficiency of the BTMS. Cold air flows through the inlet ports located on the inlet face (7) into the battery pack. Inside the battery pack, the air flows around the rings (3b) and around the uncovered part of the surfaces of the cells (1). The cold intake air extracts heat from the cells (1) and the rings (3b) by convection, while the tight fit of the rings (3b) with the surfaces of the cells (1) ensures uniform temperature distribution inside the battery pack by conductive heat transfer. Heat extracted by the stream of cool air from the cells (1), and rings (3b) is dissipated into the environment via the outlet ports located on the outlet face (8). Type 2 In type-2 (Fig. 7), plurality of rings (3b) is strategically placed in every row for inserting the cells (1) through these rings (3b), and plurality of tubes (4) are implemented in the central row. In a battery pack, maximum heat is accumulated in the central region. So, a plurality of tubes (4) is used in the centre row to transport heat from the central region of the battery pack. Cool air stream can pass through these tubes (4) and absorb the heat from the cells (1) in the central region of the battery pack and removes the heat to the environment. Furthermore, plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Type 3 Type 3 (Fig. 8) illustrates a plurality of cells (1), box (2A), plurality of rings (3b), plurality of tubes (4), plate (5) at the top of the top bus-bar (6), plate (5A) at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6), the regular inlet ports at the inlet face (7), as well as additional inlet port (9), which is located at the bottom side of the battery pack. In order to flow the air inside the battery pack via the additional inlet port (9), hole is made at the bottom face of the box (2A) and at the plate (5A) located at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). The inclusion of the additional inlet port (9) at the bottom of the battery pack results in a significant enhancement in the uniformity of temperature distribution and reduction of the maximum temperature of the battery pack. Third embodiment In a third embodiment, the present invention discloses an air-cooled Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) (300) as illustrated in figure 9 comprising the following components: cells (1), a rectangular box (2 and 2A), a plurality of perforated plates – henceforth called as fins (4’) that are fitted with rings at its holes, henceforth called rings with fins structure (3c), wherein the plurality of fins (4’) being stacked parallel to each other with perfect alignment of the rings attached to the parallel fins, each cell being inserted through the structure (3c) that is the plurality of rings attached to the plurality of parallel fins (4’) maintaining tight fit with each other, plates (5 and 5A) positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). In the structure (3c), the rings are fitted with the fins (4’) in a way that half of each ring is above the fin (4’) and remaining half of that ring is below the fin (4’). Further, the contact areas of the rings in the structure (3c), and the plates (5 and 5A) with the cells (1) are coated with a layer of electrically insulating and thermally conductive material to prevent short circuit in the battery pack. Heat generated in the cells (1) is transferred to the rings in the structure (3c) via conduction. This heat removal from the cells (1) is significantly improved due to the presence of the fins (4’) attached with the rings in the structure (3c). Parallel arrangement of the fins (4’) further helps to maintain uniform distribution of airflow by creating parallel flow channels in the battery pack. This invention of an air-cooled battery thermal management system enables improved temperature uniformity and a reduction in maximum temperature of the battery pack by the utilization of the structure (3c) that is the plurality of rings with the plurality of fins (4’) and plates (5 and 5A). Type 1 In type-1 (Fig. 10), a plurality of cells (1) is arranged inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack in a row and connected electrically in series. Also, a plurality of rows of cells (1) are arranged and connected electrically in parallel inside the rectangular box (2) of the battery pack. Each cell is inserted through the structure (3c) that is plurality of rings attached to plurality of parallel fins (4’) maintaining tight fit with each other. Significant amount of heat generated in the cells (1) is transported to the busbar (6), thereby raising the temperature of the busbar (6). Plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Inlet face (7) contains single inlet port or plurality of inlet ports for the intake of cold air inside the battery pack. Outlet face (8) contains a single outlet port or plurality of outlet ports for the outflow of hot air from the battery pack. The inlet ports on the inlet face (7) and the outlet ports on the outlet face (8) are arranged in various positions for enhanced efficiency of the BTMS. Cold air flows through the inlet ports located on the inlet face (7) into the battery pack. Inside the battery pack, the air flows around the structure (3c) of rings with fins (4’) and uncovered part of the surfaces of the cells (1). The cold intake air extracts heat from the cells (1), the structure (3c) of rings with fins (4’) by convection, while the fins (4’) and the rings fitted tightly on the surfaces of the cells (1) ensure uniform temperature distribution inside the battery pack by conductive heat transfer. Heat extracted by the stream of cool air from the cells (1), and the structure (3c) is dissipated into the environment via the outlet ports located on the outlet face (8). Type 2 In type-2 (Fig. 11), the structure (3c) wherein a plurality of rings attached with plurality of parallel fins (4’) are strategically placed inside the battery pack with cells (1) arranged in multiple rows inserted through plurality of rings attached with plurality of parallel fins (4’). Wider gap is provided between two neighbouring rows of cells (1) in the central region of the battery pack compared to the gap between the other rows of cells (1) in order to enhance the airflow and associated convective heat transfer from the central region of the battery pack. Therefore, this arrangement of the gaps between the rows of cells (1) in the central region of the battery pack prevents the accumulation of heat in the central region of the battery pack, thereby reducing the temperature rise in the battery pack. Furthermore, plates (5) are positioned at the top of the top-busbar (6) and at bottom of the bottom-busbar (6) with a tight fit to the busbar (6), thereby removing the heat from the busbar (6) via conduction. Type 3 Type-3 (Fig. 12) comprises of plurality of cells (1), box (2A), the structure (3c) of the plurality of rings attached with the plurality of parallel fins (4’), plate (5) at the top of the top bus-bar (6), plate (5A) at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6), the regular inlet ports at the inlet face (7), as well as additional inlet port (9), which is located at the bottom side of the battery pack. Wider gap is provided between two neighbouring rows of cells (1) in the central region of the battery pack compared to the gap between the other rows of cells (1). In order to flow the air inside the battery pack via the additional inlet port (9), hole is made at the bottom face of the box (2A) and at the plate (5A) located at the bottom of the bottom-busbar (6). The inclusion of the additional inlet port (9) at the bottom of the battery pack results in a significant enhancement in the uniformity of temperature distribution and reduction of the maximum temperature of the battery pack. An air-cooled battery thermal management system (BTMS) for Lithium-ion battery pack (200) comprising: a plurality of cells (1); a box (2, 2A) for arranging the cells (1) in upright position in rows in X-Y direction; wherein the plurality of cells (1) being arranged in a row and connected electrically in series and plurality of rows of cells (1) being arranged and connected electrically in parallel inside the box (2, 2A); a plurality of array of rings (3b) being inserted vertically width-wise in Z direction between the cells (1) lengthwise in X direction with a gap in between each array (3b) placed in the same row as well as for all the rows proceeding towards Y direction such that the length of each array (3b) cover the full length of the box (2, 2A), wherein the said array (3b) being arranged in all the rows, wherein said array (3b) being inserted in between the cells (1) in an interface and tight fit condition for the intimate contact between them, a pair of plates (5, 5A) being positioned at the top of a top bus-bar (6) and at the bottom of a bottom bus-bar (6) with a tight fit for heat dissipation; an inlet port on the inlet face (7) to pass the cool air therethrough and an outlet port on the outlet face (8) to release hot air after absorbing heat from the system (100) into the environment, wherein the BTMS being configured to ensure uniform and increased temperature distribution and heat dissipation by conduction whereas the cool air from the inlet extracts heat from the cells (1) via the array (3b) to dissipate into the environment by convection. 2. The battery thermal management system as claimed in claim 1, wherein plurality of tubes (4) being inserted in the centre row for absorbing heat generated at the central region of the battery pack (200) as well as from the cells (1) and removing it to the environment, wherein the tubes (4) being configured in the same manner in X-direction length-wise with a gap in between each tube (4) placed in the same row such that each tube length covers the full length of the box (2, 2A). 3. The battery thermal management system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the plates (5, 5A) removing the heat generated in the centre of the cells, the cell terminals and from the busbar (6) via conduction. 4. The battery thermal management system as claimed in claim 1, wherein an additional inlet port (9) being provided in the bottom plate (5A), located at the bottom side of the battery pack in order to flow the air from inside the battery pack into the environment by convection. 5. The battery thermal management system as clamed in claim 1, wherein the rings (3b), the tubes (4), and the plates (5, 5A) being coated with a layer of electrically insulating and thermally conductive material.

patents.abstract: An electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery including a current collector, a plurality of intermediate sections disposed on the current collector in an island shape and including a first binder, and a mixture layer disposed on the current collector and on the plurality of intermediate sections, wherein when viewed from the thickness direction of the electrode, the average distance between the peripheral edges of adjacent intermediate sections is 30-250 µm, the area S of each of the plurality of intermediate sections is 5000 µm2 to 150,000 µm2 inclusive, the mixture layer contains graphite and a second binder, and the ratio of the peak intensity corresponding to the (110) plane to the peak intensity corresponding to the (002) plane in the X-ray diffraction pattern of the graphite is 0.0040 or more.
patents.complete_specification: ] The present invention relates to an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery and a method for producing the same, and a lithium ion secondary battery. Background Art [0002] As an electrode of a lithium ion secondary battery, an electrode in which a 10 mixture layer containing an active material and a binding material is disposed on a current collector has been known. As a method for producing a mixture layer, the following production methods have been known: a production method that involves applying onto a current collector a slurry in which a material containing at least an active material and a binding material is dispersed in a solvent, 15 followed by drying; a production method including forming a layer on a current collector from composite particles containing at least an active material and a binding material and compressing the resultant molded layer; and a production method that involves compressing an amorphous kneaded product formed of a material containing at least an active material and a binding material with a 20 calender roll a plurality of times and bonding the kneaded product to a current collector, followed by compression. Further, an electrode including a predetermined-patterned layer of a binding material between a current collector and a mixture layer has also been known (e.g., see Patent Literatures 1 to 5). 25 Furthermore, an electrode containing a particulate binding material disposed so that the material is scattered between a current collector and a mixture layer has also been known (e.g., see Patent Literature 6). 30 3 Citation List Patent Literature [0003] Patent Literature 1: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2016-100303 A (corresponding publication: specification of U.S. patent application 5 publication No. 2017/279114) Patent Literature 2: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2014-078497 A Patent Literature 3: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2015-106525 A 10 Patent Literature 4: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2014-199738 A Patent Literature 5: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2013-012393 A (corresponding publication: specification of U.S. patent application publication No. 2013/004843) 15 Patent Literature 6: Japanese Patent Application Laid-Open No. 2023-082849 A (corresponding publication: specification of U.S. patent application publication No. 2023/178738) Summary of Invention 20 Problem to Be Solved by the Invention [0004] An electrode including a mixture layer on a current collector tends to lack a binding material disposed between the current collector and the mixture layer, whereby the bonding strength between the current collector and the mixture layer tends to be insufficient. Therefore, a layer containing the binding material may be 25 disposed between the current collector and the mixture layer. In particular, in the method for producing an electrode using a solid material, such as the aforementioned composite particles or the amorphous kneaded product, the bonding strength between the current collector and the mixture layer is particularly insufficient unlike an electrode produced by applying the 4 aforementioned slurry onto the current collector and subsequently drying. Therefore, it is useful to form, across the entire surface or partially, a layer containing the binding material between the current collector and the mixture layer. 5 A binding material generally has electrically insulative properties. Thus, it is conceivable to partially form the layer containing the binding material between the current collector and the mixture layer to achieve electrical conduction therebetween. However, when a layer of the binding material is disposed in a striped 10 pattern or a grid pattern between the current collector and the mixture layer, in a manner similar to that of the technologies of Patent Literatures 1 to 5, the battery may rapidly deteriorate in the case of rapid charging of the battery, that is, in the case of high-hour rate charge. Although Patent Literatures 4 and 5 also propose that the layer of the binding material is disposed in a dotted pattern between the 15 current collector and the mixture layer, both rapid charging performance and cycle characteristics are not simultaneously achieved in some cases. When a small amount or a trace amount of particulate binding material is scattered between the current collector and the mixture layer, in a manner similar to that of the technology of Patent Literature 6 (Japanese Patent Application Laid20 Open No. 2023-082849 A), the scattered particulate binding material may, in some cases, not be resistant to a change in volume of the mixture layer in a charge and discharge cycle. Consequently, the mixture layer may, in some cases, fail to be held on the current collector, resulting in detachment of the mixture layer from the current collector. In particular, in the case of an element having a structure in 25 which a positive electrode and a negative electrode are layered with a separator therebetween, a pressure applied to restrain the layered structure of the element is low, and thus battery characteristics when the mixture layer is detached from the current collector tend to be significantly impaired. 5 [0005] Accordingly, there is a desire for an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery that can achieve both excellent rapid charging performance and cycle characteristics in a lithium ion secondary battery; a method for producing such an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery; and a lithium ion secondary battery 5 that can achieve both excellent rapid charging performance and cycle characteristics. Solution to Problem [0006] The present inventor has intensively studied to solve the aforementioned 10 problems. The present inventor has presumed that a reason why the rapid charging performance of a battery tends to be low when a layer of a binding material disposed between a current collector and a mixture layer has a striped pattern or a grid pattern is as described below. 15 The binding material generally has electrically insulative properties as described above. When the layer of the binding material disposed between the current collector and the mixture layer has a striped pattern, it is considered that a conduction path from the current collector to the mixture layer is formed so as to avoid the layer of the binding material in a striped pattern. That is, it is 20 considered that a conduction path of the mixture layer disposed on the layer of the binding material has difficulty being formed in the extending direction of the striped pattern. On the other hand, it is considered that the conduction path of the mixture layer disposed on the layer of the binding material is easily formed in a direction orthogonal to the extending direction of the striped pattern. Thus, when 25 a lithium ion secondary battery having as a negative electrode an electrode including as an active material graphite in which an electric potential at which an electrochemically reversible reaction occurs is close to the oxidation-reduction potential of metal lithium is subjected to a high-hour rate electrochemical reaction, such as rapid charging, it is considered that the reaction on the electrode is uneven. 6 Then, it is considered that the battery rapidly deteriorates by a phenomenon in which metal lithium is precipitated on the negative electrode, this phenomenon impairing the battery performance. When the layer of the binding material has a grid pattern, the conduction path has difficulty being formed in the extending 5 direction of the grid pattern similarly to the striped pattern, and thus it is considered that the battery rapidly deteriorates, reducing the battery performance. [0007] The present inventor has further proceeded with investigation based on the aforementioned presumption, and as a result, completed the present invention. The present invention provides as follows. 10 [0008] <1> An electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery, comprising a current collector, a plurality of intermediate portions that are disposed on the current collector in an island shape and contain a first binding material, and a mixture layer disposed on the current collector and the plurality of intermediate portions, wherein 15 an average distance between peripheral edges of the intermediate portions adjacent to each other as viewed in a thickness direction of the electrode is 30 m or more and 250 m or less, and an area S of each of the intermediate portions is 5,000 m2 or more and 150,000 m2 or less; and the mixture layer contains graphite and a second binding material, and the 20 graphite has a ratio of a peak intensity corresponding to a (110) plane relative to a peak intensity corresponding to a (002) plane in an X-ray diffraction pattern of 0.0040 or more. <2> The electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to <1>, wherein the mixture layer further contains a silicon atom-containing active 25 material. <3> The electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to <1> or <2>, being a negative electrode. <4> A lithium ion secondary battery comprising the electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to <3>; and a positive electrode. 7 <5> The lithium ion secondary battery according to <4>, wherein a discharge capacity per unit area of a portion where the electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery, which is the negative electrode, and the positive electrode face each other, when the lithium ion secondary battery is discharged at a 10-hour rate, is 3.3 mAh/cm2 5 or more. <6> A method for producing an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery, the electrode including a current collector, a plurality of intermediate portions that are disposed on the current collector in an island shape and contain a 10 first binding material, and a mixture layer disposed on the current collector and the plurality of intermediate portions, the mixture layer containing an active material and a second binding material; an average distance between peripheral edges of the intermediate portions adjacent to each other as viewed in a thickness direction of the electrode is 30 m or more and 250 m or less, and an area S of each of the intermediate portions is 5,000 m2 or more and 150,000 m2 15 or less, and the method comprising: a step (1) of applying a binding material composition containing the first binding material onto the current collector in an island shape to form a first 20 intermediate in which the intermediate portions are formed; a step (2) of supplying composite particles containing the active material and the second binding material onto the current collector and the intermediate portions of the first intermediate to form a composite particle layer; and a step (3) of pressing the composite particle layer to form the mixture layer, 25 thereby obtaining the electrode. Advantageous Effects of Invention [0009] According to the present invention, an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery that can achieve both excellent rapid charging performance and 8 cycle characteristics in a lithium ion secondary battery; a method for producing such an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery; and a lithium ion secondary battery that may achieve both excellent rapid charging performance and cycle characteristics can be provided. 5 Brief Description of Drawings [0010] FIG.1: FIG. 1 is a schematic view of an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to an embodiment A1 as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode. 10 FIG.2: FIG. 2 is a schematic view of a cross section taken along line II-II of FIG. 1. FIG.3: FIG. 3 is a schematic view for illustrating intermediate portions adjacent to an intermediate portion M1. 15 Description of Embodiments [0011] Hereinafter, the present invention will be described in detail with reference to embodiments and examples. However, the present invention is not limited to the embodiments and examples described hereinafter, and may be freely modified for implementation without departing from the scope of claims of the present 20 invention and the scope of their equivalents. Components of the following embodiments may be appropriately combined. For example, any numerical value selected from the numerical group listed as the lower limit value and any numerical value selected from the numerical group listed as the upper limit value may be appropriately combined. In the drawings, the same components are 25 denoted by the same reference numerals, and descriptions thereof may be omitted. [0012] In the following description, unless otherwise specified, the term "(meth)acrylic acid" encompasses acrylic acid, methacrylic acid, and combinations thereof; 9 The term "(meth)acrylate" encompasses acrylates, methacrylates, and combinations thereof; The term "(meth)acrylic acid ester" encompasses acrylic acid esters, methacrylic acid ester, and combinations thereof; 5 The term "(meth)acrylamide" encompasses acrylamide, methacrylamide, and combinations thereof; The term "(meth)acryloyl" encompasses acryloyl, methacryloyl, and combinations thereof. [0013] In the following description, the structure of a structural unit that a 10 polymer has may be expressed by the term "monomer unit" immediately after the name of a monomer capable of forming its repeating unit by polymerization. For example, a structural unit that can be formed by polymerizing a (meth)acrylic acid ester is also referred to as a "(meth)acrylic acid ester monomer unit". However, the term "monomer unit" is not limited by a polymerization method to obtain the 15 monomer unit, and may represent a structural unit obtained by an optional polymerization method. The structural unit may be a repeating unit. [0014] In the following description, unless otherwise specified, the “median diameter D50” of a particle means a particle diameter at which the integrated value from the small-diameter side in the volume-based integrated particle 20 diameter distribution measured by a laser diffraction/light scattering method becomes 50%. [0015] In the following description, unless otherwise specified, a direction of an element being “parallel”, “perpendicular”, and “orthogonal” may contain errors within a range that does not impair the advantageous effect of the present 25 invention, for example, within a range of 3, 2, or 1. [0016] In the following description, unless otherwise specified, a “lithium ion secondary battery” refers to a secondary battery that uses lithium ions as a carrier for charge transfer between a positive electrode and a negative electrode. [0017] <1. Electrode for lithium ion secondary battery> 10 <1.1. Summary of electrode for lithium ion secondary battery> An electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to an embodiment of the present invention includes: a current collector; a plurality of intermediate portions that are disposed on the current collector in an island shape 5 and contain a first binding material; and a mixture layer disposed on the current collector and the plurality of intermediate portions. Further, in the electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to the present embodiment, the average distance between the peripheral edges of the intermediate portions adjacent to each other as viewed in the thickness direction 10 of the electrode is 30 m or more and 250 m or less, and the area S of each of the intermediate portions is 5,000 m2 or more and 150,000 m2 or less. The aforementioned mixture layer contains graphite and a second binding material, and the aforementioned graphite has a ratio of the peak intensity corresponding to a (110) plane relative to the peak intensity corresponding to a 15 (002) plane in an X-ray diffraction pattern of 0.0040 or more. [0018] A lithium ion secondary battery using the electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to the present embodiment as an electrode of the lithium ion secondary battery may achieve both excellent rapid charging performance and excellent cycle characteristics. 20 [0019] <1.2. Embodiment A1 of electrode> Hereinafter, an electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to an embodiment A1 of the present invention will be described using the drawings. FIG. 1 is a schematic view of the electrode for a lithium ion secondary battery according to the embodiment A1 as viewed in the thickness direction of 25 the electrode. FIG. 2 is a schematic view of a cross section taken along line II-II of FIG. 1. As shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, an electrode 100 includes a current collector 110, a plurality of intermediate portions 120, and a mixture layer 130. The electrode 100 for a lithium ion secondary battery may include a current 11 collecting member for collecting current from the current collector 110, such as a lead or a current collecting tab, which is not shown. Each of the plurality of intermediate portions is disposed on the current collector 110 in an island shape. Here, intermediate portions being disposed in an 5 island shape means that a plurality of intermediate portions are provided and disposed discretely from each other. Further, the intermediate portions being disposed on the current collector means that the intermediate portions are disposed in contact with the current collector, and preferably in direct contact with the current collector. 10 [0020] In the present embodiment, the intermediate portions 120 and the mixture layer 130 are disposed on a surface 110U, one of the two main surfaces of the current collector 110. [0021] In another embodiment, the intermediate portions and the mixture layer 15 may be disposed on each of the two main surfaces of the current collector. [0022] In the present embodiment, the intermediate portions 120 are disposed in an island shape across the entirety of the electrode. However, in still another embodiment, the intermediate portions that are not disposed in an island shape, that is, the intermediate portions that are continuously distributed, for example, in 20 a band shape may be formed in part of the electrode, or the intermediate portions that are disposed in an island shape and in which the average distance between peripheral edges and/or the area S are outside of certain numerical ranges to be described later may be formed in part of the electrode. A positive electrode and a negative electrode of a lithium ion secondary 25 battery are usually disposed so as to face each other. A portion of the surface of one of the electrodes that does not face the other electrode usually does not largely contribute to a charge and discharge reaction. Therefore, in the portion of the electrode that does not face the other electrode, the intermediate portions may not be disposed in an island shape, and the intermediate portions in which the average 12 distance between the peripheral edges and/or the area S are outside of the ranges to be described later may be disposed. For example, the intermediate portions continuously distributed or the intermediate portions in which the average distance between the peripheral edges 5 and/or the areas S are outside of the range to be described later may be disposed at a peripheral area of the electrode. When the intermediate portions continuously distributed are disposed at the peripheral area of the electrode, separation of the mixture layer from the peripheral area may be suppressed in a step of producing an electrode (e.g., cutting an electrode raw film). Further, even when the 10 intermediate portions in which the average distance between the peripheral edges is less than a lower limit to be described later or the area S is more than an upper limit to be described later are disposed at the peripheral area of the electrode, separation of the mixture layer from the peripheral area may be similarly suppressed in a step of producing an electrode (e.g., cutting an electrode raw film). 15 [0023] It is preferable that in the portion of the surface of one of the electrodes that faces the other electrode, the intermediate portions that are disposed in an island shape and in which the average distance between the peripheral edges and the area S fall within the ranges to be described later are formed. [0026] When the plurality of intermediate portions are disposed on the current collector in an island shape, the rapid charging characteristics of a battery may be 15 improved. The present inventor presumes that the reason is as described below. A binding material contained in the intermediate portions usually has low electroconductivity and usually acts as an insulating material, and thus the intermediate portions disposed between the current collector and the mixture layer prevent electrical conduction between the current collector and the mixture layer. 20 Therefore, the conduction paths of the mixture layer disposed on the intermediate portions and the current collector are formed so as to avoid the intermediate portions. When the intermediate portions have a continuous shape as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode (e.g., a band shape or a grid shape), that is, the 25 intermediate portions are not disposed in an island shape, it is considered that a conduction path connecting the mixture layer disposed on the intermediate portions to the portion of the current collector on which the intermediate portions are not disposed is not formed in a direction in which the intermediate portions are continuous. For example, when the intermediate portions are formed in a band 14 shape as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode, it is considered that the direction of the conduction path as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode is limited to a direction other than the extending direction of the intermediate portions. 5 On the other hand, when the intermediate portions are disposed on the current collector in an island shape as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode, the intermediate portions are discretely disposed on the current collector. Thus, it is considered that a specific direction in which the intermediate portions are continuous does not exist and a conduction path connecting the 10 mixture layer disposed on the intermediate portions to the portion of the current collector on which the intermediate portions are not disposed is formed in all directions from the intermediate portions as viewed in the thickness direction of the electrode. Consequently, it is considered that an uneven reaction on the electrode may be suppressed, improving the characteristics that are exhibited 15 during rapid charging of a battery. [0069] Graphite contained in the mixture layer has a ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of the peak intensity (I(110)) corresponding to a (110) plane in the crystal structure of graphite in the X-ray diffraction pattern relative to the peak intensity (I(002)) corresponding to a (002) plane in the crystal structure of graphite in the X-ray 10 diffraction pattern of usually 0.0040 or more, preferably 0.0050 or more, and more preferably 0.0055 or more. The upper limit thereof is not particularly limited, but is preferably 0.0150 or less, and more preferably 0.0115 or less. [0070] The (002) plane in the crystal structure of graphite is a plane in a c-axis direction of a graphite crystal, and the (110) plane of graphite is a plane in an a15 axis direction perpendicular to the (002) plane. In the measurement of the X-ray diffraction pattern of graphite, a peak attributed as the diffraction line from the (002) plane of graphite and a peak attributed as the diffraction line from the (110) plane of graphite are detected. The ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of the peak intensity (I(110)) corresponding to 20 the (110) plane relative to the peak intensity (I(002)) corresponding to the (002) plane is a numerical value involved in the orientation of graphite. A higher ratio (I(110)/I(002)) means a lower degree of orientation. Here, the orientation of graphite represents the degree to which the crystal plane (002) of graphite particles aligns with the plane direction of the current collector. 25 [0071] When the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) is equal to or more than the aforementioned lower limit, the rapid charging characteristics can be improved in a lithium ion secondary battery including the electrode. The reason is presumed as described below. 32 [0072] Graphite is an anisotropic material and slips easily in an in-plane direction. Thus, when a layer (mixture layer) containing graphite is subjected to a pressing operation with a roll press machine to increase the electrode density in a step of producing an electrode, graphite particles contained in the mixture layer are likely 5 to be oriented along the plane of the current collector. When graphite is highly oriented in the in-plane direction of the current collector, the path of voids inside the mixture layer from the electrode surface to the current collector (tortuous path length) is increased. When the void structure of the electrode is in such a state, the transport (electrophoresis) of lithium ions from the surface layer of the 10 mixture layer of the electrode to the deep portion of the mixture layer near the current collector is hindered at rapid charging. As a result, a charging reaction occurs in a concentrated manner on the electrode surface, and thus the charge capacity is reduced. In addition, it is possible that metal lithium precipitates on the electrode surface, causing irreversible capacity degradation. 15 In contrast, when the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) involved in orientation is equal to or more than the aforementioned lower limit, that is, the orientation of the graphite particles towards the plane of the current collector is restricted, the path of voids from the electrode surface to the deep portion of the electrode near the current collector (tortuous path length) can be shortened, and the charging 20 performance in rapid charging can be improved. [0073] The ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of graphite contained in the mixture layer may be adjusted by adjusting the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of graphite used as the material for the mixture layer and production conditions of the mixture layer. For example, the mixture layer may be formed by producing composite particles containing 25 graphite and the binding material as a powder and pressing a layer of the composite particles as this powder, and as a result, the mixture layer in which the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of graphite falls within the aforementioned range may be formed. Graphite contained in the composite particles is present in the composite particles in a state of low degree of orientation. Thus, when the mixture layer is 33 formed on the current collector using the graphite and a pressing step is performed, the degree of orientation can be reduced as compared with that achieved by a method in which a liquid composition containing graphite, the binding material, and a solvent is applied onto the current collector, dried, and pressed to produce 5 the mixture layer and the electrode. Furthermore, in a conventional method for producing an electrode in which a liquid composition containing graphite, the binding material, and a solvent is applied onto the current collector, dried, and pressed, the liquid composition is simply applied and dried to orient the graphite particles on the current collector to some degree, and thus the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) 10 of graphite falling within the aforementioned range generally cannot be achieved. The ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of graphite can be changed, for example, by 15 selecting a method for producing composite particles. In particular, when a spray drying method capable of forming composite particles instantaneously is selected as the method for producing composite particles, the degree of orientation of graphite in the electrode can be reduced. [0074] The ratio (I(110)/I(002)) of graphite may be measured by the following 20 method. For the mixture layer, an X-ray diffraction pattern is obtained with an Xray diffraction device. A peak intensity I(110) and a peak intensity I(002) of the respective peaks are obtained, and the ratio (I(110)/I(002)) may be determined. X-ray diffraction measurement may be performed, for example, by a concentration method under conditions of a tube voltage of 45 kV, a tube current 34 of 200 mA, a measurement angle of 20 to 90, and a scanning speed of 20/min. [0111] <Characteristics of lithium ion secondary battery> The lithium ion secondary battery including the electrode according to the embodiment described above has excellent rapid charging characteristics and cycle characteristics. 15 [0112] (Rapid charging characteristics: Charge rate) The rapid charging characteristics of the lithium ion secondary battery may be evaluated by the percentage (charge rate) Rc of a battery capacity after a 0.25-hour rate charge of the lithium ion secondary battery when the battery capacity before charging is defined as 100%. Specifically, Rc may be determined 20 by the following method. A lithium ion secondary battery after the capacity (C0) is achieved by a 10-hour rate discharge in measurement of capacity after initial formation is allowed to stand at a temperature of 25C and a lower limit cell voltage for 1 hour, and then charged to a cell voltage of 4.2 V at a 4.0 C rate, that is, by a 0.25-hour 25 rate constant current method. The lithium ion secondary battery is allowed to stand for 30 minutes, and then discharged to the lower limit cell voltage at a temperature of 25C at a 0.2 C rate, that is, by a 5-hour rate constant current method. The battery capacity C1 at that time is measured. The charge rate Rc (%) may be determined by expression: Rc = (C1/C0)  100. 48 [0113] In an example, higher Rc, which represents the rapid charging characteristics of a lithium ion battery, is preferable. [0114] (Rapid charging characteristics: Rapid charge-discharge cycle characteristics) 5 The lithium ion secondary battery described above has excellent rapid charge-discharge cycle characteristics. The rapid charge-discharge cycle characteristics of the lithium ion secondary battery can be evaluated, for example, by a cycle capacity retention ratio in a rapid charge-discharge cycle test in which rapid 0.25-hour rate charge and discharge are performed for a plurality of cycles 10 (e.g., 50 cycles). As the cycle capacity retention ratio is higher, the rapid charge cycle characteristics are more excellent. [0115] (Cycle characteristics) The cycle characteristics of the lithium ion secondary battery can be evaluated as a cycle capacity retention ratio in a cycle test in which 200 cycles of 15 charging and discharging at a temperature of 45C are performed. In an example, the cycle capacity retention ratio of the lithium ion secondary battery is preferably 80% or more, more preferably 85% or more, and still more preferably 88% or more. The upper limit thereof is ideally 100%, but may be 100% or less. The cycle capacity retention ratio represents a ratio of the "200-cycle discharge 20 capacity" relative to the "first cycle discharge capacity" in the aforementioned cycle test, and may be measured by a method described in the section <Evaluation method" (Cycle characteristics) of Examples to be described later. [0116] (Discharge capacity per unit area) The discharge capacity per unit area is a ratio of the capacity when a 10-25 hour rate discharge is performed within a voltage range from the upper limit voltage to the discharge voltage of the battery, relative to the total area of the portion where the positive electrode faces the negative electrode. From the viewpoint of energy density, a higher discharge capacity per unit area is preferable. 49 The upper limit voltage and the lower limit voltage of a battery vary depending on the positive electrode active material and the negative electrode active material that are used. When the specification of the battery is known, it is preferable that the upper and lower limit voltages of the battery are set according 5 to the specification. Further, when materials to be used are known, it is preferable that the upper and lower limit voltages of the battery are set according to the materials. For example, when the positive electrode active material contains lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide or lithium cobalt oxide, the upper limit voltage of a general battery cell is usually 4.2 V. When the positive electrode 10 active material is lithium iron phosphate, the upper limit voltage of the battery cell is usually 3.8 V. When two or more types of positive electrode active materials are used, the upper limit voltage of the battery cell is determined according to the material to be operated at a higher voltage. In the case of a novel material, reference to technical documents and the like may be made. 15 The lower limit voltage varies depending on the positive electrode active material and the negative electrode active material. When lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide is used as the positive electrode active material and graphite is used as the negative electrode active material, the lower limit voltage of the battery cell is usually 3.00 V. When the positive electrode active material 20 contains lithium iron phosphate, the lower limit voltage of the battery is usually 2.40 V. Further, when graphite and the silicon atom-containing active material are used in combination as the negative electrode active material, it is preferable that the lower limit voltage is set to be lower than the aforementioned voltage value. 25 When an active material used in the battery is unclear, the type of an active material used can be found from a diffraction pattern based on the crystal structure of the active material by analyzing the battery with a high-energy X ray. When the lower limit voltage is unclear, it is preferable that from a rated voltage, a current value that is reduced by application to a voltage lower than the 50 rated voltage by 0.1 V over 30 minutes is discovered, discharging is further continued at the current value, a point at which the slope (V/t) of voltage change relative to time change is 15 times or more the slope of voltage change relative to time change until the voltage is decreased by 0.1 V from the rated 5 voltage is set to the lower limit voltage of the battery. The upper and lower limit voltages of the battery are determined as described above, and charging and discharging are then performed within the range of the upper and lower limit voltages while changing the current value. Thus, the discharge capacity of the battery at a 10-hour rate can be determined. 10 When the area of the portion where the positive electrode faces the negative electrode is unclear, the capacity of the battery is determined by a 10-hour rate discharge, and the area can be obtained by measurement of the size of the electrode inside the battery, after disassembly of the battery or using an X-ray CT. 15 [0117] The discharge capacity per unit area (battery capacity) of the portion where the negative electrode and the positive electrode face each other, when the lithium ion secondary battery is discharged at a 10-hour rate, is preferably 3.3 mAh/cm2 or more, more preferably 3.5 mAh/cm2 or more, and still more preferably 4.0 mAh/cm2 or more. 20 Even when the discharge capacity per unit area is equal to or more than the aforementioned lower limit, the lithium ion secondary battery according to the present embodiment may achieve excellent rapid charging characteristics and cycle characteristics. [0118] For example, when the entirety of the surface of the positive electrode 25 faces part of the surface of the negative electrode, the "area of the portion where the negative electrode and the positive electrode face each other" is equal to the area of the positive electrode, and specifically the area of the positive electrode mixture layer of the positive electrode. 51 When one (e.g., the negative electrode) of the positive electrode and the negative electrode of the lithium ion secondary battery is an electrode in which the mixture layer (e.g., the negative electrode mixture layer) is formed on each of the surfaces of the current collector, the "area of the portion where the negative 5 electrode and the positive electrode face each other" is a sum (A1 + A2) of an area A1 of a portion where the mixture layer formed on a surface of the current collector faces the mixture layer (e.g., the positive electrode mixture layer) of the other electrode (e.g., the positive electrode), and an area A2 of a portion where the mixture layer formed on another surface of the current collector faces the mixture 10 layer of the other electrode. Rc (%) = (C1/C0)  100 [0169] (Cycle characteristics) 5 A battery cell separate from the battery cell used in the evaluation of rapid charging characteristics was prepared.
