A positive electrode for lithium ion secondary batteries according to the present invention comprises the positive electrode active material layer. The positive electrode active material layer is characterized by containing a positive electrode active material and an aqueous polymer binder that is derived from a latex, and having a thickness of 150 µm or more. A lithium ion secondary battery according to the present invention is provided with the positive electrode, a negative electrode, a separator, and a nonaqueous electrolyte.
patents.complete_specification: TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] 5 The present invention relates to a positive electrode for a lithium-ion secondary battery and a lithium-ion secondary battery. BACKGROUND ART [0002] 10 A positive electrode active material layer of a lithium ion battery is usually produced by applying a slurry containing positive electrode active material particles, a PVdF-based binder, N-methylpyrrolidone, and a conductive additive onto a current collector, and drying the coating layer. 15 SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION PROBLEMS TO BE SOLVED BY THE INVENTION [0003] N-methylpyrrolidone is included in a list of restricted substances under the REACH Regulation due to concerns about its toxicity. 20 The present invention has been made in view of such circumstances and provides a positive electrode including a positive electrode active material layer that can be formed using a positive electrode active material slurry that is free from N-methylpyrrolidone. 25 SOLUTION TO PROBLEM [0004] The present invention provides a positive electrode for a lithium-ion secondary battery comprising a positive electrode active material layer, the positive electrode active material layer including a positive electrode active 3 material and a latex-derived aqueous polymer binder and having a thickness of 150 μm or more. EFFECTS OF THE INVENTION 5 [0005] Since the positive electrode active material layer includes the latexderived aqueous polymer binder, a favorable positive electrode active material layer can be formed using the positive electrode active material slurry (dispersion medium: water) that is free from N-methylpyrrolidone. 10 BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0006] Fig. 1 is a schematic cross-sectional view of a lithium-ion secondary battery according to an embodiment of the present invention. 15 Fig. 2 (a) is a schematic plan view of a positive electrode included in the lithium-ion secondary battery according to an embodiment of the present invention, and Fig. 2 (b) is a schematic cross-sectional view of the positive electrode taken along a broken line A-A in Fig. 2 (a). Fig. 3 (a) is a schematic plan view of a negative electrode included in the 20 lithium-ion secondary battery according to an embodiment of the present invention, and Fig. 3 (b) is a schematic cross-sectional view of the negative electrode taken along a broken line B-B in Fig. 3 (a). Fig. 4 is a schematic structural view of an electrode assembly included in the lithium-ion secondary battery according to an embodiment of the present 25 invention. 4 EMBODIMENT OF THE INVENTION [0007] Hereinafter, an embodiment of the present invention will be described 5 with reference to drawings. The configurations shown in the drawings and the following description are merely examples, and the scope of the present invention is not limited to those shown in the drawings or the following description. A positive electrode 5 for a lithium-ion secondary battery according to the present embodiment includes a positive electrode active material layer 2, the 10 positive electrode active material layer 2 including a positive electrode active material and an aqueous polymer binder derived from latex and having a thickness of 150 μm or more. A lithium-ion secondary battery 30 according to the present embodiment includes the positive electrode 5 according to the present embodiment, a negative 15 electrode 32, a separator 34, and a non-aqueous electrolyte 15. [0008] The positive electrode 5 for a lithium-ion secondary battery is the positive electrode 5 included in the lithium-ion secondary battery 30 or the positive electrode 5 used for producing the lithium-ion secondary battery 30. 20 The positive electrode 5 for a lithium-ion secondary battery includes a positive electrode current collector 3 and the porous positive electrode active material layer 2 provided on the positive electrode current collector 3. The positive electrode current collector 3 is a sheet serving as a substrate on which the positive electrode active material layer 2 is provided, and the 25 positive electrode current collector 3 is a conductor that electrically connects a positive electrode connection member 13 and the positive electrode active material layer 2 to each other. The positive electrode current collector 3 is, for example, an aluminum foil. The positive electrode connection member 13 is electrically connected to an external connection terminal 18a. The positive 5 electrode active material layer 2 may be provided on one side of the positive electrode current collector 3 or may be provided on both sides of the positive electrode current collector 3. [0009] 5 The positive electrode active material layer 2 is a layer containing a positive electrode active material. A thickness of the positive electrode active material layer 2 (after pressing) is 150 μm or more, and preferably 200 μm or more. This can increase the amount of the positive electrode active material contained in the positive electrode 5, thereby increasing battery capacity of the 10 lithium-ion secondary battery 30. Furthermore, since the current collector 3 included in the lithium-ion secondary battery 30 can be reduced, a gravimetric energy density of the lithium-ion secondary battery 30 can be increased. On the other hand, if the thickness of the positive electrode active material layer 2 is excessively large, a distance between the surface of the positive 15 electrode active material layer 2 and the current collector 3 becomes too large, which may increase the electrode resistance. Accordingly, the thickness of the positive electrode active material layer 2 is preferably 500 μm or less, and more preferably 400 μm or less. [0010] 20 The positive electrode active material layer 2 includes the positive electrode active material and the latex-derived aqueous polymer binder. Also, the positive electrode active material layer 2 may include CMC (sodium carboxymethyl cellulose or calcium carboxymethyl cellulose). The positive electrode active material layer 2 may also include a thickening agent. The positive 25 electrode active material layer 2 may also include a conductive agent. Further, the positive electrode active material layer 2 may include a surfactant. [0011] As the positive electrode active material, lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) is preferable. Other positive electrode materials can also be used, 6 provided that they have good compatibility with the solvent of the positive electrode slurry. As the lithium iron phosphate, lithium iron phosphate secondary particles that are secondary particles in which primary particles of lithium iron phosphate 5 (LiFePO4) are aggregated are preferable. Further, the positive electrode active material primary particles may have a conductive film on the surface. This can improve conductivity of the surfaces of the fine particles on which an intercalation reaction is progressing and can reduce the internal resistance of the positive electrode. The conductive film is, for example, a carbon film. The primary 10 particles of lithium iron phosphate have an average particle size of, for example, 30 nm or more and 400 nm or less. The average particle size can be calculated by measuring particle sizes of 100 primary particles randomly selected in a crosssectional photograph of the positive electrode active material layer 2 and arithmetically averaging these particle sizes. 15 [0012] The positive electrode active material layer 2 can include larger-diameter lithium iron phosphate secondary particles as a first positive electrode active material and smaller-diameter lithium iron phosphate secondary particles as a second positive electrode active material having a smaller particle size than the 20 first lithium iron phosphate secondary particles. The larger-diameter lithium iron phosphate secondary particles are lithium iron phosphate secondary particles having a particle size of 10 μm or more among a plurality of lithium iron phosphate secondary particles included in the positive electrode active material layer 2 and have an average particle size of 25 15 μm or more and 22 μm or less. The smaller-diameter lithium iron phosphate secondary particles are lithium iron phosphate secondary particles having a particle size of less than 10 μm among the plurality of lithium iron phosphate secondary particles included 7 in the positive electrode active material layer 2 and have an average particle size of 2 μm or more and 7 μm or less. [0013] For example, the average particle size of the larger-diameter lithium iron 5 phosphate can be obtained by measuring the particle sizes of 100 lithium iron phosphate secondary particles randomly selected in a cross-sectional photograph of the positive electrode active material layer 2 and arithmetically averaging the particle sizes of the secondary particles having a particle size of 10 μm or more among the secondary particles whose particle sizes have been measured; and the 10 average particle size of the smaller-diameter lithium iron phosphate can be obtained by arithmetically averaging the particle sizes of the secondary particles having a particle size of less than 10 μm among the secondary particles whose particle sizes have been measured. [0014] 15 For example, when the particle sizes of 100 lithium iron phosphate secondary particles randomly selected in the cross-sectional photograph of the positive electrode active material layer 2 are measured, and a particle size distribution of the lithium iron phosphate secondary particles is created with particle size on the horizontal axis and number of particles on the vertical axis, a 20 peak for the smaller-diameter lithium iron phosphate can be present in a range of 2 μm or more and 7 μm or less, and a peak for the larger-diameter lithium iron phosphate can be present in a range of 15 μm or more and 22 μm or less. This particle size distribution may not have a peak other than the two peaks of the peak for the larger-diameter lithium iron phosphate and the peak for the smaller25 diameter lithium iron phosphate. [0015] It is preferable that a ratio a:b of mass (b) of the second positive electrode active material to mass (a) of the first positive electrode active material be 7:3 to 9:1 (i.e., a ratio (b/a) of (1/9) or more and (3/7) or less). This ratio stabilizes the 8 positive electrode slurry and the positive electrode active material layer 2. This ratio also improves the pressing characteristics of the positive electrode active material layer 2 and facilitates control of porosity. The masses of the first positive electrode active material and the second 5 positive electrode active material can be calculated from the density and particle size of the positive electrode active material particles. The density of the positive electrode active material particles can be measured and calculated using a positive electrode active material (powder) equivalent to the positive electrode active material particles included in the positive electrode active material layer 2. In 10 addition, the measurement can be performed by dissolving the positive electrode active material layer 2 in a solvent or the like and recovering and classifying the positive electrode active material. [0016] The conductive agent is, for example, fine particles of furnace black, 15 acetylene black, carbon black, and coke-based soft carbon. By containing the conductive agent, the positive electrode active material layer 2 can improve conductivity and reduce the internal resistance of the positive electrode 5. [0017] The latex-derived aqueous polymer binder is a polymer binder that can 20 be colloidally dispersed in an aqueous dispersion medium. The aqueous polymer binder is, for example, an acrylic polymer binder, styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), or the like. By using such a polymer binder, it is possible to use water or an aqueous solution as the dispersion medium for the positive electrode active material slurry used for forming the positive electrode active material layer 2. A 25 glass transition temperature Tg of a polymer compound serving as the polymer binder is, for example, 20°C or less, preferably 10°C or less, and more preferably 0°C or less. This allows the polymer binder to exhibit flexibility and further improves binding properties. 9 Inclusion of the aqueous polymer binder in the positive electrode active material layer 2 can suppress peeling of the positive electrode active material layer 2 from the positive electrode current collector 3 and cracking of the positive electrode active material layer 2. 5 [0018] A ratio (d/c) of mass (d) of the latex-derived aqueous polymer binder included in the positive electrode active material layer 2 to mass (c) of the positive electrode active material contained in the positive electrode active material layer 2 (the sum of the mass of the first positive electrode active material and the mass of 10 the second positive electrode active material) is, for example, (1/98.7) or more and (1.6/97.8) or less. This allows favorable binding properties to be obtained. Furthermore, since the amount of the binder is small, output characteristics of the lithium-ion secondary battery 30 can be improved. The mass of the latex-derived aqueous polymer binder included in the positive electrode active material layer 2 15 can be calculated, for example, from the mass of the aqueous polymer binder extracted from the positive electrode active material layer 2. In addition, the positive electrode active material layer 2 can be produced with a smaller amount of binder than in a solvent-based system. Further, the binding properties of positive electrode active material 20 layer 2 to the positive electrode current collector 3 can be improved. [0019] CMC (sodium carboxymethyl cellulose or calcium carboxymethyl cellulose) has a function of increasing the viscosity of the positive electrode active material slurry used for forming the positive electrode active material layer 2. 25 CMC may function as a binder of the positive electrode active material layer 2. Inclusion of CMC in the positive electrode active material slurry can increase the viscosity of the positive electrode active material slurry and enable the positive electrode active material layer 2 to have a uniform thickness. Further, the positive electrode active material slurry can be applied in a thick coating, and the positive 10 electrode active material layer 2 having a large thickness (for example, a thickness of 150 μm or more (after pressing)) can be formed. [0020] A ratio (e/c) of mass (e) of CMC included in the positive electrode active 5 material layer 2 to mass (c) of the positive electrode active material included in the positive electrode active material layer 2 (the sum of the mass of the first positive electrode active material and the mass of the second positive electrode active material) is, for example, (0.3/98.7) or more and (0.6/97.8) or less. This can suppress cracking of the positive electrode active material layer 2 during drying of 10 a coating layer of the positive electrode active material slurry. [0021] A total of the percentage of the latex-derived aqueous polymer binder and the percentage of CMC in the positive electrode active material layer 2 is, for example, 1.3 wt% or more and 2.0 wt% or less. This can suppress binding failure 15 of the positive electrode active material layer 2 even when the positive electrode active material slurry is thickly applied by a single application to form a positive electrode active material layer having a thickness (after pressing) of 150 μm or more. This can also increase the battery capacity of the lithium-ion secondary battery including the positive electrode active material layer 2. 20 [0022] A ratio (d/e) of mass (d) of the polymer binder to mass (e) of CMC included in the positive electrode active material layer 2 may be 2.25 or more and 4.0 or less. This can suppress cracking of the positive electrode active material layer 2 even when the positive electrode active material slurry is applied in a thick 25 coating by a single application to form a positive electrode active material layer having a thickness (after pressing) of 150 μm or more. [0023] As for the positive electrode, the positive electrode active material layer 2 can be formed, for example, by mixing and kneading: the larger-diameter 11 lithium iron phosphate secondary particles as the first positive electrode active material having an average particle size D50 in a range of 15 μm or more and 22 μm or less; the smaller-diameter lithium iron phosphate secondary particles as the second positive electrode active material having an average particle size D50 5 in a range of 2 μm or more and 7 μm or less; a latex of the aqueous polymer binder (an emulsion in which a polymer compound serving as the binder is colloidally dispersed in water); the CMC; and water or the aqueous solution to prepare the positive electrode active material slurry, applying the slurry onto the positive electrode current collector 3, and drying the coating layer. If necessary, a 10 thickener may be added to the positive electrode active material slurry, or a small amount of a surfactant may be added to the positive electrode active material slurry. Further, the positive electrode active material layer 2 may be pressed. In the pressing treatment, for example, pressure may be applied to the positive electrode active material layer 2 such that a porosity of the positive electrode 15 active material layer 2 falls within a range of 20% to 40%. An excessively low porosity leads to poor impregnation of an electrolytic solution 15, whereas an excessively high porosity increases the thickness of the positive electrode active material layer 2, thereby decreasing the volumetric energy density. The porosity is preferably 30% to 40%. 20 [0024] The positive electrode active material layer 2 may be produced by repeatedly applying thin layers in a coating process; however, in the positive electrode active material layer 2 produced by such repeated coating, contact resistance may occur at interfaces between the layers, which may increase the 25 resistance. In addition, in repeated coating, the coated and dried layer may be dissolved by a solvent contained in the subsequently applied slurry, which may also cause deformation of the coating film. From the above, it is preferable that the positive electrode active material layer 2 be produced as a uniform thick layer by a single application. 12 As a reference example, the DCR resistance values of electrodes having a thickness of about 200 μm formed by one coating and two coatings are described below. The single-layer electrode shows a resistance of 1.483 mΩ, whereas the 5 two-layer electrode shows a resistance of 1.523 mΩ, indicating that the resistance is higher in the latter. [0025] A negative electrode 32 is an electrode including a porous negative electrode active material layer 36. The negative electrode active material layer 36 10 is, for example, a porous layer including a negative electrode active material provided on a sheet-shaped negative electrode current collector 38. The negative electrode current collector 38 is electrically connected to a negative electrode connection member 14. The negative electrode connection member 14 is electrically connected to an external connection terminal 18b. The negative 15 electrode current collector 38 is, for example, a copper foil. The negative electrode active material is a substance that is directly involved in the transfer of electrons accompanying charge transfer in the negative electrode. The negative electrode active material is, for example, graphite, partially graphitized carbon, hard carbon, soft carbon, lithium titanate (LTO), or a 20 Sn alloy. The negative electrode active material layer 36 can include one or more of these negative electrode active materials, either alone or in combination. [0026] The separator 34 has a sheet shape and is disposed between the positive electrode 5 and the negative electrode 32. Further, the separator 34 can configure, 25 together with the positive electrodes 5 and the negative electrodes 32, an electrode assembly 22 as shown in Fig. 4. By providing the separator 34, it is possible to prevent a short-circuit current from flowing between the positive electrode 5 and the negative electrode 32. 13 There is no particular limitation on the separator 34 if a short-circuit current can be prevented from flowing and if ions conducting between the positive electrode and the negative electrode can pass through the separator 34, and a microporous film of polyolefin, a cellulose sheet, or an aramid sheet can be used, 5 for example. In addition, the separator 34 may be a nonwoven fabric including at least one of cellulose fiber, polyester fiber, polypropylene fiber, polyacrylonitrile fiber, and polyethylene terephthalate fiber. [0027] As shown in Fig. 4, the electrode assembly 22 may have a structure in 10 which a plurality of positive electrodes 5 and a plurality of negative electrodes 32 are stacked such that the positive electrodes 5 and the negative electrodes 32 are alternately disposed. In addition, the electrode assembly 22 may have a structure in which the separator 34 is disposed between the adjacent positive electrode 5 and negative electrode 32. 15 [0028] As the solvent for the non-aqueous electrolyte 15, carbonates, lactones, ethers, esters, ionic liquids, and the like can be used, and two or more of these solvents can also be mixed and used. In particular, a cyclic carbonate and a chain carbonate of these solvents are preferably mixed and used. The non-aqueous 20 electrolyte 15 is, for example, a solution in which a lithium salt solute such as LiCF3SO3, LiAsF6, LiClO4, LiBF4, LiPF6, LiBOB, LiN (CF3SO2)2, or LiN(C2F5SO2) is dissolved in an organic solvent. If necessary, additives such as VC (vinylene carbonate), PS (propane sultone), VEC (vinyl ethyl carbonate), PRS (propene sultone), and a flame retardant may be blended alone or in combination 25 of two or more. [0029] A battery cell case 11 is a battery cell outer casing that houses the electrode assembly 22 (including the positive electrode 5, the negative electrode 32, and the separator 34) and the nonaqueous electrolyte 15. The battery 14 cell case 11 may be made in a pouch shape made by welding a laminated film at a welding portion. In this case, the lithium-ion secondary battery 30 is a pouch battery. Alternatively, the battery cell case 11 may be a metal case or a hard resin case. The battery cell case 11 may have a lid member 12. 5 [0030] Production 1 of Positive Electrode for Lithium-Ion Secondary Battery Mixture was prepared by mixing carbon-coated lithium iron phosphate secondary particles A (average particle size (D50): 18 μm) and carbon-coated lithium iron phosphate secondary particles B (average particle size (D50): 4 μm) 10 at a mass ratio of 9:1, an acrylic polymer binder solution (latex-dispersed aqueous solution, AXA391, effective component concentration: 40 wt%, glass transition temperature Tg: −35°C, pH: 7–9, B-type viscosity: 5–50 cP, average particle size: 180 μm, particle size distribution having a peak at 170 μm (100–500 μm)), and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC; BSH6, manufactured by Dai-ichi Kogyo 15 Seiyaku Co., Ltd.; degree of etherification: 0.65–0.75; viscosity of 1% CMC aqueous solution at 25°C: 3000–4000 mPa·s; average degree of polymerization: 1200–1350; average molecular weight: 255,000–270,000). Table 1 shows the mass percentages of the total positive electrode active materials, the CMC (solid content), the acrylic polymer binder (solid content), and total of the CMC (solid 20 content) and the acrylic polymer binder (solid content) in the produced positive electrode active material layers. These materials were mixed and kneaded with water as a dispersion medium to prepare positive electrode active material slurry. The positive electrode active material slurry was applied once onto an aluminum foil (positive electrode current collector sheet), and the coating film was dried and 25 further pressed to form a positive electrode active material layer having a thickness of 221 μm on one surface of the positive electrode current collector sheet, thereby producing positive electrodes. No cracking was observed in the positive electrode active material layers after drying. 15 [0031] [Table 1] [0032] Production 2 of Positive Electrode for Lithium-Ion Secondary Battery 5 Positive electrodes were prepared by changing the mass ratio of lithium iron phosphate secondary particles A to lithium iron phosphate secondary particles B to 7:3. Table 2 shows the mass percentages of the total positive electrode active materials, the CMC (solid content), the acrylic polymer binder (solid content), and total of CMC (solid content) and the acrylic polymer binder 10 (solid content) in the produced positive electrode active material layers, as well as the mass ratio (b/a) of the acrylic polymer binder (b) to CMC (a). The positive electrodes were prepared in the same manner as in Production 1, thereby forming positive electrode active material layers having a porosity of 34% and a thickness 16 of 214 μm on one side of the positive electrode current collector sheet. No cracking was observed in the positive electrode active material layers after drying. [0033] [Table 2] 5 [0034] Next, the produced positive electrode, a polyolefin separator, a metallic lithium negative electrode, and a non-aqueous electrolyte (a 1M LiPF6 electrolyte (carbonate-based solvent)) were placed in a coin cell case to produce lithium ion secondary batteries (coin cells) of Working Examples 1 to 8 and Comparative 10 Examples 1 to 6. [0035] Charge-Discharge Test A charge/discharge test was performed using the lithium-ion secondary batteries of Working Examples 1 to 8 and Comparative Examples 1 to 6. 15 Specifically, charge–discharge was performed at 1 C with an upper cut-off voltage of 3.6 V and a lower cut-off voltage of 2.0 V, and battery capacity (discharge capacity) per unit mass of the positive electrode active material layer (mAh/g) was calculated from the discharge current value. It was also found that a favorable electrode can be obtained by setting the ratio (b/a) of the mass (b) of the acrylic polymer binder to the mass (a) of CMC included in the positive electrode active material layer to 2.25 or more and 4.0 or less. 10 [0036] Tape Peeling Test A tape peeling test was performed using the positive electrodes of Working Examples 1 and 4 and the positive electrodes of Comparative Examples 1, 3, and 4. 15 The positive electrode was cut into a size of 5 cm × 5 cm. [0040] In addition, a plurality of positive electrodes including positive electrode active materials different from each other in the positive electrode active material 10 layer were fabricated and subjected to a tape peeling test. Ltd., EP) were mixed. Water was added to the mixed powder and kneaded to prepare a negative electrode active material slurry. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to a use of collector composition for the beneficiation of lithium-containing minerals from an ore, and the process for beneficiation of lithium-containing minerals using said collector composition.
patents.complete_specification: FIELD OF THE INVENTION The present invention relates to a collector composition for the beneficiation of lithium–containing minerals, from an ore, their use in flotation processes and the 5 process for beneficiation of lithium containing minerals using said collector composition. STATE OF ART Lithium is an important strategic resource substance which is widely applied to 10 emerging fields of batteries, ceramics, glass, lubricants, refrigerants, nuclear industry, photoelectricity and the like, and is an indispensable important raw material of modern high-tech products. In recent years, the continuous development of high and new technologies, growth of lithium battery electric vehicles and lithium battery mobile electronic products, lithium and lithium salt products are 15 more and more widely applied, and the demand of the international market for the lithium products is continuously increasing. Lithium does not occur in elemental form in nature because of its reactivity. However, there are more than 100 known minerals that may contain lithium, 20 although only a few of these are currently economic to extract. The most common lithium-bearing minerals found in economic deposits are Spodumene, Lepidolite, Petalite, Eucryptite, Amblygonite, Hectorite, Bikitaite, Zinnwaldite, and Jadarite. Among them, due to its high lithium content, spodumene is considered the most important lithium ore mineral. A typical run of mine ore can contain 0,5-2% Li2O, 25 while a typical Spodumene concentrate suitable for lithium carbonate production contains 5,5-7% Li2O (68%-87% spodumene). Higher grade concentrates with 7.6% Li2O and low iron content are used in ceramics and more demanding industries. Nowadays, global resources of lithium have been estimated to be approximately 41 30 million tons, with the largest resources held by Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, the USA, 3 China, Brazil, Portugal, Zimbabwe and Australia. Spodumene which is basically LiAlSi2O6 contains approximately 8% Li2O and is the most abundant lithiumcontaining mineral. Spodumene is associated with other gangue minerals, such as feldspar, quartz and muscovite, from which it must be separated to be useable in 5 chemical and ceramic applications. Global supply of lithium is currently sourced from brines or hard rock deposits. In the former, lithium is concentrated as soluble salts by solar evaporation. Lithium produced from brines is generally of a low grade and, while the capital 10 input for brine production is high, operating costs are low. In the case of hard rock deposits conventional mining and beneficiation techniques are used to produce high grade spodumene concentrate or other mineral concentrates in which the grade is greater than that of the parent are. It is possible 15 to obtain lithium chemicals of technical, battery grade (99.5%) from various acidroasting and lime-roasting processes. It is well-known from the state of the art to separate the valuable minerals from gangue minerals by using flotation. 20 The mineral, which can be dry ground, but preferably wet-ground, is previously crumbled and suspended in water for the flotation. Collectors are normally added to the mineral, frequently in combination with foaming agents and where appropriate, other auxiliary reagents such as regulators, depressors (deactivators) 25 and/or enhancers (activators), to favor the separation of the valuable minerals from the unwanted mineral gangue components in the subsequent flotation. These reagents are usually allowed to act for a certain time on the finely ground (conditioned) mineral before insufflating air into the suspension (flotation) so as to generate a froth. In this case, the collector is in charge of causing a 4 hydrophobization of the surface of the minerals such that these minerals are adhered to the gas bubbles formed during the air insufflation. The hydrophobization of the mineral components is carried out selectively such that the mineral components which are not to be floated are not adhered on the gas bubbles. The froth containing 5 the mineral is separated and subsequently prepared. The object of the flotation is to separate the valuable mineral from the minerals with the highest possible yield, and to simultaneously obtain, in this case, the best possible enrichment. Flotation comprises differentiated processes, such as direct or reverse flotation. In direct flotation the desired minerals are collected in the froth while the unwanted minerals 10 remains dispersed. In reverse or inverse flotation the unwanted minerals are collected in the froth and the desired minerals remain dispersed in the flotation cell underflow. The beneficiation of lithium-containing minerals such as Spodumene, Lepidolite, 15 Petalite, Eucryptite, Amblygonite, Hectorite, Bikitaite, Zinnwaldite, Elbaite and Jadarite from their associated gangue minerals (e.g., quartz(SiO2) and iron oxides (Fe2O3,Fe3O4) is difficult due to their similar surface chemical properties. Due to the fact that most lithium deposits in the world are deposits that also contain 20 silicates, the selective separation of lithium containing minerals from their associated gangue minerals (e.g. quartz (SiO2) and iron oxide (Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) is a process that has been intensively studied. Anionic surfactants are used as collectors in known processes for the beneficiation 25 lithium containing minerals, such as fatty acids. Known anionic collectors are, for example, saturated and unsaturated fatty acids, oleic acid fatty acids, linoleic acids, linolenic acids, resin acids, tall oil fatty acids, phosphoric esters, especially optionally alkoxylated phosphoric esters derived from 5 fatty alcohols or from fatty alcohol mixtures, alkyl sulfates, especially alkyl sulfates derived from fatty alcohols or from fatty alcohol mixtures, alkylaryl sulfonates, alkyl sulfosuccinates, alkylsulfosuccinimates and acyl lactylates. 5 WO2021038017 describes a collector composition, comprising at least one component a) selected from N-oleoyl sarcosine; and at least one component b) selected from the group consisting of di(isononyl)phthalate, di(2-ethylhexyl)phthalate, di(2-propylheptyl) phthalate, di(isononyl)adipate, di(2-ethylhexyl)adipate, di(2-propylheptyl)adipate and isotridecanol for the 10 beneficiation of lithium silicates and magnesium silicates from an ore comprising different silicate minerals, their use in flotation processes and a method for the beneficiation of lithium silicates-and magnesium silicates-containing minerals using said collector composition. 15 The use of fatty acids as collector/co-collector for the beneficiation of lithium ores is known in the literature. However high doses of the collector compositions and long conditioning times are required. There are several other flotation processes which are disclosed in literature for the beneficiation of lithium. 20 However, none of the known techniques is sufficient to produce an economically viable solution for the beneficiation of lithium ore. From the state of art set forth above, it can be seen that there is still a need of improvement in the field of beneficiation of lithium containing minerals such as 25 lithium silicates, particularly spodumene, from an ore, in which collectors for the beneficiation of lithium containing minerals from gangue minerals are used. Thus, it is an object of the present invention to provide a collector composition that can be used to produce high-grade lithium-containing minerals which can be 6 isolated in high yield with high recovery and with low iron content, as well as good wettability, water dispersibility and suitable froth. The present invention relates a process for the beneficiation of lithium-containing 5 minerals, such as lithium silicates, from ore comprising lithium-containing minerals and gangue minerals, wherein the process comprises the steps of: a) mixing the ore comprising lithium-containing minerals and gangue minerals with water to obtain an aqueous mixture, 10 b) adding the collector composition as previously described to the aqueous mixture obtained in step a), c) agitating the mixture obtained in step b) (conditioning step) d) introducing air injection to the mixture c to generate a froth, and e) collecting the lithium-containing minerals, such as lithium silicates, in the 15 froth. patents.abstract: Lithium sulphate single crystals doped with urea (ULS), thiourea (TLS), and cupric chloride (CuLS) were successfully grown from aqueous solution using the slow evaporation technique at room temperature. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed the incorporation of dopants into the lithium sulphate lattice, resulting in minor lattice modifications while maintaining good crystalline quality. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy verified the presence of lithium sulphate functional groups along with characteristic vibrational modes of the incorporated dopants. Optical absorption studies revealed high transparency across the visible region, indicating suitability for optoelectronic applications. Elemental composition and dopant incorporation were further confirmed through Energy Dispersive X-ray Analysis (EDAX) and CHN elemental analysis. Dielectric studies conducted as a function of frequency and temperature exhibited low dielectric loss and ferroelectric behavior, highlighting the potential of the grown crystals for optoelectronic and ferroelectric device applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:NLO-active ferroelectric single crystals of urea-, thiourea-, and cupric chloride-doped lithium sulphate monohydrate (ULS, TLS, and CuLS) were grown from aqueous solution using the slow evaporation technique. Single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction analyses confirmed that all doped crystals crystallize in the monoclinic system with slight lattice modifications due to dopant incorporation. FTIR and EDAX analyses verified the presence of dopants in the crystal lattice. Optical absorption studies revealed low absorption in the visible region, with UV cut-off wavelengths of 210 nm (ULS), 220 nm (TLS), and 210 nm (CuLS), indicating enhanced optical quality. Dielectric measurements showed low dielectric constant and loss at high frequencies, confirming the ferroelectric nature of the crystals. These results demonstrate that doped lithium sulphate monohydrate crystals are promising candidates for nonlinear optical and optoelectronic applications. , C , Claims:We claim the 1. A doped lithium sulphate (LS) single crystal, wherein X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirms successful incorporation of one or more dopants into the lithium sulphate crystal lattice without altering its fundamental crystal structure, while exhibiting minor variations in lattice parameters due to dopant inclusion. 2. The doped lithium sulphate crystal as claimed in claim 1, wherein the XRD pattern exhibits sharp and intense diffraction peaks, indicating high crystallinity with minimal structural defects and near dislocation-free crystal growth, and wherein the interplanar spacing (d-values) for all observed diffraction peaks are calculated and indexed to their corresponding (hkl) planes. 3. The doped lithium sulphate crystal as claimed in claim 1, wherein the ultraviolet (UV) cut-off wavelengths are approximately 210 nm for undoped lithium sulphate (ULS), 220 nm for thiourea-doped lithium sulphate (TLS), and 210 nm for copper-doped lithium sulphate (CuLS), and wherein the crystals exhibit low optical absorption across the visible region, making them suitable for optoelectronic device applications. 4. The doped lithium sulphate crystal as claimed in claim 1, wherein Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectral analysis confirms the presence of lithium sulphate functional groups along with characteristic vibrational modes corresponding to the incorporated dopants. 5. The doped lithium sulphate crystal as claimed in claim 1, wherein Energy Dispersive X-ray Analysis (EDAX) confirms the elemental composition of the crystal, including weight and atomic percentages, thereby validating the successful incorporation of dopant elements into the lithium sulphate lattice. 6. The doped lithium sulphate crystal as claimed in claim 1, wherein CHN elemental analysis confirms the presence of carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen elements in the grown crystals, further substantiating the incorporation of organic or dopant species within the crystal lattice.

patents.abstract: This project proposes a novel volumetric heat management architecture designed to address the critical thermal bottlenecks of fast-charging Lithium-ion battery packs. Unlike conventional surface-cooling methods, this system integrates an internal lattice of Hollow Heat Pipe fabricated from Aluminum 6063 and charged with an acetone working vapour into the seperator region of cathode-anode interface in case of a solid block cuboidal lithium ion battery of high volume or to the central rod in case of a cylindrical ion battery for heat dissipation. This configuration significantly reduces system mass while maintaining high effective thermal conductivity. To address the mechanical stress caused by electrode expansion ("breathing") during cycling, the OHPs utilize a flexible, flow mechanism supported by a copper sintered wick structure. Critical electrical isolation is achieved via a Aluminum Nitride (AlN) ceramic coating on the OHP surface, which acts as a high-k dielectric barrier, decoupling the electrical path from the thermal flux (q) governed by Fourier’s Law. Low thermal contact resistance is ensured through vacuum potted viscoelastic thermal interface materials, creating a module that tolerates mechanical vibration and expansion. To manage transient thermal loads and mitigate thermal runaway propagation, the lattice is embedded within a Flexible Composite Phase Change Material (FCPCM) matrix. This buffer consists of paraffin wax encapsulated into a porous Expanded Graphite (EG) skeleton, encapsulated within a Boron Nitride-doped Polyurethane elastomer shell. This engineered shell provides a thermal conductivity of 3 w/mK approximately. while possessing sufficient elasticity to accommodate the volumetric expansion of the paraffin during phase transition, effectively neutralizing the risk of hydrostatic shell rupture. The FCPCM utilizes the latent heat of fusion to clamp temperature spikes during peak discharge rates, acting as a thermal capacitor. This hybrid active-passive architecture effectively eliminates internal hotspots, prevents thermal propagation, and maximizes volumetric energy density by minimizing passive structural mass.
patents.complete_specification: Description:This system utilizes a vascular grid of seven-layer composite heat pipes to extract heat from the internal regions of large-volume batteries and transport it to an external manifold. The manifold is cooled through a dual-stage process involving natural air convection and an active refrigeration unit to chill the acetone working fluid. The architecture incorporates ceramic dielectric coatings for insulation, phase-change materials for thermal buffering, and viscoelastic gels to manage mechanical electrode expansion. , Claims:I/We claim: 1.“Multiphase Internal Cooling System For High Volume Lithium Ion Batteries” is a product that focus to increases the effficiency of the user’s machinery. 2.The product is capable of taking the battery to higher discharge rates. 3.The product is designed with room for modifications and upgrades.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A Cathode Material For Lithium-Ion Batteries and a Preparation Method Thereof The present invention discloses an energy storage system; more particularly, lithium-ion battery cathode material consisting of chromium phosphate-chitosan composite material within a voltage window of 0.3–2.5 V versus Li/Li⁺, exhibiting high reversibility, diffusion-assisted lithium intercalation, and long-term cycling stability. This invention further discloses a porous nanostructured chromium phosphate uniformly incorporated within a chitosan biopolymer matrix, forming an inorganic–organic Cr-P-C hybrid cathode with enhanced electronic conductivity, mechanical stability, and ion-transport characteristics. Also discloses a method for synthesizing the chromium phosphate-chitosan composite cathode material resulting in a three-dimensional porous architecture that promotes efficient lithium-ion diffusion and structural integrity during repeated cycling. For lithium-ion batteries, chromium phosphate-chitosan composite material exhibits high energy efficiency and provides desired capacity and rate capability with long-term cycling performance. Dated this 22nd day of January 2026.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION: [001] The present invention relates to the technical field of energy storage systems and particularly relates to lithium-ion batteries, a chromium phosphate-chitosan composite, a cathode material for lithium-ion batteries, and a preparation method thereof. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION: [002] A lithium-ion secondary battery typically consists of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, a separator, and an electrolyte, with both electrodes containing active materials that facilitate the intercalation and deintercalation of lithium ions. [003] Lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2), lithium nickel oxide (LiNiO2), lithium manganese oxide (LiMnO2 or LiMn2O4), or lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) has been utilized as the active material for the positive electrode in lithium secondary batteries. Lithium cobalt oxide possesses the advantages of high working voltage and exceptional capacity characteristics; yet, its practical use is challenging for a high-capacity battery owing to the elevated cost and supply volatility of cobalt as a raw ingredient. [004] The structural instability of lithium nickel oxide complicates the attainment of adequate longevity properties. Lithium manganese oxide demonstrates exceptional stability; nonetheless, it is hindered by inadequate capacity attributes. Consequently, lithium composite transition metal oxides comprising two or more varieties of transition metals have been formulated to address the issues associated with lithium transition metal oxides containing only Ni, Co, or Mn. Notably, lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide, which includes Ni, Co, and Mn, has gained extensive application in electric vehicle batteries. [005] A common lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide typically exists as a spherical secondary particle composed of an aggregation of tens to hundreds of primary particles. Nonetheless, concerning the lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxide structured as a secondary particle comprising numerous aggregated primary particles, a significant issue arises: particle fragmentation, wherein primary particles displace during the rolling process in the preparation of the positive electrode, is predisposed to occur, leading to the formation of cracks within the particles during charge and discharge cycles. In instances where the positive electrode active material has particle breaking or cracking, the contact area with the electrolyte solution is Enhanced breakdown of active material and gas production due to an adverse interaction with the electrolyte solution are intensified, resulting in deteriorated lifespan characteristics. [006] Furthermore, the need for high-output and high-capacity batteries, particularly those used in electric vehicles, has recently surged, leading to a progressive increase in the nickel concentration of the positive electrode active material. In instances where the nickel concentration in the positive electrode active material is elevated, initial capacity characteristics are enhanced; however, the repeated charging and discharging processes generate a significant quantity of highly reactive Ni4+ ions, leading to structural degradation of the positive electrode active material. Consequently, this results in an increased degradation rate, adversely affecting the longevity of the material. [007] Traditional transition metal oxides and phosphate-based electrode materials exhibit inherently low electronic conductivity, sluggish lithium-ion diffusion kinetics, and inadequate structural stability during repeated charge-discharge cycles. These limitations lead to low reversible capacity, limited active surface area, and poor rate capability. [008] Therefore, there is a requirement for an alternative efficient cathode material for lithium-ion batteries to fulfil the enhanced active surface area and superior cycling stability. OBJECTIVES OF THE INVENTION: [009] The primary object of the present invention is to develop an environmentally friendly, cost-effective chromium phosphate-chitosan (hereinafter known as CrPC) composite material by a simple solution combustion method. [010] Another object of the present invention is the use of an as-prepared composite nanoparticle as a cathode material for a lithium-ion battery. [011] Another object of the present invention is to produce energy-efficient, desired-capacity, rate-capable, and long-term cyclic performance of lithium-ion batteries. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION: A cathode material for lithium-ion batteries is described, consisting of a chromium phosphate-chitosan composite (CrPC) with porous nanostructured chromium phosphate particles embedded in a chitosan biopolymer matrix. Lithium-ion storage occurs via reversible intercalation and deintercalation within the chromium phosphate lattice, with a charge/discharge process following a solid-solution electrochemical mechanism. The chitosan matrix enhances lithium-ion diffusion and electronic conductivity through interconnected porous pathways. The preparation method includes stirring a mixture of chromium nitrate, urea, orthophosphoric acid, and chitosan, heating it, and then calcining to obtain the CrPC material. A lithium-ion battery utilizing this cathode operates within a voltage range of 0.3–2.5 V versus Li/Li+, showing a reversible specific capacity of 130–135 mAh/g and maintaining stable capacity during charge–discharge cycling. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION: [036] According to the first embodiment, the present invention discloses a chromium phosphate-chitosan composite employed as cathode material for a lithium-ion battery. [037] The second embodiment of the present invention discloses the porous nanostructured chromium phosphate particles embedded within a chitosan biopolymer matrix increase redox activity, surface area, electronic pathways, and mechanical strength, thereby enhancing lithium intercalation capacity (130 mAh/g-135 mAh/g). [038] Figure 1 illustrates the method of synthesis of CrPC composite material by a simple solution combustion method. The solution combustion method involves vigorous stirring of the precursors, like chromium nitrate [Cr(NO3)3], ortho-phosphoric acid [H3PO4], and urea [CO(NH2)2] as a fuel, in a minimum quantity of deionized water. Simultaneously, chitosan was dissolved for eight hours in 100 mL of 1% v/v acetic acid in deionized water at the ambient temperature and stirred with a magnetic stirrer. Both the solutions were mixed in a silica crucible and placed in a preheated muffle furnace at 540oC-550oC for about 15-20 minutes. Further CrPC NPs were calcinated at 700oC for 3 hours. [039] The synthesized CrPC composite was confirmed by different analytical techniques like XRD, FTIR, SEM, EDX, and XPS. Figure 2(a) illustrates the XRD patterns of CrP, chitosan, and CrPC composite. CrP and CrPC composites XRD patterns illustrates broad peaks at 2θ around 12.5o, 20o and 29.7o, whereas chitosan and CrPC exhibits a sharp peaks at 2θ around 20o and 29.2o corresponding to the (011), (020) and (023) planes. [040] Figure 2(b) illustrates FTIR spectrum of CrP, chitosan, and CrPC composite material, which reveals the chemical nature of CrPC composite material. The broadband of the spectrum is due to symmetric stretching vibrations of the-OH,-NH2 functional groups appears at 3354 cm-1. The peaks at 2943 cm-1, 1656 cm-1, 1432 cm-1, is due to the presence of C-H, C=O, and N-H stretching vibrations respectively. Another band at 1030 cm-1, 712 cm-1 is due to the presence of stretching vibrations of P-O in CrP and CrPC and C-O-C in chitosan and Cr-O and C-H bending vibrations of CrP, CrPC, and chitosan, respectively. Thus, XRD and FTIR data support the formation of CrPC composite material. [041] Figure 3(a) illustrates XPS survey spectra that identify all primary components inside the CrPC composite. The peaks identified at 575-590 eV correspond to Cr 2p, 133-138 eV to P 2p, 530-535 eV to O 1s, 283-289 eV to C 1s, and 399-405 eV to N 1s associated with chitosan-amine functionality. The presence of all expected elements verifies the effective synthesis ofCrP and its integration with chitosan (CrPC). The absence of a metallic chromium peak signifies that chromium is present in its oxidized state. Elevated O 1s intensity is indicative of phosphate oxygen, hydroxyl groups, and the functional groups of chitosan. The C and N peaks indicate a significant contribution of the organic matrix from chitosan. [042] Figure 3(b) illustrates the Cr 2p spectrum. It exhibits two major peaks: Cr 2p3/2 ≈ 577–579 eV Cr 2p1/2 = 586–588 eV. The binding energies are indicative of Cr3+ species, commonly present in chromium phosphate (CrPO4). No peaks at approximately 574 eV (Cr⁰) or 576 eV (Cr²⁺) are observed, hence verifying full oxidation. Minor peak broadening may suggest surface hydroxylation interaction between CrP nanoparticles and the chitosan matrix. Chromium primarily exists as Cr(III) coupled with phosphate and possibly interacting with the amine groups of chitosan. [043] Figure 3© illustrates a pronounced P 2p peak detected at 133-135 eV. This BE range is indicative of phosphate (PO43-) groups. The solitary symmetric apex signifies the absence of mixed oxidation states, and excellent chemical uniformity. [044] Figure 3(d) illustrates the C 1s spectrum. The C 1s area exhibits: 284.5 eV: C-C / C-H bonds; 285.5–286.5 eV: C-N / C-O (derived from chitosan); and 287–289 eV: O-C=O or carbonyl moieties. This verifies the existence of a chitosan backbone within the composite. Elevated energy peaks signify-NHCO-groups,-C-O-(alcohols/ethers), and C=O bonding. The increase in BE relative to pure chitosan indicates a connection between the functional groups of the polymer and CrP nanoparticles. [045] Figure 3€ illustrates the O 1s spectrum. The O 1s region typically deconvolutes into 530-531 eV: Metal-O (Cr-O-P); 531.5-532.5 eV: P=O / PO43-; 533+ eV: C-O / O-H (chitosan). A strong lower-energy oxygen peak confirms the formation of Cr-O-P species. Higher-energy components correspond to chitosan’s hydroxyl groups and surface-adsorbed water. This mixture confirms successful inorganic-organic hybridization. [046] Figure 3(f) illustrates the N 1s spectrum. The N 1s area has peaks at approximately 399-400 eV:-NH₂ moieties of chitosan: 401-402 eV: protonated ammonium ion (-NH3+). This verifies the existence of amine groups, of chitosan. Minor increases in binding energy suggest interaction between amine groups and phosphate surfaces and potential weak coordination between-NH₂ groups and Cr3+ ions. Chromium is present as Cr3+ in a stable chromium phosphate configuration. Chitosan is effectively incorporated, preserving its amine and hydroxyl functional groups. Significant interactions between CrP nanoparticles and chitosan are shown by peak shifts. The CrPC composite exhibits chemical homogeneity and robust bonding, confirming the effective synthesis of the composite. [047] Figure 4(a & b) illustrates the morphology of CrP at 1 μm and 20 μm. CrP manifests as irregular shapes. The morphology indicates heterogeneous precipitation, which is characteristic of the synthesis of inorganic phosphate. Despite having a moderate surface area, its shape lacks the porosity required for significant electrochemical activity. [048] Figure 4(c) illustrates the EDX spectrum that confirms the elemental composition of CrP. The O and P peaks confirm formation of phosphate groups. The Cr peak confirms incorporation of chromium into the phosphate framework. The relative atomic ratios align well with chromium phosphate, indicating successful synthesis with no major impurities. [049] Figures 4(d & e) illustrate the morphology of CrPC composite material. Which is much higher porosity than CrP. CrP clusters are finely dispersed within the chitosan matrix. CrPC composite appears less compact, forming a 3D interconnected structure. Thereby enhancing surface area, better electrolyte diffusion pathways, and more uniform particle distribution. This morphology is more favourable for electrochemical applications. [050] Figure 4(f) illustrates the EDX spectrum that confirms the presence of chitosan along with CrP. C, H, and N peaks appear due to the chitosan polymer. O and P remain dominant because of the phosphate groups. Cr percentage decreases because CrP is now diluted within chitosan. Overall the EDX confirms successful formation of a CrPC with uniform distribution of organic and inorganic components. Electrochemical Study [051] The cyclic voltammograms of CrP reveal distinct anodic and cathodic peaks indicative of a reversible Li⁺ insertion/deinsertion process. The broad cathodic peak (0.16–0.1 V) is linked to Li⁺ intercalation, with peak current rising proportionally with scan rate, signifying fast reaction kinetics. The anodic peak (0.27–0.35 V) represents Li⁺ deinsertion, with decreasing peak separation at lower scan rates suggesting low polarization and favorable reversibility. Log(i)–log(scan rate) analysis yields b ≈ 1, indicating that the electrode lacks deep bulk lithium intercalation; only the exposed surface participates in redox; there is low active material utilization, which lowers capacity; and CrP behaves like a surface-limited pseudocapacitive material because of the following: poor electronic conductivity, high charge-transfer resistance, limited ability for Li⁺ to penetrate the bulk. Therefore, CrP exhibits capacitive response not because it is highly active, but rather because bulk participation is restricted. [052] CrPC demonstrates superior performance compared to CrP, showing higher current density and sharper peaks, indicative of enhanced kinetics due to the chitosan matrix. For lithium insertion, cathodic peaks shift positively by 0.13–0.17 V, reflecting a lowered energy barrier for Li⁺ insertion attributed to the chitosan network, with increased accommodation sites indicated by higher peak currents. During lithium deinsertion, anodic peaks shift by 0.27–0.33 V, signifying faster Li⁺ extraction while maintaining stable peak shapes at high scan rates, confirming structural robustness. Additionally, b-values for CrPC was found to be 0.576 is nearer 0.5, indicating Li⁺ insertion/extraction under diffusion control. In CrPC, lithium ions migrate within the active material, is demonstrated by the current increasing more slowly with scan rate. The carbon covering makes it possible for: improved conductivity of electricity, reduced resistance to charge transfer, and more consistent distribution of current. As a result, Li⁺ has access to the bulk redox sites, which CrP did not. Diffusion behaviour indicates that CrPC improves actual capacity and stability by using more of the internal volume. A b-value that is not precisely 0.5 but is marginally above indicates that CrPC has a mixed mechanism: controlled by dominant diffusion, intercalation. A small contribution from pseudocapacitors. For high-energy and high-rate performance, this combination is perfect. [053] Because of its poor conductivity and sluggish ion diffusion, CrP shows purely capacitive surface-limited behaviour (b = 1.0), suggesting that lithium storage is limited to the material's surface. Following CrPC displays a diffusion-dominated kinetic profile (b = 0.576), demonstrating that the carbon layer facilitates Li⁺ intercalation into the bulk by improving electronic channels. The carbon coating is directly responsible for this change in behaviour from capacitive to diffusion-controlled, indicating a novel improvement in the storage mechanism. [054] Figure 5(c) illustrates, CrP exhibits greater charge-transfer resistance (Rct) due to a larger semicircle at high frequencies. Slower diffusion of Li⁺ due to a longer Warburg tail. Whereas CrPC exhibits faster electron/ion transport is indicated by a very narrow semicircle and a low Rct. Porous chitosan channels result in a reduced Warburg slope and an increased Li⁺ diffusion coefficient. This demonstrates that CrPC offers an interface for interfacial Li⁺ exchange that is more effective. [055] Figures 6(a, b) illustrates GCD curves for first five cycles and last five cycles of CrP, show distinct charge and discharge plateaus between-0.15 and 0.5 V. Stable Li⁺ intercalation–deintercalation is shown by the curves' symmetrical and flat profiles. A small IR drop is seen when the number of cycles rises to 5000 cycles because of: slow diffusion of Li⁺ in dense CrP. However, the overall cycling behaviour exhibits strong structural integrity and reversible Li⁺ exchange. [056] Figures 6(c, d) illustrate GCD curves for first five cycles and last five cycles of CrPC, sharper plateaus, and less IR drop. The charge-discharge shapes are almost the same even after 5000 cycles, proving: outstanding mechanical stability, enhanced transfer of ions, inhibition of the pulverization of electrodes, increased conductivity as a result of chitosan. Superior slope stability is demonstrated by CrPC, demonstrating exceptional long-term retention and Li⁺ kinetics. [057] The invention describes a chromium phosphate-based cathode system in which the extraction (deintercalation) happens after anodic polarization, and the lithium-ion insertion happens through reversible intercalation of Li⁺ into the CrP host lattice. Rapid Li⁺ diffusion and decreased polarization are made possible by the addition of a chitosan polymer matrix to CrP, which increases surface capacitance and adds more ion-transport channels. Because of its dominating capacitive-assisted intercalation storage, the composite architecture offers superior cycling stability over 5000 cycles, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and increased current response. Improved lithium-ion kinetics, structural flexibility, and long-term durability make the combination of CrP and chitosan ideal for advanced lithium-ion battery applications. [058] Figure 7 illustrates the galvanostatic charge-discharge profile of CrPC for a lithium-ion battery. It illustrates the relationship between specific capacity (mAh/g) and potential (V versus Li/Li⁺) during lithiation (discharge: Li⁺ insertion) and delithiation (charge: extraction of Li+). In the figure charge and discharge profiles are shown by the two opposite-direction curves. Specific Capacity (mAh/g) on the X-axis varies between 0 and 135 mAh/g, shows the amount of charge that the electrode is capable of holding. More Li⁺ can be added or removed from the cathode with a larger capacity. The CrPC provides 130 mAh/g when discharging and also during charging. Y-axis indicates the working potential of the material 0.3 V to 2.5 V. The cathode material exhibits a charge-discharge process of the solid-solution type. Low lattice strain and high cyclability are indicated by voltage sloping behaviour without a plateau. High-rate Li⁺ intercalation is promoted by a carbon-supported Cr–P framework. [059] As lithium ions are introduced into the CrPC lattice, the discharge curve demonstrates a progressive drop in potential from 2.5 V to 0.3 V. During lithium-ion extraction, the charge curve increases from 0.3 V to 2.5 V, following a nearly symmetrical reversal route. Stable Li⁺ insertion–extraction processes are confirmed by the near overlap and symmetry between the charge and discharge curves, which show strong reversibility and good coulombic efficiency. [060] Specific Capacity: Within the above-mentioned voltage range, the CrPC composite provides a specific capacity of roughly 120-130 mAh/g. The following are responsible for the capacity contribution: action of chromium centers in redox process, contribution of the carbon matrix produced from chitosan to surface-assisted pseudocapacitance, enhanced accessibility of electrolytes via the porous composite structure. [061] Low polarization and quick response kinetics are suggested by the minimal voltage difference between the charge and discharge curves. This is due to the presence of effective channels for electron transport in the chitosan matrix, increased diffusion of lithium ions in the porous CrPC network, decreased impedance to charge transport at the electrode-electrolyte contact. The CrPC composite is an electrochemically active lithium storage material with stable voltage profiles, strong reversibility, and improved kinetics because of its inorganic-organic hybrid structure, as demonstrated by the galvanostatic charge-discharge behaviour. patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A TRANSACTION BURST ENERGY CONTROLLED DIGITAL PAYMENT NOTIFICATION DEVICE EMPLOYING LITHIUM TITANATE BATTERY The present invention provides a transaction notification device is disclosed. The device comprises a lithium titanate battery, a lithium titanate specific battery management system, a charging circuit, a transaction burst energy controller, an intermediate energy buffer, a control circuit, an audio playback subsystem, and a trigger interface configured to receive a payment confirmation signal. Energy is discharged predominantly during transaction triggered audio playback events, while the intermediate energy buffer supplies peak playback current and is replenished between transactions. The transaction burst energy controller dynamically adjusts charging current, recharge timing, wake window duration, and audio parameters based on detected and predicted transaction frequency.
