The plurality of modules 112 exchange datasets through the database 110 and the server 108, thereby enabling automated propagation of computational results between successive stages of the modelling pipeline. In one embodiment, the system 100 generates a large synthetic dataset comprises approximately 3000 defect-containing supercell configurations derived from pristine LiFePO₄ crystal structures, including lithium vacancies, iron antisite defects, lithium antisite defects, oxygen vacancies, and lithium interstitial defects. The dataset generation, first-principles calculations, machine-learning model training, and simulation stages are coordinated through automated workflow management scripts implemented using Python-based pipeline frameworks. The task dependencies, execution states, and computational outputs are automatically monitored and logged to ensure reproducible execution of the computational modelling workflow. [0082] The disclosed system 100 is implemented as a computational system for modelling physical defect phenomena in lithium-ion battery cathode materials. The machine-learning model operates in conjunction with first-principles simulation engines and atomistic simulation modules to predict physical properties including defect formation energy, lattice distortion behaviour, and ionic diffusion dynamics within LiFePO₄ structures. The system 100 therefore provides a technical solution for materials-science simulation and battery material analysis rather than a standalone computer program. The computational system is configured to model atomic-scale defect energetics in LiFePO₄ crystal structures using first-principles simulation and machine-learning-assisted interatomic potential modelling. [0083] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 is configured to operate as a defect-centric computational module integrated within battery material research and development workflows. The system 100 interfaces with external computational platforms, material databases, and simulation environments to support defect analysis and material optimization of LiFePO₄ crystal structures. In one embodiment herein, the system 100 enables high-throughput screening of intrinsic defect configurations by processing large volumes of defect-containing supercell structures and predicting corresponding defect formation energies and atomistic properties, thereby facilitating rapid evaluation of multiple candidate material configurations within battery development pipelines. [0084] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 is configured to integrate with simulation-driven material design frameworks. Predicted defect energetics and atomistic simulation outputs are utilized to guide iterative material optimization processes for improving electrochemical performance, ionic transport characteristics, and structural stability of lithium-ion battery cathode materials. In one embodiment herein, the system 100 supports real-time evaluation of defect behaviour by utilizing the trained defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model to predict defect energetics and atomic interactions with reduced computational latency relative to first-principles calculations, thereby enabling rapid decision-making during material design and analysis workflows. [0085] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 is configured to integrate with digital twin systems representing battery materials and electrochemical systems, predicted defect energetics, diffusion behaviour, and structural characteristics are incorporated into virtual representations of battery materials for monitoring, simulation, and performance prediction under operational conditions. In one embodiment herein, the system 100 is further configured to interface with automated material discovery pipelines. The active learning control module 120 continuously refines the defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model using newly generated defect configurations, thereby enabling adaptive improvement of prediction accuracy within automated material screening and discovery workflows. [0086] In one embodiment herein, the integration of the system 100 within battery development workflows enables accelerated innovation in lithium-ion battery material design by reducing computational time associated with defect analysis, improving prediction reliability, and enabling continuous model refinement through active learning. [0087] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 implements a defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model trained using defect-containing atomic configurations of LiFePO₄ crystal structures. The training dataset comprises intrinsic defect configurations including lithium vacancies, iron antisite defects, lithium antisite defects, oxygen vacancies, and lithium interstitial defects. The defect-aware training enables the interatomic potential model to learn atomic interaction behaviour associated with defect-induced lattice distortions and local structural variations within the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. [0088] In one embodiment herein, the defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model prioritizes defect-state representations over pristine lattice configurations during the training process, thereby improving prediction accuracy of intrinsic defect formation energies, atomic forces, and defect-induced lattice distortions. The trained model captures defect-specific atomic environment variations and charge-state dependent behaviour associated with Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ oxidation states, thereby enabling accurate modelling of defect energetics and defect-driven structural transformations within LiFePO₄ crystal structures. [0089] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 enables scalable prediction of defect-driven phenomena including lithium-ion diffusion behaviour, defect migration pathways, and defect-induced structural instability using the trained defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model, thereby reducing dependence on repeated first-principles quantum mechanical calculations. The computational framework enables prediction of defect energetics and atomistic behaviour across large supercell configurations within reduced computational time while maintaining near first-principles accuracy. [0090] In one embodiment herein, the system 100 provides a technical effect comprises accelerated computational evaluation of intrinsic defect energetics and defect-driven material behaviour in LiFePO₄ crystal structures, thereby enabling efficient design and optimization of defect-engineered lithium-ion battery cathode materials. The improved prediction capability facilitates identification of energetically favorable defect configurations and defect-induced transport characteristics, thereby improving electrochemical performance, structural stability, and operational lifespan of lithium-ion battery systems. [0091] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 2 refers to an overall workflow diagram of the system 100. The workflow begins at step 202, where the computing device 102 retrieves atomic structure datasets associated with perfect LiFePO₄ crystal structures from the database 110 and initializes the computational modelling process through the processor 104. At this stage, intrinsic defect types including lithium vacancies, iron antisite defects (Fe on Li), lithium antisite defects (Li on Fe), oxygen vacancies, and lithium interstitial defects are identified for generating synthetic defect configurations. [0092] At step 204, the processor 104 executes the atomic structure generation module 114, which expands primitive LiFePO₄ unit cells into supercell representations and programmatically inserts intrinsic defect configurations using computational libraries. Multiple synthetic defect configurations are generated either sequentially or in parallel using message-passing routines. In one embodiment herein, each generated structure is automatically evaluated for lattice stability, charge neutrality, and structural validity. When invalid configurations arise due to excessive lattice distortion or charge imbalance, the module regenerates and revalidates the supercell until a stable configuration is achieved. All validated defect structures are stored in the database 110 together with metadata describing defect type, defect position, and defect charge state, thereby forming a heterogeneous defect configuration dataset. [0093] At step 206, the heterogeneous defect configuration dataset is provided to the first-principles computation module 116, which performs first-principles quantum mechanical calculations using density functional theory with on-site Coulomb correction to determine total energies, atomic forces, magnetic moments, and lattice relaxation parameters associated with the defect configurations. The defected structures are processed using first-principles calculation frameworks and the resulting output state files are harvested to produce a machine-learning compatible dataset containing atomic energies, forces, and stress parameters. When convergence errors or energy instabilities occur during computation, the module automatically adjusts simulation parameters and repeats the calculation until valid results are obtained. The validated results are stored in the database 110 as reference energy-force data representing intrinsic defect energetics of the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. [0094] At step 208, the reference energy-force data is supplied to the machine-learning interatomic potential training module 118, which trains a defect-aware interatomic potential model capable of predicting atomic interactions, atomic forces, defect formation energies, and charge-state dependent defect energetics associated with the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. In one embodiment herein, the module trains graph-based machine-learning models to learn local atomic environments and defect-induced lattice distortions. A multi-objective loss function is implemented to optimize accuracy of total atomic energy prediction, per-atom force prediction, and reconstruction of defect formation energies. When validation loss exceeds predefined thresholds, the module automatically performs hyperparameter adjustments or retraining using augmented datasets. The resulting trained model serves as a computationally efficient surrogate for predicting defect energetics across large configuration spaces. The machine-learning interatomic potential training module 118 implements a graph-based neural network architecture trained using first-principles energy-force datasets to generate predicted atomic interaction parameters for defect-containing LiFePO₄ crystal structures. [0095] At step 210, the active learning control module 120 utilizes the trained model to evaluate additional defect configurations and estimate prediction uncertainty. Configurations associated with high uncertainty are automatically transmitted to the first-principles computation module 116 for additional quantum mechanical calculations. The newly generated results are incorporated into the training dataset, thereby iteratively refining the model through an active-learning feedback loop until prediction uncertainty across defect classes falls below a predefined threshold. In one embodiment herein, the refined model is subsequently provided to the defect simulation module 122, which performs atomistic simulations of LiFePO₄ crystal structures containing intrinsic defects within a molecular dynamics simulation environment to evaluate lithium-ion migration behaviour, defect diffusion pathways, lattice strain evolution, and defect clustering interactions. Simulation errors or instabilities are monitored and may trigger retraining cycles to further improve model robustness. [0096] In one embodiment herein, the simulation outputs are processed by the analysis and visualization module 124, which generates defect energetics analysis data including predicted defect formation energies, atomic displacement behaviour, lattice strain distributions, and defect interaction characteristics. The results are visualized through scientific visualization tools to display atomic relaxations, defect migration trajectories, and local stress fields within the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. This sequential workflow enables autonomous generation, training, and validation of a defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential model with minimal human intervention, thereby providing a scalable and reproducible computational pipeline for defect informatics in lithium-ion battery cathode materials. [0097] In one embodiment herein, the term “defect-aware machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP)” as used in the present specification refers to a data-driven atomic interaction model trained using first-principles reference data corresponding to defect-containing LiFePO₄ crystal structures. The MLIP is configured to approximate total energies, atomic forces, and defect formation energetics for configurations containing intrinsic point defects including lithium vacancies (VLi), iron antisites (FeLi), lithium antisites (LiFe), oxygen vacancies (VO), and lithium interstitials. The model learns atomic environment descriptors from defect-containing configurations such that both bulk crystal interactions and defect-induced lattice distortions are represented within a unified potential framework. [0098] The defect-aware machine learning interatomic potential is trained using the DFT-derived dataset through a multi-objective learning scheme that minimizes prediction errors in total energy, atomic forces, and defect formation energies simultaneously. Representative validation metrics demonstrate that the trained model achieves energy prediction errors on the order of a few hundredths of an electron-volt per atom and force prediction errors below approximately one-tenth of an electron-volt per angstrom, indicating near-first-principles accuracy for defect energetics prediction. [0099] Table 1: Parameter Value DFT engine ABINIT 10 / Quantum ESPRESSO 7 Exchange–correlation PBE + U (Fe U = 4 eV, J = 0 eV) Pseudopotentials PAW – PBE (from PseudoDojo) Cutoff energy 50 Ry (wfc) / 400 Ry (rho) k-mesh 2×2×2 Monkhorst–Pack Spin polarization Enabled (Fe) Electronic convergence 10⁻⁶ Ry Force tolerance < 0.05 eV Å⁻¹ Relaxations Atomic + cell (ISIF = 3 / ionmov = 3) [0100] Table 1 depicts computational parameters used for performing first-principles calculations of defect configurations in LiFePO₄ crystal structures. The calculations are carried out using open-source DFT engines including ABINIT 10 and Quantum ESPRESSO 7, employing the PBE + U exchange–correlation functional with Fe U = 4 eV to accurately capture Fe²⁺and Fe³⁺ charge transitions and the associated local lattice relaxations. The simulations utilize PAW-PBE pseudopotentials from PseudoDojo, a 50 Ry wavefunction cutoff and 400 Ry charge density cutoff, and a 2×2×2 Monkhorst–Pack k-point mesh, with spin polarization enabled for Fe atoms. Electronic convergence is set to 10⁻⁶ Ry with a force tolerance below 0.05 eV Å⁻¹, while both atomic and cell relaxations are performed to obtain stable defect structures. In one embodiment herein, the calculations produce total energies, atomic forces, stresses, and magnetic moments for each defected configuration, and the resulting energy–force–structure triples serve as ground-truth reference data for training the machine-learning interatomic potential model. [0101] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 3 refers to a graph 300 depicting a relationship between defect formation energy and iron magnetic moment for various intrinsic defect configurations in the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. The graph 300 shows a scatter plot that illustrates computed data points obtained from first-principles calculations, where the horizontal axis represents defect formation energy (eV) and the vertical axis represents the magnetic moment of Fe atoms (μB). Multiple colored markers correspond to distinct intrinsic defect types including lithium vacancies (V_Li), lithium antisite defects (Li_Fe), iron antisite defects (Fe_Li), lithium–iron swap defects, and oxygen vacancies (V_O). In one embodiment herein, the graph 300 demonstrates the variation of magnetic properties of Fe atoms as a function of defect energetics within the LiFePO₄ lattice. The distribution of data points highlights how different defect configurations influence local magnetic moments and electronic states of iron atoms, thereby providing insight into the coupling between defect formation energetics and magnetic behavior in the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. This relationship assists in understanding defect-induced electronic structure modifications relevant to lithium-ion battery cathode performance. [0102] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 4 refers to a graph 400 depicting training and validation loss curves of the machine-learning interatomic potential models across multiple training epochs for the LiFePO₄ defect datasets. Multiple curves correspond to different machine-learning interatomic potential frameworks including MACE, NequIP, and DeepMD, each trained using the DFT-derived defect dataset representing intrinsic defect configurations within LiFePO₄ crystal structures. In one embodiment herein, the training process employs a multi-objective loss function that simultaneously optimizes prediction accuracy for total atomic energy, per-atom forces, and defect formation energies. The gradual decrease in both training and validation loss values across epochs indicates improved convergence and predictive capability of the trained models. [0103] In one embodiment herein, the generated defect dataset contains numerous supercell configurations representing intrinsic point defects in LiFePO₄, including lithium vacancies (VLi), iron antisites (FeLi), lithium antisites (LiFe), and oxygen vacancies (VO). Each configuration stores structural coordinates, defect identity, charge-state information, total system energy, and atomic force vectors obtained from first-principles calculations. The dataset therefore forms a structured reference database linking atomic geometry with defect energetics for machine-learning training and validation. [0104] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 5 refers to a graph 500 depicting progressive reduction in validation loss across successive active learning cycles during training of the machine-learning interatomic potential model for the LiFePO₄ defect datasets. [0105] During each cycle, configurations exhibiting high prediction uncertainty are selected for first-principles re-evaluation, and the resulting data is integrated into the training dataset to refine the model. The gradual reduction in loss values demonstrates enhanced model convergence and robustness in predicting defect energetics and atomic interactions within LiFePO₄ crystal structures. The trained machine-learning interatomic potential is integrated with a molecular-dynamics simulation engine to model defect diffusion and structural relaxation in LiFePO₄ at finite temperatures. Simulation outputs include time-dependent atomic trajectories, defect migration pathways, and diffusion coefficients derived from mean-square-displacement analysis. These simulations enable large-scale atomistic analysis of defect dynamics beyond the computational limits of direct first-principles calculations. [0106] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 6 refers to a graph 600 depicting lithium vacancy diffusion dynamics based on mean squared displacement as a function of simulation time for the LiFePO₄ crystal structures. In one embodiment herein, the simulation is conducted at an elevated temperature condition of approximately 600 K, allowing observation of lithium-ion migration behaviour mediated by lithium vacancies within the LiFePO₄ lattice. The increasing MSD trend over time indicates progressive atomic displacement of lithium ions, reflecting defect-assisted diffusion pathways within the crystal structure. The observed step-like variations in the curve correspond to discrete lithium-ion hopping events between adjacent lattice sites, thereby illustrating vacancy-mediated lithium transport dynamics. The MSD profile is further utilized to estimate lithium-ion diffusion coefficients and migration characteristics, providing quantitative insight into defect-driven ion transport behaviour relevant to lithium-ion battery cathode performance. [0107] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, FIG. 7 refers to a snapshot 700 depicting atomistic structures of the LiFePO₄ crystal configurations containing intrinsic defects as observed during simulation. [0109] According to an exemplary embodiment of the invention, the system 100 implements an automated computational workflow for defect informatics in LiFePO₄ crystal structures. In one implementation, workflow orchestration for automated dataset generation, first-principles calculations, and machine-learning training may be coordinated through workflow management frameworks such as Snakemake or FireWorks, which organize sequential computational tasks, manage dependencies between simulation steps, and enable reproducible execution of the defect-modelling pipeline across computational resources. [0110] In one embodiment herein, libraries such as atomic simulation environment (ASE) and Pymatgen are employed for automated supercell construction, defect configuration generation, and metadata logging, while workflow execution is managed through reproducible pipeline frameworks. patents.abstract: High-Entropy Multicomponent Transition Metal Oxide Anode for Long-Life Lithium-Ion and Sodium-Ion Batteries 2. Abstract This invention relates to a high-entropy multicomponent transition metal oxide containing three or more transition metals for use as an anode material in rechargeable batteries. The oxide comprises a single-phase solid solution of Ni, Co, Mn, Fe, and Cu synthesized by a sol–gel assisted calcination process to produce a structurally stable lattice with severe lattice distortion. The presence of multiple redox-active metal centers increases the theoretical capacity, while the high-entropy structure suppresses volume expansion during repeated charge–discharge cycles. The material exhibits improved cycling stability, high reversible capacity, and enhanced rate performance in lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. The invention further includes compositional tuning and thermal treatment methods for achieving phase stability and long-term electrochemical durability. Keywords High-entropy oxide, ternary oxide, battery anode, lithium-ion battery, multicomponent oxide, energy storage.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Preamble The present invention relates to the field of advanced electrochemical energy storage devices and particularly to a binder-free heterostructure electrode comprising a ternary transition metal oxide integrated with a two-dimensional conductive MXene material for ultrafast charge storage applications. With the increasing demand for portable electronics, wearable systems, electric vehicles, and smart sensors, there is a strong need for energy storage devices capable of delivering high power density, rapid charging, long cycle life, and mechanical durability. Conventional batteries generally offer high energy density but suffer from slow charging rates, while traditional supercapacitors provide fast charge-discharge capability but often possess lower energy density. To overcome these limitations, transition metal oxides have been widely explored due to their high theoretical capacitance and multiple oxidation states that enable Faradaic charge storage. In particular, ternary transition metal oxides such as nickel-cobalt-molybdenum oxide and zinc-nickel-cobalt oxide provide superior electrochemical activity, enhanced conductivity, and abundant redox sites compared with single-component oxides. However, their practical application is often limited by poor intrinsic conductivity, particle agglomeration, structural instability, and the use of insulating binders that reduce performance. The present invention addresses these drawbacks through a binder-free architecture in which the ternary oxide is directly grown on Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene sheets using a one-step hydrothermal synthesis route, thereby eliminating inactive binders and ensuring strong interfacial adhesion. MXene serves as a highly conductive and flexible substrate with layered morphology, hydrophilic surface terminations, and rapid electron transport pathways, while the ternary oxide contributes high pseudocapacitance through reversible redox reactions. The synergistic interaction between the two components significantly lowers charge transfer resistance, enhances ion diffusion, prevents MXene restacking, and improves utilization of electroactive sites. The resulting heterostructure electrode exhibits high specific capacitance, excellent rate capability, long-term cycling stability, and strong mechanical integrity under repeated bending or deformation. The invention is particularly suitable for flexible supercapacitors, hybrid capacitors, wearable electronics, portable energy systems, micro-storage devices, and next-generation high-power applications. Thus, the disclosed binder-free ternary transition metal oxide/MXene heterostructure provides an efficient, scalable, and cost-effective solution for advanced charge storage technologies. 4. Methodology Fig. 1 Working flow of Proposed Methodology. 1. Selection of Raw Materials Choose high-purity metal precursor salts of nickel, cobalt, manganese, iron, and copper such as nitrates, acetates, or chlorides. These metals are selected in near-equimolar ratios to obtain a high-entropy multicomponent oxide composition suitable for battery anode applications. 2. Preparation of Precursor Solution Dissolve the measured quantities of each metal precursor separately in deionized water or ethanol. Combine all metal solutions in a single beaker under continuous magnetic stirring to form a homogeneous mixed-metal solution. 3. Addition of Chelating Agent Add citric acid, ethylene glycol, or another suitable chelating agent to the mixed solution. The chelating agent binds with metal ions and ensures uniform molecular-level mixing, preventing phase separation during synthesis. 4. pH Adjustment Adjust the pH of the solution to around 6–8 using ammonia or sodium hydroxide solution. Proper pH control improves gel formation and stabilizes the dissolved metal complexes. 5. Sol–Gel Formation Heat the solution at 70–90°C under constant stirring until the liquid gradually transforms into a viscous gel. Continued heating removes excess solvent and produces a uniform precursor matrix containing all metal ions. 6. Drying of Gel Transfer the gel into a drying oven and heat at 100–120°C for several hours to remove residual moisture. A dry porous precursor mass is obtained after complete dehydration. 7. Grinding of Dried Precursor Crush and grind the dried precursor using a mortar and pestle or ball mill to obtain a fine powder. Uniform particle size improves subsequent calcination efficiency. 8. Primary Calcination Place the precursor powder in an alumina crucible and calcine in a furnace at 450–600°C for 3–5 hours. This step decomposes organic matter and initiates oxide phase formation. 9. Secondary Calcination / Annealing Further heat the powder at 700–900°C for 4–8 hours to develop a stable single-phase high-entropy crystal structure. Controlled heating and cooling rates help avoid unwanted secondary phases. 10. Cooling and Collection Allow the furnace to cool naturally to room temperature. Collect the calcined high-entropy multicomponent oxide powder and store in airtight containers. 11. Material Characterization Analyze the synthesized powder using XRD for phase confirmation, SEM/TEM for morphology, EDX for elemental distribution, and BET analysis for surface area. Uniform distribution of all metals confirms successful entropy stabilization. 12. Electrode Slurry Preparation Mix the active high-entropy oxide powder with conductive carbon black and binder such as PVDF in a suitable solvent like NMP to form a homogeneous slurry. Typical composition may be 80:10:10 by weight. 13. Coating on Current Collector Apply the slurry uniformly onto copper foil using doctor blade coating. Dry the coated foil at 80–100°C and then vacuum dry at 120°C to remove solvent completely. 14. Electrode Punching and Pressing Punch circular electrode discs and press them gently to improve contact density and adhesion. 15. Cell Assembly Assemble coin cells inside an argon-filled glove box using the prepared anode, separator, electrolyte, and lithium or sodium metal counter electrode depending on the battery system. 16. Electrochemical Testing Perform charge–discharge cycling, cyclic voltammetry, rate capability, and impedance studies to evaluate reversible capacity, cycling stability, and fast charging performance of the high-entropy oxide anode. 17. Optimization Repeat synthesis by varying metal ratios, calcination temperature, or particle size to achieve the best electrochemical performance for lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. 5. Result and Discussion Result The synthesized high-entropy multicomponent oxide anode exhibited a stable single-phase crystalline structure confirmed by XRD analysis, while SEM images revealed uniformly distributed particles with porous morphology favorable for electrolyte penetration. Elemental mapping confirmed homogeneous dispersion of Ni, Co, Mn, Fe, and Cu throughout the oxide matrix. The electrode delivered a high initial discharge capacity in lithium-ion battery testing and retained a high reversible charge capacity after the first few formation cycles. Coulombic efficiency rapidly increased and stabilized above 98% during repeated cycling. The anode maintained excellent structural integrity after long-term charge–discharge cycles, with capacity retention above 90% after 500 cycles at moderate current density. Even at high current rates, the material showed strong rate capability with minimal polarization loss. Fast lithium-ion diffusion was observed due to lattice distortion and multiple ion pathways. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy showed reduced charge transfer resistance after cycling activation. The multiredox metal centers contributed to enhanced total storage capacity. In sodium-ion cells, the electrode demonstrated stable sodium insertion and extraction behavior and retained significant capacity despite the larger ionic radius of sodium ions. Volume expansion during repeated cycling was effectively suppressed by the entropy-stabilized lattice, and no major phase collapse or particle pulverization was observed after extended operation. Thermal stability tests indicated safe performance under elevated operating temperatures. Compared with conventional graphite anodes, the developed material delivered higher specific capacity, while compared with single-metal oxides, it showed superior cycling life and improved rate response. Overall, the results confirm that the proposed high-entropy oxide is a promising long-life anode material for next-generation lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. Resulting graph 1. Discussion The experimental results demonstrate that the synthesized high-entropy multicomponent transition metal oxide is a highly effective anode material for rechargeable lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. The formation of a stable single-phase crystal lattice confirms the successful entropy-driven stabilization of multiple transition metal cations within one oxide framework. This unique structure plays an important role in minimizing phase segregation and structural collapse during repeated electrochemical cycling. The porous and uniformly distributed particle morphology observed through microscopic analysis provides a larger active surface area and short diffusion pathways for electrolyte ions, thereby improving charge storage kinetics. The high initial discharge capacity and strong reversible capacity retention indicate that the presence of multiple redox-active metals contributes significantly to enhanced charge storage. Unlike conventional single-metal oxides, the combined redox reactions of Ni, Co, Mn, Fe, and Cu generate additional active sites for lithium and sodium ion insertion and extraction. The gradual increase and stabilization of coulombic efficiency above 98% confirm the formation of a stable electrode–electrolyte interface and reduced parasitic side reactions during long-term operation. The excellent cycling retention after hundreds of cycles proves that the entropy-stabilized lattice effectively suppresses volume expansion and particle pulverization, which are common failure mechanisms in traditional alloy and oxide anodes. Strong rate capability at higher current densities suggests fast ion transport and improved electronic conductivity caused by lattice distortion and defect-rich pathways. Electrochemical impedance analysis further supports this behavior by showing reduced charge transfer resistance after cycling activation. In sodium-ion batteries, the material also exhibits promising performance despite the larger ionic radius of sodium ions. This indicates that the expanded and flexible lattice of the high-entropy oxide can accommodate repeated sodium insertion without severe degradation. Therefore, the developed material provides a versatile platform for both lithium and sodium storage technologies. Overall, the study confirms that compositional entropy engineering is an advanced strategy for designing next-generation battery electrodes with high capacity, long life, and stable fast-charging capability. 6. Conclusion The present invention successfully developed a high-entropy multicomponent transition metal oxide anode material for advanced lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries. The entropy-stabilized single-phase structure containing multiple transition metals provides high reversible capacity, superior cycling durability, enhanced rate capability, and reduced impedance. The material effectively suppresses structural degradation and volume expansion during repeated charge–discharge cycles, leading to long operational life. Its excellent electrochemical behavior in both lithium-ion and sodium-ion systems demonstrates broad applicability for future energy storage devices. Hence, the proposed high-entropy oxide anode offers a promising and scalable solution for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and grid-level storage applications. , Claims:Claims 1. We claim that the invention provides a high-entropy multicomponent transition metal oxide anode material comprising three or more transition metals for rechargeable battery applications. 2. We claim that the anode material comprises nickel, cobalt, manganese, iron, and copper distributed in a single-phase crystalline oxide lattice. 3. We claim that the high configurational entropy of the material stabilizes the crystal structure and prevents phase segregation during cycling. 4. We claim that the multiredox metal centers enhance reversible charge storage capacity compared with conventional single-metal oxide anodes. 5. We claim that the invention suppresses volume expansion, particle cracking, and structural collapse during repeated lithiation and sodiation processes. 6. We claim that the material exhibits high coulombic efficiency, long cycling life, and excellent capacity retention over extended charge–discharge cycles. 7. We claim that the anode demonstrates strong rate capability and fast ion diffusion under high current density conditions. 8. We claim that the material is synthesized through a sol–gel assisted calcination method followed by controlled thermal treatment to obtain phase purity. 9. We claim that the developed anode is suitable for both lithium-ion batteries and sodium-ion batteries with stable electrochemical performance. 10. We claim that the invention is applicable for electric vehicles, portable electronics, renewable energy storage, and other high-performance energy storage systems.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT The present invention discloses a Solar Lithium Ion Drone that integrates solar energy harvesting with lithium-ion battery storage to achieve extended flight duration and improved energy efficiency. The system utilizes photovoltaic panels to generate power during flight and stores excess energy in batteries for continuous operation. The hybrid energy approach enhances drone performance, reduces reliance on ground charging, and enables long-duration missions. The invention provides a sustainable, efficient, and advanced solution for modern UAV applications.
patents.complete_specification: Description:The Solar Lithium Ion Drone comprises a lightweight drone frame integrated with high-efficiency solar panels positioned to maximize sunlight exposure. The photovoltaic panels convert solar energy into electrical energy, which is regulated through a power management module. The module ensures proper voltage regulation and distributes energy between the propulsion system and the lithium-ion battery pack. The lithium-ion batteries serve as an energy reservoir, storing excess power and supplying energy when solar input is insufficient. The drone includes brushless motors and propellers for efficient flight, along with a flight controller for navigation and stability. Additional components such as GPS modules, sensors, and communication systems enable autonomous operation and real-time data transmission. The system is designed to optimize energy consumption through intelligent algorithms that balance power generation and usage. The overall design ensures durability, lightweight construction, and efficient performance for extended missions. , C , Claims:WE CLAIM We claim a Solar Lithium Ion Drone comprising photovoltaic panels, a lithium-ion battery pack, a power management system, propulsion motors, and a control unit, wherein the system is configured to generate, store, and utilize solar energy for extended flight operations. We further claim that the drone utilizes a hybrid energy system combining solar power and battery storage for continuous operation. We also claim that the system includes intelligent energy management for optimizing power distribution and efficiency. We claim that the drone is suitable for long-duration and remote applications. Finally, we claim that the invention improves flight time and reduces dependency on conventional charging methods compared to existing drone systems.

patents.abstract: [047] The present invention provides a passive thermal regulation system for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles. The system comprises a plurality of lithium-ion battery cells arranged within a battery pack enclosure, a heat-spreading assembly thermally coupled to the cells, encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements positioned adjacent to thermally critical regions, passive heat discharge pathways extending toward external enclosure surfaces, and thermal isolation barriers arranged between selected cell groups. Heat generated by the cells is transferred through compliant thermal interface layers to directional heat-spreading members, distributed away from local hot spots, temporarily absorbed by phase-change materials during peak thermal loading, and gradually released through conductive bridges and natural convection channels. The system reduces cell-to-cell temperature variation, improves fast-charging thermal stability, reduces dependence on powered pumps, fans or liquid coolant loops, and slows thermal propagation during abnormal heating conditions. The invention provides a compact, energy-efficient and safety-enhancing battery thermal management architecture suitable for electric vehicle battery packs. Accompanied Drawing [FIGS. 1-2]
patents.complete_specification: Description:[001] The present invention relates to the field of battery thermal management systems for electric vehicles, and more particularly relates to a passive thermal regulation system for lithium-ion battery packs configured to control heat accumulation, reduce cell-to-cell temperature variation, delay thermal runaway propagation, and maintain safe operating temperature ranges without relying primarily on active liquid cooling, forced refrigeration, or continuously powered thermal conditioning components. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [002] Lithium-ion battery packs used in electric vehicles are required to operate under highly variable charging, discharging and environmental conditions. During rapid acceleration, regenerative braking, fast charging, hill climbing, high ambient temperature exposure and repeated drive cycles, individual battery cells generate heat due to internal resistance, electrochemical reactions and current concentration. If such heat is not effectively managed, the battery pack may experience accelerated ageing, reduced charge acceptance, capacity fading, safety risks and uneven performance among cells. [003] Conventional electric vehicle battery packs commonly use active thermal management arrangements such as liquid cooling plates, coolant loops, pumps, valves, fans, compressors, heat exchangers and electronic control units. While such arrangements can provide controlled cooling under many conditions, they increase vehicle cost, packaging complexity, energy consumption, maintenance requirements, leakage risk and failure modes. The dependence on powered components also means that thermal regulation may be compromised when auxiliary power is limited, when the vehicle is parked, or when active cooling components malfunction. [004] Air-cooled systems have also been used for certain battery pack architectures. However, simple air-cooled battery systems often suffer from non-uniform airflow distribution, local hot spots, dust ingress, noise generation and limited cooling capacity during fast charging or high-power operation. In densely packed lithium-ion battery modules, airflow may not reach thermally critical regions located between inner cells, thereby creating temperature gradients between peripheral cells and central cells. [005] Liquid-cooled battery plates provide improved heat extraction compared with air-only systems, but such systems typically require precise sealing, coolant compatibility, corrosion control, pumping energy and leak detection. Even a minor coolant leak within or near a high-voltage battery enclosure may create electrical insulation concerns, service complexity and reliability issues. Further, liquid cooling components add weight and occupy valuable space within the vehicle platform. [006] Phase change materials have been proposed for battery cooling because they absorb latent heat during melting. However, many known phase change material-based systems suffer from low thermal conductivity, excessive weight, volume constraints, slow heat release after saturation, leakage during phase transition, poor mechanical stability, and difficulty in maintaining uniform contact with cylindrical, prismatic or pouch cells over long-term vibration and thermal cycling. [007] Heat pipes, graphite sheets and metallic heat spreaders have also been explored for thermal management. These components can transfer heat away from hot regions, but conventional arrangements often fail to integrate heat spreading, heat buffering, passive venting and thermal runaway isolation in a compact battery pack structure. Merely placing heat spreaders between cells may move heat laterally but may not sufficiently absorb transient heat spikes or discharge stored heat to the external casing. [008] Another significant problem in electric vehicle battery packs is the propagation of heat from an overheated cell to adjacent cells. When one cell enters an abnormal thermal condition, heat transfer to neighbouring cells may trigger a cascading failure. Many known cooling systems are designed for normal operating heat removal and are not sufficiently configured to slow down thermal propagation under abuse, impact, overcharge or internal short-circuit conditions. [009] There remains a practical need for a passive battery thermal regulation system that can operate without continuous energy consumption, provide uniform heat distribution, buffer peak thermal loads, guide heat toward external dissipation zones, reduce cell-to-cell temperature variation, and improve safety during abnormal heating events. Such a system should be compatible with different lithium-ion cell formats, capable of being integrated into existing electric vehicle battery trays, and should reduce dependence on pumps, fans, coolant circuits or complex active cooling equipment. [010] Therefore, the present invention provides a passive thermal regulation architecture in which thermally conductive pathways, encapsulated phase change members, directional heat-spreading layers, passive airflow or ventilation channels, and thermal isolation barriers are structurally integrated within a lithium-ion battery pack. The invention addresses the above limitations by combining heat absorption, heat redistribution, controlled passive dissipation and thermal propagation resistance in a compact and manufacturable battery pack configuration. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [011] The present invention provides a passive thermal regulation system for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles, wherein the system comprises a plurality of battery cells arranged within a battery module housing, a heat-spreading assembly thermally coupled to selected surfaces of the cells, one or more encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements positioned adjacent to thermally critical regions of the battery pack, and a passive heat discharge pathway configured to transfer stored and distributed heat toward an external heat dissipation surface of the battery enclosure. [012] In one aspect of the invention, the heat-spreading assembly comprises a multilayer thermal transfer structure including at least one anisotropic thermally conductive layer, at least one metallic or graphite-based heat distribution plate, and at least one compliant thermal interface layer. The anisotropic layer directs heat preferentially away from high-temperature cell zones and toward passive dissipation channels, thereby reducing localised hot spots and maintaining improved temperature uniformity across the battery pack. [013] In another aspect of the invention, the phase-change thermal buffer elements are encapsulated within leak-resistant containment pockets, sleeves, cartridges or laminated panels. The phase-change material may be selected to undergo phase transition within a predetermined temperature range suitable for lithium-ion battery safety and performance. The encapsulation prevents leakage during melting and solidification, while the thermal interface with the heat-spreading assembly enables rapid absorption of peak heat generated during fast charging or high-load discharge. [014] In yet another aspect of the invention, the system includes passive airflow channels or natural convection passages formed between a battery module frame and an enclosure wall. These channels are configured to promote movement of air due to temperature-induced density differences, vehicle motion, or pressure variation without requiring a powered fan. The passive airflow channels may include fin structures, ribbed surfaces, louvered inlets, protected vent paths or heat-dissipating surfaces for improving heat release to the surrounding environment. [015] In a further aspect of the invention, thermal isolation barriers are placed between selected cell groups or module segments to reduce lateral thermal propagation during an abnormal heating event. The barriers may comprise ceramic fibre layers, aerogel-based insulating layers, mica sheets, intumescent material, flame-resistant polymer composites or combinations thereof. These barriers are positioned so that normal heat transfer to the passive thermal regulation pathway is allowed while rapid propagation toward adjacent cells is restricted. [016] The invention further provides a structurally integrated battery pack architecture in which heat generated by battery cells is first received by thermal interface layers, laterally distributed through heat spreaders, temporarily absorbed by phase-change buffer elements, and subsequently transferred through passive conduction and natural convection paths to the battery enclosure. This sequence enables effective thermal control without continuous operation of pumps, compressors, forced-air blowers or liquid coolant loops. [017] The passive thermal regulation system of the invention may be configured for cylindrical, prismatic or pouch-type lithium-ion cells. The system may be integrated in electric cars, electric buses, electric two-wheelers, electric three-wheelers, hybrid vehicles, stationary charging buffers and modular energy storage units associated with electric vehicle platforms. The invention improves battery safety, reduces auxiliary power consumption, lowers system complexity and enhances long-term battery pack reliability. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [018] The accompanying drawings are provided for illustrating exemplary embodiments of the present invention and for facilitating understanding of the structural and functional arrangement of the passive thermal regulation system. The drawings are not intended to limit the scope of the invention, and equivalent configurations, shapes, proportions and arrangements may be adopted without departing from the inventive concept. [019] Figure 1 illustrates a schematic sectional view of a lithium-ion battery pack having a plurality of battery cells, heat-spreading layers, encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements, passive airflow channels and thermal isolation barriers arranged within a battery enclosure according to an embodiment of the present invention. [020] Figure 2 illustrates a functional heat-flow diagram showing the transfer of heat from battery cells to thermal interface layers, heat-spreading members, phase-change buffer elements, passive conduction paths, natural convection channels and external enclosure dissipation surfaces according to an embodiment of the present invention. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION [021] The present invention will now be described in detail with reference to exemplary embodiments. The embodiments described herein are provided to explain the principles of the invention and should not be construed as limiting the invention to the exact structural arrangement disclosed. The terms “comprising,” “including,” “having” and similar expressions are intended to be open-ended and do not exclude the presence of additional elements, layers, components or functional features. Passive Thermal Regulation Architecture [022] In an embodiment, the passive thermal regulation system comprises a battery pack enclosure, a plurality of lithium-ion battery cells disposed within the enclosure, a module support frame, heat-spreading members positioned in thermal communication with the cells, encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements disposed adjacent to the heat-spreading members, and one or more passive heat discharge pathways extending toward external surfaces of the enclosure. The arrangement is designed to receive heat from the cells, distribute the heat across a larger area, absorb sudden thermal peaks and gradually reject heat to the surrounding environment. [023] The battery cells may be cylindrical cells, prismatic cells, pouch cells or a combination thereof. In the case of cylindrical cells, the heat-spreading members may be positioned between rows of cells or along tangential contact regions. In the case of prismatic or pouch cells, the heat-spreading members may be arranged along broad side surfaces of the cells to maximise thermal contact. The cell arrangement may be selected according to vehicle platform requirements, voltage requirements, pack capacity and packaging constraints. [024] The battery pack enclosure may be formed from aluminium alloy, steel, magnesium alloy, fibre-reinforced composite material, thermally conductive polymer composite or any suitable structural material. At least one portion of the enclosure is configured as a passive heat dissipation surface. The dissipation surface may include fins, ribs, corrugations, surface texturing, thermally conductive inserts or exposed heat-releasing panels for increasing the effective heat transfer area. Heat-Spreading Assembly [025] In an embodiment, the heat-spreading assembly includes one or more thermally conductive plates, strips, foils, sheets or laminated members placed in contact with or near the battery cells. The heat-spreading assembly may include aluminium sheets, copper foils, graphite sheets, pyrolytic graphite layers, carbon-based thermal sheets, thermally conductive polymer composites or hybrid metallic-carbon laminates. The heat-spreading assembly functions to reduce temperature concentration at individual cells by transferring heat laterally toward cooler zones and toward the phase-change buffer elements. [026] The heat-spreading assembly may include an anisotropic thermal layer having a higher in-plane thermal conductivity than through-plane thermal conductivity. This configuration allows heat to be guided along a preferred direction away from local hot spots while limiting direct heat transfer toward adjacent cells in certain directions. By controlling directional heat flow, the system helps maintain thermal uniformity during normal operation and reduces the possibility of rapid heat propagation during abnormal events. [027] A compliant thermal interface layer may be provided between each battery cell and the heat-spreading assembly. The compliant layer compensates for dimensional tolerances, vibration, thermal expansion and surface irregularities. The compliant layer may comprise silicone-based thermal pad material, thermally conductive elastomer, graphite-loaded polymer, ceramic-filled polymer, boron nitride-filled polymer or other electrically insulating and thermally conductive materials. This layer improves heat transfer without creating electrical short-circuit risks. Phase-Change Thermal Buffer Elements [028] The phase-change thermal buffer elements are configured to absorb transient heat generated during high-current operation. Each phase-change element may comprise a phase-change material encapsulated within a thermally conductive and leak-resistant containment structure. The phase-change material may include paraffin-based materials, fatty acid-based materials, hydrated salt compositions, polymeric phase-change materials, eutectic mixtures or composite phase-change materials having thermally conductive additives. [029] In a preferred embodiment, the phase-change material is selected to have a melting temperature within a range corresponding to a safe upper operating temperature of the lithium-ion battery cells. For example, the phase transition range may be selected such that latent heat absorption begins before the cells reach a temperature associated with accelerated degradation or safety risk. This allows the phase-change material to function as a thermal buffer during fast charging, rapid discharge, high ambient temperature exposure and temporary heat accumulation. [030] The phase-change material may be enhanced with thermally conductive fillers such as expanded graphite, graphene, carbon nanotubes, aluminium nitride, boron nitride, graphite flakes, metal foam, carbon fibre or ceramic particles. These fillers improve heat absorption rate and heat release rate by reducing the thermal resistance of the phase-change element. The phase-change material may be impregnated into a porous matrix, honeycomb carrier, foam structure or laminated containment member to maintain mechanical stability during repeated melting and solidification cycles. [031] The containment structure of the phase-change thermal buffer element may be formed as a cartridge, pouch, sealed panel, sleeve, capsule, laminated sheet or modular insert. The containment structure prevents leakage of the phase-change material and maintains reliable thermal contact with adjacent heat spreaders. The containment structure may include an aluminium laminate, polymer-metal laminate, flame-retardant polymer film, coated metallic casing or thermally conductive composite shell. Passive Airflow and Heat Discharge Pathways [032] In an embodiment, the passive heat discharge pathway includes one or more natural convection channels formed between the battery module frame and the battery enclosure. The channels are dimensioned to allow air movement caused by thermal buoyancy, pressure differences during vehicle motion, or passive exchange through protected inlet and outlet passages. The channels may be located along side walls, bottom walls, top cover regions or corner regions of the enclosure. [033] The passive airflow channels may include internal fins, ribbed plates, staggered guide walls, inclined ducts or thermal chimney structures. These features promote heat transfer from internal heat-spreading members to air within the channels. The channels are preferably designed to avoid direct exposure of battery cells to dust, water, debris or road contaminants. Therefore, the airflow path may include labyrinth passages, hydrophobic vent membranes, protective covers or one-way venting structures. [034] In another embodiment, the passive heat discharge pathway includes conductive thermal bridges extending from the heat-spreading assembly to one or more exterior dissipation regions of the battery enclosure. The thermal bridges may comprise metallic ribs, graphite bars, conductive composite beams, embedded heat pipes operating passively, or thermally conductive fasteners. These bridges provide a controlled path for heat movement from internal battery regions to external surfaces without requiring a circulating coolant. Thermal Isolation and Safety Barriers [035] The passive thermal regulation system may include thermal isolation barriers arranged between adjacent cell groups, between module partitions, or around high-risk zones of the battery pack. The barriers are configured to slow the movement of excessive heat from a thermally distressed cell group to neighbouring cell groups. The barriers may include mica, ceramic fibre, aerogel, glass fibre, intumescent sheet, mineral-based insulation, flame-retardant polymer composite or multilayer combinations thereof. [036] The thermal isolation barriers may be selectively interrupted or shaped to allow heat to flow toward the heat-spreading assembly while resisting direct lateral heat transfer between cells. This directional arrangement permits normal thermal management during regular operation while reducing propagation speed during abnormal heating. In one embodiment, the barrier includes a thermally conductive window facing the heat-spreading member and an insulating surface facing an adjacent cell group. [037] The system may further include pressure relief pathways, gas diversion channels or flame-resistant vent regions to guide gases away from neighbouring cells in the event of a cell venting condition. These features may be integrated with the passive airflow channels while maintaining separation between routine thermal airflow and emergency venting flow. The arrangement reduces the possibility that hot gases will directly impinge upon adjacent cells. Battery Module Integration [038] The battery module support frame may include slots, recesses, grooves or receiving pockets for retaining the heat-spreading members and phase-change thermal buffer elements. The support frame may be made of flame-retardant polymer, composite material, aluminium or hybrid structures. The frame maintains mechanical positioning of the cells and thermal regulation components under vibration, vehicle shock and repeated thermal expansion. [039] In one embodiment, the phase-change buffer elements are removable modular cartridges inserted into corresponding receiving spaces in the battery module frame. This allows service replacement, inspection or adaptation of thermal capacity according to vehicle type. For example, a battery pack intended for high-performance driving or fast charging may use higher-capacity phase-change cartridges, while a light electric vehicle may use thinner laminated buffer members. [040] The passive thermal regulation system may also include temperature sensors for monitoring purposes, although the core thermal regulation is passive. The sensors may be used by a battery management system to observe cell temperatures, detect abnormal temperature rise, estimate phase-change saturation state, or limit charging and discharging when required. The invention does not require the sensors to actively drive a pump or coolant circuit for normal heat regulation. Functional Operation [041] During normal electric vehicle operation, heat generated by the lithium-ion cells is transferred through the compliant thermal interface layers to the heat-spreading assembly. The heat-spreading assembly laterally distributes the heat and reduces local temperature peaks. When the heat load increases, the phase-change thermal buffer elements absorb additional heat through latent heat during phase transition. As the vehicle continues operating or later enters a lower-load condition, the stored heat is gradually transferred through conductive bridges and passive airflow channels to external dissipation surfaces. [042] During fast charging, the system reduces rapid temperature rise by combining thermal spreading and phase-change absorption. During parking after a high-load drive cycle, the passive airflow channels and conductive enclosure regions continue to release heat without requiring powered cooling. During an abnormal heating event, the thermal isolation barriers reduce lateral heat propagation, while the heat-spreading members and phase-change elements draw heat toward safer dissipation zones. [043] The passive thermal regulation system thereby provides a balanced thermal response: it distributes heat during ordinary operation, absorbs heat during transient peaks, dissipates heat during low-load or parked conditions, and resists heat propagation during abuse conditions. The system is particularly useful in electric vehicles where energy efficiency, safety, weight reduction and maintenance reduction are important. Advantages of the Invention [044] The present invention reduces dependence on active liquid cooling systems and thereby decreases auxiliary energy consumption, leakage risk, maintenance complexity and manufacturing cost. The system provides thermal buffering without requiring continuous power input and maintains improved temperature uniformity across the battery pack. [045] The directional heat-spreading arrangement reduces hot spots within densely packed modules, while the encapsulated phase-change material absorbs peak heat loads. The passive airflow and conductive discharge pathways release heat to the battery enclosure, and the thermal isolation barriers reduce the risk of thermal runaway propagation. The resulting architecture is compact, safe, modular and suitable for integration into different electric vehicle platforms. [046] Although the invention has been described with reference to lithium-ion battery packs for electric vehicles, the same passive thermal regulation principles may be applied to hybrid vehicle batteries, stationary energy storage systems, portable power modules, charging buffer units and other electrochemical energy storage assemblies requiring safe and efficient temperature control. , Claims:1. A passive thermal regulation system for a lithium-ion battery pack in an electric vehicle, comprising a plurality of lithium-ion battery cells arranged within a battery pack enclosure, a heat-spreading assembly thermally coupled to the lithium-ion battery cells, one or more encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements thermally connected to the heat-spreading assembly, and at least one passive heat discharge pathway extending toward an external heat dissipation surface of the battery pack enclosure. 2. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the heat-spreading assembly comprises an anisotropic thermally conductive layer configured to direct heat preferentially away from a local high-temperature cell region toward the one or more encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements. 3. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the heat-spreading assembly comprises at least one metallic, graphite-based, carbon-based or thermally conductive composite heat distribution member positioned between adjacent cell groups or along a surface of the lithium-ion battery cells. 4. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein a compliant thermal interface layer is positioned between the lithium-ion battery cells and the heat-spreading assembly to improve thermal contact while electrically insulating the lithium-ion battery cells from the heat-spreading assembly. 5. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein each encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer element comprises a phase-change material sealed within a leak-resistant containment structure selected from a cartridge, pouch, sleeve, capsule, laminated panel or modular insert. 6. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 5, wherein the phase-change material comprises one or more thermally conductive fillers selected from expanded graphite, graphene, boron nitride, aluminium nitride, graphite flakes, carbon fibre, metal foam or ceramic particles. 7. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the passive heat discharge pathway comprises at least one natural convection channel formed between a battery module frame and the battery pack enclosure for releasing heat without a powered fan, pump or coolant circulation loop. 8. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, further comprising one or more thermal isolation barriers positioned between adjacent cell groups to restrict lateral heat propagation during an abnormal heating event while allowing heat transfer toward the heat-spreading assembly. 9. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 8, wherein the one or more thermal isolation barriers comprise mica, ceramic fibre, aerogel, intumescent material, flame-retardant polymer composite or a multilayer combination thereof. 10. The passive thermal regulation system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the heat-spreading assembly, the encapsulated phase-change thermal buffer elements and the passive heat discharge pathway are structurally integrated within a battery module frame such that heat generated by the lithium-ion battery cells is distributed, temporarily absorbed and passively dissipated through the battery pack enclosure without continuous powered cooling.

patents.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a method (200) and system (102) for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module. The system (102) includes a controller (104) to receive energy storage module data during charging of the energy storage module, estimate an anode potential of the energy storage module and compare a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator. The controller (104) computes an incremental capacity signal to generate a second plating indicator, computes a differential voltage signal to generate a third plating indicator and combines the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator to generate a single plating severity index (PSI). The controller (104) classifies a lithium plating condition of the energy storage module based on the generated PSI.
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present disclosure generally relates to the field of energy storage. In particular, the present disclosure relates to a method and system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module during charging by estimating anode potential using an electrochemical model and analyzing a voltage-capacity characteristics using incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA). BACKGROUND [0002] Lithium plating during charging is a critical degradation mechanism in lithium-ion energy storage modules that can lead to capacity loss, internal short circuits, and safety hazards. Early detection of lithium plating during operation is therefore important for safe and efficient energy storage management. [0003] Commercial battery management systems (BMSs) typically rely on voltage, current, and surface temperature measurements combined with static heuristics, such as maximum allowable C-rate versus temperature or fixed voltage limits. While these heuristics are simple to implement, they are unable to observe the internal electrochemical state of the energy storage module, particularly the anode potential. As a result, such approaches cannot reliably distinguish between safe operating conditions and conditions that are prone to lithium plating, even when voltage and temperature values appear acceptable. [0004] Model-based approaches have also been explored for predicting plating risk. In particular, reduced-order Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) electrochemical models are used to estimate the internal anode potential and infer the likelihood of lithium plating in an energy storage module. However, DFN-type models can exhibit significant estimation errors under practical operating conditions, such as strong cooling, in-plane current inhomogeneity, and high-rate charging. These errors may reach several tens of millivolts, which is comparable to the safety margin relative to the plating threshold. Consequently, model inaccuracies may result in either false plating alarms or failure to detect actual plating events. [0005] Electrochemical diagnostic techniques such as Incremental Capacity Analysis (ICA), represented by dQ/dV, and Differential Voltage Analysis (DVA), represented by dV/dQ, are also widely used to analyse ageing mechanisms, phase transitions, and loss of lithium inventory in energy storage modules. However, these techniques are commonly applied offline using laboratory cycling data. Implementing ICA and DVA in real time under field conditions is challenging due to measurement noise, partial charge cycles, varying current profiles, and temperature dependence. Moreover, many existing implementations focus on general ageing diagnostics rather than specifically identifying lithium plating, and they are typically not integrated with fast-charging control systems. [0006] Other approaches include impedance-based diagnostics, such as electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) or pulse resistance tests, which can indicate degradation and, in certain cases, lithium plating in energy storage modules. However, such methods often require specialised hardware or interruptions to normal operation, making them unsuitable for continuous in-situ monitoring during fast charging of the energy storage module. [0007] Accordingly, existing techniques suffer from several limitations. Current BMS heuristics are unable to detect incipient lithium plating before it becomes severe in an energy storage module. Model-based anode potential estimation methods are sensitive to modelling assumptions and operating conditions, resulting in uncertain plating thresholds. Real-time ICA and DVA implementations remain challenging in practical operating environments due to noise and partial cycling conditions. Furthermore, conventional systems lack a unified diagnostic metric capable of combining multiple indicators into a single actionable signal for charging control. Therefore, there remains a need for an integrated, real-time lithium plating detection system for energy storage modules that combines electrochemical model-based estimation with voltage-capacity diagnostic features, while accounting for model errors and adapting to varying operating conditions. [0008] Therefore, there is, a need to address at least the above-mentioned drawbacks and any other shortcomings, or at the very least, provide a valuable alternative to the existing assemblies. OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0009] A general object of the present disclosure is to provide a method and system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module during charging by estimating an anode potential using an electrochemical model and analyzing a voltage-capacity characteristics using incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA). [0010] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for estimating the anode potential of the energy storage module based on energy storage module data comprising voltage, current, and temperature received during charging of the energy storage module. [0011] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for generating a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module. [0012] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for identifying a lithium plating condition by comparing the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a plating indicator. [0013] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for computing an incremental capacity (ICA) signal from the energy storage module data and extracting at least one ICA feature associated with lithium plating. [0014] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for computing a differential voltage (DVA) signal from the energy storage module data and extracting at least one DVA feature associated with lithium plating. [0015] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for combining a plurality of plating indicators obtained from anode potential estimation, ICA features, and DVA features using a fusion logic module to generate a plating severity index (PSI). [0016] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide the method for classifying a lithium plating condition of the energy storage module based on the generated plating severity index (PSI). SUMMARY [0017] Aspects of the present disclosure relates to the field of energy storage. In particular, the present disclosure relates to a method and system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module during charging by estimating anode potential using an electrochemical model and analyzing a voltage-capacity characteristics using incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA). [0018] An aspect of the present disclosure relates to the method for detecting lithium plating in the energy storage module. The method includes receiving by a controller, energy storage module data comprising voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module. The method includes estimating by the controller, an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model. The method includes generating by the controller, a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential, wherein the error-correction is applied based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module. The method includes comparing by the controller, the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated to a lithium plating condition. The method includes computing, by the controller, an incremental capacity (ICA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of an ICA feature to generate a second plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The method includes computing by the controller, a differential voltage (DVA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a DVA feature to generate a third plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The method includes combining by the controller, the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator using a fusion logic module to generate a single plating severity index (PSI). The method includes classifying by the controller, the lithium plating condition of the at least one energy storage module based on the generated PSI. [0019] In an embodiment, the electrochemical model comprises at least one of a Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model, a Multi-Species Multi-Reaction (MSMR) model, a Single-Particle Model (SPM), and a Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (PTD)-SPM hybrid model. [0020] In an embodiment, the error-correction comprises applying at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module based on a temperature dependent safety buffer and a cooling dependent safety buffer respectively. The method includes estimating the anode potential associated with in-plane inhomogeneity and cooling conditions of the energy storage module, to generate the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module. [0025] In an embodiment, extracting the at least one DVA feature comprises identifying at least one of changes in trough position, trough depth, peak symmetry, or formation of low-voltage features associated with lithium plating.
