The method includes weights of the weighted combination depend on at least one of temperature, C-rate, state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), or energy storage module chemistry of the energy storage module. [0027] In an embodiment, the method includes classifying the lithium plating condition comprises assigning the PSI into predefined severity classes including at least one of a safe condition, an incipient plating condition, an active plating condition, or a severe plating condition. [0028] An aspect of the present disclosure relates to a system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module, the system comprising: a controller, and a fusion logic module. The system includes receive energy storage modules data comprising at least one of voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module. The system includes estimate an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model. The system includes generate a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential, wherein the error-correction is applied based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module. The system includes compare the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated to a lithium plating condition. The system includes compute an incremental capacity (ICA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a ICA feature to generate a second plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The system includes compute a differential voltage (DVA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a DVA feature to generate a third plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The system includes combine the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator using a fusion logic module to generate a single plating severity index (PSI). The system includes classify the lithium plating condition of the at least one energy storage module based on the generated PSI. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0029] The accompanying drawings are included to provide a further understanding of the present disclosure and are incorporated in and constitute a part of this specification. The drawings illustrate exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure and, together with the description, serve to explain the principles of the present disclosure. [0031] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary flow diagram of a method for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0032] The following is a detailed description of embodiments of the disclosure depicted in the accompanying drawings. The embodiments are in such detail as to clearly communicate the disclosure. However, the amount of detail offered is not intended to limit the anticipated variations of embodiments; on the contrary, the intention is to cover all modifications, equivalents, and alternatives falling within the scope of the present disclosures as defined by the appended claims. [0033] Embodiments of the present disclosure relates to the field of energy storage. In particular, the present disclosure relates to a method and system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module during charging by estimating anode potential using an electrochemical model and analyzing a voltage-capacity characteristics using incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA). [0034] An embodiment of the present disclosure relates to the method for detecting lithium plating in the energy storage module. The method includes receiving by a controller, energy storage module data comprising voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module. The method includes estimating by the controller, an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model. The method includes generating by the controller, a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential, wherein the error-correction is applied based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module. The method includes comparing by the controller, the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated to a lithium plating condition. The method includes computing, by the controller, an incremental capacity (ICA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of an ICA feature to generate a second plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The method includes computing by the controller, a differential voltage (DVA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a DVA feature to generate a third plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. The method includes combining by the controller, the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator using a fusion logic module to generate a single plating severity index (PSI). The method includes classifying by the controller, the lithium plating condition of the at least one energy storage module based on the generated PSI. [0035] The term “energy storage module”, can be interchangeably used with “battery”, “battery module”, “batteries” and meaning of the terms remain same throughout the document. [0036] The term “energy storage modules management system”, can be interchangeably used “battery management system (BMS)”, and meaning of the terms remain same thorough out the document. [0037] Various embodiments with respect to the present disclosure will be explained in detail with reference to FIGs 1 to 2. [0038] FIG. 1 illustrates a block diagram 100 of a system 102 for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0039] FIG. 2 illustrates a flow diagram of a method 200 for detecting lithium plating in the energy storage module, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0040] Referring to FIGs. 1 to 2, the system 102 may be configured to detect lithium plating in the energy storage module, using an an energy storage module data comprising voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module. [0041] As shown in FIG. 1, the block diagram 100 of the system 102 comprises a controller 104, a memory 106, a data acquisition module 108, an anode potential generation module 110, a signal computation module 112, a PSI generation module 114, a fusion logic module 116, a classification module 118, and a database 120. [0042] The controller 104 may be configured to execute instructions stored in the memory 106 to perform lithium plating detection operations in the energy storage module. The controller 104 may execute instructions stored in the memory 106 to process the received energy storage module data and coordinate operations of the data acquisition module 108, the anode potential generation module 110, the signal computation module 112, the PSI generation module 114, the fusion logic module 116, and the classification module 118. [0043] In an embodiment, the controller 104 may be implemented as one or more microprocessors, microcomputers, microcontrollers, digital signal processors, central processing units, logic circuitries, and/or any devices that manipulate data based on operational instructions. Among other capabilities, the controller 104 may be configured to fetch and execute computer-readable instructions stored in a memory. The memory may store one or more computer-readable instructions or routines, which may be fetched and executed to create or share the data units over a network service. The memory may include any non-transitory storage device, including, for example, volatile memory such as a Random Access Memory (RAM), or a non-volatile memory such as an Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory (EPROM), a flash memory, and the like. [0044] The data acquisition module 108 may be configured to receive energy storage module data during charging of the energy storage module. The received energy storage module data may comprise at least one of voltage, current, and temperature associated with the energy storage module. The received data may be stored in the database 120 and may be provided to subsequent modules for further processing. [0045] The anode potential generation module 110 may be configured to estimate an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model. In an embodiment, the electrochemical model may comprise at least one of a Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) model, a Multi-Species Multi-Reaction (MSMR) model, a Single-Particle Model (SPM), or a Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (P2D)-SPM hybrid model. The anode potential generation module 110 may further generate a corrected anode potential by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect associated with the energy storage module. The error-correction may include applying a temperature dependent safety buffer and a cooling dependent safety buffer for receiving errors associated with in-plane inhomogeneity and cooling conditions. The corrected anode potential may be compared with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated with a lithium plating condition. [0046] The signal computation module 112 may be configured to compute electrochemical diagnostic signals from the received energy storage module data. In an embodiment, the signal computation module 112 may compute an incremental capacity (ICA) signal corresponding to variations of charge with respect to voltage during charging of the energy storage module. The signal computation module 112 may further compute a differential voltage (DVA) signal corresponding to variations of voltage with respect to charge during charging of the energy storage module. [0047] The signal computation module 112 may further extract diagnostic features from the computed ICA and DVA signals. In an embodiment, ICA features may include at least one of peak position shifts, peak amplitude changes, suppression of graphite staging peaks, or formation of additional features associated with lithium plating. Similarly, DVA features may include at least one of changes in trough position, trough depth, peak symmetry, or formation of low-voltage features associated with lithium plating. Based on the extracted ICA and DVA features, the system 102 may generate a second plating indicator and a third plating indicator associated with the lithium plating condition. [0048] The PSI generation module 114 may be configured to process the plating indicators generated from the anode potential estimation and the signal computation modules. In particular, the PSI generation module 114 may generate a plating severity index (PSI) that represents a combined indication of lithium plating risk in the energy storage module. [0049] The fusion logic module 116 may be configured to combine the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator to generate the PSI. In an embodiment, the fusion logic module 116 may generate the PSI as a weighted combination of the plating indicators derived from the corrected anode potential, the ICA signal features, and the DVA signal features. The weights of the weighted combination may depend on at least one of temperature, C-rate, state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), or chemistry of the energy storage module. [0050] The classification module 118 may be configured to classify the lithium plating condition of the energy storage module based on the generated PSI. In an embodiment, the PSI may be assigned to predefined severity classes including at least one of a safe condition, an incipient plating condition, an active plating condition, or a severe plating condition. [0051] In an embodiment, the PSI generated by the fusion logic module 116 may be used by the controller 104 associated with the energy storage module to regulate charging operation. When the PSI exceeds predefined thresholds, the charging current may be reduced, limited to a safe value, or the charging process may be terminated to prevent further lithium plating and associated degradation of the energy storage module. [0052] In an embodiment, the system 102 may estimate the anode potential of the energy storage module using the reduced-order electrochemical-thermal model. The electrochemical model may be corrected using temperature-dependent safety buffers and calibration against experimental data to provide a conservative estimate of the anode potential relative to a plating threshold. Such correction may be employed for modelling deviations associated with operating conditions of the energy storage module. [0053] In an embodiment, the system 102 may compute incremental capacity (ICA) and differential voltage (DVA) signals from the received energy storage module data during charging of the energy storage module. The system 102 may extract diagnostic features from the ICA and DVA signals in real time. The extracted ICA and DVA features may include at least one of peak positions, peak amplitudes, derivatives, and morphological changes associated with lithium plating. The feature extraction may be performed using adaptive filtering to manage measurement noise and partial charge cycles. [0054] In an embodiment, the fusion logic module 116 may combine a model-based anode potential deviation, an ICA anomaly score, and a DVA anomaly score to generate a plating severity index (PSI). The fusion-based combination of multiple plating indicators may provide a more robust detection of lithium plating compared to using the indicator and may be adaptable to different operating conditions and energy storage module. [0055] In an embodiment, the generated PSI may be used by the controller 104 associated with the energy storage module to regulate charging operation. When the PSI exceeds predefined thresholds, the charging current may be reduced, limited to a safe value, or the charging process may be halted to prevent further lithium plating and associated degradation of the energy storage module. [0056] In another embodiment, the system 102 may be configured for detecting lithium plating in the energy storage module during charging. The system 102 may include the energy storage module such as a lithium-ion cell or pack equipped with sensing elements configured to measure voltage, current, and temperature. The system 102 may further include the reduced-order electrochemical-thermal model configured to estimate internal states of the energy storage module, including anode potential and other electrochemical parameters. [0057] In an embodiment, the reduced-order electrochemical-thermal model may include at least one of a Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) model, a Multi-Species Multi-Reaction (MSMR) model, or a Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (P2D)–Single Particle Model (SPM) hybrid model. The model may receive measured current I(t), terminal voltage V(t), and temperature T(t) as inputs. Based on these inputs, the model may generate estimates of internal parameters including state of charge (SOC), anode potential, electrolyte potential, and internal temperature of the energy storage module. [0058] Another embodiment as disclosed herein, to receive deviations associated with in-plane inhomogeneity and cooling variations, the system 102 may apply an error-correction layer to the estimated anode potential. The error-correction may include applying a temperature-dependent offset based on pre-characterized model and experimental discrepancies, and applying a cooling-topology-dependent safety buffer ΔΦ. For example, larger safety buffers may be applied for energy storage modules having limited cooling capability. The corrected anode potential Φ*_anode may then be compared with the plating threshold. The plating threshold may correspond to a lithium plating potential limit adjusted by the safety buffer ΔΦ. A decrease in the corrected anode potential relative to the plating threshold may indicate an increased likelihood of lithium plating. [0059] In another embodiment, the system 102 may compute the incremental capacity signal corresponding to dQ/dV using measured charging data of the energy storage module. The incremental capacity signal may be obtained through numerical differentiation of charge with respect to voltage and may include smoothing operations to reduce noise. The system 102 may maintain a database of reference incremental capacity curves obtained under standard operating conditions. During operation, the system 102 may identify variations in the incremental capacity signal, including shifts or suppression of graphite staging peaks and the formation of additional signal features associated with lithium plating. These deviations may be quantified as an ICA anomaly metric. [0060] In another embodiment, the system 102 may also compute the differential voltage signal corresponding to dV/dQ from the measured relationship between voltage and charge. Similar smoothing operations may be applied to reduce measurement noise. The system 102 may analyze the differential voltage signal to detect changes in characteristic signal features. Such features may include variations in the position and depth of characteristic troughs, symmetry of DVA peaks, and the appearance of low-voltage signal features associated with lithium plating and loss of cyclable lithium. Differences between the computed differential voltage signal and reference curves may be summarized as a DVA anomaly metric. [0061] In another embodiment, each diagnostic channel may generate indicator associated with lithium plating detection. The first indicator may correspond to the proximity of the corrected anode potential to the plating threshold. The second indicator may correspond to the ICA anomaly metric derived from the incremental capacity signal. The third indicator may correspond to the DVA anomaly metric derived from the differential voltage signal. [0062] The fusion logic module 116 may combine the indicators obtained from the anode potential estimation, ICA signal analysis, and DVA signal analysis to generate the plating severity index (PSI). In an embodiment, the PSI may be calculated as the weighted combination of the indicators. The weights applied in the combination may depend on operating conditions of the energy storage module, including temperature, C-rate, state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), and chemistry of the energy storage module. [0063] In an embodiment, the generated PSI may be mapped to predefined severity classes representing lithium plating conditions. For example, PSI value below a predetermined threshold may indicate a safe operating condition. A PSI within an intermediate range may indicate an incipient lithium plating condition, while higher PSI values may correspond to active or severe lithium plating conditions. [0064] For an instance, during fast-charging operation, the system 102 may continuously execute the electrochemical model and signal analysis modules in real time. For example, during charging at a high charging rate, the corrected anode potential may initially remain above the plating threshold and the ICA and DVA anomaly metrics may remain minimal, indicating low PSI and safe operating condition. As the state of charge increases, the corrected anode potential may approach the plating threshold and deviations in ICA and DVA signals may appear, resulting in an increase in the PSI and corresponding adjustment of the charging current. If the PSI exceeds a severe threshold due to adverse operating conditions such as low ambient temperature or insufficient cooling, the controller 104 may significantly reduce the charging rate or terminate charging to prevent lithium plating. [0065] In an embodiment, PSI values generated during operation may be stored in the database 120 and may be used for monitoring degradation trends, updating predictive lifetime models, or informing future charging limits of the energy storage module. [0066] In an embodiment, the system 102 may operate at sampling rates suitable for real-time operation. For example, ICA and DVA signal updates may occur at approximately 1–10 Hz, while the reduced-order electrochemical model may operate at approximately 10–100 Hz. The ICA and DVA computations may utilize sliding window techniques and smoothing filters, such as Savitzky–Golay filtering, to mitigate measurement noise and handle partial charging cycles. [0067] In an embodiment, the fusion logic module 116 used to generate the PSI may be implemented using analytic computation or may be augmented using a machine-learning classifier trained on labelled lithium plating and non-plating events to improve detection performance under varying operating conditions. [0068] In another embodiment, the system 102 may implement a fusion-based lithium plating detection algorithm that jointly utilizes corrected model-based anode potential estimation, incremental capacity analysis (ICA) features, and differential voltage analysis (DVA) features to generate a single plating severity index (PSI). The fusion of multiple indicators may provide a unified representation of lithium plating risk associated with the energy storage module. [0069] In another embodiment, PSI values generated during operation may be stored and analyzed over the lifetime of the energy storage module. The PSI trajectory obtained during repeated charging cycles may be used for lifetime prognosis, warranty assessment, and evaluation of second-life suitability of the energy storage module. [0070] In another embodiment, the lithium plating detection algorithm implemented by the system 102 may be deployed in different computing environments. For example, the algorithm may be executed within a battery management system (BMS) associated with the energy storage module, within an edge controller supervising multiple energy storage modules, or within a cloud-assisted architecture where PSI inference is performed using data received from the energy storage module. [0071] In another embodiment, lithium plating detection may be performed over a state-of-charge window of approximately 10% to 95% SOC. In some implementations, the detection may be primarily active within a preferred SOC window of approximately 20% to 90% SOC. [0072] In another embodiment, the system 102 may operate across a temperature range of approximately −10 °C to 55 °C. In certain implementations, fast-charging operation may preferably occur within a temperature range of approximately 10 °C to 40 °C. [0073] In another embodiment, the corrected anode potential estimation may include application of a dynamic safety buffer ΔΦ relative to a model-predicted plating threshold. The safety buffer ΔΦ may range approximately between 5 mV and 20 mV and may be scaled based on operating conditions including charging rate and cooling characteristics of the energy storage module. [0074] In another embodiment, the algorithm implemented by the system 102 may operate at sampling and update rates suitable for real-time detection. The reduced-order electrochemical model and fusion logic computations may operate at update rates of approximately 5 Hz to 50 Hz. Incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA) computations may operate using effective update windows of approximately 1 second to 10 seconds depending on measurement noise. [0075] In another embodiment, the plating severity index (PSI) generated by the fusion logic module 116 may be classified into predefined operating regions. For example, a PSI value below approximately 0.3 may correspond to a safe operating condition. A PSI value between approximately 0.3 and 0.6 may correspond to a moderate derating condition. A PSI value between approximately 0.6 and 0.8 may correspond to a strong derating condition. A PSI value greater than or equal to approximately 0.8 may correspond to a shut-down or fault condition associated with lithium plating. [0076] FIG. 2 illustrates an exemplary flow diagram of a method 200 for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module, in accordance with an embodiment of the present disclosure. [0077] Referring to FIG. 2, at step 202, the method 200 may include receiving an energy storage module data comprising voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module. [0078] At step 204, the method 200 may include estimating an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model. [0079] At step 206, the method 200 may include generating a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module. [0080] At step 208, the method 200 may include comparing the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated to a lithium plating condition. [0081] At step 210, the method 200 may include computing an incremental capacity (ICA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and to generate a second plating indicator. [0082] At step 212, the method 200 may include computing a differential voltage (DVA) signal based on the received energy storage module data to generate a third plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition. [0083] At step 214, the method 200 may include combining the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator using a fusion logic module to generate a PSI. [0084] At step 216, the method 200 may include classifying the lithium plating condition of the at least one energy storage module based on the generated PSI. [0085] While the foregoing describes various embodiments of the disclosure, other and further embodiments of the invention may be devised without departing from the basic scope thereof. The scope of the disclosure is determined by the claims that follow. The disclosure is not limited to the described embodiments, versions, or examples, which are included to enable a person having ordinary skill in the art to make and use the disclosure when combined with information and knowledge available to the person having ordinary skill in the art. ADVANTAGES OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE [0086] The present disclosure provides a method and system for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module during charging. [0087] The present disclosure provides lithium plating detection, performed using a combination of model-based anode potential estimation and signal-based diagnostic techniques, including incremental capacity analysis (ICA) and differential voltage analysis (DVA). The integration of these complementary indicators improves the reliability of detecting lithium plating conditions in the energy storage module. [0088] The present disclosure utilizes an error-corrected anode potential estimation mechanism that incorporates temperature-dependent and cooling-dependent safety buffers. , Claims:1. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the electrochemical model comprises at least one of: a Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model, a Multi-Species Multi-Reaction (MSMR) model, a Single-Particle Model (SPM), and a Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (PTD)-SPM hybrid model. 3. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the error-correction comprises: applying, by the controller (104), at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module based on a temperature dependent safety buffer and a cooling dependent safety buffer respectively; and estimating, by the controller (104), the anode potential associated with in-plane inhomogeneity and cooling conditions of the energy storage module, to generate the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module. 4. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein the plating threshold is selected based on a lithium plating potential limit and a safety buffer configured to maintain operating conditions of the energy storage module. 5. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein computing the ICA signal comprises varying charge with respect to voltage during charging of the energy storage module. 6. The method (200) as claimed in claim 5, wherein extracting the at least one of the ICA feature comprises identifying, by the controller (104), at least one of peak position shifts, peak amplitude changes, suppression of graphite staging peaks, or formation of additional features associated with lithium plating of the energy storage module. 7. The method (200) as claimed in claim 7, wherein extracting the at least one DVA feature comprises identifying, by the controller (104), at least one of changes in trough position, trough depth, peak symmetry, or formation of low-voltage features associated with lithium plating. 9. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, comprising: generating, using the fusion logic module (116), the PSI as a weighted combination of the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator; and wherein weights of the weighted combination depend on at least one of temperature, C-rate, state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), or energy storage module chemistry of the energy storage module. 10. The method (200) as claimed in claim 1, wherein classifying the lithium plating condition comprises assigning, by the controller (104), the PSI into predefined severity classes including at least one of a safe condition, an incipient plating condition, an active plating condition, or a severe plating condition. 11. A system (102) for detecting lithium plating in an energy storage module, the system (102) comprising: a data acquisition module (108); an anode potential generation module (110); a signal computation module (112); a PSI generation module (114); a fusion logic module (116); a memory (106); and a controller (104) configured to: receive energy storage module data comprising at least one of voltage, current, and temperature during charging of the energy storage module; estimate an anode potential of the energy storage module based on the received energy storage module data using an electrochemical model; generate a corrected anode potential of the energy storage module by applying an error-correction to the estimated anode potential, wherein the error-correction is applied based on at least one temperature and at least one cooling effect of the energy storage module; compare the corrected anode potential of the energy storage module with a plating threshold to generate a first plating indicator associated to a lithium plating condition; compute an incremental capacity (ICA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a ICA feature to generate a second plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition; compute a differential voltage (DVA) signal based on the received energy storage module data and extracting at least one of a DVA feature to generate a third plating indicator associated to the lithium plating condition; combine the first plating indicator, the second plating indicator, and the third plating indicator using a fusion logic module to generate a single plating severity index (PSI); and classify the lithium plating condition of the at least one energy storage module based on the generated PSI.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT ADVANCED FAST-CHARGING LITHIUM-ION BATTERY SYSTEM WITH MULTI-COMPONENT COMPOSITE ANODE AND DUAL-ELECTRODE REDUCED GRAPHENE OXIDE. The present disclosure relates to a lithium-ion battery system. The system includes a composite anode electrode formed by dispersing at least two lithium-ion intercalation materials and at least one conductive additive within a binder matrix. The composite anode electrode is coated onto a current collector. The system further includes a cathode electrode comprising a lithium-containing transition metal oxide active material together with at least one conductive additive. The cathode electrode is also dispersed in a binder matrix and coated onto a current collector. A porous separator is positioned between the anode electrode and the cathode electrode. An electrolyte is provided in ionic communication with both electrodes. The electrolyte comprises a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent along with at least one film-forming additive. patents.complete_specification: Description:BACKGROUND Field of Invention: [0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage. More particularly, the disclosure relates to lithium-ion battery systems. Discussion of prior arts: [0002] Lithium-ion battery technology has been widely adopted for portable electronics and electric vehicles since its introduction. However, existing battery systems continue to face limitations in simultaneously achieving high energy density, high power density, extended cycle life, rapid charging capability, thermal stability, and cost-effective manufacturing at a practical cell scale. Despite extensive research and development efforts, conventional systems exhibit trade-offs among these performance parameters. [0003] In the domain of composite anode design, prior approaches have employed graphite, silicon, lithium titanate, and conductive carbon materials either individually or in limited combinations. Such configurations exhibit constraints in charge rate capability, structural stability, and electrochemical performance, particularly when scaled beyond laboratory conditions. Additionally, conventional fabrication methodologies often require controlled environments, including dry-room infrastructure, thereby increasing complexity and cost. [0004] Further, known techniques for incorporating surface-modifying materials, including metal oxides, involve processes such as atomic layer deposition or other non-scalable methods. These approaches are generally limited to small-scale cells and do not readily integrate into conventional electrode fabrication processes. Similarly, the use of conductive additives has largely been restricted to individual electrodes, resulting in non-uniform charge transport characteristics within full-cell configurations. [0005] In addition, prior lithium-ion pouch cell configurations demonstrate limitations in capacity, energy density, and manufacturing conditions. High-rate charging performance is often accompanied by reduced cell capacity or reliance on specialised processing environments. Ambient-condition fabrication approaches reported in the art are typically associated with lower voltage chemistries and reduced energy densities, thereby limiting their applicability to high-performance battery systems. [0006] In light of the foregoing, there exists a need for a lithium-ion battery system that addresses the above-mentioned limitations and provides improved electrochemical performance, scalable fabrication, and enhanced operational characteristics. SUMMARY [0007] The present disclosure relates to a lithium-ion battery system. The system includes a composite anode electrode formed by dispersing at least two lithium-ion intercalation materials and at least one conductive additive within a binder matrix. The composite anode electrode is coated onto a current collector. The system further includes a cathode electrode comprising a lithium-containing transition metal oxide active material together with at least one conductive additive. The cathode electrode is also dispersed in a binder matrix and coated onto a current collector. A porous separator is positioned between the anode electrode and the cathode electrode. An electrolyte is provided in ionic communication with both electrodes. The electrolyte comprises a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent along with at least one film-forming additive. The anode electrode, cathode electrode, separator, and electrolyte are enclosed within a cell enclosure that is hermetically sealed. The battery system is configured to operate at a charge current of at least 3 amperes per ampere-hour of rated capacity, with a surface temperature rise of up to 15°C above ambient temperature during charging. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0008] Figure 1 illustrates a schematic cross-sectional view of a single-layer pouch cell assembly comprising an anode, a separator, and a cathode arranged in a layered configuration within an enclosure. [0009] Figure 2 illustrates an exploded schematic of a composite anode electrode comprising multiple active materials distributed within a binder matrix, together with a fabrication process flow. [0010] Figure 3 illustrates a graph of open-circuit voltage as a function of state of charge across a plurality of operating temperature conditions. [0011] Figure 4 illustrates a graph of direct current internal resistance as a function of state of charge. [0012] Figure 5 illustrates a graph showing variation in cell surface temperature with respect to time during a charging operation. [0013] Figure 6 illustrates a graph of discharge capacity in ampere-hours as a function of cycle number at a plurality of charge-discharge rates. [0014] Figure 7 illustrates constant-current constant-voltage charging profiles at a plurality of charge rates plotted as cell voltage versus time. [0015] Figure 8 illustrates a graph of capacity retention as a percentage of initial rated capacity as a function of cycle number at a plurality of charge-discharge rates. [0016] Figure 9 illustrates a microstructural analysis panel comprising phase maps, thickness comparison, phase distribution, porosity comparison, and volumetric distribution of cell layers. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0017] The foregoing detailed description includes references to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of the detailed description. The drawings show illustrations in accordance with example embodiments. These example embodiments, which may be herein also referred to as “examples” are described in enough detail to enable those skilled in the art to practice the present subject matter. However, it may be apparent to one with ordinary skill in the art, that the present disclosure may be practiced without these specific details. In other instances, well-known methods, procedures and components have not been described in detail so as not to unnecessarily obscure aspects of the embodiments. The embodiments can be combined, other embodiments can be utilized, or structural, logical, and design changes can be made without departing from the scope of the claims. The foregoing detailed description is, therefore, not to be taken in a limiting sense, and the scope is defined by the appended claims and their equivalents. [0018] In this document, the terms “a” or “an” are used, as is common in patent documents, to include one or more than one. In this document, the term “or” is used to refer to a nonexclusive “or” such that “A or B” includes “A but not B,” “B but not A,” and “A and B,” unless otherwise indicated. [0019] Referring to Figure 1, there is disclosed an embodiment of a lithium-ion battery system configured as a single-layer pouch-format cell assembly. The battery system comprises a stacked electrochemical structure including an anode assembly, a separator, and a cathode assembly arranged in a layered configuration to facilitate ionic transport and electronic conduction during operation. [0020] In one embodiment, the anode assembly comprises a first current collector, which may include a copper foil, and a composite anode electrode coated on at least one surface of the current collector. The composite anode electrode may comprise a plurality of lithium-ion intercalation materials and conductive additives dispersed within a binder matrix. The composite anode may include, but is not limited to, graphite, lithium titanate, silicon-based materials, carbonaceous conductive networks, and metal oxide particulates. The coating may be applied using slurry casting, doctor blade coating, slot-die coating, or equivalent deposition techniques. [0021] Disposed adjacent to the anode assembly is a separator layer. The separator may comprise a porous polymeric membrane, such as a polyolefin-based separator, including commercially available materials such as Celgard-type separators. The separator provides electrical insulation between the electrodes while permitting ionic conduction of lithium ions. [0022] On the opposite side of the separator is provided a cathode assembly. The cathode assembly comprises a second current collector, which may include an aluminium foil, and a cathode electrode coating disposed on at least one surface of the current collector. The cathode electrode may comprise a lithium-containing transition metal oxide active material together with one or more conductive additives and binders. In certain embodiments, the cathode active material may include nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide compositions, optionally combined with carbonaceous conductive agents. [0023] The stacked arrangement of the anode assembly, separator, and cathode assembly is enclosed within a flexible pouch enclosure. The enclosure may comprise a laminated aluminium-polymer film configured to provide mechanical support and environmental isolation. In one embodiment, the pouch is sealed along multiple edges using heat-sealing techniques following introduction of an electrolyte. The electrolyte may comprise a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent system including one or more film-forming additives. The electrolyte may be introduced prior to final sealing, and sealing may be performed under reduced pressure conditions. [0024] In certain embodiments, the electrode layers define an active area selected based on design requirements. The anode and cathode dimensions may be configured such that the anode extends beyond the cathode perimeter to ensure complete overlap and uniform electrochemical interaction. The dimensions and geometry of the electrodes may vary depending on application requirements and manufacturing considerations. [0025] During operation, lithium ions migrate through the electrolyte and separator between the cathode and anode, while electrons flow through an external circuit, as schematically illustrated in Figure 1. The layered structural configuration enables reversible electrochemical intercalation processes for energy storage and release. [0026] In alternative embodiments, the current collectors may comprise other conductive materials including nickel, stainless steel, or coated metallic foils. The separator may include multilayer, composite, or ceramic-coated configurations. The enclosure may alternatively comprise rigid or semi-rigid housings including prismatic or cylindrical formats. The electrode coatings may be applied on one or both sides of the respective current collectors, and multiple stacked layers may be employed to form multi-layer cell architectures. [0027] It will be understood that the configuration illustrated in Figure 1 is exemplary, and various modifications, substitutions, and structural variations may be implemented without departing from the scope of the disclosure. [0028] Figure 2 illustrates the complete fabrication process flow for the 3500 mAh single-layer pouch cell embodiment of the lithium-ion battery system of the present disclosure. The figure depicts two parallel fabrication tracks, namely an upper track for the composite anode electrode and a lower track for the cathode electrode, which converge at the assembly and electrochemical testing stages. Each step in the process flow corresponds to a distinct manufacturing operation that, taken together, enables the complete lithium-ion battery system as disclosed herein. All steps illustrated in Figure 2 are performed at an ambient temperature in the range of 25°C to 30°C and a relative humidity of less than 55%, without requiring a dry-room facility, an inert atmosphere, or any specialised humidity control infrastructure. [0029] The upper track of Figure 2 begins with the identification of the five functionally distinct active materials that together constitute the composite anode electrode of the present disclosure. The anode composition illustrated in Figure 2 comprises graphite, lithium titanate (Li₄Ti₅O₁₂), aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) nanoparticles, silicon nanoparticles, and reduced graphene oxide, collectively referred to herein as the five-component composite anode. The cathode component is identified in Figure 2 as rGO@NMC₅₃₂, indicating that in one embodiment the nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide active material of the stoichiometric composition NMC532 is combined with reduced graphene oxide as a conductive additive. [0030] In one embodiment, the composite anode electrode may comprise graphite particles at 61 weight percent serving as the primary lithium-ion intercalation host material. The graphite particles serve as the dominant capacity-providing component of the composite anode electrode, accepting and releasing lithium ions reversibly during charge and discharge cycles. In another embodiment, lithium titanate (Li₄Ti₅O₁₂) may be present at 18 weight percent as a zero-volumetric-strain fast-charge sublattice material. The lithium titanate sublattice may operate at a fixed electrochemical intercalation plateau of approximately 1.55 volts measured against a lithium metal reference electrode and may exhibit a volumetric strain of approximately 0.2% during lithiation and delithiation. This near-zero volumetric strain characteristic of the lithium titanate sublattice is a critical structural feature that enables the composite anode electrode to accept charge currents of 5 to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity, corresponding to full charge times of 12 minutes to 10 minutes respectively, without any risk of metallic lithium nucleation or deposition at any state of charge during said charging. [0031] In one embodiment, silicon nanoparticles may be present at 5 weight percent as a secondary high-capacity lithium-ion intercalation material. The silicon nanoparticles may provide significantly higher theoretical specific capacity relative to graphite, and their nanoparticulate morphology may limit the absolute volumetric expansion during lithiation, thereby reducing mechanical stress on the composite anode electrode structure. In a further embodiment, reduced graphene oxide may be present at 7 weight percent as a three-dimensional electron-transport network and mechanical buffer additive. The reduced graphene oxide incorporated in the composite anode electrode may have an electrical conductivity in the range of 1,000 to 10,000 siemens per metre and may be thermally stable above 500°C. At this weight fraction, the reduced graphene oxide may reduce the electrical resistivity of the composite anode electrode by a factor of approximately 7 relative to a corresponding anode formulation that does not contain reduced graphene oxide, and may form a continuous three-dimensional conductive network that distributes a charge current of 21 amperes, corresponding to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity, uniformly across the active area of the composite anode electrode without localised current hotspots or voltage collapse. [0032] In one embodiment, aluminium oxide nanoparticles may be present at 2 weight percent as an artificial inorganic solid electrolyte interphase precursor. The aluminium oxide nanoparticles may have a particle diameter in the range of 5 nanometres to 50 nanometres, a melting point of at least 2,072°C, and may be chemically inert with respect to the electrolyte within an operating voltage window of 0 volts to 4.35 volts measured against a lithium metal reference electrode. In one embodiment, the aluminium oxide nanoparticles may coat both the graphite particle surfaces and the silicon nanoparticle surfaces simultaneously during slurry preparation, thereby forming an artificial inorganic solid electrolyte interphase layer on both particle types. This simultaneous dual-surface coating may reduce the first-cycle irreversible capacity loss of the composite anode electrode from approximately 15 percent to approximately 8 percent of the initial charge capacity, representing a significant improvement in initial coulombic efficiency. [0033] The upper track of Figure 2 further illustrates the sieving of the NMC active material followed by the weighing of the PVDF binder, constituting the initial preparation steps for the cathode electrode. In one embodiment, the NMC powder may be sieved prior to weighing to remove agglomerates and to ensure a uniform particle size distribution suitable for homogeneous slurry preparation. The PVDF binder may be weighed separately and may subsequently be dissolved in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone solvent prior to the mixing step. In one embodiment, the cathode electrode may comprise nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide in the stoichiometric composition NMC532 at 82 weight percent, reduced graphene oxide at 6 weight percent as a conductive additive, carbon black at 4 weight percent, and polyvinylidene fluoride binder at 8 weight percent. [0034] Following preparation of the composite anode slurry and its application onto the current collector, Figure 2 illustrates a drying step in the upper track. In one embodiment, the composite anode electrode coating, once applied to the current collector, may be dried to remove the aqueous carrier medium from the water-based binder system. The composite anode electrode may be prepared from an aqueous slurry comprising graphite particles, lithium titanate, silicon nanoparticles, reduced graphene oxide, aluminium oxide nanoparticles, and a water-based binder system comprising carboxymethyl cellulose at 4 weight percent and styrene-butadiene rubber at 3 weight percent. The water-based binder system of the composite anode electrode does not require N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone solvent, which constitutes a significant processing and environmental advantage relative to conventional anode fabrication methodologies. [0035] In one embodiment, the drying step may be performed at an ambient temperature in the range of 25°C to 30°C and a relative humidity of less than 55%, without requiring a dry-room facility. It may be noted that the fabrication of a nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide cathode-based 3.5 ampere-hour lithium-ion battery capable of a charge current of 5 to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity outside a conventional dry-room environment represents the first demonstrated fabrication of this kind, the dry-room environment otherwise requiring capital investment in the range of Rs. 5 crore to Rs. 20 crore. This ambient-condition fabricability constitutes a central feature of the present disclosure and distinguishes the disclosed battery system from all prior art identified in the structured review of more than 500 peer-reviewed research articles published between 2001 and 2025. [0036] The lower track of Figure 2 begins with a material characterization step designated as solid-state material characterization. The illustrated components in this step include reduced graphene oxide, carbon black, and NMC active material, which are shown being combined in a manner indicative of solid-state mixing or pre-characterization operations. In one embodiment, each material may undergo characterization techniques that may include but are not limited to X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, or Raman spectroscopy, to confirm material identity, crystallinity, morphology, and purity prior to electrode fabrication. [0037] This characterization step may ensure that the reduced graphene oxide incorporated into the cathode electrode possesses the electrical conductivity in the range of 1,000 to 10,000 siemens per metre and the thermal stability above 500°C required for high-rate electrode operation. The dual-electrode reduced graphene oxide configuration, wherein reduced graphene oxide is present simultaneously in both the composite anode electrode at 7 weight percent and in the cathode electrode at 6 weight percent, is a central feature of the present disclosure. In one embodiment, the reduced graphene oxide at 6 weight percent in the cathode electrode may improve cathode electrical conductivity by a factor of approximately 80 relative to a corresponding cathode formulation that does not contain reduced graphene oxide, enabling the cathode electrode to accept and deliver the charge and discharge currents specified herein without excessive polarisation losses. [0038] Figure 2 depicts a mixing step in the lower track, illustrating a mechanical mixer or overhead stirrer apparatus combining the NMP solvent, PVDF binder, and cathode active materials into a homogeneous cathode slurry. In one embodiment, the cathode slurry may be prepared by first dissolving the PVDF binder in NMP solvent to form a homogeneous binder solution, followed by addition of NMC532 active material, reduced graphene oxide, and carbon black conductive additive to the binder solution, and subsequent mixing under controlled conditions to achieve a uniform, homogeneous slurry suitable for coating. The mixing step enables uniform dispersion of all cathode components within the slurry, including NMC532 at 82 weight percent, reduced graphene oxide at 6 weight percent, carbon black at 4 weight percent, and polyvinylidene fluoride at 8 weight percent. It may be noted that unlike the composite anode electrode, which employs a water-based binder system comprising carboxymethyl cellulose and styrene-butadiene rubber and requires no N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, the cathode electrode in one embodiment may employ polyvinylidene fluoride dissolved in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone as the binder system, consistent with established cathode processing practices for nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide active materials. [0039] Following the mixing step, Figure 2 illustrates a coating step wherein the cathode slurry is cast onto a current collector substrate using a doctor blade or slot-die coating apparatus, as depicted in the figure. In one embodiment, the current collector for the cathode electrode may comprise an aluminium foil. The coating may be applied to one or both surfaces of the current collector depending on the cell architecture and capacity requirements of the specific embodiment. The coating step may enable the cathode electrode to be formed with the precise composition described herein, and with the active electrode area required to support the ionic flux of 21 amperes across a combined active electrode area of approximately 1,600 square centimetres at a charge current of 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity. [0040] Following the coating step, the cathode electrode undergoes a drying step as illustrated in the lower track of Figure 2. In one embodiment, the drying step may remove the N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone solvent from the cathode coating, leaving behind a dense, adherent cathode electrode film on the aluminium current collector. The drying may be performed under conditions compatible with the ambient-temperature fabrication approach of the present disclosure. [0041] Following the independent fabrication of the composite anode electrode via the upper track and the cathode electrode via the lower track, Figure 2 illustrates the convergence of the two tracks at the assembly step. In one embodiment, the assembly of the lithium-ion battery system may comprise positioning the porous separator between the composite anode electrode and the cathode electrode. The separator thickness of approximately 22 micrometres is consistent with commercially available polyolefin-based porous polymeric separators that provide the requisite electrical insulation while maintaining sufficient ionic permeability to sustain the lithium-ion flux of 21 amperes corresponding to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity across the combined active electrode area of approximately 1,600 square centimetres during fast charging. [0083] The lower centre sub-panel of Figure 9 presents a histogram of the phase value distribution across the full microstructural volume of the lithium-ion battery system. In one embodiment, the phase value distribution histogram may be observed to exhibit a broad and approximately unimodal distribution centred in the mid-phase value range, with a high-frequency tail extending toward phase values approaching 1.0, consistent with the multi-component nature of the lithium-ion battery system disclosed herein. The upper right sub-panel of Figure 9 presents a horizontal bar chart comparing the target porosity and the actual measured porosity for each of the three layers. In one embodiment, the composite anode electrode may be observed to have a target porosity of approximately 0.35 to 0.40 and an actual measured porosity closely consistent with this target value. The porous separator may be observed to have a target porosity of approximately 0.40 to 0.45 and an actual measured porosity closely consistent with this target. The close agreement between target and actual porosity values for all three layers confirms the process control and reproducibility of the ambient-temperature fabrication process disclosed herein. [0084] The lower right sub-panel of Figure 9 presents a pie chart illustrating the volumetric distribution of the three layers of the lithium-ion battery system, with the composite anode electrode occupying approximately 43.1 percent of the total cell volume, the cathode electrode occupying approximately 45.7 percent of the total cell volume, and the porous separator occupying approximately 11.2 percent of the total cell volume. [0085] The lithium-ion battery system of the present disclosure may offer several significant advantages over prior art battery systems, as supported by the experimental data, electrochemical characterisation, and microstructural analysis presented herein. [0086] In one embodiment, a primary advantage of the present disclosure resides in the elimination of the dry-room fabrication requirement for a high-performance nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide cathode-based lithium-ion battery system capable of fast charging. The complete fabrication of the 3.5 ampere-hour pouch cell at ambient temperature in the range of 25°C to 30°C and relative humidity below 55%, without a dry-room facility otherwise requiring capital investment in the range of Rs. 5 crore to Rs. 20 crore, may substantially reduce the manufacturing infrastructure cost and enable fabrication in standard laboratory or production environments without specialised humidity-controlled infrastructure. This ambient-condition fabricability, confirmed by the microstructural integrity data presented in Figure 9 and the electrochemical performance data presented in Figures 3 through 8, represents the first demonstrated fabrication of an NMC532-based 3.5 ampere-hour lithium-ion battery capable of 5 to 6 amperes per ampere-hour charge rate outside a conventional dry-room environment. [0087] In one embodiment, a further advantage of the present disclosure resides in the five-component composite anode electrode design, wherein the synergistic combination of graphite at 61 weight percent, lithium titanate at 18 weight percent, silicon nanoparticles at 5 weight percent, reduced graphene oxide at 7 weight percent, and aluminium oxide nanoparticles at 2 weight percent within a single electrode may simultaneously deliver high gravimetric energy density of at least 195 watt-hours per kilogram, fast-charge capability at 5 to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity corresponding to full charge times of 12 minutes or less as confirmed in Figure 7, extended cycle life projecting greater than 80 percent capacity retention at 3,000 cycles as supported by the capacity retention data of Figure 8, and complete elimination of metallic lithium deposition risk at any state of charge during charging or discharging by virtue of the lithium titanate sublattice operating at its fixed intercalation plateau of 1.55 volts versus a lithium reference electrode. [0088] In one embodiment, a further advantage may reside in the dual-electrode reduced graphene oxide configuration, wherein reduced graphene oxide present simultaneously in both the composite anode electrode at 7 weight percent and the cathode electrode at 6 weight percent provides a factor of approximately 7 reduction in composite anode electrode resistivity and a factor of approximately 80 improvement in cathode electrode conductivity, collectively enabling the uniform distribution of charge currents of up to 21 amperes across the active electrode area without localised current hotspots, voltage collapse, or excessive polarisation losses, as confirmed by the smooth and continuous constant-current charging profiles observable in Figure 7 at all five charge rate conditions from 1C to 5C. [0089] In one embodiment, a further advantage may reside in the triple-layer solid electrolyte interphase protection system of the composite anode electrode, wherein the reduced graphene oxide mechanical buffer layer, the aluminium oxide nanoparticle artificial inorganic solid electrolyte interphase layer formed by scalable slurry mixing without requiring atomic layer deposition or vapour-phase coating processes, and the fluoroethylene carbonate and vinylene carbonate derived organic-inorganic protective films collectively limit direct current internal resistance growth to approximately 0.5 milliohms per 100 cycles, as illustrated by the internal resistance profile of Figure 4. This represents a six-fold improvement over unprotected silicon-containing anode systems and supports the capacity retention performance observable in Figure 8. [0090] In one embodiment, a further advantage may reside in the broad operating temperature stability of the lithium-ion battery system, wherein the well-defined and monotonically increasing open-circuit voltage versus state of charge relationship confirmed across the temperature range of −10°C to 55°C in Figure 3, including at the elevated temperatures of 45°C to 55°C generated during fast charging at 5 to 6 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity, confirms the thermal and electrochemical stability of the advanced electrolyte formulation across a wide operational temperature window relevant to both consumer and industrial applications. [0091] The lithium-ion battery system of the present disclosure may find application across a wide range of fields requiring high energy density, fast-charging capability, extended cycle life, and thermally stable operation. [0092] In one embodiment, the lithium-ion battery system may find application in electric vehicles and hybrid electric vehicles, wherein the fast-charge capability corresponding to full charge times of 12 minutes or less at 5 amperes per ampere-hour of rated cell capacity, the gravimetric energy density of at least 195 watt-hours per kilogram, and the projected cycle life of greater than 80 percent capacity retention at 3,000 cycles may address the key requirements of driving range, charge time, and battery pack longevity for automotive applications. [0093] In one embodiment, the lithium-ion battery system may find application in portable consumer electronics including smartphones, laptop computers, tablet computers, and wearable devices, wherein the combination of high gravimetric energy density and fast-charging capability of 12 minutes or less at 5C corresponding to 17.5 amperes may enable extended device operation with significantly reduced charging duration relative to conventional lithium-ion battery systems. patents.abstract: A Cell-Level Predictive Thermal Runaway Detection System with Embedded Analysis and Risk-Based Diagnostic Generation for Lithium-Ion Battery Packs. The present invention relates to a system for detecting thermal anomalies in lithium-ion battery packs using cell-level temperature monitoring. The system comprises a plurality of temperature sensors, an embedded control unit, a signal processing and feature extraction module, a predictive analysis module, a diagnostic generation module, a risk classification module, and a communication interface. The system processes temperature data to extract thermal features and evaluates thermal behavior using a predictive model to identify abnormal conditions prior to threshold violation. Predictive diagnostic trouble codes and associated risk levels are generated and transmitted to a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard for display and logging. The invention enables real-time embedded monitoring and early detection of thermal anomalies without reliance on external processing systems. (FIG. 1)
patents.complete_specification: Description:TECHNICAL FIELD [0001] The present invention relates to battery management systems and embedded diagnostic technologies for electric vehicles. More particularly, the invention relates to a cell-level predictive thermal monitoring system configured to detect abnormal thermal behavior in lithium-ion battery packs using embedded analysis and to generate predictive diagnostic outputs with risk classification. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION [0002] Lithium-ion battery packs used in electric vehicles are susceptible to thermal anomalies that may lead to thermal runaway, resulting in safety hazards and performance degradation. Conventional battery management systems primarily rely on threshold-based monitoring of temperature and voltage parameters, which detect faults only after a predefined limit is exceeded. [0003] Existing approaches employing machine learning or data-driven techniques for battery monitoring are generally implemented in external computing environments and are not integrated within embedded control units. Further, such approaches do not provide structured mechanisms for generating predictive diagnostic outputs prior to threshold violation or for classifying risk levels associated with detected anomalies. [0004] Additionally, existing systems typically monitor battery packs at an aggregate level rather than at an individual cell level, thereby limiting early detection of localized thermal events. There is therefore a need for an embedded system capable of real-time cell-level monitoring, predictive analysis of thermal behavior, and generation of actionable diagnostic information prior to occurrence of critical conditions. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION [0005] The present invention provides a cell-level predictive thermal runaway detection system configured for lithium-ion battery packs of electric vehicles. [0006] An object of the invention is to provide a system capable of acquiring real-time temperature data from individual battery cells using a plurality of cell temperature sensors. [0007] Another object of the invention is to provide a signal processing and feature extraction mechanism for deriving thermal indicators including rate of temperature rise, deviation from pack-level average temperature, and duration above a predefined threshold. [0008] A further object of the invention is to provide a predictive analysis module implemented within an embedded control unit for evaluating thermal behavior of battery cells. [0009] Another object of the invention is to provide a diagnostic generation mechanism for generating predictive diagnostic trouble codes prior to exceeding a predefined thermal runaway threshold. [0010] A further object of the invention is to provide a risk classification mechanism for categorizing detected thermal anomalies into predefined severity levels. [0011] Another object of the invention is to provide a communication interface for transmitting diagnostic information to a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard. [0012] A further object of the invention is to provide a system capable of real-time embedded operation without reliance on external processing infrastructure. [0013] The invention achieves these objectives through integration of cell-level sensing, embedded signal processing, predictive analysis, diagnostic generation, and risk classification within a unified architecture, thereby enabling early detection of thermal anomalies and improved safety in battery-operated electric vehicles. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0014] FIG. 1 illustrates a cell-level predictive thermal runaway detection system comprising a plurality of cell temperature sensors, an embedded control unit, a signal processing and feature extraction module, a predictive analysis module, a diagnostic generation module, a risk classification module, a communication interface, and a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard configured for real-time monitoring and diagnostic reporting. [0015] FIG. 2 illustrates a predictive thermal fault detection workflow including acquisition of cell temperature data, preprocessing and validation of signals, extraction of thermal features including rate of temperature rise, deviation from pack-level average, and duration above threshold, evaluation of thermal behavior using a predictive model, identification of abnormal thermal conditions, generation of predictive diagnostic trouble codes, classification of risk levels, transmission via a communication interface, and display and logging of faults. DETAILED DESCRIPTION [0016] The present invention relates to a predictive thermal runaway detection system for a lithium-ion battery pack of a two-wheeler electric vehicle, configured to detect abnormal thermal behavior at a cell level and generate predictive diagnostic outputs prior to occurrence of a thermal runaway condition. [0017] Referring to FIG. 1, the system comprises a plurality of cell temperature sensors (100), an embedded control unit (110), a signal processing and feature extraction module (120), a predictive analysis module (130), a diagnostic generation module (140), a risk classification module (150), a communication interface (160), and a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard (170). [0018] The cell temperature sensors (100) are configured to measure temperature values of individual battery cells in real time. In one embodiment, the sensors are positioned at multiple locations across the battery pack to enable cell-level monitoring. The sensed temperature data is transmitted to the embedded control unit (110). [0019] The embedded control unit (110) is configured as an automotive-grade microcontroller-based system capable of performing real-time processing under resource constraints. The embedded control unit (110) receives temperature data from the sensors and forwards the data to the signal processing and feature extraction module (120). [0020] The signal processing and feature extraction module (120) is configured to preprocess and normalize the received temperature signals and to derive thermal features indicative of cell behavior. The derived features include rate of temperature rise over a predefined time interval, deviation of a cell temperature from an average temperature of the battery pack, and duration for which a cell temperature exceeds a predefined warning threshold. [0021] The predictive analysis module (130) is configured to evaluate the derived thermal features using a predictive model to identify patterns associated with abnormal thermal behavior. The predictive analysis module operates within the embedded control unit and processes data in real time without reliance on external computing infrastructure. [0022] In one embodiment, the predictive analysis module is implemented within the embedded control unit [0023] The diagnostic generation module (140) is configured to generate a predictive diagnostic trouble code corresponding to a battery cell exhibiting abnormal thermal behavior. The diagnostic trouble code is generated prior to the cell temperature exceeding a predefined thermal runaway threshold. [0024] The risk classification module (150) is configured to assign a risk level to the detected abnormal condition. In one embodiment, the risk levels include medium risk, high risk, and critical risk. The classification is based on severity of the thermal behavior and associated predictive indicators. [0025] The communication interface (160) is configured to transmit the predictive diagnostic trouble code and associated risk classification to a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard (170). In one embodiment, the communication interface comprises a controller area network (CAN) interface or a universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART) interface. [0026] The secondary electronic control unit or dashboard (170) is configured to receive the transmitted diagnostic information and display fault status, cell identification, and associated risk level to a user. The system may further log the diagnostic information for subsequent analysis. [0027] Referring to FIG. 2, the operational workflow of the system is illustrated. The system acquires cell temperature data from the sensors and preprocesses and validates the signals to remove noise and ensure signal consistency. Thermal features are extracted from the processed signals, including rate of temperature rise, deviation from pack-level average temperature, and duration above a predefined threshold. [0028] The extracted thermal features are evaluated using a predictive model to assess thermal behavior of individual cells. Based on the evaluation, abnormal thermal conditions are identified prior to occurrence of a threshold violation. Upon detection of such abnormal conditions, a predictive diagnostic trouble code is generated corresponding to the affected cell. [0029] The system then classifies the identified condition into a predefined risk level based on severity of the predicted thermal behavior. The predictive diagnostic trouble code and associated risk classification are transmitted via a communication interface to a secondary electronic control unit or dashboard, where the fault is displayed and logged. [0030] In one embodiment, the system operates using a combination of predictive analysis and threshold-based validation to improve reliability of fault detection. The system enables early identification of thermal anomalies and provides real-time diagnostic information for preventive action. [0031] The described system provides a cell-level predictive monitoring framework integrated within an embedded control unit, enabling real-time detection of abnormal thermal behavior, predictive diagnostic generation, and risk-based classification without reliance on external processing systems. [0032] Although the invention has been described with reference to specific modules and operational steps, it will be understood that variations and modifications may be made without departing from the scope of the invention as defined in the appended claims. , Claims:I/We Claim: 1. A predictive thermal runaway detection system for a lithium-ion battery pack of a two-wheeler electric vehicle comprising a plurality of cell-level temperature sensors configured to acquire real-time temperature data from individual battery cells; an embedded control unit configured to receive the temperature data and perform signal processing including extraction of derived thermal features comprising rate of temperature rise, deviation from pack-level average temperature, and duration of operation above a predefined warning threshold; a predictive analysis module implemented within the embedded control unit and configured to analyze the derived thermal features to identify abnormal thermal behavior prior to exceeding a predefined thermal runaway threshold; a diagnostic generation module configured to generate a predictive diagnostic trouble code associated with a corresponding battery cell before occurrence of a threshold violation; a risk classification module configured to classify the identified abnormal thermal behavior into predefined risk levels; and a communication interface configured to transmit the predictive diagnostic trouble code and associated risk classification to a secondary electronic control unit for real-time display and logging. 2. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the embedded control unit comprises a resource-constrained automotive-grade microcontroller configured for real-time processing. 3. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the predictive analysis module comprises a machine learning-based model configured to evaluate thermal behavior of individual battery cells. 4. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the derived thermal features include rate of temperature rise calculated over a predefined time window. 5. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the risk classification module classifies thermal conditions into multiple levels including medium, high, and critical risk. 6. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the predictive diagnostic trouble code includes cell identification, fault type, and associated risk level. 7. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the communication interface comprises a controller area network or universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter interface. 8. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the system is configured to generate predictive diagnostic trouble codes prior to exceeding a predefined temperature threshold. 9. The system as claimed in claim 1, further comprising a secondary electronic control unit configured to receive transmitted diagnostic information and display fault status and risk level to a user. 10. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein the system operates using a hybrid predictive and threshold-based fault detection mechanism.
