patents.abstract: High-Performance Lithium-Sulfur Battery with Carbon Nanotube Reinforced Sulfur Cathode Abstract The present invention discloses a high-performance lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery employing a carbon nanotube (CNT) reinforced sulfur cathode for enhanced electrochemical performance and long-term stability. The cathode comprises 70-80 wt.% sulfur uniformly embedded within a conductive CNT network possessing a specific surface area of 450-650 m2 g_I. The developed battery delivers an initial specific discharge capacity of 1450-1650 mAh g“J at 0.1 C and retains more than 88% of its capacity after 500 charge­discharge cycles. The CNT framework improves electrical conductivity to approximately 12-18 S cmH and effectively suppresses polysulfide dissolution. The cell exhibits a coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.2% and an energy density of 420-520 Wh kg-1. The reinforced cathode architecture enables sulfur utilization above 85% while maintaining excellent rate capability up to 5 C. The invention provides a cost-effective and scalable approach for developing next­generation high-energy-density rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and grid-scale energy storage applications.
patents.complete_specification: BACKGROUND OF INVENTION The present invention relates to the field of electrochemical energy storage devices and, more specifically, to lithium-sulfur battery technology employing a carbon nanotube reinforced sulfur cathode for achieving high energy density, improved electrochemical stability, and enhanced cycle performance. The invention is directed toward overcoming the limitations associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries and existing lithium-sulfur battery systems by developing a cathode architecture that facilitates efficient electron transport, improved sulfur utilization, and suppression of polysulfide migration during battery operation The increasing consumption of energy throughout the world has generated a strong demand for advanced energy storage technologies capable of delivering higher performance than currently available battery systems. The widespread adoption of electric vehicles, portable electronic devices, medical equipment, aerospace systems, renewable energy installations, and smart grid networks requires rechargeable batteries with high energy density, long service life, fast charging capability, and reliable operational stability. 109-Jun-2026/85362/202641071453/Form 2(Title Page) Although lithium-ion batteries have achieved remarkable commercial success over the past several decades, their energy storage capacity is approaching the theoretical limits of the cathode materials commonly used in commercial cells. This limitation has encouraged researchers and industrial manufacturers to investigate alternative battery chemistries that can provide significantly greater energy storage capabilities while maintaining economic viability and environmental sustainability [1-3]. Among the various next-generation battery technologies under investigation, lithium­sulfur batteries have emerged as one of the most promising candidates due to their exceptionally high theoretical specific capacity and energy density. Sulfur possesses a theoretical specific capacity of approximately 1675 mAh g_1 and offers a theoretical energy density substantially higher than that of conventional lithium-ion battery cathode materials. In addition, sulfur is naturally abundant, inexpensive, environmentally friendly, and readily available from industrial processes. These advantages make sulfur an attractive active material for the development of cost-effective and high-performance rechargeable batteries suitable for large-scale applications. Consequently, significant research efforts have been devoted to the development of lithium-sulfur battery systems capable of meeting future energy storage requirements [4-7]. Despite their attractive characteristics, lithium-sulfur batteries continue to face several technical challenges that restrict their commercial implementation. One of the major obstacles arises from the intrinsically low electrical conductivity of elemental sulfur and its lithiation products. Sulfur is an electrical insulator, and this poor conductivity hinders efficient electron transfer during electrochemical reactions. As a result, only a fraction of the active sulfur material may participate effectively in charge storage processes, leading to reduced capacity utilization and lower overall battery performance. The conductivity limitation becomes even more significant at high sulfur loading levels, where charge transport pathways become increasingly restricted [8-10]. Another significant challenge associated with lithium-sulfur batteries is the formation and dissolution of intermediate lithium polysulfide species during battery operation. During discharge, sulfur undergoes a series of electrochemical conversion reactions that produce soluble lithium polysulfides. These intermediates can dissolve into the electrolyte and migrate between the cathode and anode. 209-Jun-2026/85362/202641071453/Form 2(Title Page) The continuous movement of polysulfides leads to active material loss and causes the well-known shuttle effect. The shuttle effect results in self-discharge, reduced coulombic efficiency, increased internal resistance, and rapid capacity degradation over repeated charge­discharge cycles. The uncontrolled migration of polysulfides remains one of the primary factors limiting the practical lifespan and efficiency of lithium-sulfur batteries [11]. A further challenge is associated with the substantial volume variation experienced by sulfur during electrochemical cycling. When sulfur reacts with lithium ions, significant structural expansion occurs within the cathode material. The repeated expansion and contraction of sulfur particles generate mechanical stress within the electrode structure, leading to cracking, pulverization, and eventual loss of electrical contact between active materials and conductive components. These structural changes contribute to progressive deterioration of battery performance and reduced cycle life. Therefore, maintaining the structural integrity of sulfur-based cathodes throughout prolonged operation is essential for achieving reliable and durable battery systems [12-13]. To address these limitations, researchers have explored numerous cathode engineering strategies involving conductive carbon materials, porous frameworks, metal oxides, metal sulfides, conductive polymers, and hybrid nanostructures. Various forms of carbon materials, including activated carbon, mesoporous carbon, graphene, carbon nanofibers, and carbon aerogels, have been investigated as sulfur host matrices. These materials provide conductive pathways and porous structures capable of accommodating sulfur and partially restricting polysulfide migration. Although such approaches have demonstrated improvements in battery performance, many existing systems still suffer from insufficient conductivity, inadequate polysulfide confinement, complex fabrication procedures, or limited long-term stability. Consequently, there remains a need for advanced cathode structures that can simultaneously enhance conductivity, improve sulfur utilization, and maintain structural durability [14]. Carbon nanotubes have attracted considerable attention as promising materials for advanced battery applications due to their unique combination of electrical, mechanical, and structural properties. Carbon nanotubes exhibit excellent electrical conductivity, high aspect ratio, superior mechanical strength, and remarkable chemical stability. Their nanoscale tubular structure enables the formation of interconnected conductive networks capable of facilitating rapid electron transport throughout the cathode. 3Furthermore, carbon nanotubes possess large surface areas that can support uniform sulfur dispersion and improve the accessibility of electrochemically active sites. These characteristics make carbon nanotubes highly suitable for incorporation into sulfur-based cathodes. The integration of carbon nanotubes within sulfur cathodes offers multiple benefits that directly address the key challenges of lithium-sulfur battery technology. The conductive nanotube network provides continuous pathways for electron transport, thereby reducing charge transfer resistance and enhancing electrochemical reaction kinetics. Simultaneously, the porous and interconnected architecture of carbon nano tubes can physically confine sulfur and intermediate polysulfides within the cathode structure. This confinement helps reduce polysulfide dissolution and suppresses shuttle-related capacity losses. In addition, the mechanical flexibility of carbon nanotubes enables the cathode to accommodate volumetric expansion during cycling, thereby preserving structural integrity and maintaining electrical connectivity over extended operational periods [15]. Although several studies have reported carbon nanotube-based sulfur composites, many existing designs fail to achieve an optimal balance between sulfur loading, conductivity enhancement, polysulfide immobilization, and mechanical stability. In many cases, limited sulfur content reduces practical energy density, while insufficient interaction between sulfur and the conductive framework results in gradual performance degradation. Moreover, some fabrication methods require expensive materials, specialized equipment, or complicated processing techniques that limit scalability and industrial adoption. These batteries provide reliable performance, high operating voltage, and relatively long cycle life. However, the energy density of conventional lithium-ion batteries is approaching the practical limits imposed by commonly used cathode materials such as lithium cobalt oxide, lithium manganese oxide, and lithium iron phosphate. As modem applications demand greater energy storage capacity, researchers have increasingly focused on alternative battery chemistries capable of delivering significantly higher specific energy while maintaining acceptable safety, cost, and durability characteristics. Among these alternatives, lithium-sulfur batteries have emerged as promising candidates due to the exceptionally high theoretical capacity of sulfur and the abundance of sulfur resources. Early lithium—sulfur battery systems utilized elemental sulfur directly as the cathode material because of its high theoretical specific capacity and low cost. While these systems demonstrated substantial energy storage potential, practical implementation was limited by several intrinsic material challenges. Sulfur possesses extremely low electrical conductivity, which restricts electron transport within the cathode and reduces the utilization of active material during electrochemical reactions. As a result, batteries employing pure sulfur cathodes often exhibited low rate capability, poor power performance, and significant capacity loss during repeated cycling. 7 H p p T p p p U p M h !■ 7'-J p s .> p! c ? ■'; | j Z p-i p „ .To address conductivity limitations, various conductive carbon materials were investigated as sulfur host structures. However, the irregular pore structure and limited conductivity of activated carbon often resulted in insufficient sulfur confinement and moderate electrochemical performance. Although some improvements in capacity retention were achieved, long-term cycling stability remained inadequate for practical applications. These materials possess well-defined pore structures capable of accommodating sulfur within interconnected channels. Several studies reported improved sulfur utilization and better capacity retention using mesoporous carbon structures. Nevertheless, the physical confinement provided by mesoporous carbon alone was often insufficient to completely suppress polysulfide migration, particularly at high sulfur loading levels. Consequently, capacity fading continued to occur over extended charge-discharge cycles. Graphene-based materials have also been extensively investigated as conductive hosts for sulfur cathodes. Owing to their high electrical conductivity, large specific surface area, and mechanical flexibility, graphene sheets can create conductive networks that improve electron transport throughout the cathode. Researchers developed graphene-sulfur composites using various synthesis approaches to enhance sulfur distribution and increase active material utilization. While graphene-based cathodes demonstrated promising electrochemical properties, challenges associated with sheet restacking, limited sulfur loading, and relatively complex fabrication procedures restricted their large-scale applicability. In many cases, the interaction between sulfur species and graphene surfaces was not sufficiently strong to prevent long-term polysulfide dissolution. Carbon nanofibers have likewise been explored as conductive frameworks for lithium­sulfur battery cathodes. Their elongated morphology and interconnected structure provide efficient pathways for electron transport while offering mechanical reinforcement to the electrode. In addition to carbon­based materials, researchers have investigated metal oxide additives such as titanium dioxide, manganese dioxide, aluminum oxide, and silicon dioxide to improve sulfur cathode performance. These materials possess polar surfaces capable of interacting with lithium polysulfides through chemical adsorption mechanisms. By anchoring polysulfides within the cathode structure, metal oxides can reduce active material loss and improve cycling stability. Despite these advantages, many metal oxides exhibit relatively low electrical conductivity, which can negatively affect charge transfer kinetics and reduce rate capability. Materials such as molybdenum, disulfide, cobalt sulfide, nickel sulfide, titanium nitride, and vanadium nitride exhibit strong chemical affinity toward polysulfides while simultaneously providing improved electrical conductivity. These materials demonstrated enhanced catalytic activity and accelerated sulfur conversion reactions. However, their synthesis frequently involves complex preparation techniques, expensive precursors, and strict processing conditions, which may increase manufacturing costs and limit large-scale commercialization. patents.abstract: “STAGGERED CELL ARRANGEMENT SYSTEM FOR ENHANCED NATURAL CONVECTION THERMAL MANAGEMENT IN LITHIUM-ION BATTERY” A passive battery thermal management system comprises a plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells arranged in a staggered configuration of alternating rows offset laterally by half of a transverse pitch ($St/2$) to form a triangular lattice pattern defining passive natural convection cooling channels. The staggered configuration is defined by a transverse pitch ratio ($St/d$) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio ($Sl/d$) of 1.19. The cooling channels direct ambient air along a tortuous path to disrupt thermal boundary layers, induce localized vortex structures, and eliminate thermal wake effects. This configuration reduces peak cell temperatures, improves temperature uniformity across the pack, and increases effective thermal resistance between adjacent cells to passively delay thermal runaway propagation. patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION 1. The present disclosure relates generally to the field of battery thermal management systems (BTMS) for electrochemical energy storage applications, and more particularly to passive thermal management architectures for high-density cylindrical lithium-ion battery packs. Specifically, the disclosure relates to passive natural convection cooling systems designed to optimize heat dissipation, minimize peak operating temperatures, and maintain temperature uniformity across multi-cell battery assemblies, particularly for electric vehicle applications and other high-discharge operating environments. 2. More specifically, the present disclosure relates to the geometric optimization of cell positioning within a battery pack to enhance convective heat transfer. This technical domain encompasses the design of staggered, non-inline cell arrangements configured to disrupt thermal boundary layers, induce localized vortex structures, and eliminate thermal wake effects in the inter-cell spaces. The disclosure focuses on the configuration of specific transverse and longitudinal pitch ratios that define a tortuous flow path for ambient air through a triangular lattice pattern, thereby enhancing the effective heat transfer coefficient under natural convection conditions without the integration of active cooling components such as fans, pumps, or liquid circulation subsystems. 3. Furthermore, the present disclosure pertains to systems and methods for mitigating and containing thermal runaway propagation within multi-cell battery assemblies. By geometrically optimizing the spatial relationships and increasing the effective thermal resistance between adjacent cylindrical cells, the system establishes a passive containment mechanism that delays the propagation of thermal runaway events from a compromised cell to neighboring cells. The technical field also extends to the validation of these geometric and thermal parameters through computational thermal simulation models, utilizing natural convection correlations and array correction factors to predict and optimize pack-level thermal performance and safety. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION 4. The present disclosure relates generally to battery thermal management systems (BTMS) for electric vehicle applications, and more particularly to passive natural convection cooling systems utilizing optimized cell arrangements to enhance heat dissipation and contain thermal runaway propagation in cylindrical lithium-ion battery packs. Lithium-ion batteries have become the dominant energy storage technology for electric vehicles; however, maintaining these batteries within an optimal temperature range is critical for safety and longevity. Operating temperatures exceeding 45°C are known to accelerate capacity degradation, whereas temperatures exceeding 60°C drastically elevate the risk of catastrophic thermal runaway. Conventional thermal management approaches predominantly rely on active cooling methods, such as liquid circulation loops, forced air convection, and thermoelectric systems, or passive methods utilizing phase change materials (PCMs) and standard inline cell arrangements. 5. Various attempts have been made to address these thermal challenges, as evidenced by several prior art disclosures. For instance, active liquid cooling systems, such as those disclosed in US10960785B2 and US10903536B2, utilize complex circulation subsystems, onboard heat exchangers, and pumps to maintain temperature uniformity. Similarly, US8758924B2 and US8263250B2 describe liquid cooling manifolds with serpentine coolant tubes and contoured channels, which introduce significant manufacturing complexity, parasitic power consumption, and potential fluid leakage risks. To avoid the complexity of active systems, passive thermal management systems utilizing phase change materials (PCMs) have been proposed, such as in US8273474B2 and US20090004556A1. However, these PCM-based systems suffer from limited latent heat capacity, weight penalties, and material degradation over repeated thermal cycles. Furthermore, alternative approaches like US20220021046A1 focus on endothermic functionalities within battery housings to mitigate temperature rises, but fail to provide continuous, convective heat dissipation during normal high-current operations. 6. When passive natural convection is employed in conventional battery packs, the cells are typically arranged in inline (aligned) configurations. These inline arrangements suffer from severe thermal wake effects, where downstream cells are positioned directly in the heated thermal plume of upstream cells. This phenomenon leads to significant temperature non-uniformity across the pack, elevated peak temperatures that limit safe operating currents, and accelerated differential aging of downstream cells. While some staggered cell configurations have been explored to disrupt flow, they fail to optimize or validate the geometric parameters—specifically the transverse and longitudinal pitch ratios—for natural convection conditions, often focusing instead on forced air cooling. Consequently, without forced convection, these configurations do not achieve the necessary boundary layer disruption or vortex generation required to effectively dissipate heat under passive conditions. Furthermore, conventional designs do not geometrically optimize the cell spacing to delay the propagation of thermal runaway to adjacent cells. 7. In summary, the collective state of the prior art reveals several critical deficiencies. Active cooling systems introduce undesirable system complexity, parasitic power draw, and additional failure modes, while passive PCM systems introduce weight penalties and suffer from degradation. On the other hand, conventional passive natural convection systems fail to eliminate thermal wake effects, lack systematically optimized geometric parameters validated specifically for natural convection, and do not address thermal runaway propagation containment through cell spacing geometry. Therefore, there exists a critical need for an improved passive battery thermal management system and method that enhances natural convection heat transfer, eliminates thermal wake effects, improves temperature uniformity across the pack, and delays thermal runaway propagation, all without the need for active cooling components or heavy, degradable materials. OBJECTIVES 8. To reduce peak cell temperatures through enhanced natural convection heat transfer using staggered arrangement 9. To improve temperature uniformity (reduce Delta-T) across the battery pack 10. To delay thermal runaway propagation through optimized cell spacing geometry 11. To eliminate requirement for active cooling components (fans, pumps, liquid systems), reducing system complexity and parasitic power 12. To provide design parameters validated through computational thermal simulation SUMMARY 13. An object of the invention is to reduce peak cell temperatures in a cylindrical lithium-ion battery pack by utilizing a passive staggered cell arrangement that enhances natural convection heat transfer, thereby achieving an average peak temperature reduction of 5.33 deg C across a discharge current operating range of 10A to 50A. 14. Another object of the invention is to improve temperature uniformity across the battery pack by reducing the temperature gradient (Delta-T) by an average of 67.9% through continuous disruption of thermal boundary layers and the induction of vortex structures in the inter-cell spaces. 15. A further object of the invention is to delay thermal runaway propagation to neighboring cells by optimizing the cell spacing geometry, thereby increasing the time to first propagation by 96%, from 75 seconds to 147 seconds, and reducing the number of affected cells by 40% during a thermal runaway event. 16. Yet another object of the invention is to eliminate the requirement for active cooling components such as fans, pumps, and liquid circulation systems, thereby reducing system complexity, weight, and parasitic power consumption through a purely passive natural convection design. 17. Still another object of the invention is to provide systematically optimized geometric parameters for natural convection, specifically a transverse pitch ratio (St/d) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio (Sl/d) of 1.19, which establish a triangular lattice pattern that forces air through a tortuous path to eliminate thermal wake effects. 18. To achieve these objects, the present invention provides an integrated passive battery thermal management system comprising an array of cylindrical lithium-ion cells arranged in a staggered configuration. The system architecture utilizes cylindrical cells, such as 18650 format cells, positioned in alternating rows offset laterally by half the transverse pitch distance. This offset creates a triangular lattice pattern that defines passive natural convection cooling channels. The geometric parameters of the pack are optimized with a transverse pitch ratio (St/d) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio (Sl/d) of 1.19, which are specifically configured to disrupt thermal boundary layers and induce vorticity under natural convection conditions. 19. In operation, the staggered cell arrangement forces ambient air to follow a tortuous path through the battery pack. As air flows through the triangular lattice, each row of cells interrupts the thermal boundary layer developed on the preceding row, preventing the formation of thick, insulating boundary layers. Simultaneously, the staggered geometry induces vortex structures in the inter-cell spaces, which enhances convective mixing of cooler ambient air with heated air from the cell surfaces. By offsetting the downstream cells relative to the upstream cells, the thermal wake effect is eliminated, ensuring that downstream cells receive fresh cooling air rather than pre-heated air. This configuration yields an array correction factor (C_arr) of 1.25, representing a 67% relative improvement in the effective heat transfer coefficient over conventional inline arrangements. Furthermore, the geometric offset increases the effective thermal resistance between adjacent cells, which reduces the heat absorption rate of neighboring cells during a runaway event and significantly delays thermal runaway propagation. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FIGURES 20. FIG. 1 illustrates a visual comparison of inline, staggered, and honeycomb cell arrangements from thermal simulation, showing temperature reduction across all test conditions. 21. FIG. 2 illustrates the peak temperature versus discharge current for inline, staggered, and honeycomb arrangements, showing the temperature reduction of the staggered configuration compared to the inline configuration across various discharge currents. 22. FIG. 3 illustrates the staggered versus inline temperature reduction across discharge currents, further detailing the comparative thermal performance and peak temperature variations for inline, staggered, and honeycomb cell arrangements. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE DISCLOSURE 23. The present disclosure details a passive battery thermal management system utilizing an optimized staggered cell arrangement to enhance natural convection heat transfer and contain thermal runaway propagation in cylindrical lithium-ion battery packs. The system is designed to operate entirely passively, eliminating the need for active cooling components such as fans, pumps, liquid circulation loops, or complex manifolds, thereby reducing system complexity, weight, and parasitic power consumption. System Architecture and Component Specifications 24. The battery pack architecture comprises a plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells arranged in a structured array. In an exemplary embodiment, the system is configured as an 8x8 cell array containing 64 cylindrical cells. The individual cells are cylindrical lithium-ion cells, specifically of the 18650 format. Each cell possesses a nominal diameter ($d$) of 18.5 mm and a height of 65 mm. The physical and thermal properties of each cell include a mass of approximately 46 g, a specific heat capacity of 1020 J/(kg-K), an internal resistance of 45 mOhm at 25°C, and a surface emissivity of 0.85. The battery pack is designed to operate in an ambient temperature environment of approximately 25°C (298.15 K). Geometric Parameters and Spacing 25. The spatial configuration of the cells within the pack is defined by highly optimized geometric parameters. The cells are arranged in alternating rows that are offset laterally relative to one another, forming a staggered (zig-zag) configuration. This arrangement defines a triangular lattice pattern that establishes passive natural convection cooling channels. 26. The geometric spacing is characterized by a transverse pitch ($St$) of 25 mm, which represents the center-to-center distance between adjacent cells within a single row. The longitudinal pitch ($Sl$) is 22 mm, representing the center-to-center distance between cells in adjacent rows. The lateral offset between adjacent rows is exactly half of the transverse pitch, which equates to a stagger offset of 12.5 mm ($St/2$). 27. These physical dimensions yield specific, optimized pitch ratios relative to the cell diameter ($d$): 28. A Transverse Pitch Ratio ($St/d$) of 1.35. 29. A Longitudinal Pitch Ratio ($Sl/d$) of 1.19. 30. These precise ratios are systematically configured to maximize natural convection heat transfer while maintaining a high packing density. Working Principle and Heat Transfer Enhancement Mechanisms 31. The core operational principle of the staggered cell arrangement is the geometric optimization of cell positioning to enhance natural convection heat transfer. This is achieved by forcing the passively rising ambient air to follow a tortuous path through the triangular lattice of the battery pack. The heat transfer enhancement operates through three primary physical mechanisms: 32. Boundary Layer Disruption: In conventional inline arrangements, thick, insulating thermal boundary layers develop along the rows of cells, restricting heat dissipation. In the present staggered configuration, each row of cells physically interrupts the thermal boundary layer developed on the preceding row, preventing boundary layer growth and maintaining high local heat transfer rates. 33. Induced Vorticity: The staggered geometry induces localized vortex structures in the inter-cell spaces. These vortices promote convective mixing of cooler ambient air with the heated air adjacent to the cell surfaces, accelerating heat dissipation. 34. Wake Effect Elimination: In inline configurations, downstream cells reside directly within the heated thermal wake of upstream cells, leading to elevated temperatures and non-uniformity. The staggered offset ensures that downstream cells are positioned out of the direct thermal path of upstream cells, allowing each cell to receive fresh, unheated cooling air from the gaps between the cells of the previous row. 35. The convective heat transfer performance is quantified using an effective heat transfer coefficient ($h{eff}$), which incorporates an array correction factor ($C{arr}$) applied to a single-cylinder heat transfer correlation (such as the Churchill-Chu natural convection correlation). For the staggered arrangement of the present disclosure, the array correction factor ($C{arr}$) is 1.25, representing a 25% enhancement in heat transfer due to convective mixing. In contrast, a conventional inline arrangement exhibits a $C{arr}$ of 0.75, representing a 25% reduction in heat transfer due to thermal wake effects. This results in a 1.67x (or 67% relative) improvement in the effective heat transfer coefficient for the staggered configuration over the inline configuration. Thermal Runaway Propagation Containment 36. In addition to normal-operation cooling, the optimized geometric spacing serves as a passive containment mechanism to delay thermal runaway propagation. When a cell undergoes thermal runaway, it releases a substantial amount of heat. The staggered cell arrangement mitigates propagation through two primary effects: 37. Enhanced Neighboring Cell Cooling: The superior natural convection cooling of the surrounding cells keeps their baseline temperatures lower, thereby increasing their sensible heat capacity and reducing their rate of heat absorption during a runaway event. 38. Increased Thermal Resistance: The geometric offset and optimized pitch ratios increase the effective thermal resistance between adjacent cells compared to tightly packed inline configurations. 39. This combined thermal resistance and enhanced cooling delays the time to first propagation (the duration from thermal runaway initiation in a trigger cell to the onset of thermal runaway in the first neighboring cell) by 96%, extending the propagation time from 75 seconds (as observed in inline configurations) to 147 seconds. Furthermore, the total number of cells affected during a runaway event is reduced by 40%, decreasing from 64 cells to an average of 38.4 cells. Performance Validation and Comparative Analysis 40. The thermal performance of the staggered cell arrangement has been validated through computational thermal simulations utilizing the Churchill-Chu natural convection correlation over a 300-second discharge duration across five distinct discharge current levels (10A, 20A, 30A, 40A, and 50A). 41. Referring to FIG. 1, a visual comparison of inline, staggered, and honeycomb cell arrangements from thermal simulation illustrates the temperature distribution and reduction across all test conditions. The staggered configuration consistently demonstrates lower peak temperatures and superior temperature uniformity compared to the inline configuration. 42. The peak temperature ($T{max}$) performance across various discharge currents is illustrated in FIG. 2. At a low discharge current of 10A, the inline configuration reaches a $T{max}$ of 45.48°C, whereas the staggered configuration limits $T{max}$ to 44.46°C, representing a reduction of 1.02°C (5.0%). As the discharge current increases, the thermal benefits of the staggered arrangement become more pronounced. At 20A, the staggered configuration reduces $T{max}$ from 79.29°C to 76.07°C (a 3.21°C or 5.9% reduction). At 30A, $T{max}$ is reduced from 110.36°C to 104.90°C (a 5.46°C or 6.4% reduction). At 40A, the reduction is 7.54°C (6.7%), bringing $T{max}$ down from 137.76°C to 130.22°C. At the maximum test current of 50A, the staggered configuration achieves a peak temperature reduction of 9.43°C (6.9%), maintaining a $T{max}$ of 152.82°C compared to 162.25°C for the inline configuration. Across all five test conditions, the staggered arrangement achieves an average $T{max}$ reduction of 5.33°C, representing an average thermal performance improvement of 6.2%. 43. The system also significantly improves temperature uniformity across the pack, which is critical for preventing differential aging and extending battery life. Temperature uniformity is evaluated using Delta-T ($\Delta T = T {max}-T{min}$), where a lower Delta-T indicates a more uniform temperature distribution. FIG. 3 illustrates the staggered versus inline temperature reduction and comparative temperature uniformity across the discharge currents. 44. At 10A, the inline configuration exhibits a Delta-T of 0.32°C, while the staggered configuration reduces this gradient to 0.11°C, representing a 66.7% improvement. At 20A, the Delta-T is reduced from 1.03°C to 0.33°C (67.5% improvement). At 30A, the gradient is reduced from 1.76°C to 0.56°C (68.1% improvement). At 40A, the Delta-T is lowered from 2.45°C to 0.77°C (68.5% improvement). At 50A, the staggered configuration limits the temperature gradient to 0.96°C compared to 3.07°C for the inline configuration, achieving a 68.7% improvement. Across all operating currents, the staggered cell arrangement achieves an average temperature uniformity improvement of 67.9%. , Claims:WE CLAIM: 1. A passive battery thermal management system for a cylindrical battery pack, comprising: a plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells arranged in an array of alternating rows; wherein adjacent rows of the plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells are offset laterally by a stagger offset equal to half of a transverse pitch ($St/2$) to form a staggered configuration defining a triangular lattice pattern with passive natural convection cooling channels; wherein the staggered configuration is defined by a transverse pitch ratio ($St/d$) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio ($Sl/d$) of 1.19, where $St$ is the transverse pitch, $Sl$ is the longitudinal pitch, and $d$ is a nominal diameter of each cylindrical electrochemical cell; and wherein the passive natural convection cooling channels are configured to direct ambient air along a tortuous path through the triangular lattice pattern to passively dissipate heat from the plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells. 2. The passive battery thermal management system of claim 1, wherein each of the plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells is an 18650 format lithium-ion cell having a nominal diameter ($d$) of 18.5 mm and a height of 65 mm; and wherein the transverse pitch ($St$) is 25 mm, the longitudinal pitch ($Sl$) is 22 mm, and the stagger offset is 12.5 mm; and wherein the array comprises an 8x8 configuration of 64 cylindrical electrochemical cells. 3. The passive battery thermal management system of claim 1, wherein the staggered configuration is characterized by an array correction factor ($C_{arr}$) of 1.25, providing a 67% relative improvement in an effective heat transfer coefficient compared to an inline cell arrangement having an array correction factor of 0.75; and wherein the system is entirely passive and devoid of active cooling components, including fans, pumps, and liquid circulation loops; and wherein the staggered configuration is configured to achieve an average peak temperature reduction of 5.33°C and an average temperature uniformity improvement of 67.9% across a discharge current range of 10A to 50A compared to an inline cell arrangement. 4. A method for passive thermal management in a cylindrical battery pack, the method comprising: arranging a plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells in an array of alternating rows offset laterally by a stagger offset equal to half of a transverse pitch ($St/2$) to form a staggered configuration defining a triangular lattice pattern; establishing passive natural convection cooling channels within the triangular lattice pattern using a transverse pitch ratio ($St/d$) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio ($Sl/d$) of 1.19, where $St$ is the transverse pitch, $Sl$ is the longitudinal pitch, and $d$ is a nominal diameter of each cylindrical electrochemical cell; and directing ambient air passively along a tortuous path through the passive natural convection cooling channels to disrupt thermal boundary layers and induce localized vortex structures in inter-cell spaces of the array. 5. The method of claim 4, wherein directing the ambient air along the tortuous path eliminates thermal wake effects by ensuring downstream cells receive unheated ambient air from gaps between cells of a preceding row; and wherein the plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells are 18650 format lithium-ion cells, and wherein the transverse pitch ($St$) is 25 mm, the longitudinal pitch ($Sl$) is 22 mm, and the stagger offset is 12.5 mm; and wherein the staggered configuration provides an array correction factor ($C_{arr}$) of 1.25 to enhance convective heat transfer. 6. The method of claim 4, wherein the passive thermal management is performed without active cooling components, reducing parasitic power consumption of the battery pack to zero; and wherein the staggered configuration reduces a peak operating temperature of the battery pack by 1.02°C to 9.43°C across a discharge current range of 10A to 50A compared to an inline cell arrangement. 7. A passive thermal runaway propagation containment assembly for a battery pack, comprising: a plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells arranged in a staggered array of alternating rows, wherein adjacent rows are offset laterally by half of a transverse pitch ($St/2$) to form a triangular lattice pattern; wherein the staggered array is defined by a transverse pitch ratio ($St/d$) of 1.35 and a longitudinal pitch ratio ($Sl/d$) of 1.19, where $St$ is the transverse pitch, $Sl$ is the longitudinal pitch, and $d$ is a nominal diameter of each cylindrical electrochemical cell; and wherein the transverse pitch ratio and the longitudinal pitch ratio are configured to increase effective thermal resistance between adjacent cells and enhance natural convection cooling of neighboring cells, thereby delaying thermal runaway propagation from a compromised cell to adjacent cells. 8. The passive thermal runaway propagation containment assembly of claim 7, wherein the increased effective thermal resistance and enhanced natural convection cooling delay a time to first propagation of thermal runaway by 96% compared to an inline cell arrangement. 9. The passive thermal runaway propagation containment assembly of claim 8, wherein the time to first propagation is extended from 75 seconds to 147 seconds. 10. The passive thermal runaway propagation containment assembly of claim 7, wherein the staggered array is configured to reduce a total number of cells affected during a thermal runaway event by 40% compared to an inline cell arrangement; and wherein each of the plurality of cylindrical electrochemical cells is an 18650 format lithium-ion cell having a nominal diameter ($d$) of 18.5 mm, a height of 65 mm, a mass of 46 g, and an internal resistance of 45 mOhm at 25°C.

patents.abstract: ABSTRACT A PROCESS FOR SELECTIVE RECOVERY OF LITHIUM CARBONATE FROM SPENT LITHIUM IRON PHOSPHATE BATTERIES The invention relates to hydrometallurgical recycling of lithium iron phosphate battery waste, and particularly to a process for selective recovery of lithium carbonate from lithium iron phosphate battery black mass. A spent lithium iron phosphate battery is discharged, dismantled to isolate a cathode sheet, and processed to obtain black mass containing LiFePO4, carbon, and binder. The black mass is leached with an aqueous dual-sulfate medium containing sulfuric acid and sodium sulfate under controlled solid-to-liquid ratio, temperature, time, and agitation to preferentially dissolve lithium while suppressing iron dissolution by increased sulfate ion concentration and ionic strength. After solid-liquid separation, dissolved iron species are removed from the pregnant leach filtrate by sodium hydroxide addition under pH control, optionally with oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+. The purified lithium-rich filtrate is reacted with sodium carbonate at elevated temperature and pH to precipitate lithium carbonate, which is recovered by filtration, washing, and drying, with purity of at least about 99%.

PREAMBLE TO THE DESCRIPTION: The following specification particularly describes the nature of this invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. A PROCESS FOR SELECTIVE RECOVERY OF LITHIUM CARBONATE FROM SPENT LITHIUM IRON PHOSPHATE BATTERIES Field of the Invention The present invention generally relates to battery recycling and hydrometallurgical resource recovery, and more particularly to a process for selective recovery of lithium carbonate from lithium iron phosphate battery black mass by sodium sulfate-assisted sulfuric acid leaching. Background of the Invention The invention relates to the field of hydrometallurgical recycling of lithium-ion batteries, and more particularly to recovery of lithium values from black mass derived from spent lithium iron phosphate batteries. The need for such processing arises as electric mobility, stationary storage, and consumer applications generate increasing volumes of end-of-life LFP cells that must be rendered safe, dismantled, and treated in an economically viable manner. In industrial practice, discharged and mechanically processed batteries produce mixed solid fractions in which lithium-bearing cathode material is present along with conductive carbon, binder residues, metallic contaminants, and other process-derived impurities. Recovery of lithium from such material in a usable chemical form has become important both for waste minimization and for reintroduction of secondary raw materials into the battery supply chain. Among known recycling routes, hydrometallurgical treatment is commonly considered for LFP black mass because it can be performed at moderate temperatures and can generate lithium-bearing liquors suitable for further conversion. Conventional practice generally employs mineral acid leaching, particularly sulfuric acid, to dissolve lithium from the phosphate cathode matrix into aqueous solution. After leaching, the slurry is subjected to solid-liquid separation, and the resulting pregnant leach solution is treated through impurity removal, pH adjustment, and subsequent precipitation steps intended to obtain a lithium compound such as lithium carbonate. Such workflows are attractive from a process standpoint, but their practical performance depends heavily on the selectivity of the leaching stage. In sulfuric-acid-only leaching systems used for lithium iron phosphate black mass, dissolution is often not limited to lithium species. Iron from the cathode framework can also pass into solution to a significant extent, producing an impurity-rich leach liquor rather than a predominantly lithium-bearing solution. Once iron is dissolved, downstream purification commonly requires addition of alkali, such as sodium hydroxide, to raise pH and precipitate iron-containing solids before lithium precipitation can be attempted. In larger recycling operations, this sequence increases reagent demand, generates additional solid residues for handling, and complicates process control from batch scale to pilot and plant scale. A substantial technical difficulty associated with such conventional processing is that high dissolved iron loads adversely affect both recovery efficiency and product quality. Iron precipitation stages may consume considerable quantities of neutralizing reagent, thereby increasing operating cost and salt burden in the process stream. Further, lithium can be lost during impurity removal due to entrainment, retention, or co-associated losses with iron-rich precipitates, which reduces overall lithium recovery unless additional washing or reprocessing steps are introduced. Impurities remaining in the liquor may also carry through to the lithium precipitation stage and make it more difficult to consistently obtain lithium carbonate of acceptable purity. These limitations are particularly significant in recycling environments where safe battery handling, selective metal extraction, chemical economy, and scale-up practicality must all be addressed together. A leaching route that performs adequately at laboratory level may become commercially unattractive if impurity dissolution causes excessive alkali consumption, increased sludge generation, and yield penalties in downstream purification. The problem is more pronounced for LFP feedstocks because the target value is principally lithium, whereas dissolution of iron does not improve process economics and instead enlarges the purification burden. Accordingly, the art has continued to face a need for a leaching and recovery approach that provides better lithium selectivity from LFP black mass while limiting impurity transfer into solution. In view of the foregoing, there remains a requirement for an industrially relevant hydrometallurgical process that can treat spent lithium iron phosphate black mass safely and economically, with lower impurity loading in the pregnant leach solution, reduced downstream chemical consumption, and improved suitability for producing battery-grade or high-purity lithium carbonate. There is also a need for such a process to be based on accessible reagents and to remain practical across laboratory, pilot, and larger commercial operations. Objects of the Invention An object of the invention is to provide a hydrometallurgical recycling process for spent lithium iron phosphate batteries in which lithium is selectively transferred from LFP black mass into solution by means of a dual-sulfate leaching medium comprising sulfuric acid and sodium sulfate. Another object of the invention is to provide a leaching system in which sulfuric acid acts to decompose the LiFePO4 structure and release lithium, while sodium sulfate increases sulfate ion concentration and ionic strength so as to improve Li/Fe selectivity and suppress excessive iron dissolution relative to sulfuric-acid-only leaching. Another object of the invention is to provide a process for recovering lithium from LFP black mass that yields a lithium-rich pregnant leach solution having a lower impurity burden, thereby simplifying downstream purification and improving overall process efficiency. Another object of the invention is to provide a recycling route in which the reduction of iron dissolution at the leaching stage correspondingly reduces alkali consumption during subsequent iron removal by pH-controlled precipitation, thereby lowering reagent demand and operating cost. Another object of the invention is to provide a process in which dissolved iron is removed selectively by controlled addition of sodium hydroxide, with lithium remaining in solution, so that purification of the lithium-bearing liquor is achieved without substantial sacrifice of lithium recovery. Another object of the invention is to provide a lithium recovery methodology wherein iron precipitate formed during impurity removal is washed with hot water to recover entrained or adsorbed lithium values, thereby minimizing lithium loss and increasing overall yield. Another object of the invention is to provide an integrated process in which the purified lithium-bearing solution is converted into lithium carbonate by reaction with sodium carbonate under controlled temperature and pH conditions, so as to obtain lithium carbonate of improved purity from LFP battery waste. Another object of the invention is to provide a recycling process including prior discharge of spent batteries to near zero voltage before dismantling, thereby improving handling safety and reducing the risk of short circuit, spark generation, and thermal events during opening and component separation. Another object of the invention is to provide a process in which dismantling and cathode coating removal are carried out to form an LFP black mass enriched in active lithium-bearing material, thereby reducing dilution by current collector foil and improving the effectiveness of the subsequent selective leaching step. Yet another object of the invention is to provide a technically practical and scalable recycling route for laboratory, batch, pilot, and larger-scale implementation, wherein conventional unit operations are combined with the aforesaid dual-sulfate leaching chemistry to achieve high lithium extraction, reduced impurity carryover, lower processing cost, and improved final lithium carbonate quality. Summary of the Invention The present invention is described in the following sections by various embodiments. However, it should be understood that the invention can be implemented in various forms and is not limited to the specific embodiment provided herein.In the context of the present disclosure, it should be understood that the described embodiments in this section are put forth for illustrative purposes only. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that various modifications, adaptations, and alternative designs may be employed without departing from the scope and spirit of the invention. Accordingly, the present invention should not be limited to the specific embodiments illustrated herein, but rather should be construed according to the claims and description that follow. Embodiments of the present invention provide a process for selective recovery of lithium carbonate from lithium iron phosphate battery black mass, wherein a spent lithium iron phosphate battery is first discharged until battery voltage is reduced to below about 0.1 V, the discharged battery is then dismantled to isolate a cathode sheet having LiFePO4 active material supported on aluminum foil, and a cathode coating is physically separated from the aluminum foil to obtain a black mass that comprises, but not limited to, LiFePO4, carbon, and binder. The black mass is contacted with an aqueous dual-sulfate leaching medium comprising sulfuric acid in a concentration range of about 0.5-1 M and sodium sulfate in a concentration range of about 0.5-1.5 M, at a solid-to-liquid ratio of about 1:10, at a temperature of about 60-80°C for about 2-4 hours under stirring of about 400-500 RPM, thereby forming a leach slurry. In addition, the sodium sulfate increases sulfate ion concentration and ionic strength of the leaching medium so as to enhance dissolution of lithium from LiFePO4 while limiting dissolution of iron species, after which the leach slurry is subjected to solid-liquid separation to obtain a lithium-containing pregnant leach filtrate and an insoluble residue. Dissolved iron species are removed from the pregnant leach filtrate by controlled addition of sodium hydroxide under pH regulation to form an iron precipitate, the iron precipitate is separated from a lithium-rich filtrate, and the lithium-rich filtrate is reacted with sodium carbonate at about 80-90°C while maintaining pH at about 10-11 to precipitate lithium carbonate, which is thereafter recovered by filtration, washing, and drying. The sequence of discharge, dismantling, black mass generation, selective dual-sulfate leaching, impurity removal, and carbonate precipitation forms an integrated hydrometallurgical route in which each stage prepares a more suitable feed for the next stage, thereby enabling efficient conversion of lithium present in spent LiFePO4 cathode material into a high-value lithium carbonate product. The aforesaid process provides a technical advancement particularly because the dual-sulfate leaching medium modifies the chemistry of acid leaching at the source of dissolution itself, rather than relying only on downstream purification of an impurity-rich liquor. By using sulfuric acid together with sodium sulfate, proton-assisted decomposition of the LiFePO4 lattice proceeds in a manner that promotes transfer of lithium into solution while suppressing excessive transfer of iron, thereby improving Li/Fe selectivity in the pregnant leach solution. This selective dissolution behavior reduces impurity loading, decreases sodium hydroxide consumption during iron precipitation, limits lithium losses associated with impurity removal, and supports formation of lithium carbonate having improved purity. The process further remains amenable to implementation at laboratory, pilot, and larger recycling scales because the individual unit operations are conventional in format while their coordinated arrangement around the dual-sulfate leach chemistry provides the inventive effect. Additionally, the words 'a' or 'an' signify at least one, and the word 'plurality' signifies 'one or more' unless otherwise specified.
