The present invention relates to a hydrometallurgical recycling process for lithium iron phosphate battery waste, particularly for recovery of lithium from lithium iron phosphate black mass as lithium carbonate. In the present process, lithium is selectively transferred from lithium iron phosphate black mass into an aqueous phase and is thereafter recovered as lithium carbonate, while dissolution of iron at the leaching stage is limited. The technical basis of the invention lies in use of a dual-sulfate leaching medium comprising sulfuric acid and sodium sulfate, instead of sulfuric acid alone. The invention addresses the process limitation encountered in sulfuric-acid-only leaching of lithium iron phosphate black mass, namely that although lithium may dissolve to a high extent, iron also dissolves to a significant extent and contaminates the pregnant leach solution. Such iron loading increases downstream sodium hydroxide consumption, increases lithium loss during impurity removal, and affects lithium carbonate purity. In the present invention, sodium sulfate is intentionally introduced into the sulfuric acid leach system to increase sulfate ion concentration and ionic strength of the leaching medium so as to promote decomposition of LiFePO4 while selectively inhibiting excessive iron dissolution. The result is a lithium-rich pregnant leach solution of reduced impurity burden and a more efficient overall recovery route to lithium carbonate. The invention utilizes a dual-sulfate leaching step which involves sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) to improve lithium extraction from the LFP black mass. The use of Na2SO4 leads to an increase in the concentration of the ions in the solvent system, making it easier for the decomposition of the LiFePO4 compound to occur. At the same time, this leaching procedure is capable of limiting the dissolving of impurities like iron. The result is the generation of a relatively pure lithium-containing solution. As a consequence of the above characteristics, the lithium recovery process becomes more efficient because there is no need for further purification stages. Therefore, this technique makes it possible to obtain lithium carbonate (Li2CO3) efficiently. In an embodiment of the present invention, the process begins with a spent lithium iron phosphate battery feed. The spent battery acts as the upstream source material from which the cathode active material is recovered. Prior to opening the battery, the battery is discharged to near zero voltage so that the electrochemical driving force remaining in the cell is substantially removed. This initial conditioning step is not merely a handling precaution but a functional preparatory operation, because safe access to the cathode fraction is necessary for obtaining a black mass feed suitable for controlled selective leaching. In an embodiment of the present invention, discharge may be carried out using a saline medium or a resistance-based discharge arrangement. Where a saline medium is used, the spent battery is immersed in about 5 wt% sodium chloride solution at room temperature until the battery voltage falls below about 0.1 V. The sodium chloride solution serves as a discharge medium by enabling controlled dissipation of residual electrical charge, thereby converting stored electrochemical energy to heat under benign conditions and stopping further lithium-ion shuttling during normal handling. In another embodiment of the present invention, a resistance-based discharge arrangement may be used to achieve the same low-voltage condition. The disclosed scale-specific discharge examples provide practical implementation support. One battery of about 0.835 kg may be discharged in 150 mL of 5 wt% sodium chloride solution for about 6-8 hours. Ten batteries may be discharged in 1.5 L of 5 wt% sodium chloride solution for about 8-12 hours. A larger batch of 50-100 batteries may be discharged in 10-20 L of 5 wt% sodium chloride solution for about 12-24 hours. In each case the battery is maintained in the discharge environment until the voltage is reduced to below about 0.1 V, thereby reducing risk of short circuit, spark generation, and thermal events during dismantling. After discharge, the spent lithium iron phosphate battery is dismantled to isolate the internal material fractions. The dismantling stage physically separates the cathode sheet containing LiFePO4 supported on aluminum foil, the anode containing graphite supported on copper foil, the separator, and casing or structural elements. This separation is based on differences in form, adhesion, density, and mechanical response of the battery components. By isolating the cathode-bearing fraction, the process enriches the material stream that carries the target lithium-bearing compound and prevents avoidable contamination of the later leaching stage by unrelated structural materials. In an embodiment of the present invention, dismantling may be performed manually, by assisted tools, or by shredding followed by classification. For laboratory-scale operation a discharged battery may be manually cut open and the cathode sheet may be separated from casing and internal parts with minimal disturbance. For a batch of 10 batteries, assisted tools may be used to improve speed and uniformity of component segregation. For larger throughput, such as 50-100 batteries, a shredding and classification system may be employed so that cathode fractions are recovered by physical separation at larger scale. These alternative embodiments preserve the same material objective, namely recovery of a cathode-derived feed suitable for black mass formation. The isolated cathode sheet comprises a cathode coating attached to aluminum foil. The cathode coating is physically stripped from the aluminum foil to produce black mass. This black mass comprises LiFePO4, carbon, and binder. The stripping operation acts as a concentration step because it removes bulk foil material that would otherwise dilute the feed to the chemical treatment stage and potentially consume reagents without contributing lithium recovery. The separated aluminum foil may therefore be kept out of the principal leaching step, while the black mass becomes the principal feedstock for lithium extraction. The black mass has an important functional role in the present invention because it concentrates the lithium-bearing active phase in a powder form that may be efficiently contacted with the dual-sulfate leaching medium. The carbon and binder present in the black mass remain relevant during downstream filtration, because these relatively insoluble constituents form part of the residue separated after leaching. The process therefore uses black mass not as a generic waste powder but as a deliberately enriched cathode-derived feed that supports selective phase transfer of lithium into solution. The core of the present invention is the dual-sulfate leaching stage. In this stage, the black mass is contacted with an aqueous leaching medium comprising sulfuric acid in a concentration range of about 0.5-1 M and sodium sulfate in a concentration range of about 0.5-1.5 M. The contacting is carried out at a solid-to-liquid ratio of about 1:10, at a temperature of about 60-80°C, for about 2-4 hours, under constant stirring. The leaching medium therefore comprises, but not limited to, an acidic component that promotes decomposition of LiFePO4 and a sulfate salt component that modifies the leaching environment to improve selectivity. Sulfuric acid performs the proton-assisted decomposition function in the dual-sulfate system. LiFePO4 has a stable olivine crystal structure, and the protons supplied by sulfuric acid attack this structure so that lithium may be released from the solid phase into the aqueous phase. According to the disclosed scientific basis, this proton-driven decomposition may also liberate iron species and phosphate species from the solid. Sulfuric acid is therefore the active chemical agent responsible for disrupting the LiFePO4 lattice and enabling dissolution of lithium from the black mass. Sodium sulfate is not an inert background salt in the present invention. Sodium sulfate is intentionally added to increase sulfate ion concentration and ionic strength of the leaching medium. According to the disclosure, this altered solvent chemistry promotes decomposition of LiFePO4 while selectively inhibiting excessive iron dissolution. The operative effect is not merely increased overall dissolution but an improved Li/Fe selectivity in which lithium is transferred efficiently into solution and the amount of dissolved iron is reduced relative to sulfuric-acid-only leaching. This selective inhibition of iron dissolution is the central scientific and technical feature that distinguishes the present invention from conventional sulfuric-acid-only systems. The interaction between sulfuric acid and sodium sulfate within the same aqueous medium is functionally significant. Sulfuric acid creates the acidic environment necessary for structural attack on LiFePO4, while sodium sulfate modifies the ionic environment during that structural breakdown. Because the black mass, the sulfuric acid, and the sodium sulfate are all present together under heat and agitation, the decomposition and selective dissolution occur in an integrated manner rather than as separate operations. The resulting pregnant leach liquor is richer in lithium and carries a reduced impurity load, and this cleaner solution directly improves subsequent iron removal and lithium carbonate precipitation. In an embodiment of the present invention, the black mass may be charged at different scales while maintaining the same solid-to-liquid ratio and general operating window. Disclosed examples include about 50 g black mass in 500 mL of the dual-sulfate solution, about 100 g black mass in 1 L of the dual-sulfate solution, and about 500 g black mass in 5 L of the dual-sulfate solution. Stirring may be about 400 RPM for the 50 g scale, about 400-500 RPM for the 100 g scale, and about 500 RPM for the 500 g scale. Temperature is maintained within about 60-80°C and the residence time is about 2-4 hours. These examples show that the selective dual-sulfate chemistry may be implemented from smaller to larger batches without altering the central leaching principle. The heating condition of about 60-80°C contributes to process intensification during leaching. Increased temperature improves reaction kinetics and supports the acid-promoted decomposition of LiFePO4, thereby helping lithium transfer into solution within the disclosed residence time of about 2-4 hours. The stirring condition of about 400-500 RPM keeps the black mass suspended, refreshes liquid-solid interfacial contact, and reduces mass transfer limitations within the slurry. The combined use of heat and agitation therefore supports reproducible contact between the black mass and the dual-sulfate medium, which is important for maintaining high lithium extraction while preserving selectivity against excessive iron dissolution. The disclosed empirical result from the dual-sulfate leaching stage is about 95% lithium extraction. The substrate is lithium iron phosphate black mass, the leaching medium comprises about 0.5-1 M sulfuric acid and about 0.5-1.5 M sodium sulfate, the solid-to-liquid ratio is about 1:10, the temperature is about 60-80°C, the time is about 2-4 hours, and stirring is about 400-500 RPM depending on scale. The disclosure further teaches that, although sulfuric acid alone may dissolve slightly more lithium in some cases, it also dissolves significantly more iron and impurities. The present invention therefore values selective extraction performance rather than maximum indiscriminate dissolution. After leaching, the resulting leach slurry comprises a dissolved ionic phase and an undissolved solid phase. The dissolved phase contains lithium ions and some iron ions, described as Fe2+ and Fe3+, while the undissolved phase contains mainly carbon and impurities. The slurry is subjected to solid-liquid separation so that the dissolved species are transferred into a clear filtrate and the insoluble species are retained in a solid residue. This phase separation relies on solubility contrast between dissolved ionic species and undissolved carbonaceous or impurity-bearing solids. In an embodiment of the present invention, the solid-liquid separation may be performed by Buchner vacuum filtration. Disclosed filtration examples include use of filter media with about 11 µm pore size at about 0.6-0.8 bar vacuum and use of filter media with about 5 µm pore size at about 1-2 bar vacuum. The filter retains the insoluble residue while allowing the lithium-bearing liquor to pass through as a pregnant leach filtrate. This separation is technically important because carbonaceous residue and undissolved impurity phases are kept from entering the downstream precipitation stages where they could interfere with pH control and product isolation. The insoluble residue formed after leaching is influenced by the selectivity of the dual-sulfate system. Because sodium sulfate selectively inhibits excessive iron dissolution, a greater fraction of undesired iron-containing material may remain outside the solution phase relative to sulfuric-acid-only leaching. The residue therefore represents not only undissolved carbon and inert material but also the retained impurity burden that has been prevented from loading the pregnant leach filtrate. This upstream retention of impurities is one reason why the later purification sequence requires less chemical intervention. The pregnant leach filtrate is then purified by controlled iron removal using sodium hydroxide. The filtrate still contains dissolved iron species, although at a lower level than in sulfuric-acid-only systems. Sodium hydroxide is added under pH regulation so that iron forms insoluble hydroxide precipitates while lithium remains dissolved in the aqueous phase. This stage uses a solubility-based selective precipitation principle, since iron hydroxides have much lower solubility than lithium salts over appropriate pH ranges. The present invention distinguishes precipitation conditions for different oxidation states of iron. In an embodiment of the present invention, Fe3+ may be precipitated at about pH 3.5-4.5. In another embodiment of the present invention, Fe2+ may be precipitated at about pH 6-8, and where required Fe2+ may first be oxidized before precipitation. The disclosure also states a practical embodiment in which Fe2+ is oxidized and precipitation is carried out at about pH 6-7 under continuous agitation. These pH windows support selective removal of iron from the lithium-bearing solution while preserving lithium in dissolved form for later recovery. During iron precipitation the solution may be stirred at about 400-500 RPM so that addition of sodium hydroxide does not create local zones of excessive alkalinity. Controlled agitation improves uniform pH distribution and formation of filterable iron precipitate. The amount of sodium hydroxide consumed in this stage is directly linked to the amount of iron previously dissolved during leaching. Because the dual-sulfate leaching medium lowers iron dissolution relative to sulfuric acid alone, the present invention reduces sodium hydroxide demand at this purification step. This interdependence between upstream leach selectivity and downstream reagent consumption is a central process integration advantage of the invention. After iron precipitation, the slurry is subjected to a further solid-liquid separation to isolate the iron precipitate from a lithium-rich filtrate. In disclosed examples, after stirring is stopped, filtration may be performed using filter paper of about 11 µm pore size under about 0.6-0.8 bar vacuum for the smaller scale; filter paper of about 8-11 µm pore size under about 0.8-1 bar vacuum for an intermediate scale; and filter paper of about 5-10 µm pore size under about 1-2 bar vacuum for a larger scale. This produces a clear lithium-rich filtrate suitable for lithium carbonate precipitation and an iron precipitate cake that still may contain entrained lithium-bearing liquor. The present invention includes a lithium recovery feature associated with the iron precipitate. The iron precipitate obtained after sodium hydroxide treatment may entrap solution within the cake pores or may carry lithium-bearing species adsorbed on or within the precipitated mass. If this precipitate were discarded without treatment, lithium would be lost from the process. The invention therefore subjects the iron precipitate to hot-water washing using deionized water at about 70-90°C under agitation so that lithium salts are selectively redissolved while the iron hydroxide remains substantially insoluble. This wash operation relies on differential solubility. Lithium salts are highly soluble in water, particularly under hot conditions, whereas the iron precipitate remains insoluble to a significant extent under the disclosed washing conditions. As a result, the hot deionized water extracts entrained or adsorbed lithium-bearing species from the precipitate without materially reversing the iron removal operation. The wash liquor obtained from this step is then recombined with the lithium-rich filtrate, thereby improving overall lithium recovery efficiency. In disclosed working examples, the iron precipitate may be washed with hot deionized water at about 70-80°C under thorough stirring of about 300-400 RPM, followed by filtration using filter paper of about 8-11 µm pore size. Vacuum may be about 0.6-0.8 bar for a smaller quantity, about 0.8-1 bar for an intermediate quantity, and about 1-2 bar for a larger quantity. The disclosure also states generally that the washing temperature may be about 70-90°C. Multiple washing stages may be employed to maximize lithium recovery, and the lithium-bearing wash liquor is added to the filtrate from iron precipitation. The purified lithium-rich solution, which may include the recombined lithium-bearing wash liquor, is then converted into lithium carbonate by reaction with sodium carbonate. In this stage the solution is heated to about 80-90°C and the pH is maintained at about 10-11. Under these conditions lithium ions react with carbonate ions to form lithium carbonate. The precipitation is promoted by the relatively low solubility of lithium carbonate and by the disclosed elevated temperature conditions under which lithium carbonate precipitation is efficient. In an embodiment of the present invention, sodium carbonate may be added to the lithium-rich filtrate at about 80-85°C with stirring at about 400 RPM while maintaining pH at about 10-11. In another embodiment of the present invention, sodium carbonate may be added at about 80-90°C with stirring at about 500 RPM while maintaining pH at about 10-11. The agitation promotes uniform mixing and avoids local excess of carbonate reagent. The thermal condition supports effective formation and growth of lithium carbonate solids. Because the upstream leach and purification sequence reduces iron and other impurity levels, the lithium carbonate precipitated in this stage is of high purity. The disclosure supports a lithium carbonate product having a purity of at least about 99%. The purity benefit is attributable to the coordinated sequence of selective dual-sulfate leaching, iron removal under controlled pH, recovery of lithium from the iron precipitate by hot-water washing, and final washing of the lithium carbonate cake. The present invention thus does not rely on the precipitation stage alone for product quality, but on controlled impurity management beginning at the initial leaching chemistry. The lithium carbonate precipitate is recovered by filtration and then washed with hot deionized water to remove residual sodium and sulfate species. This wash step is again based on differential solubility, since sodium salts and sulfate-containing soluble species dissolve readily in hot water whereas lithium carbonate remains as an insoluble solid under the disclosed conditions. The wash therefore improves product purity by reducing sodium ion and sulfate ion contamination associated with the mother liquor adhering to the filter cake. Disclosed examples for product isolation include filtration of the lithium carbonate precipitate using filter paper of about 11 µm pore size under about 0.6-0.8 bar vacuum, followed by washing with hot deionized water at about 60-70°C. Another disclosed example uses filter paper of about 5 µm pore size under about 1-2 bar vacuum, followed by washing with hot deionized water at about 70-80°C. These examples illustrate alternative filtering conditions suited to different scales or solids-handling requirements while maintaining the same purification function. After washing, the lithium carbonate product is dried at about 100-120°C to remove moisture and stabilize the final product. Disclosed examples include drying at about 100°C for about 6-8 hours, at about 110°C for about 4-6 hours, and at about 120°C for about 3-41 hours. The drying step converts the wet lithium carbonate cake into a dry product suitable for storage, handling, or subsequent use. Moisture removal at this stage preserves product quality achieved through the preceding selective recovery sequence. In an embodiment of the present invention, the best mode presently disclosed is a sequence in which a spent lithium iron phosphate battery is first discharged in about 5 wt% sodium chloride solution until the voltage is below about 0.1 V, then dismantled to recover the cathode sheet, and the cathode coating is stripped from aluminum foil to obtain black mass comprising LiFePO4, carbon, and binder. The black mass is then leached in an aqueous medium comprising about 0.5-1 M sulfuric acid and about 0.5-1.5 M sodium sulfate at a solid-to-liquid ratio of about 1:10, at about 60-80°C for about 2-4 hours under stirring of about 400-500 RPM. The leach slurry is filtered to obtain a lithium-containing pregnant leach filtrate and insoluble residue. Dissolved iron is removed from the filtrate by sodium hydroxide addition under pH control, the iron precipitate is filtered and washed with hot deionized water at about 70-90°C, and the lithium-bearing wash liquor is recombined with the lithium-rich filtrate. The purified solution is heated to about 80-90°C and reacted with sodium carbonate at pH about 10-11 to precipitate lithium carbonate, which is filtered, washed with hot deionized water, and dried at about 100-120°C. A representative implementation of the leaching stage uses about 50 g black mass in 500 mL of the dual-sulfate leaching medium, stirred at about 400 RPM and maintained at about 60-80°C for about 2-4 hours. Another representative implementation uses about 100 g black mass in 1 L of leaching medium under about 400-500 RPM stirring. A further representative implementation uses about 500 g black mass in 5 L of leaching medium under about 500 RPM stirring. Across these disclosed examples, the solid-to-liquid ratio remains about 1:10 and the dual-sulfate chemistry remains unchanged, demonstrating scalability of the selective lithium extraction principle. A representative implementation of the downstream purification and recovery stages comprises filtering the leached slurry by Buchner vacuum filtration, adjusting the pH of the filtrate with sodium hydroxide so that Fe3+ precipitates at about pH 3.5-4.5 and Fe2+ precipitates at about pH 6-8, washing the resulting iron precipitate with hot deionized water at about 70-80°C under about 300-400 RPM agitation, and combining the recovered lithium-bearing wash liquor with the lithium-rich filtrate. Sodium carbonate is then added to the heated purified solution at about 80-90°C under stirring of about 400-500 RPM while maintaining pH about 10-11, thereby forming lithium carbonate, which is filtered, washed with hot deionized water at about 60-80°C, and dried at about 100-120°C. In an embodiment of the present invention, variations may be adopted without departing from the disclosed selective dual-sulfate principle. The discharge may be performed in 5 wt% sodium chloride solution or by resistance-based discharge. Dismantling may be manual, assisted, or based on shredding and classification. Filtration may use pore sizes disclosed as about 11 µm, about 8-11 µm, about 5-10 µm, or about 5 µm, with corresponding vacuum conditions disclosed as about 0.6-0.8 bar, about 0.8-1 bar, or about 1-2 bar. Iron precipitation may involve direct precipitation of Fe3+ or oxidation-assisted precipitation of Fe2+, depending on the oxidation state present in solution. Lithium carbonate precipitation may be conducted within the disclosed ranges of about 80-90°C, about 400-500 RPM stirring, and pH about 10-11. Such embodiments preserve the sequence and functional cooperation of the disclosed stages. In an embodiment of the present invention, the process is scalable from laboratory-scale operation to pilot and larger recycling operation because the unit operations themselves are conventional in format while the selective chemistry is embedded in the dual-sulfate leaching stage. The discharge stage may handle one battery, ten batteries, or 50-100 batteries. The leaching stage may treat about 50 g, about 100 g, or about 500 g black mass with proportionate solution volumes. The process architecture therefore remains consistent while throughput is adjusted by batch size, stirring condition, filtration capacity, and vacuum level. The technical benefits obtained by the invention arise from the interaction of the disclosed features rather than from any isolated operation. Discharging improves handling safety before dismantling. Dismantling and black mass formation enrich the cathode-derived feed. The dual-sulfate leaching medium comprising sulfuric acid and sodium sulfate selectively transfers lithium into solution while limiting iron dissolution. Filtration isolates insoluble residue from the lithium-bearing liquor. Sodium hydroxide treatment removes dissolved iron under controlled pH conditions. Hot-water washing of the iron precipitate recovers lithium that would otherwise be lost. Sodium carbonate precipitation converts purified dissolved lithium into lithium carbonate, and product washing and drying yield a dry high-purity product. By using sodium sulfate as a selective leaching modifier, the invention provides improved Li/Fe selectivity, lower iron dissolution, lower sodium hydroxide consumption, lower lithium loss, reduced overall chemical burden, higher lithium carbonate purity, and a more economical and ecologically friendly recycling route for lithium iron phosphate battery black mass. Various experiments as mentioned below have been performed to determine the steps to achieve the best results. Example 1: Battery Discharging: 1. One LFP battery (0.835 Kg) is discharged in 150 mL of 5 wt% NaCl solution at room temperature. The system is kept undisturbed for about 6-8 hours until voltage drops below 0.1 V. The battery becomes fully inactive and safe for dismantling. 2. Ten LFP battery (8.35 Kg) is discharged in 1.5 L of 5 wt% NaCl solution at room temperature. The system is kept undisturbed for about 8-12 hours until voltage drops below 0.1 V. The battery becomes fully inactive and safe for dismantling. 3. A large batch (50-100 batteries) is discharged in 10-20 L of 5 wt% NaCl solution at room temperature. The system is kept undisturbed for about 12-24 hours until voltage drops below 0.1 V. The battery becomes fully inactive and safe for dismantling. Example 2: Battery Dismantling: 1. A single discharged LFP battery is manually cut open to access internal components. The cathode sheet is separated from the casing and other parts with minimal disturbance. This method ensures precise recovery of active material for laboratory-scale processing. 2. A batch of 10 batteries is dismantled using assisted tools to improve speed and uniformity. Components such as cathode, anode, and separator are segregated systematically. This reduces cross-contamination and enhances consistency of collected cathode material. 3. Multiple batteries (50-100 units) are processed using a shredding and classification system. Post-shredding, physical separation techniques are applied to recover cathode fractions. This approach enables efficient large-scale dismantling with improved material recovery. Example 3: Leaching: 1. 50 g of black mass is leached using 500 ml of solution containing 0.5 M-1M H2SO4 and 0.5 M-1.5 M Na2SO4. The process is carried out at 60°C-80°C with stirring at 400 RPM for 2-4 hours with proper agitation in a reactor system. High lithium recovery is achieved with controlled iron dissolution. 2. 100 g of black mass is leached using 1 L of solution containing 0.5 M-1M H2SO4 and 0.5 M-1.5 M Na2SO4. The process is carried out at 60°C-80°C with stirring at 400-500 RPM for 2-4 hours with proper agitation in a reactor system. High lithium recovery is achieved with controlled iron dissolution. 3. 500 g of black mass is leached using 5 L of solution containing 0.5 M-1M H2SO4 and 0.5 M-1.5 M Na2SO4. The process is carried out at 60°C-80°C with stirring at 500 RPM for 2-4 hours with proper agitation in a reactor system. High lithium recovery is achieved with controlled iron dissolution. Example 4: Solid–Liquid Separation: 1. The leached slurry is filtered using Buchner vacuum filtration with Whatman filter paper (11 µm pore size) at 0.6-0.8 bar pressure. Efficient separation of carbon residue and undissolved solids is achieved without clogging. A clear lithium-bearing filtrate and solid residue are obtained. 2. The leached slurry is filtered using Buchner vacuum filtration with Whatman filter paper (5 µm pore size) at 1-2 bar pressure. Efficient separation of carbon residue and undissolved solids is achieved without clogging. A clear lithium-bearing filtrate and solid residue are obtained. Example 5: Iron Removal using NaOH: 1. The solution is stirred at 400–500 RPM while adjusting pH to 3.5-4.5 for Fe3+ removal. For Fe2+, oxidation is carried out followed by pH adjustment to 6-7 under continuous agitation. Maintained RPM improves reaction kinetics and prevents localized over-precipitation. Example 6: Filtration after Fe Removal: 1. For 50 g the precipitate is filtered using Whatman filter paper (11 µm pore size) under vacuum (0.6-0.8 bar). Stirring (300-400 RPM) is stopped before filtration to allow proper settling. A clear lithium-rich filtrate is obtained with minimal iron carryover. 2. For 100 g the precipitate is filtered using Whatman filter paper (8-11 µm pore size) under vacuum (0.8-1 bar). Stirring (300-400 RPM) is stopped before filtration to allow proper settling. A clear lithium-rich filtrate is obtained with minimal iron carryover. 3. For 500 g the precipitate is filtered using Whatman filter paper (5-10 µm pore size) under vacuum (1-2 bar). Stirring (500 RPM) is stopped before filtration to allow proper settling. A clear lithium-rich filtrate is obtained with minimal iron carryover. Example 7: Precipitate Washing After Fe Removal: 1. For 10 g the iron precipitate is washed with hot deionized water (70-80°C) under thorough stirring (300-400 RPM) to recover dissolved lithium trapped within the solids. The suspension is filtered using Whatman filter paper (8-11 µm pore size) under vacuum (0.6-0.8 bar). Iron precipitate remains insoluble, while lithium-rich washings are collected. 2. For 100 g the iron precipitate is washed with hot deionized water (70-80°C) under thorough stirring (300-400 RPM) to recover dissolved lithium trapped within the solids. The suspension is filtered using Whatman filter paper (8-11 µm pore size) under vacuum (0.8-1 bar). Iron precipitate remains insoluble, while lithium-rich washings are collected. 3. For 500 g the iron precipitate is washed with hot deionized water (70-80°C) under thorough stirring (300-400 RPM) to recover dissolved lithium trapped within the solids. The suspension is filtered using Whatman filter paper (8-11 µm pore size) under vacuum (1-2 bar). Iron precipitate remains insoluble, while lithium-rich washings are collected. Example 8: Lithium Precipitation: 1. Na2CO3 solution is added to the lithium-rich filtrate at 80-85°C with stirring 400 RPM. The pH is maintained at 10-11 to ensure complete precipitation of Li2CO3. White lithium carbonate precipitate forms with high purity due to low impurity content. 2. Na2CO3 solution is added to the lithium-rich filtrate at 80-90°C with stirring 500 RPM. The pH is maintained at 10-11 to ensure complete precipitation of Li2CO3. White lithium carbonate precipitate forms with high purity due to low impurity content. Example 9: Filtration & Washing: 1. Li2CO3 precipitate is filtered using Whatman filter paper (11 µm) under vacuum (0.6-0.8 bar). The cake is washed with hot DI water (60-70°C) to remove Na⁺ and SO42-impurities. A clean Li2CO3 cake with improved purity is obtained. 2. Li2CO3 precipitate is filtered using Whatman filter paper (5 µm) under vacuum (1-2 bar). The cake is washed with hot DI water (70-80°C) to remove Na⁺ and SO42-impurities. A clean Li2CO3 cake with improved purity is obtained. Example 10: Drying: 1. Drying is carried out at 100°C for 6-8 hours to ensure gradual moisture removal and stable product formation. 2. Drying is carried out at 110°C for 4-6 hours to ensure gradual moisture removal and stable product formation. 3. Drying is carried out at 120°C for 3-41 hours to ensure gradual moisture removal and stable product formation. Example 11: In the process of leaching of black mass containing LFP, a solution of 0.5-1 M of H2SO4 and 0.5-1.5 M of Na2SO4 is used to ensure effective and highly selective separation of lithium into the aqueous medium. In this experiment 95% of lithium is extracted through leaching, giving rise to an extract containing significant amounts of lithium, thus making its extraction easy. The addition of Na2SO4 causes an increase in both the concentration of the sulfate ion and ionic strength, resulting in the increased dissolution of lithium but at the same time minimizing excess dissolution of iron ions and other impurity. This minimizes impurities, thereby reducing the amount of chemicals required for the process, especially NaOH. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to an integrated process for producing fibre-embedded graphitic or partially graphitic carbon-coated olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials including lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium iron manganese phosphate (LiFexMn(1-x)PO4) and lithium manganese phosphate (LiMnPO4). The process comprises wet precursor homogenization, high-shear slurry conditioning, spray drying, densification, controlled calcination, particle-size engineering and post-synthesis mechano-fusion processing. The mechano-fusion treatment simultaneously embeds conductive carbon and conductive fibres onto active-material particles while promoting particle spheroidisation, densification and conductive-network formation. The resulting cathode material exhibits improved tap density, electrode compaction density, electronic conductivity, rate capability, cycling stability and low-temperature electrochemical performance. The invention further provides cathode materials, cathode electrodes and lithium-ion cells produced according to the disclosed process.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Field of Invention: [001] The present invention relates generally to lithium-ion battery cathode active materials and industrial manufacturing methods thereof. More particularly, the invention relates to lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials and scalable processes for their manufacture thereof. Background of the Invention: [002] Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) is widely recognized as a promising cathode material for lithium-ion batteries due to its excellent thermal stability, long cycle life, safety characteristics, and relatively low cost compared with other cathode chemistries. [003] However, conventional LiFePO4 materials suffer from relatively low electronic conductivity and moderate tap density, which limit their energy density and high-rate performance. To overcome these limitations, various approaches have been developed, including carbon coating, particle size reduction, conductive additives, and particle morphology engineering. [004] For instance, US9755234 discloses a glycothermal method for producing lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) nanopowders using lithium, iron and phosphorus precursors in a triethanolamine solvent. The process operates under elevated temperature and pressure conditions and is reported to provide improved control over particle size and particle-size distribution as compared to conventional glycothermal synthesis routes. The resulting LiFePO4 material is suitable for use as a cathode active material in lithium-ion batteries. [005] Further, WO 2011/057646 discloses a hydrothermal process for producing lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) powder. The process utilizes aqueous precursor solutions containing lithium, iron and phosphate sources in the presence of an organic surfactant, and further employs a co-solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol during hydrothermal synthesis. The reference teaches that the use of the co-solvent influences particle morphology and improves electrochemical performance, particularly at high discharge rates. The resulting LiFePO4 powder may be subjected to heat treatment to obtain crystalline olivine-phase material and a carbon coating derived from the organic surfactant and/or additional carbon sources. However, the reference does not disclose densification of spray-dried spherical precursor granules, nor does it teach post-synthesis mechanical embedding of graphitic or fibrous conductive carbon into the surfaces of olivine phosphate particles. [006] In particular, carbon-coated LiFePO4 materials have been developed to improve electronic conductivity. While such approaches can enhance electrochemical performance, many existing processes suffer from several limitations, including: • Non-uniform carbon coating, low particle packing density; • Poor control of particle morphology; • Discontinuous or batch-based production processes, and • Excessive carbon loading that reduces energy density [007] Furthermore, many conventional synthesis methods produce irregularly shaped LiFePO4 particles, which result in lower tap density and poor electrode compaction density, thereby limiting volumetric energy density. [008] Recent developments in high-density Generation-4 LiFePO4 cathode materials require advanced particle engineering techniques capable of simultaneously improving particle morphology, tap density, electrode compaction density and electrical conductivity. However, existing manufacturing processes do not adequately integrate continuous synthesis, particle spheroidisation, and advanced carbon coating techniques in a scalable industrial process. In particular, conventional coating methods often fail to produce uniform conductive carbon networks at low carbon loading, and they do not effectively enable simultaneous particle densification and spheroidisation during post-processing steps. [009] Furthermore, existing technologies do not adequately employ high-energy mechano-fusion techniques capable of embedding conductive carbon materials onto LiFePO4, LiFexMn(1-x)PO4 or other olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate particle surfaces under controlled mechanical conditions. In particular, conventional conductive-carbon coating and blending technologies generally fail to achieve simultaneous conductive-carbon embedding, conductive-fibre interconnection, particle densification and spheroidisation through a single dry surface-engineering operation. Conventional carbon black blending, slurry coating and pyrolytic coating approaches typically leave conductive additives physically mixed or superficially deposited on active-material particles and therefore do not provide the mechanically anchored conductive-carbon architecture, conductive-bridge formation and cooperative morphology modification achieved by the mechano-fusion processing disclosed herein. [010] Accordingly, there remains a need for an improved and scalable process capable of producing high tap-density LiFePO4 cathode materials with enhanced electrical conductivity, controlled particle morphology, and improved electrode compaction density suitable for high-performance lithium-ion batteries. [011] Lithium iron manganese phosphate (LFMP/LMFP) materials are structurally related olivine phosphate cathode materials in which manganese partially substitutes iron to increase operating voltage and energy density. However, manganese-containing olivine phosphate materials may suffer from lower electronic conductivity, manganese-related resistance growth, non-uniform carbon coating, irregular morphology, poor powder packing, lower tap density and processing instability. [012] Accordingly, there is a need for a common industrial process platform capable of producing both LiFePO4 and LiFexMn(1-x)PO4 cathode materials using the same integrated wet precursor homogenization, spray granulation, densification, controlled calcination and post-synthesis mechano-fusion conductive embedding sequence. [013] Although various hydrothermal, solvothermal, glycothermal, solid-state, spray-drying and carbon-coating methods for producing olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials have been reported, such methods generally do not provide an integrated industrial manufacturing process combining precursor homogenization, spherical granule formation, pressure-assisted densification, controlled multi-zone calcination, particle-size engineering and post-synthesis mechano-fusion conductive-carbon embedding and spheroidisation within a coordinated production platform. Furthermore, conventional approaches generally rely upon carbonization, pyrolytic carbon coating, surface deposition or physical carbon blending techniques and do not simultaneously generate mechanically anchored conductive-carbon networks, conductive-fibre interconnections, particle densification, conductive-network formation and spheroidised particle morphology while maintaining low conductive-carbon loading and high active-material content. Existing technologies also do not provide a common industrial process platform capable of producing lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium iron manganese phosphate (LiFexMn(1-x)PO4), lithium manganese phosphate (LiMnPO4) and related olivine phosphate cathode materials using substantially the same integrated manufacturing sequence. Objects of the Invention: [014] In a primary object, the invention intends to provide an integrated continuous or semi-continuous industrial process for producing Generation-4 LiFePO4 cathode material having high tap density, high electrode compaction density, high electrical conductivity and improved electrochemical performance. [015] In a second object, the invention intends to provide a hybrid route that combines wet ball-milling or solution/slurry homogenization, high-shear slurry conditioning, spray drying, densification, controlled multi-stage calcination and post-synthesis mechano-fusion in a coordinated manufacturing sequence. [016] In a third object, the invention provides LiFePO4 particles having a uniform in-situ carbon layer from carbon precursors and a post-synthesis graphitic or partially graphitic carbon network mechanically fused to the particle surface. [017] In a fourth object, the invention intends to provide a mechano-fusion step configured to simultaneously embed about 0.3 wt% to about 3 wt% conductive carbon, including vapour-grown carbon fibre, carbon nanotube, carbon black, graphite, soft carbon or combinations thereof, while spheroidising and compacting the particles. [018] In a fifth object, the invention intends to improve particle packing efficiency, reduce internal porosity, enhance powder flowability and increase tap density without sacrificing high-rate discharge performance. [019] In a sixth object, the invention intends to maintain Fe2+ stability and minimize impurity phase formation by controlling pH, oxygen exposure, dew point, furnace atmosphere and cooling conditions. [020] In a seventh object, the invention intends to provide a product suitable for EV and ESS lithium-ion cells, including materials having tap density of at least about 1.35 g/cm³, electrode compaction density of at least about 2.55 g/cm³, electronic conductivity of at least about 1 x 10-2 S/cm and, in preferred embodiments, capacity retention of at least about 90% at 5 °C. [021] In an eighth object, the invention intends to provide manufacturing controls and quality control gates that enable scale-up from laboratory to pilot and production lines, while maintaining morphology, particle size distribution, carbon content and electrochemical consistency. [022] In a ninth object, the invention intends to provide the same integrated industrial process platform for manganese-containing olivine phosphate cathode materials including LiFexMn(1-x)PO4, LFMP/LMFP and lithium manganese phosphate, thereby reducing the possibility of design-around by merely substituting manganese for part of the iron in the olivine phosphate composition. [023] In a tenth and final object, the invention intends to provide high-density mixed Fe/Mn olivine phosphate cathode materials having mechanically embedded graphitic or partially graphitic conductive-carbon networks and spheroidised morphology using the same post-synthesis mechano-fusion processing route. Summary of the Invention: [024] In view of the above objects, the invention, in its primary aspect, provides an integrated continuous hybrid manufacturing process for producing fibre-embedded graphitic or partially graphitic carbon-coated Generation-4 olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials, including lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium iron manganese phosphate (LiFexMn(1-x)PO4), lithium manganese phosphate (LiMnPO4), and mixed Fe/Mn olivine phosphate derivatives having high tap density, high electrode compaction density, improved electrical conductivity, enhanced rate capability, and improved low-temperature electrochemical performance. [025] In one aspect, the invention provides a coordinated multi-step process comprising: (1) wet ball-milling of lithium, iron, and phosphate precursor materials in a liquid medium to achieve homogeneous precursor dispersion and intimate reactant contact to form a precursor slurry; (2) high-shear or high-speed conditioning of slurry of step (1) to improve dispersion stability, rheology control, and particle uniformity; (3) spray drying of the conditioned slurry of step (2) to produce substantially spherical precursor granules having controlled moisture content, morphology, and particle-size distribution; (4) densification of the precursor granules of step (3) through pelletisation and/or cold isostatic pressing (CIP) to reduce internal voids, improve particle packing efficiency, and promote formation of high-density secondary structures; (5) controlled multi-stage calcination of the structures of step (4) under inert, reducing, or controlled atmosphere to form phase-pure olivine LiFePO4 with in-situ carbon coating derived from carbon precursors; (6) controlled milling and particle-size classification of the particles of step (5) to obtain optimized D10/D50/D90 particle-size distribution suitable for cathode fabrication; and (7) post-synthesis mechano-fusion processing of the particles of step (6) configured to simultaneously embed graphitic or partially graphitic conductive carbon onto LiFePO4 particle surfaces and spheroidise the particles, thereby forming an interconnected conductive carbon network while improving particle roundness, packing behaviour, tap density, and electrode compaction density. [026] In an aspect the invention provides an integrated process platform for olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials represented by LiMPO4 or LiFexMn(1-x)PO4, wherein M comprises Fe, Mn, Fe/Mn combinations or substituted transition-metal combinations, and wherein x is greater than 0 and less than 1, preferably about 0.05 to about 0.95. The same coordinated process sequence is applicable to LiFePO4, LiMnPO4, LFMP/LMFP, and doped or substituted olivine phosphate derivatives. Brief Description of Drawings: [027] Figure (001) illustrates the overall integrated industrial process flow for producing Generation-4 lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4/C) cathode material including raw-material feeding, wet milling, slurry conditioning, spray drying, densification, staged calcination, cooling, jet milling, mechano-fusion conductive embedding, spheroidisation and final packaging. [028] Figure (002) illustrates precursor preparation comprising wet ball milling and high-shear slurry homogenization of lithium source, iron source, phosphate source, carbon precursor and liquid medium. [029] Figure (003) illustrates spray drying for producing substantially spherical precursor granules from conditioned precursor slurry. [030] Figure (004) illustrates a continuous multi-zone furnace configured for controlled thermal processing and olivine LiFePO4 formation under inert or controlled atmosphere. [031] Figure (005) illustrates post-calcination particle engineering comprising jet milling, conductive-carbon pre-mixing and post-synthesis mechano-fusion conductive embedding and spheroidisation. [032] Figure (006) illustrates the mechanism of mechano-fusion carbon embedding and particle spheroidisation, including particle acceleration, shear and compression, frictional heating, carbon anchoring, particle rounding, densification and formation of an embedded conductive-carbon network around spheroidised LiFePO4 or LiFexMn(1-x)PO4 particles. [033] Figure (007) illustrates representative particle-size distribution (PSD) analysis including D10, D50 and D90 particle-size values. [034] Figure (008) illustrates representative X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis and crystal-structure confirmation of the LiFePO4 material. [035] Figure (009) illustrates representative scanning electron microscopy (SEM) morphology before and after conductive-carbon embedding and mechano-fusion spheroidisation. [036] Figure (009) illustrates representative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images showing embedded conductive-carbon fibres and conductive-network formation surrounding spheroidised LiFePO4 particles. [037] Figure (010) illustrates representative electrochemical charge-discharge performance at different C-rates and temperatures including 25°C, 0°C and 45°C together with 0.1C reversibility behaviour. [038] Figure (011) illustrates representative cycling stability and capacity-retention performance during extended electrochemical cycling. [039] Figure (012) illustrates representative industrial quality-control (QC) and process-control (PC) architecture including raw-material QC, slurry QC, spray-dryer QC, calcination QC, mechano-fusion QC and electrochemical cell testing. [040] Unless otherwise specified, the drawings and representative LFP data may also illustrate the same integrated process platform as applied to manganese-containing olivine phosphate materials, including LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4, with suitable adjustment of iron and manganese precursor feed ratios. Detailed Description of Drawings: [041] 6.1 Figure (001) – Integrated Industrial Process Flow [042] Figure (001) illustrates the complete integrated manufacturing route starting from raw-material feeding and proceeding through wet milling, high-speed/high-shear mixing, spray drying, pelletisation, multi-zone furnace calcination, controlled cooling, jet milling, pre-mixing, jet spheroidisation/mechano-fusion and final packing. The figure supports the industrial process character of the invention and shows how the unit operations are coordinated to obtain high tap density, improved compaction density, improved conductive-network formation and scalable production consistency. [043] 6.2 Figure (002) – Precursor Preparation, Wet Milling and High-Shear Homogenization. [044] Figure (002) illustrates preparation of a uniform precursor slurry from lithium salts, iron salts, manganese salts where applicable, phosphate source, carbon source, additives and water or other liquid medium. Wet ball milling provides intimate precursor contact and particle-size reduction, while high-shear homogenization improves dispersion stability, slurry uniformity and downstream spray-drying consistency. This stage contributes to uniform Li/Fe/P or Li/Fe/Mn/P distribution and supports phase-pure olivine phosphate formation after calcination. [045] 6.3 Figure (003) – Spray-Drying Process for Spherical Precursor Granules [046] Figure (003) illustrates conditioned precursor slurry being fed to a spray dryer through an atomizer nozzle to form fine droplets and dried spherical precursor granules. The cyclone separator and fines collection system assist powder recovery. The spray-drying stage improves granule morphology, powder flowability, downstream densification behaviour and uniform thermal conversion. [047] 6.4 Figure (004) – Continuous Multi-Zone Furnace for Controlled Thermal Processing [048] Figure (004) illustrates a continuous multi-zone pusher tray furnace configured for olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode material processing, including LiFePO4 and LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4, under N2/Ar/H2 or other controlled atmosphere. Representative zones include pre-drying at about 120-180°C, binder pyrolysis/degassing at about 300-450°C, solid-state reaction at about 600-650°C, high-temperature sintering/crystallization at about 750-850°C, controlled cooling at about 350-200°C and rapid cooling/discharge at about 200-50°C. Atmosphere control, inert gas flow, exhaust handling and sealed discharge assist transition-metal oxidation-state control and impurity reduction. [049] 6.5 Figure (005) – Jet Milling, Carbon Pre-Mixing and Post-Synthesis Mechano-Fusion [050] Figure (005) illustrates post-calcination particle engineering in which cooled olivine phosphate material is jet milled to control D10, D50 and D90 particle size, pre-mixed with graphitic or partially graphitic conductive carbon, and processed in a post-synthesis mechano-fusion device. This stage prepares the material for simultaneous conductive-carbon embedding, spheroidisation, surface conductive-network formation, inter-particle resistance reduction and tap-density improvement. [051] Figure (006)-Mechanism of Mechano-Fusion Carbon Embedding and Particle Spheroidisation [052] Figure (006) schematically illustrates the mechanism by which conductive carbon is embedded into and around LiFePO4, LiFexMn(1-x)PO4 or other olivine phosphate particles during post-synthesis mechano-fusion processing. [053] In the particle acceleration stage, olivine phosphate particles and conductive-carbon particles are introduced into a high-speed mechano-fusion chamber comprising a rotating rotor, stator wall and high-shear processing zone. Rotation of the rotor accelerates the particles and repeatedly drives them through narrow shear and compression regions. [054] In the shear and compression stage, intense high-shear force and compressive stress act on the powder mixture. Conductive-carbon particles including graphitic carbon, partially graphitic carbon, carbon black, soft carbon, vapour-grown carbon fibre, carbon nanotubes, graphene-derived carbon or combinations thereof are pressed against active-material particle surfaces and become mechanically anchored or embedded. [055] The carbon embedding shown in Figure (006) is different from ordinary dry blending because the conductive carbon is not merely physically mixed with the active material. Instead, shear and compression cause carbon particles, fibres or nanotubes to be fused, wrapped, bridged or mechanically locked onto the particle surfaces, thereby forming more stable conductive contacts. [056] In the frictional heating stage, repeated particle-particle and particle-wall contact generates localized surface heating. Representative localized temperatures may be within about 80°C to about 400°C depending on rotor speed, residence time, powder loading, chamber clearance and carbon concentration. This localized frictional heating activates particle surfaces and improves adhesion or bonding of conductive carbon to the olivine phosphate particles. [057] The localized thermal and mechanical energy assists formation of mechanically stabilized carbon bonding regions, improves conductive-carbon spreading over the particle surface, reduces carbon segregation and improves conductive-network continuity. [058] In the particle spheroidisation stage, continued shear, compression and frictional processing progressively round angular particles, smooth rough edges, compact loose agglomerates, collapse internal voids and densify secondary particles. This produces substantially spheroidised particles with improved packing behaviour and lower inter-particle void volume. [059] The spheroidised morphology generated by the mechanism of Figure (006) contributes to increased tap density, improved electrode compaction density, improved powder flowability, improved calendaring behaviour, reduced electrode porosity and improved volumetric energy density. [060] In the embedded carbon-network stage, graphitic or partially graphitic carbon domains, carbon nanotubes, vapour-grown carbon fibres and other conductive-carbon components form an interconnected network around the spheroidised olivine phosphate core. The network provides conductive bridges between neighbouring active-material particles and reduces inter-particle electronic resistance. [061] The final particle structure shown in Figure (006) includes a spheroidised olivine phosphate core, an embedded conductive-carbon layer and an external conductive-carbon network. This combined structure improves electronic conductivity, charge-transfer kinetics, high-rate discharge capability, fast-charging behaviour, low-temperature performance and cycling stability. [062] The cooperative mechanism of Figure (006) therefore demonstrates that mechano-fusion simultaneously performs conductive-carbon embedding, localized frictional surface activation, conductive-network formation, particle densification and spheroidisation in a single post-synthesis particle-engineering operation. [063] Figure (007) illustrates post-calcination particle engineering in which cooled olivine phosphate material, including LFP or LFMP/LMFP material, is jet milled to control D10, D50 and D90 particle size, pre-mixed with graphitic or partially graphitic conductive carbon, and processed in a post-synthesis mechano-fusion device. This stage simultaneously embeds conductive carbon, promotes particle spheroidisation, improves surface conductive-network formation, reduces inter-particle resistance and improves tap density and electrode compaction behaviour. [064] 6.6 Figure (007) – Particle-Size Distribution Analysis [065] Figure (007) illustrates representative particle-size distribution of the processed LiFePO4/C powder. The measured values shown are D10 = 0.2721 μm, D50 = 1.0943 μm and D90 = 3.6716 μm. The narrow and controlled distribution supports improved electrode coating uniformity, reduced oversized agglomerates, effective lithium-ion diffusion and improved rate capability. [066] 6.7 Figure (008) – XRD Structural Analysis [067] Figure (008) illustrates representative XRD analysis for the LiFePO4 material together with crystal-structure information. The pattern corresponds to an orthorhombic olivine LiFePO4 structure with Pnma space group. Representative lattice parameters shown include a = 10.32 Å, b = 6.00 Å, c = 4.69 Å, α = β = 90°, γ = 90°, and unit-cell volume of about 290.85 Å3. The refinement parameters shown include Rw = 9.321% and GOF = 1.49, supporting successful olivine phase formation and reduced impurity contribution. [068] 6.8 Figure (009) – SEM Morphology Before and After Mechano-Fusion Spheroidisation [069] Figure (009) illustrates representative SEM morphology comparison before and after conductive-carbon embedding and mechano-fusion spheroidisation processing according to preferred embodiments of the present invention. [070] Before conductive-carbon embedding and mechano-fusion spheroidisation processing, the lithium iron phosphate particles exhibit relatively irregular, angular and loosely packed morphology with comparatively porous and lower-density secondary particles. The untreated material further exhibits rough particle surfaces, non-uniform particle-size distribution, increased inter-particle void regions and partial agglomeration, which may contribute to reduced powder packing efficiency, lower tap density and higher inter-particle resistance. [071] After conductive-carbon embedding and mechano-fusion spheroidisation processing, the inventive Generation-4 LiFePO4/C material exhibits substantially more rounded, compact and densified spheroidised secondary-particle morphology with improved particle-contact uniformity and reduced agglomeration. [072] The SEM observations further indicate formation of a more uniform conductive-carbon distribution surrounding and interconnecting the LiFePO4 particles. The graphitic or partially graphitic conductive carbon becomes mechanically embedded and anchored onto the particle surfaces during high-shear mechano-fusion processing, thereby improving conductive-network continuity and conductive-contact stability. [073] The combined effects of conductive-carbon embedding and particle spheroidisation contribute to: • increased tap density; • improved electrode compaction density; • improved powder flowability; • improved particle packing behaviour; • reduced inter-particle voids; • reduced electrode porosity; • reduced inter-particle resistance; • improved electron-transport pathways; • improved conductive-network formation; • improved calendaring behaviour; and • improved volumetric energy density. [074] The rounded and densified secondary-particle morphology generated through mechano-fusion processing further improves electrode structural uniformity and enhances electrochemical reproducibility during high-rate charge-discharge operation. [075] Accordingly, the SEM morphology results demonstrate that the integrated conductive-carbon embedding and spheroidisation process provides significant structural, conductivity and electrochemical advantages compared with conventional lithium iron phosphate materials lacking post-synthesis mechano-fusion treatment. [076] 6.9 Figure (009) – TEM Analysis of Conductive-Carbon Embedded Network and Spheroidised LiFePO4 Particles: [077] Figure (009) illustrates representative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) morphology of the inventive Generation-4 LiFePO4/C material after conductive-carbon embedding and mechano-fusion spheroidisation processing. [078] The TEM images demonstrate formation of an interconnected conductive-carbon architecture surrounding and interconnecting the LiFePO4 particles. Embedded graphitic or partially graphitic conductive fibres, including vapour-grown carbon fibres (VGCF), carbon nanotubes (CNT), graphitic carbon and conductive-carbon networks, are mechanically anchored and distributed throughout the spheroidised LiFePO4 particle structure. [079] The TEM observations further indicate that the conductive carbon forms a substantially continuous electron-transport pathway between neighbouring LiFePO4 particles, thereby improving conductive-network continuity and reducing inter-particle electronic resistance. [080] Compared with untreated or conventionally blended LiFePO4 materials, the inventive material exhibits: • improved conductive-carbon distribution; • improved conductive-network uniformity; • improved conductive-fibre interconnection; • improved particle-contact conductivity; • reduced conductive-network discontinuity; • reduced inter-particle resistance; • improved electron transport pathways; and • improved electrochemical reaction uniformity. [081] The TEM images further support that mechano-fusion processing simultaneously: • embeds conductive carbon; • promotes conductive-fibre interconnection; • densifies secondary particles; • reduces internal void regions; • improves spheroidisation; and • improves conductive-contact stability during cycling. [082] The embedded conductive-fibre architecture contributes to: • increased electronic conductivity; • improved high-rate discharge capability; • improved fast-charging performance; • improved low-temperature electrochemical behaviour; • improved cycling stability; • improved tap density; • improved electrode compaction density; and • improved volumetric energy density. [083] Accordingly, the TEM analysis confirms that the integrated mechano-fusion conductive embedding process forms a mechanically stabilized conductive-carbon network not achievable through conventional physical carbon blending processes. [084] 6.10 Figure (010) – Electrochemical Charge-Discharge and Temperature Performance [085] Figure (010) illustrates charge-discharge profiles at different C-rates at about 25°C, 0°C and 45°C, and 0.1C cycle-to-cycle reversibility. The profiles demonstrate a stable LiFePO4 plateau near about 3.4 V, high reversible capacity, reduced polarization and improved high-rate behaviour. Representative capacities are about 160–165 mAh/g at 0.1C, about 148–155 mAh/g at 1C and about 125–135 mAh/g at 5C at room temperature, with stable low-temperature and elevated-temperature behaviour. [086] 6.11 Figure (011) – Cycling Stability and Capacity Retention [087] Figure (010) illustrates 100-cycle stability at 0.1C. Representative values shown include an initial discharge capacity of about 164.3 mAh/g, an intermediate capacity of about 163.21–163.56 mAh/g, and a final capacity of about 162.02 mAh/g after 100 cycles, corresponding to approximately 98.61% capacity retention. The cycling profile demonstrates stable reversible lithium insertion/extraction, stable conductive-network retention and improved electrochemical durability. [088] 6.12 Figure (011) – Cycling Stability and Capacity-Retention Performance [089] Figure (011) illustrates representative cycling stability, discharge capacity retention and electrochemical durability of the Generation-4 LiFePO4/C material. The cycling profile supports stable lithium insertion and extraction, reduced polarization growth and retention of the conductive-carbon network during repeated charge-discharge operation. [090] 6.13 Figure (012) – Industrial Quality-Control and Process-Control Architecture [091] Figure (012) illustrates a representative industrial QC/PC architecture for the integrated Generation-4 LiFePO4/C manufacturing line. The architecture includes sequential QC gates at raw-material receiving, wet milling and slurry conditioning, spray drying, densification, calcination, jet milling/classification, mechano-fusion carbon embedding, final powder packaging and electrochemical cell testing. [092] At the raw-material QC gate, precursor purity, moisture content, trace metals and impurity levels are verified before release to production. During wet milling and slurry conditioning, pH, viscosity, solids loading, slurry stability and Fe2+/Fe3+ indicators are monitored to maintain precursor dispersion and minimize oxidation. During spray drying, granule particle-size distribution, morphology, residual moisture, outlet temperature and collection efficiency are controlled to obtain free-flowing spherical precursor granules. [093] The densification QC gate monitors green density, compact integrity and granule strength. The calcination QC gate monitors furnace temperature profile, oxygen concentration, dew point, inert-gas flow, residence time, XRD phase purity, carbonization behaviour and residual lithium or impurity phases. Jet milling and classification QC monitor D10, D50, D90, oversized particles, fines and agglomerate control. [094] The mechano-fusion QC gate monitors conductive-carbon loading, carbon distribution, particle spheroidisation, tap density, powder conductivity and morphology after graphitic or partially graphitic carbon embedding. Final powder QC includes tap density, residual moisture, flowability, magnetic contamination screening, carbon content, electronic conductivity and packaging under dry-room or inert atmosphere conditions. [095] The PC architecture further includes a central PLC/SCADA or equivalent control system configured to receive inline and offline QC data and adjust feed rate, atomization conditions, furnace atmosphere, gas flow, milling/classifier settings, mechano-fusion parameters and reject/recycle loops. Electrochemical release testing verifies discharge capacity, rate capability, cycling stability, EIS response, first-cycle efficiency and low-temperature retention before product batch release. [096] This integrated QC/PC architecture supports industrial reproducibility, batch traceability, morphology consistency, carbon-network uniformity, tap-density control, conductivity control and electrochemical consistency during scale-up from laboratory to pilot and production-scale manufacture. Detailed Description of the Invention: [097] In order to provide a clear and consistent understanding of the terms used in the present specification, a number of definitions are provided below. Moreover, unless defined otherwise, all technical and scientific terms as used herein have the same meaning as commonly understood by the person of ordinary skill in the art to which this invention pertains. [098] The use of the word “a” or “an” when used in conjunction with the term “comprising” in the claims and/or the specification may not only mean “one”, but also encompasses the meaning of “one or more”, “at least one”, and “one or more than one”. Similarly, the word “another” may mean at least a second or more. [099] As used in this specification and claim(s), the words “comprising” (and any form of comprising, such as “comprise” and “comprises”), “having” (and any form of having, such as “have” and “has”), “including” (and any form of including, such as “include” and “includes”) or “containing” (and any form of containing, such as “contain” and “contains”), are inclusive or open-ended and do not exclude additional, unrecited elements or process steps. [100] Definitions: For the purposes of the present invention, the following terms are defined as follows: “Tap density” refers to the tapped bulk density of a powder material measured using a standardized mechanical tapping method, typically expressed in grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). “Electrode compaction density” refers to the density of a cathode electrode after calendaring or compression during electrode fabrication, typically expressed in g/cm³. “Generation-4 lithium iron phosphate” (Generation-4 LFP) refers to an engineered LiFePO4 cathode material characterized by high tap density, high electrode compaction density, improved electrical conductivity, enhanced rate capability, and improved electrochemical stability achieved through controlled particle morphology, phase purity, and conductive carbon coating. “Mechano-fusion processing” refers to a high-energy mechanical treatment in which particles are subjected to intense shear, compression, and friction forces within a rotating chamber, enabling conductive carbon materials to be mechanically fused and embedded onto the surface of LiFePO4 particles while simultaneously promoting particle spheroidisation and densification. “Conductive carbon network” refers to a conductive layer or interconnected carbon structure formed on or around LiFePO4 particles that enhances electron transport and electrical conductivity within the cathode material. “Lithium transition-metal phosphate” refers to olivine-structured phosphate cathode materials including LiFePO4, LiMnPO4, LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4, lithium iron manganese phosphate (LFMP/LMFP), and doped or substituted olivine phosphate derivatives containing Fe, Mn, Mg, Ti, Zr, Nb, V, Al or combinations thereof. “Generation-4 olivine phosphate cathode material” refers to a high-density engineered olivine cathode material selected from LiFePO4, LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4, LiMnPO4 or substituted derivatives thereof, characterized by controlled phase purity, spheroidised secondary morphology, high tap density, high electrode compaction density and an embedded graphitic or fibrous conductive-carbon network. [101] The invention describes olivine-type lithium transition-metal phosphate cathode materials, including lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium manganese phosphate (LiMnPO4), lithium iron manganese phosphate (LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4), mixed Fe/Mn olivine phosphate systems, and substituted olivine phosphate derivatives. [102] In certain embodiments, the cathode material comprises lithium iron manganese phosphate having a general formula LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4, where x ranges from about 0.05 to about 0.95. The relative Fe:Mn ratio may be selected according to voltage, capacity, conductivity and stability requirements, while the integrated process sequence remains materially the same. [103] Further, the invention intends to provide an integrated process platform not only for LiFePO4 but also for manganese-containing olivine phosphate cathode materials, including lithium iron manganese phosphate, manganese-rich lithium iron manganese phosphate, lithium manganese phosphate and other mixed-metal olivine phosphate derivatives processed by the same coordinated manufacturing sequence. [115] Accordingly, the process utilizes a precursor slurry containing lithium, iron, manganese where applicable, and phosphate precursor materials in stoichiometric proportions corresponding to lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4), lithium iron manganese phosphate (LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4), lithium manganese phosphate (LiMnPO4) or substituted olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate materials, optionally with slight stoichiometric adjustments to compensate for process losses during subsequent processing steps. [116] The precursor slurry is subjected to wet ball-milling in a liquid medium using ceramic or other chemically inert milling media to achieve fine particle dispersion, homogeneous mixing of the precursor components, and mechano-chemical activation of the reactants. [117] Typical milling conditions may include a rotational speed in the range of about 300-600 rpm, a milling duration of about 2-6 hours, a ball-to-powder ratio of about 5:1 to 15:1, and a solids loading of about 20-35 wt% in the slurry.
