[118] In preferred embodiments, the milling vessel is maintained under an inert atmosphere such as nitrogen or argon to minimize oxygen exposure and preserve the oxidation state of iron in the Fe2⁺ form, thereby preventing undesirable oxidation reactions during precursor preparation. [119] The wet milling process facilitates uniform dispersion of the lithium, iron, manganese where applicable, and phosphate precursors, reduces particle agglomeration, and improves reactant contact at the microscopic level. Solution-phase milling also reduces dust formation and improves process safety compared with dry powder handling. [120] The output of Step (1) is a homogeneous precursor slurry exhibiting stable rheological properties, reduced agglomerate size, and improved compositional uniformity, which is suitable for subsequent slurry conditioning and spray-drying steps. The improved slurry uniformity contributes to the formation of consistent spherical granules during spray drying and enhanced densification during downstream processing steps. [121] Following wet milling, the precursor slurry is subjected to high-speed or high-shear conditioning in order to improve dispersion stability and rheological uniformity prior to spray drying. [122] The mixing operation may be performed using high-shear rotor-stator mixers, homogenizers, or equivalent mixing equipment. In certain embodiments, the mixing speed may be in the range of about 2000-8000 rpm, depending on slurry viscosity, solids loading, and dispersion requirements. [123] In preferred embodiments, the pH of the slurry may be controlled within a range of about 6.5 to 8.5, and more preferably about 7.0 to 8.0, in order to maintain precursor stability, prevent undesirable precipitation or agglomeration, and ensure uniform dispersion of lithium, iron, and phosphate species within the slurry. [124] The viscosity of the conditioned slurry may be adjusted to a suitable range for spray-drying atomization, typically about 300-700 centipoise (cP). Viscosity control may be achieved by adjusting solids loading, solvent composition, dispersant concentration, or other rheology-modifying additives. [125] In certain embodiments, entrained air bubbles may be removed from the slurry using de-foaming agents, vacuum de-aeration, or other degassing techniques in order to prevent foaming, nozzle instability, or inconsistent droplet formation during spray drying. [126] The conditioned slurry may further be subjected to inline filtration, for example using filters having pore sizes of about 50-200 µm, in order to remove foreign particles, oversized agglomerates, or contaminants. Such filtration improves spray-dryer nozzle reliability and contributes to consistent spherical granule formation. [127] The output of Step (2) is a well-dispersed and homogeneous precursor slurry having controlled viscosity, stable rheological properties, and minimal agglomeration, suitable for efficient atomization and spherical particle formation in the subsequent spray-drying process. [128] In accordance with the above embodiment, the precursor slurry of Step (2) is then subjected to spray-drying in step (3). [129] Step (3) comprises converting the conditioned precursor slurry obtained from Step (2) into free-flowing spherical precursor granules using a spray-drying process. Spray drying facilitates controlled particle morphology, uniform granule formation, and improved powder handling characteristics. [130] In this step, the slurry is atomized into fine droplets within a spray-drying chamber, where rapid solvent evaporation produces spherical granules having controlled particle size distribution and internal microstructure. [131] Atomization may be achieved using two-fluid nozzles, pressure nozzles, rotary atomizers, or equivalent atomization devices capable of generating uniform droplets. In certain embodiments, the spray dryer may be operated with an inlet gas temperature in the range of about 180-430 °C and an outlet temperature in the range of about 90-120 °C, although other temperature conditions may be used depending on slurry composition, solvent system, and desired drying characteristics. [132] The feed rate, atomization pressure, and gas flow rate may be adjusted to obtain stable droplet formation and to reduce the residual moisture content of the granules, typically to less than about 0.2 wt%. [133] In certain embodiments, the resulting granules may have a median particle size (D50) in the range of about 10-50 µm, although other particle size distributions may be produced depending on atomization conditions and downstream processing requirements. [134] The spray-drying system may further include cyclone separators, bag filters, or equivalent particle recovery systems to capture fine particles and improve overall material yield. In certain embodiments, heat recovery systems may be incorporated to improve the energy efficiency of the spray-drying operation. [135] The spherical precursor granules produced by this step exhibit improved flowability, uniform packing behaviour, and controlled internal porosity, which contribute to enhanced densification, uniform thermal treatment, and improved particle morphology during subsequent pelletisation and calcination steps. [136] The spray-dried granules obtained from step (3) may thereafter be subjected to densification prior to thermal treatment. The densification through cold isostatic pressing (CIP) at pressures of about 100 MPa to about 300 MPa significantly reduces internal porosity and enhances precursor packing uniformity prior to calcination. The combined effect of spray-granule engineering, CIP densification, and post-synthesis spheroidisation enables production of high-density Generation-4 LiFePO4 particles exhibiting substantially improved tap density and electrode compaction density compared with conventional LiFePO4 materials. [137] In certain embodiments, the spray-dried granules may be placed in flexible moulds or sealed elastomeric containers and subjected to hydrostatic pressure within a pressure vessel filled with a suitable pressure-transmitting fluid. Typical pressing conditions may include pressures in the range of about 100-300 MPa applied for a duration of about 1-3 minutes, although other pressures and holding times may be employed depending on granule properties and desired densification levels. [138] Following the CIP treatment, the densified compacts may optionally be lightly crushed, granulated, or sieved to obtain a suitable particle size distribution for subsequent thermal processing while retaining the densification benefits obtained during pressing. [139] The CIP densification step significantly reduces internal porosity within the granules, improves particle-to-particle contact, and enhances the packing efficiency of the precursor material. These characteristics contribute to more uniform phase formation during subsequent calcination and facilitate the production of lithium iron phosphate particles with improved morphology and higher tap density. [140] The inclusion of the CIP densification step enables enhanced final tap density and improved electrode compaction density without requiring excessive high-temperature sintering, which could otherwise lead to undesirable coarsening of the primary particles. [141] The densified material of step (4) is then subjected to a continuous multi-zone thermal treatment for formation of phase-pure olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate. [142] Step (5) comprises subjecting the densified precursor material obtained from Step (4) to a continuous multi-zone thermal treatment in order to convert the precursor composition into phase-pure olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate including LiFePO4, LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4 or LiMnPO4 while controlling particle morphology and minimizing undesirable grain coarsening. [143] The thermal treatment may be carried out in a multi-zone furnace system, including but not limited to a rotary kiln furnace, belt furnace, pusher furnace, or other continuous conveying furnace, operating under a controlled atmosphere such as nitrogen, argon, or mixtures thereof. In certain embodiments, the furnace operates in a continuous processing mode, wherein the precursor material is conveyed through a plurality of sequential temperature zones configured to perform drying, precursor reaction, crystallization, and cooling processes. [144] In preferred embodiments, the overall residence time of the material within the multi-zone furnace ranges from about 30 minutes to about 600 minutes, depending on furnace configuration, heating rate, material throughput, and the desired crystallinity and morphology of the LiFePO4 particles. [145] In certain embodiments, the multi-zone thermal treatment comprises the following temperature regions: [146] Drying Zone: The precursor material is exposed to a temperature in the range of about 120-180°C for approximately 30-120 minutes to remove residual moisture and volatile components originating from the spray-drying and densification steps. [147] Pre-Reaction Zone The material is subsequently heated to a temperature in the range of about 300-450°C for approximately 30-120 minutes, during which decomposition of organic components and carbon precursors occurs and intermediate lithium-iron-phosphate precursor phases begin to form. [148] Primary Reaction Zone The precursor material is further heated to a temperature in the range of about 600-650°C for approximately 15-120 minutes, enabling formation of the olivine LiFePO4 crystal structure and initiation of in-situ carbon formation from the carbon precursor. [149] Crystallization Zone The material is subsequently exposed to a higher temperature region in the range of about 750-850°C for approximately 5-120 minutes to complete crystallization of the olivine LiFePO4 phase, improve crystal ordering, and enhance electronic conductivity through carbonization of the carbon precursor. [150] Controlled Cooling Zone Following the crystallization stage, the material is gradually cooled within a controlled cooling zone to a temperature typically below about 200 °C, preferably within the range of about 50-200°C, while maintaining an inert or controlled atmosphere. Cooling within the cooling zone may be achieved through one or more cooling mechanisms including water-chiller assisted cooling jackets, water-cooled furnace walls or heat exchangers, and circulating cooled gas streams within the cooling zone. In certain embodiments, cooled inert gases such as nitrogen or argon may be circulated to remove heat from the material while preventing oxidation. [151] Controlled cooling prevents undesirable oxidation reactions, preserves the desired LiFePO4 crystal structure, and minimizes thermal stress that could otherwise lead to particle fracture or morphology degradation. [152] During the thermal treatment, gas flow rate, oxygen concentration, and furnace atmosphere may be carefully controlled to minimize formation of impurity phases and to maintain the desired chemical environment for LiFePO4 formation. [153] The continuous multi-zone thermal treatment enables controlled phase formation, improved crystallinity, optimized carbon coating, and stable particle morphology suitable for achieving high tap density, improved electrode compaction density, enhanced electrical conductivity, and superior electrochemical performance, including improved rate capability and improved performance at low operating temperatures in lithium-ion battery applications. [154] Accordingly, calcination is carried out through multiple thermal zones comprising pre-calcination, olivine phase formation, crystallization/stabilization, and controlled inert cooling stages. Controlled thermal treatment improves phase purity, preserves Fe²⁺ stability, suppresses impurity formation, and enhances carbon-assisted crystallization behaviour. [155] The calcined olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate material of step (5) is subjected to jet milling and classification in order to reduce soft agglomerates and achieve a controlled particle size distribution suitable for subsequent carbon coating and particle morphology engineering. [156] Jet milling may be performed using a fluidized-bed jet mill, spiral jet mill, or other high-energy gas milling system, wherein compressed gas streams such as nitrogen or air accelerate particles to induce inter-particle collisions and fragmentation. This process effectively breaks down soft agglomerates formed during calcination while largely preserving the primary particle structure. [157] After milling, the material may be subjected to air classification, centrifugal classification, or dynamic classifier systems to remove oversized particles and regulate the proportion of fine particles. In certain embodiments, oversized fractions separated during classification may be recycled to the jet milling stage for further size reduction. [158] In preferred embodiments, the resulting lithium iron phosphate powder exhibits a particle size distribution with a median particle size (D50) in the range of about 0.1-6 µm, with controlled D10 and D90 values suitable for downstream particle engineering and cathode material processing. [159] The jet milling and classification step enables precise control of particle size distribution, improved powder flowability, and uniform particle morphology, thereby preparing the lithium iron phosphate particles for the subsequent carbon coating and particle spheroidisation process. [160] In yet another embodiment, the invention further provides a post-synthesis mechano-fusion process configured to simultaneously perform carbon embedding and particle spheroidisation, thereby forming a conductive graphitic or partially graphitic carbon network on the LiFePO4 particle surface and improving particle packing density, electrical conductivity, and electrochemical performance. The process comprises: 1. carbon coating the lithium transition-metal phosphate material of step (6) as above; and 2. spheroidising the carbon-coated lithium transition-metal phosphate material obtained from the carbon coating step. [161] In one of the embodiments, the conductive-carbon network comprises graphitic carbon particles and fibrous conductive carbon bridging adjacent olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate particles to form a mechanically anchored three-dimensional conductive network on and between adjacent cathode-material particles. [162] Accordingly, following the jet milling and classification step described in Step (6), the olivine lithium transition-metal phosphate powder, including LiFePO4 or LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4 powder, is subjected to a carbon coating and particle spheroidisation process using mechano-fusion processing. [163] In this step, the olivine phosphate particles are processed in a mechano-fusion or high-shear mechanical processing system in which conductive carbon materials are mechanically embedded onto the particle surfaces while simultaneously promoting particle densification and spheroidisation. [164] In certain embodiments, the carbon source may comprise graphitic carbon, partially graphitic carbon, soft carbon, or combinations thereof. The carbon material may be introduced in an amount of about 0.3 wt% to about 3 wt% relative to the total weight of the olivine phosphate material, sufficient to form a conductive carbon network on the surface of LiFePO4, LiFe_xMn_(1-x)PO4 or related olivine phosphate particles while maintaining high active material loading. [165] During mechano-fusion processing, intense mechanical shear forces and compressive stresses are applied to the powder mixture, resulting in mechanical fusion of carbon particles onto the LiFePO4 particle surfaces. This process enables the formation of a conformal carbon coating layer while simultaneously promoting particle rounding and spheroidisation, thereby improving particle packing characteristics. [166] In preferred embodiments, the mechano-fusion process may be operated at rotational speeds ranging from about 5,000 to about 15,000 rpm, enabling efficient carbon embedding and controlled modification of particle morphology. [167] The mechano-fusion coating and spheroidisation process provides several advantages, including: • Formation of a uniform conductive carbon coating; • Improved electronic conductivity of the cathode material; • Enhanced particle spheroidisation; • Increased tap density; and • Improved electrode compaction behaviour during cathode fabrication. [168] In certain embodiments, the integrated sequence of jet milling, carbon pre-dispersion, and mechano-fusion-assisted spheroidisation facilitates increased tap density, enhanced electronic conductivity, and reduced particle aggregation, thereby yielding LiFePO4/C cathode materials demonstrating improved electrochemical characteristics, including superior rate capability and improved performance under low-temperature operating conditions in lithium-ion batteries. [169] Following the mechano-fusion coating and spheroidisation step, the processed material may be subjected to final quality control evaluation and packaging under controlled dry-room conditions prior to use in lithium-ion battery cathode manufacturing. [170] In certain embodiments, a rotational processing chamber comprising a high-shear compression rotor, a stator wall, and controlled feed ports generates intense compressive, shear, and frictional forces capable of mechanically embedding conductive carbon materials onto the surfaces of LiFePO4 particles. Preferably, about 0.3 wt% to about 3 wt% of graphitic or partially graphitic carbon, including vapour-grown carbon fibre (VGCF), carbon nanotubes, graphite, soft carbon, or combinations thereof, is embedded to form a substantially conformal conductive carbon network without introducing excessive inactive carbon loading. [171] Simultaneously, the mechano-fusion operation promotes rounding of angular particles, reduction of rough agglomerates, improved particle spheroidisation, enhanced secondary-particle packing behaviour, and reduced inter-particle resistance. The resulting fibre-embedded conductive carbon network further improves electron transport pathways, lowers charge-transfer resistance, and enhances high-rate electrochemical performance. [172] In accordance with the above embodiment, the mechano-fused product may subsequently be lightly classified to remove oversized agglomerates. Thereafter, the powder may be packaged under dry-room conditions or an inert atmosphere. Final moisture content is preferably controlled below about 500 ppm, and more preferably below about 300 ppm, depending on application requirements. [173] The disclosed process, in accordance with the various embodiments, enables industrial-scale, scalable production of LiFePO4 cathode materials exhibiting improved particle morphology, high tap density, enhanced electrode compaction density, improved low-temperature electrochemical performance, and consistent product quality. [190] Experimental Example 1: Laboratory Preparation of Gen-4 LFP/C: [191] A precursor slurry is prepared by combining lithium carbonate, ferric phosphate, glucose and one or more auxiliary carbon/chelating agents selected from citric acid, ascorbic acid, sucrose, lactose, fructose or combinations thereof in deionized water or an aqueous solvent medium. The slurry is wet ball-milled using zirconia media at about 300–600 rpm for 2–6 hours, preferably around 450 rpm for 4 hours, at about 20–40 wt% solids. The slurry pH is adjusted preferably within 6.5–8.5, more preferably around 7.0–8.0, and the viscosity is controlled to a range suitable for spray atomization. [192] The slurry is high-shear mixed at about 3,000–8,000 rpm for 10–60 minutes and filtered through a suitable screen before spray drying. The slurry is spray dried to form spherical precursor granules having D50 of about 10–50 µm and residual moisture below about 0.2–1.0 wt%. [193] The spray-dried granules are densified by pelletisation, roller compaction or cold isostatic pressing, followed by staged calcination under nitrogen or argon. The precursor material undergoes continuous multi-zone thermal treatment comprising: a Drying Zone (120–180 °C, 30–120 min) for moisture removal; a Pre-Reaction Zone (300–450 °C, 30–120 min) for decomposition of organic components and precursor phase formation; a Primary Reaction Zone (600–650 °C, 15–120 min) for olivine LiFePO₄ formation and in-situ carbon generation; a Crystallization Zone (750–850 °C, 5–120 min) for crystal growth and carbonization; and a Controlled Cooling Zone (<200 °C, preferably 50–200 °C) under an inert atmosphere. Controlled gas composition, oxygen concentration, and cooling conditions ensure high crystallinity, optimized carbon coating, stable morphology, enhanced conductivity, high tap density, and superior electrochemical performance. [194] The calcined powder is milled/classified to D50 of about 1–6 µm and then mechano-fused with 0.3–3 wt% conductive carbon, such as graphite, VGCF, CNT, carbon black or partially graphitic carbon, at about 5,000–15,000 rpm. The mechano-fusion step improves carbon embedding, spheroidisation, tap density, compaction density, conductivity and particle uniformity. [202] Experimental Example 7: Experimental Characterization and Measurement Methods: [203] The Generation-4 LiFePO4/C material and comparative control materials were evaluated using a coordinated set of powder, structural, surface, electrical and electrochemical characterization methods. The purpose of these methods was to verify the process-structure-property-performance relationship generated by the integrated wet milling, spray granulation, densification, staged calcination, jet milling/classification and post-synthesis mechano-fusion sequence. [204] X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Cu Kα radiation over a representative 2θ scan range suitable for LiFePO4 phase identification. The measured diffraction pattern was compared with the olivine LiFePO4 reference structure, and phase purity was evaluated by confirming the presence of dominant orthorhombic olivine LiFePO4 reflections and the absence or substantial reduction of impurity reflections such as Fe2O3, Fe3O4, FePO4, Li3PO4, Li4P2O7 and Fe2P. [205] Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to evaluate particle morphology, agglomerate condition, secondary-particle shape, surface compactness, particle-contact uniformity and spheroidisation after mechano-fusion. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to confirm the presence of conductive carbon fibres, graphitic or partially graphitic carbon bridges, carbon anchoring and conductive-network continuity around the LiFePO4 particles. The tap density was calculated as powder mass divided by tapped volume. [210] Powder electronic conductivity was measured using a four-probe method or compressed pellet conductivity fixture. In one representative method, a known mass of powder was pressed into a pellet or compressed powder bed under controlled pressure, and electrical resistance was measured using a four-point probe configuration. Conductivity was calculated from sample geometry and measured resistance. [211] Experimental Example 8: Cathode Electrode Preparation for Half-Cell Testing: [212] For electrochemical evaluation, cathode electrodes were prepared by mixing the Generation-4 LiFePO4/C active material with a conductive additive and a polymer binder. In one representative formulation, the electrode contained about 90-96 wt% LiFePO4/C active material, about 2-6 wt% conductive carbon and about 2-6 wt% binder. The conductive additive may comprise carbon black, acetylene black, Super P, graphite, CNT, VGCF or combinations thereof. The binder may comprise polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), carboxymethyl cellulose/styrene-butadiene rubber (CMC/SBR), PTFE or another cathode-compatible binder. [213] For PVDF-based electrodes, the active material, conductive additive and PVDF binder were dispersed in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) to form a uniform cathode slurry. The slurry was mixed until homogeneous and coated onto aluminium foil using a doctor blade, slot-die coating head or equivalent coating method. The coated electrode was dried at about 80-120°C to remove solvent, followed by vacuum drying at about 100-140°C to reduce residual solvent and moisture. [214] The dried electrode was calendared to a desired electrode density and punched into circular electrodes or cut into electrode strips depending on the cell format. Electrode mass loading may be selected according to the test purpose, for example about 2-5 mg/cm2 for high-precision laboratory rate testing or higher loading for practical electrode evaluation. Electrode compaction density was determined from electrode coating mass, electrode area and coating thickness after calendaring. [215] Experimental Example 9: Coin Cell / Half-Cell Assembly Procedure: [216] Half-cell testing was carried out using coin cells, pouch-type laboratory cells or equivalent lithium half-cell formats. In a representative CR2032 coin-cell procedure, the LiFePO4/C cathode electrode was used as the working electrode and lithium metal foil was used as both counter electrode and reference electrode. A porous polyolefin separator, glass-fibre separator or equivalent separator was placed between the cathode and lithium metal electrode. [217] The electrolyte may comprise 1 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate/diethyl carbonate, ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate, ethylene carbonate/ethyl methyl carbonate, or other carbonate solvent mixtures, optionally containing additives such as vinylene carbonate, fluoroethylene carbonate or lithium difluoro(oxalato)borate depending on cell-design requirements. Cell assembly was performed in a dry room or argon-filled glove box with low moisture and low oxygen levels. [218] The assembled cells were rested for electrolyte wetting and then subjected to formation cycling before rate-capability and cycling tests. The voltage window for LiFePO4 half-cell testing may be about 2.5-4.2 V versus Li/Li+, preferably about 2.5-4.0 V or about 2.7-3.8 V depending on the test protocol. C-rate was calculated based on the theoretical capacity of LiFePO4 or measured low-rate capacity, and discharge capacities were normalized to active-material mass. [219] Experimental Example 10: Electrochemical Testing Protocol: [220] Electrochemical testing included, low-rate formation, rate capability, cycling retention, temperature-dependent discharge and impedance evaluation. In one representative protocol, cells were cycled at 0.1C for formation and low-rate capacity determination, followed by sequential cycling at 0.2C, 0.5C, 1C, 3C and 5C to evaluate rate capability. Capacity retention at high rate was calculated relative to 0.1C or another defined reference rate. [221] Cycling stability was evaluated at 0.5C, 1C or another selected industrially relevant rate for 100, 500 or 1000 cycles. Coulombic efficiency, discharge capacity, capacity retention and voltage polarization were recorded. Low-temperature performance was evaluated by conditioning cells at about 0°C or-10°C before discharge testing. Elevated-temperature performance may be evaluated at about 45°C to assess stability and impedance growth. [222] Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was measured over a frequency range suitable for resolving electrolyte resistance, interfacial resistance and charge-transfer resistance. The inventive Generation-4 LiFePO4/C material exhibited reduced polarization and lower charge-transfer resistance relative to comparative control materials lacking post-synthesis conductive-carbon embedding and spheroidisation. patents.abstract: The present invention relates to the development of an integrated energy system of an electric vehicle that consists of a high-capacity lithium-ion battery pack and intelligent wireless charging system. This battery pack applies advanced technologies of electrodes, thermal management systems, and intelligent battery management algorithms to increase energy density, charging efficiency, safety during operation, and lifetime cycles. Wireless charging system is equipped with resonant transmitter and receiver coils, adaptive sensing of alignment, dynamic frequency tuning, and machine learning for charging control in order to optimize charging efficiency and minimize losses during the process. Communication between the battery management system and the charging control system allows for predicting and controlling charging and regulating temperature as well as for diagnostics and maintenance of battery health. The integrated system is able to work in the stationary and dynamic modes as well as to have the capabilities of electromagnetic interference protection and foreign object detection. FIG.1
patents.complete_specification: Description:[0002] The growing popularity of electric cars has led to an increase in the need for effective energy storage systems. The existing lithium-ion batteries utilized in electric cars have some drawbacks such as energy density constraints, thermal stability problems, degradation during charging process, limited lifetime, and inefficiency of material use. The current battery packs consume considerable space and require frequent recharging. [0003] Wireless charging technologies have been introduced as alternatives to wired charging. Current wireless chargers use inductive coupling methods. In any case, such methods have numerous problems such as power transfer losses, inductor alignment, electromagnetic interference, excess heat production, and low charging efficiency. Moreover, most of the currently available wireless charging methods require precise placement of vehicles and cannot adjust the process of charging depending on the state of the battery. Numerous prior art solutions have described methods for battery management systems and wireless charging technologies separately. Nevertheless, there is a lack of coordination between the advanced high density battery designs and intelligent wireless charging. An integrated solution that can boost battery energy density while also enhancing wireless charging effectiveness, safety, and operational dependability for electric vehicles is therefore required. SUMMARY [0004] In view of the foregoing, an embodiment herein provides a method for innovations in high-density lithium-ion batteries and efficient wireless power transfer systems for EVs. In some embodiments, wherein a method for designing an integrated electric vehicle energy management system including a high-capacity lithium-ion battery pack and a smart wireless power delivery system. The lithium-ion battery pack comprises advanced electrode designs, nanostructured active materials, solid or semi-solid-state electrolytes, thermal management systems, and a smart battery management controller. The design allows for better energy density, faster charge rates, improved cycle life, and better thermal stability. [0005] The wireless power delivery system consists of a transmitting coil assembly, receiving coil assembly, adaptive resonance tuning circuitry, alignment sensors, EMF optimization circuits, and machine learning algorithms to optimize charging process based on the state-of-charge of the battery pack, temperature, condition, and vehicle position. Moreover, the system includes an interface between the battery management system and the wireless charging controller that allows for optimized energy delivery, lower charging losses, predictive maintenance and higher safety. The proposed system allows for higher charging efficiency, longer driving range, shorter charging time, lower thermal stresses and higher user convenience. [0006] These and other aspects of the embodiments herein will be better appreciated and understood when considered in conjunction with the following description and the accompanying drawings. It should be understood, however, that the following descriptions, while indicating preferred embodiments and numerous specific details thereof, are given by way of illustration and not of limitation. Many changes and modifications may be made within the scope of the embodiments herein without departing from the spirit thereof, and the embodiments herein include all such modifications. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS [0007] The embodiments herein will be better understood from the following detailed description with reference to the drawings, in which: [0008] FIG. 1 illustrates a method for innovations in high-density lithium-ion batteries and efficient wireless power transfer systems for EVs according to an embodiment herein. DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS [0009] The embodiments herein and the various features and advantageous details thereof are explained more fully with reference to the non-limiting embodiments that are illustrated in the accompanying drawings and detailed in the following description. Descriptions of well-known components and processing techniques are omitted so as to not unnecessarily obscure the embodiments herein. The examples used herein are intended merely to facilitate an understanding of ways in which the embodiments herein may be practiced and to further enable those of skill in the art to practice the embodiments herein. Accordingly, the examples should not be construed as limiting the scope of the embodiments herein. [0010] FIG. 1 illustrates a method for innovations in high-density lithium-ion batteries and efficient wireless power transfer systems for EVs according to an embodiment herein. In accordance with the preferred embodiment, the process consists of using a high-energy lithium-ion battery pack designed specifically for electric vehicle applications. The battery pack consists of several electrochemical cells connected in series and in parallel. Each individual cell is made of high-performance anode material composed of silicon graphite compounds, and high-performance cathode material made of nickel-containing layer oxides. Such compositions of materials substantially enhance the capacity of energy storage when compared to traditional lithium-ion batteries. [0011] The electrochemical cells are housed in a thermally-efficient enclosure utilizing phase change materials and liquid cooling channels. The thermal management system constantly detects the temperature changes by means of distributed sensors that are located across the entire battery pack. This information is sent to the battery management system which can trigger cooling or protection processes in case of any abnormal operation. [0012] The battery management system (BMS) serves as an integral part of the invention. The BMS contains voltage monitors, current sensors, state-of-charge estimators, state-of-health predictors, and fault detectors. Machine learning algorithms process the operation data to predict the degradation trends and adjust the charging schedules to ensure long battery life. [0013] In some embodiment, the wireless power transmission system is composed of a ground-based transmitting unit and a vehicle-based receiving unit. The transmitting unit consists of a high-frequency inverter feeding into a resonant transmitting coil. The receiving unit consists of a resonant receiving coil coupled to rectification and power conditioning circuitry. The transmitting and receiving coils are designed with optimized geometry for achieving the highest possible efficiency of magnetic coupling. In one design variant, multi-layer litz-wire coils are used to minimize the skin-effect losses. There is an alignment detection unit that constantly detects the positional deviation of the transmitter and receiver coils. Alignment is determined by the use of ultrasonic sensors, magnetic field sensors, optical sensors, or computer vision units. With the help of detected positioning data, adaptive tuning circuits adjust the resonant frequencies and compensations for maximum energy transfer efficiency. [0014] In some embodiment, the wireless charging controller has intelligent prediction algorithms that are trained using past charging data. The prediction algorithm determines the optimal charging power based on the battery temperature, past charging experience, energy need, and environment. [0015] In another embodiment, a two-way communication is maintained between the wireless charger and the vehicle battery management system by using wireless communication techniques. There is constant exchange of real-time data such as state-of-charge, battery temperature, charging needs, and faults. It provides for both static and dynamic charging procedures. In the case of static charging, the vehicle obtains power while standing above charging pads. On the other hand, in dynamic charging, power is transmitted by charging modules embedded on the road surface to vehicles moving above them. Control algorithms intelligently adjust the level of transferred power depending on the velocity of the car, its alignment and battery requirement. To increase the safety, electromagnetic shields are built around the transmitter and receiver apparatuses. These shields decrease the level of electromagnetic radiation and make sure that the limits set by relevant regulations are adhered to. Moreover, foreign object detection system detects metallic objects existing in the charging area and stops the process of transmitting energy. This invention also incorporates the feature of predictive maintenance. Parameters obtained from battery modules and charging stations are analyzed using cloud computing technology. [0016] Renewable energy sources such as solar photovoltaics and wind power systems can also be incorporated into the wireless charging system. The storage of energy and smart grid connectivity will ensure that renewable energy is effectively utilized for charging applications of the electric vehicles. This architecture ensures effective coordination among all the various components in terms of energy storage, wireless charging, thermal management, safety and intelligent control systems. It results in an efficient electric vehicle energy ecosystem that offers increased efficiency, faster charging, increased battery life, and user convenience. , Claims:I/We Claim: 1. A method for innovations in high-density lithium-ion batteries and efficient wireless power transfer systems for EVs, wherein the method comprising: a high-density lithium-ion battery pack, a battery management system, a wireless power transmission system, and an intelligent charger, wherein the battery management system and the wireless power transmission system communicate with each other for efficient charging and operation. 2. The system according to claim 1, wherein the lithium-ion battery pack includes silicon-graphite composite anode materials and rich-nickel cathode materials designed to maximize energy density and battery capacity. 3. The system according to claim 1, wherein the battery pack comprises components for managing temperature, which include temperature sensors, heat sink systems, phase-changing materials, and temperature control algorithms. 4. The system according to claim 1, wherein the wireless charging subsystem includes resonant transmission and receiving coils for transferring electrical energy using the principle of magnetic coupling. 5. The system according to claim 4, wherein the tuning circuitry automatically changes the resonant frequency and compensation based on the alignment of the coils.

patents.abstract: A hybrid energy management system for electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure is disclosed. The system comprises a grid interface unit (110), an AC/DC converter (120), a DC bus stabilization module (130), a lithium battery energy module (140) coupled via a DC/DC converter (150), a supercapacitor bank (160) connected through a high-speed DC/DC interface (170), and an energy management controller (180). The controller dynamically classifies load events and allocates power between the lithium battery and supercapacitor bank. Transient high-power spikes are supplied by the supercapacitor bank (160), while sustained loads are delivered by the lithium battery module (140). The system enhances grid stability, reduces battery degradation, mitigates peak demand charges, and improves fast-charging efficiency.
patents.complete_specification: Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION: The present invention relates to electric vehicle charging infrastructure systems. More particularly, the present invention relates to a hybrid energy storage management system integrating supercapacitor banks and lithium-ion battery modules for stabilizing, buffering, and optimizing high-power fast-charging electric vehicle stations. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has led to a significant increase in demand for high-power fast-charging infrastructure. Modern fast-charging stations are designed to deliver power levels ranging from 50 kW to 350 kW and beyond. Such ultra-fast charging systems are essential for reducing charging times and improving user convenience. However, the deployment of these high-power charging stations presents multiple technical challenges related to grid stability, infrastructure cost, safety, power quality, and energy efficiency. Conventional EV charging stations typically draw power directly from the electrical grid. When a vehicle initiates a fast-charging session, the charging station demands a sudden high-power load. This creates transient spikes in current draw, leading to voltage sag, grid instability, and increased stress on distribution transformers and upstream infrastructure. In areas with weak grid networks, such sudden loads may result in breaker trips or voltage collapse. To mitigate such issues, some charging stations incorporate battery energy storage systems (BESS). These systems store energy during off-peak periods and discharge during peak charging events. Lithium-ion battery modules are commonly used for this purpose due to their high energy density and mature manufacturing ecosystem. However, lithium-ion batteries exhibit inherent limitations. They are not optimized for handling extremely high transient power spikes. Repeated exposure to high charge/discharge rates accelerates degradation, increases internal resistance, reduces cycle life, and elevates thermal risks. Supercapacitors, also known as ultracapacitors, offer an alternative storage solution for handling transient high-power loads. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, supercapacitors possess extremely high power density and can undergo rapid charge and discharge cycles with minimal degradation. However, they have low energy density, making them unsuitable for sustained long-duration energy supply. Existing hybrid systems combining batteries and supercapacitors often operate with simple parallel coupling arrangements. In many implementations, passive power sharing is used without intelligent coordination. Such systems suffer from poor energy balancing, inefficient power transfer, uncontrolled current spikes, and thermal mismatches between storage components. Additionally, many prior systems lack real-time predictive load management, resulting in inefficient utilization of storage resources. Another limitation of current charging infrastructures lies in grid interconnection agreements. Utilities often impose demand charges based on peak load usage. A single high-power charging event can significantly increase operational costs due to peak demand penalties. Traditional battery-only buffering systems do not effectively mitigate millisecond-scale power transients that contribute to peak measurements. Further challenges include thermal runaway risks in lithium batteries under high current stress, complex battery management systems (BMS) not optimized for hybrid energy coordination, and inadequate DC bus stabilization during simultaneous multi-vehicle charging. In addition, scalability remains an issue. Many systems are not modular, making it difficult to expand station capacity without redesigning the entire architecture. The absence of intelligent hierarchical control between energy storage elements reduces reliability and overall infrastructure resilience. The present invention addresses these limitations by introducing a coordinated hybrid architecture in which a supercapacitor bank manages transient and high-frequency load variations, while a lithium battery module supplies sustained energy demands. The system incorporates a real-time energy management controller configured to dynamically allocate power based on load prediction, state-of-charge balancing, and thermal parameters. Technically, the invention overcomes prior limitations by: • Isolating transient spikes from lithium battery modules using a high-speed DC/DC interface • Implementing hierarchical control logic that prioritizes supercapacitor discharge for high C-rate events • Incorporating predictive load smoothing algorithms • Integrating a bidirectional grid interface with active demand shaping • Introducing a thermal equalization subsystem to improve battery life By separating transient and steady-state power roles, the present invention significantly extends battery life, improves grid stability, reduces demand charges, enhances safety, and enables scalable fast-charging infrastructure deployment. OBJECT OF THE INVENTION: The principal object of the present invention is to provide a hybrid supercapacitor–lithium battery energy management system for stabilizing high-power electric vehicle fast-charging stations. Another object of the present invention is to reduce transient grid stress by isolating sudden load spikes through a high-power supercapacitor buffer layer. Another object of the present invention is to extend lithium battery lifespan by minimizing exposure to high C-rate transient loads. Yet another object of the present invention is to reduce peak demand charges through intelligent load shaping and predictive discharge coordination. Yet another object of the present invention is to provide a modular, scalable, and thermally balanced energy storage architecture suitable for multi-vehicle ultra-fast charging environments. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION: The present invention discloses a hybrid energy buffering architecture for electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure that integrates a supercapacitor bank and a lithium battery module through a coordinated power management controller. The system is configured to decouple transient power demands from sustained energy requirements, thereby stabilizing the DC bus of a fast-charging station. The architecture comprises a grid interface unit, a bidirectional AC/DC converter, a lithium-ion battery module, a supercapacitor bank, DC/DC converters for independent control of each storage medium, and a central energy management controller. The controller dynamically monitors load demand, state-of-charge, temperature parameters, and grid constraints to determine optimal power flow distribution. During sudden high-power charging initiation, the supercapacitor bank delivers instantaneous current to maintain DC bus voltage stability. The lithium battery module provides steady-state energy replenishment while operating within safe current limits. The system further includes predictive algorithms to pre-charge the supercapacitor bank prior to anticipated high-load events. The invention also discloses a method for coordinated hybrid energy allocation involving load detection, transient classification, dynamic current allocation, and thermal balancing. The architecture improves efficiency, reliability, safety, and scalability of fast-charging infrastructure. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS Fig.1: System Block Diagram Fig.2: Method Flow Diagram DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION The present invention is related to a hybrid energy storage architecture for high-power electric vehicle charging stations integrating supercapacitor buffering and lithium battery energy modules under coordinated management. The present invention introduces a hierarchical power buffering structure designed to isolate transient load dynamics from steady-state energy delivery. The system ensures optimal distribution of energy between high-power density and high-energy density storage elements. The system comprises a grid interface unit (110) configured to connect to an external utility grid. The grid interface unit (110) includes protective relays, EMI filters, surge suppressors, and isolation transformers to ensure safe interconnection. An AC/DC bidirectional converter (120) is electrically coupled to the grid interface unit (110). The AC/DC converter (120) converts grid AC power into a regulated DC bus voltage. It includes active power factor correction circuitry and insulated-gate bipolar transistor switching modules operating at high switching frequencies between 20 kHz and 100 kHz. A DC bus stabilization module (130) is connected downstream of the AC/DC converter (120). The DC bus stabilization module (130) includes high-voltage capacitors rated between 800V and 1000V DC to maintain voltage uniformity during rapid load changes. A lithium battery energy module (140) is connected to the DC bus via a bidirectional DC/DC converter (150). The lithium battery energy module (140) comprises multiple series-parallel lithium-ion cells arranged to provide nominal storage between 50 kWh and 500 kWh depending on installation size. The bidirectional DC/DC converter (150) regulates charge and discharge current and limits maximum C-rate to below 2C during standard operation. A supercapacitor bank (160) is coupled to the DC bus through a high-speed DC/DC interface (170). The supercapacitor bank (160) comprises multiple ultracapacitor cells arranged to deliver power bursts exceeding 10C discharge rates. The high-speed DC/DC interface (170) operates with sub-millisecond response time to instantaneously inject current into the DC bus during load spikes. An energy management controller (180) is electrically connected to the lithium battery energy module (140), supercapacitor bank (160), AC/DC converter (120), and DC bus module (130). The energy management controller (180) comprises a microprocessor, memory module, predictive load algorithm engine, SOC estimation module, and thermal monitoring circuitry. The energy management controller (180) continuously monitors load demand from EV charging dispensers (190). When a vehicle initiates fast charging, the controller classifies the load event as transient or sustained based on rate-of-change of current and duration thresholds. If the load change exceeds a predefined gradient threshold, typically 50 A/ms, the controller directs the high-speed DC/DC interface (170) to discharge the supercapacitor bank (160). Simultaneously, the lithium battery DC/DC converter (150) ramps output gradually to sustain energy supply after the transient phase. A thermal management system (200) includes liquid cooling channels integrated within battery modules and forced-air cooling around supercapacitor arrays. Temperature sensors relay real-time data to the energy management controller (180), which dynamically adjusts current allocation to prevent overheating. Fig.1 illustrates the system architecture showing the grid interface unit (110), AC/DC converter (120), DC bus module (130), lithium battery module (140), battery DC/DC converter (150), supercapacitor bank (160), supercapacitor DC/DC interface (170), energy management controller (180), EV charging dispensers (190), and thermal management system (200). Fig.2 illustrates the operational method flow beginning with load detection, transient classification, SOC evaluation, current allocation, thermal check, controlled discharge, sustained energy supply, and rebalancing cycle. In operation, when no vehicle is charging, the lithium battery module (140) charges the supercapacitor bank (160) through controlled transfer via DC/DC converters. When multiple vehicles connect simultaneously, the system distributes transient load among supercapacitors first, reducing grid peak draw. In a first embodiment, the system is configured for a 150 kW charging station with a 100 kWh lithium battery pack and 5 kWh supercapacitor array rated for 300 kW instantaneous output. In a second embodiment, the system is implemented in a 350 kW ultra-fast charger with modular lithium battery racks and scalable supercapacitor modules arranged in parallel banks. The described architecture ensures reduced battery stress, improved grid interaction, minimized voltage sag, and extended storage lifespan. The advantages include peak shaving, demand charge reduction, improved energy efficiency above 95%, enhanced safety, modular scalability, and superior transient handling capability. The protected system defines a coordinated hybrid buffering architecture in which energy roles are functionally segregated between high-energy-density storage and high-power-density storage. The defining structural feature lies in the controlled interconnection of a grid interface unit (110), a bidirectional AC/DC converter (120), a DC bus stabilization module (130), a lithium battery energy module (140) coupled through a bidirectional DC/DC converter (150), a supercapacitor bank (160) coupled through a high-speed DC/DC interface (170), and an energy management controller (180) configured to dynamically allocate current based on load classification. The uniqueness does not lie merely in combining batteries and supercapacitors, but in the architectural hierarchy, response timing constraints, and power-role segregation logic. The grid interface unit (110) serves as the physical and electrical boundary between utility infrastructure and the charging station. It includes isolation transformers, surge arresters, high-speed breakers, EMI suppression filters, and grid synchronization circuitry. This module ensures that harmonic distortion remains within IEEE 519 standards and that any fault within the station does not propagate upstream. By providing protective and conditioning functionality before power conversion, it establishes a controlled input environment for downstream power electronics. The bidirectional AC/DC converter (120) transforms grid AC power into a regulated high-voltage DC supply suitable for EV fast charging. Unlike conventional rectifiers, this converter includes active power factor correction and controllable switching bridges. Its bidirectionality allows controlled energy feedback when necessary, such as regenerative grid support or storage rebalancing. The converter maintains DC bus voltage within ±2% tolerance under fluctuating grid conditions. The coordinated communication between this converter and the energy management controller (180) enables demand shaping and peak mitigation. The DC bus stabilization module (130) functions as the central energy highway of the system. It includes high-voltage electrolytic and film capacitors rated between 800–1000 V DC. This module absorbs microsecond-scale ripple and maintains voltage continuity during sub-millisecond transitions. Without this module, switching transitions between storage elements could cause voltage oscillations harmful to vehicle charging electronics. The lithium battery energy module (140) provides sustained energy delivery. It consists of series-parallel cell arrays forming high-capacity packs ranging from 50 kWh to 500 kWh. The battery management system embedded within monitors cell voltage, balancing states, temperature gradients, and internal resistance. The associated bidirectional DC/DC converter (150) regulates current flow to ensure that discharge rates remain below 2C during steady supply. This limitation protects lithium cells from thermal stress and electrochemical degradation. The supercapacitor bank (160) is structurally distinct and electrically decoupled from the battery module through a high-speed DC/DC interface (170). The supercapacitor cells are arranged to achieve rapid discharge capability exceeding 10C. The high-speed interface (170) incorporates fast-switching MOSFET or SiC-based devices capable of responding within microseconds. This interface allows near-instantaneous current injection into the DC bus when sudden load increases are detected. Because of this configuration, transient spikes never directly stress the lithium battery module. The energy management controller (180) is the central intelligence core. It continuously samples load current gradients, DC bus voltage fluctuations, state-of-charge values, and thermal readings. Using predefined threshold parameters such as rate-of-change-of-current exceeding 50 A/ms, it categorizes load events as transient or sustained. Upon detecting a transient event, it immediately commands the high-speed DC/DC interface (170) to discharge the supercapacitor bank (160), thereby shielding the lithium battery module (140) from abrupt current spikes. After the transient window, typically 100–500 milliseconds, the controller gradually ramps battery discharge through the converter (150) to assume steady-state supply. This functional separation between transient and sustained energy delivery forms the core inventive distinction. The supercapacitor bank absorbs high-frequency energy fluctuations, while the lithium battery module handles long-duration load. The controller ensures no simultaneous uncontrolled discharge occurs. This coordinated timing mechanism enhances system lifespan, safety, and grid compliance. In-Depth Explanation of the Method Protection Scope The protected operational method defines a structured sequence beginning with load detection from EV charging dispensers (190). The energy management controller (180) monitors instantaneous current and calculates the derivative of load increase. When a vehicle initiates fast charging, the load gradient is analyzed. If the gradient exceeds a predefined threshold, the event is classified as transient. The controller then activates the high-speed DC/DC interface (170) to discharge the supercapacitor bank (160). This discharge maintains DC bus voltage stability within narrow tolerance bands. During this phase, lithium battery output is intentionally limited. As the load stabilizes and current demand becomes sustained rather than impulsive, the controller ramps lithium battery discharge through the bidirectional DC/DC converter (150). The ramp rate is carefully controlled to avoid overshoot and minimize internal resistance heating. Simultaneously, thermal parameters from the thermal management system (200) are evaluated. If temperature exceeds safe limits, the controller dynamically reduces discharge rates or shifts energy allocation back toward the supercapacitor bank. After transient events subside, the supercapacitor bank is gradually recharged from the lithium battery module or directly from grid supply during low-demand intervals. This cyclical balancing ensures readiness for the next high-power event. This structured process ensures deterministic load handling rather than passive parallel sharing, which distinguishes it technically from prior loosely-coupled hybrid systems. In-Depth Explanation of Fig. 1 Fig.1 illustrates the structural architecture of the hybrid energy buffering system. At the top of the diagram, the utility grid supplies AC power to the grid interface unit (110). This unit protects and conditions incoming power before forwarding it to the bidirectional AC/DC converter (120). The converter transforms AC to DC and feeds the DC bus stabilization module (130). From the DC bus module (130), two independent branches extend. One branch connects through the battery DC/DC converter (150) to the lithium battery energy module (140). The second branch connects through the high-speed DC/DC interface (170) to the supercapacitor bank (160). This dual-branch configuration ensures independent controllability of energy sources. The energy management controller (180) communicates with all major modules, receiving voltage, current, and temperature data. It sends gating signals to converters (150) and (170) to regulate discharge behavior. The EV charging dispensers (190) draw power from the DC bus module (130), and the thermal management system (200) monitors environmental conditions. The diagram visually demonstrates the isolation principle—supercapacitor and battery modules do not directly parallel each other but are mediated through controlled power electronics interfaces. In-Depth Explanation of Fig. 2 Fig.2 represents the operational process flow. The process begins with load detection at the charging dispenser (190). The energy management controller (180) evaluates whether the load change is transient or sustained. If transient, control logic directs energy draw from the supercapacitor bank (160). If sustained, lithium battery output (140) is ramped via DC/DC converter (150). Throughout operation, DC bus voltage stabilization is maintained via module (130). Thermal monitoring (200) occurs concurrently. After load stabilization, the controller initiates a rebalancing cycle, gradually restoring supercapacitor charge. The process then resets to standby monitoring mode. This flowchart captures the dynamic energy role segregation that forms the system’s technical foundation. Technical Significance and Advantages The architecture reduces lithium battery degradation by eliminating high C-rate stress cycles. It enhances grid compliance by smoothing instantaneous load spikes. It lowers demand charges through peak shaving. It improves safety by limiting battery thermal runaway risks. It enables modular scalability by allowing independent expansion of battery and supercapacitor modules. It achieves response times in microseconds for transient handling and controlled ramping for sustained loads. , Claims:A hybrid energy management system for electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure, comprising: a) a grid interface unit (110) configured to receive AC power from a utility grid; b) a bidirectional AC/DC converter (120) coupled to said grid interface unit (110); c) a DC bus stabilization module (130) connected to said AC/DC converter (120); d) a lithium battery energy module (140); e) a bidirectional DC/DC converter (150) electrically coupling said lithium battery energy module (140) to said DC bus stabilization module (130); f) a supercapacitor bank (160); g) a high-speed DC/DC interface (170) coupling said supercapacitor bank (160) to said DC bus stabilization module (130); h) an energy management controller (180) configured to classify load events and dynamically allocate current between said lithium battery energy module (140) and said supercapacitor bank (160); wherein transient load spikes are supplied primarily by said supercapacitor bank (160) and sustained energy demand is supplied by said lithium battery energy module (140). The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein said energy management controller (180) includes predictive load estimation algorithms. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein said high-speed DC/DC interface (170) operates with sub-millisecond response time. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein said lithium battery energy module (140) operates within a maximum discharge rate of 2C. The system as claimed in claim 1, further comprising a thermal management system (200). The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein said supercapacitor bank (160) delivers discharge rates exceeding 10C. The system as claimed in claim 1, wherein said energy management controller (180) performs peak demand shaping. A method for managing hybrid energy storage in electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure, comprising: a) detecting load demand from charging dispensers (190); b) classifying load as transient or sustained using an energy management controller (180); c) discharging a supercapacitor bank (160) during transient events; d) gradually ramping lithium battery output through a DC/DC converter (150); e) stabilizing DC bus voltage via a DC bus module (130); f) recharging said supercapacitor bank (160) during low-load conditions. The method as claimed in claim 8, wherein thermal parameters are continuously monitored. The method as claimed in claim 8, wherein predictive algorithms pre-charge said supercapacitor bank (160) before anticipated load events.

patents.abstract: Abstract A battery employing lithium-oxygen chemistry may include an anode comprising lithium, an electrolyte, and a porous cathode which is known as electrochemical profile. The electrolyte may include a lithium-containing salt; a partially fluorinated ether, such as 2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-dioxolane; and a co-solvent selected from the group consisting of ethers, amides, nitriles, and combinations thereof. In some examples, the electrolyte does not include a cyclic carbonate ester, a sulfolane, or a sulfolane derivative. The porous cathode allows oxygen to come into contact with the electrolyte.
patents.complete_specification: Description:Li—O2 batteries may provide a relatively high gravimetric energy density (watt-hours per kg; Wh/kg), e.g., compared to lithium ion or lead-acid batteries. The theoretical gravimetric energy density of a Li—O2 battery is about 11,680 Wh/kg, which is calculated using the oxidation of 1 kg of lithium metal. This energy density compares favorably to the gravimetric energy density of gasoline, the current fuel of choice for vehicles, which is about 13,000 Wh/kg. Other considerations also impact the design and function of Li—O2 batteries. For example, the power density (measured in watt per kilogram; W/kg) is important for propulsion of a vehicle. The power density of Li—O2 batteries is currently low. While not wishing to be bound by any theory, current research results indicate that the mechanism of energy discharge in a Li—O2 battery is reduction of oxygen in the presence of lithium ions to form lithium oxides (such as lithium peroxide). Hence, very large surface areas are required to provide high power. For example, a battery with 100 kW power output at a cell voltage of 2.5 volts (V) and a current density of 25 milliamps per square centimeter (mA/cm2) may require an internal surface area of 160 m2. A Li—O2 battery may include one of four chemistries: aprotic liquid electrolyte, aqueous electrolyte, a mixed system including an aqueous electrolyte immersing the cathode and an aprotic electrolyte immersing the anode, and a solid-state battery including a solid electrolyte. The fundamental chemistry of energy storage and discharge is affected by the electrolyte surrounding the cathode. The Li—O2 battery described in this disclosure includes a Li metal and/or alloy anode, a cathode including a conductive, porous material, and a lithium ion (e.g., Li+) conducting, nonaqueous, aprotic liquid electrolyte, which is in contact with both the anode and the cathode. Li—O2 batteries operate by reduction of O2 to form lithium peroxide (Li2O2) on the cathode during discharge, with the process being reversed on charge. Because the chemistry during battery operation is related to generation of superoxides and peroxides (e.g., Li2O2), which are highly reactive, the chemical stability of the aprotic electrolyte affects whether the Li—O2 battery is stable over repeated charges and discharges. In some aprotic electrolytes, the electrolyte may decompose during operation of the battery as a result of proton abstraction from, and oxidative instability of, the liquid organic solvent in the presence of the active cathode electrochemistry (namely 2(Li++e−)+O2→Li2O2), which limits the battery's rechargeability. , C , C , Claims:Claims 1. A battery employing lithium-oxygen chemistry comprising: an anode comprising lithium; an electrolyte comprising: a lithium-containing salt, 2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-dioxolane, and a co-solvent selected from the group consisting of ethers, amides, nitriles, and combinations thereof, wherein the electrolyte does not include a cyclic carbonate ester, a sulfolane. 2. Wherein the volume ratio of 2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-dioxolane to the co-solvent is between about 30:1 and about 1:1. 3. Wherein the lithium salt is selected from the group consisting of LiPF6, LiClO4, LiTFSI, LiBF4, LiAsF6, LiN(SO2CF3)2, LiSO3CF3, and combinations. 4. Wherein the co-solvent is selected from the group consisting of 1,2-dimethoxyethane, diglyme, triglyme, tetraglyme, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), dimethyl acetamide, pivalonitrile, acetonitrile, and combinations. 5. Wherein the volume ratio of 2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-di oxolane to the co-solvent is between about 20:1 and about 10:1. 6. The battery of which, wherein the volume ratio of 2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-dioxolane to the co-solvent is between about 30:1 and about 5:1.

patents.abstract: The present invention discloses a machine learning-based intelligent lithium battery charging and health management system for electric vehicles. The system is configured to continuously monitor battery operational parameters including voltage, current, temperature, charging cycles, internal resistance, and environmental conditions to intelligently optimize battery charging operations. A machine learning analytics engine predicts battery state-of-health, remaining useful life, and degradation characteristics to generate adaptive charging profiles and predictive maintenance recommendations. The system further incorporates thermal management and anomaly detection mechanisms to improve charging safety and battery reliability. By utilizing cloud, edge, or on-board computing architectures, the invention supports real-time battery analytics and scalable deployment for individual and fleet electric vehicle applications. The disclosed system enhances charging efficiency, extends battery lifespan, minimizes degradation, and enables intelligent battery health management across diverse operating environments.
patents.complete_specification: Description:The present invention relates to electric vehicle battery management technologies and, more particularly, to a machine learning-based intelligent lithium battery charging and health management system for electric vehicles. The invention is directed towards the intelligent monitoring, predictive analysis, adaptive charging control, thermal management, and battery health estimation of lithium-based batteries using machine learning techniques. The disclosed system is configured to optimize charging operations, improve battery lifespan, enhance charging safety, predict battery degradation patterns, and facilitate efficient battery utilization across various electric vehicle applications through real-time and historical battery performance analytics. BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION The following description of related art is intended to provide background information pertaining to the field of the disclosure. This section may include certain aspects of the art that may be related to various features of the present disclosure. However, it should be appreciated that this section be used only to enhance the understanding of the reader with respect to the present disclosure, and not as admissions of prior art. The rapid adoption of electric vehicles has significantly increased the demand for efficient and reliable lithium battery management technologies. Lithium batteries serve as the primary energy source in electric vehicles and directly influence vehicle performance, charging efficiency, operational safety, and battery lifespan. Conventional battery management systems are predominantly based on predefined charging algorithms and static threshold mechanisms that are incapable of dynamically adapting to varying battery conditions. Such systems often fail to address battery aging, environmental variations, and user-specific charging patterns, thereby affecting the overall efficiency and longevity of electric vehicle batteries. Modern electric vehicles are subjected to diverse operating conditions, including fluctuating ambient temperatures, frequent fast charging cycles, varying discharge rates, and inconsistent user charging behaviors. These operational variations contribute significantly to battery degradation and may adversely impact battery performance over time. Existing battery charging methodologies generally employ fixed charging profiles that do not account for real-time battery health indicators or predictive degradation models. Consequently, batteries may experience accelerated wear, reduced energy storage capacity, and increased maintenance requirements. Battery degradation is influenced by multiple factors such as electrochemical aging, thermal stress, charge and discharge cycle frequency, internal resistance variations, and environmental conditions. Traditional battery management systems lack the capability to continuously analyze these factors using intelligent predictive models. As a result, they are unable to provide accurate estimations of battery state-of-health, remaining useful life, or optimal charging strategies. The inability to proactively identify degradation patterns may lead to unexpected battery failures and increased replacement costs for electric vehicle owners and fleet operators. Recent advancements in machine learning technologies have demonstrated significant potential for predictive analytics and intelligent decision-making across various industrial applications. Machine learning models are capable of processing large volumes of real-time and historical data to identify complex relationships among battery parameters that may not be detectable using conventional analytical methods. By incorporating machine learning techniques into battery charging and health management systems, it becomes possible to dynamically optimize charging operations, predict battery anomalies, and improve overall battery performance through adaptive learning mechanisms. Despite ongoing developments in battery management technologies, existing solutions remain limited in providing comprehensive intelligent charging optimization, predictive maintenance capabilities, and adaptive thermal management within a unified framework. Most currently available systems focus on isolated battery monitoring functions and do not effectively integrate predictive battery analytics, charging profile optimization, anomaly detection, and personalized charging recommendations. Furthermore, there is limited support for scalable deployment across individual vehicles and electric vehicle fleets utilizing cloud or edge computing infrastructures. There is therefore a need in the art to provide a machine learning-based intelligent lithium battery charging and health management system for electric vehicles that is capable of continuously monitoring battery operational parameters, predicting battery degradation trends, dynamically optimizing charging profiles, enhancing thermal and operational safety, estimating battery health and remaining useful life, and supporting intelligent and adaptive battery management across multiple deployment environments to improve charging efficiency, battery longevity, and overall electric vehicle performance. OBJECTIVE OF THE INVENTION Some of the objects of the present disclosure, which at least one embodiment herein satisfies are listed herein below. The primary objective of the present invention is to provide a machine learning-based intelligent lithium battery charging and health management system for electric vehicles that intelligently monitors battery parameters and dynamically optimizes charging operations to improve battery efficiency, reliability, and operational safety. Another objective of the present invention is to provide a predictive battery health management mechanism configured to estimate battery state-of-health, remaining useful life, and degradation trends using machine learning models trained on historical and real-time battery performance data. Another objective of the present invention is to provide an adaptive charging optimization framework capable of determining optimal charging current, charging voltage, charging duration, and charging sequences based on battery operating conditions and user charging behavior. Another objective of the present invention is to provide an intelligent thermal management module configured to predict and mitigate thermal abnormalities during charging and discharging operations to enhance battery safety and prevent thermal stress-related degradation. Another objective of the present invention is to provide an anomaly detection mechanism for identifying battery faults, charging irregularities, and performance deviations through continuous machine learning-based analytics and predictive maintenance capabilities. Another objective of the present invention is to provide a scalable battery analytics platform that supports cloud-based, edge-based, and on-board deployment architectures for individual electric vehicles as well as fleet-level battery management applications. Another objective of the present invention is to provide an adaptive and continuously learning battery management system that improves charging strategies and battery utilization by incorporating environmental factors, charging history, operational conditions, and machine learning-driven feedback mechanisms. SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION This section is provided to introduce certain objects and aspects of the present disclosure in a simplified form that are further described below in the detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify the key features or the scope of the claimed subject matter. The present invention provides a machine learning-based intelligent lithium battery charging and health management system configured for electric vehicle applications. The system integrates battery sensing modules, machine learning analytics engines, charging optimization mechanisms, predictive battery health management modules, thermal management components, and computing platforms for intelligent battery monitoring and control. The system continuously acquires battery operational parameters including voltage, current, temperature, state-of-charge, charging cycles, internal resistance, charging history, and environmental conditions. These parameters are analyzed using one or more machine learning models to generate predictive insights relating to battery health, degradation patterns, charging efficiency, and safety indicators. The disclosed invention enables adaptive and intelligent battery charging operations that are responsive to real-time battery conditions and operational requirements. The present invention facilitates predictive maintenance and personalized battery management by dynamically modifying charging profiles and thermal control parameters based on machine learning-generated outputs. The system supports cloud, edge, and hybrid deployment environments to enable scalable battery analytics across electric vehicle ecosystems. Through intelligent data processing and adaptive learning mechanisms, the invention improves battery lifespan, minimizes degradation, enhances charging safety, and optimizes energy utilization. The disclosed architecture is particularly advantageous for fast-charging applications, fleet management systems, and next-generation electric vehicle platforms that require accurate battery health estimation and intelligent charging optimization to maximize operational performance and reduce battery replacement and maintenance costs.
